additional_notes: Passé composé of *comprendre* with *avoir* (used after subjects like *je*): *j'ai compris* = “I understood / I’ve understood.” Often used to confirm you understood instructions: *D’accord, j’ai compris.* With object pronouns before the verb (as in *Je l’ai compris / Je vous ai compris*), it means “I understood it/you.” Note: *compris* looks like English “comprise” (to include), but it means “understood.”
target_language_example: D'accord, j'ai compris.
native_language_example: Okay, I got it.

additional_notes: Used with *avoir* + past participle (*j’ai cru*) to talk about what you believed/thought at a specific moment in the past. Often followed by a pronoun object: *Je l’ai cru* (I believed it), *Je vous ai cru* (I believed you), *J’y ai cru* (I believed in it / I believed it). It can also be used with an infinitive to mean “I thought I…”: *J’ai cru entendre…* (I thought I heard…), *J’ai cru voir…* (I thought I saw…).
target_language_example: J’ai cru que tu venais ce soir.
native_language_example: I thought you were coming tonight.

additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular passé composé of *croire* used before a clause introduced by *que*: *J’ai cru que…*. Very often it implies you were mistaken or surprised (similar to “I thought (but I was wrong)…”). In most cases, English won’t translate it literally as “I have believed that”.
target_language_example: J’ai cru que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

meaning: "I thought it was" / "I believed it was".
additional_notes: Used with "je" in the passé composé: "J’ai cru que c’était…" to say you believed something in the past (often later found out it wasn’t true). You can change the subject: "Il a cru que c’était…" (= He thought it was…). In more formal French you may also hear "j’ai pensé que c’était…"; "j’ai cru" often emphasizes a mistaken belief.
target_language_example: J’ai cru que c’était le bon arrêt, mais on est descendus trop tôt.
native_language_example: I thought it was the right stop, but we got off too early.

additional_notes: Passé composé of demander: auxiliary avoir (ai) + past participle demandé. Used to say you asked for something or requested something in the past. Note the false friend with English “demand”: French demander usually means “to ask (for)” rather than “to demand.” Often followed by a direct object (Je l’ai demandé) or by de + infinitive / que + clause (J’ai demandé de venir / J’ai demandé qu’il vienne).
target_language_example: J’ai demandé une table pour deux.
native_language_example: I asked for a table for two.

additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression; it’s usually part of a longer sentence. It combines: (j’)ai dit = “I said” (passé composé of dire) + ce que je = “what I / that which I…”. It normally needs something after it, for example: « J’ai dit ce que je pensais » (“I said what I thought”) or « J’ai dit ce que je voulais dire » (“I said what I meant to say”).
target_language_example: J’ai dit ce que je pensais.
native_language_example: I said what I thought.

ai dit de ne pas le faire

target_language_multi_word_term: ai dit de ne pas le faire
additional_notes: This is usually part of a full sentence with the subject "Je" ("J’ai dit…"). It uses the passé composé: "ai dit" = "said/told". "Dire à quelqu’un de + infinitive" means "to tell someone to + verb"; with negation, "de ne pas + infinitive" means "not to + verb". "le" refers to "it" (a masculine singular thing/action). Often you’ll see who you told with "à + person" (e.g., "Je lui ai dit…" or "J’ai dit à Paul…").
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit de ne pas le faire.
native_language_example: I told him/her not to do it.

ai dit de ne pas venir

target_language_multi_word_term: ai dit de ne pas venir
meaning: “(I) said / have said not to come.”
additional_notes: This is usually part of a full sentence like “J’ai dit de ne pas venir.” It uses the passé composé of dire: “j’ai dit” = “I said / I’ve said,” followed by “de” + infinitive. The negative infinitive “ne pas venir” means “not to come.”
target_language_example: J’ai dit de ne pas venir aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I said not to come today.

meaning: “(I) said that I was going to…”
additional_notes: Sentence fragment built from **j’ai dit** (passé composé of *dire*: “I said”) + **que** (“that”) + **j’allais** (imperfect of *aller*). **j’allais + infinitive** commonly expresses a future-in-the-past (“was going to / was going to do”). You typically complete it with an infinitive verb: *J’ai dit que j’allais partir* (“I said I was going to leave”). Note: as written without **J’** at the start, it’s usually only seen as a fragment/continuation, not a standalone sentence.
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit que j'allais partir tôt.
native_language_example: I told him/her that I was going to leave early.

ai dit tout ce que je

target_language_multi_word_term: ai dit tout ce que je
meaning: "(I) said everything that I…" (an incomplete phrase that needs a verb to finish the idea).
additional_notes:
This is usually part of a longer sentence: « J’ai dit tout ce que je savais / pensais / pouvais. »
- « j’ai dit » = “I said” (from dire)
- « tout ce que » = “everything that / all that”
You normally add another verb after « je » (e.g., savais = knew, pensais = thought, pouvais = could). On its own, « ai dit tout ce que je » is not a complete sentence; it’s missing the subject « j’ » (or « je ») before « ai » and the final verb after « je ».
target_language_example: J’ai dit tout ce que je savais.
native_language_example: I said everything I knew.

additional_notes: This is the *passé composé* of *donner*: **j’ai donné** = *I gave / I have given*. It’s built with **avoir** (j’ai) + the past participle **donné**. It’s usually followed by what was given (*J’ai donné des ordres*) or by an indirect/direct object pronoun (*Je le leur ai donné* = “I gave it to them”). On its own (*J’ai donné.*), it can mean “I gave (it)” when the context is already clear.
target_language_example: Je t’ai donné tout ce que j’avais.
native_language_example: I gave you everything I had.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb 'avoir' in the passé composé to say something has already happened. The adverb 'déjà' typically comes right after the auxiliary (ai/ as/ a/ avons/ avez/ ont): « J’ai déjà + participe passé ». The exact form of 'avoir' changes with the subject (e.g., « tu as déjà… », « il a déjà… », « nous avons déjà… »).
target_language_example: J’ai déjà fini mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I’ve already finished my homework.

additional_notes: Used with the verb dire in the passé composé: j'ai dit = “I said / I have said”. Adding déjà means “already”. Very often you’ll see it with object pronouns placed before the verb: Je te l’ai déjà dit (“I already told you”), Je vous l’ai déjà dit (“I already told you”); l’ = “it/that”.
target_language_example: Je t’ai déjà dit que je ne pouvais pas venir.
native_language_example: I already told you that I couldn’t come.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *entendre* (to hear): **j’ai entendu** = “I heard / I’ve heard.” Often takes a direct object: *Je l’ai entendu* (“I heard it/him/her”), *J’ai entendu ça* (“I heard that”). Don’t confuse with **écouter** (“to listen”). Also note **entendu** can sometimes mean “understood/OK” (e.g., *Entendu !*), but in these examples it means “heard.”
target_language_example: J’ai entendu ton message, je te rappelle ce soir.
native_language_example: I heard your message; I’ll call you back tonight.

additional_notes: *Ai eu* is the 1st person singular **passé composé** of **avoir** (helper verb **avoir** + past participle **eu**). It’s used in many expressions: **J’ai eu l’idée** = “I had the idea”; **Je vous ai eu au téléphone** = “I reached/got hold of you on the phone”; **Je vous ai eu / Je t’ai eu !** can mean “I got you!” (I tricked you / I caught you / I got the better of you), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Je t’ai eu !
native_language_example: I got you!

additional_notes: Passé composé of "avoir de la chance" (to be lucky). Used to talk about being lucky in a specific past situation. You can change the subject: "tu as eu de la chance" (you were lucky), "on a eu de la chance" (we got lucky).
target_language_example: J’ai eu de la chance : le bus est arrivé tout de suite.
native_language_example: I was lucky: the bus arrived right away.

additional_notes: Used with the subject "je" in the passé composé: "j’ai fait". Very common in the causative structure "faire + infinitive" to mean "to make/have someone do something": "Je vous ai fait monter" = "I made you / had you come up." Depending on context, some expressions with "faire" can have special meanings (e.g., "faire marcher quelqu’un" often means "to trick/lead someone on").
target_language_example: Je t’ai fait attendre cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I made you wait five minutes.

additional_notes: This is usually part of the longer phrase "j’ai fait ce que…" ("I did what…"). It uses the passé composé: "ai fait" = "have done/did" (from "faire"). "ce que" means "what/that which" and must be followed by a clause: "J’ai fait ce que tu as demandé."
target_language_example: J’ai fait ce que tu as demandé.
native_language_example: I did what you asked.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer sentence. It’s most often said as: « J’ai fait ce que vous m’avez dit » (“I did what you told me”). « ai fait » is the passé composé of *faire* (“to do/make”) used with *j’* (I). « ce que » means “what / that which,” and « vous » is “you” (formal or plural).
target_language_example: J’ai fait ce que vous m’avez demandé.
native_language_example: I did what you asked me (to do).

meaning: 'have done everything that…' (with 'je': 'j’ai fait tout ce que…').
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment in the passé composé (past tense). It’s most commonly used as part of a longer sentence with a following clause: "J’ai fait tout ce que je pouvais" (I did everything I could) or "J’ai fait tout ce que tu m’as dit" (I did everything you told me). It needs a subject before it (usually "j’") and usually something after "ce que" to complete the idea.
target_language_example: J’ai fait tout ce que je pouvais pour t’aider.
native_language_example: I did everything I could to help you.

additional_notes: This is the negative expression "(n')ai jamais" with the "ne" commonly dropped in informal spoken French. It’s used with the verb "avoir" in the passé composé: "Je n’ai jamais…" = "I have never…". When there’s a direct object, it usually goes before the verb: "Je les (n’)ai jamais vus" = "I’ve never seen them."
target_language_example: Je l’ai jamais rencontré.
native_language_example: I’ve never met him.

meaning: 'have never said' / 'never said' (spoken French, with the 'ne' often dropped).
additional_notes: This is part of the negative past tense of "dire" (to say): "je (ne) l’ai jamais dit" = "I have never said it." In casual speech, "ne" is often omitted ("je l’ai jamais dit"), but in writing and more formal speech you usually keep "ne": "je ne l’ai jamais dit." Object pronouns often come before the verb: "Je ne te l’ai jamais dit" (I never told you), "Je ne le lui ai jamais dit" (I never told him/her).
target_language_example: Je l’ai jamais dit à mes parents.
native_language_example: I never told my parents.

additional_notes: Usually used with negation: « je n’ai jamais entendu parler de … » (= I’ve never heard of …). It’s the past form of « entendre parler de » (“to hear about/of”), and you can change the subject and tense: « tu n’as jamais entendu parler de… », « il n’avait jamais entendu parler de… ». Follow it with a noun, name, or thing after « de ».
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais entendu parler de ce film.
native_language_example: I’ve never heard of that movie.

additional_notes: This is the perfect tense of **avoir** with **jamais** (never): **(je) n’ai jamais eu…** = “I have never had…”. In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: **j’ai jamais eu…** (informal). It often appears with pronouns: **j’en ai jamais eu** = “I’ve never had any / I’ve never had one (of those)”; **je ne l’ai jamais eu** = “I never had it / never got it”; **je n’en ai jamais eu l’occasion** = “I never had the chance.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais eu de voiture.
native_language_example: I’ve never had a car.

meaning: “have never anything” (part of the negative: “I have never had anything / I never have anything”).
additional_notes:
This is not usually used by itself; it’s typically part of a full sentence like « Je n’ai jamais rien (eu) ».
- « ne ... jamais ... rien » is a common “double negative” structure: ne + verb + jamais (“never”) + rien (“nothing/anything”).
- In everyday spoken French, « ne » is often dropped: « J’ai jamais rien (eu) ».
- Add « eu » (past participle of avoir) to make it clearly past: « Je n’ai jamais rien eu » = “I’ve never had anything.” Without « eu », it can sound present/ongoing in speech: « J’ai jamais rien » = “I never have anything.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais rien eu d’aussi cher.
native_language_example: I’ve never had anything that expensive.

additional_notes: Used with the subject "je": "Je n’ai jamais voulu…" = the standard form with negation "ne… jamais". In everyday spoken French, the "ne" is often dropped: "J’ai jamais voulu…". It’s followed by an infinitive clause ("…que ça arrive" = "…for that to happen") or by an object pronoun: "Je ne l’ai jamais voulu" (I never wanted it), "Je n’en ai jamais voulu" (I never wanted any / I never wanted it of that kind).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais voulu te faire de mal.
native_language_example: I never wanted to hurt you.

additional_notes: This is part of the common negative pattern **ne…jamais** = “never.” In full it’s usually **je n’ai jamais vu…** (“I have never seen…”). The order in French is typically: **subject + ne + object pronoun(s) + avoir (ai/as/a/avons/avez/ont) + jamais + past participle (vu)**. Examples: **Je n’en ai jamais vu…** (“I’ve never seen any…”), **Je ne t’y ai jamais vu** (“I’ve never seen you there”).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais vu ce film.
native_language_example: I have never seen this movie.

additional_notes: "Ai lu" is the passé composé of lire (to read): j’ai lu = I have read / I read. It’s used with a direct object, often replaced by a pronoun: Je l’ai lu = I read it / I’ve read it ("l’" = "it"). You can add where you read it with dans (in) or quelque part (somewhere).
target_language_example: J’ai lu ce livre pendant les vacances.
native_language_example: I read this book during the vacation.

additional_notes: First-person singular in the passé composé of oublier (to forget): j’ai + oublié. Often followed by de + infinitive to say you forgot to do something (J’ai oublié de + verb), or by que to say you forgot that… (J’ai oublié que…).
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai oublié ton anniversaire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot your birthday.

meaning: "(I) spoke" / "(I) have spoken" (past tense of parler).
additional_notes: Used in the passé composé: avoir (ai) + past participle (parlé). You’ll usually see it with the subject pronoun: « j’ai parlé ». In the examples « Je lui en ai parlé », « lui » means “to him/her” and « en » means “about it / some (of it)”, so the whole phrase often means “I told him/her about it.”
target_language_example: Je lui en ai parlé ce matin.
native_language_example: I told him/her about it this morning.

additional_notes: informal spoken French for "n'ai pas" after je/j'. In everyday speech, the ne is often dropped: j'ai pas = je n'ai pas. It is usually part of a negative past tense with avoir, so English often uses "didn't" rather than a literal "haven't." Not used in formal writing.
target_language_example: J'ai pas compris.
native_language_example: I didn't understand.

additional_notes: This is the negative past tense of « demander » (to ask / request), usually said as « J’ai pas demandé » in casual speech (dropping « ne » from « Je n’ai pas demandé »). It can take object pronouns: « Je te l’ai pas demandé » = “I didn’t ask you for it / I didn’t ask you that.” Often used defensively to mean “I didn’t ask for this.” Note: « demander » can look like English “demand,” but it often means “ask for / request.”
target_language_example: J’ai pas demandé qu’on m’aide.
native_language_example: I didn’t ask for anyone to help me.

meaning: 'didn’t say' / 'haven’t said' (negated passé composé of dire, “to say”).
additional_notes: Used with a subject like "j’" (je): "Je ne l’ai pas dit" = formal/written; "J’ai pas dit" = very common in speech (drops "ne"). Pronouns can come before the verb: "Je ne le lui ai pas dit" = “I didn’t tell it to him/her.” "dit" is the past participle of "dire".
target_language_example: J’ai pas dit ça !
native_language_example: I didn’t say that!

additional_notes: *Ai pensé* is the **passé composé** of *je pense* (first person singular): *penser* → *j’ai pensé*. It often appears with **y** (*j’y ai pensé*) meaning “I thought about it/that” (where **y** replaces *à + thing/idea*).
target_language_example: J’y ai pensé, mais je ne suis pas sûr.
native_language_example: I thought about it, but I’m not sure.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of penser used with que to introduce what you thought (a full clause): most often you’ll see it as "j’ai pensé que...". In everyday English it’s usually translated as "I thought (that)...". It’s followed by a verb phrase (e.g., "j’ai pensé que c’était vrai").
target_language_example: J’ai pensé que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the full phrase "j’ai pensé que c’était…" to introduce something you believed in the past. "ai pensé" is the passé composé (past tense) of "penser" (to think) with "avoir", and "c’était" means "it was" (imperfect of "être"). Often followed by a noun or an adjective: "…que c’était une erreur" / "…que c’était fini".
target_language_example: Je lui ai pensé que c'était une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I thought it was a good idea.

additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own: it normally continues with a verb after **tu** (e.g., *ai pensé que tu étais… / que tu avais… / que tu voulais…*). It’s built from **j’ai pensé** (past tense of *penser*, “I thought”) + **que** (“that”) + **tu** (“you”, informal singular). In a full sentence you’d typically write **J’ai pensé que tu…** with **J’** at the start.
target_language_example: J’ai pensé que tu étais malade.
native_language_example: I thought you were sick.

additional_notes: Used with j’ to form the passé composé: j’ai pris = “I took / I got / I grabbed.” Prendre is very flexible: prendre du café = “get/have some coffee”; prendre rendez-vous (pour…) = “make/book an appointment (for…)”; prendre quelqu’un pour… = “mistake someone for…”.
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai pris ton stylo par erreur.
native_language_example: Sorry, I took your pen by mistake.

meaning: "have always" (1st person singular with avoir, often in the past: "I have always …").
additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb avoir in compound tenses (especially the passé composé) to say you have always done/felt something. Word order: subject + ai + toujours + past participle (e.g., « J’ai toujours aimé… »). Object pronouns can come before « ai »: « Je t’ai toujours fait confiance. »
target_language_example: J’ai toujours voulu vivre à Paris.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to live in Paris.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of *vouloir* with *je*: **j’ai toujours voulu...**. It expresses a long-standing desire up to now. Commonly followed by an infinitive (**j’ai toujours voulu voyager**) or a noun (**j’ai toujours voulu une voiture rouge**).
target_language_example: J’ai toujours voulu apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to learn French.

additional_notes: *Ai trouvé* is used with **je/j’** to talk about something you found in the past: **j’ai trouvé…** = “I found / I’ve found…”. It often appears with object pronouns: **Je l’ai trouvé** (“I found it”), **J’en ai trouvé un** (“I found one (of them)”).
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé tes clés sous la table.
native_language_example: I found your keys under the table.

additional_notes: Used in the passé composé: j’ai vu = “I saw / I’ve seen.” Often followed by a direct object (j’ai vu ça) or used with negation (je n’ai vu personne = “I didn’t see anyone”). With an object pronoun, it comes before the verb: Je l’ai vu. (“I saw him/it.”).
target_language_example: J’ai vu ton message hier soir.
native_language_example: I saw your message last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *voir* (to see): **j’ + ai + vu**. In most cases you’ll see **j’ai vu**. You may see **j’ai vue** with **-e** when the direct object is feminine and placed before the verb (agreement), e.g., *la première chose que j’ai vue*.
target_language_example: Je l’ai vue à la télé.
native_language_example: I saw her on TV.

additional_notes: Inversion of the verb "avoir" ("j’ai" → "ai-je") used to ask a question in a more formal/literary style. Often followed by a noun (Ai-je le droit… ?) or used with pronouns: "en ai-je" = "do I have any (of it/them)?" and can also mean "do I need any?" depending on the verb phrase (e.g., "besoin" → "en ai-je besoin ?").
target_language_example: Ai-je oublié mon passeport ?
native_language_example: Have I forgotten my passport?

additional_notes: *Ai* is the 1st-person singular of **avoir** (I have). The full structure is **avoir besoin de + noun / pronoun / infinitive**: *J’ai besoin de toi* (I need you), *J’ai besoin d’aide* (I need help), *J’ai besoin de partir* (I need to leave). In negatives, French often uses **ne... que** to mean “only”: *Je n’ai besoin que d’une chose* (I only need one thing).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de ton aide maintenant.
native_language_example: I need your help right now.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say you need a small amount of something. It’s part of the longer structure: « J’ai besoin d’un peu de + noun ». « d’ » is used instead of « de » before a vowel or silent h (e.g., d’eau, d’argent). Note: in correct French typography/orthography, this is normally written with curly apostrophes: « ai besoin d’un peu d’ ».
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un peu d'argent pour le bus.
native_language_example: I need a little money for the bus.

additional_notes: This is usually used with the subject pronoun: « J’ai besoin de savoir… » = “I need to know…”. It literally uses the verb avoir (“to have”): avoir besoin de + infinitive = “to need to + verb”. You can change the subject: « Tu as besoin de savoir… » (you need to know), « Il/Elle a besoin de savoir… » (he/she needs to know).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de savoir où tu vas.
native_language_example: I need to know where you're going.

additional_notes: This is part of the phrase "avoir besoin de" (= to need). It’s usually used with the subject: "J’ai besoin de vous". "Vous" can mean either "you" (formal, one person) or "you" (plural). You can replace "vous" with a thing: "J’ai besoin de ton aide" (I need your help).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de vous pour remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: I need you to fill out this form.

additional_notes: This is the start of the structure « j’ai besoin que + subject + verb (subjunctive) ». It’s used to express a need/requirement and is typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive: « J’ai besoin que tu viennes » (“I need you to come”).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin que tu m’aides ce soir.
native_language_example: I need you to help me tonight.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer sentence: « J’ai besoin que tu me + [verb] … ». After « avoir besoin que », French normally uses the subjunctive: « que tu me fasses / que tu me dises / que tu m’aides ». The « me » is the object pronoun (“to me / me”) placed before the verb.
target_language_example: J’ai besoin que tu me dises la vérité.
native_language_example: I need you to tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Form of **avoir**: **j’ai** = “I have” + **des** = “some” (plural). Very often used with **en**: **j’en ai des…** = “I have some (of them)/I’ve got … of them,” where **en** replaces what you’re talking about (“some of it/them”). Common with quantities: **J’en ai des centaines / des tonnes** (“I have hundreds / tons of them”).
target_language_example: J’en ai des nouvelles.
native_language_example: I have some new ones.

additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular present form of the phrase "avoir envie de" (to feel like / to want). It’s followed by an infinitive: "J’ai envie de dormir" (I feel like sleeping). With a noun, you also use "de": "J’ai envie de chocolat" (I want chocolate). Note: French "envie" usually means desire/craving, not English "envy" (jealousy).
target_language_example: J’ai envie de rester à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: I feel like staying home tonight.

meaning: "I have faith in" / "I believe in" (I trust).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **avoir foi en + someone/something** = “to have faith in.” It’s often used in religious contexts (faith in God), but it can also mean strong trust or confidence in a person. With pronouns: **J’ai foi en toi** (in you, informal singular), **J’ai foi en vous** (in you, formal or plural).
target_language_example: J’ai foi en toi, tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: I have faith in you; you’re going to make it.

meaning: "I just need to" / "I only need to".
additional_notes: Used to say you only need one thing. It’s the 1st-person singular form of « avoir besoin de » (to need): « j’ai (juste) besoin de + noun » or « j’ai (juste) besoin de + infinitive » (de becomes d’ before a vowel: « j’ai juste besoin d’appeler… »).
target_language_example: J’ai juste besoin de cinq minutes pour finir.
native_language_example: I just need five minutes to finish.

meaning: "I have the impression" / "I feel like" / "I get the feeling".
additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase **avoir l’impression** (“to have the impression / to feel”). **ai l'impression** is the **1st person singular present** ("I have the impression"). Common patterns: **J’ai l’impression que + clause** ("I feel like / I get the feeling that...") and **J’ai l’impression de + infinitive** ("I feel like + verb"). Often used to make an opinion sound less direct or less certain. Note: you’ll commonly see it with the elision **j’ai**; the core term here is **ai l'impression**.
target_language_example: Je crois que je me trompe, mais j'ai l'impression que tu es fatigué.
native_language_example: I think I might be wrong, but I get the feeling that you're tired.

meaning: "I feel like…" / "I have the impression that…"
additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular present form inside the common verb phrase «avoir l’impression de». It’s typically used as «J’ai l’impression de + infinitive» to express a subjective feeling/perception (often with some uncertainty): “I feel like…” / “I get the sense that…”. You can also use «J’ai l’impression que + clause» (e.g., «J’ai l’impression que tu es fatigué.»).
target_language_example: Je pense que je suis prêt, mais j'ai l'impression de me tromper.
native_language_example: I think I’m ready, but I feel like I might be wrong.

meaning: "I feel like" / "it seems to me that" / "I have the impression that."
additional_notes: Most often used as **j'ai l'impression que ...** (with *j'* = “I”). It introduces a personal impression or a tentative opinion and often sounds softer than stating something as a fact. It’s typically followed by the **indicative**: *J'ai l'impression qu'il est en retard.*
target_language_example: J'ai l'impression que tu es fatigué.
native_language_example: I feel like you’re tired.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French as part of negation: “je n’ai pas …” → “j’ai pas …” (“I don’t have …”). Often seen with “en”: “j’en ai pas” = “I don’t have any / I haven’t got any.” It can also be used in expressions like “j’en ai pas l’impression” (“I don’t get the impression / I don’t feel like that”). In formal writing, include “ne”: “je n’ai pas …”.
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai pas d’argent sur moi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have any money on me.

meaning: "(I) don’t feel like it / (I) don’t want to."
additional_notes: This is a shortened, informal form of « je n’ai pas envie (de…) » (dropping « je » and « ne »). « Avoir envie de + infinitive/noun » means “to feel like / want to (do something).” You can also say « je n’en ai pas envie » where « en » replaces « de + something » (“I don’t feel like it / I don’t want any”).
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai pas envie de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Typically used with the subject pronoun "j'" to form "J'ai quelque chose d'important à + infinitive". Often followed by an indirect object pronoun (e.g., "à te / à vous / à lui") and then an infinitive such as "dire", "faire", or "demander".
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose d'important à te dire.
native_language_example: I have something important to tell you.

ai quelque chose à te dire

target_language_multi_word_term: ai quelque chose à te dire
additional_notes: Usually said as a full sentence with the subject: « J’ai quelque chose à te dire. » The structure is « avoir + quelque chose à + infinitive » (“to have something to do/say”). « te » = “to you” (informal singular). For formal or plural “you,” use « vous »: « J’ai quelque chose à vous dire. »
target_language_example: J’ai quelque chose à te dire : je déménage bientôt.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you: I’m moving soon.

meaning: I have something to… / I’ve got a thing to…
additional_notes: Used (usually with "j’") to introduce an action you need/want to do: « J’ai un truc à faire/te dire/te demander ». « Truc » is very common and informal, meaning “thing/stuff” when you don’t want to be specific or can’t find the exact word. In careful French, you can replace it with « quelque chose à » (“something to”).
target_language_example: J’ai un truc à te dire.
native_language_example: I’ve got something to tell you.

additional_notes:
Imperative of aider (“to help”) + the object pronoun moi (“me”). Used to ask someone to help you; can be followed by:
- avec + noun: Aide-moi avec ces munitions. (“Help me with this ammo.”)
- à + infinitive: Aide-moi à faire mes devoirs. (“Help me do my homework.”)
It can sound urgent or frustrated depending on tone (e.g., Alors aide-moi ! = “Then help me!”).
target_language_example: S'il te plaît, aide-moi à porter ces sacs.
native_language_example: Please help me carry these bags.

additional_notes: Imperative of aider (to help) + moi (me) + à + an infinitive verb. Used to ask someone to help you do an action or accomplish a task. In everyday English you often drop “to”: “Help me choose.” You can add an object after the infinitive: « Aide-moi à le soulever » (help me lift it).
target_language_example: Aide-moi à remplir ce formulaire, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Help me fill out this form, please.

additional_notes: Imperative of "aider" + object pronoun "moi". Used to ask for help, often politely; you can add "s'il vous plaît" or "je vous en prie" to make it more pleading. More informal alternatives include "aide-moi" (to one person you use tu) and "aidez-moi" is also used when speaking to several people.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, aidez-moi à porter ces sacs, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Excuse me, help me carry these bags, please.

additional_notes: "Aidez" is the formal or plural command form of "aider" (to help). "moi" is the object pronoun (me), and "à" is followed by an infinitive verb to say what you need help doing (e.g., "aidez-moi à apprendre"). In informal singular you’ll also hear "aide-moi à".
target_language_example: Aidez-moi à remplir ce formulaire, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Help me fill out this form, please.

meaning: "(that) you were able to come" / "(that) you could come".
additional_notes: This is the past subjunctive of "pouvoir" + "venir" ("que tu aies pu venir"). It’s used after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (emotion, doubt, necessity, etc.), and it refers to a completed past possibility (you managed to come). Often used with "que": "Je suis content que tu aies pu venir."
target_language_example: Je suis content que tu aies pu venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m happy you were able to come tonight.

additional_notes: This is the verb–subject inversion used to ask a yes/no question in more formal French: "aime" (likes) + "il" (he). The extra "-t-" is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel sound (aime) and the subject pronoun starts with a vowel (il): "aime-t-il". In everyday speech, people often use "Est-ce qu'il aime… ?" or "Il aime… ?" instead.
target_language_example: Aime-t-il ce film ?
native_language_example: Does he like this movie?

additional_notes: "Aimer" means "to like/love" and "beaucoup" means "a lot." With objects/things (music, school), it’s usually "really like." With people (Je t'aime beaucoup / Je les aime beaucoup), it means strong affection ("I like you a lot"), and is generally less intense than "Je t’aime" ("I love you"). Word order: subject + aimer (conjugated) + beaucoup + object (or object pronoun before the verb: "Je t’aime beaucoup").
target_language_example: J'aime beaucoup cette chanson.
native_language_example: I really like this song.

meaning: likes (quite) a lot; is fond of.
additional_notes: "Aimer" alone can mean "to love" (people) or "to like" (things). Adding "bien" often softens it and clearly means "to like" / "to be fond of" someone or something (not romantic love). It can also suggest "rather/quite a lot" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je t'aime bien, mais je ne suis pas amoureux.
native_language_example: I like you, but I’m not in love.

additional_notes: "aime" is the 3rd-person singular of "aimer" (to like/love). Used with a subject (il/elle/on or a name): "Cathy aime la musique." For "I like music," say "J’aime la musique." You can add a style or adjective after "musique" (e.g., "musique acoustique", "musique country", "musique lente").
target_language_example: Mon frère aime la musique classique.
native_language_example: My brother likes classical music.

additional_notes: aime is the il/elle/on form of aimer. With les + a plural noun, it often means someone likes a type or category of things in general; in English, you usually do not translate les as "the" here. Depending on context, aimer can also mean "to love."
target_language_example: Elle aime les chats.
native_language_example: She likes cats.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject (ils/elles) + the verb aimer in the present tense (aiment) + the plural definite article les before a plural noun. In French, aimer can mean both 'to like' and 'to love' depending on context; with things in general, it often means 'to like'.
target_language_example: Ils aiment les films français.
native_language_example: They like French movies.

meaning: to like; to quite like (less strong than « aimer »).
additional_notes: Used to express liking or enjoyment without the stronger sense of love/being in love. Common with things and activities (« J’aime bien ce film. ») and also with people to mean you like them as a person/friend (often implying not romantic love).
target_language_example: Je vais souvent dans ce café parce que j’aime bien l’ambiance.
native_language_example: I often go to this café because I quite like the atmosphere.

additional_notes: This is the conditional form of aimer (“to like/love”) with inversion (-tu), used to ask a polite question: “Would you like…?” It can be followed by a noun (Aimerais-tu un café ?), an infinitive (Aimerais-tu venir ?), or a question word like où (Où aimerais-tu aller ?). More formal than Tu veux… ?
target_language_example: Aimerais-tu venir dîner ce soir ?
native_language_example: Would you like to come for dinner tonight?

additional_notes: Conditional form of « aimer » used to make polite offers or questions. It’s the formal/plural « vous » form, common with strangers, in customer service, or when speaking to more than one person. Often followed by an infinitive (aimeriez-vous discuter ?) or by « que » + subjunctive (aimeriez-vous que Marie fasse… ?).
target_language_example: Aimeriez-vous prendre un café ?
native_language_example: Would you like to have a coffee?

meaning: "do you like" / "do you love" (asked to one person).
additional_notes: This is the verb "aimer" (to like/love) in the present tense with inversion for questions: "aimes-tu...?" = "do you like...?" It’s addressed to one person you call "tu" (informal singular). In everyday speech, people also commonly ask "Tu aimes...?" (intonation) or "Est-ce que tu aimes...?". "Aimer" can mean "like" (things/activities) or "love" (people), depending on context.
target_language_example: Aimes-tu la musique française ?
native_language_example: Do you like French music?

meaning: "Do you like the …?" (asking if you like something).
additional_notes: This is a question using inversion: verb + “-tu” (Aimes-tu…?). It’s equivalent to “Est-ce que tu aimes… ?” and means “Do you like…?”. “Le” is the masculine singular “the,” often used with general likes/dislikes (e.g., aimes-tu le café ? = do you like coffee?). Use “la” for feminine nouns and “les” for plural nouns.
target_language_example: Aimes-tu le café ?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee?

meaning: "Do you like (the)…?" (asking about liking something in general).
additional_notes: This is the verb–subject inversion form of a question: "aimes" (you like) + "tu" (you). It’s slightly formal/standard compared with "Tu aimes les… ?". "Les" is used with plural nouns and also when talking about things in general (e.g., "les maths").
target_language_example: Aimes-tu les films d’horreur ?
native_language_example: Do you like horror movies?

meaning: Do you like…? / Do you love…? (formal).
additional_notes: This is the verb *aimer* (“to like/love”) in the **vous** form (*aimez*) with **inversion** (*-vous*) to make a question. It’s a **formal** or more “bookish” way to ask; in everyday speech you often hear *Vous aimez… ?* or *Est-ce que vous aimez… ?*. Depending on context, *aimer* can mean “to like” (e.g., food, activities) or “to love” (people). It can be followed by a noun (*Aimez-vous Boston ?*) or an infinitive (*Aimez-vous faire du sport ?*).
target_language_example: Aimez-vous le café ?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they like something feminine singular (“la” = “the” for feminine nouns). This is the formal question style with inversion (verb + “vous”). For masculine nouns, use “aimez-vous le… ?”; for plural, “aimez-vous les… ?”.
target_language_example: Aimez-vous la musique classique ?
native_language_example: Do you like classical music?

meaning: "Do you like the…?" (asking if someone likes a specific thing).
additional_notes: This is the formal/question form with inversion: verb + subject (aimez-vous). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun with le (e.g., le football, le piano). For feminine nouns you’d use "aimez-vous la…?"; for plural, "aimez-vous les…?" In everyday speech, people often say "Vous aimez le… ?"
target_language_example: Aimez-vous le café ?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee?

meaning: "Do you like the..." (asking if someone likes a type of thing).
additional_notes: "Aimez-vous" is the formal/inverted way to ask "Do you like...?". "Les" is used for plural nouns or general categories (e.g., movies, strawberries). In casual speech, you’ll often hear: "Vous aimez les… ?" or "Tu aimes les… ?".
target_language_example: Aimez-vous les desserts au chocolat ?
native_language_example: Do you like chocolate desserts?

additional_notes: Often links two items or people to add information: X ainsi que Y = “X as well as Y” (similar to “et aussi”). It can also introduce a comparison, especially with a pronoun or clause: ainsi que vous le savez = “as you already know” / “just as you know.”
target_language_example: J’ai invité Marie ainsi que Paul.
native_language_example: I invited Marie as well as Paul.

additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun to describe a place that has air conditioning: une chambre avec air conditionné (a room with air conditioning), un bureau à air conditionné (an air-conditioned office). Also used with appareil to mean an air-conditioning unit (appareil de climatisation is another common way to say this).
target_language_example: Est-ce que l'hôtel a l'air conditionné ?
native_language_example: Does the hotel have air conditioning?

additional_notes: Used before a noun starting with a vowel sound (air de → air d’). Often found in phrases like “un/une air d’…” to say something has a certain vibe or reminds you of something (e.g., un air d’été). Also appears in “avoir l’air de …” (“to seem to / to look like”), but that’s a longer expression.
target_language_example: Cette chanson a un air d'été.
native_language_example: This song has a summer vibe.

additional_notes: Usually appears within the larger pattern **avoir l’air d’aller bien** (“to look/seem like you’re doing well”). It’s most natural with an article: **l’air** (not *air* alone). You can vary what follows **avoir l’air de**: **avoir l’air fatigué** (to look tired), **avoir l’air d’être malade** (to seem to be sick).
target_language_example: Après tes vacances, tu as l’air d’aller bien.
native_language_example: After your vacation, you seem to be doing well.

meaning: 'the look of a…' / 'looks like a…' (usually in « avoir l’air d’un/une… »).
additional_notes: Most often used with « avoir l’air de + noun » to describe what someone/something seems like: « Il a l’air d’un professeur » (“He looks like a teacher”). Note: French « air » means “look/appearance” here, not “air” (the gas). Use « d’un » before a masculine singular noun and « d’une » before a feminine singular noun.
target_language_example: Il a l’air d'un médecin.
native_language_example: He looks like a doctor.

additional_notes: Used for travel (train/plane/bus): « Aller-retour ou aller simple ? » = “Round trip or one-way?” It can mean the ticket itself (« un aller-retour ») or the act of going somewhere and coming back (« faire un aller-retour »). Often used with destination: « un aller-retour à Paris » / « un aller-retour chez toi ».
target_language_example: Je voudrais un aller-retour pour Lyon, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a round-trip ticket to Lyon, please.

additional_notes: Used in travel/transport when buying tickets. Often said as "un aller simple" or with "billet" ("un billet aller simple"). Contrasts with "aller-retour" (round trip/return ticket).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un billet aller simple pour Marseille, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a one-way ticket to Marseille, please.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: aller au + [place/event] (au = à + le). For feminine singular, use aller à la (aller à la piscine). For plural, use aller aux (aller aux États-Unis). Before a vowel sound, use aller à l' (aller à l'école). Note: "aller au petit coin" is a polite/euphemistic way to say “to go to the bathroom.”
target_language_example: Nous aimons aller au musée.
native_language_example: We like to go to the museum.

meaning: to go to the movies; to go to the cinema.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to watch a movie at a movie theater. Conjugate "aller" to match the subject (je vais, tu vas, il/elle va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont). Often paired with a time: "On va au cinéma ce soir."
target_language_example: On va aller au cinéma samedi soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to go to the movies on Saturday night.

aller au cinéma ou au théâtre

target_language_multi_word_term: aller au cinéma ou au théâtre
meaning: to go to the movies or to the theater.
additional_notes: Uses aller (to go) + au (= à + le) before masculine singular places: au cinéma, au théâtre. Common in invitations or preferences: Tu veux… ? / Vous voulez… ? and Tu préfères… ? / Vous préférez… ? (tu = informal singular, vous = formal or plural).
target_language_example: Ce soir, on va aller au cinéma ou au théâtre ?
native_language_example: Tonight, are we going to go to the movies or to the theater?

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to bed (usually to sleep). Common with devoir (“Tu dois aller au lit”) and in questions (“Tu es prêt à aller au lit ?”).
target_language_example: Je vais aller au lit tôt ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to go to bed early tonight.

meaning: to go to the bathroom (to use the toilet).
additional_notes: Common, polite way to say you need to use the toilet. Used with devoir/je dois (I have to) or as a request: « Je peux / Puis-je aller aux toilettes ? » (Can/May I go to the bathroom?). Literally “to go to the toilets,” and it’s typically plural in French: « les toilettes ». In casual speech you may also hear « aller aux WC ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je dois aller aux toilettes.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have to go to the bathroom.

meaning: 'to go with' (to match / to pair well with).
additional_notes: Used to say that two things match or look good together (often clothes, colors, accessories). It can also mean that something is compatible or fits well with something else. Very common in the negative: « ne pas aller avec » = 'not to go with / not to match'.
target_language_example: Cette cravate ne semble pas aller avec ta chemise.
native_language_example: That tie doesn’t seem to go with your shirt.

additional_notes: Used when you leave your current place to fetch or pick up someone or something (often implying you’ll bring it/them back). Common with an object: « aller chercher mon portefeuille », « aller chercher Maria » (pick Maria up).
target_language_example: Je vais aller chercher les clés dans la voiture.
native_language_example: I’m going to go get the keys from the car.

meaning: to fit perfectly; to suit someone perfectly (“fit like a glove”).
additional_notes: Used primarily for clothing/accessories that fit extremely well (size and shape), and by extension for something that suits someone very well (a role, a style, etc.). Commonly used with a clothing item as the subject: « Cette veste va comme un gant. »
target_language_example: Cette veste va comme un gant.
native_language_example: This jacket fits like a glove.

meaning: to move forward; to move on (make progress).
additional_notes: Used when you want to continue, make progress, or stop dwelling on the past and take the next step. Very common with expressions like "Il est temps de..." (It’s time to...) and "Il faut..." / "On doit..." (We have to...). Often about life decisions or a situation, not just physical movement.
target_language_example: Après cette erreur, on doit aller de l'avant.
native_language_example: After that mistake, we have to move on.

meaning: to be obvious; to go without saying.
additional_notes: Used to say something is self-evident or taken for granted. Commonly appears in impersonal constructions such as « Il va de soi que… » or as a standalone reassurance « Ça va de soi. ». The base expression is « aller de soi » (infinitive).
target_language_example: Pour elle, aider ses amis, c’est aller de soi.
native_language_example: For her, helping her friends is a given / goes without saying.

meaning: “come on!” / “go on!” (urging someone to do something).
additional_notes: Often used as an imperative; in real speech you more commonly see it conjugated (« Va donc ! », « Allez donc ! »). Using the infinitive « aller donc » can sound like a brusque instruction (e.g., on a sign or in clipped speech). « donc » adds insistence or impatience, similar to “just” or “come on.” Tone depends on context: it can be encouraging or annoyed.
target_language_example: Aller donc, dis-moi la vérité !
native_language_example: Come on, tell me the truth!

meaning: to go to; to go on
additional_notes: Used with en before many places, especially feminine countries, regions, and continents (for example en France, en Europe). It also appears in some set expressions like aller en promenade, where it means going on an activity or outing.
target_language_example: Pourquoi veux-tu aller en Europe ?
native_language_example: Why do you want to go to Europe?

meaning: to go to prison; to be sent to jail.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the possibility or consequence of being imprisoned (often after breaking the law). Common with pouvoir (could/might) or devoir (must/have to).
target_language_example: Si tu fais ça, tu risques d'aller en prison.
native_language_example: If you do that, you risk going to prison.

meaning: to come and go; to go back and forth (often freely).
additional_notes: Used to talk about moving in and out of a place or moving around without restrictions: “Tu peux aller et venir…” = “You can come and go…”. It can be literal (physical movement) or more abstract (people/characters coming and going in a story).
target_language_example: Ici, les visiteurs peuvent aller et venir librement.
native_language_example: Here, visitors can come and go freely.

meaning: to go for a walk/ride; to go out for a bit.
additional_notes: Used for taking a short outing, often for fresh air, a change of scenery, or to clear your head. You can specify how: "aller faire un tour en voiture" (go for a drive), "à pied" (on foot), "dans le quartier" (around the neighborhood). Often said on its own: "Je vais aller faire un tour" = "I’m going to go out for a bit."
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on va aller faire un tour dans le quartier.
native_language_example: After dinner, we’re going to go for a walk around the neighborhood.

meaning: to go all the way; to see it through to the end.
additional_notes: Used to say you will continue until the end of a process, effort, or goal (not giving up). It can also mean going “all the way” with a decision or action, depending on context. Often appears with verbs like vouloir, devoir, falloir, tenir à.
target_language_example: Même si c'est difficile, je vais aller jusqu'au bout.
native_language_example: Even if it’s hard, I’m going to see it through to the end.

meaning: to go far; (figuratively) to go too far; to have a lot of potential/success.
additional_notes: Literal use: physical distance (“go far”). Figurative use: to exceed acceptable limits (“to go too far”), or to indicate future success (“He’ll go far”). Note: "loin" means "far" and is a false friend with English "loin" (meat).
target_language_example: Avec ce talent, il peut aller loin.
native_language_example: With that talent, he can go far.

additional_notes: “Aller” means “to go.” “Là-bas” means “over there / to that place” (often a place not right here, sometimes a bit far away). You can change the verb to match the subject: je vais là-bas, tu vas là-bas, il/elle va là-bas, etc. You can also use “y aller” to mean “to go there” when the place is already known from context.
target_language_example: On peut aller là-bas demain ?
native_language_example: Can we go there tomorrow?

meaning: to go faster; to speed up.
additional_notes: Used to compare speed (plus vite = faster). Often with a subject (Je/Nous) to mean “go faster,” or with faire + infinitive (faire aller) to mean “make something/someone go faster” (e.g., a car, machine, or person).
target_language_example: On peut aller plus vite si on prend l'autoroute.
native_language_example: We can go faster if we take the highway.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to an unspecified place. Often followed by another action: « aller quelque part et + verb » (“go somewhere and …”). In questions/invitations, it can suggest going to a quieter or more private place to talk.
target_language_example: On peut aller quelque part de plus calme pour discuter ?
native_language_example: Can we go somewhere quieter to talk?

meaning: to go without saying; to be obvious.
additional_notes: Used to say something is self-evident and doesn’t need to be stated. Common patterns: « Ça va sans dire. » (“That goes without saying.”) and « Il va sans dire que… » (“It goes without saying that…”). Note: the infinitive form « aller sans dire » is less common in full sentences than the conjugated forms « ça va sans dire » / « il va sans dire ».
target_language_example: Ça devrait aller sans dire : je serai là à l’heure.
native_language_example: It should go without saying: I’ll be there on time.

meaning: to go and get (something) done; to go get yourself + [verb].
additional_notes:
Usually used as a pattern: **aller se faire + infinitive** (often with a verb like *couper, soigner, masser*), meaning you go somewhere to have something done for you: *aller se faire couper les cheveux* = “to go get your hair cut.”

It can also introduce rude expressions like **aller se faire voir** (“go away / get lost”) or the very vulgar **aller se faire foutre**.
target_language_example: Je vais aller se faire couper les cheveux.
native_language_example: I'm going to go get my hair cut.

meaning: to go alone / by oneself (all alone).
additional_notes: Used to say someone goes without help or without company. Very common when talking about children doing something independently. You’ll often hear it with pronouns: « y aller tout seul » (to go there alone) or « Je vais y aller tout seul ». You can also agree with the subject: « toute seule » (feminine), « tout seuls / toutes seules » (plural).
target_language_example: Il veut aller tout seul à l’école.
native_language_example: He wants to go to school by himself.

meaning: to go too far (to overdo it; to cross a line).
additional_notes: Used literally for distance or figuratively for behavior, words, jokes, or actions that are excessive or unacceptable. Often said as a warning or criticism: « Tu vas trop loin » (You’re going too far).
target_language_example: Je plaisantais, mais là, tu vas aller trop loin.
native_language_example: I was joking, but now you’re going to go too far.

additional_notes: A common, compositional phrase meaning to go and see someone or something. With a person, it often means "go see" or "go visit"; with a film or show, it means "go watch"; and without a direct object, it can mean "go check" or "go see for oneself."
target_language_example: Je vais aller voir le médecin demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to go see the doctor tomorrow.

meaning: to look elsewhere; to go somewhere else (instead).
additional_notes: Used when you should search for something in another place or choose another option. In the imperative it can sound dismissive: « Va voir ailleurs ! » = “Go away / Look somewhere else!”
target_language_example: Si ce magasin n’a plus ta taille, on peut aller voir ailleurs.
native_language_example: If this store doesn’t have your size anymore, we can look elsewhere.

additional_notes: In standard French, the usual form is « y aller », not « aller y ». The sequence « aller y » is generally not used in normal sentence word order, so this entry is best understood as a reference to the components of the expression rather than a standard standalone phrase. In commands, related forms like « vas-y » or « allez-y » can mean « go ahead ».
target_language_example: On dit « y aller », pas « aller y » en français standard.
native_language_example: People say "y aller," not "aller y" in standard French.

additional_notes: Used for going to a place or destination. Often contracts with articles: à + le = au, à + les = aux (for example, aller au cinéma, aller aux États-Unis).
target_language_example: Peux-tu aller à la mer demain ?
native_language_example: Can you go to the seaside tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used with "aller" (to go) + "à" to express going to a place. "à l'hôpital" means going to the hospital (for treatment, a visit, or work depending on context). Common with "devoir" (must/need to) or "il faut" (it’s necessary to).
target_language_example: Je dois aller à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: I have to go to the hospital.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "aller" (to go) + the preposition "à" (to/at) + "l'école" (the school). Depending on context, it can mean physically going to school at a given moment or (especially with children/obligations) having to attend school.
target_language_example: Je dois aller à l'école demain matin.
native_language_example: I have to go to school tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun, especially for places: la mairie, la gym, la fac, la patinoire. With masculine nouns, French usually uses aller au; with plural nouns, aller aux; and before a vowel sound, aller à l’. In some cases, English may drop "the" in translation, for example aller à la fac = "to go to college."
target_language_example: Je veux aller à la patinoire.
native_language_example: I want to go to the ice rink.

meaning: to go to the train station.
additional_notes: Used when talking about getting to the train station (la gare). Often appears in questions asking for directions: « Comment aller à la gare ? » or « Des indications pour aller à la gare ». To express the means of transport, you can add « en bus » (by bus) or « en métro » (by metro). You may also hear « à la gare » alone after a verb like « aller » or « être ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, comment puis-je aller à la gare ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how can I get to the train station?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "aller" (to go) + "à la" because "plage" is feminine (la plage). It often refers to going for leisure/swimming/sunbathing. You can change the subject to match who is going (je vais, tu vas, on va, nous allons, etc.).
target_language_example: Cet été, on va aller à la plage tous les week-ends.
native_language_example: This summer, we're going to go to the beach every weekend.

meaning: "are you going" / used to form a polite question: "are you going to…?"
additional_notes: This is the verb "aller" (to go) in the present tense (vous allez) with subject–verb inversion to make a formal/polite question: "Allez-vous + infinitive… ?" It can mean literal movement (going somewhere) or the near future ("going to" do something). Common in writing and formal speech; in everyday conversation people often use "Est-ce que vous allez… ?" or "Vous allez… ?"
target_language_example: Allez-vous me rappeler demain ?
native_language_example: Will you call me back tomorrow?

meaning: "Go, go, go!" / "Come on!" (to urge or cheer someone on).
additional_notes: Repetition of the imperative "allez" (from "aller", to go). Used in spoken French to push people to act faster, keep going, or to encourage a team (like chanting). Often said with an exclamation mark and strong intonation; similar to English "Come on!" or "Let’s go!" depending on context.
target_language_example: Allez, allez, allez ! On y va !
native_language_example: Come on, come on, come on! Let’s go!

meaning: "Come on, let's…" (to urge or encourage action).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French to get things moving or motivate someone. "Allez" literally means "go" (imperative of aller), but here it functions like "come on". Often followed by "on y va" (let’s go) or a verb phrase: "Allez, on le fait" (come on, let’s do it).
target_language_example: Allez, on commence !
native_language_example: Come on, let’s start!

additional_notes: This is the verb "aller" (to go) in the present tense + "vous" (you) with inversion to form a formal/plural question. It can be literal about going somewhere ("Allez-vous à Paris ?"), and it also appears in the common expression "Comment allez-vous ?" meaning "How are you?" (literally "How are you going?").
target_language_example: Allez-vous au travail en métro ?
native_language_example: Do you go to work by subway?

meaning: Go ahead; go there; go for it (formal/plural).
additional_notes: Imperative of « aller » with « y » (“there/at it”). Used to encourage or invite someone to act (“Go ahead!”), to tell someone to go to a place (“Go there!”), or to give permission (“If you want to go, go ahead.”). Addressed to « vous » (one person formally or several people). Often repeated for emphasis: « Allez-y, allez-y ! ».
target_language_example: Allez-y, je vous écoute.
native_language_example: Go ahead, I’m listening.

meaning: "who knows?" / "go figure." (used to say it’s impossible to know or explain).
additional_notes: Often used as a rhetorical comment when the reason/explanation is unknown or hard to understand. It can stand alone ("Allez savoir.") or be followed by a question word: "Allez savoir pourquoi...", "Allez savoir ce que...", "Allez savoir ce qui...". Common in spoken, conversational French.
target_language_example: Il n’est pas venu, allez savoir pourquoi.
native_language_example: He didn’t come—who knows why.

meaning: “Oh, alright then / okay, fine.” (also: “come on then”).
additional_notes: Informal interjection used to agree reluctantly, to concede, or to wrap things up and move on. Often said with a sigh or a shrug, similar to “alright, fine” or “come on then” in English. You’ll also hear close variants like “allez, va !” or just “allez !”.
target_language_example: Bon, allez va, j’arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Alright then, I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: Extremely offensive insult. Uses the imperative with « vous » (addressing one person formally or several people). A common variant with « tu » is « Va te faire foutre ». Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start or escalate conflict.
target_language_example: Je suis furieux : allez vous faire foutre.
native_language_example: I’m furious: go fuck yourself.

meaning: 'are we going…?' / 'are we going to…?' (question form).
additional_notes: This is the verb *aller* (nous form: *allons*) followed by *nous* in an inverted order to form a question (more formal/written style): *Allons-nous + infinitive ?* or used with question words: *Où allons-nous… ? Quand allons-nous… ?* In everyday speech, people often say *On va… ?* or *Est-ce que nous allons… ?* instead.
target_language_example: Allons-nous prendre le bus ou marcher ?
native_language_example: Are we going to take the bus or walk?

meaning: 'are we going to do' (what will we do?).
additional_notes: Used in questions with inversion: verb + “-nous” (Allons-nous…) and often preceded by “Qu’…”: “Qu’allons-nous faire ?” = “What are we going to do?” It uses the near-future construction “aller + infinitive” (here, “faire”). You can also add details: “Qu’allons-nous faire maintenant ?” (now) / “Qu’allons-nous faire de lui ?” (what are we going to do with him?).
target_language_example: Qu’allons-nous faire si le train est annulé ?
native_language_example: What are we going to do if the train is canceled?

additional_notes: This is the 1st-person plural present of aller (“to go”) with inversion (verb + nous) to form a question: Allons-nous au cinéma ? (“Are we going to the movies?”). It can also mean “How are we?” in Comment allons-nous ? You may see it with pronouns like y or en: Y allons-nous ? (“Are we going there?”) and Allons-nous-en ! (“Let’s go / Let’s leave!”). In everyday speech, people often prefer Est-ce que nous allons… ? or On va… ? instead of inversion.
target_language_example: Allons-nous au restaurant ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to the restaurant tonight?

additional_notes: Common encouragement to start or move on. Literally “let’s go there” (aller + y), but it’s used like “come on, let’s go” or “go ahead.” Often said on its own, or followed by a short instruction: « Allons-y, … ». Can also mean “let’s get started” in a non-literal sense.
target_language_example: Bon, allons-y : on commence maintenant.
native_language_example: Alright, let’s go: we’re starting now.

additional_notes: Past tense of "aller" with être: "je suis allé(e)" = "I went / I've been". "au" is the contraction of "à + le" and is used before a masculine singular place or destination (au restaurant, au stade). Agree "allé" with the subject: "il est allé", "elle est allée", "ils sont allés", "elles sont allées".
target_language_example: Je suis allé au musée dimanche.
native_language_example: I went to the museum on Sunday.

meaning: went to the park / gone to the park.
additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the verb aller in the passé composé: je suis allé(e) au parc (I went to the park). With être, allé agrees with the subject: allé (masc.), allée (fem.), allés/allées (plural). Au = à + le (to the).
target_language_example: Je suis allé au parc après l’école.
native_language_example: I went to the park after school.

meaning: “went to” / “has gone to” (used with **en** for feminine countries, countries starting with a vowel, or continents).
additional_notes: Past tense of **aller** formed with **être**: **être allé(e)(s) + en + place**. Use **en** with feminine countries (e.g., *en France*), countries starting with a vowel (e.g., *en Italie*), and continents (e.g., *en Europe*). With masculine countries, you usually use **au** (*au Canada*), and with plural places **aux** (*aux États-Unis*). The past participle **allé** agrees with the subject: *il est allé*, *elle est allée*, *ils sont allés*, *elles sont allées*.
target_language_example: Il est allé en France.
native_language_example: He went to France.

additional_notes: Used with the verb “aller” in the past tense (passé composé): “être” + past participle “allé” + destination introduced by “à”. It can mean a completed trip (“went to”) or life experience (“have/has been to”). The past participle agrees with the subject: “il est allé”, “elle est allée”, “ils sont allés”, “elles sont allées”. With “à” + articles: “à” + “le” → “au” (au cinéma), “à” + “les” → “aux” (aux États-Unis).
target_language_example: Je ne suis jamais allé à Istanbul.
native_language_example: I have never been to Istanbul.

meaning: “went to the” (said to/for a woman or girl).
additional_notes: Past tense of aller (to go): je/tu/vous/elle est allée… The -e in allée agrees with a female subject. Au = à + le, used before a masculine singular noun (au travail, au garage, au stade). With a feminine noun, you usually use à la (allée à la piscine).
target_language_example: Elle est allée au supermarché après le travail.
native_language_example: She went to the supermarket after work.

additional_notes: "Allés" is the past participle of "aller" used with "être" in the passé composé. It agrees with a plural subject (vous/ils/nous) and is masculine here; feminine plural would be "allées". "Au" = "à + le" and is used before masculine singular nouns (au restaurant, au stade, au Japon). For feminine singular, use "à la" (allées à la maison); for plural places, use "aux" (allés aux États-Unis).
target_language_example: Nous sommes allés au marché ce matin.
native_language_example: We went to the market this morning.

meaning: "So, it's..." / "Well then, it's..." (to introduce a conclusion, decision, or next step).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to move things along: to sum up, confirm a decision (Alors, c'est décidé.), check an answer (Alors, c'est oui ?), react to a situation (Alors, c'est parfait.), or ask what comes next (Alors, c'est quoi la suite ?). Often sounds like "OK, so..." in conversation.
target_language_example: Alors, c'est bon, on y va ?
native_language_example: So, it’s settled—are we going?

meaning: “So, I…” / “Then, I…” (used to introduce what you did or will do).
additional_notes: “Alors” is a very common connector at the start (or in the middle) of a sentence to show a consequence, next step, or conclusion. With “je”, it often continues a story or explains what happens next: “Alors, je suis venu.” It can also be used in questions: “Alors, je viens ?” = “So, should I come?” In faster speech you may hear it without a clear pause/comma.
target_language_example: Alors, je vais essayer une autre solution.
native_language_example: So, I’m going to try another solution.

meaning: "So, shall we…?" / "So, we…" (to start or move things along).
additional_notes: Common conversational opener used to transition, prompt action, or tease/comment on a situation. It’s often followed by a verb with "on" meaning "we" (e.g., "Alors, on commence ?" = "So, shall we start?"). The tone depends on context: it can sound friendly, impatient, or joking.
target_language_example: Alors, on y va ?
native_language_example: So, are we going?

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to move the conversation along: asking what’s happening, what’s wrong, or what to do next. Depending on tone, it can sound neutral, encouraging, or a bit impatient. Often followed by: « qu’est-ce qu’on fait ? », « qu’est-ce qu’il y a ? », « qu’est-ce qui se passe ? ».
target_language_example: Alors, qu'est-ce que tu veux faire maintenant ?
native_language_example: So, what do you want to do now?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to start a question, often as a follow-up or to prompt someone to explain. "Alors" means "so/then" and adds a conversational tone (like “So,”). It’s followed by "qu’est-ce que" + subject + verb: « Alors, qu’est-ce que tu veux ? »
target_language_example: Alors, qu'est-ce que tu veux faire ce soir ?
native_language_example: So, what do you want to do tonight?

meaning: “So, what are you…?” / “So, what’s up with you…?” (used to introduce a question, typically followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Common conversational lead-in to a question. It can convey impatience (“come on, then…”), curiosity, or simply move the conversation forward. It’s usually followed by a verb: « alors, qu'est-ce que tu attends ? », « …deviens ? », « …décides ? », « …veux faire ? ». You may also see it without the comma in writing: « Alors qu'est-ce que tu… ? »
target_language_example: Alors, qu'est-ce que tu attends ?
native_language_example: So, what are you waiting for?

additional_notes: Used as a conversational opener before a question, often to move things along, ask for an update, or prompt someone to respond. In writing you’ll often see a comma after alors: « Alors, que… ? ». It can sound a bit insistent depending on tone (like “So…?”).
target_language_example: Alors, que faisons-nous maintenant ?
native_language_example: So, what are we doing now?

meaning: "So, you…" / "Well, are you…?" (used to start a question or prompt).
additional_notes: Very common conversational opener. It uses "alors" to introduce what comes next (often a question, conclusion, or decision) and addresses someone directly with "tu" (informal "you"). Often implies “so, what now?” or “so, do you see?”.
target_language_example: Alors, tu viens avec nous ?
native_language_example: So, are you coming with us?

meaning: “So…?” / “So, how is it?” (to ask for a reaction or result).
additional_notes: Common spoken lead-in before a question, often about how something went or what someone thinks of something: “Alors, ça donne quoi ?” (So, what’s the result?), “Alors, ça fait quoi ?” (So, what does it do / how does it feel?), “Alors, ça te plaît ?” (So, do you like it?). You can also use it on its own to prompt someone to answer: “Alors, ça ?” ≈ “Well?”
target_language_example: Alors, ça s’est bien passé ?
native_language_example: So, did it go well?

meaning: “So, what…?” / “So, what is it (that)…?” (used to launch a question).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to move things along, often after a pause or to ask what happens next. Commonly followed by “que” + subject + verb (via the structure “qu’est-ce que …”): “Alors qu'est-ce qu'on fait ?”, “Alors qu'est-ce que tu veux ?”. Note the apostrophe in “qu'est-ce”.
target_language_example: Alors qu'est-ce qu'on fait ici ?
native_language_example: So, what are we doing here?

meaning: 'So what…?' / 'So what is it that…?' (to start a question).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to move the conversation forward, ask for an update, or ask what to do next. Often followed by a subject + verb (e.g., « Alors qu'est-ce qu'on fait ? »). In speech it’s very common; in more formal writing you might drop « alors » or use a more formal question form.
target_language_example: Alors qu'est-ce qu'on fait maintenant ?
native_language_example: So what do we do now?

meaning: “So/then what…?” (used to ask what happened/what it was/what to do next).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to prompt an explanation or the next step. Typically followed by a clause (often with a verb phrase): « alors qu'est-ce que je dois faire ? » (“So what should I do?”). « alors » can correspond to “so” or “then” depending on context.
target_language_example: Alors qu'est-ce que tu vas faire maintenant ?
native_language_example: So what are you going to do now?

additional_notes: Commonly introduces a contrast between two facts (often translated as “whereas” or “even though”): « Mes chaussures sont vieilles, alors que les siennes sont neuves. » It can also mean “when/while” to situate one action during another: « Il est parti alors que je dormais. » With the imperfect, it often describes an ongoing background situation.
target_language_example: Elle est sortie alors que je préparais le dîner.
native_language_example: She went out while I was making dinner.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “one of my …”: un ami à moi / une amie à moi. It’s often used to introduce someone as belonging to your circle without sounding as possessive or as specific as mon ami (“my friend”). Very common in speech; you can also say un de mes amis.
target_language_example: Tom est un ami à moi.
native_language_example: Tom is a friend of mine.

additional_notes: A romantic expression for the person you love most (your ideal or main partner). Often used when talking about someone (“C’est l’amour de ma vie”) or as an affectionate form of address (“mon amour de ma vie”). You’ll also see it with other possessives: "amour de ta vie" (the love of your life), "amour de sa vie" (the love of his/her life).
target_language_example: Je pense que tu es l’amour de ma vie.
native_language_example: I think you’re the love of my life.

meaning: in love with (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used with the verb « être »: « Je suis amoureuse de … » = “I’m in love with …”. It agrees with the speaker: a man says « amoureux de », and plural is « amoureux/amoureuses de ». « de » becomes « d’ » before a vowel or silent h (e.g., « amoureuse d’Alex »).
target_language_example: Elle est amoureuse de son voisin.
native_language_example: She’s in love with her neighbor.

meaning: (for a woman speaking) in love with him.
additional_notes: Used with the verb être: « Je suis amoureuse de lui. » It describes a woman/girl who is in love; masculine form is « amoureux de lui ». You also commonly see « tomber amoureuse de lui » = “to fall in love with him.”
target_language_example: Je crois que je suis amoureuse de lui, mais je n'ose pas lui dire.
native_language_example: I think I'm in love with him, but I don't dare tell him.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" (e.g., "Je suis amoureux/amoureuse de...") to say you are in love with a person. Adjective agreement: "amoureux" (male) / "amoureuse" (female). For a crush/liking someone (not necessarily love), French often uses "avoir un béguin pour" or "craquer pour" (more informal).
target_language_example: Tom est amoureux de Marie.
native_language_example: Tom is in love with Marie.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is in love with you: « Il/Je suis amoureux de toi ». Adjective agreement: a man says « amoureux », a woman says « amoureuse ». With formal/polite “you,” use « amoureux/amoureuse de vous ». In the negative you may see « ne … pas » and « plus »: « Je ne suis plus amoureux de toi » = “I’m not in love with you anymore.”
target_language_example: Je suis amoureux de toi depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: I’ve been in love with you for a long time.

meaning: Have fun! (to one person you address as “tu”).
additional_notes: Imperative form of “s’amuser” (to have fun). You say it to wish someone a good time: before a party, a trip, an outing, etc. For more than one person or a formal “you,” use: “Amusez-vous bien.”
target_language_example: Amuse-toi bien pendant ton voyage !
native_language_example: Have fun on your trip!

additional_notes: Imperative with "vous" (polite to one person or to a group). Often used as a friendly send-off: "Allez, amusez-vous bien !" You can also ask "Vous amusez-vous bien ?" = "Are you having fun?"
target_language_example: Merci, amusez-vous bien ce soir !
native_language_example: Thanks, have fun tonight!

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to say “pet.” Often used with the verb avoir: « J’ai un animal de compagnie » (I have a pet). You can specify the type with « comme animal de compagnie » (as a pet): « un lapin comme animal de compagnie ».
target_language_example: On a un chat comme animal de compagnie.
native_language_example: We have a cat as a pet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about animals kept by people, usually at home (e.g., a cat or dog). In everyday conversation, you may also hear just "un animal" when the context is clearly pets. Agreement: masculine singular "un animal domestique", feminine singular "une chèvre domestique", plural "des animaux domestiques".
target_language_example: Le chat est un animal domestique.
native_language_example: A cat is a domestic animal (a pet).

additional_notes: Used after a number to state an age difference: « X a [nombre] ans de plus que moi » = “X is [number] years older than me.” You can change the pronoun: que toi (than you), que lui/elle (than him/her), que nous/vous/eux/elles (than us/you/them). Opposite: « ans de moins que moi » = “years younger than me.”
target_language_example: Ma sœur a trois ans de plus que moi.
native_language_example: My sister is three years older than me.

additional_notes: A common way to say “camera” in French, especially for still photos. Often used with possessives: mon/ton/son appareil photo (“my/your/his/her camera”). In casual speech you may also hear “un appareil” when the context is clear, but “appareil photo” is the safe, clear term.
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon appareil photo à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my camera at home.

additional_notes: "Appareil photo" means "camera." Add the correct possessive before it (mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur), then use "est" ("is") to describe the camera: état (cassé = broken), qualité (mieux = better), caractéristiques (étanche = waterproof), taille (plus petit = smaller), etc. In many cases you’ll also hear it with an article: "L’appareil photo est…" = "The camera is…".
target_language_example: Mon appareil photo est trop lourd pour voyager.
native_language_example: My camera is too heavy for traveling.

additional_notes: Used when you want to contact the police (usually by phone) to report something, ask for help, or to say you will report someone. Common with "je vais" / "on va" (I’m going to / we’re going to).
target_language_example: Si tu vois quelque chose de suspect, on va appeler la police.
native_language_example: If you see something suspicious, we’re going to call the police.
