additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of appeler addressed to vous (one person formally, or more than one person). Often used to ask someone to phone you later: Appelez-moi ce soir / demain / après… You can also use it to mean “call me [a name]”: Appelez-moi Marie.
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, appelez-moi demain matin.
native_language_example: If you have questions, call me tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: A polite/formal way to invite someone to contact you if a situation comes up. Uses the imperative of appeler (“appelez” = “call”, addressing one person with vous) + moi (“me”) + si (“if”) + vous avez (“you have”). Commonly followed by a noun phrase like besoin (“need”), des questions (“questions”), des problèmes (“problems”), du nouveau (“news/updates”). Informal version: « Appelle-moi si tu as… »
target_language_example: Appelez-moi si vous avez des questions.
native_language_example: Call me if you have any questions.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of appeler + the object pronoun moi (“me”). Used to ask someone to phone you, often with a time or condition: appelle-moi quand… (call me when…), appelle-moi si… (call me if…), appelle-moi à… (call me at…). Commonly paired with s’il te plaît to be more polite.
target_language_example: Appelle-moi quand tu arrives.
native_language_example: Call me when you arrive.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to phone you later, when a certain condition is met (e.g., quand tu as fini / as le temps / es prêt / seras à Paris). “Appelle-moi” is the informal (tu) command form; with someone you address as vous, say “Appelez-moi quand vous…”.
target_language_example: Appelle-moi quand tu arrives à la maison.
native_language_example: Call me when you get home.

meaning: “Call me if you have…” / “Call me if you need…”
additional_notes: Common sentence starter used to offer help or stay in touch. **Appelle-moi** is the informal (tu) command “call me.” After **si** (“if”), French typically uses the **present tense**: *si tu as besoin…* (not “will have”). You can finish it with many things: **besoin (de…)** = need (something), **un/des problème(s)** = a problem/problems, **du nouveau** = news/updates.
target_language_example: Appelle-moi si tu as besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: Call me if you need help.

additional_notes: Used in inverted question form with the impersonal subject "on" (meaning “one/people/we” in general). Very common after "Comment" to ask for the name of something: "Comment appelle-t-on X ?" = “What do you call X?” / “What is X called?” You can replace "cela" with "ça" for a more casual tone, but "appelle-t-on" itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Comment appelle-t-on ce plat en français ?
native_language_example: What do you call this dish in French?

additional_notes: "Appelle" is the informal singular command (imperative) of appeler, used when speaking to one person you know well (tu). For "you" formal or plural, use "Appelez la police". You’ll also see it in other tenses: "On appelle la police ?" (Should we call the police?) and "J'appelle la police" (I’m calling the police).
target_language_example: Vite, appelle la police !
native_language_example: Quick, call the police!

additional_notes: This is the past form (passé composé) of the verb phrase « appeler la police » (“to call the police”): « (subject) + avoir + appelé ». Example: « J’ai appelé la police. » In questions you may see « As-tu… ? / Avez-vous… ? » (tu vs vous), or the informal spoken form « T’as… ? ». « On a appelé la police » often means “someone/we called the police.”
target_language_example: Il a appelé la police tout de suite.
native_language_example: He called the police right away.

additional_notes: Imperative of the verb *apporter* (“to bring”) + the indirect object pronoun *moi* (“to me”). Used to ask/order someone to bring something to you. Often followed by a noun: *Apporte-moi mes lunettes.* You can swap the pronoun: *apporte-lui* (bring him/her), *apporte-nous* (bring us).
target_language_example: Apporte-moi un verre d’eau, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Bring me a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Uses the verb apprendre (“to learn”) with a language. You can swap in other languages: apprendre l’anglais, apprendre l’espagnol, etc. If you want to say you’re currently doing it, French commonly uses the present tense: J’apprends le français (“I’m learning French”).
target_language_example: Je devrais apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I should learn French.

additional_notes: A common phrase for studying a language that isn’t your native language. "Apprendre" means “to learn,” and "une langue étrangère" means “a foreign language.” You can add which language with "apprendre le français / l’espagnol", or say "apprendre une langue" (learn a language).
target_language_example: J’essaie d’apprendre une langue étrangère pour voyager.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn a foreign language to travel.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb: « apprendre à + infinitif » (e.g., apprendre à conduire). It can mean learning a skill or learning how to behave/cope (apprendre à vivre avec). With an indirect object, it can mean “to teach someone to”: « apprendre à quelqu’un à + infinitif » (Je lui apprends à nager).
target_language_example: Elle va apprendre à conduire.
native_language_example: She’s going to learn to drive.

additional_notes: Used with apprendre + à + infinitive to talk about learning how to do something. You’ll most often see it in the past with avoir (passé composé): j’ai appris à…, il/elle a appris à…. Agreement can change with gender/number in some contexts (e.g., elle a appris à…, elles ont appris à…; also apprise/appris in certain constructions). Common in questions like « Quand avez-vous appris à… ? ».
target_language_example: J’ai appris à conduire l’année dernière.
native_language_example: I learned to drive last year.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with "avoir" in the passé composé: "j'ai appris à nager" = "I learned to swim." More generally, French uses "apprendre à + infinitive" to mean "to learn to (do something)": "apprendre à conduire" (learn to drive), "apprendre à cuisiner" (learn to cook). You can also use it with an indirect object to mean "to teach someone to": "Je lui ai appris à nager" = "I taught him/her to swim."
target_language_example: J’ai appris à nager à l’école.
native_language_example: I learned to swim at school.

additional_notes: Used for pressing a physical or on-screen button. "Appuyer sur" means "to press" (literally "to press on"). Often appears in instructions or requests: "Il faut…" (you must…), "Veuillez…" (please…), "Puis-je… ?" (may I…?).
target_language_example: Veuillez appuyer sur le bouton pour ouvrir la porte.
native_language_example: Please press the button to open the door.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening two days from now. It can be placed at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., « Après-demain, je pars » / « Je pars après-demain »).
target_language_example: On se voit après-demain à 10 heures.
native_language_example: See you the day after tomorrow at 10 o’clock.

additional_notes: Means the part of the day after midday (after 12:00) and before evening. Often used with time expressions: « trois heures de l’après-midi » (3 p.m.). You can also say « dimanche après-midi » (Sunday afternoon). It’s usually masculine: « un/cet après-midi »; however, in casual speech some people also say « cette après-midi ».
target_language_example: On se voit cet après-midi à 15 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other this afternoon at 3 p.m.?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an earlier action (avoir + past participle) that happens before the main action in the sentence. Common pattern: après avoir + past participle (parlé, étudié, vu, etc.). It refers to the subject of the main clause (e.g., Je vais me coucher après avoir étudié = I studied, then I go to bed).
target_language_example: Après avoir fini le travail, on est rentrés à la maison.
native_language_example: After finishing work, we went home.

après avoir marché un moment, nous

target_language_multi_word_term: après avoir marché un moment, nous
meaning: after walking for a while, we…
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to say that one action happened after another. Pattern: « Après avoir + past participle…, + subject + verb ». Here, « après avoir marché » = “after having walked,” and « un moment » = “for a while.” In speech you can also say « Après avoir marché un moment, on… » (more general/less formal than « nous »).
target_language_example: Après avoir marché un moment, nous avons trouvé un café.
native_language_example: After walking for a while, we found a café.

additional_notes: Used to say something is realized, felt, or judged only later (often with regret or hindsight). With events, it can mean something happened too late or arrived after everything was already over.
target_language_example: Après coup, j’ai compris que c’était une mauvaise idée.
native_language_example: Afterwards, I realized it was a bad idea.

meaning: "after the" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than an event or time: après le dîner, après le travail, etc. If the next word starts with a vowel or silent h, it becomes "après l'" (après l'école). For feminine singular nouns, use "après la"; for plural, "après les".
target_language_example: On ira se promener après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: We’ll go for a walk after breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than lunchtime. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence to set the time (“Après le déjeuner, …”) or after the verb (“… après le déjeuner”). You can also say “juste après le déjeuner” = “right after lunch.”
target_language_example: On se voit après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: See you after lunch.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens after the evening meal. Often appears with timing words like "juste" (right) or "tout de suite" (immediately): "juste après le dîner" = right after dinner; "tout de suite après le dîner" = immediately after dinner.
target_language_example: On fera une promenade après le dîner.
native_language_example: We'll go for a walk after dinner.

meaning: after work (after finishing your job for the day).
additional_notes: Used to say what happens once the workday is over. Often comes at the beginning or end of a sentence as a time expression (e.g., « après le travail, je… » / « je… après le travail »).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au café après le travail.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the café after work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause: « après que + subject + verb ». In careful/standard French, « après que » is followed by the indicative (often a past tense in narratives). In everyday speech you may also hear the subjunctive after « après que », but many speakers consider it nonstandard.
target_language_example: Nous sommes rentrés à la maison après que le film a commencé.
native_language_example: We went home after the movie started.

meaning: "after you" (polite: "you first"), or "after you" (later than you).
additional_notes: Used literally for time/sequence: "Elle est sortie après toi" = she left after you. Also used as a polite way to let someone go first: "Après toi." Common related expressions: "d’après toi" = "according to you / in your opinion"; "en avoir après toi" = "to have it in for you" (to be angry at you / hold a grudge).
target_language_example: Vas-y, après toi !
native_language_example: Go ahead, after you!

après tout ce que j'ai fait

target_language_multi_word_term: après tout ce que j'ai fait
meaning: “after all I’ve done” (often said to express disappointment, indignation, or a sense of unfairness/ungratefulness).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize your efforts and imply the other person is being unfair or ungrateful. Common as a rhetorical question: « Après tout ce que j'ai fait (pour toi/vous/lui/elle) ? » You can add « pour + pronoun/name » to specify who you did it for.
target_language_example: Tu me laisses tomber, après tout ce que j'ai fait pour toi ?
native_language_example: You’re abandoning me after all I’ve done for you?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a final thought, justification, or change of mind after considering the situation. It can appear at the start of a sentence (Après tout, …) or at the end (…, après tout) and often supports an argument: “he has the right…, after all.”
target_language_example: Après tout, on peut toujours essayer.
native_language_example: After all, we can always try.

additional_notes: Often said as a polite way to let someone go ahead of you (e.g., holding a door): « Après vous. » Literally means 'after you.' Don’t confuse it with « d’après vous », which means 'according to you / in your opinion.'
target_language_example: Après vous, madame.
native_language_example: After you, ma’am.

additional_notes: Means the time after midday (after lunch) until early evening. Often used with the article: l’après-midi (“in the afternoon”), or without an article after certain prepositions: cet après-midi (“this afternoon”), demain après-midi (“tomorrow afternoon”). You can also say de l’après-midi (“in the afternoon/afternoon-time”) depending on context.
target_language_example: Je te rappelle cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I'll call you back this afternoon.

additional_notes: Refers to the decorated tree used for Christmas. You can say "décorer l’arbre de Noël" (to decorate the Christmas tree) and "sous l’arbre de Noël" (under the Christmas tree), where gifts are often placed.
target_language_example: On met les cadeaux sous l’arbre de Noël.
native_language_example: We put the gifts under the Christmas tree.

additional_notes: A common noun; usually masculine: (un) arc-en-ciel. Often used with weather contexts, especially after rain: « après la pluie ». It can be used literally (a rainbow in the sky) and in expressions like « au bout de l’arc-en-ciel » (“at the end of the rainbow”). Plural: des arcs-en-ciel.
target_language_example: Après l’orage, on a vu un arc-en-ciel au-dessus de la ville.
native_language_example: After the storm, we saw a rainbow above the city.

additional_notes: Used for weapons that fire bullets using an explosive charge (e.g., a pistol, rifle). More formal/technical than "pistolet" (handgun) or the broad word "arme" (weapon). Often used in questions about owning or carrying a gun: "posséder/avoir une arme à feu", "porter une arme à feu".
target_language_example: Il est interdit de porter une arme à feu ici.
native_language_example: It’s forbidden to carry a firearm here.

additional_notes: Refers to weapons that shoot bullets using an explosion (e.g., pistols, rifles). Usually used in the plural (des/les armes à feu). Often appears in rules/signs like « Pas d’armes à feu » (“No firearms”).
target_language_example: Il est interdit d’avoir des armes à feu dans ce bâtiment.
native_language_example: It’s forbidden to have firearms in this building.

meaning: “does it happen?” / “what happens?” or “does he arrive?” (in a question).
additional_notes: This is the verb *arriver* in an inverted question with *il* (“he/it”): *arrive-t-il ?* The extra *-t-* is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (like *arrive*) and the subject pronoun starts with a vowel (*il/elle/on*): *arrive-t-il*, *arrive-t-elle*, *arrive-t-on*. Depending on context, *arriver* can mean “to arrive” (reach a place) or “to happen/occur” (especially in questions like *Qu’arrive-t-il ?* = “What’s happening?”). This inversion style is fairly formal; in everyday speech you often hear *Il arrive à quelle heure ?* / *Qu’est-ce qui arrive ?*
target_language_example: Pourquoi arrive-t-il toujours en retard ?
native_language_example: Why does he always arrive late?

meaning: happens from time to time; occasionally.
additional_notes: Used to say something occurs occasionally (not regularly). Often with "ça/cela" as the subject: "Ça arrive de temps en temps." With an indirect object, it means “it happens to me/you/etc.”: "Ça m'arrive de temps en temps."
target_language_example: Ça arrive de temps en temps, ne t'inquiète pas.
native_language_example: It happens from time to time, don’t worry.

additional_notes: Used to say someone will come or arrive very soon. Most often heard as a reply when someone calls you (e.g., from another room): « J’arrive tout de suite ! » You can change the subject to match who’s coming: j’arrive / il arrive / on arrive / nous arrivons.
target_language_example: Attends-moi deux minutes, j’arrive tout de suite.
native_language_example: Wait for me two minutes, I’m coming right away.

additional_notes: With a place or abstract noun, arriver à often means "arrive at" or "reach" (for example, arriver à la station, arriver à une conclusion). With an infinitive, it often means "manage to" or "succeed in" doing something: je n'arrive pas à comprendre = "I can't manage to understand."
target_language_example: Combien de temps cela prend-il pour arriver à la station ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to arrive at the station?

meaning: can you (manage to) / are you able to.
additional_notes: From the verb "arriver à" + infinitive, meaning "to manage to do" or "to succeed in doing". Often implies difficulty or effort. In questions, inversion gives "Arrives-tu à…?"; you can also say "Tu arrives à…?" (more common in speech).
target_language_example: Arrives-tu à comprendre cette phrase sans aide ?
native_language_example: Can you manage to understand this sentence without help?

additional_notes:
Used with an infinitive: « Arrivez-vous à + infinitive ? » asks whether someone succeeds in doing something (often like “can you manage to…?”). Example: « Arrivez-vous à lire ça ? » = “Can you read that?”

Note: if it’s followed by a place (no infinitive), « arrivez-vous à + place ? » can mean “are you arriving in/to…?” (e.g., « Quand arrivez-vous à Paris ? » = “When do you arrive in Paris?”).
target_language_example: Arrivez-vous à comprendre cette phrase sans traduction ?
native_language_example: Can you manage to understand this sentence without a translation?

additional_notes: Used to say someone reached a place later than expected/scheduled. Commonly also said as « être en retard » (to be late). With « être » in the past tense, « arrivé » agrees with the subject: « arrivée » (f.), « arrivés » (m. pl.), « arrivées » (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis arrivé en retard à cause des embouteillages.
native_language_example: Sorry, I arrived late because of traffic.

meaning: "arrived … ago" (arrived a certain amount of time ago).
additional_notes: Used to say when someone arrived in the past: **arrivé il y a + time period** (e.g., *deux jours*, *une semaine*). It agrees with the subject when used with *être*: *arrivé* (masc. sing.), *arrivée* (fem. sing.), etc., though this entry is for the fixed written form **arrivé il y a**. Often appears in the full structure **Je suis arrivé(e) il y a …**.
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé il y a trois jours.
native_language_example: I arrived three days ago.

additional_notes: On its own, **« arrivé quelque chose »** is incomplete in standard French. You normally say **« Il est arrivé quelque chose (à quelqu’un) »** or **« Il est arrivé quelque chose de + adjective »** (e.g., *de bizarre*). Although **arriver** can mean “to arrive,” in this structure it often means **“to happen,”** which can confuse English speakers.
target_language_example: Il est arrivé quelque chose de bizarre hier soir.
native_language_example: Something strange happened last night.

meaning: “arrived in/at/to” (depending on the place); also “came to / reached”.
additional_notes: Past participle of **arriver à** (“to arrive at/to”, “to reach”). With **être** in compound tenses: *il est arrivé*, *elle est arrivée* (agreement in gender/number). Used for physical arrival (*arrivé à Tokyo*, *arrivé à destination*) and for reaching a point/result (*en être arrivé à cette conclusion* = “to have come to that conclusion”; *arrivé à un moment important* = “reached an important moment”). For cities/countries, French uses **à** where English often uses “in”.
target_language_example: Je suis enfin arrivé à destination.
native_language_example: I finally arrived at my destination.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has reached the train station. It’s built from the past participle of *arriver* + *à* + *la gare*. Often used with *être*: *Je suis arrivé(e) à la gare.* The past participle can agree: *arrivé* (masc.), *arrivée* (fem.), *arrivés/arrivées* (plural).
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à la gare à huit heures.
native_language_example: I arrived at the station at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say you reached a place earlier than another person: « arriver + là-bas + avant + [person] ». « Arrivés » is the past participle of *arriver* with *être* (e.g., *nous sommes arrivés* / *vous êtes arrivés*) and it agrees with the subject (arrivés/arrivées/arrivé/arrivée). After *avant*, you typically use a stressed pronoun: *avant moi, avant toi, avant lui/elle, avant nous, avant vous, avant eux/elles*.
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés là-bas avant nous.
native_language_example: They arrived there before us.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the place where buses stop to pick up and drop off passengers. Very common with location phrases like « où est… ? » (where is…?), « il y a… » (there is…), and « à l’arrêt de bus » (at the bus stop).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à l’arrêt de bus à 8 heures.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the bus stop at 8 o’clock.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to tell one person to stop doing something. arrête is the tu-form imperative; with vous, use arrêtez de.
target_language_example: Arrête de te plaindre.
native_language_example: Stop complaining.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop an action or behavior. It’s the imperative of arrêter + de + infinitive (arrête de + verb). Often followed by a noun phrase with faire (e.g., faire le bébé = act like a baby; faire semblant = pretend). Can sound bossy depending on tone; for a softer version you can say « Arrête de… s’il te plaît. »
target_language_example: Arrête de faire ça, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop doing that, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone ("tu") to stop an action that’s affecting you. It’s followed by an infinitive: "Arrête de me + infinitive" (e.g., "arrête de me regarder"). "me" is the object pronoun meaning "me" placed before the infinitive. Note: "arrêter" can mean "to stop" (not "to arrest" in these contexts).
target_language_example: Arrête de me déranger, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop bothering me, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop speaking. Can be a firm command; adding "s’il te plaît" makes it more polite. Pattern: "Arrête de" + infinitive (e.g., "Arrête de crier" = Stop shouting).
target_language_example: Arrête de parler et écoute-moi deux minutes, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop talking and listen to me for two minutes, please.

meaning: "Stop (yourself) ..." (telling one person informally to stop doing something).
additional_notes: Used in the tu imperative: arrête + de + reflexive infinitive (te + verb), especially with reflexive verbs like se disputer (argue), se débattre (struggle), se quereller (quarrel). It’s a common way to tell someone to stop an action. Note: arrêter usually means “to stop,” not “to arrest.”
target_language_example: Arrête de te plaindre !
native_language_example: Stop complaining!

arrête de tourner autour du pot

target_language_multi_word_term: arrête de tourner autour du pot
meaning: 'Stop beating around the bush' / stop avoiding the point.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop being vague or indirect and to say what they really mean. Often followed by a request like « et dis-moi la vérité » (and tell me the truth) or « viens-en au fait » (get to the point). You can also say « Arrêtez de tourner autour du pot » for 'you' (plural/formal).
target_language_example: Arrête de tourner autour du pot : tu veux venir ou non ?
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush: do you want to come or not?

additional_notes: Used with the verb arrêter de + infinitive (“to stop doing something”). Here, fumer = “to smoke.” Often used with advice/obligation expressions like devoir (“must”), il faut (“it’s necessary”), and (tu/vous) devrais/devriez (“should”).
target_language_example: J’essaie d’arrêter de fumer depuis le mois dernier.
native_language_example: I’ve been trying to stop smoking since last month.

meaning: "Stop" + verb (telling people to stop doing something).
additional_notes: This is the command form (imperative) of "arrêter" addressed to "vous" (you plural or polite you). It’s followed by an infinitive: "Arrêtez de crier" = “Stop shouting.” Can sound firm or annoyed depending on tone; for a more polite request you can add "s’il vous plaît".
target_language_example: Arrêtez de courir dans le couloir !
native_language_example: Stop running in the hallway!

additional_notes: Used to tell one person formally (vous) or several people to stop doing something that affects you. It’s typically followed by an infinitive: « Arrêtez de me + infinitif » (e.g., regarder, fixer, tirer). Note: « arrêter » often means “to stop,” and is not the same as English “to arrest” in this context.
target_language_example: Arrêtez de me parler comme ça !
native_language_example: Stop talking to me like that!

additional_notes: Used as an imperative with *vous* (talking to more than one person, or to one person politely). It’s followed by an infinitive reflexive verb: *Arrêtez de vous disputer* (“Stop arguing”), *Arrêtez de vous moquer de moi* (“Stop making fun of me”). Literally “stop yourselves from …”. Note: *arrêter* looks like English “arrest,” but here it means “to stop.”
target_language_example: Arrêtez de vous inquiéter, tout ira bien.
native_language_example: Stop worrying; everything will be fine.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "arrêter de" + infinitive = "to stop (doing something)". It’s the past participle "arrêté" used with "avoir" (j’ai/il a/elle a arrêté...). You can replace "fumer" with another verb: "arrêter de boire" (stop drinking), "arrêter de travailler" (stop working).
target_language_example: J’ai arrêté de fumer l’année dernière.
native_language_example: I quit smoking last year.

additional_notes: Used for a fighting discipline or combat sport (often taught in a school/dojo), e.g., kung-fu, judo, karate. Usually masculine: un art martial; plural: des arts martiaux.
target_language_example: Elle pratique un art martial depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: She has been practicing a martial art for three years.

additional_notes: Question form of tu as, made with inversion. It is common in more formal or written yes/no questions. When followed by a past participle, English often translates it as 'did you ... ?' rather than 'have you ... ?'.
target_language_example: As-tu fini tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Did you finish your homework?

meaning: 'did you buy' / 'have you bought' (informal question form).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of "tu as acheté" (you bought / you have bought). It uses inversion: verb + "-tu" + past participle. Often used in writing or more formal speech; in everyday conversation you may hear "Tu as acheté… ?" or "Est-ce que tu as acheté… ?".
target_language_example: As-tu acheté du pain en rentrant ?
native_language_example: Did you buy bread on your way back?

meaning: "have you brought" (asking if someone brought something).
additional_notes: This is a question using inversion: "tu as apporté" (you brought / you have brought) becomes "as-tu apporté… ?" In the passé composé, "apporter" uses "avoir" + past participle "apporté". With "Qu'…" it becomes "Qu'as-tu apporté ?" (= "What did you bring?").
target_language_example: As-tu apporté ton passeport ?
native_language_example: Did you bring your passport?

meaning: "did you learn" / "have you learned" (informal question: "have you found out").
additional_notes: This is the inverted-question form of "tu as appris" (you learned / you have learned). It uses the past tense with "avoir" (passé composé): "tu as" + past participle "appris". With "apprendre", it can mean (1) learn something (a poem, a language, a skill), or (2) learn/find out some news or information ("apprendre une nouvelle", "apprendre cela"), often with question words like "comment", "de qui", "par qui", "quand".
target_language_example: Où as-tu appris le français ?
native_language_example: Where did you learn French?

additional_notes: Question form of *tu as dit* (passé composé of **dire**, “to say/tell”) using inversion (**as-tu**). Often followed by what was said (*As-tu dit “salut” ?*) or by **à + person** to mean “tell someone” (*As-tu dit à Thomas… ?*). Can also appear as **Qu’as-tu dit… ?** (“What did you say…?”).
target_language_example: As-tu dit la vérité à tes parents ?
native_language_example: Did you tell your parents the truth?

additional_notes: Used to ask in the tu form whether someone has ever done something (at any time) or has already done it (by now). Built with inversion: "as-tu" = "have you" (from avoir) + "déjà" = "already/ever". Often followed by a past participle (passé composé): « As-tu déjà + participe passé… ? »
target_language_example: As-tu déjà visité Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has heard something before. It’s the inversion form of a yes/no question (as-tu = have you). “Déjà” means “already/ever,” and with questions it often translates as “ever.” Follow it with the thing heard: ce mot (this word), cette histoire (this story), les informations (the news).
target_language_example: As-tu déjà entendu parler de ce chanteur ?
native_language_example: Have you ever heard of this singer?

additional_notes: Question in the passé composé used to ask about past experience. Literally “have you already eaten,” but with déjà it often means “ever” (at any time before now). You can add the food after it: « As-tu déjà mangé + [food] ? ».
target_language_example: As-tu déjà mangé des escargots ?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten snails?

additional_notes: A question in the passé composé using inversion (verb–subject): as (avoir) + tu + déjà + vu (past participle of voir). Used to ask if someone has ever seen something before. If you’re speaking more formally or to more than one person, use « Avez-vous déjà vu… ? ».
target_language_example: As-tu déjà vu Paris la nuit ?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen Paris at night?

meaning: "have you ever seen a" (asking someone if they have seen something before).
additional_notes: A common question pattern: « As-tu déjà vu un/une … ? » = “Have you ever seen a …?” Use « un » with masculine nouns and « une » with feminine nouns. « As-tu » is informal/singular “you” (tu); in more formal situations use « Avez-vous déjà vu … ? ».
target_language_example: As-tu déjà vu une girafe ?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a giraffe?

meaning: "have you ever been…?" (asking about past experience).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever had an experience up to now. Built from inversion for questions (as-tu = "have you") + déjà ("ever/already") + été (past participle of être, "been"). Often followed by an adjective (malade), or by a past participle in the passive voice (été trahi/embrassé/traité) meaning "been betrayed/kissed/treated". Agreement: été is followed by forms that may change for gender/number (blessé/blessée, trahi/trahie, traité/traitée).
target_language_example: As-tu déjà été à Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

additional_notes: Inverted question form of "tu as entendu" (from entendre = to hear). Used to ask if someone heard a sound, a question, news, a story, or something about a topic. Often followed by a noun or clause: "As-tu entendu ce bruit ?", "As-tu entendu parler de… ?" (have you heard about…?).
target_language_example: As-tu entendu parler du nouveau restaurant ?
native_language_example: Have you heard about the new restaurant?

meaning: “did you have…?” / “have you had…?” (past of avoir, in a question).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of **tu as eu** (passé composé of *avoir*). It’s used to ask whether someone **had/experienced** something: *As-tu eu des ennuis ?* (“Did you get in trouble?”), *As-tu eu du café ?* (“Did you have/Did you get some coffee?”). The **-tu** inversion is common in more formal or neutral questions; in everyday speech you’ll also hear **Est-ce que tu as eu…** or **Tu as eu… ?**
target_language_example: As-tu eu le temps de déjeuner ?
native_language_example: Did you have time to eat lunch?

meaning: "have you done" / "did you do" (passé composé question).
additional_notes: This is an inversion question form: **as** (from *avoir*) + **tu** + **fait** (past participle of *faire*). It asks about something completed in the past, often translated as either **“Did you do...?”** or **“Have you done...?”** depending on context. *Faire* is very broad in French and can mean **do**, **make**, or **get (something) done** (e.g., *faire la vaisselle* “do the dishes”, *faire les achats* “do the shopping”).
target_language_example: As-tu fait tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Did you do your homework?

additional_notes: Question form with inversion (more formal than "Tu as fini ?"). Often followed by "de" + infinitive to say what you finished doing: "As-tu fini de + verbe ?" (Have you finished + -ing?). You can also use it with a direct object: "As-tu fini ta journée ?" (Have you finished your day?). "En as-tu fini ?" means "Are you done with it/with that?" (the "en" refers to something already mentioned).
target_language_example: As-tu fini de faire tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Have you finished doing your homework?

additional_notes: Question in the passé composé: "As-tu…?" = "Have you…?". "fini de" + infinitive means "finished (doing)" something. Used to ask if someone is done reading a book, the newspaper, etc. (Informal singular "tu" form; for formal/plural use: "Avez-vous fini de lire… ?")
target_language_example: As-tu fini de lire ce magazine ?
native_language_example: Have you finished reading this magazine?

additional_notes: Uses inversion for a yes/no question: "as" (tu as) + "-tu" + past participle, often with "jamais" meaning "ever" in questions. More neutral/standard than "tu as déjà... ?"; in casual speech you’ll also hear "T’as jamais... ?".
target_language_example: As-tu jamais voyagé seul(e) à l’étranger ?
native_language_example: Have you ever traveled abroad alone?

meaning: "have you ever eaten" (asked to one person, informal "tu").
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s past experience. It’s a question with inversion ("as-tu" = "have you"). In questions, "jamais" often means "ever" (not "never"). Follow it with a place or food: "As-tu jamais mangé ici ?" / "As-tu jamais mangé des huîtres ?"
target_language_example: As-tu jamais mangé des sushis ?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten sushi?

additional_notes: A common way to ask about life experiences. It uses inversion for a question: « as-tu… ? » = “have you…?”. « jamais » in questions usually means “ever” (not “never”). « été » is the past participle of « être » (to be). With « être », some past participles agree with the subject (e.g., « arrêtée » for a woman, « arrêté » for a man).
target_language_example: As-tu jamais été à Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

meaning: 'have you ever been…?' (asking about past experience).
additional_notes: Question form with inversion: "as" (= "have") + "tu" (you) + "jamais" (ever) + "été" (been). Used to ask if someone has ever visited a place or ever done something. Often followed by a place ("au Caire", "en Afrique") or by an infinitive: "As-tu jamais été te baigner nu(e) ?" (= Have you ever gone skinny-dipping?). You can also use "Y as-tu jamais été ?" where "y" replaces the place (= "Have you ever been there?").
target_language_example: As-tu jamais été au Canada ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Canada?

additional_notes: This is the inversion form used to ask a question in the passé composé: as (have) + tu (you) + lu (read). It’s addressed to one person you’re on “tu” terms with (friend, child, etc.). Often followed by a direct object: As-tu lu ce livre ?
target_language_example: As-tu lu cet e-mail ?
native_language_example: Have you read this email?

additional_notes: A yes/no question using inversion (verb + -tu). It’s the passé composé of manger: "tu as mangé" (you ate / you have eaten). In everyday speech, you’ll also hear: "Tu as mangé ?" or "T’as mangé ?"
target_language_example: As-tu mangé avant de venir ?
native_language_example: Have you eaten before coming?

additional_notes: Question form (inversion) of the past tense of **mettre** (“to put/place/apply”). Used to ask if someone put/applied/posted/placed something: *As-tu mis de la crème solaire ?* In the pattern **Combien de temps as-tu mis à + infinitive ?**, it means **“How long did you take to…?”**
target_language_example: As-tu mis ton manteau avant de sortir ?
native_language_example: Did you put on your coat before going out?

meaning: 'did you get' / 'have you obtained' (you, informal singular).
additional_notes: Question form using inversion: "as" (tu as = you have) + "tu" + past participle "obtenu" (from obtenir). It’s the passé composé and often translates as “did you get?” in English. Used with a direct object: As-tu obtenu une réponse ? (“Did you get an answer?”).
target_language_example: As-tu obtenu ce que tu voulais ?
native_language_example: Did you get what you wanted?

additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of the passé composé: « Tu as parlé ? » → « As-tu parlé ? ». It literally means “have you spoken?” and is used to ask if someone spoke/talked (at some point in the past). It can take different prepositions depending on meaning: « parler à » (to speak to), « parler avec » (to speak with), « parler de » (to talk about). With an indirect object pronoun: « lui as-tu parlé ? » = “have you spoken to him/her?”.
target_language_example: As-tu parlé à ton professeur après le cours ?
native_language_example: Did you speak to your teacher after class?

additional_notes: This is a question in the passé composé: « parler à + person » = to talk to/speak to someone. « As-tu… ? » is the inverted (more formal) way to ask a yes/no question; in casual speech you often hear « Tu as parlé à… ? » or « Est-ce que tu as parlé à… ? ». Add a time expression after the person: « As-tu parlé à Tom hier ? ».
target_language_example: As-tu parlé à la prof après le cours ?
native_language_example: Did you talk to the teacher after class?

meaning: "did you spend" / "how was" (used to talk about time/holidays/trips).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of the passé composé: « tu as passé » → « as-tu passé… ? ». With « passer » + a time period or event (Noël, la journée, un bel été), it usually means “to spend” that time, and often translates naturally as “How was…?” rather than “Did you pass…?”. You can add an object like « Noël », « la journée », « un agréable voyage ».
target_language_example: As-tu passé une bonne soirée ?
native_language_example: Did you have a nice evening?

additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of **tu as pensé**. It’s used to ask what someone thought or whether they remembered to think about something. Common patterns: **as-tu pensé à + noun/infinitive ?** (Did you think about…?/Did you remember to…?), **qu’as-tu pensé de + noun ?** (What did you think of…?), **pourquoi as-tu pensé ça ?** (Why did you think that?), **y as-tu pensé ?** (Did you think about it?), **à quoi as-tu pensé ?** (What did you think about?).
target_language_example: As-tu pensé à m’appeler hier ?
native_language_example: Did you remember to call me yesterday?

additional_notes: Question form of the verb *perdre* (to lose) in the *passé composé*: **as** (you have) + **perdu** (lost). Used with a direct object (keys, ticket, money, weight) or in expressions like **As-tu perdu la tête ?** (“Are you crazy?/Have you lost your mind?”). With **Combien…?**, it often means “How much did you lose?” (money, weight).
target_language_example: As-tu perdu ton téléphone ?
native_language_example: Did you lose your phone?

meaning: "did you take" / "have you taken" (formal/inverted question form).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of the passé composé of **prendre**: **tu as pris** (you took/you have taken) → **as-tu pris… ?** (did you take…?). It’s used in more formal written/spoken French than **Tu as pris… ?** or **Est-ce que tu as pris… ?**. The exact meaning depends on context: taking something (photos), having something (breakfast), taking a side (**prendre parti**), taking a measurement (**prendre sa température**).
target_language_example: As-tu pris tes médicaments aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Did you take your medicine today?

meaning: "were you able to" / "did you manage to".
additional_notes: Question form with inversion: **as** (= *avoir*, present) + **tu** + **pu** (past participle of *pouvoir*). It’s usually followed by an infinitive: **As-tu pu + infinitive ?** It asks whether something was possible or whether someone succeeded (often implying there may have been difficulty).
target_language_example: As-tu pu trouver une solution ?
native_language_example: Were you able to find a solution?

additional_notes: Question form with inversion: "as" (auxiliary avoir, present) + "tu" + past participle "regardé" (passé composé of regarder). Used to ask if someone watched something (a film, a show, a game) or looked at/checked something (e.g., under the car).
target_language_example: As-tu regardé le match à la télé ?
native_language_example: Did you watch the game on TV?

meaning: "have you noticed" (asking someone if they observed something).
additional_notes: This is a question using inversion: "as-tu" = "have you" + past participle "remarqué". It’s used to check whether someone has observed a change, detail, or sign. Often followed by a noun or clause: "As-tu remarqué un changement ?" / "As-tu remarqué que… ?".
target_language_example: As-tu remarqué que la porte est ouverte ?
native_language_example: Have you noticed that the door is open?

meaning: "have you met" / "did you meet" (informal singular "you"), in the past.
additional_notes: This is a question form using inversion: "as-tu" = "have you" (tu). It uses the passé composé: avoir (tu as) + past participle (rencontré). Used to ask if/how/where you met someone, or whether you met someone at an event.
target_language_example: Où as-tu rencontré tes meilleurs amis ?
native_language_example: Where did you meet your best friends?

additional_notes: Inversion question with "tu" (to one person you address as tu). Used with "recevoir" to ask if someone got/received something (a note/grade, letter, message, reply). The past participle is "reçu"; you can also ask "As-tu reçu… ?" + object.
target_language_example: As-tu reçu le mail que je t’ai envoyé hier ?
native_language_example: Did you get the email I sent you yesterday?

meaning: "did you manage to…?" / "were you able to…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone succeeded in doing something (often something difficult, uncertain, or requiring effort). It’s the verb "réussir" + "à" + infinitive: "Tu as réussi à finir ?" = "Did you manage to finish?" (You can also use other subjects: "a-t-il réussi à…", "avez-vous réussi à…".)
target_language_example: As-tu réussi à trouver l’adresse ?
native_language_example: Did you manage to find the address?

additional_notes: Question form with inversion: **as** (from *avoir*) + **tu** + **trouvé** (past participle of *trouver*). Used to ask if someone found a person/thing, or found an answer/solution. In casual speech, you’ll often hear **Tu as trouvé… ?** instead. With inversion, a **-t-** can be added for pronunciation with *il/elle/on* (e.g., *A-t-il trouvé… ?*), but not with *tu*.
target_language_example: As-tu trouvé une solution ?
native_language_example: Did you find a solution?

additional_notes: Inversion question form of "tu as vu" (you have seen). Used to ask whether someone saw a person/thing, often with a time expression: « As-tu vu ça ? » / « Quand as-tu vu … pour la dernière fois ? ». In casual speech, you’ll also hear « T’as vu… ? ».
target_language_example: As-tu vu mes clés ?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

meaning: "Have you seen my..." (to a male person, informally).
additional_notes: This is a question in the informal ("tu") form: "As-tu" = "Have you" (inverted for a question), "vu" = "seen". "ma" means "my" for feminine singular nouns (ma bouteille, ma maman, ma voiture, ma plume). If the noun is masculine, use "mon" (As-tu vu mon livre ?).
target_language_example: As-tu vu ma clé ?
native_language_example: Have you seen my key?

meaning: 'Have you seen my …?' (asking if someone has seen your item).
additional_notes: Used to ask a friend, family member, etc. if they’ve seen something you’re looking for. "As-tu" is the informal singular (tu) form of "as-tu vu" = "have you seen". "Mon" means "my" before a masculine noun (mon stylo) or before a feminine noun starting with a vowel sound (mon amie). In formal situations, use "Avez-vous vu mon/ma … ?".
target_language_example: As-tu vu mon téléphone ? Je ne le trouve pas.
native_language_example: Have you seen my phone? I can’t find it.

additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of "tu as été" (passé composé of "être" with "avoir"). It’s used to ask if someone has been in a state (sage, seul/seule, amoureux) or has experienced something (invité, maltraité, piqué, vacciné). Often corresponds to English "Have you been…?" or, depending on context, "Were you…?".
target_language_example: As-tu été fatigué hier ?
native_language_example: Were you tired yesterday?

additional_notes: This is a question form of the passé composé of *être*: **tu as été** → **as-tu été ?** (subject–verb inversion). It’s used to ask about where someone went/was in the past (often with places: *en Europe, en prison, à la fête*, or with **y** = “there”). Depending on context, it can mean either “have you been (to) …?” or “how long were you …?”
target_language_example: Où as-tu été hier soir ?
native_language_example: Where were you last night?

additional_notes: Used with "tu": "tu as dit" is the passé composé of "dire" (to say/tell). It often appears with an indirect object pronoun: "tu leur as dit" = "you told them", and it can introduce a clause: "Tu as dit où vous alliez ?" = "You said where you were going?"
target_language_example: Tu leur as dit la vérité ?
native_language_example: Did you tell them the truth?

additional_notes: This is a fragment you’ll usually see in a full sentence like: « Tu as dit que tu voulais… » It uses the passé composé: « tu as dit » = “you said,” followed by « que » = “that,” and then « tu voulais » (imparfait) = “you wanted.” The subject « tu » is often present before « as dit ».
target_language_example: Tu as dit que tu voulais un café.
native_language_example: You said you wanted a coffee.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French in questions, often with the shortened form "t'as déjà…" (= "tu as déjà…"). Used with the passé composé ("as" + past participle) to ask about past experience; in this kind of question, "déjà" often corresponds to English "ever" ("Have you ever…?") rather than strictly "already".
target_language_example: T'as déjà visité Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Paris?

additional_notes: Spoken form of **(tu) as déjà vu … ?** = “have you already/ever seen … ?”. Very common in conversation, often with contractions like **T’as déjà vu… ?** or with **en** to mean “one/some/any of it”: **T’en as déjà vu ?** = “Have you ever seen any (of them)?”
target_language_example: T’as déjà vu ce film ?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this movie?

meaning: 'you heard' / 'have you heard?' (and sometimes: 'do you understand?').
additional_notes: This is from the verb entendre (“to hear”), in the passé composé: (tu) as entendu = “you heard / you have heard.” Very common in speech with the subject dropped: t’as entendu…? = “Did you hear…?” It can also be used to check understanding or to warn/insist: Tu m’as entendu. = “Do you understand me? / Are we clear?”
target_language_example: T’as entendu ce qu’il a dit ?
native_language_example: Did you hear what he said?

additional_notes: “As eu” is the passé composé of avoir with “tu” (tu as eu = you had / you got). It’s used in many common patterns: “Comment tu as eu… ?” = “How did you get…?”, “Tu en as eu assez ?” = “Have you had enough?”, and “Tu l’as eu ?” often means “Did you get it?” (depending on context, it can also mean “Did you manage to get him/it?”).
target_language_example: Tu as eu mon message ?
native_language_example: Did you get my message?

additional_notes: Passé composé of faire for "tu" (avoir + fait). Used to talk about something you did in the past, often with a direct object: "Tu as fait quoi ?" / "Qu’est-ce que tu as fait ?" It can mean "did" or "made" depending on context (e.g., "as fait ce bruit" = "made that noise"). In speech, it’s often contracted: "t’as fait".
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu as fait ça ?
native_language_example: Why did you do that?

additional_notes: Passé composé of **faire** with **tu**: **tu as fait ça** = “you did that.” In speech and informal writing, **tu** often drops and words contract: **t’as fait ça ?**; after **que**, **tu as** becomes **qu’as**: **C’est toi qu’as fait ça ?** (= *C’est toi qui as fait ça ?*).
target_language_example: Comment t’as fait ça ?
native_language_example: How did you do that?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression on its own: as is the tu form of avoir. In patterns like tu n'as jamais + past participle, it means "you have never ...". Words like en, y, or lui can come before as, as in the examples. In questions, it can also sound surprised, like "you've never...?"
target_language_example: Tu n'as jamais essayé le ski ?
native_language_example: You've never tried skiing?

additional_notes: Formed with **avoir + parlé** (passé composé) for **tu**: *tu as parlé*. Used for a completed past action. Very common with **en** to mean “talked about it”: *Tu en as parlé ?* = “Did you talk about it?” You can also specify the person with **à**: *Tu en as parlé à lui/à Marie ?*
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu ne m'en as pas parlé ?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me about it?

meaning: "you talked/spoke to" (have spoken to), usually with a person after à.
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of parler (tu as parlé). It’s commonly used in questions like « Tu en as parlé à … ? » = “Did you talk about it to … ?”. Use « parler à quelqu’un » for talking *to* someone, and « parler de quelque chose » for talking *about* something. The pronoun « en » often replaces « de + thing » (parler de ça → en parler).
target_language_example: Tu en as parlé à ton ami ?
native_language_example: Did you talk about it to your friend?

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: the first part of negation “ne” is dropped, so **tu n’as pas** → **tu as pas**. Used with **avoir** as an auxiliary or main verb, so the English meaning depends on context: **Tu m’as pas aidée** = “You didn’t help me,” **Tu n’y as pas pensé ?** = “You didn’t think about it?”. Often appears with pronouns: **m’/t’/l’/en/y** (e.g., **Tu m’as pas entendu(e) ?**, **T’en as pas eu assez ?**).
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu m’as pas dit la vérité ?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me the truth?

meaning: 'did you have a good …?' / 'did you spend a nice …?' (start of a question).
additional_notes: This is a common fragment in questions like: « Tu as passé une bonne journée ? » (Did you have a good day?) or « Vous avez passé une bonne soirée ? » (Did you have a nice evening?). It uses « passer » to mean 'to spend' (time) or 'to have' (a good time), not 'to pass' in English—so it can be confusing. Usually followed by a noun like « journée », « soirée », « nuit », « semaine », « vacances », etc.
target_language_example: Tu as passé une bonne journée ?
native_language_example: Did you have a good day?

additional_notes: Used with many meanings depending on context: taking something (Tu as pris mon stylo.), taking photos (Tu as pris des photos.), gaining weight (Tu as pris du poids.), or taking someone in your arms = hugging (Tu m'as pris dans tes bras.). In speech, "tu as" is often shortened to "t'as". Spelling note: with "avoir", the past participle usually stays "pris", but it agrees if the direct object comes before: « les photos que tu as prises » (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Tu as pris un café ce matin ?
native_language_example: Did you have a coffee this morning?

additional_notes: Used with « tu » to talk to one person informally: « Tu as trouvé… » = “You found/you’ve found…”. In speech it’s very often contracted to « t’as trouvé… », especially in questions like « Où t’as trouvé ça ? » (“Where did you find that?”).
target_language_example: T’as trouvé tes clés où ?
native_language_example: Where did you find your keys?

additional_notes: Second-person singular in the passé composé of voir (tu as vu). Used to talk about what someone saw (“ce que tu as vu”, “tu m’as vu ?”) and in questions like “T’as vu… ?” meaning “Have you seen… (recently)?” In speech it’s often contracted to “t’as vu”.
target_language_example: Tu as vu mes clés ?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

meaning: "have you seen what…" (to react to or point something out).
additional_notes: Common in casual spoken French as part of a longer sentence: « Tu as vu ce que… ? » It’s the verb « voir » in the passé composé (« tu as vu » = “you saw / you’ve seen”) followed by « ce que » (“what/that which”). You can add a noun or a full clause after it.
target_language_example: Tu as vu ce que j’ai trouvé dans la rue ?
native_language_example: Did you see what I found in the street?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of the verb être for “tu”: avoir (tu as) + past participle été. It’s used with adjectives (Tu as été courageux. = You were brave.) and very often in the passive voice (Tu as été banni/agressé/traité… = You were banned/assaulted/treated…). In spoken English it often translates as “you were,” even though French uses the “have” past.
target_language_example: Tu as été très gentil avec moi.
native_language_example: You were very kind to me.

additional_notes: Question form of tu as (“you have”), used when speaking to one person informally. This inverted form with a hyphen is common in writing and more formal speech; in everyday conversation, tu as ... ? is often more common.
target_language_example: As-tu les clés ?
native_language_example: Do you have the keys?

meaning: 'do you need' (to ask what someone needs).
additional_notes: This is the question form (with inversion) of **tu as besoin de...** = “you need ...”. It’s usually followed by **de** + a noun (**As-tu besoin de mon aide ?**) or **de** + an infinitive (**As-tu besoin de partir ?**). To ask “How much do you need?” you can use **De combien as-tu besoin ?** and “What do you need?” is **De quoi as-tu besoin ?**.
target_language_example: As-tu besoin de quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Do you need anything?

additional_notes: Question form of **avoir besoin de** (“to need”). Used with **de + noun/infinitive**: *As-tu besoin de ce livre ?* (“Do you need this book?”), *As-tu besoin de boire ?* (“Do you need to drink?”). This is the **tu** form (informal singular). More formal: **Avez-vous besoin de… ?**
target_language_example: As-tu besoin de mon aide ?
native_language_example: Do you need my help?

additional_notes: "As-tu" is the inverted question form of "tu as" (you have). Use "des" before a plural noun (often meaning "some" or just indicating an unspecified amount/number): "As-tu des frères ?" = "Do you have (any) brothers?" In very formal speech, prefer "Avez-vous des... ?".
target_language_example: As-tu des questions ?
native_language_example: Do you have any questions?

meaning: “do you have any … ?” (asking if someone has some of something).
additional_notes: This is the question form of **tu as du … ?** (“you have some …?”) with **inversion**: **as-tu … ?** = “do you have … ?”. **du** is the **partitive article** (**de + le**) and is used with uncountable nouns or things thought of as a quantity (e.g., **du papier**, **du temps**, **du thon**). For feminine nouns it becomes **de la** (e.g., **as-tu de la farine ?**), and before a vowel it becomes **de l’** (e.g., **as-tu de l’eau ?**).
target_language_example: As-tu du sucre pour le café ?
native_language_example: Do you have any sugar for the coffee?

meaning: 'Do you feel like…?' / 'Do you want to…?'.
additional_notes: Question form of **avoir envie de** + infinitive (or sometimes a noun): it asks about a desire or urge in the moment. More casual/neutral than **veux-tu…** (“do you want…?”), and often closer to “feel like.” Used with **de** before a verb: *As-tu envie de sortir ?*
target_language_example: As-tu envie de manger quelque chose ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you feel like eating something tonight?

as-tu la moindre idée de qui

target_language_multi_word_term: as-tu la moindre idée de qui
meaning: "Do you have the slightest idea who…"
additional_notes: Used to ask (often with surprise or disbelief) whether someone knows a person’s identity. "As-tu" is the inverted form of "tu as" (more formal/written than "Tu as… ?"). "la moindre" means "the slightest" and is often used in questions or negatives. "de qui" introduces an indirect question; it’s followed by a normal statement word order (e.g., "de qui il est", "de qui a fait ça").
target_language_example: As-tu la moindre idée de qui a envoyé ce message ?
native_language_example: Do you have the slightest idea who sent this message?

meaning: "do you have any … at all?" / "do you have the slightest …?"
additional_notes: Used to insist on the smallest amount or the slightest thing, often implying doubt or surprise. It’s the inverted-question form of "tu as" ("do you have"). Usually followed by a noun: "As-tu le moindre + nom ?" (e.g., argent, idée, plan, tatouage).
target_language_example: As-tu le moindre doute ?
native_language_example: Do you have the slightest doubt?

additional_notes: Question form of "tu as peur" (“you are afraid”). Often followed by "de" + noun/infinitive: "As-tu peur de moi ?" (Are you afraid of me?), "As-tu peur de parler ?" (Are you afraid to speak?). You can also use "En as-tu peur ?" to mean “Are you afraid of it/that?” referring back to something already mentioned.
target_language_example: As-tu peur de voler en avion ?
native_language_example: Are you afraid of flying on a plane?

additional_notes: Common question pattern: **As-tu quelque chose à + infinitive ?** (ajouter, dire, montrer, déclarer, etc.). It uses **inversion** (as-tu = as + tu) and is a bit more formal than **Tu as quelque chose à… ?** or **Est-ce que tu as quelque chose à… ?**. Often used to ask if someone has anything more to say/do, or in official contexts (**à déclarer ?**).
target_language_example: As-tu quelque chose à boire ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to drink?

meaning: "do you have a" (asking if someone has something; masculine singular).
additional_notes: This is the verb "avoir" (to have) in the "tu" form (as) with inversion to make a question: "As-tu… ?" It’s used before a masculine singular noun: "As-tu un sac ?" For feminine singular, use "as-tu une… ?"; for plural, "as-tu des… ?".
target_language_example: As-tu un stylo pour écrire ?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen to write?

meaning: “do you have a…?” (addressing one person; before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Question formed with inversion: "as" (you have) + "tu" (you) + a noun phrase. Used with "une" because the following noun is feminine (e.g., une opinion, une suggestion). For masculine nouns, use "as-tu un…?".
target_language_example: As-tu une question ?
native_language_example: Do you have a question?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **avoir besoin (de)** = “to need.” **Tu as besoin de + noun**: *Tu as besoin d’aide* (“You need help”). **Tu as besoin de + infinitive**: *Tu as besoin de dormir* (“You need to sleep”). Very often you’ll see **en** with it (**tu en as besoin**) meaning “you need **it/that**,” where **en** replaces something previously mentioned (often introduced with **de**).
target_language_example: Si tu en as besoin, je peux venir avec toi.
native_language_example: If you need it, I can come with you.

additional_notes: This is the informal (tu) form of **avoir besoin de** (“to need”). It’s most often used in a question like **Tu as besoin de quelque chose ?** (“Do you need anything?”). With **ne...pas** it becomes **Tu n’as pas besoin de…** (“You don’t need…”).
target_language_example: Tu as besoin de quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Do you need anything?

as besoin de quoi que ce soit

target_language_multi_word_term: as besoin de quoi que ce soit
additional_notes: Used most often after **si** (“if”): **si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit…** = “if you need anything (at all)…”. **Quoi que ce soit** means “anything at all / whatever it may be” and is common in conditional sentences and with negation (e.g., *je n’ai besoin de rien / je n’ai besoin de quoi que ce soit* depending on style).
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit, envoie-moi un message.
native_language_example: If you need anything, send me a message.

additional_notes: From the verb "avoir" (to have): "tu as de la chance" = “you’re lucky.” Often used as an exclamation: "Comme tu as de la chance !" (“You’re so lucky!”). In casual speech you may hear "T’en as de la chance" (= "Tu en as, de la chance"), which adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Tu as de la chance d’avoir des amis comme ça.
native_language_example: You’re lucky to have friends like that.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean you possess or have a certain amount of something: « Tu as des + nom pluriel ». Very common in questions and conditions: « si tu as des … » = “if you have any …”.
target_language_example: Si tu as des questions, je peux t’aider.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, I can help you.

meaning: you look well / you seem in good shape.
additional_notes: Usually appears as **Tu as l’air en forme** when addressing one person informally. **Avoir l’air** means “to look / to seem” (not literally “to have the air”). You can swap the adjective: *tu as l’air fatigué(e)* (you look tired), *tu as l’air content(e)* (you look happy). Note: in careful French, use the curly apostrophe **l’air**; **l'air** is common in plain text.
target_language_example: Tu as l'air en forme aujourd'hui !
native_language_example: You look well today!

meaning: Non-standard French; typically a misspelling/phonetic spelling of « jusqu’à » (“until / up to”).
additional_notes: « as qu’à » is not considered correct French spelling. If you see it in a text message or informal writing, the person almost certainly means « jusqu’à » (jusque + à), used for time (“until”), limits (“up to”), or distance (“as far as”). In standard writing, replace it with « jusqu’à » (e.g., « jusqu’à demain », « jusqu’à 10 personnes », « jusqu’à Paris »).
target_language_example: Je travaille as qu'à 18 h.
native_language_example: I work until 6 p.m. (intended meaning: « Je travaille jusqu’à 18 h. »)

additional_notes: Used with the verb *avoir* (to have). Most often heard as **Tu as quelque chose à dire ?** (“Do you have something to say?”), especially when you think someone wants to speak up. You can change the subject and verb: **J’ai / Il a / Vous avez quelque chose à dire**.
target_language_example: Tu as quelque chose à dire ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to say?

additional_notes: Used with a subject (often "tu") to agree with someone or say they are correct: "Tu as raison." = "You’re right." It’s the verb "avoir" (tu as) + "raison". In French you literally “have reason,” but in English we usually say “be right.”
target_language_example: Tu as raison, je me suis trompé.
native_language_example: You’re right, I was wrong.

meaning: "you have a" (or in a question: "do you have a…?").
additional_notes: Form of the verb *avoir* (to have): **tu as un + noun**. Very often in speech it’s contracted to **t’as un…?** Especially common for asking if someone has something: **T’as un… ?**. Use **un** before a masculine singular noun (for feminine: **une**).
target_language_example: T’as un stylo ?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen?

additional_notes: This is the form of **avoir** with **tu**: **tu as une + noun** (feminine singular). Very often in speech it’s shortened to **t’as une…**. It can be a statement (**Tu as une voiture.**) or a question (**Tu en as une meilleure ?** = “Do you have a better one?”). With **en**, **tu en as une** means “you have one (of them)”.
target_language_example: T’as une minute ?
native_language_example: Do you have a minute?

additional_notes: Imperative form of « s’asseoir » used when speaking to one person politely (vous) or to more than one person. Often used on its own, or after another instruction: « Venez… et asseyez-vous. »
target_language_example: Asseyez-vous, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please sit down.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about quantity: assez de + noun (assez de temps, assez de gens, assez de fibres). With adjective + noun, you often see: assez de + adjective + noun (assez de bon sens). It can also be used as an exclamation meaning “Enough!” (Assez !), and with “de” it can introduce what you’ve had enough of in a complaint (Assez de ça ! / Assez de…!).
target_language_example: On n’a pas assez de place dans la voiture.
native_language_example: We don’t have enough room in the car.

additional_notes: Used to say there is sufficient time to do something. Very common with "pour" + infinitive ("assez de temps pour + verb"). You can also use it in questions like "Assez de temps ?" / "Avons-nous assez de temps ?".
target_language_example: On a assez de temps pour manger avant le film.
native_language_example: We have enough time to eat before the movie.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something has sufficient size, age, or maturity to do something. Pattern: « être assez grand(e)(s) pour + infinitif ». With people it often means “old enough” or “grown-up enough.” « grand » agrees with the subject (grand, grande, grands, grandes).
target_language_example: Il est assez grand pour voyager seul.
native_language_example: He is old enough to travel alone.

additional_notes: Used to cut off a discussion or change the subject. Often followed by **de + noun/pronoun**: **Assez parlé de moi** (“Enough about me”). Can be said on its own (**Assez parlé !**) as a firm “That’s enough talking.”
target_language_example: Assez parlé de travail, on passe au dessert ?
native_language_example: Enough about work—shall we move on to dessert?

additional_notes: Imperative form of **s’asseoir** (“to sit down”), used when speaking to someone you address as **tu** (a friend, child, etc.). For a more polite or plural version, use **asseyez-vous** (“sit down”). Often followed by details like **avec moi** (with me) or **plus près** (closer).
target_language_example: Assieds-toi ici, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Sit here, please.

additional_notes: "assis" is the past participle of "s’asseoir" (to sit down) and is used like an adjective. It agrees with the person: "assis" (masc.), "assise" (fem.), "assis" (plural masc./mixed), "assises" (plural fem.). Often used with "être": "Il est assis…", "Elle est assise…". The fixed segment "assis sur le banc" is masculine singular; for a woman you would typically say "assise sur le banc".
target_language_example: Il est encore assis sur le banc et il attend le bus.
native_language_example: He is still sitting on the bench and waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to ask or suggest continuing to wait for some extra time. You can make it more polite with « Pouvez-vous… ? » (Can you…?) or « Veuillez… » (Please…). In conversation, « Attendez un peu plus longtemps » is the imperative (Wait a little longer).
target_language_example: Désolé, le médecin est en retard : pouvez-vous attendre un peu plus longtemps ?
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor is running late: can you wait a little longer?

additional_notes: Means not deciding or acting yet, and seeing what happens first. In modern usage, « attendre et voir » is more common, but « attendre voir » can be encountered, especially in more informal or elliptical speech.
target_language_example: On va attendre voir ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: We'll wait and see what happens.

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of clauses in legal or official documents (contracts, court decisions) to introduce background facts or reasons before a conclusion. It’s very formal and mostly written; in everyday French you’d usually say “comme”, “puisque”, or “étant donné que”.
target_language_example: Attendu que le locataire n’a pas payé le loyer, le contrat peut être résilié.
native_language_example: Whereas the tenant has not paid the rent, the contract may be terminated.

additional_notes: Used as a warning about something potentially dangerous or something you might bump into. "Aux" = "à + les", so it’s followed by a plural noun (e.g., aux marches, aux portes). For a singular noun you’ll often see "attention au" (masc.) or "attention à la" (fem.).
target_language_example: Attention aux vélos !
native_language_example: Watch out for bikes!

additional_notes: Used after the noun "attention" (often with "faire" or "porter") to say what you pay attention to: "faire attention à" = to pay attention to / to be careful about; "porter une (grande) attention à" = to pay (close) attention to. In the negative, "ne ... pas faire attention à" often means "to ignore / not pay attention to."
target_language_example: Fais attention à la marche !
native_language_example: Watch your step!

additional_notes: Used to warn someone or to stress that something must be done (or avoided): **Attention à ce que + subject + verb**. It often takes the **subjunctive** after *ce que* (especially in careful/formal French): *Attention à ce que tu dises… / à ce qu’il fasse…*.
target_language_example: Attention à ce que tu dises à Paul.
native_language_example: Be careful what you say to Paul.

attention à ce que tu dis

target_language_multi_word_term: attention à ce que tu dis
meaning: "Watch what you say" / "Be careful what you say."
additional_notes: A warning telling someone to be careful with their words. Uses the pattern "attention à" + "ce que" + subject + verb (here: "tu dis" = "you say"). You can change "tu" to be more polite: "Attention à ce que vous dites."
target_language_example: Attention à ce que tu dis : il y a des enfants ici.
native_language_example: Watch what you say: there are children here.

meaning: "be careful not to" / "watch out not to".
additional_notes: Used to warn someone to avoid doing something. Usually followed by an infinitive: « Attention à ne pas + verb » (e.g., « Attention à ne pas tomber »). Often shortened in speech to « Attention, ne… » or simply « Attention ! » when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Attention à ne pas oublier ton passeport.
native_language_example: Be careful not to forget your passport.

meaning: to catch a cold; to get chilled.
additional_notes: Literally “to catch cold.” Commonly used as a warning (often in the near future): « Tu vas attraper froid ! » It can mean either getting sick (a cold) or simply getting too cold from exposure, depending on context. Often used with « ne pas »: « Pour ne pas attraper froid ».
target_language_example: Mets ton manteau, tu vas attraper froid.
native_language_example: Put your coat on, you’re going to catch a cold.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going past a limit in space ("au-delà du fleuve" = on the other side of the river) or in a more abstract sense (looking beyond appearances, beyond distance, etc.). Often followed by "de" + noun: "au-delà de ...".
target_language_example: Il faut penser au-delà des apparences.
native_language_example: You have to think beyond appearances.

additional_notes: Used to express going past a limit (physical, numerical, or figurative). It can mean a place “past” something (Au-delà de la gare), a quantity/age “over” something (au-delà de cent ans), or an idea “beyond” a certain point (au-delà de…). Often contrasts with “en-deçà de” (below/under).
target_language_example: Au-delà de 50 euros, la livraison est gratuite.
native_language_example: Over 50 euros, delivery is free.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower position (on a page, in a building, etc.): « au-dessous » = “below/underneath.” Often followed by « de » to compare levels/standards: « au-dessous de… » (below…). In the fixed expression « au-dessous de tout », it means “beneath everything / beyond unacceptable” (very bad, disgraceful).
target_language_example: Le garage est au-dessous de l'appartement.
native_language_example: The garage is below the apartment.

additional_notes: Often used with **de** to say what something is above: **au-dessus de + noun/pronoun** (e.g., *au-dessus de moi* = above me). It can also be used alone to mean “up above/overhead.” Contrast with *sur* (“on top of,” in contact).
target_language_example: Il y a un pont au-dessus de la rivière.
native_language_example: There is a bridge above the river.

additional_notes: Used for physical position ("above/over" something): « au-dessus de la rivière », « juste au-dessus de zéro ». Figuratively, it can mean being "beyond" something (not affected by it) or thinking you are "above" rules/criticism: « Je suis au-dessus de tout ça », « se croire au-dessus de tout ». Note the opposite: « au-dessous de » = below/under.
target_language_example: L’appartement est au-dessus de la boulangerie.
native_language_example: The apartment is above the bakery.

additional_notes: Used to compare position or level. Literally “above the” (feminine singular), so it’s followed by a feminine noun: au-dessus de la moyenne (above average), au-dessus de la richesse (above wealth). For masculine singular, use “au-dessus du” (au-dessus du lit). For plural, use “au-dessus des” (au-dessus des nuages). Can be physical (location) or figurative (priority/value).
target_language_example: Le tableau est accroché au-dessus de la porte.
native_language_example: The painting is hung above the door.

meaning: beyond my (strength/means), more than I can handle/afford.
additional_notes: Used with a noun after "mes" to say something exceeds your capacity. Common set phrases: "au-dessus de mes forces" = too difficult for me / I can’t manage it; "au-dessus de mes moyens" = too expensive for me / I can’t afford it. With "vivre au-dessus de ses moyens" it means living beyond one’s means (spending more than you have).
target_language_example: Désolé, ce restaurant est au-dessus de mes moyens.
native_language_example: Sorry, this restaurant is beyond my means (I can’t afford it).

additional_notes: Literally “above our heads.” Used for something physically higher than the people speaking/being referred to (clouds, the sun, bullets flying, a helicopter). Often implies something passing overhead (e.g., a helicopter flew over our heads).
target_language_example: Un avion est passé au-dessus de nos têtes.
native_language_example: A plane flew over our heads.

additional_notes: Used to describe something located or happening higher than where you are (in the sky, on a higher floor, etc.). Often answers “Where?” (Où ?) and can be used with movement verbs like voler (“to fly”).
target_language_example: Un avion passe au-dessus de nous.
native_language_example: A plane is flying over us.

additional_notes: Used to locate something higher than and usually not touching something else. "Au-dessus de" becomes "au-dessus des" before a plural noun (de + les = des): au-dessus des vagues/des arbres. Common with verbs like flotter (to float), voler (to fly), and voir (to see).
target_language_example: Un avion passe au-dessus des nuages.
native_language_example: A plane is flying above the clouds.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is higher than or positioned over something else. Often expresses physical location (au-dessus du lit) but can also be figurative, meaning 'beyond' or 'not subject to' (au-dessus du soupçon = above suspicion). Contraction: au-dessus du = au-dessus de + le; also au-dessus de la, au-dessus des.
target_language_example: Le tableau est accroché au-dessus du canapé.
native_language_example: The painting is hanging above the couch.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like aller/venir to invite someone: « Tu veux aller/venir au bal avec moi ? ». « bal » is a formal dance or, in many learner contexts, a school prom. Choose « tu » (Viendras-tu…?) for someone you know well, and « vous » (Viendrez-vous…?/Voulez-vous…?) for polite or plural situations.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu veux venir au bal avec moi ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to the prom with me?

meaning: "(to/in) baseball"; used after jouer to mean "to play baseball."
additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb jouer: jouer au base-ball = to play baseball. It’s the contraction of à + le (au) + base-ball. For feminine sports you often use à la (e.g., jouer à la pétanque).
target_language_example: On joue au base-ball ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Are we playing baseball this weekend?

additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le" and is used with many sports/activities after "jouer". So "jouer au baseball" = "to play baseball". With preferences/comparisons: "préférer X au baseball" = "prefer X to baseball".
target_language_example: Le week-end, on joue souvent au baseball au parc.
native_language_example: On weekends, we often play baseball at the park.

meaning: right in the middle of; smack in the middle of.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens at the exact middle of a time period or place, often suggesting it’s surprising or inconvenient (e.g., in the middle of the night / day). Often followed by a noun: au beau milieu de la nuit, au beau milieu de la journée, au beau milieu de la rue.
target_language_example: Il m’a appelé au beau milieu de la réunion.
native_language_example: He called me right in the middle of the meeting.

additional_notes: Often used as an adverbial phrase meaning “if needed” (Je suis là, au besoin. = “I’m here if you need me.”). It can also appear with a noun to mean “to meet (someone’s) needs”: répondre au besoin du client = “to meet the customer’s needs.”
target_language_example: Tu peux m’appeler au besoin.
native_language_example: You can call me if necessary / if you need to.
