additional_notes: Used to say someone is (or has arrived) where they should be. Often appears in reassuring phrases like « Vous êtes au bon endroit » (“You’re in the right place”) or « Vous êtes venu au bon endroit » (“You came to the right place”). Also common in « au bon endroit, au bon moment » (“in the right place at the right time”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tu es au bon endroit.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re in the right place.

au bon endroit au bon moment

target_language_multi_word_term: au bon endroit au bon moment
meaning: in the right place at the right time.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone’s location and timing were perfect, often thanks to luck or coincidence (e.g., being there when something happened or when an opportunity appeared). Commonly used with se trouver / se trouver / se trouver ("to be / to find oneself").
target_language_example: On a eu le poste parce qu’on était au bon endroit au bon moment.
native_language_example: We got the job because we were in the right place at the right time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at an appropriate or convenient time. Common in set phrases like « au bon endroit, au bon moment » (“in the right place at the right time”) and « Tu arrives au bon moment » (“You’re arriving just in time / at the perfect moment”).
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé au bon moment pour t’aider.
native_language_example: I arrived at the right time to help you.

meaning: “in the good old days” (nostalgically referring to an earlier time in the past).
additional_notes: Used to evoke the past with nostalgia. Common after verbs like penser à (to think about) and se souvenir de (to remember): « Je pense au bon vieux temps. » Can also be used alone as an exclamation: « Au bon vieux temps ! »
target_language_example: À chaque fois que je vois cette photo, je pense toujours au bon vieux temps.
native_language_example: Every time I see this photo, I still think about the good old days.

meaning: at the edge of; on the verge of.
additional_notes: Used for a physical location near the edge of something (au bord de la rivière = by the riverbank) and also figuratively for being very close to a situation happening (au bord de la guerre = on the brink of war). Often followed by a noun with a definite article (de la, du, des) or a place name (au bord de Paris).
target_language_example: Le village est au bord de la mer.
native_language_example: The village is on the edge of the sea (by the seaside).

meaning: on the verge of; at the edge of (the).
additional_notes: Used both literally (being next to something, like a river) and figuratively (being very close to a bad situation happening): au bord de la faillite (on the verge of bankruptcy), au bord de la famine (on the brink of famine). Often you’ll also see it as "au bord de" (without "la"), depending on the noun that follows: au bord du lac (by the lake), au bord d’un accident (on the verge of an accident).
target_language_example: J’étais au bord de la panique, mais tout s’est bien passé.
native_language_example: I was on the verge of panicking, but everything went fine.

meaning: by the sea; at the seaside.
additional_notes: Literally “at the edge of the sea.” Used to talk about being near the sea (a seaside town, the coast, the beach area). Common after verbs like aller (to go), vivre/grandir (to live/grow up), or être (to be).
target_language_example: On a loué une maison au bord de la mer pour le week-end.
native_language_example: We rented a house by the sea for the weekend.

meaning: by the lakeside; at the edge of the lake.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located right next to a lake (on its shore). It commonly follows verbs like être, habiter, rester, camper, or nouns like maison/hôtel: « une maison au bord du lac ». You can swap in other places: « au bord de la mer » (by the sea), « au bord de la rivière » (by the river).
target_language_example: On va se promener au bord du lac après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: We’re going to take a walk by the lake after lunch.

additional_notes: "Boulot" is an informal word for "work/job." "Au boulot !" is a common way to say “Back to work!” or “Let’s get to work!” With verbs of movement like "aller", it means going to work ("aller au boulot"), and with "être" it means being at work ("être au boulot").
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas répondre : je suis au boulot.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't reply: I'm at work.

meaning: at the end (of); after (a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching the end of something in space or in time. Very common patterns: **au bout de + noun** (“at the end of…”: *au bout de la file*), and **au bout de + duration** (“after…”: *au bout de trois ans*). Can also be figurative: **aller au bout de** (“go all the way through; follow through to the end”).
target_language_example: Au bout de la rue, il y a une boulangerie.
native_language_example: At the end of the street, there’s a bakery.

meaning: after (a period of time); at the end of (a place/thing).
additional_notes: With time expressions, it means “after”: « au bout de trois jours » = “after three days.” With locations/objects, it means “at the end of”: « tout au bout de la rue » = “at the very end of the street,” « au bout de la table » = “at the end of the table.” It’s often followed by a duration (quelques jours/semaines, trois jours, combien de temps) or a noun (la rue, la table).
target_language_example: Au bout de dix minutes, le bus est enfin arrivé.
native_language_example: After ten minutes, the bus finally arrived.

meaning: at the end of the (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the end point of a place, path, or duration. It must be followed by a feminine singular noun: au bout de la rue (street), au bout de la journée (day). With a masculine noun, use "au bout du"; with plural, use "au bout des".
target_language_example: La pharmacie est au bout de la rue.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is at the end of the street.

additional_notes: Used to sum up the final outcome after considering everything (similar to “when all is said and done”). Often appears at the start or end of a sentence as a conclusion.
target_language_example: Au bout du compte, on a décidé de rester à la maison.
native_language_example: In the end, we decided to stay at home.

meaning: at the end of the hallway/corridor.
additional_notes: Used to give directions indoors (hotels, apartments, offices). Often followed by "à droite" (on the right) or "à gauche" (on the left): "Au bout du couloir, à droite." It can describe where a room or door is: "La salle de bains est au bout du couloir."
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont au bout du couloir, à gauche.
native_language_example: The restrooms are at the end of the hallway, on the left.

meaning: completely exhausted; at the end of your rope.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say someone is mentally or physically worn out, sometimes because of stress or difficult circumstances. Often used with "être" (Je suis / Il est / Vous êtes au bout du rouleau) or after "avoir l’air" (Elle a l’air au bout du rouleau).
target_language_example: Après trois nuits sans dormir, je suis au bout du rouleau.
native_language_example: After three nights without sleeping, I'm at the end of my rope.

meaning: at the office; to the office.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". With verbs of being/location (être, rester, arriver), it often means "at the office" (arriver au bureau = arrive at the office). With verbs of movement (aller, se rendre), it means "to the office".
target_language_example: Je suis au bureau aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm at the office today.

additional_notes: Used to express a precaution or possibility: you do something now because something might happen later. Often followed by a clause with the conditional (e.g., « au cas où vous voudriez… »), or used alone (« au cas où ») meaning “just in case.”
target_language_example: Prends un parapluie, au cas où il pleuvrait.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella, in case it rains.

meaning: "in case it…" / "if it happens that…" (to prepare for a possible situation).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a precaution for something that might happen. It’s often followed by the conditional (e.g., « au cas où il ferait froid ») or a present-tense situation (« au cas où il se passe quelque chose »). The subject « il » can be real (“he”) or the impersonal « il » meaning “it” (weather/events).
target_language_example: Garde mon numéro au cas où il y aurait un problème.
native_language_example: Keep my number in case there’s a problem.

meaning: in case it rains / if it should rain.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a precaution you take because something might happen. After **au cas où**, French often uses the **conditional** (like **pleuvrait**) in everyday speech, even though the subjunctive is also possible depending on context. Common pattern: **Prends… au cas où…** (“Take … in case …”).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre une veste au cas où il pleuvrait.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a jacket in case it rains.

additional_notes: Used to locate something in the middle of a place or object: au centre du parc/de la ville/de la cible. Can also refer to a “center” as a place people go (e.g., au centre-ville = downtown, au centre commercial = the shopping mall).
target_language_example: Le restaurant est au centre de la ville.
native_language_example: The restaurant is in the center of the city.

meaning: in/to downtown; in/to the city center.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a location in the central part of a town/city, or movement there. Often follows verbs like être/se situer/se trouver (to be/located) and aller (to go). With motion, English may use “to” (aller au centre-ville).
target_language_example: On va au centre-ville ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going downtown tonight.

additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le" and is used with masculine singular places ("le centre commercial"). It can mean either being there (location: "Il est au centre commercial") or going there (destination: "Je vais au centre commercial").
target_language_example: On se retrouve au centre commercial à 15 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the shopping mall at 3 p.m.?

meaning: (to be/keep) warm; in a warm place.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/rester (to be/stay), garder (to keep), or mettre (to put) to talk about staying warm or keeping someone/something warm (often indoors, out of the cold). Common in instructions: « Restez au chaud » = “Stay warm / Stay inside where it’s warm.” « Bien au chaud » emphasizes extra warmth/coziness.
target_language_example: Il fait froid dehors, alors on reste bien au chaud à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s cold outside, so we’re staying nice and warm at home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" to say someone doesn't currently have a job: "être au chômage". It can refer to being unemployed in general, and sometimes implies being registered for unemployment benefits.
target_language_example: Depuis janvier, elle est au chômage et cherche un poste.
native_language_example: Since January, she’s been unemployed and is looking for a position.

meaning: at the movie theater; to the movies.
additional_notes: Literally “at the cinema” (au = à + le). Used after verbs like aller/venir (going) or être (being there): « Aller au cinéma », « être au cinéma ». It can also be used figuratively to mean “like in a movie / you think this is a movie?” depending on context.
target_language_example: On va au cinéma ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to the movies tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say you went (or are going) to the cinema together with someone. "Au cinéma" = "to the cinema / to the movies" (à + le = au). "Avec" is followed by a person or group (avec Marie, avec mes amis).
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec mes amis ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my friends tonight.

meaning: to the cinema or to the theater.
additional_notes: Often used after a verb of going/being (especially « aller »): « Je vais au cinéma ou au théâtre. » « Au » is the contraction of « à + le » (masculine singular places/venues: « le cinéma », « le théâtre »).
target_language_example: Ce soir, on va au cinéma ou au théâtre ?
native_language_example: Tonight, are we going to the cinema or the theater?

meaning: clear; clarified (used in expressions meaning “to clear things up”).
additional_notes: Mostly used with verbs like **mettre au clair** or **tirer au clair**: **mettre/tirer quelque chose au clair** = “to clarify/clear up/sort out something,” often after confusion or a misunderstanding. Commonly appears with **les choses** (“things”): **mettre les choses au clair** = “to set things straight.”
target_language_example: Avant de partir, j’aimerais mettre un point au clair.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I’d like to clear one thing up.

meaning: by moonlight; in the light of the moon.
additional_notes: Used to describe something happening outdoors at night, lit by the moon. Often has a romantic or poetic feel (walks, kisses, scenery).
target_language_example: On a dîné sur la terrasse au clair de lune.
native_language_example: We had dinner on the terrace by moonlight.

meaning: at/on the corner (of a street, building, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for a physical corner or nearby spot: *au coin* = “at the corner”; *juste au coin* = “right around the corner”; *au coin suivant* = “at the next corner”. Often followed by **de** to name what the corner belongs to (*au coin de la rue*, *au coin de Michigan Avenue*, *au coin du bois*). With verbs like **tourner**, it means turning at the corner (*Il a tourné au coin*).
target_language_example: Le café est juste au coin de la rue.
native_language_example: The café is right around the corner.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located right at the corner where streets meet. Very common for giving directions or describing where a place is (shops, cafés, where you live). Often follows verbs like être (to be), habiter (to live), se situer (to be located).
target_language_example: Le café est au coin de la rue, juste à côté de la boulangerie.
native_language_example: The café is on the street corner, right next to the bakery.

additional_notes: Used to say that everyone who is expected is there (a group is complete), or that a place/organization is fully staffed/occupied. Common in announcements or roll-call contexts: « Au complet ! » = “Everyone’s here / All present.”
target_language_example: Pour la réunion, nous sommes au complet.
native_language_example: For the meeting, everyone is here.

meaning: to the account of; in the name of (an account).
additional_notes: Mostly used in banking/accounting contexts to say money is credited/transferred to someone’s account (often followed by a name or account number). Related expression: « mettre quelque chose au compte de + noun » = “to attribute something to …” (e.g., fatigue, chance).
target_language_example: Veuillez verser la somme au compte de Marie Dupont.
native_language_example: Please transfer the amount to Marie Dupont’s account.

meaning: On the contrary; quite the opposite.
additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct what was just said or implied. Often comes at the start of a sentence ("Au contraire, ...") or as a short reply ("Au contraire !", "Non, au contraire."). You can strengthen it with "bien": "Bien au contraire" = "Quite the contrary".
target_language_example: Tu penses que je suis fâché ? Au contraire, je suis très content.
native_language_example: You think I’m angry? On the contrary, I’m very happy.

meaning: at sunset; when the sun goes down.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a time of day (sunset). Often appears in time expressions like "du lever au coucher du soleil" (= from sunrise to sunset / all day).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au coucher du soleil sur la plage.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at sunset on the beach.

meaning: aware; in the know; up to date.
additional_notes: Usually used with être: « Je suis au courant » = “I know/I’m aware.” Often followed by de + noun/verb: « être au courant de quelque chose » = “to be aware of something.” Not a literal translation of “current.”
target_language_example: Je suis au courant de la réunion de demain.
native_language_example: I’m aware of tomorrow’s meeting.

meaning: aware; informed; up to date (about something).
additional_notes: Used with "être" to mean "to be aware/informed" (often followed by "de" + noun: "être au courant de..."), and with "tenir" to mean "to keep someone informed" ("tenir quelqu’un au courant"). Very common in everyday and professional contexts.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas au courant des changements, tu peux m’expliquer ?
native_language_example: I’m not aware of the changes—can you explain?

additional_notes: Used to say someone knows about something: « être au courant de ». Very common with verbs like « mettre quelqu’un au courant (de) » (to inform someone) and « tenir quelqu’un au courant (de) » (to keep someone updated). Often followed by a noun or by « de ce que… ».
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas au courant de ce changement, tu peux m’expliquer ?
native_language_example: I wasn’t aware of this change—can you explain it to me?

additional_notes: Used to situate something within a period of time or during an event (a conversation, a discussion, a century, a year, etc.). Often followed by a noun phrase: au cours de la journée / au cours de la réunion. Common in more formal or written French; in everyday speech you can often use "pendant" instead.
target_language_example: Au cours de la soirée, j’ai rencontré ses parents.
native_language_example: During the evening, I met his parents.

additional_notes: An exclamation used to reject, dismiss, or curse someone/something: "Au diable + noun" = "To hell with + noun" (Au diable Noël !). Said to a person, it’s an insult roughly like "Go to hell." Can also be used alone (Au diable !) to show anger or frustration. Strong/impolite; often sounds a bit old-fashioned.
target_language_example: Au diable les excuses, on y va !
native_language_example: To hell with excuses, let’s go!

additional_notes: Used to talk about the start of a time period, story, process, or relationship. Often sets the scene at the start of a narration (Au début, …). It can also refer back to someone’s initial opinion or feeling (Je pensais ça au début = “I thought so at first”), and in expressions like Reprenons au début (“Let’s go back to the beginning”) or Pas au début (“Not at first”).
target_language_example: Au début, je ne comprenais rien, mais maintenant ça va mieux.
native_language_example: At first, I didn’t understand anything, but now it’s better.

meaning: at first; initially; at the start (of something).
additional_notes: Often used to contrast an initial situation/feeling/idea with what happens later: « Au départ…, mais ensuite… ». It can also mean returning to the starting line/position, especially in contexts like sports, races, or games (« On se remet au départ »).
target_language_example: Au départ, je pensais que ce serait compliqué, mais finalement c’était simple.
native_language_example: At first, I thought it would be complicated, but in the end it was simple.

meaning: by the way; actually (come to think of it).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a new question or topic, often as a quick aside or to remember something. Common in conversation; it can also sound like “so, about that…” when returning to a point.
target_language_example: Au fait, tu as eu des nouvelles de Marie ?
native_language_example: By the way, have you heard from Marie?

meaning: “to/at the fire”; also “at the traffic light.”
additional_notes: “Au” = “à + le” (“to the / at the”). With real fire, context decides the best English translation: **mettre/jeter X au feu** = “to throw/put X into the fire,” while **(se détendre) face au feu** is “(relax) by/in front of the fire.” In directions, **au feu** refers to a traffic light: **Tourne à droite au feu** = “Turn right at the light.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve au feu, puis on tourne à gauche.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the traffic light, then we’ll turn left.

meaning: over the course of; as time goes by; gradually over time.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that unfolds or changes gradually during a period of time. It is followed by a noun introduced by de (which often contracts: de + le → du; de + les → des), e.g., au fil de la journée (over the course of the day), au fil des années (over the years).
target_language_example: Au fil de la journée, j’ai commencé à mieux comprendre le français.
native_language_example: Over the course of the day, I started to understand French better.

additional_notes: Used to sum up or give the final outcome after considering everything. Often placed at the start of a sentence as a discourse marker ("Au final, ..."), but it can also appear at the end ("... au final") or even stand alone as a short conclusion ("Au final, oui.").
target_language_example: Au final, on a décidé de rester à la maison.
native_language_example: In the end, we decided to stay home.

meaning: at the back; deep down (at heart).
additional_notes: Used for physical location to mean “at the back”/“in the far end” of a place: Au fond à gauche ! (“At the back on the left!”), Restez au fond (“Stay in the back”). With de + noun (au fond de…), it means “at the back/bottom of”: au fond de la classe (“at the back of the classroom”). Figuratively, it means “deep down/at heart”: bon au fond de leur cœur (“good at heart”).
target_language_example: La salle de bain est au fond du couloir.
native_language_example: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.

meaning: at the back/bottom of; deep inside.
additional_notes: Used for both literal place (“at the back of the room,” “at the bottom of the bottle”) and figurative meaning (“deep down inside me”). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: au fond de la bouteille, au fond de la mosquée, au fond de moi.
target_language_example: Au fond de mon sac, j'ai retrouvé mes clés.
native_language_example: At the bottom of my bag, I found my keys again.

additional_notes: Used to give directions inside a building. Often followed by extra details like "à gauche" (on the left) or "à droite" (on the right).
target_language_example: La salle de réunion est au fond du couloir, à droite.
native_language_example: The meeting room is at the end of the hallway, on the right.

additional_notes: Short for « au football ». Used after verbs like « jouer » (jouer au foot = to play soccer) and with « être bon au foot » = to be good at soccer. In France, « foot » normally means soccer (not American football).
target_language_example: On joue au foot après l'école.
native_language_example: We play soccer after school.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like jouer (à) to talk about playing the sport: jouer au football. It can also describe someone’s ability at the sport, often with être bon/nul au football (“to be good/terrible at soccer”). In France, football usually means “soccer” (not American football).
target_language_example: Mon frère joue au football le samedi.
native_language_example: My brother plays soccer on Saturdays.

meaning: in the oven; into the oven.
additional_notes: Used with cooking verbs like mettre/enfourner (to put in the oven) and cuire (to bake/roast): « mettre au four » = put into the oven; « être au four » = be in the oven (currently baking). It can also be used jokingly/threateningly in a literal sense (“I’ll put you in the oven”).
target_language_example: Mets le gâteau au four pendant 30 minutes.
native_language_example: Put the cake in the oven for 30 minutes.

additional_notes: Literally describes a horse (or rider) moving at a gallop: « Le cheval va au galop. » By extension it can be used figuratively for doing something quickly or rushing: « Il est parti au galop. » Can also be used as a command: « Au galop ! » (= “Gallop!” / “Hurry up!”).
target_language_example: On est rentrés au galop avant la pluie.
native_language_example: We got back quickly before the rain.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like jouer (à) to say someone plays golf: jouer au golf. In a question like « Au golf ? », it can mean “To the golf course?” or “Golf?” depending on context. « au » is a contraction of « à + le ».
target_language_example: On va au golf cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We’re going to the golf course this afternoon.

meaning: in broad daylight; out in the open (publicly).
additional_notes: Often used literally for something happening in daylight, but very commonly used figuratively to mean something is revealed publicly or done openly (not hidden): « dévoiler/mettre au grand jour », « la vérité éclate au grand jour ».
target_language_example: Ils ont enfin mis la fraude au grand jour.
native_language_example: They finally brought the fraud out into the open.

meaning: according to; at the mercy of (depending on).
additional_notes: Used to say something changes or happens depending on someone’s wishes (“as X pleases”) or depending on circumstances like the weather or events (“as things go”). Often followed by a noun: au gré du vent (with the wind), au gré des envies (as one feels like), au gré des saisons (according to the seasons).
target_language_example: Nous changerons de programme au gré de la météo.
native_language_example: We’ll change the plan depending on the weather.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done without a plan, selection, or specific target. Common with verbs like choisir/tirer (to choose/draw), poser (des questions) (to ask), and can also describe moving or wandering with no direction (errer au hasard).
target_language_example: J’ai choisi un livre au hasard dans la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: I picked a book at random from the library.

meaning: day by day; from one day to the next.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that changes daily (prices, schedules, weather) or a way of living without planning ahead—just getting through each day. Often used with vivre: « vivre au jour le jour » = to live day to day.
target_language_example: Avec ce travail instable, je vis au jour le jour.
native_language_example: With this unstable job, I live day to day.

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to press for precise information or to clarify what someone really means. It can sound a bit insistent depending on tone. Often placed after the word or clause it clarifies: « Qui, au juste ? », « Où, au juste ? ».
target_language_example: Tu veux dire quoi, au juste ?
native_language_example: What exactly do you mean?

meaning: offshore; out at sea (away from the coast).
additional_notes: Used with places to mean “off (the coast) of …”: au large du Chili = offshore of Chile. Can describe something located or happening at sea, away from land. As an exclamation (“Au large !”), it can mean “Set sail!/Head out to sea!” or “Off you go!” depending on context.
target_language_example: On peut apercevoir des dauphins au large de la côte.
native_language_example: You can spot dolphins offshore (off the coast).

meaning: off (the coast of); out at sea near.
additional_notes: Used mainly with places (often coastal) to indicate something is offshore, away from the coast: « au large de Marseille » = off the coast of Marseille. Common with verbs like « naviguer », « se trouver », « être », and in news/weather reports. Not used for general distance on land (use « loin de » for “far from”).
target_language_example: Un voilier se trouve au large de la Bretagne.
native_language_example: A sailboat is off the coast of Brittany.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens when the sun rises (early in the morning). Often used with verbs like se réveiller (to wake up), partir/quitter (to leave), or commencer (to start). You can also hear jusqu'au lever du soleil (“until sunrise”).
target_language_example: On est partis au lever du soleil pour éviter la chaleur.
native_language_example: We left at sunrise to avoid the heat.

additional_notes: Used to replace one option/action with another. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive: «au lieu de + nom» (au lieu de ça/cela) or «au lieu de + verbe» (au lieu de travailler). You can also use it at the start of a sentence: «Au lieu de ça/cela, ...».
target_language_example: Au lieu de prendre la voiture, on va marcher.
native_language_example: Instead of taking the car, we're going to walk.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like aller (to go) and être/rester (to be/stay): aller au lit = “to go to bed,” être au lit = “to be in bed,” rester au lit = “to stay in bed.” Also used in the fixed expression faire pipi au lit (“to wet the bed”).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué(e), je vais au lit.
native_language_example: I’m tired, I’m going to bed.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happening far from where you are. Often comes after the verb (voir, entendre, apercevoir, distinguer): « Je vois une ville au loin. »
target_language_example: On entendait de la musique au loin.
native_language_example: We could hear music in the distance.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something stretches alongside a place (often written/said as **le long de** in modern French: *le long de la rivière* = along the river). With **tout au long de + time period**, it means “throughout/over the whole course of”: *tout au long de l’année*, *tout au long de nos études*.
target_language_example: Je l’ai soutenu tout au long de son traitement.
native_language_example: I supported him throughout his treatment.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of location or movement. "au" is the contraction of "à + le" and is used because "lycée" is masculine (le lycée). Refers to the French high school level (roughly ages 15–18).
target_language_example: Je suis au lycée, mais je veux aller à l’université l’an prochain.
native_language_example: I’m in high school, but I want to go to university next year.

meaning: to the store; at the store.
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le" and is used with masculine singular places like "le magasin". With verbs of movement, it often means "to the store" (Je vais au magasin). With other verbs, it can mean "at the store" (Je suis au magasin / J’étais au magasin).
target_language_example: Je vais au magasin acheter du lait.
native_language_example: I'm going to the store to buy milk.

additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le" (to/at + the). Used with "aller", "venir", "se rendre" to say you’re going to the (open-air) market; it can also mean being there depending on context.
target_language_example: On se retrouve au marché samedi matin.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the market Saturday morning.

meaning: to the maximum; as much as possible.
additional_notes: Used to mean doing something to the fullest extent. With verbs like « utiliser / informer », it means “as much as possible.” With states like « Je suis au maximum », it can mean “I’m at my limit / maxed out.” It can also describe an action pushed to the furthest point (e.g., sliding as far as you can).
target_language_example: Profite au maximum de tes vacances !
native_language_example: Make the most of your vacation!

meaning: as best as possible; at one’s best.
additional_notes: Used to say you did what you could in the circumstances: « J’ai fait au mieux » (I did my best). It can also mean “at best” when talking about the best-case outcome. In the expression « être au mieux de sa forme », it means “to be at one’s best / in top form.”
target_language_example: Je ferai au mieux avec le temps qu’on a.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best with the time we have.

additional_notes: Used to locate someone/something in the center of a place or group: au milieu de + noun (au milieu des arbres). It can also mean 'amid' in a more figurative sense (au milieu de cette jungle). Often interchangeable with 'au centre (de)' for a physical center, but 'au milieu' is also common for being surrounded by things/people.
target_language_example: Je t’attends au milieu de la place.
native_language_example: I’m waiting for you in the middle of the square.

additional_notes: Used to locate something/someone in the center of a place or situation (au milieu de la route, au milieu de la fête). With groups, it often means “among/in the midst of” (au milieu de la foule). Can also sound like “right in the middle of” when expressing surprise (Qu’est-ce que tu fais au milieu de… ?).
target_language_example: Je l’ai rencontré au milieu de la foule.
native_language_example: I met him in the middle of the crowd.

meaning: "in the middle of" / "in the middle of the" (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to locate something at the center of a place/object, or to say something happens partway through an activity (a discussion, a sentence, etc.). It’s the feminine form: au milieu de la + noun (la discussion). Other forms: au milieu du (masc.), au milieu des (plural), au milieu de l’ (before a vowel sound).
target_language_example: Je l’ai appelé au milieu de la réunion.
native_language_example: I called him in the middle of the meeting.

meaning: in the middle of the night.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens during the night, typically when most people are asleep. Often implies an inconvenient or surprising time (e.g., waking someone up). You can also use it on its own to describe the time: « On est au milieu de la nuit. »
target_language_example: J'ai entendu un bruit au milieu de la nuit.
native_language_example: I heard a noise in the middle of the night.

additional_notes: Used to say a place is very remote/isolated, far from towns or anything familiar. Often expresses inconvenience or surprise (e.g., being stuck or wondering why someone is there).
target_language_example: On a pris la mauvaise route et on s'est retrouvés au milieu de nulle part.
native_language_example: We took the wrong road and ended up in the middle of nowhere.

meaning: in the middle of; halfway through.
additional_notes: Used to place something in the center of a location ("au milieu du parc") or to say something happens halfway through a period or event ("au milieu du mois", "au milieu du film/concert/cours"). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (du = de + le). For feminine, use "au milieu de la"; for plural, "au milieu des"; before a vowel, "au milieu de l’".
target_language_example: On s’est rencontrés au milieu du voyage.
native_language_example: We met halfway through the trip.

additional_notes: Used to state a minimum amount/number or lower limit. Often placed after the quantity it refers to ("sept heures, au minimum") or before it ("au minimum sept heures"). Can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “at least/minimum.”
target_language_example: Il faut économiser 50 € par mois, au minimum.
native_language_example: You need to save €50 a month, at least.

additional_notes: Used to give a minimum amount, time, or degree. It can also add emphasis in questions or suggestions, like 'at least' in English: Est-ce que tu m'écoutes au moins ? = 'Are you at least listening to me?'
target_language_example: On peut au moins essayer.
native_language_example: We can at least try.

au moins une fois par semaine

target_language_multi_word_term: au moins une fois par semaine
additional_notes: Used to say the minimum frequency something happens. Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also appear after the verb. You can swap in other time periods: « au moins une fois par jour / par mois / par an ».
target_language_example: J’appelle ma grand-mère au moins une fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I call my grandmother at least once a week.

additional_notes: Introduces a time clause to say something happens exactly as/when something else happens. Often used with the imperfect to describe an action in progress that another action happens during (e.g., « au moment où je sortais… »). You’ll also see it with emphasis like « juste au moment où » (“just as / right when”).
target_language_example: Au moment où je m’endormais, le téléphone a sonné.
native_language_example: Just as I was falling asleep, the phone rang.

additional_notes: Literally “to the world,” but it’s commonly used to mean “in the world,” especially after superlatives: « le/la plus … au monde » (“the most … in the world”). It also appears in set phrases like « mettre au monde » (to give birth to) and « n’avoir que [quelqu’un] au monde » (to have only [someone] in the world).
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur restaurant au monde.
native_language_example: It’s the best restaurant in the world.

additional_notes: Used to express the method, instrument, or means by which something is done. It’s a fairly formal way to say "using" (often close to "à l’aide de" in many contexts). Pattern: au moyen de + noun/noun phrase. Note the spelling is fixed: "au moyen de" (no apostrophe).
target_language_example: Les oiseaux volent au moyen de leurs ailes.
native_language_example: Birds fly by means of their wings.

meaning: on the wall; against the wall.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". With "au mur", French often uses "à" where English uses "on" (e.g., "accrocher au mur" = "hang on the wall"). It can also mean facing/with your front toward the wall: "Face au mur" = "Facing the wall."
target_language_example: Il y a une photo au mur, juste au-dessus du canapé.
native_language_example: There’s a photo on the wall, just above the couch.

meaning: in the same place; in the same spot.
additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone stays in one location or that two things happen at one identical location. Often used with verbs like habiter (to live), travailler (to work), rester (to stay), and with toujours (still/always): « Tu habites toujours au même endroit ? ».
target_language_example: On se retrouve au même endroit demain à midi.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in the same place tomorrow at noon.

meaning: "in the name of" / "on behalf of"; also "in (someone's) name" (registered under).
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) to speak or act for someone/a group: « Au nom de tous, merci… » = “On behalf of everyone…”. (2) to say something is officially registered under a person’s name: « un compte au nom de Marie » = “an account in Marie’s name.” With « répondre au nom de », it means “to go by the name of.”
target_language_example: Je signe ce document au nom de mon entreprise.
native_language_example: I’m signing this document on behalf of my company.

meaning: 'in the name of' (invoking an authority, principle, or group; sometimes used as an emphatic exclamation like 'for heaven’s sake').
additional_notes: Used to invoke an authority, principle, person, or group as justification: *Au nom du peuple* (“in the name of the people”). Common in religious formulas: *Au nom du Père, du Fils et du Saint-Esprit…* Also used as an exclamation to express surprise/indignation: *Au nom du Ciel !* ≈ “For heaven’s sake!” Note the form varies with gender/number of the following noun (*au nom du* + masculine singular; *au nom de la* + feminine singular; *au nom des* + plural; *au nom de l’* before a vowel).
target_language_example: Au nom du peuple, je vous demande de vous taire.
native_language_example: In the name of the people, I ask you to be quiet.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a total count (often with a number): « Ils étaient au nombre de dix » = “There were ten of them.” Also used with « compter (qqn) au nombre de… » to mean “to count (someone) among…” (a group, friends, participants, etc.). In negative form: « Il ne compte pas au nombre de… » = “He doesn’t count as one of… / He isn’t among…”.
target_language_example: Nous étions au nombre de cinq à la réunion.
native_language_example: There were five of us at the meeting.

meaning: to the north; in the north.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a northern direction or location. Common patterns: « au nord de + place » = “north of (a place)”; « plus au nord » = “further north.”
target_language_example: Le village est au nord de la rivière.
native_language_example: The village is north of the river.

meaning: to the park / at the park.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à" + "le" (used before masculine singular nouns like "le parc"). With movement verbs (aller, se rendre, conduire), it usually means "to the park"; with context about location, it can mean "at the park."
target_language_example: On se retrouve au parc à 15 h.
native_language_example: Let's meet at the park at 3 p.m.

meaning: at a walking pace; (in “attention au pas”) watch your step.
additional_notes: Literally “at the step.” Common in instructions and signs: “rouler au pas” = drive very slowly (walking speed), especially in parking lots or near pedestrians. In the expression “mettre (quelqu’un) au pas,” it means “to bring (someone) into line / make them obey.” In “attention au pas,” “pas” means a step/ledge (e.g., when getting off a train).
target_language_example: Dans cette zone piétonne, il faut rouler au pas.
native_language_example: In this pedestrian area, you have to drive at walking pace.

meaning: “heel!” (to a dog) / “at the foot (of), at the base (of)”.
additional_notes: As a command to a dog, « Au pied ! » tells it to come next to you and walk close by your leg (like “heel!”). In location phrases, it’s usually « au pied de + noun »: « au pied du lit » (at the foot of the bed), « au pied de la pente » (at the bottom of the slope), « au pied du mont… » (at the base of the mountain).
target_language_example: Le chien est resté au pied pendant toute la promenade.
native_language_example: The dog stayed at heel for the whole walk.

meaning: at the foot of the hill (at the bottom of the hill).
additional_notes: Used to describe a location right where a hill begins—down at the base, not on top or halfway up. Often used with "il y a" or "se trouve" to say what is located there (e.g., a lake, a bus stop, a building).
target_language_example: Il y a un petit café au pied de la colline.
native_language_example: There is a small café at the foot of the hill.

meaning: at the foot/base of the mountain.
additional_notes: Describes a location at the bottom of a mountain (right next to it). Uses "au pied de" + a place: "au pied de la tour" (at the base of the tower), "au pied des Alpes" (at the foot of the Alps).
target_language_example: Nous avons planté la tente au pied de la montagne.
native_language_example: We pitched the tent at the foot of the mountain.

meaning: at the picnic; to the picnic.
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le". With "pique-nique" it commonly indicates location (being at the picnic) after verbs like "s'amuser" (to have fun), and can also indicate destination (going to the picnic) after verbs of motion like "aller" or "retourner".
target_language_example: On se retrouve au pique-nique vers midi.
native_language_example: We'll meet up at the picnic around noon.

meaning: for the worst; in the worst case.
additional_notes: Most often used with verbs like se préparer à / être prêt(e) à to mean “prepare for the worst.” You can also use it to introduce a fallback scenario: Au pire, on prendra un taxi (“Worst case, we’ll take a taxi”).
target_language_example: Au pire, on restera à la maison.
native_language_example: Worst case, we'll stay at home.

meaning: “Looking forward to it/seeing you again.” (as a goodbye)
additional_notes: Used as a polite closing, often after “au revoir” or with an infinitive: “Au plaisir de vous revoir.” It can also appear in the literal sense “to the pleasure” after verbs like “ajouter” (“ajoute au plaisir” = “adds to the pleasure”).
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide — au plaisir de vous revoir.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help — I look forward to seeing you again.

meaning: at most; to the most (in set phrases like “au plus offrant/bas/haut”).
additional_notes: Commonly used after a number to mean “at most” (maximum): « Deux, au plus » = “Two at most.” It also appears in fixed expressions with an adjective/noun, e.g. « au plus offrant » (to the highest bidder), « au plus bas/haut » (at its lowest/highest point).
target_language_example: On en aura trois, au plus.
native_language_example: We’ll have three at most.

meaning: no later than; at the latest.
additional_notes: Used to set the latest acceptable time for something to happen (a deadline). It often follows the time/date: « à 18 h au plus tard ». Also common with « au plus tard à + time » or « au plus tard le + date ». Similar in meaning to « au maximum » when talking about time.
target_language_example: Envoie-moi le document demain au plus tard.
native_language_example: Send me the document by tomorrow at the latest.

meaning: as early/soon as possible; at the earliest.
additional_notes: Used to express the earliest possible time something can happen. Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence. Can also follow a time phrase: « la semaine prochaine au plus tôt » = “next week at the earliest” (not before next week). Common in scheduling and planning questions: « Quand pouvez-vous… au plus tôt ? »
target_language_example: Je peux vous rappeler demain au plus tôt.
native_language_example: I can call you back tomorrow at the earliest.

meaning: as quickly as possible; as soon as possible.
additional_notes: Used to express urgency. Often said alone as an instruction (“Au plus vite !”), or after a verb: “faire au plus vite” = to do it as fast as possible. Can also follow an infinitive: “à faire/à écraser au plus vite” = to do/crush as soon as possible.
target_language_example: Envoyez-moi le document au plus vite, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Send me the document as quickly as possible, please.

additional_notes: Very common informal expression to say that something is exactly right or works perfectly (often as a quick reaction: « Au poil ! »). Used for things, situations, or results: « tout est au poil » = “everything is great / all set.”
target_language_example: Ton idée est au poil, on fait comme ça.
native_language_example: Your idea is spot on; let's do it that way.

meaning: 'at this point/stage'; also 'ready/accurate' (depending on the expression).
additional_notes: Often used in set phrases: **au point où j'en suis / on en est** = “at this stage (given where I/we are)”; **mettre (qqch) au point** = “to finalize, work out, clarify/straighten out (a plan, details, a misunderstanding)”; **être au point** (or **une réponse est au point**) = “to be ready, correct, well-prepared/accurate.”
target_language_example: Au point où on en est, autant finir aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: At this point, we might as well finish today.

meaning: to the point of (doing something); so much that…
additional_notes: Used to show degree/intensity that leads to a result, often with an infinitive: « au point de + infinitif » (e.g., « fatigué au point de s’endormir »). Can also be followed by « que »: « au point que + phrase » (e.g., « au point que je ne pouvais plus parler »).
target_language_example: Il était épuisé au point de s’endormir dans le train.
native_language_example: He was exhausted to the point of falling asleep on the train.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives that take « à » (e.g., « jouer à » = to play, « être bon/mauvais à » = to be good/bad). « Au » is the contraction of « à + le »: « jouer au poker », « être bon au poker ».
target_language_example: Il joue souvent au poker avec ses amis.
native_language_example: He often plays poker with his friends.

additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le" and is used with masculine singular places like "le poste". Depending on the verb, it can mean being there ("Je suis au poste de police") or going there ("Je dois me rendre au poste de police"). You can also say "au commissariat" for "at/to the police station" (common in France).
target_language_example: On va au poste de police pour déposer une plainte.
native_language_example: We’re going to the police station to file a report.

additional_notes: Used about people or groups who currently control the government or have authority. Common patterns: « le parti au pouvoir » (the ruling party), « être au pouvoir » (to be in power), « arriver/venir au pouvoir » (to come to power), « revenir au pouvoir » (to return to power), « porter quelqu’un au pouvoir » (to bring someone to power).
target_language_example: Le nouveau président est au pouvoir depuis 2024.
native_language_example: The new president has been in power since 2024.

meaning: on the first floor (France: the level above the ground floor).
additional_notes: Used to say where something/someone is located or where to carry/take something. In France and many French-speaking places, "le rez-de-chaussée" is the ground floor, so "le premier étage" is one floor up (what Americans often call the second floor). Often used with verbs like "monter" (go up), "descendre" (go down), "porter" (carry), and "se situer" (to be located).
target_language_example: La salle de réunion est au premier étage, juste à gauche de l’ascenseur.
native_language_example: The meeting room is on the first floor, just to the left of the elevator.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens in spring in general (a recurring season). You can use it at the start of a sentence to set the time: « Au printemps, … ». Similar patterns: « en été » (in summer), « en automne » (in autumn), « en hiver » (in winter).
target_language_example: Au printemps, il commence souvent à faire plus chaud.
native_language_example: In spring, it often starts to get warmer.

meaning: at the cost of; at the expense of.
additional_notes: Introduces a sacrifice or negative consequence that is the “price” paid to achieve something (health, time, lives, privacy, etc.). Often used with nouns like sa santé, sa vie, de gros efforts, leur vie privée. Can also appear with même au prix de… (“even at the cost of…”).
target_language_example: Elle a obtenu ce poste au prix de nombreuses heures de travail.
native_language_example: She got that job at the cost of many hours of work.

additional_notes: Used mainly on public transport (train/metro/bus) to say what will happen at the next stop: getting off (descendre) or changing trains (changer de train). It can also be used more generally to mean the next time the vehicle stops.
target_language_example: On descend au prochain arrêt, d'accord ?
native_language_example: We’re getting off at the next stop, OK?

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen earlier, before another action or event. Common with verbs like demander (to ask), prévenir (to warn), téléphoner (to call), or discuter/parler de (to discuss). It’s a fairly formal way to say "avant" / "d’abord".
target_language_example: Merci de me prévenir au préalable si vous êtes en retard.
native_language_example: Please let me know beforehand if you’re going to be late.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens regularly in your daily routine (habits, work, life). Often follows verbs like vivre, faire, utiliser, aider, or donner la force: « vivre au quotidien », « au quotidien, je… ». It’s close to « tous les jours », but emphasizes the day-to-day reality rather than a specific calendar day.
target_language_example: Au quotidien, je prends le métro pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: Day to day, I take the subway to go to work.

meaning: in slow motion; at a slow pace.
additional_notes: Used with videos/images/scenes to mean “in slow motion” (e.g., passer/repasser une scène au ralenti). Also used more generally for things running sluggishly or operating below normal speed (e.g., le travail marche au ralenti, mon cœur bat au ralenti, une ville fonctionne au ralenti).
target_language_example: Depuis la panne, l’usine tourne au ralenti.
native_language_example: Since the breakdown, the factory has been running at a slow pace.

meaning: at the restaurant; to the restaurant.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". With a verb of location (être, manger, travailler), it often means "at the restaurant"; with a verb of movement (aller), it can mean "to the restaurant". Used for a general place rather than a specific named restaurant (otherwise you might use "dans ce restaurant" or name it).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au restaurant à 19 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the restaurant at 7 p.m.

additional_notes: A common time + place phrase. **Au** = **à + le** (“at the”). Often used with **aller** (“to go”): *aller au restaurant* = “to go to a restaurant / go out to eat.” In questions with **aller** in the past, you may see agreement in **allé/allée/allés/allées** depending on who went (male/female, singular/plural), e.g. *Êtes-vous allée… ?* (to one woman), *Êtes-vous allées… ?* (to several women).
target_language_example: On est allés au restaurant hier soir.
native_language_example: We went to a restaurant last night.

additional_notes: A standard, polite way to say goodbye when leaving or ending a conversation. It is more neutral/formal than salut.
target_language_example: Je dois partir maintenant, au revoir !
native_language_example: I have to leave now, goodbye!

meaning: “Goodbye, my …” (said to a male person, often affectionately).
additional_notes: Used when saying goodbye while adding a term of address after mon (my): mon ange (my angel), mon petit (my little one), mon vieil ami / mon vieux (my old friend / my buddy). Because mon agrees with a masculine noun, you’ll often hear it with male people or with masculine nicknames; with a feminine noun you’d use ma (e.g., Au revoir, ma chérie).
target_language_example: Au revoir, mon ami, à bientôt !
native_language_example: Goodbye, my friend—see you soon!

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dire or faire: dire au revoir à quelqu’un = to say goodbye to someone. The à introduces the person/people you’re saying goodbye to (au revoir à Lydia, au revoir à tout le monde). Often shortened to just au revoir when the person is obvious.
target_language_example: On doit partir : dis au revoir à tes amis.
native_language_example: We have to leave: say goodbye to your friends.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located on the building’s street-level floor (the level you enter from outside). In French, the ground floor is the "rez-de-chaussée" (the next level up is the "premier étage"), which can differ from US English where the "first floor" is usually street level.
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont au rez-de-chaussée, juste à gauche de l’entrée.
native_language_example: The bathrooms are on the ground floor, just to the left of the entrance.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to call for help in an emergency or urgent situation. It can be said alone ("Au secours !") or used with verbs like "crier" ("Il/Elle a crié au secours"). Stronger/more dramatic than "à l’aide" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Au secours ! Je n’arrive pas à sortir d’ici !
native_language_example: Help! I can’t get out of here!

meaning: within; in the heart of (a group/organization/family).
additional_notes: Used to locate something inside a group, institution, or community (often in a formal tone): au sein de l’entreprise, au sein du gouvernement, au sein de la famille. It emphasizes being part of the group rather than just physically inside a place. Common pattern: jouer un rôle au sein de + group.
target_language_example: Au sein de l’équipe, chacun a une tâche différente.
native_language_example: Within the team, everyone has a different task.

meaning: on the ground; on the floor.
additional_notes: Literally “to the ground” (à + le = au, sol = ground). Common with verbs like tomber (to fall) or être (to be): tomber au sol = “fall to the ground.” In some contexts (e.g., aviation/military), it means “ground” as opposed to “in the air”: unité au sol = “ground unit,” remettre au sol = “bring/put back on the ground” (e.g., land). Often similar to par terre in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Après l’explosion, tout le monde s’est retrouvé au sol.
native_language_example: After the explosion, everyone ended up on the ground.

meaning: at the top/summit of the mountain.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le" (at the). "Sommet" means the highest point (summit/peak). Used to say something is located at, or someone arrives/spends time at, the mountain’s highest point. You can swap in another place: "au sommet de la colline" (at the top of the hill).
target_language_example: On s'est retrouvés au sommet de la montagne pour admirer le lever du soleil.
native_language_example: We met at the top of the mountain to watch the sunrise.

meaning: to the sound of; to the rhythm of.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens while a sound is playing or accompanying it (music, radio, someone’s breathing, etc.). Often used with verbs like danser (to dance), s’endormir (to fall asleep), marcher (to walk). Literally “at the sound of.”
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillé au son des oiseaux.
native_language_example: I woke up to the sound of birds.

meaning: in the basement; downstairs (in the basement).
additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is located or stored in a building’s basement. Often follows a verb like être (to be), se trouver (to be located), ranger (to put away/store), or enfermer (to lock up). You can specify which building with “au sous-sol de + place” (e.g., au sous-sol de cet immeuble).
target_language_example: Les vélos sont au sous-sol.
native_language_example: The bikes are in the basement.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is located in the basement level of a building. Often with places like un parking (parking garage), la buanderie (laundry room), la cave (cellar). With feminine nouns you may also see: « à la cave » (in the cellar).
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont au sous-sol.
native_language_example: The restrooms are in the basement.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the subject or topic of what you’re talking about, often in slightly formal or neutral contexts (e.g., phone calls, emails, meetings). It’s similar to "à propos de" and "concernant". Followed by a noun or noun phrase: "au sujet de votre frère", "au sujet de ce rapport".
target_language_example: Je vous appelle au sujet de votre rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I'm calling you about your appointment.

meaning: at the supermarket; to the supermarket.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". Use it with places (being there or going there): Je suis au supermarché (I’m at the supermarket) / Je vais au supermarché (I’m going to the supermarket). For a feminine place you’d use "à la" (e.g., à la boulangerie).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au supermarché à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the supermarket at 6 p.m.?

meaning: seriously (in « prendre … au sérieux » = “to take … seriously”).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb « prendre »: « prendre quelqu’un/quelque chose au sérieux » (to take someone/something seriously). Very often appears in the negative: « ne pas prendre … au sérieux » (not to take … seriously).
target_language_example: Il faut prendre ce problème au sérieux.
native_language_example: We need to take this problem seriously.

additional_notes: Used to place something in a past era, often before a person, period, or generation: au temps de Napoléon, au temps de mes grands-parents. It often refers to 'back when' something was the case.
target_language_example: Au temps de mes grands-parents, il n'y avait pas d'internet.
native_language_example: In my grandparents' time, there was no internet.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jouer" (to play): "jouer au tennis" = to play tennis. You can also use it after adjectives to talk about ability: "bon/mauvais/médiocre au tennis" = good/bad/average at tennis.
target_language_example: Je ne joue pas souvent au tennis, mais je suis assez bon au tennis.
native_language_example: I don’t play tennis often, but I’m pretty good at tennis.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing tennis (or going to a tennis activity) with someone. Often appears after verbs like: **jouer au tennis avec** (to play tennis with), **aller au tennis avec** (to go to tennis with). **Au** = **à + le** and is commonly used with sports/activities: **au tennis**, **au foot**.
target_language_example: Je joue au tennis avec mon frère le samedi.
native_language_example: I play tennis with my brother on Saturdays.

additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase on its own. It’s typically used with a time expression after it: « au tennis tous les samedis / tous les week-ends / tous les soirs ». « au tennis » means “(to) tennis / (to) play tennis” in context (often short for « aller au tennis »). « tous les » means “every” with plural time words (days, weekends, evenings).
target_language_example: Je vais au tennis tous les samedis.
native_language_example: I go/play tennis every Saturday.

meaning: to the theater; at the theater.
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le" and is used with masculine singular places. With verbs of movement (aller, aller/venir), it often means "to the theater" (destination): « Je vais au théâtre. » With location/context, it can mean "at the theater": « Il y avait trop de monde au théâtre. » Note the past participle agreement in « aller » with "être": « ma femme et moi sommes allés » (mixed or all men) vs « sommes allées » (all women).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au théâtre à 19 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the theater at 7 p.m.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or stating the final sum/number after everything is counted or added up. Often placed at the end of a sentence: « Combien ça fait au total ? »
target_language_example: Nous avons trois tickets, donc ça fait 45 € au total.
native_language_example: We have three tickets, so that comes to €45 in total.

additional_notes: Most often means “at work” (at your workplace or working): Êtes-vous au travail ? / une présentation au travail. It can also be used after verbs like se mettre (or se remettre) to mean “to get to work” or “to start working”: se mettre au travail.
target_language_example: Je suis au travail jusqu'à 18 h.
native_language_example: I'm at work until 6 p.m.

meaning: through; across (often through something, or via a medium).
additional_notes: Used to describe movement or passage from one side to the other (through a door, a city, a road), or seeing/understanding something via a “filter” (e.g., "au travers de ses yeux" = “through his/her eyes”). Often interchangeable with "à travers"; "au travers de" can sound a bit more emphatic about going through/around an obstacle or passing through something.
target_language_example: On est passé au travers de la forêt pour rentrer plus vite.
native_language_example: We went through the forest to get back faster.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is speaking or doing something via a telephone call. Common with verbs like parler (à quelqu’un) au téléphone (to talk to someone on the phone) and répondre au téléphone (to answer the phone). In casual speech you may hear dropped words: « Je suis pas au téléphone » can mean “I’m not on the phone / I’m not currently talking on the phone.”
target_language_example: Je te rappelle : je suis au téléphone.
native_language_example: I’ll call you back: I’m on the phone.

additional_notes: Means someone is in the driver’s seat and controlling the vehicle. Commonly used with verbs like être (être au volant = to be driving) or to describe a person (le type au volant = the guy driving).
target_language_example: Je suis au volant, donc je ne peux pas répondre au téléphone.
native_language_example: I’m driving, so I can’t answer the phone.

additional_notes: A shouted warning/cry for help when you see someone stealing or running off with something. Often used with an exclamation mark: « Au voleur ! ».
target_language_example: Au voleur ! On m’a volé mon sac !
native_language_example: Thief! Someone stole my bag!

meaning: to the zoo / at the zoo.
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le". Use "au zoo" after verbs like aller (to go), être (to be), venir (to come), and emmener (to take/bring someone). The meaning can be "to the zoo" (direction) or "at the zoo" (location), depending on the verb and context.
target_language_example: On se retrouve au zoo à 14 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the zoo at 2 p.m.

meaning: no doubt; no question about it.
additional_notes: Used to say there is zero uncertainty. Often appears with negatives like « Je n’ai aucun doute » (I have no doubt) or in fixed expressions like « (ne) faire aucun doute » / « (ne) laisser aucun doute » meaning “to leave no doubt.” « Là-dessus » means “about that / on that point.”
target_language_example: Il n’y a aucun doute : elle viendra ce soir.
native_language_example: There’s no doubt: she’ll come tonight.

additional_notes: Often used with people or organizations. It can mean being physically close to someone ("go be by/with him"), or dealing with/asking a person or institution for something ("from/with" them: e.g., demander un renseignement auprès de la mairie = ask the town hall for information).
target_language_example: J’ai pris des renseignements auprès de la mairie.
native_language_example: I got information from the town hall.

meaning: 'will it have...?' / 'will he have...?' (formal inverted question form).
additional_notes: This is the future tense of *avoir* (il/elle/on **aura**) used in an inverted question: **aura-t-il ... ?** The **-t-** is inserted for pronunciation when a verb ending in a vowel is followed by **il/elle/on** (e.g., *aura-t-il*, *aura-t-elle*). Used to ask about outcomes or effects: *Quel effet cela aura-t-il ?*
target_language_example: Quel effet cela aura-t-il sur le bébé ?
native_language_example: What effect will this have on the baby?

additional_notes: Future form of « avoir lieu » (literally “to have place”), used for scheduled or planned events (meetings, conferences, parties, competitions). It agrees with the subject: « l’événement aura lieu… ». Often followed by a time and/or place: « demain », « dimanche prochain », « à Tokyo », etc.
target_language_example: Le concert aura lieu samedi à 20 h.
native_language_example: The concert will take place on Saturday at 8 p.m.

meaning: "should have" (regret about what you did or didn’t do).
additional_notes: This is the conditional form of devoir (“to have to / should”): j’aurais dû = “I should have…”. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (often a past infinitive idea in English): j’aurais dû te le dire (“I should have told you”). With negation: je n’aurais pas dû… (“I shouldn’t have…”). Also used with other persons: tu aurais dû, il/elle aurait dû, nous aurions dû, etc.
target_language_example: J’aurais dû écouter ton conseil.
native_language_example: I should have listened to your advice.

additional_notes: Used to express regret or criticism about a past action that didn’t happen. It’s the conditional perfect of devoir ("to have to / should"): tu aurais dû + infinitive. The pronoun le (“it”) refers to something already known from context and comes before the infinitive: « Tu aurais dû le faire » (You should have done it).
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû le dire plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have said it earlier.

additional_notes: Uses the past conditional of devoir to express regret or criticism about something that wasn’t done in the past. It usually changes with the subject: j’aurais dû le faire (I should have done it), tu aurais dû le faire (you should have done it), il/elle aurait dû le faire (he/she should have done it). Often used with a past-time context (hier, plus tôt, etc.).
target_language_example: J’aurais dû le faire plus tôt.
native_language_example: I should have done it earlier.

meaning: “should have” (referring to me/myself + “of it/about it/some of it,” depending on the verb that follows).
additional_notes: Often a fragment that must be followed by an infinitive: **j’aurais dû m’en + infinitive** (e.g., *m’en souvenir, m’en occuper, m’en rendre compte*). **aurais dû** is the conditional perfect of *devoir* and typically expresses regret (“I should have…”). **m’** = “to me / myself,” and **en** can mean “of it/about it” or “some (of it)” depending on the construction.
target_language_example: J'aurais dû m'en rendre compte plus tôt.
native_language_example: I should have realized it sooner.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer sentence, most often with the subject "j'": "J'aurais dû…". It uses the conditional past of "devoir" to express regret or that something was advisable in the past. The "me" is an object/reflexive pronoun placed before the infinitive that follows (often a reflexive verb): "J'aurais dû me lever" (I should have gotten up), "J'aurais dû me calmer" (I should have calmed down).
target_language_example: J'aurais dû me coucher plus tôt.
native_language_example: I should have gone to bed earlier.

additional_notes: Conditional perfect of devoir: (je/tu/il/on/nous/vous/ils) + "aurais/aurait/aurions/auriez/auraient" + "dû" + infinitive. Used to express regret ("J'aurais dû venir plus tôt") or reproach ("Tu aurais dû venir hier"). Common negative: "Tu n'aurais pas dû venir" = "You shouldn't have come."
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû venir plus tôt pour éviter la foule.
native_language_example: You should have come earlier to avoid the crowd.

additional_notes: Past conditional of devoir ("to have to / should") + voir ("to see"). Used to express regret or that something was the right thing to do, but didn’t happen. Changes with the subject: j’aurais dû voir, tu aurais dû voir, il/elle aurait dû voir, etc.
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû voir ce film, il est génial.
native_language_example: You should have seen that movie; it’s great.

additional_notes: "Aurais pu" is the conditional perfect of "pouvoir" (to be able to). It often expresses a missed possibility, regret, or reproach: "Tu aurais pu appeler" = "You could have called" (implying you didn’t). It can also describe an unreal/hypothetical past: "tout ce que j’aurais pu espérer" = "all I could have hoped for." In speech you often hear contractions like "T’aurais pu…" for "Tu aurais pu…".
target_language_example: J’aurais pu te prévenir, mais j’ai oublié.
native_language_example: I could have warned you, but I forgot.

additional_notes: Form of « devoir » in the conditional perfect: « il/elle/on » + « aurait dû » + infinitive (e.g., « On aurait dû partir plus tôt. »). Used to express regret, criticism, or that something was expected but didn’t happen. It can also indicate that something was supposed to happen or have an expected effect: « Ça aurait dû le tuer. »
target_language_example: On aurait dû téléphoner avant et réserver une table.
native_language_example: We should have called ahead and reserved a table.

meaning: "could have" (would have been able to), for something possible in the past.
additional_notes: This is the conditional perfect: avoir in the conditional (aurait) + past participle of pouvoir (pu). It’s used to talk about a past possibility that didn’t happen, or to say something almost happened: Elle aurait pu y rester = She could have stayed/ended up there (but didn’t). Often used for regrets, warnings, or near-misses (e.g., Il aurait pu se briser le cou = He could have broken his neck).
target_language_example: On aurait pu se perdre sans ton aide.
native_language_example: We could have gotten lost without your help.

meaning: could have been / might have been.
additional_notes: Past conditional: "aurait" (would have) + "pu" (been able to) + "être" (to be). Used to talk about an unreal past possibility—often to say a situation was possible but didn’t happen, or to express a near miss ("It could have been worse/you").
target_language_example: L'accident aurait pu être très grave.
native_language_example: The accident could have been very serious.

additional_notes: Used to compare: **aussi bien … que …** = “as well … as …” (Je parle aussi bien français que Tom.). With **tout aussi bien**, it often means “might as well / just as well” to suggest an option is equally acceptable (Tu pourrais tout aussi bien rester ici.). It can sound dismissive or sarcastic depending on context.
target_language_example: S'il pleut, on peut aussi bien rester à la maison.
native_language_example: If it rains, we might as well stay at home.

meaning: as well as; just as well as.
additional_notes: Used for comparisons. (1) To say two things/people are included equally: « les adultes aussi bien que les enfants » = “adults as well as children.” (2) To say someone does something at the same level as someone else: « Elle skie aussi bien que son frère » = “She skis as well as her brother.” Often intensified with « tout » (tout aussi bien que = “just as well as”) or softened with « presque » (presque aussi bien que = “almost as well as”).
target_language_example: Il cuisine tout aussi bien que sa sœur.
native_language_example: He cooks just as well as his sister.

additional_notes: Used to compare height or size. Pattern: aussi + adjective (grand) + que + noun/pronoun. With a negative, it becomes “not as … as”: pas aussi grand que…. You can also add approximations like presque / à peu près (“almost / about”) before aussi.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas aussi grand que lui.
native_language_example: I’m not as tall as him.

additional_notes: Used to compare equality: aussi + adjective (here grande) + que + noun/pronoun. It agrees with the person/thing described (grand/grande/grands/grandes). For other adjectives, replace grande: aussi petit(e) que, aussi important(e) que, etc.
target_language_example: Ma chambre est aussi grande que la tienne.
native_language_example: My room is as big as yours.

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen at the earliest time you can manage. Common after verbs like faire, commencer, quitter, répondre. Often abbreviated as “ASAP” in English, but in French you usually say the full phrase.
target_language_example: Appelez-moi aussi tôt que possible.
native_language_example: Call me as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used to compare speeds or how quickly two actions happen: aussi + adverb (vite) + que + the reference (a person, thing, or clause). It can mean equality ("as fast as") and often implies a limit with pouvoir: « aussi vite que je peux / que tu le peux » = "as fast as I/you can."
target_language_example: On va avancer aussi vite que possible.
native_language_example: We’ll move forward as fast as possible.

additional_notes: Used to say you will do something with maximum speed. It can stand alone as an instruction/request (“As quickly as possible.”). Often used after a verb: courir/venir/se préparer/répondre aussi vite que possible. You can also hear "le plus vite possible" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Envoyez-moi les documents aussi vite que possible, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please send me the documents as quickly as possible.

additional_notes: Introduces a time clause for something that happens immediately after another event. Use it with a conjugated verb: « aussitôt que tu arrives ». In instructions, it’s common with the imperative: « Téléphone-moi aussitôt que tu arrives ! ». Don’t confuse with « aussitôt que possible » = “as soon as possible / as quickly as possible.”
target_language_example: Aussitôt que j’ai fini, je te rappelle.
native_language_example: As soon as I’m done, I’ll call you back.

meaning: “as much as / as many as”; “as … as” (for quantity or degree).
additional_notes: Used to compare quantity or intensity: *pas autant que* = “not as much as.” With *vouloir/pouvoir* it often means “as much as you want/can” (*autant que tu veux / autant que tu peux*). Also used in comparisons like *autant que toi* (“as much as you”).
target_language_example: Tu peux en prendre autant que tu veux.
native_language_example: You can take as much as you want.

meaning: "as far as I know" (to the best of my knowledge).
additional_notes: Used to qualify what you’re saying and show you’re not 100% certain. It can stand alone as a short answer (“Autant que je sache.”), appear at the start (“Autant que je sache, oui.”), or be inserted in the middle with commas (“Il est, autant que je sache, un ami fiable.”). The negative form is common: “Pas autant que je sache.” = “Not that I know of.”
target_language_example: Autant que je sache, le magasin est encore ouvert.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the store is still open.

meaning: as much as possible; as far as possible.
additional_notes: Used to say you should do something to the maximum extent you can. It often follows a verb (e.g., voir/lire/éviter autant que possible) or can be used alone as a short answer. With verbs, it means “as much as possible,” and in some contexts it can mean “as far as possible” (to the greatest extent feasible).
target_language_example: Parle français autant que possible pendant le cours.
native_language_example: Speak French as much as possible during class.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “around” in a physical sense (surrounding something or moving around it): s’asseoir autour de la table, mettre son bras autour de quelqu’un. It can also be used figuratively with verbs like tourner (“to revolve”) to mean “everything is centered on”: Le monde ne tourne pas autour de vous. In other contexts, it can mean “about/roughly”: autour de 10 minutes, autour de 30 euros.
target_language_example: On arrive autour de 18 h.
native_language_example: We’ll arrive around 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to express something surrounding/encircling something (a belt around the waist, a rope around a beam) or moving in a circle/orbit around something (the Moon around the Earth). It’s the feminine form: autour du (masc. singular), autour des (plural).
target_language_example: Il y a un parc autour de la gare.
native_language_example: There is a park around the train station.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or position around something masculine singular: autour du lac (= around the lake). With feminine singular, use "autour de la"; with a vowel sound, "autour de l'"; with plural, "autour des". Also common in set phrases like "autour du monde" (= around the world).
target_language_example: On s'est promenés autour du parc.
native_language_example: We went for a walk around the park.

additional_notes: Used to say people are gathered/sitting/dancing in a circle near a fire. Common with verbs like s’asseoir (to sit), être assis (to be sitting), danser (to dance).
target_language_example: Le soir, on raconte des histoires autour du feu.
native_language_example: In the evening, we tell stories around the fire.

additional_notes: Used to describe people gathered in a circle around a campfire, often for relaxing, singing, talking, or dancing. "Autour de" + noun = "around" something; "feu de camp" means "campfire."
target_language_example: On raconte des histoires autour du feu de camp.
native_language_example: We tell stories around the campfire.

meaning: indirectly; “around the bush” (usually in tourner autour du pot).
