additional_notes: Used mostly about water depth: if you « as pied », the water is shallow enough for your feet to touch the bottom. Can also be used figuratively to mean you’re on solid ground / not overwhelmed (e.g., in a new situation). Often appears in negatives: « Ici, on n’a pas pied. »
target_language_example: Est-ce qu’on peut avoir pied ici ?
native_language_example: Can we stand here (is it shallow enough)?

meaning: to feel sorry for; to have pity (on).
additional_notes: Usually used with **de**: **avoir pitié de + noun/pronoun** (“to feel sorry for / take pity on”). In requests or strong appeals it can mean “have mercy”: **Ayez pitié !**
target_language_example: Je vais avoir pitié de lui.
native_language_example: I’m going to feel sorry for him.

meaning: “to have something to” (followed by an infinitive); often used in set phrases to mean “to have something to do with / to be related to.”
additional_notes: Structure: avoir quelque chose à + infinitif (e.g., « avoir quelque chose à dire » = to have something to say; « avoir quelque chose à faire » = to have something to do). Very common with « à voir avec » / « à faire avec » to express a connection: « avoir quelque chose à voir avec X » = to have something to do with X. Negative: « n’avoir rien à + infinitif » = to have nothing to…
target_language_example: Tu disais avoir quelque chose à me montrer.
native_language_example: You said you had something to show me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is correct. Because this entry is listed under the infinitive form, example sentences often place it after another verb, as in "Tu dois avoir raison." Although it looks like "to have reason," that literal translation is usually not how the expression is understood; for "to have a reason," French more often uses "avoir une raison de ...". The opposite is "avoir tort".
target_language_example: Tu dois avoir raison.
native_language_example: You must be right.

meaning: “to be right to” / “to have good reason to” (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is justified in doing something or thinking something. It’s followed by an infinitive: « Tu as raison de partir » (You’re right to leave). Conjugate « avoir » to match the subject (j’ai, tu as, il/elle a, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu vas avoir raison de partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You’re going to be right to leave now.

meaning: to have an appointment; to be meeting someone (at a set time).
additional_notes: Used with "avec" + person and often a time/place: "J’ai rendez-vous avec le médecin à 15 h". Also common for a planned meet-up (including a date): "J’ai rendez-vous avec Léa". In the negative: "Je n’ai pas rendez-vous aujourd’hui". You can add "chez" for where (e.g., "chez le dentiste").
target_language_example: Je vais avoir rendez-vous avec le dentiste demain matin.
native_language_example: I’m going to have an appointment with the dentist tomorrow morning.

meaning: to have your period (to be menstruating).
additional_notes: Common, neutral way to say someone is menstruating. Used with possessive + plural: « j’ai mes règles », « elle a ses règles ». Even though « règles » also means “rules,” here it refers to menstrual periods (a potential confusion for English speakers).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas aller à la piscine aujourd’hui : j’ai mes règles, donc j’ai ses règles.
native_language_example: I can’t go to the pool today: I’m on my period.

additional_notes: Uses the verb avoir (to have) in French where English uses “to be”: j’ai soif (I’m thirsty), tu as soif, il/elle a soif, nous avons soif, vous avez soif, ils/elles ont soif. It can also be used figuratively with de + noun to mean “to thirst/crave for” something: avoir soif de sang (to thirst for blood).
target_language_example: Après la marche, je vais avoir soif, alors je vais boire de l’eau.
native_language_example: After the walk, I’m going to be thirsty, so I’m going to drink some water.

meaning: to be sleepy (to feel like sleeping).
additional_notes: Literally “to have sleep.” It’s commonly used with devoir (“must/probably”) or sembler (“seem”) to make a guess about someone’s state: Tu dois avoir sommeil (“You must be sleepy”). Often contrasted with avoir sommeil vs. avoir envie de dormir (similar meaning, slightly more explicit: “feel like sleeping”).
target_language_example: Je commence à avoir sommeil, je vais me coucher.
native_language_example: I’m starting to feel sleepy, I’m going to bed.

meaning: to have had enough; to have had one’s fill (sometimes: to get what one deserves).
additional_notes: Often used with « en »: « j’en ai eu mon compte » = “I’ve had enough / I’ve had my fill (of it).” It can also be said about someone else: « Il a eu son compte » can mean “He’s had enough,” or in some contexts “He got what was coming to him.”
target_language_example: Après trois réunions d’affilée, j’ai eu mon compte.
native_language_example: After three meetings in a row, I’ve had enough.

meaning: to have (something) on your conscience; to feel guilty about (something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone feels (or should feel) guilt or remorse for something they did or failed to do. Often followed by what causes the guilt: « avoir ça / quelque chose sur la conscience ».
target_language_example: Il dit qu’il a ce mensonge sur la conscience depuis des années.
native_language_example: He says he’s had that lie on his conscience for years.

additional_notes: Means to be mistaken; opposite of « avoir raison » (to be right). Very common in conversation, especially in questions or with modal verbs/expressions like « devoir », « pouvoir », « sembler »: « Tu peux avoir tort ? » (Could you be wrong?), « Il doit avoir tort » (He must be wrong).
target_language_example: As-tu envisagé que tu puisses avoir tort ?
native_language_example: Have you considered that you might be wrong?

additional_notes: A very common, compositional chunk: avoir + un + masculine singular noun. It means "to have a/an" depending on the following English word. In real sentences, avoir is often conjugated (for example: a, avait, aura, aurait, etc.). Use avoir une before a feminine singular noun.
target_language_example: J'aimerais avoir un jardin.
native_language_example: I'd like to have a garden.

additional_notes: Used to say you have an additional one of the same thing. In real sentences it’s usually completed with a noun or pronoun: « avoir un autre café » (to have another coffee), « en avoir un autre » (to have another one). Agreement can change: « avoir une autre… » (feminine), « avoir d’autres… » (plural).
target_language_example: Je peux avoir un autre café, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I have another coffee, please?

meaning: to have a baby; to be expecting a baby (pregnant).
additional_notes: Common way to say someone is going to have a baby. With "va" (near future), it often means "is going to have a baby" and can imply either being pregnant now or that the birth is coming. Also used in the past: "Elle a eu un bébé" = "She had a baby."
target_language_example: Ils vont avoir un bébé en juin.
native_language_example: They’re going to have a baby in June.

meaning: 'to have a' / 'to get a' (a thing, a seat/table, a connection, a talk, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: avoir une + noun. Depending on context it can mean possession ("have") or request/obtain ("get/can we have...")—common in travel/restaurant situations: "Puis-je avoir une correspondance ?" (a connection), "Pourrions-nous avoir une table ?" (a table), "Pouvons-nous avoir une fourchette ?" (a fork). Also used for events/actions: "avoir une discussion/une conversation" (to have a discussion/conversation), and for abstract nouns: "avoir une raison" (to have a reason).
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux avoir une minute, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I have a minute, please?

meaning: to hear about; to get wind of (something).
additional_notes: Usually used as **avoir vent de + noun/phrase** to mean you learned something indirectly or unofficially (through rumors, whispers, the press, etc.). Often implies the information wasn’t meant to be public: *Les journalistes ont eu vent de l’affaire.*
target_language_example: Je pense avoir vent de ton projet, mais je ne sais pas si c’est vrai.
native_language_example: I think I’ve heard about your plan, but I don’t know if it’s true.

meaning: to have to; to need to (be required to).
additional_notes: Used like a modal verb and followed by an infinitive: « avoir à + infinitive ». In the negative (« ne pas avoir à ») it means “not have to / not need to.” Very common in « sans avoir à + infinitive » (“without having to…”). Don’t confuse with « avoir affaire à » (“to be dealing with”), which is a different expression.
target_language_example: Nous pouvons nous y rendre sans avoir à les informer.
native_language_example: We can go there without having to inform them.

meaning: to keep an eye on; to watch closely.
additional_notes: Used to say you are monitoring someone/something to make sure nothing goes wrong (or to watch someone suspicious). Common with an object pronoun: « Je l’ai à l’œil. » or « Je l’ai à l'œil. » Note the optional apostrophe in « l’œil / l'œil » depending on typography.
target_language_example: Je vais avoir à l'œil ton sac pendant que tu commandes.
native_language_example: I’ll keep an eye on your bag while you order.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Often used with negation: « n’avoir rien à voir (avec…) » = “to have nothing to do (with…)”. You can also say « Qu’est-ce que ça a à voir avec… ? » = “What does that have to do with…?”
target_language_example: Ça n’a rien à voir avec toi : ça n’a pas à voir avec toi.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with you: it has nothing to do with you.

meaning: "have we" (present) / "did we" (past), in an inverted question.
additional_notes: "Avons-nous" is the inversion form of "nous avons" used to ask a formal or written question. It’s from "avoir" (to have): present tense = "Avons-nous ... ?" (Have we...?), and in the passé composé it appears as the auxiliary: "Comment avons-nous fait ... ?" (How did we do...?). In everyday speech, people often use "Est-ce que nous avons... ?" or "On a... ?" instead.
target_language_example: Avons-nous assez de temps pour finir ?
native_language_example: Do we have enough time to finish?

meaning: 'we did' / 'we have done' (past tense of faire).
additional_notes: Used with the subject nous in the passé composé: nous + avons (present of avoir) + fait (past participle of faire). It can mean “we did” or “we have done,” depending on context. Common with expressions like faire un rêve (to have a dream) and in phrases like Nous l'avons fait. (“We did it.”).
target_language_example: Nous avons fait nos devoirs hier soir.
native_language_example: We did our homework last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of parler for nous: avoir (avons) + past participle (parlé). Often used with « en » to mean "talked about it/that": « Nous en avons parlé » = "We talked about it."
target_language_example: Nous en avons parlé hier soir.
native_language_example: We talked about it last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *trouver* with *nous*: **nous avons trouvé** + object. Often used with an object pronoun: **nous l’avons trouvé** = “we found it / we’ve found it.”
target_language_example: On a enfin une solution : nous avons trouvé un moyen de partir.
native_language_example: We finally have a solution: we found a way to leave.

additional_notes: Fragment built with the passé composé of **voir** (to see): **nous avons vu** = “we saw / we have seen”. **Un** means “a/an” before a masculine singular noun (use **une** for feminine). Often followed by a noun: *Nous avons vu un film / un chien / un accident.*
target_language_example: Nous avons vu un chien dans le parc.
native_language_example: We saw a dog in the park.

additional_notes: This is the passive voice in the past (passé composé): *avons été* ("have been") + past participle *attaqués* (agrees with the subject: *attaqués/attaquées/attaqué/attaquée*) + *par* introduces who/what did it (the agent). *des* means "some" or just plural "(the/a)" depending on context.
target_language_example: Nous avons été attaqués par des chiens errants.
native_language_example: We were attacked by some stray dogs.

meaning: 'do we have?' / 'have we?' (inverted question form of 'nous avons').
additional_notes: Used to form questions by inverting the verb and subject pronoun: "Nous avons..." → "Avons-nous...?" It’s formal/standard in writing and careful speech; in everyday conversation you often hear "Est-ce que nous avons...?" or "On a...?". Can also appear with "en": "En avons-nous...?" = "Do we have any? / Do we have the means for it?".
target_language_example: Avons-nous assez d'argent pour partir ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Do we have enough money to leave this weekend?

additional_notes: English loanword used in French for a person who looks after children for a few hours (often in the evening). Usually used with the article: une baby-sitter / un baby-sitter. Can also refer to the person directly (e.g., « la baby-sitter »).
target_language_example: On a trouvé une baby-sitter pour ce soir.
native_language_example: We found a babysitter for tonight.

additional_notes: Used for a wizard’s/fairy’s wand in stories, costumes, and games. "Baguette" can also mean a loaf of French bread, but "baguette magique" means the wand (not bread). Often used with verbs like avoir (to have), mettre (to put), and trouver (to find).
target_language_example: J'ai perdu ma baguette magique avant le spectacle.
native_language_example: I lost my magic wand before the show.

meaning: a bloodbath; a massacre (a situation with a lot of bloodshed).
additional_notes: Used to describe a very violent event where many people are hurt or killed. Often used as a strong, dramatic warning ("Ce sera un bain de sang") or with verbs like "éviter" (to avoid) and "finir en" (to end in). Can be literal or figurative (e.g., predicting extreme violence).
target_language_example: Ils ont annulé la manifestation pour éviter un bain de sang.
native_language_example: They cancelled the protest to avoid a bloodbath.

additional_notes: Used mainly in the phrase «prendre un bain de soleil» = “to sunbathe / to take a sunbath,” meaning to lie or sit in the sun to get some sun (often to tan).
target_language_example: On va à la plage pour prendre un bain de soleil.
native_language_example: We’re going to the beach to sunbathe.

meaning: to give up; to stop trying.
additional_notes: An idiom meaning you quit or lose heart in the face of difficulties. Often used in the negative to encourage someone: « Ne baisse pas les bras ! » (= Don’t give up!).
target_language_example: Après plusieurs refus, il a fini par baisser les bras.
native_language_example: After several rejections, he eventually gave up.

additional_notes: Usually used literally to describe someone being shot in the head (often in news/crime contexts). You’ll also see it in common phrases like « se tirer une balle dans la tête » (to shoot oneself in the head) or « il/elle a reçu une balle dans la tête » (he/she was shot in the head).
target_language_example: Il a reçu une balle dans la tête.
native_language_example: He was shot in the head.

meaning: "a bunch of" / "a gang of" (often used to insult a group).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to refer to a group of people. Very common in insults: "Bande de + [insult] !" (“You bunch of …!”). It can also be neutral, like "une bande de copains" (“a group of friends”). Note: "bande" is feminine (une bande), but you often hear it as an exclamation without an article: "Bande de…!"
target_language_example: Arrêtez de faire du bruit, bande de gamins !
native_language_example: Stop making noise, you bunch of kids!

meaning: comic (book); comic strip (as a genre/work); graphic narrative.
additional_notes: Refers to a comic work (often a comic book/album). Commonly abbreviated as « BD » (e.g., « une BD »). Literally: « bande » = strip/band + « dessinée » = drawn, i.e., a “drawn strip.” Plural: « des bandes dessinées ».
target_language_example: Elle est allée acheter une bande dessinée.
native_language_example: She went to buy a comic book.

additional_notes: A strong, often rude command telling someone to stop touching, messing with, or trying to take something. You can add what they should not touch with "de" + noun: "Bas les pattes de mon sac !" (Hands off my bag!). Commonly used in arguments; not polite in formal situations.
target_language_example: Bas les pattes de mon téléphone !
native_language_example: Hands off my phone!

additional_notes: A noun for the sport. Often used with the verb jouer: jouer au base-ball (“to play baseball”). The final -ll is usually pronounced like an English “l” sound: /bɛz.bɔl/.
target_language_example: On joue au base-ball après l'école.
native_language_example: We play baseball after school.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the sport. Common with the verb phrase "jouer au basket-ball" (to play basketball). You can also say "une équipe de basket-ball" (a basketball team).
target_language_example: On joue au basket-ball après l'école.
native_language_example: We play basketball after school.

additional_notes: Used mainly in military or formal contexts ("to beat a retreat"). Can also be used figuratively to mean backing off or withdrawing from a situation. Note: "retraite" often means "retirement" in other contexts, but here it means "retreat."
target_language_example: Devant l’ennemi, l’armée a dû battre en retraite.
native_language_example: Facing the enemy, the army had to retreat.

additional_notes: Usually refers to either your spouse’s brother or your sibling’s husband. It can also mean a stepbrother in blended families. Often used with a possessive: « mon beau-frère », « son beau-frère ».
target_language_example: Mon beau-frère habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My brother-in-law lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Usually means either your spouse’s father (father-in-law) or your mother’s new husband (stepfather). It’s used with possessives like mon/ton/son beau-père; the feminine form is belle-mère.
target_language_example: Mon beau-père arrive ce soir.
native_language_example: My father-in-law / stepfather is arriving tonight.

additional_notes: Colloquial way to praise someone’s work or the result of what they did. Often used as an exclamation (“Beau boulot !”) or with the partitive “du” (“C’est du beau boulot”, “Tu as fait du beau boulot”). Tone can be genuinely complimentary, or sarcastic depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Beau boulot, tu as réglé le problème en cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Nice work—you fixed the problem in five minutes.

additional_notes: Informal/slang. Used to describe a man or as a direct form of address (like “hey, handsome”), often flirtatious or teasing. You can say it alone (“Beau gosse.”) or with an article (“un/le beau gosse”).
target_language_example: Hé, beau gosse, tu fais quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: Hey, handsome, what are you doing tonight?

meaning: a beautiful day in my life; a great day of my life.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a particularly happy or memorable day. Very often you’ll see it as "le plus beau jour de ma vie" ("the best day of my life"). You can also pluralize it: "des beaux jours de ma vie" ("some of the best days of my life").
target_language_example: C’était un beau jour de ma vie.
native_language_example: That was a great day of my life.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone for what they did. Often said on its own (“Beau travail !”) or with the verb faire: “Tu as fait du beau travail” (“You did a good job”). You’ll also hear “du beau travail” when it means “some fine work” in general.
target_language_example: Beau travail ! Tu as réglé le problème en cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Nice work! You fixed the problem in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to show a large quantity: beaucoup de travail, beaucoup de bruit. In English, it can correspond to either “many” or “much” depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Elle a beaucoup de patience.
native_language_example: She has a lot of patience.

meaning: a lot of luck; very lucky.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has been lucky (often about a situation or outcome). Common pattern: avoir beaucoup de chance = “to be very lucky.” You can also say Tu as beaucoup de chance / Vous avez beaucoup de chance (“You’re very lucky”).
target_language_example: On a eu beaucoup de chance avec la météo aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We were very lucky with the weather today.

meaning: a lot of things; many things.
additional_notes: Used to talk generally about a large number of things (events, objects, facts, activities). Often follows verbs like faire (do), acheter (buy), révéler (reveal), se passer (happen): « Il s’est passé beaucoup de choses. » It can also appear in « avoir beaucoup de choses en commun » (“to have a lot in common”).
target_language_example: J'ai encore beaucoup de choses à faire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I still have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: a lot of things have changed.
additional_notes: Common phrase to talk about how life, a situation, or a place is different now than before. Often followed by a time expression like « ces dernières années » (in recent years) or « depuis… » (since…). « Beaucoup de choses » = “a lot of things”; « ont changé » is the past tense (passé composé) of « changer » = “to change.”
target_language_example: Depuis la pandémie, beaucoup de choses ont changé dans notre façon de travailler.
native_language_example: Since the pandemic, a lot of things have changed in the way we work.

additional_notes: Used to say there are many tasks or items to do/see/discuss/etc. It is usually followed by an infinitive verb (voir, faire, discuter, rattraper): « beaucoup de choses à + infinitive ». You can add « encore » to mean “still a lot of things to …”.
target_language_example: J’ai beaucoup de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: a lot of things to do.
additional_notes: Used to say you have many tasks/errands or a busy schedule. Often used with avoir (“to have”): « J’ai beaucoup de choses à faire. » It can also be used with il y a (“there is/are”): « Il y a beaucoup de choses à faire. » You can add timing words like encore (“still”) or today: « J’ai encore beaucoup de choses à faire aujourd’hui. »
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j’ai beaucoup de choses à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have a lot of things to do.

meaning: many people; a lot of people.
additional_notes: Common way to talk about a large number of people in general. Often used as the subject at the start of a sentence: « Beaucoup de gens + verb » (e.g., Beaucoup de gens pensent que…). « Beaucoup » can also modify a specific group: « beaucoup de mes amis » (many of my friends).
target_language_example: Beaucoup de gens veulent apprendre le français.
native_language_example: Many people want to learn French.

meaning: a lot of books; many books.
additional_notes: “Beaucoup de” means “a lot of / many” and is followed by a noun: beaucoup de livres, beaucoup de temps, beaucoup de gens. In negative sentences, it often becomes “pas beaucoup de” (“not many”): Je n’ai pas beaucoup de livres.
target_language_example: J’ai beaucoup de livres à la maison.
native_language_example: I have a lot of books at home.

meaning: a lot of people; lots of people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general (a crowd), not “many worlds.” Often used with quantities: « Il y a beaucoup de monde » (It’s crowded / There are lots of people). You can also use it as the subject: « Beaucoup de monde est venu » (Many people came).
target_language_example: Il y avait beaucoup de monde au marché ce matin.
native_language_example: There were lots of people at the market this morning.

meaning: many people; a lot of people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general. Often followed by a verb: « Beaucoup de personnes + verbe ». You can also say « beaucoup de gens » (more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Beaucoup de personnes pensent que c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: Many people think it's a good idea.

additional_notes: "Beaucoup de" means "many/a lot of". "Beaucoup de questions" is used to say there are many questions, or that someone is asking many questions. Common with verbs like "poser" (to ask): "poser beaucoup de questions" = "to ask a lot of questions". You can add a topic with "à propos de" or "au sujet de" (about): "beaucoup de questions au sujet de…".
target_language_example: J’ai encore beaucoup de questions sur ce projet.
native_language_example: I still have a lot of questions about this project.

meaning: a lot of time; much time.
additional_notes: Used to say something takes a long time, or that someone spends a long time doing something. Often follows verbs like prendre (to take) or passer (to spend): « prendre beaucoup de temps », « passer beaucoup de temps à + infinitive », « passer beaucoup de temps avec/ensemble/devant… ».
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas beaucoup de temps, je dois partir.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time; I have to leave.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say someone spends (or wastes) a lot of time doing something: « passer / consacrer / perdre beaucoup de temps à + infinitif ». Often implies the activity takes longer than expected or is not very productive (especially with « perdre »).
target_language_example: On passe beaucoup de temps à attendre ici.
native_language_example: We spend a lot of time waiting here.

meaning: a lot of work; lots of work.
additional_notes:
Used to say there is a large amount of work to do. Often used with:
- "C’est beaucoup de travail" = “It’s a lot of work.”
- "Il y a beaucoup de travail" = “There’s a lot of work (to do).”
- "J’ai/On a encore beaucoup de travail" = “I/We still have a lot of work.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j’ai beaucoup de travail.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have a lot of work.

meaning: a lot of work to do.
additional_notes: Used to say there’s a large amount of work that still needs to be done. Very common with "il y a..." (there is/are...) or "avoir..." (to have...). You can swap the subject: "J’ai / Nous avons / On a..."
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j’ai beaucoup de travail à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have a lot of work to do.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" (to have): "avoir beaucoup en commun" = to share many interests/traits/experiences. It can refer to people (friends, couples, coworkers) or even things (two ideas/products can have things in common). Often appears with "nous", "toi et moi", "vous deux", etc.
target_language_example: On a vraiment beaucoup en commun, c’est drôle !
native_language_example: We really have a lot in common—it’s funny!

additional_notes: Used to strongly compare improvement (health, quality, situation, etc.). Often follows a verb like "être" (C'est beaucoup mieux), "se sentir" (Je me sens beaucoup mieux), or "sonner" (Ça sonne beaucoup mieux). It can also mean "deserves better" / "could do better" depending on context (Il mérite beaucoup mieux; Tu pourrais faire beaucoup mieux).
target_language_example: Après une bonne nuit de sommeil, je me sens beaucoup mieux.
native_language_example: After a good night’s sleep, I feel much better.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a comparison with plus: beaucoup plus + adjective/adverb (beaucoup plus simple = much simpler), or beaucoup plus de + noun (beaucoup plus de temps = much more time). Common in comparisons: beaucoup plus ... que (much more ... than).
target_language_example: Ce film est beaucoup plus intéressant que le premier.
native_language_example: This movie is much more interesting than the first one.

additional_notes: Used to say someone still needs to learn many things (often implying they’re not very experienced yet). Common patterns: “J’ai beaucoup à apprendre” (I have a lot to learn) and “Tu as encore beaucoup à apprendre” (You still have a lot to learn).
target_language_example: On débute tous un jour : j’ai encore beaucoup à apprendre.
native_language_example: We all start someday: I still have a lot to learn.

additional_notes: Used to say you have many tasks/things to take care of. Often with forms of "avoir" (j’ai / tu as / il y a) or "rester" (il reste...) to mean there’s still a lot left to do.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j’ai beaucoup à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have a lot to do tonight.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural to mean “parents-in-law” (both of them together): *mes beaux-parents* = “my in-laws.” Singular forms are *beau-père* (father-in-law) and *belle-mère* (mother-in-law). Note: *beaux-parents* can also mean “step-parents” in some contexts, but “in-laws” is the most common meaning for beginners.
target_language_example: Je dîne chez mes beaux-parents ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m having dinner at my in-laws’ place tonight.

meaning: fine days; good weather (often: the warmer months).
additional_notes: Literally “beautiful days.” Often used to talk about spring/summer returning or the period when the weather is nice: « aux beaux jours » (when the weather is nice), « pour les beaux jours » (for the warm season), « le retour des beaux jours » (the return of nice weather).
target_language_example: On sortira davantage aux beaux jours.
native_language_example: We’ll go out more when the weather is nice.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s eyes. It’s the plural form: beau → beaux (masculine plural) + yeux (eyes). You often hear it with a possessive: tes beaux yeux / vos beaux yeux, and intensifiers like si / tellement. Note: in the expression « pour les beaux yeux de quelqu’un », it means “just to please someone / for no real reason,” not literally about eyes.
target_language_example: Je pourrais te regarder toute la journée : tu as de beaux yeux.
native_language_example: I could look at you all day: you have beautiful eyes.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm that something is true or has actually happened (often after doubt or to emphasize a conclusion). Common with statements like "C’est bel et bien..." or in the past tense: "Il est bel et bien parti." It adds emphasis, similar to “really”/“well and truly.”
target_language_example: Elle a bel et bien reçu mon message.
native_language_example: She really did receive my message.

additional_notes: Usually means your son’s wife (your daughter-in-law), especially in phrases like « la belle-fille de quelqu’un ». It can also mean a stepdaughter (your spouse’s daughter). Even though it looks like « belle » (pretty) + « fille » (girl), it does not mean “pretty girl.”
target_language_example: Ma belle-fille vient dîner dimanche.
native_language_example: My daughter-in-law is coming for dinner on Sunday.

additional_notes: Usually means your spouse’s mother (mother-in-law). It can also mean a stepmother depending on context; if you need to be extra clear, you can say "la mère de mon mari" / "la mère de ma femme" (my husband’s/wife’s mother). Used with possessives: "ma/ta/sa belle-mère".
target_language_example: Je dîne chez ma belle-mère ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m having dinner at my mother-in-law’s tonight.

additional_notes: Refers to a spouse’s sister, or (also) your sibling’s wife. Usually used with a possessive: ma/ta/sa belle-sœur. Hyphenated; feminine form (masculine: beau-frère).
target_language_example: Ma belle-sœur habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My sister-in-law lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Means an attractive/pretty woman. You’ll most often see it with an article (une belle femme = “a beautiful woman”, la belle femme = “the beautiful woman”) or as an exclamation (Quelle belle femme ! = “What a beautiful woman!”).
target_language_example: C'est une belle femme, mais surtout une personne très gentille.
native_language_example: She's a beautiful woman, but above all a very kind person.

meaning: need (to have/for), used before a vowel sound.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb: « avoir besoin de » = “to need.” « besoin d’ » is the form of « besoin de » before a word starting with a vowel or silent h (e.g., « d’un », « d’autres », « d’eau »). Common expression: « Pas besoin de… » = “No need to…” / “You don’t have to…”.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'aide, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need help, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone needs something additional, often in shops, restaurants, or customer service. It can be phrased informally with "Tu as... ?" or "T'as... ?" and more formally/politely with "Vous avez... ?" / "Avez-vous... ?".
target_language_example: Vous avez besoin d'autre chose, ou c'est tout ?
native_language_example: Do you need anything else, or is that all?

additional_notes: Used with avoir: "avoir besoin d'un/une + noun" = "to need a/an + noun." It indicates necessity or requirement. Contracts to "d'un" before a masculine singular noun (or a vowel sound); use "d'une" for feminine singular, and "de"/"d'" with plural or after negation (often: "Je n'ai pas besoin de..." rather than "d'un").
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un stylo, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need a pen, please.

additional_notes: Common way to offer or ask for help with a task. Often used as a question: « Tu as besoin d'un coup de main ? » = “Do you need a hand?” Note: « T'as besoin… ? » is a very common spoken contraction of « Tu as besoin… ? ».
target_language_example: Tu as besoin d'un coup de main pour porter ces cartons ?
native_language_example: Do you need a hand carrying these boxes?

additional_notes: Fixed chunk used inside the construction **avoir besoin de + noun** (“to need”) combined with **un peu de** (“a little (of)”). Written here with apostrophes to show elision in casual typing: **d'un** = **de un**, and the final **d'** is **de** before a vowel sound (e.g., **d’eau, d’aide**). Typical frame: **J’ai besoin d'un peu d' + [vowel-starting noun]**.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un peu d'eau, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need a little water, please.

meaning: need a drink (often an alcoholic drink).
additional_notes: Literally “need of a glass,” but it’s used like English “need a drink.” Common with avoir besoin de: « Tu as besoin d’un verre ? » / « J’aurais besoin d’un verre. » It can mean you’re thirsty, but very often implies wanting alcohol (to relax, after a stressful day, etc.).
target_language_example: Après cette journée, j'ai besoin d'un verre.
native_language_example: After this day, I need a drink.

additional_notes: Usually appears in the expression avoir besoin de = "to need." It is followed by a noun (J'ai besoin de sommeil) or an infinitive verb (J'ai besoin de parler).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de ton aide.
native_language_example: I need your help.

additional_notes: Used mainly in the structure « avoir besoin de + infinitive »: « J’ai besoin de faire… » = “I need to do…”. In the negative, « pas besoin de + infinitive » means “no need to…” / “you don’t have to…”.
target_language_example: Tu as besoin de faire une pause ?
native_language_example: Do you need to take a break?

meaning: need him / need him (to be there).
additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase « avoir besoin de »: « (quelqu’un) a besoin de lui » = “(someone) needs him.” You can also say « pas besoin de lui » = “no need for him / we don’t need him.” « lui » is an indirect object pronoun meaning “him” (or “to him”), and it refers to a male person (or “to them” as a formal singular).
target_language_example: On a besoin de lui pour finir ce projet.
native_language_example: We need him to finish this project.

meaning: need me / need me for something.
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: "avoir besoin de [quelqu’un/quelque chose]" = "to need [someone/something]". The pronoun changes depending on who is needed: besoin de toi (need you, informal), besoin de vous (need you, formal/plural), besoin de lui/d’elle (need him/her), besoin de nous/de vous/d’eux/d’elles (need us/you/them).
target_language_example: Tu as besoin de moi ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you need me tonight?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir": "avoir besoin de" + noun = "to need" something. It’s often used in questions ("As-tu besoin de notre aide ?") and can be modified with words like "encore" (still/again), "toujours" (still/always), or "vraiment" (really). The "de" usually becomes "d'" before a vowel: "besoin d'aide".
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin de notre aide, appelle-nous.
native_language_example: If you need our help, call us.

additional_notes: Used after a form of "avoir" (e.g., "j'ai / il a / elles ont") to express a need: "avoir besoin de + noun". The noun phrase "de nouvelles chaussures" means "(some) new shoes" (plural, feminine).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de nouvelles chaussures pour l'hiver.
native_language_example: I need new shoes for the winter.

additional_notes: Used within the construction "avoir besoin de" + a person to express needing someone (for help, support, presence, etc.). With pronouns, French typically uses stressed pronouns (moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles): e.g., "J’ai besoin de toi." In contrast, "besoin de quelqu'un" uses the indefinite pronoun "quelqu'un" (“someone”).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de quelqu'un pour m’aider ce soir.
native_language_example: I need someone to help me tonight.

additional_notes: Used to offer help or check if someone wants/needs anything. Very common in questions: « Besoin de quelque chose ? » (short for « Vous/tu avez besoin de quelque chose ? »). « avoir besoin de + noun » = “to need + noun.”
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin de quelque chose, je suis là.
native_language_example: If you need anything, I'm here.

besoin de quoi que ce soit

target_language_multi_word_term: besoin de quoi que ce soit
additional_notes: Used mostly in questions and conditional/negative contexts to mean “anything at all.” It’s common in polite offers: « Si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit… » = “If you need anything…”. Often interchangeable with « besoin de quelque chose » (“need something”), but « quoi que ce soit » is more general/emphatic (“anything at all”).
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit, je suis là.
native_language_example: If you need anything at all, I’m here.

additional_notes: Used after forms of the verb "avoir" (to have): "avoir besoin de" + noun = "to need" + noun. "Repos" means "rest" (often physical rest). You’ll commonly say it with a subject pronoun: "J’ai besoin de repos", "Tu as besoin de repos", "Il/Elle a besoin de repos", etc.
target_language_example: Après le voyage, j’ai besoin de repos.
native_language_example: After the trip, I need some rest.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: « avoir besoin de temps pour + infinitive ». It expresses that someone needs a certain amount of time in order to do something (understand, relax, plan, etc.). The « pour » is followed by an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de temps pour y réfléchir.
native_language_example: I need time to think about it.

additional_notes: Used after forms of "avoir besoin de" (to need) + "toi" (you, stressed pronoun). Common with "j'ai / tu as / il(elle) a / on a / nous avons / vous avez / ils(elles) ont besoin de toi". Means someone needs your help, presence, or support. Note: with formal/plural "you," use "besoin de vous."
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de toi maintenant.
native_language_example: I need you right now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" (to have): "avoir besoin de" + noun = "to need". "Ton" agrees with the thing you have ("ton aide" because "aide" is feminine but starts with a vowel sound; compare: "ta voiture", "ton ami"). Can change tense/person: "j'ai / j'avais / j'aurai besoin de ton aide"; and often followed by "pour" + infinitive: "... pour faire ça".
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de ton aide pour porter ces cartons.
native_language_example: I need your help to carry these boxes.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir": "avoir besoin de" + noun means "to need". "Votre" is the polite/plural form of "your" (vs. informal singular "ton/ta"). Common patterns: "J’ai besoin de votre aide" (I need your help), "Nous avons besoin de votre aide pour…" (We need your help to/for…).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de votre aide pour remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: I need your help to fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used with the expression "avoir besoin de" (to need). "Vous" can mean either (1) "you" in a formal/polite way to one person, or (2) "you" to several people. You can also use "avoir besoin de" + infinitive: "Vous avez besoin de vous reposer" = "You need to rest."
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de vous parler un instant.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: « avoir besoin de ça » = “to need that/this.” Often used for practical needs (“Do I need that?”), and in negatives like « je n’ai plus besoin de ça » = “I don’t need that anymore.” In speech, « ça » can mean either “that” or “this,” depending on context.
target_language_example: On n'a pas besoin de ça maintenant.
native_language_example: We don't need that right now.

additional_notes: Usually used after a verb like "avoir" ("avoir besoin urgent de..."). It is followed by a noun ("besoin urgent de repos" = an urgent need for rest) or by an infinitive ("besoin urgent de partir" = an urgent need to leave).
target_language_example: J’ai un besoin urgent de parler au médecin.
native_language_example: I have an urgent need to speak to the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the food/spread. You’ll also see the plural in stores: « beurre de cacahuètes ». « Cacahuète » = peanut; « beurre de… » often means a spread/paste made from something (not necessarily dairy butter).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un sandwich au beurre de cacahuète, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a peanut butter sandwich, please.

meaning: "Well, I…" (used to start a response or transition).
additional_notes: Often written and said as **« Eh bien, je… »** (also **« Et bien, je… »**). It’s a discourse marker used to react (surprise, realization), to hesitate, or to move the conversation along before saying what you’re going to do/think. The comma is typical: **Eh bien, je…**
target_language_example: Eh bien, je pense qu’on devrait partir maintenant.
native_language_example: Well, I think we should leave now.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective before or after a noun (mon fils bien-aimé = my beloved son) or as a noun meaning “(my) beloved” (Qui était ce bien-aimé ? = Who was this beloved person?). It agrees in gender and number: bien-aimée (f.), bien-aimés (m. pl.), bien-aimées (f. pl.). Often sounds a bit literary/solemn in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: J’ai retrouvé une lettre de ma bien-aimée.
native_language_example: I found a letter from my beloved.

additional_notes:
Used when *bien* reinforces *ce que* (“what/that which”) to show certainty or emphasis.
- **C’est bien ce que…** = “That’s exactly what…” / “That is indeed what…”
- Often appears after verbs like **écouter** or **savoir**: **Écoute bien ce que je te dis** (“Listen carefully to what I’m telling you”).
target_language_example: C’est bien ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I meant.

meaning: 'exactly what I…' / 'indeed what I…' (emphasis before finishing the sentence).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches what you thought/said/feared, etc. It’s usually part of a longer structure like: « C’est bien ce que je pensais / disais / voulais dire. » Here, « bien » means “indeed/exactly,” and « ce que je… » introduces “what I…”.
target_language_example: C’est bien ce que je pensais.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I thought.

bien ce que je veux dire

target_language_multi_word_term: bien ce que je veux dire
meaning: exactly what I mean / what I'm trying to say.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize or confirm your point, often after explaining something. Common in phrases like: « C’est bien ce que je veux dire » (“That’s exactly what I mean”), « Tu/Vous sais bien ce que je veux dire » (“You know what I mean”), « Tu vois bien ce que je veux dire » (“You see what I mean”). « bien » adds emphasis (“really/clearly/exactly”).
target_language_example: Oui, c’est bien ce que je veux dire : on doit partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: Yes, that’s exactly what I mean: we need to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used especially for meat (steak, burger, etc.) to say it’s cooked a lot with little/no pink inside. When ordering, you’ll often hear: saignant (rare), à point (medium), bien cuit (well done). Literally means “well cooked.”
target_language_example: Pour moi, un steak bien cuit, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: For me, a well-done steak, please.

meaning: “well said”; also “(I) did tell you so / I told you.”
additional_notes: As an exclamation, it praises what someone just said: « Bien dit ! » (“Well said!”). In « Je te/l’avais bien dit », *bien* emphasizes that you really did say it earlier—often with an “I told you so” feeling. With *dire de* + infinitive: « Je vous avais bien dit de ne pas entrer » = “I told you not to come in.”
target_language_example: Bien dit ! C’est exactement ça.
native_language_example: Well said! That’s exactly it.

additional_notes: Most often used as a comment meaning “of course/obviously,” sometimes with irony (e.g., « Mais bien entendu ! » = “Yeah, of course!”). It can also be literal with the verb entendre: « J’ai (très) bien entendu » / « Tu m’as bien entendu ? » = “I heard (very) clearly” / “Did you hear me clearly?”
target_language_example: —Tu viens demain ? —Bien entendu !
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course!

additional_notes: Literally means “well tried,” but it’s most commonly used as a reaction to someone’s attempt—often implying it didn’t work or that you’re not fooled (similar to “nice try!”). You can also use it sincerely to encourage someone after an effort.
target_language_example: Tu pensais que je n’allais pas remarquer ? Bien essayé !
native_language_example: You thought I wouldn’t notice? Nice try!

meaning: well done; well made; (sometimes) serves you right.
additional_notes: Often describes something made or done with quality: « C’est (très) bien fait », « un travail bien fait », « si le tour est bien fait ». With « pour toi/vous » (« C’est bien fait pour toi/vous ! »), it becomes ironic and means “serves you right!” after someone gets the consequence of their actions.
target_language_example: Ton exposé est très bien fait.
native_language_example: Your presentation is very well done.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate someone on a good move, performance, or result (often in games, sports, or work). You can strengthen it with adverbs: "Très bien joué !" / "Vraiment bien joué !" You’ll also hear it said on its own as an exclamation: "Bien joué !"
target_language_example: Bien joué ! Tu as trouvé la bonne réponse.
native_language_example: Well played! You found the right answer.

meaning: (if you would) excuse me; (if you don’t mind) excuse me.
additional_notes: Used as a polite set phrase—often in the pattern « Si tu/vous veux/ voulez bien m’excuser… »—to interrupt briefly, ask to be excused for a moment, or to politely leave. « bien » here means “kindly / if you don’t mind.”
target_language_example: Si vous voulez bien m'excuser, je dois prendre cet appel.
native_language_example: If you’ll excuse me, I have to take this call.

additional_notes: Usually used to criticize people or opinions seen as conformist, morally self-righteous, or aligned with mainstream “proper” views (often close to the idea of “politically correct” or “bourgeois”). It can be an adjective (des idées bien pensantes) or a noun (un(e) bien-pensant(e)). Often written with a hyphen: bien-pensant.
target_language_example: Il critique la presse bien pensante.
native_language_example: He criticizes the conventional, “respectable” press.

meaning: much more; far more (used to intensify a comparison).
additional_notes: Often placed before a comparative adjective/adverb or before a quantity: "bien plus chaud" (much warmer), "bien plus bas" (much lower). It can also appear with "que" to compare: "bien plus que ça" (much more than that), "bien plus malin que..." (much smarter than...). Here, "bien" means “much/far” (an intensifier), not “well.”
target_language_example: Ce film est bien plus intéressant que le premier.
native_language_example: This movie is much more interesting than the first.

additional_notes: Describes someone who is doing well physically (often used in a fairly formal or neutral tone, e.g., in writing or polite conversation). It agrees in gender and number: bien portante (f.), bien portants (m. pl.), bien portantes (f. pl.). Often used with "être": "Il est bien portant."
target_language_example: Malgré son âge, elle est encore bien portante.
native_language_example: Despite her age, she’s still in good health.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast: **bien que + subjunctive** (e.g., *bien qu’il soit…, bien que je sache…*). Note: in phrases like **montrer bien que** (“to show clearly that”) or **je pensais bien que…** (“I was pretty sure that…”), **bien** is just an adverb meaning “clearly/really,” and **que** means “that”—this is not the conjunction *bien que* meaning “although.”
target_language_example: Bien que je sois fatigué, je vais continuer.
native_language_example: Although I’m tired, I’m going to keep going.

meaning: to go well; to happen successfully.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how an event/situation is unfolding. Very common with "ça" or "tout" (e.g., "Ça va bien se passer" = “It’s going to be fine / It will go well”). "se passer" = “to happen / to take place”; adding "bien" means it happens without problems. The "se" is part of the verb (pronominal verb).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, l'entretien va bien se passer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the interview will go well.

additional_notes: Used to agree, confirm something, or say something is obvious or expected. It often appears at the start of a sentence, but it can also come after the noun or answer it refers to.
target_language_example: Tu peux compter sur moi, bien sûr.
native_language_example: You can count on me, of course.

meaning: "Of course, I…" / "Sure, I…" (strong agreement or confirmation).
additional_notes: Used to reassure or confirm what you’re about to say or do. You’ll often hear it at the start of a sentence: “Bien sûr, je peux…” (“Of course I can…”). The comma is optional in writing; in speech there’s usually a short pause. "Bien sûr" can also sound like “obviously,” depending on tone (it can feel a bit blunt if said sharply).
target_language_example: Bien sûr, je peux vous aider.
native_language_example: Of course, I can help you.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something about “he” (il). The extra **que** adds emphasis (similar to “of course he does/is/can”). It’s common in answers or when correcting someone. Often followed by a pronoun object like **le/l’** (“it/him”) or by **y en a** (“there is/are some/one”). You can also just say **Bien sûr.**
target_language_example: Bien sûr qu'il vient ce soir !
native_language_example: Of course he’s coming tonight!

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is obvious or certain, followed by a full clause (bien sûr que + subject + verb). It can also be used in answers like “Bien sûr que oui” (of course) or “Bien sûr que non” (of course not), often with an indignant or emphatic tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Bien sûr que je viendrai demain.
native_language_example: Of course I’ll come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something you’re about to say about yourself. It’s often followed by a verb: « Bien sûr que je viens ! » (“Of course I’m coming!”). « Que » introduces the clause and adds emphasis; you can also say « Bien sûr, je … » (slightly more neutral).
target_language_example: Bien sûr que je peux t’aider.
native_language_example: Of course I can help you.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something you think/can do/are/want, etc. The pattern is: « Bien sûr que je le + verb(e) » where « le » replaces the thing already mentioned (it/that). Often more emphatic than just « Bien sûr. »
target_language_example: — Tu peux venir ce soir ? — Bien sûr que je le peux.
native_language_example: — Can you come tonight? — Of course I can.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny something, often as a response to a question or accusation. It can sound reassuring (“of course not, honey/dad”) or indignant (“of course not—who do you take me for?”). You may also hear it after an initial “Non,”: “Non, bien sûr que non.”
target_language_example: —Tu as oublié mon anniversaire ? —Bien sûr que non !
native_language_example: —Did you forget my birthday? —Of course not!

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something about the person addressed: **bien sûr que tu + verb**. Often shortened to **bien sûr !** (“of course!”). In careful/formal speech you may also hear **bien sûr que oui** (“of course, yes”).
target_language_example: Bien sûr que tu peux venir avec nous.
native_language_example: Of course you can come with us.

additional_notes: Used to compliment something someone just said or came up with (a joke, a witty remark, a smart idea, a good choice of words). Often stands alone as a reaction (“Bien trouvé !”), or with “C’est…” (“C’est bien trouvé.”).
target_language_example: — On devrait l’appeler “Plan B”. — Bien trouvé !
native_language_example: — We should call it “Plan B.” — Good one!

additional_notes: As a standalone comment ("Bien vu." / "C’est bien vu."), it praises someone’s observation, idea, or quick thinking (“Good point”, “Nice one”). With the verb avoir ("j’ai bien vu", "vous l’avez bien vu ?"), it usually means you saw something clearly/indeed (“I saw it well”, “Did you see it properly?”).
target_language_example: Ah, bien vu ! Je n’avais pas remarqué ce détail.
native_language_example: Ah, good catch! I hadn’t noticed that detail.

meaning: well-mannered; well brought up (about a person/child).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who behaves politely because they were raised well. It agrees with the person: bien élevée (f.), bien élevés (m. pl.), bien élevées (f. pl.). Often said about children: « un enfant bien élevé ».
target_language_example: C'est un enfant bien élevé : il dit toujours bonjour et merci.
native_language_example: He’s a well-mannered child: he always says hello and thank you.

additional_notes: Refers to someone’s physical and mental comfort, health, and overall quality of life. Common in formal or neutral contexts: "le bien-être de + person/group" (the well-being of...). Also used in topics like public health, work, and family responsibilities.
target_language_example: Nous faisons tout pour assurer le bien-être des patients.
native_language_example: We do everything to ensure the patients’ well-being.

additional_notes: Used to welcome someone to a specific place or situation, followed by a noun phrase: « Bienvenue à la maison », « Bienvenue à Paris ». Also common: « Bienvenue chez moi/nous » (“welcome to my/our place”) and « Bienvenue dans … » (“welcome in/into …”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Bienvenue à notre fête !
native_language_example: Welcome to our party!

meaning: to drink a lot (to drink like a fish).
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to say someone drinks excessively, usually alcohol. Often used to criticize or joke about someone’s drinking habits (e.g., "Il peut boire comme un trou").
target_language_example: Il peut boire comme un trou quand il est stressé.
native_language_example: He can drink like a fish when he’s stressed.

additional_notes: Uses the verb *boire* (to drink) + *du* (= *de + le*, meaning “some”) + *vin* (wine). Very common with offers/invitations: *Tu veux boire du vin ?* / *Voulez-vous boire du vin ?* You can specify the type of wine: *du vin blanc*, *du vin rouge*, *du vin rosé*, *du vin sec*.
target_language_example: On va boire du vin ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to drink wine tonight.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase used when offering or asking for a drink. It can take an adjective or extra detail: « boire quelque chose de froid » (to drink something cold), « boire quelque chose sans alcool » (something non-alcoholic). In offers/questions you’ll often hear: « Tu veux/Voulez-vous boire quelque chose ? » (Do you want something to drink?).
target_language_example: On peut boire quelque chose avant de partir ?
native_language_example: Can we have something to drink before leaving?

additional_notes: Literally “to drink a glass,” but it’s commonly used to mean going out to have a drink together (often alcohol, but it can also be something non-alcoholic depending on context). Very common in invitations: « On va boire un verre ? », « Tu veux boire un verre ? ». You can also specify what: « un verre d’eau », « un verre de vin ».
target_language_example: Après le travail, on peut boire un verre ?
native_language_example: After work, can we go have a drink?

additional_notes: Literally “box of tools.” Used for a physical toolbox, and also figuratively for a set of resources or methods (e.g., a “toolkit” for learning, management, software). Note: the standard spelling includes accents (« boîte à outils »), but this entry uses the exact form requested: « boite à outils ».
target_language_example: J'ai laissé ma boite à outils dans la voiture.
native_language_example: I left my toolbox in the car.

additional_notes: A formal, literal term for a very powerful weapon using nuclear reactions. Often used with verbs like fabriquer (to make), détruire (to destroy), or in historical contexts (e.g., Hiroshima). You may also hear "bombe nucléaire" as a common synonym.
target_language_example: Personne ne veut qu'une bombe atomique soit utilisée.
native_language_example: No one wants an atomic bomb to be used.

meaning: Time bomb; (figuratively) a situation that is likely to cause serious trouble later.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: a bomb set to explode after a delay. Often used figuratively for a hidden problem or tense situation that could “blow up” at any moment (e.g., a political crisis, a fragile system, a dangerous relationship).
target_language_example: Cette crise est une bombe à retardement : tôt ou tard, ça va exploser.
native_language_example: This crisis is a time bomb: sooner or later, it will blow up.

additional_notes: Often used as an interjection to show surprise, shock, impatience, etc.: « Bon Dieu ! » Similar in tone to “Good God!” In a religious/literal sense, it’s usually « le Bon Dieu » meaning “God / the Good Lord.” Capitalization can vary, but « le Bon Dieu » commonly treats it like a title.
target_language_example: Bon Dieu, j'ai oublié mes clés !
native_language_example: Good God, I forgot my keys!

additional_notes: Used to wish someone a happy birthday. You can say it on its own, or add the person’s name or a term of affection (e.g., Bon anniversaire, papa !). It’s common to also say "Joyeux anniversaire" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Bon anniversaire, Julie !
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Julie!

additional_notes: Most often said to someone right before they start eating (like "Enjoy your meal!"). It can also be used literally with "avoir" to describe someone’s appetite: "avoir bon appétit" = to have a good appetite.
target_language_example: Bon appétit ! J’espère que tu vas aimer ce plat.
native_language_example: Enjoy your meal! I hope you’ll like this dish.

additional_notes: Used as a polite greeting in the afternoon, and also commonly as a goodbye/wish (especially when you’re leaving). Works with titles like monsieur/madame/capitaine or in the plural: « Bon après-midi, mesdames. »
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide — bon après-midi !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help — have a good afternoon!

meaning: a good job (good work); a good job (a good job/position).
additional_notes: "Boulot" is a common, informal word for "job/work" (more casual than "travail" or "emploi"). "Un bon boulot" often means a good job/position (e.g., stable, well-paid). "Faire du bon boulot" means "to do good work" and is used to compliment someone on the quality of what they did.
target_language_example: Bravo, vous avez fait du bon boulot !
native_language_example: Well done, you did a good job!

additional_notes: Used to say someone chose well. Often said alone as a quick reaction ("Bon choix !") or with a verb like faire: "faire un bon choix" = "to make a good choice." You can intensify it with "très" ("Très bon choix").
target_language_example: Tu as pris le gâteau au chocolat ? Bon choix !
native_language_example: You got the chocolate cake? Good choice!

meaning: “Good luck / hang in there” (encouragement for something difficult).
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone who has a hard task ahead (work, an exam, a stressful situation). Often said on its own as a friendly send-off: « Bon courage ! ». You can add « pour… » + noun/infinitive: « Bon courage pour ton examen / pour réviser ».
target_language_example: Bon courage pour demain, ça va bien se passer.
native_language_example: Good luck for tomorrow—you’ll be fine.

additional_notes: Most often used in the full phrase « C’est bon de te voir » to greet someone you’re happy to see again. « te » is the informal “you” (said to one person you know well); for a formal or plural “you,” use « bon de vous voir ». You can add intensifiers like « si / tellement / vraiment » (“so / really”). In the past: « C’était bon de te voir » (“It was good to see you”).
target_language_example: C’est vraiment bon de te voir après tout ce temps !
native_language_example: It’s really good to see you after all this time!

meaning: a good place; the right place.
additional_notes: Means a place that is suitable for something. Often used with « pour + infinitive » (e.g., « un bon endroit pour dormir » = a good place to sleep). With « le bon endroit », it often means “the right place” (the correct location).
target_language_example: On cherche un bon endroit pour manger dehors.
native_language_example: We're looking for a good place to eat outside.

meaning: the right place at the right time.
additional_notes: Often said as « au bon endroit au bon moment » (with « au » = “in the/at the”). It means that luck/timing helped something happen (meeting someone, getting an opportunity, avoiding a problem).
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé ce job parce que j’étais au bon endroit au bon moment.
native_language_example: I got this job because I was in the right place at the right time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about food/drink flavor with « avoir bon goût » (to taste good): « Ça a bon goût. ». Can also describe someone’s sense of style or preferences: « Tu as bon goût. » (You have good taste). Often intensified with « très / vraiment / assez »; negation: « pas bon goût » (doesn’t taste good).
target_language_example: Ce plat a vraiment bon goût, tu as bon goût !
native_language_example: This dish tastes really good—you have good taste!

additional_notes: Used mainly as an adjective meaning “inexpensive”: un hôtel bon marché. It’s invariable (no feminine/plural change): bon marché / bon marché / bon marché. With a person (e.g., Il est bon marché), it can mean “stingy/cheap (with money)”.
target_language_example: On cherche un restaurant bon marché près d’ici.
native_language_example: We’re looking for an inexpensive restaurant near here.

additional_notes: Often used with "le" as "le bon moment" to mean the most suitable time for an action: "C'est le bon moment pour + infinitive" (It's the right time to...). It can also simply mean a pleasant time, but in many everyday contexts it means "the right moment" rather than "a fun time."
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas le bon moment pour partir.
native_language_example: This isn’t the right time to leave.

meaning: the right word; a witty remark (a “one-liner”).
additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) "le bon mot" = the correct/right word to use (including in phrases like "le bon mot de passe" = the correct password). (2) "un bon mot" = a clever, funny remark (often something you say to make people laugh).
target_language_example: Il a toujours un bon mot quand l’ambiance est tendue.
native_language_example: He always has a witty remark when the atmosphere is tense.

meaning: a good plan/idea; a good deal (a useful tip).
additional_notes: Often used in conversation to approve a suggestion: « Ça a l’air d’un bon plan » = “That sounds like a good plan.” It can also mean “a good deal” (e.g., a bargain or a helpful recommendation): « C’est un bon plan pour manger pas cher » = “It’s a good tip/deal for eating cheaply.” Common in everyday, fairly informal speech.
target_language_example: Ça a l’air d’un bon plan : on y va demain matin.
native_language_example: That sounds like a good plan: let’s go tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something is healthy or beneficial (food, habits, activities). Often in the pattern: « C’est bon pour la santé. » You can also specify whose health: « bon pour ta/ma/sa santé ».
target_language_example: Faire une promenade chaque jour, c’est bon pour la santé.
native_language_example: Taking a walk every day is good for your health.

meaning: "damn!" / "for goodness’ sake!" (an exclamation of anger, impatience, or surprise).
additional_notes: Used like a mild swear word to vent frustration or to urge someone to do something (often at the start of a sentence: « Bon sang, dépêche-toi ! »). Literally it means “good blood,” but it’s not used with that literal meaning. Strength varies by speaker/context; it’s common in spoken French and can sound rude depending on tone.
target_language_example: Bon sang, tu pourrais répondre quand je te parle !
native_language_example: For goodness’ sake, could you answer when I’m talking to you!

additional_notes: Often used with "avoir du bon sens" (to have common sense) and "une personne de bon sens" (a sensible person). You can also say "dans le bon sens du terme" to mean "in the proper sense of the word" (the intended/positive meaning).
target_language_example: Fais preuve de bon sens et mets ton casque à vélo.
native_language_example: Use common sense and wear your bike helmet.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s work (often as an exclamation: « Bon travail ! »). It can also describe the quality of work (« C’est un bon travail. ») or refer to a good/steady job position (« Il a besoin d’un bon travail. »).
target_language_example: Bon travail, vous avez terminé plus vite que prévu !
native_language_example: Good job, you finished faster than expected!

additional_notes: Used as a farewell to wish someone a good journey (especially by boat, but also more generally). In the expression « Quel bon vent t’amène ? / vous amène ? », it’s a slightly old-fashioned, friendly way to say “What brings you here?” (as if a favorable wind brought you).
target_language_example: Bon vent, et à bientôt !
native_language_example: Safe travels, and see you soon!

additional_notes: Usually used with the definite article: "le bon vieux temps". It refers to an earlier period remembered fondly (often implying things were better/simpler then). Common with verbs like "parler de" / "discuter de" (to talk about).
target_language_example: On se rappelle souvent le bon vieux temps.
native_language_example: We often remember the good old days.

meaning: “Have a good trip!” / “Have a safe journey.”
additional_notes: Used to wish someone well before they leave on a trip. You can say it on its own (“Bon voyage !”) or with verbs like souhaiter (“Je te souhaite bon voyage.”) or faire (“Tu as fait bon voyage ?” = “Did you have a good trip?”).
target_language_example: Bon voyage, et à bientôt !
native_language_example: Have a good trip, and see you soon!

meaning: worth taking; good to accept (even if it’s small).
additional_notes: Used after phrases like « c’est… », « tout… », « toujours… » to mean something is beneficial to take/accept because it can help (money, opportunities, advantages, etc.). Can also be used more literally to mean someone/something is an easy or acceptable “catch” (e.g., « Tout suspect est bon à prendre » = any suspect will do).
target_language_example: Une petite réduction, c’est toujours bon à prendre.
native_language_example: A small discount is always worth taking.

additional_notes: A strong insult used to say someone is worthless or useless. It can also be used about yourself (often with self-blame): « Je suis bon à rien ». Often preceded by insults like « espèce de… » or used as a noun: « ce bon à rien ».
target_language_example: Arrête de me traiter de bon à rien !
native_language_example: Stop calling me a good-for-nothing!

meaning: a good student (a well-behaved / hard-working student).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who does well at school or is diligent and well-behaved. Often with an article: « C’est un bon élève », « Il/Elle est un(e) bon(ne) élève ». Without an article (e.g., « Il est bon élève ») is also possible but more formal/literary.
target_language_example: John est un bon élève.
native_language_example: John is a good student.

meaning: “Well, I…” (to introduce what you’re about to do/say, often to wrap up or move on).
additional_notes: Used as a conversational transition, similar to “Well,” “Alright,” or “Okay then,” before stating your next action or conclusion (e.g., leaving, deciding to go home, admitting something). The comma/pause is important: “Bon, je…” is more about organizing the conversation than saying “good.”
target_language_example: Bon, je vais y aller, il se fait tard.
native_language_example: Well, I’m going to go, it’s getting late.

meaning: "Alright, (so) we…" / "Well, (so) we…" (used to start a decision or next step).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to move things along: to wrap up, change topic, or propose the next action. It often introduces a suggestion or decision with "on" (= "we" / informal "you" meaning "let’s"). Not literally "good, we" here—"bon" works like a filler meaning "okay/well".
target_language_example: Bon, on y va ?
native_language_example: Alright, shall we go?

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question as a conversational opener. "Bon" here means "well/okay" and can show you’re ready to act, checking the situation, or sometimes mild impatience. It’s very common in spoken French (you can also hear "Bon, qu’est-ce qu’on fait ?" / "Bon, qu’est-ce qui se passe ?").
target_language_example: Bon, qu'est-ce qu'on fait maintenant ?
native_language_example: Okay, what do we do now?

meaning: 'Well then…' / 'Alright then…' (to start, react, or move things along).
additional_notes: Common spoken filler used to open a conversation, change topic, wrap up, or show mild impatience/urgency. Said alone or with a question ("Bon alors ?") it can mean "So?" or "Well?" to prompt someone to answer or act.
target_language_example: Bon alors, on y va ?
native_language_example: Alright then, shall we go?

additional_notes: Used for a snow figure made by packing snow (often with a carrot nose, scarf, etc.). You can say "faire un bonhomme de neige" (to make a snowman). It’s masculine: "un/le bonhomme de neige".
target_language_example: Les enfants ont fait un bonhomme de neige dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The kids made a snowman in the garden.

meaning: "Hello/Good morning, Mrs./Ms." (polite greeting to a woman).
additional_notes: Used in formal or polite situations, followed by a woman’s last name: « Bonjour, Mme Dupont. ». « Mme » is the abbreviation of « Madame » and is always capitalized in writing; it’s pronounced like « madame » (often shortened in speech to « bonjour madame »).
target_language_example: Bonjour, Mme Martin. Comment allez-vous ?
native_language_example: Hello, Mrs. Martin. How are you?

additional_notes: Used to greet someone directly followed by a noun: a person (Bonjour, mon ami.), a role (Bonjour, mon professeur.), or a term of endearment (Bonjour, mon cœur.). "Mon" is the possessive "my" used with masculine singular nouns (mon ami, mon nom).
target_language_example: Bonjour, mon professeur.
native_language_example: Hello, my teacher.

additional_notes: Means an act of kindness or charity. Commonly used with the verb faire: « faire une bonne action » (to do a good deed). You can also say « une bonne action par jour » (a good deed a day).
target_language_example: J’essaie de faire une bonne action chaque jour.
native_language_example: I try to do a good deed every day.

meaning: a good year; (in “une bonne année”) a full/solid year (about a year).
additional_notes: Literally “good year.” With the article, it’s very common to say “depuis une bonne année” = “for a good year now,” meaning for roughly a year or a bit more (emphasizing it’s been quite a while). Without an article, “Bonne année !” is also a New Year’s greeting (“Happy New Year!”).
target_language_example: Je travaille ici depuis une bonne année.
native_language_example: I’ve been working here for a good year (about a year).

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck before an exam, trip, job interview, adventure, etc. Often followed by « pour + noun » (Bonne chance pour ton examen) or « à + person » (Bonne chance à tous / à toi). You can also say « Bonne chance ! » on its own, or add a name (Bonne chance, Harry.).
target_language_example: Bonne chance pour ton entretien demain !
native_language_example: Good luck with your interview tomorrow!

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck about an upcoming event, task, or goal. It’s typically followed by a noun (Bonne chance pour ce soir / pour la prochaine fois) or an infinitive (Bonne chance pour la convaincre / pour obtenir la permission). You can also say « Je te/vous souhaite bonne chance pour… » for a slightly more formal phrasing.
target_language_example: Bonne chance pour ton entretien demain !
native_language_example: Good luck with your interview tomorrow!

meaning: a woman (often in a dismissive/sexist way); sometimes ‘wife’.
additional_notes: Colloquial and often derogatory, similar to “broad” / “that woman” / “old woman” depending on context. It can also mean someone’s wife (“sa bonne femme”), especially in informal speech, but it still has a familiar or disrespectful tone—avoid in polite conversation. In exclamations like “Sacrée bonne femme !”, it can mean “What a woman!” (admiring or ironic depending on tone).
target_language_example: Il est encore parti avec sa bonne femme.
native_language_example: He left again with his wife.

meaning: 'good girl' / 'nice girl' (a well-behaved or kind-hearted girl/woman).
additional_notes: Literally "good girl." With children (or when talking about behavior), it often means "well-behaved" (like praising/rewarding someone). Said to an adult woman, it more often means "a nice, good-natured person," but it can also sound patronizing/infantilizing depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: C'est vraiment une bonne fille, toujours prête à aider les autres.
native_language_example: She’s really a nice person, always ready to help others.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well for a celebration or special day. Often followed by "de" + the event ("Bonne fête du Canada !") or "à" + a person ("Bonne fête à toi !"). In Quebec and some French-speaking areas, "Bonne fête !" is commonly used to mean "Happy birthday!"; in France, people usually say "Joyeux anniversaire !" for birthdays.
target_language_example: Bonne fête à ta sœur !
native_language_example: Happy birthday to your sister!

additional_notes: Usually used with être de/en bonne humeur (to be in a good mood). You can also talk about someone’s bonne humeur to mean their cheerful attitude (e.g., “plein de bonne humeur” = “full of cheer”).
target_language_example: Elle est de bonne humeur aujourd'hui, alors tout se passe bien.
native_language_example: She’s in a good mood today, so everything is going well.

additional_notes: Used to say something is a good suggestion/plan (often as a reaction: « Bonne idée ! »). With emphasis it can be « Quelle bonne idée ! » (“What a great idea!”). Can also be used with articles like « une bonne idée » (“a good idea”) or « la bonne idée » (“the good idea/right idea”).
target_language_example: Bonne idée : on peut y aller en métro.
native_language_example: Good idea: we can go by metro.

additional_notes: Used as a polite goodbye or well-wish, especially at the end of a conversation (Alors, bonne journée.). With a comma and often a name/title, it works like “Have a nice day, …” (Bonne journée, madame Clara.). It can also be a normal noun phrase meaning “a good day” in past or descriptive contexts (Hier était une bonne journée; On a passé une bonne journée).
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide — bonne journée !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help — have a nice day!

additional_notes: Used to announce or react to positive information. Often said on its own as an interjection (“Bonne nouvelle !”) or with emphasis like “très bonne nouvelle” (“very good news”). You can also start a sentence with it to introduce the news: “Bonne nouvelle : …”
target_language_example: Bonne nouvelle : j’ai trouvé tes clés.
native_language_example: Good news: I found your keys.

additional_notes: A common farewell said in the evening or before going to sleep. Often used alone or with a name (e.g., « Bonne nuit, Tom ! »). You can also say « Bonne nuit ! » right before bed; it’s different from « Bonsoir », which is used as a greeting or early-evening goodbye.
target_language_example: Bonne nuit, à demain !
native_language_example: Good night, see you tomorrow!

meaning: "Good night, my …" (followed by a term of endearment).
additional_notes: Used when saying good night to someone you care about. "Mon" is "my" used before a noun (e.g., mon ange, mon bébé, mon cœur). Even when talking to a woman, you still say "mon" before a vowel sound (mon ange). Common in romantic/family contexts.
target_language_example: Bonne nuit, mon amour.
native_language_example: Good night, my love.

additional_notes: Used as a polite goodbye to someone who’s leaving by car or traveling (similar to *bon voyage*). It can also be literal: *la bonne route* = “the right road/route.” In wishes, it’s often said without a verb (*Bonne route !*) or with *souhaiter* (*Je te/vous souhaite bonne route*).
target_language_example: Bonne route, et tiens-moi au courant quand tu arrives !
