native_language_example: Safe travels, and let me know when you arrive!

additional_notes: Often used with the verb "être" to describe someone’s health: "être en bonne santé" = "to be in good health." It’s also used more generally to talk about health as a state or goal (sleep, lifestyle, etc.).
target_language_example: Après l’opération, il est enfin en bonne santé.
native_language_example: After the operation, he’s finally in good health.

additional_notes: A common polite goodbye used in the late afternoon/evening (when the evening is starting). You can say it on its own (“Bonne soirée !”) or add a person (“Bonne soirée, messieurs.”). Typically used when you’re parting ways, not when arriving.
target_language_example: Je rentre chez moi — bonne soirée !
native_language_example: I’m heading home — have a good evening!

additional_notes: Used to talk about social etiquette—how you’re expected to behave (saying please/thank you, not interrupting, being respectful). Often said in a scolding or reminder: « Où sont tes bonnes manières ? » = “Where are your manners?”
target_language_example: Il faut de bonnes manières à table.
native_language_example: You need good manners at the table.

additional_notes: Means positive information or an update. Very common in questions like « Tu as des bonnes nouvelles ? » (“Do you have any good news?”). Often used with an article: « des bonnes nouvelles » (some good news) or intensified: « de très bonnes nouvelles » (very good news). Note: You may also hear « de bonnes nouvelles » (without « des »), especially after « avoir » in careful French.
target_language_example: J'espère que tu as de bonnes nouvelles.
native_language_example: I hope you have good news.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well before they go on vacation or for a holiday break. Often said with the verb "passer": "Passe de bonnes vacances" (informal singular), "Passez de bonnes vacances" (formal or plural). You can also say it on its own: "Bonnes vacances !"
target_language_example: Bonnes vacances ! On se revoit en septembre.
native_language_example: Have a nice vacation! See you again in September.

additional_notes: Literally “good friends.” Often used to mean people you’re friendly with and know well. Adjective agreement: masculine plural bons amis; feminine plural bonnes amies; mixed group typically uses masculine plural (bons amis). You can also say un bon ami / une bonne amie.
target_language_example: On est de bons amis depuis le lycée.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends since high school.

meaning: “Goodness!” / “Good heavens!” (an exclamation of surprise, shock, or amazement).
additional_notes: Used as a standalone interjection or with “Oh,” to react to something unexpected (good or bad). It’s a mild, somewhat old-fashioned-sounding expression; not really about religion in everyday use.
target_language_example: Bonté divine, j’ai complètement oublié mes clés !
native_language_example: Good heavens, I completely forgot my keys!

additional_notes: Used to locate something along the edge or side of a place or object. It’s the feminine form of “bord de” and is followed by a feminine noun (la route, la table, la mer, etc.). Often appears in set phrases like “au bord de la mer” (by the seaside) or “sur le bord de la route” (on the side of the road).
target_language_example: On s’est assis au bord de la piscine.
native_language_example: We sat down by the edge of the pool.

additional_notes: Used to describe a place right next to a cliff drop-off. Often appears with a preposition like "au bord de la falaise" (at the edge of the cliff) or "près du bord de la falaise" (near the edge of the cliff).
target_language_example: Ne t'approche pas du bord de la falaise.
native_language_example: Don’t go near the edge of the cliff.

additional_notes: Literally “edge of the sea.” Often used with prepositions like "au bord de la mer" (by the sea) or "le long du bord de la mer" (along the seashore).
target_language_example: On a loué une maison au bord de la mer.
native_language_example: We rented a house by the sea.

meaning: 'the edge/side of the' or 'on board the' (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun after it: (au) bord du trottoir = at the edge of the sidewalk; (à) bord du bateau/train = on board the boat/train. With this pattern you usually see it after prepositions: au bord du (= à + le), à bord du. For feminine singular, you use "de la" (bord de la mer), and for plural "des" (bord des routes).
target_language_example: Il y a un café au bord du lac.
native_language_example: There’s a café by the lake.

additional_notes: A very strong, very vulgar expletive used to express anger, frustration, surprise, or to insult someone. It’s made of swear words (“bordel” + “merde”) and should be avoided in polite conversation, with strangers, at work, or in formal settings. Often said as an outburst: « Oh, bordel de merde ! »
target_language_example: Oh, bordel de merde, j’ai encore raté le bus !
native_language_example: For fuck’s sake, I missed the bus again!

meaning: to kick someone’s ass (to beat up / punish harshly).
additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive. Used as a threat (“Je vais te botter le cul !”) or to say someone can/can’t beat someone up (“Il ne va pas te botter le cul.”). You can also specify the target with “botter le cul de + [person]”. Often implies physical violence, so avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Si tu continues, je vais te botter le cul.
native_language_example: If you keep going, I’m going to kick your ass.

additional_notes: Usually used after verbs like « rester » or « se tenir » to describe someone frozen in surprise: « Il est resté bouche bée. » It agrees in gender/number in modern French: « bouche bée » for everyone (not *bouche bé* / *bouche bées*).
target_language_example: Quand j’ai vu le prix, je suis resté bouche bée.
native_language_example: When I saw the price, I was left open-mouthed.

additional_notes: Informal, spoken negative of “bouger” (“to move”), short for “Ne bouge pas.” Used to tell someone not to move (often in a firm or urgent way). You can also see it in longer negatives like “ne bouge pas de + place” = “doesn’t leave/doesn’t move from + place.”
target_language_example: Bouge pas, j’arrive tout de suite.
native_language_example: Don’t move, I’ll be right there.

meaning: a piece/bit/end of (something); also “a while” in time expressions (un bout de temps).
additional_notes: “Un bout de + noun” often means a piece or bit of something: un bout de corde (a piece/end of rope), un bout de gâteau (a piece of cake), un bout de bois (a piece of wood). With time, “un bout de temps” means “a while,” and “Ça fait un bout de temps” means “It’s been a while” (more idiomatic than the literal “a bit of time”).
target_language_example: Attends un bout de temps, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: Wait a while, I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Literally “bit of paper.” Used for any small piece of paper (a note, scrap, receipt, etc.). Often in phrases like « un bout de papier » (a piece of paper) or « sur un bout de papier » (on a piece of paper).
target_language_example: J’ai noté ton numéro sur un bout de papier.
native_language_example: I wrote down your number on a piece of paper.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the end, tip, or far side of something: le bout du doigt (the tip of the finger), le bout du fil (the end of the thread), à l'autre bout du… (at the other end of…). Note: du = de + le, so bout du = bout de le. Also appears in the common idiom mener quelqu’un par le bout du nez (“to lead someone by the nose,” i.e., to control/manipulate them).
target_language_example: Le bout du câble est cassé.
native_language_example: The end of the cable is broken.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a location at the far end of a hallway. Very common with the preposition: « au bout du couloir » (“at the end of the hallway”).
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont au bout du couloir, à droite.
native_language_example: The bathrooms are at the end of the hallway, on the right.

meaning: the end of the world; a very remote place.
additional_notes: Usually used in the expression « au bout du monde » to mean “very far away / in the middle of nowhere” (often with the idea of an isolated place). « bout » = “end” and « monde » = “world.”
target_language_example: Ils habitent au bout du monde, loin de tout.
native_language_example: They live at the end of the world, far from everything.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a quantity/container: "une bouteille de vin" (one bottle of wine). You can use it after verbs like acheter (to buy), boire (to drink), apporter (to bring). In French, "de" links the container to what’s inside.
target_language_example: On apporte une bouteille de vin pour le dîner.
native_language_example: We’re bringing a bottle of wine for dinner.

additional_notes: Refers to the box where you receive mail (at home or in an apartment building). It can also mean a public mailbox where you drop letters to be sent, depending on context (déposer une lettre dans la boîte aux lettres).
target_language_example: J’ai reçu une lettre dans ma boîte aux lettres ce matin.
native_language_example: I got a letter in my mailbox this morning.

additional_notes: A place that’s open late at night where people go to dance and drink. It’s feminine: une boîte de nuit; in the plural: des boîtes de nuit. Often used with verbs like aller en/dans une boîte de nuit (to go to a nightclub) and entrer dans une boîte de nuit (to get into a nightclub).
target_language_example: On va en boîte de nuit samedi soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to a nightclub Saturday night?

additional_notes: A fixed storage compartment in a car’s dashboard (usually in front of the passenger seat). Used with "dans la boîte à gants" (“in the glove compartment”) or "regarder dans la boîte à gants" (“look in the glove compartment”). Not necessarily for gloves—people often keep papers, keys, etc. there.
target_language_example: Mes papiers d’assurance sont dans la boîte à gants.
native_language_example: My insurance papers are in the glove compartment.

additional_notes: A container (often portable) used to store and carry tools like a hammer (marteau) or pliers (pince). In everyday speech it’s usually literal, but it can also be used figuratively (e.g., a “set of methods/resources”).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de ma boîte à outils pour réparer la chaise.
native_language_example: I need my toolbox to fix the chair.

meaning: right arm; (figurative) right-hand man / trusted assistant.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: the physical right arm (often with possessives: mon/ton/son bras droit). Figurative meaning: someone’s main helper or second-in-command ("être le bras droit de quelqu’un", "Sois mon bras droit").
target_language_example: Au travail, Sarah est mon bras droit : elle m’aide sur tout.
native_language_example: At work, Sarah is my right-hand woman: she helps me with everything.

additional_notes: Used for causing someone strong emotional pain, often in love or disappointment. Common patterns include « briser le cœur à quelqu’un » (to break someone’s heart) and « Ça me brise le cœur » (It breaks my heart) for something sad.
target_language_example: Il a brisé le cœur de Marie.
native_language_example: He broke Marie’s heart.

additional_notes: A common everyday item. Uses the structure "[object] à [purpose]" (a brush for teeth). Often used with possessives: "ma/ta/sa brosse à dents". In speech, you’ll also hear: "Je me brosse les dents" (I brush my teeth).
target_language_example: N'oublie pas ta brosse à dents avant de partir.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your toothbrush before leaving.

additional_notes: An imperative (command) using the verb "brosser" (to brush) in the "tu" form with a reflexive pronoun: "brosse-toi" = "brush (yourself)". "Les dents" means "the teeth" (French commonly uses "the" where English uses "your"). Often used with time expressions like "après chaque repas" (after each meal) or "au moins deux fois par jour" (at least twice a day).
target_language_example: Avant d'aller au lit, brosse-toi les dents.
native_language_example: Before going to bed, brush your teeth.

additional_notes: From the verb « brosser » (to brush) + « les dents » (the teeth). Often used with a reflexive pronoun to mean “brush your own teeth”: « se brosser les dents » (e.g., « Mon fils se brosse les dents. »). Without « se », it usually means brushing someone else’s teeth: « Je lui brosse les dents. »
target_language_example: Je me brosse les dents avant de me coucher.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth before going to bed.

additional_notes: Usually used reflexively with a person: « se brosser les dents » (je me brosse…, tu te brosses…, il/elle se brosse…, nous nous brossons…, vous vous brossez…, ils/elles se brossent…). Often used as an instruction: « Va te brosser les dents ! »
target_language_example: Va te brosser les dents avant d'aller te coucher.
native_language_example: Go brush your teeth before going to bed.

additional_notes: Past tense with the verb « boire » (to drink): « bu » is the past participle used with « avoir » (e.g., j’ai bu, il a bu, ils ont bu). It doesn’t change for gender/number here because it’s used with « avoir » and the direct object (« une tasse de café ») comes after the verb. « une tasse de café » = a cup of coffee.
target_language_example: Ce matin, j’ai bu une tasse de café avant de partir.
native_language_example: This morning, I drank a cup of coffee before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where you mail letters/packages and buy stamps. Very common in directions: "au bureau de poste" (to the post office), "près du bureau de poste" (near the post office), "à côté du bureau de poste" (next to the post office).
target_language_example: Je dois passer au bureau de poste pour envoyer un colis.
native_language_example: I need to stop by the post office to send a package.

additional_notes: Contraction of ce + est. Very common for identifying or pointing out a person, thing, or idea. Depending on context, it can mean 'this is', 'that is', or 'it's'.
target_language_example: C'est mon ami.
native_language_example: This is my friend.

meaning: nonstandard French form; often intended as either « c'est ce » ('it is this/that') or part of « est-ce » in questions
additional_notes: « c'est-ce » with a hyphen is not standard French as a standalone expression. In most contexts, the writer likely means « c'est ce » (without a hyphen) or another standard pattern such as « est-ce ». Because it is nonstandard, it is best treated as a spelling error or typo rather than a normal phrasebook entry.
target_language_example: On voit parfois « c'est-ce » en ligne, mais ce n'est pas l'orthographe standard.
native_language_example: You sometimes see "c'est-ce" online, but it is not the standard spelling.

additional_notes: Used to clarify, specify, or rephrase what you just said. Often followed by a noun/pronoun (C'est-à-dire moi / nous / toi / tout le monde) or a more precise explanation.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à huit heures, c'est-à-dire à 20 h.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at eight o’clock, that is, at 8 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation of how something happens or how things are, often with a sense of “that’s just how it is” or “that’s how it should be.” Common patterns: « c'est ainsi que + [event/action] » (That’s how + something happened) and « c'est ainsi que + être/devoir + … » (That’s how it is/should be).
target_language_example: c'est ainsi que tout a commencé.
native_language_example: That's how it all started.

additional_notes: Past tense of "arriver" used impersonally to describe an event that took place. Often followed by time expressions ("une fois", "tellement vite") or by "à + person" to mean it happened to someone ("C'est arrivé à quelqu'un"). In questions, you’ll commonly hear: "Quand est-ce que c’est arrivé ?"
target_language_example: C'est arrivé tellement vite.
native_language_example: It happened so fast.

meaning: “it’s quite / it’s rather” (with an adjective); or “that’s enough / it’s enough” (depending on context).
additional_notes: With an adjective, *assez* means “quite/rather/fairly”: *C'est assez clair / important / incroyable / simple.* It can also mean “That’s enough” or “It’s enough (for now)” when *assez* stands alone or is followed by *pour...*: *Je crois que c'est assez pour l'instant.*
target_language_example: Je crois que c'est assez pour l'instant.
native_language_example: I think that’s enough for now.

meaning: “That’s also what I…” / “That’s what I … too.”
additional_notes: Used to agree with someone or say you share the same thought, belief, or desire. It’s followed by a verb such as pense (think), crois (believe), croyais/pensais (thought/believed), veux (want), etc. Common pattern: « c'est aussi ce que je + verbe ».
target_language_example: — Je pense qu'il va pleuvoir. — c'est aussi ce que je pense.
native_language_example: — I think it’s going to rain. — That’s what I think too.

additional_notes: Often used to confirm or emphasize something (“it really is…” / “it is indeed…”), especially with another clause: « C'est bien ce que… ». It can also express approval or acceptance: « C'est bien noté » (“Noted / Understood”) and « Et c'est bien comme ça » (“And that’s fine that way / That’s how it is”). The exact meaning depends on context and tone.
target_language_example: D'accord, c'est bien ce que j'avais compris.
native_language_example: Okay, that’s indeed what I understood.

meaning: “That is indeed what… / So that’s what…” (used to confirm or verify something).
additional_notes: Used to confirm or check that something is correct, often with a verb of thinking, believing, or wanting: “C'est bien ce que je pensais” (= “That’s exactly what I thought”). In questions, it means “Is that really what…?” (e.g., “C'est bien ce que tu veux ?” = “Is that really what you want?”). Here, “bien” adds emphasis (“indeed / really / exactly”).
target_language_example: C'est bien ce que je pensais.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I thought.

meaning: "that's exactly what I…" / "that's indeed what I…" (introduces what you thought/meant/said, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to confirm or insist that something matches what you thought/said/meant. It’s typically followed by a verb phrase: « c'est bien ce que je pensais » (that's exactly what I thought), « c'est bien ce que je voulais dire » (that's exactly what I meant). Here « bien » means “indeed/exactly,” not “good.”
target_language_example: c'est bien ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: That's exactly what I meant.

meaning: "It's good/nice that you (are / have ...)" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express a positive opinion about something the other person is/has done. After « c'est bien que », French uses the subjunctive: « que tu sois… ». In the examples with a past action, you often get the subjunctive of « être » + a past participle: « que tu sois revenu(e) / rentré(e) / venu(e) ». Add -e for feminine (« venue », « revenue », « rentrée »).
target_language_example: C'est bien que tu sois venu m'aider.
native_language_example: It’s nice that you came to help me.

additional_notes: Very common, with several meanings depending on context: (1) taste/quality: « C'est bon. » = “It’s good (tasty / good quality).” (2) suitability/benefit: « C'est bon pour toi. » = “It’s good for you.” (3) confirmation/acceptance: « C'est bon. » = “That’s fine / OK.” (4) “I understand / I’ve seen”: « C'est bon, j'ai vu. » = “OK, I saw / I get it.” Often used in conversation as a quick, informal-sounding acknowledgment, but not slang.
target_language_example: C'est bon, on y va !
native_language_example: OK, let’s go!

meaning: "it feels good to be…" / "it’s nice to be…"
additional_notes: Used to express pleasure or relief about a situation or state (often after being away or after something difficult): C'est bon d'être chez soi (It feels good to be home). You can also use it with an exclamation for emphasis: Que c'est bon d'être… = How good it feels to be…
target_language_example: C'est bon d'être en vacances.
native_language_example: It feels good to be on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to express that you’re happy or pleased about doing something or experiencing something (often meeting, seeing, hearing someone again, or learning information). In these examples, it’s followed by an infinitive: c’est bon de + infinitive (l’entendre, le savoir, t’avoir…). Can also imply “it feels good to…” depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est bon de te revoir après tout ce temps.
native_language_example: It’s nice to see you again after all this time.

additional_notes: A friendly greeting used when you’re happy to see someone (often again, after some time). You can add words like « aussi » (too) or « de retour » (back), and informal add-ons like « mec » / « mon pote » (buddy/mate).
target_language_example: C'est bon de te voir de retour !
native_language_example: It’s good to see you back!

additional_notes: Used to say something is beneficial (for health, traffic, etc.) or suitable/acceptable in a situation. With "c'est bon pour cette fois", it means "okay this time" (accepting/allowing it). With "c'est bon pour ce que tu as", it can mean "good enough for what you have" or "fine given what you have."
target_language_example: Un peu de marche, c'est bon pour la santé.
native_language_example: A little walking is good for your health.

additional_notes: Usually followed by a relative word such as que, qui, dont, or à quoi: c'est ce que..., c'est ce qui..., etc. It points to the specific thing being identified, and English often translates the whole pattern as 'that's what ...'.
target_language_example: C'est ce dont j'ai besoin.
native_language_example: That's what I need.

meaning: “That’s what…” / “That’s what it is/was…” (used before a vowel sound).
additional_notes: Shortened form of « c’est ce que » used before a word starting with a vowel or a silent h: « c’est ce qu’elle… », « c’est ce qu’on… », « c’est ce qu’il… ». It introduces the thing being identified, explained, or reported (“That’s what she meant,” “That’s what we have to do,” etc.).
target_language_example: C'est ce qu'elle voulait dire.
native_language_example: That’s what she meant.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what a woman/girl (elle) says, thinks, believes, does, etc. Very common pattern: “C’est ce qu’elle + verb …” = “That’s what she + verb …”. Often followed by a verb in various tenses (dit/disait/a dit, pense, croit, fait, voudrait).
target_language_example: C'est ce qu'elle a dit hier soir.
native_language_example: That's what she said last night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause explaining what a man (il = he) did, said, thinks, wants, etc.: "c'est ce qu'il + verb…". It refers back to a situation or idea just mentioned (or implied). You can swap the pronoun: "c'est ce que je…" (that’s what I…), "c'est ce qu'elle…" (that’s what she…), "c'est ce qu'on…" (that’s what we/people…).
target_language_example: c'est ce qu'il cherche.
native_language_example: That’s what he’s looking for.

meaning: "that's what they…" / "it’s what they…" (introduces what they do/think/said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that explains what “they” (ils) are doing, thinking, looking for, or have said. Often followed by a verb in the present (cherchent, pensent) or the past (ont dit).
target_language_example: C'est ce qu'ils veulent entendre.
native_language_example: That's what they want to hear.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that explains what was said/thought/expected. "C'est" = "it is/that's" and "ce que" = "what/that which." "On" is very common in spoken French and can mean "we" (often instead of "nous"), or "people/they/someone" in a general sense. Often followed by a past tense: « C'est ce qu'on avait dit » (That's what we had said).
target_language_example: C'est ce qu'on avait prévu.
native_language_example: That’s what we had planned.

additional_notes: A common sentence frame: **C'est** (it is/that's) + **ce que** (what/that which) + **on** (we/people in general) + **a** (has/have, from *avoir*). Very often followed by a **past participle** to form the passé composé: *C'est ce qu'on a décidé* = “That’s what we decided.” Using **on** instead of **nous** is very common in spoken French.
target_language_example: C'est ce qu'on a promis.
native_language_example: That's what we promised.

additional_notes: Used to report what people say in general (a rumor, common belief, received wisdom). Often carries a nuance of distance, skepticism, or “supposedly,” depending on context and intonation. « on » here means “people / they / we (in general)”.
target_language_example: Il paraît qu’il va démissionner… enfin, c'est ce qu'on dit.
native_language_example: Apparently he’s going to resign… anyway, that’s what they say.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to the aim or point under discussion. It is followed by an infinitive (a “to …” verb): c'est ce qu'on essaie de comprendre / faire / savoir / déterminer. Literally: “it’s that which we’re trying to …”.
target_language_example: c'est ce qu'on essaie de comprendre.
native_language_example: That's what we're trying to understand.

meaning: "That's what we do." / "That's what people do."
additional_notes: Used to say something is normal, expected, or the right thing to do in a situation (often referring to group/family/clan values). "on" is an informal subject meaning "we" or "people/you" in general. Often has a tone of justification: "we do this because it's the way things are done."
target_language_example: On aide nos voisins quand ils ont besoin : c'est ce qu'on fait.
native_language_example: We help our neighbors when they need it: that's what we do.

meaning: "That’s what we’re going to …" (used before a verb).
additional_notes: This is usually an incomplete chunk that needs a verb after it, most often with an infinitive: « c'est ce qu'on va faire / voir / dire. » It’s built from « c'est » (it is/that’s), « ce que » (what/that which), and « on va » (we’re going to / people are going to). In more formal/careful speech you may also hear « c’est ce que nous allons … ». Note: in French, « c'est » is typically written with an apostrophe, and capitalization varies by position in the sentence; the fixed chunk here is given in lowercase to match the term.
target_language_example: D'accord, c'est ce qu'on va faire maintenant.
native_language_example: Okay, that’s what we’re going to do now.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an idea, fact, or thing and identify it: 'that's what ...'. It is usually followed by a clause such as je pense, j'ai compris, or tout le monde veut.
target_language_example: C'est ce que je veux dire.
native_language_example: That's what I mean.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about what a group typically does. It’s usually followed by a plural noun (e.g., « les gens », « les mères », « les partenaires »). Structure: « c'est ce que » = “that’s what/that which,” and « font » is the 3rd person plural of « faire » (“to do/make”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : c'est ce que font les amis.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: that’s what friends do.

meaning: "That's what I…" (introduces what you do/mean/like, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to point to something specific and then add a verb with “je” (I): *C'est ce que je + verb* = “That’s what I + verb.” Before a verb starting with a vowel or silent h, *je* becomes *j’* (elision): *j’aime, j’entends, j’essayais, j’écris*. You’ll often see it when explaining or clarifying: “That’s what I meant / was trying to say / wrote.”
target_language_example: C'est ce que j'ai dit hier.
native_language_example: That's what I said yesterday.

meaning: “That’s what I …” (introduces exactly what you did/said/wrote/felt, etc.).
additional_notes: Commonly used to clarify or emphasize the precise thing you did/said/felt. Typical pattern: **c'est ce que j'ai + past participle** (dit, fait, écrit, ressenti, compris…). Note: the correct past participle of *dire* is **dit** (“said”), not *dis* (which is the present tense: *je dis*).
target_language_example: c'est ce que j'ai écrit.
native_language_example: That’s what I wrote.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or remind someone of what you previously said. Often said alone as a full sentence; it can also take an add-on like “non ?” (right?) or “oui” (yes). Literally: “it is what I have said.”
target_language_example: Tu vois ? C'est ce que j'ai dit hier.
native_language_example: See? That’s what I said yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or clarify the specific action you took, often in response to a question or after describing what happened. Literally "it is what I did" / "it is what I have done" (passé composé: j'ai fait). Example exchange: « Tu as appelé la police ? » — « Oui, c'est ce que j'ai fait. »
target_language_example: Tu m’as demandé de vérifier, et c'est ce que j'ai fait.
native_language_example: You asked me to check, and that's what I did.

meaning: "That's what I like" / "That's what I like about ..."
additional_notes: Used to point out the specific thing you like. Often followed by a complement like chez elle/lui/toi (about her/him/you), dans ... (in ...), en toi (in you), or an infinitive to say what you like doing/hearing: C'est ce que j'aime entendre (That's what I like to hear).
target_language_example: C'est ce que j'aime dans cette ville : il y a toujours quelque chose à faire.
native_language_example: That's what I like about this city: there's always something to do.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific trait you appreciate. It’s typically followed by a person or pronoun (chez toi, chez lui/elle, chez vous) or a noun (chez Marie). Here, “chez” doesn’t mean “at someone’s home”; it means “in/about someone” (their personality, behavior, style, etc.).
target_language_example: c'est ce que j'aime chez toi : tu dis toujours les choses franchement.
native_language_example: That’s what I like about you: you always say things frankly.

meaning: “that’s what I …” (introduces what you do/did/would do, said, thought, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned or understood, then add your own action/opinion with a verb: « c'est ce que je disais » (that’s what I was saying), « c'est ce que je compte faire » (that’s what I plan to do). Typically followed by a verb; tense/mood changes with meaning (present, imperfect, conditional, etc.).
target_language_example: c'est ce que je compte faire.
native_language_example: That’s what I plan to do.

meaning: "That's what I thought" / "That's what I believed."
additional_notes: Used to say your earlier understanding was (or may have been) wrong, often followed by a correction or new information. You can add words like "au début" (at first), "aussi" (too), or "du moins" (at least) to nuance it. Literally: "it is what I believed."
target_language_example: Il n'était pas français—enfin, c'est ce que je croyais.
native_language_example: He wasn’t French—well, that’s what I thought.

additional_notes: Used to say that the thing just mentioned is what you do (often habitually), or to confirm what you’re doing. You can add adverbs like d’habitude (usually), toujours (always), tout le temps (all the time), or le mieux (best). Can also be used as a confirming question: « c’est ce que je fais, non ? » = “That’s what I do, right?”
target_language_example: C'est ce que je fais d'habitude.
native_language_example: That’s what I usually do.

meaning: "that's what I … to myself" (start of a phrase).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete fragment that’s normally followed by a reflexive verb, especially **dire**: **c'est ce que je me dis** (“That’s what I tell myself”). It introduces what you tell/ask/think to yourself as a reaction to a situation. Note: in standard French, **C’est** is usually capitalized at the start of a sentence; the term here is given in lowercase exactly as written.
target_language_example: Quand je doute, c'est ce que je me dis chaque matin : « Tu peux y arriver ».
native_language_example: When I doubt, that’s what I tell myself each morning: “You can do it.”

additional_notes: Used to say that something confirms what you already believed or expected. Often said in response to new information (similar to “I knew it” / “That’s what I figured,” but usually more neutral).
target_language_example: Ah, tu as annulé la réunion ? C'est ce que je pensais.
native_language_example: Oh, you canceled the meeting? That’s what I thought.

additional_notes: Used to state your opinion or belief about something just mentioned. You can add softeners like “du moins” (at least), “enfin” (well/anyway), or “aussi” (too) to nuance it. In a question (“Est-ce que c’est ce que je pense ?”), it means “Is it what I think it is?”
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas sûr, mais c'est ce que je pense.
native_language_example: I'm not sure, but that's what I think.

meaning: "That's what I am" / "That's who I am."
additional_notes: Used to state or accept your identity, role, or nature. Often appears inside a longer sentence (e.g., "C'est ce que je suis censé faire" = "That's what I'm supposed to do"). "Ce que" means "what/that which," so the structure is literally "it’s what I am."
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas le changer : c'est ce que je suis.
native_language_example: I can't change it: that's who I am.

c'est ce que je vais faire

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est ce que je vais faire
additional_notes: Used to confirm a decision or agree with a suggestion/instruction. Often said after someone tells you what to do, or after you’ve just decided on a plan. It can sound polite/obedient with titles like "Monsieur/Madame". Literally: "it is what I am going to do."
target_language_example: D'accord, c'est ce que je vais faire tout de suite.
native_language_example: Okay, that’s what I’m going to do right away.

meaning: “That’s what I want.” / “It’s what I want.”
additional_notes: Used to clearly state that a specific thing (already mentioned or understood) is what you want. Often followed by an intensifier or add-on such as « aussi » (too), « plus que tout » (more than anything), « pour toi » (for you), or by an infinitive to specify an action: « c'est ce que je veux découvrir / te dire » (that’s what I want to discover / tell you). Note: although it’s common to write « C’est… » with a capital letter and apostrophe, the exact term here is « c'est… ».
target_language_example: c'est ce que je veux te dire.
native_language_example: That’s what I want to tell you.

meaning: “That’s what I wanted.” / “That’s what I wanted to…”
additional_notes: Refers back to a specific thing you wanted (often just mentioned or shown). Very commonly followed by an infinitive to specify what you wanted to do: « c'est ce que je voulais voir/dire/faire ».
target_language_example: c'est ce que je voulais vous dire.
native_language_example: That’s what I wanted to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that explains what “we” expected, thought, planned, meant, wanted, etc. It’s very common in explanations or confirmations: C’est ce que nous + verb (attendions, pensions, voulions dire…). Often translates naturally as “That’s what we…” rather than the more literal “It is what we…”.
target_language_example: C'est ce que nous devons faire maintenant.
native_language_example: That's what we have to do now.

c'est ce que tout le monde

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est ce que tout le monde
additional_notes: Common sentence starter meaning “that’s what everybody/everyone…”. It is typically followed by a verb such as croit (believes), dit (says), fait (does), pense (thinks), or voit (sees): « c'est ce que tout le monde + verbe ». Used to express a widely held belief, a common claim, or typical behavior. Note: your term is written with lowercase « c'est »; in normal French orthography at the beginning of a sentence you’ll usually see « C’est », but the wording is the same.
target_language_example: c'est ce que tout le monde pense.
native_language_example: That’s what everyone thinks.

meaning: “is that what you…?” / “that’s what you…” (introduces what you say/think/do), usually followed by a verb.
additional_notes: Informal-register subject (tu). Typically followed by a verb phrase to specify the action/thought/speech: « c'est ce que tu dis/penses/veux/fais ». Very common in questions to confirm understanding: « c'est ce que tu essaies de me dire ? ». Note: capitalize at the start of a sentence (« C'est… »), but the multi-word term itself is « c'est ce que tu ».
target_language_example: c'est ce que tu essaies de me dire ?
native_language_example: Is that what you’re trying to tell me?

meaning: "that's what you have" / "that's what you've got."
additional_notes: Used to point out or confirm what someone possesses/has (often followed by more context). In spoken French you may also hear: "C'est ce que t'as" (more informal, dropped "u").
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : c'est ce que tu as, et c'est déjà bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: that’s what you have, and that’s already good.

meaning: "that's what you do" / "is that what you do?"
additional_notes: Used to comment on, confirm, or mildly challenge someone’s behavior or habit. It can be a statement (c'est ce que tu fais.) or a question with rising intonation or a question mark (c'est ce que tu fais ?). Commonly extended with time/frequency phrases (e.g., tout le temps, le vendredi soir) or with "de mieux / le mieux" to mean "that’s what you do best."
target_language_example: c'est ce que tu fais tout le temps.
native_language_example: That’s what you do all the time.

meaning: "that’s what you want" / "is that what you want?"
additional_notes: Used to state or (more often) confirm someone’s desire/choice, frequently as a question. In writing, you’ll often see it followed by a confirmation tag like « non ? » or « pas vrai ? ». It can also be expanded with what the person wants: « c'est ce que tu veux entendre » (that’s what you want to hear) or « c'est ce que tu veux que je dise ? » (is that what you want me to say?). Note: « tu » makes it informal/familiar; for formal you’d use « c'est ce que vous voulez ».
target_language_example: C'est ce que tu veux, non ?
native_language_example: That’s what you want, right?

meaning: “is that what you wanted?” / “that’s what you wanted.”
additional_notes: Used to confirm (often with a questioning intonation) that something matches what the other person wanted or intended. Can be a question (“Is that what you wanted?”) or a statement (“That’s what you wanted.”). Often followed by a tag such as “non ?” (right?) or “pas vrai ?” (isn’t that true?). Literally: “it’s what you wanted.”
target_language_example: C'est ce que tu voulais, non ?
native_language_example: That’s what you wanted, right?

additional_notes: Set phrase meaning “it’s what you…” and commonly used to confirm or check something about the listener (formal/plural « vous »). Typically followed by a verb phrase: « c'est ce que vous cherchez ? » (present), « c'est ce que vous cherchiez ? » (imperfect), « c'est ce que vous lui avez fait » (past), etc. Often used in questions, but can also be a statement.
target_language_example: c'est ce que vous cherchez ?
native_language_example: Is that what you’re looking for?

meaning: "Is that what you want?" / "That's what you want." (used to confirm)
additional_notes: Literally “it’s what you want.” Often said as a question (with rising intonation or a question tag like « non ? ») to check/confirm someone’s choice or request. « Vous » is the polite or plural “you.”
target_language_example: C'est ce que vous voulez, ou vous préférez autre chose ?
native_language_example: Is that what you want, or would you prefer something else?

meaning: "Is that what you wanted?" / "That's what you wanted."
additional_notes: Used to check or confirm what someone wanted, meant, wanted to hear, or wanted you to do/know. Often followed by an infinitive or clause: « C'est ce que vous vouliez dire ? » (Is that what you meant?), « C'est ce que vous vouliez que je fasse. » (That's what you wanted me to do.). Very common in polite/formal speech because of « vous ».
target_language_example: D'accord, je comprends : c'est ce que vous vouliez dire ?
native_language_example: Okay, I understand: is that what you meant?

meaning: “That’s what/which…”; “That’s the thing that…” (introduces the element that causes or explains something)
additional_notes: Used to highlight the key factor behind a result or feeling: “That’s what makes…”, “That’s what scares me…”. It’s typically followed by a verb, because “ce qui” is the subject (the thing that does the action). Contrast: “c’est ce que” is followed by a direct object (“That’s what I want / what I did”), since “ce que” is the object of the verb. Note the spelling: the literal term includes an apostrophe (c'est), and the register is neutral.
target_language_example: C'est ce qui me fait le plus peur.
native_language_example: That’s what scares me the most.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the key point or takeaway after something is mentioned. Often said to reassure someone or to refocus on what’s most important (e.g., effort, result, being safe). You can add intensity with "le plus" ("what matters most").
target_language_example: On est arrivés en retard, mais on est arrivés : c'est ce qui compte.
native_language_example: We arrived late, but we arrived—that’s what matters.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or identify something (“Yes, that’s it/that’s correct”), or to conclude/close a point (“That’s that.”). Often said alone as a short reply. Similar to “c’est ça” (more common and slightly more casual).
target_language_example: — Alors, on se retrouve à 18 h devant la gare ? — Oui, c'est cela.
native_language_example: — So, we’re meeting at 6 p.m. in front of the station? — Yes, that’s right.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a comparison or analogy. It can be followed by a noun (C'est comme un jeu), an infinitive (C'est comme avoir...), or a full clause (C'est comme si...). Often used to explain what something feels like or resembles.
target_language_example: C'est comme si on était en vacances.
native_language_example: It's as if we were on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to state that something is (and will remain) that way—often with a sense of acceptance, resignation, or “no further explanation.” It can refer to a current situation (“It’s been like that for an hour”) or a general truth (“That’s life”). In speech you may also hear it without the subject: « Comme ça. »
target_language_example: On ne peut pas changer les règles : c'est comme ça.
native_language_example: We can’t change the rules: that’s how it is.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation of how something happened or how something is done, often followed by a clause starting with a subject (il/elle/on/je, etc.). The qu’ is the shortened form of que before a vowel sound (e.g., qu’il, qu’on).
target_language_example: C'est comme ça qu'on apprend le français : un peu chaque jour.
native_language_example: That's how you learn French: a little every day.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation of the way someone does something. Pattern: « c'est comme ça que + subject + verb ». With « il », it becomes « c'est comme ça qu'il + verb » (often with elision: « qu'il »). Note: in standard French writing, this is usually capitalized at the start of a sentence (« C'est… »), but the fixed term here is given in lowercase as provided.
target_language_example: c'est comme ça qu'il a appris le français.
native_language_example: That’s how he learned French.

meaning: "That’s how we/people…" (that’s the way it’s done/said/happened).
additional_notes: Used to explain a method, a usual way of doing things, or how something happened. "On" is very common and often means "we" (in everyday speech) or "people/one" in a general sense. It’s frequently followed by a verb: "C’est comme ça qu’on fait" (That’s how you do it), "C’est comme ça qu’on l’appelle" (That’s what it’s called).
target_language_example: C'est comme ça qu'on apprend le français : un peu chaque jour.
native_language_example: That’s how you learn French: a little every day.

meaning: 'that's how' / 'that's the way' (it happens, works, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation of the way something happens or is done: "That's how + clause." Often followed by a verb: "C'est comme ça que ça marche" (That's how it works). Can also sound judgmental or surprised in questions: "C'est comme ça que tu me remercies ?" (Is that how you thank me?).
target_language_example: C'est comme ça que j'ai appris le français : un peu chaque jour.
native_language_example: That's how I learned French: a little bit every day.

additional_notes: Used to explain your way of doing something (how you work, live, do a job, etc.). Often followed by a verb: « C’est comme ça que je fonctionne / que je fais les choses. » It can sound like a simple explanation, or like “that’s just how I am/that’s how it works (for me)” depending on tone.
target_language_example: C'est comme ça que je prends mes décisions.
native_language_example: That’s how I make my decisions.

meaning: “Is that how you…?” / “So that’s how you…?” (often expressing surprise, disapproval, or criticism).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or question someone’s way of doing/saying something. Often rhetorical and can sound judgmental, implying “your way is wrong/odd.” It’s typically followed by a verb phrase: « c'est comme ça que tu réponds ? » = “Is that how you answer?”
target_language_example: c'est comme ça que tu réponds ?
native_language_example: Is that how you answer?

meaning: “that’s how you…” / “that’s the way you…” (introducing an explanation of how someone does something).
additional_notes: Used to explain a method or process, typically followed by a verb: « c'est comme ça que vous faites… / que vous pouvez… ». In writing, you may also see the capitalized form « C’est comme ça que vous… ». It can be shortened to « c’est comme ça que… » when the subject is clear.
target_language_example: c'est comme ça que vous pouvez réserver une table en ligne.
native_language_example: That’s how you can book a table online.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens in a particular (often fixed, expected, or accepted) way. Common pattern: « c'est comme ça que ça + [verb] » (with « ça » = “it/that”), often with « se passer » (“to happen”) or « se faire » (“to be done”).
target_language_example: c'est comme ça que ça se passe ici.
native_language_example: That’s how it happens / That’s how things are done here.

c'est comme ça que ça marche

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est comme ça que ça marche
meaning: “That’s how it works.” / “That’s just how it is.”
additional_notes: Used to explain or justify how a system, rule, or situation operates—often with a resigned or firm tone (“whether you like it or not”). Common in conversation. You can add context after it (e.g., « ici », « dans cette entreprise »). Variants: « C'est comme ça que ça marche ici. », « Parce que c'est comme ça que ça marche. », « Mais c'est comme ça que ça marche. »
target_language_example: Je sais que ce n’est pas idéal, mais c'est comme ça que ça marche ici.
native_language_example: I know it’s not ideal, but that’s how it works here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something can be found within a place, text, document, or file. Often followed by a noun like "le contrat" (the contract), "le livre" (the book), "le dossier" (the file).
target_language_example: C'est dans le mail que je t'ai envoyé.
native_language_example: It’s in the email I sent you.

meaning: "it’s about… / it’s (from) … / it’s (of) …" (used to introduce what something is about, where it comes from, or what it belongs to).
additional_notes: Common in cleft sentences to emphasize the element introduced by « de »: « C'est de là que… » = “It’s from there that…”. With « de cela », it introduces the topic: « C'est de cela qu'il s'agit » = “That’s what it’s about.” It can also mark possession or category in context: « C'est de la mienne » = “It’s mine (one of mine).” With « de + âge », it expresses approximate sameness of age: « C'est de son âge » = “He/She is about the same age as him/her.”
target_language_example: C'est de cela qu'il s'agit.
native_language_example: That’s what it’s about.

additional_notes: This is the pattern **c'est + partitive article** (**du / de la / de l' / des**) to talk about what something is made of, what kind of thing it is, or an unspecified amount (often with uncountable nouns like water) and with languages: *C'est de l'anglais.* The **l'** is used because the next word starts with a vowel sound (e.g., *anglais, eau, allemand*).
target_language_example: C'est de l'huile d'olive.
native_language_example: It's (some) olive oil.

additional_notes: Used to locate something across a boundary or divider (a street, river, border, city, etc.). Typically followed by a noun: « c’est de l’autre côté de la rue / de la rivière / de la frontière ».
target_language_example: La gare ? C'est de l'autre côté de la rivière.
native_language_example: The train station? It’s on the other side of the river.

additional_notes: Used to identify what something is made of or what substance it is. It’s the structure: c’est + de la + [feminine mass noun]. For masculine: c’est du (C’est du sucre). For plural: c’est des (C’est des pâtes). In English you often just say “It’s mud/morphine/silk” without “some.”
target_language_example: Attention, c'est de la peinture fraîche.
native_language_example: Careful, it’s fresh paint.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation/thing isn’t the same as before or isn’t the same as another one. You can add details with time or comparison words: "cette fois-ci" (this time), "maintenant" (now), "pour moi" (for me).
target_language_example: Je comprends ton idée, mais pour moi, c'est différent.
native_language_example: I understand your idea, but for me, it’s different.

meaning: “which is to say” / “that’s saying something” (used to emphasize what was just said and draw a conclusion from it).
additional_notes: Used after a statement to underline its significance or the implication you should draw. Often set off by a comma or dash. Close in tone to “which is to say…”, “so you can imagine…”, or “that tells you something”.
target_language_example: Il n’a pas dormi depuis deux jours — c'est dire comme il est fatigué.
native_language_example: He hasn’t slept for two days—that’s how tired he is.

meaning: “it’s (some) …” / “that’s …” (used before a masculine noun, often uncountable).
additional_notes: "C'est du" = "c'est de + le" (du). It’s used before a masculine singular noun, very often a mass/uncountable noun, to say what something is (material, substance, type, or category): "C'est du chocolat" (It’s chocolate), "C'est du bénévolat" (It’s volunteer work). It can also be evaluative/emphatic to classify something by its quality: "C'est du grand art" (That’s great art). In questions like "C'est du vrai ?", "du vrai" means “the real thing / something real.”
target_language_example: C'est du grand art.
native_language_example: That’s great art.

meaning: “It’s she who…” / “She’s the one who…”, used for emphasis.
additional_notes: This is a cleft sentence used to emphasize the subject (elle). It highlights who did something or who is responsible: c'est elle qui décide = She’s the one who decides. You can swap elle for other pronouns/nouns: c’est lui qui…, c’est Marie qui…. In questions, it can express surprise or confirm information: c'est elle qui te l'a dit ? = Was it her who told you?
target_language_example: c'est elle qui décide.
native_language_example: She’s the one who decides.

meaning: "that's exactly what" / "that's exactly the thing that".
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches perfectly. It’s usually followed by a relative construction such as: ce que (what/that which), ce qui (what/that which as the subject), ce dont (what/that which… of/that you need), or ce à quoi (what/that which… to which). You’ll often see it in phrases like: C’est exactement ce dont j’ai besoin. (That’s exactly what I need.)
target_language_example: C'est exactement ce que je voulais entendre.
native_language_example: That's exactly what I wanted to hear.

meaning: “That’s exactly what …” (used with verbs that take "de").
additional_notes: Used to say something matches perfectly. "Ce dont" uses "dont" (= “of which/that which”) and is required when the following verb or expression normally takes "de" (e.g., avoir besoin de → "ce dont j’ai besoin"; parler de → "ce dont je parle"). Typically followed by a subject + verb phrase.
target_language_example: C'est exactement ce dont j'ai besoin.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I need.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches perfectly: "That’s exactly what she said / what we need / what they did." The form "ce qu'" is a contraction of "ce que" before a vowel sound (e.g., "c'est exactement ce qu'il faut").
target_language_example: C'est exactement ce qu'on cherchait.
native_language_example: That's exactly what we were looking for.

additional_notes: Expression used to emphasize that something matches perfectly what a man did/said/needs, etc. It is the beginning of a sentence and must be followed by a verb phrase after "il" (e.g., "c'est exactement ce qu'il a dit", "c'est exactement ce qu'il lui faut"). Note: in standard French spelling you usually write "C’est" (with apostrophe) rather than "C'est"; both represent the same pronunciation.
target_language_example: C'est exactement ce qu'il a dit.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what he said.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something matches perfectly (what someone said, did, is, or means). It’s typically followed by a clause: « c'est exactement ce que + subject + verb ». Often used to agree or confirm precisely. Note: in writing, it may also appear with a capital letter at the start of a sentence (« C'est exactement ce que… »), but the phrase itself is the same.
target_language_example: c'est exactement ce que tu as dit.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what you said.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something matches perfectly with what you think/said/want. It must be completed with a verb clause: « c'est exactement ce que je pense / voulais / cherchais / dis. » Note: in careful writing, you may see « c’est » with an apostrophe instead of « c'est », but both represent the same spoken form.
target_language_example: c'est exactement ce que je pense.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I think.

additional_notes: Used to say a task is finished or an action has been completed. Common after instructions ("Call me when it’s done") or as reassurance ("Consider it done"). In "Eh bien, c’est fait", it can also mean “Well, it’s done now” (often after something you finally did).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, c'est fait.
native_language_example: Don't worry, it's done.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has ended or is done. In relationships, "c'est fini entre nous" means “we’re over / it’s over between us.” It can also be used as a firm warning: "Si tu en parles, c'est fini" = “If you talk about it, it’s over.”
target_language_example: Si tu en parles, c'est fini entre nous.
native_language_example: If you talk about it, it’s over between us.

additional_notes:
Used to thank someone or comment positively on a kind gesture. Often followed by:
- "de + infinitive": "C'est gentil d'être venu" (It’s kind of you to have come).
- "de la/leur part": "C'est gentil de leur part" (That’s kind of them).
- "à toi": "C'est gentil à toi" (That’s kind of you).
It can also be said politely before refusing or adding a caveat: "C'est gentil, mais…" (That’s nice, but…).
target_language_example: C'est gentil, mais je n'ai pas besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: That’s kind, but I don’t need help.

additional_notes: Used to thank or show appreciation for an action. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., dire, aider, venir). You can specify the recipient with an indirect object pronoun: c'est gentil de me le dire (“it’s kind of you to tell me”). A common variant is « c'est gentil de ta part » (“that’s very kind of you”).
target_language_example: C'est gentil de me le dire.
native_language_example: It’s kind of you to tell me.

additional_notes: Used to express enthusiasm or strong approval about a situation, idea, or experience. Very common in spoken French. You can also add what is great with “C’est génial de + infinitive” (e.g., “C’est génial d’être de retour.”).
target_language_example: C'est génial de te revoir !
native_language_example: It's great to see you again!

additional_notes: A cleft sentence structure used to highlight the location of an action or event: c'est + place (ici/là/bas/à Paris, etc.) + que + rest of the sentence. Often used for important moments or to confirm a place (e.g., asking "Is this where…?").
target_language_example: C'est ici que je prends le bus tous les matins.
native_language_example: This is where I take the bus every morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something matters or is significant. Very common with "pour" + a person (e.g., "C'est important pour moi/toi/vous") to mean it’s important to someone. In questions, it often appears as "Est-ce que c'est important ?" (= Is it important?). Note: you may also see "C’est" with a curly apostrophe; it’s the same expression.
target_language_example: Je sais combien c'est important pour toi.
native_language_example: I know how important it is for you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is important to someone or for a purpose. Typically followed by a person/thing: « C'est important pour moi/toi/nous » or « C'est important pour + noun ». You can also add an infinitive with « de »: « C'est important pour moi de comprendre. »
target_language_example: C'est important pour moi de te voir ce soir.
native_language_example: It’s important for me to see you tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t important or serious, or that it’s “nothing more than” what follows. Often followed by a noun phrase (e.g., du bruit, un accident). Note: "juste" can also mean "fair/right" in other contexts (e.g., "Ce n'est pas juste" = "That's not fair"), but in "c'est juste + noun" it usually means "just/only."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, c'est juste une blague.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s just a joke.

meaning: “It’s just a…” / “It’s only a…” (used to downplay or minimize something).
additional_notes: Often used to reassure someone or to say something isn’t a big deal or isn’t important. It’s commonly followed by a masculine singular noun: un boulot, un contrôle, un costume, etc. For feminine nouns, you’ll say: « C’est juste une… ». Note: « c’est » is frequently written with a capital and apostrophe (« C’est ») in normal French writing, but the phrase here is kept exactly as provided: « c'est juste un ».
target_language_example: Je te promets, c'est juste un contrôle de routine.
native_language_example: I promise you, it’s just a routine check.

meaning: “it’s just a” (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something, often to reassure, correct an exaggeration, or emphasize that something is not serious/important. Structure: c’est (“it is”) + juste (“just/only”) + une (“a/an” for feminine singular nouns). For a masculine singular noun, use: c’est juste un…
target_language_example: c'est juste une fête.
native_language_example: It’s just a party.

meaning: "it's the…" / "this is the…" (before a vowel sound).
additional_notes: Contraction of "c'est" + "le/la" before a word that starts with a vowel or silent h: "c'est l'ami", "c'est l'été", "c'est l'essentiel". Used to identify, introduce, or point out what something is.
target_language_example: C'est l'heure de partir.
native_language_example: It’s time to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say it’s the birthday of a female person (or a feminine noun): *ma femme* (my wife), *ma fille* (my daughter), *ma mère/maman* (my mother/mom). In French, **anniversaire** commonly means **birthday** (not just “anniversary” in the English sense).
target_language_example: C'est l'anniversaire de ma sœur aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It’s my sister’s birthday today.

additional_notes: Used to say that the moment has arrived to do something or that it’s the scheduled time for an activity. Very common with "de" + infinitive (C'est l'heure de partir.) or with "de" + noun (C'est l'heure de ma sieste / des visites.). On its own, it can mean “I think it’s time.”
target_language_example: C'est l'heure de dîner, on y va ?
native_language_example: It's time for dinner—shall we go?

additional_notes: Used to say that now is the appropriate/expected time to leave or to go do the next activity. It’s typically followed by an infinitive with "de" (e.g., "d’aller") and often a destination or purpose: "aux toilettes" (to the bathroom), "se coucher" (go to bed), "travailler" (go to work), "à l’école" (to school).
target_language_example: C'est l'heure d'aller à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s time to go home.

additional_notes: Used to say that the moment has come to do an action. Usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "C'est l'heure de partir"). You may also see "C'est l'heure du/de la/des + noun" to mean “it’s time for …” (e.g., "C'est l'heure du dîner").
target_language_example: C'est l'heure de partir, on y va !
native_language_example: It’s time to leave; let’s go!

meaning: “It’s time for the…” (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to announce that it’s time for a scheduled activity or event. It’s followed by a feminine noun: « c'est l'heure de la sieste / c'est l'heure de la photo ». With a masculine noun, you usually use « c'est l'heure du ... » (e.g., « c'est l'heure du déjeuner »).
target_language_example: C'est l'heure de la sieste.
native_language_example: It’s time for the nap.

meaning: "It's time for..." (said when it's time to do/eat something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to announce the appropriate time for something, especially meals or bedtime. Grammar changes with gender/sound: c'est l'heure du + masculine noun (du déjeuner), c'est l'heure de la + feminine noun (de la sieste), c'est l'heure de l' + vowel sound (de l'école), c'est l'heure des + plural (des vacances).
target_language_example: Les enfants, c'est l'heure du bain !
native_language_example: Kids, it's bath time!

additional_notes: Used to identify or point to something: c'est la + noun. Common in emphasis/cleft sentences like « Le problème, c'est la fatigue » (“The problem is the tiredness/fatigue”). Use « c'est le » for masculine nouns and « ce sont les » for plural.
target_language_example: Le souci, c'est la météo.
native_language_example: The issue is the weather.

meaning: “That’s the right one.” / “That’s the correct one.”
additional_notes: Refers to a feminine noun understood from context (e.g., la réponse, la taille, la décision). Used when you’ve identified the correct choice/answer/option. In “Cette fois, c’est la bonne”, it often means “This time it’s the right one” (the successful attempt). For a masculine noun, use: “c’est le bon”.
target_language_example: On a essayé plusieurs tailles, et maintenant, c'est la bonne.
native_language_example: We tried several sizes, and now this is the right one.

additional_notes: Used when the implied or stated noun is feminine (e.g., la chose, la fois, l’étape, la page, la bouteille). Often said with the noun omitted when context makes it obvious (“It’s the last one”). It can also imply “the final time” when the omitted noun is fois (e.g., under the surface: c’est la dernière (fois)). For a masculine noun: c’est le dernier. Note: In writing you may also see the apostrophe form c’est la dernière; the term is commonly typed without the apostrophe as c'est la dernière.
target_language_example: J’espère que c'est la dernière.
native_language_example: I hope it’s the last one.

c'est la dernière chose que je

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est la dernière chose que je
meaning: "That's the last thing I (want/would do)" (the thing I want least).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that you really don’t want something, or that something is the least likely/least desired option. It’s commonly followed by a verb ("…que je veux faire") or left implied ("…que je veux"). Tense can change ("que je voulais" = "that I wanted").
target_language_example: C'est la dernière chose que je veux entendre maintenant.
native_language_example: That’s the last thing I want to hear right now.

additional_notes: Used to say something will not happen again. Often followed by a clause with "que" (e.g., "C'est la dernière fois qu'on se voit" = "It’s the last time we’re seeing each other"). Said alone, it can sound like a warning or a firm boundary ("C'est la dernière fois, compris ?" = "This is the last time, understood?") or like a promise ("C'est la dernière fois, promis.").
target_language_example: C'est la dernière fois que je t'attends aussi longtemps.
native_language_example: This is the last time I wait for you for so long.

additional_notes: Used to say something will not happen again. It’s often a firm warning or a final decision: « c'est la dernière fois que tu me touches. » With the present tense (« c'est la dernière fois que je t'appelle. ») it means “I’m not calling you again.” With the imperfect (« c'est la dernière fois que je le voyais. ») it describes a last time in the past (“That was the last time I saw him”).
target_language_example: c'est la dernière fois que je t'appelle.
native_language_example: This is the last time I’m calling you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is over (an era, a story, a show, etc.). Very common with "de" + noun: "c'est la fin de notre émission" (the end of our show). You can also use it alone: "C'est la fin."
target_language_example: C'est la fin du film, on peut partir.
native_language_example: It's the end of the movie; we can leave.

additional_notes: Used to say something feminine (an idea, piece of news, option, part, etc.) is the best. Can also be used on its own as an enthusiastic reaction: « c'est la meilleure. » Context determines whether it means “It’s the best one” (a feminine item) or “She’s the best” (a woman). Masculine equivalent: « c'est le meilleur. »
target_language_example: Parmi toutes les options, c'est la meilleure.
native_language_example: Among all the options, it’s the best.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is first in order, rank, or sequence. Because “première” is feminine, it typically refers to a feminine noun that is stated or implied (e.g., “la première chose/étape/porte”). It can also imply “the first time” when “fois” is understood from context: “C’est la première depuis un bon moment” = “It’s the first time in quite a while.”
target_language_example: C'est la première chose que j'ai faite.
native_language_example: It’s the first thing I did.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done/experienced something before. Very often followed by **que + subject + verb**: *C'est la première fois que j'entends ça.* You can also add details like **de ma vie** (“in my life”) or ask a question: *C'est la première fois que vous venez ?*
target_language_example: C'est la première fois que je viens ici.
native_language_example: It's the first time I've come here.

additional_notes: Used to say you are doing/experiencing something for the first time. It’s followed by a clause describing the action/experience; French commonly uses the present tense here even when English uses the present perfect (e.g., « c'est la première fois que je vois… » = “it’s the first time I’ve seen…”). It can also be used as a question: « c'est la première fois que vous venez ? ».
target_language_example: c'est la première fois que je vois ça.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve seen that.

c'est la première fois que je

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est la première fois que je
meaning: "This is the first time that I..."
additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing/feeling/saying something for the first time. It’s often followed by the present tense in French (e.g., « C'est la première fois que je viens ici. »), where English would use the present perfect (“it’s the first time I’ve come here”). You can change « je » to another subject: « c'est la première fois qu'il/elle/on/nous... ».
target_language_example: C'est la première fois que je prends le métro à Paris.
native_language_example: This is the first time I’m taking the subway in Paris.

additional_notes: Used when the “only one” is feminine (une personne/une chose). For a masculine noun, say "c'est le seul"; for plural, "ce sont les seuls/les seules". Often followed by extra information: "C'est la seule en qui j'ai confiance" (the only one I trust), "C'est la seule raison" (the only reason), "C'est la seule faveur que je te demande" (the only favor I’m asking).
target_language_example: Ne le dis à personne : c'est la seule personne qui le sait.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone: she’s the only person who knows.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that only one thing is true/important/works. It introduces a relative clause with "qui". After "la seule chose qui", you may see either the indicative (common for facts: "C'est la seule chose qui a du sens") or the subjunctive (often to stress uniqueness/subjectivity: "... qui ait du sens").
target_language_example: C'est la seule chose qui me rassure.
native_language_example: It's the only thing that reassures me.

meaning: “That’s life.” (used to accept a situation, often with resignation).
additional_notes: Literally “it’s the life,” but most often used as a fixed expression meaning “that’s how it is.” It can be used alone as a comment (c'est la vie.) or reinforced (c'est la vie, c'est tout.). In other contexts, it can also be literal: “c'est la vie de…” = “it’s the life of…”.
target_language_example: On a raté le train… c'est la vie.
native_language_example: We missed the train… that’s life.

additional_notes: Used to insist that what you’re saying is true, often to reassure someone or add emphasis. You can strengthen it with additions like « et tu le sais » (and you know it) or « je le jure » (I swear). « La vérité vraie » is a deliberately emphatic/redundant way to say “the real truth.”
target_language_example: C'est la vérité, je le jure.
native_language_example: It’s the truth, I swear.

additional_notes: Used to identify, point out, or define a masculine singular noun or idea. It combines c'est ('it is/this is/that is') with le ('the'). In context, it can also mean 'this is the'. Before a vowel sound, French usually uses c'est l' instead.
target_language_example: C'est le début de l'histoire.
native_language_example: It's the beginning of the story.

meaning: 'It's the right one.' / 'That's the correct one.'
additional_notes: Used to confirm you have chosen the correct thing (number, road, method, etc.). "Le bon" refers to a masculine noun (often implied/omitted, like "numéro" or "chemin"). For feminine nouns, use "c'est la bonne"; for plural, "ce sont les bons / les bonnes".
target_language_example: On a essayé plusieurs numéros : c'est le bon.
native_language_example: We tried several numbers: this is the right one.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that a statement or situation is true. Common in questions (Est-ce que c'est le cas ? = “Is that the case?”), in conditionals (Si c'est le cas… = “If that’s the case…”), and as a short confirmation (Oui/Si, c'est le cas. = “Yes, that’s the case.”).
target_language_example: Je suppose que c'est le cas.
native_language_example: I suppose that’s the case.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the best possible result/effort in the circumstances. It’s typically followed by a subject + a verb of ability (e.g., peux/pouvais/ai pu) or, very often after a superlative, the subjunctive (e.g., puisse/puissions): « c'est le mieux que je puisse faire ».
target_language_example: Désolé, c'est le mieux que je puisse faire pour l’instant.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s the best I can do for now.

meaning: “now is the time” / “this is the moment.”
additional_notes: Used to say that the right time has come to do something, often suggesting “now (or never)” or “this is your chance.” Common in prompts like: « Si vous avez des questions, c’est le moment » (= now’s the time to ask).
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, c'est le moment.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, now’s the time.

meaning: 'it's time to' / 'now is the time to'.
additional_notes: Used to say that the right time has come to do something, often for emphasis or to prompt someone to act. It can sound encouraging/urgent (C'est le moment de dire la vérité.) or rhetorical/critical as a question (C'est le moment de parler de ça ? = Is this really the right time to talk about that?). Followed by an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: C'est le moment de partir, sinon on va rater le train.
native_language_example: It's time to leave, otherwise we'll miss the train.

c'est le plus beau jour de

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est le plus beau jour de
additional_notes: Used to say something is the happiest or most wonderful day (often for weddings or major celebrations). It’s usually followed by a possessive phrase like « ma/ta/sa/notre/votre vie » (“my/your/his/her/our/your life”). Note: in normal French spelling, this is written « C’est » rather than « c'est ».
target_language_example: c'est le plus beau jour de notre vie.
native_language_example: it’s the best day of our life.

additional_notes: Used to identify a male person (pointing out who someone is). Often answers the question « Qui est-ce ? » or confirms an identity: « Est-ce que c'est lui ? ». With a noun phrase, it can mean “He’s the one…”: « C'est lui le responsable » = “He’s the one responsible.” Variations: « c'est elle » (her), « c'est eux/elles » (them).
target_language_example: Je suis presque sûr que c'est lui.
native_language_example: I'm almost sure it's him.

meaning: 'It’s him who…' / 'He’s the one who…' (used to emphasize that he is the person who did/said something).
additional_notes: Common French emphasis pattern (a “cleft sentence”): c’est + [person/thing] + qui + verb. It highlights or clarifies who is responsible or being singled out (often implying “not someone else”). You can replace lui with another pronoun or noun: c’est elle qui…, c’est Paul qui…. Note: in writing, you’ll often see C’est with a capital letter at the start of a sentence, but the fixed term here is c'est lui qui.
target_language_example: c'est lui qui a fait tout le travail.
native_language_example: He’s the one who did all the work.

meaning: “It’s him who has / who did (it)” (used for emphasis).
additional_notes: This is a cleft sentence (c’est X qui…) used to strongly emphasize the subject. Here, “lui” = “him”. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the passé composé starting with “a” (e.g., “a fait”, “a dit”, “a pris”). You can replace “lui” with other pronouns: “c’est moi qui ai…”, “c’est elle qui a…”, “c’est eux qui ont…”. Note: in writing, you’ll usually see “c’est” (with an apostrophe), but the fixed term here is given as "c'est".
target_language_example: c'est lui qui a cassé le verre.
native_language_example: He’s the one who broke the glass.

meaning: “It was him who…” / “He’s the one who…” (with emphasis on him).
additional_notes: French uses this emphasis pattern (a cleft sentence): c’est + person + qui + verb. It highlights the person responsible for the action (to identify, blame, or give credit). Here, “m’a” is the contraction of “me” + “a” (has), introducing a past action: e.g., “C’est lui qui m’a aidé” = “He’s the one who helped me.”
target_language_example: C'est lui qui m'a fait ça.
native_language_example: He’s the one who did this to me.

meaning: “it’s there / it’s (right) here”; also “that’s where/when” (with **que**), and “that’s the key point” (in set phrases).
additional_notes: Common patterns: **C'est là que…** = “That’s where/when …” (introduces the place/time something happened). Set phrases like **C'est là toute la différence / toute la question** mean “That’s the whole difference / the whole question,” i.e., “that’s the crux.” It can also simply confirm location: **Je sais que c'est là** = “I know it’s there.”
target_language_example: C'est là que ça devient intéressant.
native_language_example: That’s where it starts to get interesting.

meaning: “That’s where …” / “That’s when …” (focuses attention on the specific point—usually a place, sometimes a moment).
additional_notes: Literally “it’s there that …”. Used for emphasis to point out the precise place (and in some contexts, the moment) where something is/occurs. The apostrophe in qu’ is used before a vowel or mute h (que → qu’): c'est là qu'il travaille, c'est là qu'on doit aller. Often translates naturally as “that’s where …” (place) or sometimes “that’s when …” (time) depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est là qu'il travaille.
native_language_example: That’s where he works.

additional_notes: Used to point to the exact place (là = there) or moment in a story and emphasize it: « c'est là que… ». « on » often means “we” in everyday French, or “people/you” in general. Common with actions, turning points, or discoveries: « c'est là qu'on l'a trouvé » (“That’s where we found it”).
target_language_example: c'est là qu'on se retrouve après le travail.
native_language_example: That’s where we meet up after work.

meaning: 'that's where' (introduces the place where something happens).
additional_notes: Used to point out a specific place and then add what happened there or what/who is there. Very common in answers and explanations: *C'est là que + subject + verb*. Often corresponds to English “That’s where…”.
target_language_example: C'est là que j'ai appris le français.
native_language_example: That's where I learned French.

meaning: 'That’s where I…' / 'That’s when I…' (introduces what you do at that point/place).
additional_notes: Expression used to highlight the exact place or moment when your action happens, often as a punchline or key point in a story. It can be literal (« C’est là que j’habite » = “That’s where I live”) or figurative (« C’est là que j’entre en jeu/en scène » = “That’s where/when I come in”). The apostrophe in « j’ » shows elision before a vowel or silent h (e.g., j’habite, j’entre, j’arrive).
target_language_example: Regarde cette rue : c'est là que j'habite.
native_language_example: Look at that street: that’s where I live.

meaning: "That's where I have it" / "That's where I got it" / "That's when I got it" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to point out the exact place (là) or moment (là = ‘then/at that point’) where you have/found/obtained something, often as a sudden realization. "je l’ai" = "I have it / I got it" with the direct-object pronoun "l’" (‘it’). In many contexts the implied idea is "je l’ai trouvé" (I found it) or "je l’ai eu" (I got it).
