additional_notes: Used to introduce the specific information you’re looking for. Often followed by "c’est..." ("what I want to know is...") or placed before an embedded question/clause.
target_language_example: Ce que je veux savoir, c’est si tu viens demain.
native_language_example: What I want to know is whether you’re coming tomorrow.

ce que je viens de dire

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que je viens de dire
additional_notes: Used to refer back to your immediately previous statement. Often appears after c’est (“that’s what I just said”) or with verbs like oublier (“forget”), ajouter (“add”), etc. Note that venir de + infinitive means “to have just done” something.
target_language_example: Ne déforme pas ce que je viens de dire.
native_language_example: Don’t twist what I just said.

additional_notes: "Ce que" means "what/that which" and introduces a clause. Used to refer to the thing(s) you are seeing, often for emphasis or contrast (e.g., believing what you see vs. what you hear). In questions like "Vois-tu ce que je vois ?", it means "Do you see what I see?".
target_language_example: Je décris ce que je vois dans la rue.
native_language_example: I describe what I see in the street.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like faire, avoir, donner, savoir, etc. to refer to the thing you wanted: "Il a fait ce que je voulais" (He did what I wanted), "J'ai eu ce que je voulais" (I got what I wanted). Literally "that which I wanted" (ce que + subject + verb). Here, "voulais" is the imperfect of "vouloir" and often describes an ongoing desire in the past.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas ce que je voulais.
native_language_example: That’s not what I wanted.

meaning: "what I meant" / "what I was trying to say."
additional_notes: Used to clarify your meaning, confirm understanding, or correct a misunderstanding (often in "C'est ce que je voulais dire" = "That's what I meant"). Uses the imperfect ("je voulais") to sound a bit softer than "je veux dire" ("I mean").
target_language_example: Attends, ce n’est pas ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: Wait, that’s not what I meant.

meaning: “what I’m telling you” / “what I’m saying to you.”
additional_notes: Used after verbs like comprendre (to understand), entendre (to hear), écouter (to listen to), and faire (to do) to refer to the message/instructions the speaker is giving. "Vous" is the formal/plural "you"; with one person informally you’d say "ce que je te dis". Often used when giving instructions or insisting: "Faites (juste) ce que je vous dis."
target_language_example: S’il vous plaît, écoutez bien ce que je vous dis.
native_language_example: Please listen carefully to what I’m telling you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause where "ce que" means "what" (the thing that), and "nous" is the subject of the following verb: "ce que nous faisons" (what we do), "ce que nous avons" (what we have). Often refers to an action, decision, or thing already known from context.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que nous devons faire.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what we have to do.

additional_notes: Used to introduce, emphasize, or point to a plan/next step. Often appears after expressions like « C'est… », « Voici… », « Voilà… » to mean “This is what we’re going to do.” Grammatically, « ce que » = “what/that which,” and « nous allons faire » uses the near future (aller + infinitive) to talk about what will happen soon.
target_language_example: D'accord, voilà ce que nous allons faire : tu appelles le taxi et je prends les valises.
native_language_example: Okay, here’s what we’re going to do: you call the taxi and I’ll take the suitcases.

meaning: "what we have" / "what we" (introduces a clause like “what we said/did/started”).
additional_notes: Used with **ce que** (“what/that which”) followed by **nous avons** (we have) as the start of a relative clause. Very often **avons** is the auxiliary in the passé composé, so it’s followed by a past participle: **ce que nous avons dit** (what we said), **ce que nous avons fait** (what we did), **ce que nous avons commencé** (what we started).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que nous avons décidé hier.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what we decided yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the relative pronoun "ce que" + a clause to refer to an unknown or general thing: "what we have (here/so far/available)". Often appears in expressions like "Voyons ce que nous avons" (Let’s see what we’ve got) or "travailler avec ce que nous avons" (work with what we have).
target_language_example: Faisons avec ce que nous avons pour l’instant.
native_language_example: Let’s make do with what we have for now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action or activity done by “us” (nous). It often appears after verbs like comprendre, aimer, savoir, expliquer, etc. The structure is: ce que + subject + verb (e.g., ce que je fais, ce que tu fais, ce que nous faisons).
target_language_example: Je suis fier de ce que nous faisons ici.
native_language_example: I'm proud of what we do here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific thing or information that “we” want. It often follows verbs like savoir (to know), dire (to say), donner (to give), obtenir (to obtain): e.g., savoir ce que nous voulons (to know what we want), donne-nous ce que nous voulons (give us what we want).
target_language_example: Je sais enfin ce que nous voulons pour le dîner.
native_language_example: I finally know what we want for dinner.

meaning: "what you" / "that which you" (short for "ce que tu" before a vowel).
additional_notes: "t'" is an elision of "tu" used in front of a vowel or silent h (e.g., "t'as" = "tu as", "t'es" = "tu es"). So "ce que t'..." commonly appears in speech as the start of phrases like "ce que t'as dit" (what you said) or "ce que t'es en train de faire" (what you’re doing). In careful writing you may see "ce que tu..." more often.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que t'as dit.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you said.

additional_notes: Spoken/informal: "t'as" is the contraction of "tu as" (you have), used here to form the past tense "tu as fait" (you did / you have done). Often appears after verbs like "voir" (to see), "savoir" (to know), or in phrases like "C'est…" to point to an action: "J'ai vu ce que t'as fait" = "I saw what you did." In more formal French, you’d say: "ce que tu as fait".
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que t'as fait, mais ce n'était pas une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I understand what you did, but it wasn't a good idea.

additional_notes: Informal spoken French: "t'as" is short for "tu as". Used after verbs like "dis", "montre-moi", "fais voir" to ask someone to show or say what they have/know/can do. With "dans le ventre" it means “show what you’re made of.”
target_language_example: Allez, montre-moi ce que t'as !
native_language_example: Come on, show me what you've got!

meaning: "what everyone" / "the thing that everyone" (introduces a clause).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what is common to everyone, and it’s usually followed by a verb and the rest of the clause: « ce que tout le monde + verb… ». Example patterns: « Ce que tout le monde veut… » (What everyone wants…), « Ce que tout le monde sait… » (What everyone knows…).
target_language_example: Ce que tout le monde veut, c’est être heureux.
native_language_example: What everyone wants is to be happy.

additional_notes: A clause starter meaning the thing(s) that you do, want, know, deserve, etc. It is normally followed by a verb: ce que tu fais, ce que tu veux, ce que tu sais.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Built from ce que ('what/that which') + tu as ('you have'). It introduces a clause about something the person has, has done, or has experienced. Very often tu as is the auxiliary in the passé composé: ce que tu as mangé = 'what you ate / what you have eaten'.
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce que tu as choisi.
native_language_example: Tell me what you chose.

meaning: what you said; the thing(s) you said.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to someone’s words as a noun phrase. It can be the subject or object of a sentence: « Ce que tu as dit est… » (What you said is…), « J’ai fait ce que tu as dit » (I did what you said). Literally “that which you have said.”
target_language_example: Je suis d’accord avec ce que tu as dit.
native_language_example: I agree with what you said.

additional_notes: Uses **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **tu as fait** (past tense of *faire*, “you did/have done”) to refer to an action as a thing: *for what you did*, *realize what you’ve done*, *see what you did*. Often used after expressions like **être reconnaissant pour…**, **réaliser…**, **voir…**.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que tu as fait, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I understand what you did, but I don’t agree.

ce que tu as fait pour moi

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu as fait pour moi
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action or favor the person did for you. Often appears after verbs like savoir (to know), dire (to say/tell), or in thanks: Merci de ce que tu as fait pour moi (Thank you for what you did for me).
target_language_example: Je n'oublierai jamais ce que tu as fait pour moi.
native_language_example: I will never forget what you did for me.

ce que tu as toujours voulu

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu as toujours voulu
additional_notes: Used to refer to a thing (an idea, an object, an experience) that someone has wanted for a long time. Often appears after phrases like "C’est..." ("It’s...") or "Pour t’offrir..." ("To offer you..."). "Ce que" introduces a relative clause meaning “what/that which,” and "tu as voulu" is the past tense (passé composé) of "vouloir" (to want).
target_language_example: Je vais enfin t’acheter ce que tu as toujours voulu.
native_language_example: I’m finally going to buy you what you’ve always wanted.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the thing(s) the person saw. It can appear in a question (C’est ce que tu as vu ?), as the subject of a sentence (Ce que tu as vu était…), or after a verb like dire/savoir (Dis-lui / Je dois savoir ce que tu as vu).
target_language_example: Raconte-moi ce que tu as vu.
native_language_example: Tell me what you saw.

additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun phrase "ce que" (“what/that which”) + "tu as" (“you have”). It refers to an unspecified thing or things in the context (often an object someone is holding or possesses): "Donne-moi ce que tu as" = “Give me what you have.”
target_language_example: Je peux réparer ce que tu as cassé.
native_language_example: I can fix what you broke.

ce que tu as à faire

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu as à faire
meaning: “what you have to do” / “what you need to do.”
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s task, responsibility, or the thing they’re expected to do. Common in advice, instructions, or reminders, and can sound firm depending on tone (e.g., “Just do what you have to do.”). Often appears after verbs like faire, savoir, se concentrer sur.
target_language_example: Concentre-toi sur ce que tu as à faire, et tout ira bien.
native_language_example: Focus on what you have to do, and everything will be fine.

ce que tu as à faire est de

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu as à faire est de
meaning: "what you have to do is to…"
additional_notes: Used to introduce an instruction or next step: it sets up a general task, followed by an infinitive verb. Often you’ll also hear the more common structure: « Ce que tu as à faire, c’est de + infinitif ». You can change the subject/pronoun (ce que je/nous/vous avons à faire…) and the time (ce que tu auras à faire…).
target_language_example: Ce que tu as à faire est de remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: What you have to do is fill out this form.

meaning: "what you're looking for" / "what you’re searching for."
additional_notes: Uses **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **tu cherches** (“you’re looking for”). It refers to an unknown thing the other person wants or needs, and can appear in questions (often after *C’est… ?* or *Est-ce que… ?*) or statements like *Je sais…* / *J’espère que tu trouveras…*.
target_language_example: Si tu n’as pas trouvé ce que tu cherches, je peux t’aider.
native_language_example: If you haven’t found what you’re looking for, I can help you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of someone’s words. It’s built with **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **tu dis** (“you say”). Often follows verbs like *comprendre* (to understand), *croire* (to believe), *faire attention à* (to pay attention to), *réaliser* (to realize), *penser* (to think). You can change **tu** to other subjects: *ce que vous dites* (what you say), *ce qu’il dit* (what he says), etc.
target_language_example: Je suis d’accord avec ce que tu dis.
native_language_example: I agree with what you’re saying.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement about the content of what someone is saying. It’s built from: "ce que" (what/that which) + "tu dis" (you say) + "est" (is). Often followed by an adjective or noun: "Ce que tu dis est vrai/faux/incroyable."
target_language_example: Ce que tu dis est très clair.
native_language_example: What you’re saying is very clear.

meaning: "what you have to do" / "what you should do."
additional_notes: Built with **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **tu dois** (“you must/have to”) + **faire** (“to do”). It’s used to point to the correct or necessary action. Often appears after verbs like **savoir** (“to know”), **dire** (“to tell”), or **montrer** (“to show”): *Je sais ce que tu dois faire.* It can also stand alone as an instruction/title (*Ce que tu dois faire.*).
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que tu dois faire.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you what you have to do.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your nature/identity, often after verbs like aimer: « Je t’aime pour ce que tu es » (“I love you for who you are”). It can also appear in an exclamation with an adjective (often written « Qu’est-ce que tu es + adjectif ! »): « (Qu’est-ce que) tu es drôle ! » = “You’re so funny!”
target_language_example: Je t’apprécie pour ce que tu es.
native_language_example: I appreciate you for who you are.

ce que tu essaies de faire

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu essaies de faire
additional_notes: Built with **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **tu essaies de faire** (“you’re trying to do”). Used to talk about an action in a general way, often after phrases like **je sais…** (I know…), **je vois…** (I see…), **merci pour…** (thanks for…), **je suis reconnaissant(e) pour…** (I’m grateful for…).
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que tu essaies de faire, mais ça ne marchera pas.
native_language_example: I understand what you're trying to do, but it won't work.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to someone’s action/activity. With the present tense (fais), it can mean what you’re doing right now or what you do in general—context decides. Common in questions (Tu peux me dire ce que tu fais ?) and warnings like Fais attention à ce que tu fais (“Be careful what you’re doing”).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu fais.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you’re doing.

ce que tu lui as fait

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu lui as fait
additional_notes: Used to point to (or accuse someone of) an action they did to another person. "Ce que" means "what/that which" and introduces a clause. "Lui" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" or "to her"; in English you usually translate it as "him/her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas croire ce que tu lui as fait.
native_language_example: I can’t believe what you did to him/her.

additional_notes:
Used to introduce a clause meaning “what you have [done/said/asked/taught] to me.”
- **ce que** = “what/that which”
- **tu** = “you” (informal singular)
- **m’** = “to me / me” (short for *me*)
- **as** = “have” (present of *avoir*), used to form the **passé composé**
Typically followed by a **past participle**: *ce que tu m'as dit / demandé / appris / expliqué* = “what you told/asked/taught/explained me (i.e., to me).”
Note: the French often places the indirect object pronoun **m’** before the auxiliary: *tu m'as dit* = “you told me.”
target_language_example: J'ai fait ce que tu m'as demandé.
native_language_example: I did what you asked me to do.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something the person said earlier. It can follow verbs like dire (say/tell), faire (do), savoir (know), penser à (think about), se rappeler (remember). Grammar note: “m’as dit” = “told me” (past tense: tu + me + as + dit).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas oublié ce que tu m'as dit.
native_language_example: I haven't forgotten what you told me.

meaning: "what you’re telling me" / "what you tell me."
additional_notes: Uses the structure **ce que + subject + verb** to mean “what/that which…”. Here, **tu** is “you,” **me** is “to me,” and **dis** is “say/tell” (from *dire*). Often used after another verb: *Je ne sais que ce que tu me dis* = “I only know what you tell me.” It can also be used for emphasis or disbelief: *C’est ce que tu me dis ?* = “Is that what you’re telling me?”
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que tu me dis, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I understand what you’re telling me, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s thoughts/opinion, often after verbs like dire (to say/tell), savoir (to know), or demander (to ask). It’s common in indirect questions or statements (e.g., Dis-moi ce que tu penses. = Tell me what you think.).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu penses de ce film.
native_language_example: I want to know what you think about this movie.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the actions or tasks someone is able to do. Often appears after verbs like "savoir" (to know), "voir" (to see), or in sayings like "Ne remets pas à demain ce que tu peux faire aujourd'hui" (“Don’t put off until tomorrow what you can do today”).
target_language_example: Montre-moi ce que tu peux faire.
native_language_example: Show me what you can do.

meaning: “what you can” / “as much as you can.”
additional_notes: Used to mean doing/paying/saving only what is possible for you. It often follows a verb like faire (Tu fais ce que tu peux.), payer (Paie ce que tu peux.), or mettre de côté (Mets de côté ce que tu peux.). In formal writing, you may also see « ce que vous pouvez ».
target_language_example: Tu peux m’aider ce que tu peux, merci.
native_language_example: Help me as much as you can, thanks.

additional_notes: Literally “that which you feel.” Used after verbs like dire (to tell), comprendre (to understand), savoir (to know), or être attentif à (to pay attention to) to refer to someone’s feelings. The verb "ressentir" here means to feel/experience an emotion (not physical touch).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu ressens, sans te juger.
native_language_example: I want to know what you’re feeling, without judging you.

meaning: "what you can do" / "what you know how to do."
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s abilities or skills. Often appears after verbs like montrer (to show) or voir/voyons (to see/let’s see): « Montre-moi ce que tu sais faire » = “Show me what you can do.” Here « ce que » means “what/that which,” and « savoir faire » means “to know how to do (something).”
target_language_example: D'accord, voyons ce que tu sais faire !
native_language_example: Okay, let’s see what you can do!

additional_notes: Used to introduce an object clause meaning “the thing(s) that you know,” often after verbs like savoir (to know), dire (to say/tell), ignorer (to be unaware of), répéter (to repeat). It can also be used as a standalone subject: “Ce que tu sais…” = “What you know…”.
target_language_example: Je veux entendre ce que tu sais.
native_language_example: I want to hear what you know.

meaning: "what you’re going to …" (introduces what someone is going to do/say).
additional_notes: This chunk is usually incomplete on its own: it normally continues with an infinitive verb (e.g., faire, dire, manger). It combines **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **tu vas** (“you’re going”), used in the near future: **tu vas + infinitive**. Example pattern: **Je sais ce que tu vas faire.**
target_language_example: Je sais ce que tu vas faire ce soir.
native_language_example: I know what you’re going to do tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an upcoming action by the person you’re speaking to (tu = informal singular “you”). Often appears in questions (C’est ce que tu vas faire ? = “Is that what you’re going to do?”), in statements (Je sais ce que tu vas faire. = “I know what you’re going to do.”), or to introduce instructions (Voici ce que tu vas faire. = “Here’s what you’re going to do.”).
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que tu vas faire après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you what you’re going to do after lunch.

additional_notes: A compositional phrase built from ce que ('what/that which') + tu veux ('you want'). It refers to the thing, action, or idea someone wants. Depending on context, it can be a simple 'what you want' or a freer 'whatever you want,' especially after verbs like faire, prendre, or choisir.
target_language_example: Tu peux manger ce que tu veux ce soir.
native_language_example: You can eat whatever you want tonight.

meaning: "what you mean" / "what you’re trying to say."
additional_notes: Used after verbs like comprendre (to understand), savoir (to know), or voir (to see) to refer to the meaning of what someone said. Literally “that which you want to say,” but in English it’s usually “what you mean.”
target_language_example: D'accord, je comprends ce que tu veux dire maintenant.
native_language_example: Okay, I understand what you mean now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the action or plan someone wants to do. Often appears after verbs like savoir (to know), dire (to say/tell), or in questions like C’est ce que tu veux faire ? / Est-ce ce que tu veux faire ? It refers to a thing/idea (ce que = what/that which), followed by tu veux faire (you want to do).
target_language_example: Je peux t'aider à préparer ce que tu veux faire.
native_language_example: I can help you prepare what you want to do.

ce que tu viens de dire

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu viens de dire
additional_notes: Used to refer back to the other person’s most recent words. Built with **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **venir de + infinitive** (the recent past: “to have just done”): **tu viens de dire** = “you just said.” Often used when reacting (surprise, disagreement) or asking someone to repeat or take back their words.
target_language_example: Je n'arrive pas à croire ce que tu viens de dire.
native_language_example: I can't believe what you just said.

additional_notes: Uses **ce que** to mean “what/that which,” followed by **tu vois** (“you see”). Common when pointing something out or explaining that appearances can differ from reality. In more formal contexts you may hear **ce que vous voyez** (“what you see,” formal/plural).
target_language_example: Ce que tu vois n’est pas toujours la réalité.
native_language_example: What you see isn’t always reality.

meaning: whatever you want / whatever you’d like.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified thing that the other person will choose (often after words like « tout » or after verbs like « faire » or « donner »). « Voudras » is the future of « vouloir » (to want), and it often sounds a bit softer/politer than « ce que tu veux » depending on context.
target_language_example: Choisis ce que tu voudras, ça me va.
native_language_example: Choose whatever you want; it’s fine with me.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific thing (an object, result, or situation) that the person wanted. It often comes after verbs like trouver (to find), être (to be), or penser (to think): « Tu as trouvé ce que tu voulais ? » / « C’était ce que tu voulais. » The core structure is « ce que » = “what/that which” + « tu voulais » (“you wanted,” imperfect), and the verb can change with tense/person (e.g., « ce que je veux », « ce que tu voulais »).
target_language_example: J'espère que tu as eu ce que tu voulais.
native_language_example: I hope you got what you wanted.

ce que tu étais en train de

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu étais en train de
meaning: "what you were in the middle of (doing)".
additional_notes: This is the start of a clause meaning “what you were doing at that moment,” and it must be followed by an infinitive verb: « ce que tu étais en train de faire / dire / préparer… ». Structure: « ce que » + subject (« tu ») + « étais en train de » + infinitive. It’s a common way to emphasize an action in progress in the past.
target_language_example: J’ai oublié ce que tu étais en train de dire.
native_language_example: I forgot what you were in the middle of saying.

additional_notes: Usually followed by a verb: ce que vous dites, ce que vous voulez, ce que vous cherchez. It introduces a clause meaning the thing that you do, say, want, think, etc. Use ce que when "you" is not the subject of the whole sentence but the object idea being referred to.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que vous voulez dire.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean.

meaning: "what you are going to do" (or "what you will do").
additional_notes: Used to introduce or refer to an action the listener is expected to do. Very common in instructions and explanations (e.g., "Here’s what you’re going to do..."). Literally "that which" + "you are going to do"; you may also see it with other subjects (ce que je vais faire, ce qu’ils vont faire) or with the near future replaced by the future (ce que vous ferez).
target_language_example: Écoutez bien : voici ce que vous allez faire.
native_language_example: Listen carefully: here’s what you’re going to do.

meaning: "what you have" (what you did/what you’ve done/what you’re holding), depending on context.
additional_notes: "Ce que" means "what" / "that which" and introduces a clause. "vous avez" is the polite/plural "you have" (passé composé when followed by a past participle: "vous avez caché / commis / accompli / prévu" = "you hid/committed/accomplished/planned"). Often used with verbs like cacher, faire, dire, prévoir, accomplir, etc.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que vous avez dit.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the thing(s) someone requested. Often appears after verbs like faire (do), donner (give), avoir (have/get): « J’ai fait ce que vous avez demandé. » You can add « tout » for emphasis: « tout ce que vous avez demandé » = “everything you asked for.” Note: « demander » usually means “to ask (for)” or “to request,” not “to demand.”
target_language_example: Voici ce que vous avez demandé.
native_language_example: Here is what you asked for.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to the content of what someone said. It often comes after verbs like répéter (repeat), comprendre (understand), entendre (hear): «Pouvez-vous répéter ce que vous avez dit ?». «Vous» is the formal/plural 'you'.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas bien compris ce que vous avez dit.
native_language_example: I didn't understand well what you said.

additional_notes: Literally “that which you have done.” Used to refer to an action or thing the person did. Often follows verbs like voir (to see), savoir (to know), comprendre (to understand), apprécier (to appreciate). Can also be expanded: « tout ce que vous avez fait » = “everything you’ve done.”
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que vous avez fait, mais je ne suis pas d'accord.
native_language_example: I understand what you did, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified thing or event that someone saw. "ce que" means "what" (literally "that which"), and "vous" is the formal "you" or plural "you". "avez vu" is the past tense of "voir" (to see) in the passé composé; depending on context it can be translated as either "you saw" or "you have seen".
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous décrire ce que vous avez vu ?
native_language_example: Can you describe what you saw?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a thing (or situation) the listener possesses/has. Often appears after an imperative: « Donnez-moi ce que vous avez… » (Give me what you have…), « Montrez-moi ce que vous avez » (Show me what you have). You can add details after it: « ce que vous avez dans la main » (what you have in your hand), « ce que vous avez à dire » (what you have to say).
target_language_example: Je peux vous aider avec ce que vous avez.
native_language_example: I can help you with what you have.

ce que vous avez à faire

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que vous avez à faire
meaning: "what you have to do" / "what you need to do."
additional_notes: Used to refer to the task(s) expected of someone. Built with **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **avoir à + infinitive** (“to have to do”). **Vous** is the formal or plural “you,” so it can address one person politely or a group.
target_language_example: Je vous ai expliqué ce que vous avez à faire.
native_language_example: I explained to you what you need to do.

ce que vous avez à faire est de

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que vous avez à faire est de
meaning: "what you have to do is to…"
additional_notes: Used to introduce instructions or advice. Structure: **Ce que + subject + avoir à faire + est de + infinitive**. (You can also hear **c’est de + infinitive**.) The **vous** form is polite/plural; with **tu**: *Ce que tu as à faire, c’est de…*
target_language_example: Ce que vous avez à faire est de remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: What you have to do is fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of what someone is saying. Often appears after verbs like comprendre (to understand) or savoir (to know), and in warnings like Faites attention à / Prenez garde à ce que vous dites (“Watch what you say”). Vous at the start makes it formal or plural (“you”).
target_language_example: Je vois ce que vous dites, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I see what you’re saying, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion about something already mentioned ("en" = "about it/that"). Often follows verbs like dire/savoir/vouloir savoir/aimerais savoir: « Dites-moi ce que vous en pensez. » You can change « vous » to « tu », « en » to match what you're referring to, and the verb tense as needed: « ce que tu en penses », « ce que vous en penserez ».
target_language_example: Après la réunion, dites-moi ce que vous en pensez.
native_language_example: After the meeting, tell me what you think about it.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the action someone (vous = you, formal or plural) is doing. Often appears after verbs like savoir (to know), voir (to see), comprendre (to understand), or in polite questions: « Puis-je demander ce que vous faites ? » = “May I ask what you’re doing?”
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que vous faites.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you’re doing.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to information the person previously said. Literally "that which you have told to me" (ce que = "what/that which"; vous m'avez dit = "you told me"). Often appears after verbs like savoir (to know), croire (to believe), répéter (to repeat), dire (to say), faire (to do) to report or repeat what was said.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas oublié ce que vous m'avez dit.
native_language_example: I haven't forgotten what you told me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the content of someone’s thoughts/opinion, often after verbs like *savoir* (to know), *dire* (to say), *comprendre* (to understand): *Je sais ce que vous pensez (de moi).* Adding *tous* means “all of you”: *ce que vous pensez tous*.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que vous pensez, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I understand what you think, but I don’t agree.

meaning: what you feel (what you’re experiencing emotionally/physically).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like dire / expliquer to introduce the content of your feelings: « Dites-lui ce que vous ressentez » (“Tell him/her what you feel”). « Ressentir » can mean feeling emotions (sadness, stress) or physical sensations (pain). « Vous » is formal or plural; in informal singular you’ll often hear « ce que tu ressens ».
target_language_example: Je veux comprendre ce que vous ressentez.
native_language_example: I want to understand what you’re feeling.

additional_notes: Uses **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **vous savez** (“you know,” formal or plural). It introduces the thing/information the other person knows: *Dites-nous ce que vous savez* (“Tell us what you know”). Can also be followed by an infinitive to mean “what you know how to do”: *ce que vous savez faire* (“what you can do / what you know how to do”).
target_language_example: Expliquez-moi ce que vous savez sur ce sujet.
native_language_example: Explain to me what you know about this topic.

meaning: whatever you want (me to do); as you wish.
additional_notes: Uses the formal/plural "vous". Often follows verbs like "faire" in phrases such as "Faites-en ce que vous voudrez" (“Do whatever you want with it”) or "Je ferai tout ce que vous voudrez" (“I’ll do whatever you want”). "Ce que" means “what/that which,” and "voudrez" is the future of "vouloir" (“to want”), but in English it’s usually translated as “whatever you want” rather than literally.
target_language_example: Prenez ce que vous voudrez et laissez le reste.
native_language_example: Take whatever you want and leave the rest.

additional_notes: Literally “that which you want.” Used to refer to the thing(s) someone wants, often after verbs like donner (to give) or manger (to eat), or in questions like « Est-ce ce que vous voulez ? » (“Is this what you want?”). « Ce que vous voulez » can also mean “whatever you want,” especially in imperatives like « Mangez ce que vous voulez » (“Eat whatever you want”). In « Faites de moi ce que vous voulez », it means “Do what you want with me.”
target_language_example: Choisissez ce que vous voulez dans le menu.
native_language_example: Choose whatever you want from the menu.

meaning: what you mean; what you’re trying to say.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or clarify someone’s meaning. Literally “that which you want to say,” but in English it’s usually “what you mean.” Often appears in questions (C’est ce que vous voulez dire ?) or after verbs like savoir/comprendre/expliquer (Je veux savoir/comprendre ce que vous voulez dire). "Vous" is formal or plural; informally you’ll hear "ce que tu veux dire".
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que vous voulez dire.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action or plan the person (vous) wants to do. It’s built with **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **vous voulez** (“you want”) + **faire** (“to do”). Common in questions (C’est/Est-ce ce que… ?) and in statements like **Je sais…** (“I know…”) or requests like **Dites-moi…** (“Tell me…”).
target_language_example: Dites-moi ce que vous voulez faire demain.
native_language_example: Tell me what you want to do tomorrow.

meaning: "what you wanted" (or "what you were looking for").
additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun phrase "ce que" (= "what/that which") plus "vous vouliez" (imperfect of "vouloir"). Often used to confirm something matches the other person’s request: "C’est bien ce que vous vouliez ?" (= "Is this what you wanted?"). "Vous" can be formal singular or plural.
target_language_example: Voilà ce que vous vouliez, n’est-ce pas ?
native_language_example: Here’s what you wanted, right?

ce que vous étiez en train de

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que vous étiez en train de
meaning: "what you were (in the middle of) doing".
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone was doing at that moment in the past. It combines: "ce que" (what/that which) + "vous étiez" (you were) + "être en train de" (to be in the process of doing). It must be followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., faire, dire, regarder).
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas compris ce que vous étiez en train de dire.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what you were saying (what you were in the middle of saying).

meaning: "what you are" / "what kind of person you are."
additional_notes: Built with the relative pronoun "ce que" + "vous êtes". It’s used to talk about someone’s nature/identity in a general way (often with an implied judgment), or more neutrally in phrases like "ce que vous êtes en train de faire" (“what you are doing”).
target_language_example: Je sais ce que vous êtes, mais je veux entendre la vérité de votre bouche.
native_language_example: I know what you are, but I want to hear the truth from you.

meaning: "what it/that" (introduces a clause about what something does, says, gives, implies, etc.).
additional_notes: Used when "ça" (= it/that) is the subject of the verb in the following clause: "ce que ça donne" (what it gives/results in), "ce que ça dit" (what it says), "ce que ça implique" (what it implies). Very common after verbs like voir/lire/savoir to mean “see/read/know what it …”.
target_language_example: On va voir ce que ça change.
native_language_example: We’ll see what it changes / what difference it makes.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or explain the meaning or implications of something. Very common after verbs like savoir (to know), dire (to tell), comprendre (to understand), or in questions like « Qu’est-ce que ça signifie ? ». « ça » = “that/it” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce mot : qu’est-ce que ça signifie ?
native_language_example: I don’t understand this word: what does it mean?

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to the meaning of a word, phrase, sign, situation, etc. Very common in questions: « Ça veut dire quoi ? » and « Qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ? » mean the same thing. Can also be used in statements: « Je sais/Je ne sais pas ce que ça veut dire. »
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce mot : qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ?
native_language_example: I don’t understand this word: what does it mean?

additional_notes: Very common in embedded questions and relative clauses. With an antecedent it often appears as "ce que" = "what/that which": "Ce que tu dis" (what you’re saying). In questions you’ll often see it inside "est-ce que" (a question marker): "Pourquoi est-ce que... ?" and "Qu’est-ce que... ?"
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I don't understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to define, identify, or convey the lived experience of something, often after verbs like savoir, comprendre, ignorer: « Je sais ce que c'est que la peur » (= I know what fear is / what it’s like). This is a more emphatic/heavier form of « ce que c’est » and is common in speech.
target_language_example: Tu ne sais pas ce que c'est que d’attendre pendant des heures.
native_language_example: You don’t know what it’s like to wait for hours.

meaning: “what is this …?” / “what’s this …?” (often showing surprise, disbelief, or annoyance).
additional_notes: Spoken, reactive pattern used when you notice something unexpected and want to question or complain about it. It is typically followed by a noun: « ce que c'est que ce + nom ». Close alternatives (often more common/neutral) include: « Qu’est-ce que c’est que ça ? » and « C’est quoi, ça ? ». The structure is idiomatic and not usually translated word-for-word.
target_language_example: Ce que c'est que ce bazar, dans ta chambre !
native_language_example: What is this mess in your room?!

meaning: "What is that?" / "What the heck is that?"
additional_notes: An emphatic, colloquial way to ask what something is, often expressing surprise, annoyance, or disbelief. It’s based on the pattern "Qu’est-ce que c’est que… ?"; in everyday speech you’ll also hear "C’est quoi, ça ?". More expressive than the neutral "Qu’est-ce que c’est ?".
target_language_example: Ce que c'est que ça ?!
native_language_example: What the heck is that?!

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression on its own. It is usually just the sequence ce que followed by ce, as in longer sentences like ce que ce mot veut dire (“what this word means”).
target_language_example: Je sais ce que ce mot veut dire.
native_language_example: I know what this word means.

additional_notes: Usually the beginning of a longer clause, not a complete expression by itself. It is typically followed by a verb, as in ce que cela veut dire ('what that/it means'). cela is more formal than ça and often refers to something previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que cela veut dire.
native_language_example: I don't understand what that means.

meaning: "what I have to" / "what I must" (what I’m supposed to do).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause meaning “the thing(s) that I have to…”. It’s often followed by an infinitive (e.g., « ce que je dois faire » = “what I have to do”), but the verb can also be implied from context.
target_language_example: Je sais ce que je dois faire.
native_language_example: I know what I have to do.

meaning: “what I can … you” (start of a sentence: “what I can tell you / offer you / give you”).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete chunk that typically continues with an infinitive or verb phrase, e.g. « ce que je peux te dire » (what I can tell you), « ce que je peux te proposer » (what I can offer you). « ce que » means “what/that which,” and « te » is “to you” (informal singular). Word order stays the same when you add the verb after it.
target_language_example: Voilà ce que je peux te proposer.
native_language_example: Here’s what I can offer you.

meaning: “what I can … for you / what I can … to you” (start of a sentence).
additional_notes: This is not a complete expression by itself; it’s a sentence starter. **Ce que** means “what/that which,” **je peux** means “I can,” and **vous** is the object pronoun (“you” singular formal or plural). It’s commonly followed by a verb like *dire* (to tell), *proposer* (to offer), *conseiller* (to recommend), etc.: *Ce que je peux vous dire/proposer…*
target_language_example: Ce que je peux vous dire, c’est que le magasin est fermé.
native_language_example: What I can tell you is that the store is closed.

meaning: "what I … you" / "what I … to you" (start of a sentence).
additional_notes: This is not a complete expression by itself; it’s the beginning of a clause that needs a verb after it. It’s used to introduce “what I (do/say/tell/give) you.” Common continuations: “ce que je te dis” (what I’m telling you), “ce que je te propose” (what I’m proposing to you), “ce que je te demande” (what I’m asking you).
target_language_example: Écoute ce que je te dis.
native_language_example: Listen to what I’m telling you.

meaning: “what I … you” (a sentence starter meaning “what I … to you”).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase fragment: **ce que** = “what/that which,” **je** = “I,” **vous** = “you” (formal or plural). It’s used before a verb to introduce the thing you are talking about, e.g. **ce que je vous dis** (“what I’m telling you”), **ce que je vous propose** (“what I’m proposing to you”).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que je vous dis.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what I’m telling you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning “what + the + noun/pronoun” (e.g., *ce que le professeur dit* = “what the teacher says”). It’s not usually a fixed phrase on its own—you complete it with a noun (le + noun) and then a verb. Note: before a vowel, *le* becomes *l’* (e.g., *ce que l’homme fait*).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que le professeur explique.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what the teacher is explaining.

meaning: "what you … about it" (start of a question).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete but very common spoken pattern, usually followed by a verb like *penses* / *dis* / *sais*: **Ce que t'en penses ?** (= *What do you think of it?*). **t'** is a contraction of **tu** before a vowel, and **en** often means “of it/about it” or “some/any (of it)”, depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Ce que t'en penses ?
native_language_example: What do you think of it?

ce que tout le monde est

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tout le monde est
additional_notes: This is a clause (often a fragment) meaning “what everybody is,” typically used to describe a shared characteristic. It’s commonly followed by an adjective or noun: « C’est ce que tout le monde est : … » (= “That’s what everyone is: …”). In a full sentence you often see it as part of « ce que + clause » (“what/that which…”).
target_language_example: Il a peur de ce que tout le monde est capable de faire.
native_language_example: He’s afraid of what everyone is capable of doing.

meaning: 'what you…' / 'that you…' (introduces a clause with tu).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone (tu = “you”) does, says, thinks, etc. Very common in questions with inversion: « Qu’est-ce que tu + verb(e)s ? » = “What are you + verb-ing?” (e.g., « Qu’est-ce que tu racontes ? » = “What are you talking about?”). It can also appear after expressions like « tenir à ce que… »: « Je tiens à ce que tu… » = “I want you to… / It matters to me that you…”.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning “the thing(s) that you like.” Often follows a verb like dire (to say), savoir (to know), demander (to ask), montrer (to show): Dis-moi ce que tu aimes. If you’re speaking more formally or to more than one person, replace tu with vous: ce que vous aimez.
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce que tu aimes comme musique.
native_language_example: Tell me what kind of music you like.

meaning: Usually part of « ce que tu aimes le plus » = “what you like most”.
additional_notes: As written, « ce que tu aimes le » is incomplete in standard French. You most often see « ce que tu aimes » (“what you like”) or « ce que tu aimes le plus » (“what you like most”). « ce que » means “what/that which,” and it introduces the thing you like.
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce que tu aimes le plus.
native_language_example: Tell me what you like the most.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the thing(s) someone found. It’s built with **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **tu as trouvé** (past tense of *trouver*, “you found/you have found”). Often appears in longer sentences, e.g. *Montre-moi ce que tu as trouvé* (“Show me what you found”).
target_language_example: Montre-moi ce que tu as trouvé.
native_language_example: Show me what you found.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; usually a speech error or an unfinished start of “ce que tu as …” (“what you have …”), where “un” is mistakenly inserted or the speaker is about to name a noun (“un livre”, “un problème”, etc.).
additional_notes:
Correct, standard forms include:
- “ce que tu as” = “what you have” (e.g., “Montre-moi ce que tu as.”)
- “ce que tu as + past participle” = “what you have done/said” (e.g., “ce que tu as fait/dit”).

If “un” is intended, it normally belongs to the following noun, but you would typically not say “ce que tu as un …” in careful French. You’d say instead: “Tu as un …” (“You have a …”) or “Qu’est-ce que tu as ?” (“What’s wrong/What do you have?”).
target_language_example: Euh… je comprends pas ce que tu as un… un problème ?
native_language_example: Uh… I don’t understand—do you have a… a problem?

meaning: "what you have to …" (introduces something you must do).
additional_notes: This is usually followed by an infinitive, most often with a verb like faire: « ce que tu as à faire » = “what you have to do.” Here, « avoir à + infinitive » means “to have to / to need to.”
target_language_example: Je sais ce que tu as à faire.
native_language_example: I know what you have to do.

additional_notes: Built with **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **tu comprends** (“you understand”). Used to refer to the information or meaning that the listener has understood (often in phrases like *Explique-moi ce que tu comprends* or *Je veux savoir ce que tu comprends*).
target_language_example: Explique-moi ce que tu comprends.
native_language_example: Explain to me what you understand.

additional_notes: Built with **ce que** + subject (**tu**) + verb (**connais**). It’s used to refer to an unknown or general thing ("what") rather than a specific noun. Often appears after verbs like *dire*, *expliquer*, *montrer*, *oublier*: *Dis-moi ce que tu connais.*
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce que tu connais de ce sujet.
native_language_example: Tell me what you know about this topic.

additional_notes: Uses **ce que** (= “what/that which”) to introduce a clause where **tu crois** (“you believe/think”) explains or identifies something. Often used to contrast belief vs reality: *Ce que tu crois n’est pas forcément vrai.* You can also hear similar patterns: *ce que je crois*, *ce qu’il croit*, *ce que tu penses*.
target_language_example: Ce que tu crois n’est pas toujours la vérité.
native_language_example: What you believe isn’t always the truth.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning “the thing that you think/believe (that) …”. It’s a relative structure: **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **tu crois** (“you think/believe”) + **que** (introduces the following clause). In everyday French you’ll also often see **ce que tu crois** without the extra **que**, depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Ce que tu crois que j’ai dit n’est pas ce que j’ai dit.
native_language_example: What you think I said isn’t what I said.

meaning: "what you … about it" (introduces what you think/say/know about something).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete but very common pattern: **ce que tu en + verb**. The pronoun **en** refers back to something already mentioned (often meaning “about it / of it / some”). You’ll often see it in questions like **Qu’est-ce que tu en penses ?** (“What do you think about it?”) or statements like **Je ne sais pas ce que tu en sais.** (“I don’t know what you know about it.”).
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu en penses ?
native_language_example: What do you think about it?

additional_notes: Used to ask (sometimes with surprise or suspicion) about someone’s presence or actions in a place. Often appears after verbs like savoir/comprendre: « Je ne sais pas ce que tu fais ici. » You can change the subject/pronoun: « ce que vous faites ici », « ce qu’il fait ici », etc.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu fais ici.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you’re doing here.

meaning: "what you’re doing there" / "what are you doing there".
additional_notes: Used to ask (often with surprise, concern, or disapproval) about someone’s presence or actions in a place. Literally: "that which you are doing there." In a full question you’ll often hear: « Qu’est-ce que tu fais là ? » (= "What are you doing there?").
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu fais là ? Je te croyais à la maison.
native_language_example: What are you doing here? I thought you were at home.

additional_notes: From the verb "foutre" (very informal, can be vulgar), used like "faire" = “to do.” Often heard in questions like "Qu’est-ce que tu fous ?" meaning “What are you doing?” with an annoyed or shocked tone. Use "Qu’est-ce que tu fais ?" for a neutral/polite version.
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu fous ici ?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here?

meaning: "What the hell are you doing here/there?"
additional_notes: Very informal and often rude. Uses the verb "foutre" ("fous" = "tu fous"), which is a coarse way to say "do" (similar to "the hell" / "the fuck" in English). "là" can mean "here" or "there" depending on context. In polite speech, use: « Qu’est-ce que tu fais ici/là ? »
target_language_example: Mais ce que tu fous là à cette heure-ci ?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here at this hour?

meaning: An incomplete fragment meaning “what you … it/him”.
additional_notes: This sequence isn’t a complete expression by itself; it’s usually the start of a longer sentence. “ce que” means “what/that which,” “tu” = “you,” and “le” is an object pronoun meaning “him” or “it.” You need a verb after it (e.g., “ce que tu le sais” is not natural; more natural would be “ce que tu sais” = “what you know,” or “ce que tu lui dis” = “what you tell him”).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce que tu le vois dans ce film.
native_language_example: I don’t know what you see in this movie.

meaning: "what you have (to him/her)" (start of a clause).
additional_notes: This is a phrase fragment that typically comes right before a past participle (e.g., dit, donné, envoyé). Structure: **ce que** = “what/that which” + **tu** = “you” + **lui** = “to him/to her” + **as** (avoir) = “have” (used to form the passé composé). Common continuation: *ce que tu lui as dit* (“what you told him/her”).
target_language_example: Je sais ce que tu lui as dit.
native_language_example: I know what you told him/her.

meaning: “what you (… to) me” (start of a clause).
additional_notes: This is not a complete expression by itself; it’s a common fragment that introduces a relative clause with **ce que** (“what/that which”), followed by **tu** (“you”) and the indirect object **me** (“to me”). It’s usually completed by a verb: **ce que tu me dis** (what you tell me), **ce que tu me donnes** (what you give me), **ce que tu me demandes** (what you ask me for), etc.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que tu me dis.
native_language_example: I understand what you’re telling me.

additional_notes: Usually said as an exclamation: « Ce que tu parles ! ». It’s a sarcastic way to reject what someone just said (similar to “as if!”). You’ll often also hear « Ce que tu racontes ! » with the same meaning. Not used to literally mean “what you’re talking about” (that would be « De quoi tu parles ? »).
target_language_example: — Il va sûrement me rappeler ce soir. — Ce que tu parles !
native_language_example: — He’ll definitely call me back tonight. — Yeah, right!

additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone believes/opines before stating a clause: « ce que tu penses que + phrase » often continues with a verb (e.g., « ce que tu penses que je vais dire » = “what you think I’m going to say”). In everyday French, you’ll also often hear a simpler version without « ce que »: « tu penses que… » (“you think that…”).
target_language_example: Ce que tu penses que je veux n’est pas ce que je veux vraiment.
native_language_example: What you think I want isn’t what I really want.

meaning: “what you can … me” (start of a longer phrase like “what you can tell/show/give me”).
additional_notes: This is a fragment, not a complete expression by itself. It usually introduces a clause with a verb after it: **ce que tu peux me dire** (what you can tell me), **ce que tu peux me montrer** (what you can show me), **ce que tu peux me donner** (what you can give me). **ce que** means “what/that which,” **tu peux** means “you can,” and **me** means “to me / me” (object pronoun placed before the verb in French).
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce que tu peux me dire sur ce quartier.
native_language_example: Tell me what you can tell me about this neighborhood.

meaning: "what you … to yourself" (introduces a clause; needs a verb after it).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed expression by itself: it’s the start of a relative clause. **Ce que** = “what/that which,” **tu** = “you,” and **te** is an object/reflexive pronoun (“to you / yourself”) that goes before the verb. You must add a verb after **te** (e.g., *ce que tu te dis* = “what you tell yourself”, *ce que tu te demandes* = “what you ask yourself”).
target_language_example: Je sais ce que tu te dis.
native_language_example: I know what you're telling yourself.

ce que tu veux que je

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu veux que je
meaning: "what you want me to…" (used before a verb).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone wants you to do. It’s usually followed by a verb in the subjunctive: « ce que tu veux que je fasse / dise / sois ». If you address someone formally, use « ce que vous voulez que je… ». On its own it sounds unfinished—you normally complete it with an action.
target_language_example: Je peux faire ce que tu veux que je fasse.
native_language_example: I can do what you want me to do.

meaning: "what you just…" (usually: "ce que tu viens de" + infinitive).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete fragment on its own. In real French you most often see it as **ce que tu viens de + infinitive** to mean “what you just did/said” (recent past): *ce que tu viens de dire* = “what you just said.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas compris ce que tu viens de dire.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what you just said.

additional_notes: Used with "vous" (formal singular or plural "you"). Very common inside the question pattern "Qu’est-ce que vous… ?" = "What are you…? / What do you…?". It can also appear in statements: "Je sais ce que vous voulez" = "I know what you want."
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que vous dites.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you’re saying.

additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun phrase "ce que" to mean “what/that which,” followed by "vous aimez" (“you like”). "Vous" can be formal singular (“you”) or plural (“you all”). Often appears after verbs like "dire" (to say), "montrer" (to show), "choisir" (to choose), or in questions about preferences.
target_language_example: Dites-moi ce que vous aimez.
native_language_example: Tell me what you like.

meaning: "what you are going to (do)" / "what you’re about to".
additional_notes: This is usually an unfinished phrase that needs something after it, often an infinitive (or implied "faire"): « ce que vous allez faire » (what you’re going to do). « Vous allez + infinitive » is the common near-future in French (like "going to" in English).
target_language_example: Dites-moi ce que vous allez faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Tell me what you’re going to do tonight.

meaning: "what you are doing there" / "what you're doing there."
additional_notes: Uses the structure "ce que" (= "what/that which") + a clause. "Là" usually means "there" (a place), but it can also mean "right now" or "in that situation," depending on context. Often appears in a longer sentence (e.g., after "je sais" / "je ne comprends pas"), and it can also be used as part of a question like "Qu'est-ce que vous faites là ?" (= "What are you doing here/there?").
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que vous faites là.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you’re doing there.

meaning: "what you can" (what you are able to).
additional_notes: This phrase is usually followed by a verb or action: « ce que vous pouvez faire / dire / apporter ». « ce que » means “what/that which,” and « vous pouvez » is the polite/plural “you can.”
target_language_example: Dites-moi ce que vous pouvez faire.
native_language_example: Tell me what you can do.

additional_notes: Built with **ce que** (“what/that which”) + **vous voyez** (“you see”). It’s used to refer to the thing(s) being seen: *Ce que vous voyez, c’est…* (“What you see is…”). **Vous** can be formal singular or plural.
target_language_example: Ce que vous voyez ici, c’est le centre-ville.
native_language_example: What you see here is downtown.

additional_notes: Often used at the start of a clause to introduce a guess or question about something: "ce que ça peut + infinitive/verb" (e.g., être, faire, vouloir dire). Uses "ça" (= "that/it"), which is very common in speech and more informal than "cela".
target_language_example: Je me demande ce que ça peut être.
native_language_example: I wonder what it could be.

meaning: “what it … to you” (start of a phrase; needs a verb after).
additional_notes:
This is an incomplete chunk that usually introduces a clause about how something affects you or what you think/feel about it. It is commonly followed by a verb, e.g.:
- « ce que ça te fait » = what it does to you / how it makes you feel
- « ce que ça te dit » = whether you feel like it (lit. what it tells you)
- « ce que ça te rappelle » = what it reminds you of
On its own, « ce que ça te » sounds unfinished.
target_language_example: Je sais ce que ça te fait.
native_language_example: I know how it makes you feel.

meaning: "what it's going to…" (introduces an indirect question about what will happen).
additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive or a verb phrase, e.g. « ce que ça va donner » (how it will turn out), « ce que ça va être » (what it’s going to be like). It’s common after verbs like « je me demande », « je ne sais pas », « on verra ».
target_language_example: Je me demande ce que ça va donner.
native_language_example: I wonder how it will turn out.

additional_notes: used to mean “what/that which” when it is the subject of the following verb. Compare with ce que, which is used when “what” is the object of the verb.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: I understand what's happening.

additional_notes: "Ce qui" means “what” (literally “that which”). Adding "a" is the start of the passé composé ("a" = “has”) before a past participle: "ce qui a déclenché" = “what triggered”. Used to refer to an unknown or unspecified thing/event: "Je sais ce qui a…" = “I know what … (happened/occurred)”.
target_language_example: Personne ne sait encore ce qui a causé l'accident.
native_language_example: No one knows yet what caused the accident.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event or situation (often something unclear or being investigated). Literally built from "ce qui" (what/that which) + the past of "avoir lieu" (to take place), but in English you normally say "what happened" rather than "what took place" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Personne ne sait exactement ce qui a eu lieu hier soir.
native_language_example: No one knows exactly what happened last night.

additional_notes: “Ce qui” means “what/that which” and refers to an unspecified thing or situation. With “arrive,” it means “what happens”; in set phrases like “Peu importe ce qui arrive,” it means “whatever happens.” You can add an indirect object/complement: “ce qui arrive à Tom” = “what happens to Tom.”
target_language_example: Peu importe ce qui arrive, je serai là.
native_language_example: Whatever happens, I’ll be there.

additional_notes: Used to highlight what is most important in a situation. Often followed by a verb phrase with "c’est…" (Ce qui compte, c’est toi.) or by "c’est que + clause" (Ce qui compte, c’est qu’on soit ensemble.).
target_language_example: Ce qui compte, c’est de faire de son mieux.
native_language_example: What matters is doing your best.

meaning: "what must be done" / "what needs to be done".
additional_notes: Used to talk about the necessary action in a situation. Often sounds serious or duty-focused (doing the right/necessary thing). Grammatically, "ce qui" means "what/that which," and "doit être fait" is passive: "must be done."
target_language_example: Même si c'est difficile, je ferai ce qui doit être fait.
native_language_example: Even if it's difficult, I will do what must be done.

additional_notes: Used with the relative pronoun **ce qui** (“what/that which”) + **est** (“is”) to introduce a clause about an unspecified thing or situation. Often followed by a past participle or adjective (e.g., **ce qui est écrit** = “what is written”, **ce qui est rare** = “which is rare”). It can also appear as a parenthetical comment: **Il était, ce qui est rare chez lui, ...** (“He was, which is rare for him, ...”).
target_language_example: Je vais faire ce qui est possible.
native_language_example: I'm going to do what is possible.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event or situation that occurred. It’s a relative clause: ce qui (“what/that which”) + est arrivé (“happened/has happened”). Often used after verbs like dire (to say), savoir (to know), entendre (to hear).
target_language_example: Personne ne comprend ce qui est arrivé hier soir.
native_language_example: Nobody understands what happened last night.

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event affecting a person/thing. "Ce qui" = "what" (the thing that), "est arrivé" = "happened" (passé composé of arriver), and "à" introduces who/what it happened to (e.g., à Tom, à Alicia). Often follows verbs like dire/tell or savoir/know: "Dis-moi...", "Je veux savoir...".
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce qui est arrivé à mon téléphone.
native_language_example: I don't understand what happened to my phone.

additional_notes: Used when "ce qui" (= what/that which) is the subject of the verb, and "lui" means “to him/to her” (indirect object). Often followed by a verb: « ce qui lui faut » (what he/she needs), « ce qui lui plaît » (what he/she likes), « ce qui lui revient » (what is due to him/her). In the fixed expression « ce qui lui a pris », it means “what came over him/her?”.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce qui lui fait peur.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what scares him/her.

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about an event that happened to someone. "Ce qui" means “what” (as the subject of the verb), "lui" means “to him/to her,” and "est arrivé" is the past of "arriver" (“happened/has happened”). You can change "lui" to "moi / toi / lui / elle / nous / vous / leur" depending on who it happened to.
target_language_example: Personne ne comprend ce qui lui est arrivé.
native_language_example: No one understands what happened to him/her.

meaning: 'what/that which' + 'me' (as the object of the verb).
additional_notes: Used before a verb to mean “what/that which … (verb) me,” referring to a thing or idea rather than a person. Common with verbs like intéresser (to interest), effrayer (to scare), appartenir (to belong to), etc. It’s often part of: C’est (bien) ce qui m’… / Ce n’est pas ce qui m’… . Note the contraction: m’ is short for me before a vowel sound (m’effraie, m’intéresse).
target_language_example: Ce qui m'inquiète, c'est le manque de temps.
native_language_example: What worries me is the lack of time.

additional_notes: Built with **ce qui** (“what/that which,” as the subject of the verb) + **m'est arrivé** (“happened to me,” past tense of *arriver* with *être*). Common in storytelling or explanations: **Tu sais ce qui m'est arrivé ?** = “Do you know what happened to me?” You can extend it with emphasis: **C'est ce qui m'est arrivé de mieux** = “That’s the best thing that ever happened to me.”
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qui m'est arrivé ?
native_language_example: Do you know what happened to me?

meaning: "what" / "the thing that" (followed by a verb affecting me).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause where the subject is an unspecified thing (“what/that which”), and *me* is the object (“to me / for me”). Pattern: **Ce qui me + verb...** → “What/That which + verb + me...”. Common with verbs like **faire peur** (scare), **venir à l'esprit** (come to mind), **revenir** (be owed/come back), **rendre heureux** (make happy).
target_language_example: Ce qui me manque le plus, c'est ma famille.
native_language_example: What I miss the most is my family.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause where "ce" refers to an unspecified thing (“what/that which”), "qui" is the subject of the verb that follows, and "nous" means “us” (often as an object: *ce qui nous arrive* = “what happens to us”, *ce qui nous manque* = “what we’re missing”, *ce qui nous attend* = “what awaits us”).
target_language_example: Je n'oublierai jamais ce qui nous est arrivé.
native_language_example: I will never forget what happened to us.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event/situation (often something important or unclear) that occurred in the past. Common after verbs like dire (to tell), savoir (to know), apprendre (to learn/find out), découvrir (to discover), and in apologies (Désolé pour…). Literally “that which happened,” and you can add a time expression after it: ce qui s’est passé hier soir.
target_language_example: Explique-moi ce qui s'est passé, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Explain to me what happened, please.

additional_notes: Refers to an event in the past, before another past moment (pluperfect: « s'était passé » = “had happened”). Used after verbs like apprendre (to learn), savoir (to know/find out), raconter (to tell), dire (to say), and in questions: « Qu'est-ce qui s'était passé ? » = “What had happened?”
target_language_example: Personne ne comprenait ce qui s'était passé.
native_language_example: Nobody understood what had happened.

additional_notes: Usually not complete on its own: it is followed by another verb, as in ce qui se passe, ce qui se dit, or ce qui se fait. It introduces 'what ...' with a pronominal or passive-like verb, so the exact English translation depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: I don't understand what's happening.

additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun "ce qui" (“what/that which” as the subject of the verb) + "se passer" (“to happen, to take place”). Common after verbs like "voir" (to see) or "savoir" (to know): "voir ce qui se passait" = “see what was going on.”
target_language_example: Je ne comprenais pas ce qui se passait.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what was happening.

additional_notes: Used to refer to events or the current situation (often something unclear or surprising). It can be a question (Ce qui se passe ?) or part of a longer sentence after verbs like comprendre, savoir, expliquer, dire. Often corresponds to English “what is happening.”
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce qui se passe ici.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what’s going on here.

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the situation regarding someone or something. "Ce qui" means "what" (as the subject of the verb), and "se passer" means "to happen". Often used in questions: « Qu’est-ce qui se passe avec … ? » or statements: « Je ne sais pas ce qui se passe avec … ».
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce qui se passe avec mon téléphone : il s’éteint tout le temps.
native_language_example: I don’t know what’s going on with my phone: it keeps turning off.

meaning: "what happens in" / "what’s going on in" (a place or situation).
additional_notes: Built with the relative pronoun "ce qui" (= what/that which, as the subject) + "se passer" (= to happen) + "dans" (= in). Used to introduce information about events or situations inside a place (a city, a room, a company) or within a topic (a story, a meeting). Often followed by a noun: "ce qui se passe dans la ville", "ce qui se passe dans cette histoire".
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce qui se passe dans cette entreprise.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what’s going on in this company.

meaning: "what's happening here" / "what is going on here".
additional_notes: Used to refer to the situation or events happening in this place. Built from: « ce qui » = “what/that which” + « se passe » (from « se passer ») = “happens/goes on” + « ici » = “here”. Often appears in phrases like « Je vois ce qui se passe ici » (“I see what's going on here”).
target_language_example: Explique-moi ce qui se passe ici.
native_language_example: Explain to me what's going on here.

additional_notes: Built with **ce qui** (“what/that which”) + **se passer** (“to happen”) in the **future tense** (**se passera** = “will happen”). Often used after verbs like *voir* (to see), *savoir* (to know), or in expressions like *On verra (bien) ...* (“We’ll see ...”).
target_language_example: Personne ne sait ce qui se passera demain.
native_language_example: No one knows what will happen tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used before a verb that starts with a vowel or silent h: **t’** is the elided form of **te** (to you). The typical pattern is **ce qui t’ + verb**: *ce qui t’arrive* (what’s happening to you), *ce qui t’empêche…* (what’s stopping you…), *ce qui t’attend* (what awaits you). Here **ce qui** means “what/that which” and functions as the subject of the following verb; **t’** is an object pronoun attached to that verb.
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce qui t'arrive.
native_language_example: Tell me what’s happening to you.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the cause or reason for someone’s action or feeling. It’s made of **ce qui** (“what/that which”) + **t’a fait** (passé composé of *faire*: “made you/caused you”). It’s usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., *rire, changer d’avis*) or sometimes an adjective (e.g., *peur* in *avoir peur* is expressed differently: *Qu’est-ce qui t’a fait peur ?*).
target_language_example: Ce qui t'a fait changer d'avis ?
native_language_example: What made you change your mind?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event that happened to the person you're speaking to. "ce qui" means "what/that which" (the subject of the verb), and "t'est arrivé" is the past tense of "arriver à quelqu'un" = "to happen to someone" (passé composé with "être": "est arrivé"). You can change the pronoun: "ce qui m'est arrivé" (what happened to me), "ce qui lui est arrivé" (what happened to him/her).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce qui t'est arrivé hier.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what happened to you yesterday.

meaning: "what" / "that which" (followed by something that happens to you or concerns you).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about you: **ce qui** = “what/that which,” and **te** is the object pronoun “to you/you.” Common patterns: **ce qui te fait...** (what makes you...), **ce qui te concerne/regarde** (what concerns you / what’s your business), **ce qui te semble...** (what seems ... to you). Often translated as “what” in English rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce qui te dérange.
native_language_example: I understand what’s bothering you.

additional_notes: Informal, idiomatic way to say someone is free to choose. Often used after verbs like faire or manger: « Fais/Mange ce qui te chante. » It’s close in meaning to « ce que tu veux », but a bit more casual/colloquial. Literally it’s like “what sings to you,” so it’s not a literal translation in English.
target_language_example: Prends ce qui te chante, je m’en fiche.
native_language_example: Take whatever you want, I don’t care.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the cause of someone’s reaction or action. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb: ce qui te fait rire (what makes you laugh), ce qui te fait peur (what scares you), ce qui te fait penser que… (what makes you think that…). You can change the pronoun: ce qui me fait / ce qui lui fait / ce qui nous fait, etc.
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce qui te fait croire ça ?
native_language_example: What makes you believe that?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause explaining the cause of a feeling, state, or change: *ce qui* = “what/which” (as the subject of the verb), *te* = “you” (object pronoun), *rend* = “makes” or “renders.” Often followed by an adjective or noun: *ce qui te rend heureux(se)* (“what makes you happy”), *ce qui te rend malade* (“what makes you sick”).
target_language_example: C’est ce qui te rend si stressé.
native_language_example: That’s what makes you so stressed.

meaning: “what is going to…” (what will happen/what’s coming next).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or verb phrase to introduce an expected future event or consequence: « ce qui va arriver », « ce qui va se passer », « ce qui va survenir ». Often used to warn someone or to say you know what will help/cause something.
target_language_example: Attends, je vais te montrer ce qui va se passer.
native_language_example: Wait, I’m going to show you what’s going to happen.

meaning: "what is going to happen" / "what will happen".
additional_notes: Used to talk about a future event or outcome (often something unknown or expected). Literally "that which is going to happen." Note: "arriver" can mean "to happen" (not just "to arrive"), so this phrase is about events, not someone arriving somewhere.
target_language_example: On verra ce qui va arriver demain.
native_language_example: We'll see what happens tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about upcoming events (often with uncertainty or suspense). Grammatically it’s a relative clause: **ce qui** = “what/that which,” **va** (aller) + infinitive = near future “is going to,” and **se passer** means “to happen/take place” (not “to pass”).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce qui va se passer demain.
native_language_example: I don’t know what’s going to happen tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about the person(s) addressed (vous = you). Often appears in phrases like « ce qui vous amène ici » (“what brings you here”) or « ce qui vous plaît » (“what you like”). It refers to “the thing that … you” or “what … you.”
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce qui vous inquiète.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what worries you.

additional_notes: An idiomatic way to say someone is free to do anything they please. Often used after verbs like faire: « Faites ce qui vous chante ! » = “Do whatever you want!” It can sound casual and a bit dismissive depending on tone.
target_language_example: Si vous voulez rester, restez : faites ce qui vous chante.
native_language_example: If you want to stay, stay: do whatever you want.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to an event that happened to someone. Here, **ce qui** means “what/that which” (the subject of the verb), and **vous est arrivé** is the passé composé of *arriver* (“happened to you”), with **vous** as the formal/plural “you.” You’ll often see it after verbs like *savoir* (to know), *dire* (to tell), or in questions.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé d’apprendre ce qui vous est arrivé.
native_language_example: I’m sorry to hear what happened to you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause referring to an idea or thing (often the object of a verb): *ce qu’il veut* (what he wants), *ce qu’il a dit* (what he said), *ce qu’il pense* (what he thinks). It’s a very common pattern: **ce que + subject pronoun** → *ce qu’il*, *ce qu’elle*, *ce qu’on*, etc. In more formal writing, **en ce qu’il...** can mean “in that / because” (explaining a reason).
target_language_example: Je comprends ce qu’il essaie de dire.
native_language_example: I understand what he’s trying to say.
