additional_notes: Future form of c'est / ce + être. It is used to say what something will be like or to identify something in the future. In English, ce can become it, this, or that depending on context.
target_language_example: Demain, ce sera plus facile.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it will be easier.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a hypothetical situation, to make a suggestion, or to express an opinion more softly. Often followed by an adjective (Ce serait génial.), an infinitive (Ce serait dommage de partir.), or a clause with "que" (Ce serait bien que tu viennes.).
target_language_example: Ce serait mieux de partir maintenant.
native_language_example: It would be better to leave now.

meaning: "that would be nice / good" (a suggestion, wish, or approval).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of «être» (serait) to sound polite or hypothetical: «Ce serait bien de + infinitive…» (It would be nice to…), «Ce serait bien que + subjunctive…» (It would be good if…), «Ce serait bien si + imperfect…» (It would be nice if…). In «Ce serait bien la première fois», it means “That would be a first” (often ironic).
target_language_example: Ce serait bien qu’on parte plus tôt.
native_language_example: It would be nice if we left earlier.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of être (serait) with ce to talk about a possibility, suggestion, or imagined situation. Often used to sound polite or cautious: Ce serait un plaisir / Ce serait un honneur. Can also be followed by a noun starting with a vowel using "ce serait un" + noun (e.g., un honneur).
target_language_example: Ce serait un bon moment pour en parler.
native_language_example: It would be a good time to talk about it.

additional_notes: Used with the conditional of être (serait) to talk about a possibility, hypothesis, or imagined result: « Ce serait une erreur » = “That would be a mistake.” It’s also common for softer, more polite opinions or warnings. « Une » is the feminine form of “a,” so it’s followed by a feminine noun (une erreur, une honte, une première).
target_language_example: Ce serait une bonne idée d'appeler avant de venir.
native_language_example: It would be a good idea to call before coming.

additional_notes: “Ce soit” is the present subjunctive of « c’est » (= « ce + être »). It’s used after « que » (or in fixed expressions) when the sentence expresses a wish, necessity, importance, possibility, doubt, etc.: « Je veux/Il faut/Il se peut que ce soit… ». You also see it in expressions like « où que ce soit » = “anywhere / wherever (it may be)”.
target_language_example: Il faut que ce soit fini avant demain.
native_language_example: It has to be finished before tomorrow.

meaning: “that it’s a good idea” (often with doubt: “that it’s a good idea”).
additional_notes: This is a clause used after expressions like *être sûr(e) que…*, *penser que…*, *pas sûr que…*, etc. Because these sentences often express doubt or a question, French commonly uses the subjunctive: *que ce soit…* (from *être* → *soit*). You’ll often hear it in questions like *Tu es sûr(e) que ce soit une bonne idée ?* (“Are you sure that’s a good idea?”).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas sûr que ce soit une bonne idée de partir si tard.
native_language_example: I’m not sure it’s a good idea to leave so late.

meaning: "it be" (subjunctive of être), used in phrases like "que ce soit" / "où que ce soit".
additional_notes: "Soit" is the subjunctive form of "être" (to be). You often see "ce soit" after "que" in set patterns: (1) "où que ce soit" = "anywhere / wherever" (often used in questions like "Vous êtes blessé où que ce soit ?" = "Are you hurt anywhere?"); (2) "que ce soit" in concessive or indefinite expressions, e.g. "C'est bien que ce soit comme ça" = "It's good that it's like that"; also in "quoi que ce soit / qui que ce soit" = "anything at all / anyone at all".
target_language_example: Je n’ai mal nulle part, je ne suis blessé où que ce soit.
native_language_example: I don’t hurt anywhere; I’m not injured anywhere.

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns or pronouns. Pattern: "Ce sont + noun/pronoun" (Ce sont nos livres. / Ce sont eux.) and in emphasis/cleft sentences: "Ce sont ... qui/que ..." (Ce sont eux qui...). Often translates as “these/those are” when pointing things out, or “it is/they are” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ce sont mes amis.
native_language_example: These are my friends.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe plural people/things with a noun: "Ce sont des + noun". It’s the plural form of "c’est" (singular). Often followed by an adjective + noun: "Ce sont des bonnes idées."
target_language_example: Ce sont des amis de ma sœur.
native_language_example: They’re friends of my sister.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that *they* (and not someone else) are the ones doing something. This is a French “cleft sentence” pattern: **Ce sont + [plural noun/pronoun] + qui + verb**. Use **eux** for “them/they” in an emphatic position. (Singular equivalent: **c’est lui/elle/moi/toi qui…**.)
target_language_example: Ce sont eux qui ont décidé de partir.
native_language_example: They’re the ones who decided to leave.

meaning: "these are the" / "those are the" (plural: "it’s the" + plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or point out specific people/things in the plural. Often appears in emphasis structures like "Ce sont les X qui..." (“It’s the X that...”), and in questions: "Est-ce que ce sont les... ?" (“Are these the... ?”). For singular, use "c’est le / la".
target_language_example: Ce sont les clés de Marie.
native_language_example: These are Marie’s keys.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out things/people that belong to you. It’s the plural form: **ce sont** + **mes** + plural noun/adjective. Common in questions: **Ce sont mes… ?** / **Est-ce que ce sont mes… ?**
target_language_example: Ce sont mes amis.
native_language_example: These are my friends.

meaning: Fragment/incomplete chunk; typically appears inside « C’est tout ce que vous + verbe… » meaning “That’s all that you … / That’s all you …”.
additional_notes: As written (« ce tout ce que vous ») isn’t a standard standalone phrase in French; it’s usually part of the fixed frame « C’est tout ce que vous + verbe » (e.g., *savez, voulez, pouvez faire, devez faire*). Note: « ce » here is normally preceded by « C’ » (as in « C’est »).
target_language_example: C’est tout ce que vous devez faire : c’est tout ce que vous.
native_language_example: That’s all you have to do: that’s all you.

meaning: "what" / "that which" (after a verb or idea that takes "à").
additional_notes: Used when the thing you’re referring to is introduced with the preposition "à" (e.g., s’attendre à, penser à, ressembler à). It often corresponds to English “what …” in sentences like “what I expected” or “what it looks like,” but in French you keep the "à": "ce à quoi je m’attendais" = “what I was expecting.”
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce à quoi il pense.
native_language_example: I don’t know what he’s thinking about.

additional_notes: Used to point to something specific or present (often in writing, presentations, instructions, or when indicating an object). “Ceci” is a more formal/neutral “this” than “ça”; in everyday speech people often say “C’est …” instead.
target_language_example: Ceci est la dernière page du document.
native_language_example: This is the last page of the document.

additional_notes: Used to point something out or define/identify it. Very common in explanations, labels, presentations, or when showing an object. For feminine nouns, use "ceci est une"; for plural, "ce sont des". In everyday speech, people often use "c'est un/une" instead of the more formal "ceci est un/une".
target_language_example: Ceci est un livre très intéressant.
native_language_example: This is a very interesting book.

additional_notes: Used for the belt you fasten in a car, plane, etc. Common with the verbs "attacher" (to fasten) and "porter" (to wear). Often said in instructions: "Veuillez attacher votre ceinture de sécurité."
target_language_example: N'oublie pas d'attacher ta ceinture de sécurité.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to fasten your seat belt.

additional_notes: Used in more formal French to ask a question by inverting the verb and subject pronoun: « Cela a-t-il… ? ». The « -t- » is added for pronunciation between two vowels (« a » and « il »). It’s most often seen with the passé composé (auxiliary « avoir »), e.g. « Cela a-t-il marché ? » = “Did that work?”.
target_language_example: Cela a-t-il marché comme prévu ?
native_language_example: Did that work as planned?

additional_notes: Used as a transition to add a contrast, nuance, or exception to what was just said—similar to “that said,” “still,” or “however” in English. Often followed by a comma: « Cela dit, … ».
target_language_example: Cela dit, je préfère attendre demain.
native_language_example: That said, I’d rather wait until tomorrow.

meaning: “does that … ?” / “how much does that make (in total)?” (formal question form).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of **cela fait** (“that makes/does”). It’s used to ask about an effect or result (e.g., **Cela fait-il mal ?** = “Does it hurt?”; **Cela fait-il une différence ?** = “Does it make a difference?”) or about a total amount with **combien** (**Combien cela fait-il en tout ?** = “How much is it altogether?”). In everyday speech, people often use **ça** and no inversion: **Ça fait mal ?** / **Ça fait une différence ?** / **Ça fait combien ?**.
target_language_example: Combien cela fait-il par personne ?
native_language_example: How much is that per person?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a possibility or something uncertain. Here, pourrait is the conditional form of pouvoir, so the phrase often corresponds to English "could" or sometimes "might." In everyday speech, people often say ça pourrait instead of cela pourrait.
target_language_example: Cela pourrait marcher.
native_language_example: That could work.

additional_notes: Used to say something is possible but not certain. "Cela" = "that/it"; "pourrait" is the conditional of "pouvoir" (could/might); "être" = to be. Often followed by an adjective (dangereux, faux) or a noun phrase (n'importe qui). In speech, you’ll often hear "ça pourrait être" instead of "cela pourrait être".
target_language_example: Cela pourrait être une erreur, vérifie encore une fois.
native_language_example: It could be a mistake—check one more time.

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning or implication of something. Often appears in questions: « Qu’est-ce que cela signifie ? » (What does that mean?), « Cela signifie-t-il que… ? » (Does that mean that…?). In casual speech, « cela » is often replaced by « ça »: « Ça signifie… ».
target_language_example: Si tu ne réponds pas, cela signifie que tu n’es pas disponible.
native_language_example: If you don’t reply, that means you’re not available.

meaning: "will it" / "is it going to" (in a formal question).
additional_notes: This is an inverted question form: "cela" (that/it) + "va" (goes/is going) + "-t-" (linking sound) + "il" (it). It’s used to ask about what will happen or how something will be (often with another verb in the infinitive: "Cela va-t-il prendre…?", "Cela va-t-il faire…?"). More formal than "Est-ce que ça va…?" or "Ça va…?".
target_language_example: Cela va-t-il marcher si on change de plan ?
native_language_example: Will it work if we change plans?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask for permission or to request someone do something. It’s built on the conditional of déranger (“to bother”), so it literally means “Would that bother you…?”. Often followed by de + infinitive (Cela vous dérangerait-il de…?) or si + imperfect (Cela vous dérangerait-il si je…?).
target_language_example: Cela vous dérangerait-il de parler un peu moins fort ?
native_language_example: Would you mind speaking a little more quietly?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a nuance, limitation, or contrast with what was just said. Often comes after a statement, like: "..., cela étant, ..." It’s fairly formal and can be replaced by "cependant" or "toutefois" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Je comprends ton point de vue ; cela étant, je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I understand your point of view; that being said, I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Feminine singular demonstrative pronoun used to point out a specific item close to the speaker or the one being indicated. It replaces a feminine noun you don’t repeat: « Cette boîte est grande. Celle-ci est plus petite. » For masculine, use « celui-ci »; plural: « celles-ci » / « ceux-ci ». Often contrasted with « celle-là » (“that one”).
target_language_example: Entre ces deux robes, je prends celle-ci.
native_language_example: Between these two dresses, I’ll take this one.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative pronoun **celle-ci** (“this one”, feminine) + **est** (“is”) to point out a specific item/person, often in contrast with others (e.g., *celle-là* = “that one”). For masculine, you’d use **celui-ci est**.
target_language_example: Celle-ci est la meilleure option.
native_language_example: This one is the best option.

meaning: "that one" (feminine; the one there / the one you mean).
additional_notes: Demonstrative pronoun used to point out or identify a specific feminine thing/person already known from context. It often contrasts with "celle-ci" (this one). It can stand alone as a short answer: "Celle-là." Use "celui-là" for masculine.
target_language_example: Prends celle-là, pas celle-ci.
native_language_example: Take that one, not this one.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific thing/person and describe it. « celle-là » is a demonstrative pronoun meaning “that one” for feminine nouns (contrast: « celui-là » for masculine; « celles-là / ceux-là » for plural). Often used when comparing or choosing between several options (e.g., “This one is nice, but that one is different.”).
target_language_example: Celle-là est la meilleure, à mon avis.
native_language_example: That one is the best, in my opinion.

additional_notes: Demonstrative pronoun used to point to specific items already known from context. It replaces a feminine plural noun (e.g., des erreurs → celles-ci). Often contrasts with celles-là (“those ones” over there / the other ones).
target_language_example: Parmi toutes les robes, je préfère celles-ci.
native_language_example: Among all the dresses, I prefer these ones.

additional_notes: "Celles-ci" is a feminine plural demonstrative pronoun meaning “these ones” (used for things that are feminine nouns or understood from context). It points to specific items nearby or just mentioned, and it’s often contrasted with "celles-là" (“those ones”). "Sont" is the plural form of "être" (“to be”).
target_language_example: Celles-ci sont plus chères que celles-là.
native_language_example: These ones are more expensive than those ones.

meaning: "those (ones)" (feminine plural), often meaning “those there / those ones.”
additional_notes: Demonstrative pronoun used to point to specific items that are feminine plural (replacing a noun like *chaussures*, *robes*, *fleurs*). Often used when choosing or comparing: *celles-là* (“those”), vs *celles-ci* (“these”). You can use it alone as an answer: *Celles-là.* = “Those.”
target_language_example: Je préfère celles-là, pas celles-ci.
native_language_example: I prefer those ones, not these.

meaning: “this one” (the one here / the one you’re pointing at).
additional_notes: Used to point out a specific item/person close to the speaker (contrast with “celui-là” = “that one” over there). It replaces a noun and agrees in gender/number: celui-ci (m. sg.), celle-ci (f. sg.), ceux-ci (m. pl.), celles-ci (f. pl.). Often used when choosing or comparing things.
target_language_example: Je vais prendre celui-ci, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll take this one, please.

meaning: "this one is" (referring to a specific masculine item/person).
additional_notes: "Celui-ci" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "this one" (masculine singular), often contrasted with "celui-là" ("that one"). It replaces a noun you don’t want to repeat: "Lequel ? — Celui-ci." For feminine, use "celle-ci"; for plural, "ceux-ci / celles-ci". "Est" is the verb "to be" (il est).
target_language_example: Je prends celui-ci : celui-ci est moins cher.
native_language_example: I’ll take this one: this one is cheaper.

additional_notes: masculine singular demonstrative pronoun. Used to point to or single out a specific person or thing, often in contrast with another option. It can refer to someone with a slightly dismissive tone depending on context. Related forms: celle-là, ceux-là, celles-là.
target_language_example: Je prends celui-là.
native_language_example: I'll take that one.

meaning: “that one is …” (referring to a specific person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to point out or contrast one specific item/person with another (often vs. “celui-ci est…” = “this one is…”). “Celui-là” is masculine singular; common related forms: “celle-là” (fem.), “ceux-là” (masc. pl.), “celles-là” (fem. pl.). In casual speech you may hear “celui-là est pas …” instead of the more standard “celui-là n’est pas …”.
target_language_example: Je préfère ce modèle, mais celui-là est moins cher.
native_language_example: I prefer this model, but that one is cheaper.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person identified by the clause that follows. It can point to a specific person ("Tom est celui qui...") or make a general statement ("Celui qui..."). The form changes with gender and number: "celle qui," "ceux qui," "celles qui."
target_language_example: Celui qui arrive en dernier ferme la porte.
native_language_example: Whoever arrives last closes the door.

additional_notes: Used to identify a specific person (male/masculine singular) who did something: « celui qui a + past participle ». Often translates as “the one who…” or “the person who…”. Feminine: « celle qui a »; plural: « ceux qui ont / celles qui ont ».
target_language_example: Je veux parler à celui qui a envoyé ce message.
native_language_example: I want to talk to the person who sent this message.

additional_notes: Used to express an exact percentage (100%) or strong agreement/certainty (like “absolutely”). Often said as an adverb: « Je suis cent pour cent d’accord » (I 100% agree). You can also use « à cent pour cent » meaning “100% / completely.”
target_language_example: Je suis cent pour cent sûr que c’est la bonne adresse.
native_language_example: I’m 100% sure this is the right address.

meaning: one hundred and seven years (107 years).
additional_notes: Used to state an age or a duration in years. In French you often say the number directly before "ans" (years). You may also hear it without "et": "cent sept" (107).
target_language_example: Le musée a cent sept ans.
native_language_example: The museum is 107 years old.

additional_notes: Used to express an approximate quantity in the hundreds. Often appears with determiners like "des centaines de" (hundreds of) or "plusieurs centaines de" (several hundred). It’s followed by a noun (usually plural): "des centaines de personnes".
target_language_example: Il y avait des centaines de spectateurs dans la salle.
native_language_example: There were hundreds of spectators in the hall.

additional_notes: Refers to a facility (often large-scale) that produces electricity for a city/region. Used with articles like « une/la centrale électrique ». Can also be used figuratively about a very energetic person or place (« Une vraie centrale électrique ! »).
target_language_example: Cette ville dépend d’une centrale électrique près de la rivière.
native_language_example: This city depends on a power plant near the river.

additional_notes: Refers to the central part of a town/city where many shops, offices, and services are. Common with directions and location: « aller au centre-ville » (go downtown), « en centre-ville » (in downtown), « en plein centre-ville » (right in the heart of downtown).
target_language_example: Je te retrouve au centre-ville devant la mairie.
native_language_example: I'll meet you downtown in front of city hall.

additional_notes: A common noun for a building/complex with many stores (magasins). Often used with prepositions like « dans/au centre commercial » (in/at the mall).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au centre commercial à 15 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the mall at 3 p.m.

meaning: a vicious circle; a self-reinforcing negative cycle.
additional_notes: Used when a bad situation causes more of itself (problem → effect → worsens the problem). Often with verbs like « sortir de », « briser », « être piégé dans » un cercle vicieux.
target_language_example: Sans aide, il risque de rester dans un cercle vicieux de dettes.
native_language_example: Without help, he risks staying in a vicious circle of debt.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning a toy/object that flies in the wind, usually attached to a string (une ficelle). Often used with verbs like faire du cerf-volant (to fly kites) and voler (to fly). Despite the literal parts (cerf = deer, volant = flying), it simply means “kite.”
target_language_example: On va au parc pour faire du cerf-volant.
native_language_example: We’re going to the park to fly a kite.

meaning: “the icing on the cake” / an extra bonus that makes something even better.
additional_notes: Used to introduce or point out a final positive detail on top of something already good (often as a set phrase: « C’est la cerise sur le gâteau. »). It can also be used at the start of a sentence like “To top it all off, …”. Depending on context and tone, it can be slightly ironic.
target_language_example: On a eu des places gratuites, et la cerise sur le gâteau, on a rencontré l’acteur principal.
native_language_example: We got free tickets, and to top it all off, we met the lead actor.

additional_notes: Plural phrase used when you don’t want (or don’t need) to be specific about which things you mean. It often introduces a general statement (“some things never change”) or refers to a few particular items in context (“review certain things”). Common patterns: « certaines choses ne… », « il y a certaines choses qui… », « en certaines choses » (believe in certain things), « avoir certaines choses en commun » (have some things in common).
target_language_example: Je dois te dire certaines choses avant de partir.
native_language_example: I need to tell you some things before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified group of people (not everyone). Often introduces a general statement, opinion, or tendency. Feminine plural because it agrees with the feminine noun "personnes"; with masculine/mixed "gens" you’d use "certaines gens" (or "certains" + a masculine noun).
target_language_example: Certaines personnes préfèrent travailler tôt le matin.
native_language_example: Some people prefer to work early in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to point out specific shoes that are close by, being shown, or already known in the conversation. "Ces" is the plural demonstrative determiner (these/those), and "chaussures" is feminine plural. Often used when shopping, asking about size, ownership, fit, or repairs.
target_language_example: J’aime beaucoup ces chaussures, mais elles sont trop grandes.
native_language_example: I really like these shoes, but they’re too big.

additional_notes: Used to describe a pair of shoes you’re talking about. *Ces* = “these” (plural), *chaussures* = “shoes” (feminine plural), and *sont* is the plural form of “to be” (être) for “they are.” Often followed by an adjective or description (e.g., *trop chères* “too expensive,” *trop petites* “too small,” *un peu grandes* “a bit big”).
target_language_example: Ces chaussures sont confortables, mais elles sont un peu grandes.
native_language_example: These shoes are comfortable, but they’re a bit big.

additional_notes: Plural demonstrative phrase: "ces" = "these" (also can mean "those" depending on context) + "choses" = "things." Used for objects, stuff, or abstract matters ("these kinds of things"). Questions often use inversion ("Ces choses sont-elles… ?" = "Are these things…?").
target_language_example: Je n'aime pas ces choses-là.
native_language_example: I don't like those things.

meaning: "those things" / "those kinds of things" (the things we’re talking about).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to specific things already known from context. Adding "-là" puts extra emphasis on which things you mean (similar to “those particular things” or “that sort of thing”). It can also be used vaguely or as a mild euphemism when you don’t want to name something directly.
target_language_example: Je n'aime pas trop ces choses-là.
native_language_example: I don't really like those kinds of things.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most recent days up to now (a short, recent period). It often corresponds to English “lately” in context. You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence: « Ces derniers jours, ... » / « ..., ces derniers jours. »
target_language_example: Je suis très fatigué ces derniers jours.
native_language_example: I've been very tired these last few days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a recent period up to now (often with the present tense or passé composé). Can be placed at the start of the sentence for emphasis or at the end as a time expression.
target_language_example: Ces derniers temps, je dors mal à cause du stress.
native_language_example: Lately, I’ve been sleeping badly because of stress.

meaning: these last (few) years; in recent years.
additional_notes: Used to talk about changes or trends over a recent period up to now. Often goes at the end of the sentence. Can also be phrased as « ces dernières années, ... » at the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ces dernières années, j’ai beaucoup voyagé pour le travail.
native_language_example: In recent years, I’ve traveled a lot for work.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to point out exactly two items or people nearby or already mentioned. It agrees with the noun’s gender: use "ces" for masculine plural and for feminine plural before a vowel sound (e.g., "ces deux hommes", "ces deux étudiantes", "ces deux écoles"), but use "ces deux" (not *ces*) before feminine plural nouns starting with a consonant: "ces deux" is still correct because "ces" is the plural demonstrative for both genders.
target_language_example: Ces deux livres sont très intéressants.
native_language_example: These two books are very interesting.

additional_notes: Used to point out or refer to two specific people already known from context. The "-là" adds emphasis (like “those two (there) / those two in particular”). Often said with a pointing/identifying tone: « Ils vont bien, ces deux-là. »
target_language_example: Je ne les connais pas bien, mais ces deux-là ont l'air sympas.
native_language_example: I don’t know them well, but those two seem nice.

additional_notes: "Ces" is the plural demonstrative determiner meaning "these" (for nouns that are masculine or feminine plural). Used to point out specific flowers you’re talking about or showing. Often followed by a relative clause like "ces fleurs que tu vois..." ("these flowers that you see...").
target_language_example: Ces fleurs sentent bon, mais elles sont fragiles.
native_language_example: These flowers smell nice, but they’re fragile.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative plural "ces" (= these/those) with "gens" (= people). Often refers to a specific group of people; depending on tone/context, it can sound distancing or judgmental (like “those people”). You may also hear "ces gens-là" for extra emphasis (“those people/that bunch”).
target_language_example: Pourquoi ces gens sont-ils si en colère ?
native_language_example: Why are these people so angry?

additional_notes: Used to describe a group of people (“ces gens” = “these people”) with a verb/adjective that follows. Often introduces an opinion or description (e.g., dangereux, fous, bizarres). Note: “ces gens” is generally masculine plural for agreement (e.g., “Ces gens sont dangereux”).
target_language_example: Ces gens sont très gentils.
native_language_example: These people are very nice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the current period of time (recently, nowadays), not literally “on these specific days.” Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Je travaille beaucoup ces jours-ci.
native_language_example: I’ve been working a lot lately.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative determiner “ces” (= “these”) with a plural noun. “Ces” is used before both masculine and feminine plural nouns (ces livres, ces tables). Often points to specific books that are known, visible, or previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Tu peux me prêter ces livres ?
native_language_example: Can you lend me these books?

additional_notes: "Ces livres" means "these books" (plural). "Sont" is the verb "to be" (ils/elles sont = they are). Use this to describe the books (adjectives like neufs/vieux), to say who they belong to (les miens / à moi), or to add information (disponibles).
target_language_example: Ces livres sont très intéressants.
native_language_example: These books are very interesting.

additional_notes: Demonstrative adjective + noun: **ces** means “these” (or “those”) before a plural noun. It refers to specific photos the speaker and listener can identify (e.g., in your hand, on a screen, in an album). You can add **-là** for emphasis or contrast: *ces photos-là* = “those photos (right there) / those specific photos.”
target_language_example: Tu peux m'envoyer ces photos ?
native_language_example: Can you send me these photos?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the current period of time (recent weeks/months), often when asking how someone has been or describing a change in habits. It can be placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: « Ces temps-ci, … » or « …, ces temps-ci. »
target_language_example: Je suis un peu fatigué ces temps-ci.
native_language_example: I’ve been a bit tired lately.

additional_notes: "Truc" is a very common, informal word for an object, something unspecified, or "stuff" (often like "thingy"). Depending on context, it can also mean a tip/trick or a gadget. Use "ces" for plural "these" with a noun (ces + noun).
target_language_example: Tu peux ranger ces trucs dans la boîte ?
native_language_example: Can you put this stuff away in the box?

additional_notes: From the verb **cesser (de)** = “to stop (doing)”. **Cesse de + infinitive** is often used as a command: *Cesse de parler !* (“Stop talking!”). With **ne cesse de + infinitive**, it means “keeps (on) … / won’t stop …”: *Il ne cesse de se plaindre.* (“He keeps complaining.”).
target_language_example: Cesse de faire ça, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop doing that, please.

additional_notes: “Appareil photo” means “camera.” “Cet” is the masculine singular form of “this” used before a word starting with a vowel sound (like a- in appareil): cet appareil photo (this camera).
target_language_example: J’aime bien cet appareil photo, il prend de très belles photos.
native_language_example: I really like this camera; it takes very nice photos.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the afternoon of today. It’s the masculine form of "ce/cet" because "après-midi" is masculine and starts with a vowel sound (so you say "cet" not "ce"). You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence: "Cet après-midi, je…" / "Je… cet après-midi."
target_language_example: On se voit cet après-midi ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other this afternoon?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the afternoon of today. �Cet�e0 is the masculine form of �b4ce�b4 used before a vowel sound (apr�e8s-midi). You can use it for asking about plans or availability today: �ab Tu es libre cet apr�e8s-midi ? �bb
target_language_example: On se voit cet après-midi ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other this afternoon?

additional_notes: "Cet" is the masculine singular demonstrative adjective used before a masculine noun that starts with a vowel sound (like arbre). It can mean either “this” or “that” depending on context.
target_language_example: Regarde cet arbre, il est énorme !
native_language_example: Look at that tree, it's huge!

meaning: "this money" (a specific sum/amount being talked about).
additional_notes: "Cet" is the masculine singular demonstrative used before a vowel sound (here: argent). It points to a particular money amount already known from the context (e.g., the money we found, the money you owe, the money from the deal). Note: French "argent" means "money" in general; it can look like English "argent" (= silver), but the meaning here is "money."
target_language_example: On doit utiliser cet argent pour payer le loyer.
native_language_example: We have to use this money to pay the rent.

additional_notes: “Cet” is the masculine singular form of “ce” used before a vowel sound (article starts with a vowel). “Article” can mean a newspaper/online article, or an item for sale/a product; the context usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: J’ai lu cet article ce matin et je l’ai trouvé très utile.
native_language_example: I read this article this morning and found it very useful.

additional_notes: Used with the demonstrative adjective **cet** (a form of **ce**) before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel sound (e.g., *endroit*). Often used to refer to a specific place that’s nearby, visible, or already known in the context. Compare: *ce lieu* (more formal), *cet endroit* (common, everyday).
target_language_example: J'aime beaucoup cet endroit, c'est calme.
native_language_example: I really like this place; it's quiet.

additional_notes: Used to describe a place you’re in or talking about. It’s followed by an adjective (génial, incroyable, parfait, super) or a longer description. "Cet" is used because "endroit" is masculine and starts with a vowel sound (you’d say "ce lieu est" but "cet endroit est").
target_language_example: Cet endroit est trop bruyant pour moi.
native_language_example: This place is too noisy for me.

additional_notes: "Cet" is the masculine singular demonstrative adjective used before a vowel sound (or silent h): "cet enfant". With other masculine nouns, you usually use "ce" ("ce garçon"), and with feminine nouns you use "cette" ("cette enfant" is rare; normally "cette fille"). The choice between "this" and "that" depends on context.
target_language_example: Cet enfant a besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: This child needs help.

additional_notes: Time expression used to talk about the current/coming winter (depending on context). It uses the demonstrative adjective "cet" (a form of "ce") because "hiver" is masculine and starts with a vowel sound. Often placed at the start of a sentence as a time marker: "Cet hiver, ..."
target_language_example: Cet hiver, je veux aller à la montagne.
native_language_example: This winter, I want to go to the mountains.

additional_notes: "Cet" is the masculine singular demonstrative adjective used before a vowel sound (h muet) or a silent h: cet homme. It points to a specific man the speaker has in mind; in conversation it can mean either "this man" (near/just mentioned) or "that man" (referring back or pointing).
target_language_example: Qui est cet homme près de la porte ?
native_language_example: Who is that man near the door?

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe a specific man (“cet homme” = “this man”), followed by the verb “est” (is) and then a description or identity. With a job/role: often no article (e.g., « Cet homme est docteur. »). With a specific known person/unique title: use « le/la » (e.g., « Cet homme est le roi. »). With a noun meaning “a …”: use « un/une » (e.g., « Cet homme est un génie. »).
target_language_example: Cet homme est très gentil.
native_language_example: This man is very kind.

additional_notes: “Cet” is the masculine singular demonstrative adjective used before a noun that starts with a vowel sound (hôtel has a silent H). You use it to point out a specific hotel: Cet hôtel est cher. (For most other masculine nouns, use “ce” (ce restaurant); for feminine, “cette” (cette chambre).)
target_language_example: J’aime bien cet hôtel, il est calme.
native_language_example: I like this hotel, it’s quiet.

additional_notes: Used to point out or refer to a specific bird. “Cet” is the demonstrative adjective “this/that” used before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel sound (like oiseau). It can mean “this bird” (near) or “that bird” (far), depending on context.
target_language_example: Regarde cet oiseau dans l'arbre !
native_language_example: Look at that bird in the tree!

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative determiner **cet** (= “this/that”) because **ordinateur** is masculine singular and starts with a vowel sound (o-). With most other masculine singular nouns, you use **ce** (e.g., **ce livre**).
target_language_example: Cet ordinateur est très rapide.
native_language_example: This computer is very fast.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the summer of the current year (the upcoming summer or the one happening now, depending on context). It’s the demonstrative adjective “ce/cet” + “été”; “cet” is used because “été” starts with a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Je vais travailler à Paris cet été.
native_language_example: I’m going to work in Paris this summer.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific situation, issue, or case already known in the conversation. Common in formal contexts (a matter/issue) and also in crime/investigation contexts (a case). It can also mean an 'affair' as in a situation/incident, not necessarily a romantic affair.
target_language_example: On doit régler cette affaire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: We need to settle this matter today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the current calendar year, often for plans, events, or comparisons with other years. It can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Cette année, je veux apprendre le français.
native_language_example: This year, I want to learn French.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the afternoon of today. Note: the standard form is **cet après-midi** (masculine **cet** before a vowel sound: *après-midi*). **Cette après-midi** is sometimes heard/used, but **cet après-midi** is generally recommended in careful French.
target_language_example: Pleuvra-t-il cette après-midi ?
native_language_example: Will it rain this afternoon?

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific feminine noun (boîte). Often refers to a physical container (a box), but can also mean a tin/can depending on context (e.g., a food container). You may hear it with emphasis forms: « cette boîte-ci » (this one here) and « cette boîte-là » (that one there).
target_language_example: Tu peux poser cette boîte sur la table ?
native_language_example: Can you put this box on the table?

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific song (one you’re talking about, hearing, or have in mind). "Cette" is the feminine singular form of "this" and agrees with "chanson" (feminine).
target_language_example: J'adore cette chanson !
native_language_example: I love this song!

additional_notes: Used to point out or refer back to a particular woman (someone present, shown in a photo, or already mentioned). In questions like « C’est qui, cette femme ? », it often means “Who is that woman?” even though it literally uses “this.” « cette » is the feminine singular form of “this/that” (masc.: « cet/cette homme »).
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas cette femme, mais elle me semble sympathique.
native_language_example: I don’t know this/that woman, but she seems nice.

additional_notes: "Cette" is the feminine singular form of "ce/cet/cette" (this/that). In French, "cette" can mean either "this" or "that" depending on context. Often used to point out a specific girl already known or identified in the conversation; tone can be neutral or negative (e.g., in "Je déteste cette fille").
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu parles toujours de cette fille ?
native_language_example: Why do you always talk about that girl?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the present/most recent occurrence of a repeated situation, often to contrast with other times (e.g., “not like last time”). It can be placed at the start (“Cette fois, …”) or at the end (“…, cette fois.”).
target_language_example: Cette fois, je vais le faire correctement.
native_language_example: This time, I’m going to do it properly.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the present/next attempt or occasion, often contrasting with previous times (e.g., "not this time"). It can be placed at the start or end of the sentence for emphasis. Refers to a specific occasion, not a general habit (contrast with "d'habitude" = usually).
target_language_example: Cette fois-ci, je vais arriver à l'heure.
native_language_example: This time, I’m going to be on time.

additional_notes: Literally “this story,” but in everyday speech it often refers to an ongoing situation or problem (“this business/this affair”), especially when someone is tired of it or it’s dragging on: « Cette histoire commence à durer. » Also note that « histoire » can mean both “story” and “history,” so the meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: On en a assez de cette histoire, ça traîne depuis des semaines.
native_language_example: We’ve had enough of this whole thing; it’s been dragging on for weeks.

meaning: “this story is …” (used to describe a story).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective or past participle to give an opinion or description: « Cette histoire est absurde / triste / monotone »; « … est basée sur des faits réels ». « Cette » is feminine singular (“this”), because « histoire » is feminine. In exclamations you may see « Que cette histoire est … ! » = “How … this story is!”
target_language_example: Cette histoire est vraiment intéressante.
native_language_example: This story is really interesting.

additional_notes: "Cette" is the feminine demonstrative adjective meaning "this/that" used with feminine singular nouns like "information." It often refers to information already mentioned or understood from context. Common with verbs like "obtenir" (to obtain), "tenir de" (to get/learn from), "donner" (to give), and "garder pour soi" (to keep to yourself).
target_language_example: Je peux te transmettre cette information par e-mail.
native_language_example: I can send you this information by email.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific letter you have, see, or are talking about. "Cette" agrees with the feminine noun "lettre". Often appears in simple phrases like "Cette lettre est pour toi/vous" (This letter is for you) or questions like "De qui est cette lettre ?" (Whose letter is this?).
target_language_example: Garde cette lettre, elle est importante.
native_language_example: Keep this letter; it’s important.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific machine you’re talking about (one nearby, just mentioned, or understood from context). "Cette" agrees with the feminine noun "machine". Common with verbs like "utiliser", "faire fonctionner" (to operate/get working), "tomber en panne" (to break down), and "se servir de" (to use).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas comment réparer cette machine.
native_language_example: I don’t understand how to fix this machine.

additional_notes: Used to point out or refer to a particular house. “Cette” is the feminine singular form of “this” (ce/cet/cette). Use it when the noun is feminine and singular, like “maison”. Often followed by descriptions (size, age, number of rooms) or questions about it.
target_language_example: J’aime bien cette maison, mais elle est trop grande.
native_language_example: I like this house, but it’s too big.

additional_notes: Used to describe or give information about a specific house. "Cette" means "this" (feminine singular), "maison" is feminine, and "est" is the verb "être" (to be) in the present tense (he/she/it is). What follows often agrees with the feminine noun (e.g., "Cette maison est belle").
target_language_example: Cette maison est trop chère pour nous.
native_language_example: This house is too expensive for us.

meaning: "this shit" (vulgar): this mess / this crap / this thing (said angrily).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used to complain about a situation ("all this shit"), to insult something you think is worthless ("this crap"), or to refer to an object when you’re annoyed ("Open this thing"). Often said with impatience or anger; avoid in polite/company settings.
target_language_example: J’en ai marre de cette merde.
native_language_example: I’m sick of this shit.

additional_notes: Means “this night” and depends on context: for something happening later today it’s “tonight”; for something that happened during the previous night it’s “last night.” Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence as a time expression.
target_language_example: Cette nuit, il va neiger.
native_language_example: Tonight, it’s going to snow.

meaning: that night (the specific night being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to point back to a particular night already known from context (often in storytelling, reports, or when asking about a past event). It contrasts with "cette nuit" (tonight/last night depending on context) by adding "-là" to mean “that one (not another)”.
target_language_example: Cette nuit-là, on a entendu un bruit étrange dans la rue.
native_language_example: That night, we heard a strange noise in the street.

additional_notes: Used to point out a particular photo that’s nearby, being shown, or already known in the conversation. « cette » is the feminine singular demonstrative adjective (“this/that”), used because « photo » is feminine; plural would be « ces photos ». Depending on context, it can mean “this” or “that.”
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de cette photo ?
native_language_example: Do you remember this photo?

additional_notes: Uses the passive voice in the past: **a été prise** (from *prendre*), meaning someone took the photo (the person isn’t specified). Often followed by **dans/à/en** + place (*dans un zoo*, *à Nara*) or **il y a / en / pendant** + time (*il y a trois ans*, *en mai*, *pendant mon enfance*).
target_language_example: Cette photo a été prise à Paris en 2019.
native_language_example: This photo was taken in Paris in 2019.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific sentence/phrase that’s being discussed or shown. "Cette" is the feminine singular demonstrative adjective (“this/that”), and "phrase" is feminine, so you say "cette phrase" (not *ce* phrase). Common in instructions about language: *Lisez/Traduisez/Supprimez cette phrase*.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous expliquer cette phrase ?
native_language_example: Can you explain this sentence?

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific phrase/sentence. "Cette" is the feminine singular form of “this,” because "phrase" is feminine. After "est" (from "être", “to be”), you typically add an adjective or description, which usually agrees in gender/number with "phrase" (e.g., "cette phrase est intéressante").
target_language_example: Cette phrase est difficile à comprendre.
native_language_example: This sentence is hard to understand.

meaning: "this room" (also: "this piece" / "this coin," depending on context).
additional_notes: Pièce can mean a room in a house/apartment (common in everyday speech: peindre cette pièce = paint this room). It can also mean a piece/object or a coin (une pièce de monnaie). The exact meaning depends on context. Note that it looks like English “piece,” but often means “room.”
target_language_example: On va ranger cette pièce avant l’arrivée des invités.
native_language_example: We’re going to tidy up this room before the guests arrive.

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific room (pièce) that’s close by or being talked about. Follow it with an adjective (agréable, sale, lumineuse), a superlative (la plus froide), or a phrase like sous surveillance. Note: pièce can also mean a “piece” (of something) or a “coin,” but here it clearly means “room.”
target_language_example: Cette pièce est trop bruyante pour dormir.
native_language_example: This room is too noisy to sleep in.

meaning: "this door" (a specific door nearby or just mentioned).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "cette" (feminine singular) + the noun "porte". Use it to point out or refer back to one particular door: asking for the key, saying where it leads ("donne sur" / "mène à"), or asking someone to open it.
target_language_example: Ne ferme pas cette porte, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t close this door, please.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a noun in a rude/angry way, like English “this fucking + noun.” Very strong and offensive in many situations; avoid in polite/company settings. It agrees with the noun: ce putain de + masculine noun (ce putain de problème), cet putain d’ + vowel sound (cet putain d’ordinateur), cette putain de + feminine noun (cette putain de porte), ces putains de + plural (ces putains de clés).
target_language_example: Éteins cette putain de musique, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Turn off this fucking music, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular question that is being asked now or has already been mentioned. "Cette" is the feminine singular demonstrative adjective used with "question" (feminine): cette question = this question (nearby/in focus).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas encore la réponse à cette question.
native_language_example: I don't have the answer to this question yet.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific dress that’s near you, being shown, or already mentioned. "Cette" agrees with the feminine noun "robe"; for a masculine noun you’d use "ce" (or "cet" before a vowel sound). Often used while shopping or giving compliments about clothing.
target_language_example: J’aime beaucoup cette robe, elle est très élégante.
native_language_example: I really like this dress; it’s very elegant.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the current week (the week you are in now). It can also mean “earlier this week” when combined with a time phrase like "plus tôt".
target_language_example: On se voit cette semaine ?
native_language_example: Are we seeing each other this week?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "cette" (feminine singular) + "ville" (city/town). It points to a specific city understood from context, or one you’re talking about/looking at; in a question it can express surprise or criticism ("Qu'est-ce que c'est que cette ville ?" = “What kind of place is this?”).
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas bien cette ville, mais elle a l'air sympa.
native_language_example: I don't know this city very well, but it seems nice.

meaning: “this car” (a specific car nearby or already mentioned).
additional_notes: "Cette" is the feminine singular form of "ce/cet/cette" (= this/that). It agrees with the feminine noun "voiture". Often used when pointing at a car or referring back to one you’ve been talking about; in questions like "À qui est cette voiture ?", it means "Whose car is this?".
target_language_example: Cette voiture est à mon voisin.
native_language_example: This car belongs to my neighbor.

meaning: 'this car is …' (used to describe or identify a specific car).
additional_notes: "Cette voiture" means "this car" (feminine singular). "Est" is the verb "to be" (he/she/it is). You typically follow it with an adjective (couleur, état: "noire", "comme neuve"), a noun phrase to identify/claim it ("la mienne", "la sienne"), or possession with "à + stress pronoun" ("à lui", "à elle").
target_language_example: Cette voiture est très pratique en ville.
native_language_example: This car is very practical in the city.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific period in the past that’s already known from context (similar to “back then” or “in those days”). Often appears with time expressions like « depuis cette époque » (“since that time”). « époque » can mean an era in history or simply a period in someone’s life.
target_language_example: Depuis cette époque, beaucoup de choses ont changé.
native_language_example: Since that time, a lot of things have changed.

additional_notes: Used to point to specific items/people that are close in space/time or in the conversation. It replaces a noun (e.g., 'those books' → 'ceux-ci' if 'books' is already understood). Typically refers to masculine plural nouns; for feminine plural, use 'celles-ci'. Often contrasts with 'ceux-là' = 'those (ones)' farther away / the other ones.
target_language_example: Parmi tous les modèles, je préfère ceux-ci.
native_language_example: Among all the models, I prefer these ones.

meaning: “those (ones)”, referring to specific masculine plural items (not near the speaker).
additional_notes: Masculine plural demonstrative pronoun: ceux (ones) + -là (over there / the ones you mean). Used to point out or contrast items: « Ceux-ci …, ceux-là … ». For feminine plural, use « celles-là ». Often used with « de »: « un de ceux-là » = “one of those.”
target_language_example: Je préfère ceux-là, pas ceux-ci.
native_language_example: I prefer those (ones), not these.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by what follows in the relative clause with qui. It can stand alone (“Ceux qui…” = “Those who…”) or follow de (“faire partie de ceux qui…” = “to be among those who…”). Feminine form: celles qui; singular: celui qui / celle qui.
target_language_example: Ceux qui veulent venir peuvent s’inscrire ici.
native_language_example: Those who want to come can sign up here.

meaning: "those who have" (the people who have done/experienced something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by what they have done or what has happened to them. It’s followed by a past participle (e.g., "ceux qui ont quitté", "ceux qui ont vécu"). You’ll often see it contrasted with "ceux qui n’ont pas…" (“those who haven’t…”). Feminine plural is "celles qui ont".
target_language_example: Je remercie ceux qui ont aidé pendant la crise.
native_language_example: I thank those who helped during the crisis.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific group of people defined by what they are like or their condition/location, often followed by an adjective, a prepositional phrase, or a further description: « Ceux qui sont devant… », « ceux qui sont prêts… ». It contrasts with « ceux qui ont » (“those who have”) and can be feminine: « celles qui sont ».
target_language_example: Ceux qui sont en retard doivent s'excuser.
native_language_example: Those who are late have to apologize.

additional_notes: "Ceux-ci" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning “these ones” (plural, usually masculine or mixed group). It’s used to point out specific items close to you or in the current context, often contrasted with "ceux-là" (“those ones”). For a plural feminine group, use "celles-ci sont". In questions, invert: "Ceux-ci sont-ils… ?"
target_language_example: Ceux-ci sont mes chaussures, pas les tiennes.
native_language_example: These are my shoes, not yours.

meaning: "every man for himself" / "each person for themselves."
additional_notes: Said when people stop cooperating and everyone looks out for their own interests (often in a negative or resigned tone). Often heard as part of the proverb: « Chacun pour soi, Dieu pour tous » (“Every man for himself, God for everyone”).
target_language_example: Quand la nourriture a manqué, c'était chacun pour soi.
native_language_example: When the food ran out, it was every man for himself.

additional_notes: Used to describe the little bumps on your skin when you’re cold, scared, or moved (e.g., by music). Very common with the verb phrase "avoir la chair de poule" (to have goosebumps).
target_language_example: J'ai la chair de poule quand j'écoute cette chanson.
native_language_example: I get goosebumps when I listen to that song.

meaning: sharing a room with his brother.
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like « être en chambre avec … » (to be rooming with) or « partager une chambre avec … » (to share a room with). « Chambre » usually means a bedroom/room (not an English “chamber”).
target_language_example: À l'internat, il est en chambre avec son frère.
native_language_example: At the boarding school, he shares a room with his brother.

additional_notes: Refers to a heavily secured room used to store valuables (money, documents, jewelry), especially in banks or secure buildings. Often used with prepositions like « dans la chambre forte » (in the vault).
target_language_example: Les documents confidentiels sont gardés dans la chambre forte.
native_language_example: The confidential documents are kept in the vault.

additional_notes: A more specific/neutral way to say “bedroom,” especially in contexts like describing a home or asking what’s in the room. In everyday speech, people also often just say “chambre.”
target_language_example: La chambre à coucher est au bout du couloir.
native_language_example: The bedroom is at the end of the hallway.

meaning: gas chamber (a room where people are killed with poison gas).
additional_notes: Used mainly in historical contexts (notably Nazi extermination camps during WWII) or to refer to a method of execution. Very heavy, sensitive term.
target_language_example: Pendant la Seconde Guerre mondiale, des prisonniers ont été tués dans une chambre à gaz.
native_language_example: During World War II, prisoners were killed in a gas chamber.

meaning: battlefield; (figuratively) a place of intense conflict.
additional_notes: Literally “field of battle.” Used for a real battlefield in war (“sur le champ de bataille” = on the battlefield). It’s also common figuratively to describe a chaotic or hostile situation (e.g., streets, politics, the workplace).
target_language_example: Après la manifestation, le centre-ville ressemblait à un champ de bataille.
native_language_example: After the protest, downtown looked like a battlefield.

additional_notes: Used for a person or team that has won the top international title in a sport or competition. Often used with an article (le champion du monde / la championne du monde) or as a title after the noun (Ayrton Senna, champion du monde). Feminine: championne du monde.
target_language_example: Il a le potentiel pour devenir un champion du monde.
native_language_example: He has the potential to become a world champion.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used in news, politics, and science to talk about long-term changes in the climate. Often used with verbs like parler de (talk about), agir contre (act against), être menacé par (be threatened by), and faire contre (do something about).
target_language_example: On doit réduire nos émissions pour lutter contre le changement climatique.
native_language_example: We need to reduce our emissions to fight climate change.

additional_notes: Used when someone revises a decision or opinion. The structure is: changer d’avis (no article). It often appears with verbs like pouvoir/devoir/faire: Tu peux changer d’avis (You can change your mind), Il a dû changer d’avis (He must have changed his mind), Je vais te faire changer d’avis (I’m going to make you change your mind).
target_language_example: Si tu veux, tu peux encore changer d'avis.
native_language_example: If you want, you can still change your mind.

additional_notes: Used with the verb changer: "changer d’avis" = to change your mind/opinion/decision. It’s the past participle "changé" + the preposition "de" (contracted to "d'" before a vowel) + "avis". In the passé composé, it is usually formed with "avoir" (e.g., "j'ai changé d'avis", "nous avons changé d'avis"). Neutral/polite in most contexts.
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai changé d'avis : je ne peux pas venir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I changed my mind: I can’t come.

additional_notes: A very common, literal phrase: "chanter" = to sing, "une chanson" = a song. Often followed by extra details like "en français" (in French), "pour tout le monde" (for everyone), or "de plus" (one more). After verbs like "venir", "commencer à", "entendre", French uses the infinitive: "venir chanter", "commencer à chanter", "entendre quelqu’un chanter".
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on peut chanter une chanson ensemble.
native_language_example: After dinner, we can sing a song together.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually (a repeated habit or regular event). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: « Chaque année, … » / « … chaque année. ».
target_language_example: Nous visitons mes grands-parents chaque année.
native_language_example: We visit my grandparents every year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens repeatedly. Very often followed by **chaque fois que** + a clause: *Chaque fois que je viens, il est absent.* It can also stand alone: *Chaque fois, il oublie ses clés.*
target_language_example: Chaque fois que je vais à Paris, je visite un musée.
native_language_example: Every time I go to Paris, I visit a museum.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a repeated situation or habit. It’s followed by a verb (often in the present for general habits, or in the past for repeated past events). The second clause can be separated by a comma in writing.
target_language_example: Chaque fois que je voyage, j’achète une carte postale.
native_language_example: Every time I travel, I buy a postcard.

chaque fois que je vois cette

target_language_multi_word_term: chaque fois que je vois cette
additional_notes: Used to introduce something that happens repeatedly whenever you see a specific thing. Common pattern: « Chaque fois que + subject + verb » (“every time that ...”). Here, « je vois » = “I see” and « cette » is a feminine singular demonstrative (“this”), so it’s followed by a feminine noun like « photo », « image », « pièce ». With a masculine noun, use « ce/cet » (e.g., « chaque fois que je vois ce film... »).
target_language_example: Chaque fois que je vois cette photo, je souris.
native_language_example: Every time I see this photo, I smile.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens daily (a regular habit). You can modify it with words like "presque" (almost) or "tous les jours" is a common alternative meaning the same thing.
target_language_example: Je fais du sport chaque jour.
native_language_example: I exercise every day.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens each morning regularly or as a habit. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Chaque matin, ..."), or after the verb ("Elle le salue chaque matin.").
target_language_example: Je fais du café chaque matin.
native_language_example: I make coffee every morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens weekly. « chaque » means “each/every” and is followed directly by a singular noun (chaque semaine, chaque jour, chaque année).
target_language_example: Je vais à la piscine chaque semaine.
native_language_example: I go to the pool every week.

additional_notes: Refers to someone paid a reward (une prime) to track down and capture/bring in a person (often a criminal). Often used with être: « Il est chasseur de primes. » Note: « prime » here means a reward/bonus, not “prime” (as in primary) or prime numbers.
target_language_example: Ils ont engagé un chasseur de primes pour le retrouver.
native_language_example: They hired a bounty hunter to track him down.

additional_notes: A feminine noun: une chauve-souris, des chauve-souris. Despite the literal parts ("bald" + "mouse"), it simply means the animal "bat" in everyday French. Often used when talking about caves, night, and hunting insects.
target_language_example: J’ai vu une chauve-souris voler près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I saw a bat flying near the window.

additional_notes: Plural noun in French; the singular is usually "une chauve-souris" (one bat). Despite the name (literally “bald mice”), chauves-souris are mammals, not birds. Often used when talking about caves (caverne/grotte) where they live and about hanging upside down.
target_language_example: On a vu des chauves-souris sortir de la grotte au coucher du soleil.
native_language_example: We saw bats coming out of the cave at sunset.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific channel you watch on TV (often numbered: la première/deuxième chaîne) or a broadcaster (locale/nationale). Often said as "une chaîne" when the context is TV.
target_language_example: Tu regardes quelle chaîne de télévision ce soir ?
native_language_example: Which TV channel are you watching tonight?

meaning: a masterpiece (a great work of art).
additional_notes: Used for an outstanding work (a painting, book, film, etc.). Often appears with articles: « un chef-d'œuvre » (a masterpiece), « le chef-d'œuvre de… » (the masterpiece of…). Can also be used more broadly for something exceptionally well done.
target_language_example: Ce film est un vrai chef-d'œuvre.
native_language_example: This film is a real masterpiece.

additional_notes: A common way to say “the railway/railroad” as a system/industry (often with "le"). Used in related phrases like "un pont de chemin de fer" (a railway bridge).
target_language_example: Elle travaille dans le chemin de fer depuis dix ans.
native_language_example: She has worked in the railway industry for ten years.

meaning: the way back (home); the return journey.
additional_notes: Literally “path/route of the return.” Used to talk about the route you take back to where you started (often back home). You’ll also commonly hear: « sur le chemin du retour » (“on the way back”) and « faire le chemin du retour » (“to make the way back / to head back”).
target_language_example: Sur le chemin du retour, on s’est arrêtés pour acheter du pain.
native_language_example: On the way back, we stopped to buy some bread.

additional_notes: With "aller" (e.g., "Je vais chercher…"), it commonly means you’re going to fetch something (bring it back), not “search for” it. You can add an indirect object pronoun to show who it’s for: "lui" (for him/her), "te" (for you), "vous" (for you, formal/plural): "Je vais lui/te/vous chercher de l'eau." You can also add an adjective: "de l'eau fraîche" (cold/fresh water).
target_language_example: Je vais chercher de l'eau.
native_language_example: I’m going to get some water.

meaning: to try to; to seek to (do something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive: « chercher à + infinitive ». It often implies making an effort or attempting to achieve something, sometimes with the idea of aiming for a result (not literally “searching”). Example: « Il cherche à comprendre » = he’s trying to understand.
target_language_example: Je vais chercher à améliorer mon français.
native_language_example: I’m going to try to improve my French.

meaning: "are you looking for…?" / "what are you looking for?" (formal question form).
additional_notes: This is the verb "chercher" (to look for/seek) with "vous" in inverted question order: "Cherchez-vous… ?" = "Are you looking for…?" It’s fairly formal; in everyday speech you often hear "Vous cherchez… ?" or "Qu’est-ce que vous cherchez ?". It can also mean "to seek" in a broader sense (e.g., "Que cherchez-vous à prouver ?" = "What are you trying to prove?").
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, cherchez-vous quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, are you looking for something?

additional_notes: Literally “white hair.” Used to talk about someone’s hair color (often with age). In expressions like « se faire des cheveux blancs » or « donner des cheveux blancs à quelqu’un », it means “to worry a lot” / “to make someone worry” (as if stress could make hair turn white).
target_language_example: Depuis qu’il a pris ce nouveau travail, il se fait des cheveux blancs.
native_language_example: Since he started this new job, he’s been worrying a lot.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s hair color. Often appears with "avoir" (Elle a les cheveux blonds) or after "aux" to mean "with" (le garçon aux cheveux blonds = the blond-haired boy). Note: "cheveux" is plural in French, so you usually say "les cheveux" or "des cheveux" (not *le cheveu* in this context).
target_language_example: J’ai les cheveux blonds, mais mon frère a les cheveux bruns.
native_language_example: I have blond hair, but my brother has brown hair.

additional_notes: Usually used as a noun phrase to describe someone’s hair (often with "avoir": "Elle a les cheveux longs" = "She has long hair"). You’ll also see it after "aux" to mean "with": "une fille aux cheveux longs" = "a girl with long hair". In French, "cheveux" is plural, so you typically say "les cheveux longs".
target_language_example: Elle a les cheveux longs et bouclés.
native_language_example: She has long, curly hair.

additional_notes: Used with the plural noun **les cheveux** (“hair”), so French uses **sont** (they are), even though English usually says **hair is**. Common with possessives: **mes/tes/ses/nos/vos/leurs cheveux sont…** + adjective (longs, courts, bleus, etc.).
target_language_example: Mes cheveux sont trop courts.
native_language_example: My hair is too short.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: (un/le) chewing-gum. Used for the sweet you chew; common with the verbs mâcher (to chew) and vouloir (to want).
target_language_example: Tu as un chewing-gum à la menthe ?
native_language_example: Do you have a mint chewing gum?

meaning: at her place; to her place (her home).
additional_notes: “Chez” means “at/to someone’s place (home, office, etc.).” With “elle,” it refers to a female person: je vais chez elle (I’m going to her place), je suis chez elle (I’m at her place). Often used with verbs like aller (to go), rentrer (to go back/come home), rester (to stay), raccompagner (to escort back).
target_language_example: Je passe chez elle ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m stopping by her place tonight.

meaning: at their place / at their home; to their place (home).
additional_notes: Used with **chez + stressed pronoun** to talk about being **at someone’s house** or going **to someone’s house**. Here **eux** = “them” (for a group or for “they”). Common with verbs like **être** (to be), **vivre** (to live), **rentrer** (to go back/come home), **arriver** (to arrive), **travailler depuis** (to work from).
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on est allés chez eux.
native_language_example: After dinner, we went to their place.

meaning: at the hairdresser’s (salon); to the hairdresser’s.
additional_notes: "Chez" means "at/to someone’s place" or "at/to a business". "Le coiffeur" is the hairdresser (the person); in everyday French, "aller chez le coiffeur" means going to the hairdresser’s salon. Often used with verbs like aller (to go) and se faire couper les cheveux (to get your hair cut).
target_language_example: On se retrouve après, je vais d’abord chez le coiffeur.
native_language_example: Let’s meet up afterward; I’m going to the hairdresser’s first.

meaning: at the dentist’s (office); to the dentist.
additional_notes: Uses "chez" to mean "at/to someone’s place" (here: the dentist’s office). Very common with appointments: "J’ai rendez-vous chez le dentiste". You can also say "aller chez le dentiste" / "se rendre chez le dentiste" = "to go to the dentist".
target_language_example: Demain matin, je vais chez le dentiste pour un contrôle.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning, I’m going to the dentist for a check-up.

meaning: at the doctor’s (office); to the doctor.
additional_notes: Uses "chez" to mean “at/to someone’s place,” so "chez le médecin" means at the doctor’s office (going there or being there). Common with verbs like "aller" (to go) and "avoir rendez-vous" (to have an appointment).
target_language_example: Je dois passer chez le médecin demain matin.
native_language_example: I have to stop by the doctor’s tomorrow morning.

meaning: at his place / at his home.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "chez" + a stressed pronoun (lui = him) to mean “at someone’s place (home, or sometimes their business/office).” Often used with verbs of going/being: "aller chez lui" (go to his place), "être chez lui" (be at his place), "sortir de chez lui" (leave/get out of his place).
target_language_example: Je passe chez lui après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m stopping by his place after work.

additional_notes: Used with chez + a stressed pronoun to talk about someone's home or place. With verbs like être or rester, it means being at your place; with aller or venir, it can mean going to your place.
target_language_example: On peut dîner chez moi ce soir.
native_language_example: We can have dinner at my place tonight.

meaning: at our place; to our place; in our home/country (depending on context).
additional_notes: “Chez” + a pronoun means “at/to someone’s place.” So “chez nous” is often “at our place / (back) to our place (home).” It can also mean “in our home” as in “in our household” (where something happens regularly). More broadly, it can mean “in our country/among us,” especially in contrasts like “chez nous, on…” or when talking about foreigners/armies being ‘chez nous.’
target_language_example: Tu peux dormir chez nous ce soir si tu veux.
native_language_example: You can sleep at our place tonight if you want.

meaning: at home; at one’s own place.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition chez (“at someone’s place”) + the reflexive stress pronoun soi (“oneself”) to mean being at your own home. Very common with verbs like être (to be) and rentrer (to go/come back): être chez soi, rentrer chez soi. It can also be used in general sayings/proverbs about “in one’s own home.”
target_language_example: Après le travail, je suis content d'être chez moi, chez soi c'est plus calme.
native_language_example: After work, I’m happy to be at my place; at home it’s calmer.

meaning: 'at your place/home' (at your house; to your home).
additional_notes: Uses "chez" + a stressed pronoun (moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles) to mean someone’s place/home. With verbs of motion (rentrer/aller), it often means going back/going to that person’s home: "Rentre chez toi" = "Go home" (to your place). It can also mean "about you" in certain contexts: "Ce que j’aime chez toi" = "what I like about you".
target_language_example: Après le dîner, je rentre chez toi.
native_language_example: After dinner, I’m going back to your place.

meaning: at your place; at your home (formal/plural “you”).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s home or household. Common with verbs like aller/venir (go/come), rentrer (go back), accompagner (walk/drive with), and être (to be): « Je vous raccompagne chez vous » (I’ll take you home), « Vous êtes chez vous ? » (Are you at home?). It can also mean “in your household/at your place” for habits (language spoken, who cooks, etc.).
target_language_example: Je peux passer chez vous demain soir ?
native_language_example: Can I stop by your place tomorrow evening?

additional_notes: Used to compliment a man (“type” = “guy”). It’s familiar/colloquial and often said as a warm opinion: « C’est un chic type. » With a woman you’d typically say « une chic fille » or « une chic personne ».
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il est vraiment un chic type.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, he’s really a great guy.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: it’s simply the noun **chien** (“dog”) followed by **est**, the **il/elle/on** form of **être** (“to be”). In real sentences you’ll usually see a determiner before *chien* (e.g., **mon chien est…**, **le chien est…**, **tout chien est…**). *Est* is used with singular subjects; plural would be **les chiens sont…**.
target_language_example: Mon chien est très gentil.
native_language_example: My dog is very nice.

meaning: “the dog is currently / is in the middle of (doing).”
additional_notes: This is the expression **être en train de + infinitive** (“to be in the middle of doing”), here with the subject **chien** (“dog”) and the verb **est** (“is”). It’s not a fixed idiom with *chien*; you can replace the subject (e.g., *je suis en train de…*, *il est en train de…*) and change tense.
target_language_example: Le chien est en train de dormir dans le salon.
native_language_example: The dog is in the middle of sleeping in the living room.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the Roman numeral system (I, V, X, L, C, D, M). You’ll see it in book chapters, centuries (le XXIe siècle), monarch names (Louis XIV), and sometimes clock faces. Singular: un chiffre romain; plural: des chiffres romains.
target_language_example: Dans ce livre, les chapitres sont numérotés en chiffre romain.
native_language_example: In this book, the chapters are numbered using Roman numerals.

additional_notes: A common food item. Usually used with the definite article: "le chocolat blanc". In preferences you’ll often see verbs like "aimer" (to like) and "préférer" (to prefer), e.g., "préférer le chocolat blanc" or "préférer le chocolat blanc au chocolat (noir)" (prefer white chocolate to (dark) chocolate).
target_language_example: Je prends une glace au chocolat blanc, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have a white chocolate ice cream, please.

additional_notes: A common drink order. Often used with an article: "un chocolat chaud" (one hot chocolate) or "du chocolat chaud" (some hot chocolate). In a café, you can order by saying simply: "Un chocolat chaud, s'il vous plaît."
target_language_example: Je prendrai un chocolat chaud, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a hot chocolate, please.

meaning: something like that; that kind of thing.
additional_notes: Used in casual speech to refer vaguely to an unspecified thing or category (often when you don’t want or need to be precise). Often appears as "une chose comme ça" or in the plural: "des choses comme ça" (= things like that).
target_language_example: On pourrait manger une pizza ou une chose comme ça.
native_language_example: We could eat a pizza or something like that.

additional_notes: Usually used with a determiner: most often « quelque chose d’autre » (“something else”) or « une chose d’autre » (“another thing”). Very common alternative word order is « autre chose ». « autre » agrees in gender/number with the noun: « une autre chose », « d’autres choses ».
target_language_example: Je veux une chose d'autre.
native_language_example: I want something else.

additional_notes: Used with **de** to link a noun (**chose**) to what it belongs to or comes from: *la plus belle chose de ta vie* (“the most beautiful thing in your life”). In commands you often see **Enlève/Enlevez … de moi** (“Take … off me / away from me”). Very common fixed phrase: **(Voilà) une bonne chose de faite** = “That’s one good thing done / out of the way.”
target_language_example: C’est la meilleure chose de la journée.
native_language_example: It’s the best thing about the day.
