additional_notes: “De la” is the common contraction of “de + la” and often means “of the” (linking something to a feminine noun). “Une tempête” is a (usually violent) storm, often at sea or on the coast, and can also be used figuratively for turmoil (e.g., “une tempête politique”).
target_language_example: On voit encore les traces de la tempête sur la plage.
native_language_example: You can still see the traces of the storm on the beach.

meaning: "with your head" / "of the head" (often used with gestures and in set expressions).
additional_notes: Most often seen in fixed phrases: «faire oui/non de la tête» = to nod/shake your head; «malade de la tête» = mentally ill / (informally) crazy; «ne pas savoir où donner de la tête» = to feel overwhelmed; «coûter les yeux de la tête» = to cost a fortune.
target_language_example: Elle a fait non de la tête.
native_language_example: She shook her head no.

meaning: from head to toe; all over.
additional_notes: Used to mean completely, covering the whole body. Common with being wet/dirty ("trempé/couvert… de la tête aux pieds") and with looking someone up and down ("regarder/examiner quelqu’un de la tête aux pieds").
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, j’étais sale de la tête aux pieds.
native_language_example: After the hike, I was dirty from head to toe.

additional_notes: Used with food to mean an unspecified quantity: "de la" + feminine noun (la viande). After a negation, it often becomes "de viande" (e.g., "Je ne mange pas de viande"). Can also be used in "avoir de la viande" meaning you have some meat (e.g., in your fridge or on your plate).
target_language_example: On achète de la viande pour le dîner.
native_language_example: We’re buying some meat for dinner.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something is about life in general (e.g., le caractère ordinaire de la vie = “the ordinary nature of life”), or in set expressions like profiter de la vie (“enjoy life”). In au péril de la vie, it means “at the risk of one’s life” (very high danger).
target_language_example: Il veut profiter de la vie et voyager un peu.
native_language_example: He wants to enjoy life and travel a bit.

meaning: of the city; from/out of the city.
additional_notes: "De la" is a contraction of "de + la" (feminine singular). With "ville" it can mean (1) belonging to the city: "le moins cher de la ville" = the cheapest in the city; (2) movement/origin: "sortir/partir/venir de la ville" = to leave/come from the city; or (3) location relative to the city: "au nord de la ville" = north of the city.
target_language_example: On vient de la ville, mais on préfère vivre à la campagne.
native_language_example: We’re from the city, but we prefer living in the countryside.

meaning: (to) have visitors; company (someone has come to see you).
additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "avoir": "J’ai de la visite" / "Tu as de la visite" / "Vous avez de la visite" meaning someone is here (or coming) to visit. It can be said as an announcement (“You have a visitor”). With "le début de la visite" or "le jour de la visite," "la visite" means “the visit” (e.g., a tour/appointment/visiting time), but "avoir de la visite" is specifically about receiving visitors.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas parler longtemps : j’ai de la visite.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk long: I have visitors.

meaning: “of the car” / “from the car” (depending on context).
additional_notes: "De la" is the contraction of "de + la" (feminine singular). With a noun like "la voiture" (the car), it can mean possession/relationship ("la porte de la voiture" = the car door) or movement from inside/out of ("sortir de la voiture" = to get out of the car).
target_language_example: Je prends mon sac de la voiture.
native_language_example: I’m taking my bag from the car.

additional_notes: Used with quantities/containers (une brique de lait, une bouteille de lait) and comparisons (plus de lait que de café). After negative expressions or amounts like peu, you often see "de lait" (Il reste peu de lait).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café avec un peu de lait, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee with a little milk, please.

additional_notes: Made of **de** + infinitive (**dire**) with the object pronoun **le** (“it”). Common after expressions like **c’est facile pour toi de le dire** (“easy for you to say”), **il suffisait de le dire** (“you only had to say so”), **pardonnez-moi de le dire** (“forgive me for saying so”), or **à toi de le dire** (“you tell me / it’s for you to say”).
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû de le dire plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have said it earlier.

meaning: 'to do it' (after a verb that uses "de" + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used when a verb is followed by **de + infinitive** (e.g., *proposer de, essayer de, décider de*). **Le** is an object pronoun meaning “it/him” and goes before the infinitive (*faire*). It can change with gender/number: *de la faire* (to do it—feminine), *de les faire* (to do them).
target_language_example: Je vais essayer de le faire demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to try to do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives that take **de + infinitive** (e.g., *promettre de...*, *désespérer de...*, *avoir la permission de...*). The direct object pronoun **le** (“him/it”) is placed **before** the infinitive: *le rencontrer* = “meet him.” (Not to be confused with *du* = *de + le* as an article.)
target_language_example: J'espère de le rencontrer bientôt.
native_language_example: I hope to meet him soon.

additional_notes: Used with a plural “they” (ils/elles) to show possession or origin. Common patterns: "de leur part" (on their part / from them), "la date de leur mariage" (the date of their wedding), "au fond de leur cœur" (deep down in their heart), "libérer … de leur cage" (free … from their cage).
target_language_example: Je me souviens du nom de leur professeur.
native_language_example: I remember the name of their teacher.

meaning: 'to read' (used after certain verbs/expressions with "de + infinitive").
additional_notes: "De" is often required before an infinitive after some verbs and expressions, e.g. "continuer de lire" (to keep reading), "arrêter de lire" (to stop reading), "finir de lire" (to finish reading), and "ça vaut la peine / le coup de lire" (it’s worth reading). In English, you usually just say "to read" without "of".
target_language_example: J’ai promis de lire ce livre ce week-end.
native_language_example: I promised to read this book this weekend.

additional_notes: Used with verbs/expressions that take **de + infinitive**, e.g. **finir de + infinitive** (“to finish doing…”) and **valoir la peine / valoir le coup de + infinitive** (“to be worth doing…”). Here, **de** links to the infinitive **lire** (“to read”); in English you usually just say “to read this book.”
target_language_example: Ça vaut la peine de lire ce livre avant le film.
native_language_example: It’s worth reading this book before the movie.

meaning: to read a book (used as an infinitive phrase after “de”).
additional_notes: This is a fragment you’ll see after certain verbs or expressions that require **de + infinitive** (e.g., *essayer de*, *avoir envie de*, *avant de*). The core action is **lire un livre** (“to read a book”); **de** links it to what comes before.
target_language_example: J’essaie de lire un livre en français.
native_language_example: I’m trying to read a book in French.

meaning: "(some/any) books" or "of books" (used after a quantity).
additional_notes: “De livres” is “de” + “livres” (“books”). You see it after quantities or expressions like beaucoup/trop/plus/un choix/un nombre, meaning “(of) books”: « un large choix de livres » = “a wide choice of books”, « trois fois plus de livres » = “three times more books”. After a negative, French often uses “de” instead of “des”: « Elles ne lisent pas de livres » = “They don’t read any books.” (Note: « livre » can also mean “pound” as a unit in some contexts, but « livres » in these examples means “books.”)
target_language_example: Il y a trop de livres dans ce sac.
native_language_example: There are too many books in this bag.

additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) distance: « de loin / vu de loin » = from far away, often about how something looks at a distance; can also mean coming from far away (« je viens de loin »). (2) emphasis/comparison: « de loin le meilleur » = by far the best. In « cousins, mais de loin », it means a distant relationship (not close).
target_language_example: De loin, on dirait un château, mais c’est juste un vieux bâtiment.
native_language_example: From far away, it looks like a castle, but it’s just an old building.

additional_notes: de + lui uses the stressed pronoun lui after the preposition de. It often follows verbs or adjectives that require de, as in parler de lui ('talk about him'), être fier de lui ('be proud of him'), or se moquer de lui ('make fun of him'). In phrases like faire de lui..., it means 'make ... of him.' In de lui avoir donné..., lui is instead the pronoun 'to him' before an infinitive, not the same fixed pattern.
target_language_example: On parle souvent de lui en classe.
native_language_example: People often talk about him in class.

meaning: of himself; (also) by himself / on his own.
additional_notes: Uses the stressed pronoun "lui-même" (= "himself") after "de". Common after nouns/adjectives about how someone sees themselves: "une opinion de lui-même" (an opinion of himself), "satisfait de lui-même" (pleased with himself). It can also be used on its own or with a verb to mean someone acts without help: "Il l’a fait de lui-même" (= he did it on his own).
target_language_example: Il a réparé le vélo de lui-même.
native_language_example: He fixed the bike by himself.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something luxurious or top-quality: un hôtel de luxe, une voiture de luxe, un appartement de luxe. It can also be used alone as a short comment meaning “deluxe / fancy!”
target_language_example: On a réservé une chambre de luxe pour notre anniversaire.
native_language_example: We booked a deluxe/luxury room for our anniversary.

meaning: Contraction of "de le" / "de la" meaning "of the", "from the", or "some (of)" before a vowel or silent h.
additional_notes: Used before a noun that starts with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u) or a silent h: de l’océan (of the ocean), de l’école (of the school), de l’orage (some storm / stormy weather). It can express possession/relationship ("habitudes de l’Ombre" = habits of the Shadow) or an indefinite amount, especially in expressions like "de l’orage" (some storm / thunderstorm).
target_language_example: On a parlé de l’hôtel près de la gare.
native_language_example: We talked about the hotel near the station.

meaning: 'for having (done something to/for me)' (introduces a past action).
additional_notes: Used with the past infinitive: « de m'avoir + past participle » (e.g., « de m'avoir invité(e) », « de m'avoir sauvé la vie »). It commonly follows expressions like « merci de… / je te remercie de… » (thanks for…), « c’est gentil/adorable de… » (it’s kind of you to…), or « tu as de la chance de… » (you’re lucky to…). Note: in French typography you may also see « de m’avoir » with a curly apostrophe; it’s the same expression.
target_language_example: Je te remercie de m'avoir sauvé la vie.
native_language_example: Thank you for saving my life.

meaning: 'of my' (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: "de" + the possessive adjective "ma" (“my” for feminine singular nouns) expresses possession or belonging, like English “of my.” In everyday French you’ll often also see "de mon" (masculine) and "de mes" (plural). In the example "Vous vous foutez de ma gueule ?", the full expression "se foutre de la gueule de quelqu’un" means “to make fun of someone” (informal).
target_language_example: Je suis fier de ma sœur.
native_language_example: I'm proud of my sister.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to show possession or a relationship: something/someone connected to your daughter (e.g., "la copine de ma fille" = "my daughter's friend", "une invitée de ma fille" = "a guest of my daughter's"). It can also follow commands to mean "away from my daughter" (e.g., "Tenez-vous à distance de ma fille" = "Stay away from my daughter").
target_language_example: C'est l'anniversaire de ma fille aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It's my daughter's birthday today.

additional_notes:
Used with a noun to show possession or a close relationship: 
- le copain de ma mère = my mom’s boyfriend
- les yeux de ma mère = my mother’s eyes
It also appears in strong oath expressions with sur ("on"), like Sur la tête de ma mère ! / Sur la vie de ma mère ! = “I swear on my mother’s life!” (very emphatic, often informal/colloquial).
target_language_example: La voiture de ma mère est garée devant la maison.
native_language_example: My mother's car is parked in front of the house.

meaning: "from me" / "on my behalf" (when sending greetings, thanks, congratulations, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to pass along a message or sentiment to another person (often with verbs like dire bonjour, saluer, remercier, féliciter). It agrees with the speaker: de ma part (from me), de ta part (from you), de sa part (from him/her), de notre part (from us), de votre part (from you formal/plural), de leur part (from them).
target_language_example: Remercie-les de ma part, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Thank them for me, please.

meaning: “in my life” / “of my life” (often: “ever in my life”).
additional_notes: Literally “of my life.” It commonly follows nouns like *l’amour (de ma vie)* (“the love of my life”) or *les personnes les plus importantes de ma vie* (“the most important people in my life”). In negative statements it can add emphasis, meaning “ever in my life” (e.g., *Je n’ai jamais vu ça de ma vie* = “I’ve never seen that in my life”). In imperatives like *Disparais de ma vie !*, it means “Get out of my life!”
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais entendu une histoire pareille de ma vie.
native_language_example: I’ve never heard such a story in my life.

meaning: In "homme(s) de main": a henchman; hired thug.
additional_notes: On its own, "de main" literally means "of (the) hand", but beginners will most often meet it in the set phrase "un homme de main / des hommes de main" = someone who does dirty work for a boss (enforcer, goon). It’s usually plural when talking about a group working for someone.
target_language_example: Le trafiquant est venu avec deux hommes de main.
native_language_example: The trafficker came with two henchmen.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like « faire »: « faire de mal (à quelqu’un) » = to do harm (to someone). Also in set phrases like « (ne) pas faire de mal » (to not hurt), « se faire de mal » (to hurt yourself), « Rien de mal » (nothing wrong), and after « quelque chose »: « quelque chose de mal » (something bad/wrong).
target_language_example: Je ne voulais pas te faire de mal.
native_language_example: I didn’t mean to hurt you.

additional_notes: Very common in informal spoken French to emphasize how extreme something is (good or bad). Often used after a noun or adjective: « un truc de malade » (something insane), « c’est beau de malade » (it’s insanely beautiful). It doesn’t mean someone is literally sick in these uses.
target_language_example: Ce concert était bien de malade !
native_language_example: That concert was insanely good!

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something marked by bad luck or tragedy: un jour de malheur (an ill-fated day), des rumeurs de malheur (rumors of tragedy/bad news). With "plus que ta part de malheur", it means “more than your share of misfortune.”
target_language_example: Depuis ce jour de malheur, elle a perdu tout espoir.
native_language_example: Since that ill-fated day, she has lost all hope.

meaning: 'to eat' (used after certain verbs, e.g. finir de + infinitive).
additional_notes: Often follows verbs that take **de + infinitive**, especially **finir de** to mean “to finish doing (something)”: **Finis de manger** = “Finish eating.” Here **de** doesn’t translate as “of”; it’s a required connector before the infinitive.
target_language_example: J'ai fini de manger.
native_language_example: I finished eating.

meaning: in a (certain) way; in a (certain) manner.
additional_notes: Used to describe *how* something is done, often followed by an adverb or adjective: **de manière + adverb/adjective** (e.g., *de manière élégante, de manière bizarre*). In everyday speech, **de façon** is a very common equivalent.
target_language_example: Il a répondu de manière calme.
native_language_example: He replied in a calm way.

meaning: so as to; in such a way as to.
additional_notes: Used to express purpose or intended result. Very often followed by an infinitive ("de manière à + infinitif": De manière à éviter…, De manière à pouvoir…). It can also be followed by "ce que" + subjunctive ("de manière à ce que + subjonctif": De manière à ce qu’il/elle puisse…).
target_language_example: Je parle lentement de manière à ce que tout le monde comprenne.
native_language_example: I speak slowly so that everyone understands.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" (and "avoir été" in the past): "Je suis/Il est/Elles sont de mauvaise humeur". It describes someone’s mood/temper, often implying they’re irritable or cranky. You can intensify it with words like "très" or add a duration: "toute la journée".
target_language_example: Je suis de mauvaise humeur ce matin, je n'ai pas assez dormi.
native_language_example: I'm in a bad mood this morning; I didn’t sleep enough.

additional_notes: Usually not a fixed expression by itself: de often belongs to the verb or pattern before it (such as essayer de, avoir besoin de, or venir de), while me is the object or reflexive pronoun placed before the infinitive. With reflexive verbs like me concentrer or me détendre, English often does not translate 'myself' separately.
target_language_example: Essaie de me comprendre.
native_language_example: Try to understand me.

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs/expressions that take **de + infinitive** (e.g. *ça vous dérangerait de…*, *merci de…*, *avant de…*). **Me** is the indirect object pronoun (“to me”) placed before the infinitive **dire**. In other contexts, French may use **à me dire** instead, depending on the verb (e.g. *commencer à me dire*).
target_language_example: Merci de me dire la vérité.
native_language_example: Please tell me the truth.

meaning: "to make me" / "to have me" (with faire, after a verb + de).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern **[verb] + de + me faire + [infinitive / noun]**. Common with verbs like **essayer de** (to try to), **prendre le temps de** (to take the time to), **faire exprès de** (to do it on purpose). With an infinitive, it means “make me + verb” (e.g., *de me faire rire* = make me laugh). With a noun phrase, it can mean “cause me” something (e.g., *de me faire des ennuis* = cause me trouble / give me trouble).
target_language_example: Il essaie de me faire peur.
native_language_example: He’s trying to scare me.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive phrase "dire" (to say/tell) with object pronouns: "me" = to me, and "le" = it (or "that"). It’s often used after another verb or expression that takes "de + infinitive" (e.g., "Merci de me le dire" / "Tu as bien fait de me le dire" / "Inutile de me le dire"). Pronoun order matters in French: "me" + "le" come before the verb ("me le dire"), unlike English word order (“tell me it/that”).
target_language_example: Merci de me le dire tout de suite.
native_language_example: Thanks for telling me right away.

additional_notes: Very vulgar. Used after a noun to insult it or show strong contempt/anger: « X de merde ! » = “you/that fucking X!” Often combined with other swear words (e.g., « putain de… »). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: J'en ai marre de ce boulot de merde.
native_language_example: I’m sick of this shitty job.

additional_notes: Used after "de" (meaning "of/from/about") + "mes" ("my", plural). Often appears after expressions that take "de" (e.g., "au-dessus de" = "above", "se moquer de" = "make fun of", "douter de" = "doubt").
target_language_example: Je suis fier de mes enfants.
native_language_example: I'm proud of my children.

additional_notes: Used after quantities or expressions like "un/une" (one), "aucun" (none), "certains" (some), etc., to mean "(one/none/some) of my friends". Often appears as part of a longer phrase: "un de mes amis" (one of my friends), "aucun de mes amis" (none of my friends).
target_language_example: Deux de mes amis habitent à Paris.
native_language_example: Two of my friends live in Paris.

meaning: a rude put-down: “my ass”, “lousy / pathetic” (used after a noun).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Said after a noun to mock or insult the person/thing: "X de mes deux !" ≈ “X, my ass!” / “Some X you are!” / “You lousy X!”. The "mes deux" implies "my two (balls)" and is used for emphasis; avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Héros de mes deux !
native_language_example: Hero, my ass!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you saw something yourself and can confirm it, not just heard about it. It often comes after a verb of seeing (voir, avoir vu, etc.). You can change the possessive to match the subject: de tes propres yeux (your), de ses propres yeux (his/her), de nos propres yeux (our), de leurs propres yeux (their).
target_language_example: Je n’y croyais pas, mais je l’ai vu de mes propres yeux.
native_language_example: I didn’t believe it, but I saw it with my own eyes.

additional_notes: Used after another verb or expression that requires "de" (e.g., "décider de…", "essayer de…", "il est temps de…"). The core phrase is "mettre fin à + noun/infinitive" (e.g., "mettre fin à la guerre", "mettre fin à fumer").
target_language_example: Il est temps de mettre fin à cette dispute.
native_language_example: It’s time to put an end to this argument.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, thing, or someone’s condition is improving over time. Often used with verbs like aller ("ça va de mieux en mieux" = "it’s getting better and better") or devenir ("ça devient de mieux en mieux"). Can also be said alone as a short reaction: "De mieux en mieux."
target_language_example: Depuis le traitement, mon père va de mieux en mieux.
native_language_example: Since the treatment, my dad is getting better and better.

meaning: appropriate; called for; expected (in the situation).
additional_notes: Used mainly with "être": "c’est/ce serait de mise" = it’s/it would be appropriate; "n’est pas de mise" = it’s not appropriate / not the done thing. Often refers to behavior, attitudes, or actions that fit (or don’t fit) a context, and has a fairly formal tone.
target_language_example: Dans ce genre de réunion, la discrétion est de mise.
native_language_example: In this kind of meeting, discretion is expected.

additional_notes: Used after the preposition de with the stressed pronoun moi. In many expressions, it may sound more natural in English as just "me," depending on the verb: for example, se moquer de moi = "make fun of me."
target_language_example: C'est une photo de moi.
native_language_example: It's a photo of me.

additional_notes: Used to show a gradual decrease over time in frequency, intensity, amount, or speed. It often follows the verb (e.g., « Il sort de moins en moins » = He goes out less and less).
target_language_example: Je comprends de moins en moins quand il parle vite.
native_language_example: I understand less and less when he speaks fast.

additional_notes: A compositional phrase made of de + mon. It often means "of my," but after certain verbs and expressions it can be translated more naturally as "about my," "from my," etc. mon is used with singular masculine nouns, and also with feminine singular nouns that begin with a vowel or mute h, as in de mon idée. Unlike de + le → du, de + mon does not contract.
target_language_example: C'est la photo de mon chien.
native_language_example: It's a photo of my dog.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or a relationship to your son. Common after a noun (e.g., l'anniversaire de mon fils = my son's birthday; la mère/le père de mon fils = the mother/father of my son). In questions like Qu'as-tu fait de mon fils ?, de can also mean "with" in the sense of "what did you do with my son?".
target_language_example: Je cherche la photo de mon fils.
native_language_example: I'm looking for my son's photo.

meaning: as best as I can; to the best of my ability.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like faire/essayer/promettre to say you’re putting in your best effort (often as reassurance or an apology). It agrees with the speaker: de mon mieux (I), de ton mieux (you singular informal), de son mieux (he/she).
target_language_example: Je vais faire de mon mieux pour être à l’heure.
native_language_example: I’m going to do my best to be on time.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to show possession, origin, or connection: "un ami de mon père" (a friend of my father), "la cabane de mon père" (my father’s cabin). It often comes after a noun, and it can also be used alone as a short answer when the context is clear (e.g., "Celui de mon père." = "My father’s one.").
target_language_example: C'est le vieux manteau de mon père.
native_language_example: It's my father's old coat.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re recalling something without looking it up (often as a quick disclaimer meaning “as far as I remember”). Common with verbs like dire, réciter, dessiner: « Il te le dit/dessine de mémoire. ». Related expressions: « avoir des trous de mémoire » = to have memory lapses; « perte de mémoire » = memory loss.
target_language_example: De mémoire, le rendez-vous est à 15 h.
native_language_example: As far as I remember, the appointment is at 3 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is the same or does the same thing. Common patterns: **faire de même** = “to do the same (thing)”; **de même + noun** = “of the same + noun” (e.g., *de même couleur* = “the same color”). Also appears in **tout de même** (very common) meaning “all the same / anyway / still,” and in some informal regional speech (e.g., Quebec) like *en face de même* = “to my face like that.”
target_language_example: Si tu prends un café, j’en prendrai de même.
native_language_example: If you have a coffee, I’ll have one too (the same).

additional_notes: Used after a noun or adjective to say something is your birthplace (ville/lieu de naissance), something you’ve had since you were born (aveugle de naissance), or something you were born with (marque de naissance = birthmark).
target_language_example: Il est français de naissance, mais il vit au Canada.
native_language_example: He’s French by birth, but he lives in Canada.

de ne le dire à personne

target_language_multi_word_term: de ne le dire à personne
additional_notes: Used after verbs like promettre (to promise) or dire à quelqu’un de… (to tell someone to…). The pronoun le means “it” (the secret/info). In everyday French you often also hear: « de ne le dire à personne » = « de ne le dire à personne (du tout) » / « de ne le dire à personne ». (With a different verb: « de ne le dire à personne » ≈ « de ne le raconter à personne » = not to tell anyone.)
target_language_example: Je te demande de ne le dire à personne.
native_language_example: I'm asking you not to tell anyone.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to make it negative, often after a verb, adjective, or expression that takes de: promettre de ne pas..., recommander de ne pas..., être en colère de ne pas pouvoir.... The de usually depends on the previous word, so the whole phrase is often best understood as part of a larger pattern rather than by itself.
target_language_example: J'ai essayé de ne pas rire.
native_language_example: I tried not to laugh.

meaning: "for not having" (followed by a past participle).
additional_notes: Used to apologize or express regret about something you did not do in the past, often after expressions like « Désolé(e) de… », « Excuse-moi de… », « Pardon de… ». It introduces a negative past infinitive: « de » + « ne pas » + « avoir » + past participle (e.g., répondu, été, pu, gagné).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de ne pas avoir appelé hier.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for not calling yesterday.

meaning: 'to not have been' / 'for not having been'.
additional_notes: Used after many verbs/adjectives that take "de" (e.g., être déçu de…, regretter de…, être sûr de…) to introduce a negative past infinitive. It refers to something that did not happen earlier: "de" + "ne pas" + "avoir été" + past participle/adjective (invité, suivi, attentif, etc.).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de ne pas avoir été disponible hier.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for not having been available yesterday.

meaning: “to not do” (negative infinitive), often after “to ask/tell/try to”.
additional_notes: Used when a verb is followed by an infinitive introduced by **de** (e.g., *demander de*, *dire de*, *tâcher de*). The negation wraps around the infinitive: **ne pas + faire** → *de ne pas faire*. Often followed by a noun (*de ne pas faire de bruit* = “not to make noise”).
target_language_example: Je te prie de ne pas faire ça ici.
native_language_example: I’m asking you not to do that here.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like dire (to tell), demander (to ask), prier/supplier (to beg) to give a negative instruction. It’s the negative infinitive: de + ne pas + infinitive. Often refers to something just mentioned or a gesture/specific action (“ça” = “that/this”).
target_language_example: Je t’ai demandé de ne pas faire ça ici.
native_language_example: I asked you not to do that here.

meaning: to not do it / not to do it.
additional_notes: Used after verbs and expressions that take **de + infinitive** (e.g., *choisir de*, *promettre de*, *des raisons de*). **ne...pas** negates the infinitive (*ne pas faire* = “not do”), and **le** replaces a thing/action already mentioned (“it/that”). In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: *de pas le faire*.
target_language_example: Je te conseille de ne pas le faire.
native_language_example: I advise you not to do it.

additional_notes: Used after a verb like dire, demander, conseiller, interdire, etc., to introduce a negative infinitive: "dire à quelqu’un de ne pas venir" = "tell someone not to come." The "ne ... pas" wraps around the infinitive (venir).
target_language_example: Je lui ai demandé de ne pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I asked him/her not to come tonight.

meaning: “to not go there” / “not to go (to that place)” (in an infinitive clause).
additional_notes: This is an infinitive phrase often used after a verb or expression that requires **de** (e.g. *décider de…*, *essayer de…*, *promettre de…*). **ne…pas** makes the infinitive negative, and **y** replaces a place or thing introduced with **à** (e.g. *à Paris* → *y*). Word order stays: **de + ne + y + infinitive + pas**.
target_language_example: J’ai décidé de ne pas y aller ce soir.
native_language_example: I decided not to go there tonight.

additional_notes: Used when a verb/adjective/noun is followed by an infinitive introduced by "de" (e.g., "essayer de", "promettre de", "désolé de", "heureux de"). In the negative infinitive, "ne ... pas" goes before the infinitive: "de ne pas être" + adjective/noun/place (e.g., "de ne pas être en retard", "de ne pas être si tendu").
target_language_example: Je te remercie de ne pas être en colère.
native_language_example: Thank you for not being angry.

de ne pas être en retard

target_language_multi_word_term: de ne pas être en retard
additional_notes: Used after many verbs that take "de" + infinitive (e.g., dire à quelqu’un de…, rappeler à quelqu’un de…, mettre en garde quelqu’un de…). The negative goes around the infinitive: "ne pas être". "en retard" means "late" (not related to the English insult).
target_language_example: N'oublie pas de ne pas être en retard au rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Don’t forget not to be late for the appointment.

meaning: to never … again (in an infinitive clause).
additional_notes: Used after a verb like promettre (to promise), décider (to decide), essayer (to try), etc., followed by an infinitive: « promettre de ne plus jamais + infinitif ». The negative is « ne … plus jamais » = “never again / not ever again.” Example: « Il a promis de ne plus jamais être en retard » = “He promised to never be late again.”
target_language_example: J’ai décidé de ne plus jamais retourner là-bas.
native_language_example: I decided to never go back there again.

meaning: to not say anything; to keep quiet (about it).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like promettre (to promise), jurer (to swear), dire à quelqu’un de… (to tell someone to…), meaning “to say nothing.” Structure: de + ne…rien + infinitive (dire). In informal spoken French, the “ne” is often dropped: promettre de rien dire.
target_language_example: Elle a juré de ne rien dire à personne.
native_language_example: She swore not to say anything to anyone.

meaning: 'of snow' / 'covered with snow' (after certain adjectives like couvert).
additional_notes: Used with "de" to specify a substance or material (here, snow). Very common in the structure "être couvert(e)(s) de + noun" = "to be covered in/with + noun": "couverte de neige" (feminine), "couvert de neige" (masculine). Also used in quantity expressions like "beaucoup de neige" = "a lot of snow".
target_language_example: Les routes sont couvertes de neige ce matin.
native_language_example: The roads are covered with snow this morning.

additional_notes: Used after words like « quelque chose » or « rien » to mean “new (information/developments)”: « quelque chose de neuf » = “something new”, « rien de neuf » = “nothing new.” Common fixed expressions include « Quoi de neuf ? » (“What’s new?”) and « Rien de neuf (sous le soleil). » (“Nothing new (under the sun).”).
target_language_example: Tu as des nouvelles ? — Non, rien de neuf.
native_language_example: Any news? — No, nothing new.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “many/a lot of” (e.g., de nombreuses personnes, de nombreuses difficultés). It’s the feminine plural form of nombreux; masculine plural is de nombreux. Common in more formal writing, but also fine in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Elle a de nombreuses idées pour améliorer le projet.
native_language_example: She has many ideas to improve the project.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a long duration. Often appears with "depuis" (since/for) to mean someone has been doing something for many years: "depuis de nombreuses années". Literally "numerous years"; in everyday English this is usually "many years".
target_language_example: Je travaille ici depuis de nombreuses années.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for many years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in a fairly formal/neutral way. It often introduces a general statement or observation (similar to “for many people…”). “Nombreuses” agrees with “personnes” (feminine plural).
target_language_example: De nombreuses personnes pensent que ce film est trop long.
native_language_example: Many people think this movie is too long.

additional_notes: means a large number of and is used before a plural noun. This is the masculine plural form; with feminine plural nouns, use de nombreuses. It is often a bit more formal or written than beaucoup de.
target_language_example: De nombreux étudiants prennent le bus le matin.
native_language_example: Many students take the bus in the morning.

additional_notes: “De nombreux” is a common, slightly formal way to say “many” (often used in writing and news). It agrees with the noun: de nombreux (masc. plural), de nombreuses (fem. plural). Here it means “in/with many countries,” often in general statements.
target_language_example: De nombreux pays ont signé cet accord.
native_language_example: Many countries signed this agreement.

additional_notes: Used to show that something belongs to “us” when it comes after another word (often a quantity or a noun like un, chacun, quelques-uns): « chacun de nos anniversaires » = “each of our anniversaries”, « quelques-uns de nos rapports » = “some of our reports”. Also used for emphasis in set phrases like « de nos propres yeux » (“with our own eyes”).
target_language_example: J'ai perdu deux de nos clés.
native_language_example: I lost two of our keys.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how things are in the present time (often compared with the past). It can go at the start or end of a sentence: “De nos jours, …” / “…, de nos jours.”
target_language_example: De nos jours, beaucoup de gens travaillent à distance.
native_language_example: Nowadays, many people work remotely.

additional_notes: A fragment used before a singular noun: de notre maison = 'of our house'. In some sentences, de can also be understood more broadly as 'about' or another relation depending on the adjective or verb before it.
target_language_example: C'est une photo de notre école.
native_language_example: It's a photo of our school.

meaning: as best we can; our best.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like faire (faire de notre mieux) to mean “to do our best.” It refers to a group including the speaker (nous / on). You can change it to match the subject: de mon mieux (my best), de ton mieux (your best), de son mieux (his/her best), de votre mieux (your best/plural/formal), de leur mieux (their best).
target_language_example: On va faire de notre mieux pour arriver à l'heure.
native_language_example: We’ll do our best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Nourriture means “food.” De nourriture is used to link food to another noun (e.g., restes de nourriture = “food leftovers,” source de nourriture = “food source,” bagarre de nourriture = “food fight”). It can also appear after an expression of quantity (beaucoup de nourriture = “a lot of food,” assez de nourriture = “enough food”). In everyday speech, the partitive can change with negation (on a de la nourriture, but on n’a pas de nourriture).
target_language_example: Il reste un peu de nourriture pour demain.
native_language_example: There’s a bit of food left for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take **de + infinitive** (e.g., *prévoir de…* “to plan to…”, *accepter de…* “to agree to…”). **Nous** is the object pronoun (“us”) placed before the infinitive **aider**.
target_language_example: Merci d'avoir accepté de nous aider.
native_language_example: Thanks for agreeing to help us.

additional_notes: Used to say an action happens another time (repeat). Often placed after the verb: « Fais-le de nouveau ! » It can also mean “back/again” in states like « être de nouveau amis » (to be friends again) or « être de nouveau sur pieds » (to be back on your feet). Don’t confuse with « à nouveau », which is very similar and also means “again.”
target_language_example: On peut essayer de nouveau demain.
native_language_example: We can try again tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means that something happens a second time or returns to a previous state. Common with verbs like être (to be), venir (to come), commencer (to start), etc. Often interchangeable with « encore » (again), but « de nouveau » emphasizes repetition/renewal ("anew") rather than "still".
target_language_example: Je vais essayer de nouveau demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to try again tomorrow.

meaning: some new (feminine plural) / new (before a feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun: de nouvelles idées, de nouvelles chansons. Often appears instead of des nouvelles when an adjective comes before the noun (des + adjective + noun → de): des nouvelles chansons → de nouvelles chansons. Also used after quantities: beaucoup de nouvelles idées. Note: "des nouvelles" can also mean "(some) news," but in these examples nouvelles is an adjective meaning "new."
target_language_example: On cherche de nouvelles solutions.
native_language_example: We’re looking for some new solutions.

additional_notes: Often used after a noun to mean “night-time” or “night shift” (équipe de nuit = night shift). It can also mean “bedside” in set phrases like table de nuit (bedside table).
target_language_example: Je préfère conduire de nuit quand il fait moins chaud.
native_language_example: I prefer to drive at night when it’s less hot.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something appears suddenly and unexpectedly, or seems to come from no identifiable place or source. Often with verbs like sortir (to come out), surgir (to spring up), venir (to come). You can also say au milieu/au centre de nulle part to mean “in the middle of nowhere.”
target_language_example: Un chat a sauté de nulle part et m’a fait peur.
native_language_example: A cat jumped out of nowhere and scared me.

additional_notes: Uses "de" to indicate the material something is made from (often with "être fait(e) de"), or the amount/type of a substance: "un morceau de papier" (a piece of paper), "un peu de papier" (a bit of paper).
target_language_example: Cette décoration est faite de papier.
native_language_example: This decoration is made of paper.

additional_notes: This is the pattern **de + infinitive**. Many verbs and expressions are followed by **de** before an infinitive, e.g. **arrêter de parler** (to stop speaking), **avoir envie de parler** (to feel like speaking), **c'est à mon tour de parler** (it's my turn to speak), **inutile de parler** (no point in speaking), **il lui arrive de parler** (he happens to speak...). Here **de** doesn’t mean “of”; it’s just the preposition required before the infinitive.
target_language_example: Je te promets d'arrêter de parler.
native_language_example: I promise I'll stop talking.

meaning: true to your word; who keeps their promises.
additional_notes: Most often used in the set phrase "(être) un homme/une femme de parole" to praise someone as reliable and trustworthy—someone who does what they said they would do. It follows a noun (homme/femme/personne) rather than being used alone.
target_language_example: Elle a dit qu’elle viendrait, et elle est venue : c’est une femme de parole.
native_language_example: She said she would come, and she did: she keeps her word.

meaning: 'to leave' / 'to go away' (as an infinitive after 'de').
additional_notes: Used when French requires **de + infinitive** after certain words/expressions, often meaning “to …”. Common patterns include **l’heure de partir** (“time to leave”), **(il est) temps de partir** (“(it’s) time to leave”), **envie de partir** (“feel like leaving”), **idée de partir** (“the idea of leaving”). Here, **de** is grammatical and usually isn’t translated as “of” in English.
target_language_example: On n’a pas le temps de partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We don’t have time to leave now.

meaning: just passing through; only here briefly.
additional_notes: Used after forms of « être » (je suis / on est / vous êtes) to say you’re not staying long (you’re visiting temporarily, stopping by, or in transit). Often implies you don’t live there or won’t remain.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas m’engager : je suis juste de passage.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t commit: I’m just passing through.

meaning: “of (a) pass/password” (used in phrases like "mot de passe").
additional_notes: "De passe" is rarely used on its own; it most commonly appears in fixed expressions like "mot de passe" (password) and sometimes "numéro de passe" (pass number). It uses "de" to mean “of,” linking two nouns: mot + de + passe.
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon mot de passe.
native_language_example: I forgot my password.

meaning: to think of/about; to remember to.
additional_notes:
You often see **de penser à** after expressions that require **de + infinitive** (e.g., **il suffit de…**, **merci de…**, **ça me rend triste de…**). The core verb is **penser à**:
- **penser à + noun/pronoun** = to think about/of someone/something (*penser à lui*, *penser à sa mort*)
- **penser à + infinitive** = to remember to do something (*penser à allumer la lumière*).
target_language_example: J’ai oublié de penser à fermer la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I forgot to remember to close the window.

additional_notes: Often used after another verb that requires "de" (e.g., essayer de, conseiller de, décider de): "essayer de perdre du poids". Literally "to lose (some) weight"; "du" is the partitive and is commonly used in this phrase.
target_language_example: J’essaie de perdre du poids avant l’été.
native_language_example: I’m trying to lose weight before the summer.

additional_notes: Used after expressions of quantity (a number, 'beaucoup', 'peu', 'plusieurs', 'une dizaine', etc.) to say how many people: 'des millions de personnes' (millions of people), 'peu de personnes' (few people). 'Personnes' is usually plural here.
target_language_example: Beaucoup de personnes travaillent à distance aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: A lot of people work remotely today.

additional_notes: Used to say something almost happened (a near miss). Common patterns: « échapper de peu à… » (to narrowly escape…), « manquer de peu » (to just miss), and « Il s’en est fallu de peu » (It was a close call / It almost happened).
target_language_example: J’ai raté mon train de peu.
native_language_example: I just missed my train.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, state, or behavior is progressively worsening over time. Often goes with verbs like « aller », « devenir », or « être »: « ça va de pire en pire », « ça devient de pire en pire », « c’est de pire en pire ».
target_language_example: Depuis quelques semaines, ça va de pire en pire au travail.
native_language_example: For the past few weeks, things have been getting worse and worse at work.

meaning: of your own free will; voluntarily.
additional_notes: A fairly formal set phrase meaning someone does something willingly, without being forced. Often used with verbs like faire / venir / accepter: « Il est venu de plein gré. »
target_language_example: Il a signé le contrat de plein gré.
native_language_example: He signed the contract of his own free will.

meaning: "to cry" (used with another verb: "to stop/avoid/try… crying").
additional_notes: This is the infinitive "pleurer" introduced by "de" after certain verbs and expressions, especially: "arrêter de…" (to stop …ing), "cesser de…" (to stop …ing), and "ça ne sert à rien de…" (there’s no point in …ing). It often translates to an English -ing form ("crying") rather than "of crying."
target_language_example: Ça ne sert à rien de pleurer maintenant.
native_language_example: There’s no point in crying now.

additional_notes: Often used after a quantity, noun, or question word to mean an additional amount: une heure de plus = "one more hour", quelques jours de plus = "a few more days", que dire de plus ? = "what more is there to say?" It does not translate literally word-for-word into natural English.
target_language_example: Je voudrais une minute de plus.
native_language_example: I'd like one more minute.

meaning: even more; more than before (with renewed intensity).
additional_notes: Often used after a verb to say something starts again or continues more strongly than before, especially with expressions like « reprendre de plus belle » (to start up again even more). Common with things like rain, wind, arguing, crying, laughing, etc.
target_language_example: Après une courte pause, la pluie a repris de plus belle.
native_language_example: After a short break, the rain started up again even harder.

additional_notes: Used to show a gradual change that keeps growing over time (often with an adjective/adverb: « de plus en plus + adjectif/adverbe »). It can describe weather, resemblance, attitudes, etc. The opposite is « de moins en moins » (less and less).
target_language_example: Je suis de plus en plus fatigué ces derniers temps.
native_language_example: I'm getting more and more tired lately.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to say the quantity is increasing over time. Often appears at the start of a sentence for emphasis ("De plus en plus de...") or after "il y a" ("Il y a de plus en plus de...").
target_language_example: De plus en plus de gens travaillent à distance.
native_language_example: More and more people work remotely.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “pocket(-size)” or “portable”: une lampe de poche = a flashlight/torch (literally “pocket lamp”); de l’argent de poche = pocket money/allowance; une édition/un livre de poche = a paperback (a cheaper “pocket edition”).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté l’édition de poche : elle est plus légère et moins chère.
native_language_example: I bought the paperback edition: it’s lighter and cheaper.

additional_notes: Most often used with "perdre" to talk about losing weight: "perdre du/de la" + noun → "lose some" (e.g., "perdre du poids"). After quantities, you typically use "de": "beaucoup de poids", "un peu de poids". It can also be used figuratively: "manquer de poids" = "to lack weight/force" (an argument isn’t convincing).
target_language_example: Depuis janvier, elle a perdu un peu de poids.
native_language_example: Since January, she has lost a little weight.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on the noun it follows. In "l’heure/les heures de pointe", it means the busiest time (rush hour). With things like "technologie/équipement/industrie de pointe", it means very advanced, at the highest level. It usually comes after the noun.
target_language_example: Le métro est bondé aux heures de pointe.
native_language_example: The subway is packed during rush hour.

meaning: first-year (as in « de première année »); first-rate/top-quality (in « de première qualité/classe »).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as part of a longer phrase, especially « de première année » = “first-year” (a first-year student). « Première » agrees with a feminine noun (année, classe, qualité). With other nouns you may see the masculine form « de premier … » (e.g., « de premier ordre » = “of the highest order”).
target_language_example: C’est une étudiante de première année.
native_language_example: She’s a first-year student.

additional_notes: "De" + infinitive is used after certain verbs/expressions (e.g., "accepter de", "avoir le temps de") to introduce the action: "accepter de prendre…" = “agree to take…”, "avoir le temps de prendre…" = “have time to have/take…”. "Prendre" often means “to take,” but in everyday French it can also mean “to have” (a drink/meal), as in "prendre un café".
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de prendre l’air.
native_language_example: I need to get some fresh air.

meaning: to take photos / to take pictures.
additional_notes: Used after certain verbs/adjectives that require "de" before an infinitive, e.g. "Il est permis de…" (it’s allowed to…), "Veuillez vous abstenir de…" (please refrain from…), or "Mon passe-temps est de…" (my hobby is to…). In many contexts you can also say simply "prendre des photos"; the "de" depends on the grammar of what comes before.
target_language_example: Il est interdit de prendre des photos à l’intérieur du musée.
native_language_example: It’s forbidden to take photos inside the museum.

meaning: 'up close' / 'closely' (at short distance; with close attention).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like voir/regarder/observer/surveiller to mean "closely" (carefully, attentively), and after verbs like suivre to mean "closely" (staying right behind or monitoring someone/something closely). Often contrasts with "de loin" (from far away).
target_language_example: Regarde ce document de près avant de le signer.
native_language_example: Look at this document closely before signing it.

additional_notes: Used to state a preference or recommended option. It can appear at the beginning as a standalone answer (“De préférence.” = “Preferably.”), or in a sentence: “Je vais de préférence…” (I preferably / I prefer to…), and in instructions like “Servir de préférence…” (preferably serve…).
target_language_example: On se voit demain, de préférence le matin.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow, preferably in the morning.

meaning: a very vulgar insult (roughly “of a whore/whore’s”), used to intensify an insult.
additional_notes: Very offensive and vulgar. Common in insults like « fils de pute » (“son of a bitch”) or after a noun to mean “shitty/awful” in a harsh way (e.g., « ce boulot de pute »). Avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: C’est un fils de pute.
native_language_example: He’s a son of a bitch.

additional_notes: Used to ask about direction or which side something/someone is on or going toward. Common in giving/asking for directions: "De quel côté est… ?" = "Which way is…?" You can also use it more generally about someone’s position or situation: "De quel côté tu es ?" can mean "Which side are you on?" (whose side/support).
target_language_example: Je suis perdu : de quel côté est le centre-ville ?
native_language_example: I'm lost: which way is downtown?

additional_notes: Used to challenge someone’s authority or legitimacy to do/say something. Often expresses indignation or protest. Can be used alone as a sharp question (“De quel droit ?”). Typically followed by a verb: « De quel droit + verbe… ? »
target_language_example: De quel droit entres-tu ici sans frapper ?
native_language_example: Who says you can come in here without knocking?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask about the color of something. Common patterns: « De quelle couleur est + singular noun ? » and « De quelle couleur sont + plural noun ? ». You can also use it after a pronoun: « Il/Elle est de quelle couleur ? ».
target_language_example: De quelle couleur est cette voiture ?
native_language_example: What color is this car?

additional_notes: Question used to ask the color of something. It’s typically followed by a noun phrase (e.g., ce chat, cette fleur, la pomme) and agrees with the thing described: use "est" for singular and "sont" for plural ("De quelle couleur sont ces fleurs ?").
target_language_example: De quelle couleur est ta voiture ?
native_language_example: What color is your car?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the color of multiple things. It agrees with a plural subject (e.g., les murs, tes yeux, ses cheveux). For a singular subject, use “De quelle couleur est … ?”
target_language_example: De quelle couleur sont les rideaux ?
native_language_example: What color are the curtains?

meaning: “of someone” / “someone’s” (and sometimes “from someone,” depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with **de** to indicate an unspecified person as the owner, relation, or source of something: **la fille de quelqu'un** (“someone’s daughter”), **l'anniversaire de quelqu'un** (“someone’s birthday”). It can also mean “from someone” in contexts like receiving something: **un message de quelqu'un** (“a message from someone”).
target_language_example: C'est l'anniversaire de quelqu'un ?
native_language_example: Is it someone’s birthday?

meaning: someone else’s; belonging to another person.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something belongs to another person (not you/the person being discussed). It typically follows the thing owned: « le sac de quelqu'un d'autre » (someone else’s bag). You can also use it with abstract nouns: « l'avis de quelqu'un d'autre » (someone else’s opinion).
target_language_example: Ce manteau est à moi, mais ce chapeau est de quelqu'un d'autre.
native_language_example: This coat is mine, but this hat belongs to someone else.

additional_notes: Used after many verbs and expressions that take the preposition "de" to introduce what they’re about (often an unspecified thing). Common patterns: parler de quelque chose (talk about something), se douter de quelque chose (suspect something), se souvenir de quelque chose (remember something), se plaindre de quelque chose (complain about something), être coupable de quelque chose (be guilty of something).
target_language_example: On doit te parler de quelque chose.
native_language_example: We need to talk to you about something.

meaning: (any) questions; questions (used after negation or quantities).
additional_notes: Often used after negation with an indefinite meaning: «ne ... pas de questions» = “no/any questions.” Also used after expressions of quantity: «une montagne de questions» = “a ton of questions.” With a noun, «questions de ...» can mean “questions from ...” or “questions about ...,” depending on context (e.g., «des questions de la presse» = “questions from the press”).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas de questions, merci.
native_language_example: I don't have any questions, thanks.

additional_notes: Literally "of what." After verbs or adjectives followed by de, English often says "what ... about/of?" instead: De quoi parlez-vous ? = What are you talking about? Before an infinitive, it often means "something to" or "enough to" do something: de quoi manger, de quoi vivre.
target_language_example: Tu as de quoi écrire ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to write with?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the topic of a conversation. "avez-vous" is the formal (or plural) inversion form of "vous avez". Often followed by "avec + person" (De quoi avez-vous parlé avec elle ?). In a less formal style you can say: "De quoi avez-vous parlé ?" → "De quoi vous avez parlé ?" or "Vous avez parlé de quoi ?"
target_language_example: De quoi avez-vous parlé pendant la réunion ?
native_language_example: What did you talk about during the meeting?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or explain the subject/topic of something. Often follows verbs like dire, savoir, voir: « Dis-moi de quoi il s’agit » (Tell me what it’s about), « Je sais/vois de quoi il s’agit » (I know/see what it’s about). « Voilà de quoi il s’agit » means “That’s what it’s about / That’s the point.”
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas de quoi il s'agit.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what it’s about.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like savoir (“to know”) or voir (“to see/understand”) to refer back to a topic, often with an implied “you know what I mean.” Common in: « Tu sais (exactement / très bien) de quoi je parle » and « Tu vois de quoi je parle ? » = “You know/see what I’m talking about?”
target_language_example: On a tous eu ce prof strict… tu sais de quoi je parle.
native_language_example: We’ve all had that strict teacher… you know what I’m talking about.

additional_notes: Used mostly with negatives (ne…pas / ne…jamais / personne / rien) or in questions to mean “anything whatsoever.” It often comes after verbs like se plaindre de, se souvenir de, se débarrasser de, parler de, etc. The "que ce soit" part is fixed and reinforces the idea of “at all/whatever it may be.”
target_language_example: Je n'ai besoin de quoi que ce soit.
native_language_example: I don't need anything at all.

additional_notes: A fairly formal way to ask what the topic/issue is. Often used when someone starts explaining something and you want clarification: « de quoi s'agit-il (exactement / au juste / vraiment) ? ». It comes from the verb « s’agir de » (“to be about / to concern”).
target_language_example: Alors, de quoi s'agit-il vraiment ?
native_language_example: So, what is it really about?

meaning: “What are you talking about?” / “What do you mean?”
additional_notes: Informal phrasing with "tu" (often sounds skeptical, surprised, or confrontational depending on tone). More standard/formal: "De quoi parles-tu ?" In a longer sentence: "Je ne vois pas de quoi tu parles" = "I don’t see/know what you’re talking about."
target_language_example: De quoi tu parles ? Je n’ai jamais dit ça.
native_language_example: What are you talking about? I never said that.

additional_notes: Used after a noun, especially for animals: un chien/cheval/chat de race = a purebred dog/horse/cat. Can also be used figuratively for people to mean “a natural/true [type]”: un sportif de race = a born athlete.
target_language_example: Ils ont adopté un chien de race.
native_language_example: They adopted a purebred dog.

meaning: to go back / to go home; to come back (after).
additional_notes: Used after a verb or expression that requires “de” (e.g., être impatient de, avoir envie de, il est temps de) + infinitive. “Rentrer” often means going back home (rentrer chez moi/chez elle), but it can also mean coming back from a place (venir de rentrer de …) or entering somewhere (rentrer dans une maison).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, j’ai hâte de rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I’m tired, I can’t wait to go home.

meaning: 'to go back home/to someone’s place' (as in 'before going back to…').
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after a preposition like avant de / après / parce que to mean “(before/after) going back.” It’s usually completed with a person or possessive: rentrer chez moi (go back to my place), chez toi, chez lui/elle, chez Paul. On its own, “de rentrer chez” sounds incomplete because chez needs a complement.
target_language_example: Avant de rentrer chez moi, je passe à la boulangerie.
native_language_example: Before going back home, I stop by the bakery.

additional_notes: Used with another verb that is followed by de (e.g., "dire à quelqu’un de…", "être pressé de…", "avoir hâte de…"). "Rentrer" means to return (often to the place you live). In English you choose "go" vs "come" depending on viewpoint; French keeps "rentrer".
target_language_example: Après le travail, je suis content de rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: After work, I’m happy to go home.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something meant for rest or time off: *un jour de repos* (a day off / day of rest), *une soirée de repos* (a night off). Also used with **être**: **Je suis de repos** = “I’m off / I’m not working (today).”
target_language_example: Demain, je suis de repos.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, I’m off.

additional_notes: Used as an infinitive after expressions that take **de + verb**, such as **essayer de** (to try to), **dire à quelqu’un de** (to tell someone to), or **(le plus important est) de** ((the most important thing is) to). In English, you usually translate it simply as “to stay/to remain” (you don’t translate **de** as “of”).
target_language_example: On te demande de rester ici quelques minutes.
native_language_example: They’re asking you to stay here for a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used after a verb like être to say someone/something has come back (often home or to a place/situation): « Je suis de retour », « Il est déjà de retour ». Also common to welcome someone back: « Content que tu sois de retour ».
target_language_example: Je suis de retour à la maison.
native_language_example: I'm back home.

additional_notes: Most often appears in negative structures with **ne ... rien**: **ne ... de rien** = “(not) ... anything” / “... nothing.” For example: **Je ne me souviens de rien** (“I don’t remember anything.”). With verbs like **douter**: **ne douter de rien** = “to doubt nothing” (can imply being very confident or even reckless). As a reply to **merci**, **De rien** means “You’re welcome / No problem.”
target_language_example: — Merci ! — De rien.
native_language_example: — Thanks! — You’re welcome.

meaning: required; expected (as a matter of etiquette or custom).
additional_notes: Used mostly in formal/written French to say something is considered obligatory in a given situation (e.g., greetings, tips, dress code). It often follows the noun: « Les remerciements sont de rigueur. » It’s related to « rigueur » (strictness/rigor), but « de rigueur » is an idiomatic set phrase meaning “expected/required.”
target_language_example: Pour un entretien, une tenue correcte est de rigueur.
native_language_example: For a job interview, proper attire is required/expected.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to show the cause is laughing (e.g., éclater de rire = burst out laughing; mourir de rire = die laughing; se plier de rire = double over laughing; se tenir les côtes de rire = hold your sides laughing).
target_language_example: Quand il a raconté la blague, on a éclaté de rire.
native_language_example: When he told the joke, we burst out laughing.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the normal rule or usual practice, often in the pattern « Il est de règle de + infinitive » (“It’s standard practice to…”). You may also see « comme de règle » (“as usual / as is customary”).
target_language_example: Il est de règle d’arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: It’s standard practice to arrive on time.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive form used after many verbs or expressions that require **de** (e.g., *éviter de*, *essayer de*, *il est difficile de*). The verb **répondre** is followed by **à**: **répondre à une question / à une lettre / à un besoin** (answer a question / reply to a letter / meet a need).
target_language_example: Je vais essayer de répondre à ton message ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to try to reply to your message tonight.

additional_notes: This is a fragment used after verbs or expressions that take **de + infinitive**, such as *essayer de* (to try to), *avoir besoin de* (to need to), *être capable de* (to be able to), *avant de* (before). On its own, it typically needs something before it (e.g., *J’essaie de résoudre ce problème.*).
target_language_example: J’essaie de résoudre ce problème.
native_language_example: I’m trying to solve this problem.

meaning: to solve the problem (with “de” used before an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used after certain verbs/expressions that are followed by **de + infinitive**, like **tenter de** (to try to) or **c’est facile de** (it’s easy to). The core action is **résoudre le problème** = “to solve the problem.”
target_language_example: J’essaie de résoudre le problème avant demain.
native_language_example: I’m trying to solve the problem before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as “dreamlike” or “the dream/ideal version” of it: un corps de rêve (a dream body), des photos de rêve (amazing photos), l’équipe de rêve (the dream team), un couple de rêve (a perfect couple). It’s a positive, common expression (not slang).
target_language_example: On a passé des vacances de rêve au bord de la mer.
native_language_example: We had a dream vacation by the sea.

additional_notes: Used after many expressions with de (e.g., profiter de…, être responsable de…, être en tête de…, le jour de…, tout est de… faute). The possessive agrees with the noun that follows: de sa + feminine singular (de sa classe), de son + masculine singular or feminine starting with a vowel (de son ami / de son école), de ses + plural (de ses amis).
target_language_example: Il est fier de sa sœur.
native_language_example: He is proud of his sister.

meaning: about his/her family; in his/her family.
additional_notes: With "parler de ...", it means "about" (topic): "parler de sa famille" = to talk about his/her family. With comparisons or groups ("le plus...", "tous les membres..."), "de sa famille" means "in his/her family" (among family members). "Sa" can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je suis la plus jeune de sa famille.
native_language_example: I’m the youngest in his/her family.

additional_notes: Uses **de** (“of/about”) + **sa** (“his/her”) + **mort** (“death”) to refer to someone’s death: *la date de sa mort* (the date of his/her death), *la rumeur de sa mort* (the rumor of his/her death), *être informé(e) de sa mort* (to be informed of his/her death). **Sa** can mean “his” or “her” depending on who is being talked about.
target_language_example: Ils parlent encore des circonstances de sa mort.
native_language_example: They still talk about the circumstances of his/her death.

additional_notes:
Uses **de** + a possessive (sa = her) to link something to someone. Common meanings:
- **of** (possession/relationship): *l’enterrement de sa mère* (her mother’s funeral), *le portrait de sa mère* (a portrait of her mother)
- **from** (origin/coming from): *elle tient de sa mère* (she takes after her mother)
- After certain phrases like **rien de …**: *rien de sa mère* (nothing about her mother).
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas de nouvelles de sa mère.
native_language_example: I have no news from/about her mother.

additional_notes: Used with a possessive (de sa vie, de ma vie, de ta vie, de notre vie, etc.) to talk about something belonging to or happening during someone’s life. Common after nouns like années, moment, amour, aspect, partie/la plupart. It can also appear in emphatic negatives like « de ma vie ! » (“in my life!” / “ever!”), but here it’s the literal meaning.
target_language_example: C'était le meilleur jour de sa vie.
native_language_example: It was the best day of his/her life.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it belongs to the science‑fiction genre: un film de science-fiction (a sci‑fi movie), un roman de science-fiction (a sci‑fi novel), de la littérature de science-fiction (sci‑fi literature). Often hyphenated in French: science-fiction.
target_language_example: Tu préfères les séries de science-fiction ou les séries policières ?
native_language_example: Do you prefer sci‑fi series or crime series?

additional_notes: de se is de + the pronoun se before an infinitive. It is not a fixed expression by itself; it shows that the infinitive is a pronominal/reflexive verb after expressions like il est temps de..., avoir l'occasion de..., or dire à quelqu'un de.... In English, this is often just translated with 'to' plus the verb, sometimes with 'oneself' or 'each other', and sometimes with no separate reflexive word at all (for example, se préparer = get ready). With other persons, se changes to me, te, nous, or vous.
target_language_example: Ils promettent de se revoir bientôt.
native_language_example: They promise to see each other again soon.

meaning: “to (get) oneself …” / reflexive “faire” after “de” (e.g., “de se faire + noun/verb”).
additional_notes: Used when an infinitive is introduced by **de** (after many verbs/adjectives/expressions) and the action happens **to the subject** or is done **by/for the subject**. Common patterns: **de se faire des amis** = “to make friends”; **de se faire + infinitive** can mean “to get (something) done to you” (e.g., **de se faire sortir** = “to get thrown out / made to leave”).
target_language_example: Elle essaie de se faire des amis dans sa nouvelle classe.
native_language_example: She’s trying to make friends in her new class.

meaning: “to get married” (used after a verb/expression that takes *de* + infinitive).
additional_notes: *Se marier* is a reflexive verb meaning “to get married” (not “to marry someone”). You use it as *de se marier* after verbs/expressions that require *de* before an infinitive (e.g., *prévoir de…*, *décider de…*, *être content de…*, *avoir peur de…*). The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject, so *de se marier* becomes: *de me marier* (je), *de te marier* (tu), *de se marier* (il/elle/on), *de nous marier* (nous), *de vous marier* (vous), *de se marier* (ils/elles).
target_language_example: Ils prévoient de se marier demain.
native_language_example: They’re planning to get married tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used as an infinitive after certain verbs that take **de** (e.g. **décider de**, **tenter de**, **essayer de**) and means **“to commit suicide / to kill oneself.”** The verb is reflexive: **se suicider**; it changes with the subject (je **me** suicide, tu **te** suicides, il/elle **se** suicide, etc.).
target_language_example: Il a décidé de se suicider.
native_language_example: He decided to commit suicide.

meaning: backup; emergency; rescue (used after a noun).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean it’s there “in case of need” (a backup/extra solution) or related to emergencies/rescue services. Common in: plan de secours (backup plan), système de secours (backup system), kit de secours (first-aid/emergency kit), clé de secours (spare/emergency key), hélicoptère(s) de secours (rescue helicopter(s)).
target_language_example: J’ai une batterie de secours dans mon sac.
native_language_example: I have a backup battery in my bag.

meaning: "service" / "for staff" / "for a department" (used after a noun).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean it’s related to a service/department or intended for staff use: "porte de service" = service/back door (staff entrance), "carte de service" = service ID card/badge, "numéro(s) de service" = service/department contact number(s). The exact translation depends on the noun it follows.
target_language_example: L’entrée de service est derrière le bâtiment.
native_language_example: The service entrance is behind the building.

meaning: “of his/her/its/their” (referring to something that belongs to someone; plural noun).
additional_notes: Used with a plural noun after another noun or a quantity: "une de ses chansons" (one of his/her songs), "de ses nouvelles" (news from him/her), "sept pour cent de ses phrases" (seven percent of his phrases). It refers back to a person already known from context.
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas entendu parler de ses projets récemment.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard about his/her plans recently.

meaning: of his/her parents; from his/her parents.
additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective «ses» (= his/her/its, plural) because «parents» is plural. «De» often means “of” (e.g., «le souhait de ses parents» = “his/her parents’ wish”), and it can also be translated as “from” after certain expressions like «dépendre de» (to depend on) and «être indépendant(e) de» (to be independent from).
target_language_example: Elle a reçu de ses parents un cadeau pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: She received a gift from her parents for her birthday.

additional_notes: de + son is used before a following singular noun. son can mean his, her, or its depending on context, and it agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner. Depending on the verb or expression before it, de is often translated as 'of' or 'about'.
target_language_example: On parle souvent de son travail.
native_language_example: We often talk about his/her work.

meaning: as best as he can; to do his best.
additional_notes: Used after a verb (often "faire") to say someone tried their hardest: "faire de son mieux" = "to do one’s best." It changes with the person: de mon mieux (my best), de ton mieux (your best), de notre mieux (our best), etc.
target_language_example: Il a fait de son mieux pour exécuter le plan.
native_language_example: He did his best to carry out the plan.

additional_notes: Used most often with the verb *faire*: *faire de son mieux pour + infinitive* = “to do one’s best to (do something).” The possessive changes with the subject: *de mon mieux* (my best), *de ton mieux* (your best), *de son mieux* (his/her best), *de notre mieux*, *de votre mieux*, *de leur mieux*.
target_language_example: Elle a fait de son mieux pour le sauver.
native_language_example: She did her best to save him.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to show possession, origin, or source. Common in family resemblance expressions: "Il a les yeux de son père" (he has his father's eyes) and with verbs like "tenir de" (to take after): "Il tient de son père" (he takes after his father).
target_language_example: Il a hérité de son père son sens de l’humour.
native_language_example: He inherited his sense of humor from his father.

meaning: (Non standard / usually incorrect) Intended meaning: “so that / so as to.”
additional_notes:
"De sorte de" is not the standard form in modern French and will usually be perceived as incorrect. In practice, you should use:
- "de sorte que" + indicative = “so that / with the result that” (followed by a conjugated verb): « Il a crié, de sorte que tout le monde l’a entendu. »
- "de sorte à" + infinitive = “so as to / in order to” (followed by an infinitive): « Il parle lentement de sorte à être compris. »
If you see "de sorte de" in writing, it is typically a mistake for one of the two forms above.
target_language_example: Il parle lentement de sorte de être compris. (forme non standard)
native_language_example: He speaks slowly so as to be understood. (non-standard form in French)

meaning: 'to go out' / 'to leave' (used after certain verbs + de).
additional_notes: "De" + infinitive is common after many verbs (e.g., proposer de…, refuser de…, demander de…). With "sortir", it can mean going out (socially) or leaving a place; in "Je vous demande de sortir", it means "to leave" and can sound like a firm request/command.
target_language_example: On m’a demandé de sortir de la salle.
native_language_example: I was asked to leave the room.

additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) After a command/request, it means “immediately / right now”: « Rappelle-moi de suite ! »
2) With a number + time period, it means “in a row / consecutively”: « cinq jours de suite » = “five days in a row.”
target_language_example: Je te rappelle de suite.
native_language_example: I’ll call you back right away.

meaning: 'of safety' or 'security' (used to describe something related to safety/protection).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that it’s for safety/protection or part of a security system (e.g., système de sécurité, contrôle de sécurité, code de sécurité, lunettes de sécurité, raisons de sécurité). Meaning can lean toward 'security' (protection from threats) or 'safety' (preventing accidents), depending on context.
target_language_example: Pour des raisons de sécurité, l'entrée est interdite.
native_language_example: For safety reasons, entry is forbidden.

meaning: “to have (done something) to/for you” / “for having (done something) to you” (used with a past infinitive to refer to a completed action).
additional_notes: Used after expressions like « (être) désolé(e), content(e), ravi(e), heureux(se) de + infinitif passé » to talk about something that already happened: « Désolé(e) de t’avoir fait peur » = “Sorry to have scared you.” Here « t’ » is the object pronoun « te » (you), elided before a vowel sound; it comes before « avoir » in the past infinitive structure: « t’avoir + participe passé » (e.g., « t’avoir vu », « t’avoir aidé »).
target_language_example: Ravi de t'avoir vu.
native_language_example: Delighted to have seen you.

additional_notes: Used after an adjective like content, heureux, ravi, etc. to mean “(I’m) happy/glad to have met you.” Literally: “of having met you.” You’ll also hear the plural/polite version: « de vous avoir rencontré(s) ».
target_language_example: Je suis ravi de t'avoir rencontré.
native_language_example: I’m delighted to have met you.

additional_notes: Used when a word requires the preposition "de" (e.g., être certain de…, être jaloux de…, parler de…) and the following noun is feminine singular, so you use "ta" (your). If the noun were masculine singular, you’d usually say "de ton"; with a plural noun, "de tes".
target_language_example: Je suis fier de ta décision.
native_language_example: I’m proud of your decision.
