additional_notes: It’s the preposition "de" + "ta mère" (your mother). Depending on context, it can mean possession ("la voiture de ta mère" = your mother’s car) or origin ("une lettre de ta mère" = a letter from your mother). It also appears inside very vulgar insults like "(fils de) ta mère" or "enculé de ta mère"; in those cases it’s not a neutral phrase.
target_language_example: J’ai reçu un appel de ta mère ce matin.
native_language_example: I got a call from your mother this morning.

additional_notes: Used to comment on someone’s action or attitude, often in patterns like « C’est gentil/sympa/noble de ta part » (“That’s kind/nice/noble of you”) or « Je m’attendais à mieux de ta part » (“I expected better from you”). « De ta part ? » can express surprise: “From you?”
target_language_example: C’est vraiment gentil de ta part de m’aider.
native_language_example: It’s really kind of you to help me.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s whole lifetime, often in set phrases and superlatives: "pour le reste de ta vie" (for the rest of your life), "la meilleure/la pire … de ta vie" (the best/worst … of your life). In "Il y va de ta vie", it means your life is at stake (it’s a matter of life and death).
target_language_example: C’est le meilleur voyage de ta vie.
native_language_example: It’s the best trip of your life.

meaning: table; for the table / at the table (in set phrases).
additional_notes: Literally “of (the) table,” used to specify something connected to eating at a table. Common in fixed expressions like: « serviette de table » (napkin), « se lever de table » (to get up/leave the table), « sel de table » (table salt), and « chef de table » (person in charge of a dining table / head waiter in some contexts).
target_language_example: Il s'est levé de table avant le dessert.
native_language_example: He got up from the table before dessert.

meaning: of (a certain) size; (être) capable / up to the task ("not a match for").
additional_notes: Used to describe size: "de taille moyenne" (medium-sized), "une surprise de taille" (a big/major surprise). In the expression "être de taille à + infinitive" or "être de taille pour + noun", it means being capable/strong enough to do something or to compete with someone: "Je ne suis pas de taille à me mesurer à lui" = "I’m not a match for him."
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas de taille à porter ce canapé tout seul.
native_language_example: I’m not strong enough to carry this couch by myself.

additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom, but a very common combination of de + te before an infinitive: de te voir, de te lever, de te dire. te is the informal singular object/reflexive form of tu, so it means 'you' or, with reflexive verbs, 'yourself'. The de usually comes from the previous word or expression and often is not translated directly into English.
target_language_example: Je suis content de te voir.
native_language_example: I'm happy to see you.

meaning: to meet you / meeting you (as in “nice to meet you”).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives like heureux/heureuse, ravi/ravie, content(e), etc.: « Ravi(e) de te rencontrer » = “Nice to meet you” (informal because te = “you” singular/informal). With « de » + infinitive, it literally means “to meet you,” but in greetings it functions like the English phrase “nice to meet you.” Use « de vous rencontrer » for formal or plural “you.”
target_language_example: Ravi de te rencontrer, je m'appelle Alex.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you, my name is Alex.

additional_notes: Used after many expressions with an infinitive introduced by de (e.g., « C’est bon/super de… », « Quelle joie de… », « J’ai le plaisir de… », « Il nous tarde de… », « Je suis impatient(e) de… »). « te » is the informal singular “you” (someone you call tu). Note: « revoir » looks like English “review,” but here it means “to see again.”
target_language_example: Je suis très contente de te revoir.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you again.

meaning: "to see you" (used after an adjective to say how you feel about seeing someone).
additional_notes: Often comes after expressions like « C’est + adjectif » or « Je suis + adjectif »: « C’est cool de te voir », « Je suis heureux/heureuse de te voir », « Je suis surpris(e) / étonné(e) de te voir ». Here « de » links the feeling/adjective to the action « voir » (to see), and « te » means “you” (informal singular object).
target_language_example: Je suis ravi de te voir ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you tonight.

additional_notes: A common fragment used after another word or expression, as in un peu de temps, besoin de temps, or une question de temps. In English, the "of" is often not translated directly, depending on the phrase.
target_language_example: Il nous faut encore un peu de temps.
native_language_example: We still need a little more time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes, but not regularly. Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence ("De temps en temps, …" / "… de temps en temps"). It can be strengthened with "que" to mean "only occasionally" ("ne… que de temps en temps").
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma de temps en temps.
native_language_example: I go to the movies from time to time.

meaning: (some/a certain amount of) time to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say how much time is available or needed before doing an action: "avoir de temps pour" (to have time to), "il faut de temps pour" (it takes time to), "donner/prendre du temps pour" (to give/take time to). Often appears with quantities like "un peu de", "assez de", "plein de", "combien de".
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de temps pour finir ce projet.
native_language_example: I need time to finish this project.

meaning: “(some/too/no) time to (do something)” (used before an infinitive).
additional_notes: Most common with quantifiers: **du temps à + infinitive** (“some time to…”), **trop de temps à + infinitive** (“too much time to…”), **pas de temps à + infinitive** (“no time to…”). Often expresses how much time someone spends on an activity: *consacrer/passer + (trop) de temps à faire…*. In *Pas de temps à perdre*, **à perdre** means “to waste/lose.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas beaucoup de temps à consacrer à ce projet cette semaine.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time to devote to this project this week.

meaning: from time to time; once in a while.
additional_notes: An adverbial phrase meaning something happens occasionally (not regularly). It can be placed at the beginning of the sentence (followed by a comma) or after the verb. Close in meaning to "parfois" (sometimes) and "occasionnellement" (occasionally).
target_language_example: De temps à autre, je prends le train au lieu de la voiture.
native_language_example: From time to time, I take the train instead of the car.

meaning: "of the earth/soil"; used to mean "earth/ground" in set phrases.
additional_notes: Literally "of earth/soil" (de + terre). Very common in fixed expressions, especially: une pomme de terre (a potato), un ver de terre (an earthworm), un cochon de terre (a woodlouse/pill bug). In these cases, you usually learn the whole phrase as vocabulary rather than translating word-by-word each time.
target_language_example: Après la pluie, il y a beaucoup de vers de terre sur le trottoir.
native_language_example: After the rain, there are lots of earthworms on the sidewalk.

meaning: 'of your' (talking to one person, before a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition **de** + the possessive adjective **tes** (= 'your' to one person). **Tes** is used before a **plural** noun (masculine or feminine): *tes nouvelles, tes voisins, tes efforts, tes responsabilités*. Contrast: **de ton** (of your + singular masculine), **de ta** (of your + singular feminine), **de tes** (of your + plural).
target_language_example: Je suis fier de tes progrès en français.
native_language_example: I’m proud of your progress in French.

meaning: 'some'/'any' tea; 'of tea' (used to talk about an amount of tea).
additional_notes: Used after a word showing quantity (un peu, beaucoup, une livre, davantage, encore) or after verbs like avoir/besoin/boire to refer to an unspecified amount of tea. It’s the partitive/genitive use of de: un peu de thé = “a little tea,” beaucoup de thé = “a lot of tea,” une livre de thé = “a pound of tea,” besoin de thé = “need (some) tea.”
target_language_example: Je voudrais un peu de thé, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a little tea, please.

additional_notes: Uses the stressed pronoun toi after the preposition de. The exact English translation depends on the expression: it can mean of you, about you, or sometimes something more idiomatic, as in amoureuse de toi = in love with you.
target_language_example: Je parle souvent de toi.
native_language_example: I talk about you often.

additional_notes: Compositional: de + ton. Usually means "of your," but after some verbs and expressions it can also be "about your" (for example parler de ton voyage = "talk about your trip"). Ton is the singular informal/form-to-one-person "your," used before masculine singular nouns, and also before feminine singular nouns starting with a vowel or mute h.
target_language_example: Nous avons parlé de ton projet hier.
native_language_example: We talked about your project yesterday.

meaning: "of your help" / "your help" (after a verb like "need").
additional_notes: Most often used after expressions like "avoir besoin de" (to need): « J’ai besoin de ton aide » = “I need your help.” The preposition « de » is required by the verb/expression before it, and « ton » agrees with « aide » (feminine singular) but uses the masculine form because « aide » starts with a vowel sound (ton aide, not *ta aide*).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de ton aide pour remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: I need your help to fill out this form.

meaning: as best as you can; your best.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is doing the best they can. Very common after "faire": "faire de ton mieux" = "to do your best." It changes with the possessive: "de mon mieux" (my best), "de son mieux" (his/her best), "de notre mieux" (our best), etc.
target_language_example: Quoi que tu fasses, tu dois le faire de ton mieux.
native_language_example: Whatever you do, you have to do it as best as you can.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate origin (un message de ton père = a message from your father) or relationship/possession (l’avocat de ton père = your father’s lawyer; l’écriture de ton père = your father’s handwriting). In expressions like « le fils de ton père », it can emphasize that someone is like their father.
target_language_example: J’ai reçu une lettre de ton père hier.
native_language_example: I received a letter from your father yesterday.

additional_notes: Common patterns: (1) After certain nouns/adjectives + de + infinitive, where toujours adds the idea of “always”: une habitude de toujours + infinitive, être gentil(le) de toujours + infinitive, promettre de toujours + infinitive. (Here, de is required by the construction; toujours is the adverb.) (2) After a noun, X de toujours means a “lifelong/longtime” X: mon ami de toujours, mon compagnon de toujours.
target_language_example: C’est une amie de toujours.
native_language_example: She’s a lifelong friend.

meaning: to beat around the bush; to avoid saying something directly.
additional_notes: Usually used as part of a larger phrase, especially after another verb: « Arrête de tourner autour du pot » (“Stop beating around the bush”). You’ll also often see it without « de »: « tourner autour du pot ». It means someone is being indirect, hesitating, or avoiding the main point.
target_language_example: Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-moi la vérité.
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me the truth.

meaning: “of all the” (referring to the whole set, masculine plural).
additional_notes: Used to mean “from/among all the …” or “of all the …” before a plural noun (e.g., de tous les journaux = of all the newspapers). It’s also common in superlatives: le plus … de tous les … (“the most … of all the …”). Agreement changes with gender/number: de toutes les (feminine plural), de tout le / de toute la (singular), or simply de tous when the noun is implied (e.g., le plus rapide de tous = the fastest of all).
target_language_example: C’est le meilleur de tous les films que j’ai vus.
native_language_example: It’s the best of all the movies I’ve seen.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe ordinary, routine, typical things (not special or formal): la vie de tous les jours (everyday life), la conversation de tous les jours (everyday conversation), le vin de tous les jours (table wine you drink regularly).
target_language_example: Je cherche des vêtements de tous les jours, pas quelque chose de chic.
native_language_example: I’m looking for everyday clothes, not something fancy.

additional_notes: Used after a superlative or ranking (le/la/les meilleur(e)(s), le plus…, parmi les plus grands…) to mean the best/greatest ever, across all historical periods. Often refers to famous people, records, or achievements.
target_language_example: C’est l’un des films les plus populaires de tous les temps.
native_language_example: It’s one of the most popular movies of all time.

additional_notes: Used to express strong, sincere support, thanks, or sympathy. Often appears with verbs like soutenir (to support), remercier (to thank), être avec quelqu’un (to stand with someone), or as an exclamation: « Merci de tout cœur ! ».
target_language_example: Je te remercie de tout cœur pour ton aide.
native_language_example: I thank you wholeheartedly for your help.

additional_notes: Means “from/by everybody.” Often used after adjectives and passive forms to show who feels or does something: « respecté de tout le monde » = “respected by everyone.” Literally “of all the world,” but in everyday French it usually just means “everyone.”
target_language_example: Elle est appréciée de tout le monde au bureau.
native_language_example: She is liked by everyone at the office.

meaning: always; for a very long time (since time immemorial).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for as long as anyone can remember. Often used with the present tense: « Les humains ont de tout temps… » (= Humans have always…).
target_language_example: De tout temps, on raconte cette légende dans le village.
native_language_example: People have told this legend in the village for as long as anyone can remember.

meaning: about all that / about all this.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an entire situation, story, or set of events already mentioned ("all of this/that"). Very common after verbs like parler de (talk about), savoir de (know about), dire de (say about), and in questions like "Quel est le but de tout ça ?" (What’s the point of all this?).
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus entendre parler de tout ça.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hear about all that anymore.

additional_notes: Used to add that something remains true regardless of what happens, or to move on in the conversation (often like English “anyway”). It can be placed at the beginning of a sentence (De toute façon, …) or at the end (… de toute façon).
target_language_example: On peut y aller demain ; de toute façon, aujourd’hui je suis trop fatigué.
native_language_example: We can go tomorrow; anyway, I'm too tired today.

additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence to say the previous point doesn’t change the outcome (“Anyway, …”). It can also follow a noun to mean “in any case/by nature,” especially with c’est/être (e.g., « C’est ma langue de toute manière » = “It’s my language anyway”).
target_language_example: De toute manière, on n’a plus le temps.
native_language_example: Anyway, we don’t have time anymore.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something is clear from the facts or from what you can see. It can appear at the start of a sentence (“De toute évidence, …”), in the middle (“… est de toute évidence …”), or alone as a short reply (“De toute évidence.”).
target_language_example: De toute évidence, elle ne dit pas la vérité.
native_language_example: Obviously, she’s not telling the truth.

meaning: with all his/her strength; as hard as possible.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize maximum effort or intensity with actions like crier (shout), pousser (push), tirer (pull), se débattre (struggle). The possessive changes with the subject: de toutes mes forces (my), de toutes tes forces (your), de toutes ses forces (his/her), de toutes nos forces (our), de toutes vos forces (your plural/formal), de toutes leurs forces (their).
target_language_example: Il tira de toutes ses forces, mais le rocher ne bougea pas.
native_language_example: He pulled with all his strength, but the rock didn’t move.

meaning: with all your strength; as hard as you can.
additional_notes: Used to say you should use maximum physical effort (hold tight, hit, jump) or more generally to try your absolute hardest. It often follows a verb (tenir, frapper, sauter, protéger, essayer). You can change the possessive to match the person: de toutes mes forces, de toutes ses forces, de toutes nos forces, etc.
target_language_example: Tiens ma main de toutes tes forces !
native_language_example: Hold my hand as tight as you can!

additional_notes: Literally “of work.” You use it to specify that something is related to someone’s job or workplace: accident de travail (work accident), compagnons de travail (coworkers), cabinet de travail (study/office). Note: travail means “work,” not “travel.”
target_language_example: C’est une réunion de travail.
native_language_example: It’s a work meeting.

meaning: '(some) work to do' / 'work that needs doing'.
additional_notes: Usually appears after an amount/quantity word: « du travail à faire » (some work to do), « beaucoup de travail à faire » (a lot of work to do), « pas de travail à faire » (no work to do). « à faire » means “to do / to be done” and describes « travail ».
target_language_example: J’ai beaucoup de travail à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: I have a lot of work to do tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically askew (not straight) or that something is going wrong ("ça va de travers", "aller de travers"). Often after a noun/adjective: "Le tableau est de travers". In "Pas un cheveu de travers", it means everything is perfectly in place (not a hair out of place).
target_language_example: Mon col est de travers, tu peux le remettre droit ?
native_language_example: My collar is crooked—can you straighten it?

de traverser la rivière à la nage

target_language_multi_word_term: de traverser la rivière à la nage
additional_notes: The core expression is usually **traverser la rivière à la nage** (“to cross the river by swimming”). The leading **de** often appears because of another verb that requires **de** before an infinitive, e.g. **décider de**, **essayer de**, **avoir peur de**: *Il a décidé de traverser la rivière à la nage.*
target_language_example: Elle a peur de traverser la rivière à la nage.
native_language_example: She’s afraid to swim across the river.

meaning: too much / too many; unnecessary; one too many.
additional_notes: Used in a few common patterns: (1) after a quantity to mean “too many/much”: «deux de trop» = “two too many”; (2) with a noun to mean “an extra/unnecessary” thing: «un mot de trop» = “a word too many”; (3) with «se sentir de trop» meaning “to feel out of place / not wanted”; and (4) with «trop» + verb (without «de») to mean “to do too much”: «trop manger / trop fumer».
target_language_example: On a acheté une chaise de trop, alors on va la rendre.
native_language_example: We bought one chair too many, so we’re going to return it.

meaning: “of (the) phone/telephone” (used to form phrases like “phone number”, “phone booth”, “phone call”).
additional_notes: It’s the structure **noun + de téléphone** to mean “phone/telephone + noun” in English: **numéro de téléphone** (phone number), **cabine de téléphone** (phone booth), **coup de téléphone** (phone call), **ligne de téléphone** (phone line). You rarely use **de téléphone** alone; it usually completes the noun before it.
target_language_example: J’ai perdu mon numéro de téléphone.
native_language_example: I lost my phone number.

additional_notes:
Often appears in fixed noun phrases:
- "la voiture de tête" = the leading car (first in a line/procession).
- "(être) dépourvu(e) de tête" = (to be) without a head / headless.
- "fromage de tête" is a traditional dish ("head cheese"), usually made from pork head meat set in jelly.
Meaning depends heavily on the noun it follows.
target_language_example: Le coureur de tête est déjà loin devant.
native_language_example: The lead runner is already far ahead.

additional_notes: Usually seen when un is the numeral 1 in a larger expression, especially for counting ranges: de un à dix = 'from one to ten'. It can also appear in counting or score phrases like et de un ! ('and that's one!'). In most other contexts, de + un is normally contracted to d'un.
target_language_example: Les enfants apprennent à compter de un à vingt.
native_language_example: The children are learning to count from one to twenty.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that has significant value (often monetary, historical, or symbolic): un objet de valeur, des bijoux de valeur. Also appears in comparisons with "avoir" (to have): "avoir plus/moins de valeur (que ...)" = "to be worth more/less (than ...)".
target_language_example: Ne laisse pas d’objets de valeur dans la voiture.
native_language_example: Don’t leave valuables in the car.

meaning: 'to come' (used after another verb to introduce an action).
additional_notes: Used after many verbs to introduce what someone should/will do: e.g., dire à quelqu’un de venir (to tell someone to come), demander à quelqu’un de venir (to ask someone to come). After "merci", "merci de venir" means "thanks for coming" (or "please come" depending on context).
target_language_example: Je te demande de venir demain matin.
native_language_example: I’m asking you to come tomorrow morning.

meaning: 'to come here' (used after a verb + de + infinitive).
additional_notes: You often see this after verbs or expressions that require **de + infinitive**, especially to report what someone is told/asked or to give a reason: **Dire à quelqu’un de venir ici** (to tell someone to come here), **être reconnaissant de venir ici** (to be grateful to come here), **bien faire de venir ici** (to do well to come here). The **de** doesn’t translate directly into English; it’s part of the French grammar pattern.
target_language_example: Merci de venir ici avec moi.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming here with me.

additional_notes: Used after a verb (often “oublier de…”, “penser à…”, “essayer de…”) to express the action of locking a door. “Verrouiller” means to lock/bolt (often with a lock or bolt).
target_language_example: N'oublie pas de verrouiller la porte avant de sortir.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to lock the door before you go out.

additional_notes: Used after a negation (ne…pas/jamais/plus) with verbs like boire to mean “any wine”: Je ne bois pas de vin. In affirmative sentences, you usually say du vin (“some wine”). Also used after a quantity: un verre de vin (“a glass of wine”).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas de vin, merci.
native_language_example: I don’t want any wine, thanks.

meaning: 'to live' (used after certain expressions that take **de + infinitive**).
additional_notes: **Vivre** means “to live.” You often see it preceded by **de** when it follows another word/expression that requires **de + verb** (infinitive), e.g. **valoir la peine de vivre** (to be worth living), **une raison de vivre** (a reason to live), **avoir de la chance de vivre** (to be lucky to live), **préférer … que de vivre** (to prefer … rather than live).
target_language_example: Il a décidé de vivre à Paris pendant un an.
native_language_example: He decided to live in Paris for a year.

additional_notes: Used with the possessive determiner "vos" (your, plural / formal) after "de". Common after verbs and expressions that take "de" (e.g., "apprendre de vos erreurs" = to learn from your mistakes). "Vos" is used with plural nouns (vos erreurs, vos paroles). For singular nouns, use "de votre" (e.g., de votre voiture).
target_language_example: Merci de vos conseils.
native_language_example: Thank you for your advice.

additional_notes: Used before a noun with votre, the possessive for formal singular 'you' or plural 'you'. In other contexts, de can also mean 'from', but in these examples it means 'of your'.
target_language_example: J'aime le son de votre voix.
native_language_example: I like the sound of your voice.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/phrases like « remercier », « être reconnaissant », « merci » to specify what you’re thanking someone for. « votre » is the polite/formal “your” (to one person, or to a group). In negative contexts it can mean you don’t need the person’s help: « se passer de votre aide » = “do without your help.”
target_language_example: Je vous remercie de votre aide, c’était très gentil.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help; that was very kind.

additional_notes: Used after an adjective to comment on someone’s kind action: « C’est très gentil/aimable/attentionné de votre part. » It can also mean “on your behalf/from you” when passing on a message: « Je lui dirai bonjour de votre part. »
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide, c’est très gentil de votre part.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, that’s very kind of you.

additional_notes: Used to show a relationship or connection to someone’s father. In these examples, it means “of your father” (e.g., un ami de votre père = your father’s friend; les yeux de votre père = your father’s eyes). "Votre" is the formal/plural form of “your” (to one person you address as vous, or to multiple people).
target_language_example: C’est une photo de votre père.
native_language_example: It’s a photo of your father.

meaning: to want to (after a verb/adjective that requires “de” + infinitive).
additional_notes: “Vouloir” normally goes directly with another verb (e.g., « Je veux partir. » = “I want to leave”). You see « de vouloir » when the word before it uses the pattern « de + infinitive », such as « avoir l’air de… » (to seem to…), « être sûr/sûre de… » (to be sure to…), or « loin de moi de… » (far be it from me to…). In these cases, « de » belongs to the earlier expression, and « vouloir » stays in the infinitive: « Tu as l’air de vouloir… », « Tu es sûr de vouloir… ».
target_language_example: Tu es sûr de vouloir continuer ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to continue?

meaning: “to have (done) … to/with you” (formal “you”), used before a past participle.
additional_notes: This is a very common structure: **de + vous + avoir + past participle** (the *perfect infinitive*). It often follows an adjective or expression like **content/ravi/désolé de…** to talk about something that happened earlier (e.g., *content de vous avoir rencontré* = happy to have met you). **Vous** is the formal/plural “you.”
target_language_example: Je suis ravi de vous avoir aidé.
native_language_example: I’m delighted to have helped you.

meaning: "for having made you wait" / "for keeping you waiting."
additional_notes: Used after an apology to say you’re sorry you caused a delay. It’s formal/polite because of "vous" (to you). Structure: "(Désolé(e) / Excusez-moi / Pardon) + de + avoir fait + infinitive". If you’re speaking to one person informally, you can say: "de t’avoir fait attendre."
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de vous avoir fait attendre, le métro avait du retard.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for keeping you waiting; the subway was delayed.

additional_notes: Used after many expressions like "être content/enchanté/heureux" or "avoir l'honneur" to say you’re pleased/happy/honored to meet someone. "Vous" is the formal way to say "you" to one person (polite) or to several people; for friends you often hear "de te rencontrer" instead.
target_language_example: Je suis ravi de vous rencontrer, Monsieur Dupont.
native_language_example: I’m delighted to meet you, Mr. Dupont.

additional_notes: Used after adjectives or nouns to say you’re happy/excited/glad to see someone again (e.g., Heureux/Heureuse, ravi/ravie, impatient(e), Quelle joie). “Vous” is the polite or plural “you.”
target_language_example: Je suis très heureux de vous revoir.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you again.

additional_notes: Used after many feelings/reactions, especially with adjectives like content(e), heureux/heureuse, ravi(e): « Je suis heureux de vous voir » (“I’m happy to see you”). Literally « de » + « voir » (“to see”) + « vous » (“you” formal/plural).
target_language_example: Je suis ravi de vous voir ce matin.
native_language_example: I’m delighted to see you this morning.

meaning: “from sight/view”; used in set phrases about seeing and viewpoints.
additional_notes: Common in expressions like: (1) « point(s) de vue » = viewpoint(s)/opinion(s) (e.g., « à tous points de vue » = in every respect), (2) « perdre … de vue » = to lose sight of (someone/something), (3) « connaître … de vue » = to know someone by sight (recognize them, but not know them personally).
target_language_example: Je l’ai perdu de vue pendant une seconde.
native_language_example: I lost sight of him for a second.

additional_notes: Literally combines de + ça. The exact English translation depends on the verb or expression: it can mean of that, about that, from that, or with that. Very common in spoken French; de cela is more formal or written.
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus parler de ça.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about that anymore.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "être" or "rester" to say someone stayed awake the whole night; literally “standing all night,” but it usually means being awake rather than physically standing.
target_language_example: Je suis resté debout toute la nuit à réviser pour l’examen.
native_language_example: I stayed up all night studying for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen the afternoon of the next day. Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., « Demain après-midi, ... » / « ... demain après-midi. »).
target_language_example: On se retrouve demain après-midi à 15 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet tomorrow afternoon at 3 p.m.?

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in the morning of the next day. Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: « Demain matin, … » / « … demain matin ».
target_language_example: On se retrouve demain matin à 9 heures.
native_language_example: We’ll meet again tomorrow morning at 9 o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in the evening (typically after work/school, or later in the day) on the day after today. Often used when making plans: « Qu'est-ce que tu fais demain soir ? »
target_language_example: On se voit demain soir ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other tomorrow evening?

additional_notes: « demanda » is the literary/simple past (passé simple) of « demander ». Use « à son/sa » + the person you’re asking (e.g., « à son ami », « à sa mère »). Common in written narrative; in everyday speech you’d more often say « a demandé conseil à son/sa… ».
target_language_example: Elle demanda conseil à son ami.
native_language_example: She asked her friend for advice.

meaning: a marriage proposal (a proposal to marry).
additional_notes: Used for the act of asking someone to marry you. Common with verbs like faire (faire une demande en mariage = to propose), demander (demander quelqu’un en mariage = to ask someone to marry you), and accepter/refuser (to accept/refuse a proposal).
target_language_example: Il lui a fait sa demande en mariage au restaurant.
native_language_example: He proposed to her at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Imperative of *demander* (“to ask”) + *lui* (“to him/her”). Used to tell someone to ask another person for information (*Demande-lui son nom*), advice (*Demande-lui conseil*), or to do something (*Demande-lui de venir*). In negatives: *Ne le/la lui demande pas* (“Don’t ask him/her”). For “ask them,” use *demande-leur*.
target_language_example: Demande-lui s’il peut t’aider.
native_language_example: Ask him/her if they can help you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question about a thing (not a person): "Demande ce que + subject + verb". Here "demande" can be the command form (tu): "Demande…" = "Ask…". It’s often followed by "tu veux / il veut / elle veut", etc. For a person, you’d usually use "demande qui…" (ask who…).
target_language_example: Demande ce que tu veux manger.
native_language_example: Ask what you want to eat.

additional_notes: Built with **demander** (“to ask”) + **pourquoi** (“why”). Very common in indirect questions: **Elle demande pourquoi il est parti** (“She asks why he left”). With **se demander pourquoi**, it means “to wonder why” (**Je me demande pourquoi…**). Note that **demander** is a common false friend: it usually means **“to ask (for)”**, not “to demand.”
target_language_example: Je demande pourquoi tu es en retard.
native_language_example: I’m asking why you’re late.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **demander** + **si** to introduce an indirect yes/no question: **Je demande si...** = “I’m asking whether/if...”. With the reflexive form **se demander si...**, it means “to wonder if...”. Note: **demander** is a false friend of English **to demand**; it usually means “to ask” or “to request.”
target_language_example: Je me demande si tu as raison.
native_language_example: I wonder if you’re right.

additional_notes: Used with a person after à: « Demande à Paul ». Often followed by « de + infinitive » to ask someone to do something: « Demande à Tom de venir ». It can also introduce a question you want them to answer: « Demande à ta sœur ». Note: « demander » looks like English “to demand” but usually means “to ask/request”.
target_language_example: Demande à la serveuse si on peut payer par carte.
native_language_example: Ask the waitress if we can pay by card.

additional_notes: Used when you consult someone for guidance. Often followed by "à" + person ("demander conseil à Tom") or "à" + professional ("à un médecin"). It can also be used without saying who you ask ("demander conseil").
target_language_example: Avant de choisir, je vais demander conseil à ma sœur.
native_language_example: Before choosing, I'm going to ask my sister for advice.

additional_notes: Used when someone asks a person to marry them (i.e., proposes). The person being proposed to is usually a direct object: « Je vais la demander en mariage » / « Il l’a demandée en mariage ». You may also see the more formal expression « demander la main de quelqu’un (à ses parents) » (ask for someone’s hand).
target_language_example: Je vais la demander en mariage ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to propose to her tonight.

meaning: to apologize; to ask for forgiveness.
additional_notes: Used when you are asking someone to forgive you for something you did. Often followed by "pour" + a noun ("demander pardon pour ça") or by "de" + infinitive ("demander pardon d’être en retard"). You can also add an indirect object ("te/vous/lui demander pardon") to specify who you’re apologizing to.
target_language_example: Je suis revenu(e) pour demander pardon.
native_language_example: I came back to apologize.

meaning: to ask (for) something; to request something.
additional_notes: Used when you want to ask for a thing, information, or a favor. Often followed by "à + person" to show who you’re asking (e.g., "demander quelque chose à Marie"). Common polite form: "Permettez-moi de vous demander quelque chose" (“Allow me to ask you something”).
target_language_example: Je peux te demander quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Can I ask you something?

additional_notes: A polite way to request help from someone. Common in formal or courteous phrasing with "je peux… ?" / "puis-je… ?" or "j'aimerais…". You can also say "demander un service" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, puis-je vous demander une faveur ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I ask you a favor?

additional_notes: Imperative of demander (“to ask”) + indirect object pronoun lui (“to him/her”). Used to tell one or more people to ask someone a question, or to request something from someone. For “ask them,” use demandez-leur.
target_language_example: Demandez-lui où il habite.
native_language_example: Ask him where he lives.

additional_notes: Most often used in the pattern **demander à + person + de + infinitive**: *Il m’a demandé de venir.* The **de** introduces the verb in the infinitive. Don’t confuse **demander** with English **to demand** (it usually means “to ask/request,” though it can sometimes mean “to demand” depending on context).
target_language_example: Je lui ai demandé de m’aider demain.
native_language_example: I asked him/her to help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past participle of "demander" used with "à" to introduce the person you ask. Common patterns: "demander à [person] si..." (ask if), "demander à [person] de + infinitive" (ask someone to do something), and "demander à [person] + noun" (request/ask for something).
target_language_example: J’ai demandé à mon professeur de répéter la question.
native_language_example: I asked my teacher to repeat the question.

additional_notes: Used for a brother you share only one parent with (same mother or same father). Feminine: « demi-sœur » (half-sister). Often used with possessives: « mon/ton/son demi-frère ». Can be followed by an adjective like « cadet » (younger) or « aîné » (older).
target_language_example: Tom est mon demi-frère.
native_language_example: Tom is my half-brother.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or amount of time. Often appears with an article: « une demi-heure » (half an hour). Common in time estimates: « On en a pour une demi-heure » = “It’ll take about half an hour.” You may also hear « une petite demi-heure » meaning “about half an hour” (roughly, a little less/more depending on context).
target_language_example: Je serai là dans une demi-heure.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in half an hour.

meaning: “runt/shorty” (an insult for someone seen as small or weak).
additional_notes: Used as a mocking nickname or insult when addressing someone directly (often to belittle them). Literally “half-portion,” but in practice it means something like “little guy” in a nasty way. You’ll often see it alone as a form of address (like “Hey, runt!”).
target_language_example: Arrête de faire le malin, demi-portion !
native_language_example: Stop acting tough, runt!

additional_notes: Used for a sister who shares only one parent with you (same mother or same father). Often used with possessives: « ma/ta/sa demi-sœur » or with « avoir »: « Il/Elle a une demi-sœur ». Hyphenated: demi-sœur.
target_language_example: J’ai une demi-sœur qui habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: I have a half-sister who lives in Lyon.

meaning: a U-turn; to turn around (go back the way you came).
additional_notes: Used a lot in driving directions and signs: « Faites demi-tour » = “Make a U-turn.” You can also use it in everyday situations to mean turning back/going back. Common with the verb « faire »: « faire demi-tour » (je fais / on fait / il a fait demi-tour). On signs you may see « Demi-tour interdit » = “No U-turn.”
target_language_example: On s'est trompés de route, on fait demi-tour.
native_language_example: We took the wrong road, we’re turning around.

additional_notes: Used with “depuis” to say something started this morning and has continued up to now (often with the present tense in French: « Elle est là depuis ce matin. »).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué depuis ce matin.
native_language_example: I've been tired since this morning.

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration starting from a point in the past up to now. It typically pairs with the present tense in French (e.g., « Depuis combien de temps tu travailles ici ? »). The word « depuis » can also be used alone with a time expression: « depuis deux ans » = “for two years” / “since two years ago.”
target_language_example: Depuis combien de temps tu habites ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you lived here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of a state or situation that started in the past and is still true now. It’s commonly followed by an adjective or a past participle used like an adjective (e.g., amoureuse, marié(e), sorti(e) de prison). You can change the verb for formality or person: « depuis combien de temps êtes-vous… ? », « depuis combien de temps suis-je… ? ».
target_language_example: Depuis combien de temps es-tu ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you been here?

meaning: "How long have you…?" / "For how long have you…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of something up to now. It’s an informal question start (because of "tu" and no inversion); it must be followed by a verb: "Depuis combien de temps tu travailles ici ?" In more formal French you’ll often hear "Depuis combien de temps est-ce que tu… ?" or inversion: "Depuis combien de temps travailles-tu… ?"
target_language_example: Depuis combien de temps tu habites ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you lived here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of a current situation or state. It’s typically followed by an adjective/participle or a complement (e.g., ensemble, mariés, ici, éloigné de…). In informal speech, people often say « Depuis combien de temps êtes-tu… » (incorrect) or more naturally « Ça fait combien de temps que vous êtes… ? » / « Depuis quand êtes-vous… ? ».
target_language_example: Depuis combien de temps êtes-vous ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you been here?

meaning: for years; for many years (up to now).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to describe something that started in the past and is still true/continuing now. It answers “since when/how long?” and emphasizes duration.
target_language_example: Je travaille ici depuis des années.
native_language_example: I've been working here for years.

meaning: for ten years; since ten years ago.
additional_notes: Used with "depuis" to express a duration starting in the past and continuing up to the present (often with the present tense: "Elle vit… depuis dix ans") or up to a point in the past (often with the imperfect: "Nous vivions… depuis dix ans lorsque…"). In English, this is usually "for ten years" (duration) or "had been … for ten years" when another past event happens.
target_language_example: Je travaille ici depuis dix ans.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for ten years.

meaning: since the beginning; from the start.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to mean something started in the past and is still true now (e.g., Je suis là depuis le début = I’ve been here since the beginning). Can also be used to mean “starting from the beginning” when talking about restarting/explaining again (e.g., Reprenons tout depuis le début = Let’s start over from the beginning).
target_language_example: On se connaît depuis le début de l’année.
native_language_example: We’ve known each other since the beginning of the year.

meaning: after all this time; it’s been so long.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a long time has passed. Very common as « depuis le temps que + subject + verb » (“considering how long…” / “given that you’ve been…”): « Depuis le temps qu’on se connaît… » (“after all the time we’ve known each other…”). It can also stand alone as an exclamation (« Depuis le temps ! », « Super, depuis le temps ! ») to show impatience or relief that something is finally happening.
target_language_example: On devrait se tutoyer, depuis le temps qu’on travaille ensemble.
native_language_example: We should use “tu” with each other, after all this time we’ve worked together.

meaning: for a long time; for a long while (since a long time ago).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to describe something that started in the past and is still true now (Je le cherche depuis longtemps = I’ve been looking for him for a long time). With the negative (ne... pas), it often means “not in a long time” (Il ne leur a pas écrit depuis longtemps). It can also describe a state that began long ago (Ils sont divorcés depuis longtemps).
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas vu Paul depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen Paul in a long time.

meaning: for only a short time; recently (since not long ago).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say something started not long ago and is still true now (e.g., Je travaille ici depuis peu). Often implies “only recently” or “not very long.”
target_language_example: J’habite à Paris depuis peu.
native_language_example: I’ve only been living in Paris for a short time.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the starting point of a situation in time (“Since when has this been true?”). With an ongoing action/state, it often means “how long have you been…?” or “for how long…?”. Can sound surprised or challenging depending on tone: « Depuis quand est-ce un crime ? » = “Since when is it a crime?”
target_language_example: Depuis quand habites-tu ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you been living here?

meaning: "Since when have you been…?" (how long have you been…?).
additional_notes: Used to ask from what point in the past a state or situation started (being there, being with someone, having a role, etc.). It’s followed by an adjective, a place/status, or another complement (e.g., "depuis quand es-tu ici ?", "depuis quand es-tu professeur ?").
target_language_example: Depuis quand es-tu à Paris ?
native_language_example: How long have you been in Paris?

meaning: 'since when have you…?' / 'how long have you been…?' (question).
additional_notes: Used to ask when something started. In careful/formal French you often add a question form: « Depuis quand est-ce que tu… ? » or use inversion: « Depuis quand apprends-tu… ? ». You can answer with « Depuis… » (Depuis hier / Depuis 2020) or « Il y a… » (Il y a deux ans).
target_language_example: Depuis quand tu habites à Paris ?
native_language_example: How long have you been living in Paris?

meaning: “Since when have you been…?” / “How long have you been…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask when something started and is still true now. It’s followed by a place, a situation, or an adjective: « Depuis quand êtes-vous au Japon / ici / ensemble / mariés ? ». In English it often corresponds to “How long have you been…?” (duration) or “Since when have you been…?” (start point).
target_language_example: Depuis quand êtes-vous en France ?
native_language_example: How long have you been in France?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause (with a verb) that marks the starting point of a situation that continues up to the present or up to another reference point: Depuis que je travaille… (“Since I’ve been working…”). Contrast: depuis + a noun/time expression (depuis lundi, depuis 2019).
target_language_example: Depuis que j’habite ici, je prends le bus tous les jours.
native_language_example: Since I’ve lived here, I take the bus every day.

meaning: for as long as I can remember; forever (up to now).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for a very long time and is still true now. Often with the present tense (Je le connais depuis toujours) or with expressions like j’ai l’impression + infinitive. Can be said alone as a surprised question: « Depuis toujours ? » = « Since when / all this time? ».
target_language_example: Elle habite dans ce quartier depuis toujours.
native_language_example: She’s lived in this neighborhood for as long as I can remember.

meaning: for three years; since three years ago.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say something started three years ago and is still true now (duration up to the present): e.g., Il vit ici depuis trois ans. Can also appear alone as a short answer to “Depuis quand ?” (Since when?/How long?).
target_language_example: Je travaille ici depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: I've worked here for three years.

meaning: 'final word' / 'last word' (a final decision or final comment).
additional_notes: Used to say something is final: « C'est mon dernier mot. » = “That’s final.” Common in « avoir le dernier mot » (“to have the final say”), meaning the person who decides or who ends the discussion. Can also mean a brief closing remark at the end of a conversation or speech: « Un dernier mot ? » = “Any last words?” / “A final comment?”
target_language_example: Laisse-moi dire un dernier mot avant de partir.
native_language_example: Let me say one last thing before leaving.

additional_notes: Most often used as « ces derniers temps » (= “lately / in recent times”), usually to talk about a period from the recent past up to now. Example patterns: « Ces derniers temps, je… » or « Je… ces derniers temps. »
target_language_example: Ces derniers temps, je suis très fatigué.
native_language_example: Lately, I’ve been very tired.

additional_notes: Used to warn or emphasize that there will be no more opportunities after this one. Often appears with "C'est ta..." (It’s your...), "Je te laisse une..." (I’ll give you one last...), or "Dernière chance de + infinitive" (Last chance to...).
target_language_example: Je te donne une dernière chance d'expliquer.
native_language_example: I’m giving you one last chance to explain.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the most recent action or thought, typically followed by a relative clause (often in the past): « la dernière chose que je + verbe ». In speech and writing you may also see: « La dernière chose que j’ai faite, c’est… ».
target_language_example: La dernière chose que je fais avant de partir, c’est d’éteindre la lumière.
native_language_example: The last thing I do before leaving is turn off the light.

meaning: "last time" (the previous/most recent time), or "the last time".
additional_notes: Often used with an article: **la dernière fois** = “the last time.” Very common pattern: **la dernière fois que + subject + verb** (“the last time that…”). You may also hear **pour la dernière fois** (“for the last time,” meaning “one final time”). **Fois** is feminine, so it takes **dernière** (not *dernier*).
target_language_example: La dernière fois que je suis allé à Paris, il pleuvait.
native_language_example: The last time I went to Paris, it was raining.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about the most recent occasion something happened. Often followed by the imperfect or passé composé depending on context: « La dernière fois que je suis allé(e)… » (last time I went…), « La dernière fois que j'étais à Paris… » (the last time I was in Paris…).
target_language_example: La dernière fois que je t’ai vu, tu étais très fatigué.
native_language_example: The last time I saw you, you were very tired.

meaning: the final stretch (the last phase before finishing).
additional_notes: Used figuratively for the final part of a project, process, or period of time when you’re close to the end (like the last straight part of a race track). Often appears with verbs like "entrer dans" or "être dans" (to enter/be in the final stretch).
target_language_example: On entre dans la dernière ligne droite avant les examens.
native_language_example: We’re entering the final stretch before the exams.

additional_notes: Often used in phrases like **à la dernière minute** (“at the last minute”) or **de dernière minute** (“last-minute,” used like an adjective): *un changement de dernière minute* (“a last-minute change”).
target_language_example: On a décidé ça à la dernière minute.
native_language_example: We decided that at the last minute.

additional_notes: Refers to the most recent years before now. Often used with a number or a time marker: « ces dernières années » (these last few years), « dans les dernières années » (in recent years), « les dernières années de sa vie » (the final years of his life), « ces quatre dernières années » (these last four years).
target_language_example: Ces dernières années, j'ai beaucoup voyagé pour le travail.
native_language_example: In recent years, I've traveled a lot for work.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) is located or hiding in the space on the other side of the door, often out of sight (e.g., to hang a coat or to hide). It describes position: "derrière" + a noun with the article ("la porte").
target_language_example: Le chat dort derrière la porte.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping behind the door.

meaning: behind the head; (idiom) in mind / up your sleeve (a plan or intention).
additional_notes: Literal use: body position or a command meaning to put your hands behind your head (e.g., "Les mains derrière la tête !"). Idiomatic use with "avoir" or "une idée": "avoir une idée derrière la tête" means you have a hidden plan, intention, or something you’re thinking about.
target_language_example: Je sais que tu as quelque chose derrière la tête.
native_language_example: I know you’ve got something in mind (a plan up your sleeve).

additional_notes: An idiomatic way to say someone is in prison or will be sent to prison. Often used with verbs like « être » (to be), « passer X ans » (to spend X years), or « mettre » (to put/send someone) + « derrière les barreaux ».
target_language_example: S'il continue comme ça, il finira derrière les barreaux.
native_language_example: If he keeps that up, he'll end up behind bars.

additional_notes: Uses "de" + "les" → "des" before "autres" (plural). Common after a noun or adjective to compare or distinguish: "différent des autres" = "different from the others". In questions like "Qu’en est-il des autres ?", it means "What about the others?".
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas être comme les autres : je veux être différent des autres.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be like the others: I want to be different from the others.

additional_notes: Used to compare or choose between exactly two options. Common after a superlative/comparative (e.g., « le plus … des deux » = “the most … of the two”) and in « l’un des deux » (“one of the two”).
target_language_example: Je préfère celui de gauche des deux.
native_language_example: I prefer the one on the left of the two.

additional_notes: "Des" is often the plural of "un/une" (= “some/any”), but after expressions like "autour de", "prendre soin de", or in "la chambre/jardin des …", it usually means "de + les" (= “of the / the”), referring to a specific group of children. So "s’occuper/prendre soin des enfants" usually means “take care of the children” (not just “some children”).
target_language_example: Ce soir, je garde des enfants.
native_language_example: Tonight, I’m babysitting some kids.

additional_notes: "Gens" means "people" (in general). "Des" is often the plural indefinite article, so "des gens" commonly means "some people" or just "people" in a general sense. Very often you’ll also see "les gens" = "people" / "the public" in general. Note that "gens" is usually masculine plural for agreement (e.g., "des gens heureux"), but if an adjective comes before it, it can be feminine (e.g., "de bonnes gens").
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui parlent très vite.
native_language_example: There are people who speak very fast.

additional_notes: Plural of « un ami / une amie » (“a friend”). « Des » is an indefinite plural article, used when talking about an unspecified number of friends: « Je suis avec des amis » (“I’m with friends”). Contrast: « les amis » = “the friends / friends in general”; « mes amis » = “my friends”. In speech, you’ll also hear « C’est des amis à moi » meaning “They’re friends of mine” (more formal: « Ce sont des amis à moi »).
target_language_example: Ce week-end, je sors avec des amis.
native_language_example: This weekend, I’m going out with some friends.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article: it often means "some" or "(any)" in general statements. "Des animaux" can refer to animals in general (Je déteste voir des animaux souffrir.) or to unspecified animals (Ils ont des animaux.). In sentence 1, it’s also used to describe what something is: "Ce sont des animaux" = "They are animals."
target_language_example: Ils ont des animaux à la ferme.
native_language_example: They have animals on the farm.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration lasting many years, often to emphasize that something took a long time ("Ça fait des années", "Ça m'a pris des années", "pendant des années"). It can also mean "years of" in expressions like "des années de pratique" or "des années de données".
target_language_example: Ça fait des années que je veux apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I've been wanting to learn French for years.

additional_notes: Plural indefinite article (des) + armes. Often translated simply as “weapons” in English (“Il y a des armes…” = “There are weapons…”). Note the potential confusion with English “arms” (body parts): in French, « les bras » are your arms, while « des armes » are weapons.
target_language_example: La police a trouvé des armes dans la voiture.
native_language_example: The police found weapons in the car.

additional_notes: “Des” is the plural partitive/indefinite article, used to mean “some” or “(any)”. “Biscuits” in French usually refers to sweet cookies; you can specify the type (e.g., biscuits pour chiens = dog biscuits/treats). Common with verbs like apporter (bring), faire (make/bake), and in offers like « Veuillez vous servir… » (“Please help yourself…”).
target_language_example: Tu veux des biscuits avec ton café ?
native_language_example: Do you want some cookies with your coffee?

additional_notes: Plural: un cadeau (a gift) → des cadeaux (some gifts). Used when the number isn’t specified, or after talking about an unspecified amount (e.g., buying, wrapping, sending gifts). Often appears with holiday words like « de Noël » (Christmas) and in phrases like « emballer des cadeaux » (to wrap gifts).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté des cadeaux pour ma famille.
native_language_example: I bought some gifts for my family.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb « faire »: « faire des cauchemars » = to have nightmares / to have bad dreams. Often appears with time expressions like « la nuit » (at night) or frequency words like « souvent » (often), « régulièrement » (regularly).
target_language_example: Depuis ce film, je fais des cauchemars.
native_language_example: Since that movie, I’ve been having nightmares.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a large number (in the hundreds) followed by a noun: « des centaines de livres/personnes/voitures ». Often also used loosely for emphasis, like English “hundreds of times” (« Je te l’ai dit des centaines de fois. »).
target_language_example: Il y a des centaines de messages dans ma boîte mail.
native_language_example: There are hundreds of messages in my inbox.

additional_notes: Indefinite plural: used for unspecified or vague “things” (objects, facts, actions, etc.). Often used when you don’t want to be specific: « Il cache des choses. » In negatives, « des » usually becomes « de »: « Je ne sais pas de choses comme ça. »
target_language_example: J’ai des choses à te dire.
native_language_example: I have some things to tell you.

additional_notes: Very common in the pattern **avoir des choses à + infinitive**: *J’ai des choses à faire* (“I have things to do”). The **à** introduces what the “things” are for (to do/to say/to tell). Often you’ll see an object pronoun before the infinitive: **des choses à te dire / à vous raconter / à se dire**. You can also add **encore** (“still”) for “still have things to…”. In **J’en ai des choses à…**, **en** is used for emphasis (“I really have a lot of things to…”).
target_language_example: J’ai encore des choses à terminer avant ce soir.
native_language_example: I still have things to finish before tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you have tasks/errands or obligations. Often with avoir (“to have”): « J’ai des choses à faire » = “I have things to do.” With « Il y a… » it means “There are things to do” (work remains). You can add words like « encore » (still) or a place like « ici » (here).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j’ai des choses à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have things to do tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the sound or occurrence of gunfire. Very common with verbs like entendre (to hear) and tirer (to fire): « On a entendu des coups de feu » / « Des coups de feu ont été tirés ». « Il y a des coups de feu » means “There are gunshots / There’s gunfire.”
target_language_example: J’ai entendu des coups de feu près de la gare.
native_language_example: I heard gunshots near the train station.

meaning: phone calls (typically several; calls you need to make).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like « passer » or « donner »: « passer des coups de fil » = “to make some phone calls.” Very common in everyday speech, usually implying multiple calls. Singular: « un coup de fil » = “a phone call.”
target_language_example: Je dois passer des coups de fil cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I have to make some phone calls this afternoon.

additional_notes: In everyday French, "faire des courses" means to go shopping, especially for groceries and everyday items. "J’ai des courses à faire" means you still have errands/shopping to do (things to pick up). It can also include shopping for specific items like gifts.
target_language_example: Je fais des courses après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m doing some shopping after work.

meaning: to have trouble (doing something); to have difficulty (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb: « avoir des difficultés à + infinitif » (e.g., « des difficultés à comprendre »). Often implies something is hard for someone to do; can vary in intensity depending on context.
target_language_example: J’ai des difficultés à prononcer certains mots en français.
native_language_example: I have trouble pronouncing certain words in French.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having trouble breathing, often in health/medical contexts (doctor, emergency, pharmacy). Typically used with "avoir" (Tu as des difficultés à respirer ?) or the slightly more formal verb "éprouver" (Vous éprouvez des difficultés à respirer). You can add time words like "récemment" (recently).
target_language_example: Depuis ce matin, j’ai des difficultés à respirer.
native_language_example: Since this morning, I’ve had trouble breathing.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article ("some"). Use "des enfants" when talking about children in general or an unspecified number (e.g., having kids: "On a des enfants"). In questions or exclamations, it can also mean simply "children?" / "There are children!" It can be used figuratively to mean "(you/they) are being childish" (e.g., "Mes amis sont vraiment des enfants").
target_language_example: Dans ce parc, il y a toujours des enfants qui jouent.
native_language_example: In this park, there are always children playing.

additional_notes: Most common in set phrases like **avoir des ennuis (avec …)** = “to be in trouble (with …)” (e.g., *avec la loi*, *avec ses parents*). You can also say **causer / créer des ennuis** = “to cause trouble” and **faire des ennuis à quelqu’un** = “to give someone trouble.” Note: French **ennui** can also mean “boredom,” but **des ennuis** often means “trouble/problems.”
target_language_example: J’ai des ennuis au travail en ce moment.
native_language_example: I’m having trouble at work right now.

additional_notes: Plural of "une erreur". Used with "faire des erreurs" (to make mistakes) and "commettre des erreurs" (to commit/make mistakes). Often means mistakes in general, not specific ones; to be specific you can say "ces erreurs" (these mistakes) or "des erreurs dans..." (mistakes in...).
target_language_example: J’ai fait des erreurs, mais j’apprends.
native_language_example: I made mistakes, but I’m learning.

additional_notes: Plural form of « une excuse » (an apology/an excuse). With verbs like « vouloir » and « devoir », it commonly means asking for or owing an apology: « vouloir des excuses » = to want an apology; « devoir des excuses (à quelqu’un) » = to owe someone an apology.
target_language_example: Je te présente des excuses pour mon retard.
native_language_example: I apologize to you for being late.

additional_notes: Plural of « une famille ». « des » is an indefinite plural article meaning “some” or “(a few)”, but in English it’s often just translated as “families.” In phrases like « Ils ont des familles », it can mean they have families/relatives (often implying responsibilities or dependents).
target_language_example: Ils ne peuvent pas partir, ils ont des familles à nourrir.
native_language_example: They can’t leave; they have families to feed.

additional_notes: “Des” is the plural indefinite article, usually meaning “some” or just indicating an unspecified plural (“women”). In general statements it can translate as “women” (e.g., “men and women”). Compare: “des femmes” = some/unspecified women; “les femmes” = women in general / the women (specific group).
target_language_example: Il y a des femmes dans la salle d’attente.
native_language_example: There are (some) women in the waiting room.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural of the indefinite article (roughly “some”), so "des films" can mean “some movies” (unspecified). In many everyday contexts it also just means “movies” generally, especially after verbs like regarder/voir/aimer: "regarder des films" = “watch movies.”
target_language_example: On peut regarder des films ce soir.
native_language_example: We can watch some movies tonight.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural of the indefinite/partitive article (often translated as “some”). You use "des fleurs" when you mean an unspecified number of flowers (buying, bringing, picking). Contrast: "les fleurs" = “the flowers” (specific/generic), "deux fleurs" = “two flowers.”
target_language_example: Je vais acheter des fleurs pour la fête.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy some flowers for the party.

additional_notes: Used to say there are (or someone is growing/planting/picking) flowers located in the garden. "Des" means an unspecified plural amount (“some”), and "dans le jardin" tells the place (“in the garden”).
target_language_example: Il y a des fleurs dans le jardin.
native_language_example: There are some flowers in the garden.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech as a shorter, more informal alternative to « parfois ». It can be used at the beginning or end of a sentence. In questions like « …, des fois ? », it often means “by any chance?”
target_language_example: Des fois, je me couche tard.
native_language_example: Sometimes I go to bed late.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French and fairly informal. Often followed by the subjunctive: « Des fois qu’il pleuve… » = “in case it rains…”. You’ll also see it after an instruction/advice: « Prends ton parapluie, des fois qu’il pleuve. » A more neutral/formal equivalent is « au cas où ».
target_language_example: Prends un chargeur, des fois que ton téléphone n’ait plus de batterie.
native_language_example: Take a charger, just in case your phone runs out of battery.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural partitive/indefinite article, used to talk about an unspecified quantity or some items in general. You’ll often see it in shopping/eating contexts: acheter des fruits (buy some fruit), manger des fruits (eat fruit). In French it stays plural (des fruits), even though English often uses "fruit" as an uncountable noun.
target_language_example: Je prends des fruits pour le dessert.
native_language_example: I’m having some fruit for dessert.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article (some). "Gens" means "people" and is very common when talking about people in general or an unspecified group. Often used with adjectives: "des gens sympas" (nice people).
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui n’aiment pas le café.
native_language_example: There are people who don’t like coffee.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing a group of people. Very common after expressions like « il y a » / « il existe » / « je connais » / « nous avons ». It can be general (“there are people who…”) or refer to a specific group depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui parlent très vite.
native_language_example: There are people who speak very fast.

additional_notes: Refers to good times (des hauts) and bad times (des bas) in life, a situation, or a relationship. Often used with "il y a eu..." (there were...) or "on a eu..." (we had...) to describe a period with mixed experiences.
target_language_example: Notre relation a eu des hauts et des bas, mais on s'aime toujours.
native_language_example: Our relationship has had ups and downs, but we still love each other.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a long duration (“for hours”), often after verbs like durer, attendre, parler, pleuvoir. Common patterns: « pendant des heures », « durant des heures », and the literary/emphatic « des heures durant » (= “for hours on end”).
target_language_example: On a discuté des heures sans voir le temps passer.
native_language_example: We talked for hours without noticing the time go by.

meaning: stories; (also) nonsense or trouble (in some expressions).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: “some stories.” Often used in set expressions: « Raconte pas des histoires » = “Don’t make things up / Don’t give me that.” « Chercher des histoires » = “to look for trouble / pick a fight.” « Se raconter des histoires » = “to fool yourself / kid yourself.”
target_language_example: Raconte pas des histoires, je sais que tu mens.
native_language_example: Don’t make things up—I know you’re lying.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article (like "some"). Use "des hommes" when you mean men in general or an unknown/unspecified set of men. It contrasts with "les hommes" (men in general / the men) and "d'hommes" after negation or certain expressions (e.g., "Je n'ai pas vu d'hommes").
target_language_example: Dans ce village, des hommes travaillent dans les champs.
native_language_example: In this village, some men work in the fields.

additional_notes: Plural indefinite article: "des" + "idées". Often used after "avoir": "avoir des idées" = to have ideas/thoughts/opinions (e.g., "des idées différentes" = different ideas/views). Can be modified to judge the ideas: "des idées pareilles" (ideas like that), "des idées tordues" (twisted/weird ideas).
target_language_example: J'ai des idées pour le projet, mais je ne suis pas sûr.
native_language_example: I have some ideas for the project, but I’m not sure.

meaning: some information; information (plural form in French).
additional_notes: In French, *information* is usually used in the plural (*des informations*) even when English would use uncountable “information.” Use it when asking for or giving details: *Je veux des informations*, *On a des informations pour vous*. In negative sentences, it often becomes *d’informations*: *Je n’ai pas d’informations*.
target_language_example: Pourriez-vous me donner des informations sur les horaires ?
native_language_example: Could you give me some information about the schedules?

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article (roughly “some/any”). Use "des livres" when you mean an unspecified number of books, or just “books” in general (e.g., what someone reads). If you mean specific books, use "les livres" (“the books”). After a negation, it often becomes "de livres" (e.g., "Je ne lis pas de livres").
target_language_example: J’achète des livres pour le voyage.
native_language_example: I’m buying some books for the trip.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article ("some"). "Lunettes" is usually used in the plural in French to mean eyeglasses. Common verbs: "porter des lunettes" (to wear glasses), "mettre des lunettes" (to put on glasses). You can add a type: "des lunettes de soleil" (sunglasses), "des lunettes de sécurité" (safety glasses).
target_language_example: Tu portes des lunettes ?
native_language_example: Do you wear glasses?

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article, so this phrase often refers to sunglasses in a nonspecific sense (not a particular pair). Commonly used with "porter" (to wear): "porter des lunettes de soleil".
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce que tu portes des lunettes de soleil la nuit ?
native_language_example: Why are you wearing sunglasses at night?

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural of the indefinite/partitive article (often translated as “some”), used before plural nouns when you mean an unspecified amount. In English you might just say “vegetables” without “some.” Common in food/shopping contexts (e.g., buying, eating, growing vegetables).
target_language_example: Je vais acheter des légumes pour la soupe.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy some vegetables for the soup.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a very large number (in the thousands). Often followed by a plural noun: « des milliers de personnes / gens ». Can also be used more loosely to mean “countless/so many” in everyday speech: « des milliers de fois » (“thousands of times”).
target_language_example: Des milliers de personnes attendent devant le stade.
native_language_example: Thousands of people are waiting in front of the stadium.

additional_notes: Used to express a large number of people (at least 2,000, often meaning “very many”). It commonly appears as the subject of a sentence with a plural verb: « Des milliers de personnes sont/ont… ». You can swap the noun: « des milliers de visiteurs », « des milliers de fois », etc.
target_language_example: Des milliers de personnes ont assisté au concert.
native_language_example: Thousands of people attended the concert.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to emphasize a very large number: des millions de personnes (millions of people). It can also be used more loosely/exaggeratedly to mean “really far,” often with distances: à des millions de kilomètres d’ici (millions of kilometers from here).
target_language_example: Il y a des millions de raisons de voyager.
native_language_example: There are millions of reasons to travel.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural partitive/article, meaning “some” (or just plural “-s” in English). "Des médicaments" is used for medicines in general or an unspecified quantity. With specific meds, French often uses "les médicaments" (the medicines) or names the medicine. Common with verbs like acheter (to buy), prendre (to take), and questions like "Prenez-vous des médicaments ?" (= Do you take any medications?).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'acheter des médicaments pour le rhume.
native_language_example: I need to buy some medicine for a cold.

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like « avoir » (to have/get news) or « donner » (to give news), and often with « de »: « des nouvelles de + someone/something » = news about/from. Can also mean recent developments: « des nouvelles récentes ? ».
target_language_example: Tu as des nouvelles de Marie ?
native_language_example: Do you have any news from/about Marie?

additional_notes: Used to ask if you’ve heard from someone (“Tu as des nouvelles de… ?”) or to request an update (“Donne(z)-moi des nouvelles de…”). Often implies contact or information about how someone is doing. In questions, it can be shortened to just “Des nouvelles de … ?” meaning “Any news from … ?”.
target_language_example: Tu as des nouvelles de Julie ?
native_language_example: Have you heard from Julie?

additional_notes: Plural of « un ordre ». Used for official or military-style instructions (« recevoir des ordres », « agir selon des ordres »), or more generally to talk about telling people what to do (« donner des ordres »). In the set phrase « Tes désirs sont des ordres ! », it means “whatever you want, I’ll do it” (often polite, sometimes ironic).
target_language_example: On a reçu des ordres de ne pas entrer.
native_language_example: We received orders not to go in.

additional_notes: “Des” is the plural indefinite article meaning “some” (or it can be left untranslated in English). Used when talking about photos in general or an unspecified number: prendre des photos (to take photos), faire des photos (to take photos / do a photo shoot), j’ai des photos (I have some photos). In the negative, it usually becomes “de”: je ne prends pas de photos (I don’t take any photos).
target_language_example: On a pris des photos pendant le voyage.
native_language_example: We took some photos during the trip.

additional_notes: Used to say what the photos are of. "Des" is the plural indefinite article (some), and "de" introduces the subject of the photos. Often used with "avoir" (to have) or "prendre" (to take): "J’ai des photos de…", "Je prends des photos de…".
target_language_example: J’ai des photos de Paris sur mon téléphone.
native_language_example: I have some pictures of Paris on my phone.

additional_notes: Indefinite plural: used when talking about an unspecified amount of potatoes, often as a food you eat or buy. You’ll also see it without the article: “pommes de terre” = “potatoes” in general.
target_language_example: On achète des pommes de terre pour le dîner.
native_language_example: We’re buying some potatoes for dinner.

additional_notes: Plural of « une preuve » (“a piece of evidence/proof”). Often used with verbs like « avoir » (to have), « fournir / présenter » (to provide/show), « chercher » (to look for), or « dissimuler » (to hide). In legal or formal contexts, « des preuves » = evidence supporting a claim; in everyday speech it can also mean “proof” (e.g., proof that something is true).
target_language_example: On n'a pas encore des preuves suffisantes.
native_language_example: We don’t have enough evidence yet.

additional_notes: Plural of "un problème". Used with "avoir" (avoir des problèmes = to have problems/trouble) and "il y a" (il y a des problèmes = there are problems). Often followed by "avec" (problems with someone/something) or "de" (type of problem: des problèmes de circulation = traffic problems).
target_language_example: On a des problèmes de connexion aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We’re having connection problems today.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone/something has recurring or notable difficulties: health/body issues (des problèmes de dos, de prostate, de sinus), relationship issues (des problèmes de couple), or practical/social issues (des problèmes de circulation/transport). Often follows avoir: « avoir des problèmes de … ».
target_language_example: J'ai des problèmes de sommeil en ce moment.
native_language_example: I’m having sleep problems at the moment.
