additional_notes: Plural of "une question". "Des" is an indefinite article meaning "some" (or just plural "a/an"). Common in polite contexts: "Avez-vous des questions ?" = "Do you have any questions?" Also used after verbs like "poser" (to ask): "poser des questions" = "to ask questions".
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, je peux y répondre.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, I can answer them.

additional_notes: Literally “centuries.” Often used with "depuis" to mean “for centuries / for ages” (sometimes exaggerated in everyday speech: "Je suis ici depuis des siècles" = “I’ve been here forever”). Can also mean a duration (“vivre des siècles” = “to live for centuries”) or appear in time expressions like "des siècles plus tard" = “centuries later.”
target_language_example: On attend depuis des siècles !
native_language_example: We’ve been waiting for ages!

meaning: lots of; a ton of; loads of.
additional_notes: Means “a lot of / many” before a noun. Common in spoken French and casual writing. It works with countable nouns (des tas de gens = lots of people) and uncountable nouns too (des tas de choses = lots of things). Often implies a large quantity, like “loads of.”
target_language_example: Il y a des tas de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: There are loads of things to do today.

additional_notes: Very common, informal way to refer to things when you don’t want to be specific or don’t know the exact word. Often used for objects (“J’ai acheté des trucs”) or events (“Il s’est passé des trucs” = “some things happened”). In more formal French, prefer “des choses”.
target_language_example: J’ai encore des trucs à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: I still have some stuff to do tonight.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase using the partitive/indefinite plural article "des" to mean an unspecified quantity (“some”). Often used with verbs like "porter" (to wear) and can be followed by an adjective ("des vêtements noirs") or a description ("des vêtements qui sont passés de mode").
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’acheter des vêtements pour l’hiver.
native_language_example: I need to buy some clothes for the winter.

additional_notes: "Des" is the plural indefinite article (often like “some” or just “(plural)”). It’s used when you’re talking about an unspecified quantity of eggs (shopping, what’s in a box, ingredients). After a negation, it often changes to "de" ("Je n’ai pas d’œufs").
target_language_example: On a acheté des œufs au marché.
native_language_example: We bought some eggs at the market.

additional_notes: Used for animated TV shows and movies; also in phrases like "personnage de dessin animé" (cartoon character). Often used with the article: "un/le dessin animé".
target_language_example: Je regarde le dessin animé !
native_language_example: I’m watching the cartoon!

additional_notes:
**dessus** means “top/upper side,” and **dessus de** most often appears inside longer expressions rather than alone.

Common patterns:
- **sur le dessus de + nom** = **on the top of** (on a surface): *sur le dessus de la voiture / de la table*.
- **au-dessus de + nom** = **above / over** (higher level, not necessarily touching). Spelling is typically **au-dessus de** (with a hyphen); you may also see **au dessus de**.

Figurative use exists with **au-dessus de**: *Je suis au-dessus de ça* = “I’m above that.”
target_language_example: Il plaça les skis sur le dessus de la voiture.
native_language_example: He put the skis on top of the car.

meaning: the top/upper side of the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the upper surface/outer top part of something feminine: *le dessus de la table* (the top of the table), *le dessus de la boîte* (the top of the box). It’s made of *dessus* (“top/upper side”) + *de la* (“of the” for a feminine singular noun). If the following noun is masculine, use *du* (*le dessus du livre*). If it starts with a vowel, use *de l’* (*le dessus de l’armoire*).
target_language_example: J’ai posé les clés sur le dessus de la table.
native_language_example: I put the keys on top of the table.

target_language_multi_word_term: tous les deux / toutes les deux
additional_notes: Used to refer to exactly two people/things together (="the two of you/them"). Agreement: **tous les deux** (masculine or mixed group), **toutes les deux** (two females). It can be set off by commas for emphasis: *vous, tous les deux,* and it often appears before **de + infinitive**: *arrêtez, tous les deux, de…* / *cessez, toutes les deux, de…*.
target_language_example: Arrêtez, tous les deux, de vous disputer !
native_language_example: Both of you, stop arguing!

additional_notes: Used to talk about age ("deux ans" = two years old) or a duration ("depuis deux ans" = for/since two years; "ça fait deux ans" = it’s been two years). Also appears in comparisons: "de deux ans plus/moins" = two years older/younger.
target_language_example: J’habite ici depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve been living here for two years.

additional_notes: Used to state the number 200. In counting, *cent* usually takes an -s (*deux cents*), but it drops the -s when another number follows (e.g., *deux cent un* = 201). In front of a noun, it stays the same: *deux cents personnes* (two hundred people).
target_language_example: Ça coûte deux cents euros.
native_language_example: It costs two hundred euros.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens two times, or to compare amounts/sizes ("deux fois + noun" = twice as much; "deux fois plus + adjective" = twice as + adjective). Also common with time expressions: "deux fois par jour/an" = twice a day/year.
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma deux fois par mois.
native_language_example: I go to the movies twice a month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency. It’s usually followed by a time period: "deux fois par semaine" (twice a week), "deux fois par mois" (twice a month), "deux fois par an" (twice a year).
target_language_example: Je vais à la piscine deux fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I go to the pool twice a week.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in a day. Often follows the verb or comes at the end of the sentence (e.g., Je prends ce médicament deux fois par jour).
target_language_example: Je prends ce médicament deux fois par jour.
native_language_example: I take this medicine twice a day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how often something happens. You can change the number: « une fois par semaine » (once a week), « trois fois par semaine » (three times a week). « Une ou deux fois par semaine » means “once or twice a week.”
target_language_example: Je vais à la salle de sport deux fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I go to the gym twice a week.

meaning: twice as much / twice as many; twice as + adjective.
additional_notes: Used to express a 2× comparison. Pattern: « deux fois plus de + noun + que… » (twice as many/much + noun as…), « deux fois plus que… » (twice as much/many as…), and « deux fois plus + adjective + que… » (twice as + adjective as…). Note: « deux fois plus » means 2× (double), not “two times more” in the sense of +200%.
target_language_example: Cette voiture coûte deux fois plus cher que l’autre.
native_language_example: This car is twice as expensive as the other one.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or time interval. With prepositions it changes meaning: “dans deux heures” = in two hours (from now); “depuis deux heures” = for two hours/for the past two hours (starting two hours ago and continuing); “toutes les deux heures” = every two hours.
target_language_example: On se voit dans deux heures.
native_language_example: See you in two hours.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (pour deux jours = for two days), or a point in time relative to something else (deux jours après = two days later). With chaque: chaque deux jours = every two days (i.e., every other day).
target_language_example: Je serai à Paris pendant deux jours.
native_language_example: I’ll be in Paris for two days.

additional_notes: Used to say someone speaks/learns two languages that are not their native language. Often follows verbs like "parler" (to speak) or "apprendre" (to learn). "Deux" agrees in number (deux is the same for masculine/feminine), while "langues étrangères" is plural.
target_language_example: J'apprends deux langues étrangères à l'école.
native_language_example: I'm learning two foreign languages at school.

additional_notes: Literally means “two minutes,” but it’s commonly used to ask someone to wait briefly, similar to “give me a minute.” It can also be used more literally for a short amount of time (“in two minutes”).
target_language_example: Attends deux minutes, j’arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m coming.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for two months), a time from now/past (in two months; two months ago), frequency (every two months), or a stage of pregnancy (two months pregnant). Common patterns: « dans deux mois » (in two months), « ça fait deux mois que… » (it’s been two months since…), « tous les deux mois » (every two months), « enceinte de deux mois » (two months pregnant).
target_language_example: Ça fait deux mois qu’on habite ici.
native_language_example: We’ve been living here for two months.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate small number, often meaning “a couple” or “a few,” not necessarily exactly 2 or 3. It can refer to items (deux ou trois personnes / stylos) or frequency (deux ou trois fois par semaine). Often matches “something like two or three” / “about two or three.”
target_language_example: Je vais rester ici deux ou trois jours.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for two or three days.

additional_notes: Used to count items that come in twos (shoes, socks, gloves, etc.). Often followed by "de" + a plural noun: "deux paires de chaussettes". Can also refer to the poker hand "two pair" ("deux paires").
target_language_example: Je vais prendre deux paires de chaussures, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll take two pairs of shoes, please.

additional_notes: Used to organize people or things into pairs (often for lining up: «En rang deux par deux»). It can also describe doing something two at a time or taking steps two at a time (e.g., climbing stairs quickly).
target_language_example: On entre dans la salle deux par deux.
native_language_example: We go into the room two by two (in pairs).

additional_notes: Often used to describe something that has two dot-like markings (e.g., a ladybug species: « la coccinelle à deux points » = the two-spot ladybug). In punctuation, « deux points » also means a colon (:).
target_language_example: Mets deux points avant la liste : pain, fromage, fruits.
native_language_example: Put a colon before the list: bread, cheese, fruit.

additional_notes: A basic time expression used to say a duration (pour deux semaines = for two weeks) or a point in the future (dans deux semaines = in two weeks). Can also be used as an exclamation/title for a trip: Deux semaines à Bali !
target_language_example: Je serai en vacances pendant deux semaines.
native_language_example: I’ll be on vacation for two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about being given another opportunity after a mistake or failure. Very common with verbs like donner/accorder (to give/grant) and mériter (to deserve), and in expressions like avoir droit à une deuxième chance (to have a right to a second chance).
target_language_example: Peux-tu me donner une deuxième chance ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a second chance?

meaning: “was supposed to be” / “must have been” (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Form of **devoir** (imparfait, il/elle/on) + **être**. It can express:
- **obligation/expectation/plan**: *Elle devait être là…* = “She was supposed to be there…”
- **deduction/likelihood about the past**: *Laura devait être malade.* = “Laura must have been sick.”
Often used with **ça** or **on** to comment on how something was expected or assumed to be.
target_language_example: Il devait être fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: He must have been tired after the trip.

meaning: in front of everyone; in public.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens where other people can see/hear it (often implying it’s embarrassing, inappropriate, or too personal). You’ll also hear variations like « pas devant tout le monde » (“not in front of everyone”) or « devant tout le monde ? » to express surprise.
target_language_example: Je préfère te parler devant tout le monde après la réunion.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk to you in public after the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that changes gradually over time and intensifies. It’s the imperfect tense of "devenir" (to become): "devenait" = "was becoming". The pattern is "de plus en plus" + adjective/adverb (e.g., sombre, violent, fort) to mean "more and more". You can swap the subject: "La situation devenait de plus en plus difficile."
target_language_example: Le bruit devenait de plus en plus fort au fil de la soirée.
native_language_example: The noise was getting louder and louder as the evening went on.

additional_notes: Used with être (auxiliary) to form the past tense: « être devenu(e) fou/folle ». It can be a real description (someone truly went insane) or, very often, an exaggerated reaction meaning “Are you crazy?!” Agreement: masculine singular « devenu fou », feminine singular « devenue folle », plural « devenus fous / devenues folles ».
target_language_example: Tu es devenu fou de faire ça ?
native_language_example: Have you gone crazy to do that?

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment built with **devoir** (to have to / must) in the **vous** form (**vous devez**) + **être** (to be) + **très** (very). It’s typically followed by an adjective: *Vous devez être très fatigué(e).* It can mean a logical assumption (“you must be…”) or a strong guess from context.
target_language_example: Vous devez être très fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: You must be very tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective (difficile, populaire, fort, grande, compliqué) to show that something is changing over time and increasing in degree. It’s the 3rd-person singular of "devenir" (to become): "X devient de plus en plus + adjectif". You can also use other forms: "deviennent de plus en plus" (they are becoming) or past tense "est devenu(e) de plus en plus" (became more and more).
target_language_example: Avec le temps, ce travail devient de plus en plus stressant.
native_language_example: Over time, this job is becoming more and more stressful.

additional_notes: Used in conversation to introduce news or something surprising/funny. Often rhetorical (you’re not really asking the other person to guess), and it can be said with or without a question mark. You’ll also hear: « Et devine quoi… » (“And guess what…”) or « Mais devine quoi ? » (“But guess what?”).
target_language_example: Devine quoi ? J’ai retrouvé tes clés !
native_language_example: Guess what? I found your keys!

additional_notes: From the verb devoir ("to have to/must"). "Devons-nous… ?" is the inverted (more formal) way to ask a question; in everyday speech you often hear "On doit… ?" or "Est-ce que nous devons… ?". Used to ask about obligation or necessity.
target_language_example: Devons-nous partir tout de suite ?
native_language_example: Do we have to leave right away?

meaning: "must we do" / "do we have to do" (sometimes "should we do").
additional_notes: From the verb *devoir* (to have to / must). *Devons-nous… ?* is an inverted, more formal way to ask a question; in everyday speech you’ll often hear *On doit faire… ?* or *Est-ce qu’on doit faire… ?*. It’s typically followed by the thing to do: *Devons-nous faire tout cela ?*
target_language_example: Devons-nous faire une réservation à l’avance ?
native_language_example: Do we have to make a reservation in advance?

meaning: "must we / do we have to" (formal question form).
additional_notes: This is the inverted (question) form of the verb *devoir* ("to have to / must") with the subject *nous* ("we"). In correct spelling, it’s usually written with a hyphen: **devons-nous ?** You can also ask the same question more commonly as **Est-ce que nous devons… ?** or **Nous devons… ?** (rising intonation).
target_language_example: Devons nous partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do we have to leave now?

additional_notes: "Devraient" is the conditional of devoir (must/should). With "être" it expresses what is expected, recommended, or logically likely about a state or situation. Often used for opinions/advice (Les criminels devraient être punis.) or expectations (Ils devraient être là. = They should be there by now).
target_language_example: À cette heure-ci, ils devraient être à la maison.
native_language_example: By this time, they should be at home.

meaning: "should I?" (polite way to ask what you ought to do).
additional_notes: From the verb "devoir" (to have to / should) in the conditional + inverted "je" to form a question. The conditional often makes the question more polite or tentative than "dois-je". Used to ask for advice or instructions: "Devrais-je fermer ?" = "Should I close?"
target_language_example: Devrais-je vous appeler plus tard ?
native_language_example: Should I call you later?

additional_notes: "Devrais" is the conditional form of "devoir" (must/should). With an infinitive like "aller" it expresses what would be a good idea to do (often used to ask for or give advice): "Je devrais aller…" = "I should go…". Can also be used after "je pense que / il dit que" (I think / he says) or in questions: "Penses-tu que je devrais aller… ?"
target_language_example: Tu penses que je devrais aller au médecin ?
native_language_example: Do you think I should go to the doctor?

additional_notes: A common combination of devoir + faire, usually used to talk about what someone should do. Devrais is the conditional form, so with a subject it can mean either "I should do" or "you should do" depending on context: je devrais faire / tu devrais faire. It often appears in questions like ce que je devrais faire = "what I should do."
target_language_example: Tu devrais faire attention.
native_language_example: You should be careful.

additional_notes: Made of the conditional of devoir ("tu devrais" = "you should") + peut-être ("maybe/perhaps"). It’s used to give gentle, less direct advice or a suggestion. Often addressed to "tu" (one person, informal), but you can change the subject: je devrais peut-être (I should maybe), vous devriez peut-être (you should maybe, formal/plural).
target_language_example: Tu devrais peut-être appeler ton médecin.
native_language_example: You might want to call your doctor.

meaning: "I should" + "you" (object), as in “I should [do something] to/for you.”
additional_notes: Used mainly as "je devrais te" + infinitive: "Je devrais te remercier" (I should thank you), "Je devrais te réveiller" (I should wake you up). "Devrais" is the conditional form of "devoir" (must/should), often expressing what would be the right thing to do, advice, or a mild obligation. "Te" is an unstressed object pronoun meaning "you" (informal singular) and comes before the infinitive.
target_language_example: Je devrais te le dire maintenant.
native_language_example: I should tell you now.

additional_notes: From the verb devoir (“to have to / must”) in the conditional (devrait) + pas + être (“to be”). Often expresses expectation, advice, or that something is not supposed to happen. In informal speech, people often drop ne: ça devrait pas être… / il devrait pas être… In more formal French you’ll see ne devrait pas être.
target_language_example: Ça devrait pas être un problème.
native_language_example: It shouldn’t be a problem.

additional_notes: Form of the verb devoir in the conditional (il/elle/on devrait) + être. Used to express what ought to be the case, what is recommended, or what is expected to be true. Can imply obligation (Cela devrait être fait immédiatement) or expectation/probability (Tom devrait être prêt à présent).
target_language_example: Ça devrait être assez facile.
native_language_example: That should be pretty easy.

additional_notes: Used to ask what would be the right thing to do: *Devrions-nous… ?* = “Should we…?” It’s formed with inversion (*devrions* + *nous*) and is a bit more formal than *On devrait… ?* or *Est-ce qu’on devrait… ?*. You can also use it for advice or recommendations in a group setting.
target_language_example: Devrions-nous partir maintenant ou attendre encore un peu ?
native_language_example: Should we leave now or wait a bit longer?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say an action is hard: « Difficile de + infinitif ». It’s a shortened form of « C’est difficile de… » and often appears as a stand-alone comment (e.g., « Difficile de résumer. »). You can also use it after « être »: « Il a été difficile de… ».
target_language_example: C'est difficile de choisir un restaurant ce soir.
native_language_example: It’s hard to choose a restaurant tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say something is hard to do: **difficile à + infinitive** (e.g., *difficile à comprendre*, *difficile à ouvrir*). The subject is usually the thing that is difficult (book/door/person), and the verb stays in the infinitive.
target_language_example: Ce formulaire est difficile à remplir.
native_language_example: This form is hard to fill out.

additional_notes: Used with two items linked by "et" (and): "la différence entre A et B". Often appears in patterns like "C’est la différence entre..." or "Il y a une (grande/subtile/énorme) différence entre...".
target_language_example: Quelle est la différence entre ce modèle et l’autre ?
native_language_example: What’s the difference between this model and the other one?

additional_notes: Uses the noun « adieu » (“farewell”). It can be emotional or final (leaving a place, ending a relationship, or not seeing someone again). You can also use it reflexively: « se dire adieu » = “to say goodbye to each other.” Common patterns: « dire adieu à + [person/place/thing] » and « venir dire adieu » (“to come say goodbye”).
target_language_example: Avant de partir, je suis passé dire adieu à mes collègues.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I stopped by to say goodbye to my coworkers.

additional_notes: Used when you are leaving or ending a conversation. You can use it without an object (Je dois dire au revoir.) or with a person: dire au revoir à quelqu’un. Very common is the reflexive form se dire au revoir (“to say goodbye to each other”).
target_language_example: Je vais te laisser : je dois dire au revoir à tout le monde.
native_language_example: I’m going to go: I have to say goodbye to everyone.

additional_notes: Used for taking leave of a person. The "à" introduces the person you’re saying goodbye to (dire au revoir à Marie). Often used with "aller" (aller dire au revoir à...) or in the imperative (Va dire au revoir à...).
target_language_example: Je dois dire au revoir à mes collègues avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have to say goodbye to my coworkers before leaving.

meaning: to say/tell what…, to say whatever…
additional_notes: Used with relative pronouns: **dire ce que + subject + verb** (“say/tell what…”) and **dire ce qui + verb** (“say/tell what… [is/does]”). Often implies freedom of speech/choice: **dire ce qu’il veut** = “say whatever he wants.” Note the difference: **ce que** is usually the object (“what” someone says/does), while **ce qui** is usually the subject (“what” is true/what happens).
target_language_example: Je vais dire ce que je pense.
native_language_example: I’m going to say what I think.

meaning: to say/tell what’s happening (what’s going on).
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to explain a situation: "Tu peux me dire ce qu'il se passe ?" (= Can you tell me what’s going on?). "ce qu'il se passe" means “what is happening/going on”; it’s very common with verbs like dire (to tell), expliquer (to explain), or savoir (to know).
target_language_example: Peux-tu me dire ce qu'il se passe ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what’s going on?

meaning: to say/tell what (someone did, wants, thinks, etc.).
additional_notes: "Dire" means "to say" or "to tell." "Ce que" introduces the thing being said/told as a clause ("what …"). Very often used with an indirect object: "dire à quelqu’un ce que…" (to tell someone what…). In questions, you’ll often see: "Peux-tu / Pouvez-vous me dire ce que… ?"
target_language_example: Tu peux me dire ce que tu cherches ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what you’re looking for?

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you want to express about yourself, but it’s normally followed by a verb or a full clause (e.g., « dire ce que je pense » = “say what I think”, « dire ce que je veux » = “say what I want”). On its own, it feels unfinished in French.
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que je pense.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you what I think.

additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase that introduces a clause starting with **ce que** (“what/that which”). It’s commonly completed with a verb like **veux** (want), **penses** (think), **sais** (know), etc.: **Dis-moi ce que tu veux** (“Tell me what you want”), **Tu peux dire ce que tu penses** (“You can say what you think”). Word order: **dire + ce que + subject + verb**.
target_language_example: Tu peux dire ce que tu penses.
native_language_example: You can say what you think.

meaning: to say/tell what; to say which (thing) …
additional_notes: “Ce qui” means “what” or “the thing(s) that” and is used when it’s the subject of the following verb: « dire ce qui est arrivé » (to say what happened). Often used when the exact information is unknown or uncertain: « On ne peut pas dire ce qui se passera » (We can’t say what will happen). In « dire ce qui lui chante », it means “to say whatever they like.”
target_language_example: Personne ne peut dire ce qui va se passer demain.
native_language_example: No one can say what will happen tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to explain an event or situation. « ce qui » means “what/that which” and refers to the thing that happened. « s'est passé » is the past tense (passé composé) of « se passer » (“to happen”), often used for specific past events.
target_language_example: Peux-tu me dire ce qui s'est passé ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what happened?

meaning: to tell/say what’s going on (what’s happening).
additional_notes: Used when you want an explanation of a situation. Very common in questions and requests: « Peux-tu me dire ce qui se passe ? » / « Dis-moi ce qui se passe. » Here « ce qui » means “what” as the subject of the verb « se passe » (“is happening”).
target_language_example: Tu peux me dire ce qui se passe ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what’s going on?

meaning: to speak badly of (someone); to badmouth; to say negative things about (someone).
additional_notes: Used with "de" + a person/thing: "dire du mal de quelqu’un/de quelque chose". Often implies criticizing, gossiping, or talking behind someone’s back. Common in advice or rules: "Ne dis pas du mal des autres."
target_language_example: Il a pour règle de ne jamais dire du mal des autres.
native_language_example: He has a rule never to speak badly of others.

meaning: to speak ill of the dead.
additional_notes: A common moral saying meaning you shouldn’t criticize someone after they have died (often out of respect, or because they can’t defend themselves). Often used with negation: « Il/On ne faut/pas… », « On ne doit pas… ».
target_language_example: Même s'il n'était pas parfait, je préfère ne pas dire du mal des morts.
native_language_example: Even if he wasn’t perfect, I’d rather not speak ill of the dead.

meaning: to say the same thing; (with "vouloir dire") to mean the same thing.
additional_notes: Used for repeating an idea in different words or pointing out that two statements have the same meaning. Common patterns: "Ça veut dire la même chose" = "It means the same thing." / "Je pourrais dire la même chose de toi" = "I could say the same thing about you" (i.e., make the same comment/criticism/praise). You may also see "Je pourrais dire la même chose pour toi" meaning roughly "the same applies to you" / "I could say the same for you."
target_language_example: En d’autres mots, je vais dire la même chose.
native_language_example: In other words, I’m going to say the same thing.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being honest (not lying). It’s an infinitive phrase, so it often follows verbs like devoir/pouvoir/oser: « Vous devez dire la vérité » (You must tell the truth). You can add the person you’re telling with « à + someone »: « dire la vérité à Tom ». You can also use indirect object pronouns: « leur dire la vérité » = tell them the truth.
target_language_example: Je vais te dire la vérité : je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you the truth: I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause after dire. Most often it means "say/tell that" (often as dire à quelqu’un que = "tell someone that"), but after verbs like vouloir it can mean "mean that". Very common for reporting information, opinions, or messages.
target_language_example: Je voulais te dire que je pars demain.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you that I'm leaving tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you’re stating about yourself. Often comes after another verb: “Je veux/je dois/je vais te/vous dire que je…” (“I want/I have/I’m going to tell you that I…”). In “Ça ne veut pas dire que je…”, it means “That doesn’t mean that I…”. It’s normally followed by the indicative (not the subjunctive).
target_language_example: Je dois te dire que je suis fatigué.
native_language_example: I have to tell you that I’m tired.

meaning: “to say that I am” / “to say I’m …”.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement about yourself, often with verbs like « je dois dire que… » (I have to say…), « je tiens à dire que… » (I want to make it clear…), or « on devrait dire que… » (you could say…). It’s frequently followed by an adjective or noun phrase: « dire que je suis impressionné / un homme nouveau ».
target_language_example: Je dois dire que je suis un peu surpris.
native_language_example: I have to say I’m a bit surprised.

meaning: to say something; to tell someone something.
additional_notes: Very common, neutral phrase. Often used when someone wants to speak up ("Laisse-moi dire quelque chose...") or when you suspect there is an implied message ("Comme si on voulait nous dire quelque chose" = as if someone wanted to tell us something). You can add who you’re speaking to with an indirect object: « dire quelque chose à quelqu’un » (to say/tell something to someone).
target_language_example: Je dois te dire quelque chose.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something.

meaning: “say what?” / “what am I supposed to say?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone means or what you’re expected to say, often as a short question: « Dire quoi ? » = “Say what?” It can refer to past or future speech (« Je viens de dire quoi ? » = “What did I just say?” / « J’aurais dû dire quoi ? » = “What should I have said?”). Very common in spoken French. Also appears in « Tu veux dire quoi par là ? » = “What do you mean by that?”
target_language_example: Je dois dire quoi, moi ?
native_language_example: What am I supposed to say, me?

additional_notes: Uses the expression « quoi que ce soit » (“anything whatsoever”) after « dire ». Very common in negative contexts (ne…pas / ne…plus / ne…jamais) or with refusal/ability: « refuser de dire quoi que ce soit », « être trop… pour dire quoi que ce soit ». It emphasizes that nothing is said.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas dire quoi que ce soit pour l’instant.
native_language_example: I can’t say anything for now.

meaning: to always say; to keep saying.
additional_notes: Literally “to say always.” As written, *dire toujours* is an infinitive phrase, so it most naturally appears after a conjugated verb (e.g., *Je vais dire toujours…*, *Il veut dire toujours…*), though many speakers prefer rephrasing to place *toujours* after the conjugated verb (*Il dit toujours…*). It can express a habit (always saying something) or repetition (keeping saying the same thing).
target_language_example: Il va dire toujours la même chose.
native_language_example: He is going to always say the same thing.

meaning: to say a word; to say anything (often: to have a quick word).
additional_notes: Very common in the fixed phrase «sans dire un mot» = “without saying a word” (in silence). With an indirect object («te/vous dire un mot»), it often means “to have a quick word (with you),” sometimes suggesting a brief, private comment rather than literally one word.
target_language_example: Tu peux attendre deux minutes ? J’aimerais te dire un mot.
native_language_example: Can you wait two minutes? I’d like to have a quick word with you.

additional_notes: Very common spoken phrasing. "un truc" is an informal, vague word meaning “a thing / something,” often used when what you’re about to say is casual, unspecified, or you don’t want to name it yet. Often appears as a question to get permission or attention: "Je peux te/vous dire un truc ?" = “Can I tell you something?”
target_language_example: Attends, je dois te dire un truc important.
native_language_example: Wait, I have to tell you something important.

meaning: to tell you something; to say one thing.
additional_notes: Often used to introduce an important point, a warning, or a personal comment. Common patterns: « Je dois te dire une chose » (I have to tell you something), « Je veux juste dire une chose » (I just want to say one thing), « Permettez-moi de vous dire une chose » (Allow me to tell you something). Uses indirect object pronouns like te/vous depending on who you’re speaking to.
target_language_example: Attends, je dois te dire une chose avant de partir.
native_language_example: Wait, I have to tell you something before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to express shock, disapproval, or disbelief at what someone has said. Very common in questions like « Comment peux-tu / pouvez-vous dire une chose pareille ? » (“How can you say such a thing?”). « pareille » here means “like that / such,” referring back to the (usually offensive or surprising) remark.
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à croire que tu aies pu dire une chose pareille.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you could say such a thing.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific comment, opinion, or idea: ça means “that.” It is often literal (“say that”), but in context it can also mean “mean that,” especially in questions like Veux-tu vraiment dire ça ? In Comment dire ça ?, it means “how should I put this?”
target_language_example: Je ne voulais pas dire ça.
native_language_example: I didn't mean to say that.

meaning: straight to bed; directly to bed.
additional_notes: Means going to bed immediately, without doing anything else first. Often used with verbs of movement like aller (to go) or partir (to leave/go off). Word order: verb + directement + au lit. Note: you usually say "aller au lit" (to go to bed) rather than *aller au lit* meaning getting into bed; "se coucher" is another common verb meaning "to go to bed / lie down to sleep."
target_language_example: Après le dîner, je suis allé directement au lit.
native_language_example: After dinner, I went straight to bed.

meaning: "heads toward" / "moves toward" (goes in the direction of).
additional_notes: Used with "se diriger vers" = to head toward a person or place (often suggesting a clear direction or intention). Conjugate "diriger" to match the subject: "je me dirige vers…", "il/elle se dirige vers…", "nous nous dirigeons vers…". You can also use it in instructions or reports (e.g., radio/mission context).
target_language_example: Je me dirige vers la sortie.
native_language_example: I'm heading toward the exit.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *dire* (“to say/tell”) + the direct object pronoun *le* (“it”), joined with a hyphen. Used to tell someone to say something out loud or to tell a piece of information. If you add an indirect object too, it becomes *dis-le-lui* (“tell it to him/her”).
target_language_example: Si tu sais la vérité, dis-le maintenant.
native_language_example: If you know the truth, say it now.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) with tu: dis = “tell/say”, le = “it” (direct object), moi = “to me”. In French imperatives, object pronouns come after the verb and are linked with hyphens. You can swap le for another direct object: Dis-la-moi (tell me it/her), Dis-les-moi (tell me them). Often used to urge someone to speak frankly: Dis-le-moi franchement.
target_language_example: Si tu sais la vérité, dis-le-moi.
native_language_example: If you know the truth, tell me.

additional_notes: Imperative form of dire addressed to one person (tu): dis = “tell/say”; leur = “to them.” It’s used to give an instruction like “Tell them to leave,” “Tell them what you know,” or “Tell them that…”. For a formal/plural command, use “Dites-leur.”
target_language_example: Dis-leur que j'arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Tell them I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *dire* (to say/tell) + the indirect object pronoun *lui* (to him/to her). Used to give an order: *Dis-lui de partir* (“Tell him/her to leave”). Can also stand alone as an encouragement/command: *Dis-lui !* (“Tell him/her!”). For more than one person, use *dites-lui* (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Dis-lui la vérité.
native_language_example: Tell him/her the truth.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction that someone should pass on to another person: "Dis-lui de + infinitive". "Lui" can refer to either "to him" or "to her"; for more than one person, you’d use "Dis-leur de...".
target_language_example: Dis-lui de m’envoyer un message ce soir.
native_language_example: Tell him/her to send me a message tonight.

additional_notes: "Dis" is the informal (tu) command form of dire (to say/tell). "Lui" means “to him/to her” (an indirect object pronoun), and "que" introduces what you’re telling them. It’s used to pass on a message: Dis-lui que + full sentence. For a formal or plural command, use: Dites-lui que…
target_language_example: Dis-lui que je vais arriver en retard.
native_language_example: Tell him/her that I'm going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to pass on a message to someone (lui = “to him/her”). Often followed by a place or a state/activity: ici (“here”), occupé(e) (“busy”), en train de + infinitive (“in the middle of” doing something). Agreement: occupé (male) / occupée (female). In the past, you may hear dis-lui que je suis passé (“tell him I stopped by / came by”).
target_language_example: S’il te plaît, dis-lui que je suis en réunion.
native_language_example: Please tell him/her that I’m in a meeting.

additional_notes: Imperative of *dire* + the object pronoun *moi* (“me”), linked with a hyphen. Used when speaking to one person you address as *tu*. Often followed by a noun (*Dis-moi la vérité.*) or by *que* + a sentence (*Dis-moi que tu viens.*).
target_language_example: Dis-moi où tu habites.
native_language_example: Tell me where you live.

meaning: 'tell me what…' (asking someone to tell you something).
additional_notes: "Dis-moi" is the informal singular imperative of "dire" (used when speaking to one person you call "tu"). It’s commonly followed by "ce que" + a full clause: "Dis-moi ce que tu sais" (Tell me what you know), "Dis-moi ce que tu en penses" (Tell me what you think about it). For a more formal/polite version, use "Dites-moi ce que…".
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce que tu veux manger ce soir.
native_language_example: Tell me what you want to eat tonight.

meaning: “tell me what you …” (telling someone to say what they did/think/decide, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to start an instruction/request: « Dis-moi » = “Tell me”, followed by « ce que » = “what/that which”, and « tu » = “you” (informal singular). It’s typically followed by a verb in the past or present: « Dis-moi ce que tu as vu » (what you saw), « Dis-moi ce que tu en penses » (what you think of it), « Dis-moi ce que tu décides » (what you decide). For a formal/polite version, use « Dites-moi ce que vous… ».
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce que tu veux faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Tell me what you want to do tonight.

meaning: "Tell me what you have / what’s going on (with you)."
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to tell you what they have to say or what information they have. Depending on context, it can mean: (1) “tell me what you’ve got (on someone)” = tell me what evidence/info you have; (2) “tell me what you have in mind/on your heart” = tell me what you’re thinking/feeling; (3) “tell me what you have” said alone can also mean “tell me what’s wrong.”
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce que tu as, et on trouvera une solution.
native_language_example: Tell me what’s going on, and we’ll find a solution.

additional_notes: An imperative (command/request). It’s made of: « dis-moi » = “tell me” (literally “say to me”), « ce que » = “what/that which,” and « tu vois » = “you see.” Often used when asking someone to look at something (e.g., around them, at a picture, or at you) and describe what they notice. « Dis-moi » can take a hyphen when followed by an object pronoun (moi).
target_language_example: Regarde la photo et dis-moi ce que tu vois.
native_language_example: Look at the photo and tell me what you see.

meaning: Tell me what’s happening / what’s going on.
additional_notes: "Dis-moi" is the informal singular command form of "dire" (you say this to one person you call "tu"). "Ce qui se passe" means "what is happening". You can add a name before it to address someone directly: "Tom, dis-moi ce qui se passe."
target_language_example: Je suis inquiet—dis-moi ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: I’m worried—tell me what’s going on.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (informal/familiar: tu) to explain the way to do something or how something happened. Often followed by an infinitive (Dis-moi comment faire…) or a full clause (Dis-moi comment tu as fait…). You can also say it alone: Dis-moi comment !
target_language_example: Dis-moi comment tu as fait ça.
native_language_example: Tell me how you did that.

additional_notes: An imperative (command) meaning “tell me the truth.” Used to insist on honesty, often when you think someone is hiding something. You can soften it with “s'il te plaît” (Dis-moi la vérité, s'il te plaît.) or make it more forceful with “Allez,” / “Non mais” or an exclamation mark.
target_language_example: Dis-moi la vérité : tu as oublié le rendez-vous ?
native_language_example: Tell me the truth: did you forget the appointment?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a location or place in an indirect question. Often followed by a clause (e.g., « Dis-moi où tu habites. »), and in formal written French you may also see inversion (e.g., « Dis-moi où es-tu né ? »). It can also be left hanging as « Dis-moi où. » when the rest is understood from context.
target_language_example: Dis-moi où tu as mis mes clés.
native_language_example: Tell me where you put my keys.

additional_notes: Imperative of *dire* + indirect object *nous* (“us”), followed by *ce que tu* (“what you…”). Used to ask someone to say what they think/know/see, etc. It’s followed by another verb: *Dis-nous ce que tu penses / sais / vois…*
target_language_example: Dis-nous ce que tu veux faire maintenant.
native_language_example: Tell us what you want to do now.

meaning: "do you say/tell" (question form of « tu dis »).
additional_notes: This is the verb–subject inversion used to ask a question with « tu » (from the verb « dire », to say/tell): « dis-tu ? ». It often appears after a question word or phrase: « qu’en dis-tu ? » (what do you think?), « comment dis-tu… ? » (how do you say…?), « pourquoi dis-tu… ? » (why do you say…?).
target_language_example: Qu’en dis-tu si on se retrouve à 19 h ?
native_language_example: What do you say if we meet up at 7 p.m.?

meaning: "hey" / "say" (to get someone’s attention, often with surprise or reproach).
additional_notes: Very common spoken interjection. Used to call someone (“Dis donc, toi !”), to react with surprise (“Dis donc, vous vous êtes levés tôt !”), or to scold/complain (“Dis donc, ça commence à faire…”). Often followed by a comma and said with emphasis. Informal.
target_language_example: Dis donc, tu pourrais au moins dire bonjour !
native_language_example: Hey, you could at least say hello!

additional_notes: Imperative form (tu) of dire: “dis” = “(you) tell/say.” Used to urge someone to be honest. You can also use “Dire la vérité” (infinitive) and other forms like “Je dis la vérité” (I’m telling the truth) or “Dis-moi la vérité” (Tell me the truth).
target_language_example: Dis la vérité, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Tell the truth, please.

additional_notes: Used with *dire* (“to say/tell”) in the negative: **ne … dis pas** = “don’t say/tell …” (especially as an order: *Ne leur dis pas.*). In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Dis pas ça !* / *Tu dis pas bonjour ?* (“You’re not saying hello?” / “Aren’t you going to say hello?”). *Dis* is the **tu** form (spoken to one person you address as *tu*).
target_language_example: Dis pas ça, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t say that, please.

additional_notes: Imperative of *dire* (“to say/tell”) used to stop someone from saying something. In careful/standard French you’ll usually see the full negation: **Ne dis pas ça** (or with an object: **Ne me/lui dis pas ça** = “Don’t tell me/him/her that”). Without **ne** (“Dis pas ça”) is common in casual spoken French.
target_language_example: S'il te plaît, ne dis pas ça à Marie.
native_language_example: Please don’t tell Marie that.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *dire* (“to say/tell”) used to urge someone to speak (often because they’re being silent). Can sound impatient or pleading depending on tone (e.g., *Enfin !* = “Come on!/At last!”). Also: *Dites quelque chose* (formal/plural), *Dis-moi quelque chose* (“Tell me something”).
target_language_example: Dis quelque chose, je t'écoute.
native_language_example: Say something—I'm listening.

additional_notes: Used for a computer’s storage device. You’ll often see it with adjectives like externe (external) or plein (full), and with verbs like enregistrer (to save/record) and perdre des données (to lose data).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un disque dur externe pour faire une sauvegarde.
native_language_example: I bought an external hard drive to make a backup.

meaning: to tell right from wrong; to distinguish good from evil.
additional_notes: Uses the verb « distinguer » (“to distinguish”) with « le bien » (“good/right”) and « le mal » (“evil/wrong”). Often used about moral judgment or maturity (e.g., whether someone understands what is right vs. wrong). You can also say « distinguer le vrai du faux » (“tell true from false”).
target_language_example: À son âge, il devrait déjà savoir distinguer le bien du mal.
native_language_example: At his age, he should already know right from wrong.

additional_notes: Used to mean an automated bank machine where you withdraw cash. Often shortened in speech to "un distributeur". Common related phrases: "retirer de l’argent" (withdraw money), "Le distributeur est en panne" (The ATM is out of order), "Le distributeur a avalé ma carte" (The machine kept my card).
target_language_example: Je vais au distributeur de billets pour retirer de l’argent.
native_language_example: I’m going to the ATM to withdraw cash.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase « dire au revoir » = “to say goodbye.” You’ll also often see it with « se »: « on se dit au revoir » / « ils se sont dit au revoir » = “we/they say said goodbye (to each other).” Used when leaving someone or ending a conversation.
target_language_example: Avant de partir, elle m’a dit au revoir.
native_language_example: Before leaving, she said goodbye to me.

additional_notes: Used with dire + de + infinitive to report an instruction, order, or advice. In English, this is often translated with “tell someone to do something,” even though French uses dire. The person receiving the instruction is often shown with an indirect object: m'a dit de..., lui a dit de....
target_language_example: Le professeur nous a dit de finir nos devoirs.
native_language_example: The teacher told us to finish our homework.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to report an instruction/advice in the negative: « dire à [quelqu’un] de ne pas + infinitif ». In real sentences you’ll often see a pronoun before « dit » (e.g., « il me dit de ne pas… », « elle lui a dit de ne pas… »). « dit » can be present (« il dit ») or past with « a dit ».
target_language_example: Elle m’a dit de ne pas parler pendant le film.
native_language_example: She told me not to talk during the movie.

additional_notes: Used with the verb dire to report an instruction: « (Je/On) ai/a dit de ne pas bouger » = “(I/We/Someone) told (them) not to move.” Often includes an indirect object pronoun to show who was told: « Je t’ai dit… » (I told you…), « Je vous ai dit… » (I told you…), « On nous a dit… » (We were told…).
target_language_example: Le policier m’a dit de ne pas bouger.
native_language_example: The police officer told me not to move.

dit de ne pas le faire

target_language_multi_word_term: dit de ne pas le faire
additional_notes: Used with a person (often as an indirect object) to report that someone was instructed not to do something: « Je lui ai dit de ne pas le faire. » = “I told him/her not to do it.” In everyday French, you’ll also hear « dire à quelqu’un de ne pas… » (more explicit: “tell someone not to…”).
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit de ne pas le faire, mais il l’a fait quand même.
native_language_example: I told him not to do it, but he did it anyway.

additional_notes: Usually used in the pattern **dire à quelqu’un de + infinitive** (“to tell someone to do something”). With an infinitive, the negation goes **before the verb**: **ne pas venir** = “not to come.” The person you’re telling is often shown with an indirect object pronoun: **lui** (to him/her), **leur** (to them), **nous** (to us), etc. In natural English, this is usually **“tell”**, not “say.”
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit de ne pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I told him/her not to come tonight.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "dire" (to say/tell) in the past ("il/elle a dit…" = he/she said…) or present ("il/elle dit…" = he/she says…). "La même chose" means "the same thing" and can also refer to someone repeating the same comment about a person: "Il a dit la même chose de vous" = "He said the same thing about you." In "Je me suis dit la même chose", it means "I told myself the same thing."
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit la même chose hier.
native_language_example: I told him/her the same thing yesterday.

additional_notes: From the verb dire (to say/tell) + la vérité (the truth). In context you’ll usually change the verb form: il dit la vérité (he tells the truth), elle dit la vérité (she tells the truth), il a dit la vérité (he told the truth), merci de m’avoir dit la vérité (thanks for telling me the truth). Often used after verbs like croire (to believe): Je crois qu’il dit la vérité.
target_language_example: Je pense qu’elle dit la vérité, même si c’est difficile à entendre.
native_language_example: I think she’s telling the truth, even if it’s hard to hear.

additional_notes: Used in indirect/reported speech to introduce what someone says about a woman (“elle”). Typically follows a subject (Il/Elle/on, a name, a role): « Il dit qu'elle… », « Elle dit qu'elle… », « Le médecin dit qu'elle… ». Tense and context determine whether it’s “says” or “said” (e.g., « il dit » vs « il a dit »). Written French often elides « que elle » to « qu'elle ».
target_language_example: Le médecin dit qu'elle peut voyager.
native_language_example: The doctor says that she can travel.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man says: **dire que** + a clause. **qu'il** is the contraction of **que + il**. The tense can change depending on context (e.g., **il a dit qu'il...**, **on m'avait dit qu'il...**).
target_language_example: Il dit qu'il n'a pas le temps aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He says that he doesn't have time today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **dire** + **que** to report what someone says or said: *X dit que…* = “X says/says that…”. The tense can change with context (e.g., *il dit que…* = “he says that…”, *il a dit que…* = “he said that…”).
target_language_example: Elle dit que le train est en retard.
native_language_example: She says that the train is late.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech: dire + que + clause. "c'était" is the imperfect of "c'est" (ce + être), often used to describe or identify something in the past. The verb "dire" can change with the subject/tense (j’ai dit / tu as dit / on a dit / il a dit), but the structure stays the same: [someone] a dit que c’était + adjective/noun.
target_language_example: Il a dit que c'était une erreur.
native_language_example: He said that it was a mistake.

additional_notes: Used with reported speech after dire que (“to say that”). In a past context, French often uses the imperfect (j’étais) to describe an ongoing state at that time (“I was …”). The subject can change (j’ai dit…, il a dit…, tu as dit… → dit que j’étais).
target_language_example: Il a dit que j'étais trop fatigué pour sortir.
native_language_example: He said that I was too tired to go out.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says or said: **dire + que + subject**. **dit** is the 3rd-person singular present of *dire* (“he/she says”), but you’ll also see it after auxiliaries in the past: *il m’a dit que tu…* (“he told me that you…”). The verb after **que** is conjugated normally depending on the time: *dit que tu viens* / *a dit que tu venais*.
target_language_example: Il dit que tu arrives à huit heures.
native_language_example: He says you’re arriving at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used after a subject (e.g., il/elle/on, tu, elles) to report what someone said: « [subject] a/ont dit que tu étais… ». « étais » is the imperfect of être, often used in indirect speech to shift back in time ("you are" → "you were"). What follows can change for gender/number (e.g., « viré » / « virée »).
target_language_example: Il a dit que tu étais fatigué(e).
native_language_example: He said that you were tired.

meaning: “(he/she) said that you …” / “(someone) tells me that you …” (reported speech).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about “you” (vous). With a subject it can be: « Il/Elle dit que vous… » (He/She says that you…) or « Il/Elle a dit que vous… » (He/She said that you…). In questions: « Comment avez-vous dit que vous vous appeliez ? » = “What did you say your name was?”
target_language_example: Il m’a dit que vous viendriez demain.
native_language_example: He told me that you would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech: *dire que* + clause. After *dit que*, French often uses the imperfect (*vous étiez*) to describe a past state or situation (“you were”). The adjective/past participle that follows agrees with who *vous* refers to (e.g., *viré/virée*, *heureux/heureuses*).
target_language_example: Il a dit que vous étiez prêts.
native_language_example: He said that you were ready.

additional_notes: A common pattern with verbs like **dire** (to say/tell) or **se dire** (to tell oneself/think): **[verb] + que + ça + [verb]**. In context, **ça** often means “it/that” (not always “that” literally). Example: **Je me suis dit que ça…** = “I thought/told myself that it…”.
target_language_example: Je me suis dit que ça valait la peine d’essayer.
native_language_example: I thought it was worth trying.

meaning: "said something"; with "ça/ce nom…", "(it) rings a bell / sounds familiar".
additional_notes: Literally from *dire* (to say) + *quelque chose* (something). Used in questions like **Avez-vous dit quelque chose ?** (“Did you say something?”). Very common in the expression **Ça te dit quelque chose ? / Est-ce que ce nom vous dit quelque chose ?** meaning “Does that ring a bell?” or “Does that name sound familiar?” (not literally “say something”).
target_language_example: Ce nom te dit quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Does that name ring a bell?

additional_notes: Very common in spoken, informal French to ask what someone said: « Il/Elle t’a dit quoi ? » (= « Qu’est-ce qu’il/elle t’a dit ? »). You can also use it about yourself: « J’ai dit quoi ? / J’avais dit quoi ? » (= “What did I say?”). It often comes at the end of the question, after the verb « dire » and sometimes an object pronoun like « te » (to you).
target_language_example: Il t’a dit quoi exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly did he tell you?

additional_notes: Used with the verb *dire* (“to say/tell”) plus *quoi que ce soit* (“anything at all”). Very common in questions and negatives to ask whether someone said something: *A-t-il/Elle dit quoi que ce soit ?* (“Did he/she say anything?”). The form of *dire* can change (e.g., *a dit*, *ont dit*, *avez dit*), but *quoi que ce soit* stays the same.
target_language_example: Il n’a rien dit : il n’a pas dit quoi que ce soit.
native_language_example: He didn’t say anything at all.

additional_notes: Past form of **dire** (“to say”), used to refer back to something someone said. Often appears in questions (**Ils ont dit ça ?** = “They said that?”) and in negation (**Tu n’as pas dit ça.** = “You didn’t say that.”). The informal contraction **T’as pas dit ça** is common in speech.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu as dit ça ?
native_language_example: Why did you say that?

additional_notes: Imperative of dire ("to say/tell") + the direct object pronoun le ("it"). Used when telling one or more people what to say or to tell someone. Other pronouns can be added after it, e.g. Dites-le-moi ("Tell me"), Dites-le-lui ("Tell him/her"), Dites-le-nous ("Tell us").
target_language_example: Si vous êtes d’accord, dites-le clairement.
native_language_example: If you agree, say it clearly.

additional_notes: Imperative of **dire**: **dites** = “tell/say” (to **vous**: one person formally or several people). **le** = “it” (a masculine direct object; often used generically for “it/that”), **moi** = “to me.” Common in requests: **S'il vous plaît, dites-le-moi** (“Please tell me”). For an informal singular command, you’d say **dis-le-moi**.
target_language_example: Si tu le sais, dites-le-moi maintenant, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: If you know it, tell me now, please.

additional_notes: Imperative of dire (“to say/tell”) + indirect object pronoun leur (“to them”). Used to give an instruction to one person you address as vous (one person formally, or several people): Dites-leur de… (“Tell them to…”) / Dites-leur que… (“Tell them that…”) / Dites-leur qui… (“Tell them who…”).
target_language_example: Dites-leur que j'arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Tell them I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: Imperative of **dire** (“to say/tell”) + indirect object pronoun **lui** (“to him/to her”). Used to tell someone what to say to a third person. With **lui**, it can mean either “him” or “her” (context makes it clear). For an informal singular command, you’d say **dis-lui**.
target_language_example: Dites-lui de me rappeler ce soir.
native_language_example: Tell him/her to call me back tonight.

additional_notes: "Dites" is the vous-form imperative of dire (used for politeness or when speaking to more than one person). "-lui" means “to him/her” (indirect object). It’s followed by "de" + infinitive: dites-lui de + verb (e.g., venir, attendre, appeler).
target_language_example: Dites-lui de revenir demain matin.
native_language_example: Tell him/her to come back tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Imperative of "dire" + "moi". Used to address one person politely (vous) or to speak to multiple people. Often followed by a question word: « Dites-moi qui/où/quand/pourquoi… ».
target_language_example: Dites-moi où est la gare, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Tell me where the train station is, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask for information with the polite/formal command form (imperative) of *dire* to *vous*: *dites*. Often followed by a full clause: *Dites-moi ce que vous savez / ce que vous voulez / ce que vous avez*. For an informal version with friends/family, you’ll often hear *Dis-moi ce que …*.
target_language_example: Dites-moi ce que vous cherchez, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Tell me what you’re looking for, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (politely or formally, with "vous") for a location or place. It’s the imperative of "dire" (dites) + "moi" (to me) + "où" (where), and is usually followed by a clause like "elle est" (she is) or "je peux le/la trouver" (I can find him/her/it).
target_language_example: Dites-moi où se trouve la gare, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Tell me where the train station is, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (politely or formally) to share information, an opinion, or what they want. It’s the imperative of *dire* (vous-form): *Dites…* + *nous* (“to us”) + *ce que vous…* (“what you…”). Common with verbs like *pensez* (think), *savez* (know), *voulez* (want).
target_language_example: Dites-nous ce que vous recherchez, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please tell us what you’re looking for.

additional_notes: This is the question form (inversion) of « vous dites » (“you say/you tell”). It’s used in polite speech or when speaking to more than one person. Often followed by a direct object: « Dites-vous la vérité ? » (“Are you telling the truth?”). Note: it can also mean “do you tell yourself…?” in reflexive contexts, but in these examples it’s simply the inverted question form.
target_language_example: Que dites-vous exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly are you saying?

additional_notes: Literally “say, then,” but used as an interjection. Often placed at the start of a sentence to call someone’s attention (“Dites donc, Monsieur…”) or to react with surprise/admiration/annoyance (“Mais dites donc !”, “Enfin, dites donc !”). It uses the polite/plural imperative of *dire* (dites).
target_language_example: Dites donc, vous avez vu l’heure ?
native_language_example: Hey, have you seen what time it is?

additional_notes: The number 18. Used for counting, giving ages, prices/amounts, results in math, and in phone numbers (often said digit by digit). Hyphenated in French: dix-huit.
target_language_example: J'ai dix-huit ans.
native_language_example: I am eighteen years old.

additional_notes: Used with age: "avoir dix-huit ans" = "to be 18 (years old)". You’ll often see it with modifiers like "à peine" (barely) or "au plus" (at most), or with time expressions: "à dix-huit ans" (at 18), "aura dix-huit ans en mai" (will turn 18 in May).
target_language_example: Je vais avoir dix-huit ans le mois prochain.
native_language_example: I’m going to turn 18 next month.

additional_notes: Used to tell time using the 24-hour clock, common in schedules and announcements. In everyday speech you might also hear "six heures (du soir)" for 6 p.m. You can add minutes after it: "dix-huit heures trente" = 6:30 p.m.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à dix-huit heures devant le cinéma.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at 6:00 p.m. in front of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Used for the number 19 (age, counting, etc.). In time expressions with "heures", it means 19:00 (7 p.m.) in the 24-hour clock: "dix-neuf heures". Note the hyphen in spelling.
target_language_example: Il a dix-neuf ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He is nineteen years old today.

additional_notes: The number 17. Often used for age ("J'ai dix-sept ans" = "I'm seventeen") or in times/durations ("quatre heures et dix-sept minutes" = "4 hours and 17 minutes"). Hyphenated in French: "dix-sept".
target_language_example: J'ai dix-sept ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I turn seventeen today.

additional_notes: Used to express a duration of time (for ten years / ten years ago: « Il a vécu là dix ans », « Ça fait dix ans ») or someone’s age (« un fils de dix ans » = a ten-year-old son). With age, it can appear after a noun: « une fille de dix ans ».
target_language_example: Ça fait dix ans que j’habite ici.
native_language_example: I’ve been living here for ten years.

additional_notes: Used to tell the time (à dix heures = at ten o’clock) or a duration/quantity of time (pendant dix heures = for ten hours; dix heures par jour = ten hours per day). Often appears with prepositions like à (at), pendant (for), and par (per).
target_language_example: Le train part à dix heures.
native_language_example: The train leaves at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (depuis dix minutes = for ten minutes; après dix minutes de marche = after ten minutes of walking) or a time difference (dix minutes en avance = ten minutes early; ma montre avance de dix minutes = my watch is ten minutes fast).
target_language_example: Attends-moi dix minutes, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Wait for me ten minutes, please.

meaning: "must I...?" / "do I have to...?" (formal question form of *devoir*).
additional_notes: Used to ask what you are required or supposed to do. It’s the inverted (more formal/written) way to form a question with *je*: *dois-je + infinitive ?* (e.g., *Dois-je partir ?*). In everyday speech, people often say *Est-ce que je dois... ?* or *Je dois... ?*
target_language_example: Dois-je remplir ce formulaire maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do I have to fill out this form now?

additional_notes: This is the verb inversion form used for questions: **dois-je** = “must I / should I” (from **devoir**), followed by **faire** (“to do/make”). It’s commonly used to ask what action is required or expected, and it can sound slightly formal. In everyday speech, you’ll often hear **Qu’est-ce que je dois faire ?** instead.
target_language_example: Alors, que dois-je faire pour confirmer la réservation ?
native_language_example: So, what do I need to do to confirm the reservation?

meaning: "Should I / must I … (to/for you)?" (very formal question form).
additional_notes: Uses inversion for questions: "Dois-je" = "must/should I" + "vous" as the object ("you" formal/plural). It’s used before an infinitive verb: "Dois-je vous appeler ?" (Should I call you?), "Dois-je vous informer… ?" (Should I inform you…?). Common in polite, formal, or written French; in everyday speech you often hear "Est-ce que je dois vous… ?" or "Je dois vous… ?".
target_language_example: Dois-je vous envoyer un e-mail ce soir ?
native_language_example: Should I send you an email tonight?

additional_notes: "Dois" is the 1st-person singular (je) form of **devoir** (to have to / must). It’s followed by an infinitive: **je dois + aller**. You can add a place after **aller** (e.g., **aller à** l’aéroport, **aller chez** le coiffeur).
target_language_example: Désolé, je dois aller au travail maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go to work now.

additional_notes: Used with **tu**: **Tu dois aller à + place** (devoir = must/need to; aller à = to go to). Often followed by a specific place: **à l’école**, **au travail**, **à la banque**. With a city: **à Paris**. With a feminine country: **en France** (not *à France*).
target_language_example: Tu dois aller à la banque aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You have to go to the bank today.

additional_notes: "Dois" is the present tense of "devoir" (to have to / must) for "je" (I). It’s followed by an infinitive: "je dois faire + [something]". Used to express obligation or necessity, often in questions like "Qu’est-ce que je dois faire ?" (What do I have to do?).
target_language_example: Désolé, je dois faire mes devoirs ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to do my homework tonight.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression on its own. `dois` is a form of `devoir` and can mean "must / have to" or "owe," while `le` means "it" or "him." You will usually see this as part of a longer sentence, for example `tu dois le faire` = "you have to do it."
target_language_example: Tu dois le faire maintenant.
native_language_example: You have to do it now.

additional_notes: Built from **devoir** (to have to/must) + the direct object pronoun **le** (“it”) + **faire** (to do). Most often seen as **je dois le faire** (“I have to do it”). **Le** replaces something already mentioned (an action/task). In speech you may hear **je sais pas** instead of **je ne sais pas**.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas, mais je dois le faire.
native_language_example: I don’t want to, but I have to do it.

meaning: "I have to" / "I must" (when the verb is reflexive: "I have to ___ myself").
additional_notes: "dois" is the 1st-person singular present of devoir (to have to / must): je dois = I have to. "me" is the reflexive pronoun used before a reflexive infinitive, e.g. je dois me reposer (I have to rest), je dois me rendormir (I have to fall back asleep). In full sentences it’s typically followed by an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: Je dois me dépêcher, on est en retard.
native_language_example: I have to hurry, we’re late.

additional_notes: Usually used with the subject pronoun: « Je dois parler à + person » = “I have to talk to + person.” « dois » is the 1st-person singular of « devoir » (to have to / must). « parler à » is used for talking to someone (e.g., « parler à Marie »). You can also use « Je dois lui parler » (“I have to talk to him/her”).
target_language_example: Je dois parler à mon professeur après le cours.
native_language_example: I have to talk to my teacher after class.

additional_notes: "Dois" is the present-tense form of "devoir" for "tu" (you), meaning obligation/necessity. It’s often followed by an infinitive like "partir" (to leave/go). You can also use it as a question: "Tu dois partir ?" = "Do you have to leave?"
target_language_example: Désolé, je dois partir maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to leave now.

meaning: 'must know' / 'need to know' (said to one person: tu).
additional_notes: Uses the verb devoir (tu dois = you must/you have to) + savoir (to know). Common in phrases like « C’est tout ce que tu dois savoir » (“That’s all you need to know”) or « Il y a une/deux choses que tu dois savoir » (“There’s one/two thing(s) you need to know”).
target_language_example: Avant de commencer, tu dois savoir que je n’ai pas beaucoup de temps.
native_language_example: Before we start, you need to know that I don’t have much time.

additional_notes: Usually short for « je dois y aller » (“I have to go”). « dois » is from « devoir » (to have to / must). « y aller » literally means “to go there,” but in everyday French « je dois y aller » is a common way to say you need to leave/you’ve got to go (to whatever place or obligation is understood from context). Often spoken as « j’dois y aller » (informal contraction).
target_language_example: Désolé, je dois y aller : j’ai un rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go: I have an appointment.

meaning: 'you must be' / 'you have to be' (also: 'you must be' = 'you’re probably').
additional_notes: “Dois” is the 2nd-person singular present of devoir (tu dois). It’s followed by an infinitive: tu dois être + adjective/place (“you must be…”). It can express (1) obligation/necessity (Tu dois être honnête. = You must be honest.) or (2) a strong guess/inference (Tu dois être fatigué. = You must be tired.).
target_language_example: Tu dois être prêt à 8 heures.
native_language_example: You have to be ready at 8 o’clock.

additional_notes: Built with **devoir** (“to owe / to have to”) + **des excuses** (“apologies”). Very common to admit you were wrong. You can add the person with **à**: *Je dois des excuses à Marie.* With an object pronoun: *Je **lui** dois des excuses* (to him/her), *Je **te** dois des excuses* (to you), *Je **vous** dois des excuses* (to you/formal or plural).
target_language_example: Je te dois des excuses pour mon retard.
native_language_example: I owe you an apology for being late.

additional_notes: Used to express strong likelihood or assumption. Literally built from devoir (must) + bien (adds emphasis like “surely”) + y avoir (there is/are). Commonly followed by a noun: « Il doit bien y avoir une solution. » It can change with person/tense: « Il devait bien y avoir… », « Il doit bien y avoir eu… ». Often used when you expect something to exist even if you haven’t found it yet.
target_language_example: Il doit bien y avoir un moyen d'y arriver.
native_language_example: There must be a way to do it.

additional_notes: "Devoir" expresses obligation/necessity ("must/have to"). "Y" often means "there" or "to it" and typically refers to a place or situation already understood from context. "Doit y aller" is third-person singular (il/elle/on). In everyday speech, "On doit y aller" can imply "We should get going" (time to leave).
target_language_example: Allez, on doit y aller.
native_language_example: Come on, we have to go.

meaning: “there must be / there has to be”.
additional_notes: Used with the impersonal expression **il y a** (“there is/are”) to express deduction or strong likelihood. You’ll most often see it as **il doit y avoir + noun**: *Il doit y avoir un problème.* In speech, **il** is sometimes dropped: *Doit y avoir un problème.* (more informal/colloquial style, but the phrase itself isn’t slang).
target_language_example: Il doit y avoir une erreur dans la réservation.
native_language_example: There must be a mistake in the booking.

meaning: 'there must be a…' / 'there should be a…'.
additional_notes: Usually part of the full structure **Il doit y avoir un/une…** (or **Doit y avoir un/une…** in casual speech), used to guess or deduce that something exists. **y avoir** means “to be/there is.” Use **un** (masc.) or **une** (fem.), and plural **des**: *Il doit y avoir des…*
target_language_example: Il doit y avoir une erreur.
native_language_example: There must be a mistake.

additional_notes: Usually used with “il”: « Il doit y avoir un moyen (de…) » = “There must be a way (to…).” It expresses a strong belief that a solution exists. In casual speech, “il” is sometimes dropped: « Doit y avoir un moyen. »
target_language_example: Il doit y avoir un moyen d’ouvrir cette porte sans clé.
native_language_example: There must be a way to open this door without a key.

meaning: “there must be another (one)” / “there has to be another (one)”
additional_notes: Usually part of a longer sentence: **Il doit y avoir une autre…** + noun (e.g., *une autre solution, une autre façon, une autre option*). It expresses a strong assumption or logical conclusion. In careful French you often add **il**: **Il doit y avoir une autre…**
target_language_example: Il doit y avoir une autre solution.
native_language_example: There must be another solution.

additional_notes: This is usually said as **Il doit y avoir une explication** (“There must be an explanation”). In casual spoken French, **il** is sometimes dropped. Uses **devoir** (doit) to express a strong assumption/likelihood (“must”).
target_language_example: Il doit y avoir une explication : le train est presque toujours à l’heure.
native_language_example: There must be an explanation: the train is almost always on time.

meaning: “there must be (some)” / “there should be (some)” (guessing a quantity or existence).
additional_notes: Usually you’ll hear it as **il doit y en avoir** in full. It’s used to make an estimate: **il doit y en avoir + number/quantity** (“there must be about…”). The **y** refers to “there/in it”, and **en** means “some/of it/them”. Dropping **il** is common in casual spoken French.
target_language_example: Il doit y en avoir une dizaine dans la boîte.
native_language_example: There must be about ten in the box.

additional_notes: Usually expresses a deduction or strong probability in sentences like these, not an obligation. It is the 3rd-person singular form of devoir + être.
target_language_example: Ce bruit doit être le vent.
native_language_example: That noise must be the wind.

additional_notes: Expresses obligation in the passive voice: something needs to be completed (often without saying who will do it). Used for tasks, deadlines, or requirements. In spoken French, you may also hear the active version: « Il faut le faire » (It has to be done).
target_language_example: Le rapport doit être fait avant midi.
native_language_example: The report must be done before noon.

meaning: 'must be a' (it has to be a...).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong deduction or obligation: *Il/Ça doit être un + noun* (“It must be a …”). It’s built from **devoir** (to have to / must) in the present tense (**doit**) + **être** (to be) + **un** (a, masculine). Change **un** to **une** for a feminine noun: *doit être une*. For plural, you’ll often see *doivent être des*.
target_language_example: Ça doit être un nouveau professeur.
native_language_example: He/That must be a new teacher.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject to express obligation or necessity. Very often followed by a past participle to make a passive meaning: "doivent être + past participle" = "must be + past participle" (e.g., doivent être changées = must be changed; doivent être rendus = must be returned).
target_language_example: Les documents doivent être signés avant demain.
native_language_example: The documents must be signed before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *donner* + indirect object pronoun *lui* (“to him/to her”). Used to tell someone to give something to a person: *Donne-lui le livre.* = “Give him/her the book.” *Lui* can refer to either “him” or “her” (singular), based on context. Often followed by a direct object (*donne-lui une chance*) or by *en* (“some/any”): *Donne-lui en.* = “Give him/her some.”
target_language_example: Donne-lui ce livre, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give him/her this book, please.

additional_notes: From the verb donner (“to give”) in the imperative (donne) + the indirect object pronoun moi (“to me”). Used to tell one person you address as tu to give you something: Donne-moi la carte. It can also mean “get me/bring me” in context (e.g., Donne-moi à boire = “Get me something to drink”). For a polite/formal version use Donnez-moi; for talking to a friend with “something to drink” you can also say Donne-moi quelque chose à boire.
target_language_example: Donne-moi ton numéro, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your number, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone you call “tu” to hand you a specific thing. Structure: Donne-moi + ce (masculine singular noun) / cette (feminine singular) / ces (plural). Often corresponds to English “Give me that/this …”.
target_language_example: Donne-moi ce stylo, s'il te plaît.
