native_language_example: Give me that pen, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (informal "tu" form) to hand you something. It’s the imperative of "donner" + the indirect object pronoun "moi" (me) + the feminine singular definite article "la". You must add the noun after it: "Donne-moi la caméra." For a masculine noun, use "donne-moi le"; for plural, "donne-moi les".
target_language_example: Donne-moi la clé, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me the key, please.

additional_notes: Common command using the informal singular "tu" form (to one person you know well, a child, etc.). It’s made of: "donne" (give) + "moi" (to me) + "le" (the, masculine). Use "donne-moi la" for a feminine noun, and "donne-moi l’" before a vowel sound (e.g., "donne-moi l’eau"). For polite/formal or plural "you," use "donnez-moi le…".
target_language_example: Donne-moi le stylo, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me the pen, please.

meaning: “Give me your …” (to one person you address as tu).
additional_notes: Imperative of donner (“to give”) + moi (“to me”) + ta (“your”, feminine singular). Use it when asking/telling someone to hand you an item. Ta changes with the noun: ta + feminine (ta veste), ton + masculine (ton manteau), tes + plural (tes clés).
target_language_example: Donne-moi ta carte, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your card, please.

meaning: "give me your" (to one person; for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: "Donne" is the informal (tu) command form of *donner* (to give). "Moi" means "to me." "Ton" means "your" before a masculine singular noun (e.g., *ton numéro*, *ton manteau*) and also before some feminine nouns that start with a vowel sound (e.g., *ton amie*). This phrase can sound like an order; to make it more polite, you can add *s'il te plaît*.
target_language_example: Donne-moi ton adresse, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your address, please.

meaning: "give me a" (for a masculine singular thing).
additional_notes: Imperative form of donner (to give) + indirect object pronoun moi (to me) + un (a/an). Used to ask someone for an item or something you want (un crayon, un indice, un pourboire). For a feminine singular thing, use « donne-moi une … ». For plural, use « donne-moi des … ». Often said as a direct request; adding « s’il te plaît » makes it more polite.
target_language_example: Donne-moi un verre d’eau, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Common, friendly way to ask for help. Literally “give me a hand,” but it usually means to help with a task (often briefly). You can change the person: « Donnez-moi un coup de main » (formal/plural), « Donne-lui un coup de main » (help him/her). Often followed by « pour… » or « avec… » to say what you need help with.
target_language_example: Donne-moi un coup de main avec mes valises, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a hand with my suitcases, please.

meaning: "give me a" (addressing one person; before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Imperative form of donner (“to give”) + moi (“to me”) + une (“a/an” for feminine nouns). Used to ask or tell someone (informally, with tu) to hand you one item: donne-moi une orange, une feuille, une couverture. For a masculine noun, use "donne-moi un"; in more polite speech you can use "donnez-moi…" (vous).
target_language_example: Donne-moi une minute, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a minute, please.

meaning: “give me a minute” / “give me a moment.”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait briefly or to give you a short amount of time (to think, to do something, or to talk to someone). It’s in the informal tu form (donne-moi); a more formal/polite version is « Donnez-moi une minute. »
target_language_example: Donne-moi une minute, je finis ce message.
native_language_example: Give me a minute, I’m finishing this message.

additional_notes: Used when something makes you shiver or react physically (goosebumps), often because it’s scary, creepy, or very moving. Frequently used with an indirect object: « Ça me donne la chair de poule » (It gives me goosebumps). You can also use other pronouns: te / lui / nous / vous / leur. The idea is idiomatic; a word-for-word translation sounds unnatural in English.
target_language_example: Ce film d’horreur me donne la chair de poule.
native_language_example: This horror movie gives me the creeps / gives me goosebumps.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (tu form) to give everything that matches a description. It must be followed by a clause like: « donne tout ce que tu peux / tu veux / tu as ». For other levels of formality: « donnez tout ce que… » (polite/plural), « donne tout ce que… » (informal singular).
target_language_example: Donne tout ce que tu peux pour m’aider.
native_language_example: Give everything you can to help me.

additional_notes: Common, friendly way to offer or describe help. The full expression is usually “donner un coup de main (à quelqu’un)”. “donne” is the present tense form for il/elle/on (and also the imperative for tu). If you need another subject: je donne, tu donnes, nous donnons, vous donnez, ils/elles donnent.
target_language_example: Elle me donne un coup de main.
native_language_example: She gives me a hand.

meaning: to make (someone) want to; to make (someone) feel like (doing something).
additional_notes: Often used as **donner envie de + infinitive** (to make you want to do something): *Ça me donne envie de voyager.* It can also be used with a noun: **donner envie de + noun** (to make you want something): *Ça me donne envie de chocolat.* Usually takes an indirect object pronoun like **me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur**: *Ça lui donne envie de…* Note: **envie** means “desire/craving,” not “envy” (which is **jalousie**).
target_language_example: Cette photo me donne envie de donner envie aux autres de voyager.
native_language_example: This photo makes me want to make others want to travel.

meaning: to hold someone’s hand; to give someone your hand (e.g., to help them up).
additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object: « donner la main à quelqu’un ». In everyday French, a handshake is more commonly « serrer la main (à quelqu’un) » (to shake hands). « Donner la main » is frequently about holding hands (walking together) or offering your hand to help someone.
target_language_example: Tu veux me donner la main pour traverser la rue ?
native_language_example: Do you want to hold my hand to cross the street?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone (or an animal) having a baby: « donner naissance à un enfant ». In a broader, figurative sense, it can mean “to give rise to / lead to” an idea, movement, or event: « donner naissance à un projet / un mouvement ».
target_language_example: Elle va donner naissance à une petite fille en mai.
native_language_example: She is going to give birth to a baby girl in May.

additional_notes: "Donner" means "to give". It’s often followed by an indirect object (à + person) or an object pronoun: "donner quelque chose à Tom" (give something to Tom), "me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur donner quelque chose" (give me/you/him… something). You may also see "en" replacing "de + something" or referring to an unspecified amount/thing: "vous en donner" = "give you some / give you some of it".
target_language_example: Je vais te donner quelque chose après le cours.
native_language_example: I’m going to give you something after class.

meaning: to say (someone) is right; to agree with (someone).
additional_notes: Most often used as "donner raison à quelqu’un" (to side with someone / acknowledge they’re right). Past tense is very common: "Je t’ai donné raison" (I agreed with you / I admitted you were right).
target_language_example: Je vais te donner raison : tu avais raison depuis le début.
native_language_example: I’ll admit you’re right: you were right from the start.

meaning: to face / overlook / open onto (a view, street, courtyard, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to describe where a room, window, balcony, building, etc. has its view or opens. Common patterns: « La chambre donne sur la mer. » (has a sea view), « La fenêtre donne sur la cour. » (faces the courtyard). It does not mean “to give on.”
target_language_example: Notre appartement va donner sur une rue calme.
native_language_example: Our apartment is going to face a quiet street.

additional_notes: A very common pattern meaning "to give a/an" before a masculine singular noun: donner un ordre, donner un conseil, donner un exemple. In some expressions, the most natural English translation may be less literal, such as donner un coup de chiffon = "give something a quick wipe."
target_language_example: Je vais te donner un exemple simple.
native_language_example: I'm going to give you a simple example.

meaning: to give a hand; to help out.
additional_notes: Common, friendly way to offer or ask for help, especially with a task. Often used with an indirect object (me/te/nous/lui/leur): « Je vais te donner un coup de main. » It can be used in requests: « Tu peux / pourrais-tu me donner un coup de main ? »
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner un coup de main avec les valises ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with the suitcases?

meaning: 'to give a…' / sometimes 'to do/hold a…' (with events like a talk or an interview).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun: donner une + nom. Literal meaning is 'to give', but with certain nouns it’s the natural French way to say you’re doing or delivering something (e.g., donner une conférence = give a talk; donner une interview = do/give an interview). With objects or reasons it stays closer to 'give' (donner une plante, donner une raison).
target_language_example: Peux-tu me donner une minute ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a minute?

meaning: to teach someone a lesson (often: to punish or reprimand to make them learn).
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to learn from a mistake, often with the idea of disciplining, scolding, or "showing them" so they won’t do it again. Can be serious or threatening depending on tone ("Je vais te/vous donner une leçon"). Also used more neutrally for actually giving instruction, but in everyday speech it often implies punishment.
target_language_example: Il faut lui donner une leçon pour qu’il arrête de mentir.
native_language_example: He needs to be taught a lesson so he’ll stop lying.

additional_notes: Imperative of donner + indirect object pronoun lui (“to him/to her”). Used to tell someone politely (vous) or to address multiple people: Donnez-lui + [thing]. In writing it’s hyphenated. Without a noun after it (“Donnez-lui !”), the “something” is understood from context.
target_language_example: Donnez-lui ce livre, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please give him/her this book.

additional_notes: Imperative of donner (“to give”) + moi (“to me”), used to ask someone to hand you something or provide information/time. It’s commonly used in requests; adding “s’il vous plaît” makes it more explicitly polite, and “donne-moi” is the informal (tu) version.
target_language_example: Donnez-moi votre passeport, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your passport, please.

additional_notes: Imperative of **donner** addressed to **vous** (someone you’re speaking to formally, or more than one person). **-moi** means “to me,” and **le** is the masculine singular “the.” Use it before a masculine noun: *Donnez-moi le numéro.* (For feminine/plural: *Donnez-moi la… / Donnez-moi les…*).
target_language_example: S’il vous plaît, donnez-moi le passeport.
native_language_example: Please give me the passport.

additional_notes: Uses the imperative of donner addressed to vous (a polite or plural "you"). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (un + noun): Donnez-moi un chocolat / un baiser. For a feminine noun, use "Donnez-moi une..."; for plural, "Donnez-moi des...". "Donnez-moi un anneau" can also mean "Give me a ring" (call me).
target_language_example: Donnez-moi un café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to hand you one item (feminine noun) or to request something in a more formal/polite way. "Donnez" is the vous-form (to one person you don’t know well, or to several people). You normally follow it with a feminine noun (une cuillère, une orange) or a feminine phrase like "une table". For masculine nouns, use "Donnez-moi un…"
target_language_example: Donnez-moi une bouteille d’eau, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a bottle of water, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to hand over something or provide information. It uses the imperative of "donner" (donnez) with "moi" (to me) and "votre" (your). "Donnez" is also used for "vous" (polite singular or plural), so it can sound polite but still quite direct depending on context (e.g., a request from staff, or a firm instruction).
target_language_example: Donnez-moi votre passeport, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your passport, please.

meaning: given/gave a/an (past participle used with an auxiliary verb, usually in the passé composé).
additional_notes: This is the past participle form of **donner** (“to give”), used most often with **avoir**: **(j’ai / tu as / il a / elle a / on a / nous avons / vous avez / ils ont / elles ont) donné un + nom**. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., *un os, un nom, un conseil, un discours*). The recipient is often introduced with **à** (*donné un os au chien*) or an indirect object pronoun (*lui*): *Je lui ai donné un nom.*
target_language_example: Elle a donné un os au chien.
native_language_example: She gave a bone to the dog.

meaning: 'that I need' / 'which I need' (used after a noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase « avoir besoin de » (“to need”). « dont » replaces « de + which/that » and links back to something mentioned: « la chose dont j'ai besoin » = “the thing (that) I need.” You can also use it after words like « quelque chose », « ce », etc.: « ce dont j'ai besoin » = “what I need.”
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé le livre dont j'ai besoin pour le cours.
native_language_example: I found the book I need for the class.

meaning: "that I told you about" / "that I mentioned to you."
additional_notes: Used in a relative clause with the pronoun « dont » (often = “about which/that”). It’s especially common after verbs that take « de », like « parler de » (to talk about), « avoir besoin de » (to need), « se souvenir de » (to remember). Example pattern: « C’est [quelqu’un/quelque chose] dont je t’ai parlé. »
target_language_example: Voici le livre dont je t'ai parlé.
native_language_example: Here’s the book I told you about.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to refer back to something you mentioned earlier. It uses the relative pronoun **dont**, which replaces **de + [person/thing]** (“about whom/which,” “whose,” etc.). Here it usually corresponds to **parler de** (“to talk about”): *l’ami dont je vous ai parlé* = “the friend (that) I told you about.” More informal: *dont je t’ai parlé* (“I told you about”).
target_language_example: C’est le restaurant dont je vous ai parlé la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: It’s the restaurant I told you about last week.

additional_notes: Used after a noun or idea to refer back to it. Here, "dont" replaces "de + [thing]" because the verb phrase is "avoir besoin de" (to need). So it means "(the thing) that we need" or "(the thing) we need."
target_language_example: Voici les documents dont nous avons besoin pour la demande.
native_language_example: Here are the documents we need for the application.

additional_notes: Used after a noun or an indefinite word like tout/ce to refer back to something required. It uses dont because the verb phrase is "avoir besoin de" (to need / to have need of): "le temps dont tu as besoin" = "the time you need"; "tout ce dont tu as besoin" = "everything you need."
target_language_example: Voici les documents dont tu as besoin pour t'inscrire.
native_language_example: Here are the documents you need to sign up.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “(that) you need,” especially with **avoir besoin de** (“to need”). **dont** replaces **de + [thing]**: *le temps dont vous avez besoin* = *le temps (de) lequel vous avez besoin* (not used in modern French) → “the time you need.” You can swap the pronoun for different people: *dont j’ai besoin* (that I need), *dont tu as besoin* (that you need), etc.
target_language_example: Voici les informations dont vous avez besoin.
native_language_example: Here is the information you need.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense "passé composé" of dormir: "(avoir) dormi". You change the helper verb to match the subject (j'ai / tu as / il-elle-on a / nous avons / vous avez / ils-elles ont) + "dormi". "Toute la journée" means "all day" and often implies you spent the whole day sleeping.
target_language_example: J'ai dormi toute la journée parce que j'étais malade.
native_language_example: I slept all day because I was sick.

meaning: to sleep very soundly (to sleep like a baby).
additional_notes: Common idiom used to say you slept extremely well, often through the night without waking up. Conjugate the verb dormir as needed: « J’ai dormi comme un bébé » (I slept like a baby).
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, dormir comme un bébé a été facile.
native_language_example: After the hike, sleeping like a baby was easy.

additional_notes: Used when offering or asking to sleep on a couch (often as a place to stay for the night). You can change the article depending on context: "sur un canapé" (on a couch), "sur mon/ton/son canapé" (on my/your/his/her couch).
target_language_example: Si tu veux, tu peux dormir sur le canapé ce soir.
native_language_example: If you want, you can sleep on the couch tonight.

meaning: To sleep very deeply (to be fast asleep).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression: literally “to sleep with clenched fists,” but it means you’re sleeping so soundly that nothing wakes you up. Used in everyday spoken and written French; not slang.
target_language_example: Après le long voyage, il semblait dormir à poings fermés.
native_language_example: After the long trip, he seemed to be fast asleep.

meaning: a cold shower; (figuratively) a harsh shock / rude awakening.
additional_notes: Often used literally with the verb « prendre »: « prendre une douche froide » = “to take a cold shower.” Figuratively, « une douche froide » means disappointing news or a sudden setback that brings you back to reality (similar to “a cold shower” or “a rude awakening” in English).
target_language_example: Apprendre qu’on a perdu le contrat a été une vraie douche froide.
native_language_example: Finding out we lost the contract was a real shock.

meaning: “Good Lord!” / “Jesus!” (an exclamation of shock, surprise, or exasperation).
additional_notes: Used as a standalone interjection (often with “Oh”) to react emotionally—similar to invoking Jesus in English. It can sound dramatic or old-fashioned, and some people may find it rude or blasphemous because it uses a religious name as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Doux Jésus, j’ai oublié mon passeport !
native_language_example: Good Lord, I forgot my passport!

meaning: red flag; (in racing) a red-flag stoppage.
additional_notes: Literally “red flag.” Used for an actual red flag (e.g., waved by a marshal/official). In motorsports, being “sous drapeau rouge” means the session/race is stopped or suspended for safety (accident, debris, bad weather, etc.). Often shouted as a warning: « Drapeau rouge ! »
target_language_example: On est sous drapeau rouge, la course est interrompue.
native_language_example: We’re under red flag; the race has been stopped.

meaning: straight to the point; directly to the goal.
additional_notes: Used with the verb « aller »: « aller droit au but » means to speak or act without wasting time, skipping extra details and getting to what matters. Common in requests or announcements like « Je vais aller droit au but » or « Peux-tu aller droit au but ? ».
target_language_example: On va droit au but : je n’ai plus de budget pour ce projet.
native_language_example: Let’s get straight to the point: I don’t have any more budget for this project.

additional_notes: Used to say you want something said plainly and without unnecessary details. Literally “straight to the goal,” so you may also hear it in sports contexts to mean playing/acting very directly.
target_language_example: Je vais aller droit au but : je ne suis pas intéressé.
native_language_example: I’ll get straight to the point: I’m not interested.

meaning: "the right to" (to do something), or a "fee/duty" (as in an official charge).
additional_notes: Most commonly used in **avoir le droit de + infinitive** to say someone is allowed/has the right to do something: *J’ai le droit de… / Tu as le droit de…* It can also appear in fixed expressions meaning a fee or duty, especially in administrative contexts (e.g., *droits de douane* = customs duties, *droit de passage* = right of way/fee to pass).
target_language_example: Tu as le droit de dire non.
native_language_example: You have the right to say no.

meaning: 'the right to know' (the right to be informed).
additional_notes: Often used in legal, administrative, or public-debate contexts about transparency and access to information. Commonly appears with an article: « le droit de savoir ». Can refer to a general principle (people have the right to know) or to someone’s entitlement to receive information in a given situation.
target_language_example: Les citoyens ont le droit de savoir comment l’argent public est dépensé.
native_language_example: Citizens have the right to know how public money is spent.

meaning: the right to vote; voting rights.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the legal right/permission to vote in an election. Often appears with verbs like avoir (to have), exercer (to exercise/use), donner (to give/grant), retirer (to take away), and with "le" or "son" (le droit de vote, son droit de vote).
target_language_example: Dans ce pays, on a le droit de vote à dix-huit ans.
native_language_example: In this country, you have the right to vote at eighteen.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to comment that something feels unusual, unexpected, or questionable: « une drôle de façon », « un drôle de goût ». Often expresses mild criticism or surprise. It agrees with the noun: « un drôle de… » (masc.) / « une drôle de… » (fem.).
target_language_example: C'est drôle de dire ça maintenant.
native_language_example: That's a strange time to say that.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + le Sud**. Use **venir du Sud** = “to come from the South,” and **quelque chose du Sud** = “something from/of the South” (southern food, a southern name, the men of the South, southern seas, etc.). Often refers to a southern region within a country or a broadly defined “the South,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Elle vient du Sud de la France.
native_language_example: She comes from the south of France.

meaning: from the edge of the cliff.
additional_notes: A common prepositional phrase used after a verb to say something happens starting at the cliff’s edge (e.g., fall, jump, look). "Du" is the contraction of "de + le" and often translates as "from the" here. Compare: "au bord de la falaise" = "at the edge of the cliff."
target_language_example: Il a glissé du bord de la falaise.
native_language_example: He slipped from the edge of the cliff.

additional_notes: Literally “from the sky/heaven” (de + le ciel → du ciel). Common in fixed expressions like « tomber du ciel » (“to fall from the sky”), often used to say someone seems to appear out of nowhere or to react as if they don’t know what’s going on. Also used in phrases like « pirates du ciel » (“sky pirates/air pirates”), « êtres du ciel » (“beings from the sky/heaven”), and « un signe du ciel » (“a sign from heaven”).
target_language_example: Il a reçu une aide du ciel au dernier moment.
native_language_example: He got help from heaven at the last moment.

meaning: nearby; local; from around here (the area).
additional_notes: Often used with a place or shop: « le café / le supermarché du coin » = the nearby/local one (the one around the corner). With people: « Être du coin » means to be from the local area/around here.
target_language_example: On va au café du coin après le travail.
native_language_example: We’re going to the café nearby (around the corner) after work.

meaning: "of the body" (sometimes "of the corpse/body" depending on context).
additional_notes: “du” = “de + le” and usually means “of the” or “some.” With “corps,” it most often refers to the (living) body: *une partie du corps*, *un organe du corps*, *les mouvements du corps*. In crime/death contexts, *le corps* can mean “the body/corpse,” as in *se débarrasser du corps*. Also note the fixed phrase *garde(s) du corps* = “bodyguard(s).”
target_language_example: Le cerveau est une partie du corps.
native_language_example: The brain is a part of the body.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or association with a specific hallway: *la porte du couloir* (the hallway door), *la lumière du couloir* (the hallway light). It’s the contraction of **de + le** → **du**. (Not to be confused with **dans le couloir** = in the hallway.)
target_language_example: La porte du couloir est fermée.
native_language_example: The hallway door is closed.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + le = du**. Used to link something to a specific crime: **le lieu du crime** (the crime scene), **l'arme/les armes du crime** (the murder weapon(s)), **la raison du crime** (the reason for the crime). With adjectives like **innocent de**, it means “innocent of (a crime)” → **innocent du crime**.
target_language_example: La police a trouvé une preuve du crime.
native_language_example: The police found evidence of the crime.

meaning: on the side of; from the side of (someone/somewhere).
additional_notes: Used to indicate (1) which “side” or viewpoint you support in a disagreement (“être/se tenir du côté de …”), or (2) which family branch someone comes from (“du côté de mon père” = “on my father’s side”). It can also mean “toward/on the side of” a place (“du côté de Paris” = “toward Paris/in the Paris area”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Dans ce débat, je suis du côté des étudiants.
native_language_example: In this debate, I'm on the students' side.

meaning: from beginning to end; all the way through.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done completely, without skipping anything (reading, telling a story, watching something). It can also mean something was true the whole time (e.g., "Elle a menti du début à la fin" = she lied the entire time). Often answers a question on its own: "Du début à la fin."
target_language_example: J’ai regardé le film du début à la fin.
native_language_example: I watched the movie from beginning to end.

additional_notes: "Du" is the contraction of "de + le". So "du feu" often appears after prepositions or phrases that use "de" (e.g., "près du feu" = near the fire, "à distance du feu" = away from the fire). It can also mean “some fire” in other contexts (partitive), but in these examples it refers to a specific fire.
target_language_example: On s'est assis près du feu.
native_language_example: We sat near the fire.

meaning: from the bottom of my heart; with deep sincerity.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a feeling or statement is truly sincere and deeply felt. It often follows verbs like dire (to say), penser (to think), remercier (to thank), and can be used with positive or negative feelings (e.g., love, gratitude, hatred). You can change the pronoun in context: du fond du cœur = “from the bottom of (my) heart.”
target_language_example: Je suis désolé du fond du cœur.
native_language_example: I'm sorry from the bottom of my heart.

meaning: overnight; all of a sudden (very quickly, unexpectedly).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very fast, sometimes unexpectedly—almost from one day to the next. Often with verbs like changer, devenir, perdre. Can also be used in negative statements to mean “it won’t happen overnight” (it will take time).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : on ne peut pas tout apprendre du jour au lendemain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you can’t learn everything overnight.

meaning: of the lake / from the lake.
additional_notes: "Du" is the contraction of "de + le". You use "du" before a masculine singular noun like "lac" (lake) to mean "of the" or "from the" (e.g., "près du lac" = near the lake; "la profondeur du lac" = the depth of the lake).
target_language_example: La vue du lac est magnifique.
native_language_example: The view of the lake is magnificent.

meaning: “in the morning” / “of the morning” (used with a time or thing from the morning).
additional_notes: Used after an exact time to mean “in the morning”: « à six heures du matin » = “at 6 a.m.” Also used after a noun to mean “the morning [noun]”: « le journal du matin » = “the morning newspaper,” « le premier train du matin » = “the first train in the morning.” Often contrasts with « du soir » (in the evening).
target_language_example: J'ai un rendez-vous à huit heures du matin.
native_language_example: I have an appointment at 8 a.m.

meaning: from morning to night; all day long.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something lasts the whole day, from the morning until the evening/night. Often used with verbs like travailler (to work) or se plaindre (to complain). It can describe a habit (present/imparfait) or a one-time situation (passé composé).
target_language_example: Je suis en réunion du matin au soir aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm in meetings from morning to night today.

meaning: "at least" / "or rather" (to correct or soften what you just said).
additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement: you add a limitation, correction, or weaker version of what you just said (often after a pause). Common pattern: “..., du moins, ...” or at the start of a sentence to mean “at least, anyway”.
target_language_example: Il va venir demain — du moins, il l’a dit hier.
native_language_example: He’s coming tomorrow—or at least, that’s what he said yesterday.

additional_notes: Literally combines de + le + monde. It often means "of the world" after a noun (les régions du monde), but after a superlative it is usually translated as "in the world" (le plus grand du monde). It also appears in expressions like tout le temps du monde = "all the time in the world."
target_language_example: C'est le plus beau château du monde.
native_language_example: It's the most beautiful castle in the world.

meaning: from (all over) the whole world; worldwide.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say where people/things come from or that something is known everywhere (e.g., des touristes du monde entier = tourists from all over the world; connu du monde entier = known worldwide). Often follows plural nouns like gens/personnes/touristes.
target_language_example: Des étudiants du monde entier viennent étudier à Paris.
native_language_example: Students from all over the world come to study in Paris.

additional_notes: “Du” = “de + le” (of the / from the). With “pays” (country), it often means something is national in scope: *les journaux du pays* (the country’s newspapers), *les amateurs de sport du pays* (sports fans in the country), *la situation économique du pays* (the country’s economic situation), or superlatives like *la plus heureuse du pays* (the happiest in the country).
target_language_example: C’est l’un des meilleurs restaurants du pays.
native_language_example: It’s one of the best restaurants in the country.

additional_notes: Most often, this is the contraction of **de + le = du**, meaning **“of the”**: *la chaleur du soleil* (“the heat of the sun”), *la planète la plus proche du soleil* (“the planet closest to the sun”). In other contexts, **du** can also mean **“some”** with an uncountable noun (e.g., *avoir du soleil* = “to have some sun/sunshine”).
target_language_example: On a besoin de la lumière du soleil pour que les plantes poussent.
native_language_example: We need sunlight for plants to grow.

meaning: "(some) time" / "of the time" (sometimes "weather," depending on context).
additional_notes: “Du” is the contraction of “de + le”. So “du temps” can mean “(some) time” after verbs like avoir: “J’ai du temps” = “I have time.” It’s also used to mean “of the time” in expressions like “la moitié du temps” (half the time) or in phrases like “couloir/tunnel du temps” (time corridor/tunnel). With “à cause du temps,” it often means “because of the weather.”
target_language_example: J’ai du temps ce soir, on peut se voir.
native_language_example: I have time tonight; we can see each other.

additional_notes: Used with an uncountable noun in the partitive form (du = de + le) to mean “some butter” or “any butter,” especially in questions and statements about ingredients or availability. In negatives, it often becomes “de beurre” (e.g., Je n’ai pas de beurre.).
target_language_example: Je voudrais du beurre, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some butter, please.

meaning: good; something beneficial (often in « faire du bien » / « dire du bien de »).
additional_notes: « Du » is the partitive article (“some”), so « du bien » means “(some) good.” Common uses: « dire du bien de quelqu’un » = to speak well of someone; « faire du bien (à quelqu’un) » = to do someone good / help them; « ça fait du bien » = it feels good / it does you good. Often used with negation: « ça ne fait pas du bien » = it’s not good for you / it doesn’t do you any good.
target_language_example: Après cette journée stressante, une promenade m’a fait du bien.
native_language_example: After that stressful day, a walk did me good.

meaning: “good things about” (in phrases like *dire/parler/penser du bien de*).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like *dire*, *parler*, *penser* to express a positive opinion about someone/something: *dire du bien de quelqu’un* = “to say good things about someone.” Often contrasted with *du mal de* (“bad things about”). Not to be confused with *faire du bien à* (“to do good to / to make someone feel better”), which takes *à* rather than *de*.
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas parler du mal des autres ; je préfère dire du bien de mes collègues.
native_language_example: I don’t like speaking badly about others; I prefer saying good things about my colleagues.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (du) + bon to mean “some good …” or “good-quality …”, often before a noun: du bon café (good coffee), du bon bois (good wood). It can also stand on its own to mean “the good stuff” (often informally): Du bon ! You may also see the contrast: Il y a du bon et du moins bon. (“There’s good and less good.”)
target_language_example: On a trouvé du bon vin pour pas cher.
native_language_example: We found some good wine for cheap.

meaning: good work; a job well done.
additional_notes: Uses the informal noun "boulot" (work/job). "Faire du bon boulot" = to do good work; it’s often said to praise someone’s results (like “Nice work!”).
target_language_example: Merci, vous avez fait du bon boulot !
native_language_example: Thanks, you did a great job!

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like « passer » (passer du bon temps = to have a good time) or « se payer » (se payer du bon temps = to treat yourself to some fun). « Du » is the partitive article here, meaning “some,” so it often translates naturally as “a good time” rather than word-for-word “some good time.”
target_language_example: On a passé du bon temps ensemble hier soir.
native_language_example: We had a good time together last night.

additional_notes: Used to praise the quality of someone’s work or what they achieved. It can stand alone as a compliment (“Du bon travail !”) or appear in sentences with faire: “faire du bon travail” = “to do good work.” Note: “du” here is the partitive article (some), so the idea is “(some) good-quality work,” not “of the good work.”
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide : c'est du bon travail !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help: that's good work!

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (du = “some”) with bon (“good”). Often used to say there is something positive in a situation or in a person: « Il y a du bon en lui » (“There’s some good in him”). Also common with « avoir du bon » to mean “to have its good points”: « Le changement a du bon ». In « C’est du bon », it’s a more colloquial way to say “That’s good stuff / That’s good.”
target_language_example: Même si c’est difficile, il y a du bon dans cette expérience.
native_language_example: Even if it’s hard, there’s something good in this experience.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article: du = de + le, meaning “some” with uncountable nouns like café. Common when offering, ordering, or talking about making coffee. In negatives, it usually becomes de: Je ne bois pas de café.
target_language_example: Je voudrais du café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used as a short interjection to tell someone (or a group) to relax, stop panicking, or lower their voice. Often preceded by “Hé/Eh” (“Hey”) and followed by a comma and an instruction (e.g., “Du calme, laisse-le faire.”). Literally “some calm,” but in English you’d usually translate it as an imperative.
target_language_example: Du calme, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Calm down, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French to connect what was just said to the next idea (often like filler: “so…/and so…”). It can be placed at the start (“Du coup, …”) or at the end (“…, du coup.”). In more formal writing, you’ll more often see "donc", "alors", or "par conséquent" instead.
target_language_example: Il pleuvait, du coup on est rentrés tôt.
native_language_example: It was raining, so we went home early.

meaning: a hard time; something difficult to deal with.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like « donner » (to give) or « avoir » (to have): « donner du fil à retordre à quelqu’un » = to give someone a hard time / be a tough challenge for them; « avoir du fil à retordre » = to have a lot to deal with. It’s a common idiom (not usually translated word-for-word).
target_language_example: Ce problème nous a donné du fil à retordre.
native_language_example: This problem gave us a hard time.

additional_notes: "Fric" is a common slang word for "money". It’s often used with the partitive article "du" to mean an unspecified amount (like "some cash"). Use it in casual speech; in more neutral/formal contexts, prefer "de l’argent".
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de du fric pour payer le loyer.
native_language_example: I need some money to pay the rent.

meaning: some (fruit/vegetable) juice; juice made from; juice of.
additional_notes: Used before the ingredient the juice comes from: du jus de citron (lemon juice), du jus de pomme (apple juice). Here, "du" = "de + le" and often functions like "some" with an uncountable noun. After "du jus de", you typically put the fruit/vegetable name without an article (citron, pomme, tomate). Note: before a vowel sound, "de" can contract to "d’" (e.g., du jus d’orange), but that would not display the exact string "du jus de".
target_language_example: Je bois du jus de pomme.
native_language_example: I drink apple juice.

additional_notes: "Du" is the partitive article (de + le) used for uncountable things like "lait" (milk). Use "du lait" when you mean an unspecified quantity: "Je bois du lait." With a specific amount, use a number: "un verre de lait" (a glass of milk). In negatives, it often becomes "de": "Je ne bois pas de lait."
target_language_example: Vous voulez du lait dans votre thé ?
native_language_example: Do you want some milk in your tea?

additional_notes: Used to say there is (or you want/put) an unspecified amount of milk inside something. It’s made of the partitive article "du" (some) + "lait" (milk) + "dans" (in). It must be followed by a place/container (e.g., "du lait dans le café", "du lait dans le frigo").
target_language_example: Je veux du lait dans mon café, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: I want some milk in my coffee, please.

additional_notes:
Most often used in set phrases: 
- « faire du mal (à quelqu’un) » = to hurt someone / do harm.
- « se faire du mal » = to hurt yourself.
- « dire du mal (de quelqu’un/de quelque chose) » = to speak badly about / criticize (often behind their back).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas te faire du mal.
native_language_example: I don't want to hurt you.

additional_notes: Most often used with **avoir**: **avoir du mal à + infinitive** = “to have a hard time / struggle to do.” Example: *J’ai du mal à comprendre.* It can also appear in the question **Il y a du mal à ça ?** meaning “Is there any harm in that?” (more like “anything wrong with that?” than physical pain).
target_language_example: Elle a du mal à se concentrer quand il y a du bruit.
native_language_example: She has trouble concentrating when there’s noise.

additional_notes: Often used with « il y a » / « il y avait » to mean a place is busy or crowded: « Il y a du monde ce soir. » = “It’s crowded tonight.” In other contexts, it can simply mean “some people” or “people around” (e.g., « devant du monde ? » = “in front of people?”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas parler maintenant : il y a du monde.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now: there are people around.

meaning: Come on—move it! / Show some energy!
additional_notes: An exclamation used to urge someone (or a group) to speed up, make an effort, or act with more energy. Often said on its own ("Du nerf !") or with "Allez" / "Alors" or someone’s name. It can sound a bit brusque/commanding. Note: although it looks like English “nerve,” here it’s closer to “energy/pep.”
target_language_example: Du nerf, on est en retard !
native_language_example: Come on, move it—we’re late!

additional_notes: Used to say there is new information or a new development, often in the pattern « Il y a du nouveau » (There’s something new) or « Tu as du nouveau ? / Vous avez du nouveau ? » (Any news/updates?). « Du » is the partitive (“some”), and « nouveau » means “new.”
target_language_example: Appelle-moi si tu as du nouveau.
native_language_example: Call me if you hear anything new.

additional_notes: "Du" = "de + le" and is a partitive article used for an unspecified amount (some). With food, it often means you want/ate/bought bread in general, not one specific loaf. Contrast: "le pain" = bread in general/as a concept or a specific bread already known; "un pain" = a (whole) loaf of bread.
target_language_example: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some bread, please.

meaning: a lot of work to do; lots to get done (ahead).
additional_notes: An idiom used to say you’re very busy or have many tasks ahead. Often used with avoir or il y a: «J’ai du pain sur la planche», «On a du pain sur la planche», «Il y a du pain sur la planche». It doesn’t literally mean bread on a board.
target_language_example: Avec ce déménagement, on a du pain sur la planche ce week-end.
native_language_example: With this move, we’ve got a lot to do this weekend.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article "du" (de + le) with the uncountable noun "papier" to mean an unspecified quantity: "As-tu du papier ?" = "Do you have any paper?" It’s also used for paper as material, often with a type specified (e.g., "du papier de soie" = tissue paper). In comparisons you may see "mince comme du papier à cigarette" (“thin as cigarette paper”).
target_language_example: Tu as du papier pour écrire ?
native_language_example: Do you have any paper to write on?

meaning: '(the) piano' (used after *jouer de* to mean “play the piano”).
additional_notes: With musical instruments, French uses **jouer de + [instrument]**: *jouer du piano, jouer de la guitare, jouer des tambours*. Here **du** = **de + le**, so *jouer du piano* literally looks like “to play of the piano,” but it simply means **to play the piano**.
target_language_example: Je joue du piano depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: I've been playing the piano for three years.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like prendre / perdre / gagner to talk about gaining or losing weight (body weight). It’s the partitive article “du” + “poids” (“weight”), meaning an unspecified amount of weight.
target_language_example: Depuis l’été, j’ai pris du poids.
native_language_example: Since the summer, I’ve gained weight.

additional_notes: “Du” is the partitive article (de + le) used with an uncountable or unspecified amount. With food, it often means you’re having/eating “(some) fish” without saying how much. If you mean one whole fish (a countable item), you’d often say “un poisson”. After negation, “du poisson” usually becomes “de poisson” (e.g., « Je ne mange pas de poisson. »).
target_language_example: Ce soir, on mange du poisson.
native_language_example: Tonight, we're having fish.

additional_notes: "Du" is the partitive article (de + le) used to talk about an unspecified amount of something you eat or drink. In questions and offers it often means “some/any popcorn?” You can also use it after "vouloir" (to want) or with "faire" (to make): "Tu veux du pop-corn ?" / "Va faire du pop-corn."
target_language_example: On achète du pop-corn pour le film ?
native_language_example: Shall we buy some popcorn for the movie?

additional_notes: “Du” is the partitive article (de + le) used for an unspecified quantity of something uncountable. With food, “manger du riz” often just means “to eat rice” in general. In negatives, it usually becomes “de” (e.g., « Je ne mange pas de riz. »).
target_language_example: Je voudrais du riz, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some rice, please.

additional_notes: Refers to lipstick as an uncountable product (using the partitive du). You’ll hear it when asking if something is lipstick, saying you have lipstick somewhere (e.g., on your teeth), or talking about wearing/applying it. The base noun is « le rouge à lèvres » (lipstick).
target_language_example: Tu as du rouge à lèvres sur la joue.
native_language_example: You have some lipstick on your cheek.

additional_notes: Often used with an indefinite amount: *Il y a du sang…* (“There’s blood…”). It can also be part of set expressions like *avoir du sang sur les mains* (“to have blood on your hands,” i.e., be responsible for someone’s death) and *avoir du sang de + origin* (“to have + origin/lineage,” e.g., *du sang noble*).
target_language_example: Il y a du sang sur ta chemise.
native_language_example: There’s blood on your shirt.

additional_notes: Most often used with *faire*: *se faire du souci (pour…)* means “to worry (about…)”. It commonly appears with reflexive pronouns: *je me fais du souci*, *il/elle se fait du souci*, *nous nous faisons du souci*, etc. You can intensify it with *beaucoup de souci* (“a lot of worry”).
target_language_example: Ne te fais pas du souci pour moi.
native_language_example: Don't worry about me.

additional_notes: Most often used in the expression **(se) faire du souci pour [quelqu’un/quelque chose]** = “to worry about [someone/something].” It’s usually reflexive (**je me fais du souci**, **nous nous faisons du souci**) to mean “I/we worry.” You can also say **(se) faire du souci pour rien** = “to worry for nothing.”
target_language_example: Je me fais du souci pour toi.
native_language_example: I’m worried about you.

meaning: some sugar (an unspecified amount of sugar).
additional_notes: "Du" is the partitive article (de + le) used for uncountable things like sugar. Common in food/drink contexts (coffee/tea, baking). In questions and offers: "Tu veux du sucre ?" / "Vous mettez du sucre ?".
target_language_example: Je voudrais du sucre, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some sugar, please.

additional_notes: "Du" is the partitive article (de + le), often implying an unspecified quantity. "Du temps" is common in questions ("Tu as du temps ?" = Do you have time?), in set phrases like "Il faut du temps" (It takes time / It needs time), and with verbs like "passer du temps" (to spend time). In the negative, it often becomes "de temps" (e.g., "Je n’ai pas de temps").
target_language_example: As-tu du temps, maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you have time now?

additional_notes: Usually used with a verb like passer: « passer du temps avec quelqu’un » = “to spend time with someone.” « du temps » often means “some time” (an unspecified amount), and « avec » introduces the person you’re with.
target_language_example: J’aimerais passer du temps avec toi ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’d like to spend time with you this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has or needs time in order to do something. Often appears with verbs like « donner » (Donnez-moi du temps pour…), « avoir » (Vous avez du temps pour…), and « il faut »/« il me faut »/« il lui faut » (Il me faut du temps pour…). The « du » is part of the partitive article, meaning “some.”
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de du temps pour finir ce travail.
native_language_example: I need some time to finish this work.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article "du" (= "de + le") to talk about an uncountable quantity. Common when offering, making, pouring, or drinking tea: "Tu veux du thé ?" In the negative, it often becomes "de": "Je ne bois pas de thé."
target_language_example: Tu veux du thé ou du café ?
native_language_example: Do you want some tea or coffee?

additional_notes: Used when offering or asking someone to choose between tea and coffee. With drinks, French often uses the partitive article (du/de la/de l’) to mean “some” (an unspecified amount). In polite offers you’ll often hear: « Je voudrais… », « Aimeriez-vous… ? », « Vous désirez… ? ».
target_language_example: Pour le petit-déjeuner, je prends du thé ou du café.
native_language_example: For breakfast, I have tea or coffee.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “(some) thunder,” used with weather: « Il y a eu du tonnerre et des éclairs » (“There was thunder and lightning”). In informal speech, « du tonnerre » can also mean “really great/awesome” to praise something: « un concert du tonnerre », « une idée du tonnerre », « Ça marche du tonnerre » (“It’s going really well / It’s a huge success”).
target_language_example: On a passé une soirée du tonnerre !
native_language_example: We had an awesome evening!

additional_notes: Most often used with negation: "ne ... pas du tout" = "not at all" (stronger than just "ne ... pas"). It can also appear after "rien": "rien du tout" = "nothing at all." In casual speech, "ne" is often dropped: "c'est pas du tout ça".
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas du tout fatigué.
native_language_example: I'm not tired at all.

additional_notes: "Du" = "de + le" and is used as a partitive article, meaning an unspecified amount: "du travail" = "some work". In everyday French it can mean either work to do (tasks) or having employment, depending on context: "chercher/ trouver du travail" = "look for / find a job".
target_language_example: Je cherche du travail depuis deux semaines.
native_language_example: I’ve been looking for a job for two weeks.

meaning: some work to do; work that needs to be done.
additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (du) to mean an unspecified amount of work. Often used with verbs like avoir (J'ai du travail à faire) or in the structure Il y a du travail à faire (“There’s work to be done”). You can change du to beaucoup de / pas de / trop de, etc.: J'ai beaucoup de travail à faire.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j'ai du travail à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have some work to do.

meaning: 'some very good work' (a job well done).
additional_notes: Used to praise the quality of someone’s work. "Du" here is the partitive article, meaning an unspecified amount of work (not a specific piece of work). Common with verbs like "faire" or "effectuer": "Il/Elle a fait du très bon travail."
target_language_example: Vous avez fait du très bon travail sur ce projet.
native_language_example: You did very good work on this project.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: *du* is the partitive article (“some”), so *il y a du vent* = “it’s windy / there’s wind.” With weather reports you’ll often see *du vent* or *il y aura du vent*. As a standalone exclamation (*Du vent !*), it’s a brusque, informal way to dismiss someone (like “Get lost!”).
target_language_example: Demain, il y aura du vent sur la côte.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it will be windy on the coast.

meaning: some wine; (in questions) any wine / would you like some wine?
additional_notes: "Du" is the partitive article ("some") used with uncountable nouns like "vin". It often means an unspecified amount: "Apporte du vin" = "Bring some wine." In questions, it can mean "any" or "some": "Voulez-vous du vin ?" = "Would you like some wine?" The negative usually changes it to "de" (or "d'"): "Je ne bois pas de vin."
target_language_example: Nous allons acheter du vin pour le dîner.
native_language_example: We’re going to buy some wine for dinner.

additional_notes: *Du* is the contraction of **de + le**. In French you usually say **jouer du + instrument** for many instruments: *jouer du violon, du piano, de la guitare, des percussions*. In English you typically drop the article: “to play violin / to play the violin.”
target_language_example: Mon frère joue du violon depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: My brother has been playing the violin for three years.

additional_notes: A fairly formal/literary way to talk about sustained, difficult work and effort. Often used with expressions like « par un dur labeur » (through hard work), « exige un dur labeur » (requires hard work), and « le dur labeur a payé » (hard work paid off).
target_language_example: Après des années de dur labeur, elle a enfin réussi.
native_language_example: After years of hard work, she finally succeeded.

meaning: tough; hard as nails (a tough person).
additional_notes: An idiom (literally “hard to cook”) used to describe someone who is very tough, resilient, or not easily intimidated. It can be an adjective (Il est dur à cuire.) or a noun for “a tough guy” (C’est un dur à cuire.). Often slightly teasing or admiring. Feminine form: dure à cuire.
target_language_example: Je sais que Tom est un dur à cuire.
native_language_example: I know Tom is a tough guy.

additional_notes: Introduces an action that happens immediately after another one. Common pattern: main clause + dès que + clause (or the reverse). In French, use a normal tense after « dès que » (often present for future meaning: « Je t’appelle dès que j’arrive »).
target_language_example: Je te le dirai dès que je le saurai.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you as soon as I know.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something that will happen immediately after you do something. It’s built from "dès que" (as soon as) + "je" (I). In French, after "dès que", you often use the present tense even when talking about the future: "Dès que je termine, je sors" = “As soon as I finish, I’m going out.”
target_language_example: Dès que je rentre, je t'appelle.
native_language_example: As soon as I get home, I'll call you.

meaning: "as soon as I can" / "as soon as I’m able."
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something at the earliest possible time, as soon as you’re free or able. It often follows another clause: Je t’appelle dès que je peux (I’ll call you as soon as I can). You can replace the verb to match the subject: dès que tu peux (as soon as you can), dès que possible (as soon as possible).
target_language_example: Je te réponds dès que je peux.
native_language_example: I’ll reply as soon as I can.

additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something at the earliest opportunity. Often follows the main clause: « Je le ferai dès que possible. ». You can also use it alone as a reply meaning “ASAP.”
target_language_example: Je te rappelle dès que possible.
native_language_example: I'll call you back as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an action that should happen immediately after another one. It’s followed by a verb (often in the present tense even when talking about the future): « Dès que tu arrives, appelle-moi. »
target_language_example: Appelle-moi dès que tu peux.
native_language_example: Call me as soon as you can.

meaning: from now on; as of now.
additional_notes: Used to say that something starts immediately and continues into the future. Common in formal or official messages (similar to « dès maintenant »). Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: « Dès à présent, … » / « … dès à présent. »
target_language_example: Dès à présent, merci d’envoyer vos demandes par e-mail.
native_language_example: From now on, please send your requests by email.

meaning: to get rid of (something); to dispose of/remove (something unwanted).
additional_notes: Most often used in the reflexive form: **se débarrasser de + nom** = “to get rid of.” Conjugates with the subject: **je me débarrasse de**, **tu te débarrasses de**, **il/elle se débarrasse de**, **nous nous débarrassons de**, **vous vous débarrassez de**, **ils/elles se débarrassent de**. The thing removed follows **de** (often **de + article**: *de ça, de ces livres, de mes vêtements*). Can imply throwing away, donating, selling, or otherwise eliminating something unwanted.
target_language_example: Je veux me débarrasser de tous ces livres.
native_language_example: I want to get rid of all these books.

additional_notes: Uses the past simple (passé simple) of *décider* ("elle/il décida"), common in written storytelling and formal narration. It is followed by *de* + an infinitive; *ne...pas* negates that infinitive: *décida de ne pas partir* = "decided not to leave." In everyday speech, French more often uses the passé composé: *elle a décidé de ne pas y aller*.
target_language_example: Après la dispute, elle décida de ne pas répondre.
native_language_example: After the argument, she decided not to reply.

meaning: “decided to” (made the decision to do something).
additional_notes: Used as part of the verb phrase « décider de + infinitive »: « J’ai décidé de partir » = “I decided to leave.” In questions you’ll often see « As-tu décidé de… ? » / « Pourquoi avez-vous décidé de… ? ». Note: « décider » can also take a direct object without « de » when meaning “decide on” something: « Ils ont décidé la date du voyage » = “They decided on the trip date.”
target_language_example: J’ai décidé de prendre le train demain.
native_language_example: I decided to take the train tomorrow.

meaning: 'decided not to' (made a decision not to do something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb décider: "(avoir) décidé de" + infinitive. Add "ne pas" before the infinitive to make it negative: "J'ai décidé de ne pas partir" = "I decided not to leave." In conversation, the "ne" is often dropped: "J'ai décidé de pas partir" (informal).
target_language_example: Nous avons décidé de ne pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: We decided not to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pattern « décider de + infinitive » to say someone makes a decision to do something. Here, « rester » means to stay/remain (not leave). In speech you often hear it as « a décidé de rester » (past decision).
target_language_example: On a décidé de rester à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: We decided to stay home tonight.

meaning: "have already been to" / "have ever been to" (a place).
additional_notes: Used with the verb aller in the passé composé (être + allé) to talk about past experience of visiting a place. In questions, "déjà" often means "ever" in English: « Tu es déjà allé à Boston ? » = "Have you ever been to Boston?" With être, the past participle agrees with the subject (allé / allée / allés / allées). You can also use it in negatives: « Je ne suis jamais allé(e) à Paris. » = "I've never been to Paris."
target_language_example: Je suis déjà allé à Montréal, mais je ne suis jamais allé à Toronto.
native_language_example: I've already been to Montreal, but I've never been to Toronto.

additional_notes: Used to say an action began before now or before another past moment. It’s built from déjà (“already”) + commencé (past participle of commencer, “to start/begin”). Often appears with the auxiliary avoir: j’ai déjà commencé (I’ve already started), le cours avait déjà commencé (the class had already started).
target_language_example: Je suis en retard : le film a déjà commencé.
native_language_example: I’m late: the movie has already started.

additional_notes: Used to say something has been said before. Often appears with an object pronoun: « Je te l’ai déjà dit » (I already told you), « Tu l’as déjà dit » (You already said it). On its own (« Déjà dit. »), it’s an elliptical reply meaning “Already said / Been said already.”
target_language_example: Je te l’ai déjà dit : on part à huit heures.
native_language_example: I already told you: we’re leaving at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used with the passé composé of *manger* (usually *avoir + mangé*): *j’ai déjà mangé*, *tu as déjà mangé*, *il/elle a déjà mangé*. In questions it often means “yet/already” depending on context: *Tu as déjà mangé ?* can mean “Have you eaten yet?” or “Have you already eaten?”
target_language_example: J’ai déjà mangé, merci.
native_language_example: I’ve already eaten, thanks.

additional_notes: Used with être (je suis / il est / le bus est) to say someone or something has already left. It can be followed by a destination with à (déjà parti à la gare = already left for the station) or pour (déjà parti pour Boston = already left for Boston). With non-people (bus, report), it means it has already departed/been sent.
target_language_example: Désolé, elle est déjà partie.
native_language_example: Sorry, she has already left.

meaning: a “déjà vu” (the feeling you’ve seen/experienced this before).
additional_notes: Used as a noun for the familiar sensation that something is happening again. Very common in French and also used in English; often preceded by "un": "C'est un déjà vu." Related structure: "avoir déjà vu" = "to have already seen" (literal).
target_language_example: Quand je suis entré dans cette rue, j'ai eu un déjà vu.
native_language_example: When I walked into this street, I had a déjà vu.

meaning: already saw a / have already seen a (masculine noun)
additional_notes: This is the ordinary past participle phrase of **voir** in the passé composé: **j’ai déjà vu** = “I’ve already seen.” It’s followed by **un + masculine noun** (e.g., *un film, un endroit, un homme*). Note this is different from the noun **un déjà-vu** (“a déjà vu” feeling), which is usually written with a hyphen.
target_language_example: J’ai déjà vu un film comme ça.
native_language_example: I’ve already seen a movie like that.

meaning: “have/has already been” (been before; used to be).
additional_notes: Used with the verb être in the past (“été”) plus déjà (“already”) to say someone has previously been in a state or had a role. Often appears in the passé composé (e.g., j’ai déjà été…, il a déjà été…). Depending on context, it can mean “has already been” or “has been before / in the past.”
target_language_example: J’ai déjà été à Paris.
native_language_example: I’ve already been to Paris.

meaning: common denominator; shared factor (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Used literally in math (especially in the set phrase « le plus petit dénominateur commun » = the least common denominator). Also used figuratively to mean the shared cause/element linking different things: « Le dénominateur commun de… ». Note spelling: « dénominateur » (not *dénomination*).
target_language_example: Dans ces deux histoires, le dénominateur commun, c’est la peur.
native_language_example: In these two stories, the common denominator is fear.

meaning: To go too far; to cross the line.
additional_notes: Used to say someone’s behavior, words, or demands are unacceptable (they’ve overstepped the limits). Often said as a criticism: « Là, tu dépasses les bornes ! »
target_language_example: Tu vas dépasser les bornes si tu continues à parler comme ça.
native_language_example: You’re going to go too far if you keep talking like that.

meaning: went too far; crossed the line.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone their behavior is unacceptable or excessive. Very common in spoken French (also seen as the infinitive: « dépasser les bornes »). Often intensified with words like « complètement ».
target_language_example: Là, tu as dépassé les bornes : excuse-toi.
native_language_example: You’ve crossed the line: apologize.

additional_notes: Imperative of the reflexive verb « se dépêcher » (“to hurry”). « -toi » is the stressed pronoun “yourself/you,” used when telling one person to hurry. Often paired with « allez » (“come on”) or followed by « ou… » (“or…”) to warn about a consequence: « Dépêche-toi, ou tu vas rater le train. » Also common: « Dépêchez-vous ! » (to several people or formal “you”).
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi, on va être en retard.
native_language_example: Hurry up, we’re going to be late.

meaning: "Hurry up!" (to more than one person, or formal).
additional_notes: Imperative form of "se dépêcher" (= to hurry). "-vous" is the reflexive pronoun and also indicates you’re speaking to a group or using the polite/formal "vous". Often followed by "de" + infinitive ("Dépêchez-vous de venir !" = Hurry up and come!), or used alone as an urgent command. In "Dépêchez-vous, les mecs !" the "vous" matches the plural "you"; "les mecs" is informal (“guys”).
target_language_example: Dépêchez-vous, on va être en retard !
native_language_example: Hurry up, we’re going to be late!

additional_notes: From the verb **déranger** = to bother, disturb, inconvenience. **Dérange pas** is a common spoken shortening of **Ne … dérange pas** (dropping **ne**). Used (1) as a negative command: **Dérange pas ta sœur.** = Don’t bother your sister. (2) to ask if something is OK: **Ça ne te dérange pas ?** = Does that bother you?/Is that okay with you?
target_language_example: Dérange pas, je vais le faire moi-même.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about it, I’ll do it myself.

additional_notes: Usually used in the full question: « Ça te dérange si je … ? » (informal, with friends) or « Ça vous dérange si je … ? » (polite/formal). Literally it’s about “bothering” someone, and it’s a common way to ask permission politely.
target_language_example: Ça vous dérange si je m’assois ici ?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I sit here?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for permission or check if it bothers someone. Most often you’ll hear it as: « Ça te dérange si je fume… ? » (informal, to one person) or « Ça vous dérange si je fume… ? » (formal / to strangers / to more than one person). You can add a place (« ici ») or specify « une cigarette ».
target_language_example: Ça vous dérange si je fume dehors ?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I smoke outside?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask what someone wants (common in shops, restaurants, hotels). It’s the verb *désirer* (“to want / to desire”) with subject–verb inversion (*-vous*) to form a question. In everyday casual speech, people often use *vous voulez… ?* or *tu veux… ?* instead.
target_language_example: Désirez-vous payer par carte ou en espèces ?
native_language_example: Would you like to pay by card or in cash?

meaning: “Sorry, I…” (apologizing before saying what you have to do / can’t do).
additional_notes: Used to soften a refusal, interruption, or bad news: “Désolé, je dois y aller.” It’s short for “Je suis désolé(e).” If you’re a woman speaking about yourself, you usually say “Désolée, je…”.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come tonight.

désolé de vous avoir fait attendre

target_language_multi_word_term: désolé de vous avoir fait attendre
additional_notes: A polite apology used when someone had to wait because of you. Uses "vous" (formal/plural) and the past infinitive "avoir fait attendre" (“to have made [you] wait”), so it refers to something that already happened. You can add emphasis with "si longtemps" (“so long”).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de vous avoir fait attendre, je suis arrivé en retard.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for keeping you waiting; I arrived late.

additional_notes: Used to apologize for a situation, event, or something that happened: “Désolé pour + noun/phrase” (Désolé pour le retard. / Désolé pour ce qui s’est passé.). You may also hear/see it with a person when expressing sympathy rather than apologizing: “(Je suis / Je me sens) désolé pour lui/elle/toi/vous” = “I feel sorry for him/her/you.” Add emphasis with “vraiment/sincèrement” (really/sincerely).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé pour le retard.
native_language_example: I’m sorry about the delay.

additional_notes: Used to apologize for something (a situation, mistake, delay, etc.). "Désolée" is the feminine form (said by a woman); "désolé pour" is masculine. You’ll also hear "je suis désolé(e) pour…" for a slightly fuller, more explicit apology. It can also mean feeling sympathy: "Je me sens désolée pour vous" = "I feel sorry for you."
target_language_example: Désolée pour le retard, j’ai raté le bus.
native_language_example: Sorry about the delay, I missed the bus.

additional_notes: Refers to a detective who works independently (not police), typically hired by clients to investigate or follow someone. Often used with être (Je suis détective privé) or with engager/embaucher (hire) and faire suivre quelqu’un par un détective privé (have someone followed by a private investigator).
target_language_example: Elle a engagé un détective privé pour retrouver son frère.
native_language_example: She hired a private investigator to find her brother.

meaning: Relax; calm down. (to one person you address as “tu”)
additional_notes: Imperative form of the reflexive verb « se détendre » (“to relax”). The hyphen + « toi » is used in affirmative commands (e.g., « Détends-toi ! »). Often said to tell someone to stop stressing or getting upset; can range from friendly to a bit sharp depending on tone/context (e.g., « Détends-toi, mec. »).
target_language_example: Détends-toi, tout va bien se passer.
native_language_example: Relax, everything is going to be fine.

additional_notes: “déteste” is the present tense (he/she/it) of **détester** (“to hate / to detest”). It’s followed by **les** when the thing disliked is plural (“the”). You can swap **les** for **le** (masc. singular) or **la** (fem. singular): *Il déteste le café. Elle déteste la pluie.*
target_language_example: Elle déteste les embouteillages.
native_language_example: She hates traffic jams.

meaning: "should have told me" / "ought to have told me".
additional_notes: Used with the verb « devoir » in the past (« dû » is the past participle). Very common in phrases like « Tu aurais dû me le dire » (You should have told me). « me » = to me, « le » = it, and « dire » = to tell/say. You’ll usually see it after an auxiliary like « avoir »: « j’ai dû… » (I had to…), « tu aurais dû… » (you should have…).
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû me le dire plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have told me earlier.

meaning: "must have been" / "had to be" (and in the conditional: "should have been").
additional_notes: From the verb *devoir* (to have to / must). Most often you’ll see it as **a dû être** (he/she/it must have been; he/she/it had to be), expressing either a past necessity or a logical deduction about the past. With the conditional perfect (**aurais dû être**, **aurions dû être**, etc.), it expresses regret or criticism: “should have been.”
target_language_example: Il a dû être très fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: He must have been very tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Often used with "par e-mail" (by email) or "via e-mail" (via email) to say how you send something or how you contact someone. You can also say "un e-mail" (an email) or "un mail" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Je t’envoie les documents par e-mail ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m emailing you the documents tonight.

additional_notes: Common in everyday French, alongside « email » and « courriel » (more common in Canada). Used like in English: « envoyer un e-mail » (to send an email), « recevoir un e-mail » (to receive an email), « une adresse e-mail » (an email address).
target_language_example: Je t’envoie un e-mail ce soir.
native_language_example: I'll send you an email tonight.

additional_notes: Refers to water that comes from the faucet (not bottled water). Often used when talking about whether the water is safe to drink: « L’eau du robinet est potable ? » (= Is the tap water drinkable/safe?)
target_language_example: Je préfère l’eau du robinet à l’eau en bouteille.
native_language_example: I prefer tap water to bottled water.

additional_notes: Most often used in the plural: « effets personnels » = your personal items (e.g., clothes, wallet, phone). Common in travel, hospitals, police reports, or lost-and-found contexts: « récupérer ses effets personnels », « garder vos effets personnels avec vous ». In the singular (« effet personnel »), it refers to one personal item.
target_language_example: Veuillez déclarer tout effet personnel manquant à la réception.
native_language_example: Please report any missing personal item to the front desk.

meaning: side effect (especially of a medicine or treatment).
additional_notes: Used for an unintended or additional effect besides the main desired one. Common in medical contexts: « Quel est l’effet secondaire le plus fréquent ? » or « J’ai eu un effet secondaire ». It can also be used more generally for an unintended consequence (e.g., of a decision), but the health/medicine meaning is the most common.
target_language_example: Ce médicament peut provoquer un effet secondaire.
native_language_example: This medicine can cause a side effect.

meaning: (Their/your/etc.) efforts were in vain; were futile/unsuccessful.
additional_notes: Used to say that attempts didn’t work or had no result. The adjective agrees: "efforts" is plural masculine, so "vains". Often used with a possessive before it: "Mes/Tes/Ses/Leurs/Vos efforts ont été vains."
target_language_example: J’ai essayé de le convaincre, mais mes efforts ont été vains.
native_language_example: I tried to convince him, but my efforts were in vain.

meaning: "well," (to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used as a spoken-style transition to start a sentence, react to something, or introduce a conclusion or suggestion. Often followed by a pause/comma: “Eh bien, …”.
target_language_example: Eh bien, on y va ?
native_language_example: Well, shall we go?

meaning: “Well, it’s…” / “So, it’s…” (used to react, conclude, or introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: "Eh bien" is a very common transition in spoken French meaning “well/so,” often signaling you’re thinking, reacting (surprise, resignation), or wrapping up. It’s frequently followed by "c’est" to launch a statement: "Eh bien, c’est tout" (“Well, that’s all”).
target_language_example: Eh bien, c'est ton jour de chance.
native_language_example: Well, it’s your lucky day.

meaning: "Well, I..." (to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to react, transition, or gently emphasize your response (sometimes with a slight pause, hesitation, or surprise). It’s neutral in tone and common in conversation. Often followed by a verb phrase: « Eh bien, je vais… », « Eh bien, je l’espère. »
target_language_example: Eh bien, je ne sais pas quoi dire.
native_language_example: Well, I don't know what to say.

additional_notes: Reflexive emphatic pronoun used to refer back to a feminine subject (elle). Often used for emphasis ("the embassy itself"), after prepositions ("après elle-même" = "at herself"), or with "par" to mean doing something alone/without help ("par elle-même" = "by herself"). In "ne pas être elle-même", it means not being in her normal state ("not herself").
target_language_example: Elle a réparé son vélo par elle-même.
native_language_example: She fixed her bike by herself.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that it’s the woman in question personally (not someone else). It can come after the subject pronoun (Elle préfère… elle-même) or after a noun (Marie elle-même). It can also be used alone as a short reply meaning “her, herself.”
target_language_example: Elle a réparé son vélo elle-même.
native_language_example: She fixed her bike herself.

additional_notes: Composed of elle + a (the 3rd-person singular of avoir, “to have”). Very often it is used before a past participle to form the passé composé: elle a dansé, elle a laissé, elle a esquivé. In those cases, English often translates it with the simple past (“she danced,” “she left,” “she avoided”) rather than literally “she has.”
target_language_example: Elle a oublié son téléphone.
native_language_example: She forgot her phone.

additional_notes: "Acheter" means "to buy". "Elle a acheté" is the passé composé (common past tense) and can translate either as simple past ("she bought") or present perfect ("she has bought"), depending on context. "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article ("a"/"an"); for feminine nouns you use "une" (e.g., "Elle a acheté une voiture").
target_language_example: Elle a acheté un cadeau pour son ami.
native_language_example: She bought a gift for her friend.

additional_notes: Past tense of dire (“to say/tell”): elle (she) + a dit (has said). Use it to report what a woman/girl said, often followed by a quote (« … ») or by que (“that”). With yes/no answers: Elle a dit oui/non. If you mention the person she spoke to, French often uses an indirect object pronoun like lui (“to him/her”): Elle lui a dit oui.
target_language_example: Elle a dit qu’elle était fatiguée.
native_language_example: She said that she was tired.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman/girl said about herself. It’s the start of reported speech: **elle a dit** (she said) + **que** (that) + **elle** (she). **Que** becomes **qu’** before a vowel sound (élision): **qu’elle**. The verb that follows is often in the past/imperfect (e.g., *qu’elle était…*) or conditional/future-in-the-past (e.g., *qu’elle viendrait*).
target_language_example: Elle a dit qu'elle n'avait pas le temps.
native_language_example: She said that she didn’t have time.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of "devoir" (to have to / must). With an infinitive, it often expresses necessity/obligation in the past: "Elle a dû partir" = "She had to leave." It can also express a strong guess/deduction about the past: "Elle a dû tomber" = "She must have fallen." Context usually tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Elle a dû partir tôt, parce qu’elle était fatiguée.
native_language_example: She must have left early because she was tired.
