native_language_example: My neighbor is very kind to the children.

additional_notes: Used to say something has high importance. It’s the verb être ("to be") in the 3rd-person singular (est) + très ("very") + important. Change est to sont for a plural subject: « Ces détails sont très importants. » You can also change the adjective for gender/number: importante (fem. singular), importants (masc. plural), importantes (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Pour réussir, la pratique est très importante.
native_language_example: To succeed, practice is very important.

meaning: 'is very pretty' (said of a feminine person/thing).
additional_notes: Uses the verb être ("to be") + très ("very") + the adjective joli/jolie ("pretty"). Jolie is the feminine form, used with feminine nouns (une fille, une maison, une montre, la vue) or with "elle" / a woman’s name. For masculine, use "est très joli" (e.g., "Il est très joli.").
target_language_example: Cette robe est très jolie.
native_language_example: This dress is very pretty.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is liked by many people. Changes with the subject: "sont très populaires" (they are very popular). "Populaire" agrees in gender/number: populaire (m/f singular), populaires (plural).
target_language_example: Cette chanteuse est très populaire en France.
native_language_example: This singer is very popular in France.

additional_notes: Used to identify or classify someone or something with a masculine singular noun: for example, Tom est un jockey. It is made of est ("is") + un ("a"). In some contexts, un may instead belong to another expression, like un peu ("a little").
target_language_example: Mon frère est un médecin.
native_language_example: My brother is a doctor.

additional_notes: Used with **il/elle** or a noun to state that someone or something is an animal: **X est un animal**. Often followed by an adjective or a relative clause: **un animal nocturne**, **un animal puissant**, **un animal qui vit en mer**. It can also be used **figuratively** about a person (often jokingly or as an insult) to mean they’re behaving like an animal or are very rough/uncivilized.
target_language_example: Ce chat est un animal très calme.
native_language_example: This cat is a very calm animal.

meaning: “is an art” (a skill or practice requiring talent, technique, or finesse).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is a true art form (dance, sculpture, etc.) or that doing it well takes special skill and subtlety (often in proverbs like « Écouter est un art »). You can also use it ironically for habits: « Remettre à plus tard est un art. »
target_language_example: Négocier, c’est un art.
native_language_example: Negotiating is an art.

additional_notes: A descriptive phrase used before a singular masculine noun: est + un + bon + noun. It means someone or something has a positive quality in that role, as in est un bon acteur ('is a good actor'). For feminine nouns, French usually uses est une bonne.
target_language_example: Mon frère est un bon cuisinier.
native_language_example: My brother is a good cook.

additional_notes: Used with a subject to describe what something is like as a place, often followed by an adjective (idéal, dangereux, super) or a relative clause (qui attire…). The noun is usually “un endroit” (a place), but it can change with gender/number (e.g., « est un endroit », « est une ville », « sont des endroits »).
target_language_example: Ce parc est un endroit calme pour lire.
native_language_example: This park is a quiet place to read.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" (to be) + "un garçon" to describe someone as a boy/young male person. Often followed by an adjective (e.g., "un garçon intelligent") or a description with "de" (e.g., "un garçon de la campagne", "un garçon de treize ans"). Note: French "garçon" means "boy"; in English, "garçon" is sometimes used to mean a waiter, which can be confusing.
target_language_example: Il est un garçon très sympa.
native_language_example: He is a very nice boy.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: *X est un grand + nom* can mean “X is a great (excellent) …” (e.g., *un grand sportif*) or “a big/major …” (e.g., *un grand malentendu*). With feminine nouns, it becomes *est une grande*; in plural: *sont de grands / de grandes*. Note that *grand* can also mean “tall” depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est un grand moment pour notre équipe.
native_language_example: It's a big moment for our team.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *être* (to be) to identify someone as a man: *Il est un homme.* In descriptions, French often puts the adjective after *homme*: *un homme âgé* (an old/elderly man), *un homme marié* (a married man). Some adjectives can also come before the noun (e.g., *un bon homme* can mean “a good-natured man”), but *un homme bon* means “a good man.”
target_language_example: Mon professeur est un homme très patient.
native_language_example: My teacher is a very patient man.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or activity to say it’s something you do for fun in your free time: « X est un passe-temps. » You can add an adjective to describe it: « un passe-temps bon marché » (inexpensive), « coûteux/onéreux » (expensive), « populaire » (popular).
target_language_example: Lire le soir est un passe-temps relaxant.
native_language_example: Reading in the evening is a relaxing hobby.

additional_notes: Used with a place name + « est un pays » + adjective/noun phrase to describe that country. « pays » is masculine, so it takes « un » and adjectives agree (e.g., « un pays magnifique », « un pays neutre »).
target_language_example: Le Canada est un pays très grand.
native_language_example: Canada is a very large country.

meaning: “is a bit / is a little / is somewhat.”
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to mean “a little” and often to soften a statement (understatement). It’s the 3rd-person singular of « être » + « un peu » (e.g., « c’est un peu… », « il/elle est un peu… »).
target_language_example: C'est un peu compliqué, mais je peux t'aider.
native_language_example: It’s a bit complicated, but I can help you.

meaning: 'is a bit' / 'is a little' (used to soften what you’re saying).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or expression to make it less direct: « Il/elle est un peu + adjectif » (e.g., timide, nerveux, fatigué) or « être un peu à sec » = to be a bit short on money. Often implies “kind of / somewhat.”
target_language_example: Je sais que Tom est un peu timide.
native_language_example: I know that Tom is a bit shy.

additional_notes: Used in polite, formal contexts, usually as part of a longer phrase like: « C’est un plaisir de vous rencontrer / de vous voir / de vous aider » (“It’s a pleasure to meet/see/help you”). With « vous », it addresses one person formally or multiple people. By itself (« est un plaisir de vous ») sounds incomplete; you normally need « C’est » at the start and an infinitive after it.
target_language_example: C’est un plaisir de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to meet you.

meaning: “is a very good …” (said about a person, usually before a job/role).
additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns (un) to praise someone’s ability in a role: « Il/elle est un très bon + noun ». For a feminine noun, use « une très bonne » (e.g., « Elle est une très bonne prof. »). You can also use it with other subjects (e.g., « Mon frère est un très bon… »).
target_language_example: Elle est un très bon médecin.
native_language_example: She is a very good doctor.

meaning: 'is a real/true (noun)' (used to emphasize what someone is like).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to stress that someone really fits that description (positive or negative): « Il est un vrai héros » = he truly is a hero. Agreement: vrai changes with gender/number (un vrai…, une vraie…, des vrais…, des vraies…). Often stronger than just « il est un … ».
target_language_example: Tom est un vrai héros.
native_language_example: Tom is a true hero.

additional_notes: "est" is the third-person singular of être ("to be"), and "une" is the feminine singular form of "a/an". Use this chunk before a feminine singular noun: for example, "Londres est une grande ville." In phrases like "est une des...", it can mean "is one of the...".
target_language_example: Ma sœur est une étudiante très sérieuse.
native_language_example: My sister is a very serious student.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns: **être + une + belle + noun** (e.g., *une belle ville*, *une belle région*). With masculine nouns, you use **un beau** (e.g., *C'est un beau pays.*). Often followed immediately by the noun; *belle* is an adjective here (not the English noun “belle”).
target_language_example: Paris est une belle ville.
native_language_example: Paris is a beautiful city.

additional_notes: Used to describe a place positively. It follows a subject (a city name or “c’/ce”) + “être” (est) + “une belle ville”. You can change the adjective: “est une grande ville” (is a big city), “est une petite ville” (is a small town/city).
target_language_example: Lyon est une belle ville, surtout au printemps.
native_language_example: Lyon is a beautiful city, especially in spring.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun to describe someone/something as good at something or being a good person/thing: « Il/Elle est une bonne + nom ». « bonne » agrees with a feminine noun (ex. « une bonne nageuse », « une bonne personne »). In « C'en est une bonne ! », it means “That’s a good one!” (often reacting to a joke/story/surprising remark).
target_language_example: Elle est une bonne professeure.
native_language_example: She’s a good teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is beneficial or positive. Very often you’ll see it with an impersonal subject: « C’est une bonne chose » (“That’s a good thing”). With a specific subject, use « X est une bonne chose » (“X is a good thing”). « chose » is feminine, so it’s « une bonne » (not *un bon*).
target_language_example: Faire une pause, c’est une bonne chose.
native_language_example: Taking a break is a good thing.

additional_notes: "Est" is the 3rd-person singular of "être" (to be). Use "X est une femme" to describe someone as a woman; add adjectives after "femme" (e.g., "une femme intelligente"). Contrast: "une fille" = a girl/daughter. For a female teacher, modern French often prefers the feminine form: "La professeure est une femme."
target_language_example: Elle est une femme très gentille.
native_language_example: She is a very kind woman.

meaning: “is a big / great …” (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with **être** (“to be”) + **une** + **grande** to describe a **feminine noun** (e.g., *une grande île*, *une grande économie*). **Grande** agrees with the noun: masculine *un grand …*, feminine *une grande …*. Meaning depends on context: **physically large** (*une grande île*) or **important/impressive** (*une grande vertu*, *une grande motivation*). With *fille*, *une grande fille* often means “a grown-up girl / big girl.”
target_language_example: Paris est une grande ville.
native_language_example: Paris is a big city.

additional_notes: Used to identify something as a language: “[X] est une langue …” (“[X] is a … language”), often followed by an adjective (difficile, sympathique) or a category/origin (slave, berbère). The verb is present tense of être (“to be”).
target_language_example: Le français est une langue très utile.
native_language_example: French is a very useful language.

additional_notes: Used to say that a language is hard to learn. You can add details like "à apprendre" (to learn): "Le japonais est une langue difficile à apprendre." "Langue" is feminine, so you say "une langue"; the adjective "difficile" stays the same in masculine/feminine singular.
target_language_example: Je pense que l’arabe est une langue difficile.
native_language_example: I think Arabic is a difficult language.

meaning: “is a person” (used to describe someone or define a job).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe someone (e.g., "est une personne bizarre/bavarde") or with "qui..." to define what someone does ("Un fleuriste est une personne qui..."). Often interchangeable with "il/elle est + adjectif" when describing someone, but "être une personne + adjectif" can sound a bit more general.
target_language_example: Ma sœur est une personne très gentille.
native_language_example: My sister is a very kind person.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity isn’t worth doing because it doesn’t bring enough benefit. It often follows an infinitive (e.g., “Regarder la télévision est une perte de temps.”). You can also use it with something: “Twitter est une perte de temps.”
target_language_example: Pour moi, faire la queue ici est une perte de temps.
native_language_example: For me, waiting in line here is a waste of time.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say that something depends mainly on one factor or perspective. Very common with abstract nouns like temps (time), point de vue (point of view), choix (choice), patience (patience): « C’est une question de + nom ». You can also use « Tout est une question de… » to mean “It’s all a matter of…”.
target_language_example: Réussir, c’est une question de pratique.
native_language_example: Succeeding is a matter of practice.

meaning: "is a kind/sort of" (used to compare or describe something approximately).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something belongs to a category or is similar to something: « X est une sorte de Y ». Often implies an approximate comparison (“sort of”), sometimes slightly ironic or skeptical depending on tone (e.g., « une sorte de blague »).
target_language_example: Ce petit café est une sorte de musée, avec toutes ses vieilles affiches.
native_language_example: That little café is kind of a museum, with all its old posters.

additional_notes: Used with a singular feminine noun to identify a place: [Place] + est une ville + adjective (calme, tranquille) or + de + country/region (“une ville de Russie” = a city in Russia). For plural, use “sont des villes.” For masculine nouns like “village,” use “est un …”.
target_language_example: Lyon est une ville très agréable.
native_language_example: Lyon is a very pleasant city.

additional_notes: Passé composé of venir, formed with être. It is used with a masculine singular subject; other forms include est venue, sont venus, sont venues. Depending on context, it can mean either "came" or "has come," as in le temps est venu = "the time has come."
target_language_example: Mon frère est venu hier soir.
native_language_example: My brother came last night.

meaning: “came to see me” / “came to visit me.”
additional_notes: Passé composé of **venir** with **être**: **il est venu** + **me voir** (“to come see me/come visit me”). The past participle agrees with the subject: **il est venu / elle est venue / ils sont venus / elles sont venues** (so the exact string **est venu me voir** is masculine singular). In negatives: **Personne n’est venu me voir** (“Nobody came to see me”). Note: **venir + infinitif** often implies coming in order to do something.
target_language_example: Mon oncle est venu me voir hier soir.
native_language_example: My uncle came to see me last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of venir for a feminine singular subject (elle / ma sœur / la police, etc.). It describes someone (or something) coming/arriving, or coming to do something: « Elle est venue me voir » = “She came to see me.” It can also be used more figuratively with time: « Ton heure est venue » = “Your time has come.” Note: « venue » is a false friend with English “venue” (place).
target_language_example: Elle est venue à la maison hier soir.
native_language_example: She came to the house last night.

additional_notes: Used with singular subjects to say something contains nothing or has no people/space left (e.g., a can, box, jar, park). For batteries, it means the battery is dead/has no charge. Feminine form: "est vide" also (same spelling/pronunciation), e.g., "La boîte est vide."
target_language_example: Le frigo est vide.
native_language_example: The fridge is empty.

additional_notes: A straightforward combination of est ("is") and votre ("your"). It often appears in questions or descriptions about someone's name, role, relationship, or belongings. Votre is used for one person in a formal way or for more than one person.
target_language_example: Quel est votre nom ?
native_language_example: What is your name?

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement/fact is true. Often appears after “que” in longer sentences (e.g., “Je crois que … est vrai”). For emphasis you can also say “C’est vrai !” (“That’s true!”).
target_language_example: Ce que tu dis est vrai.
native_language_example: What you're saying is true.

additional_notes: "est" is the 3rd-person singular of "être" + "vraiment". It is used with a person or thing to add emphasis ("is really very beautiful") or to mean "actually/truly" ("is really dangerous"). Depending on context, the subject can be "he," "she," "it," or a named person or thing.
target_language_example: Ce film est vraiment intéressant.
native_language_example: This movie is really interesting.

meaning: is because of; is due to.
additional_notes: Built on the preposition phrase "à cause de" (= because of). It’s most often used to explain a cause, frequently with a negative idea (problem, delay, accident). Very common with "C’est à cause de…" (It’s because of…). For neutral/positive causes, French often prefers "grâce à" (= thanks to). Note the fixed structure: "est à cause de" + noun phrase (e.g., "est à cause de la pluie").
target_language_example: Le retard est à cause de la circulation.
native_language_example: The delay is because of traffic.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is within a building/space (indoors) or within an area. Often answers “Where is … ?” → « Il/Elle est à l'intérieur. » Can also appear with a complement: « est à l'intérieur de… » / « est à l'intérieur des terres » (inland).
target_language_example: Ma femme est à l'intérieur.
native_language_example: My wife is inside.

meaning: “is at the / is to the” (être + à + la).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (la). Often indicates location (Tom est à la salle de bain. = Tom is in the bathroom) or appears in fixed expressions like être à la recherche de (“to be looking for”), être à la racine de (“to be at the root of”), and La parole est à X (“The floor goes to X / It’s X’s turn to speak”). Not the same as English “à la” meaning “in the style of”.
target_language_example: La parole est à la défense.
native_language_example: The floor goes to the defense.

additional_notes: Used with être to say someone is at home (physically at their house). For questions, keep the same structure and raise intonation or add a question mark: « Il est à la maison ? ». You can change the subject and the verb form: « je suis / tu es / il est / elle est / on est / nous sommes / vous êtes / ils sont / elles sont à la maison ».
target_language_example: Ma sœur est à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: My sister is at home tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express possession/ownership: *X est à moi* = “X is mine.” Often contrasts with *c’est mon/ma/mes* (“it’s my...”), which is used directly before a noun (e.g., *c’est mon sac*). Here, *à moi* emphasizes who the owner is and can sound insistent (e.g., “It’s mine!”).
target_language_example: Ce livre est à moi, pas à toi.
native_language_example: That book is mine, not yours.

additional_notes: Used to say what the topic/subject of something is. Often followed by a noun or a verb in the infinitive: « C’est à propos de mon travail » (about my job), « C’est à propos de venir demain » (about coming tomorrow). In everyday French, you’ll very often see « c’est à propos de… ».
target_language_example: Ce livre est à propos de la cuisine française.
native_language_example: This book is about French cooking.

additional_notes: Used to show ownership/possession with être + à + stressed pronoun: « C’est à moi / à toi / à lui / à elle / à nous / à vous / à eux / à elles ». With plural: « sont à toi ». For formal or plural “you,” use « est à vous ».
target_language_example: Ce livre est à toi.
native_language_example: This book is yours.

meaning: Not a standard phrase by itself; likely meant to be part of “C’est ça que tu… ?” = “Is that what you…?”
additional_notes:
On its own, “est ça que tu” is ungrammatical in French. In real usage you’ll most often see:
- “C’est ça que tu veux ?” = “Is that what you want?”
- “C’est ça que tu dis ?” = “Is that what you’re saying?”
“C’est” means “it is/that is”, and “que” introduces what follows (“that/which”). In questions, French often uses “C’est ça que tu + verb… ?” to check or confirm something.
target_language_example: C’est ça que tu veux ?
native_language_example: Is that what you want?

additional_notes: Used at the end of a list to mean there are more similar items (often implying “you get the idea”). Can also be said alone (“Et ainsi de suite.”) to mean “and so on.”
target_language_example: On a visité Paris, Lyon, Marseille, et ainsi de suite.
native_language_example: We visited Paris, Lyon, Marseille, and so on.

additional_notes:
Used to react to what someone just said.
- To ask for what happens next or to prompt someone to continue: “Et alors, après ?” (“And then, after that?”).
- To express “so what?” (often a bit challenging or dismissive): “Je sais, et alors ?” (“I know—so what?”).
Often placed at the start of a sentence; can also be followed by a question word (quoi, après, pourquoi…).
target_language_example: Tu n’aimes pas ce film ? Et alors ?
native_language_example: You don’t like this movie? So what?

meaning: "and it’s / and that’s" (used to introduce, point to, or emphasize what follows).
additional_notes: Composed of et (“and”) + c’est (“it is/that is”). Common in speech and writing to link to a conclusion, explanation, identification, or the key point: « et c'est ce que… », « et c'est comme ça que… », « et c'est à cause de… ». The emphasis can sound insistent or pointed depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Et c'est ce que tu fais.
native_language_example: And that’s what you do.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to continue the conversation or ask for more detail (often after something was just mentioned). It’s basically “and how about…?” / “so, how…?”. You can often drop et and just say comment.
target_language_example: Et comment tu as appris le français ?
native_language_example: And how did you learn French?

additional_notes: Used after a feminine time/quantity word to add “half”: une heure et demie (1.5 hours), cinq heures et demie (5:30). The masculine form is “et demi” (e.g., un an et demi). In telling time, it’s common because “heure” is feminine.
target_language_example: On se voit à six heures et demie.
native_language_example: See you at six thirty.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. et means "and"; des usually introduces a plural noun. In English, des may be translated as "some" or often left untranslated: et des sandales = "and sandals." In some cases, des can instead be part of another structure, as in des deux côtés ("on both sides").
target_language_example: J'ai acheté du fromage et des tomates.
native_language_example: I bought cheese and some tomatoes.

meaning: and another / and more; also “and yet / however”.
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) adding one more item or a bit more of something: « Et encore un peu de sucre » (“And a bit more sugar”). (2) correcting/qualifying what you just said: « Et encore, pas pour longtemps » (“And yet, not for long”). (3) alone (« Et encore. ») can mean “And what’s more / And yet” depending on context.
target_language_example: On a déjà beaucoup marché… et encore, ce n’est pas fini.
native_language_example: We’ve already walked a lot… and yet, it’s not over.

meaning: and there is / and there are; and also (there’s…).
additional_notes: Used to add another thing to a list, description, or situation: “and there’s…” / “and then there’s…”. It can introduce an extra example (“Et il y a ça aussi.”), a person/thing (“Et il y a moi…”), or a point (“Et il y a pire.” = “and it can be worse / and there’s worse”). The verb is always singular (il y a) even when referring to plural things.
target_language_example: On a du pain, du fromage, et il y a des fruits aussi.
native_language_example: We have bread, cheese, and there’s fruit too.

meaning: "and I" (in the past), introducing a reflexive verb in the passé composé.
additional_notes: Used to link two past actions with "et" (and). "Je me suis" is the passé composé form used with many reflexive verbs (verbs with "se"), e.g. "je me suis habillé(e)" (I got dressed), "je me suis séché(e)" (I dried myself), "je me suis foulé..." (I sprained...). The past participle may agree with the subject in some cases (e.g. "je me suis retrouvé(e)").
target_language_example: Je suis rentré chez moi et je me suis couché tôt.
native_language_example: I came home and went to bed early.

meaning: 'and I don't / and I do not' (starting a negative clause).
additional_notes: Used to continue a sentence and add what *you* do not do/think/want/know, etc. It’s normally followed by a verb, and often completes the negation with words like **pas**, **plus**, **jamais**, **rien**, etc. (e.g., *Et je ne sais pas…*, *Et je ne veux plus…*).
target_language_example: Et je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: And I can't come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to add information about yourself, often after a previous statement. "Je suis" means "I am" (from the verb "être"). In speech, "et je" is often pronounced with a liaison: "et je suis" → sounds like "é j(e) suis". The adjective that follows usually agrees with the speaker (e.g., "doué" masculine, "douée" feminine).
target_language_example: Et je suis prêt(e) à partir.
native_language_example: And I'm ready to leave.

meaning: "and I (to you)" / "and I will (to you)" (introduces what I do/say to you).
additional_notes: Used to link to the next action: « et » = “and”, « je » = “I”, « te » = “to you” (informal singular object pronoun). It’s very common before a verb: « et je te promets… » (and I promise you…), « et je te rendrai… » (and I’ll make you…). With threats it often sounds like “and I’ll … you”. For formal “you,” use « et je vous … ».
target_language_example: D’accord, et je te rappelle ce soir.
native_language_example: Okay, and I’ll call you back tonight.

additional_notes: A basic combination of et + le, used before a masculine singular noun. It can simply join two nouns or noun phrases, and in short questions like Et le père ? it often means "what about the ...?" Before a vowel or mute h, French usually uses et l' instead.
target_language_example: Je prends la soupe et le sandwich.
native_language_example: I'll have the soup and the sandwich.

meaning: “and the” (plural); also “and what about the …?” in questions.
additional_notes: Most often it simply links two plural noun phrases: « X et les Y ». At the start of a question (« Et les … ? »), it can mean “What about …?” or “And the …?” (bringing up something not yet answered). « les » is the plural “the.”
target_language_example: Et les billets, tu les as achetés ?
native_language_example: And the tickets—did you buy them?

meaning: "and now" / "now" (to move on to the next moment or step).
additional_notes: Used to transition to what happens next, often after something has changed or after waiting/doing something. It can also introduce a new problem or question ("and now I don’t know what to do"). Often set off by a comma: "Et maintenant, ...".
target_language_example: Et maintenant, qu’est-ce qu’on fait ?
native_language_example: And now, what do we do?

meaning: “and gentlemen” (used in the phrase “Mesdames et messieurs” = “Ladies and gentlemen”).
additional_notes: Very formal, used to address an audience in speeches, announcements, or presentations. Usually comes after “Mesdames” (ladies). On its own, it sounds incomplete unless the previous part (“Mesdames”) is implied.
target_language_example: Mesdames et messieurs, bienvenue à bord.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome aboard.

additional_notes: Used to add yourself to another person or group. French uses the stressed pronoun moi after et, even when English would often say "and I" as the subject: for example, mon frère et moi avons....
target_language_example: Paul et moi allons au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: Paul and I are going to the movies tonight.

meaning: “and I, we…” (spoken way to say “X and I…” as the subject).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French: after a subject like “Tom et moi”, speakers often add “on” (meaning “we”) before the verb: “Tom et moi, on + verbe”. It emphasizes the group and sounds natural in conversation, but in more formal writing you’d usually say “Tom et moi, nous + verbe” (or simply “Tom et moi + verbe” without repeating the subject).
target_language_example: Ma sœur et moi, on part à huit heures.
native_language_example: My sister and I are leaving at eight o’clock.

meaning: 'and I, we’re…' (meaning 'X and I are…' in casual speech).
additional_notes: Common spoken pattern with left-dislocation for emphasis: “X et moi, on…” = “X and I, we…”. Here “on” is used instead of “nous” and the verb is in 3rd person singular (on est). In more formal/written French you’d usually say “X et moi, nous sommes…”.
target_language_example: Ma sœur et moi, on est fatigués ce soir.
native_language_example: My sister and I are tired tonight.

additional_notes: Used to bring the focus back to yourself—often to complain, defend yourself, or ask what you should do next. It’s followed by a full question (e.g., "Et moi, qu'est-ce que je peux faire ?"). Similar in tone to "What about me?" or "And what am I supposed to do?".
target_language_example: Et moi, qu'est-ce que je peux faire ?
native_language_example: What about me—what can I do?

meaning: “and I have” (as part of “X et moi avons…” = “X and I have…”).
additional_notes: Used in a compound subject with another person/name: “Tom et moi avons…” means “Tom and I have…”. French uses the stressed pronoun “moi” (not “je”) after “et”. The verb is plural (avons) because the subject is two people. Often you’ll see the full pattern: “Lui/Elle/Tom/Mes amis et moi avons …”.
target_language_example: Ma sœur et moi avons réservé une table.
native_language_example: My sister and I booked a table.

meaning: “and I are” (used after a name/noun: “X and I are …”).
additional_notes: This appears in patterns like “Tom et moi sommes …” to make a subject with two people. French uses **moi** (not *je*) after **et**: “Paul et moi…”. The verb is **sommes** (1st person plural, “we are”), and adjectives/past participles agree in plural (e.g., “ma femme et moi sommes **allées** …” if the group is feminine/mixed with a feminine speaker).
target_language_example: Mes parents et moi sommes contents de te voir.
native_language_example: My parents and I are happy to see you.

meaning: “and I went” (past tense, with a male or mixed-gender “we”).
additional_notes: Used when the subject is “X et moi” (= “X and I”), so the verb is conjugated like **nous**: **nous sommes allés** (passé composé of *aller* uses **être**). **Allés** agrees with the group: use **allées** if the group is all female (e.g., *Ma sœur et moi sommes allées...*). Often you’ll see the full pattern: **[Name/person] et moi sommes allés + place/verb**.
target_language_example: Mes amis et moi sommes allés au restaurant après le travail.
native_language_example: My friends and I went to the restaurant after work.

et moi sommes dans la même classe

target_language_multi_word_term: et moi sommes dans la même classe
meaning: “and I are in the same class.”
additional_notes: Used after naming another person (e.g., « Marie et moi… ») to say you and that person are in the same class. « et moi » (“and me/I”) is part of the subject, so the verb is plural: « sommes » (we are).
target_language_example: Paul et moi sommes dans la même classe.
native_language_example: Paul and I are in the same class.

et moi sommes du même âge

target_language_multi_word_term: et moi sommes du même âge
additional_notes: Used to say you and someone else have the same age. Because the subject is “X et moi” (“X and I”), the verb is in the 1st person plural: *nous sommes* → *sommes*. The person comes before *et moi* (e.g., *Elle et moi…*, *Toi et moi…*).
target_language_example: Mon frère et moi sommes du même âge.
native_language_example: My brother and I are the same age.

additional_notes: Used when you list yourself with someone else as the subject (X et moi). Even though it uses “moi,” the meaning is “X and I.” The verb is in the plural: “étions” is the imperfect (past) form of être for “nous,” often used for background description in the past.
target_language_example: Ma sœur et moi étions fatigués après le voyage.
native_language_example: My sister and I were tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Often used to continue a story or add an extra point. It can introduce the next event in time (“and then…”) or add a new element (“and also / besides”). In speech it can work like a soft transition (“and then, anyway…”).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un café, et puis je rentre à la maison.
native_language_example: I’m going to have a coffee, and then I’m going home.

meaning: "So/and what…?" (used to introduce a follow-up question).
additional_notes:
Often used at the start of a question to continue a conversation or ask for the next detail, similar to “So what did…?” / “And what does…?”. It’s usually followed by:
- **qu’est-ce que + subject + verb**: *Et qu’est-ce que tu fais ici ?* (“So what are you doing here?”)
- **qu’est-ce qui + verb**: *Et qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?* (“So what happened?”)
It’s neutral in tone; not slang.
target_language_example: Et qu'est-ce que tu veux dire par là ?
native_language_example: So what do you mean by that?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to ask for the next detail: “And/so what did she say/do/want…?” It’s the start of the longer structure “Et qu’est-ce que + subject + verb… ?”. In writing you may also see the full form “et qu’est-ce que …”. You can omit “et” if you’re not continuing a story: “Qu’est-ce qu’elle a dit ?”.
target_language_example: Et qu'est-ce qu'il a répondu ?
native_language_example: So what did he reply?

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to continue the conversation or react to what was just said, often to ask for more information: « Et qu’est-ce que tu as vu ? » (“And what did you see?”). Depending on tone, it can sound neutral, surprised, or a bit impatient (like “So what are you going to do?”).
target_language_example: D'accord, et qu'est-ce que tu veux faire maintenant ?
native_language_example: Okay, so what do you want to do now?

meaning: "And what did that do / lead to / bring?" (asking about the result or point).
additional_notes:
Used to start a follow-up question, often after someone mentions an action or event. The exact meaning depends on the verb that follows: 
- « Et qu'est-ce que ça a donné ? » = What was the outcome?
- « Et qu'est-ce que ça m'apporte ? » = What’s in it for me?/What do I get out of it?
- « Et qu'est-ce que ça peut faire ? » = What difference does it make?/So what?
Common in spoken French; it can sound skeptical or challenging depending on tone.
target_language_example: Tu as tout essayé ? Et qu'est-ce que ça a changé ?
native_language_example: You tried everything? And what did that change?

additional_notes: An informal, often humorous command used to hurry people up or demand immediate action (similar to “chop-chop!”). Often said on its own as an impatient prompt, or after naming what you want done (e.g., an order, a task, bringing food). Not literally about jumping; it’s an idiomatic way to say “right now!”
target_language_example: Allez, on se dépêche : et que ça saute !
native_language_example: Come on, hurry up—get moving!

meaning: “and a few (more)” (used to make a number approximate).
additional_notes: Used right after a number to mean “plus a small additional amount,” similar to “-something” or “and a bit” in English. Common with age, time, money, etc.: « vingt ans et quelques » = “twenty-something”; « deux heures et quelques » = “two hours and a bit.”
target_language_example: Il a trente ans et quelques.
native_language_example: He’s thirty-something.

meaning: "what if he/it…?" (introduces a hypothetical idea or worry).
additional_notes: Used to ask about a possibility, make a suggestion, or express concern. It’s often followed by a verb in the imperfect to imagine a scenario: « Et s’il venait ? » (“What if he came?”). Literally it’s “and if he…”, but in English it’s usually translated as “what if…”.
target_language_example: Et s'il pleuvait demain ?
native_language_example: What if it rained tomorrow?

meaning: "What if he/it doesn’t…?" / "What if there isn’t/aren’t…?"
additional_notes: Used to introduce a worried or hypothetical question. It’s built from **et si** (“what if”) + **il** (“he/it”) + **n’y… pas** (negation with **y**, referring to a place/there). The verb changes depending on what follows: *Et s’il n’y arrive pas ?* (doesn’t manage), *Et s’il n’y en a pas ?* (there aren’t any), *Et s’il n’y est pas ?* (isn’t there).
target_language_example: Et s'il n'y a plus de batterie ?
native_language_example: What if there’s no battery left?

meaning: “and what if he doesn’t…?” / “and if he doesn’t…?”
additional_notes: Used to raise a concern or possibility about a negative outcome. It introduces a conditional question: et + si (“and if”) + il (“he”) → s’il, followed by the negative ne (usually with pas/jamais/plus, etc.): “Et s’il ne vient pas ?” = “What if he doesn’t come?”
target_language_example: Et s'il ne répond pas ?
native_language_example: What if he doesn’t answer?

additional_notes: Used to add “his/her friends” as an extra subject along with someone already mentioned (e.g., “Elle et ses amis…” = “She and her friends…”). Note: “ses” is a possessive meaning “his/her/their” and is used here because “amis” is plural; the owner is understood from context.
target_language_example: Paul et ses amis vont au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: Paul and his friends are going to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: Often used at the start of a question to introduce a possibility, worry, or suggestion: "what if...?" In other contexts, it can simply link clauses and mean "and if."
target_language_example: Et si on restait à la maison ce soir ?
native_language_example: What if we stayed home tonight?

meaning: 'what if it were…?' (introduces a hypothetical possibility).
additional_notes: Used to imagine an alternative or to question a situation: “What if that wasn’t the case?”, “What if it was true?”, etc. Very often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (vrai, trop tard, toi, lui). In speech it can sound like a suggestion, doubt, or worry. Uses the imperfect (c'était) for “were/was” in hypothetical questions.
target_language_example: Et si c'était une erreur ?
native_language_example: What if it were a mistake?

meaning: "What if I..." (to suggest or imagine a possibility).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical idea, proposal, or concern about what might happen if you do something. Often followed by a verb in the imperfect or present, depending on context: « Et si je courais ? » (proposal) / « Et si je refuse ? » (worry/question).
target_language_example: Et si je prenais le train au lieu de conduire ?
native_language_example: What if I took the train instead of driving?

meaning: "and if I don't…" (to introduce a worry or condition).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question or sentence to introduce a hypothetical situation, often expressing concern: « Et si je ne + verb… ? » (“What if I don’t…?”). It’s usually followed by another verb in the present tense (e.g., « comprends », « peux », « trouve »).
target_language_example: Et si je ne comprends pas ?
native_language_example: What if I don’t understand?

additional_notes: Used to propose an idea or option, often gently or spontaneously. It’s usually followed by the imperfect tense in French (e.g., « Et si on partait ? ») even though it refers to a possible action now or soon.
target_language_example: Et si on allait boire un café ?
native_language_example: What if we went to get a coffee?

meaning: "what if you…" (to imagine a situation or make a suggestion).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical question or a gentle suggestion. Very common pattern: « Et si tu + imparfait ? » to suggest an action (e.g., « Et si tu restais ? » = “What if you stayed?”). Can also be used for worried/serious hypotheticals (« Et si tu n’y arrives pas ? » = “What if you can’t do it?”).
target_language_example: Et si tu venais avec nous ?
native_language_example: What if you came with us?

meaning: “and you?” (asking the question back, to one person informally).
additional_notes: Used after you answer or comment, to ask the other person the same thing: « Je vais bien, et toi ? » It uses « toi » (singular informal “you”), so it’s for someone you address with « tu ». For a formal/plural version, say « et vous ? ». In other contexts, « et toi » can also simply mean “and you” (adding the person to a statement).
target_language_example: Moi, ça va bien—et toi ?
native_language_example: I’m doing well—and you?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to turn the question back to the other person. "Et toi" means "and you" (informal singular), and "qu'est-ce que" introduces a question like "what did you do / what do you have / what are you becoming (how’s it going) / what are you going to do / what do you want". Often followed by "tu" and a verb; in casual speech you may hear "t'as" instead of "tu as".
target_language_example: J'ai fini tôt. Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu fais ce soir ?
native_language_example: I finished early. And you, what are you doing tonight?

meaning: "and you?" / "what about you?" (often to turn the question back to someone).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to shift focus to the other person, often after you’ve been talking about someone else or after answering a question. "Et toi" is very common; adding "tu" sets up the verb that follows and can sound a bit more insistent or challenging depending on tone (e.g., "Et toi, tu m'aimes ?").
target_language_example: Moi, j’ai fini. Et toi, tu as déjà commencé ?
native_language_example: I’m done. And you, have you started already?

additional_notes: Used to add that something involves all people in a group. It can appear in the middle of a sentence, or at the beginning ("Et tout le monde…") to emphasize what happens to everyone or what everyone knows/does.
target_language_example: On part à 8 h, et tout le monde doit être à l'heure.
native_language_example: We’re leaving at 8, and everyone has to be on time.

additional_notes: Used to add information about the person you’re speaking to, often after another clause: "…, et tu es …". It can also start a question meaning "And are you…?". "Tu es" is the singular informal "you are" (to one person you address as "tu").
target_language_example: Tu dis que tu ne peux pas venir, et tu es sûr(e) ?
native_language_example: You say you can’t come—are you sure?

additional_notes: Used as an instruction in the imperative (vous form), often by security staff or police during a check. It’s frequently paired with other commands like « Enlevez/Retirez/Ôtez votre manteau… ». Singular informal would be « et vide tes poches »; polite singular is still « videz vos poches ».
target_language_example: Avant de passer au contrôle de sécurité, enlevez votre ceinture et videz vos poches.
native_language_example: Before going through security, take off your belt and empty your pockets.

additional_notes: Used to add information about the person you’re speaking to, or to ask a follow-up question. It can introduce a statement ("…, et vous êtes adorable.") or a question ("Et vous êtes d’accord ?", "Et vous êtes ?" meaning "And you are…?" / "And who are you?"). The verb form changes depending on what follows (e.g., "vous êtes allé(e)(s)").
target_language_example: Et vous êtes ici depuis longtemps ?
native_language_example: And have you been here long?

additional_notes: Inversion of the verb “être” (to be) with “vous” to form a question: “etes-vous … ?”. Used for polite/formal singular (“you”) or for addressing more than one person. In casual speech, French often uses “vous etes … ?” or “est-ce que vous etes … ?”. Note: in standard French spelling, accents are normally required (“Êtes-vous”).
target_language_example: Etes-vous sérieux ?
native_language_example: Are you serious?

additional_notes: Used with the verb « avoir » (to have): « j’ai eu de la chance » = “I was lucky.” « eu » is the past participle, so it’s most often seen in the past tense (passé composé): « avoir eu de la chance ». You can add details with « avec… », « pour… », etc.: « On a eu de la chance avec lui » = “We were lucky with him / He worked out well for us.”
target_language_example: On a eu de la chance : il n’y avait pas de bouchons.
native_language_example: We were lucky: there was no traffic.

additional_notes: Used in the passé composé with avoir: j’ai eu / tu as eu / il a eu / nous avons eu / etc. + des + plural noun. It often translates as “had” or sometimes “got/experienced” depending on the noun (e.g., avoir des vertiges = to feel dizzy). Note: “eu” doesn’t agree with the subject (it stays eu) unless there’s a preceding direct object (advanced).
target_language_example: J’ai eu des problèmes avec ma voiture.
native_language_example: I had some problems with my car.

additional_notes: Used with « avoir » to talk about an event occurring: « a eu lieu » (it took place), « n’a pas eu lieu » (it didn’t happen). Often found in formal or neutral contexts (events, meetings, incidents). In questions: « Quand cela a-t-il eu lieu ? » = “When did that happen?”
target_language_example: La réunion a eu lieu hier soir.
native_language_example: The meeting took place last night.

additional_notes: Used with « avoir » in the past (passé composé): « j’ai eu un… / il a eu un… ». In questions with « déjà », it often means “have you ever had…?”. The noun after « un » tells what was had or experienced (e.g., « un animal », « un malaise »).
target_language_example: J’ai eu un problème avec ma carte.
native_language_example: I had a problem with my card.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « avoir » (to have) to talk about an accident in the past: « j’ai eu un accident » (I had an accident), « tu as eu un accident ? » (Did you have an accident?). It can refer to a car accident or another kind of accident; add « grave » to mean a serious accident (« un accident grave »).
target_language_example: Ça va ? J’ai appris que tu as eu un accident.
native_language_example: Are you okay? I heard you had an accident.

eu un accident de la route

target_language_multi_word_term: eu un accident de la route
additional_notes: This is the past participle phrase used with an auxiliary, most often in the passé composé: « J’ai eu un accident de la route » (I had / was in a traffic accident). On its own, « eu » is incomplete—you normally need « avoir » (e.g., « j’ai » / « il a » / « elle a »). You can also say « avoir un accident » (to have an accident) or « avoir un accident de voiture » (a car accident).
target_language_example: J’ai eu un accident de la route hier, mais je vais bien.
native_language_example: I had a traffic accident yesterday, but I’m fine.

additional_notes: This is the past participle phrase used with the verb "avoir" in the passé composé: "avoir un accident de voiture" = "to have a car accident." It agrees with the subject only through the auxiliary (j'ai eu, elle a eu, nous avons eu, etc.). You can also say "un accident" or "un accident de la route" depending on context.
target_language_example: Heureusement, elle a eu un accident de voiture sans gravité.
native_language_example: Luckily, she had a minor car accident.

additional_notes: You usually see this as part of a larger phrase with the verb *avoir*: **il y a eu un tremblement de terre** (“there was an earthquake”) or **on a eu un tremblement de terre** (“we had an earthquake”). By itself, **eu** is the past participle of *avoir* (“had”).
target_language_example: Il y a eu un tremblement de terre cette nuit.
native_language_example: There was an earthquake last night.

additional_notes: Used in the passé composé: *avoir* → *j’ai / tu as / il a…* + *eu* + a noun with an article. *Eu* does not change for gender/number here (it stays *eu*). You’ll see it before many feminine nouns: *eu une idée, eu une amende, eu une relation*, etc.
target_language_example: J’ai eu une bonne nouvelle ce matin.
native_language_example: I had some good news this morning.

additional_notes: A formal expression (often in writing or administrative/legal contexts) meaning “taking into account.” It’s usually followed by a noun phrase: « eu égard à votre situation », « eu égard aux circonstances ».
target_language_example: Eu égard à la météo, la réunion est annulée.
native_language_example: Given the weather, the meeting is canceled.

additional_notes: Stressed pronoun (masculine plural) used for emphasis, often after the verb: « Ils l’ont fait eux-mêmes » = “They did it themselves.” With « par eux-mêmes », it means “by themselves / on their own” (without help). In « laissés à eux-mêmes », it means “left to themselves” (left alone to manage).
target_language_example: Ils veulent résoudre le problème eux-mêmes.
native_language_example: They want to solve the problem themselves.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a woman you were married to in the past. Often used with a possessive: « mon/ton/son/votre ex-femme ». The hyphen is common in French (ex-femme), though you may also see « ex femme ».
target_language_example: Il ne parle jamais de son ex-femme.
native_language_example: He never talks about his ex-wife.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a man you were married to in the past (after divorce or separation). Often used with a possessive: mon/ton/son ex-mari. The prefix « ex- » can also be used with other relationships (ex-femme, ex-petit ami).
target_language_example: Je vais déposer les enfants chez mon ex-mari ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m going to drop off the kids at my ex-husband’s this weekend.

additional_notes: Used right before a relative pronoun like **que** or **qui**: **exactement ce que…** = “exactly what…”, **exactement ce qui…** = “exactly what… (as the subject)”. Common for emphasizing that something is the precise thing needed or the precise action to do: **J’ai exactement ce qu’il faut** (“I have exactly what’s needed”), **Faites exactement ce que je vous dis** (“Do exactly what I tell you”).
target_language_example: C’est exactement ce que je cherchais.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I was looking for.

additional_notes: Introduces a relative clause to specify something precisely: exactement ce qu'il + verb/expression (e.g., exactement ce qu'il faut, exactement ce qu'il me fallait). "Il" can mean “he” or “it” depending on context; here it’s often an impersonal "il" (as in "il faut").
target_language_example: C’est exactement ce qu'il faut pour réussir.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what it takes to succeed.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is precise or matches perfectly. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): « exactement ce que je dois faire », « exactement ce que je pensais ». It can also be used as a short reply/fragment to mean “exactly what I thought/wanted.”
target_language_example: Je vais te dire exactement ce que tu dois faire.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you exactly what you have to do.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that specifies precisely what you ("je") think/want/need/mean, etc. It is usually followed by a verb: « exactement ce que je veux », « exactement ce que je pensais ». « ce que » means “what/that which.”
target_language_example: C’est exactement ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I wanted to say.

additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase fragment: it must be followed by a verb (and often an object), e.g. « exactement ce que tu veux » (exactly what you want), « exactement ce que tu as dit » (exactly what you said). « ce que » means “what/that which,” and « tu » is the informal singular “you.”
target_language_example: C’est exactement ce que tu voulais.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what you wanted.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or state the precise details of an event. Often follows verbs like "savoir" (to know) or "dire" (to say/tell): "Je sais exactement ce qui s'est passé" / "Dis-moi exactement ce qui s'est passé." Here, "ce qui" means “what (that)” and "s'est passé" is the past tense of "se passer" (“to happen,” “to take place”).
target_language_example: Explique-moi exactement ce qui s'est passé hier soir.
native_language_example: Explain to me exactly what happened last night.

additional_notes: A formal phrase for a health examination done by a doctor. Often used with verbs like "passer" (to have/take an exam) or in questions like "À quand remonte... ?" meaning "How long ago was... ?" / "When was the last time... ?".
target_language_example: J'ai un examen médical demain matin.
native_language_example: I have a medical check-up tomorrow morning.

meaning: “Excuse me” / “sorry” (to apologize or get someone’s attention).
additional_notes: Used with people you address as tu (friends, family, kids, someone your age in an informal setting). Often followed by de + infinitive: « Excuse-moi de te déranger » (“Sorry to bother you”). You can also say it alone to interrupt politely (« Excuse-moi, … ») or to ask someone to wait (« Excuse-moi un instant / un moment »). For formal you, use « excusez-moi ».
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, je peux te poser une question ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you a question?

meaning: “Excuse me” / “sorry” (polite; to get someone’s attention or apologize).
additional_notes: Very common polite phrase. Use it to address a stranger, ask a question, get past someone, or briefly interrupt: “Excusez-moi, …”. You can also add time words like “un instant / une seconde”. It’s the formal/plural form (vous); with friends you often hear “excuse-moi”.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je cherche la gare.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’m looking for the train station.

meaning: "Excuse me, I…" (polite way to start an apology or make a request).
additional_notes: Used to politely get someone’s attention before explaining what you need or why you’re interrupting/leaving. "Excusez-moi" is the formal/polite form (to a stranger, in public, or in customer service). It’s often followed by "je + verb" (je dois…, je suis…, je vous ai…).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je dois y aller.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have to go.

meaning: “Excuse me, I have to…” (polite way to interrupt or leave).
additional_notes: Used to politely get someone’s attention and explain you need to do something or go somewhere. Very common before an infinitive verb: je dois y aller (I have to go), je dois vous laisser (I have to leave you), je dois descendre (I have to get off). Can also be used to move past people: je dois circuler (I need to get through).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je dois partir maintenant.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have to leave now.

meaning: “Excuse me, could you…?” (polite way to ask someone to do something).
additional_notes: Very formal/polite: use it to get someone’s attention and make a request (asking for directions, help, information, or asking someone to repeat). "Excusez-moi" is the polite “excuse me,” and "pourriez-vous" is the conditional form of "pouvoir" (“could you”). Often followed by an infinitive (pourriez-vous répéter) or by "me dire" / "me montrer".
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, pourriez-vous m’aider à trouver cette adresse ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you help me find this address?

additional_notes: Used in driving/police contexts: "être en excès de vitesse" (to be speeding) and "un excès de vitesse" (a speeding offense). Often associated with "une amende" (a fine) or "un radar" (speed camera).
target_language_example: Il a eu une amende pour excès de vitesse.
native_language_example: He got a fine for speeding.

additional_notes: This is the inverted (more formal) question form of « il existe » (“there is/there exists”). It’s used to ask whether something exists or is available: « Existe-t-il une solution ? » = “Is there a solution?” You’ll often see it followed by a noun phrase (un moyen, une option, une version…).
target_language_example: Existe-t-il une autre façon de faire ?
native_language_example: Is there another way to do it?

meaning: Explain to me / tell me (so I understand).
additional_notes: "Explique-moi" is the imperative (command/request) form of "expliquer" (to explain) + "moi" (to me). It’s used to ask someone for an explanation; tone depends on context and can range from polite to impatient. With a noun: "Explique-moi la règle" (Explain the rule to me). With a question word: "Explique-moi pourquoi..." (Explain to me why...).
target_language_example: Explique-moi comment ça marche, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Explain to me how it works, please.

additional_notes: A noun for a being from another planet. The word itself doesn’t change for masculine/feminine (un/une extra-terrestre); only the article changes. Common with verbs like ressembler à (to look like) and on dirait (you’d think / it looks like).
target_language_example: Il est déguisé en extra-terrestre pour la fête.
native_language_example: He’s dressed up as an alien for the party.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun. In a physical/spatial sense it means 'facing' or 'across from' (Face à la cheminée. / Face à moi.). In a figurative sense it means 'faced with' or 'up against' a situation, problem, or opponent (face à la vie; face à des rats). Often interchangeable with "en face de" for the purely physical meaning.
target_language_example: Face à ce problème, on doit rester calme.
native_language_example: Faced with this problem, we have to stay calm.

additional_notes: Used as a noun phrase in expressions like « la face cachée de X » (the side you can’t see). With cards or objects, « (mettre/poser) … face cachée » means placing it with the front/visible side against the surface (face down). You may also see it set off by commas: « la carte, face cachée, sur la table ».
target_language_example: Il a retourné la feuille pour montrer sa face cachée.
native_language_example: He flipped the sheet over to show its hidden side.

additional_notes: Used to say two people are physically facing each other or that you want to speak directly in person rather than by phone/message. Can be used as an adverb phrase (parler face à face) or as a noun phrase (un face-à-face = a face-to-face meeting/confrontation).
target_language_example: Je préfère en discuter face à face.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk about it face to face.

additional_notes: Used to describe that something is easy to do: facile à + infinitive (facile à utiliser, facile à comprendre). It also appears in the set phrase “Facile à dire” (“Easier said than done”). Feminine: facile; plural: faciles.
target_language_example: Ce logiciel est facile à apprendre.
native_language_example: This software is easy to learn.

meaning: to take (someone/something) out; to make (someone/something) go out.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object: faire sortir quelqu’un (to make someone go out / to take someone out), faire sortir quelque chose (to take something out / bring something out). Often followed by de + place: faire sortir le chat de la chambre (get the cat out of the room). In the imperative: Fais sortir les poubelles ! (Take the trash out!).
target_language_example: Peux-tu faire sortir le chien ?
native_language_example: Can you take the dog out?

meaning: an announcement card/notice (birth, wedding, death, etc.).
additional_notes: Used mainly as a noun: un faire-part. Often refers to a printed card sent to family/friends to announce a birth (faire-part de naissance), a wedding (faire-part de mariage), or a death/funeral (faire-part de décès). It can also mean a formal notice/announcement in general.
target_language_example: Nous avons envoyé un faire-part de naissance à toute la famille.
native_language_example: We sent a birth announcement to the whole family.

meaning: to get by; to manage; to make do (to keep things going).
additional_notes: Used mostly in everyday conversation to say you’re coping or managing despite difficulties. Often heard in the set reply to « Ça va ? »: « On fait aller. » (meaning “We’re getting by.”). It’s idiomatic rather than literal—literally it’s “to make (something) go,” but the usual sense is “to keep things going / make do.”
target_language_example: En ce moment, c’est un peu compliqué, mais on va faire aller.
native_language_example: Right now it’s a bit complicated, but we’re going to get by.

meaning: to allude to; to refer to indirectly.
additional_notes: Usually used with « à »: « faire allusion à quelque chose / à quelqu’un ». It means mentioning something indirectly (hinting) rather than stating it openly.
target_language_example: Il a fait allusion à notre conversation d'hier, mais il n'a rien dit clairement.
native_language_example: He alluded to our conversation yesterday, but he didn’t say anything clearly.

meaning: to call on; to seek/use help (usually: faire appel à).
additional_notes: Often used with **à** + a person/thing: **faire appel à quelqu’un** = to call on someone for help/expertise; **faire appel à une entreprise/un service** = to use their services. It can also mean **to appeal** (e.g., in a legal sense: **faire appel d’une décision** = to appeal a decision).
target_language_example: On va faire appel à un plombier.
native_language_example: We’re going to call a plumber.

meaning: to be careful; to pay attention (watch out).
additional_notes: Often used as a warning or reminder: Faire attention ! = “Be careful!” You can add what to watch for with à: faire attention à + noun (“watch out for…”), or with an infinitive: faire attention en descendant (“be careful when getting off”). Common in safety/traffic contexts.
target_language_example: Les conducteurs doivent faire attention aux enfants qui traversent la route.
native_language_example: Drivers must watch out for children crossing the road.

meaning: to pay attention to; to be careful about.
additional_notes: Commonly used to warn or advise someone. Pattern: faire attention à + noun/pronoun (Il faut faire attention à la marche. / Faire attention à toi.) or faire attention à + infinitive (faire attention à ne pas… = be careful not to…). Frequently used with devoir/il faut and in the imperative (Fais attention ! / Faites attention !).
target_language_example: Il nous faut faire attention à nos dépenses.
native_language_example: We need to watch our spending.

meaning: to do one’s best; to do as best as possible.
additional_notes: Used when you want to say you’ll try to achieve the best possible result given the situation, limits, or available time/resources. Common in reassuring phrases like « Je vais faire au mieux » or « On fera au mieux » (= We’ll do our best).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé pour le retard, je vais faire au mieux pour arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: Sorry about the delay—I’ll do my best to arrive on time.

meaning: to make do (with); to cope with; to manage with.
additional_notes: Used when you have to accept a situation or use what you have, even if it’s not ideal: « Il faut faire avec » = “we have to deal with it / make do.” It can also be a literal question about what you will do with something: « Qu’est-ce que je vais faire avec ça ? » = “What am I going to do with that?”
target_language_example: On n’a pas de voiture, alors on va faire avec les transports en commun.
native_language_example: We don’t have a car, so we’ll make do with public transportation.

additional_notes: Used mainly in the impersonal weather expression « Il va faire beau » / « Il va faire beau demain » (future) or « Il faisait beau » (past) to mean the weather is/was pleasant/sunny. The base term is « faire beau » (used with « il » as the subject). You can contrast it with « faire mauvais » / « Il fait mauvais » (bad weather).
target_language_example: Demain, il va faire beau, alors on ira se promener.
native_language_example: Tomorrow it’s going to be nice out, so we’ll go for a walk.

meaning: to look good; to be appropriate (socially); to do something nicely.
additional_notes: Used when something gives a good impression (“Ça fait bien” = “It looks good / It’s proper / It’s the right thing to do socially”). It can also mean doing something in a neat/satisfactory way (“faire bien son travail” = “do your job well”). Often appears as “ça fait bien” or “ça ne fait pas bien” (it doesn’t look good / it’s not proper).
target_language_example: Pour l'entretien, ça va faire bien de porter une chemise.
native_language_example: For the interview, it will look good to wear a shirt.

meaning: to be right to (do); to do well to (do).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: « faire bien de + infinitif ». It means it’s a good idea / the right choice to do something, often as advice or a mild reproach. Very common in the past: « Tu as bien fait de… » (= You did the right thing to…). Note that the verb is conjugated, but the multi-word term is « faire bien de » (infinitive form).
target_language_example: Tu vas faire bien de prendre un parapluie.
native_language_example: You’re going to do well to take an umbrella.

additional_notes: Used mainly in the impersonal weather expression **Il fait bon.** It means the weather/temperature feels pleasant (often mild or warm), not “to do good.” You can also say **Il fait bon dehors/ici** (“It’s nice out/in here”).
target_language_example: Quand il commence à faire bon, on peut marcher au parc.
native_language_example: When it starts to be nice out, we can walk in the park.

meaning: to have a good trip (to travel safely and pleasantly).
additional_notes: Usually used after verbs like souhaiter/espérer: « Je te souhaite de faire bon voyage. » More commonly, people simply say « Bon voyage ! » as a send-off before someone leaves.
target_language_example: Je te souhaite de faire bon voyage et de profiter de tes vacances.
native_language_example: I hope you have a good trip and enjoy your vacation.

additional_notes: Used when you want to be seen positively (at a first meeting, a job interview, meeting someone’s parents, etc.). Often said as advice: « Essaie de faire bonne impression » (“Try to make a good impression”).
target_language_example: À l’entretien, je vais faire bonne impression.
native_language_example: At the interview, I'm going to make a good impression.

additional_notes: Common with young children or in casual, family contexts; it’s less formal than "aller aux toilettes" or "aller à la selle". Often used with "Je dois faire caca" (I need to poop) or "Il/Elle a fait caca" (He/She pooped).
target_language_example: Je dois faire caca, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: I need to poop; I’ll be right back.

meaning: to give (something) as a gift; to give (something) to someone for free.
additional_notes: Usually used as **faire cadeau de + quelque chose + à + quelqu’un** or with an indirect object pronoun: **Je te fais cadeau de…** = “I’m giving you … as a gift / you can have … for free.” It can also be used figuratively to mean “to waive” or “to let someone off” (e.g., *Je vous fais cadeau des frais* = “I’ll waive the fees”).
target_language_example: Je vais te faire cadeau de ce livre.
native_language_example: I’m going to give you this book as a gift.

meaning: to have a career; to become successful in a profession/field.
additional_notes: Used with a job or field, often with "comme" (as) or "dans" (in): "faire carrière comme chanteuse", "faire carrière dans la publicité". It can mean building a long-term professional path, and often implies achieving success or recognition.
target_language_example: Elle veut faire carrière dans le journalisme.
native_language_example: She wants to have a career in journalism.

additional_notes: A compositional pattern meaning to do the thing named in the following clause: faire ce que tu veux, faire ce qu'on dit, faire ce qu'on demande. Depending on context, English may also use 'do whatever'.
target_language_example: Je vais faire ce que tu proposes.
native_language_example: I'm going to do what you suggest.

meaning: "to do what I…" (start of a sentence).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase that normally needs a verb right after it, most often: "faire ce que je veux" (do what I want), "faire ce que je peux" (do what I can), "faire ce que je dois" (do what I must), "faire ce que je pense" (do what I think). It’s used to introduce what you (je) want/can/must/think you should do.
target_language_example: Je vais faire ce que je peux.
native_language_example: I’m going to do what I can.

additional_notes: Used to express freedom (or frustration about not having freedom) to choose your own actions. Often appears after verbs like laisser/empêcher (e.g., "ne pas me laisser faire ce que je veux" = "not let me do what I want"). You can swap the subject pronoun: faire ce que tu veux (do what you want), faire ce qu’il/elle veut (do what he/she wants), etc.
target_language_example: Ce week-end, je vais faire ce que je veux.
native_language_example: This weekend, I'm going to do what I want.

additional_notes: Used to give permission or express that someone is free to choose their actions. Often follows verbs like peux/peux, pourrais, pourras (“you can / you could / you will be able to”). In “Tu peux me faire ce que tu veux”, it means “You can do whatever you want to me” (can sound intense depending on context).
target_language_example: Ce soir, tu peux faire ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: Tonight, you can do whatever you want.

meaning: to do whatever you want (to do).
additional_notes: Uses the formal/plural "vous". Often follows verbs like "pouvoir" (can) or "avoir le droit de" (have the right to) to give permission or freedom of choice. "Ce que" here means "what/that which" (the thing that you want).
target_language_example: Ici, vous pouvez faire ce que vous voulez.
native_language_example: Here, you can do whatever you want.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase used to refer to a specific action (“this”). It often follows another verb (e.g., devoir, pouvoir, laisser, forcer). In the causative construction, it can appear as “faire + [person] + faire ceci” = “to make/have someone do this.”
target_language_example: Tu peux faire ceci maintenant ?
native_language_example: Can you do this now?

additional_notes: Means 'to do that.' It is a straightforward combination of faire + cela. Cela is more formal or written than ça, so in everyday speech, faire ça is more common.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas faire cela encore une fois.
native_language_example: I don't want to do that again.

additional_notes: Commonly used in the idiomatic sense “to blackmail,” often with a person as the object: « Il/Elle me fait chanter. » You may also hear the literal meaning “to make (someone/something) sing” (e.g., a child or an instrument), but the “blackmail” meaning is very frequent in news/crime contexts.
target_language_example: Il a essayé de me faire chanter avec ces photos.
native_language_example: He tried to blackmail me with those photos.

additional_notes: Used with the impersonal subject "il" to talk about temperature: "Il fait chaud" = "It’s hot." You can change tense ("il faisait chaud", "il va faire chaud", "il a fait chaud") or add a place ("Il doit faire chaud à Paris"). Not used for people; for a person say "J’ai chaud" (I’m hot).
target_language_example: Il va faire chaud demain.
native_language_example: It’s going to be hot tomorrow.

meaning: to piss (someone) off; to annoy (someone) a lot.
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Often used as an angry command: « Arrête de (me) faire chier ! » = “Stop pissing (me) off!” Can also mean “to be a pain / to hassle” someone: « Ils viennent nous faire chier » = “They’re coming to mess with us / give us trouble.”
target_language_example: Tu peux arrêter de me faire chier, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you stop pissing me off, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe behaving as though something were true, often even when it isn’t. Usually followed by a clause introduced by "comme si" (e.g., "comme si j'étais…"); after "comme si," French often uses the imperfect (imparfait) to express an unreal or hypothetical situation: "Il fait comme s'il ne savait pas."
target_language_example: Elle va faire comme si tout allait bien.
native_language_example: She’s going to pretend that everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object: faire confiance à + person/thing (Je fais confiance à Marie. / Je fais confiance à cette équipe.). Often used with pouvoir (can) or devoir (must): Je peux/je dois te/vous faire confiance. You can also say se faire confiance (reflexive) to mean “to trust each other” or “to trust oneself,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Comment puis-je vous faire confiance�?
native_language_example: How can I trust you?

meaning: to trust (someone); to have confidence in (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you trust a person or can rely on them. It is followed by a person or pronoun with « à »: faire confiance à Tom / faire confiance à quelqu’un / faire confiance à lui/elle. Common negative: ne faire confiance à personne = to trust nobody.
target_language_example: Peut-on faire confiance à Tom pour faire ça ?
native_language_example: Can we trust Tom to do that?

meaning: to meet someone (for the first time); to get acquainted.
additional_notes: Used when you are introduced and start getting to know someone. Often followed by "avec" + a person: "faire connaissance avec toi". Very common with "venir de" to mean "to have just met": "Nous venons de faire connaissance."
target_language_example: Enchanté ! On va faire connaissance autour d’un café ?
native_language_example: Nice to meet you! Shall we get acquainted over a coffee?

meaning: to make (someone/something) known; to introduce oneself; to get known.
additional_notes: Often used reflexively: « se faire connaître » = to make yourself known (e.g., to identify yourself, introduce yourself, or become well-known). It can also be used with an object: « faire connaître X » = to make X known / to let people know about X.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous vous faire connaître, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you identify yourself, please?

meaning: to get a haircut; to have your hair cut.
additional_notes: Uses the pattern (se) faire + infinitive to mean “have something done (by someone else).” Most often you’ll hear it reflexively: « Je dois me faire couper les cheveux » (“I need to get my hair cut”). You can add details like style/length: « courts », « juste les pointes », etc.
target_language_example: Je vais me faire couper les cheveux demain matin.
native_language_example: I’m going to get my hair cut tomorrow morning.

meaning: to do something else; what else can/should I do?
additional_notes: Mostly used in questions (often with « que », « qu’est-ce que », « qu’aurais-je… ») to ask about an alternative: « Que faire d’autre ? » = “What else can I do?” Here « d’autre » means “else/other (thing)”. Very close in meaning to « faire autre chose » (often more common). Note: it’s usually « faire *d’autre chose* » or « faire *quelque chose d’autre* » in many contexts; « faire d’autre » is most natural in these question patterns where the “thing” is implicit.
target_language_example: On n’a plus d’argent pour le taxi : qu’est-ce qu’on pourrait faire d’autre ?
native_language_example: We don’t have any more money for the taxi: what else could we do?

meaning: to make someone sad; to upset someone.
additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur): « Ça me fait de la peine » = “That makes me sad / I feel sorry about that.” It can also express sympathy or regret about a situation: « Ça fait de la peine de voir ça ».
target_language_example: Ça me fait de la peine de te voir comme ça.
native_language_example: It makes me sad to see you like that.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as « faire du mal à quelqu’un » (“to hurt someone”), but « faire de mal » appears in negative or general constructions (e.g., « ne pas faire de mal », « ne peut pas faire de mal »). Fixed reassuring phrase: « Ça ne peut pas faire de mal » = “It can’t hurt” / “It won’t do any harm (to try).”
target_language_example: Je ne vais pas vous faire de mal.
native_language_example: I’m not going to hurt you.

additional_notes: Used to promise effort even if success isn’t guaranteed. Often follows verbs like "aller" (Nous allons...) or "devoir" (Nous devons...), and can be followed by "pour" + infinitive to say what you’re trying to achieve ("faire de notre mieux pour..." = "do our best to..."). You can change the possessive to match the subject: "faire de mon mieux" (my best), "de ton mieux" (your best), "de son mieux" (his/her best), "de leur mieux" (their best).
target_language_example: On va faire de notre mieux pour arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: We’re going to do our best to arrive on time.

meaning: to do one’s best; to try as hard as one can.
additional_notes: Used to express that someone is making their best effort, even if the outcome isn’t perfect. The possessive changes with the subject: faire de mon mieux (my best), de ton mieux (your best, informal), de son mieux (his/her/one’s best), de notre mieux (our best), de votre mieux (your best—formal or plural), de leur mieux (their best). Common in reassurance or explanations: Il/Elle fait de son mieux. / Je fais de mon mieux.
target_language_example: Il fait de son mieux pour terminer le projet à temps.
native_language_example: He’s doing his best to finish the project on time.

meaning: To turn around; to make a U-turn; to go back.
additional_notes: Used when changing direction to return the way you came (walking, driving, etc.). Very common in directions: « Tu peux faire demi-tour » (you can turn around/U-turn). Can also be figurative: « faire demi-tour » = to change your mind and go back on a decision.
target_language_example: On s'est trompés de route : il faut faire demi-tour.
native_language_example: We took the wrong road: we need to turn around.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk about doing/making things in general: faire des tests (do tests), faire des efforts (make efforts), faire des fautes (make mistakes), faire des compromis (make compromises). With an adjective before the noun, you often use de instead of des: faire de grands efforts. In the negative, des often becomes de: ne pas faire de fautes.
