additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone traveled a long distance or made a big effort, often with surprise, frustration, or to highlight the importance of the goal. It’s commonly used with the passé composé: « J’ai fait tout ce chemin pour… » (I came all this way to…).
target_language_example: J’ai fait tout ce chemin pour te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I came all this way to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause after a singular subject (il/elle/on/ça + fait): "Il fait tout ce que tu dis." For other subjects, the verb changes: "Je fais tout ce que…", "Ils font tout ce que…". Often followed by a verb (tu dis, tu veux, il peut, etc.).
target_language_example: Il fait tout ce que tu lui demandes.
native_language_example: He does everything you ask him to do.

additional_notes: Used with the verb faire to talk about doing or making something: "faire un gâteau" (make a cake), "faire un voyage" (take/make a trip). "fait" can be the past participle in the passé composé (j’ai fait un…) or the 3rd-person singular present (il/elle fait un…).
target_language_example: J’ai fait un choix difficile.
native_language_example: I made a difficult choice.

additional_notes: From **faire un rêve** (“to have a dream”). Very common in the **past tense**: **J’ai fait un rêve** = “I had a dream.” You can also use the verb **rêver**: **J’ai rêvé** = “I dreamed.” Literally it’s “made a dream,” but the natural meaning is “had a dream.”
target_language_example: J’ai fait un rêve étrange cette nuit.
native_language_example: I had a strange dream last night.

additional_notes: This is the present tense form of *faire* with *une* (he/she/it: *il/elle fait une…*). It’s commonly used in medical/health expressions: *faire une allergie* (to have/get an allergic reaction), *faire une overdose* (to overdose), *faire une crise* (to have an attack/episode), etc. It does not translate literally as “makes a.”
target_language_example: Elle fait une réaction allergique aux noix.
native_language_example: She has an allergic reaction to nuts.

meaning: '(has) done a good deed' (done something kind/helpful).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "faire" + "une bonne action" to say someone did something morally good or helpful. It’s commonly used in the passé composé: "a fait une bonne action" (he/she did a good deed), "j’ai fait une bonne action" (I did a good deed).
target_language_example: J’ai fait une bonne action en aidant ma voisine à porter ses courses.
native_language_example: I did a good deed by helping my neighbor carry her groceries.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "faire une erreur" (to make a mistake). It changes with subject and tense: je fais / j’ai fait, il fait / il a fait, vous faites / vous avez fait. Often used to point out an error: "Je pense que vous avez fait une erreur."
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai fait une erreur dans le numéro de téléphone.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake in the phone number.

additional_notes: From **faire** (to do/make). **fait** is the 3rd person singular present: *il/elle/on fait ça* = “he/she/one does that.” Used to refer to an action that’s understood from context. You can change the subject: *je fais ça* (I do that), *tu fais ça* (you do that), etc.
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce qu'il fait ça ?
native_language_example: Why does he do that?

additional_notes: Imperative (command) with **vous** form of *faire* (“to do/make”) + the direct object pronoun **le** (“it/him”), joined with a hyphen. Often means **“do it”** (e.g., *Faites-le sans attendre.*). With an infinitive, it can be the causative *faire*: **faites-le + infinitive** = “make him/it + verb” (e.g., *Faites-le parler* = “Make him talk”).
target_language_example: Si tu es prêt, faites-le maintenant.
native_language_example: If you’re ready, do it now.

additional_notes: Imperative of **faire** for **vous** (“faites…”) + the direct object pronoun **les** (“them”). Very often used in the causative pattern **faites-les + infinitive**: *Faites-les entrer* (“Have them come in”), *Faites-les taire* (“Make them be quiet”). The pronoun **les** comes before the infinitive it affects.
target_language_example: Faites-les attendre ici, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Have them wait here, please.

additional_notes: From the polite command form of *faire* (“faites”) + *moi* (“me”). It’s often followed by an infinitive or set phrases: **faites-moi connaître** = “let me know”, **faites-moi part de…** = “tell me / share… with me”, **faites-moi voir** = “show me”. You can also add **s’il vous plaît** for extra politeness.
target_language_example: Faites-moi savoir quand vous arrivez, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please let me know when you arrive.

additional_notes: This is the verb "faire" (vous form: "faites") with inversion "-vous" to form a question in formal/polite French: "Faites-vous… ?" = "Do you…?" It can also appear with pronouns: "Comment le faites-vous ?" (How do you do it?) and with a reflexive verb: "Où vous faites-vous coiffer ?" (Where do you get your hair done?). In a command, "Faites-vous plaisir" means "Treat yourself" (literally "Make yourself pleasure").
target_language_example: Que faites-vous ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight?

additional_notes: Imperative (vous form) of « faire attention ». Often followed by « à » + noun or clause: « Faites attention à la voiture » (Watch out for the car) or « Faites attention à ce que vous dites » (Be careful what you say). Used both as a warning and as advice to be mindful.
target_language_example: Faites attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: Be careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Polite/plural command (vous form) used to warn someone to avoid a bad outcome. Pattern: « Faites attention à ne pas + infinitive » (e.g., « … ne pas tomber »). For one person you know well: « Fais attention à ne pas … ».
target_language_example: Faites attention à ne pas oublier votre passeport.
native_language_example: Be careful not to forget your passport.

additional_notes: Imperative using "vous" (polite singular or plural). It can sound genuinely permissive ("you’re free to choose") or, depending on tone/context, dismissive/annoyed ("fine, do whatever you want"). Often used with objects too: "Faites ce que vous voulez de X" = "Do whatever you want with X" (including people, in a figurative sense).
target_language_example: Si ça te convient, tant mieux; sinon, faites ce que vous voulez.
native_language_example: If it suits you, great; if not, do what you want.

additional_notes: A polite, welcoming phrase said to guests to tell them to feel comfortable and act naturally. Grammatically it’s the imperative of "faire" + "comme" + "chez vous" (using "vous" either for several people or for one person politely).
target_language_example: Entrez, posez vos affaires et faites comme chez vous.
native_language_example: Come in, put your things down, and make yourself at home.

additional_notes: Colloquial/informal negative command meaning "(you) don’t…" or "don’t do…". It’s a shortened form of the more standard/polite **ne faites pas** (often heard as **faites pas** in speech). Used before a verb or phrase: **Faites pas attention** = "Don’t pay attention," **Faites pas ça** = "Don’t do that."
target_language_example: Faites pas de bruit, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t make noise, please.

additional_notes: Fixed expression said by a dealer or announcer in gambling contexts (casino, roulette, etc.) to invite players to bet. It uses the formal/plural command form (faites = “do/make” to you all / to a customer). Not used much outside betting contexts.
target_language_example: Au casino, le croupier a dit : « Faites vos jeux ! »
native_language_example: At the casino, the dealer said, “Place your bets!”

meaning: 'made for each other' (a perfect match, especially as a couple).
additional_notes: Used with **être**: *Ils/Nous/On/Vous êtes faits l'un pour l'autre.* It agrees with the people involved: **faits** (masc. plural or mixed group), **faites** (fem. plural). You can also change **l'un** to **l'une** if the person referred to is female: *Ils sont faits l'un pour l'autre* / *Elles sont faites l'une pour l'autre*. Common in romantic contexts, but can also describe a great pairing in general.
target_language_example: Je pense que vous êtes faits l'un pour l'autre.
native_language_example: I think you’re made for each other.

meaning: to have to; to be necessary that
additional_notes: Usually appears in conjugated forms such as il faut que or il va falloir que, followed by a subjunctive verb. It expresses necessity, obligation, or something that needs to be done.
target_language_example: Il va falloir que tu finisses tes devoirs.
native_language_example: You’re going to have to finish your homework.

meaning: "will it be necessary" / "will we need to" (question form).
additional_notes: Future tense of the impersonal verb « falloir » (“to be necessary”), used in questions with inversion (« -t-il » = “will it”). Often appears with « combien » (“how many/how much”) or « combien de temps » (“how long”) to ask what will be needed or how long something will take. You can translate it as “will it be necessary…?” or more naturally “will we need to…?”.
target_language_example: Faudra-t-il réserver à l’avance ?
native_language_example: Will we need to book in advance?

additional_notes: Used with the verb faire: faire une fausse couche = to have a miscarriage. It’s a sensitive medical/personal topic; in everyday conversation, people may also say "perdre le bébé" (lose the baby) or use medical terms like "interruption spontanée de grossesse".
target_language_example: Elle a fait une fausse couche l’année dernière.
native_language_example: She had a miscarriage last year.

additional_notes: From the verb "falloir" ("il faut" = "it’s necessary"). Very often used as "il faut faire + infinitive" (e.g., "Il faut faire vite" = "We/you have to do it quickly"). It can also change with an indirect object pronoun: "Il me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faut faire..." = "I/you/he/we/you/they need to do...". Dropping "il" ("Faut faire...") is common in casual spoken French.
target_language_example: Faut faire attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when crossing the street.

meaning: “(We/you) have to do something”; “something must be done.”
additional_notes: Usually you’ll see this as **il faut faire quelque chose** (impersonal **il faut** = “it’s necessary / you have to”). In everyday speech, **il** is often dropped: **Faut faire quelque chose !** It expresses obligation/necessity and is often used to urge action.
target_language_example: Faut faire quelque chose, ça ne peut pas continuer comme ça.
native_language_example: We have to do something; it can’t go on like this.

additional_notes: From the idea of *il faut le faire* (“you have to do it”), but in everyday speech it’s often an exclamation reacting to something surprising, bold, or outrageous. Frequently used with **Il**: **Il faut le faire !** Tone can be admiring or (more often) critical/ironic.
target_language_example: Il a encore oublié mon anniversaire… faut le faire !
native_language_example: He forgot my birthday again… you’ve got some nerve!

meaning: We have to go / We’ve got to get going.
additional_notes: Short for "(il) faut y aller". "Il faut" expresses necessity (“it’s necessary / you have to”), and "y aller" means “to go there / to go (to it).” Very common when it’s time to leave or when you must go do something. "Y" can refer to a place (there) or to an activity you need to go to (e.g., an appointment).
target_language_example: Bon, faut y aller, sinon on va être en retard.
native_language_example: Alright, we’ve got to go, otherwise we’ll be late.

additional_notes: Usually appears as **il faut être + adjective/noun** (“you/one must be…”) or with an object pronoun: **il me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faut être…** (“I/you/he… must be…”). Often expresses necessity or advice: *Il faut être prudent* = “You have to be careful.”
target_language_example: Pour ce travail, il faut être patient.
native_language_example: For this job, you need to be patient.

meaning: need to be more (…); have to be more (…).
additional_notes: Used in the common structure « Il me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faut + infinitive » to express necessity: « Il te faut être davantage patient » = “You need to be more patient.” « davantage » means “more” (often a bit more formal than « plus »). Adjectives agree with the person: « organisé/organisée », « patient/patiente », etc. Note: « davantage » looks like “advantage” but it doesn’t mean that.
target_language_example: Il te faut être davantage prudent si tu conduis la nuit.
native_language_example: You need to be more careful if you drive at night.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the structure « Il faut être plus + adjective/adverb » to say someone should improve or change their behavior: « Il faut être plus patient » (You need to be more patient). Often heard in advice, instructions, or criticism. On its own, « faut être plus » sounds incomplete—you normally add what you should be more of.
target_language_example: Il faut être plus prudent sur la route.
native_language_example: You need to be more careful on the road.

additional_notes: This is the question form (inversion) of "il faut" ("it’s necessary / we need"). It’s often used in real questions (e.g., asking what’s needed) and also in rhetorical questions expressing doubt or surprise ("Faut-il…?" = "Do we really have to…?").
target_language_example: Faut-il réserver à l’avance ?
native_language_example: Do we need to book in advance?

meaning: “(Well,) you have to / it has to be done” (resigned necessity).
additional_notes: Short for spoken/written informal "(il) faut bien". Used to express that there’s no real choice: something is necessary even if you don’t like it. Often followed by "que" + subjunctive: "Faut bien que je parte" (“I have to go”). Can also stand alone: "Faut bien." / "Oui, il faut bien." (“Well, you have to.”).
target_language_example: Faut bien que j’y aille, demain je travaille tôt.
native_language_example: I have to go—tomorrow I start work early.

meaning: “we have to / we need to” (short for « il faut qu’on »).
additional_notes: Very common spoken shortcut to express necessity/obligation. It’s typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive: « faut qu'on parte », « faut qu'on puisse… ». In everyday French, « on » often means “we”. In more careful speech or writing, you’ll often see « il faut qu'on… ».
target_language_example: Faut qu'on file maintenant.
native_language_example: We have to head off now.

additional_notes: Very common spoken phrase, short for « Il faut qu’on parle » (from « il faut » = “it’s necessary / we must”). Often introduces a serious or important conversation. « qu’on » is the contraction of « que + on ».
target_language_example: faut qu'on parle ce soir, c'est important.
native_language_example: We need to talk tonight—it's important.

additional_notes: Very common spoken shortcut for « il faut que … » (from the verb « falloir », “to be necessary”). It’s followed by the subjunctive: « Faut que je parte. » = “I have to leave.” You may also hear « y faut que … » in casual speech.
target_language_example: Faut que je rentre avant huit heures.
native_language_example: I have to get home before eight o’clock.

meaning: “it has to be” / “it must be” (introduces a requirement).
additional_notes: Short for “il faut que ce soit…”. Very common in spoken French (“faut que…”). It’s followed by the subjunctive: “que ce soit” (from “être”). Used to say something is necessary/required.
target_language_example: Faut que ce soit prêt avant midi.
native_language_example: It has to be ready before noon.

meaning: “I have to go (to…)” / “I need to go (to…).”
additional_notes: Informal spoken version of **« Il faut que j’aille… »** (“It’s necessary that I go…”). It expresses an obligation/need and is followed by **j’aille** (subjunctive of *aller*) plus a destination (**au boulot, en cours, à l’hôpital**) or an action (**voir ma mère, boire une bière**). Often used to mean you should leave or you have something you must do.
target_language_example: Faut que j'aille au boulot, je suis en retard.
native_language_example: I have to go to work, I’m late.

additional_notes: Very common spoken shortening of "Il faut que j’aille au…" (= “I need to / I have to go to the…”). "au" = "à + le" and is used before a masculine singular place or destination (e.g., au travail, au cinéma, au supermarché). In more formal speech/writing, include "il": "Il faut que j’aille au…"
target_language_example: faut que j'aille au supermarché.
native_language_example: I have to go to the supermarket.

meaning: “I have to go / I need to go (there).”
additional_notes: Short for “(il) faut que j’y aille,” built from the impersonal expression “il faut que…” + subjunctive (“j’aille”). “y” means “there / to it,” referring to a place or situation already mentioned or understood. Often used to excuse yourself: “Bon, faut que j’y aille.”
target_language_example: Désolé, faut que j'y aille maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

additional_notes: Informal spoken short form of "il faut que je". It expresses necessity or obligation, and the verb after it is normally in the subjunctive: "faut que je parte", "faut que je réponde".
target_language_example: Faut que je parte maintenant.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

meaning: "I have to / I need to (do something)."
additional_notes: Short for "(Il) faut que je fasse…" meaning a necessity/obligation. "Il faut que" is normally followed by the subjunctive, so you get "je fasse" (not *je fais*). Dropping "il" ("Faut que…") is common in spoken French and sounds informal.
target_language_example: Faut que je fasse mes devoirs avant de sortir.
native_language_example: I have to do my homework before going out.

meaning: "I have to / I need to" (with "it/him" as the object), as in "Il faut que je le…"
additional_notes: Almost always used as part of the longer structure **il faut que + subject + verb (subjunctive)**: **Il faut que je le fasse** (“I have to do it”). **faut** here comes from **falloir** (“to be necessary”) and needs **il** (impersonal “it”): you normally say **il faut que…**, not *faut que…* by itself. **le** is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” or “him,” placed before the verb: **je le + verb**.
target_language_example: Il faut que je le fasse aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have to do it today.

additional_notes: Spoken/informal start of a sentence, shortened from **« Il faut que je m’en … »**. **Il faut que** is followed by the **subjunctive** (e.g., *je m’en aille* = “I have to go/leave”). **m’en** combines **me** + **en** (“me” + “from there/of it”), and its exact meaning depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: faut que je m'en aille, je suis en retard.
native_language_example: I have to go, I’m late.

meaning: "I have to / I need to" (followed by a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Short, informal spoken version of « il faut que je me… ». It’s used to say something is necessary/urgent. It’s typically followed by a reflexive verb in the present (je me + verb): « Faut que je me repose » (I need to rest), « Faut que je me dépêche » (I have to hurry). In more careful speech/writing, use « Il faut que je me… ».
target_language_example: Faut que je me dépêche, je suis en retard.
native_language_example: I have to hurry, I'm late.

additional_notes: Common in speech as a shortened form of “Il faut que je retourne…”. Uses the verb “falloir” (il faut que…) to express necessity (“have to / need to”), followed by “je retourne” (“I go back”). Often used with places or activities: au travail/au boulot, bosser.
target_language_example: Faut que je retourne au bureau, on m’attend.
native_language_example: I have to go back to the office; they’re waiting for me.

meaning: "I need to know" / "I have to know."
additional_notes: Usually used as part of "Il faut que je sache…" (= “I need to know…”). After "il faut que", French uses the subjunctive: "je sache" (from "savoir", to know). Common for expressing necessity/urgency before asking for information.
target_language_example: Il faut que je sache à quelle heure tu arrives.
native_language_example: I need to know what time you’re arriving.

meaning: "I have to get out / I need to leave."
additional_notes: Spoken, informal shortening of **« il faut que je sorte »**. Uses the structure **(il) faut que + [subjunctive]**: *je sorte* (not *je sors*). Often used for urgency (e.g., leaving a place, escaping danger, stepping outside).
target_language_example: Désolé, faut que je sorte tout de suite.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to get out right now.

meaning: "I have to / I need to (tell you / do something for you)."
additional_notes: This is a common spoken fragment of « il faut que je te … » (“I have to …”). It’s usually followed by a verb in the subjunctive, often « dire »: « Faut que je te dise… » (“I have to tell you…”). « te » is the informal object pronoun meaning “to you” (singular).
target_language_example: Faut que je te parle, c’est important.
native_language_example: I have to talk to you; it’s important.

meaning: "I have to tell you" / "I need to tell you."
additional_notes: Usually used as part of the full phrase "Il faut que je te dise…" (literally: "It’s necessary that I tell you…"). It introduces something important, sometimes a warning, a secret, or news. In casual speech, "il" is often dropped: "Faut que je te dise…".
target_language_example: Il faut que je te dise quelque chose.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something.

meaning: “I need to talk to you / I have to talk to you.”
additional_notes: Short for **(Il) faut que je te parle**. Uses **falloir** (“to be necessary”) in the common pattern **il faut que + [subject] + verb (subjunctive)**. In conversation, dropping **il** (**faut que…**) is very common and informal. Often used to introduce an important or serious topic; you can add **de + noun/pronoun**: *Faut que je te parle de ça / d’un truc.*
target_language_example: Faut que je te parle après le cours.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you after class.

meaning: "I have to / I need to … (you, formal)" (start of a sentence).
additional_notes: Usually part of the structure "Il faut que je vous + verb" to express necessity/obligation in a polite or formal way when speaking to one person (vous) or a group. It’s incomplete on its own and needs a verb after "vous" (e.g., "dire", "parler", "demander"). In everyday speech, people may drop "Il": "Faut que je vous…"
target_language_example: Il faut que je vous parle.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you.

meaning: “I need to talk to you” / “I have to talk to you.”
additional_notes: Short for « (Il) faut que je vous parle » (“It’s necessary that I talk to you”). Dropping « il » is common in spoken French and sounds informal. Uses « vous » for a polite/formal “you” (to a boss, stranger, etc.). Often introduces a serious or important conversation; you can add an adverb like « franchement » (honestly/frankly).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, faut que je vous parle un instant.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Short, spoken form of "il faut que tu". It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "Faut que tu comprennes", "Faut que tu signes"). Common for giving strong advice, instructions, or saying something is necessary.
target_language_example: Faut que tu fasses attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when crossing the street.

meaning: “you have to/need to … (to) me” (usually in: « Il faut que tu me … »).
additional_notes: This is part of the common structure « Il faut que + [subject] + [verb in the subjunctive] ». It expresses necessity/obligation: « Il faut que tu me dises… » = “You need to tell me…”. The « me » is the indirect object pronoun (“to me”). On its own, « faut que tu me… » is incomplete—you normally continue with a verb.
target_language_example: Il faut que tu me dises la vérité.
native_language_example: You need to tell me the truth.

meaning: "you have to be / you need to be" (said as part of "Il faut que tu sois...").
additional_notes: Almost always used with an implied or stated "il": "Il faut que tu sois..." = "You have to be...". It’s a common way to express necessity/obligation and it triggers the subjunctive, so you’ll see "sois" (subjunctive of "être") rather than "es".
target_language_example: Il faut que tu sois à l’heure.
native_language_example: You have to be on time.

meaning: "You need to be more…" / "You have to be more…" (followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone it’s necessary that they change their behavior or attitude. It comes from "(il) faut que" + a verb in the subjunctive: "tu sois" (from être) + "plus" + adjective (e.g., plus patient(e), plus organisé(e)). Without "il" ("Faut que…") is common in speech and more informal; "Il faut que…" is more standard.
target_language_example: Faut que tu sois plus prudent.
native_language_example: You need to be more careful.

meaning: “you have to / you need to (… yourself)” (start of a sentence).
additional_notes: This is usually part of the structure: « Il faut que tu te + verb (subjunctive) … ». It expresses necessity/obligation. « te » is a reflexive pronoun (“yourself/to yourself”), used with many common verbs: se lever (to get up), se dépêcher (to hurry), se calmer (to calm down), etc. Often the « il » is omitted in casual speech: « Faut que tu te dépêches. »
target_language_example: Faut que tu te dépêches, on est en retard.
native_language_example: You have to hurry up, we’re late.

meaning: "you have to / you must" (short for "il faut que vous").
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: people often drop "il" and say "faut que...". It introduces what someone is required/needed to do, and it’s followed by the subjunctive: "Faut que vous veniez" (not *"vous venez"). In more formal writing/speech, use "Il faut que vous...".
target_language_example: Faut que vous veniez tout de suite.
native_language_example: You have to come right away.

meaning: "You need to be more..." / "You have to be more..."
additional_notes: Shortened from "Il faut que..." ("it’s necessary that..."). It introduces a requirement or strong advice and is followed by the subjunctive: "vous soyez" + an adjective (e.g., "plus organisé(e)(s)"). The adjective agrees with who you’re talking to: "organisé" (one man), "organisée" (one woman), "organisés" (group/mixed or men), "organisées" (group of women). Common in spoken French; "Il faut que" is a bit more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Faut que vous soyez plus patients avec les enfants.
native_language_example: You need to be more patient with the kids.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **falloir** (almost always as **il faut…**). With an indirect object pronoun, it means someone needs something: **Il lui faut un manteau** = “He needs a coat” (literally: “To him, a coat is necessary”). Common patterns: **Il faut un + noun** (“You need a/an…”) and **Il me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faut un/une + noun** (“I/you/he… need a/an…”).
target_language_example: Il nous faut une carte pour entrer.
native_language_example: We need a ticket/card to get in.

additional_notes: Used to explain what happens because something is missing or because you didn’t manage to do something. Common patterns: **faute de + noun** (for lack of something): *Faute de temps…*; **faute de + infinitive** (failing to do something): *Faute de comprendre…*. Not the same as **une faute** (= a mistake/error).
target_language_example: Faute de preuves, la police a classé l’affaire.
native_language_example: For lack of evidence, the police closed the case.

additional_notes: Means a wheelchair (a chair with wheels used by someone who has difficulty walking). Often used with the verb "être" (to be) or with "en" to mean being transported in one: "être dans un fauteuil roulant", "être évacué en fauteuil roulant". You may also hear "chaise roulante" (more common in Canada).
target_language_example: Après l’accident, il se déplace en fauteuil roulant.
native_language_example: After the accident, he gets around in a wheelchair.

meaning: a way of; a way to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a method/means (“une façon de + infinitive” = “a way to + verb”) or someone’s manner/style (“une façon de + verb/noun” = “a way of …”). Often preceded by an article or quantity: « la/une seule/une autre façon de… ».
target_language_example: Il n’y a pas d’autre façon de comprendre sans demander.
native_language_example: There’s no other way to understand without asking.

meaning: a figure of speech; (also) someone’s way of speaking.
additional_notes: Often used to correct or soften what you just said: « C’était / Ce n’était qu’une façon de parler » = “I didn’t mean it literally; it was just an expression.” You can also use it parenthetically: « Il est, façon de parler, un robot » (“so to speak”). In a more literal sense, « sa façon de parler » means “his/her way of speaking / manner of speaking.”
target_language_example: Je dis ça, mais c’est une façon de parler : je ne le pense pas vraiment.
native_language_example: I say that, but it’s just a figure of speech—I don’t really mean it.

additional_notes: Used to describe how someone (or a group/culture) typically thinks or approaches ideas. Often followed by a possessive adjective: « ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur façon de penser ».
target_language_example: Sa façon de penser a beaucoup changé depuis l'année dernière.
native_language_example: His/Her way of thinking has changed a lot since last year.

meaning: a housewife; a stay-at-home woman who runs the household.
additional_notes: Used to describe a woman whose main activity is managing the home (housework, childcare, etc.), rather than having paid work outside the home. Often used after être: « Je suis femme au foyer » (no article). With an article it’s treated like a noun: « une femme au foyer », « les femmes au foyer ».
target_language_example: Depuis la naissance de son bébé, elle est femme au foyer.
native_language_example: Since her baby was born, she has been a stay-at-home mom.

additional_notes: Refers to a woman who cleans and tidies rooms and may bring items (soap, towels) in a hotel or private household. Historically it can also mean a lady’s maid/maidservant for a wealthy woman. Plural: femmes de chambre.
target_language_example: La femme de chambre passera tout à l’heure pour refaire la chambre.
native_language_example: The chambermaid will come by later to make up the room.

additional_notes: Refers to a woman whose job is cleaning (in a home, hotel, office, etc.). It does not mean “housewife” (a woman who manages her own household). In some contexts it can sound a bit old-fashioned; you may also hear more neutral terms like « agent(e) d’entretien ».
target_language_example: La femme de ménage arrive tous les lundis matin.
native_language_example: The cleaner comes every Monday morning.

meaning: 'woman is' (usually in a longer sentence: 'La femme est…').
additional_notes: On its own, "femme est" sounds incomplete in French. You normally need an article before "femme" (most often "la" for a general statement or "une" for a specific/unspecified woman): "La femme est…" / "Une femme est…". Used to describe or define someone/something: "La femme est médecin."
target_language_example: La femme est très gentille.
native_language_example: The woman is very nice.

meaning: an open window (a window left open).
additional_notes: Used literally to describe a window that is open or has been left open. Often appears with verbs like laisser (to leave), dormir avec (to sleep with), or in phrases like par la fenêtre ouverte (through the open window). The adjective ouverte agrees with fenêtre (feminine): une fenêtre ouverte.
target_language_example: Peux-tu fermer la fenêtre ouverte, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you close the open window, please?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **faire du bien à [qqn]** (“to do good to someone”). It’s commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: **ça te fera du bien** (to you), **ça lui fera du bien** (to him/her), **ça nous fera du bien** (to us). Often followed by **de + infinitive** to say what will help: **Ça te fera du bien de…** (“It’ll do you good to…”).
target_language_example: Un peu d’air frais te fera du bien.
native_language_example: A bit of fresh air will do you good.

additional_notes: A common way to promise you’ll try hard. It’s the future tense of « faire de son mieux » (to do one’s best). « ferai » is the 1st-person singular future of « faire » (I will do).
target_language_example: Je ferai de mon mieux pour être à l’heure.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best to be on time.

ferai tout ce que je peux

target_language_multi_word_term: ferai tout ce que je peux
additional_notes: A strong way to promise you’ll make your best effort. It uses the future tense of faire (je ferai = I will do). You can change the subject: « Je ferai tout ce que je peux » (I’ll do everything I can), « Il/Elle fera… » (He/She will do…), « Nous ferons… » (We will do…).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je ferai tout ce que je peux pour t’aider.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll do everything I can to help you.

meaning: "I will do everything that you…" (sentence fragment).
additional_notes:
This is an incomplete phrase that normally continues with a verb (often "veux" = "want" or "demandes" = "ask"): "Je ferai tout ce que tu veux." 
- "ferai" is the future tense of "faire" (to do/make): "je ferai" = "I will do".
- The pattern "tout ce que + subject + verb" means "everything that + subject + verb".
target_language_example: Je ferai tout ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: I’ll do anything you want.

additional_notes: Question formed with inversion: conditional of *faire* ("ferais" = "would do") + *-tu*. Used to ask what someone would do, often in hypothetical situations or to challenge/confirm intentions. You’ll often see it with an object: *Le ferais-tu ?* (Would you do it?).
target_language_example: Si tu avais le choix, le ferais-tu ?
native_language_example: If you had the choice, would you do it?

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a warning. It’s built on the pattern **faire mieux de + infinitive** (“to do better to…”). **Ne pas** goes right before the infinitive: *Tu ferais mieux de ne pas parler.* You can change the person/tense: *Je ferais mieux de ne pas… / Vous feriez mieux de ne pas…*
target_language_example: Tu ferais mieux de ne pas répondre comme ça.
native_language_example: You’d better not answer like that.

meaning: "I would do anything to/for" (to achieve something).
additional_notes: Used to express willingness to do whatever it takes. "Ferais" is the conditional form of "faire" (je ferais = I would do). It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb ("...pour te revoir" / "...pour y aller") or a noun ("...pour une chance"). You can change the subject: "tu ferais", "il/elle ferait", "on ferait", etc.
target_language_example: Je ferais n'importe quoi pour te revoir.
native_language_example: I would do anything to see you again.

meaning: would do (someone) good; would be good for you.
additional_notes: Conditional of « faire du bien » (“to do good / to make someone feel better”). Used to suggest that something would help you feel better (rest, a nap, a drink, etc.). Often appears with an indirect object: « Ça me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur ferait du bien » (That would do me/you/him/her/us/you/them good).
target_language_example: Après une longue journée, une douche chaude te ferait du bien.
native_language_example: After a long day, a hot shower would do you good.

meaning: "would do such a thing" / "would do something like that."
additional_notes: Uses the conditional (ferait, from faire) to talk about a hypothetical person or to express disbelief/indignation: “Who would do such a thing?” Often used with "qui" or "quelle personne". "une chose pareille" means “such a thing” / “something like that.”
target_language_example: Je me demande qui ferait une chose pareille.
native_language_example: I wonder who would do such a thing.

meaning: “will you do … ?” (future tense of faire, in an inverted question).
additional_notes: Used to ask a question with subject–verb inversion: feras (you will do) + tu (you). Often appears in more formal or written French; in everyday speech you’ll also hear Tu feras… ? or Est-ce que tu feras… ?. It can take object pronouns: Le feras-tu ? (“Will you do it?”), Me feras-tu savoir… ? (“Will you let me know…?”).
target_language_example: Feras-tu la vaisselle ce soir ?
native_language_example: Will you do the dishes tonight?

meaning: 'will you do...?' / 'will you make...?' (formal question form of *faire*).
additional_notes: This is the **future tense** of *faire* (“to do/make”) with **inversion** (*verbe + -vous*) to ask a question: *Ferez-vous… ?* = “Will you…?” It’s more **formal** than *Vous ferez… ?* or *Est-ce que vous ferez… ?*. It can mean “do” (*Que ferez-vous ?* = “What will you do?”) or “make” (*Me ferez-vous une faveur ?* = “Will you do me a favor?”).
target_language_example: Ferez-vous le ménage demain matin ?
native_language_example: Will you do the cleaning tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: From the verb **faire** (“to do/make”) in the **conditional** (**vous feriez**) plus **inversion** (**-vous**) to form a question. Used for polite requests or hypothetical questions. Often appears with **le**: **le feriez-vous ?** = “would you do it?”
target_language_example: Feriez-vous cela pour m’aider ?
native_language_example: Would you do that to help me?

additional_notes: Informal and aggressive command telling someone to stop talking. Literally means “close it,” where “la” refers to the mouth; often written with a hyphen in the imperative: « Ferme-la ! ». Avoid in polite situations; use « Tais-toi » / « Taisez-vous » for a less harsh “be quiet.”
target_language_example: Ferme-la et laisse-moi finir.
native_language_example: Shut up and let me finish.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) of the verb *fermer* (“to close”) + *la porte* (“the door”). Often used to tell one person to close a specific door. Use *Fermez la porte* for “close the door” to more than one person or as the polite/formal form. Can be softened with *s’il te plaît* (“please”) or *je te prie* (“please/I beg you”).
target_language_example: Il fait froid : ferme la porte, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: It’s cold: close the door, please.

additional_notes: Imperative form of « fermer » addressed to one person (tu). Used as an instruction (e.g., in a game, for a photo, or to avoid seeing something). With « tu veux pas voir ça », it means “Close your eyes—you don’t want to see that.” It can also be used literally: « Il/elle ferme les yeux » = “He/She closes his/her eyes.”
target_language_example: Ferme les yeux, ça va piquer un peu.
native_language_example: Close your eyes, it’s going to sting a little.

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to shut a window. Common in polite requests: "Veuillez fermer…" (please, formal) and "Voudriez-vous…?" (would you…?, very polite). In everyday speech you might also say: "Ferme la fenêtre."
target_language_example: Tu peux fermer la fenêtre, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you close the window, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to shut a door. Very common with polite request forms like « Peux-tu… ? », « Pourrais-tu… ? », « Allez-vous… je vous prie ? » or « Veuillez… ». You can add « derrière toi » to mean “behind you” (close it after you pass through).
target_language_example: Tu peux fermer la porte derrière toi, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you close the door behind you, please?

meaning: to lock the door (with a key).
additional_notes: Used when you lock a door using a key (not just shutting it). Often said as an instruction or reminder: « N’oublie pas de fermer la porte à clé. » You can also hear « fermer à clé » without repeating the object if it’s clear what you’re locking.
target_language_example: N’oublie pas de fermer la porte à clé avant de partir.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to lock the door before you leave.

meaning: to close your eyes; (figuratively) to ignore/turn a blind eye (to something).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: physically close your eyes. Figuratively, often used with « sur/ là-dessus » to mean “to overlook something” or “to pretend not to notice,” especially in requests like « Pourrais-tu fermer les yeux là-dessus ? » (“Could you let it slide?”).
target_language_example: Je vais fermer les yeux sur cette erreur, mais pas la prochaine fois.
native_language_example: I’ll overlook this mistake, but not next time.

meaning: to lock (with a key); to lock up.
additional_notes: Used when you close something and secure it with a key (a door, a window, a suitcase, etc.). Often used in the imperative: « Ferme à clé ! » (= Lock it!). You can specify what you’re locking: « Fermer la porte à clé ».
target_language_example: Pense à fermer à clé avant de partir.
native_language_example: Remember to lock up before leaving.

additional_notes: Imperative of *fermer* (“to close”) + *la* (“it”), used as an abrupt command for someone to stop talking. Commonly felt as aggressive/insulting; in polite contexts prefer *Taisez-vous.* (formal) or *Tais-toi.* (informal).
target_language_example: Fermez-la et laissez-moi parler !
native_language_example: Shut up and let me talk!

additional_notes: This is the imperative of "fermer" addressed to "vous". Use it when speaking politely to one person (e.g., a stranger, customer, older person) or to several people. For an informal command to one person, you’d say: "Ferme la porte." You can soften it with "s’il vous plaît" or "je vous prie".
target_language_example: Fermez la porte, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

meaning: “closed the door” (past tense of “to close the door”).
additional_notes: Uses the past participle fermé of fermer (“to close”), typically with avoir to form the passé composé: j’ai/tu as/il a/nous avons fermé la porte. Often followed by details like de + place (la porte de sa chambre) or derrière nous (“behind us”).
target_language_example: J’ai fermé la porte, mais la fenêtre est restée ouverte.
native_language_example: I closed the door, but the window stayed open.

additional_notes: A fire made outdoors (often while camping, sometimes on a beach) for warmth, light, or cooking. Used with faire/allumer/construire un feu de camp (“make/light/build a campfire”).
target_language_example: On a fait un feu de camp pour se réchauffer.
native_language_example: We made a campfire to warm up.

additional_notes: Used when giving directions or talking about driving rules. In French you often say “au feu rouge” (at the red light) or “après le feu rouge” (after the red light). “Griller un feu rouge” means “to run a red light.”
target_language_example: Arrêtez-vous au feu rouge, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Stop at the red light, please.

additional_notes: Used literally for traffic lights (au feu vert = when the light is green) and figuratively for authorization (donner/avoir le feu vert = to give/get the go-ahead). Often used alone as a short confirmation: « Feu vert. »
target_language_example: On attend le feu vert avant de commencer.
native_language_example: We’re waiting for the green light before starting.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one single sheet/page of paper (not a whole notebook or stack). You can also say "une feuille" when it’s clear from context that it’s paper.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'une feuille de papier, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need a sheet of paper, please.

additional_notes: Very informal and rude. Used as an order to make someone leave (similar to "dégage !" or "va-t’en !"). Also used with other forms: "Je fiche le camp" = "I’m getting out of here / I’m leaving," and "Il faut fiche le camp" = "We/you need to get out (leave)."
target_language_example: Fiche le camp, je ne veux plus te voir ici.
native_language_example: Get lost, I don’t want to see you here anymore.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to stop bothering (someone).
additional_notes: Usually used to tell someone to stop annoying you: « Fiche-moi la paix ! » = “Leave me alone!” It’s informal and can sound rude/angry depending on tone. You can also use it with a third person: « Fiche-lui la paix » (Leave him/her alone). Similar to « laisser tranquille » (a bit more neutral).
target_language_example: Je voudrais que tu arrêtes de me déranger et que tu me laisses ficher la paix.
native_language_example: I’d like you to stop bothering me and leave me alone.

meaning: to clear off; to get lost; to run off.
additional_notes: Informal (can sound rude depending on tone). Used to tell someone to leave (often as an imperative: « Fiche le camp ! ») or to say that someone/something left suddenly (« Il/Elle a fiché le camp. »). Similar to « foutre le camp » (usually stronger/more vulgar).
target_language_example: Quand il a vu la police, il a fiché le camp.
native_language_example: When he saw the police, he cleared off.

additional_notes: Used to express pride in someone or something. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (fier de toi, fier de ça) or by an infinitive to say what you’re proud to do (fier de réussir). Agreement: fier (masc. singular), fière (fem. singular), fiers (masc. plural), fières (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Je suis fier de mon travail.
native_language_example: I’m proud of my work.

additional_notes: Used to praise or encourage someone you address as “tu.” “Fier” agrees with the speaker: a man says “je suis fier de toi,” a woman says “je suis fière de toi.” You can also use it with other people: “fier de lui/elle,” “fiers/fières de vous/eux/elles.”
target_language_example: Je suis très fier de toi pour ton travail !
native_language_example: I'm very proud of you for your work!

additional_notes: Used almost always as the pronominal verb **se fier à** + someone/something: **je me fie à...** (I trust/rely on...), **tu te fies à...**, **nous nous fions à...**. Common in advice and warnings: **Ne te fie pas à...** (Don’t trust/rely on...). Often implies depending on someone/something being reliable.
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux me fier à vous ?
native_language_example: Can I rely on you?

additional_notes: Used with plural masculine subjects, often after forms of être (e.g., nous sommes fiers de...). It agrees with the subject: fier (m. sg.), fière (f. sg.), fiers (m. pl.), fières (f. pl.). Followed by a noun or a stressed pronoun: fier/fière(s) de moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles.
target_language_example: Nous sommes fiers de lui.
native_language_example: We’re proud of him.

additional_notes: Used for thin metal wire, often for practical uses like making cages, fixing things, crafting, or tying items. With materials you’ll often see it after en (“made of”): en fil de fer. With quantities it’s usually du fil de fer (“some wire”).
target_language_example: On a réparé la clôture avec du fil de fer.
native_language_example: We repaired the fence with some wire.

additional_notes: Most literally means a red wire (or thread), especially when talking about electronics or instructions ("Cut the red wire"). Figuratively, it can also mean a “common thread” or main theme linking parts of a story or argument ("le fil rouge de l’histoire").
target_language_example: Coupe le fil rouge, pas le fil vert.
native_language_example: Cut the red wire, not the green one.

additional_notes: Usually used with "en" ("en file indienne") to tell people to line up one behind another, often in school or when moving through a narrow space. Related verb phrase: "se mettre en file indienne" = to line up single file.
target_language_example: Pour entrer dans le musée, mettez-vous en file indienne.
native_language_example: To enter the museum, line up single file.

additional_notes: Means a girl who has no brothers or sisters. Used without an article after the verb être: « Je suis fille unique. » For a male only child, say « fils unique ».
target_language_example: Ma sœur est fille unique, donc elle n'a pas de frères ni de sœurs.
native_language_example: My sister is an only child, so she has no brothers or sisters.

meaning: A very vulgar insult: “son of a bitch / you bastard.”
additional_notes: Extremely offensive and aggressive (stronger than many common insults). Used to insult someone directly ("Tu es un fils de pute") or to talk about someone ("ce fils de pute"). In the plural: "fils de pute" / "fils de putes". Literal meaning is “son of a whore,” but the closest natural English equivalent is usually “son of a bitch.” Avoid in polite or everyday situations.
target_language_example: C'est un fils de pute, il m'a volé mon téléphone.
native_language_example: He’s a son of a bitch—he stole my phone.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has no brothers (and no sisters if you mean they are the only child overall). Feminine: « fille unique » (only daughter). If someone is an only child (no siblings at all), you can also say « enfant unique ».
target_language_example: Il est fils unique, donc il n'a pas de frères.
native_language_example: He’s an only son, so he doesn’t have any brothers.

additional_notes: Used before a noun, often with an article: "fin de la journée" (end of the day), "fin du mois" (end of the month). It can refer to the ending moment/event ("Fin de la partie" = game over) or the last phase of a period ("en fin de cycle" = at the end of a cycle). Common in set phrases like "Bonne fin de journée" (have a nice rest of your day).
target_language_example: On se voit à la fin de la journée.
native_language_example: See you at the end of the day.

additional_notes: Used in headings, announcements, or narration to mark that something is finished. It’s followed by a feminine noun (la leçon, la partie, la scène). For a masculine noun, use "fin du" (e.g., fin du film).
target_language_example: Fin de la réunion !
native_language_example: End of the meeting!

additional_notes: Very common in Canadian French (especially Quebec) for “weekend”; in France you’ll often hear “week-end”. Used with or without an article: « une bonne fin de semaine », « chaque fin de semaine », « en fin de semaine » (= on the weekend). « une longue fin de semaine » = a long weekend.
target_language_example: On se voit en fin de semaine ?
native_language_example: See you this weekend?

additional_notes: Used to introduce what is ending: fin du cours (end of the class), fin du jeu (end of the game), fin du message (end of the message), fin du week-end (end of the weekend). Often appears with a preceding article: la fin du… (“the end of the…”). Note the contraction: de + le = du (so de la fin du… = “from the end of the…”).
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à la fin du film.
native_language_example: I arrived at the end of the movie.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the last days of a month, often for deadlines, paydays, rent, or bills. Common in phrases like « à la fin du mois » (at the end of the month). You may also see « fin de mois » (month-end), especially in expressions like « difficile fin de mois » (a tough end of the month financially).
target_language_example: Je paie mon loyer à la fin du mois.
native_language_example: I pay my rent at the end of the month.

additional_notes: Used literally for an apocalypse/disaster ("la fin du monde") or more loosely to exaggerate a situation ("Ce n’est pas la fin du monde" = “It’s not the end of the world”). You’ll often see it with an article: "la fin du monde".
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas la fin du monde si on est en retard.
native_language_example: It’s not the end of the world if we’re late.

meaning: "ended up" / "eventually" (after some time, effort, or events).
additional_notes: Used as the verb phrase "finir par" + infinitive: "Il/Elle a fini par comprendre" = "He/She ended up understanding." It often suggests a result that happens after a process (waiting, trying, changing, repeated actions). You’ll commonly see it in past tenses (passé composé: "a fini par"; plus-que-parfait: "avait fini par").
target_language_example: On a fini par trouver un restaurant ouvert.
native_language_example: We eventually found a restaurant that was open.

additional_notes: This is the passé simple (literary past) of « faire de son mieux pour + infinitive » (“to do one’s best to…”). In everyday speech you’ll usually see/hear « il a fait de son mieux pour… » (passé composé) or « il faisait de son mieux pour… » (imperfect). The possessive changes with the subject: « je fais de mon mieux », « elle fait de son mieux », « nous faisons de notre mieux », etc.
target_language_example: Il fit de son mieux pour exécuter le plan.
native_language_example: He did his best to carry out the plan.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" (or "se sentir") to say someone is proud of someone/something: "être fière de + noun/pronoun/verb (infinitive)". This is the feminine form; the masculine is "fier de" (Il est fier de son travail). With plural "vous" for a group of women you also use "fières" (Soyez fières de vous).
target_language_example: Je suis fière de mon travail.
native_language_example: I’m proud of my work.

meaning: proud of you (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone you’re proud of them. Agreement matters: a woman says « fière »; a man says « fier ». « de toi » is informal singular “of you”; with « vous », it’s « fier/fière de vous ».
target_language_example: Je suis fière de toi, tu as vraiment bien travaillé.
native_language_example: I’m proud of you—you really worked hard.

additional_notes: A simple noun phrase: "fleurs" (plural of *fleur*, flower) + "dans" (in) + "le jardin" (the garden). Often used with *il y a* (there is/are): *Il y a des fleurs dans le jardin.* You may also see *des fleurs* (some flowers) instead of just *fleurs*.
target_language_example: Il y a des fleurs dans le jardin.
native_language_example: There are flowers in the garden.

meaning: “... time(s), I ...” (e.g., “This time, I…”, “Sometimes, I…”, “One more time, I’ll…”).
additional_notes:
Common sentence pattern where a time/frequency phrase with *fois* comes first, followed by *je* + verb.
- **Cette fois, je…** = “This time, I…”
- **Des fois, je…** = “Sometimes, I…”
- **Encore une fois, je…** = “One more time, I…” (often a warning: “If you do it one more time, I’ll…”)
target_language_example: Encore une fois, je te le répète : je n'ai pas le temps.
native_language_example: One more time, I'm telling you: I don't have time.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens: number + « fois par » + time period (jour/semaine/mois/an). Example pattern: « deux fois par semaine » = twice a week. You can also say « une fois par jour » (once a day).
target_language_example: Je fais du sport trois fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I work out three times a week.

meaning: “times a year” (how many times per year).
additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency over a year. Often comes after a number or after “combien de” in a question: “deux fois par an” (twice a year), “Combien de fois par an… ?” (How many times a year…?). Similar patterns: “fois par mois” (times a month), “fois par semaine” (times a week).
target_language_example: Je vais à la salle de sport trois fois par an.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a year.

additional_notes: Used with a number to say how often something happens in one day: « une fois par jour » (once a day), « deux fois par jour » (twice a day), etc. It often appears in instructions (medicine, routines): « Prenez ce médicament deux fois par jour. »
target_language_example: Je me brosse les dents deux fois par jour.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth twice a day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens within a month), often after a number: « deux fois par mois » (twice a month). In questions you’ll often see « Combien de fois par mois… ? » (How many times per month…?).
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma une fois par mois.
native_language_example: I go to the movies once a month.

meaning: 'times per week' (how many times in a week).
additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency. Often comes after a number ("deux fois par semaine" = twice a week) or in questions with "combien de" ("Combien de fois par semaine…?" = How many times a week…?).
target_language_example: Je vais à la salle de sport trois fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a week.

meaning: "times bigger/larger than the" (used to compare sizes).
additional_notes: Used after a number to express a multiplicative comparison in size: « X est deux/trois fois plus grande que la Y » = X is two/three times bigger than Y. « grande » agrees with the noun being described (grande = feminine; grand = masculine). « que la » introduces a feminine noun; for a masculine noun you’d use « que le », and before a vowel/silent h: « que l’ ».
target_language_example: La nouvelle cuisine est deux fois plus grande que la précédente.
native_language_example: The new kitchen is twice as big as the previous one.

additional_notes: Most often used as **une fois pour toutes** (very common) to mean doing something definitively so it won’t need to be discussed or repeated. Often appears with verbs like **régler** (settle), **clarifier** (clear up), **en finir** (be done with it).
target_language_example: Il faut régler ça une fois pour toutes.
native_language_example: We need to settle this once and for all.

meaning: “time that / time when” (as in “the first/next/every time that…”).
additional_notes: Used after an expression with fois (une/deux/troisième fois; la prochaine fois; chaque fois) to introduce a clause with a verb: la première fois que…, chaque fois que…, la prochaine fois que…. In this structure, que links the time expression to what happens.
target_language_example: La dernière fois que je l’ai appelé, il n’a pas répondu.
native_language_example: The last time I called him, he didn’t answer.

meaning: “time(s) that I …” / “the time when I …” (used to start a clause).
additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer expression like **la première fois que je…** (the first time that I…), **la dernière fois que je…** (the last time that I…), or **chaque fois que je…** (every time I…). It introduces what you did/experienced on that occasion.
target_language_example: C’est la première fois que je viens à Paris.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come to Paris.

fois que nous nous sommes rencontrés

target_language_multi_word_term: fois que nous nous sommes rencontrés
meaning: “time that we met” / “time when we met.”
additional_notes: Used after an ordinal or expression like *la première fois*, *la dernière fois*, *la prochaine fois* to talk about an occasion in the past or future. *Fois* means “time/occasion,” and *que* introduces the clause (*when/that*). The verb is in the passé composé: *nous nous sommes rencontrés* (“we met,” literally “we met each other”).
target_language_example: Je n’oublierai jamais la première fois que nous nous sommes rencontrés.
native_language_example: I will never forget the first time we met.

meaning: 'does it work?' / 'does it run?' (question form of « il fonctionne »).
additional_notes: This is a formal/standard way to ask a yes/no question using inversion: verb + -t- + subject pronoun (« il »). The -t- is added for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel sound (fonctionne) and the pronoun starts with a vowel (il). Used for devices, systems, code, machines, etc. In everyday speech, people often say « Est-ce qu’il fonctionne ? » or « Il fonctionne ? ».
target_language_example: Ce programme fonctionne-t-il sur ton ordinateur ?
native_language_example: Does this program work on your computer?

meaning: the bottom/deepest part of the; deep down in the.
additional_notes: Literally “fond” = bottom/depth and “du” = “de + le” (“of the”). Used for a physical place (au fond du couloir/terrain = at the far end, in the back) and for figurative meanings: from the bottom of one’s heart (du fond du cœur), or the core/essence of something (le fond du problème).
target_language_example: Au fond du couloir, il y a une porte.
native_language_example: At the end of the hallway, there is a door.

meaning: the end (far end) of the hallway/corridor.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a location far away from the entrance or starting point of a hallway. Often appears with prepositions like « au fond du couloir » (at the end of the hallway) or « tout au fond du couloir » (right at the very end).
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont au fond du couloir, à gauche.
native_language_example: The bathrooms are at the end of the hallway, on the left.

meaning: the bottom of (one’s) heart; deep down.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you truly feel "deep inside." Very common in set phrases like "du fond du cœur" (from the bottom of my heart) and "au fond du cœur" (deep down, in one’s heart). Often used with strong feelings (thanks, sincerity, love, regret).
target_language_example: Merci du fond du cœur pour ton aide.
native_language_example: Thank you from the bottom of my heart for your help.

meaning: to burst into tears (to suddenly start crying).
additional_notes: Used when someone begins crying abruptly due to strong emotion (sadness, relief, shock, etc.). Conjugate « fondre » to match the subject and tense (e.g., « elle fondre en larmes » is incorrect; use « elle fond en larmes », « elle a fondu en larmes », etc.).
target_language_example: Quand il a annoncé son départ, elle a fondu en larmes.
native_language_example: When he announced he was leaving, she burst into tears.

additional_notes: "Font-ils" is the inverted question form of "ils font" (they do / they are doing). It’s used in formal or written questions, often after a question word: « Que font-ils ? » (What are they doing?), « Pourquoi font-ils… ? » (Why do they…?). In everyday speech, people often say « Qu’est-ce qu’ils font ? » or « Ils font quoi ? ».
target_language_example: Que font-ils ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What are they doing this weekend?

additional_notes: Used to specify the sport (as opposed to football = soccer in many French-speaking contexts). Often appears after prepositions like jouer au / faire du (to play) and in comparisons like préférer X au Y (to prefer X to Y).
target_language_example: Je regarde le football américain le dimanche.
native_language_example: I watch American football on Sundays.

meaning: (formal) “it must be admitted / it is necessary” (often: “force est de + infinitive”).
additional_notes: Used in formal writing to express an unavoidable conclusion or obligation. Very common in the set phrase “Force est de constater que…” (= “We/one must admit/acknowledge that…”). Usually followed by “de” + infinitive, or by “que” + clause.
target_language_example: Force est de constater que les prix ont augmenté.
native_language_example: We have to admit that prices have gone up.

meaning: to pressure someone into doing something; to twist someone’s arm.
additional_notes: Used when someone is trying to push you to agree or act against your will (e.g., insisting, guilt-tripping, not taking no for an answer). Often appears with an indirect object pronoun: « me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur forcer la main ». Can be used in the imperative: « Arrête de me forcer la main ! » (to one person) / « Arrêtez de me forcer la main ! » (formal or plural).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas, alors n’essaie pas de me forcer la main.
native_language_example: I don’t want to, so don’t try to pressure me into it.

additional_notes: Usually refers to elite military units trained for high-risk missions (often used with the definite article: « les forces spéciales »). In conversation it can also be used jokingly or as a nickname to address someone acting like a commando: « Eh, les forces spéciales ! »
target_language_example: Il rêve d'entrer dans les forces spéciales.
native_language_example: He dreams of joining the special forces.

meaning: heavy snowfall (a lot of snow falling).
additional_notes: Used in weather/news contexts to explain delays, cancellations, or blocked roads (often with en raison de / à cause de). The adjective fortes agrees with chutes (feminine plural).
target_language_example: À cause de fortes chutes de neige, l’aéroport est fermé.
native_language_example: Because of heavy snowfall, the airport is closed.

additional_notes: Used with être (or devenir) to say someone is extremely happy about something: « être fou de joie ». You can add a reason with « en + verbe » (e.g., « en apprenant la nouvelle » = “on hearing the news”). Note agreement: « fou » → « folle » for a woman (e.g., « Elle est folle de joie »).
target_language_example: Il est devenu fou de joie en apprenant la nouvelle.
native_language_example: He became overjoyed when he heard the news.

additional_notes: Used with "être" or "devenir" to say someone is extremely angry. You can use it as an exclamation ("Fou de rage !") or in a sentence ("Il est fou de rage").
target_language_example: Quand il a appris la nouvelle, il est devenu fou de rage.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, he became furious.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is "crazy" in a very emphatic way (often as an insult or harsh judgment). Literally "crazy to be tied up"—as if they’d need to be restrained. It agrees with the person: fou (masc. sing.), folle (fem. sing.), fous/folles (plural).
target_language_example: Arrête de conduire comme ça, tu es fou à lier !
native_language_example: Stop driving like that, you’re completely crazy!

meaning: “(Are you) kidding/messing with me?” or “making fun of me.”
additional_notes: Usually appears as **Tu te fous de ma gueule ?** (from **se foutre de** = to mess with / to make fun of). **Gueule** is a vulgar word for “mouth” (often used for an animal), so the whole expression is **very informal/rough** and can sound aggressive. You can use it when you feel someone is joking at your expense or not being serious.
target_language_example: Tu te fous de ma gueule ? J’ai dit la vérité !
native_language_example: Are you kidding me? I told the truth!

meaning: to mess up / ruin (something); to blow up (destroy).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar because of « foutre » (roughly like “to screw up” / “to fuck up”). Used for ruining plans (« foutre en l’air un projet »), messing something up (« foutre en l’air tout le travail »), or sometimes literally destroying/blowing something up. In polite contexts, prefer: « gâcher », « bousiller » (informal), or « ruiner ».
target_language_example: J’ai foutre en l'air ma présentation en oubliant mes notes.
native_language_example: I screwed up my presentation by forgetting my notes.

meaning: to cause trouble; to mess things up (vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used to say someone is stirring up trouble, creating chaos, or ruining a situation (intentionally or not). Common in spoken French. You can soften it with "mettre le bazar" (less vulgar) or "foutre le bazar" (informal but less crude).
target_language_example: Arrête de foutre la merde, on essaie de travailler !
native_language_example: Stop causing trouble, we’re trying to work!

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to stop bothering (someone).
additional_notes: Informal and somewhat rude/strong (because of “foutre”). Used to tell someone to stop annoying you, or to say you want to be left alone. Common in the imperative (e.g., “Fous-moi la paix !”), but can also be used with verbs like “laisser” (e.g., “Laisse-moi foutre la paix.”). A more neutral option is “Laisse-moi tranquille.”
target_language_example: Laisse-moi foutre la paix, je travaille.
native_language_example: Leave me alone, I’m working.

meaning: to scare the hell out of (someone); to really frighten.
additional_notes: Very informal (and a bit vulgar because of "foutre"). Usually used with an indirect object pronoun: "Ça m’a foutre la trouille" / "Il lui a foutre la trouille" (in practice you’ll most often hear the past participle form: "a foutu la trouille"). Used for a sudden, strong fright.
target_language_example: Ce film va te foutre la trouille.
native_language_example: That movie is going to scare the hell out of you.

meaning: to get out / leave (very informal, can be rude: “clear off!”).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French but vulgar because of the verb « foutre ». Often used to tell someone to leave (as an order, typically conjugated: « Fous le camp ! » / « Foutez le camp ! »), but it can also describe a situation that’s falling apart or going wrong: « Tout a commencé à foutre le camp » = “Everything started to go to hell / fall apart.”
target_language_example: Il me semble que vous devriez foutre le camp.
native_language_example: It seems to me that you should get out / leave.

meaning: to really scare (someone); to freak (someone) out.
additional_notes: Very informal and a bit vulgar because of "foutre". Commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: "Tu me fous les jetons" (You’re freaking me out) / "Ça me fout les jetons" (That really scares me). Stronger and slangier than "faire peur".
target_language_example: Ce film va te foutre les jetons !
native_language_example: That movie is going to really freak you out!

additional_notes: Used with a subject (often “quelqu’un”) to say there is a knock at the door. You can also ask “Qui frappe à la porte ?” (“Who’s knocking at the door?”). The verb is *frapper* (“to knock/strike”), and *à la porte* means “at the door.”
target_language_example: Quelqu’un frappe à la porte : tu peux ouvrir ?
native_language_example: Someone’s knocking at the door: can you open it?

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "frapper à la porte" (= to knock at/on the door). It’s used when you want to say someone knocked, often before entering or to get someone’s attention. You can add details like how long: "pendant cinq minutes" (for five minutes).
target_language_example: J’ai frappé à la porte, mais personne n’a répondu.
native_language_example: I knocked on the door, but nobody answered.

additional_notes: Common idiom used to emphasize that it’s extremely cold (often said about the weather or a place). It’s informal/colloquial and is often used with « Il fait un froid de canard ! » or as an exclamation: « Quel froid de canard ! ».
target_language_example: Mets ton manteau : dehors, c’est un froid de canard !
native_language_example: Put on your coat—it's freezing cold outside!

additional_notes: Means cheese made from goat’s milk. Often used after verbs like aimer/détester/préférer, or when listing types of cheese (du fromage de chèvre). You can compare it with other cheeses: fromage de vache (cow’s cheese) / fromage de lait de vache (cheese made from cow’s milk).
target_language_example: Je prends une salade avec du fromage de chèvre.
native_language_example: I’ll have a salad with goat cheese.

additional_notes: Most often used in the plural: « fruits de mer ». Common on menus and in expressions like « plateau de fruits de mer » (a seafood platter). It generally refers to shellfish (oysters, mussels, shrimp, etc.) rather than fish.
target_language_example: Ce fruit de mer est très frais.
native_language_example: This seafood item is very fresh.

meaning: seafood (shellfish and other things from the sea).
additional_notes: Usually used as an uncountable category in French: manger des fruits de mer = “to eat seafood.” Often includes shellfish like shrimp, mussels, oysters, etc. Common with partitives/articles like des, les, and with acheter/vendre/manger.
target_language_example: On a commandé des fruits de mer au restaurant.
native_language_example: We ordered seafood at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Means your siblings as a group. It’s also used as a form of address to a group (often in religious contexts): « Bien chers frères et sœurs ! » = “Dear brothers and sisters!” (like “dear friends”).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas de frères et sœurs, je suis enfant unique.
native_language_example: I don't have any brothers or sisters; I'm an only child.

additional_notes: Used in formal writing, literature, and historical narration. "Fut" is the passé simple (simple past) of "être" for "il/elle/on"; in everyday conversation, French usually uses "a été" instead. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun or adjective+noun ("fut une" for feminine).
target_language_example: Ce fut un moment décisif pour l'équipe.
native_language_example: It was a decisive moment for the team.

additional_notes: Uses the literary past tense (passé simple) of *être*: *fut* = “was.” You’ll mostly see it in formal writing (emails/letters) or in literature. In everyday speech, people usually say *Ça a été un plaisir de…* or *C’était un plaisir de…*.
target_language_example: Ce fut un plaisir de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to meet you.

additional_notes: “Fut” is the passé simple (historic/literary past) of être (“to be”), used mostly in books, formal writing, and storytelling rather than everyday conversation. “Une” is used because what follows is feminine (une étudiante, une surprise, une réussite, etc.). In everyday spoken French, you’ll usually see/hear “a été une” instead.
target_language_example: Dans le roman, elle fut une héroïne inattendue.
native_language_example: In the novel, she was an unexpected heroine.

meaning: livelihood; the work that provides your income.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the job or activity that lets someone earn a living. Often appears with possessives (mon/son/leur gagne-pain) and in the plural when many people lose their source of income (perdre son gagne-pain / perdre ses gagne-pain).
target_language_example: Il ne veut pas changer de métier : c’est son gagne-pain.
native_language_example: He doesn’t want to change jobs: it’s his livelihood.

meaning: To save time; to buy yourself time.
additional_notes: Literally “to win time.” Very common with "faire" ("faire gagner du temps à quelqu’un" = to save someone time). You can also use it on its own: "On va gagner du temps" (We’ll save time).
target_language_example: Si on prend le métro, on va gagner du temps.
native_language_example: If we take the metro, we’ll save time.

meaning: to gain ground; to make progress (often by getting an advantage).
additional_notes: Used literally (e.g., an army advancing) or figuratively (an idea becoming more popular, a business increasing market share, someone improving in a competition). Often followed by "sur" + someone/something (gagner du terrain sur ses concurrents).
target_language_example: Notre équipe commence à gagner du terrain sur ses concurrents depuis le début de la saison.
native_language_example: Our team has started to gain ground on its competitors since the start of the season.

meaning: to earn a living; to make a living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone supports themselves financially (usually through a job). Often appears with verbs like « devoir » (must), « pouvoir » (can), or questions like « Que fais-tu pour gagner ta vie ? ». The possessive changes with the subject: gagner ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur vie.
target_language_example: Elle travaille la nuit pour gagner sa vie.
native_language_example: She works at night to earn a living.

meaning: wardrobe; closet; (by extension) your clothes (your wardrobe).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a closet/wardrobe where you store clothes: «dans la garde-robe». It can also mean your whole collection of clothes: «toute ma garde-robe». In some contexts (e.g., theater/film), «la garde-robe» can also refer to the costume/wardrobe department.
target_language_example: Je dois ranger ma garde-robe ce week-end.
native_language_example: I have to tidy up my closet/wardrobe this weekend.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a person whose job is to protect someone (often a celebrity, politician, etc.). Gender/number can vary: un garde du corps (most common), une garde du corps (also used, especially if the bodyguard is a woman), des gardes du corps (plural). Often used with possessives: mon/ton/son garde du corps.
target_language_example: Le chanteur se déplace toujours avec un garde du corps.
native_language_example: The singer always travels with a bodyguard.

meaning: police custody; being held by the police for questioning.
additional_notes: Used in legal/police contexts. Most often you’ll see it with être en garde à vue (to be in police custody) or être placé en garde à vue (to be taken/placed into police custody). It refers to a temporary measure during an investigation, not a prison sentence.
target_language_example: Elle a été placée en garde à vue après son interrogatoire.
native_language_example: She was taken into police custody after her questioning.

meaning: “Keep an eye on” (watch, look after, monitor).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to watch a person/thing for a while (to make sure they’re safe, don’t leave, or nothing bad happens). Common in everyday requests and warnings. Imperative form: « Garde un œil sur … ». Other conjugations exist (e.g., « Je garde un œil sur … »).
target_language_example: Garde un œil sur ton portefeuille !
native_language_example: Keep an eye on your wallet!

meaning: to keep watch; to keep an eye out.
additional_notes: Means staying alert and watching for something. In modern usage, more common forms are « garder l’œil ouvert » (stay alert/keep your eyes open) and « garder un œil sur + [quelqu’un/quelque chose] » (keep an eye on). « garder l'œil » on its own may sound a bit incomplete without context.
target_language_example: Quand tu es à la terrasse, garde l'œil sur ton sac.
native_language_example: When you’re sitting at the café terrace, keep an eye on your bag.

meaning: 'to stay on course' / 'to stay on track' (keep pursuing the same goal).
additional_notes: Used both literally (a boat/plane keeps its heading) and figuratively (keep the same direction/plan despite difficulties). Often used with "il faut" or "on doit" to encourage perseverance: "Il faut garder le cap."
target_language_example: Malgré les difficultés, on doit garder le cap.
native_language_example: Despite the difficulties, we have to stay on track.

meaning: to keep quiet; to remain silent.
additional_notes: Used for staying silent on purpose (not speaking). Common with rules/requests (e.g., in class) and can also mean not speaking about something or to someone ("à mon égard" = "toward me / with me").
target_language_example: Merci de garder le silence dans la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: Please keep quiet in the library.

additional_notes: Means not telling other people confidential information. Often used after pouvoir (can) or savoir (know how/know how to) to say you are able to keep something confidential: « Je peux garder un secret » / « Je sais garder un secret ». In questions, « Tu peux… ? » is informal (to a friend) and « Pouvez-vous… ? » is more formal/polite.
target_language_example: Je peux garder un secret.
