The example below contains the exact string « il quelque chose que » only to match the requested term, but it is not grammatical French.
target_language_example: Il quelque chose que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: (Intended) There’s something I have to tell you.

meaning: (nonstandard/incorrect as written) Intended meaning is usually: “there is something that you…”
additional_notes: As written, **il quelque chose que tu…** is not grammatical French and is typically missing **y a**. The correct and very common phrase is **il y a quelque chose que tu…** (“there is something that you…”). If you saw **il quelque chose que tu…** in notes or a transcript, it’s likely a typo or an incomplete chunk.
target_language_example: il quelque chose que tu dois savoir.
native_language_example: (Intended) There’s something you need to know.

meaning: Un fragment non standard qui ressemble à « il y a quelque chose que vous… » = « there is something that you… ».
additional_notes: Tel quel, « il quelque chose que vous » n’est pas grammatical en français : on attend normalement « il y a quelque chose que vous… ». On peut rencontrer ce fragment comme erreur d’apprenant ou comme portion tronquée d’une phrase plus longue. Usage naturel : « Il y a quelque chose que vous devez savoir / que vous pouvez faire / que vous devriez voir », etc.
target_language_example: « il quelque chose que vous » n’est pas correct : on dit plutôt « Il y a quelque chose que vous devez savoir. »
native_language_example: “il quelque chose que vous” is not correct; you usually say “Il y a quelque chose que vous devez savoir.”

meaning: Likely meant: « quoi que ce soit » = “anything / whatever.”
additional_notes: « Il quoi que ce soit » isn’t a correct fixed phrase in French. The useful expression is « quoi que ce soit », which means “anything/whatever” and is very common with negation (ne…pas / ne…plus / ne…jamais): « Je n’ai rien dit, quoi que ce soit » (I didn’t say anything at all). It can also appear after words like « sans » or in questions/conditions: « Y a-t-il quoi que ce soit à manger ? » (Is there anything to eat?). It’s usually not used alone; it fits into a sentence.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il quoi que ce soit que je puisse faire ?
native_language_example: Is there anything I can do?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or a final point after what was just said. Often followed by a full clause (il reste que + subject + verb). Close to: « pourtant », « néanmoins », « malgré tout »; slightly formal/neutral.
target_language_example: On a beaucoup travaillé ; il reste que le résultat n’est pas parfait.
native_language_example: We worked a lot; still, the result isn’t perfect.

meaning: "he" + "s'" (= "se"), used with pronominal/reflexive verbs (often 'himself' or just part of the verb).
additional_notes: “S’” is the shortened form of “se” used before a vowel or silent h: il se → il s’ (il s’habille, il s’approche). It appears with reflexive actions (he dresses himself), reciprocal actions, and many pronominal verbs where “se/s’” is just required in French and isn’t always translated literally (il s’y connaît = he knows about it).
target_language_example: Il s'est levé tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He got up early this morning.

meaning: “it’s about…” / “it’s a question of…” / “it is…” (used to identify what or who is being talked about).
additional_notes: Often used with **de**: **Il s’agit de + noun/infinitive** = “It’s about / it’s a matter of + noun/to…” (Il s’agit d’argent = “It’s about money”). With a person, it commonly appears in **(de) qui il s’agit**: **Je sais de qui il s’agit** = “I know who it is / who you mean.” This expression is impersonal (it doesn’t refer to a specific “he”).
target_language_example: Je sais de qui il s'agit.
native_language_example: I know who it is / who you mean.

meaning: 'it's about' / 'it's a matter of' / 'this is' (used to introduce what something is).
additional_notes: Used mainly in more formal or neutral contexts to specify the subject or nature of something: Il s'agit de + noun (or de + infinitive). It doesn’t mean “it acts” in the normal sense of agir; think of it as “the point is / we’re talking about…”. Often used to clarify: « Il s'agit d'autre chose » = “It’s something else.”
target_language_example: De quoi parle ce document ? Il s'agit d'un contrat.
native_language_example: What is this document about? It's a contract.

meaning: 'it’s about…' / 'it’s a matter of…' / 'this is…' (used to introduce or specify what/who something concerns or is).
additional_notes: Impersonal, fairly formal phrase used to identify or specify the topic/subject. Common in explanations, presentations, and official contexts. Typically followed by a noun/pronoun (Il s’agit de mon fils. = This is my son.) or an infinitive (Il s’agit de comprendre. = The point is to understand.). Less common in casual everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il s'agit de mon fils.
native_language_example: This is my son.

meaning: “he … it/from it” (se + en), used with certain verbs.
additional_notes: “S’en” is the combination of the reflexive pronoun (se → s’, “himself”) + en (“of it / from it,” often replacing “de ça / de…”). It appears in many fixed verb patterns, so you translate the whole verb, not word-by-word. Common ones from your examples: s’en sortir = to manage / get through; s’en prendre à quelqu’un = to take it out on someone / attack someone; s’en occuper = to take care of it; s’en souvenir = to remember it.
target_language_example: Il s'en sortira malgré les difficultés.
native_language_example: He’ll get through it despite the difficulties.

meaning: 'he has' (used with reflexive/pronominal verbs in the past: “he …ed himself/got …”).
additional_notes: This is the start of a reflexive verb in the passé composé: il + se → s’ + être (s’est). It’s followed by a past participle: il s’est excusé (he apologized), il s’est évanoui (he fainted), il s’est disputé (he argued), il s’est moqué (he made fun), il s’est occupé de… (he took care of…). In English you often don’t translate the “se” literally; it just marks the verb as pronominal.
target_language_example: Il s'est levé tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He got up early this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the verb "se passer" (= to happen), used impersonally with "il" as a dummy subject: "Il s'est passé quelque chose" (Something happened), "Il s'est passé beaucoup de choses" (A lot happened). Often followed by "quelque chose", "des choses", "des trucs" (more informal), etc.
target_language_example: Il s'est passé quelque chose d'étrange hier soir.
native_language_example: Something strange happened last night.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to say an event occurred (often implying it was important, unexpected, or unclear). Uses the impersonal subject "il" + the verb "se passer" in the past (passé composé). It can be followed by details: "ici" (here), "d'autre" (something else), or "entre nous / entre vous" (something happened between us/you—often suggesting a personal, romantic, or tense situation).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas tout expliquer, mais il s'est passé quelque chose hier soir.
native_language_example: I can’t explain everything, but something happened last night.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. It uses **se passer** (“to happen”) in the passé composé (**il s'est passé...**) with **quoi** at the end, which is a more informal word order. More neutral/formal versions: **Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?** or **Que s’est-il passé ?**. You can add details after it: **Il s'est passé quoi entre vous ?** (“What happened between you two?”).
target_language_example: Il s'est passé quoi entre vous ?
native_language_example: What happened between you two?

additional_notes: Present tense of **savoir** (il sait). Used for knowing a fact, having information, or knowing how to do something. (For knowing a person/place, French often uses **connaître** instead.) Often followed by a question word: *il sait où/qui/ce que...*
target_language_example: Il sait que tu es ici.
native_language_example: He knows that you are here.

additional_notes: Used before a reflexive or pronominal verb. se is the third-person singular reflexive pronoun. It can sometimes mean "himself," but very often you translate the whole verb expression instead, not se by itself.
target_language_example: Il se lève tôt tous les jours.
native_language_example: He gets up early every day.

additional_notes: This is the passé simple (literary past) of "il se met à". It’s common in written stories, narration, and more formal/literary style. It’s followed by an infinitive: "il se mit à + infinitive" (e.g., "il se mit à pleuvoir" = it started to rain). In everyday speech, you’ll usually see/hear "il s’est mis à" (passé composé) instead.
target_language_example: En entendant la nouvelle, il se mit à pleurer.
native_language_example: On hearing the news, he began to cry.

additional_notes: Past simple (literary/storytelling tense) of "il se met à pleuvoir". Used to describe a sudden beginning of rain, often with time adverbs like "soudain" (suddenly), "tout à coup" (all of a sudden), or "à peine" (hardly). In everyday speech, you’ll more often hear: "il s’est mis à pleuvoir" (it started to rain).
target_language_example: Tout à coup, il se mit à pleuvoir et nous avons couru nous abriter.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, it started to rain and we ran to take shelter.

additional_notes: Used to say that events are happening (often unexpected, strange, or serious). Very common with an indefinite subject like "Il se passe quelque chose…" (Something is happening…) or in a question: "Il se passe quoi ?" (What’s going on?). Here, "il" is an impersonal/dummy subject (it doesn’t refer to a person), and "se passer" means “to happen,” not “to pass.”
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce qu’il se passe ici ?
native_language_example: What’s going on here?

meaning: things are happening (often strange or mysterious).
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "se passer" = "to happen". Very common in storytelling or when you don’t know exactly what’s going on, and it often hints that something unusual is going on ("Il se passe des choses étranges" = "Strange things are happening").
target_language_example: Ne sors pas ce soir : il se passe des choses bizarres dans le quartier.
native_language_example: Don’t go out tonight: strange things are happening in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal "il" (it) with "se passer" (to happen). Often used when you suspect something is happening, sometimes something unusual or important. You can add a place with "ici / à la maison / entre vous".
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il se passe quelque chose dans le bureau.
native_language_example: I think something is going on in the office.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. Literally “what is happening,” using se passer (“to happen”). You can add a place: « Il se passe quoi ici ? » (“What’s happening here?”). In a conditional question it can mean “what happens if…”: « Si je lis pas ça, il se passe quoi ? » (“If I don’t read that, what happens?”). More standard/written: « Que se passe-t-il ? »
target_language_example: Hé, il se passe quoi dehors ?
native_language_example: Hey, what’s going on outside?

additional_notes: Very common and informal because of "un truc" (roughly “a thing / something”). You can use it when you notice an event (“outside”, “around here”) or when there seems to be an unspoken issue/chemistry between people (“entre nous / entre vous”). Often followed by an adjective like "bizarre" or "sérieux".
target_language_example: Il se passe un truc, je ne sais pas quoi.
native_language_example: Something's going on; I don't know what.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It is followed by the subjunctive (e.g., « il se peut que je sois… », « il se peut qu’il vienne… »). Often interchangeable with « il est possible que », though « il se peut que » is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il se peut que nous soyons en retard à cause du trafic.
native_language_example: We might be late because of traffic.

additional_notes: This is the start of the common expression **il se peut que…** (“it may be that…”), used to express uncertainty. It is typically followed by the **subjunctive**: *Il se peut que je sois en retard* (not *je suis*). You can replace **je** with another subject: *il se peut qu’il/elle/nous…*
target_language_example: Il se peut que je sois en retard ce soir.
native_language_example: I might be late tonight.

il se peut que je sois

target_language_multi_word_term: il se peut que je sois
meaning: "I may be…" / "it’s possible that I am…"
additional_notes: Used to express possibility/uncertainty. It is most often part of the structure « Il se peut que + subjunctive », so it’s followed by the subjunctive form « je sois » (not *je suis*). You can then add an adjective or expression (« en retard », « obligé(e) », etc.) or sometimes a past form like « il se peut que je sois parti(e) » (“I may have left for a moment”), where « parti/partie » agrees with the speaker’s gender.
target_language_example: Il se peut que je sois déjà parti quand tu arriveras.
native_language_example: I may already have left when you arrive.

meaning: 'it’s possible that you…' / 'you may…' (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. After "il se peut que", French uses the subjunctive mood (e.g., "vous ayez", "vous fassiez", "vous restiez"). Often translates as "it may be that you…" or simply "you might…" in English.
target_language_example: Il se peut que vous soyez en retard à cause du trafic.
native_language_example: You might be late because of traffic.

meaning: "it might be that" / "it could be that" (expresses possibility).
additional_notes: Used to say something is possible but not certain. It’s fairly formal/neutral, and it is normally followed by the subjunctive: « Il se pourrait que ce soit… », « …que tu aies… », « …que vous soyez… ».
target_language_example: Il se pourrait que le train ait du retard.
native_language_example: The train might be late.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective (bien, fatigué, heureux, faible, blessé) or sometimes with a noun phrase to talk about someone’s physical or emotional state. It comes from the reflexive verb « se sentir » (to feel). In English you usually just say “he feels …”.
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, il se sent mieux.
native_language_example: Today, he feels better.

meaning: "he was standing" / "he was positioned" (was staying in a certain posture or place).
additional_notes: Imperfect of the verb "se tenir" (reflexive). Used to describe someone’s posture or where they were located for a period of time. It’s often followed by details like "debout" (standing up), "contre" (against), or a place/distance: "à quelques mètres de moi" (a few meters from me).
target_language_example: Il se tenait près de la porte et attendait en silence.
native_language_example: He was standing near the door and waiting in silence.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a fact (often unexpected or relevant to the situation), similar to “it so happens that…”. It’s followed by a clause with que: « Il se trouve que + [subject] + [verb] ». It can also be used as a short reply: « Il se trouve que oui/non » (“It turns out yes/no”).
target_language_example: Il se trouve que j’ai déjà réservé une table.
native_language_example: It turns out I already booked a table.

additional_notes: Used to express an impression or something that appears true (often with some uncertainty). It can be personal ("Il semble heureux" = "He seems happy") or impersonal with "il semble que + subjunctive" ("Il semble que ça ait cours..." = "It seems that it's common..."). With negation and infinitives, you often see: "Il semble ne pas..." / "Il semble ne rien...".
target_language_example: Il semble que le train soit en retard.
native_language_example: It seems that the train is late.

additional_notes: Used to express an impression or conclusion based on what you see/know, not full certainty. Often followed by the subjunctive in more formal French (e.g., « Il semble que Jeanne ait… »), but in everyday speech you may hear the indicative (« Il semble que Jeanne a… »). Can also be shortened to « Il semble que oui/non » (“it seems so/not”).
target_language_example: Il semble que le train ait du retard.
native_language_example: It seems that the train is delayed.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future state/identity/quality: *Il sera là* (he’ll be there), *Il sera un bon mari* (he’ll be a good husband). With negation, standard French is *Il ne sera pas…* (often spoken as *Il sera pas…*). Also appears in impersonal/passive-style phrases like *Il sera exigé de vous…* = “You will be required to…”.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il sera prêt demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’ll be ready tomorrow.

meaning: "you just need to" / "all you have to do is".
additional_notes: Used to say that something is enough to achieve a result, often implying it’s easy or requires only that one action. Structure: il suffit de + infinitive (Il suffit d’appeler). Can also be followed by "pour" + infinitive to state the purpose: Il suffit d’appuyer ici pour commencer.
target_language_example: Pour ouvrir la porte, il suffit de tourner la clé.
native_language_example: To open the door, you just have to turn the key.

additional_notes: Contraction of "il te a" → "il t'a" before a vowel sound. Common in the passé composé: "il t'a parlé" = "he spoke to you" / "he has spoken to you"; "il t'a fait quelque chose ?" = "did he do something to you?" The meaning depends on the past participle that follows (parlé, posé, fait, etc.).
target_language_example: Il t'a envoyé un message hier soir.
native_language_example: He sent you a message last night.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *dire*: **il a dit** = “he said/told”. **t'** is short for **te** (“to you”). Often used in questions with rising intonation: **Il t'a dit ?** = “Did he tell you?” You can add what was said with **que...** (“that...”) or ask for details: **Il t'a dit quoi ?** (“What did he tell you?”).
target_language_example: Il t'a dit quand il arrive ?
native_language_example: Did he tell you when he’s arriving?

additional_notes: A common pronoun pattern: il means "he" or "it", and te means "you" as an object. The exact English translation depends on the verb, for example il te parle = "he's talking to you" and il te voit = "he sees you".
target_language_example: Il te montre la photo.
native_language_example: He's showing you the photo.

additional_notes: Impersonal structure with the verb *falloir*: **il faut** + indirect object (**te**) + infinitive. It expresses necessity/requirement and is a bit more emphatic than *tu dois* in some contexts. Often followed by an infinitive: *Il te faut partir*, *Il te faut étudier*.
target_language_example: Il te faut dormir un peu si tu veux être en forme demain.
native_language_example: You need to sleep a bit if you want to be in shape tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the impersonal verb « falloir » (necessity): literally “it is necessary for you.” Used to say someone needs something (Il te faut du repos), or to ask how much/how long is needed (Il te faut combien ? / Il te faut combien de temps ?). Often followed by a noun; with a verb you use « il te faut + infinitive » (e.g., Il te faut partir).
target_language_example: Pour demain, il te faut ton passeport.
native_language_example: For tomorrow, you need your passport.

meaning: you need a / you’ll need a (masculine noun).
additional_notes: Built with the verb "falloir" (impersonal): "il faut" = "it’s necessary / you have to". With an indirect object pronoun, it means what someone needs: "il me faut…" (I need…), "il te faut…" (you need…), "il lui faut…" (he/she needs…), etc. Use "un" before a masculine singular noun; use "une" for feminine ("il te faut une voiture"). Often used as advice/requirement: "Il te faut un super mécano" = "You’ll need a great mechanic."
target_language_example: Pour ce job, il te faut un bon CV.
native_language_example: For this job, you need a good CV.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that something is pleasing to someone (with the verb "plaire" = "to please"). It often refers to a thing, idea, name, etc.: « Il te plaît, ce nom ? » = “Do you like that name?” Don’t confuse with « s’il te plaît » (with s’), which means “please” (as in a polite request).
target_language_example: Ce cadeau, il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Do you like this gift?

additional_notes: "Il" = "he" and "travaille" is the present tense of "travailler" (to work). Use it to talk about someone's job, where they work ("Il travaille dans un hôpital"), what field they work in ("dans le domaine de..."), or how much they work ("du matin au soir" = all day; "à peine" = barely/hardly).
target_language_example: Il travaille aujourd'hui, donc il ne peut pas venir.
native_language_example: He's working today, so he can't come.

additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive to express the near future: il va partir = 'he's going to leave'. Here il can mean 'he' or an impersonal 'it'. In il va y avoir, the full expression means 'there is/are going to be'.
target_language_example: Il va pleuvoir ce soir.
native_language_example: It's going to rain tonight.

meaning: "he/it is going to do/make"; also "the weather is going to be" (talking about weather).
additional_notes: This is the futur proche: aller (il va) + infinitive (faire) to talk about something that’s going to happen soon. "Il" can mean "he" (about a person) or an impersonal "it" (especially with weather: "Il va faire quel temps ?" = "What’s the weather going to be like?"). In questions you’ll often see: "Il va faire quoi ?" (What’s he going to do?) and "Il va faire quel temps ?" (What will the weather be like?).
target_language_example: Demain, il va faire beau, alors on va sortir.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it’s going to be nice out, so we’re going to go out.

meaning: "we're going to have to" / "it will be necessary to" (soon).
additional_notes: Impersonal expression using the near future of falloir ("to be necessary"). It means that something must be done, often implying obligation or necessity. Common patterns: il va falloir + infinitive (Il va falloir attendre.) and il va falloir que + subjunctive (Il va falloir que tu viennes.).
target_language_example: Il va falloir partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We’re going to have to leave now.

meaning: “(someone) is going to have to …” / “it will be necessary to …”.
additional_notes: Common way to express upcoming necessity/obligation. It’s the near future of the impersonal verb falloir (“to be necessary”): il va falloir + que + subjunctive (Il va falloir que je parle, que tu acceptes, etc.). The person who must do it appears after que.
target_language_example: Il va falloir que nous partions bientôt.
native_language_example: We’re going to have to leave soon.

additional_notes: Used to predict upcoming rain. Very common with a time marker like "demain" (tomorrow), "ce soir" (tonight), or "dans la soirée" (later in the evening). "Il" here is an impersonal subject (it doesn’t refer to a person).
target_language_example: Prends un parapluie : il va pleuvoir.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella: it’s going to rain.

meaning: “something is going to happen” / “it’s about to happen.”
additional_notes: Built with the near future: "aller" (va) + "se passer" (to happen). Often used with "quelque chose" to suggest an event is coming soon, sometimes with worry or anticipation: "Il va se passer quelque chose (de grave)." Common in questions too: "Il va se passer quoi ?" = "What’s going to happen?"
target_language_example: Il va se passer quelque chose, je le sens.
native_language_example: Something is going to happen, I can feel it.

meaning: “there is/are going to be” (there will be).
additional_notes: Very common way to say something will happen/exist soon. Built from "il va" (it is going to) + "y avoir" (to be/there to be). The thing that will exist comes after: "Il va y avoir + noun". Often used with quantities: "beaucoup de…", "des…", "de l’…".
target_language_example: Il va y avoir un problème si on arrive en retard.
native_language_example: There’s going to be a problem if we arrive late.

additional_notes: An impersonal expression used to give advice or say what is preferable. Often followed by an infinitive (Il vaut mieux partir.) or by "que" + subjunctive (Il vaut mieux que je reste.).
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux que tu prennes un taxi.
native_language_example: You’d better take a taxi.

additional_notes: Used to recommend the best option or warn someone. It’s impersonal ("il" doesn’t refer to a person). It is usually followed by the subjunctive: « Il vaut mieux que tu restes ici. » / « Il vaut mieux que je vous parle franchement. » You can make it negative: « Il vaut mieux que tu ne le saches pas. »
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux que nous partions maintenant.
native_language_example: We’d better leave now.

meaning: "I'd better…" / "it's better that I…" (introduces what you should do).
additional_notes: Used to give advice or express preference about your own action: "Il vaut mieux que je + verb (subjunctive)". Common with verbs like "parte" (leave), "fasse" (do), "reste" (stay). Similar idea to "je ferais mieux de…" (I should…).
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux que je parte maintenant.
native_language_example: I'd better leave now.

additional_notes: From vouloir. Used to say what a man or boy wants, plans, or wishes for. It is often followed by an infinitive verb (il veut partir = he wants to leave) or by que + another clause (il veut qu'on vienne = he wants us to come).
target_language_example: Il veut apprendre le français.
native_language_example: He wants to learn French.

additional_notes: From the verb « venir » (to come). It can describe movement toward someone/something (« Il vient droit vers le pont. »). Very common patterns: « il vient de + place » = he comes from (« Il vient d'une ferme… »); « il vient de + infinitive » = he has just done something (« Il vient d'entrer… », « Il vient juste de te donner… »); « il vient voir + quelqu’un » = he comes to see someone (« Il vient me voir… »).
target_language_example: Il vient avec nous ce soir.
native_language_example: He’s coming with us tonight.

meaning: "he comes from" or "he has just (done something)".
additional_notes: 1) With a place/person/thing after it, it means origin: « Il vient de Gênes. » = he comes from Genoa. 2) With an infinitive (verb) after it, « venir de + infinitif » expresses the recent past: « Il vient de prier. » = he just prayed / he has just prayed. The subject can change (je/tu/il/elle/on/nous/vous/ils) but the structure stays the same.
target_language_example: Il vient de finir ses devoirs.
native_language_example: He has just finished his homework.

additional_notes: "Il" = "he" and "vit" is the present-tense form of "vivre" (to live). Used to say where someone lives (il vit en ville, il vit au coin), or who they live with (il vit avec ses parents). Note that "vit" is pronounced like "vee" (silent t).
target_language_example: Il vit à Paris depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: He has been living in Paris for three years.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (imparfait): it often describes an ongoing desire in the past, a repeated wish, or a background intention. Very common in questions like « Qu’est-ce qu’il voulait ? » (“What did he want?”) and « Qu’est-ce qu’il voulait dire ? » (“What did he mean?”). With « que + subjunctive »: « Il voulait que… » = “He wanted (that) …”.
target_language_example: Il voulait que je vienne avec lui.
native_language_example: He wanted me to come with him.

additional_notes: Impersonal structure with the verb falloir: "il faut" = "it is necessary". "Il vous faut + infinitive" means "you need/have to + verb" and addresses "vous" (you, formal or plural). In speech you may also hear "il vous faut + noun" (you need + a thing).
target_language_example: Il vous faut être patient pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: You need to be patient to learn French.

additional_notes: Formal way to say something is necessary for “you” (vous). It’s built from falloir (“to be necessary”): il faut + indirect object (vous) + infinitive (être). Adjective agreement changes depending on who is “you” (ex: préparé/préparée/préparés). Less formal alternatives: « vous devez être… », « il faut que vous soyez… ».
target_language_example: Il vous faut être attentifs pendant la visite.
native_language_example: You need to be attentive during the visit.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal verb phrase "il faut" (= it is necessary). "Il vous faut" means "you need" (addressing one person with "vous" or multiple people). It’s followed by an infinitive: "être" (to be), then "davantage" (more), and typically an adjective that agrees with who you’re talking to (ex: organisé/organisée/organisés/organisées; patient/patiente/patients/patientes).
target_language_example: Il vous faut être davantage prudents sur la route.
native_language_example: You need to be more careful on the road.

additional_notes: Built with the impersonal verb « falloir »: « il faut » = “it is necessary / you must”. « Il vous faut… » is a polite/formal way to tell someone what they need to do. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (« être ») and then « plus » + an adjective. The adjective agrees with the person you’re talking to: organisée/patiente/polie (feminine singular), patient/poli (masculine singular), patientes/polies (feminine plural), patients (masculine plural or mixed group).
target_language_example: Pour ce travail, il vous faut être plus attentifs.
native_language_example: For this job, you need to be more attentive.

additional_notes: From the verb "falloir" (impersonal: "il faut"). Used with an object: "il vous faut + noun" = "you need + noun". "vous" is formal singular or plural; informal singular would be "il te faut". Often expresses a requirement or necessity.
target_language_example: Pour entrer, il vous faut une pièce d’identité.
native_language_example: To get in, you need an ID.

additional_notes: Used to be polite when asking for something or giving a polite instruction. Also used on its own to mean “please?” when you didn’t hear/understand, or “you’re welcome” in reply to “merci” (more formal). Often shortened to “s’il vous plaît” (“if you please”).
target_language_example: Un café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: A coffee, please.

additional_notes: This is the subject pronoun il plus y. In sentences like these, y usually means "there" and refers to a place already mentioned: Il y va = "He goes there." y can also mean "to it/them" with some verbs that use à.
target_language_example: Il y va souvent le week-end.
native_language_example: He goes there often on weekends.

additional_notes: Passé composé of the expression "il y a" ("there is/are"). Used to say that something existed or happened in the past, often to report an event: "Il y a eu un accident" (There was an accident). With plural nouns, English usually uses "there were" ("Il y a eu des problèmes" → There were problems). In questions you may hear "Il y a eu quoi ?" meaning "What happened?/What was there?" (quite conversational).
target_language_example: Il y a eu un problème hier soir.
native_language_example: There was a problem last night.

il y a eu beaucoup de

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a eu beaucoup de
meaning: “there were/there has been a lot of …”
additional_notes: Used to say that many people/things/events existed or happened. It’s the past form of “il y a” (there is/there are): present “il y a beaucoup de …” → past “il y a eu beaucoup de …”. “Eu” agrees with nothing here because “avoir” is used impersonally (the subject is “il”). Often followed by a plural noun, but it can also be used with uncountable nouns (e.g., “de la neige” → “beaucoup de neige”).
target_language_example: Il y a eu beaucoup de monde au concert hier soir.
native_language_example: There were a lot of people at the concert last night.

meaning: "there was" / "there were" (there has been) + a noun.
additional_notes: This is the past form of "il y a" (“there is/are”). You use it to say that something happened or existed: "Il y a eu de grandes inondations" = “There were big floods.” With a plural noun preceded by an adjective, French often uses "de" (instead of "des"): "il y a eu de vives réactions". Without an adjective, you’ll usually see "il y a eu des réactions".
target_language_example: Après l’annonce, il y a eu de nombreuses questions.
native_language_example: After the announcement, there were many questions.

additional_notes: Used to report that events, situations, or things occurred/existed in the past. It’s the past tense of "il y a" (there is/are) and is often followed by a plural noun: "Il y a eu des + nom(s)". Very common in news/reporting (e.g., changes, deaths, shootings, repercussions).
target_language_example: Il y a eu des problèmes pendant le vol.
native_language_example: There were some problems during the flight.

meaning: “there was a” / “there has been a” (something happened).
additional_notes: Used to say that an event occurred in the past. It’s the past tense of “il y a” (“there is/are”). Often followed by an event noun (un accident, un mariage, un scandale, un silence). With a specific time expression, it typically means simple past (“there was”); without one, it can translate as “there has been.”
target_language_example: Hier soir, il y a eu un accident sur l’autoroute.
native_language_example: Last night, there was an accident on the highway.

il y a eu un tremblement de terre

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a eu un tremblement de terre
additional_notes: Uses the past tense of « il y a » (il y a eu = “there was/there were”) to report that an event happened. « un tremblement de terre » means “an earthquake.” Often followed by a time (hier, ce matin) or a place (au Pérou).
target_language_example: Il y a eu un tremblement de terre cette nuit, mais personne n’a été blessé.
native_language_example: There was an earthquake last night, but nobody was hurt.

meaning: 'there was a' / 'there has been a' (something happened).
additional_notes: Past tense of "il y a" used to report that an event occurred. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (une enquête, une explosion). With a masculine noun, you’d use "il y a eu un". Common in news-style descriptions of events.
target_language_example: Il y a eu une panne de courant hier soir.
native_language_example: There was a power outage last night.

additional_notes: Very common fixed expression. Most often it introduces something that exists or is present: il y a un livre sur la table = there is a book on the table. It is used for both singular and plural. Before a length of time, it means 'ago': il y a deux ans = two years ago.
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de monde ici.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people here.

additional_notes: Used to add another item to a list or mention an extra thing that exists/is available. Often followed directly by a noun phrase (Il y a aussi un cadeau...), and it can refer to something in a specific place when you add a location (Il y a aussi mes photos, chez ma mère).
target_language_example: Il y a aussi une boulangerie près d'ici.
native_language_example: There’s also a bakery near here.

additional_notes: Used with "il y a" (= "there is/there are") to say there’s an additional thing, fact, or issue to mention or check. Often followed by "que..." to add details: "Il y a autre chose que tu devrais savoir." In a question ("Il y a autre chose ?"), it means “Is there anything else?”
target_language_example: Il y a autre chose dont je dois m'occuper ?
native_language_example: Is there anything else I need to take care of?

additional_notes: Used with a noun: « Il y a beaucoup de + nom » (Il y a beaucoup de travail.). It can also stand alone: « Il y a beaucoup en jeu » (“a lot is at stake”), or be followed by an infinitive with « à »: « Il y a beaucoup à faire » (“there’s a lot to do”).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, il y a beaucoup de monde au musée.
native_language_example: Today, there are a lot of people at the museum.

additional_notes: Used to say that a large number/amount of something exists or is present. With a noun: « Il y a beaucoup de + nom » (e.g., beaucoup de touristes). With an uncountable idea like space, you can say « Il y a beaucoup de place » (“There is plenty of room”). After « beaucoup de », the noun is usually plural unless it’s uncountable.
target_language_example: Dans cette ville, il y a beaucoup de restaurants.
native_language_example: In this city, there are a lot of restaurants.

il y a beaucoup de choses

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a beaucoup de choses
meaning: “there are many things / a lot of things.”
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal expression “il y a” (“there is/are”) + “beaucoup de” (“a lot of”) + “choses” (“things”). Often followed by a relative clause with “qui/que/dont” to add details: “Il y a beaucoup de choses que…”, “Il y a beaucoup de choses dont…”. “Beaucoup de” stays the same for singular/plural nouns (unlike “many”).
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de choses à apprendre quand on commence le français.
native_language_example: There are a lot of things to learn when you start French.

il y a beaucoup de choses que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a beaucoup de choses que
additional_notes: Used to introduce a list or idea of many tasks, items, or questions that follow. It’s the pattern: il y a (there is/are) + beaucoup de choses (many things) + que + subject + verb. With "que", the next clause describes the things (e.g., things I need to do/buy/ask).
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de choses que je dois finir avant demain.
native_language_example: There are many things that I need to finish before tomorrow.

il y a beaucoup de fleurs

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a beaucoup de fleurs
additional_notes: Uses the common structure “il y a” (“there is/there are”) + “beaucoup de” (“a lot of/many”) + a noun. You can swap in other nouns (Il y a beaucoup de monde = There are lots of people) or add adjectives after the noun (Il y a beaucoup de fleurs rouges = There are many red flowers).
target_language_example: Au printemps, il y a beaucoup de fleurs dans ce parc.
native_language_example: In spring, there are lots of flowers in this park.

il y a beaucoup de gens

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a beaucoup de gens
additional_notes: Used to say that many people are present somewhere. Often followed by a place: “Il y a beaucoup de gens + dans/à/sur…”. You can also use it by itself (“Il y a beaucoup de gens.”) to mean it’s crowded.
target_language_example: Le week-end, il y a beaucoup de gens au marché.
native_language_example: On weekends, there are a lot of people at the market.

meaning: 'there is indeed / surely there is' (or, with time: '... ago (really/a long time)').
additional_notes: Built on **il y a** (“there is/are” or “... ago”) plus **bien** to add emphasis/assurance. Often used to confirm something exists (**Il y a bien un problème.**) or in a confirming question (**Il y a bien un service de livraison ?** = “There *is* a delivery service, right?”). With time expressions it intensifies the duration: **il y a bien longtemps** = “a very long time ago.”
target_language_example: Il y a bien une solution, ne t’inquiète pas.
native_language_example: There is definitely a solution, don’t worry.

additional_notes: Used to say that more alternatives exist. It’s typically followed by a plural noun: « Il y a d'autres options. » (There are other options.) You can also use it without a noun when it’s understood from context: « Il y en a d'autres. » (There are others.)
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : il y a d'autres possibilités.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are other possibilities.

meaning: "there are / there is" + "some" (often before a noun, especially with an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to say that something exists/is present. With plural nouns, you often see "il y a des ..." (there are some ...), but it frequently becomes "il y a de + adjective + plural noun": "Il y a de jolies maisons". You also see it in common phrases like "Il y a de fortes/grandes chances" (= there’s a good chance / it’s quite likely). In "ce qu’il y a de mieux", it means “the best there is / the best possible.”
target_language_example: Il y a de bonnes raisons de partir tôt.
native_language_example: There are good reasons to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to state that water is present somewhere ("Il y a de l'eau ici / partout"). "De l'" is the partitive article meaning "some". In a question, intonation or "Est-ce qu'il y a de l'eau ?". In the negative, it usually becomes "Il n'y a pas d'eau."
target_language_example: Attention, il y a de l'eau par terre.
native_language_example: Careful, there’s water on the floor.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation still has a chance to improve or work out. You can add "pour + noun/pronoun" to mean "there is hope for ..." (e.g., "il y a de l'espoir pour lui").
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : il y a de l'espoir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there is hope.

additional_notes: Used to say that some amount of something exists or is present. It’s the “there is” structure (il y a) + a partitive article (de la) for feminine singular nouns that are treated as an uncountable substance or abstract idea: de la peinture, de la magie, de la force. With masculine singular it becomes "il y a du" (du feu), and with plural "il y a des".
target_language_example: Il y a de la neige sur la route.
native_language_example: There is some snow on the road.

additional_notes: Used to say that many things exist/are present. "De nombreuses" agrees with a feminine plural noun (e.g., chansons, explications, façons, rivières). With masculine plural nouns, use "il y a de nombreux" (e.g., de nombreux problèmes).
target_language_example: Il y a de nombreuses raisons de partir tôt.
native_language_example: There are many reasons to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to say that many of something exist or are present. It’s the phrase "il y a" (there is/are) + "de nombreux" (many) before a plural noun. "De nombreux" agrees with the noun: masculine plural "de nombreux" (parcs), feminine plural "de nombreuses" (animaux → masculine, but "de nombreuses choses").
target_language_example: Il y a de nombreux restaurants dans ce quartier.
native_language_example: There are many restaurants in this neighborhood.

meaning: “there’s enough / there’s something to …”; also “there’s reason to …”
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say there is enough of something or what’s needed to do it (Il y a de quoi manger = there’s something to eat / enough to eat). It can also mean there’s a good reason to feel a certain way (Il y a de quoi avoir peur / être fier = there’s reason to be scared / proud). On its own (Il y a de quoi.), it can mean “That’s true / fair enough” or “There’s plenty (of it),” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il y a de quoi manger pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, there’s enough to eat for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to say that multiple things exist or are present. It’s the plural form of "il y a" + "des" (= "some" or plural "a/an"). Often followed by a plural noun: "Il y a des + noun". In negative sentences, "des" usually becomes "de": "Il n’y a pas de…".
target_language_example: Il y a des restaurants ouverts près d’ici.
native_language_example: There are some restaurants open near here.

meaning: years ago; a long time ago.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened several years in the past, often to emphasize that it was quite a long time ago. It can stand alone (Il y a des années !) or be followed by de cela / de ça (“ago / back then”).
target_language_example: On s’est rencontrés il y a des années, mais je me souviens encore de toi.
native_language_example: We met years ago, but I still remember you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or point out items, ideas, or facts in a general way. It’s often followed by an adjective (Il y a des choses importantes…), or by a relative clause with qui/que (Il y a des choses qui… / Il y a des choses que…).
target_language_example: Il y a des choses que je ne comprends pas.
native_language_example: There are things I don’t understand.

il y a des choses que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a des choses que
additional_notes: Used to introduce an unspecified list of actions, facts, or information, followed by a relative clause with "que" (often with "je/tu/vous" + verb): "Il y a des choses que je dois faire" = "There are things I have to do." You can change the subject and verb after "que" depending on who is doing/knowing/wanting the things.
target_language_example: Il y a des choses que nous devons discuter.
native_language_example: There are things we need to discuss.

additional_notes: Built from il y a (“there is/there are”) + des gens (“people/some people”). Use it to say that people are present in a place (Il y a des gens à l’intérieur.) or to make a general statement about certain people (Il y a des gens qui… = “There are people who…”). Note: you usually don’t say *il y a les gens*; for “the people” you’d use other structures (e.g., Les gens sont…).
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui parlent anglais ici ?
native_language_example: Are there people who speak English here?

il y a des gens qui

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a des gens qui
additional_notes: Used to introduce the idea that some people do a certain thing or have a certain belief. Very common for general statements; it’s followed by a verb clause (e.g., il y a des gens qui + verb). Often implies “some people” rather than all people.
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui n’aiment pas le café.
native_language_example: Some people don’t like coffee.

additional_notes: With a time unit, it means “two [days/weeks/months/years] ago”: Il y a deux mois. With a noun, it means “there are two …”: Il y a deux voitures. Often followed by a plural noun or a time unit.
target_language_example: Je l’ai rencontré il y a deux ans.
native_language_example: I met him two years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often comes at the beginning or end of a sentence. The full pattern is "il y a + duration" (e.g., il y a trois jours = three days ago).
target_language_example: J'ai commencé ce travail il y a deux ans.
native_language_example: I started this job two years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It can come at the end of the sentence (Elle a disparu il y a deux jours.) or at the beginning (Il y a deux jours, ...).
target_language_example: On s'est vus il y a deux jours.
native_language_example: We saw each other two days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often comes at the end of the sentence (e.g., « Je suis parti il y a deux mois. ») but can also be placed earlier. « Il y a… » + a time period (un jour, une semaine, deux ans, etc.) means “... ago.”
target_language_example: On s'est rencontrés il y a deux mois.
native_language_example: We met two months ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long before now something happened. It often comes at the end of the sentence: « Je suis arrivé il y a deux semaines. ». More generally, « il y a + length of time » means “... ago” (il y a trois jours = three days ago).
target_language_example: On a déménagé il y a deux semaines.
native_language_example: We moved two weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It’s built from "il y a" (there is/ago) + a time expression; you can swap in other times (il y a deux jours, il y a trois semaines, il y a un an). Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Je l’ai vu il y a dix ans."
target_language_example: J’ai commencé le français il y a dix ans.
native_language_example: I started French ten years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that some amount of something is present. It’s the phrase “il y a” (“there is/are”) + the partitive article: du (masc. singular), de la (fem. singular), de l’ (before a vowel/h), or des (plural). Often used for things you can’t easily count (work, fog, noise, sun, frost, movement, etc.).
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, il y a du vent.
native_language_example: Today, there is some wind.

meaning: there’s something new; there are updates/news
additional_notes: Uses the partitive "du" (some) + "nouveau" (new) to mean “something new (to report).” Often said when there’s been a change or you have new information: "Il y a du nouveau ?" = “Any news?”
target_language_example: Il y a du nouveau : le rendez-vous est reporté à demain.
native_language_example: There’s news: the appointment has been moved to tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report the presence of blood, often in a medical context. "Il y a" means "there is/are" and "du sang" means "(some) blood" (partitive: an unspecified amount). You can add where the blood is: "dans mes urines" (in my urine), "dans mes selles" (in my stool), "dans mon vomi" (in my vomit), or "dessus" (on it).
target_language_example: Il y a du sang sur mon pansement.
native_language_example: There is blood on my bandage.

additional_notes: Used to say something still exists/is present, or that there are additional things left. Often followed by a noun: "Il y a encore des problèmes" (There are still problems). In questions like "Qu'est-ce qu'il y a encore ?", it means "What is it now?/What else is there?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a encore du travail à faire.
native_language_example: There’s still work to do.

meaning: "there are still some" / "there are some left".
additional_notes: Used to say that some items still exist or remain available. Often followed by a plural noun: "Il y a encore des billets" (There are still tickets). It can also mean "there are more ..." in the sense that additional ones exist beyond what was expected.
target_language_example: Il y a encore des places pour ce soir.
native_language_example: There are still seats available for tonight.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate number, amount, distance, or time. With a quantity: « Il y a environ 30 personnes » = there are about 30 people. With a time expression: « Il y a environ une heure/un an » = about an hour/a year ago.
target_language_example: Il y a environ vingt minutes, j’ai envoyé un message.
native_language_example: About twenty minutes ago, I sent a message.

additional_notes: Used with a definite noun (le/la/les) to point out that something exists or to introduce an item in a list or sequence (often like “first, there’s…”). The article changes with gender/number: il y a le musée, il y a la facture, il y a les billets.
target_language_example: Dans ce prix, il y a le petit-déjeuner.
native_language_example: In this price, there’s breakfast included.

meaning: a long time ago; for a long time (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the structure "il y a + time" to mean "... ago" (e.g., il y a deux jours = two days ago). With "longtemps", it often means "a long time ago" and can also suggest something should have happened earlier ("You should have told me a long time ago").
target_language_example: Je ne l’ai pas vu depuis longtemps : je l’ai rencontré il y a longtemps.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him in a long time: I met him a long time ago.

additional_notes: Used to point out that something exists or is present in a specific place or in what was just mentioned. Often followed by a noun: "Il y a là un problème" = "There’s a problem there / in that." Slightly formal/literary compared to plain "il y a".
target_language_example: Il y a là une contradiction.
native_language_example: There’s a contradiction there.

meaning: "there is no / there are no" (there isn’t any).
additional_notes: Informal spoken form of "il n’y a pas de" (dropping "ne"). Used to say something doesn’t exist or isn’t available. It’s followed by a noun without an article: "Il y a pas de budget" = “There’s no budget.” In more careful French (writing, formal situations), use "Il n’y a pas de…".
target_language_example: Désolé, il y a pas de place pour ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, there are no seats left for tonight.

meaning: there is/are little; not much; not many.
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say a small quantity exists or is available. With countable nouns (plural): “not many” (Il y a peu de chiens). With uncountable nouns: “not much” (Il y a peu de lait). Often implies “fewer than expected,” but can be neutral.
target_language_example: Il y a peu de temps avant le départ.
native_language_example: There isn't much time before departure.

additional_notes: Used to suggest a possibility that something exists. "Il y a" means "there is/are"; adding "peut-être" softens it to an uncertain guess ("maybe"). Often followed by a noun phrase like "quelque chose", "une solution", "un meilleur moyen".
target_language_example: Il y a peut-être une erreur dans ce document.
native_language_example: There might be a mistake in this document.

meaning: 'there are lots of' / 'there is plenty of'.
additional_notes: Uses the structure "il y a" (there is/are) + "plein de" (lots of/plenty of) + noun. Very common in spoken French to mean "a lot of"; can sound a bit informal compared with "beaucoup de". The noun after "de" is usually plural ("plein de choses"), but you can also use it with an uncountable idea like "plein de place" (plenty of space).
target_language_example: Il y a plein de bons restaurants dans ce quartier.
native_language_example: There are lots of good restaurants in this neighborhood.

meaning: “more than … ago” or “there’s more / there are more.”
additional_notes:
Common uses:
1) Time: "il y a plus de + duration" = “more than + duration ago” (e.g., "il y a plus d’un mois").
2) Adding information or comparing: "Et il y a plus." = “And there’s more.” / "Il y a plus important / plus grave" = “There’s something more important / more serious.” In these comparisons, "plus" is usually followed by an adjective or idea that’s being emphasized.
target_language_example: Il y a plus de deux ans, j’habitais à Lyon, et il y a plus : j’y retourne bientôt.
native_language_example: More than two years ago, I lived in Lyon—and there’s more: I’m going back soon.

meaning: 'there are more than' / 'there is more than'.
additional_notes: Used to say a quantity is greater than another quantity ("plus de + noun") or greater than a number ("plus de + number"). Often followed by "que" for comparisons: "Il y a plus de X que de Y" (more X than Y).
target_language_example: Il y a plus de trente personnes dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are more than thirty people in the room.

additional_notes: Used to say that more than one thing exists or is available. Often followed by a plural noun ("Il y a plusieurs possibilités") or by a plural noun + relative clause ("Il y a plusieurs étoiles qui..."). Note: "Il y a plusieurs années" can mean "several years ago" (time ago), depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a plusieurs restaurants près d'ici.
native_language_example: There are several restaurants near here.

meaning: "four ... ago" or "there are four" (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Two common patterns:
1) Time ago: « il y a + duration » = “... ago” (e.g., « il y a quatre jours » = “four days ago”).
2) Existence/quantity: « il y a + number + noun » = “there is/are ...” (e.g., « il y a quatre chaises » = “there are four chairs”). « Il y a » is used for both “there is” and “there are.”
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à Paris il y a quatre jours.
native_language_example: I arrived in Paris four days ago.

additional_notes: Uses the common structure "il y a" (there is/there are) + "quelqu'un" (someone). In a question (often said like "Il y a quelqu’un ?"), it can mean "Is anyone there?" or "Is someone here?". You can add a place (là-bas, à l’intérieur) or a clause ("qui arrive" = "who is arriving").
target_language_example: Je crois qu'il y a quelqu'un.
native_language_example: I think there’s someone.

additional_notes: Built on the very common structure **il y a** = “there is/there are.” With rising intonation (sometimes written **Il y a quelqu’un là ?**), it’s usually a question you say when checking if anyone is present (e.g., knocking on a door). As a statement (**Il y a quelqu’un là.**), it means “There’s someone there.” **là** means “there/over there” and adds emphasis; you can also just say **Il y a quelqu’un ?**
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, il y a quelqu'un là ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is anyone there?

il y a quelqu'un qui veut

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelqu'un qui veut
meaning: "Someone wants to…" / "There’s someone who wants to…"
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that another person is asking to speak to them or see them (often in a phone call, at the door, or at reception). Follow it with an infinitive like parler (to talk) or voir (to see), and add the person pronoun: te (you, informal), vous (you, formal/plural), lui (him/her).
target_language_example: Il y a quelqu'un qui veut vous parler à l'accueil.
native_language_example: Someone wants to speak to you at reception.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present somewhere (often when you’re not sure what it is). Commonly followed by a place phrase like “là-haut” (up there), “par là” (around there), “ici” (here), “dans la pièce” (in the room), etc.
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose derrière la porte.
native_language_example: There’s something behind the door.

il y a quelque chose d'autre

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose d'autre
additional_notes: Used to add an extra point or mention an additional item. Common in conversation when remembering something or continuing a list. You can also vary it: "Il y a autre chose" is a common shorter version.
target_language_example: Attends, il y a quelque chose d'autre que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: Wait, there’s something else I need to tell you.

il y a quelque chose là

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose là
additional_notes: Literally “there is something there.” Used either (1) literally, to point out that something is present in a place, or (2) figuratively, to say an idea/suspicion has some truth or potential (“You might be onto something”). Often said as: « Il y a quelque chose, là. »
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose là : ton idée pourrait marcher.
native_language_example: There’s something to it: your idea could work.

il y a quelque chose que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose que
additional_notes: Used to introduce an unspecified “something” followed by a relative clause with que. Often followed by verbs like devoir/devrait (“must/should”) or pouvoir (“can”). In a question, it can mean “Is there something I can do?” (often implying “to help”).
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: There’s something I have to tell you.

il y a quelque chose que je

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose que je
additional_notes: Used to introduce an unspecified thing you want to mention, followed by a verb phrase (often with devoir/pouvoir/vouloir): « Il y a quelque chose que je dois/pourrais/voudrais… ». « il y a » = “there is/are”, « quelque chose » = “something”, and « que » introduces the relative clause “that I…”.
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: There’s something I have to tell you.

il y a quelque chose que vous

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose que vous
additional_notes: This is a sentence starter used to introduce something the speaker wants to point out. It’s built from: **il y a** (“there is/are”) + **quelque chose que** (“something that”) + **vous** (“you”, formal or plural). It must be followed by a verb: *Il y a quelque chose que vous devez savoir.*
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose que vous devez savoir.
native_language_example: There’s something you need to know.

il y a quelque chose qui

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose qui
additional_notes: Used to point out that an unspecified thing exists or is happening, and it is followed by a relative clause with qui + a verb (qui vit, qui pue, qui vient, etc.). In questions, it can mean “Is there something you’d like?” or “Is something wrong/that you want?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose qui ne va pas ?
native_language_example: Is something wrong?

il y a quelque chose qui cloche

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose qui cloche
additional_notes: Used when you feel there’s a problem, inconsistency, or malfunction, even if you can’t identify it yet. Often followed by "avec" + thing/person: "Il y a quelque chose qui cloche avec cette télé."
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose qui cloche avec ton histoire : ça ne tient pas debout.
native_language_example: Something’s off with your story: it doesn’t add up.

il y a quelque chose qui ne va

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose qui ne va
additional_notes: Very common with the full form: « Il y a quelque chose qui ne va pas. » Used to say that a situation, a plan, a machine, or someone’s health/mood isn’t right. « ne va pas » comes from « aller » (to go), and here means “to be okay / to be going well.”
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose qui ne va pas avec mon téléphone.
native_language_example: Something’s wrong with my phone.

meaning: "a few ... ago" or "there are a few ..."
additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) with a time word (jours/semaines/mois/années): "il y a quelques + time" = "a few + time ago". (2) as "il y a" meaning "there is/there are": "il y a quelques + plural noun" = "there are a few + noun". "Quelques" is always followed by a plural noun.
target_language_example: Il y a quelques minutes, j'étais dans le métro.
native_language_example: A few minutes ago, I was on the subway.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It can come at the end of the sentence (Elle est partie il y a quelques années.) or at the beginning as a time marker (Il y a quelques années, ...). Built from il y a (“there is/there are”) + quelques (“a few”) + années (“years”).
target_language_example: J’ai commencé le français il y a quelques années.
native_language_example: I started French a few years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Place it after the verb or at the end of the sentence (e.g., « C'est arrivé il y a quelques heures. »). « il y a » literally means 'there is/are' but in time expressions it means 'ago'.
target_language_example: Je l’ai vu il y a quelques heures.
native_language_example: I saw him a few hours ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Literally “there is a few days,” but in French it means “X time ago” (il y a + duration). Often used with the past tense: Je suis arrivé / J’ai perdu / J’ai commencé…
target_language_example: On s'est parlé il y a quelques jours.
native_language_example: We talked a few days ago.

additional_notes: Common spoken/informal way to ask what something contains or what’s inside. Often followed by a place/container ("Il y a quoi dans le sac ?") or by "dedans / là-dedans" (“in there”). A more neutral/formal equivalent is "Qu’est-ce qu’il y a… ?"
target_language_example: Il y a quoi là-dedans ?
native_language_example: What’s in there?

meaning: "there are six" / "six ... ago" (with a time unit).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to state quantity: "Il y a six personnes" = "There are six people." Used with a duration (often + a time unit like "semaines", "ans") to mean "six ... ago": "Il y a six semaines" = "Six weeks ago."
target_language_example: Il y a six chaises dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are six chairs in the room.

il y a tant de choses

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a tant de choses
additional_notes: Uses the common structure **il y a** (“there is/there are”) + **tant de** (“so much/many”) + a noun. Even though **choses** is plural, French still says **il y a**. Often followed by **que + clause** (Il y a tant de choses que je veux dire…) or **à + infinitive** (Il y a tant de choses à faire…). You can swap **choses** for another noun: *Il y a tant de travail / tant de problèmes…*
target_language_example: Il y a tant de choses à apprendre en français.
native_language_example: There are so many things to learn in French.

additional_notes: Used with the expression "il y a" (there is/are) plus "toujours" (always) to say something is always present or always happens. The noun that follows determines whether English uses "is" or "are" (e.g., "de la place" → "there is"; "des armes" → "there are").
target_language_example: Il y a toujours une solution.
native_language_example: There is always a solution.

meaning: "there is always a..." (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Built from the common structure "il y a" = "there is/there are" + "toujours" = "always" + "une" = "a" (feminine). It’s often used to express a general truth or reassurance: "There’s always a solution/way out/possibility." Change "une" to "un" for masculine nouns ("il y a toujours un..."), or to "des" for plurals ("il y a toujours des...").
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : il y a toujours une solution.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s always a solution.

additional_notes: Used with a number to state how many things exist or are present: “il y a + number + (noun)”. It can refer to things in general (“There are three problems”) or in a specific place/situation (“There are three intelligent species on the planet”).
target_language_example: Dans cette ville, il y a trois musées.
native_language_example: In this city, there are three museums.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It’s built from "il y a" ("there is/are" but used for time = "ago") + a time expression ("trois ans"). Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Je suis arrivé il y a trois ans." You can also use it alone as a short answer to “When?”
target_language_example: J’ai commencé le français il y a trois ans.
native_language_example: I started French three years ago.

additional_notes: Used with a past event to say how long ago it happened. The pattern is: [past tense verb] + il y a + [time]. Example: « Je suis parti(e) il y a deux heures » = “I left two hours ago.”
target_language_example: J'ai commencé ce travail il y a trois jours.
native_language_example: I started this job three days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It typically goes after the verb (often in the past tense): « J’ai déménagé il y a trois mois. » You can swap the time amount: « il y a deux jours / une semaine / un an ».
target_language_example: J'ai commencé ce travail il y a trois mois.
native_language_example: I started this job three months ago.

meaning: there are too many / too much (of).
additional_notes: Used to say there is an excessive amount or number of something. Follow it with a noun: il y a trop de + nom. With plural countable nouns: « trop de + nom pluriel » (trop de villages). With uncountable nouns: « trop de + nom singulier » (trop de bruit). Often expresses complaint or frustration.
target_language_example: Il y a trop de monde dans le métro ce matin.
native_language_example: There are too many people on the subway this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present somewhere. In this phrase, un is the masculine singular article, so before a feminine noun you would say il y a une, and for plural nouns il y a des.
target_language_example: Il y a un chat dans le jardin.
native_language_example: There is a cat in the garden.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Very common with past tenses: « C’était il y a un an », « La maison a été construite il y a un an ». You can add precision with words like « environ » (about), or extend it: « il y a un an et demi » (a year and a half ago).
target_language_example: J’ai commencé ce travail il y a un an.
native_language_example: I started this job a year ago.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say that an additional/different one exists: "Il y a un autre chemin" (There’s another path). In questions, intonation or a question mark makes it "Is there another …?". Often followed by a noun (un autre chemin, un autre corps, un autre moyen, un autre type).
target_language_example: Il y a un autre endroit où on peut se rencontrer ?
native_language_example: Is there another place where we can meet?

il y a un besoin urgent de

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a un besoin urgent de
meaning: there is an urgent need for.
additional_notes: Used to say something is needed right away. It’s a formal, common structure: "il y a" (there is/are) + "un besoin urgent de" + noun (or "de" + infinitive if followed by a verb). Often followed by "davantage de" (more) or an uncountable noun: "de sang", "de logement", etc.
target_language_example: Il y a un besoin urgent de solutions concrètes.
native_language_example: There is an urgent need for practical solutions.

additional_notes: Uses the common structure “il y a …” to say that something exists or is present (“there is/are …”). You can add a place after it: “Il y a un chat dans la cuisine / sous la table / sur la table.” In speech, “Il y a” is often pronounced like “y a”.
target_language_example: Il y a un chat dehors.
native_language_example: There’s a cat outside.

meaning: “there is a big/large …” (introduces a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is located somewhere: **il y a** = “there is/there are”. **un grand** is the masculine singular form of “big/large”; it can also mean “tall” for people/things (e.g., a tall man, a tall tree). For a feminine noun, use **une grande** (e.g., *il y a une grande maison*).
target_language_example: Dans ce parc, il y a un grand arbre.
native_language_example: In this park, there is a big tree.

additional_notes: "Il y a" is the common way to say "there is/there are" in French. Add a place after it (e.g., "à la porte" = at the door, "dans le jardin" = in the garden, "ici" = here, "dehors" = outside). Often used to point out someone’s presence, sometimes with an adjective: "Il y a un homme bizarre…" = "There’s a strange man…".
target_language_example: Il y a un homme devant la maison.
native_language_example: There’s a man in front of the house.

additional_notes: Used to say that two people, things, or events are connected or related. Often followed by « entre … et … » (between … and …) or understood from context. « lien » can mean an emotional bond (between people) or a logical/causal connection (between ideas or events).
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il y a un lien entre ces deux histoires.
native_language_example: I think there is a connection between these two stories.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. The pattern is "il y a + time period" (e.g., il y a deux jours = two days ago). You can add "environ" to mean "about/roughly" (il y a un mois environ).
target_language_example: J'ai déménagé il y a un mois.
native_language_example: I moved a month ago.

meaning: a little while ago; it's been a while (since/that…).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened some time ago: « Il est parti il y a un moment. » = “He left a little while ago.” With « il y a un moment que + verb », it means “(someone) has been doing something for a while / it’s been a while since…”, often with an action still continuing now: « Il y a un moment qu'elle vous attend. » = “She’s been waiting for you for a while.”
target_language_example: J'ai envoyé le message il y a un moment.
native_language_example: I sent the message a little while ago.

meaning: "there is a small…" / "there is a little…"
additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present. It’s the phrase "il y a" (there is/there are) + an indefinite article (un/une/des) + the adjective "petit" (small/little). "Petit" must agree with the noun: un petit chien (masc.), une petite maison (fem.), des petits problèmes (plural). Often used to soften the idea of something negative: "un petit problème" = a minor problem.
target_language_example: Il y a un petit café au coin de la rue.
native_language_example: There’s a small café on the corner of the street.

additional_notes: Uses the common structure "il y a" (“there is/there are”) to point out that something is wrong. Often followed by "avec…" to specify what has an issue ("Il y a un problème avec les freins" = “There’s a problem with the brakes”). You can also say it on its own as a warning or to introduce bad news.
target_language_example: Il y a un problème avec la connexion internet.
native_language_example: There’s a problem with the internet connection.

meaning: "there’s something" / "there’s this thing" (a detail, object, or issue).
additional_notes: Uses the common pattern "il y a" = "there is/are" + "un truc" (informal for "a thing/stuff"). Often used when you don’t know the exact name, or when introducing an important detail: "Il y a un truc que tu dois savoir" = "There’s something you need to know." Depending on tone/context, it can also hint that something is going on or there’s a catch.
target_language_example: Attends, il y a un truc que je ne comprends pas.
native_language_example: Wait, there’s something I don’t understand.

meaning: “there is a” (introduces the existence/presence of a feminine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present. It’s the feminine singular form of “il y a” + an indefinite article: “il y a un” (masculine) / “il y a une” (feminine). Very common for pointing things out (“Il y a une porte derrière.”) or introducing something new (“Il y a une dernière chose.”).
target_language_example: Il y a une erreur dans ce document.
native_language_example: There is a mistake in this document.

additional_notes: Used to say that another person/thing exists or is available. It must be followed by a noun (e.g., "Il y a une autre porte"). "Une autre" is feminine; for a masculine noun use "il y a un autre …" and for plural "il y a d’autres …".
target_language_example: Il y a une autre solution.
native_language_example: There is another solution.

meaning: “there is one thing…” / “one thing is…” (to introduce an important point).
additional_notes: Used to bring up a specific point, often followed by a relative clause: **il y a une chose que…** (“there’s one thing that…”), **il y a une chose dont…** (“there’s one thing about which… / that…”). Can also be said alone (**Il y a une chose.**) to create a pause before explaining.
target_language_example: Il y a une chose que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: There’s one thing I have to tell you.

il y a une chose que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a une chose que
meaning: “There is one thing that …” / “There’s something that …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific thing (often important) followed by a relative clause with que. Very common pattern: Il y a une chose que + subject + verb (e.g., je dois faire / tu dois savoir). You can swap une chose for quelque chose (“something”).
target_language_example: Il y a une chose que je veux te dire.
native_language_example: There’s one thing I want to tell you.

il y a une chose que je

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a une chose que je
meaning: "there’s one thing that I…" (to introduce what you want to say)
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to highlight one specific point before continuing with a verb phrase (often with "veux" / "dois" / "n’aime pas" / "ne comprends pas"). It’s a common way to set up emphasis: "Il y a une chose que je veux te dire…".
target_language_example: Il y a une chose que je veux te dire : je pars demain.
native_language_example: There’s one thing I want to tell you: I’m leaving tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened (a point in the past). Often placed at the end of the sentence: «Tu as dit ça il y a une demi-heure.»
target_language_example: Je l’ai appelé il y a une demi-heure.
native_language_example: I called him half an hour ago.

additional_notes: Used to point out that two things are not the same. Very often followed by "entre X et Y" (between X and Y): "Il y a une différence entre toi et moi." You can add adjectives for emphasis (e.g., "une différence considérable / fondamentale").
target_language_example: Il y a une différence entre ce que tu dis et ce que tu fais.
native_language_example: There’s a difference between what you say and what you do.

additional_notes: Used to say an explanation exists (often implying there’s a reason behind something). It can be followed by an adjective (logique, simple, scientifique) or by “à + situation” (Il y a une explication à tout ça = There’s an explanation for all this). In careful writing you may add accents: “Il y a une explication scientifique à tout ça.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y a une explication.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s an explanation.

additional_notes: Uses the common phrase **il y a** (“there is/there are”) to point out that someone exists or is present somewhere. Often followed by a place (**dans la pièce**) or a relative clause (**qui veut te voir** = “who wants to see you”). In speech, it’s very often shortened to **y a une femme**.
target_language_example: Il y a une femme devant la porte.
native_language_example: There’s a woman in front of the door.

additional_notes: Used to say how much time has passed since an event happened. The pattern is: [past tense] + il y a + duration (e.g., il y a deux minutes / trois jours). Note that "il y a" literally means "there is/are" but here it means "ago".
target_language_example: Je t’ai envoyé un message il y a une heure.
native_language_example: I sent you a message an hour ago.

meaning: “a week ago” (one week in the past).
additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often comes at the end of the sentence: « Il est parti il y a une semaine. ». You can add « environ » to mean “about”: « il y a une semaine environ ».
target_language_example: On s’est vus il y a une semaine.
native_language_example: We saw each other a week ago.

meaning: "there will be" / "there is going to be".
additional_notes: Future tense of « il y a » (“there is/are”). Used to announce that something will exist or happen in the future. Very common with quantities and events: « Il y aura un contrôle demain » (There will be a test tomorrow), « Il y aura des problèmes » (There will be problems).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il y aura assez de temps pour tout faire.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, there will be enough time to do everything.
