additional_notes: Future tense of "il y a" (“there is/there are”). Used to predict or announce that something will exist/happen later. "des" is the plural indefinite article (roughly “some”), so what follows is a plural noun (des passagers, des difficultés, des patrouilles, des morts). In negatives you often see "il n’y aura pas de ...".
target_language_example: Demain, il y aura des changements.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, there will be some changes.

meaning: “there was / there were” (past of “il y a”).
additional_notes: Used to say that something existed or was present at a certain time in the past. It’s the imperfect tense, often used for description/background (setting the scene): people/things/situations that were there. Plural in English depends on what follows (“il y avait une…” = there was; “il y avait des…” = there were).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait beaucoup de monde.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there were lots of people.

additional_notes: Used to describe a large quantity in the past. "Il y avait" is the imperfect of "il y a" (there is/are). After "beaucoup de", the noun usually follows directly (no article: "beaucoup de jeunes", "beaucoup de neige").
target_language_example: Quand on est arrivés, il y avait beaucoup de monde.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there were a lot of people.

il y avait beaucoup de monde

target_language_multi_word_term: il y avait beaucoup de monde
meaning: there were a lot of people (it was crowded).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "il y a" ("il y avait") to describe a past situation/background: “there was/there were.” "Beaucoup de monde" literally means “a lot of people” (more like “a lot of folks/people around”) and is very commonly used to say a place was crowded. "Monde" here is singular but refers to people in general.
target_language_example: Hier soir, il y avait beaucoup de monde au restaurant, alors on a attendu dehors.
native_language_example: Last night, there were a lot of people at the restaurant, so we waited outside.

meaning: "there was some" / "there were (some)" (for an uncountable thing).
additional_notes: "Il y avait" is the imperfect of "il y a" (there is/are), used to describe what existed/was present in the past or to set a scene. "De la" is the partitive article (some) used with feminine singular uncountable nouns (e.g., brume, crème, peur, sueur). For masculine use "du" (il y avait du…), and for plural use "des" (il y avait des…).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait de la musique dans la rue.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was music in the street.

additional_notes: Used to say that several people/animals/things existed or were present in the past. It’s the imperfect tense of « il y a » and is followed by a plural noun: « Il y avait des + nom (pluriel) ».
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait des gens devant la porte.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there were people in front of the door.

additional_notes: Imperfect form of *il y a* (“there is/are”), used to describe what existed or what the situation/conditions were in the past (often background info): *Hier, il y avait du soleil / du brouillard.* The *du* is the partitive article (*de + le*) meaning “some” with uncountable or general quantities (fog, sun, broken glass, etc.). With feminine nouns you’ll see *de la*; with plural, *des*.
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait du monde devant le café.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there were people in front of the café.

additional_notes: Past-tense form of "il y a". Used to describe what existed or was present in a place or situation in the past. Often followed by a noun: "Il y avait un drapeau..." (= there was a flag), "Il y avait un hic" (= there was a problem/catch), "Il y avait un total de..." (= there was a total of...). You can change the article/number as needed (une / des) and it can also be negative: "il n’y avait pas de...".
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait un chat devant la porte.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was a cat in front of the door.

additional_notes: Imperfect form of "il y a". Used to describe that something existed/was present at a place or at a time in the past, often as background description (people, things, events: "il y avait une vue", "il y avait une fête"). With plural: "il y avait des..."
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait une longue file d’attente.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was a long line.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern "il y en a" to say that some exist/are present/are available. "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (e.g., "des pommes" → "il y en a" = "there are some"). Often followed by a number or quantity: "il y en a trois" (there are three of them), "il y en a une centaine" (there are about a hundred).
target_language_example: Tu as des stylos ? Oui, il y en a dans le tiroir.
native_language_example: Do you have pens? Yes, there are some in the drawer.

meaning: "There is/are some" or "there are (a number/amount of them)".
additional_notes: Used to say that some exist/are available, often followed by a number or quantity: Il y en a cinq (There are five). "en" replaces something previously mentioned (e.g., des pommes → Il y en a). With quantity words like "trop" it means "too many/too much of it/them": Il y en a trop.
target_language_example: Des chaises ? Oui, il y en a dans la salle.
native_language_example: Chairs? Yes, there are some in the room.

additional_notes: Built on the common pattern "il y en a" (= "there are some"), where "en" replaces something already mentioned (often "some of it/them"). "d'autres" means "others/more". It can stand alone ("Il y en a d'autres.") or be followed by details like "comme toi" (like you) or a relative clause: "Il y en a d'autres qui arrivent" (others are arriving).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : il y en a d'autres qui peuvent t'aider.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are others who can help you.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a lot of something exists. It’s typically followed by a number/quantity expression: des centaines (hundreds), des milliers (thousands), des tonnes/des tas (tons/loads). Built on "il y en a" = "there are some/there is some"; the extra "des" introduces the quantity phrase.
target_language_example: Des bons restaurants à Paris, il y en a des milliers.
native_language_example: There are thousands of good restaurants in Paris.

il y en a des qui

target_language_multi_word_term: il y en a des qui
additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about a subset of people or things. Built from **il y en a** (“there are/there is”) + **des… qui** (“some… who/that”). Common in spoken French; often followed by a verb describing what those people do or are like.
target_language_example: Il y en a des qui pensent que c’est facile, mais ce n’est pas vrai.
native_language_example: Some people think it’s easy, but that’s not true.

meaning: “There are still some (left)” / “There are more (of them).”
additional_notes: Uses **il y a** (“there is/are”) + **en** (“some/of it/of them,” referring to something already mentioned) + **encore** (“still/more”). Often used to say there is still some left, or that there are more remaining. You can add a quantity: **Il y en a encore un / beaucoup / plein**.
target_language_example: Tu veux un gâteau ? Il y en a encore.
native_language_example: Do you want a cake? There are still some left.

meaning: there are lots of them / there are plenty.
additional_notes: Uses the common pattern "il y a" (there is/are) + "en" (of them/of it) + "plein" (a lot). Often followed by "de" + noun: "Il y en a plein de..." = "There are lots of..." You can also say it alone as an excited emphasis: "Il y en a plein !"
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y en a plein dans le magasin.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are plenty in the store.

meaning: "there’s enough (of it) for…" / "it will last for…"
additional_notes: Used with a duration or a group to say how long something lasts or that there’s enough to cover someone/something. Common patterns: « Il y en a pour tout le monde » = there’s enough for everyone; « Il y en a pour une seconde / deux jours » = it lasts one second / two days (often about battery life, time, money, food, etc.). « en » refers to the thing you’re talking about (some of it), and « il y a » is an impersonal way to say “there is/are.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y en a pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s enough for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to point out that among a group, some people/things do a certain action or have a certain quality. Very common in speech; often implies “some… (and others don’t)”. Built from: il y a = “there is/are” + en = “of them/some” + qui = “who/that”.
target_language_example: Il y en a qui préfèrent rester à la maison.
native_language_example: There are some people who prefer to stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to say that one exists or is available. Built on **il y a** (“there is/are”) + **en** (“some/any/of them,” replacing a noun mentioned or understood) + **un** (“one”). Often answers a question like *Tu en as un ?* (“Do you have one?”) → *Oui, il y en a un.*
target_language_example: Tu cherches un chargeur ? Il y en a un sur la table.
native_language_example: Are you looking for a charger? There’s one on the table.

meaning: "There is one" / "There’s one (of them)" (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used when you mean “one of it/them” and the thing has already been mentioned or is understood. « en » replaces “of it/them” (a previously mentioned noun), and « une » shows it’s ONE and feminine (for a masculine noun, you’d say « il y en a un »). Common in counts or comparisons: « Il y en a une de moins » = “There’s one less.”
target_language_example: Tu as des piles ? Oui, il y en a une dans le tiroir.
native_language_example: Do you have batteries? Yes, there’s one in the drawer.

meaning: “there will be some / there will be (some of it/them)” (in the future).
additional_notes: Future tense of the common structure **il y a** (“there is/are”) with **en** (“some / some of it/them”), used when the thing has already been mentioned or is understood. Often followed by a quantity or place: **Il y en aura trois** (“There will be three”), **Il y en aura partout** (“There will be some everywhere”), **Il y en aura pour tout le monde** (“There will be enough for everyone”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y en aura assez pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there will be enough for everyone.

additional_notes: Imperfect past form of "il y en a". Used when "en" replaces a previously mentioned noun (meaning "some" or "(some) of it/them"): *Il y en avait beaucoup* = "There were a lot (of them)." You often add a quantity after it (beaucoup, un, deux, etc.).
target_language_example: Dans le frigo, il y en avait encore.
native_language_example: There were still some in the fridge.

additional_notes: Imperfect form of être with il. Usually used for descriptions, states, or background/ongoing situations in the past. In context, il can mean either "he" or "it".
target_language_example: Il était très content de te voir.
native_language_example: He was very happy to see you.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past tense (était) to describe an ongoing state in the past: where/ how someone was sitting, often as background description. Frequently followed by a place or position: "sur une chaise" (on a chair), "par terre" (on the floor), "entre X et Y" (between X and Y), "avec les bras/jambes croisés" (with arms/legs crossed).
target_language_example: Quand je suis entré, il était assis près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: When I came in, he was sitting near the window.

meaning: “he was in / he was on / he was wearing” (être + en + noun).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe a past state or situation: en désaccord (in disagreement), en déplacement professionnel (on a business trip), en affaires avec… (in business with…). It can also describe what someone was wearing: en uniforme (in uniform), en redingote (wearing a frock coat). The feminine form is « elle était en ».
target_language_example: Quand je l’ai vu, il était en uniforme.
native_language_example: When I saw him, he was in uniform.

meaning: 'he was in the process of' / 'he was (in the middle of) doing'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action was ongoing at that moment in the past (like English "was doing"). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « il était en train de + infinitif ». You can change the subject and tense: « je suis en train de… » (I’m doing…), « ils étaient en train de… » (they were doing…).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il était en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he was in the middle of making dinner.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (était) to describe an ongoing state, feeling, or characteristic in the past (background description). "Il" usually means "he," but it can also mean "it" (e.g., talking about a movie: "Il était très long"). Typically followed by an adjective: "Il était très content/fatigué."
target_language_example: Quand il était jeune, il était très timide.
native_language_example: When he was young, he was very shy.

meaning: "Once upon a time there was a..." (storybook opening).
additional_notes: Used at the start of fairy tales and stories to introduce a character. It’s the imperfect tense of être (il était = “he/it was”), followed by une fois (“once”), then un/une + noun. You can change un to une depending on the noun: « Il était une fois une princesse… »
target_language_example: Il était une fois un chat qui voulait devenir roi.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a cat who wanted to become king.

additional_notes: Set phrase used to begin fairy tales and stories. It’s in the imperfect tense (était) to set the scene in the past. Often followed by a character or setting: « il était une fois un roi… »
target_language_example: Il était une fois une princesse qui vivait dans une grande forêt.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a princess who lived in a big forest.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine plural, or mixed group). "Aiment" is the present tense (3rd person plural) of "aimer". It can mean "to like" (Ils aiment ça. = They like that.) or "to love" (Ils aiment leurs enfants. = They love their children.). You can follow it with a noun (ils aiment leurs enfants), an infinitive (ils aiment se plaindre = they like to complain), or a pronoun like "ça" (they like that).
target_language_example: Ils aiment regarder des films le soir.
native_language_example: They like watching movies in the evening.

additional_notes: Used to describe an ongoing state, repeated situation, or background in the past (the imperfect). Common patterns: « ils avaient peur de… » = “they were afraid to/of…”, « ils avaient besoin de… » = “they needed…”. Often appears in reported speech after « ils ont dit que… » (they said that…).
target_language_example: Quand ils étaient jeunes, ils avaient toujours peur du noir.
native_language_example: When they were young, they were always afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Present tense of **dire** (“to say/tell”) with **ils** (“they”). Often used to report what other people claim or announce, frequently followed by **que**: *Ils disent que…* In casual speech, negation may drop **ne**: *Ils disent pas…* (instead of *Ils ne disent pas…*).
target_language_example: Ils disent qu’ils vont arriver à 18 h.
native_language_example: They say they’re going to arrive at 6 p.m.

meaning: “they must / they have to” (they are required to).
additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (a group of males, or a mixed group). "Doivent" is the present tense of "devoir" (to have to / must). It’s used to express obligation or necessity, and is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "ils doivent partir"). In the negative: "ils ne doivent pas..." = "they must not / they aren’t supposed to...".
target_language_example: Ils doivent partir maintenant.
native_language_example: They have to leave now.

meaning: 'they must be' / 'they have to be' (or 'they must be' = 'they’re probably…').
additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Doivent" is the present tense of "devoir" (must/should/have to). With "être" it can express either (1) obligation/requirement: "They have to be replaced", or (2) a logical guess/probability: "They must be tired" (= they’re probably tired).
target_language_example: Ils doivent être en retard, il y a beaucoup de trafic.
native_language_example: They must be late; there’s a lot of traffic.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb « faire » (to do/to make) with « ils » (they). Very common and used broadly: doing an action (« Ils font un test. »), making/producing something (« Ils font tout le nécessaire. »), or “doing” an activity (« Ils font ça depuis… »). In informal speech you may hear « Ils font pas… » (missing « ne ») instead of the more formal « Ils ne font pas… ».
target_language_example: Ils font ça tous les jours.
native_language_example: They do that every day.

meaning: "they have" + "it/him/her" (used to form the past tense: "they ...ed it/him/her").
additional_notes: « Ils » = « they ». « l’ » is a direct object pronoun meaning “it,” “him,” or “her,” used before a verb that starts with a vowel (like « ont »). « ont » is the present tense of « avoir » (they have) and is used to build the passé composé: ils l’ont + past participle (fait, pris, emmené, etc.) → “they did it / they took him/her/it / they brought him/her, etc.” With « avoir », the past participle can agree in gender/number when the direct object pronoun comes before it: « Ils l’ont pris » (masc. “him/it”), « Ils l’ont prise » (fem. “her/it”).
target_language_example: Ils l'ont emmené à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: They took him/it to the hospital.

meaning: "they" + "to me" + "have" (used to form the past tense: "they ... to me").
additional_notes: Common start of a sentence in the passé composé: ils (they) + m’ (me, as an indirect object) + ont (have). It’s followed by a past participle: Ils m’ont dit (They told me), Ils m’ont donné (They gave me), Ils m’ont pris… (They took/caught me…). m’ is the shortened form of me before a vowel sound (ont). Meaning depends on the verb that follows (e.g., Ils m’ont eu = “They got me/fooled me”).
target_language_example: Ils m'ont envoyé un message hier.
native_language_example: They sent me a message yesterday.

additional_notes:
Past tense (passé composé) of "dire": "ils" (they) + "m'" (to me) + "ont dit" (have said/told). Often followed by:
- "que" + a clause: "Ils m'ont dit que..." (They told me that...)
- "de" + infinitive: "Ils m'ont dit de venir" (They told me to come)
Also used in "C'est ce qu'ils m'ont dit" = "That's what they told me."
target_language_example: Ils m'ont dit que le train était en retard.
native_language_example: They told me that the train was late.

meaning: 'they do not / they didn't' (start of a negation with 'ils').
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a negative sentence with the subject pronoun ils (“they”). In standard French, ne is paired with another negative word: pas (not), jamais (never), plus (no longer), rien (nothing), etc. In everyday spoken French, ne is often dropped (Ils savent pas).
target_language_example: Ils ne veulent pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: They don't want to come tonight.

additional_notes: From the verb *pouvoir* (“to be able to / can”) in the present tense: *ils peuvent* (“they can”). The standard French negation is *ne … pas*: *ils ne peuvent pas* (“they can’t”). In casual spoken French, *ne* is often dropped: *ils peuvent pas*.
target_language_example: Ils ne peuvent pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: They can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: This is the negative form of **ils sont** (“they are”) with **ne … pas** placed around the verb **être**: **ils ne sont pas + adjective / prepositional phrase / past participle**. In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **ils sont pas**.
target_language_example: Ils ne sont pas prêts pour le départ.
native_language_example: They aren’t ready to leave.

meaning: 'they have' / 'they did' (talking about what they did to us).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the passé composé: ils (they) + nous (to us) + ont (have). The object pronoun nous goes before the verb. In sentences like « Ils nous ont oubliés / saluées », the past participle can agree with nous (forgotten us / greeted us) in gender/number when nous refers to the direct object.
target_language_example: Ils nous ont aidés à trouver un hôtel.
native_language_example: They helped us find a hotel.

additional_notes: Composed of ils + ont (from avoir). It can mean possession, but it is also very commonly used as the auxiliary in the passé composé. In that case, English often translates it with a simple past: ils ont dormi = “they slept.”
target_language_example: Ils ont déjà fini.
native_language_example: They've already finished.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of *dire* with *ils* (they): *ils* + *ont* (have) + *dit* (said). Used for something they said in the past, often translated simply as “they said.” Common in reported speech: *Ils ont dit qu’ils…* (“They said that they…”).
target_language_example: Ils ont dit qu’ils viendraient demain.
native_language_example: They said they would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past of devoir ("to have to" / "must"). It can express (1) obligation in the past: « Ils ont dû partir » = “They had to leave.” It can also express a deduction (very common): « Ils ont dû avoir un accident » = “They must have had an accident.” With deduction about a completed action, you’ll often see « ont dû » + infinitive (or + avoir/être + past participle).
target_language_example: Ils ont dû oublier l'adresse.
native_language_example: They must have forgotten the address.

additional_notes: "Ils ont eu" is the passé composé of avoir (ils + ont + eu) and talks about a completed past event. Depending on context, it can mean they possessed something (Ils ont eu plusieurs enfants = they had several children), they got/received something (Ils ont eu ce qu’ils voulaient = they got what they wanted), or they experienced something (Ils ont eu de la chance = they were lucky). In "ils ont eu raison", it’s part of the fixed phrase "avoir raison" = 'to be right'.
target_language_example: Ils ont eu beaucoup de succès cette année.
native_language_example: They had a lot of success this year.

additional_notes: This is the **passé composé** of *faire* for **ils** (“they”): *ils* + *ont* (have) + *fait* (done/made). It’s used for completed actions in the past. *Faire* can mean **do** or **make** depending on context: *Ils ont fait une pause* (“They took a break”), *Ils ont fait le tour du monde* (“They travelled around the world”), *Ils ont fait de leur mieux* (“They did their best”).
target_language_example: Ils ont fait la cuisine hier soir.
native_language_example: They cooked last night.

meaning: 'they put/placed' (past tense of mettre); also 'they took (time)' and in fixed phrases like 'they put an end (to)'
additional_notes: "Ils ont mis" is the passé composé of mettre (they put/placed). Common patterns: (1) mettre + object + place: « Ils ont mis mon nom dans la Coupe » = they put my name in the Goblet. (2) mettre + object (meaning install/add): « Ils ont mis un portail » = they installed/put in a gate. (3) mettre + duration + à + infinitive: « Ils ont mis deux ans à construire… » = it took them two years to build… (4) mettre fin à + noun: « Ils ont mis fin au… » = they put an end to…
target_language_example: Ils ont mis trois heures à arriver.
native_language_example: It took them three hours to arrive.

additional_notes: Passé composé of prendre (to take). Used for many common meanings: taking/grabbing something (Ils ont pris de la nourriture), having a meal/drink (Ils ont pris leur petit-déjeuner = they had breakfast), taking a risk (Ils ont pris un gros risque), taking someone away (can imply kidnapping depending on context), and choosing a route (Qu’est-ce qu’ils ont pris comme rues ? = Which streets did they take?).
target_language_example: Ils ont pris le bus pour aller au centre-ville.
native_language_example: They took the bus to go downtown.

meaning: “they all have” / “they have all” (all of them).
additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun ils (“they”) + avoir (“have”), with tous emphasizing that every person in the group did the action. In the passé composé, tous is commonly placed between the auxiliary verb ont and the past participle: Ils ont tous changé (“They all changed”). Can also mean “they all have (something)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ils ont tous compris la question.
native_language_example: They all understood the question.

meaning: “they were / they have been” (passé composé of être; often used to form the passive).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a past participle to make the passive voice: ils ont été + participe passé (e.g., attaqués, surpris). The past participle usually agrees with ils (masculine plural: -s).
target_language_example: Ils ont été invités à la fête, mais ils n’ont pas pu venir.
native_language_example: They were invited to the party, but they couldn’t come.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say what a group possesses or has (Ils ont une voiture.). Also used in common expressions with "avoir" like "ils ont raison" (they are right), "ils ont peur" (they are afraid), and to talk about age: "Ils ont un fils de dix ans" (they have a ten-year-old son). In speech, it often sounds like "il-zon" because of the liaison (s + ont).
target_language_example: Ils ont besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: They need help.

additional_notes: “Avoir besoin de” means “to need.” After it, use a noun (Ils ont besoin de vacances) or an infinitive verb (Ils ont besoin de s’inspirer…). “De” may contract with articles: de + les → des, de + le → du, de + l’ stays de l’.
target_language_example: Ils ont besoin de temps pour réfléchir.
native_language_example: They need time to think.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "ont" is the present tense of "avoir" (to have). "des" is the plural indefinite article meaning "some" (often not translated in English). Used to say that they possess or have something available: "Ils ont des armes" = "They have weapons"; "Ils ont des bonnes nouvelles ?" = "Do they have any good news?"; "Ils ont des jumelles" = "They have binoculars."
target_language_example: Ils ont des amis à Paris.
native_language_example: They have friends in Paris.

additional_notes: From the idiom **avoir l’air (de)** = “to seem / to look.” Often followed by **de + infinitive** (e.g., *ils ont l'air de s’amuser* = they seem to be having fun) or by an **adjective** (e.g., *ils ont l'air heureux* = they look happy). You can change the subject: *j’ai l’air, tu as l’air, il/elle a l’air, nous avons l’air, vous avez l’air, ils/elles ont l’air*.
target_language_example: ils ont l'air si heureux.
native_language_example: They look so happy.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Parlent" is the present tense of "parler". It can mean speaking a language (often with no preposition: "Ils parlent français") or talking about something (use "de": "Ils parlent de musique"), and it can also be used as a question: "Ils parlent ?" = "Are they speaking/talking?"
target_language_example: Ils parlent de toi en ce moment.
native_language_example: They’re talking about you right now.

meaning: “they can / they are able to” (sometimes “they may”).
additional_notes: "Ils" = “they” (masculine or mixed group). "Peuvent" is the present tense of "pouvoir" (to be able to / can). It’s used for ability (“They can speak French”), possibility (“They can maybe start…”), or permission depending on context. In questions, it often means “Can they…?” ("Ils peuvent faire ça ?").
target_language_example: S’ils veulent, ils peuvent venir demain.
native_language_example: If they want, they can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb **savoir** (to know a fact / to know that…). **Ils** = “they” (usually a group of men, or a mixed group). Often used before **que** (“that”): *Ils savent que…* In speech, **ils** is often not strongly pronounced, and there is a liaison: *ils savent* → sounds like **[il sav]**.
target_language_example: Ils savent que c’est important.
native_language_example: They know that it’s important.

meaning: "they" + "se" (themselves / each other) used with reflexive or reciprocal verbs.
additional_notes: Used before a verb in pronominal verbs (verbs that take a reflexive pronoun). Depending on context, it can mean they do something to themselves (reflexive) or to one another (reciprocal): Ils se battent = They’re fighting (each other). Ils se détendent = They relax. With another object it can be "to each other": Ils se disent la vérité = They tell each other the truth.
target_language_example: Ils se parlent tous les jours.
native_language_example: They talk to each other every day.

meaning: “they (have) …” in the past tense with a reflexive/pronominal verb.
additional_notes: Used to start the passé composé of pronominal (often reflexive) verbs: ils (they) + se (themselves/each other) + sont (are/have, using être). The past participle usually agrees with ils (masculine plural) when applicable: Ils se sont levés. In some verbs like se noyer (“to drown”), it means “they drowned.”
target_language_example: Ils se sont réveillés tôt.
native_language_example: They woke up early.

meaning: they got married / they married (each other).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb se marier (“to get married”). Used to say that a couple married at a specific time (often with il y a…, quand…, récemment, etc.).
target_language_example: Ils se sont mariés en juin.
native_language_example: They got married in June.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se moquer de** = “to make fun of, to mock.” It’s commonly followed by a person or a thing: **se moquer de quelqu’un/de quelque chose**. In the past tense here (**passé composé**), it’s **ils se sont moqués de…** (“they made fun of…”).
target_language_example: Ils se sont moqués de mon accent, mais ça ne me dérange pas.
native_language_example: They made fun of my accent, but it doesn’t bother me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about where people will be or what they will be like in the future: Ils seront là dans quelques minutes. It can also express a guess/assumption about the present (“they must be…”), especially from context: Ils seront déjà partis. In your example « ils seront rentrés », the helper verb is in the future (« ils seront ») + past participle (« rentrés ») to form the futur antérieur (“they will have come back / they must have come back”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : ils seront prêts demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: they will be ready tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of être used with ils for a masculine or mixed-gender plural subject. For an all-female group, use elles sont.
target_language_example: Ils sont très contents aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: They are very happy today.

meaning: “they went” / “they have gone” (masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of aller with être: ils (they) + sont (are) + allés (gone). Use for a group of males or a mixed group; for all-female, say « elles sont allées » (with -es). Often followed by a place with « à/dans/au/à la/aux » or an activity: « aller + infinitive » (e.g., « allés voir » = went to see).
target_language_example: Après le travail, ils sont allés au restaurant.
native_language_example: After work, they went to the restaurant.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of arriver with être: ils + sont + arrivé(s). The -s on arrivés agrees with ils (masculine plural; for an all-female group you’d write elles sont arrivées). Used for arriving at a place (à + city, en + country) and also figuratively in “arriver à la conclusion” = “to come to the conclusion.”
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés à Paris hier soir.
native_language_example: They arrived in Paris last night.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of *arriver* with *être*: *ils sont arrivés* (“they arrived”), with agreement on *arrivés* (add -e / -es for feminine: *elles sont arrivées*). *Là-bas* means “over there / there (in that place)”. After *avant*, French typically uses a stressed pronoun: *avant elle / lui / nous / vous / eux / elles* (not *le/la/les*).
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés là-bas avant moi.
native_language_example: They arrived there before me.

meaning: “they are in …” (in a place or in a state/situation).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **être** + **en** + a noun phrase to describe a location (**en classe** = in class) or a condition/situation (**en bon état** = in good condition; **en guerre (avec …)** = at war (with …); **en bons termes** = on good terms). You replace **ils** with another subject as needed (e.g., *je suis en…*, *elle est en…*).
target_language_example: Ils sont en vacances cette semaine.
native_language_example: They are on vacation this week.

meaning: they are (currently) / they are in the middle of (doing).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize an action happening right now (French version of the English present continuous). Structure: être (conjugated) + en train de + infinitive. Here: ils sont en train de + infinitive = “they are currently …”.
target_language_example: Ils sont en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: They are preparing dinner (right now).

additional_notes: Used to point out that a group of males or a mixed group is present. Depending on context, “là” can mean either “here” (near the speaker) or “there” (at a specific place). Often said when noticing or locating someone/something: “Regarde, ils sont là.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ils sont là pour t’aider.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, they’re here to help you.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *mourir* (to die) with the auxiliary *être*. *Ils sont morts* can describe (1) the event of dying (“they died”) or (2) the resulting state (“they’re dead”). In writing, you may also see it used in a time clause: *Quand ils sont morts, …* (“When they died, …”).
target_language_example: Ils sont morts il y a dix ans.
native_language_example: They died ten years ago.

additional_notes: Past tense with the verb "être" (passé composé) of "partir" = to leave/go away. "Ils" refers to a group of males or a mixed group. Often followed by time ("il y a une heure"), purpose/duration ("pour le week-end"), direction ("par là"), or a destination ("pour Paris").
target_language_example: Ils sont partis sans dire au revoir.
native_language_example: They left without saying goodbye.

additional_notes: Used to say that all the people/things in a group are present or in the same state. In questions, you’ll often see inversion: « Où sont-ils tous ? » (“Where are they all?”). « tous » here means “all (of them)” and typically comes after the verb.
target_language_example: Ils sont tous prêts.
native_language_example: They’re all ready.

meaning: "they are very" (used to describe a group of males or a mixed group).
additional_notes: “Ils” = “they” (for a group of men/boys, or a mixed-gender group). “Sont” is the verb “être” (to be) for “they are.” “Très” means “very” and usually comes right before an adjective (très forts, très généreux). The adjective that follows generally agrees in number (plural) with “ils.”
target_language_example: Ils sont très gentils.
native_language_example: They are very nice.

meaning: 'they came' / 'they have come' (masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of venir with être: venir → ils sont venus. Used for arriving/coming to a place (chez moi, à mon appartement), coming from somewhere (depuis le Brésil), or coming at a time (la semaine passée, le lundi). Agreement: venus (masc. plural); if the group is all female: elles sont venues.
target_language_example: Ils sont venus tôt pour m’aider.
native_language_example: They came early to help me.

meaning: “they are at/in …” (location) or “they are yours/belong to you” (possession), depending on context.
additional_notes: This is the 3rd-person plural of **être à** (“to be at/to”). Most often it gives a **location**: *Ils sont à Philadelphie.* It can also show **possession/availability** with an indirect object: *Ils sont à vous* (“They’re yours / They belong to you”). It also appears in set phrases: *être à nos trousses* (“to be after us / on our tail”) and *être à portée de voix* (“within earshot”).
target_language_example: Ils sont à la maison, mais ils sont à vous si vous en avez besoin.
native_language_example: They’re at home, but they’re yours if you need them.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine plural, or mixed group). "Veulent" is the present tense of "vouloir" (to want). Often followed by an infinitive: "ils veulent apprendre" (they want to learn). It can also be followed by a noun: "ils veulent quelques heures de plus" (they want a few more hours), or by "que" + subjunctive to express what they want someone to do: "ils veulent que je vous parle" (they want me to talk to you).
target_language_example: Ils veulent partir maintenant.
native_language_example: They want to leave now.

additional_notes: Present tense of venir (to come) with ils (they). It can describe movement toward someone/somewhere (Ils viennent vers nous. = They’re coming toward us.) or be used in the near past with venir de + infinitive (Ils viennent juste de la sortir… = They just took her out…).
target_language_example: Ils viennent ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are they coming tonight?

meaning: "they go" / "they are going"; often used to form the near future ("they're going to...").
additional_notes: Subject pronoun "ils" (they, masculine or mixed group) + present tense of "aller" (to go). Very commonly followed by an infinitive to express the near future: "ils vont + infinitive" = "they are going to + verb".
target_language_example: Ils vont partir bientôt.
native_language_example: They’re going to leave soon.

meaning: “they’re going to … us” (near future with “nous” = us).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about something that’s about to happen: Ils vont + infinitive. The pronoun “nous” (us) is placed before the infinitive: « Ils vont nous voir » = “They’re going to see us.” Depending on the verb, “nous” can be a direct object (see us) or indirect object (talk to us).
target_language_example: Cache-toi : ils vont nous entendre !
native_language_example: Hide: they’re going to hear us!

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Voulaient" is the imperfect past tense of "vouloir" (to want), used for an ongoing/recurring desire in the past, background context, or what someone wanted at the time. Often followed by a noun ("ils voulaient des excuses") or by "que" + subjunctive for what they wanted someone to do ("ils voulaient que je vienne").
target_language_example: Quand ils étaient plus jeunes, ils voulaient voyager partout.
native_language_example: When they were younger, they wanted to travel everywhere.

additional_notes: “Ils” means “they” (for a group of men or a mixed group). “Étaient” is the imperfect past of “être” (to be). It’s used to describe a past situation, background, or ongoing state (where they were, how they were, what they were like), often setting the scene rather than focusing on a completed event.
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, ils étaient déjà fatigués.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were already tired.

additional_notes: Used to say that every person in a group of males or mixed gender was in the same situation/state. "Ils" = they (masc./mixed), "étaient" = were (imperfect of être), and "tous" = all. "Tous" here is an adverb meaning “all (of them)” and typically goes right after the verb: « Ils étaient tous + adjective/past participle/noun phrase » (e.g., « en uniforme », « partis »).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, ils étaient tous déjà là.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were all already there.

additional_notes: Most often used as **n’importe quoi**. In a sentence, **(n’)importe quoi** means “anything / whatever” (often with **tout**: *tout et n’importe quoi* = “anything and everything”). As an exclamation (**N’importe quoi !**), it means “Nonsense!” / “That’s ridiculous!” and is fairly informal. Common in **Tu dis n’importe quoi !** = “You’re talking nonsense!”
target_language_example: Arrête, tu racontes n’importe quoi !
native_language_example: Stop, you’re talking nonsense!

meaning: an objection/problem with the fact that…
additional_notes: Used mostly in the common pattern: « (ne pas) avoir/voir d’inconvénient à ce que + subjunctive » to mean “to (not) mind / to (not) have any objection to …”. Example: « Je ne vois pas d’inconvénient à ce que tu viennes. » = “I don’t mind you coming.” Note the subjunctive after « à ce que » (tu viennes, il fasse, nous partions, etc.).
target_language_example: Je ne vois pas d’inconvénient à ce que vous partiez plus tôt.
native_language_example: I don’t mind you leaving earlier.

meaning: “any objection to me…” / “any problem with me…”
additional_notes: Usually used in the full phrase **(ne pas) avoir d’inconvénient à ce que + subjunctive** to politely ask permission or check if something is OK: **Vous n’avez pas d’inconvénient à ce que je… ?** = “Do you mind if I…?” After **à ce que**, French uses the **subjunctive** (e.g., *je parte, je vienne, je fasse*).
target_language_example: Vous n’avez pas d’inconvénient à ce que je m’assoie ici ?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I sit here?

inconvénient à ce que je me

target_language_multi_word_term: inconvénient à ce que je me
meaning: "(to have) a problem/objection with the fact that I…" (often: "I don't mind that I…").
additional_notes: This chunk is usually part of the pattern: « (ne pas) avoir d’inconvénient à ce que + subject + verb (subjunctive) ». Example: « Je n’ai pas d’inconvénient à ce que je me joigne à vous » = “I don’t mind joining you.” After « à ce que », French typically uses the subjunctive (e.g., « je me joigne », « je me lave », « je me mette »).
target_language_example: Je n’ai aucun inconvénient à ce que je me joigne à vous.
native_language_example: I have no problem with joining you / I don’t mind joining you.

additional_notes: Used on signs and in rules to say that smoking is not allowed. Often appears as « Il est interdit de fumer » or with emphasis: « strictement interdit » (= strictly forbidden). You can add a place: « ici », « dans le bâtiment », etc.
target_language_example: Il est interdit de fumer dans le train.
native_language_example: No smoking on the train.

additional_notes: Used to say an action won’t help or isn’t worth doing. Very common in the full form: « Il est inutile de + infinitive » (“It’s pointless to…”). In speech and writing it’s often shortened to « Inutile de + infinitive » (“No point in…”).
target_language_example: Inutile de t'inquiéter, tout va bien.
native_language_example: No point in worrying, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Future tense of aller (to go) + bien (well). Used to reassure someone about a person or a situation: Il ira bien (He’ll be fine), Ça ira bien (It’ll be fine / It’ll work out). Often said as reassurance.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ça ira bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’ll be fine.

additional_notes: From the verb adorer (to love/to adore). Used to express strong enthusiasm for something (a name, a person, a hobby, a place, etc.). More intense than "j'aime" (I like), but in everyday French it’s often used casually like “I love it!” You can follow it with a noun ("J'adore le théâtre"), a person ("J'adore ce type"), or an infinitive verb ("J'adore faire..."), and you can emphasize it with "J'adore ça !".
target_language_example: J'adore ce restaurant, on y mange très bien.
native_language_example: I love this restaurant; the food is really good there.

meaning: “I love this …” (referring to a singular feminine thing).
additional_notes: Used to express strong liking/love for something. It must be followed by a noun: **j'adore cette + nom**. **cette** is the feminine singular form of “this,” used with feminine nouns (and also before a vowel sound or *h* muet: *cette amie*). For masculine nouns, use **ce/cet** (*j'adore ce film / j'adore cet endroit*).
target_language_example: j'adore cette idée.
native_language_example: I love this idea.

additional_notes: Contraction of je ai. It is the 1st-person singular form of avoir and is used both for possession/state (for example, j'ai un livre = I have a book) and as an auxiliary before a past participle to form a very common past tense, often translated as the simple past in English.
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon téléphone.
native_language_example: I forgot my phone.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of appeler: j’ + ai + appelé. Use it to say you called someone or called a place. With time expressions you can specify when: « J’ai appelé … il y a deux jours » = “I called … two days ago.”
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai appelé trop tard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I called too late.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *apprendre* with *je*: **j'ai appris**. It can mean (1) you learned something (a skill/knowledge): *j'ai appris le français* (“I learned French”), or (2) you found out/heard some information: *j'ai appris la nouvelle* (“I found out/heard the news”). It’s commonly followed by **que** (“that”) or **ce qui** (“what”): *j'ai appris que…*, *j'ai appris ce qui s’est passé*.
target_language_example: j'ai appris hier que tu étais ici.
native_language_example: I found out yesterday that you were here.

additional_notes: Past tense of attendre (“to wait”), using the passé composé: j’ + ai + attendu. Often followed by a duration (des heures, toute la journée, très longtemps) or by pour + infinitive (“in order to / to”): J’ai attendu toute ma vie pour le dire.
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai attendu longtemps, mais tu n'es pas venu.
native_language_example: Sorry, I waited a long time, but you didn’t come.

additional_notes: Past tense of comprendre (“to understand”), used to say you understood something just explained. In conversation it often means “Got it/OK, I understand,” and can sound firm depending on tone (e.g., "Ouais, j'ai compris" = “Yeah, I got it”).
target_language_example: D'accord, j'ai compris : on se retrouve à 18 h devant la gare.
native_language_example: Okay, I got it: we’re meeting at 6 p.m. in front of the station.

meaning: "I thought" / "I believed" (often: mistakenly, or for a moment).
additional_notes: Passé composé of « croire ». Very common with an infinitive (« j'ai cru entendre/voir… » = “I thought I heard/saw…”) or with « que » + a full clause (« j'ai cru qu'il allait… » = “I thought he was going to…”). It often suggests your impression wasn’t certain or turned out to be wrong.
target_language_example: J'ai cru entendre du bruit.
native_language_example: I thought I heard some noise.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of *croire* to report what you believed at that moment, often implying you later realized it was wrong or it turned out differently (surprise, fear, misunderstanding). It’s followed by a full clause with its own verb tense: *j’ai cru que + imparfait / plus-que-parfait / conditionnel*, etc. Example nuance: *J’ai cru que tu étais parti/partie* (agreement with the person addressed: *parti* to a man, *partie* to a woman).
target_language_example: J'ai cru que c'était un voleur.
native_language_example: I thought it was a burglar.

meaning: "I thought it was..." / "I believed it was..." (often a mistaken first impression).
additional_notes: Used to describe what you believed at first in the past. Very often it implies you were wrong or surprised afterward. Structure: « J'ai cru que + [imparfait] »; most commonly « c'était » = “it was”.
target_language_example: J'ai cru que c'était la bonne adresse, mais je me suis trompé.
native_language_example: I thought it was the right address, but I was mistaken.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed in the past, often implying you later realized it wasn’t true. It’s followed by a verb phrase (e.g., future-in-the-past/conditional: *tu changerais…*; past perfect: *tu t’étais…*; or a negative: *tu ne… jamais*).
target_language_example: J'ai cru que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *dire* (“to say/tell”). Use it to report something you said in the past. Often followed by a clause (*J'ai dit que…* = “I said that…”) or by *de* + infinitive when reporting an instruction (*J'ai dit de…* = “I told [someone] to…”).
target_language_example: J'ai dit de faire le tour.
native_language_example: I said to go around.

additional_notes: Used to report what you previously said, followed by a full clause. After « que », French commonly uses backshifting (e.g., conditional/past forms) in reported speech: « J'ai dit que je le ferais » (“I said I would do it”). In casual speech you may also hear no backshift: « J'ai dit que je le ferai » (“I said I will do it”), though it’s less standard in careful French.
target_language_example: J'ai dit que je le ferais.
native_language_example: I said that I would do it.

meaning: “I said that I was going to …”
additional_notes: Used to report something you previously said you intended to do. After "j'ai dit que", French often uses the imperfect ("j'allais") for “was going to / intended to,” even if in English you might say “I said I would…”. The verb after "j'allais" stays in the infinitive (e.g., essayer, le faire, m'en occuper).
target_language_example: J'ai dit que j'allais t'appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I said I was going to call you tonight.

additional_notes: Used to report something you said in the past. "J'ai dit" is the passé composé of "dire" (to say/tell). It’s followed by "que" + a full clause; after "je" you continue with the verb (e.g., "j'ai dit que je venais").
target_language_example: J'ai dit que je ne pouvais pas venir aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I said that I couldn’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to say you made a decision and are going to do something. It’s the passé composé of décider: "j’ai décidé" + "de" + infinitive (e.g., partir, revenir, profiter). The English meaning can be either simple past (I decided to) or present perfect (I've decided to), depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai décidé de changer de travail.
native_language_example: I've decided to change jobs.

additional_notes: Used to say you did something before now. Very often followed by a past participle (passé composé): « j'ai déjà + appelé / commencé / entendu ». It can also mean “I have already (experienced/known)” depending on the verb (e.g., « j'ai déjà connu ça » = “I’ve been through that before”).
target_language_example: J'ai déjà entendu cette histoire.
native_language_example: I’ve already heard that story.

additional_notes: Used to say you have previously seen something. Often followed by a direct object (e.g., « ce film ») or used with « ça » (“that/it”). « déjà » adds the idea of “already/before.”
target_language_example: J'ai déjà vu cette série, elle est super.
native_language_example: I've already seen this series; it's great.

meaning: "I had to" / "I needed to"; sometimes "I must have" (probably).
additional_notes: Passé composé of devoir (to have to). It often expresses a past obligation/necessity: « J'ai dû partir » = “I had to leave.” In some contexts it expresses a logical guess about the past: « J'ai dû m'évanouir » = “I must have fainted” (I probably fainted). The form « dû » (with the accent) can look like English “due” but it’s a different word.
target_language_example: J'ai dû annuler le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I had to cancel the appointment.

additional_notes: Passé composé of entendre (“to hear”). Used for (1) something you heard at a specific moment (J'ai entendu l'appel; J'ai entendu ça à la radio) or (2) information/rumors you learned by hearing (J'ai entendu dire que…; J'ai entendu de bonnes choses sur…). Often translates as either “I heard” or “I’ve heard” depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai entendu ça à la radio.
native_language_example: I heard that on the radio.

meaning: “I heard this/that …” (as a lead-in to what you heard; usually followed by more words).
additional_notes: On its own, "j'ai entendu ce" sounds incomplete in French because "ce" typically needs a continuation (most often "ce que" + clause, or "ce" + noun). In everyday speech, you more commonly hear "j'ai entendu ça" (“I heard that/this”). Use "j'ai entendu ce" mainly when you are about to add what it is (e.g., "… ce que tu as dit" / "… ce bruit").
target_language_example: J'ai entendu ce que tu as dit.
native_language_example: I heard what you said.

additional_notes: Used to say you know something by reputation or through what people say, not necessarily from direct experience. It comes from "entendre parler de" (to hear people talk about). You can change the subject and tense: "Tu as entendu parler de… ?" (Have you heard of…?), "J'avais entendu parler de…" (I had heard about…).
target_language_example: J'ai entendu parler de ce restaurant, il est très bien.
native_language_example: I've heard about this restaurant; it's very good.

additional_notes: Past tense of « essayer » (to try): « j'ai essayé » uses the passé composé and is often followed by « de » + infinitive (e.g., « j'ai essayé de comprendre » = I tried to understand). It can also be used without an infinitive to mean you made an attempt (e.g., « J'ai essayé deux fois » = I tried twice). In context it often implies effort, even if it didn’t work: « J'ai essayé, mais… ».
target_language_example: J'ai essayé de t'appeler hier, mais tu ne répondais pas.
native_language_example: I tried to call you yesterday, but you weren’t answering.

additional_notes: Past tense of "essayer de" + infinitive. Used to say you made an effort to do something (often implying it didn’t work, or at least it took effort). In conversation it can be followed by an infinitive: "J'ai essayé de l'appeler" (I tried to call him).
target_language_example: J'ai essayé de te joindre, mais tu ne répondais pas.
native_language_example: I tried to reach you, but you weren't answering.

additional_notes: Used to say you made an effort to do something involving the person you’re speaking to. Structure: « j’ai essayé de + infinitive » (past tense, passé composé). « te » is the object pronoun meaning “you” (informal singular) and comes before the infinitive: « j’ai essayé de te contacter / te joindre / te le dire / te trouver ». Note: « essayer » looks like English “essay” but here it means “to try” (false friend).
target_language_example: J'ai essayé de te parler hier soir, mais tu ne répondais pas.
native_language_example: I tried to talk to you last night, but you weren’t answering.

additional_notes: Passé composé of avoir (je + ai + eu). Used for completed past events. Depending on the noun, it often translates as “I had” (j’ai eu une idée), “I got” (j’ai eu le boulot = I got the job), or “I received” (j’ai eu ton SMS = I got/received your text). Pronounced roughly like “zhay-oo” (two vowel sounds).
target_language_example: J'ai eu un problème avec ma carte.
native_language_example: I had a problem with my card.

meaning: I was lucky / I had good luck.
additional_notes: Literally “I had some luck.” Uses the past tense of avoir (j’ai eu) to talk about being lucky in a specific situation. Often followed by “de + infinitive” to say what you were lucky to do (e.g., de te rencontrer = to meet you).
target_language_example: J'ai eu de la chance de ne pas rater le train.
native_language_example: I was lucky not to miss the train.

meaning: “I got a …” / “I had a …” (past: I received or experienced something).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of avoir: "j’ai eu" = "I had". It’s commonly used with things you receive ("J’ai eu un appel" = I got a call) or sudden experiences/ideas ("J’ai eu un flash" = I had a flash / sudden inspiration). It must be followed by a masculine singular noun (un + noun); for feminine, use "j’ai eu une …".
target_language_example: J'ai eu un message de mon prof ce matin.
native_language_example: I got a message from my teacher this morning.

meaning: "I had a" / "I have had a" (past tense, feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of avoir: « j’ » (I) + « ai » (have) + « eu » (had) + « une » (a, feminine). It’s used to say you had/experienced something in the past, and it must be followed by a feminine noun (e.g., « une idée », « une liaison », « une révélation »). With a masculine noun, you’d use « j’ai eu un … ». In English it’s usually rendered as simple past: “I had a …”.
target_language_example: j'ai eu une révélation.
native_language_example: I had a revelation.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: « j'ai failli + infinitif » = you came very close to doing something, but it didn’t happen (often a near miss). Despite looking like English “failed,” « faillir » means “to almost (do)” in this structure.
target_language_example: J'ai failli avoir un accident en venant.
native_language_example: I almost had an accident on my way here.

additional_notes: Used with the passé composé of faire (j’ + ai + fait). It can mean “I did” or “I have done,” depending on context. Common patterns: j'ai fait + [a thing/task] (“I did/made …”), j'ai fait + [activity] (“I did … / I went …,” e.g., j'ai fait l'armée = “I did military service”), j'ai fait + [distance/route] (“I covered …,” e.g., tout le chemin), j'ai fait de mon mieux (“I did my best”), j'ai fait n'importe quoi (“I did something stupid/whatever”). Note: the apostrophe in j'ai is required before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: J'ai fait ce qu'on m'a dit.
native_language_example: I did what I was told.

additional_notes: Used to say you carried out whatever follows—often what you thought was right/necessary, or what someone told/asked you to do. It’s typically followed by another clause (e.g., "j’ai pu" = I could; "j’avais à faire" = I had to do; "tu as dit" = you said; "vous avez demandé" = you asked).
target_language_example: J'ai fait ce que j'ai pu.
native_language_example: I did what I could.

meaning: “I did what I…” (an unfinished lead-in that must be completed).
additional_notes: This is a sentence starter that expects you to add a verb phrase after « je » (e.g., « j’ai pu », « devais faire », « pouvais »). On its own (« j’ai fait ce que je… ») sounds incomplete; it’s typically used to introduce an explanation of what you were able/required to do.
target_language_example: J'ai fait ce que je devais faire, puis je suis parti.
native_language_example: I did what I had to do, then I left.

additional_notes: Used to say you carried out what someone expected/asked. It’s usually followed by a verb phrase like « attendiez de moi » (expected of me) or « aviez demandé » / « m’aviez demandé » (had asked / had asked me).
target_language_example: J'ai fait ce que vous m'aviez demandé.
native_language_example: I did what you had asked me to do.

meaning: “I did the …” / “I have done the …” (passé composé of faire + le + masculine noun).
additional_notes: Structure: j'ai fait + le + noun (masculine singular). Used for actions/tasks you “do” or “carry out”: le boulot (the work/job), le maximum (your best/the most you can), le nécessaire (what’s necessary), le test (the test), le tour (a trip/round). In English, passé composé can translate as either “I did” or “I have done,” depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai fait le nécessaire.
native_language_example: I did what was necessary.

meaning: "I did my…" / "I’ve done my…" (used to introduce something you did: my job, my choice, my best, etc.).
additional_notes: Followed by a masculine singular noun or an expression functioning like one: « j'ai fait mon boulot » (I did my job), « j'ai fait mon choix » (I made my choice), « j'ai fait mon possible » (I did my best). Common idiom: « faire son beurre » = to make money/profit: « j'ai fait mon beurre avec… ».
target_language_example: J'ai fait mon choix.
native_language_example: I made my choice.

meaning: "I did everything that…" / "I have done everything that…"
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you did, followed by a clause (usually with a subject + verb): « J'ai fait tout ce que je pouvais. » It’s in the past tense (passé composé: j’ai fait = I did / I have done). Often implies you did your best or did all that was possible.
target_language_example: J'ai fait tout ce que je pouvais pour t'aider.
native_language_example: I did everything I could to help you.

additional_notes: Literally “I did/made a dream,” but in French you use faire (to do/make) + un rêve (a dream) to talk about dreaming. It’s typically used with a time expression like cette nuit / la nuit dernière (“last night”) and can be followed by an adjective (incroyable, merveilleux, etc.).
target_language_example: Cette nuit, j'ai fait un rêve très étrange.
native_language_example: Last night, I had a very strange dream.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "faire" with "avoir": "j'ai fait" = "I did" / "I have done." Used to state you did something; can also express emphasis, disbelief, or defensiveness in questions (e.g., "J'ai fait ça, moi ?"). "Ça" refers to something already known from context.
target_language_example: Vous pensez que j'ai fait ça ?
native_language_example: Do you think I did that?

additional_notes: With a direct object, it means you completed something: « J'ai fini mon service. » = “I finished my shift.” Used with a place (often with « ici », « au… », « dans… »), « finir » can mean “to end up”: « J'ai fini ici. » = “I ended up here.”
target_language_example: J'ai fini trop tard, alors j'ai pris un taxi.
native_language_example: I finished too late, so I took a taxi.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: people often drop "ne" in negatives. So "j'ai jamais" means the same as the standard written form "je n'ai jamais". Used with the past tense ("j'ai" / "je suis") to say you have never done/been something, or with "été aussi…" to mean "I’ve never been so…".
target_language_example: J'ai jamais vu un film aussi drôle.
native_language_example: I've never seen a movie that funny.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *lire* with *avoir*: **j'** (je) + **ai** (have) + **lu** (read). Used to say you read something (a file, report, article). Often translates to English simple past (“I read…”) or present perfect (“I have read…”), depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai lu ton message ce matin.
native_language_example: I read your message this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense of oublier (“to forget”) using the passé composé: j’ai + oublié. Often used alone as an apology (“Sorry, I forgot.”) or followed by what was forgotten: j’ai oublié + noun (j’ai oublié les paroles) or j’ai oublié ce que… (“I forgot what…”).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon mot de passe, je ne peux pas me connecter.
native_language_example: I forgot my password, I can’t log in.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t do an action because you forgot. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « j’ai oublié de + infinitive » (e.g., j’ai oublié de fermer la porte). Can also introduce something you forgot to mention: « Oh, j’ai oublié de te dire… ».
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai oublié de répondre à ton message.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to reply to your message.

meaning: “I forgot my …” (talking about a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun after it (mon + masculine noun), e.g., mon livre, mon portable, mon portefeuille. In French, the past tense is built with avoir: j’ai oublié = “I forgot / I’ve forgotten.” If the noun is feminine, you usually say: j’ai oublié ma …
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon passeport à l'hôtel.
native_language_example: I forgot my passport at the hotel.

meaning: I spoke to / I talked to.
additional_notes: Used with the passé composé of parler (j'ai parlé) to say you spoke/talked to someone in the past. The preposition à introduces the person you spoke to (e.g., j'ai parlé à ma mère). In speech, you’ll often hear it shortened to "j’ai parlé à" → "j’ai parlé à" (same spelling, faster pronunciation).
target_language_example: J'ai parlé à ton professeur après le cours.
native_language_example: I spoke to your teacher after class.

meaning: “I don’t have / I didn’t / I haven’t” (informal negative form of « j’ai »).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: it drops « ne » from the standard negative « je n’ai pas … ». Used either with a noun (« J'ai pas le temps » = I don’t have time) or before a past participle (« J'ai pas compris » = I didn’t understand / I haven’t understood). In careful writing or formal situations, use « je n’ai pas ».
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai pas le temps aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time today.

meaning: “I spent” / “I had” (a time/day/evening) / “I made” (a call) / “I struck” (a deal).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé (past tense) of *passer* with *avoir*: **j'ai passé** = “I passed / I spent / I did,” depending on what follows. Common patterns: **j'ai passé du temps** (I spent time), **j'ai passé la journée/la soirée** (I spent the day/evening), **j'ai passé un coup de fil** (I made a phone call), **j'ai passé un marché** (I made/struck a deal). Note: although *passer* can also take *être* in other meanings (e.g., *je suis passé* = I went by/passed by), **j'ai passé** is correct when *passer* takes a direct object (time, a call, an agreement, etc.).
target_language_example: Hier, j'ai passé la journée ici.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I spent the day here.

meaning: “I had / I spent a …” (talking about time, like a day or an evening).
additional_notes: Used with a time period (une journée, une soirée, une semaine, etc.) to describe how your time was. It’s the passé composé of *passer*: *j’ai passé* + adjective + time word. Even though it looks like English “I passed,” here it usually means “I spent” or “I had.”
target_language_example: J'ai passé une semaine incroyable à Paris.
native_language_example: I had an incredible week in Paris.

additional_notes: Used to express a past thought or idea. Most often followed by **que** + a sentence: *J'ai pensé que...* (“I thought that...”). With **à** + a person/thing, it means “to think about (someone/something)”: *J'ai pensé à toi* (“I thought about you”).
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que tu avais raison.
native_language_example: I thought you were right.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed or assumed (often a reason or motivation for what you did). In French, after "penser que" you normally use the indicative (e.g., "j'ai pensé que tu voulais…"). In negative form, it often takes the subjunctive: "je n'ai pas pensé que tu viennes" (I didn’t think you would come).
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que tu étais déjà parti, alors je ne t'ai pas appelé.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left, so I didn’t call you.

additional_notes: Used to describe a past belief/opinion that may or may not still be true. "J'ai pensé" is the passé composé of *penser* (a completed thought in the past). "que" introduces what you thought, and "c'était" means "it was/that was" (from *ce + était*). Often followed by an adjective or a noun phrase: *important*, *une bonne idée*, *vous*, etc.
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que c'était trop tard.
native_language_example: I thought it was too late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed/assumed about someone (often as an explanation). It’s the passé composé of penser (j’ai pensé = “I thought”), followed by que + a clause starting with tu. What follows can be in the imperfect/conditional/etc. depending on the meaning: e.g., "J’ai pensé que tu aurais faim" = “I thought you would be hungry.”
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption, expectation, or polite suggestion about the other person. Commonly followed by the conditional to soften the statement: « j'ai pensé que vous voudriez / aimeriez / auriez… ». Can be translated literally as “I thought that you…”.
target_language_example: j'ai pensé que vous voudriez le savoir.
native_language_example: I thought you’d want to know.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "penser" + "à". Use "penser à" + noun/pronoun to say you had something in mind or considered something: "J'ai pensé à toi" (I thought of you), "J'ai pensé à ça" (I thought about that). Contrast: "penser que" is followed by a full clause/opinion ("Je pense que…" = I think that…).
target_language_example: Hier, j'ai pensé à toi.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I thought of you.

additional_notes: Passé composé of prendre (je prends → j'ai pris). Very common and flexible depending on what follows: it can mean you took/grabbed something (j'ai pris de quoi manger), took notes (j'ai pris des notes), had food/drinks (j'ai pris deux verres de vin), answered a call (j'ai pris l'appel), made a decision (j'ai pris ma décision), made an appointment (j'ai pris rendez-vous), or took care of someone (j'ai pris soin de toi). The most natural English translation depends on the object/complement.
target_language_example: J'ai pris des notes pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: I took notes during the meeting.

meaning: 'I was able to' / 'I could' / 'I managed to' (in the past).
additional_notes: Past tense of "pouvoir" (passé composé). It often means you had the ability or the opportunity to do something and succeeded: "J'ai pu faire…" = "I was able to do…". In questions, it can express surprise/regret: "Comment j'ai pu… ?" = "How could I…?". Common with comparisons/time: "aussi vite que j'ai pu" (as fast as I could), "autant que j'ai pu" (as much as I could), "dès que j'ai pu" (as soon as I could).
target_language_example: Je suis parti dès que j'ai pu.
native_language_example: I left as soon as I could.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of recevoir. Used to say you received or got a message, letter, call, orders, etc. Often followed by a direct object: J'ai reçu ton message / un appel / une lettre. In formal contexts you may see: J'ai bien reçu… ("I have received…").
target_language_example: J'ai reçu ton e-mail ce matin.
native_language_example: I got your email this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of recevoir: « j’ai reçu » = I received / I’ve received. « une lettre » is a (paper) letter, not an email (use « un e-mail / un mail »). Often followed by « de » + person: « une lettre de mon père » (a letter from my father).
target_language_example: J'ai reçu une lettre de ma grand-mère hier.
native_language_example: I received a letter from my grandmother yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for you for a long time (often up to the present). Common with past participles (j'ai toujours été…) or with verbs like rêver (j'ai toujours rêvé de…). In spoken French, "j'ai" is often reduced to "j'" before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: j'ai toujours rêvé d'y aller.
native_language_example: I've always dreamed of going there.

meaning: “I always knew that” / “I’ve known all along that …”.
additional_notes: Used to say you were certain about something from the start (often even before it happened). Grammatically it’s the passé composé of *savoir* (*j’ai su*), but with *toujours* the overall sense is usually “I knew it all along” rather than “I found out.” Typically followed by a clause in the imperfect or conditional (e.g., *arriverait, pouvais, y arriverais, finirait*).
target_language_example: j'ai toujours su que ce jour arriverait.
native_language_example: I always knew that this day would come.

additional_notes: Literally "I have always wanted." Used to talk about a long-standing desire up to now. Often followed by an infinitive (j'ai toujours voulu + verb: "j'ai toujours voulu voyager") or by a noun ("j'ai toujours voulu un fils"). In more formal/written French, you may also see "j'ai toujours voulu dire" for "I've always wanted to say," but everyday speech often uses "j'ai toujours voulu te dire…".
target_language_example: J'ai toujours voulu apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I've always wanted to learn French.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of être (j'ai été) with toujours to stress that something has consistently been true up to now. It’s usually followed by a complement like avec toi (with you), de ton côté (on your side), or là pour toi (there for you). Depending on context, it can also be translated as “I was always…”.
target_language_example: J'ai toujours été de ton côté.
native_language_example: I've always been on your side.

additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence with a past participle (passé composé): **J'ai tout + past participle** = “I … everything” (e.g., *J'ai tout essayé* = “I tried everything”). On its own, **J'ai tout** can mean “I have everything / I’ve got everything,” depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai tout préparé pour ce soir.
native_language_example: I prepared everything for tonight.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *trouver* with **avoir**. Used when you located/discovered something (*j'ai trouvé une solution*), found/obtained something (*j'ai trouvé du travail*), or to express an opinion with **j'ai trouvé que + clause** (“I thought / I found that…”, e.g., *j'ai trouvé ça tout à fait normal* / *j'ai trouvé que c'était normal*). It can also be used alone to mean “I’ve got it!” / “Found it!” (*Voilà, j'ai trouvé.*).
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé une solution.
native_language_example: I found a solution.

additional_notes: Used to announce that you found something (an object, a place, a solution, etc.). Literally "I have found a" (passé composé of trouver). The noun that follows is masculine singular and usually begins with a consonant sound: un boulot, un travail, un gâteau, un point de vue. With a feminine noun, you’d say: j’ai trouvé une …
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé un bon restaurant près d'ici.
native_language_example: I found a good restaurant near here.

additional_notes: Used to say you discovered an object inside a place/container (a room, bag, pocket, someone’s things). Very common in conversation; you then add the location after "dans". In more formal writing you might also see "j’ai trouvé ceci dans…"
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé ça dans mon sac.
native_language_example: I found this in my bag.

additional_notes: Literally the passé composé of voir: "j'ai vu" = "I saw / I've seen." In conversation, especially in "C'est bon, j'ai vu", it can mean "OK, I understand" or "OK, I've got it" after someone explains or shows you something. It can also mean you noticed something ("I saw how you look at her") or discovered the truth about someone ("I saw his true face").
target_language_example: Pas besoin d'expliquer, j'ai vu.
native_language_example: No need to explain, I get it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you saw, usually followed by a full clause: « J'ai vu ce que tu as fait » (“I saw what you did”). In speech, « j'ai » is often pronounced like “zhay”. You can also use other tenses/persons: « tu as vu ce que… », « j'avais vu ce que… ».
target_language_example: J'ai vu ce que tu as écrit.
native_language_example: I saw what you wrote.

meaning: 'I saw the' / 'I've seen the' (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: "J'ai vu" is the passé composé of *voir* (to see): *j’* (I) + *ai* (have) + *vu* (seen). It’s followed by **la** when the thing you saw is feminine singular (*la photo*, *la Terre*). For masculine singular use **j’ai vu le…**, and for plural use **j’ai vu les…**. In speech, *j’ai* is often pronounced like “zhay”.
target_language_example: j'ai vu la photo sur votre livre.
native_language_example: I saw the photo on your book.

additional_notes: Literally "I have seen that" (passé composé of voir). Used to say you saw something (on TV, in the news, online, etc.) or that you’ve already seen it before. In casual speech you may also hear just "Vu ça" or "J’ai déjà vu ça" (I’ve already seen that).
target_language_example: T'inquiète, j'ai vu ça sur Internet.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I saw that on the Internet.

additional_notes: Passé composé of être (je + ai + été). Often used (1) with an adjective to describe how you were/you felt: « J'ai été content/ravi. », and (2) to form the passive voice: « J'ai été acquitté » = “I was acquitted.” In many everyday contexts it translates to English simple past (“I was”), even though the literal form is “I have been.”
target_language_example: J'ai été très fatigué hier soir.
native_language_example: I was very tired last night.

additional_notes: Contraction of je ai, from the verb avoir. Very common in everyday French for possession and in many set expressions: j'ai faim = I'm hungry, j'ai 20 ans = I'm 20 years old, j'ai rendez-vous = I have an appointment.
target_language_example: J'ai une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I have a good idea.

meaning: “I have something else.” / “I have something else to do/say/ask.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce an additional thing you want to say/ask, or to indicate you have other plans or something else on your mind (often implying you can’t do what was suggested). Frequently followed by: « de prévu » (planned), « en tête » (in mind), or « à + infinitive » (to do/say/ask).
target_language_example: J'ai autre chose de prévu.
native_language_example: I have other plans.

additional_notes: From the expression avoir besoin de, which means "to need." It is usually followed by de + noun/pronoun or de + infinitive: j'ai besoin de temps, j'ai besoin de ça, j'ai besoin de me reposer. It can also be followed by que + clause: j'ai besoin que vous m'écoutiez.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: I need help.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something. The d' (de) links to what you need: j'ai besoin d'un/une + noun (j'ai besoin d'un café / d'une carte). With a verb, use de + infinitive: J'ai besoin d'y aller (“I need to go there”). The verb is avoir, so it can change: tu as besoin de…, il/elle a besoin de…, nous avons besoin de….
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un moment pour réfléchir.
native_language_example: I need a moment to think.

meaning: "I need a" (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you need something or someone. It’s the most common way to express need in French.
