Change the article depending on the noun: j’ai besoin d’une + feminine noun; j’ai besoin de + plural/uncountable (e.g., j’ai besoin de temps); j’ai besoin d’ + vowel sound (e.g., j’ai besoin d’un avocat).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un stylo, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need a pen, please.

meaning: “I need a/an …” (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or requirement. "J'ai besoin de" = "I need"; it becomes "d'une" before a feminine singular noun (e.g., une autorisation, une signature). For a masculine noun, use "j'ai besoin d'un"; for a plural, use "j'ai besoin de" + plural noun (e.g., "j'ai besoin de clés"). Note the apostrophe: "j'ai" is the contraction of "je ai".
target_language_example: j'ai besoin d'une autorisation.
native_language_example: I need an authorization/permission.

additional_notes: Used to say that you need something or need to do something. It is followed by de + a noun (j'ai besoin de détails) or de + an infinitive (j'ai besoin de partir). This form is specifically for 'I need'.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de parler avec toi.
native_language_example: I need to talk with you.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity/urgency to obtain information. Structure: « j'ai besoin de + infinitif » (here « savoir »). Often followed by an indirect question (e.g., « pourquoi », « qui », « ce que », « où », etc.) or by a noun phrase (« quelque chose », « la vérité »). Note: You’ll also see « J’ai besoin de savoir » with capitalization and the apostrophe « J’ai » in formal writing; the term here is given in lowercase.
target_language_example: j'ai besoin de savoir pourquoi tu es parti si tôt.
native_language_example: I need to know why you left so early.

meaning: "I need to (do something) to/with you" (used before a verb).
additional_notes: This is the start of the pattern: « J'ai besoin de te + infinitive » (e.g., te parler, te voir, t'aider). « avoir besoin de » means “to need,” and « te » is the object pronoun “you” (informal singular). It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de te parler.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone’s help, support, or presence. "J’ai besoin de" is followed by a person (toi/vous/lui/elle) or a thing (ex. "J’ai besoin d’aide" = I need help). You can add a place or time: "J’ai besoin de toi là-bas" (I need you there) or "quand j’ai besoin de toi" (when I need you).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de toi maintenant, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need you now, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something from or belonging to the person you’re addressing. « votre » is the formal singular (“your” to one person politely) or plural (“your” to multiple people). It must be followed by a noun: « J'ai besoin de votre avis », « J'ai besoin de votre signature », etc.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de votre avis.
native_language_example: I need your opinion.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone's help/presence. "Vous" can mean one person you’re addressing formally, or multiple people ("you all"). You can add details like "ici" (here), "tout de suite" (right now), or "vous deux" (both of you).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, j'ai besoin de vous pour remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need you to fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone to do something. It must be followed by a verb in the subjunctive: « j'ai besoin que tu viennes », « j'ai besoin que tu fasses ça ». In speech, you may also hear « J’ai besoin de toi pour + infinitive » (e.g., « J’ai besoin de toi pour m’aider »).
target_language_example: j'ai besoin que tu viennes demain matin.
native_language_example: I need you to come tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to ask/insist that someone do something. It’s followed by **que** + **subjunctive**: *J'ai besoin que tu me croies* (croire → **croies**), *… que tu me fasses* (faire → **fasses**), *… que tu me rendes* (rendre → **rendes**). The object pronoun **me** comes before the verb (*tu me crois*, *tu me fasses*, *tu me rendes*). In everyday speech you can also say **J’ai besoin de toi pour + infinitive**: *J’ai besoin de toi pour m’aider.*
target_language_example: J'ai besoin que tu me rendes service.
native_language_example: I need you to do me a favor.

meaning: “I have what he/it …” (incomplete on its own).
additional_notes: This is typically the beginning of a longer structure: « j'ai ce qu'il + verb … » meaning “I have what he/it …”. Most commonly, it appears as « j'ai ce qu'il faut », which can mean “I have what’s needed” or “I have what it takes,” depending on context. Note: the standalone fragment « j'ai ce qu'il » is grammatically incomplete unless followed by something like « faut », « faut pour… », « faut faire », etc.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : j'ai ce qu'il faut.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I have what’s needed.

meaning: I trust (in) / I have confidence in.
additional_notes: Used to say you trust a person or thing: "J'ai confiance en toi/elle/lui/vous" (I trust you/her/him/you [formal/plural]). You can also trust someone's ability or judgment: "J'ai confiance en ton jugement" (I trust your judgment). In negatives: "Je n'ai pas confiance en..." (I don't trust...).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, j'ai confiance en toi.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I trust you.

additional_notes: Used to say you have other things/people/plans besides the ones mentioned. It’s usually followed by a plural noun: j’ai d’autres projets / d’autres patients. The full pattern is: "j’ai" + "d’autres" + plural noun. Often implies “I have more/else to do.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas rester : j'ai d'autres choses à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't stay: I have other things to do.

meaning: "I have (some)" / "I’ve got (some)" (used before a noun phrase; often appears when an adjective comes before a plural noun, where "des" becomes "de").
additional_notes: This is the beginning of the structure "j’ai + [noun phrase]". In standard French, the plural indefinite article "des" typically becomes "de" (or "d’") when an adjective precedes the plural noun: "J'ai de grands projets" (vs. *j'ai des grands projets*). It also appears in set phrases like "J'ai de tout" (“I have everything / a bit of everything”) and in relative clauses like "ce que j'ai de mieux" (“the best I have”).
target_language_example: j'ai de très bonnes nouvelles.
native_language_example: I have very good news.

meaning: "I have some…" / "I have…" (with an uncountable noun beginning with a vowel or silent h).
additional_notes: This is the partitive construction: avoir + de l' + uncountable noun (e.g., de l'eau, de l'expérience, de l'or). It often means “some” in English, but English may omit “some” (“I have asthma”). Use de l' before a vowel sound or silent h; otherwise use du (masc.) or de la (fem.).
target_language_example: J'ai de l'eau dans mon sac.
native_language_example: I have some water in my bag.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel fortunate, often followed by de + infinitive to specify what you’re lucky to do/have (e.g., j'ai de la chance de te connaître = I’m lucky to know you). Can also be said alone (j'ai de la chance.) or as a rhetorical tag (j'ai de la chance, hein ?). In Si j'ai de la chance ! it’s an emphatic “Yes, I’m lucky!” and can be ironic depending on context.
target_language_example: j'ai de la chance de te connaître.
native_language_example: I’m lucky to know you.

additional_notes: Used to say you possess or have something in general, before a plural noun: j’ai + des + noun (e.g., des projets, des infos). "J’ai" is the contraction of "je ai". "Des" often means "some" or simply marks an unspecified plural in French.
target_language_example: J'ai des questions pour toi.
native_language_example: I have some questions for you.

meaning: “I have some …” (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: “Du” is the partitive article (de + le) meaning “some” or “(a bit) of.” It’s used with many uncountable nouns (j'ai du boulot = I have some work, j'ai du respect = I have some respect) and some set phrases (j'ai du retard = I’m late / I have a delay). Don’t confuse with “j’ai dû” (with an accent), which means “I had to.”
target_language_example: J'ai du boulot aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have some work today.

meaning: "I have news" / "I have something new (to tell you)."
additional_notes: Used to announce you have new information or an update. Very common with "pour toi/vous" (for you) and in phrases like "dès que j'ai du nouveau" or "si j'ai du nouveau" meaning "as soon as I have any news" / "if I get any news." You can also say "Du nouveau ?" to ask "Any news?"
target_language_example: Je t'appelle dès que j'ai du nouveau.
native_language_example: I’ll call you as soon as I have any news.

additional_notes: Used to say you have some work/tasks, often implying you’re busy or have work waiting. You can add details: "en retard" (overdue/behind), "pour vous" (for you), "qui m’attend" (waiting for me). Structure: "J’ai du + nom" = “I have some + noun” (an unspecified amount).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j'ai du travail.
native_language_example: I can’t go out tonight: I have work to do.

meaning: "I still have" / "I have ... left" (also "I have more").
additional_notes: Used to say something remains to do/ask, time remains, or that you can add something else. Common patterns: "j'ai encore + noun" (j'ai encore du travail = I still have work), "j'ai encore + infinitive" (j'ai encore des choses à faire = I still have things to do), and "j'ai encore le temps" (I still have time). In "j'ai encore mieux", it means "I have something even better".
target_language_example: j'ai encore quelques questions à vous poser.
native_language_example: I still have a few questions to ask you.

meaning: “I feel like” / “I want (to)” (often a mild, craving-like want).
additional_notes: Literally “I have desire.” Most often followed by **de + infinitive**: *j'ai envie de parler* (I feel like talking). With a different subject or a full clause, you can use **avoir envie que + subjunctive**: *j'ai envie qu'elle soit heureuse* (I want her to be happy). In questions or negative/ironic contexts it can mean “Do you think I want to…?”
target_language_example: j'ai envie de parler.
native_language_example: I feel like talking.

meaning: "I feel like…" / "I want to…" (often: "I’m in the mood to…").
additional_notes: "Avoir envie de" expresses a desire, urge, or craving. Use **j'ai envie de + infinitive** (with **d'** before a vowel or mute h): *j'ai envie d'essayer* (I feel like trying). With a noun, use **j'ai envie de + noun** (or **d'**): *j'ai envie d'une cigarette* (I feel like a cigarette). It’s usually a more feeling-based want than **je veux**, which can sound more direct/demanding.
target_language_example: j'ai envie d'essayer.
native_language_example: I feel like trying.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire or urge. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « j'ai envie de + infinitive » (j'ai envie de sortir, j'ai envie de marcher). It can be a light preference (“I feel like…”) or a stronger desire depending on context. In a negative or rhetorical question, it can imply reluctance or annoyance: « Tu crois que j'ai envie de faire ça ? » (“Do you think I want to do that?”).
target_language_example: J'ai envie de rentrer chez moi.
native_language_example: I feel like going home.

additional_notes: A very common way to express hunger in French. Literally “I have hunger” (avoir + noun): j'ai faim (I’m hungry), tu as faim (you’re hungry), il/elle a faim (he/she is hungry), nous avons faim (we’re hungry), vous avez faim (you’re hungry/formal), ils/elles ont faim (they’re hungry).
target_language_example: J'ai faim, on peut manger maintenant ?
native_language_example: I'm hungry—can we eat now?

additional_notes: Usually followed by **de/d’**: **j'ai juste besoin de + noun** (I just need + noun) or **j'ai juste besoin de + infinitive** (I just need to + verb). *Besoin* is masculine: **un besoin**. Note: in normal French spelling, this is typically written with capitals and an apostrophe: **J’ai juste besoin**.
target_language_example: j'ai juste besoin de cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I just need five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say you only need one thing (often to reassure, minimize, or explain). Follow with an infinitive verb after d’ (before a vowel): « J’ai juste besoin d’envoyer… ». With a noun, use de/d’ + article: « J’ai juste besoin d’un moment / d’un peu d’eau ».
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai juste besoin d'appeler ma sœur.
native_language_example: Sorry, I just need to call my sister.

additional_notes: Used to express a simple or immediate need. With an infinitive (verb) it means “I just need to…”: « j'ai juste besoin de parler / prendre l’air ». With a noun it means “I just need …”: « j'ai juste besoin de temps / de toi ». Often conveys “that’s all I need” or “for now,” and can soften a request or explanation.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, j'ai juste besoin de prendre l'air.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I just need to get some air.

meaning: “I have the …” (used before a vowel sound).
additional_notes: “J’ai” means “I have.” The “l’” is the elided form of “le” or “la,” used before a word beginning with a vowel or a silent h (h muet): j'ai l'adresse, j'ai l'intention, j'ai l'œil. It’s used to say you possess something or have something available/with you, depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai l'adresse que vous vouliez.
native_language_example: I have the address you wanted.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **avoir l’air (de)** = “to look/seem (like/to)”. It describes appearance or the impression you give. Common patterns: **j'ai l'air + adjective** (J'ai l'air fatigué), **j'ai l'air de + noun** (J'ai l'air d'une banque ?), or **j'ai l'air de + infinitive** (J'ai l'air de faire quoi ?). In **Alors, de quoi j'ai l'air ?**, it can mean “What do I look like?” or, with an offended/defensive tone, “What do you take me for?”
target_language_example: Alors, de quoi j'ai l'air ?
native_language_example: So, what do I look like? / What do you take me for?

meaning: “I look like a…” / “Do I look like a…?”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase «avoir l’air de» = “to seem / to look like.” This pattern is typically followed by a noun: «J'ai l'air d'un voleur.» (“I look like a thief.”) In questions it often implies “Do I look like…?” Change «d'un» to «d'une» with feminine nouns (e.g., «J'ai l'air d'une touriste.»).
target_language_example: j'ai l'air d'un voleur ?
native_language_example: Do I look like a thief?

meaning: "I feel like…" / "I have the impression…" (I think/seems to me).
additional_notes: Used to express a subjective feeling or perception (not a certain fact). Common patterns: « J'ai l'impression de + infinitive » (I feel like doing / having done) and « J'ai l'impression que + clause » (I feel like / I get the sense that…). Often translates naturally as “I feel like…” or “It seems to me…”.
target_language_example: J'ai l'impression qu'il va pleuvoir.
native_language_example: I have a feeling it’s going to rain.

meaning: “I feel like…” / “I get the impression that…” (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to express a subjective feeling or perception about a situation. It’s typically followed by an infinitive: « j'ai l'impression de + infinitif » (e.g., « j'ai l'impression de rêver »). If you want to use a full clause with “that,” French often uses « j'ai l'impression que + (phrase conjuguée) » instead.
target_language_example: J'ai l'impression de rêver.
native_language_example: I feel like I’m dreaming.

meaning: “I feel/think that…” or “I get the impression that…”
additional_notes: Used to express a personal impression, hunch, or inference (often with some uncertainty). Commonly followed by the indicative: « j'ai l'impression que c'est lui ». Can also be used as a short reply: « j'ai l'impression que oui/non ». « j'ai l'impression que si » can contradict a negative statement (roughly “actually, yes”).
target_language_example: j'ai l'impression que tu as une idée.
native_language_example: I get the impression that you have an idea.

meaning: "I have the…" / "I've got…" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is a common starter for saying you have something (an object, a trait, or a condition): j'ai + feminine noun. It literally means “I have the…”, but in English you often translate it as “I have…” (without “the”) or sometimes “My … is …” (e.g., j'ai la peau sensible = “I have sensitive skin”). For masculine nouns, use "j'ai le"; for plural, "j'ai les"; and before a vowel sound, "j'ai l'".
target_language_example: J'ai la peau sensible.
native_language_example: I have sensitive skin.

meaning: "I have the" (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: j’ai le + nom. Often expresses possession (j’ai le numéro), having something available/under control (j’ai le contrôle, j’ai le dossier), or a condition involving a body part (j’ai le nez qui coule = my nose is running). If the noun is feminine, use « j’ai la »; plural: « j’ai les ». Before a vowel or silent h, « le/la » becomes « l’ » (j’ai l’adresse).
target_language_example: J'ai le contrôle.
native_language_example: I have control.

meaning: "I have the right to" / "I'm allowed to".
additional_notes: Used to state a right or permission to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., parler, me défendre, poser). You can change the subject: tu as le droit de… (you’re allowed to…), il/elle a le droit de… (he/she is allowed to…), on a le droit de…, nous avons le droit de…, vous avez le droit de…, ils/elles ont le droit de….
target_language_example: J'ai le droit de dire non.
native_language_example: I have the right to say no.

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns after "avoir" to talk about things you have. Very common with body parts ("J'ai les mains froides" = "My hands are cold") and it also appears in fixed expressions/idioms where the meaning isn’t literal (e.g., "J'ai les boules" = "I'm really annoyed/upset" (informal), "J'ai les crocs" = "I'm starving" (informal), "J'ai les moyens" = "I can afford it"). The adjective usually agrees in plural if you add one ("les mains froides").
target_language_example: J'ai les mains froides.
native_language_example: My hands are cold.

meaning: Informal for « je n’ai pas »: “I don’t have / I haven’t.”
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: the « ne » is dropped in the negative (« je n’ai pas » → « j’ai pas »). Used with the verb « avoir » (to have): « j’ai pas de … » = “I don’t have any …”. It can also be a short reply meaning “I don’t (have any)” or “I haven’t.”
target_language_example: J'ai pas la tête à ça.
native_language_example: I’m not in the mood for that / I can’t deal with that right now.

additional_notes:
Common everyday way to say you feel fear. Often followed by:
- "de" + infinitive: "J'ai peur de tomber." (I’m afraid of falling.)
- "que" + subjunctive: "J'ai peur qu'il soit en retard." (I’m afraid he might be late.)
You can also use it alone as a reaction: "J'ai peur !"
target_language_example: J'ai peur de parler en public.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of speaking in public.

meaning: “I have someone …” (e.g., someone in mind / someone to see).
additional_notes: Used with a complement to express that there is a specific person involved. Common patterns: “J’ai quelqu’un en tête” = “I have someone in mind”; “J’ai quelqu’un à voir” = “I have someone to see / I need to see someone.” On its own (“J’ai quelqu’un.”) it usually just means “I have someone (with me/at home/etc.)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas rester : j'ai quelqu'un à voir.
native_language_example: I can’t stay: I have someone to see.

additional_notes: Used to say you have something (an object, a problem, or something intended for someone). Often followed by extra info: **dans** + body part (j'ai quelque chose dans l'œil = something is in my eye), **pour** + person (j'ai quelque chose pour lui = I have something for him), or a relative clause **qui…** (j'ai quelque chose qui t'est destiné = I have something meant for you). Note: the contraction **j'ai** is very common in writing; you may also see **j’ai** with a typographic apostrophe.
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose pour toi.
native_language_example: I have something for you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an important action you’re about to do or say. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., dire, faire, demander) and can take an indirect object: à te… (to you, informal) / à vous… (to you, formal or plural). You can also say: J'ai quelque chose d'important à dire. / J'ai quelque chose d'important à te dire.
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose d'important à te dire avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have something important to tell you before leaving.

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to give someone something (a gift, a message, a surprise, an item you picked up). You can swap the person: « pour vous » (for you, formal/plural), « pour lui/elle » (for him/her).
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose pour toi : je t'ai acheté un petit cadeau.
native_language_example: I have something for you: I bought you a small gift.

meaning: "I have something to …" (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action you need/want to do (often something important to say, announce, show, fix, or deal with). It’s followed by the infinitive: « J'ai quelque chose à + verb » (à dire, à annoncer, à montrer, à régler, etc.).
target_language_example: Attends, j'ai quelque chose à te demander.
native_language_example: Wait, I have something to ask you.

additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase that needs an infinitive verb after it, most often: « dire » (to tell), « demander » (to ask), or « donner » (to give). The « te » is an informal object pronoun meaning “to you” (to one person you address as « tu »). For a formal/polite version: « J’ai quelque chose à vous dire. »
target_language_example: j'ai quelque chose à te dire.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you.

j'ai quelque chose à te dire

target_language_multi_word_term: j'ai quelque chose à te dire
meaning: I have something to tell you.
additional_notes: Used to introduce news or a message you want to share. Often sounds a bit serious or important (it can create suspense), especially with openers like « Écoute » or « En fait ». You can change who you’re speaking to: « à vous dire » (to you, formal/plural), « à lui dire » (to tell him/her), « à leur dire » (to tell them).
target_language_example: Avant de partir, j'ai quelque chose à te dire.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I have something to tell you.

additional_notes: Literally “I have reason,” but it means “I’m right.” Often used in conversation to confirm you’re correct: “J’ai raison, pas vrai ?” (“I’m right, aren’t I?”). In the pattern “J’ai raison ou j’ai raison ?”, it’s a rhetorical way of saying “I’m right, obviously.”
target_language_example: Tu vois ? J'ai raison, pas vrai ?
native_language_example: See? I’m right, aren’t I?

additional_notes: Used to say you have a scheduled meeting with a specific person. Very common for medical, professional, or planned personal meetups. In speech it can also imply a date depending on context (e.g., "avec une fille").
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j'ai rendez-vous avec mon médecin.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have an appointment with my doctor.

additional_notes: Used to express that you have a lot to do, say, or share. It is followed by an infinitive (e.g., dire, faire, raconter). You can insert an indirect object pronoun before the infinitive: à te dire = “to tell you,” à vous raconter = “to tell you (formal/plural) a story.”
target_language_example: J'ai tant de choses à te dire.
native_language_example: I have so many things to tell you.

meaning: “I have everything that …” (a fragment that normally continues, most often as « j'ai tout ce qu'il faut » = “I have everything I need / all that’s necessary”).
additional_notes: By itself, « j'ai tout ce qu'il » is incomplete: it sets up a relative clause that must continue (e.g., « faut », « veut », etc.). The most common completion is « j'ai tout ce qu'il faut », where « ce qu'il faut » means “what is needed / what it takes.” Note: the form « j'ai » uses an apostrophe; it’s often written with curly apostrophe « j’ai » in French typography.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, j'ai tout ce qu'il faut.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have everything I need.

meaning: "I have a" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: From "je" + "ai" (present tense of avoir, “to have”). Used to say you have/possess something, or that you have something to do (e.g., "J'ai un truc à faire" = “I’ve got something to do”). Before a feminine singular noun, say "j'ai une".
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai un rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have an appointment.

meaning: “I have a little …” / “I’ve got a small …” (often used to introduce something small, like a gift or surprise).
additional_notes: Usually followed by a noun: j’ai un petit cadeau (a small gift), j’ai un petit quelque chose (a little something). “Petit” can sound modest/affectionate and is commonly used when you’re about to give or show something. Note: in writing you may see the apostrophe (j’ai), but the term here is given as j'ai.
target_language_example: j'ai un petit cadeau pour toi.
native_language_example: I have a little gift for you.

meaning: "I have an appointment" / "I have a meeting".
additional_notes: Used to say you have a scheduled commitment at a specific time. "Un rendez-vous" can be a professional appointment (doctor, business, etc.) or sometimes a date (romantic context). Often followed by details like "chez le médecin" (at the doctor’s) or "à 15 h" (at 3 p.m.).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j'ai un rendez-vous à 14 h.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have an appointment at 2 p.m.

additional_notes: Very common and informal: "truc" is a catch-all word for an unspecified object, plan, topic, problem, or secret. Often followed by details: "j’ai un truc à te dire" (something to tell you), "j’ai un truc de prévu" (something planned), "j’ai un truc pour toi" (something for you).
target_language_example: J'ai un truc intéressant à te dire.
native_language_example: I have something interesting to tell you.

additional_notes: Uses “truc” (= “thing/something”) as a very common, casual way to refer to an unspecified task, topic, or object. It’s followed by “à” + infinitive (e.g., régler, dire, montrer). In more formal French, you might say “j’ai quelque chose à…” instead of “j’ai un truc à…”.
target_language_example: J'ai un truc à vous dire.
native_language_example: I’ve got something to tell you.

additional_notes: From the verb **avoir** (to have): **j'ai** = “I have.” It’s used to introduce something you possess or want to say, especially with announcements or information: **J’ai une annonce / une question / une idée.** The **j’** is a shortened form of **je** before a vowel sound. Use **un** instead of **une** with a masculine noun (**j’ai un problème**).
target_language_example: J'ai une question à te poser.
native_language_example: I have a question to ask you.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is feminine and is either mentioned just before or understood from context (e.g., une théorie, une faveur, une question). If you explicitly say the noun, you can add it after « autre »: « J’ai une autre théorie. » For a masculine noun, use « j’ai un autre … » (e.g., « J’ai un autre problème. »).
target_language_example: J'ai une autre théorie à vous soumettre.
native_language_example: I have another theory to put to you.

additional_notes: In French, **une bonne** is a noun meaning a (female) domestic servant/maid. The phrase **j'ai une bonne** can sound old-fashioned and socially marked; in modern everyday French people usually say **j'ai une femme de ménage** (cleaning lady/housekeeper) or **j'ai une aide à domicile** (home help), depending on the job.
target_language_example: j'ai une bonne à la maison depuis des années.
native_language_example: I’ve had a maid/housekeeper at home for years.

meaning: “I have a wife and…” (i.e., “I’m married and…”)
additional_notes: Used to state your family situation, typically followed by children (e.g., “trois enfants”, “un enfant”). French commonly uses “avoir” (“to have”) to talk about family relationships (wife/husband/children). Note: “une femme” can mean “a woman” or “a wife,” but in this pattern (“J’ai une femme…”) it usually means “a wife.”
target_language_example: J'ai une femme et trois enfants.
native_language_example: I have a wife and three children.

meaning: "I have an idea." / "I’ve got an idea."
additional_notes: Used when you suddenly think of a solution or suggestion. Very common in conversation; it can stand alone or be used after a lead-in like "Oh" or "OK". Often followed by what the idea is (e.g., "j'ai une idée : on y va demain.").
target_language_example: OK, j'ai une idée : on peut prendre le métro.
native_language_example: OK, I’ve got an idea: we can take the subway.

additional_notes: Used to get someone’s attention before asking something. Often followed by a detail: « pour toi » (for you), « à propos de… » (about…), or « à poser » (to ask). In more formal settings you can also say « J’aurais une question » (“I have a question” / “I’d like to ask a question”).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, j'ai une question : où est la gare ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question: where is the train station?

meaning: "I have to do (something)" / "I have things to do."
additional_notes: From the structure **avoir à + infinitive**, which expresses that you have something to do (often an obligation or task). It can be left incomplete in context (**j'ai à faire**) to mean “I have things to do / I’m busy,” but it’s more common to specify the verb: **J’ai à faire mes devoirs**. Often similar in meaning to **je dois + infinitive** (“I must / I have to”), with **avoir à** sounding a bit more formal or administrative.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j'ai à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have things to do tonight.

additional_notes: From aimer. The apostrophe appears because je becomes j' before a vowel or silent h. Use it to say you like or love something, someone, or doing an action: j'aime le café, j'aime danser.
target_language_example: J'aime lire le soir.
native_language_example: I like reading in the evening.

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to say you like something without it sounding as strong or intense as “j’adore” (I love it). Often used to express a positive opinion or preference: “J’aime bien ça” (I like that), “J’aime bien cet endroit” (I quite like this place). Can also be used on its own to mean “I like it” or “I’m fine with it”: “Moi, j’aime bien.”
target_language_example: J'aime bien ce film, surtout la musique.
native_language_example: I quite like this movie, especially the music.

meaning: 'I would like' / 'I'd like' (polite way to say what you want).
additional_notes: From the conditional of aimer (“to like/love”), used to make requests or wishes sound softer and more polite than je veux (“I want”). Often followed by an infinitive: j’aimerais aller…, j’aimerais te parler…. You can add bien (j’aimerais bien…) to mean “I’d really like to / I’d quite like to.”
target_language_example: J'aimerais un café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee, please.

meaning: “I was going” / “I was going to” (was about to).
additional_notes: Contraction of « je » + « allais » (imparfait of « aller »). Very common for the near future in the past: « j'allais + infinitive » = “I was going to / I was about to …” (often something planned or almost happening: « J'allais t'appeler. »). It can also mean simple past movement: “I was going (somewhere)”.
target_language_example: J'ai cru que j'allais m'évanouir.
native_language_example: I thought I was going to faint.

meaning: “I’m coming right away / I’ll be right there.”
additional_notes: Used to reply when someone is waiting for you or calling you; it means you’re on your way immediately (or very soon). In conversation it can also be used loosely to mean “in a minute.” Often paired with short replies like “Ouais,” “OK,” “J’y vais,” or “Vas-y.”
target_language_example: Ouais, j'arrive tout de suite.
native_language_example: Yeah, I’m coming right away.

additional_notes: *J'aurais* is the conditional of *j'ai* ("I have"). It’s used (1) with a past participle to talk about a hypothetical past or regret: *J'aurais compris* ("I would have understood"); (2) with certain past participles like *voulu* to express what you would have wanted to do: *J'aurais voulu parler…* ("I would have liked/wanted to talk…"); and (3) in questions about an unreal situation: *Qu'est-ce que j'aurais fait sans toi ?* ("What would I have done without you?").
target_language_example: J'aurais aimé venir, mais je travaillais.
native_language_example: I would have liked to come, but I was working.

additional_notes: This is the past conditional of "aimer" and is used to express that you would have wanted something, but it didn’t happen (or you regret it). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive ("j'aurais aimé rester") or by "que" + subjunctive ("j'aurais aimé que tu m’en parles"). It can also sound like a gentle reproach meaning "I wish you had…".
target_language_example: j'aurais aimé que tu m'en parles plus tôt.
native_language_example: I would have liked you to tell me about it earlier.

meaning: "I should have" / "I ought to have" (regret about something not done).
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of devoir: j’ (je) + aurais (would have) + dû (had to/should). Used to say you did not do something in the past and you regret it or think it would have been better. Often followed by an infinitive: j'aurais dû venir (I should have come). Can also be used in questions: J'aurais dû dire quoi ? (What should I have said?). Note: without the apostrophe (j'aurais) is acceptable in plain text, though in French typography it’s usually j’aurais.
target_language_example: j'aurais dû y penser plus tôt.
native_language_example: I should have thought of it earlier.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional perfect of devoir ("aurais dû") to express regret or criticism about a past action that wasn’t done: you think it was the right thing to do earlier. Often followed by a time expression like "depuis longtemps" (for a long time), "il y a longtemps" (a long time ago), or "plus tôt" (earlier).
target_language_example: J'aurais dû le faire hier, mais j'ai oublié.
native_language_example: I should have done it yesterday, but I forgot.

meaning: "I should have (to you)" / "I ought to have (told you, believed you, etc.)."
additional_notes: Used to express regret about something you didn’t do in the past. It’s the past conditional of devoir: "j’aurais dû" + infinitive (e.g., "dire", "croire"). "Te" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to you" (informal singular). Often continues as "j’aurais dû te + [verb]" or "j’aurais dû te le + [verb]" ("I should have told it to you").
target_language_example: J'aurais dû te demander avant de partir.
native_language_example: I should have asked you before leaving.

meaning: “I could have” / “I would have been able to.”
additional_notes: This is the past conditional of pouvoir (“can/to be able to”): j’ (je) + aurais (would have) + pu (been able). It’s used for missed possibilities, regrets, or hypothetical past situations. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., j'aurais pu le faire = I could have done it), but it can also stand alone when the action is understood from context (J'aurais pu. = I could have.)
target_language_example: J'aurais pu te le dire, mais j'ai oublié.
native_language_example: I could have told you, but I forgot.

meaning: “I had” / “I used to have” / “I was (having)” — imperfect past of « avoir »; also used to form the past perfect (plus-que-parfait): « j'avais + participe passé » = “I had + past participle”.
additional_notes: « j'avais » is « je » + « avais » (imperfect of « avoir », to have). It expresses past states, habitual actions, or ongoing situations (“I had/used to have/was having”). It also serves as the auxiliary for the plus-que-parfait: « j'avais compris » = “I had understood”. In informal speech/writing, French often drops « ne » in negation: « j'avais pas » = “I didn’t have / I hadn’t”.
target_language_example: C'est ce que j'avais compris.
native_language_example: That’s what I had understood.

additional_notes: Contraction of **je + avais** (the imperfect past tense of **avoir**, “to have”). Used for descriptions, ongoing past situations, habits, or background information. With age, French uses **avoir**: **J'avais huit ans** = “I was eight (years old)” (literally, “I had eight years”).
target_language_example: Quand j'avais dix ans, j'avais un chien.
native_language_example: When I was ten, I had a dog.

meaning: "I needed" / "I was in need of" (imperfect past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (j'avais) to describe an ongoing need or a background situation in the past. It’s typically followed by de/d’ + noun or pronoun (de toi, d’elle, de ça), or by de + infinitive (e.g., j’avais besoin de partir = I needed to leave). In expressions like « Comme si j'avais besoin de ça », it’s often ironic: “as if I needed that (on top of everything).”
target_language_example: Hier, j'étais stressé : j'avais besoin d'une pause.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I was stressed: I needed a break.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "avoir besoin de" (to need). Use it for ongoing/repeated needs in the past or to set background: "I needed...". Followed by a noun (besoin de compagnie), an infinitive (besoin de réfléchir), or a person/object + infinitive (besoin de te voir). In more formal French, say "j'avais besoin d'argent" instead of "de fric".
target_language_example: J'avais besoin de repos, alors je suis resté chez moi.
native_language_example: I needed some rest, so I stayed home.

additional_notes: Contraction of je + en. Here, en usually replaces something introduced by de, so the English translation depends on the verb: it can mean "of it," "about it," "from it," or sometimes "some." In the examples, it refers back to a thing already mentioned or understood.
target_language_example: J'en parle souvent.
native_language_example: I talk about it often.

additional_notes: Used with the pronoun "en" to replace something introduced with "de" (or an amount/quantity). It often means “some” or “(some) of it/them.” Common patterns: "j'en ai" + past participle (e.g., "j'en ai mangé" = I ate some), and "j'en ai assez" + past participle (e.g., "j'en ai assez vu/entendu" = I’ve seen/heard enough).
target_language_example: Tu veux des biscuits ? J'en ai acheté.
native_language_example: Do you want cookies? I bought some.

meaning: I’ve heard about it / I’ve heard of it.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re familiar with something because you’ve heard people talk about it (but you may not know it well). The pronoun “en” replaces the thing you’re talking about (de + noun), e.g., « Tu connais ce film ? — Oui, j'en ai entendu parler. » Often used on its own as a short reply.
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas ce musée, mais j'en ai entendu parler.
native_language_example: I don’t know that museum, but I’ve heard of it.

additional_notes: Passé composé form built from **j’ + en + ai + eu** (avoir). **En** typically replaces something previously mentioned introduced with **de / du / de la / des**, especially an amount, number, or “some of it/them.” It’s commonly completed by a quantity or fixed expression: **j'en ai eu deux/une** (“I had two/one (of them)”), **j'en ai eu assez / marre** (“I’ve had enough / I’m fed up”). On its own (**J'en ai eu.**), it means “I had some/it,” with the context understood.
target_language_example: Tu veux encore du gâteau ? — Non merci, j'en ai eu assez.
native_language_example: Do you want more cake? — No thanks, I’ve had enough.

additional_notes: Used to say you have completely ended something or want nothing more to do with it (a relationship, a situation, a task, even a person). **en** refers back to “it/that” (what you’re done with), and **avec** introduces the thing/person: *j'en ai fini avec lui / avec tout ça.* Often expresses strong finality or “I’ve had enough.”
target_language_example: J'en ai fini avec tout ça.
native_language_example: I’m done with all of this.

meaning: “I never have any (of it)” / “I’ve never had any.” (fragment; usually completed as *j’en ai jamais eu*)
additional_notes:
This is a colloquial/incomplete fragment.
- **en** means “some/any (of it/them)” and replaces something previously mentioned (often introduced by *de*).
- With **jamais** (“never”), standard French normally uses **ne … jamais**: *Je n’en ai jamais…*
- In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: *J’en ai jamais…*
- Most commonly you complete it with **eu** (“had”): *Je n’en ai jamais eu* / *J’en ai jamais eu* (casual).
target_language_example: Du café décaféiné ? J’en ai jamais eu, désolé.
native_language_example: Decaf coffee? I’ve never had any, sorry.

meaning: "I've seen some (of it/them)" / "I saw some (of it/them)"; often, by extension, "I've seen enough" depending on context.
additional_notes: `en` replaces something previously mentioned (roughly “of it/of them”). It’s very common with quantities: **j'en ai vu beaucoup** (I saw a lot of them), **j'en ai vu un peu** (I saw a bit of it), **j'en ai vu assez** often means “I’ve had enough / I’ve seen enough.” Related fixed expression: **j'en ai vu d'autres** = “I’ve seen worse / I’ve been through more than that” (said to show you’re not impressed or not shocked).
target_language_example: J'en ai vu assez.
native_language_example: I’ve seen enough.

meaning: “I have some / I’ve got some (of it/them).”
additional_notes: "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (a quantity, some of something, or "of it/them"). So "j'en ai" often means "I have some" without repeating the noun. It can also appear in set expressions like "Qu’est-ce que j’en ai à faire ?" = "What do I care? / Why should I care?" and with nouns like "intention": "J’en ai l’intention" = "I intend to."
target_language_example: Tu as du pain ? Oui, j'en ai.
native_language_example: Do you have (any) bread? Yes, I do.

additional_notes: Very common way to say you’re tired of something or that you can’t take any more. Often followed by **de** + infinitive or noun: **j'en ai assez de + verb/noun** (e.g., *d’attendre*, *de ce bruit*). **en** refers to the thing you’re fed up with (sometimes implied). You can also say it alone: **j'en ai assez !**
target_language_example: J'en ai assez d'attendre.
native_language_example: I've had enough of waiting.

meaning: "I'm fed up with" / "I've had enough of".
additional_notes: Used to say you’re tired of something and want it to stop. Pattern: « j'en ai assez de + noun/infinitive » (e.g., « j'en ai assez de ce bruit » / « j'en ai assez d'attendre »). « en » refers back to the thing you’ve had enough of (roughly “of it/of that”). You can also say « j'en ai assez ! » when the object is implied (“I’ve had enough!”).
target_language_example: j'en ai assez de tout ça.
native_language_example: I've had enough of all this.

additional_notes: From "avoir besoin de" (to need). "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (de ça, de lui/d’elle, du pain, etc.) and means “of it/of them/some.” Used when what you need is already known from context.
target_language_example: Je n'ai plus de café : j'en ai besoin pour rester éveillé.
native_language_example: I don't have any coffee left: I need it to stay awake.

meaning: "I feel like it" / "I want to (do it)".
additional_notes: From "avoir envie de…" (to feel like / want…). "En" replaces "de + something" already mentioned or understood from context. Common as a standalone reply ("J'en ai envie."), for emphasis/insistence ("Mais j'en ai envie."), or rhetorically ("Tu crois que j'en ai envie ?").
target_language_example: Tu veux sortir ce soir ? Oui, j'en ai envie.
native_language_example: Do you want to go out tonight? Yes, I feel like it.

meaning: “It’ll take me…” (a certain amount of time).
additional_notes: Used to say how long something will take you. It’s part of the expression « en avoir pour + duration »: « J'en ai pour deux minutes » = “I’ll be two minutes / It’ll take me two minutes.” You can also ask: « J'en ai pour combien de temps ? » (“How long will it take me?”).
target_language_example: J'en ai pour cinq minutes.
native_language_example: It’ll take me five minutes.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun "en" to mean "of it" / "of them" (replacing something introduced with de, du, de la, des, or a quantity). "Un" agrees with the item you mean: j'en ai un (masc.), j'en ai une (fem.), j'en ai deux/trois, etc. Often answers "Tu en as un ?" / "Vous en avez un ?"
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, j'en ai un de rechange.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have a spare one.

meaning: “I have one / I’ve got one (of it/them).”
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun **en** meaning “of it/of them,” replacing **de + noun/quantity**. **Une** replaces a feminine noun understood from context (e.g., **une idée**, **une blague**, **une nouvelle**, **une suggestion**). Often used to answer or react when someone asks for another one: **Tu en as une autre ? — J’en ai une.**
target_language_example: Tu as une autre suggestion ? j'en ai une.
native_language_example: Do you have another suggestion? I have one.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun "en" to replace something previously mentioned (often introduced with "de"/"des"), and "une" because the thing you have is feminine singular. For a masculine noun you’d say "j’en ai un"; for more than one: "j’en ai deux / j’en ai plusieurs". Common with "avoir" to avoid repeating the noun: « Tu as une voiture ? — Oui, j’en ai une. »
target_language_example: Tu as une question ? Oui, j'en ai une.
native_language_example: Do you have a question? Yes, I have one.

additional_notes: "En" replaces something previously mentioned (roughly "about it" / "of it"). Often used with quantity words: "j'en sais plus" (I know more), "j'en sais assez" (I know enough), "j'en sais peu" (I know little).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, j'en sais assez pour t'aider.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know enough about it to help you.

meaning: "I am (one)" / "I’m at that point" / "I’m (almost) sure (of it)" (with *en* = “of it/of them”).
additional_notes: *En* replaces something introduced with **de** ("of it/of them"). So **j'en suis** can mean “I’m one (of them)” (*J'en suis un/une aussi.*) or “I’m at that stage/point” depending on context. With adjectives like **sûr/sûre**, it commonly expresses certainty about something previously mentioned: *J'en suis (presque) sûr(e).*
target_language_example: J'en suis presque sûre.
native_language_example: I’m almost sure of it.

additional_notes: Used to express hope or expectation. Often followed by "que" + a full sentence: "J'espère que…" (“I hope that…”). It can also be used on its own as a short reply meaning “I hope so / hopefully,” e.g., "Bien, j'espère." Note: keep the apostrophe as in "j'espère" (from "je" + "espère").
target_language_example: Bien, j'espère.
native_language_example: Fine, I hope.

additional_notes: Used before a clause (a full idea with a verb). The apostrophe is because "que" contracts to "qu'" before a vowel sound (e.g., "qu'il", "qu'on", "qu'un"). Note: "espérer" means "to hope", not "to expect".
target_language_example: J'espère qu'on se verra bientôt.
native_language_example: I hope we’ll see each other soon.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you hope is true about a man or boy. It’s the start of a longer sentence: J’espère (que) + clause. After que, il often becomes qu’il (elision). With espérer, French usually uses the indicative (e.g., j’espère qu’il sait…), not the subjunctive.
target_language_example: J'espère qu'il sait ce qu'il fait.
native_language_example: I hope he knows what he’s doing.

meaning: "I hope that we…" / "I hope that people/one…" (used to begin a clause).
additional_notes: Introduces a hope about what will happen. « on » commonly means « we » in everyday French (instead of « nous »), but it can also mean « people/one » in a general sense depending on context. The verb after « j’espère qu’on » is usually in the future, present, or conditional depending on how certain/polite the hope is.
target_language_example: J'espère qu'on pourra se voir demain.
native_language_example: I hope we’ll be able to see each other tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express hope or expectation about what follows. It introduces a clause with a subject and verb (often in the present or past): « j'espère que tu as raison. » In casual speech, « tu as » is often shortened to « t’as ».
target_language_example: j'espère que tu as de bonnes nouvelles.
native_language_example: I hope you have good news.

meaning: "I hope it’s…" / "I hope that it is…"
additional_notes: Used to express hope about the identity, correctness, or quality of something, typically followed by an adjective or a noun phrase: « j'espère que c'est bon / vrai / la bonne adresse ». In speech and informal writing, « que c'est » may be reduced in pronunciation, but the spelling generally stays the same. You can also shift tense depending on context: « J’espère que c’était… » (I hope it was…).
target_language_example: j'espère que c'est la bonne salle.
native_language_example: I hope it’s the right room.

additional_notes: Used to express hope or a wish about what the other person will do or what will happen. It’s followed by a full clause (tu + verb), commonly in the future (tu viendras, tu pourras) or the present (tu vas, tu peux). Use “j’espère que vous” when addressing someone with “vous” (formal or plural).
target_language_example: j'espère que tu pourras me pardonner.
native_language_example: I hope you’ll be able to forgive me.

additional_notes: Used to express a hope about what the listener(s) will do, think, or feel. It is followed by a full clause: "j'espère que vous + verb…". "Vous" can mean either "you" (formal) or "you all" (plural). After "j'espère que", French typically uses the indicative (present/future), not the subjunctive.
target_language_example: j'espère que vous aimerez.
native_language_example: I hope you’ll like it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re hoping will happen. “Ça” is a very common pronoun meaning “it/that/this” (often referring to a situation or what was just mentioned). It’s typically followed by a verb clause: “j'espère que ça va”, “j'espère que ça t'ira”, “j'espère que ça vous aidera”.
target_language_example: j'espère que ça vous aidera.
native_language_example: I hope that will help you.

meaning: "I was hoping you would…" / "I hoped you would…"
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (j’espérais) to express an expectation or hope in the past. It’s usually followed by "que" + "tu" and then the subjunctive (e.g., "que tu sois", "que tu dises") or sometimes the conditional (e.g., "que tu me le dirais") depending on style and context.
target_language_example: J'espérais que tu viennes ce soir.
native_language_example: I was hoping you would come tonight.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb: j'essaie de + infinitive (e.g., j'essaie de comprendre). It expresses effort, not guaranteed success. The full form is "j'essaie de"; "j'" is short for "je" before a vowel sound (essaie).
target_language_example: J'essaie de parler français tous les jours.
native_language_example: I’m trying to speak French every day.

additional_notes: Used to express an assumption or a likely conclusion, often based on what you know (but not with complete certainty). Very common in conversation. Typically followed by a clause introduced by "que": "j'imagine que tu as raison." You may also hear/write the more informal "j'imagine que t'as..." (= "tu as").
target_language_example: j'imagine que tu as raison.
native_language_example: I guess you’re right.

additional_notes: Very common spoken/informal contraction of « je ne sais pas ». In casual speech, « je » becomes « j’ » and « ne » is usually dropped: « je sais pas » / « j'sais pas ». Note the apostrophe in writing can vary (’ vs '), but here we keep the exact form: j'sais pas.
target_language_example: Désolé, j'sais pas où il habite.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know where he lives.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: contraction of « je (ne) sais pas quoi ». Often used when you can’t name or specify something (« Il a dit j'sais pas quoi » = “He said something or other”) or when you’re unsure what exactly (« On peut faire j'sais pas quoi ce soir » = “We can do… I don’t know, something tonight”). « ne » is usually dropped in speech.
target_language_example: Il m'a demandé j'sais pas quoi, mais j'ai pas compris.
native_language_example: He asked me something or other, but I didn’t understand.

additional_notes: "y" replaces something introduced with "à" (e.g., penser à quelque chose → y penser = to think about it) or a place (aller à Paris → y aller = to go there). "j'" is just "je" shortened before a vowel sound (y, ai, etc.). Often translates as “it” in English when it stands for an idea/thing (J'y ai pensé = I thought about it), and as “there” when it stands for a place.
target_language_example: J'y vais demain.
native_language_example: I'm going there tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is a common chunk in the passé composé: j' (je) + y (pronoun meaning “there” or “to it/that”) + ai (have). Use y to replace something introduced with à (à Paris → j'y…, à ça → j'y…), or a place already known from context. It comes before the auxiliary: J'y ai pensé. (not *J'ai y pensé*).
target_language_example: J'y ai déjà été une fois.
native_language_example: I've already been there once.

additional_notes: “Y” replaces a place (there) or something introduced with à (to it/at it). In ordinary contexts, j'y suis often means “I’m there” (at that place). It also appears in the set expression “Allez/Va voir ailleurs si j'y suis”, a dismissive, fairly informal way to say “Get lost / Go away.”
target_language_example: Tu me cherches ? Je suis dans le salon : j'y suis.
native_language_example: Are you looking for me? I’m in the living room: I’m there.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun **y** to mean “there” (to a place already mentioned or understood). **J'y vais** can mean you’re going to that place (“I’m going there”) or that you’re leaving/heading out now (“Okay, I’m going”). Often appears with time or decision markers: *alors* (then), *de toute façon* (anyway), *il est tard* (it’s late), etc.
target_language_example: D'accord, j'y vais, on se voit demain.
native_language_example: Okay, I'm heading off—see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of être ("je" + "étais"). Used for background descriptions, ongoing situations, habits, or states in the past (where English often uses "was/were" or "used to"). Common in set phrases like "j'étais en train de…" (I was in the middle of…), "j'étais sur le point de…" (I was about to…), and "j'étais parti" (I had left / I was gone, depending on context).
target_language_example: Quand tu as appelé, j'étais au travail.
native_language_example: When you called, I was at work.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of « être » (j’étais) + « là » (“there”). Used to state that you were present at a time in the past, often as background information or to explain how you knew something. Very common in clauses with « que »: « Il savait que j’étais là » (“He knew I was there”).
target_language_example: Comment as-tu su que j'étais là ?
native_language_example: How did you know I was there?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: « être sur le point de + infinitive » to say something was going to happen very soon. You can change the tense/person: « je suis sur le point de… » (I’m about to…), « il était sur le point de… » (he was about to…).
target_language_example: J'étais sur le point de partir quand tu as appelé.
native_language_example: I was about to leave when you called.

additional_notes: Used as an emphatic, often exclamatory way to refuse or disagree—stronger than just « non ». It can stand alone, or be reinforced with « mais » ("Mais jamais de la vie !").
target_language_example: — Tu veux lui demander pardon ? — Jamais de la vie !
native_language_example: — Do you want to apologize to him? — No way!

additional_notes: Used with "avoir" + past participle: « Je n’en ai jamais entendu parler. » It usually appears with negation (ne...jamais), though in casual speech the "ne" is often dropped (« J’en ai jamais entendu parler. »). Often followed by « de » + a person/thing: « Je n’ai jamais entendu parler de ce film. »
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais entendu parler de ce restaurant.
native_language_example: I’ve never heard of that restaurant.

additional_notes: Often used to say you don’t know who someone is. In careful/formal French you typically include ne: « Je n’ai jamais entendu parler de lui. » In everyday speech, ne is often dropped: « J’ai jamais entendu parler de lui. » It can also be used as a short answer: « Jamais entendu parler de lui. »
target_language_example: Désolé, je n’ai jamais entendu parler de lui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’ve never heard of him.

additional_notes: In questions, **jamais** often means **“ever”** (not “never”). **Manger dans un restaurant** means “to eat at a restaurant.” You’ll often see it in questions like **As-tu/Avez-vous jamais mangé dans ce restaurant ?** = “Have you ever eaten at this restaurant?”
target_language_example: Tu as jamais mangé dans ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten at this restaurant?

additional_notes: Usually appears with **ne ... jamais ... rien** to mean someone **never says/does/understands anything**. Word order can change with pronouns: **Elle n’en a jamais rien dit** (“She never said anything about it”), **Vous ne me dites jamais rien** (“You never tell me anything”).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais rien compris à ce jeu.
native_language_example: I never understood anything about this game.

additional_notes: Used with negation (often « ne ... jamais » and very commonly « ne ... plus jamais ») to say you don't want/expect to see the person again. « plus jamais » adds the idea of “not anymore, never again” (often emphatic). In full sentences you’ll usually see: « (Je) ne veux plus jamais te revoir » = “I never want to see you again.”
target_language_example: Désolé, mais je ne veux plus jamais te revoir.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I never want to see you again.

additional_notes: Used with a negative meaning to say something has not been seen at any time. Commonly appears in the passé composé with (ne) … jamais: « Je n’ai jamais vu ça. » In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « J’ai jamais vu ça. » It can also be used as a short standalone reaction: « Jamais vu ! » (= “Never seen it!”). With « encore », « n’ai encore jamais vu » means “have still never seen / have never yet seen.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais vu un film aussi long.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen such a long movie.

meaning: “ever been” / “never been” (depending on whether there’s a negation).
additional_notes: Built from jamais (“ever/never”) + été (past participle of être, “been”). In questions without ne, jamais often means “ever” (e.g., Avons-nous jamais été…? = “Have we ever been…?”). With ne…jamais (or in common spoken French where ne is dropped: J’ai jamais été…), it means “never been.” Often used with aussi + adjective to mean “(I’ve) never been so…”: Je n’ai jamais été aussi heureux = “I’ve never been so happy.”
target_language_example: J'ai jamais été aussi heureux.
native_language_example: I’ve never been so happy.

additional_notes: Used with the past participle "été" (from "être") to say someone has never been something (state) or has never been somewhere (location/experience). Often appears in negation: "ne ... jamais été" (e.g., "Je n'ai jamais été ici"). In casual spoken French, "ne" is often dropped: "J'ai jamais été..."
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais été à Paris.
native_language_example: I've never been to Paris.

additional_notes: Not correct French as written. This entry preserves the exact input term for reference. To say 'I have a/an ...', use j'ai un ... or j'ai une .... avoir is the infinitive ('to have'); with je in the present tense, it becomes j'ai.
target_language_example: je avoir un problème.
native_language_example: I have a problem.

additional_notes: Used with a noun (Je cherche mon chat. = I’m looking for my cat) or with an idea/information (Je cherche quelle phrase écrire. = I’m trying to figure out what sentence to write). It can also mean “I’m trying to find (words)” as in Je cherche mes mots (I’m searching for the right words).
target_language_example: Je cherche une boulangerie près d'ici.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a bakery near here.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the “to ___” form): je commence à comprendre, je commence à m’y habituer. It expresses that something is beginning, often gradually. You can change the subject (tu commences à…, il/elle commence à…, etc.) and the tense (j’ai commencé à… = “I started to…”).
target_language_example: Je commence à parler français un peu mieux.
native_language_example: I’m starting to speak French a little better.

additional_notes: Used to say you understand an idea, a situation, someone’s feelings, a language, or what is happening. Often followed by a clause: « Je comprends que… » (“I understand that…”) or « Je comprends ce que… / ce qui… / comment… » (“I understand what… / what… / how…”). Can also be used alone as a reply: « Je comprends. »
target_language_example: Je comprends que tu sois fatigué, mais on doit partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I understand that you’re tired, but we have to leave now.

additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase used to begin a sentence; it must be followed by what the other person is doing/saying (often: "je comprends ce que tu veux dire" = "I understand what you mean"). "Ce que" means "what/that which".
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean.

additional_notes: From connaître. Used with people and nouns to say you know someone or are familiar with something (a place, expression, type of person, etc.). French often uses savoir instead for knowing a fact or knowing how to do something.
target_language_example: Je connais bien ce quartier.
native_language_example: I know this neighborhood well.

meaning: "I know a…" (I’m familiar with a person/thing).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say you know someone or are familiar with something: *Je connais un prêtre* (I know a priest), *Je connais un raccourci* (I know a shortcut). Use **un** before a masculine noun; use **une** for feminine (*Je connais une bonne adresse*). Often contrasts with **je sais…**, which is more for facts/information (*Je sais la réponse* = I know the answer).
target_language_example: Je connais un bon restaurant près d’ici.
native_language_example: I know a good restaurant near here.

additional_notes: Used to express worry or to politely introduce bad news or a negative answer. It is typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., « Je crains que ton plan ne fonctionne pas. »). You may also see an extra « ne » after « que » (the *ne explétif*), which is common in formal French and doesn’t mean “not” by itself. It can also be used alone as « Je crains que non. » = “I’m afraid not.”
target_language_example: Je crains que nous soyons en retard.
native_language_example: I’m afraid we’re late.

additional_notes: First-person singular of croire. Used to give an opinion or express a belief. Often followed by que (je crois que...) to mean "i think that..."; with en, it means "believe in" something.
target_language_example: Je crois que tu as raison.
native_language_example: I think you're right.

additional_notes: Used to express confidence or faith in a person, group, idea, or thing. Often followed by a noun or stressed pronoun: moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles (e.g., « Je crois en toi »). It can mean moral support/trust (« I believe in you ») or belief/faith (« I believe in that/God ») depending on context.
target_language_example: Je crois en toi, tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: I believe in you—you’re going to make it.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or what you believe is true (often with some uncertainty), followed by a clause. The apostrophe (qu') is used before a vowel sound: je crois qu'il..., je crois qu'on..., je crois qu'elle.... A more certain alternative is "je sais que" (I know that).
target_language_example: Je crois qu'il va pleuvoir ce soir.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express an opinion or belief about a woman or girl. Often followed by a verb (e.g., "est", "va", "aime"). In speech, "je crois" can sound like "j'crois".
target_language_example: Je crois qu'elle a raison.
native_language_example: I think she's right.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or what you believe about a man/boy ("il" = "he/it"). In everyday French, "je crois que" often means "I think" (a bit uncertain), not necessarily a strong belief. It’s followed by a full clause: "Je crois qu'il + verb..."
target_language_example: Je crois qu'il va rentrer bientôt.
native_language_example: I think he’s going to come home soon.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or belief about a man or boy ("il"). Often followed by an adjective, a job, or a description: "Je crois qu'il est malade" (I think he's sick), "Je crois qu'il est médecin" (I think he's a doctor). In everyday speech, "je crois" often means "I think" rather than a strong religious belief.
target_language_example: Je crois qu'il est déjà parti.
native_language_example: I think he has already left.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or guess. "Je crois que" = "I think/believe that"; before a vowel it becomes "qu'". "On" often means "we" in everyday French, but it can also mean "people" or an unspecified "they," depending on context.
target_language_example: Je crois qu'on est en retard.
native_language_example: I think we're late.

additional_notes: Used to express an opinion or guess about something that has (likely) already happened, typically followed by a past participle in the passé composé: « je crois qu'on a compris / réussi / terminé ». In everyday French, « on » often means “we” (instead of « nous »). « qu'on » is the contraction of « que on ».
target_language_example: Je crois qu'on a assez attendu.
native_language_example: I think we’ve waited long enough.

additional_notes: A common way to introduce an opinion, belief, or guess. In everyday English, it is often translated as "I think" rather than the more literal "I believe." The "that" is often omitted in English.
target_language_example: Je crois que tu as raison.
native_language_example: I think you're right.

additional_notes: Used to express a guess or belief about something. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, adjective, or prepositional phrase (e.g., « pour moi », « à toi », « prêt »). In speech, it’s commonly shortened to « je crois que c’est… ».
target_language_example: Je crois que c'est la bonne adresse.
native_language_example: I think it's the right address.

additional_notes: Used to express a belief or guess about something you did or that happened (often with a past action: *j’ai + past participle*). It sounds a bit unsure/soft, like “I think I…” rather than a firm statement. Often followed by verbs like *vu* (seen), *compris/pigé* (understood), *changé* (changed), *oublié* (forgotten), etc.
target_language_example: Je crois que j'ai oublié mes clés.
native_language_example: I think I forgot my keys.

meaning: 'I think I have' / 'I believe I have'.
additional_notes: Used to express an opinion or uncertainty about having something (an object, a plan, a right, a feeling, etc.). It’s often followed by a noun phrase: « Je crois que j’ai un plan. » You can use it when you’re not 100% sure, similar to “I think I’ve got…” in English.
target_language_example: Je crois que j'ai la réponse.
native_language_example: I think I have the answer.

additional_notes: Used to express your opinion or belief about yourself (often to soften what you’re saying). Followed by a verb: « Je crois que je peux... », « Je crois que je devrais... ». In speech, « je crois que » can sound like « j’crois que ».
target_language_example: Je crois que je vais rester à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: I think I'm going to stay home tonight.

meaning: "I think I have it" / "I think I’ve got it."
additional_notes: Used when you think you have found something (an object) or when you think you understand something. "Je crois que" = "I think / I believe". "je l’ai" means "I have it": "l’" is short for "le" or "la" ("it") before a vowel sound, and "ai" is from "avoir" (to have). Often followed by more detail: "Je crois que je l’ai trouvé" (I think I found it) or "Je crois que je l’ai compris" (I think I understood it).
target_language_example: Attends… je crois que je l'ai : la réponse est 42.
native_language_example: Wait… I think I’ve got it: the answer is 42.

meaning: "I think I can" / "I believe I can."
additional_notes: Used to express a tentative or polite level of confidence that you’re able to do something. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., je crois que je peux le faire) or a verb phrase describing what you can handle/arrange/keep.
target_language_example: Je crois que je peux venir demain.
native_language_example: I think I can come tomorrow.

meaning: "I think I am" / "I believe I am".
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a personal belief about your own state/identity/feelings, often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: « Je crois que je suis fatigué(e) », « Je crois que je suis amoureux/amoureuse ». The word for “in love” agrees with the speaker: « amoureux » (typically masculine) / « amoureuse » (typically feminine). You’ll often add « de toi » (“with you”) or « encore » (“still”).
target_language_example: Je crois que je suis perdu(e).
native_language_example: I think I’m lost.

meaning: "I think I’m going to…" (I think I will… soon).
additional_notes: Used to express an intention or something you expect will happen in the near future. It’s typically followed by an infinitive: « Je crois que je vais partir » (I think I’m going to leave). In speech, you may hear it shortened: « J’crois que j’vais… ».
target_language_example: Je crois que je vais prendre un café.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief about what “we” (nous) did, can do, are, or will do. Often translates as “I think” in everyday speech (less strong than “I’m sure”). Followed by a full clause, e.g., je crois que nous + verb (avons trouvé, pouvons, ne sommes pas, pourrons, etc.).
target_language_example: Je crois que nous sommes prêts.
native_language_example: I think we’re ready.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion, belief, or guess about what someone (tu = “you”) should do or has done. In everyday French, "je crois que" often sounds like "I think" (not necessarily strong certainty). Often followed by the conditional for advice: "Je crois que tu devrais…" (“I think you should…”).
target_language_example: Je crois que tu as raison.
native_language_example: I think you're right.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion, assumption, or polite correction. "Je crois que" can soften what follows (similar to "I think" in English). "Vous" is the formal/plural "you"; in speech, "je crois que" is often shortened to "j’crois que" (more casual).
target_language_example: Je crois que vous avez raison, mais il faut vérifier.
native_language_example: I think you're right, but we need to check.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief about a situation. “Ça” usually refers to something general (“it/that”), like a result, an idea, or a situation: Je crois que ça a marché (“I think it worked”). In everyday speech, you’ll also hear “Je crois que…” without “ça,” or “Je crois que ça…” followed by a verb like plaît, a plu, a fonctionné, etc.
target_language_example: Je crois que ça va être difficile.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to be difficult.

meaning: I think I know / I believe I know.
additional_notes: Used to express that you *probably* know something, but you’re not 100% sure. Often followed by an indirect question (ce que…, où…, pourquoi…, comment…, etc.). More cautious than “je sais” (I know).
target_language_example: Je crois savoir comment on peut t’aider.
native_language_example: I think I know how we can help you.

meaning: "I thought / I believed / I was under the impression" (in the past).
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of *croire* (“to believe/think”), used for an ongoing past belief, expectation, or assumption—often one that turned out to be wrong. Common patterns: **je croyais que + sentence** (I thought that…), **je croyais + infinitive** (I thought I could…), **je croyais + past infinitive** (I thought I had…).
target_language_example: Je croyais que le magasin était ouvert, mais il est fermé.
native_language_example: I thought the store was open, but it’s closed.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you believed before, often implying surprise or disappointment that it isn’t true. The imperfect (croyais) suggests an earlier belief. "On" can mean "we" (very common in speech) or "people/one" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je croyais qu'on avait le temps, mais le train part dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I thought we had time, but the train leaves in five minutes.

meaning: "I thought (that)…" (often: I used to think / I was under the impression that).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (croyais) to describe a past belief or assumption, often one that turned out to be wrong or was later corrected. It’s followed by a full clause: je croyais que + subject + verb (in a past or conditional tense depending on meaning).
target_language_example: Je croyais que tu étais déjà parti(e).
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

meaning: “I thought it was …” (often implying: I was mistaken / I had assumed).
additional_notes: Used to state a past belief or assumption, often when correcting yourself or realizing you were wrong. It’s in the imperfect (je croyais), which can sound softer/more tentative than “j’ai cru” (a more sudden/one-time “I thought”). You typically complete it with a noun/adjective/pronoun: “Je croyais que c’était fait / la femme / le mien / pour moi / réglé / vous.”
target_language_example: Je croyais que c'était réglé.
native_language_example: I thought it was settled.

meaning: "I thought it was the..." (about a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you were mistaken about someone/something’s identity or purpose. It’s in the imperfect (je croyais), often implying a prior assumption that turned out to be wrong. Use "le" before a masculine singular noun (le bon, le but, le chasseur, le livreur). For a feminine noun, you’d say "je croyais que c’était la..."
target_language_example: Je croyais que c'était le professeur, mais c'était un étudiant.
native_language_example: I thought it was the teacher, but it was a student.

meaning: “I thought you…” / “I believed you…” (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to say what you believed or assumed before, often implying you were wrong or surprised. It’s the imperfect tense (je croyais) followed by que + tu + verb (e.g., avais, comprenais, savais).
target_language_example: Je croyais que tu venais ce soir.
native_language_example: I thought you were coming tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you had an assumption/expectation about the other person that turns out to be wrong or surprising. "Je croyais" is the imperfect of *croire* (to believe/think), often implying “I was under the impression…”. It’s typically followed by a negative verb phrase: *je croyais que tu ne + verbe + pas/plus/jamais…*
target_language_example: Je croyais que tu ne voulais pas venir.
native_language_example: I thought you didn’t want to come.

additional_notes: Used to say your belief/assumption in the past, often when you’ve just learned it’s not true. The verb is in the imperfect (je croyais) because it describes an ongoing state of belief in the past. Followed by a clause with “tu étais” + an adjective (d’accord, occupé/occupée, retraité), a past participle (parti/partie), or an expression (à la retraite). Adjectives and past participles may change for gender: occupé/occupée, parti/partie. “Être retraité” and “être à la retraite” both mean “to be retired.”
target_language_example: Je croyais que tu étais en vacances cette semaine.
native_language_example: I thought you were on vacation this week.

meaning: 'I thought you…' / 'I believed you…' (about something in the past).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed or expected (often incorrectly). In French, after "je croyais que", you typically use the imperfect or past tenses (e.g., "vous aviez…", "vous alliez…", "vous deviez…", "vous dormiez…"). It can sound neutral or slightly reproachful depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Je croyais que vous étiez déjà parti(e).
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

meaning: “I thought you were …” (I believed, but I was mistaken or unsure).
additional_notes: Used to say what you believed in the past, often implying it may not be true now (a misunderstanding or correction). The verb tense is imperfect: « je croyais » + « que » + « vous étiez » (imperfect of être). Commonly followed by a noun/adjective: « Je croyais que vous étiez médecin. »
target_language_example: Je croyais que vous étiez déjà en route.
native_language_example: I thought you were already on your way.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of devoir ("to have to / must"). It’s used to talk about an obligation, necessity, or expectation in the past, often followed by an infinitive: je devais partir (I had to leave). Depending on context, it can mean either something you were required to do (had to) or something planned/expected (was supposed to).
target_language_example: Je devais appeler ma mère, mais j’ai oublié.
native_language_example: I was supposed to call my mom, but I forgot.
