It’s often followed by a verb: **Je sais que ça marche / que ça va marcher** (“I know it works / will work”), and it can be negated: **Je sais que ça ne le dérangerait pas** (“I know it wouldn’t bother him”).
target_language_example: Je sais que ça va te faire plaisir.
native_language_example: I know that it’s going to make you happy.

meaning: 'I know who …' (I know the person’s identity).
additional_notes: Used before an indirect question with **qui**. After **qui**, French keeps normal word order: **Je sais qui elle est** (not *je sais qui est-elle*). You can add a noun/clause after it: **Je sais qui tu es**, **Je sais qui il est**, etc.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je sais qui tu es.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know who you are.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of savoir (“to know”). It describes past knowledge or awareness, often as a background fact (“I knew that…”). In expressions like « Si seulement je savais… », it can mean “If only I knew… / I wish I knew…”.
target_language_example: Je savais déjà qu'il allait venir.
native_language_example: I already knew he was going to come.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you already knew about a man (or "it" if referring to a masculine noun). After "qu'il", you typically use the imperfect/past or conditional to talk about what you knew would happen: "Je savais qu'il viendrait" (I knew he would come).
target_language_example: Je savais qu'il allait appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I knew he was going to call tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you knew something in the past. "Je savais" is the imperfect (ongoing/background past), often introducing a clause with "que" + a full sentence: "Je savais que tu viendrais."
target_language_example: Je savais que tu allais aimer ce film.
native_language_example: I knew that you were going to like this movie.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense: « je savais » (I knew) + « je pouvais » (I could/was able to). It introduces something you were sure you were able to do, often followed by an infinitive (e.g., « je pouvais compter », « je pouvais parler »).
target_language_example: Je savais que je pouvais te faire confiance.
native_language_example: I knew that I could trust you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about what you (already) knew someone was going to do. "Je savais" is the imperfect of *savoir* (to know), often used for background knowledge, expectations, or something you suspected/anticipated. It can sound satisfied (“I knew it!”) or reproachful depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Je savais que tu finirais par appeler.
native_language_example: I knew you’d end up calling.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you already knew about the other person. It’s the imperfect past (je savais) + a clause with que + tu étais (“you were”). Often followed by an adjective (contre, faux), a place (ici), or a noun phrase (un bon soldat).
target_language_example: Je savais que tu étais fatigué.
native_language_example: I knew you were tired.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause saying what you already knew in the past. "Je savais" is the imperfect of "savoir" (a past state: “I knew / I was aware”). It’s followed by "que" + a full sentence with "vous" (often in formal situations, to a stranger, customer, etc., or when speaking to more than one person).
target_language_example: Je savais que vous aviez raison.
native_language_example: I knew you were right.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you knew or expected in the past, followed by a full clause (often with a verb like "allait" or "devait"). "Je savais" is the imperfect tense (ongoing/background past). "Ça" refers to something general (“it/that”), like an event or situation.
target_language_example: Je savais que ça finirait par arriver.
native_language_example: I knew it would eventually happen.

additional_notes: Used to say what you will be like, where you will be, or what situation you will be in at a future time. Often followed by an adjective (je serai gentil), a place (je serai sur scène), or a time clause with "quand" (quand je serai grande).
target_language_example: Demain, je serai à Paris pour le travail.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, I will be in Paris for work.

meaning: “I will be back / I’ll be back.”
additional_notes: Future tense of « je suis de retour » (“I am back”). Used to say you will return later; often followed by a time (« pour neuf heures » = by nine o’clock) or a deadline (« dès que possible » = as soon as possible). In casual speech, you can also hear « je reviens » (“I’m coming back / I’ll be right back”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je serai de retour dans une heure.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll be back in an hour.

meaning: "I’ll be back in…" (after a certain amount of time).
additional_notes: Used to say you will return after a time delay. It’s the future tense of "être" (je serai) + "de retour" (“back/returned”) + "dans" meaning “in” with a duration (dans une heure, dans deux jours). Don’t confuse this with "je serai de retour à" (“I’ll be back at [a specific time]”).
target_language_example: Je serai de retour dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in ten minutes.

meaning: "I'll be there" / "I'll be here" (future: I will be present).
additional_notes: Literally “I will be there.” Used for future presence at a place/time (Je serai là demain.) or to reassure someone you’ll be available to help/support them (Je serai là si tu as besoin de moi.). Context decides whether “là” is best translated as “there” or “here.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je serai là pour toi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll be there for you.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish, desire, or request in a fairly formal tone (more formal than “je veux”). Often followed by an infinitive (“je souhaite partir”) or by “que” + subjunctive (“je souhaite que vous veniez”). Common in emails/letters and polite speech.
target_language_example: Je souhaite réserver une chambre pour deux nuits.
native_language_example: I would like to book a room for two nights.

meaning: “I suggest that …” (to propose an idea or course of action).
additional_notes: Often followed by the subjunctive to talk about what someone should do: Je suggère que nous partions / que tu prennes / que vous vous mettiez. It’s a polite but fairly direct way to make a recommendation.
target_language_example: Je suggère que nous commencions maintenant.
native_language_example: I suggest that we start now.

additional_notes: First-person singular of être. Use it to talk about who you are, how you feel, or what you are like: je suis heureux, je suis intelligent. In other contexts, the same spelling can also mean "I follow" from suivre, but here it means "I am."
target_language_example: Je suis prêt pour le voyage.
native_language_example: I am ready for the trip.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *aller* (“to go”), formed with the auxiliary *être*: *je suis allé* (masc.), *je suis allée* (fem.). Commonly followed by a place (*je suis allé au supermarché / chez le médecin / dans une pizzeria*) or by an infinitive to say you went to do something (*je suis allé nager*, *je suis allé pêcher*, *je suis allé voir…*).
target_language_example: Samedi, je suis allé au musée avec un ami.
native_language_example: On Saturday, I went to the museum with a friend.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of *aller* with *être*: **je suis allé** (masc.) / **je suis allée** (fem.). **Au** is the contraction of **à + le** and is used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., *au Canada*, *au jardin*, *au ballet*). For feminine or plural, use **à la**, **à l’**, or **aux**.
target_language_example: Je suis allé au restaurant hier soir.
native_language_example: I went to the restaurant last night.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *aller* (“to go”) with *être*: **je suis allé** (masculine speaker) / **je suis allée** (feminine speaker). Often followed by a time expression (hier, ce matin, dimanche dernier) or a purpose (*pour* + infinitive): *Je suis allé au parc pour jouer…*
target_language_example: Je suis allé au parc après le travail.
native_language_example: I went to the park after work.

meaning: "I went to" (to a place, often a country/continent).
additional_notes: Past tense of aller (passé composé) with être: je suis allé (masc.) / je suis allée (fem.). Use en before continents and most feminine countries (en Europe, en Inde). For masculine countries use au (au Canada), and for plural places use aux (aux États-Unis).
target_language_example: Je suis allé en France l'année dernière.
native_language_example: I went to France last year.

meaning: “I went to bed” (I went to lie down/sleep).
additional_notes: Uses the past tense (passé composé) of aller: « je suis allé(e) ». Add -e if the speaker is female (« je suis allée me coucher »). « Aller se coucher » is the common way to say “to go to bed” (to lie down for the night). It’s often followed by details like « tôt » (early) or what you did before going to bed.
target_language_example: Je suis allé me coucher vers onze heures.
native_language_example: I went to bed around eleven o’clock.

meaning: "I went to see" / "I went to check (something) out."
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "aller" used before an infinitive: "aller voir" = to go and see/visit/check. You can use it with a person (je suis allé voir Tom), a place/show (je suis allé voir Café Müller), an object (je suis allé voir votre piano), or a clause to mean “go see what’s happening” (je suis allé voir ce qui se passait). If the speaker is female, it becomes "je suis allée voir".
target_language_example: Hier, je suis allé voir si le magasin était ouvert.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I went to see/check whether the store was open.

additional_notes: Past tense of "aller" (to go) with "être": je suis allé (masc.) / je suis allée (fem.). Use "à" before a place or event: a city (à Paris), a store (à ce magasin), a concert (à un concert). Often followed by extra info like transport (en train) or purpose (voir Tom).
target_language_example: Je suis allé à Montréal l'année dernière.
native_language_example: I went to Montreal last year.

meaning: “I went to the …” (past tense, to a feminine place/activity).
additional_notes: Passé composé of **aller**: **je suis allé(e)** + place/activity. Use **allé** if the speaker is male, **allée** if female. **à la** is used before feminine singular nouns (la poste, la librairie). With masculine nouns, it changes to **au** (à + le), and with plural it becomes **aux** (à + les).
target_language_example: Hier, je suis allé à la boulangerie.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I went to the bakery.

additional_notes: Past tense of "aller" (to go) in the passé composé: "je" + "être" (suis) + past participle "allé(e)". Add -e because the speaker is feminine (male: "je suis allé"). Often followed by a place with "à" (au/à la/à l’/aux), or by a person’s place with "chez" (e.g., "chez lui").
target_language_example: Je suis allée à la bibliothèque hier.
native_language_example: I went to the library yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *arriver* (to arrive). It uses **être** as the helping verb: *je suis + arrivé*. The past participle agrees with the subject: **je suis arrivé** (male speaker) / **je suis arrivée** (female speaker). Often used to announce you’ve just gotten somewhere: *Je suis arrivé !* = “I’m here / I’ve arrived!”
target_language_example: Salut ! Je suis arrivé à la gare.
native_language_example: Hi! I arrived at the station.

meaning: 'I arrived at/in' (a place), or 'I arrived' (at a time / on time).
additional_notes: Used with **arriver** in the past tense (**je suis arrivé(e)**) to say you reached a destination or arrived at a specific moment. With **cities** you typically use **à**: *Je suis arrivé à Tokyo.* For **times**, you can use **à + time** (often **à deux heures**; sometimes people shorten it to *à deux* in context). Common set phrase: **arriver à temps (pour...)** = 'to arrive on time (for...)'. You can also use **à** for some ways of getting there, e.g. **à vélo** = 'by bike'.
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à Paris à 18 h, juste à temps pour le dîner.
native_language_example: I arrived in Paris at 6 p.m., just in time for dinner.

je suis arrivé à la gare

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis arrivé à la gare
meaning: I arrived at the train station.
additional_notes: A common way to say you got to a place. With the verb *arriver* (to arrive), French uses *être* as the auxiliary in the past tense: *je suis arrivé(e)*. Add **-e** if the speaker is female: *je suis arrivée à la gare*. You can add time details: *ce matin* (this morning), *en retard* (late), *à 8h* (at 8).
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à la gare à 8h, mais le train était déjà parti.
native_language_example: I arrived at the station at 8 a.m., but the train had already left.

meaning: “I’m at the …” / “I’m in the …” (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a place or situation/state introduced by **à + le**, which contracts to **au**: **je suis au** + masculine singular noun. Common with locations (**au terrain de golf**) and some fixed expressions for states/situations (**au bord de…** = “on the verge of…”, **au régime** = “on a diet”). For feminine singular, use **à la** (je suis à la …); for plural, **aux** (je suis aux …).
target_language_example: Je suis au café du coin.
native_language_example: I’m at the café on the corner.

meaning: "I’m fine / I feel good"; also "Am I really…? / Am I in the right…?" (with a question).
additional_notes: With no extra complement, it often means you feel well or comfortable: « Je suis bien, et toi ? » / « Je suis bien là où je suis. » With a question and a place or situation, « bien » adds emphasis and asks for confirmation (similar to “really/indeed”): « Je suis bien à la poste ? » = “I’m at the post office, right?” It can also intensify an adjective: « bien décidé » = “really determined.”
target_language_example: Je suis bien ici, merci.
native_language_example: I feel good here, thanks.

additional_notes:
Used to express satisfaction or pleasure. Often followed by:
- "de + infinitive" (Je suis content de te voir. = I'm happy to see you.)
- "que + subjunctive" (Je suis content que tu sois là. = I'm glad you're here.)
Agreement: "content" changes with the speaker (female: "Je suis contente"; plural: "Nous sommes contents/contentes").
target_language_example: Je suis content d'être ici avec vous.
native_language_example: I'm happy to be here with you.

additional_notes: Used to express that you are happy about doing something or about something happening. It’s often followed by an infinitive (Je suis content de vous aider) or by de + l’/le/la + infinitive when the verb has an object (Je suis content de l’apprendre = to learn it). You can also change the subject/person: je suis / tu es / il est / elle est / nous sommes / vous êtes / ils sont / elles sont content(e)(s) de. Feminine: contente; plural: contents/contentes.
target_language_example: Je suis content de te rencontrer.
native_language_example: I'm happy to meet you.

je suis content de te voir

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis content de te voir
additional_notes: A friendly greeting when you meet someone. Literally "I am happy to see you." You can change the adjective for gender: "Je suis content(e) de te voir" (men often say/write content; women contente). "Te" is informal "you" (used with friends/family); with someone you address as "vous", say "Je suis content(e) de vous voir."
target_language_example: Je suis content de te voir, ça fait longtemps !
native_language_example: I'm happy to see you; it’s been a long time!

meaning: "I'm happy/glad (about you / to …)" or "I'm pleased with you."
additional_notes: Often followed by an infinitive to say what you’re happy to do: « Je suis content de vous voir / de vous rencontrer ». You can also use « Je suis content(e) que… » + subjunctive: « Je suis content que vous soyez ici. » Use « content » (masc.) / « contente » (fem.) to match the speaker. « vous » is formal or plural.
target_language_example: Je suis content de vous voir aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I'm happy to see you today.

meaning: “I’m glad (happy) that you …” (to someone you address as “tu”).
additional_notes: Used to express happiness/satisfaction about what the other person did/does/says. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive: Je suis content que tu aies appelé (past), que tu appelles (present/ongoing), que tu dises ça. For a woman speaker: Je suis contente que tu… For “you” formal/plural: Je suis content(e) que vous…
target_language_example: Je suis content que tu aies appelé.
native_language_example: I’m glad you called.

je suis content que tu sois

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis content que tu sois
meaning: “I’m happy that you are …” / “I’m glad you’re …”
additional_notes: Used to express happiness or relief about the other person’s state or situation. After **content que**, French requires the **subjunctive**: **que tu sois** (not *que tu es*). **Content** agrees with the speaker: **je suis content** (male speaker) / **je suis contente** (female speaker). Note that French **content** usually means “happy/glad,” not the English sense of “content” (satisfied/calm).
target_language_example: Je suis content que tu sois mon ami.
native_language_example: I’m happy you’re my friend.

meaning: I’m happy / I’m glad (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to express happiness or satisfaction. “Contente” agrees with the speaker: a man says “Je suis content”; more than one woman: “Je suis contentes”; mixed/men: “Je suis contents.” Common patterns: “Je suis contente de + infinitive” (Je suis contente de te revoir), “Je suis contente pour + person” (happy for someone), and “Je suis contente que + subjunctive” (Je suis contente que tu sois venu).
target_language_example: Je suis contente qu’on puisse se voir ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m glad we can see each other this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to express happiness or satisfaction about an action or situation. It’s followed by an infinitive (je suis contente de te voir) or, with a noun/pronoun, by de + something (je suis contente de cette nouvelle). For a man: je suis content de. More formal/plural 'you' forms in your examples: te (informal singular), vous (formal singular or plural).
target_language_example: Je suis contente de te revoir !
native_language_example: I'm happy to see you again!

je suis contente de te voir

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis contente de te voir
meaning: "I’m happy to see you." (said by a woman)
additional_notes: A common greeting when you see someone. Use it when you’re genuinely pleased to see the person. If said by a man, it’s usually "je suis content de te voir". "Te" is informal (to one person you address as "tu"); with "vous": "je suis contente de vous voir". You can add a place/time: "... ici", "... aujourd’hui".
target_language_example: Je suis contente de te voir ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you tonight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause expressing feelings. It’s followed by the subjunctive: « Je suis contente que tu sois ici. » If the speaker is a man, say « je suis content que ». You can also use « je suis ravi(e) que » (stronger).
target_language_example: Je suis contente que tu puisses venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m glad you can come tonight.

je suis contente que tu sois

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis contente que tu sois
additional_notes: Used to express happiness about something the other person did. It is followed by the subjunctive: « tu sois » (from être). You then add a past participle to say what they did: « sois passé(e) » (stopped by), « sois rentré(e) » (came home), « sois revenu(e) » (came back), « sois venu(e) » (came). « Contente » is feminine; a male speaker would usually say « Je suis content que tu sois… ». With some verbs, the past participle agrees with the person (e.g., « venu/venue », « rentré/rentrée »).
target_language_example: Je suis contente que tu sois venu ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m glad you came tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express agreement with someone or with an idea. Often followed by **avec + person** (je suis d'accord avec toi/lui/elle/eux) or by a condition with **si** (Je suis d'accord si…). In more formal contexts you can also say **Je suis d’accord.** without adding who you agree with.
target_language_example: Je suis d'accord avec toi : on part plus tôt.
native_language_example: I agree with you: we’ll leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to express agreement with a person or with what they said. You can change the subject and the tense: « Tu es d’accord avec moi ? » (Do you agree with me?), « Il/Elle est d’accord avec toi », « Nous sommes d’accord avec vous », etc. Note the preposition « avec » before the person (toi, lui, elle, vous).
target_language_example: Je suis d'accord avec toi.
native_language_example: I agree with you.

meaning: "I'm in" / "I'm inside" (in a place or situation).
additional_notes: Used for being physically inside a place (je suis dans une nouvelle maison = I’m in a new house) and also in many set expressions about a situation or state: je suis dans tous mes états (I’m really upset/agitated), je suis dans un beau pétrin (I’m in a mess/in trouble), je suis dans le film (I’m really into the movie / I’m following the movie).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas répondre : je suis dans le métro.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t answer: I’m in the subway.

meaning: "I am in the..." / "I'm inside the..." (must be followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase used to say you are inside a masculine singular place/space or vehicle: je suis dans le train (I’m on the train), je suis dans le magasin (I’m in the store). Use **dans la** for feminine nouns (dans la cuisine), **dans l’** before a vowel (dans l’hôtel), and **dans les** for plural (dans les toilettes).
target_language_example: Je suis dans le train, j’arrive dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: I’m on the train; I’ll be there in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Past tense of *devenir* (“to become”), formed with *être*: *je suis devenu* (masc.) / *je suis devenue* (fem.). It’s used for a change of state or identity: becoming a profession (*Je suis devenu avocat*), becoming someone’s friend (*Je suis devenu son ami*), or becoming tired/sick/busy (*Je suis devenu fatigué/malade/occupé*).
target_language_example: Avec le temps, je suis devenu plus patient.
native_language_example: Over time, I became more patient.

additional_notes: Used to say something has already happened or is already true. Often followed by an adjective (Je suis déjà furieux. = “I’m already furious.”) or by a past participle with **être** in the passé composé (Je suis déjà parti(e). = “I’ve already left.”). With passé composé, **déjà** usually goes between the auxiliary and the past participle: *Je suis déjà parti(e), je suis déjà devenu(e).* Past participles with **être** agree with the subject: *parti/partie, devenu/devenue, pris/prise*, etc.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je suis déjà arrivé(e).
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ve already arrived.

additional_notes:
Used to apologize or to express regret/sympathy. Often followed by:
- de + infinitive: Je suis désolé de te déranger. (“I’m sorry to bother you.”)
- que + subjunctive: Je suis désolé que tu aies faim. (“I’m sorry you’re hungry.”)
Also common on its own: Je suis désolé, mais… (“I’m sorry, but…”)
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, je n’ai pas compris.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I didn’t understand.

meaning: “I’m sorry to (you)…” (a polite way to apologize before an action).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to apologize for what you’re about to do, especially politely/formally with vous: « Je suis désolé(e) de vous + verbe » (e.g., déranger, interrompre, ennuyer). Add -e if the speaker is female: « Je suis désolée… ». On its own, « Je suis désolé(e) » = “I’m sorry.”
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de vous déranger, mais j’ai une question.
native_language_example: I’m sorry to bother you, but I have a question.

additional_notes: Used to apologize or to express sympathy. With a thing/event: "Je suis désolé pour hier/ça" = sorry about what happened. With a person: "Je suis désolé pour Mandarine" = you feel sorry for them (what they’re going through). Often followed by a noun or "ce qui..." (what...).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé pour le retard.
native_language_example: I’m sorry about the delay.

additional_notes:
Used to apologize or express sympathy/regret. 
- “Je suis désolée de + infinitive” = “I’m sorry for (doing) …” (e.g., Je suis désolée de t’avoir dérangé. = I’m sorry to have bothered you.)
- “Je suis désolée pour + person/thing” = “I’m sorry for you / about …” (sympathy or regret).
Grammar: “désolée” agrees with the speaker; a man says “je suis désolé”, and in a mixed/unspecified group you may see “désolé(e)”.
target_language_example: Je suis désolée, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to apologize or express sympathy about something (an event, a mistake, a situation) or for someone. "Désolée" is feminine; a man says "Je suis désolé pour…". Often followed by a person (pour elle) or by a thing/time/event (pour hier, pour tout).
target_language_example: Je suis désolée pour le retard.
native_language_example: I’m sorry about the delay.

meaning: “I am in / on” (in a state, situation, or location).
additional_notes: Used with **en + noun** to describe your current status or activity: *en congé* (on vacation/leave), *en formation* (in training), *en possession de…* (in possession of…). It can also introduce fixed expressions like **en plein / en pleine + noun** to mean “right in the middle of”: *en plein milieu…*, *en pleine conversation*. With some place words you’ll also see it for location: *en bas* (“downstairs / down below”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis en réunion.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m in a meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say you won’t arrive on time. Often followed by "pour" + an event/place ("Je suis en retard pour l’école") or "de" + a duration ("Je suis en retard de 10 minutes"). You can also say it as a worried exclamation: "Mon Dieu, je suis en retard !"
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis en retard pour le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late for the appointment.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action is happening right now (in progress). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « Je suis en train de + infinitif » (e.g., je suis en train de manger). In everyday French you can often just use the present tense (« Je bois du café ») unless you want to stress “right now.”
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, je suis en train de travailler.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m working (right now).

je suis en train de lire

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis en train de lire
meaning: "I'm reading" / "I'm in the middle of reading (right now)."
additional_notes: Uses the structure "être en train de" + infinitive to emphasize an action in progress at the moment of speaking (similar to the English present continuous). It’s often used to stress "right now" or "in the middle of" doing something: "Je suis en train de lire" can stand alone, or you can add what you’re reading (un livre, cette lettre, etc.).
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis en train de lire, je te réponds après.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m reading right now; I’ll reply later.

additional_notes: Said by a woman to state she is pregnant. You can add a time detail: « Je suis enceinte de trois mois » (I’m three months pregnant). Note the feminine form « enceinte » (a man wouldn’t say « je suis enceinte »).
target_language_example: Je suis enceinte de deux mois.
native_language_example: I’m two months pregnant.

meaning: "I entered the" / "I went into the" (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a place that is grammatically feminine (la chambre, la maison, la salle). "Je suis entré" is masculine; a woman would say "je suis entrée". Past tense with être: "entrer" uses "être" and the past participle agrees in gender/number (entré/entrée/entrés/entrées). Often followed by a room/building: "dans la chambre", "dans la maison", "dans la salle".
target_language_example: Je suis entré dans la cuisine et j’ai allumé la lumière.
native_language_example: I went into the kitchen and turned on the light.

additional_notes: “Fier” agrees with the speaker: “je suis fier” (male speaker) / “je suis fière” (female speaker). It’s followed by “de” + a noun/pronoun (“de toi”, “de moi”, “de mes capacités”) or by “de” + infinitive to say you’re proud to do something (“je suis fier de travailler ici”). Common also in other persons: “il/elle est fier/fière de”, “nous sommes fiers/fières de”.
target_language_example: Je suis fier de ce que j'ai fait.
native_language_example: I’m proud of what I did.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone (often for an achievement or effort). "Toi" is used when addressing one person informally (tu). For formal "you" (vous), say: "Je suis fier/fière de vous." Also note agreement: a man says "fier"; a woman says "fière."
target_language_example: Je suis fier de toi, mon pote.
native_language_example: I’m proud of you, buddy.

additional_notes: Used by a female speaker (or someone using the feminine form) because *heureuse* is feminine; a male speaker usually says **je suis heureux**. Often followed by **de + infinitive** (*Je suis heureuse de te voir* = “I’m happy to see you”) or **que + subjunctive** (*Je suis heureuse que vous soyez venu* = “I’m happy that you came”). **Je suis heureuse pour vous/toi** means “I’m happy for you.”
target_language_example: Je suis heureuse de te rencontrer enfin.
native_language_example: I’m happy to finally meet you.

additional_notes: Used to express your happiness or satisfaction. Often followed by “que” + subjunctive to say what you’re happy about: “Je suis heureux/heureuse que …”. Agree the adjective with the speaker: a man typically says “heureux”, a woman “heureuse”. You can also make it more polite/formal with “Je suis très heureux/heureuse …”.
target_language_example: Je suis heureux de te voir.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you.

additional_notes: Used to express that you’re glad about something. Most often followed by an infinitive: « Je suis heureux de te voir. » (“I’m happy to see you.”). You can also use it with a noun: « Je suis heureux de cette nouvelle. » (“I’m happy about this news.”). With a full clause, French usually switches to « je suis heureux que + subjunctive »: « Je suis heureux que tu sois ici. »
target_language_example: Je suis heureux de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: I’m happy to meet you.

meaning: "I’m happy to…" (formal/polite, used before an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with **vous** to address one person formally or several people. It’s normally followed by an infinitive, often **avoir / entendre / voir / trouver**, e.g. *Je suis heureux de vous entendre* (“I’m happy to hear you”). If you’re speaking to a friend (tu), you’d say **Je suis heureux de te…** (or **Je suis heureuse…** if the speaker is female).
target_language_example: Je suis heureux de vous aider aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I’m happy to help you today.

je suis heureux que tu sois

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis heureux que tu sois
meaning: "I’m happy that you are…" (introduces what you’re happy about).
additional_notes: Used to express happiness about someone’s state/action. After "heureux/heureuse que", French normally uses the subjunctive, so you’ll often see "que tu sois" (from "être"). You can add an adjective or phrase after it: "je suis heureux que tu sois ici / en sécurité / avec nous". For a woman speaking: "je suis heureuse que tu sois…"
target_language_example: Je suis heureux que tu sois ici aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I’m happy that you’re here today.

additional_notes: Used to say you are present at a place. Also works in a figurative sense (e.g., answering a call: "I’m here" / "I’m listening"). You can add words like "aussi" (too) or "maintenant" (now).
target_language_example: Je suis ici, ne t’inquiète pas.
native_language_example: I’m here, don’t worry.

additional_notes: Use it to say why you are present (your purpose). Follow with: (1) a noun/name = "I'm here for X" (often meaning you came because of that person/thing), or (2) an infinitive verb = "I'm here to + verb" (e.g., apprendre, faire). In polite situations you can also say "Je suis là pour..." with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Je suis ici pour vous aider.
native_language_example: I'm here to help you.

additional_notes: Here, **juste** is used like an adverb meaning **“just/only”** (to downplay what you did or who you are: *Je suis juste votre serveur* = “I’m just your waiter”) or **“right”** with places: *juste derrière / juste à côté* = “right behind / right next to.” (Note: **juste** can also mean “fair/accurate,” but that’s a different use.)
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je suis juste derrière toi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m right behind you.

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself as a specific person/thing followed by a feminine singular noun: « Je suis la bête », « Je suis la voisine », etc. « la » is the feminine form of “the” (as opposed to « le » for masculine). In careful writing it takes the accent: « je suis là » means “I am here” (different meaning).
target_language_example: Je suis la prof de français.
native_language_example: I’m the French teacher.

meaning: "I am the" (used before a masculine noun/title).
additional_notes: Used to identify yourself as a specific person/role with a masculine noun: *Je suis le + noun/title* (e.g., *le propriétaire, le père*). For feminine nouns, use *je suis la*; before a vowel or silent h, use *je suis l’* (e.g., *Je suis l’enseignant / l’enseignante*). If you mean “I am a…”, use *je suis un/une* instead.
target_language_example: Bonjour, je suis le responsable du magasin.
native_language_example: Hello, I’m the manager of the store.

additional_notes: Often used to say you’re available (e.g., for a meeting or to help) or that you’re free from an obligation (e.g., after work, after a commitment, or at a future time: « Dans deux ans, je suis libre. »). Feminine speaker typically says: « Je suis libre. » (same form).
target_language_example: Je suis libre ce soir, on peut se voir.
native_language_example: I’m free tonight; we can see each other.

additional_notes: Used to say you are physically present (“I’m here”), that you’ve been present since a certain time (“I’ve been here for two hours / since the beginning”), or to reassure someone and offer support (“I’m here for you / if you need me”). Often said as a quick response to a call or to confirm you’ve arrived: « Je suis là ! »
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je suis là si tu as besoin de moi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m here if you need me.

meaning: "I’m here for" (to do something / to support someone).
additional_notes: Used to say why you are present (purpose) or what your role is. Often followed by an infinitive (je suis là pour travailler / t’écouter / te protéger) or a noun (je suis là pour monsieur Zakharov; je suis là pour une seule raison). In a supportive context, it can mean “I’m here for you.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je suis là pour toi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m here for you.

additional_notes: Used to say where or when you were born. The past tense is formed with *être* (je suis...) + past participle. *Né* agrees with the speaker: a woman says **je suis née** (with -e). Common with places (**à** + city, **en** + country, **dans** + place) or time (**il y a** + number + years). Can also be used figuratively in a more poetic sense (e.g., **je suis né pour...** = 'I was born to...').
target_language_example: Je suis né à Paris, mais j’ai grandi à Lyon.
native_language_example: I was born in Paris, but I grew up in Lyon.

meaning: “I was born” (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: From the verb "naître" (to be born). With "être" in the past tense: "je suis né" (male) / "je suis née" (female). Used to talk about where or when you were born (place: en/à/dans; time: en + decade/year, e.g. "en 1995", "dans les années trente"). Also used in "où je suis née" = "where I was born."
target_language_example: Je suis née à Paris, mais j’ai grandi à Lyon.
native_language_example: I was born in Paris, but I grew up in Lyon.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re not available right now. The feminine form is « je suis occupée ». You can add time phrases like « pour le moment » (for the moment) or « aujourd’hui » (today).
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis occupé maintenant ; je te rappelle plus tard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm busy right now; I'll call you back later.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of partir (“to leave”), used with être: je suis parti (masc.) / je suis partie (fem.). Often followed by details like when (je suis parti tôt), why (pour ne pas…), or where (je suis parti en France / pour Paris). In the expression partir à la retraite, it means “to retire.”
target_language_example: Je suis parti à 7 heures parce que j’avais un rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I left at 7 o’clock because I had an appointment.

meaning: "I’m not" (informal for « je ne suis pas »).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: the « ne » is dropped in negatives (je (ne) suis pas…). Used to say you are not something (« je suis pas amoureux ») or not in a state/situation (« je suis pas tranquille », « je suis pas au téléphone »). In more formal writing/speech, use « je ne suis pas ».
target_language_example: Je suis pas prêt, j’arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I’m not ready, I’ll be there in five minutes.

meaning: “I’m more / I’m …-er than …” OR (in speech, without *ne*) “I’m not … anymore.”
additional_notes:
**Plus** has two common uses:
1) **Comparison**: *Je suis plus + adjective + que…* = “I’m more … than …” (e.g., *Je suis plus âgée que toi* = “I’m older than you”). Here, **plus** is usually pronounced **[plys]**.
2) **Negation (spoken French)**: *Je (ne) suis plus + adjective/noun phrase* = “I’m no longer / not … anymore.” In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je suis plus dans le coup* (= *Je ne suis plus dans le coup*). Here, **plus** is usually pronounced **[ply]**.
target_language_example: Je suis plus dans le coup.
native_language_example: I’m not in the loop anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say you are ready or willing to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., partir, te suivre). Agreement: prêt (masc.), prête (fem.); plural: prêts / prêtes. With other subjects: tu es prêt(e) à, il/elle est prêt(e) à, nous sommes prêt(e)s à, etc. You can intensify it with “à tout” (ready for anything).
target_language_example: Je suis prêt à commencer maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m ready to start now.

meaning: I'm ready to / I'm willing to.
additional_notes: Used by a woman speaking ("prête" is feminine; a man says "je suis prêt à"). Followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "faire", "recommencer", "vous suivre"). Often expresses readiness or willingness; with "à tout" it means "ready/willing to do anything".
target_language_example: Je suis prête à partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I'm ready to leave now.

additional_notes: Used in formal or polite situations with "vous". It’s usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., "vous aider", "vous annoncer", "vous revoir", "vous voir") or by "connaître" in "Je suis ravi de vous connaître" ("Nice to meet you"). For a woman speaker, "ravi" becomes "ravie": "Je suis ravie de vous…".
target_language_example: Je suis ravi de vous accueillir parmi nous.
native_language_example: I’m delighted to welcome you among us.

je suis ravi que vous soyez

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis ravi que vous soyez
additional_notes: Used to express happiness about someone’s presence or situation. It’s followed by the subjunctive: « que vous soyez… » (e.g., « là », « en sécurité », « avec nous »). « Ravi » agrees with the speaker (ravi = masculine, ravie = feminine). « Vous soyez » is addressed to one person formally or to several people.
target_language_example: Je suis ravi que vous soyez ici aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I'm glad you're here today.

additional_notes: Used to express gratitude for a person, thing, or action. It’s followed by a noun (son aide) or by something like "ce que..." + a clause (ce que tu as fait). In everyday French, you’ll also often hear "je te suis reconnaissant(e)" (I’m grateful to you) or "je suis reconnaissant(e) de/pour..."; adjective agrees with the speaker: reconnaissant (male), reconnaissante (female).
target_language_example: Je suis reconnaissant pour ton soutien.
native_language_example: I’m grateful for your support.

meaning: "I came back / I got home" (male speaker).
additional_notes: From the verb "rentrer" = to come back, to return, to go back in (often used for getting back home). It’s most common with places like "à la maison" or "chez moi" and with time/manner: "hier" (yesterday), "plus tôt" (earlier), "tard" (late), "en bus" (by bus). Agreement: a woman says "je suis rentrée". In the passé composé it uses "être" (je suis…).
target_language_example: Je suis rentré tôt ce soir parce que je suis fatigué.
native_language_example: I got home early tonight because I’m tired.

meaning: “I went home / I came back home.”
additional_notes: Uses the past tense (passé composé) of rentrer (“to come back/go back/return”). Rentrez is used with être: je suis rentré (male speaker) / je suis rentrée (female speaker). Chez moi means “at my place/home” (literally “to/at my home”). Often used after an activity to say you headed back home.
target_language_example: Après le travail, je suis rentré chez moi et j’ai dîné.
native_language_example: After work, I went home and had dinner.

meaning: "I came back / I got home" (said by a woman).
additional_notes: "Rentrer" often means to return or to come/go back home. It uses "être" in the past tense: "je suis rentré" (man) / "je suis rentrée" (woman). You can add where you’re coming from with "de" (Je suis rentrée du boulot.) or where you returned to with a place (Je suis rentrée à la maison.). It can also mean coming back earlier/later: "Je suis rentrée plus tôt."
target_language_example: Je suis rentrée tard hier soir.
native_language_example: I got home late last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of **rester** (“to stay/remain”), formed with **être**: *je suis resté* (masc.) / *je suis restée* (fem.). Often followed by a place or situation: *Je suis resté avec…* (“I stayed with…”) or *Je suis resté enfermé…* (“I stayed locked in…”). Note that **rester** means “stay/remain,” not “rest.”
target_language_example: Je suis resté à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: I stayed home tonight.

je suis resté à la maison

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis resté à la maison
additional_notes: Past tense with être (passé composé) of rester (“to stay”): je suis resté (male speaker) / je suis restée (female speaker). Often followed by a reason or duration: afin de… (in order to…), toute la journée (all day), à cause de… (because of…).
target_language_example: Je suis resté à la maison hier soir parce que je ne me sentais pas bien.
native_language_example: I stayed at home last night because I didn’t feel well.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *rester* with **être**. **Restée** agrees with a female speaker (add -e). A male speaker says **je suis resté**. Often followed by **chez** (chez moi = at my place/home), **à la maison** (at home), or a duration/comparison (plus longtemps, toute la journée).
target_language_example: Je suis restée à la maison parce que j’étais fatiguée.
native_language_example: I stayed at home because I was tired.

additional_notes: Passé composé of **revenir** (“to come back/return”), used for returning to a place or situation: *Je suis revenu à la maison* (I came back home), *Je suis revenu pour toi* (I came back for you). Uses **être** as the helping verb, so the past participle agrees with the subject: **je suis revenu** (masc.), **je suis revenue** (fem.). Not to be confused with English **revenue** (false friend).
target_language_example: Je suis revenu trop tard, le magasin était déjà fermé.
native_language_example: I came back too late; the store was already closed.

meaning: "I am so…" (very), used to intensify an adjective.
additional_notes: Use **je suis si + adjective** to emphasize a feeling or state: *Je suis si fatigué / si fatiguée.* You can also add **que + [subjunctive]** to give a result or reason: *Je suis si content(e) que tu sois là.* Make the adjective agree with the speaker (masc. *content*, fem. *contente*).
target_language_example: Je suis si stressé que je n’arrive pas à dormir.
native_language_example: I’m so stressed that I can’t sleep.

je suis si fière de toi

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis si fière de toi
meaning: I’m so proud of you. (said by a woman)
additional_notes: "Fière" agrees with the speaker: a man would say "Je suis si fier de toi." "De toi" is informal singular "of you" (to one person you’re on "tu" terms with). You can add a name or term of endearment: "mon fils", "chéri/chérie".
target_language_example: Je suis si fière de toi, tu as très bien travaillé.
native_language_example: I’m so proud of you—you worked really hard.

additional_notes: Used to express strong happiness or relief. The adjective agrees with the speaker: a man would say « je suis si heureux ». « si » means “so” (very). Often followed by: « de + infinitive » (je suis si heureuse de te revoir = I’m so happy to see you again) or « que + clause » (je suis si heureuse que tu ailles bien = I’m so happy that you’re doing well).
target_language_example: Je suis si heureuse d’être ici avec vous.
native_language_example: I’m so happy to be here with you.

meaning: "I went out" / "I got out" (I left; I exited).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *sortir* with *être*: **je suis sorti** (male speaker) / **je suis sortie** (female speaker). Often used with **de** to show what you exited (*je suis sorti de la voiture* = I got out of the car) or in general to say you went outside/left the house (*je suis sorti malgré la pluie*).
target_language_example: Désolé, je n’ai pas répondu : je suis sorti un moment.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t reply: I went out for a bit.

je suis sur le point de

target_language_multi_word_term: je suis sur le point de
meaning: “I’m about to …” / “I’m just about to …” (something is going to happen very soon).
additional_notes: Used to express an action that is imminent. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « Je suis sur le point de partir » (I’m about to leave). You can change « je suis » to other subjects/tenses: « Il est sur le point de… », « Nous sommes sur le point de… ».
target_language_example: Je suis sur le point de partir, j’arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I’m about to leave; I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to express certainty. Common patterns: **je suis sûr de + noun/pronoun** (“I’m sure about…”): *Je suis sûr de sa venue.*; **je suis sûr que + clause** (“I’m sure that…”): *Je suis sûr qu’il va marquer.* In writing, you may see agreement: **je suis sûr** (male speaker) / **je suis sûre** (female speaker).
target_language_example: Je suis sûr qu’on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: I’m sure we’ll find a solution.

additional_notes: Used to express confidence/certainty about what a man will do or what is true. It’s the pattern: je suis sûr(e) que + subject + verb. If the speaker is female, use « je suis sûre qu'il... ». Before a vowel or silent h, « que » becomes « qu' » (qu'il, qu'elle, qu'on).
target_language_example: Je suis sûr qu'il va comprendre.
native_language_example: I'm sure he'll understand.

additional_notes: Used to express strong confidence about a statement. The adjective agrees with the speaker: a woman typically says "je suis sûre que" (with -e). Common in conversation to reassure or insist: "Je suis sûr(e) que tout va bien."
target_language_example: Je suis sûr que tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: I’m sure you’ll manage to do it.

additional_notes: Used to express confidence about what the other person will do or what will happen next. Followed by a verb (often in the future): « Je suis sûr que tu trouveras. » You’ll also hear « je suis sûre » if the speaker is female.
target_language_example: Je suis sûr que tu vas réussir.
native_language_example: I’m sure you’re going to succeed.

meaning: "I’m sure that you…" (introduces something you’re certain about).
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence and is usually followed by a verb clause (e.g., "je suis sûr que vous savez…"). It expresses certainty or strong confidence. You may also hear the feminine form "je suis sûre que vous…" (said by a woman).
target_language_example: Je suis sûr que vous allez aimer ce restaurant.
native_language_example: I’m sure you’re going to like this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to express strong confidence/certainty about a statement. "Sûre" agrees with the speaker: a man says "Je suis sûr que" (no -e). Often followed by the indicative (e.g., "Je suis sûre que c’est…", "Je suis sûre que ça se passera bien").
target_language_example: Je suis sûre que tu vas réussir.
native_language_example: I’m sure you’re going to succeed.

meaning: "I’m sure that it/that…" (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to express confidence about what will happen or be true. It’s often followed by a verb phrase: « Je suis sûre que ça va s’arranger. » If a man is speaking, you write/say « je suis sûr que ça… » (no -e). « ça » usually means “it/that” and refers to a situation or thing understood from context.
target_language_example: Je suis sûre que ça va marcher.
native_language_example: I’m sure it’s going to work.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a feeling or state, typically followed by an adjective (e.g., content, désolé(e), fatigué(e)). Note gender agreement: désolé (male), désolée (female).
target_language_example: Je suis tellement fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I am so tired today.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *tomber* with **être**: *je suis tombé* (masc.), *je suis tombée* (fem.). Literal word-for-word is “I am fallen,” but natural English is “I fell / I have fallen.” Common extensions: **tomber sur** = “to run into / come across (by chance)” (*Je suis tombé sur un vieil ami*), **tomber de** = “to fall from” (*du toit*), and **tomber amoureux / tomber follement amoureux** = “to fall in love (madly)”.
target_language_example: Je suis tombé dans les escaliers.
native_language_example: I fell on the stairs.

additional_notes: Used when you meet someone by chance or find something unexpectedly. In the past tense with être: je suis tombé (male speaker) / je suis tombée (female speaker); plural: nous sommes tombés/tombées. Often followed by a person or thing: tomber sur quelqu’un / tomber sur quelque chose.
target_language_example: En rangeant mes affaires, je suis tombé sur de vieilles photos.
native_language_example: While tidying up my things, I came across some old photos.

meaning: "I came across a" / "I stumbled upon a" (by chance).
additional_notes: Used to describe finding or encountering something unexpectedly. It comes from the verb phrase "tomber sur" + a noun (e.g., un article, une photo, des gens). The past participle agrees with the subject: "je suis tombé" (male) / "je suis tombée" (female). You can change the subject too: "il est tombé sur…", "on est tombés sur…". It does not mean you literally fell.
target_language_example: Je suis tombé sur une vieille photo de nous en rangeant mes affaires.
native_language_example: I came across an old photo of us while tidying my things.

meaning: “I fell / I’ve fallen” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Past tense of **tomber** using **être** in the passé composé. **Tombée** agrees with a female speaker (a man says **je suis tombé**). Depending on what comes after it, it can be literal (**fall down/off/from a height**) or part of common expressions: **tomber amoureuse de** = “to fall in love with,” **tomber dessus** = “to come across it / run into it,” **tomber malade** = “to fall ill.”
target_language_example: Je suis tombée dans les escaliers.
native_language_example: I fell on the stairs.

meaning: "I am your" (addressing one person; before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to state identity/role: "Je suis ton + [noun]". "Ton" means "your" when the possessed noun is masculine singular (ton père, ton patron). Use "ta" with a feminine singular noun (ta mère) and "tes" with plural nouns (tes parents).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je suis ton professeur.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m your teacher.

additional_notes: With a state or situation, it often means “still” (something continues): *Je suis toujours là* = “I’m still here.” With an adjective, it can mean “still” (same as before) or “always” (a general habit), depending on context. *Toujours* usually goes after *suis* in this pattern.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je suis toujours disponible.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m still available.

meaning: “I’m too…” / “I’m so…” (often: “I’m really…” in casual speech).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb phrase: *Je suis trop fatigué(e)* (“I’m too/so tired”). In informal French, *trop* is often used as an intensifier meaning “really/so” (not always a literal “too much”). Agreement: *fatigué* (male), *fatiguée* (female). You can also use it with frequency: *Je suis trop souvent sorti le soir* (“I went out too often in the evening”).
target_language_example: Je suis trop stressé aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I’m so stressed today.

meaning: “I am very …” (to say you feel/are very something).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to intensify what you are (or how you feel): Je suis très content(e), satisfait(e), fier/fière, intéressé(e), etc. Make the adjective agree with you (e.g., content/contente; fier/fière; satisfait/satisfaite; intéressé/intéressée). In more formal or permanent descriptions, you may also hear "je suis" + adjective (e.g., Je suis très patient).
target_language_example: Je suis très fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I’m very tired today.

meaning: I’m very happy. (said by a woman)
additional_notes: Feminine form: a woman says « je suis très heureuse »; a man would say « je suis très heureux ». Common patterns: « je suis très heureuse de + infinitive » (I’m very happy to...), « je suis très heureuse que + subjunctive » (I’m very happy that...), and « je suis très heureuse pour toi/vous » (I’m very happy for you).
target_language_example: Je suis très heureuse que tu sois venu.
native_language_example: I’m very happy that you came.

additional_notes:
Used to express a strong positive feeling. Often followed by:
- "de" + infinitive: "Je suis très heureux de te voir" (I’m very happy to see you).
- "de" + noun/pronoun: "Je suis très heureux de cette nouvelle" (I’m very happy about this news).
"Heureux" agrees with the subject: a woman typically says "Je suis très heureuse".
target_language_example: Je suis très heureux d'être ici avec vous.
native_language_example: I'm very happy to be here with you.

meaning: "I’m very happy to / I’m very pleased to" (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to express strong happiness or pleasure about doing something or about the fact that something is happening. It’s a polite, common phrase. After "de", you typically use a verb in the infinitive (e.g., "te voir", "travailler"). You can also say "Je suis très heureuse de" if the speaker is female.
target_language_example: Je suis très heureux de faire votre connaissance.
native_language_example: I’m very pleased to meet you.

additional_notes: Used to express strong interest in a topic/activity. Structure: être intéressé(e) par + noun/subject. The adjective agrees with the speaker: "je suis très intéressé" (male), "je suis très intéressée" (female). You can vary intensity: "intéressé(e)" (interested), "très intéressé(e)" (very interested), "vraiment intéressé(e)" (really interested).
target_language_example: Je suis très intéressé par la musique.
native_language_example: I'm very interested in music.

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself as one thing: it comes before a singular masculine noun. For a feminine noun, use "je suis une ..." instead. With professions or nationalities, French often omits the article: for example, "je suis étudiant" or "je suis français."
target_language_example: Je suis un étudiant sérieux.
native_language_example: I'm a serious student.

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself as male (“je” = I, “suis” = am, “un homme” = a man). Often followed by an adjective or description: “Je suis un homme heureux” (a happy man), “Je suis un homme de parole” (a man of my word), or a relative clause: “Je suis un homme qui…” (I’m a man who…). In many contexts you can also say “Je suis un…” + noun/role (e.g., “Je suis un professeur”).
target_language_example: Bonjour, je m’appelle Marc et je suis un homme très occupé.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Marc and I’m a very busy man.

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself or describe your role/identity before a feminine singular noun: *Je suis une étudiante / une Française / une artiste.* For masculine nouns, use *je suis un*. Before a vowel sound, *je suis* often links to the next word (liaison), e.g., *je suis une amie*.
target_language_example: Je suis une étudiante.
native_language_example: I am a student (female student).

additional_notes: A basic way to state that you are a woman (gender/identity). Often followed by an adjective or extra info: *Je suis une femme mariée* (“I’m a married woman”), *Je suis une femme, pas une fille* (“I’m a woman, not a girl”). In some set expressions the meaning shifts: *une femme du monde* = a society/high-society woman; *une femme bien* = a respectable/good woman. You may also see it with vulgar slang like *une femme qui a des couilles* meaning a very tough/brave woman.
target_language_example: Je suis une femme et je m'appelle Claire.
native_language_example: I am a woman and my name is Claire.

meaning: "I came" / "I have come" (past tense of venir).
additional_notes: Uses the verb être in the passé composé: je suis venu. Agreement matters: venu (masc.), venue (fem.), venus/venues (plural). Often followed by an infinitive to say purpose (e.g., Je suis venu récupérer...), or a place with à (Je suis venu à Tokyo...), or a way of coming (Je suis venu à pied = I came on foot).
target_language_example: Je suis venu te parler deux minutes.
native_language_example: I came to talk to you for two minutes.

additional_notes: Passé composé of **venir** (“to come”) with **être**. **Venu** agrees with the speaker: **je suis venu** (male) / **je suis venue** (female). Often used to explain your purpose or reason for coming: *C’est pour ça que je suis venu ici.* In English you usually translate it as “I came here” (not “I am come here”).
target_language_example: Je suis venu ici pour te parler.
native_language_example: I came here to talk to you.

meaning: "I came here to" (I came here in order to…).
additional_notes: Used to state your purpose/reason for coming somewhere. It uses the past tense (passé composé) of venir: "je suis venu" (male speaker) / "je suis venue" (female speaker). For more than one person: "nous sommes venus/venues ici pour…". Follow it with an infinitive verb: "…pour apprendre / pour vous aider".
target_language_example: Je suis venu ici pour te parler un moment.
native_language_example: I came here to talk to you for a moment.

meaning: "I came to" / "I came in order to" (to do something).
additional_notes: Used to state your purpose for coming. It’s the passé composé of venir (je suis venu = “I came / I have come”); add -e if the speaker is female (je suis venue). Follow with an infinitive verb (e.g., voir, parler, aider) or a noun phrase (e.g., passer un marché).
target_language_example: Je suis venu pour t'aider.
native_language_example: I came to help you.

meaning: "I came to (you) to…" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say you came in order to do something for/to someone: « Je suis venu te + infinitive » (e.g., te prévenir, te sauver). The pronoun « te » (= you) goes before the infinitive. « Venir » uses « être » in the past: « je suis venu » (male speaker) / « je suis venue » (female speaker).
target_language_example: Je suis venu te parler.
native_language_example: I came to talk to you.

meaning: "I came" / "I have come" (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Past tense of "venir" (to come) using "être": "je suis venu" (man) / "je suis venue" (woman). The past participle agrees in gender (and sometimes number). Often means arriving somewhere: "Je suis venue le plus vite possible" = "I came as fast as possible." Note: French "venue" is not the same as English "venue" (place).
target_language_example: Je suis venue hier soir pour t'aider.
native_language_example: I came last night to help you.

additional_notes: Used by a woman speaking about herself: venir → "to come"; venue agrees with the speaker (male: "je suis venu pour"). Follow it with an infinitive to express purpose ("...pour boire" = "to drink"), or with a noun to express the reason ("...pour le travail" = "for work").
target_language_example: Je suis venue pour t’aider.
native_language_example: I came to help you.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to identify yourself in relation to the listener: Je suis votre ami (I’m your friend). With certain nouns it becomes a set, polite phrase meaning “at your service” or “I’m the person you need,” e.g. Je suis votre homme ! (“I’m your man!”) and Je suis votre serviteur. (“Your humble servant.”). Because it uses votre, it’s addressed to one person you’re speaking to using vous (formal, or plural).
target_language_example: Bonjour, je suis votre guide pour la visite.
native_language_example: Hello, I’m your guide for the tour.

meaning: “I am really / I’m truly …” (to emphasize a feeling or opinion).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective (or sometimes before a past participle used like an adjective) to add emphasis: Je suis vraiment content(e), désolé(e), déçu(e), intéressé(e). Make the adjective agree with the speaker (masc. -é / fem. -ée; masc. content / fem. contente; masc. fier / fem. fière). Often in emotional statements and apologies.
target_language_example: Je suis vraiment fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I’m really tired today.

additional_notes: Used to apologize sincerely or express regret. Often followed by **de + infinitive** to say what you’re sorry about (*Je suis vraiment désolé de partir*) or **pour + noun/pronoun** (*…pour ça*). **Désolé** agrees with the speaker: *désolée* (female speaker), *désolés/désolées* (plural).
target_language_example: Je suis vraiment désolé pour le retard.
native_language_example: I’m really sorry for the delay.

meaning: "I am at / in"; sometimes "I’m (distance/time) from" or "I’m available / with you."
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "à" to give location (Je suis à Detroit), a situation/condition (Je suis à la rue = I’m on the street / homeless), distance or time away (Je suis à une heure de mon bureau = I’m an hour from my office), and in polite customer-service style to mean you’re available for someone (Je suis à vous tout de suite / Je suis à vous = I’ll be with you right away / I’m with you).
target_language_example: Je suis à dix minutes de la gare.
native_language_example: I’m ten minutes from the train station.

additional_notes: Informal. Used to say you’re behind schedule or late (often with an exclamation: « Je suis à la bourre ! »). Note that « je suis à la … » can start other phrases too (e.g., « je suis à la recherche de… » = “I’m looking for…”), but « à la bourre » is a fixed expression meaning “late.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis à la bourre, j’arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm running late—I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a guess or assumption you think is probably true, often based on context rather than certainty. It can sound neutral or slightly tentative; in questions it can also be a polite way to check something (“Je suppose que vous… ?”).
target_language_example: Je suppose que tu es prêt(e), alors on peut y aller.
native_language_example: I suppose you’re ready, so we can go.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption or a conclusion you’re not completely sure about. Often followed by an adjective, a noun, or a clause: « je suppose que c'est vrai » (I suppose it’s true). In speech, « je suppose » can sound slightly more formal or detached than « je crois » or « je pense ».
target_language_example: Je suppose que c'est la bonne adresse.
native_language_example: I suppose it's the right address.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption, a likely conclusion, or a hesitant opinion about yourself. Often followed by a verb in the present: « Je suppose que je peux… » (“I suppose I can…”). In everyday speech, « je suppose que… » can be close to “I guess…”, sometimes sounding a bit uncertain or reluctant depending on tone.
target_language_example: Je suppose que je peux venir demain.
native_language_example: I suppose I can come tomorrow.

je suppose que je me suis

target_language_multi_word_term: je suppose que je me suis
meaning: "I guess (that) I have…" / "I suppose (that) I…" (introduces what you think happened).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a thought or admission about yourself, often followed by a reflexive verb in the passé composé (je me suis + past participle). The past participle may agree with the speaker: je me suis trompé (male) / trompée (female); je me suis laissé / laissée emporter.
target_language_example: Je suppose que je me suis mal exprimé.
native_language_example: I guess I expressed myself poorly.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption about the person you’re speaking to (tu = informal singular “you”). It’s usually followed by a verb clause: « Je suppose que tu as raison. » Can sound polite/softening, like “I guess…”. With « vous » instead: « Je suppose que vous… »
target_language_example: Je suppose que tu es fatigué(e).
native_language_example: I suppose you’re tired.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption or a polite guess about the person/people you’re addressing. The pronoun "vous" is used for one person in a formal situation or for multiple people. Often followed by a verb: "Je suppose que vous avez... / que vous êtes..."
target_language_example: Je suppose que vous avez déjà réservé une table.
native_language_example: I suppose you’ve already booked a table.

meaning: "I" + "to you" (or "to you" as a direct object) before a vowel: "I you…".
additional_notes: "Je t'" is "je" + "te" shortened to "t'" before a vowel or silent h (j(e) + t(e) → je t'). It means "I" plus the object pronoun "you" (singular informal) placed before the verb: je t'aime (I love you), je t'explique (I explain to you / explain it to you), je t'ai pris… (I took … from you / I took you … depending on context). Not used for formal/plural "you" (use "je vous…").
target_language_example: Je t'appelle ce soir.
native_language_example: I'll call you tonight.

additional_notes: Contraction of je + te + ai, used before a past participle in the passé composé. t' means 'you'. In English, this is often translated with either the simple past or the present perfect, depending on context. The past participle can sometimes agree in gender when te is a direct object, as in Je t'ai cherchée.
target_language_example: Je t'ai envoyé un message.
native_language_example: I sent you a message.

additional_notes: Passé composé of appeler: je + t’ (te, “you”) + ai appelé (“called”). Used to say you called someone (often recently). You can add details like purpose (C'est pour ça que je t'ai appelé. / Je t'ai appelé pour ça.), device/number (Je t'ai appelé sur ton portable.), or duration (Je t'ai appelé toute la nuit.).
target_language_example: C'est pour ça que je t'ai appelé.
native_language_example: That’s why I called you.

additional_notes: From the verb « apporter » (“to bring” something to someone). « t' » = « te » (“to you”). Uses the passé composé, so it often means something you brought and are presenting now (“I’ve brought you…”). You usually add the thing you brought right after: « je t'ai apporté des fleurs / ça / un cadeau ».
target_language_example: je t'ai apporté un cadeau.
native_language_example: I brought you a gift.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of demander: je + t' (te = “you”, informal singular) + ai demandé. Used to remind someone of something you asked them to do or to ask if you asked them something (“Did I ask you for your opinion?”). Often followed by what you asked: « Je t'ai demandé de + infinitive » (I asked you to...) or « Je t'ai demandé [quelque chose] » (I asked you [something]).
target_language_example: Je t'ai demandé de fermer la porte, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I asked you to close the door, please.

additional_notes: Commonly followed by **de + infinitive** to report an instruction: *Je t'ai dit d'attendre* (“I told you to wait”). It can also appear in *ce que je t'ai dit* (“what I told you”), often after verbs like *penser à* or *réfléchir à*.
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit de ne pas toucher ça !
native_language_example: I told you not to touch that!

additional_notes: Used to remind (often firmly) someone of an instruction you already gave them. Structure: je (I) + t’ (to you) + ai dit (told) + de + infinitive verb. In casual speech, negation may drop “ne” (e.g., « Je t'ai dit de pas venir » instead of « Je t'ai dit de ne pas venir »).
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit de laisser tomber.
native_language_example: I told you to drop it.

je t'ai dit de ne pas

target_language_multi_word_term: je t'ai dit de ne pas
additional_notes: Used to remind/scold someone about a negative instruction you already gave them. It’s in the past tense (passé composé) and is followed by an infinitive: “Je t'ai dit de ne pas + verb” (e.g., dire, faire, venir). In casual speech, the “ne” is often dropped: “Je t'ai dit de pas …”.
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit de ne pas en parler.
native_language_example: I told you not to talk about it.

additional_notes:
Used to remind someone of something you already said. 
- "Je t'ai dit que" is followed by a full clause (subject + verb): « Je t'ai dit que je le ferais. »
- If you don’t use "que", you can say « Je te l’ai dit. » (= I told you / I told you so).
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit que je ne voulais pas y aller.
native_language_example: I told you (that) I didn’t want to go.

additional_notes: Used to remind, insist, or emphasize something you previously said. Structure: "Je t'ai dit" (passé composé of dire = "I told you") + "que" (that) + a new clause starting with "je" (I). Typically followed by a verb phrase: "Je t'ai dit que je viens demain."
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit que je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I told you that I can’t come tonight.

meaning: "I already have (to you) / I've already… (to you)".
additional_notes: Used to start a sentence in the passé composé: **je** (I) + **t'** = **te** (to you) + **ai** (have) + **déjà** (already), followed by a past participle (e.g., *dit, demandé, laissé*). The object pronoun **te** comes before the helper verb (**ai**). Often used in questions to mean “Have I ever already…?”
target_language_example: Je t'ai déjà envoyé le lien.
native_language_example: I already sent you the link.

meaning: "I made you / I did (something) to/for you"; sometimes "I had/got you (do something)".
additional_notes: Passé composé of faire with te (you). Common patterns: (1) je t'ai fait + noun = “I made you …” (food, drink, etc.): Je t'ai fait du thé / un sandwich. (2) je t'ai fait + infinitive = “I had/got you …” (causative): Je t'ai fait inviter = “I got you invited.” (3) pour ce que je t'ai fait = “for what I did to you.” Context decides whether it’s “for you” (made something) or “to you” (did something to you).
target_language_example: Je t'ai fait un café, tu en veux ?
native_language_example: I made you a coffee—do you want it?

meaning: “I spoke to you / I talked to you” (also: “I told you”).
additional_notes: Passé composé of *parler* with an indirect object: *parler à quelqu’un* → *Je t’ai parlé* (“I spoke to you”). To say what you talked about, add *de*: *Je t’ai parlé de lui/d’elle* (“I told you about him/her”). It can also be used as a reminder (“I already mentioned it to you”) or as a question: *Je t’ai parlé ?* (“Did I talk to you?” / “Have I told you?”).
target_language_example: Je t'ai parlé de ce film hier.
native_language_example: I told you about that movie yesterday.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *voir* (to see): **j’ai vu** = “I saw.” **t’** is the shortened form of **te** (“you” as a direct object) before a vowel: **je t’ai vu** = “I saw you.” Very often followed by an infinitive to mean “I saw you do …”: *Je t’ai vu partir.*
target_language_example: Je t'ai vu sortir de la maison.
native_language_example: I saw you leave the house.

additional_notes: Used to express love or deep affection. It’s most common with romantic partners, but can also be said to close family (often with context or emphasis). "Je t'aime plus" is a common, playful way to say "I love you more."
target_language_example: Je t'aime de tout mon cœur.
native_language_example: I love you with all my heart.

additional_notes: Used to reply when someone has just said “Je t’aime.” to you. The “t’” is short for “te” (“you”), and “aussi” means “too/as well.” You can add a term of endearment after it (e.g., chéri/chérie) or use it with family (e.g., maman).
target_language_example: Je t'aime aussi, chéri.
native_language_example: I love you too, darling.

additional_notes: Used to express affection or liking in a friendly (or light romantic) way. It’s generally weaker than « je t’aime », which usually means “I love you.” You can say it to a friend, classmate, coworker, etc. (« bien » softens the meaning to “like.”)
target_language_example: Je t'aime bien, mais je ne suis pas prêt(e) pour une relation.
native_language_example: I like you, but I’m not ready for a relationship.

additional_notes: Literally “I call you” (present tense), but in everyday French it’s often used to mean “I’ll call you” when the call is planned for later, especially with a time marker (demain, quand…, dès que…, s’il y a…). Also used as a promise to call back.
target_language_example: Je t'appelle tout à l'heure.
native_language_example: I'll call you later.

additional_notes: Used to promise you’ll call immediately after something happens. It’s followed by a clause (often in the present tense in French even when referring to the future): « Je t'appelle dès que j'arrive » = “I’ll call you as soon as I arrive.”
target_language_example: Je t'appelle dès que j'ai fini.
native_language_example: I’ll call you as soon as I’m finished.

additional_notes: Uses the plus-que-parfait (j'avais dit) to refer to something you said earlier (before another past moment). Common for reminding someone of an instruction or prediction; in “Qu'est-ce que je t'avais dit ?” it corresponds to “See? I told you so.”
target_language_example: Je t'avais dit de rester dans la voiture.
native_language_example: I told you to stay in the car.

meaning: “I told you to …” (past, informal: “I’d told you to …”).
additional_notes: Uses the pluperfect ("avais dit") to refer to something you had already told someone before another moment in the past (often implying “you didn’t listen” or “remember?”). Followed by an infinitive verb: "Je t'avais dit de faire attention". In informal speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je t'avais dit de pas venir".
target_language_example: Je t'avais dit de fermer la porte à clé !
native_language_example: I told you to lock the door!

je t'avais dit de ne pas

target_language_multi_word_term: je t'avais dit de ne pas
meaning: 'I told you not to…' / 'I had told you not to…' (a reproach: you did it anyway).
additional_notes: Uses the plus-que-parfait ("j'avais dit") to refer back to a previous warning/instruction. Often said in an annoyed tone when the person didn’t follow what you said. It must be followed by an infinitive: "Je t'avais dit de ne pas + verb" (e.g., l'ouvrir, revenir, venir, y toucher).
target_language_example: Je t'avais dit de ne pas parler si fort !
native_language_example: I told you not to talk so loudly!

meaning: “I had told you that …” (often: “I told you …”).
additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (plus-que-parfait): je + t’ (to you) + avais dit (had said/told) + que (that). It introduces a clause with a past statement that happened before another past moment, and it’s also commonly used to remind someone of something you previously said (sometimes with an “I told you so” tone depending on context and intonation).
target_language_example: Je t'avais dit que j'arriverais en retard.
native_language_example: I told you (that) I would be late.

meaning: "I ... you some/one (of it/them)" (je = I, t' = to you, en = some/of it/of them).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself—it’s the beginning of a sentence with object pronouns. "t'" is the indirect object pronoun meaning “to you.” "en" replaces something introduced with "de" (de ça, de ce livre, de ces pommes, etc.) and can mean “some,” “one,” or “of it/of them.” Word order note: in simple tenses it appears as "Je t’en + verb"; in the near future: "Je vais t’en + verb"; in the past with two verbs: "Je vais t’en avoir donné" (more advanced).
target_language_example: Je t'en achèterai une autre.
native_language_example: I’ll buy you another one (of them).

additional_notes: Used to politely insist or beg someone to do (or not do) something: “Je t’en prie, + imperative” (Je t’en prie, viens / ne dis rien). It can also reply to “merci” meaning “you’re welcome,” though “de rien” is more common in everyday speech. Often expresses emotion (urgency, pleading, reassurance) depending on tone.
target_language_example: Je t'en prie, aide-moi une minute.
native_language_example: Please, help me for a minute.

additional_notes: Used to strongly and politely ask someone not to do something. "Je t’en prie" literally means "I beg you" (or "please"), and it’s followed by a negative command starting with "ne" (often completed with "pas", "jamais", etc.): "Je t’en prie, ne + [verb] + pas".
target_language_example: Je t'en prie, ne me laisse pas ici.
native_language_example: Please, don’t leave me here.
