additional_notes: Used before a verb: je = "I" and te = the informal singular object pronoun "you." In English, te may translate as either "you" or "to you," depending on the verb. Use it when speaking to one person you call tu; the formal/plural equivalent is je vous.
target_language_example: Je te vois demain.
native_language_example: I'll see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb connaître (“to know / be familiar with”) + a person (te = “you”). It can imply familiarity (“I know you well”) and is often used to say you understand how someone is or what they’ll do: « Je te connais trop bien. » Adding « toi » can make it more emphatic or pointed: « Je te connais, toi. » You’ll also see it with time expressions (« depuis longtemps » = “for a long time”) or set phrases like « par cœur » (“by heart / perfectly”).
target_language_example: Ne me mens pas, je te connais !
native_language_example: Don’t lie to me, I know you!

meaning: "I advise you to" / "I recommend that you".
additional_notes: Used to give advice to one person you address as "tu". Structure: "Je te conseille de" + infinitive (e.g., "je te conseille de partir"). Often a polite recommendation, but it can also introduce harsh advice depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Je te conseille de prendre un parapluie.
native_language_example: I recommend that you take an umbrella.

additional_notes: Literally “I believe you.” Used to say you believe what someone is saying (Je te crois.), or to express an opinion about them with an adjective or noun: Je te crois honnête (“I think you’re honest”). Can be strengthened with bien sûr (“of course”) or questioned: Pourquoi est-ce que je te crois ? (“Why do I believe you?”).
target_language_example: Je te crois, ne t’inquiète pas.
native_language_example: I believe you, don’t worry.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker asks someone directly for something (a favor, a phone number) or asks them to do something: « Je te demande de + infinitive » (I’m asking you to…). It can also introduce a question: « Je te demande qui/ce que… » (I’m asking you who/what…). Often used in set phrases like « C’est tout/ la seule chose que je te demande » (That’s all/the only thing I’m asking of you).
target_language_example: Je te demande de m'aider cinq minutes, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I’m asking you to help me for five minutes, please.

additional_notes: Future tense of « dire » (to say/tell) + « te » (to you). Used to promise or announce information you will give later: « Je te dirai plus tard » (“I’ll tell you later”), or in patterns like « … et je te dirai … » (“… and I’ll tell you …”).
target_language_example: Appelle-moi ce soir et je te dirai la vérité.
native_language_example: Call me tonight and I'll tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Used to insist on what you’re saying, give a firm instruction, or emphasize a point. Very common in speech: « Je te dis que… » (“I’m telling you that…”), « Fais ce que je te dis » (“Do what I tell you”), « Je te dis ça comme ça » (“I’m just saying / I’m telling you that just because”).
target_language_example: Je te dis que ce n’est pas une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I’m telling you it’s not a good idea.

meaning: 'I owe you' (money, a favor, a drink, an explanation, etc.).
additional_notes: Literally “I to-you owe.” Used with a person (te = “to you”) plus what you owe: Je te dois 10 euros / une bière / une explication. In questions, you can hear it as Je te dois quoi ? (“What do I owe you?”).
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide : je te dois un café.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help: I owe you a coffee.

additional_notes: "Je" = I, "te" = to you (informal singular), "donne" = give. Used for giving something concrete (money, an object) or something abstract (permission, help). In speech it can also mean "Here you go" when handing something to someone.
target_language_example: Je te donne mon numéro, appelle-moi quand tu veux.
native_language_example: I'll give you my number—call me whenever you want.

additional_notes: Future tense of donner (“to give”). Used when promising or offering to give something to one person (te = “to you” informal singular). It’s often followed by the thing being given (money, an address, information, a gift). In casual speech, ne is often dropped in negatives: Je te donnerai pas… = “I won’t give you…”.
target_language_example: Je te donnerai un coup de main demain.
native_language_example: I’ll give you a hand tomorrow.

meaning: "I’m doing/making (something) for you" or "I’m doing (something) to you," depending on what comes next.
additional_notes: It’s the verb *faire* (“to do/make”) with the object pronoun *te* (“to you/for you”). The exact meaning depends on the expression that follows: *je te fais confiance* (I trust you), *je te fais un prix* (I’ll give you a price/discount), *je te fais une omelette* (I’ll make you an omelet), *je te fais une promesse* (I’m making you a promise). Some combinations can be informal or vulgar (e.g., *je te fais chier*).
target_language_example: Je te fais un café ?
native_language_example: Shall I make you a coffee?

meaning: "I swear (to you)" / "I promise" (used to insist that what you’re saying is true).
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or strongly emphasize sincerity, often in spoken French. You can say it alone ("Je te jure !") or followed by "que" + a full statement ("Je te jure que…").
target_language_example: Je te jure que je n’ai rien fait.
native_language_example: I swear I didn’t do anything.

meaning: “I have … it to you” / “I … it to you” (start of a passé composé clause with object pronouns).
additional_notes: A common fixed pronoun+auxiliary sequence used before a past participle in the passé composé: je (I) + te (to you) + l’ (it / him / her) + ai (have). You then add the past participle: « Je te l’ai dit. » = “I told you (it).” The l’ stands for le/la/les depending on what is being referred to. With avoir, the past participle can agree with a preceding direct object pronoun (e.g., l’ = la → « Je te l’ai amenée. »).
target_language_example: Je te l'ai toujours dit.
native_language_example: I’ve always told you (that).

additional_notes: Common way to remind someone you already said something. Literally "I to you it have said" (passé composé of dire). "te" = to you; "l'" replaces the thing/idea you said (it/that). Often used as a standalone sentence ("Je te l'ai dit.") or followed by a clause: "Je te l'ai dit, …". In context it can sound insistent or impatient (like "I told you!"), especially with "cent fois / des centaines de fois."
target_language_example: Je te l'ai dit, je ne sais pas.
native_language_example: I told you, I don't know.

additional_notes: Literally “I have already said it to you.” Very common for repeating information (can sound impatient depending on tone). Breakdown: je (I) + te (to you) + l’ (it) + ai dit (have said/told) + déjà (already). Often followed by a time marker (hier, deux fois) or a tag question (non ?).
target_language_example: Je te l'ai déjà dit deux fois.
native_language_example: I already told you twice.

additional_notes: Literally “I had told it to you”: *je* (I) + *te* (to you) + *l’* (it/that) + *avais dit* (had said/told). Used to remind someone you already warned them or predicted something. Often followed by tag questions like *hein ?*, *non ?*, *n’est-ce pas ?* (“right?”). Can sound a bit smug/teasing depending on tone; adding *mec* makes it more casual.
target_language_example: Tu vois, je te l'avais dit.
native_language_example: See, I told you (so).

additional_notes:
Very common with two main uses:
1) To allow/permit: « Je te laisse + infinitive » = “I’ll let you + verb” (je te laisse partir / gagner / deviner). It can also be conditional: « Si…, je te laisse partir. »
2) To leave/end the conversation: « Je te laisse. » or « Faut que je te laisse. » = “I have to go / I’ll let you go.”
It can also mean “I’m leaving you (with someone/with something)”: « Je te laisse Paula. » (I’m leaving you with Paula) or “I’m giving you (something)” in the sense of “leaving you”: « Je te laisse une dernière chance. »
target_language_example: Désolé, je te laisse, je dois y aller.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’ve got to go—I’ll let you go.

meaning: “I … it to you” (I [verb] it to you / I [verb] you it).
additional_notes: This is a common French pronoun pattern: **je** (I) + **te** (to you) + **le** (it / him) placed **before the verb**: *Je te le demande* (I’m asking you for it / I’m asking it of you). **le** can change to **la** (it/her, feminine) or **les** (them). **te** becomes **t’** before a vowel or silent h: *Je t’en parle.* In negatives, **ne…pas** goes around the verb: *Je ne te le demande pas.*
target_language_example: Je te le montre tout de suite.
native_language_example: I’ll show it to you right away.

additional_notes: Future tense of dire (“to tell”). te = “to you” and le = “it” (the thing being told). Often followed by a time/condition: après (after), plus tard (later), un jour (one day), quand… (when…), si… (if…). In conversation it can imply “not now, later.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je te le dirai demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll tell you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to insist, reassure, or emphasize what you’re saying. Literally "I tell it to you": **te** = "to you" and **le** = "it/that" (the thing you’re talking about). Often said with emotion or conviction, sometimes followed by a pause: "Je te le dis, ..."
target_language_example: Je te le dis, tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: I’m telling you, you’re going to make it.

meaning: “I promise you (I promise it to you).”
additional_notes: Used to strongly reassure someone. Structure: je (I) + te (to you) + le (it/that) + promets (promise). The “le” often refers to what was just said: “Everything will be fine—I promise.” You can also say “Je te promets” (I promise you) without “le.”
target_language_example: Je serai là demain, je te le promets.
native_language_example: I’ll be there tomorrow, I promise you.

additional_notes: Literally “I show you” (je = I, te = to you, montre = show). Used when offering or agreeing to demonstrate something; often followed by what/how (e.g., « comment faire » = how to do it) or an object (« un truc » = something).
target_language_example: Attends, je te montre où c’est.
native_language_example: Wait, I’ll show you where it is.

meaning: "I'm talking to you" / "I'm speaking to you."
additional_notes: Used to address someone directly. Often appears in situations where you want the person to pay attention or respond (can sound firm or like a reprimand: « Regarde-moi quand je te parle ! »). Can also be softened by adding context like « en ami » (“as a friend”).
target_language_example: Écoute : je te parle sérieusement.
native_language_example: Listen: I'm talking to you seriously.

additional_notes: Used to make a request sound polite, formal, or insistent. Often placed after an imperative (command/request): « Explique-moi…, je te prie. » It’s generally more formal/earnest than « s’il te plaît ». With « te » it’s addressed to one person you use “tu” with; for “you” (formal/plural), you’ll hear « je vous prie ».
target_language_example: Ferme la porte, je te prie.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request or instruction, followed by an infinitive verb: « Je te prie de + infinitive ». Often more formal than « s’il te plaît ». With « te » it’s addressed to one person you know (tu); in very formal contexts you may also see « Je vous prie de … » for vous.
target_language_example: Je te prie de m’attendre ici une minute.
native_language_example: Please wait for me here for a minute.

meaning: “Let me introduce you to …” / “I’d like to introduce you to …”
additional_notes: Used when introducing someone to the person you’re speaking to. Literally “I present you,” but in practice it means “I’m introducing (someone) to you.” Pattern: « Je te présente + [person] » (informal singular “you”). For formal or plural “you,” use « Je vous présente … ». You can also say « Je te présente à + [person] » to introduce the listener to someone else.
target_language_example: Je te présente Léa : elle travaille avec moi.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to Léa: she works with me.

meaning: “I’ll bring it back to you / I’ll bring it to you” or “I’ll take you (back/home).”
additional_notes: From the verb **ramener** (“to bring back / to take back”). **Je te ramène + [object]** means you’re bringing something back/to the person: *Je te ramène le couteau* (“I’ll bring you back the knife”). Used alone (**Je te ramène.**), it often means “I’ll take you back / I’ll drive you home,” with the destination implied (often *chez toi* = to your place).
target_language_example: Si tu veux, je te ramène chez toi après le film.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll take you home after the movie.

meaning: I’ll take you home (give you a ride home).
additional_notes: "Ramener" means "to bring/take someone back" somewhere. With "te" it means "(I) take you". "Chez toi" means "to your place / to your home" (literally "at your place"). Common when you’re accompanying someone or driving them home.
target_language_example: Il fait nuit, je te ramène chez toi.
native_language_example: It’s dark—I'll take you home.

je te ramène à la maison

target_language_multi_word_term: je te ramène à la maison
meaning: I’ll take you home / I’ll bring you back home (give you a ride).
additional_notes: Used when you’re offering to accompany someone back to their home, often by car (but it can also mean walking them home). "ramener" here means “to bring/take back,” and "je te" is “I (to) you.” You may also hear: "Je te ramène chez toi" (I’ll take you to your place).
target_language_example: Il est tard, je te ramène à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s late, I’ll take you home.

meaning: thank you (to you); I thank you.
additional_notes: A polite way to thank someone you address with **tu** (friends, family, kids). It can sound a bit more formal/earnest than simply **merci**, and it’s often followed by **pour + noun** (Je te remercie pour ton aide.) or **de + infinitive** (Je te remercie d’être venu.). For **vous**, say **je vous remercie**.
target_language_example: Je te remercie pour ton aide.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used to arrange a meetup: it often comes with a place or time (e.g., devant = out front, dehors = outside, à l’hôtel = at the hotel, tout à l’heure = later / in a little while). Literally, retrouver means “to find again,” so it can also mean “I found you again,” but in everyday conversation it very commonly means “I’ll meet you.”
target_language_example: Je te retrouve à la sortie du métro à 18 h.
native_language_example: I’ll meet you at the metro exit at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to express good wishes to someone (te = "to you" informal singular). It’s followed by a noun phrase: Je te souhaite du succès ("success"), Je te souhaite une longue vie ("a long life"). For a formal or plural "you," use je vous souhaite.
target_language_example: Je te souhaite bon courage pour ton examen.
native_language_example: I wish you good luck/courage for your exam.

additional_notes: Used to express gratitude toward someone. The adjective agrees with the speaker: a man says « je te suis reconnaissant », a woman says « je te suis reconnaissante ». Often followed by « pour » + noun (e.g., « pour ton aide »). It’s more formal/serious than « merci ». You may also hear « je t’en suis reconnaissant(e) » = “I’m grateful to you for that.”
target_language_example: Je te suis reconnaissant pour ton travail.
native_language_example: I'm grateful to you for your work.

je te suis reconnaissant pour ta

target_language_multi_word_term: je te suis reconnaissant pour ta
meaning: “I’m grateful/thankful to you for your …” (to a woman: « Je te suis reconnaissante… »).
additional_notes: Used to express gratitude directly to someone you address with « tu » (informal singular “you”). « reconnaissant(e) » agrees with the speaker: a man says « reconnaissant », a woman says « reconnaissante ». « pour ta » is followed by a feminine noun (e.g., « gentillesse », « patience »); with a masculine noun, use « pour ton … » (e.g., « pour ton aide »). More formal: « Je vous suis reconnaissant(e) pour votre … ».
target_language_example: Je te suis reconnaissant pour ta gentillesse.
native_language_example: I’m grateful to you for your kindness.

meaning: "I'll kill you" / "I’m going to kill you."
additional_notes: Literally "I kill you" (je = I, te = you, tue = kill). In real life it can be a serious threat, but it’s also often used as exaggeration like English "I’m gonna kill you!" (said when angry or joking). You’ll also see it with a condition: "Je te tue si..." ("I’ll kill you if...").
target_language_example: Si tu touches à mon téléphone, je te tue !
native_language_example: If you touch my phone, I’ll kill you!

additional_notes: Future tense of « voir » (to see): « je verrai » = “I will see.” « te » is an object pronoun meaning “you” (informal singular). Often followed by a time/place: « demain », « bientôt », « plus tard », « là-bas », or « à mon retour ». In « Je te verrai quand je te verrai », it can mean “I’ll see you when I see you” (i.e., we’ll see / I don’t know exactly when).
target_language_example: Je te verrai ce weekend.
native_language_example: I’ll see you this weekend.

meaning: I see you. / I’ll see you (later).
additional_notes: Literally “I see you” (je = I, te = you, vois = see). In context it can mean (1) you are literally in my sight (“Je te vois là-bas.”), (2) I’m going to meet/see you at a time (“Je te vois demain.”), or (3) a friendly goodbye meaning “see you later” (“Je te vois plus tard.”). Word order: the object pronoun te (“you”) comes before the verb vois.
target_language_example: Je te vois ce soir à 20 h.
native_language_example: I’ll see you tonight at 8 p.m.

meaning: "I want to / I’d like to"; "I insist that"; or "I care about".
additional_notes:
Common, slightly formal way to emphasize something important.
- **Je tiens à + infinitive**: “I want to / I’d like to” (often for polite statements): *Je tiens à m’excuser.*
- **Je tiens à ce que + subjunctive**: “I insist that …” / “It’s important to me that …”: *Je tiens à ce que ce soit clair.*
- **Je tiens à + noun/pronoun**: “I care about” / “I’m attached to”: *Je tiens à toi / à elle.*
target_language_example: Je tiens à ce que tout le monde soit prêt à l’heure.
native_language_example: I insist that everyone be ready on time.

additional_notes: Present tense of *travailler*. You can add time expressions (*le matin*, *toute la journée*), a place (*en ville*), who you work with (*avec mon père*), or who you work for (*pour le FBI*). With *sur*, it often means “to work on” a project/case (*sur une affaire*).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : je travaille ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I’m working tonight.

meaning: “I work for” (someone/an organization) or “I work to/in order to” (a goal).
additional_notes: Used with a person or organization to say who you work for (your employer/client): « Je travaille pour Tom / pour la police. » Also used with an infinitive to express purpose: « Je travaille pour gagner ma vie / pour me payer… » (same idea as “in order to”).
target_language_example: Je travaille pour une entreprise américaine.
native_language_example: I work for an American company.

additional_notes:
Used to express your personal opinion or impression. 
- With a direct object + adjective: "Je trouve ce film intéressant." (I find this movie interesting.)
- With "que" + a full clause: "Je trouve que c'est une bonne idée." (I think it's a good idea.)
Often similar in meaning to "je pense" but focuses more on your impression/judgment.
target_language_example: Je trouve ce restaurant excellent.
native_language_example: I find this restaurant excellent.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or judgment about something, followed by a clause (je trouve que + subject + verb). Often similar to “à mon avis”. In conversation it can also introduce a short reply like “Je trouve que si” (“I think so / Actually, yes”).
target_language_example: Je trouve que ce film est trop long.
native_language_example: I think this movie is too long.

meaning: "I find that" / "I think that" (giving your opinion).
additional_notes: Used to express your personal impression or opinion about something (ça = “that/it”). Very common before an adjective: « Je trouve ça + adjectif » (drôle, fascinant, difficile à croire). In everyday English it often corresponds to “I think it’s…” or “I find it…”.
target_language_example: Je trouve ça vraiment intéressant.
native_language_example: I find that really interesting.

additional_notes: First-person singular of aller. When followed by an infinitive, it is a very common way to talk about something you are about to do or intend to do in the near future. On its own, je vais can also mean "i'm going" or "i'm doing well," depending on context.
target_language_example: Je vais appeler Marie ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to call Marie tonight.

meaning: “I’m going to go” / “I’m going to go and …”.
additional_notes: Uses the near future: aller (conjugated) + infinitive. Here, it’s literally “I go to go,” but it naturally means “I’m going to go (do something).” Often followed by another verb (je vais aller me coucher / prendre une douche / vivre…), or by a place (je vais aller à la messe / à la crique). In conversation, it’s common to shorten to “je vais” when the destination is clear (Je vais à la messe).
target_language_example: Désolé, je vais aller travailler maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to go work now.

meaning: "I’m going to get/pick up" (or "I’m going to go look for").
additional_notes: Literally "I go to fetch" (aller + infinitive chercher) and is used for a near-future action. "Chercher" often means "to get/fetch/pick up" someone/something (e.g., kids), not only "to search for." In sentence 1, it most naturally means going to pick the kids up.
target_language_example: Je vais chercher mon colis à la poste.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my package at the post office.

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to go and fetch something (often by going somewhere to pick it up). With a person/job, it means to go and get them (e.g., a doctor). The object/person comes after: je vais chercher un docteur / un bol. You can also say: je vais chercher une… (feminine) or des… (plural).
target_language_example: Je vais chercher un café, j’arrive.
native_language_example: I’m going to get a coffee, I’ll be right back.

meaning: "I'm going to have to" / "I'll have to" (I will be required to).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re obliged/forced to do something soon. It combines the near future "je vais" (I’m going to) + "devoir" (to have to/must) + an infinitive verb: "Je vais devoir partir". Can sound like a polite, matter-of-fact necessity.
target_language_example: Désolé, je vais devoir annuler notre rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm going to have to cancel our appointment.

additional_notes: "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (or a quantity/partitive idea): *en créer* = create some (of them), *en chercher un autre* = look for another one (of them), *en choisir un* = choose one (of them), *en informer* = inform (someone) about it, *en refaire* = make/do some more, *en tuer beaucoup* = kill many (of them). It usually refers back to something already mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: Il n'y a plus de café ? Je vais en acheter.
native_language_example: There’s no more coffee? I’m going to buy some.

additional_notes: Very common way to say you intend to attempt something soon. Often followed by **de + infinitive** (Je vais essayer de + verb = “I’m going to try to…”). It can also be used alone as an encouraging reply (“I’ll try!”) or followed by a direct object (Je vais essayer ça = “I’m going to try that”).
target_language_example: Je vais essayer de te rappeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to try to call you back tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you intend to make an effort to do something. It’s formed from aller (je vais) + essayer de + infinitive (e.g., appeler, le joindre, m’en souvenir, trouver). In speech it often sounds like “j’vais essayer de…”.
target_language_example: Je vais essayer de venir demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to try to come tomorrow.

meaning: “I’m going to do / I’m going to make.”
additional_notes: Uses the near future: **aller (je vais) + infinitive**. Here the infinitive is **faire** (“to do/make”). In context it can mean “I’m going to do (something)” or “I’m going to make (something/someone)…”. In questions like **Comment je vais faire ?**, it often means “How am I going to manage / What am I going to do?”
target_language_example: Je vais faire mes devoirs ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to do my homework tonight.

meaning: "I’m going to make/do a" (before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: "Je vais" expresses the near future (going to). "Faire" is a very common verb meaning "to do/make"; with many nouns it’s translated as either "make" or "do" depending on the noun: faire un discours (give/make a speech), faire un effort (make an effort), faire un essai (do an attempt / write a trial/essay), faire un pacte (make a pact), faire un rapport (write/make a report), faire un vœu (make a wish). Use "un" because the noun is masculine; for feminine nouns you’d use "je vais faire une…".
target_language_example: Je vais faire un gâteau pour ton anniversaire.
native_language_example: I’m going to make a cake for your birthday.

meaning: “I’m going to … her” / “I’m going to … it” (feminine direct object).
additional_notes: Used with the near future: **je vais + infinitive** (“I’m going to + verb”). **La** is a direct object pronoun meaning **“her”** or **“it”** (for a feminine noun like *la valise*, *la lettre*). In this structure, the pronoun usually goes **before the infinitive**: *Je vais la porter / la prévenir / la rappeler*.
target_language_example: Je vais la rencontrer demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to meet her tomorrow.

meaning: "I'm going to" + "him/it" (with the object pronoun before the verb).
additional_notes: Used with aller (je vais, tu vas, etc.) + infinitive to talk about the near future. The pronoun le (“him/it”) is placed before the infinitive verb: Je vais le faire = “I’m going to do it”; Je vais le voir = “I’m going to see him.” In your example, Je vais le draguer means “I’m going to hit on him.”
target_language_example: Je vais le faire demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the near future (aller + infinitive): je vais + dire. **Le** is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (the thing you’re telling), and **à** introduces the person you’re telling it to: *Je vais le dire à maman* (“I’m going to tell Mom”). You can replace **à + name/person** with an indirect pronoun: *Je vais lui dire* (“I’m going to tell him/her”), *Je vais leur dire* (“I’m going to tell them”).
target_language_example: Je vais le dire à Paul ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell Paul tonight.

meaning: “I’m going to do it” / “I’ll do it.”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future form: aller (je vais) + infinitive (faire) to express an intention or something about to happen. The pronoun “le” means “it” (a previously mentioned thing). In longer patterns like “je vais le faire sortir…”, “faire + infinitive” can mean “to make/force someone to do something” (e.g., “make him go out”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je vais le faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to do it tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the near future: **aller (vais) + infinitive**. **Les** is a direct object pronoun meaning **“them”** (for plural nouns), and it goes **before the infinitive**: *Je vais les chercher* (I’m going to pick them up / look for them), *Je vais les suivre* (I’m going to follow them).
target_language_example: Je vais les appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to call them tonight.

meaning: "I'm going to (to him/her)" (introduces an action done for/to him or her).
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun: "lui" = "to him" or "to her". In French, object pronouns usually come before the verb: Je vais lui parler. / Je vais lui expliquer. If you’re speaking to the person directly, you use "te" or "vous" instead: Je vais te/vous expliquer.
target_language_example: Je vais lui téléphoner ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to call him/her tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the near future (aller + infinitive): je vais + dire. "Lui" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” or “to her” (context tells you which). It goes before the verb: je vais lui dire…, je vais lui dire que…, je vais lui dire ce que….
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je vais lui dire la vérité.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to tell him/her the truth.

meaning: "I'm going to (myself)…" (used before a reflexive verb that starts with a vowel sound).
additional_notes: Used to form the near future: je vais + infinitive. With reflexive verbs (se + verb), the reflexive pronoun comes before the infinitive. "m'" is the shortened form of "me" used before a vowel or silent h: je vais m'amuser, je vais m'occuper. For consonants you keep "me": je vais me laver.
target_language_example: Je vais m'habiller et je reviens.
native_language_example: I'm going to get dressed and I'll be back.

additional_notes: This is the start of a very common pattern: **je vais m'en + verb**. Here **vais** (from *aller*) expresses the near future (“I’m going to…”). **m’** is a reflexive pronoun (“myself / to me”), used because the following verb is reflexive in French (e.g., *s’assurer de*, *se servir de*, *se débarrasser de*, *se charger de*). **en** replaces something introduced with **de** (“of it / from it / some”), so it often corresponds to “it” in English in these examples: *Je vais m’en charger* = “I’m going to take care of it.” The exact English translation depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je vais m'en occuper.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to take care of it.

meaning: "I'll take care of it." / "I'll handle it."
additional_notes: Built from the verb phrase "s'en occuper" (= to take care of it / deal with it). "m'" means "myself" (because the verb is reflexive: s'occuper), and "en" replaces "de + [thing]" (so it refers to "it" / "that"). Often used to reassure someone you will handle a task or responsibility. You can add emphasis: "moi-même" (myself), "personnellement" (personally), "tout seul" (all by myself).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je vais m'en occuper ce soir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it tonight.

meaning: “I’m going to take care of / handle …”
additional_notes: Used when you commit to dealing with a task or looking after a person. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (de + la paperasse / toi / vous). In speech you may hear contractions like: « Je vais m'occuper d'ça / d'eux ».
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je vais m'occuper de tout.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to take care of everything.

meaning: “I’m going to (do something to/for myself)” + a reflexive verb (near future).
additional_notes: Used with the near-future tense: **aller (present) + reflexive pronoun + infinitive**. It introduces what you’re about to do: *Je vais me coucher* (I’m going to go to bed), *Je vais me marier* (I’m going to get married). The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: **je vais me**, **tu vas te**, **il/elle va se**, **nous allons nous**, **vous allez vous**, **ils/elles vont se**.
target_language_example: Je vais me préparer et je reviens.
native_language_example: I’m going to get ready and I’ll be back.

meaning: "I’m going to get (something done to me)" / "I’m going to make myself (something)."
additional_notes: Built from aller (near future) + se faire + infinitive/noun. With an infinitive, it often means something will happen to you (often unpleasant): Je vais me faire disputer/virer/tuer = “I’m going to get told off/fired/killed.” With certain verbs it can mean getting something for yourself (often positive): Je vais me faire pardonner = “I’m going to get forgiven.” With a noun, it commonly means preparing something for yourself: Je vais me faire un sandwich = “I’m going to make myself a sandwich.”
target_language_example: Si je mens encore, je vais me faire gronder.
native_language_example: If I lie again, I’m going to get scolded.

meaning: "I’m going to put" / "I’m going to put on" (near future with mettre).
additional_notes: Uses the near-future tense: aller (je vais) + infinitive. Mettre is very flexible: it can mean to put/place something somewhere (mettre les assiettes à chauffer), to put something on (clothes/accessories: mettre mon chapeau), or more generally to set/arrange something (je vais mettre ça pour toi). The exact meaning depends on what follows (an object, a place, or clothing).
target_language_example: Je vais mettre la table avant le dîner.
native_language_example: I’m going to set the table before dinner.

meaning: Informal: “I’m not going to…” / “I won’t…”. Sometimes: “I’m not…” (e.g., je vais pas bien = I’m not well).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French as a shortened negation of "je ne vais pas" (the "ne" is dropped). Used to talk about what you’re not going to do or what won’t be possible: "je vais pas pouvoir…" = "I won’t be able to…". With "bien" it expresses your state/health: "je vais pas bien" = "I’m not doing well / I don’t feel well."
target_language_example: Désolé, je vais pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not going to come tonight.

meaning: “I’m going to pass/cross/go through,” and by extension “I’m going to (do/spend)” depending on what follows.
additional_notes:
This is the near-future tense: **aller (je vais) + infinitive (passer)** = “I’m going to …”. **Passer** is very flexible:
- **passer + place/thing**: to pass, go by, go through, cross (*passer la frontière* = cross the border).
- **passer par + place**: to go via/through (*passer par derrière* = go around the back).
- **passer + time/day**: to spend/have (*passer une bonne journée* = have a good day).
- **passer + call/message/etc.**: to make/put through (*passer quelques coups de fil* = make a few phone calls).
Because of these different meanings, it’s not always best translated with English “pass.”
target_language_example: Je vais passer par la boulangerie en rentrant.
native_language_example: I’m going to stop by the bakery on my way back.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future tense: "aller" (je vais) + infinitive (prendre). Very common when choosing or ordering something (Je vais prendre celui-là; Je vais prendre un verre d’eau), taking/bringing your things (Je vais prendre mon sac / mes affaires), taking transportation (Je vais prendre un taxi), or offering to take something from someone (e.g., to hold their coat: Je vais prendre votre manteau).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Uses the near future: **aller (je vais) + infinitive (rester)** to say what you plan/intend to do soon. **Rester** means “to stay” or “to remain” (often with **avec** someone, **dans** a place, or with a duration like **un petit moment / encore / un peu**). Note: **rester** can look like English “rest,” but it usually means “stay,” not “rest.”
target_language_example: Il est tard, je vais rester à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: It’s late, I’m going to stay at home tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future (aller + infinitive): je vais + rester. Often followed by a time expression (e.g., un peu plus longtemps, jusqu’à demain). To make it a question, you can keep the same word order with rising intonation: Combien de temps je vais rester ici ?
target_language_example: Je vais rester ici jusqu’à ce que tu reviennes.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here until you come back.

meaning: 'I'm going to … you' (I'm going to do something to/for you).
additional_notes: Contraction of « je vais te » used before a verb starting with a vowel sound (including many silent-h words): je vais t’expliquer, je vais t’aider, etc. It’s the near-future tense (je vais + infinitive) plus the object pronoun te/t’ (= “to you” / “you”). The exact English rendering depends on the verb: sometimes “to you” (je vais t’expliquer = I’m going to explain it to you), sometimes just “you” (je vais t’aider = I’m going to help you). Can be friendly or threatening depending on context.
target_language_example: Attends, je vais t'expliquer.
native_language_example: Wait, I’m going to explain it to you.

meaning: i'm going to [do something] to/for you
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to talk about what the speaker is about to do for or to one person. This is the near-future pattern je vais + infinitive, with te meaning 'you' placed before the infinitive: je vais te protéger = 'I'm going to protect you.'
target_language_example: Je vais te montrer le chemin.
native_language_example: I'm going to show you the way.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you’re about to say, often followed by a question word (ce que/ce qui/qui) or “autre chose.” Literally “I go to tell you,” but in French this is the near-future tense (aller + infinitive). Can sound emphatic in context (“Listen carefully…”).
target_language_example: Je vais te dire la vérité demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you the truth tomorrow.

meaning: "I’m going to tell you what…" (normally: "je vais te dire ce que…").
additional_notes: In practice, this phrase is almost always followed by **que**: **Je vais te dire ce que…** + a clause. It introduces what you’re about to tell someone (often an explanation, opinion, or instruction). You can also change **te** depending on who you’re talking to: **Je vais vous dire ce que…** (more formal / to multiple people).
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que je pense.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you what I think.

je vais te dire ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: je vais te dire ce que
additional_notes: Used to introduce the information that follows. Very common with a clause after ce que: Je vais te dire ce que je sais / ce que je veux. If you want to mention a noun directly instead of a clause, you’d usually use “ce que” + clause or switch to “ce qui/ce dont” depending on meaning; but in everyday speech, “Je vais te dire…” is often followed by whatever you’re about to explain.
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que j’en pense.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you what I think about it.

je vais te dire ce que je

target_language_multi_word_term: je vais te dire ce que je
meaning: "I’m going to tell you what I…" (sentence starter).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you think, want, know, or plan to say next. It’s often followed by a verb like "pense" (think), "veux" (want), "sais" (know), or "vais faire" (am going to do). In everyday speech, you may also hear "je vais te dire ce que j’…" before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que je pense.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you what I think.

meaning: "I'm going to give you" / "I will give you."
additional_notes: Used to say you’re about to give something to someone. Literally: je vais (I’m going) + te (to you) + donner (to give). Very common before a noun (Je vais te donner cinq dollars), or with quelque chose (something). Depending on context, it can be neutral (giving money/advice) or a threat/punishment (Je vais te donner une bonne leçon = “I’ll teach you a good lesson”).
target_language_example: Attends deux minutes, je vais te donner mon numéro.
native_language_example: Wait two minutes, I’m going to give you my number.

meaning: "I'm going to make you…" / "I'm going to do … to/for you."
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to mean “I’m going to make you (do something)” (e.g., je vais te faire sortir = I’m going to make you go out). Used with a noun to mean “I’m going to make/prepare (something) for you” (je vais te faire des œufs). It can also be used as a threat: je vais te faire très mal = I’m going to hurt you badly. Word order changes with pronouns: je vais te le faire (I’m going to do it for you).
target_language_example: Attends, je vais te faire un café.
native_language_example: Wait, I'm going to make you a coffee.

meaning: "I'm going to ... it to you" / "I'll ... it for you".
additional_notes: A common sentence starter in the near future ("je vais" + infinitive). "te" is the indirect object pronoun (to you), and "le" is the direct object pronoun (it/him). In French, these pronouns come before the infinitive: "Je vais te le donner" (not *je vais donner te le*). "le" can change to "la" (it/her), "les" (them), or "l'" before a vowel ("Je vais te l'expliquer").
target_language_example: Je vais te le dire franchement.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell you honestly.

additional_notes: Common way to announce you’re about to share information. Breakdown: je vais + infinitive = near future (“I’m going to…”); te = “to you”; le = “it” (the thing you’ll say); dire = “to tell.” Often used with emphasis or tone: "Je vais te le dire exactement" (precisely), "Je vais te le dire, hein ?" (you know?/okay?), or in a rhetorical/defensive question: "Tu crois que je vais te le dire ?" (“Do you really think I’m going to tell you?”). In casual speech you may hear "Je vais te l’dire" or "J’vais te l’dire".
target_language_example: Attends deux secondes, je vais te le dire.
native_language_example: Wait two seconds, I'm going to tell you.

additional_notes: Common near-future structure: "je vais" + infinitive. "te" means "to you" (informal singular); with "vous" it becomes "je vais vous montrer". Can be used on its own as a promise/introduction before showing something ("Viens, je vais te montrer").
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, je vais te montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to show you how it works.

additional_notes: A direct threat. Often used literally in serious contexts, but it can also be said jokingly/exaggeratedly (like “I’m gonna kill you!” in English) depending on tone and situation—still very aggressive, so avoid using it. Grammar: near future (aller + infinitive) = je vais + tuer; te = “you” (informal singular object pronoun).
target_language_example: Si tu touches à ma sœur, je vais te tuer.
native_language_example: If you touch my sister, I’m going to kill you.

meaning: "I'm going to (do) everything / I'm going to (do) it all" (before a verb).
additional_notes: Used with the near future ("aller" + infinitive): "je vais" + "tout" + verb (e.g., expliquer, dire, régler). "Tout" means "everything" and is placed before the infinitive verb. Often implies you will handle the whole situation: "Je vais tout régler" = "I’m going to take care of everything / fix everything."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je vais tout préparer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to prepare everything.

additional_notes: Uses the near future: "aller" (je vais) + infinitive (voir). Often means "I’ll check/find out" (je vais voir si/où/ce que…) and can also mean "I’m going to go see/visit" someone (je vais voir les autres). In contexts like "Je vais voir ce que ça donne", it’s like "we’ll see what happens / how it turns out."
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, je vais voir si c’est ouvert.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll check if it’s open.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to check or try something before confirming. It’s often followed by a question-style clause (with "si" = "if/whether"), and can imply making an attempt: "Je vais voir si je peux…" = "I’ll see if I can…". Common in everyday spoken French.
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, je vais voir si c’est ouvert.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll see if it’s open.

meaning: "I’m going to … you" (using vous = formal singular or plural "you").
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to form the near future: je vais + infinitive. The pronoun vous comes before the infinitive (je vais vous aider / je vais vous appeler). Vous can mean one person (formal) or several people (plural).
target_language_example: Je vais vous appeler demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you tomorrow.

meaning: "I’m going to get (fetch) it for you" / "I’ll go get you (something)."
additional_notes: With an object (e.g., « de la glace », « quelque chose »), « chercher » often means “to go get/fetch,” not “to search for.” Without an object, « je vais vous chercher » can also mean “I’m going to come pick you up” (e.g., in a car).
target_language_example: Attendez ici, je vais vous chercher un verre d’eau.
native_language_example: Wait here, I’ll go get you a glass of water.

meaning: “I’m going to tell you” (to you, formal/plural).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re about to say. Literally “I go to tell you,” but in French it’s the common near-future form: aller (vais) + infinitive (dire). “Vous” can be formal (one person) or plural (several people). Often followed by a question word or clause: ce que/ce qui (what), où (where), pourquoi (why).
target_language_example: Je vais vous dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you the truth.

meaning: “I’m going to tell you what …” (usually: “Je vais vous dire ce que …”).
additional_notes: This is typically followed by **ce que** + a full clause: **Je vais vous dire ce que j’en pense** (“I’m going to tell you what I think about it”). By itself, **je vais vous dire ce…** feels incomplete in French; most of the time you need **ce que** (what) or another completion like **ceci / cela** (“this/that”). **vous** is polite/plural “you.”
target_language_example: Je vais vous dire ce que je sais.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you what I know.

additional_notes: Used to announce what you are about to give (money, advice, information, names). "Je vais" = near future (“I’m going to / I’m about to”), and "vous" is used for one person formally or for multiple people.
target_language_example: Je vais vous donner mon numéro de téléphone.
native_language_example: I’m going to give you my phone number.

meaning: "I’m going to do/make (something) for you" / "I’m going to have you (do something)".
additional_notes:
Common with two patterns:
1) **je vais vous faire + noun** = “I’m going to make/do something for you” (e.g., *je vais vous faire à manger*, *je vais vous faire une faveur*, *je vais vous faire visiter* = “I’ll show you around”).
2) **je vais vous faire + infinitive** = “I’m going to make you / have you do something” (causative). It can also mean arranging for someone else to do it: *je vais vous faire chercher à la gare par ma sœur* = “I’ll have my sister pick you up at the station.”
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, je vais vous faire un café.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to make you a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a demonstration or to guide someone to see something. It uses the near future: "je vais" + infinitive (montrer). "Vous" is used for one person formally or for multiple people; with one friend you’d usually say "je vais te montrer".
target_language_example: Attendez une seconde, je vais vous montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to show you how it works.

additional_notes: Uses the near future: "je vais" + infinitive (aller) = "I’m going to go". "y" replaces a place or destination already understood ("there", "to it"). Often used to announce you’re leaving or deciding to go somewhere: "Alors/Dans ce cas, je vais y aller" = "Alright/In that case, I’ll go (then)."
target_language_example: Bon, je vais y aller : il est tard.
native_language_example: Alright, I'm going to go: it’s late.

meaning: “I’m going to be …” / “I will be …” (near future).
additional_notes: Built with aller (je vais) + infinitive (être). It’s used to talk about something that’s about to happen or a decision/intention: Je vais être clair/honnête/gentil (“I’m going to be clear/honest/nice”). With states/feelings it can also mean something is about to occur: Je sens que je vais être malade (“I feel like I’m going to be sick”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je vais être en retard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to be late.

meaning: "I’m going to be late" / "I’ll be late."
additional_notes: Used to warn that you won’t arrive on time. The structure is: je vais + infinitive (near future: “I’m going to…”) + être en retard (“to be late”). You can specify where you’ll be late with en/à: en cours (“for class”), à l’audience (“to the hearing”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je vais être en retard au rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to be late for the appointment.

additional_notes: From the verb aller (to go): je vais. Used for movement (“I’m going to the bathroom”) and very often for the near future as je vais + infinitive (“I’m going to do …”). In general contexts it can mean “I’m doing/heading” in life (“I know exactly where I’m going”).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un café après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to have a coffee after work.

meaning: “I’m going to the …” (to a masculine singular place, or to a place name).
additional_notes: Used to say you are going somewhere. It’s the verb aller (to go) conjugated with je: je vais. The preposition au = à + le, used before masculine singular nouns (au bar, au labo, au stade) and some fixed expressions/places (au petit coin = to the restroom). With regions/directions you can also use au (au sud-ouest du village = to the southwest of the village). Contrast: je vais à la (feminine), je vais à l’ (before vowel), je vais aux (plural).
target_language_example: Je vais au supermarché après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to the supermarket after work.

additional_notes: Used to say you are heading to your workplace. Often followed by the mode of transport: en autobus/en train/en voiture (by bus/train/car) and à bicyclette/à pied (by bike/on foot). You can add time/frequency like tous les jours (“every day”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : je vais au travail.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I’m going to work.

additional_notes: Common reply to "Ça va ?" or "Comment ça va ?" It literally means "I’m going well," but it’s used to talk about your general state (health/mood). You can add emphasis like "Je vais très bien" (very well) or reassurance like "Je vais bien, je t’assure" (I’m fine, I promise).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je vais bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m fine.

additional_notes: Used to say you are going to a destination. “Je vais” = “I go / I’m going”, and “à” is used before places (cities, specific places): Je vais à Paris, je vais à l’école. With masculine countries you often use “au” instead (Je vais au Canada). With feminine countries you use “en” (Je vais en France).
target_language_example: Je vais à la gare.
native_language_example: I’m going to the train station.

meaning: “I’m going to the …” (to a feminine place/activity).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: Je vais à la + [place/activity]. For masculine singular, use « je vais au »; for plural, « je vais aux ». Often refers to going somewhere or going to do an activity (e.g., à la pêche = going fishing).
target_language_example: Je vais à la bibliothèque après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to the library after work.

additional_notes: Used to express desire or intention. It can be followed by a noun (je veux une bière), an infinitive (je veux partir), or que + subjunctive to say what you want someone else to do (je veux que tu viennes). In requests, je voudrais is often more polite than je veux.
target_language_example: Je veux rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I want to go home.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to purchase something. Follow it with the item you want to buy (often with an article): du/de la/des for an unspecified amount (Je veux acheter du pain), or un/une/le/la/les for a specific item (Je veux acheter une maison / la robe).
target_language_example: Je veux acheter des billets pour le concert.
native_language_example: I want to buy tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you intend to purchase something. "Je veux" = "I want"; "acheter" = "to buy". "Une" is the feminine singular article (a/one), so it must match a feminine noun (une chemise, une montre). If the noun is masculine, use "je veux acheter un…" (un livre). You can also use it with quantity expressions that take "une" (une douzaine de…, une paire de…).
target_language_example: Je veux acheter une bouteille d’eau.
native_language_example: I want to buy a bottle of water.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to go somewhere or go do something. It’s often followed by a place (e.g., "dehors", "dans mon lit", "à Paris") or by an infinitive verb to express an activity ("aller dormir", "aller nager", "aller parler"). In speech you’ll also hear: "Je veux y aller" = "I want to go there."
target_language_example: Je veux aller au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to go to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to learn something. Add what you want to learn after it: "Je veux apprendre le français / une nouvelle langue". You can also add an adverb like "plus vite" (faster).
target_language_example: Je veux apprendre le français cette année.
native_language_example: I want to learn French this year.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to learn how to do an action. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (apprendre à + verb), e.g., apprendre à nager, apprendre à parler. You can add details after the verb (like an object: apprendre à parler le français).
target_language_example: Je veux apprendre à cuisiner des plats français.
native_language_example: I want to learn to cook French dishes.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want to be in the future. Pattern: « Je veux devenir + (un/une) + noun » (Je veux devenir ingénieur / Je veux devenir un médecin). With roles/jobs, French often drops the article (ingénieur), but you may still hear it with some nouns (un médecin). It can also be followed by an adjective or phrase: « Je veux devenir riche » / « Je veux devenir amie avec… ».
target_language_example: Je veux devenir professeur de français.
native_language_example: I want to become a French teacher.

meaning: "I mean…" (to clarify, explain, or correct what you’re saying).
additional_notes: Literally "I want to say," but very often used in spoken French like English "I mean" as a filler before giving clarification, adding a detail, softening a statement, or correcting yourself: "Je veux dire, c’est quoi ça ?" It also appears in the fixed question "Tu comprends ce que je veux dire ?" = "Do you know what I mean?"
target_language_example: Je veux dire, ce n’est pas grave, mais préviens-moi la prochaine fois.
native_language_example: I mean, it’s not a big deal, but let me know next time.

meaning: “I want to … from it/them” (using **en** = “of it/them / from it/them”).
additional_notes: **En** is a pronoun that usually replaces something introduced by **de** (de ça, de ce sujet, de ces choses) or a quantity (du, de la, des). So **je veux en + verb** often means “I want to do something with/from it/them,” e.g. **en entendre** (hear about it), **en tirer avantage** (benefit from it), **en venir (à …)** in **voici où je veux en venir** = “here’s what I’m getting at.” Word order: **en** goes before the verb: *Je veux en parler.*
target_language_example: Je veux en savoir plus sur ce projet.
native_language_example: I want to know more about this project.

je veux en savoir plus sur

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux en savoir plus sur
meaning: “I want to learn more about” / “I want to know more about”.
additional_notes: Used to say you want more information about someone or something. "En" refers back to the topic (roughly “about it/them”), and "sur" introduces what you’re asking about. You can change the subject and tense (e.g., "Tu veux en savoir plus sur…", "Nous voulons en savoir plus sur…").
target_language_example: Je veux en savoir plus sur ce projet.
native_language_example: I want to learn more about this project.

meaning: "I want to hear" (I want to listen to / be told).
additional_notes: Used to express that you want to hear something specific (the truth, someone’s opinion, news, etc.). It can also mean you want someone to say something out loud or tell you directly. Often followed by a noun or clause: « Je veux entendre la vérité » / « Je veux entendre ce que tu as à dire ».
target_language_example: Je veux entendre ce que tu as à dire.
native_language_example: I want to hear what you have to say.

meaning: "I want to do" / "I want to make."
additional_notes: Used to state your intention before an action. Follow it with an infinitive verb: je veux faire + (verb/noun phrase), e.g. "Je veux faire les courses" (I want to do the grocery shopping) or "Je veux faire du sport" (I want to exercise). In conversation you can also drop "faire" and say "Je veux + infinitive" (Je veux aller…, Je veux acheter…).
target_language_example: Je veux faire une pause.
native_language_example: I want to take a break.

additional_notes: Used to say you have the desire/intent to take action, either in general ("I want to do something") or with an added detail: *ce soir* (tonight), *dans ce monde* (in this world), *de ma vie* (with my life / make something of my life), *pour toi* (for you). You can replace **je** with another subject (e.g., *tu veux...*, *il/elle veut...*, *nous voulons...*).
target_language_example: Je veux faire quelque chose ce week-end.
native_language_example: I want to do something this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to soften or limit what you’re asking for or expressing ("only", "simply"). Very common before an infinitive (Je veux juste partir.) or before a que-clause (Je veux juste que tu saches…). Often implies “nothing more than that.”
target_language_example: Je veux juste te parler cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I just want to talk to you for five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to express a simple wish/request, often to soften what you’re saying (“all I want is…”). It’s followed by a full clause introduced by « que », so the next verb is typically in the subjunctive: « Je veux juste que tu viennes », « … que ça se passe bien ». In spoken French, « juste » can sometimes be dropped: « Je veux que… ».
target_language_example: Je veux juste que tout le monde soit content.
native_language_example: I just want everyone to be happy.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you want someone else to do. It is typically followed by the subjunctive (because it expresses a wish/request): « Je veux juste que tu viennes » (not *que tu viens*). In casual speech you may also hear « je veux juste que tu… » to soften a request or reassure someone.
target_language_example: Je veux juste que tu sois honnête avec moi.
native_language_example: I just want you to be honest with me.

je veux juste que tu sois

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux juste que tu sois
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or desire for someone’s state/behavior. It’s followed by the subjunctive: "tu sois" (from "être"). Often completed with an adjective or phrase: "en sécurité" (safe), "heureuse" (happy), "impliqué" (involved), "sûr" (sure/certain).
target_language_example: Je veux juste que tu sois là demain.
native_language_example: I just want you to be there tomorrow.

meaning: "I just want to... you" / "I only want to... you" (starting a sentence).
additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re about to say: *Je veux juste* = “I just/only want to…”. **Te** is an object pronoun meaning “to you” or “you” (direct object), placed before the verb it goes with: *te protéger* (protect you), *te remercier* (thank you), *te rendre la pareille* (return the favor), *te tenir dans mes bras* (hold you in my arms). Often followed by an infinitive.
target_language_example: Je veux juste te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I just want to tell you the truth.

je veux juste un peu plus de

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux juste un peu plus de
additional_notes: Use this to express a modest request for a slightly greater amount of something. It’s often followed by a noun or by “ça” (“that”). With most nouns, “plus de” is followed by no article: “plus de sommeil,” “plus de variété.”
target_language_example: Je veux juste un peu plus de temps pour finir.
native_language_example: I just want a little more time to finish.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence before an infinitive to politely soften what you’re saying: « Je veux juste vous + infinitive… » (e.g., remercier, dire, demander, souhaiter). « vous » is the formal singular “you” (to a stranger/someone you don’t know well) or the plural “you” (to several people).
target_language_example: Je veux juste vous poser une question.
native_language_example: I just want to ask you a question.

additional_notes: "Je veux" means "I want." The pronoun "le" usually means "him" or "it" (masculine singular) and is placed before the verb it refers to: "Je veux le protéger" = "I want to protect him/it." With another verb in the infinitive, "le" typically goes before that infinitive (not after it).
target_language_example: Je veux le garder pour plus tard.
native_language_example: I want to keep it for later.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to do an action (“le” = “it,” referring to something already mentioned). You can add details with prepositions, e.g., avec toi (with you), ce soir (tonight), pour vous (for you). In speech, you often hear contraction: “J’veux le faire.”
target_language_example: Je veux le faire maintenant.
native_language_example: I want to do it now.

additional_notes: "Je veux" means “I want.” "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it” (for a masculine noun). "Voir" is the infinitive “to see.” You can add time words like "maintenant" (now) or phrases like "de mes propres yeux" (with my own eyes). For a woman/ feminine noun, use "Je veux la voir"; for plural, "Je veux les voir."
target_language_example: Je veux le voir tout de suite.
native_language_example: I want to see him/it right away.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to eat (now or in general). Often followed by a food item or by something like “quelque chose de …” (something …): “Je veux manger quelque chose de salé.” You can also add “aussi” for “too”: “Moi aussi, je veux manger !”
target_language_example: J’ai faim : je veux manger maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m hungry: I want to eat now.

meaning: "I want to" + a reflexive verb ("I want to [do something] (to/for myself)").
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive with a reflexive pronoun (me = “myself/me”). Many French verbs are reflexive (e.g., se coucher = to go to bed, se débarrasser de = to get rid of, se joindre à = to join). In speech, “je” often becomes “j’” before a vowel sound: j’veux me… (informal pronunciation).
target_language_example: Je veux me reposer ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to rest tonight.

meaning: “I want to talk / I want to speak.”
additional_notes: Used with **de** to mean “to talk about” (**Je veux parler de…** = “I want to talk about…”), and with **à** to mean “to speak to” (**Je veux parler à…** = “I want to speak to…”). You’ll also see it in patterns like **C’est de ça que je veux parler** (“That’s what I want to talk about”) and **Tu sais de quoi je veux parler** (“You know what I’m talking about”).
target_language_example: Je veux parler de ce problème avec toi.
native_language_example: I want to talk about this problem with you.

meaning: "I want to speak to" / "I want to talk to".
additional_notes: Used to say you want to talk to someone. "Parler à" takes the preposition "à" before a person: parler à ma mère, parler à un avocat. In polite contexts (customer service, official situations), you may also hear "Je voudrais parler à..." (more polite).
target_language_example: Je veux parler à votre responsable, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want to speak to your manager/person in charge, please.

additional_notes: Very common spoken/informal form of "je ne veux pas" (dropping "ne"). Used to refuse something or say you don’t want something to happen: "je veux pas + infinitive" (I don’t want to...), or "je veux pas que + subjunctive" (I don’t want [someone] to...).
target_language_example: Je veux pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out tonight.

meaning: “I want us to…” / “I want people to…”
additional_notes: Used to express what you want to happen, followed by a verb in the subjunctive (je veux qu'on reste / qu'on soit / qu'on fasse…). “On” often means “we/us” in everyday French, but it can also mean “someone/people” (indefinite). If you want to be more explicit, you can say: « Je veux que nous… » (we) or « Je veux que tu… » (you).
target_language_example: Je veux qu'on reste ensemble.
native_language_example: I want us to stay together.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want someone or something else to do or be. It is followed by a new subject and usually the subjunctive: for example, Je veux que tu viennes = I want you to come. In natural English, it is often translated as 'I want someone to...' rather than the more literal 'I want that...'.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu sois honnête avec moi.
native_language_example: I want you to be honest with me.

meaning: "I want it to be…" / "I want (that) it be…"
additional_notes: Used to express what you want to happen or what you want something/someone to be. It introduces the subjunctive with être: « que ce soit » (not *que c’est*). You can follow it with a person/thing (« Je veux que ce soit toi. ») or with a past participle to mean “I want it done” (« Je veux que ce soit réparé. »).
target_language_example: Je veux que ce soit prêt avant demain.
native_language_example: I want it to be ready before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want someone else to do. In French, this structure is followed by a new subject and usually the subjunctive: je veux que tu + verb.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu viennes avec moi.
native_language_example: I want you to come with me.

meaning: "I want you to go" / "I want you to (do something)".
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do. After "je veux que", French uses the subjunctive: "tu ailles" (from "aller", to go). It can be followed by a place ("à Boston", "au bureau de poste", "chez toi") or by other expressions like "mieux" ("I want you to get better").
target_language_example: Je veux que tu ailles te reposer.
native_language_example: I want you to go rest.

meaning: "I want you to do" (addressing one person).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do. It introduces the subjunctive: after "je veux que...", the next verb is in the subjunctive (here, "tu fasses" from "faire"). Often followed by an object or details: "quelque chose", "ça lundi", etc.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu fasses tes devoirs avant de sortir.
native_language_example: I want you to do your homework before going out.

meaning: "I want you to (do it / do it to him)."
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you want someone else to do. After « je veux que… », French typically uses the subjunctive (e.g., « que tu le fasses / dises / prennes »). « le » is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (or “him”), placed before the verb: « que tu le prennes » = “that you take it.”
target_language_example: Je veux que tu le fasses maintenant.
native_language_example: I want you to do it now.

je veux que tu le fasses

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux que tu le fasses
additional_notes: Used to express a direct request or demand. After "je veux que" (I want that), French uses the subjunctive: "tu le fasses" (from "faire"). "le" = "it" (the thing already known from context). You can add an adverb like "immédiatement" (immediately) or "correctement" (properly).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu le fasses maintenant.
native_language_example: I want you to do it now.

meaning: "I want you to … (for me / to me)."
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do. After "je veux que tu…", French normally uses the subjunctive: "Je veux que tu me chantes / laisses / parles / rendes…". "me" is an object pronoun placed before the verb (it can mean "to me" or "me," depending on the verb).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu me montres tes photos.
native_language_example: I want you to show me your photos.

je veux que tu me dises

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux que tu me dises
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone to tell you. It’s often followed by a question word (quoi/ce que/où/quand/comment/pourquoi) or by “tout” (everything). After “je veux que…”, French uses the subjunctive: “tu me dises” (not *tu me dis*).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu me dises la vérité.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me the truth.

meaning: “I want you to take …” (or “I want you to …”).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do. After "je veux que" (I want that…), French uses the subjunctive: "tu prennes" is the subjunctive form of "prendre" (to take). What follows can be an object ("ce médicament", "ça") or a verb phrase ("soin de …" in "prendre soin de" = to take care of).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu prennes ton parapluie avant de sortir.
native_language_example: I want you to take your umbrella before going out.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stay somewhere or with someone. After *je veux que…* (I want that…), French normally uses the subjunctive: *tu restes* (from *rester*, “to stay/remain”). Often followed by a place or person: *là* (there), *sur la plage* (on the beach), *avec Tom* (with Tom), *à distance* (at a distance).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu restes ici jusqu’à demain.
native_language_example: I want you to stay here until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce important information you want the other person to be aware of. After it, French uses the subjunctive: savoir → que tu saches. You can follow it with que + a sentence (“…that…”) or with a question word like qui/ce qui (“…who/what…”).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu saches que je suis toujours là pour toi.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I’m always here for you.

je veux que tu saches que

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux que tu saches que
additional_notes: Used to introduce important information or reassure someone. After « je veux que », French uses the subjunctive: « tu saches ». Very often followed by feelings, beliefs, or trust: « je t’aime », « je te crois », « tu peux me faire confiance ».
target_language_example: Je veux que tu saches que je suis là pour toi.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I’m here for you.

meaning: "I want you to be…" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to be/do. After « je veux que », French uses the subjunctive: « tu sois » (from « être », to be). You can follow it with an adjective (« heureux/heureuse », « silencieux/silencieuse ») or a prepositional phrase (« avec moi », « à mon côté »). Note agreement: adjectives change with the person’s gender (heureux/heureuse, fier/fière).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu sois prêt(e) à partir.
native_language_example: I want you to be ready to leave.

meaning: “I want you to …” (with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used before a reflexive verb (a verb that uses “se”), so you see “te” (yourself) because the subject is “tu.” After “je veux que…,” French normally uses the subjunctive: « Je veux que tu te sentes / concentres / souviennes… ».
target_language_example: Je veux que tu te reposes un peu.
native_language_example: I want you to rest a bit.

additional_notes: Used to say you want someone else to come/do something. After "je veux que..." (I want that...), French uses the subjunctive: "tu viennes" (not *tu viens*). You can add an action or destination after it: "Je veux que tu viennes avec nous / travailler ici / vivre avec moi."
target_language_example: Je veux que tu viennes à la réunion demain.
native_language_example: I want you to come to the meeting tomorrow.

meaning: “I want you (to…)” (formal/plural “you”), followed by the subjunctive.
additional_notes: Used to state what you want someone (one person formally, or several people) to do. After « je veux que vous », French normally uses the subjunctive: « vous ayez », « vous chantiez », « vous parliez », « vous sortiez ». Often sounds firm or like an order depending on context.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous m’appeliez demain matin.
native_language_example: I want you to call me tomorrow morning.

meaning: “I want you to go …” (to a group or to ‘you’ formal).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do, followed by a place or direction. After « je veux que », French uses the subjunctive, so « aller » becomes « vous alliez ». « vous » can mean either ‘you (plural)’ or ‘you (formal)’.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous alliez à l’accueil, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want you to go to the reception desk, please.

meaning: "I want you to stop" (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Used to tell one person politely/formally (vous) or multiple people to stop doing something. It’s typically followed by either (1) a direct object: « Je veux que vous arrêtiez ceci » (“stop this”), or (2) « de » + infinitive: « Je veux que vous arrêtiez de faire ça » (“stop doing that”). Because it comes after « je veux que », the verb is in the subjunctive: « arrêtiez » (from « arrêter »). You may also see clarifiers like « tous les deux / toutes les deux » (“both of you”) placed in different spots for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous arrêtiez de crier, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want you to stop shouting, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person formally (vous) or several people (vous plural) to stop doing something. It’s followed by the subjunctive verb form "cessiez" because "je veux que…" expresses a desire/command. Very often you add "de" + infinitive: "Je veux que vous cessiez de me suivre" (…to stop following me). The extra phrases "tous les deux / toutes les deux" mean "both of you" (masc./mixed vs. fem.), and commas just add emphasis.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous cessiez de faire du bruit, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want you to stop making noise, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do. It’s "je veux que" + a verb in the subjunctive; here "fassiez" is the subjunctive form of "faire" for "vous". "Vous" can be formal (one person) or plural (more than one).
target_language_example: Je veux que vous fassiez attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: I want you to be careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a request or demand with a verb in the subjunctive after « je veux que ». « vous » is formal or plural “you,” and « me » means “to me / me” (e.g., je veux que vous me disiez…, je veux que vous me laissiez…).
target_language_example: Je veux que vous me répondiez aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I want you to answer me today.

je veux que vous me disiez

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux que vous me disiez
meaning: "I want you to tell me" (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Used to ask (often firmly) for information: je veux que + subject + verb in the subjunctive. Here, "vous" can mean either "you" (formal singular) or "you" (plural), and "disiez" is the subjunctive form of "dire" after "je veux que".
target_language_example: Je veux que vous me disiez ce qui s’est passé.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me what happened.

meaning: "I want you to know" (speaking to one or more people politely/formally).
additional_notes: Used to introduce important information, reassurance, or emphasis. It uses the subjunctive: « que vous sachiez » (from savoir, “to know”), because it follows « je veux que… ». Often continues with « que… » + a full idea: « Je veux que vous sachiez que… ».
target_language_example: Je veux que vous sachiez que je suis là pour vous aider.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I’m here to help you.

additional_notes: Used with **vouloir que** (“to want that…”), which is followed by the **subjunctive**: **vous soyez** (from *être*, “to be”). **Vous** can mean either **“you (plural)”** or **polite/formal “you” (singular)**. You can complete it with a noun/adjective (*je veux que vous soyez ma compagne* = “I want you to be my partner”) or with a past participle when using *être* (*je veux que vous soyez revenue* = “I want you to have come back / I want you back,” said to a woman).
target_language_example: Je veux que vous soyez à l’heure demain.
native_language_example: I want you to be on time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone ("vous" = you, formal or plural) to do. After "je veux que", French uses the subjunctive: "vous veniez" (from "venir"). You can add details like "avec moi" (with me), "ce soir" (tonight), or "seul(s)/seule(s)" (alone).
target_language_example: Je veux que vous veniez demain matin.
native_language_example: I want you to come tomorrow morning.

meaning: "I want you to…" (addressing you formally or as a group), before a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Used to express a desire/command about what someone else should do: « je veux que + [subject] + verb (subjunctive) ». Here « vous vous » appears because the verb is reflexive (e.g., « vous vous rappeliez » = “you remember”; « vous vous y mettiez » = “you get to it”). Often sounds like a firm instruction in context.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous vous dépêchiez.
native_language_example: I want you to hurry up.

meaning: "I want something (that is)…" (followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to ask for an unspecified thing with a certain quality. After "quelque chose", use "de" + adjective: "quelque chose de simple", "de doux", "de sucré". You can add an infinitive to specify the type: "quelque chose de sucré à manger" (something sweet to eat).
target_language_example: Je veux quelque chose de chaud à boire.
native_language_example: I want something hot to drink.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire to remain somewhere or not leave. It can be followed by a place (rester dans la maison = stay in the house) or by a person (rester avec lui = stay with him), or used alone (Je veux rester.)
target_language_example: Il pleut trop : je veux rester à la maison.
