target_language_example: La fête commence à huit heures.
native_language_example: The party starts at eight o'clock.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a train station (gare SNCF). Common in directions with prepositions like près de (near), en face de (opposite/across from), à côté de (next to), and questions like Où se trouve… ?
target_language_example: Je vais à la gare pour prendre le train.
native_language_example: I'm going to the station to take the train.

additional_notes: “La glace” can mean frozen water (ice) or ice cream; context makes it clear. With verbs like “fondre” (to melt), “céder / se rompre” (to give way / break), it means ice. With flavors (“au chocolat”, “à la vanille”) or verbs like “aimer / manger”, it usually means ice cream. Related: “un glaçon” = an ice cube.
target_language_example: Attention, la glace est fine ici.
native_language_example: Careful, the ice is thin here.

additional_notes: Can refer to war in general or to a specific war, depending on context. French often uses the definite article where English may simply say "war" in a general sense.
target_language_example: La guerre n'est jamais une solution.
native_language_example: War is never a solution.

meaning: slang/vulgar for “mouth” or “face” (often in insults or set expressions).
additional_notes: Very informal and often rude. Literally refers to an animal’s mouth/jaw, but in everyday slang it can mean a person’s mouth or face. Common in fixed phrases like « casser la gueule (à quelqu’un) » = “to beat someone up” and « se saouler la gueule » = “to get really drunk.” Not used in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Si tu cries, je te casse la gueule.
native_language_example: If you shout, I’ll beat you up.

additional_notes: A feminine noun. Often used with verbs like jouer de la guitare (to play the guitar) or pratiquer la guitare (to practice the guitar). You can also say à la guitare to mean “on the guitar” (e.g., playing chords on guitar).
target_language_example: Elle joue de la guitare tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She plays the guitar every evening.

additional_notes: Usually means “shame” (a painful feeling of being dishonored or humiliated), often used with de ("la honte de..." = "the shame of..."). It can also be an exclamation in everyday speech: "La honte !" = "How embarrassing!" / "So lame!" In informal French you may hear "foutre la honte (à quelqu’un)" = "to embarrass someone" / "to make someone look bad."
target_language_example: J’ai dit son nom de travers devant tout le monde… la honte !
native_language_example: I said his name wrong in front of everyone… so embarrassing!

additional_notes: Refers to a person’s leg. Common with body-related phrases: « à la jambe » (in the leg, e.g., injured), « le long de la jambe » (along the leg), and in instructions like « Lève la jambe » (Lift your leg).
target_language_example: J’ai mal à la jambe depuis hier.
native_language_example: My leg has been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: Literally “the young girl.” Used for a girl/young woman (often a teenager). It can sound a bit formal or old-fashioned compared with "la fille" in everyday speech. Feminine singular: "la" + "jeune" + "fille".
target_language_example: La jeune fille attend le bus devant l'école.
native_language_example: The young girl is waiting for the bus in front of the school.

meaning: the day (as a span of time, often daytime).
additional_notes: Refers to the course of a day as a period of time (how the day went, how long it felt, what you did during it). Often contrasts with "la nuit" (night). Can also mean "during the day/daytime" in phrases like "pendant la journée" or "dans la journée".
target_language_example: On se voit dans la journée.
native_language_example: We'll see each other during the day.

additional_notes: Can refer to the general idea of fairness and doing what’s right ("justice will come"), or more concretely to the justice system/courts ("justice is expensive"). Often used with verbs like croire en (believe in) and vouloir (want/seek).
target_language_example: Elle veut que la justice fasse son travail.
native_language_example: She wants the justice system to do its job.

additional_notes: Most often means “language” (e.g., la langue française). It can also mean the physical “tongue.” In the expression « tirer la langue », it means “to stick out your tongue” (often teasing or being silly).
target_language_example: J'apprends la langue française.
native_language_example: I'm learning the French language.

meaning: the letter (a written message sent by mail).
additional_notes: Used for a physical written message (a piece of paper) you send or receive in the mail. Common with verbs like écrire (to write), envoyer (to send), recevoir (to receive), ouvrir (to open), lire (to read), and with expressions like mettre la lettre au courrier (to mail the letter). Not to be confused with une lettre meaning “a letter” of the alphabet (A, B, C).
target_language_example: J’ai reçu la lettre ce matin.
native_language_example: I received the letter this morning.

additional_notes: A common noun usually used with the definite article: *la liberté*. Often appears in phrases like *se battre pour la liberté* (to fight for freedom) and *avoir la liberté de + infinitive* (to have the freedom to do something).
target_language_example: J’ai la liberté de choisir mon travail.
native_language_example: I have the freedom to choose my job.

additional_notes: Common with phone calls: « Restez à la ligne » = “Stay on the line / don’t hang up.” « La ligne est coupée » means the call/connection has been cut off (often due to a technical problem or bad weather). It can also mean a “line” in a more general sense (e.g., a defensive line).
target_language_example: Allô ? Je crois que la ligne est coupée.
native_language_example: Hello? I think the line got cut off.

additional_notes: Used for a written or mental set of items (names, tasks, topics, etc.). Commonly followed by "de" to say what kind of list it is: "la liste des courses" (shopping list), "la liste des sujets" (list of topics).
target_language_example: J'ai fait la liste des choses à acheter.
native_language_example: I made the list of things to buy.

additional_notes: Usually refers to legal rules made by the government. You often see it with verbs like respecter (obey), changer (change), modifier (amend), and faire respecter (enforce). In the plural, les lois = the laws.
target_language_example: Il faut respecter la loi.
native_language_example: You have to obey the law.

additional_notes: Feminine noun. Refers to light in general (daylight, a lamp’s light) or, in everyday speech, electricity/lights in a room (e.g., allumer/éteindre la lumière = turn the light on/off). In negative phrases like « Pas même la lumière », it emphasizes that there is nothing at all—not even light.
target_language_example: Tu peux allumer la lumière, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you turn on the light, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about natural light coming from the sun. Often with verbs like illuminer (to light up), entrer (to come in), profiter de (to enjoy), or without it: sans la lumière du soleil (without sunlight). Note the structure: la lumière (light) + du (= de + le) + soleil (sun).
target_language_example: Le matin, la lumière du soleil entre par la fenêtre.
native_language_example: In the morning, sunlight comes in through the window.

additional_notes: A feminine noun (la). Often used with verbs like briller (to shine) and with time expressions like pendant la nuit (during the night).
target_language_example: Ce soir, la lune est très brillante.
native_language_example: Tonight, the moon is very bright.

additional_notes: Used to describe the moon with an adjective or phrase (e.g., belle, brillante, visible, croissante). In sentence 3, “La lune est sortie …” uses « est » as the auxiliary verb with « sortir » in the passé composé: “The moon came out / appeared.”
target_language_example: Ce soir, la lune est très claire.
native_language_example: Tonight, the moon is very bright/clear.

additional_notes: Used for a physical machine/device (e.g., in a factory or at home). Common with verbs like démarrer (start), mettre en marche (turn on/start), marcher (to work/run), and travailler (to operate/work). In casual speech, it can also refer to a specific appliance everyone knows from context (e.g., la machine à laver = the washing machine).
target_language_example: La machine ne marche plus, il faut l'éteindre.
native_language_example: The machine isn’t working anymore; we need to turn it off.

additional_notes: A common household appliance used to wash clothes. With "mettre X à la machine à laver" you mean “to put X in the washing machine.” It can also refer to doing laundry in general (e.g., "mettre à la machine à laver").
target_language_example: J'ai mis mes vêtements dans la machine à laver.
native_language_example: I put my clothes in the washing machine.

additional_notes: Refers to the body part. In French, body parts often use the definite article where English uses a possessive: il me tient la main = "he's holding my hand," not usually "the hand." Also appears in expressions like mettre la main sur, meaning "to get hold of" or "to find."
target_language_example: Elle me prend la main pour traverser la rue.
native_language_example: She takes my hand to cross the street.

meaning: caught in the act; caught red-handed.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when someone is caught doing something wrong (stealing, lying, cheating) at the very moment they’re doing it. Often used with verbs like « surprendre », « attraper », or « prendre »: « Je l’ai surpris la main dans le sac. »
target_language_example: On l’a surpris la main dans le sac en train de copier à l’examen.
native_language_example: He was caught red-handed cheating on the exam.

additional_notes: Used to specify the left hand (vs. "la main droite" = the right hand). "Gauche" is an adjective meaning "left" and agrees with "main" (feminine singular). Often used in instructions (e.g., hold, write, turn) or to talk about which hand you use.
target_language_example: Je tiens le sac dans la main gauche.
native_language_example: I’m holding the bag in my left hand.

la main pour poser une question

target_language_multi_word_term: la main pour poser une question
meaning: '(raise) a hand to ask a question.'
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb « lever »: « lever la main pour poser une question » (common in class/meetings). « poser une question » = to ask a question (literally “to put/pose a question”). You can also say « lever la main pour demander une question », but « poser une question » is more natural.
target_language_example: J’ai levé la main pour poser une question, mais le prof ne m’a pas vu.
native_language_example: I raised my hand to ask a question, but the teacher didn’t see me.

additional_notes: A common way to refer to a house or home in general. maison can mean either a physical house or a home, depending on context. la is the feminine singular definite article ('the').
target_language_example: La maison est très calme le matin.
native_language_example: The house is very quiet in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to show ownership or association: "la maison de Marie" = Marie’s house. With a question word: "la maison de qui ?" = whose house? If the owner is a pronoun, French usually uses a possessive adjective instead: "ma/ta/sa maison" (not *la maison de moi*). Can also be used figuratively: "la maison de Dieu" = the house of God.
target_language_example: C'est la maison de mon oncle.
native_language_example: This is my uncle’s house.

additional_notes: Used to describe the house (color, location, condition, what it’s made of, etc.). The verb is **être** in the present tense: **La maison est + adjective** (La maison est blanche), **La maison est + location** (La maison est sur la colline), or **La maison est + past participle** for a passive description (La maison est construite / peinte).
target_language_example: La maison est très calme le soir.
native_language_example: The house is very quiet in the evening.

la maison plutôt que de sortir

target_language_multi_word_term: la maison plutôt que de sortir
meaning: at home rather than going out.
additional_notes: This is typically used with a verb (often *rester* or *préférer*): *rester à la maison plutôt que de sortir* (“stay home rather than go out”). *Plutôt que (de)* means “rather than (doing).” In natural French you usually say *à la maison* (“at home”), not just *la maison* by itself in this context.
target_language_example: Ce soir, je préfère rester à la maison plutôt que de sortir.
native_language_example: Tonight, I’d rather stay home than go out.

meaning: home all day (literally: “the house all day”).
additional_notes: In practice, French usually says **à la maison toute la journée** (“at home all day”). It’s a time expression with **toute la journée** = “all day / the whole day,” and it often answers the question *Où ?* (Where?) with *à la maison*.
target_language_example: Je suis resté(e) à la maison toute la journée.
native_language_example: I stayed home all day.

meaning: "the main/major one" (feminine), or "the major (key)" in music.
additional_notes: This looks like a misspelling: in standard French it’s usually **la majeure** (feminine of *majeur/majeure* = major, main). You’ll often see it in phrases like **la majeure partie (de...)** = “the majority/most (of...)”, or in music to mean “major” (e.g., *en do majeur* = “in C major”).
target_language_example: La majeure partie des étudiants arrive à huit heures.
native_language_example: Most of the students arrive at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about more than half of a group or quantity. It’s often followed by a plural noun (la majorité des étudiants) or an uncountable noun (la majorité du temps). The verb can agree with the idea of the group, so you’ll often see plural agreement in practice.
target_language_example: La majorité des gens préfèrent rester chez eux.
native_language_example: Most people prefer to stay at home.

meaning: the morning (as a period of time; roughly from early morning until around noon).
additional_notes: "La matinée" refers to the morning *time span* (often used with actions/events: "dans la matinée" = sometime during the morning; "passer la matinée à..." = to spend the morning doing...). It contrasts with "le matin," which more often means "in the morning" in a general/routine sense (e.g., "le matin, je bois du café").
target_language_example: On se voit dans la matinée.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other sometime in the morning.

additional_notes: Feminine form of “le/la meilleur(e)” meaning “the best.” It agrees with a feminine noun (expressed or implied): *la meilleure solution* (“the best solution”). You can also use it alone when the noun is understood: *Vous êtes la meilleure !* (“You’re the best!”). Often appears after another superlative: *la plus simple est souvent la meilleure* (“the simplest is often the best”).
target_language_example: C'est la meilleure idée aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It’s the best idea today.

la meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée

target_language_multi_word_term: la meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée
meaning: "the best thing that ever happened to me" / "the best thing that has happened to me."
additional_notes: A strong, affectionate compliment, often said to a partner or about a person/event. The verb is commonly in the subjunctive after a superlative: "la meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée". Agreement: "arrivé" (to a man speaking), "arrivée" (to a woman speaking). You can change the pronoun: "qui lui soit arrivé(e)" (that happened to him/her), etc. In speech you may hear the informal "T’es la meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée" instead of "Tu es…".
target_language_example: Depuis qu’on s’est rencontrés, tu es la meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée.
native_language_example: Since we met, you’re the best thing that ever happened to me.

additional_notes: Used for the sea as a place or what you can see/smell near the coast. It’s feminine: la mer. Common with verbs like aller à la mer (go to the seaside), voir la mer (see the sea), and sentir la mer (smell like the sea / smell of the sea).
target_language_example: En été, on va souvent à la mer.
native_language_example: In summer, we often go to the seaside.

additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive in most contexts. Often used with the partitive: **de la merde** = “(some) shit/crap” meaning something is worthless (**C’est de la merde** = “It’s crap”). Used as an insult or to tell someone off: **Mange de la merde ! / Va manger de la merde !** (“Eat shit!”), and in expressions like **chercher la merde** (“to look for trouble / start shit”).
target_language_example: Ce truc, c’est de la merde.
native_language_example: This thing is crap.

meaning: mine (a feminine thing; short for « la mienne [= la chose féminine] »).
additional_notes: Possessive pronoun used to replace a feminine singular noun already understood from context (e.g., « la calculatrice »). It agrees with what is owned (la/une + feminine singular), not with the owner. Often used after « c’est / est »: « C’est la mienne. »
target_language_example: Ce sac est la mienne ?
native_language_example: Is this bag mine?

additional_notes: Used before a noun (feminine singular) to emphasize a very small amount, often in questions, negatives, or conditional phrases: "la moindre idée" (the slightest idea), "la moindre différence" (the slightest difference), "la moindre question" (any question at all). In negatives you’ll often see "pas la moindre …" = "not the slightest …".
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas la moindre envie de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I don’t have the slightest desire to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Means 50% of something. Often used with "de" + noun ("la moitié du temps" = half the time; "la moitié de la nuit" = half the night). Can also stand alone when what you’re dividing is clear from context ("Donne-moi la moitié." = Give me half.)
target_language_example: Je veux la moitié du gâteau, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I want half of the cake, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about 50% of something. It’s part of the pattern « la moitié de + noun ». The part after « de » changes with the noun: « la moitié du » (masc. sing.), « la moitié de la » (fem. sing.), « la moitié de l’ » (before a vowel or silent h), « la moitié des » (plural).
target_language_example: J’ai mangé la moitié de la tarte.
native_language_example: I ate half of the pie.

additional_notes: Used to express 50% of a plural group or a quantity. It’s often followed by a plural noun: « la moitié des élèves ». Verb agreement varies: you’ll often see plural when focusing on the people/things (« La moitié des élèves ne sont pas là »), and singular when focusing on the fraction/amount (« La moitié des melons a été mangée »). You can also say « plus de la moitié des » = “more than half of (the)”.
target_language_example: La moitié des participants sont déjà partis.
native_language_example: Half of the participants have already left.

additional_notes: Can mean one specific mountain (e.g., “Il pointe vers la montagne.”) or, especially with activities like skiing/hiking, “the mountains” as a general destination/region (“aller à la montagne”, “faire du ski à la montagne”). Often contrasts with “la mer” (the seaside).
target_language_example: Cet hiver, on va passer une semaine à la montagne.
native_language_example: This winter, we’re going to spend a week in the mountains.

meaning: death; the act or fact of dying.
additional_notes: Usually used with the definite article in French (la mort). Common patterns: « à la mort de quelqu’un » = after/upon someone’s death; « la cause de la mort » = cause of death. It can also be personified in literature (« La mort… » = Death as a character).
target_language_example: Depuis la mort de sa grand-mère, il est très triste.
native_language_example: Since his grandmother’s death, he has been very sad.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or name to refer to a specific person’s death: « la mort de mon père », « la mort de Marie ». It often appears with verbs/phrases like « pleurer la mort de… » (to mourn), « se souvenir de la mort de… » (to remember), and « à la mort de… » meaning “upon/at the time of the death of…”.
target_language_example: À la mort de sa mère, il est parti vivre chez sa tante.
native_language_example: After his mother died, he went to live with his aunt.

meaning: “the death of his/her …” (when the next noun is masculine).
additional_notes: This is the pattern **la mort de + possessive + noun**: *la mort de son épouse / son ami / son chat* (“the death of his/her spouse/friend/cat”). It’s used to talk about someone’s or an animal’s death, often in a serious, emotional context. The possessive must agree with the noun that follows: **son** + masculine singular (*son ami*), **sa** + feminine singular (*sa mère*), **ses** + plural (*ses parents*). Use **son** before a feminine noun starting with a vowel or mute h (*son épouse*, *son amie*).
target_language_example: Elle a été bouleversée par la mort de son frère.
native_language_example: She was devastated by her brother’s death.

additional_notes: A feminine noun for a Muslim place of worship. Used with the definite article: « la mosquée ». To say “to/into the mosque,” you often use « à la mosquée » (or « dans la mosquée » for “inside the mosque”).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la mosquée après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the mosque after lunch.

additional_notes: Often used for music in general, where English usually just says "music" without "the" (for example, "il aime la musique" = "he likes music"). In some contexts it refers to specific music that is playing, as in "mettre la musique" or "baisser la musique".
target_language_example: La musique classique me détend.
native_language_example: Classical music relaxes me.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the music genre. Often used with aimer (to like/love): « J’aime la musique classique. » It usually takes the definite article « la » when talking about the genre in general.
target_language_example: J’écoute souvent de la musique classique en travaillant.
native_language_example: I often listen to classical music while working.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as another person’s mother: « Je suis la mère de … ». Also appears in sayings like « La répétition est la mère de … » meaning “repetition is the mother of …” (the source/origin of something).
target_language_example: Je suis la mère de Julien.
native_language_example: I’m Julien’s mother.

additional_notes: Feminine form of "le/la même". Used to say that a person/thing is identical or unchanged. Often used with a feminine noun: "la même caméra" (= the same camera), or with "que" for comparison: "la même … que …" (= the same … as …). Can also stand alone to mean “the same (one)” when the noun is understood: "Elle n’est plus la même" (= She’s not the same anymore).
target_language_example: On a pris la même route que vous.
native_language_example: We took the same road as you.

additional_notes: Used to say two situations, actions, or ideas are identical or unchanged. Often follows verbs like être (C’est la même chose.), faire (faire la même chose), vivre (vivre la même chose), dire (dire la même chose). You can also use it after prepositions: la même chose que… (the same thing as…).
target_language_example: On a commandé la même chose au restaurant.
native_language_example: We ordered the same thing at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to say that something you just said applies equally to another person or thing. Often followed by a pronoun or noun: « la même chose pour moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles » or « la même chose pour Paul ». In conversation, you may also hear the shorter « pareil pour … ».
target_language_example: Je prendrai un café, et la même chose pour toi.
native_language_example: I’ll have a coffee, and the same for you.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/things share an identical feeling, opinion, or situation. Often followed by a pronoun or noun: « la même chose que toi / que lui / que d’habitude ». Note that « la même chose » can also be used alone (without « que ») when the comparison is understood.
target_language_example: Je veux la même chose que toi, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: I want the same thing as you, please.

meaning: "the same thing as me" / "the same as I do".
additional_notes: Used to compare what you do, think, feel, or mean with someone else. Often follows a verb: *faire la même chose que moi* (do the same thing as me), *penser la même chose que moi* (think the same thing as me), *ressentir la même chose que moi* (feel the same thing as me). With *penser à…*, it means thinking about the same thing (*Tu penses à la même chose que moi ?*).
target_language_example: On a choisi la même chose que moi au restaurant.
native_language_example: They chose the same thing as me at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people are in the same class at school. Often with: « On est dans la même classe » (We’re in the same class) or « Ils sont dans la même classe ». Can also mean the same category/type in a broader sense, but for beginners it’s most common for school.
target_language_example: On est dans la même classe cette année.
native_language_example: We’re in the same class this year.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like faire/commettre/refaire to say someone repeats an identical mistake. Often followed by a comparison: « la même erreur que… » (“the same mistake as…”).
target_language_example: J’ai refait la même erreur que la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: I made the same mistake again as last week.

additional_notes: Used when someone repeats an identical question, or when you want to say you’re wondering exactly the same thing as someone else. Often appears with verbs like poser (to ask), se poser (to wonder/ask oneself), and reposer (to ask again). Can also be used as a comeback: Je pourrais te poser la même question (“I could ask you the same question”).
target_language_example: On a déjà répondu à la même question hier.
native_language_example: We already answered the same question yesterday.

meaning: the same size (same height, for people).
additional_notes: Used to compare size/height: « la même taille que + noun/pronoun » (Elle est de la même taille que moi). With the verb « faire » (to be, height-wise): « faire la même taille » / « faire à peu près la même taille ».
target_language_example: On fait la même taille, alors on peut échanger nos vestes.
native_language_example: We’re the same height, so we can swap jackets.

additional_notes: Refers to the natural environment (plants, animals, landscapes) rather than cities or human-made things. Often used when talking about protecting the environment: « sauver la nature », « protéger la nature », « aimer la nature ».
target_language_example: J'aime me promener dans la nature le week-end.
native_language_example: I like to go for walks in nature on the weekend.

additional_notes: A feminine noun used with the definite article (la). Common with weather and travel: à cause de la neige (because of the snow), la neige a fondu (the snow melted), la neige est profonde (the snow is deep).
target_language_example: Attention, il y a de la neige sur la route.
native_language_example: Careful, there’s snow on the road.

additional_notes: A common, general word for food (what people or animals eat). Used in everyday questions and comments: Et la nourriture ? (“And the food?”), La nourriture était bonne (“The food was good”).
target_language_example: La nourriture est incluse dans le prix.
native_language_example: Food is included in the price.

additional_notes: Used to describe the food (quality, condition, etc.) by following it with an adjective or description: « La nourriture est incroyable / gâtée / nécessaire… ». « La nourriture » is feminine singular, so adjectives usually take the feminine singular form (e.g., « bonne », « délicieuse », « nécessaire »).
target_language_example: La nourriture est délicieuse ici.
native_language_example: The food is delicious here.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns to mean “the new …” (opposite: "l’ancienne"). It agrees in gender/number: "la nouvelle école" (fem. sg.), "les nouvelles routes" (pl.). Don’t confuse with "une nouvelle" meaning “a piece of news / a short story.”
target_language_example: J’ai rencontré la nouvelle prof de français aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I met the new French teacher today.

meaning: the news; a piece of news.
additional_notes: Refers to a specific item of news or an announcement you hear/learn (good or bad): apprendre/entendre la nouvelle. It’s singular in French even when English often says “the news.” Not to be confused with une nouvelle meaning “a short story,” or with nouveau/nouvelle meaning “new.”
target_language_example: Elle a eu envie de pleurer quand elle a appris la nouvelle.
native_language_example: She felt like crying when she heard the news.

additional_notes: Used to talk about receiving/hearing the information that someone has died. Often appears with verbs like recevoir (to receive), apprendre (to learn), révéler (to reveal), and with reactions like être choqué(e) à/ par (to be shocked by).
target_language_example: J’ai appris la nouvelle de sa mort ce matin.
native_language_example: I learned the news of his death this morning.

additional_notes: Literally means "the night," but French often uses the article where English does not: je travaille la nuit = "I work at night." It can refer to the nighttime in general or to what happens during the night.
target_language_example: J'aime marcher la nuit quand il fait frais.
native_language_example: I like walking at night when it's cool.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the night immediately before today. Often placed at the end of the sentence as a time expression (e.g., "Je l’ai vu la nuit dernière").
target_language_example: J’ai très mal dormi la nuit dernière.
native_language_example: I slept very badly last night.

additional_notes: A possessive pronoun meaning “ours” that replaces a feminine singular noun already mentioned (e.g., "la maison" → "la nôtre"). It agrees with the thing possessed: le nôtre (masc. sg.), la nôtre (fem. sg.), les nôtres (plural). Don’t confuse with "notre" (possessive adjective) as in "notre maison" = "our house."
target_language_example: Ma voiture est vieille, mais la nôtre est fiable.
native_language_example: My car is old, but ours is reliable.

meaning: the page (of a book, document, website).
additional_notes: Used for a physical page (in a book, notebook, etc.) and also for a web page (une page web). In expressions: « tourner la page » literally means “to turn the page,” and figuratively “to move on / put something behind you.”
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé l'information sur la page d'accueil du site.
native_language_example: I found the information on the website’s home page.

additional_notes: Means peace in general (often without translating the article “la” in English). Common in set phrases: « faire la paix » = to make up / make peace; « la paix dans le monde » = world peace; and with verbs like « donner la paix » (to bring/give peace). In commands like « Laisse-moi la paix ! » / « Fiche-moi la paix ! », it means “Leave me alone!” (the « fiche-moi… » version is informal/stronger).
target_language_example: Après la dispute, ils ont fait la paix.
native_language_example: After the argument, they made up.

meaning: the game; the match (a single session).
additional_notes: Used to talk about one round/session of a sport or game you can watch, start, and win/lose. Common with verbs like regarder (watch), commencer (start), gagner/perdre (win/lose).
target_language_example: On a perdu la partie, mais on s'est bien amusés.
native_language_example: We lost the game, but we had fun.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “the skin” (human or animal). It’s very common in set expressions: **sauver la peau (à quelqu’un)** = “to save someone’s life”; **faire la peau (à quelqu’un)** = “to kill someone / get rid of someone” (threatening, often informal); **la peau du cul** is a vulgar phrase meaning “butt/ass skin,” used in rude expressions like **par la peau du cul** (“by the scruff of the ass,” i.e., roughly/forcibly). **la peau de + name** can mean “the hide/skin of …” (sometimes like “a bounty” in a wanted context).
target_language_example: Il m’a sauvé la peau.
native_language_example: He saved my life.

additional_notes: Very common in set phrases: « valoir la peine » = “to be worth it” (Cela en vaut la peine.), « (ce n’est) pas la peine » = “no need / don’t bother” (Non, pas la peine.), and « Tu en vaux la peine » = “You’re worth it.” Depending on context, « peine » can also mean “sorrow” or “pain” (e.g., « de la peine » = “sadness”).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas la peine de te presser.
native_language_example: There’s no need to rush.

additional_notes: Most often used in set phrases with an infinitive: **se donner la peine de + infinitive** or **prendre la peine de + infinitive** = “to take the trouble to / to bother to.” Example: *Personne n’a pris la peine de répondre.* Note: **de la peine** can also mean “sadness” (*Ça me fait de la peine…* = “It makes me sad…”), which is a different use.
target_language_example: Peux-tu prendre la peine de m’expliquer ?
native_language_example: Can you take the trouble to explain it to me?

additional_notes: A formal/legal term meaning a criminal punishment where the state executes someone. Common with verbs like « abolir » (to abolish) and in debates: « être pour/contre la peine de mort » (to be for/against the death penalty).
target_language_example: Je suis contre la peine de mort.
native_language_example: I’m against the death penalty.

additional_notes: Can mean the art/activity of painting (e.g., doing painting, studying painting, modern painting) or the liquid paint itself (especially in contexts like stirring paint or wet/fresh paint). In French it’s often used with verbs like faire (faire de la peinture) and with adjectives like fraîche (peinture fraîche = wet paint).
target_language_example: Attention, il y a de la peinture fraîche sur le mur.
native_language_example: Careful, there’s wet paint on the wall.

meaning: “the most … person” / “the person who is the most …” (superlative).
additional_notes: Used to form a superlative about a person: **la personne la plus + adjective** (e.g., *la personne la plus intelligente* = “the smartest person”). You can add a clause with **que je connaisse** (“that I know”) or a place/group with **ici / de la terre / dans…**. Feminine singular (*la personne*) is often used even when talking about a man (e.g., *Tom est la personne la plus…*).
target_language_example: C'est la personne la plus gentille de la classe.
native_language_example: She’s the nicest person in the class.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "la" (the) + "petite" (small/little) + "fille" (girl/daughter). In stories and everyday speech it usually means a young female child. "À la petite fille" means "to the little girl" (indirect object).
target_language_example: La petite fille joue dans le parc.
native_language_example: The little girl is playing in the park.

additional_notes: Common shorthand for « la photographie ». Used with verbs like « faire/prendre une photo » (to take a photo) and « sur la photo » (in the photo). In instructions, it can refer to an image in a layout (e.g., on a page/screen).
target_language_example: Tu peux m’envoyer la photo ?
native_language_example: Can you send me the photo?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a pool for swimming (public or private). Common with verbs like aller à la piscine (to go to the pool) and être à la piscine (to be at the pool).
target_language_example: On va à la piscine cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We're going to the pool this afternoon.

additional_notes: A common food noun. Uses the feminine article **la** (and **une pizza** = “a pizza”). Often used with verbs like **aimer/détester** (to like/hate), **manger** (to eat), and **rajouter** (to add) when talking about toppings/ingredients: **rajouter des ingrédients sur la pizza**.
target_language_example: Nous avons mangé la pizza.
native_language_example: We ate the pizza.

additional_notes: In everyday French, une/ la pièce often means a room (especially when talking about the size or layout of a home): une grande pièce, une pièce lumineuse. Note: une pièce can also mean “a coin” (une pièce de deux euros) or “a play” (une pièce de théâtre), depending on context.
target_language_example: La pièce est trop petite pour mettre un lit.
native_language_example: The room is too small to put a bed in.

additional_notes: Used to describe the state/condition of a room in the past; it’s followed by an adjective or past participle (e.g., rangée, verrouillée, froide). Note: "pièce" can mean "room" (not "piece"), which can be confusing for English speakers.
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, la pièce était trop sombre.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the room was too dark.

additional_notes: Very common for asking if there’s enough space: « Il y a de la place ? » = “Is there room?” / “Is there space?” It can also mean a place/spot (a seat on a bus, a spot in a car). In informal speech, « être dans la place » can mean “to be around / to be there (where the action is)”.
target_language_example: Il y a encore de la place à cette table ?
native_language_example: Is there still room at this table?

additional_notes: Most often used as **de la place pour** after *il y a* or *avoir*: *Il y a de la place pour…* / *On a de la place pour…* meaning there is enough space/capacity (in a car, a room, in your schedule, etc.). In everyday English you usually translate it as “room/space for,” not “place for.”
target_language_example: Il y a de la place pour trois personnes dans la voiture.
native_language_example: There’s room for three people in the car.

additional_notes: A feminine noun used for a seaside beach (sand/shore). Common with the preposition "à" to mean “to the beach” (aller à la plage), and with "en face de" to mean “opposite/across from” (en face de la plage).
target_language_example: On va à la plage cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We’re going to the beach this afternoon.

meaning: the planet (often meaning Earth; also any planet).
additional_notes: Used literally for an astronomical planet (often with context like orbit, space travel), and very commonly in expressions like « de la planète » meaning “in the world/on Earth” (e.g., “the best athletes on the planet”).
target_language_example: C'est l'un des meilleurs restaurants de la planète.
native_language_example: It's one of the best restaurants on the planet.

additional_notes: A common weather noun. It’s feminine: "la pluie" (the rain). Often used with weather verbs like "il pleut" (it’s raining) and with "accompagner" (to accompany) or "cesser" (to stop), as in your examples.
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas marcher sous la pluie.
native_language_example: I don’t like walking in the rain.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the largest part of a group or amount. Very often followed by **de**: **la plupart de + noun/pronoun** (la plupart des gens, la plupart d’entre vous, la plupart du temps). It’s singular in form, but the verb can be singular or plural depending on what follows (e.g., **La plupart des gens sont…** / **La plupart du temps, il est…**).
target_language_example: La plupart de mes amis habitent loin d’ici.
native_language_example: Most of my friends live far from here.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun or a quantity to mean “most of.” It’s often followed by a noun with a definite article: la plupart des gens (“most people”), la plupart du temps (“most of the time”). With a pronoun: la plupart d’entre eux/elles (“most of them”). Verb agreement is usually plural: La plupart des étudiants sont là.
target_language_example: La plupart des gens aiment le café.
native_language_example: Most people like coffee.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “the majority of.” It’s often followed by a plural verb: « La plupart des gens sont… ». With a number/percentage you’d typically use « la plupart de + number » (e.g., « la plupart de mes amis »).
target_language_example: La plupart des étudiants arrivent en retard aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Most of the students are arriving late today.

additional_notes: Means “the majority of people.” Very common with a general statement: « La plupart des gens + verbe… ». Grammatically, « la plupart » is singular but it usually takes a plural verb when it refers to multiple people: « La plupart des gens pensent… ».
target_language_example: La plupart des gens aiment quand il fait beau.
native_language_example: Most people like it when the weather is nice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens in general in typical situations. It can go at the beginning of a sentence (often followed by a comma) or after the verb: « La plupart du temps, je… » / « Je… la plupart du temps. »
target_language_example: La plupart du temps, je prends le bus pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: Most of the time, I take the bus to go to work.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective to say that a feminine singular noun/person has the highest degree of a quality: *la plus + adjectif* (e.g., *la plus simple*). Compare: *le plus* (masculine singular), *les plus* (plural). Often appears with **de**: *la plus … de la classe* (“the most … in the class”).
target_language_example: C'est la plus grande ville de la région.
native_language_example: It's the biggest city in the region.

additional_notes: Superlative form used with a feminine noun: "la plus belle + noun" (e.g., la plus belle nuit). For masculine, use "le plus beau"; for plural, "les plus belles / les plus beaux". Often follows "C’est..." or "Ça a été..." to describe something as the best/most beautiful of its kind.
target_language_example: C'est la plus belle journée de l'année.
native_language_example: It's the most beautiful day of the year.

additional_notes: Superlative form of "grande" used with feminine singular nouns: "la plus grande ville" (the biggest city). Also used in set phrases like "la plus grande partie" (the largest part/most) and with abstract nouns: "la plus grande vertu/préoccupation" (the greatest virtue/concern). For masculine, use "le plus grand".
target_language_example: C’est la plus grande erreur de ma vie.
native_language_example: It’s the biggest mistake of my life.

additional_notes: Used to express that something makes up the largest share of a whole (time, money, space, etc.). It’s often followed by a noun or noun phrase: « la plus grande partie de son argent / de la nuit / de sa chambre ». You can also say « la plupart de » in many cases (especially with people/things in general), but « la plus grande partie de » emphasizes the idea of a portion/quantity.
target_language_example: J’ai passé la plus grande partie de la journée à étudier.
native_language_example: I spent most of the day studying.

additional_notes: Superlative of proximity: proche = close/near, plus proche = closer/nearer, la plus proche = the closest (feminine singular). Used with feminine nouns like la banque, la gare, la station-service, la sortie, la zone. For masculine nouns: le plus proche (e.g., le métro le plus proche). Can also refer to emotional closeness (e.g., a family member you’re closest to).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, où est la pharmacie la plus proche ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the nearest pharmacy?

meaning: tiptoes; the front/tips of your feet (as when you tiptoe).
additional_notes: Most often used in the expression « sur la pointe des pieds » (= on tiptoe / tiptoeing), to describe walking quietly or standing on the front of your feet. Example verb: « marcher sur la pointe des pieds » (to tiptoe).
target_language_example: Elle est entrée sur la pointe des pieds pour ne pas réveiller le bébé.
native_language_example: She came in on tiptoe so as not to wake the baby.

additional_notes: Refers to the police force or police officers as a group. In French, it is commonly used with the definite article: la police.
target_language_example: La police est arrivée rapidement.
native_language_example: The police arrived quickly.

meaning: "the police has/have" (used to introduce an action in the past).
additional_notes: La police is a singular noun in French, so it uses the singular form of avoir: a. You’ll often see it at the start of a sentence in the passé composé: la police a + past participle (e.g., arrêté, capturé, poursuivi). In English, “the police” is usually treated as plural (“the police have…”).
target_language_example: La police a arrêté le suspect hier soir.
native_language_example: The police arrested the suspect last night.

meaning: "the police arrested" / "the police stopped and detained".
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of arrêter: "a arrêté" = "has/have arrested" or (more often in stories/news) "arrested." Used to say the police detained someone (un suspect, un homme, etc.). Often followed by the person arrested: "la police a arrêté le suspect / deux hommes."
target_language_example: La police a arrêté le voleur ce matin.
native_language_example: The police arrested the thief this morning.

meaning: politics; policy (an organization’s approach or set of rules).
additional_notes: Most often refers to politics as a field/activity (s’intéresser à la politique, être impliqué dans la politique, prendre ses distances avec la politique). It can also mean an organization’s policy/approach: la politique de l’entreprise = the company’s policy. Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Es-tu impliqué dans la politique ?
native_language_example: Are you involved in politics?

additional_notes: A common food noun. Gender: feminine (la/une pomme). Plural: les pommes. Often used with food phrases like "gâteau à la pomme" (apple cake) and with verbs like couper (to cut), laver (to wash), manger (to eat), and éplucher (to peel).
target_language_example: Tom a lavé la pomme avant de la manger.
native_language_example: Tom washed the apple before eating it.

meaning: the world population; the global population.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the total number of people on Earth. Often appears in statistics or discussion of growth/decline (e.g., « augmente », « est en augmentation »). « mondiale » is the adjective meaning “global/worldwide” agreeing with « population » (feminine).
target_language_example: La population mondiale dépasse aujourd’hui huit milliards d’habitants.
native_language_example: The world population is now over eight billion people.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific door. "Porte" means "door," and "la" is the singular definite article used with it. It can be a room door, front door, fridge door, etc., depending on context.
target_language_example: Ferme la porte, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

meaning: 'the door of / the door to' (usually followed by a location, like front/back).
additional_notes: Used to specify which door you mean, most often with directions: la porte de derrière (back door) and la porte de devant (front door). In everyday French, you’ll often hear the shorter forms: la porte de derrière / la porte arrière; la porte de devant / la porte d’entrée.
target_language_example: Je passe par la porte de derrière.
native_language_example: I’m going through the back door.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the door at the back of a building/house. Often contrasted with "la porte de devant" (the front door).
target_language_example: Tu peux entrer par la porte de derrière ?
native_language_example: Can you come in through the back door?

additional_notes: Used to describe the state of a specific door. It’s typically followed by an adjective or past participle (often with an agreement in -e because porte is feminine): la porte est ouverte/fermée/verrouillée, or an adjective like la porte est automatique. You’ll often see it in instructions: Assurez-vous que la porte est…
target_language_example: Désolé, la porte est déjà fermée.
native_language_example: Sorry, the door is already closed.

meaning: the open door; the door left open.
additional_notes: Literally “the door open.” Used when describing a door that is already open or that someone leaves open (often with verbs like laisser/garder “to leave/keep”).
target_language_example: J'ai laissé la porte ouverte parce qu'il faisait chaud.
native_language_example: I left the door open because it was hot.

meaning: the door locked (with a key); used in “fermer la porte à clé” = “to lock the door.”
additional_notes: Most often used after the verb in the phrase “fermer la porte à clé” (“lock the door”), meaning you close it and turn the key. You can also hear “mettre la porte à clé” with the same meaning. “À clé” literally means “with a key,” but in this context it implies locking, not just having a key nearby.
target_language_example: Avant de partir, j’ai fermé la porte à clé.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I locked the door.

additional_notes: Used for a feminine noun/person, or when the noun is implied: Elle est la première de sa classe (“the top/first in her class”). It can refer to the first person to do something (la première à venir) or the first occurrence of something (la première neige). For a masculine noun/person: le premier.
target_language_example: Elle est arrivée la première.
native_language_example: She arrived first.

meaning: “the first thing that” (or “the first thing I/you/etc. …”).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing the first action or object in a sequence: « la première chose que j’ai faite/que je vois/que nous avons achetée ». Often appears after « C’est… » to highlight what happened first. The past participle can agree with « chose » when the direct object comes before the verb: « la première chose que mes parents ont achetée ».
target_language_example: La première chose que je fais en arrivant, c’est d’allumer la lumière.
native_language_example: The first thing I do when I arrive is turn on the light.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first occasion something happens. Very common in expressions like "C’est la première fois que…" (It’s the first time that…) and with "depuis" to mean "the first time since…".
target_language_example: C’est la première fois que je viens à Paris.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come to Paris.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing an event that happened for the first time. Often comes after verbs like *se rappeler / se souvenir de* (“to remember”) or in questions about someone’s age or experience. The verb after *que* is conjugated normally (past or present depending on context).
target_language_example: C’était la première fois que je visitais Paris.
native_language_example: It was the first time I visited Paris.

additional_notes: Used to start a sentence about your first experience doing something. It’s usually followed by a verb (often in the past): « La première fois que je suis venu(e)… » / « La première fois que j’ai mangé… ». You can also use it with the present to talk generally: « La première fois que je viens ici, je suis toujours nerveux/nerveuse. »
target_language_example: La première fois que je suis allé(e) à Paris, j’étais très impressionné(e).
native_language_example: The first time I went to Paris, I was very impressed.

la première fois que nous nous sommes

target_language_multi_word_term: la première fois que nous nous sommes
meaning: "the first time that we…" (setting up a past event we did to/with each other).
additional_notes: This is the start of a longer clause that usually continues with a reflexive verb in the passé composé ("nous nous sommes" + past participle), e.g. "rencontrés" (met), "parlés" (spoke), "vus" (saw each other). You’ll typically complete it with what happened: "La première fois que nous nous sommes rencontrés…" = "The first time we met…"
target_language_example: La première fois que nous nous sommes rencontrés, c’était à Paris.
native_language_example: The first time we met, it was in Paris.

meaning: the press; the news media (especially newspapers/journalists).
additional_notes: Used as a collective noun for journalists and media organizations, often in political/public contexts: répondre aux questions de la presse (answer reporters’ questions), rencontrer la presse (meet the press). It can be specified: la presse à sensation (tabloid press), la presse étrangère (foreign press).
target_language_example: Le maire a fait une déclaration à la presse après l’incident.
native_language_example: The mayor made a statement to the press after the incident.

additional_notes: Used for a real princess (a king/queen’s daughter) or as a story/role title (e.g., in fairy tales, movies, theater). Often appears with verbs like sauver (to save), attendre (to wait), jouer le rôle de (to play the role of).
target_language_example: Dans le film, la princesse s’enfuit du château.
native_language_example: In the movie, the princess runs away from the castle.

additional_notes: Feminine form of “the next,” used with feminine nouns (often implied from context): la prochaine sortie (next exit), la prochaine gare (next station), la prochaine chose (next thing). For masculine, use “le prochain.” Can also mean “the next one” when the noun is understood (e.g., in directions).
target_language_example: On s’arrête à la prochaine station.
native_language_example: We’ll stop at the next station.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what will happen on the next occasion something happens. It can come at the end of the sentence (“… la prochaine fois.”) or at the beginning for emphasis (“La prochaine fois, …”). Often used with the future tense (je ferai / je viendrai), or as advice/warning (“Fais attention la prochaine fois.”).
target_language_example: La prochaine fois, je t’appelle avant de venir.
native_language_example: Next time, I’ll call you before coming.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you intend or promise to do on the next occasion. Often followed by the future tense (e.g., je ferai / j'essaierai / je vous emmènerai). It can sound like a friendly promise ("Next time, I'll take you") or a warning/threat depending on context.
target_language_example: La prochaine fois, je t'appelle avant de venir.
native_language_example: Next time, I’ll call you before coming.

additional_notes: Most often means the activity/hobby of fishing (aller à la pêche). In questions like « Comment était la pêche ? », it can also refer to how good the fishing was (how many fish you caught). Don’t confuse with « la pêche » meaning “peach” (the fruit) or the expression « avoir la pêche » meaning “to feel energetic”.
target_language_example: On va à la pêche demain matin.
native_language_example: We’re going fishing tomorrow morning.

meaning: "the question" (a question; the issue being discussed).
additional_notes: Most often means a literal question someone asks. It can also mean “the issue/matter at hand” in a discussion: « La question se posa… » = “The question/issue came up…”. In « Je posais juste la question », it’s a common way to say you were only asking (often to soften what you said).
target_language_example: La question, c’est de savoir si on a assez de temps.
native_language_example: The question is whether we have enough time.

additional_notes: Two common meanings: (1) a line of people waiting (often with the verb phrase « faire la queue » = to stand in line; « il y a la queue » = there’s a line), and (2) an animal’s tail. The meaning is clear from context.
target_language_example: On a fait la queue pendant trente minutes.
native_language_example: We stood in line for thirty minutes.

meaning: the radio (radio broadcasting; also the radio set).
additional_notes: Used for the medium (“on the radio”) or the device (“turn up the radio”). Often heard in expressions like « écouter la radio » (to listen to the radio) and « à la radio » (on the radio). In sentence 2, « radio kabyle » means a radio station/programming in Kabyle.
target_language_example: J'écoute la radio en voiture.
native_language_example: I listen to the radio in the car.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation, often followed by a clause (subject + verb): « la raison pour laquelle + [sentence] ». In everyday speech, people also commonly say « la raison pour laquelle… » or simpler « pourquoi… » (why).
target_language_example: Voilà la raison pour laquelle je suis en retard.
native_language_example: That’s the reason why I’m late.

meaning: the queen; (figuratively) the queen of…, the best/top one.
additional_notes: Literally refers to a female monarch (“the queen”). It’s also used figuratively to mean the best or most important of a group: “la reine des + plural noun” = “the queen of …” (e.g., the top/flagship one).
target_language_example: Pour moi, cette pâtisserie est la reine des desserts.
native_language_example: For me, this pastry is the queen of desserts.

meaning: river (a smaller natural river/stream than a fleuve).
additional_notes: In French, *une rivière* is a river that flows into another river; a *fleuve* flows into the sea. You’ll often see it with prepositions like *au bord de la rivière* (by the river) and *au-dessus de la rivière* (over the river).
target_language_example: Nous pique-niquons au bord de la rivière.
native_language_example: We’re having a picnic by the river.

meaning: (to cross) the river by swimming; to swim across the river.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb « traverser »: « traverser la rivière à la nage » = to cross the river by swimming (rather than by bridge/boat). « à la nage » literally means “by swimming.”
target_language_example: On va traverser la rivière à la nage.
native_language_example: We’re going to swim across the river.

meaning: the road; (figurative) something that holds up / makes sense.
additional_notes: Most commonly means “the road” (a street/roadway). Used in phrases like “barrer la route à quelqu’un” (to block someone’s way) and “dégager la route” (clear the road). In a common figurative expression, “ne pas tenir la route” means “not to hold up / not to make sense / not to be convincing.”
target_language_example: Attention, il y a beaucoup de brouillard sur la route.
native_language_example: Careful, there’s a lot of fog on the road.

additional_notes: Refers to a street/road in a town or city. Common with location phrases like « au bout de la rue » (at the end of the street) and movement verbs like « traverser la rue » (to cross the street).
target_language_example: La boulangerie est juste en face, de l’autre côté de la rue.
native_language_example: The bakery is right across the street.

meaning: reality; the real world; what is actually true.
additional_notes: Used to contrast what’s real with what’s imagined, believed, or fictional ("la réalité et la fiction"). Often appears with verbs like accepter (accept), refléter (reflect), correspondre à (match), and expressions like prendre conscience de (become aware of) and la réalité de + noun (the reality of…).
target_language_example: Parfois, la réalité est plus compliquée que ce qu’on imagine.
native_language_example: Sometimes, reality is more complicated than what we imagine.

meaning: the answer; the response; the reply.
additional_notes: Used for an answer to a question (la réponse à une question) or a reply to something someone said/wrote. Common collocations: avoir la réponse (to have/get the answer), connaître la réponse (to know the answer), donner la réponse (to give the answer), attendre la réponse (to wait for the answer).
target_language_example: Dans quelques heures, on devrait avoir la réponse.
native_language_example: In a few hours, we should have the answer.

additional_notes: Used to state what the answer is, often followed by an adjective (exacte/juste = correct, fausse = wrong, compliquée = complicated) or by the answer itself. Note that feminine agreement is common because *réponse* is feminine: *la réponse est exacte/juste/fausse/complicquée*.
target_language_example: La réponse est simple : tu dois remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: The answer is simple: you have to fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used for a planned meeting (work, school, association, etc.). Common verbs: "avoir lieu" (to take place), "se tenir" (to be held), "aller à une réunion" (to go to a meeting).
target_language_example: La réunion commence à 9 h, ne sois pas en retard.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at 9 a.m.; don’t be late.

meaning: “the meeting will be held / will take place.”
additional_notes: Used in formal or neutral contexts to state when/where a meeting will happen. « se tiendra » is the future of « se tenir » meaning “to be held (event takes place)”. Often followed by a time or place: « La réunion se tiendra vendredi / à 14 h / dans la salle 3 ».
target_language_example: La réunion se tiendra à 10 h dans la grande salle.
native_language_example: The meeting will be held at 10 a.m. in the main room.

additional_notes: Refers to the period of the year when it rains a lot, often with a typical start and end date. Used with verbs like commencer/débuter (to start) and se terminer/finir (to end).
target_language_example: Pendant la saison des pluies, il pleut presque tous les jours.
native_language_example: During the rainy season, it rains almost every day.

meaning: the room; the hall (a larger room/venue).
additional_notes: Used for an indoor space, often a public or rented one: a hall, venue, auditorium, or room in a building (e.g., salle de classe, salle de réunion). In contexts like "la salle éclata de rire", it means the audience/the whole room reacted. Also used in set phrases like "sortir de la salle" (leave the room/venue).
target_language_example: On se retrouve dans la salle à côté.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in the room next door.

meaning: "the … room" (used before a noun to name a room).
additional_notes: This is usually an incomplete phrase that needs a noun after it: **la salle de + noun**. Common combinations: **la salle de bains** (bathroom), **la salle de classe** (classroom), **la salle de sport** (gym). In everyday French you’ll often see **salle de bain** without the final **-s**, but **salle de bains** is also common.
target_language_example: Où est la salle de bains ?
native_language_example: Where is the bathroom?

meaning: the bathroom; the room for washing/bathing (often also the toilet).
additional_notes: Literally “the bath room.” In French, la salle de bain can refer to a bathroom with a shower/bath and may also be used when you mean you need the toilet, especially in polite requests (e.g., asking to go to the bathroom).
target_language_example: Où est la salle de bain, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Where is the bathroom, please?

additional_notes: Commonly used to ask for or indicate where the bathroom is. In many homes it can include a shower or bathtub (and sometimes a toilet), but in some places the toilet may be in a separate room (les toilettes).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, où est la salle de bains ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

additional_notes: Refers to the room where lessons take place. Often used with verbs like être (La salle de classe est vide/propre) or quitter (quitter la salle de classe). In everyday French, people may also just say "la classe" to mean the class/classroom depending on context.
target_language_example: Les élèves entrent dans la salle de classe à huit heures.
native_language_example: The students go into the classroom at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: The room where you eat meals (often at a dining table). In a house/apartment tour, it’s commonly listed with other rooms (le salon, le couloir, etc.). Literally “the room to eat” (salle + à + manger).
target_language_example: La salle à manger est juste à côté de la cuisine.
native_language_example: The dining room is right next to the kitchen.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning a person’s physical (and sometimes mental) well-being. Often used with verbs like « avoir » (to be in good health) and « être en bonne/mauvaise santé » (to be in good/bad health).
target_language_example: Je fais du sport pour garder la santé.
native_language_example: I exercise to stay healthy.

la santé est plus importante que

target_language_multi_word_term: la santé est plus importante que
additional_notes: Use this to compare priorities: “X est plus important(e) que Y” = “X is more important than Y.” Here, “la santé” is feminine, so it’s “importante.” Often followed by “la richesse” (wealth) or “tout (le reste)” (everything else).
target_language_example: Pour moi, la santé est plus importante que l'argent.
native_language_example: For me, health is more important than money.

meaning: "science" (the study of the natural world using experiments and evidence).
additional_notes: A feminine noun, usually used with the definite article: la science. It can mean science in general as a field of knowledge, or the scientific approach/method (e.g., croire en la science = trust science).
target_language_example: La science nous aide à mieux comprendre le monde.
native_language_example: Science helps us understand the world better.

additional_notes: Most literally means “the stage” (in a theater, concert, etc.): sortir de la scène = get off the stage. It can also mean “the scene” as in what’s happening in front of you or a particular situation/moment (especially in storytelling): regarder la scène = watch the scene. In informal speech, it can refer to a vibe/situation you don’t feel: Je la sens pas, la scène = I’m not feeling this situation.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas à l’aise avec la scène, alors je préfère rester dans la salle.
native_language_example: I’m not comfortable with the stage, so I’d rather stay in the audience.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where a crime happened, especially in police/investigation contexts. Often used with verbs like arriver sur (arrive at), enquêter sur (investigate), and préserver (preserve/secure).
target_language_example: Ne touchez à rien : il faut préserver la scène du crime.
native_language_example: Don’t touch anything: we need to preserve the crime scene.

additional_notes: Refers to a seven-day period. Often used with time expressions like « toute la semaine » (all week), « la semaine passée/dernière » (last week), and in set phrases like « à la semaine » meaning “per week / weekly” (e.g., being paid weekly).
target_language_example: On part en voyage la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: We’re leaving on a trip next week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the week immediately before the current one. Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also go near the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je l’ai vu la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: I saw him last week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the week after this one. It can be placed at the end of the sentence or near the verb: « la semaine prochaine, je pars » / « je pars la semaine prochaine ».
target_language_example: On se voit la semaine prochaine ?
native_language_example: Will we see each other next week?

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (la seule façon = the only way) or on its own to mean “the only one” (Suis-je la seule ? = Am I the only one?). It agrees in gender/number: le seul (masc. sing.), la seule (fem. sing.), les seuls / les seules (plural).
target_language_example: Elle est la seule qui comprend.
native_language_example: She’s the only one who understands.

additional_notes: Used to single out one unique thing. It introduces a relative clause with **qui** (meaning “that/which” as the subject of the verb that follows). Often followed by a verb in the 3rd person singular: *la seule chose qui m’aide…* / *la seule chose qui est importante…* You can also change it for gender/number: *le seul truc qui*, *les seules choses qui*.
target_language_example: La seule chose qui me manque, c’est le temps.
native_language_example: The only thing I’m missing is time.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that one point is the priority above all others. Often followed by a clause, e.g. "La seule chose qui compte, c’est que..." or "La seule chose qui compte est de + infinitive" (more formal). "Qui compte" literally means "that counts" in the sense of "that matters."
target_language_example: La seule chose qui compte, c’est que tu ailles mieux.
native_language_example: The only thing that matters is that you get better.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize what is most important, often followed by "c'est..." or "est que..." + subjunctive (e.g., "La seule chose qui importe est que tu sois..."). It can also be followed by "est si..." to introduce a yes/no condition.
target_language_example: La seule chose qui importe, c'est qu'on arrive à temps.
native_language_example: The only thing that matters is that we arrive on time.

la seule à ne pas être invitée à

target_language_multi_word_term: la seule à ne pas être invitée à
meaning: “the only one not invited to” / “the only one who wasn’t invited to”.
additional_notes: Used to express that one person was the sole exception (everyone else was invited). Feminine singular: la seule … invitée. Adjust for gender/number as needed: le seul (masc.), les seuls / les seules (plural). Pattern: « la/le seul(e) + à + infinitive »; here the infinitive is negative and passive: « ne pas être invité(e) ». The final « à » introduces the event (e.g., « à la fête », « à la soirée »).
target_language_example: Elle a été la seule à ne pas être invitée à la fête.
native_language_example: She was the only one who wasn’t invited to the party.

meaning: "his/hers/its/theirs" (feminine singular possessive pronoun): "the one that belongs to him/her/them."
additional_notes: Used to avoid repeating a noun: it replaces "sa + noun". It agrees with the thing owned (here feminine singular), not with the owner. Variants include: le sien, la sienne, les siens, les siennes.
target_language_example: Cette valise est la sienne.
native_language_example: This suitcase is hers.

meaning: the situation; the state of things.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current circumstances or condition of something (personal, political, economic, etc.). Often appears with an adjective (la situation est grave/mauvaise) or a modifier (la situation politique/financière).
target_language_example: On doit évaluer la situation avant de décider.
native_language_example: We need to assess the situation before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to describe the current state of events, usually followed by an adjective or phrase (e.g., « la situation est sous contrôle », « la situation est instable »). You can change the tense to talk about the past/future: « la situation était… » (was), « la situation sera… » (will be).
target_language_example: La situation est compliquée, mais on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: The situation is complicated, but we’re going to find a solution.

additional_notes: Often means “society” in general (people and social life as a whole): « un danger pour la société », « la société change ». It can also mean “a company/firm” in a business context, especially when it’s the subject of actions like deciding, investing, abandoning a project, etc.
target_language_example: La société a décidé d'abandonner le projet.
native_language_example: The company decided to abandon the project.

meaning: the evening (late afternoon/nighttime); also an evening event/party.
additional_notes: Often refers to the time period after the afternoon and before going to bed (e.g., «dans la soirée» = sometime this evening). It can also mean an evening spent socially or an organized evening event (like a dinner/party): «Merci pour la soirée.»
target_language_example: On se voit dans la soirée, vers 20 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other this evening, around 8 pm?

additional_notes: Most commonly means a physical exit/doorway. In contexts like schools or events, "à la sortie" means "when it lets out / at the end (as people are leaving)" or "outside by the exit." In security/police instructions, "boucler la sortie" means to secure/block off an exit.
target_language_example: Pardon, où est la sortie ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the exit?

additional_notes: A common food item. Usually used with an article (la/une): "la soupe" (the soup) or "une soupe" (a soup / a bowl of soup). Often described with adjectives like chaude (hot) or salée (salty), and with verbs like bouillir (to boil).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre la soupe, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have the soup, please.

meaning: station (train/subway/bus), or a station/base (e.g., space station).
additional_notes: In everyday travel contexts, "la station" usually means a transport station and is often specified as "la station de métro", "la station de train" / "la gare", or "la station de bus". It can also mean a facility/base such as "la station spatiale" (space station) or "la station de recherche" (research station).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la station de métro à 18 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the subway station at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Means either (1) safety (the condition of being safe) or (2) security (measures/people who protect a place). In French you can say "de la sécurité" to mean "security (staff/guards)" or "security (presence/measures)" (e.g., "Il y a de la sécurité partout").
target_language_example: La sécurité est renforcée à l'entrée du bâtiment.
native_language_example: Security has been increased at the entrance to the building.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a physical table. In meal contexts, it often means the dining table. Common expressions include mettre la table ('set the table') and quitter la table ('leave the table').
target_language_example: Le livre est sur la table.
native_language_example: The book is on the table.

additional_notes: Used for severe weather events (at sea, in the air, etc.). It can also be used figuratively to mean “turmoil” or “trouble” (e.g., causing problems and then suffering the consequences).
target_language_example: On reste à l’intérieur : la tempête arrive ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re staying inside: the storm is coming tonight.

additional_notes: “La terre” can mean the planet Earth (“la Terre”), but very often it means soil or ground, especially in gardening or when something is in/on the ground. It’s also used in a figurative sense for a region or homeland: “la terre de…” = “the land of…”.
target_language_example: Après la pluie, la terre est trop humide pour planter.
native_language_example: After the rain, the soil is too wet to plant.

additional_notes: Used to replace a feminine singular noun that belongs to the person you’re talking to (tu). It agrees with the thing owned: le tien (masc.), la tienne (fem.), les tiens/les tiennes (plural). Often used in comparisons or contrasts: « ma … / la tienne » (mine / yours).
target_language_example: Je préfère ma version à la tienne.
native_language_example: I prefer my version to yours.

additional_notes: A common, slightly literary way to refer to the time when daylight fades and night begins. Often used with prepositions like "à" (at), "après" (after), or "dès" (as soon as): "à la tombée de la nuit", "dès la tombée de la nuit".
target_language_example: On rentre à la maison à la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: We go home at nightfall.

additional_notes: Common short form of "la télévision" in everyday speech. Used with verbs like "regarder la télé" (to watch TV) and "éteindre la télé" (to turn off the TV).
target_language_example: On va regarder la télé ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to watch TV tonight?

additional_notes: Refers to the device (the TV set) and also to TV as a medium/programs. Common with verbs like regarder (to watch), allumer/éteindre (to turn on/off), and fonctionner (to work).
target_language_example: On regarde la télévision ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we watching TV tonight?

additional_notes: Usually refers to the physical head, but in some expressions it can also suggest the mind or thoughts. With body parts, French often uses the definite article where English uses a possessive: secouer la tête = shake your/her head. It also appears in many idioms, such as avoir une idée derrière la tête (to have something in mind / an ulterior motive).
target_language_example: J'ai mal à la tête.
native_language_example: I have a headache.

meaning: with your head held high; proudly/confidently.
additional_notes: Used to show pride, confidence, or dignity (often after a difficult situation). Common in encouragement like « Garde la tête haute » (“Keep your head up”). Can also be used with verbs like marcher/rentrer (walk/come home) to describe someone acting with dignity.
target_language_example: Même après cet échec, il est parti la tête haute.
native_language_example: Even after that failure, he left with his head held high.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: the animal (often in farm contexts: traire la vache = to milk the cow). In spoken French, « Oh, la vache ! » is a common, informal reaction showing surprise, shock, or admiration (similar to “Wow!”).
target_language_example: Oh, la vache ! C’est super cher !
native_language_example: Wow! It’s really expensive!

additional_notes: Refers to dishes/plates/cups/cutlery as a category, and also to the chore of washing them. Common in the phrase « faire la vaisselle » = “to do the dishes.” In a store context (« vendre de la vaisselle »), it means dishware/tableware.
target_language_example: Après le dîner, je fais la vaisselle.
native_language_example: After dinner, I do the dishes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the day immediately preceding an event or date. It’s most common with holidays or important days: « la veille de Noël » (Christmas Eve), « la veille du départ » (the day before the departure). Often followed by a noun with de/du/de la/des.
target_language_example: Je prépare tout la veille de mon voyage.
native_language_example: I prepare everything the day before my trip.

additional_notes: Used as a general word for meat (as a category) and also in specific phrases like "la viande de lapin" (rabbit meat). Often appears with cooking verbs (couper, rôtir) and can be contrasted with "la viande crue" (raw meat).
target_language_example: Coupez la viande en tranches minces.
native_language_example: Cut the meat into thin slices.

additional_notes: Usually refers to life in general or a person's life. French often uses the article here where English simply says "life." Common expressions include donner la vie (give life / give birth), perdre la vie or laisser la vie (lose one's life), coûter la vie (cost someone their life), and devoir la vie à quelqu’un (owe someone your life).
