additional_notes: Used for a physical place to shop (a market), or more generally for the market as an economic system/sector: "le marché des valeurs mobilières" = the stock market; "le marché a repris" = the market picked up/recovered; "inondé de produits" = flooded with products. In expressions like "C'est le marché", it means “that’s how the market works / that’s the way things are.”
target_language_example: Ce produit est moins cher sur le marché.
native_language_example: This product is cheaper at the market.

additional_notes: Can mean the institution/commitment of being married (“marriage”) or the ceremony/event itself (“a wedding”). Often used with: "annuler le mariage" (cancel the wedding), "avant le mariage" (before marriage), "le mariage de + name" (someone’s wedding), and "avoir lieu" (to take place).
target_language_example: Ils veulent un petit mariage, mais le mariage aura lieu en été.
native_language_example: They want a small wedding, but the wedding will take place in the summer.

additional_notes: Used for a sports match/game (soccer, baseball, etc.). Common with de + sport (un match de baseball) or between teams (un match France–Angleterre). You can talk about the result (gagner/perdre le match), timing (avant/après le match), or changes (le match a été reporté = postponed).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au stade avant le match.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the stadium before the match.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) in the passive voice: "a été" (was) + "annulé" (cancelled). Used to say an event/game did not take place, often with a reason introduced by "à cause de" / "en raison de" (because of). Note: "grâce à" usually means "thanks to" (a positive cause), so using it with bad weather is generally ironic.
target_language_example: Désolé, le match a été annulé à cause de la neige.
native_language_example: Sorry, the match was cancelled because of the snow.

additional_notes: Refers to the morning time. With the definite article "le" it often means a habitual time (“le matin” = “in the mornings / in the morning”): « Je travaille le matin. » It can also mean a specific morning when context is clear: « Le matin suivant… » (“the following morning”).
target_language_example: Je fais du sport le matin.
native_language_example: I work out in the morning.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mark the superlative: le meilleur moyen = the best way. Meilleur is the irregular form related to bon ('good'). It changes for gender and number: la meilleure, les meilleurs, les meilleures. If the noun is omitted, le meilleur can mean 'the best one.'
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur choix pour nous.
native_language_example: It's the best choice for us.

additional_notes: Used to single out the top person/thing within a group. It’s typically followed by a plural noun: « le meilleur des étudiants » (the best of the students). With things in general, French often uses it with a plural even when English might use singular: « le meilleur des cadeaux » = “the best gift.” You may also see feminine « la meilleure des… » and plural « les meilleurs/les meilleures des… ».
target_language_example: Pour moi, c’est le meilleur des films de l’année.
native_language_example: For me, it’s the best movie of the year.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the best option or outcome. Often appears with verbs like vouloir/chercher/choisir: « Nous voulons le meilleur pour toi » (“We want the best for you”). It agrees with gender/number in other forms: « la meilleure » (f.), « les meilleurs / les meilleures » (pl.).
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur restaurant du quartier.
native_language_example: It's the best restaurant in the neighborhood.

meaning: the message (a written or spoken note/information).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a message you received or want to check (text, voicemail, note, email, etc.). In conversation, “Le message ?” can mean “What does the message say?” or “Which message?” depending on context. “Prends le message” commonly means “take the message” (i.e., write it down/pass it on).
target_language_example: Tu peux prendre le message et le lui donner ?
native_language_example: Can you take the message and give it to him?

additional_notes: Possessive pronoun used to avoid repeating a masculine singular noun already mentioned or understood from context. It agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: for example, livre → le mien. Related forms are la mienne, les miens, and les miennes.
target_language_example: Ton manteau est sur la chaise, et le mien est dans la voiture.
native_language_example: Your coat is on the chair, and mine is in the car.

additional_notes: A masculine noun for an object with a reflective surface. Common with verbs like « montrer » (to show), « prendre » (to take), « tenir » (to hold), and « réfléchir » (to reflect).
target_language_example: Je me regarde dans le miroir avant de partir.
native_language_example: I look at myself in the mirror before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize even the smallest amount or detail, especially in questions and negative statements: "pas le moindre..." = "not the slightest / not any...". It agrees with the noun: "le moindre" (masc. sing.) and "la moindre" (fem. sing.). Common with nouns like "sens", "doute", "sou", "argent", "indice", "intérêt".
target_language_example: Ce que je dis a-t-il le moindre sens ?
native_language_example: Does what I'm saying make the slightest sense?

additional_notes: "Le mois" is a masculine noun meaning a month. It can refer to a specific month ("Avril est le mois…"), the whole month as a period of time ("tout le mois" = the whole month), or a relative time period ("le mois suivant" = the following/next month). Plural: "les mois" (months).
target_language_example: On se voit le mois prochain.
native_language_example: See you next month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous month. It often goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., « J’ai voyagé le mois dernier. »), but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je l’ai vu le mois dernier.
native_language_example: I saw him last month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. Often placed at the end of the sentence as a time expression, but it can also be used alone as a short answer.
target_language_example: On commence le nouveau travail le mois prochain.
native_language_example: We start the new job next month.

additional_notes: Means a point in time (now, then, a particular occasion). Very common in time expressions: « le moment de + infinitive » (the time to do something), « le moment présent » (the present moment), « ce n’est pas le moment » (it’s not the right time), « le moment est venu » (the time has come), « le moment opportun » (the opportune/right moment).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas le moment d’en parler.
native_language_example: Now isn’t the right time to talk about it.

meaning: when the time comes; when the moment arrives.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen later, at the appropriate time. Often placed at the end of a sentence as a set phrase, and can be used alone (“Le moment venu.”) to mean “When the time comes.”
target_language_example: Je te dirai la vérité le moment venu.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you the truth when the time comes.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the world in general: the planet, life on earth, or human society. In some contexts, it can also suggest people in general.
target_language_example: Je veux voyager et voir le monde.
native_language_example: I want to travel and see the world.

additional_notes: Literally, it means “the world has …” and is followed by a past participle (passé composé) or by another phrase: « Le monde a changé » (“The world has changed”), « Le monde a besoin de… » (“The world needs…”). If you mean “everyone has…”, French usually says « tout le monde a… » (more common than « le monde a… »).
target_language_example: Le monde a besoin de paix.
native_language_example: The world needs peace.

meaning: "the world has been" / "everyone has been" (depending on context).
additional_notes: This is usually not a complete sentence on its own: it typically needs what happened next (e.g., an adjective or past participle). In French, "le monde" can mean "the world" or, in many contexts, "everyone" (like "tout le monde"). "a été" is the past tense (passé composé) of "être" (to be): "has been" / "was".
target_language_example: Le monde a été surpris par la nouvelle.
native_language_example: Everyone was surprised by the news.

additional_notes: This is not a complete expression by itself; it normally needs a noun after "un" (e.g., "Le monde a un problème" = "The world has a problem"). If you meant "Le Monde", note that it can also be the name of a French newspaper, but "Le Monde a un…" would still require a complement to be complete.
target_language_example: Le monde a un gros problème : la pollution.
native_language_example: The world has a big problem: pollution.

meaning: "the world must" (often intended as "everyone must" in "Tout le monde doit…").
additional_notes: On its own, "le monde doit" is uncommon/awkward in everyday French. To say "everyone must/has to…", French normally uses "Tout le monde doit…" (literally "all the world must"). "doit" is the 3rd-person singular of "devoir" (must/has to).
target_language_example: Tout le monde doit montrer son passeport à l'entrée.
native_language_example: Everyone has to show their passport at the entrance.

additional_notes: Literally “the entire world.” Used to emphasize that something is known, involved, or affected worldwide, or (more loosely) that everybody knows/does something. Often used with verbs like savoir (to know), être au courant (to be aware), or in emotional statements like détester le monde entier (to hate everyone/the whole world).
target_language_example: Il a posté la vidéo, et le monde entier l’a vue.
native_language_example: He posted the video, and the whole world saw it.

additional_notes: Used to state an opinion or fact about the world (le monde). It’s often followed by an adjective (Le monde est compliqué), a noun phrase (Le monde est un endroit dangereux), or a verb phrase like "en train de" to show something in progress (Le monde est en train de changer). Don’t confuse with "tout le monde" (= everyone), which can also appear as "Tout le monde est ..." (= everyone is ...).
target_language_example: Le monde est parfois injuste.
native_language_example: The world is sometimes unfair.

additional_notes: Said when you run into someone unexpectedly, discover a surprising connection, or realize people/places are linked in an unexpected way. Often used as an exclamation: « Comme/Que le monde est petit ! » (similar to “How small the world is!”). « hein ? » can be added to seek agreement (“right?”).
target_language_example: On se retrouve encore ici ? Le monde est petit !
native_language_example: We end up here again? It’s a small world!

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; as written it looks incomplete or like a typo (often people mean “le monde” = “the world” / “people”, or “tout le monde” = “everyone”).
additional_notes: “Le monde le” doesn’t have a conventional meaning in French. You may be missing a following word (e.g., “le monde, le …”) or have words in the wrong order. Common correct alternatives: “le monde” (the world; also “people/crowd” depending on context) and “tout le monde” (everyone).
target_language_example: Dans ton message, tu as écrit « le monde le », mais cette suite de mots n’est pas correcte en français.
native_language_example: In your message, you wrote “le monde le”, but that sequence of words isn’t correct in French.

additional_notes: Literally “the world knows it,” used to emphasize that something is widely known. More common in everyday French is "tout le monde le sait" (“everyone knows it”). The "le" refers back to what was just mentioned (it/that).
target_language_example: Tout le monde le sait : il adore le chocolat.
native_language_example: Everyone knows it: he loves chocolate.

additional_notes: This is a literal combination of **le monde** (“the world”) + **peut** (he/she/it “can”, from *pouvoir*). In everyday French, to mean “everyone can…”, you usually say **tout le monde peut…** (“everyone can…”). **Le monde peut…** is less common on its own and often sounds incomplete unless the context is really about “the world” (e.g., the planet, society).
target_language_example: Tout le monde peut se tromper.
native_language_example: Everyone can make mistakes.

additional_notes: Used to say something is common knowledge. In everyday French, "tout le monde sait" is much more common than "le monde sait" on its own.
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que Paris est la capitale de la France.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that Paris is the capital of France.

meaning: "everyone knows that" (used to stress something as obvious).
additional_notes: Often used as an emphatic, sometimes exaggerated way to say something is common knowledge. In everyday French, you’ll more commonly hear/see: « Tout le monde sait que… » (Everyone knows that…).
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que ce restaurant est excellent.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that this restaurant is excellent.

additional_notes: This isn’t really a complete set phrase on its own: it’s usually the start of a sentence before a reflexive verb (a verb that uses *se*, like *se lever*, *se souvenir*, *se rencontrer*). *Le monde* can mean “the world,” but it can also mean “people/everyone” depending on context (more commonly you’ll see *tout le monde* = “everyone”).
target_language_example: Le monde se souvient de ce moment.
native_language_example: People remember that moment.

additional_notes: In everyday speech, "(tout) le monde" often means "everyone" or "people". So "le monde veut..." is used to talk generally about what people want. More standard: "tout le monde veut...". If you mean the literal "world" (planet), you’d usually add context (e.g., "le monde entier").
target_language_example: Tout le monde veut partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: Everyone wants to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s mood/mental state, especially when it’s high or low. Common patterns: « avoir le moral » (to be in good spirits), « remonter le moral (à quelqu’un) » (to cheer [someone] up / lift [someone’s] spirits), and the idiom « avoir le moral dans les chaussettes » (to feel very down).
target_language_example: Après une mauvaise journée, j’écoute un podcast pour me remonter le moral.
native_language_example: After a bad day, I listen to a podcast to lift my spirits.

additional_notes: Used for a computer/account password or a secret code to access something. Often appears with verbs like changer (to change), demander (to ask for), oublier (to forget), or entrer/saisir (to enter/type).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié le mot de passe, je dois le réinitialiser.
native_language_example: I forgot the password; I have to reset it.

additional_notes: Refers to an engine in a vehicle or machine. Common with verbs like tourner (run), fonctionner (work), être bruyant (be noisy), and éteindre (turn off/shut down).
target_language_example: Le moteur de la voiture démarre enfin.
native_language_example: The car’s engine finally starts.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: (un) mur. Used for a wall in a building (inside or outside), or a barrier/fortification (e.g., a stone wall). Plural: les murs. Common phrases: contre le mur (against the wall), sur le mur (on the wall).
target_language_example: Il y a une fenêtre dans le mur.
native_language_example: There is a window in the wall.

additional_notes: Refers to a medical doctor; often used with verbs like appeler (call), consulter (see/consult), and arriver (arrive). In French, you usually use the article: le médecin (the doctor), un médecin (a doctor).
target_language_example: J’ai rendez-vous chez le médecin demain matin.
native_language_example: I have an appointment at the doctor’s tomorrow morning.

meaning: "the doctor has" / "the doctor" + a past action (past tense).
additional_notes: Used to start a sentence in the passé composé: "Le médecin" (the doctor) + "a" (has) + past participle (e.g., examiné, prescrit, prononcé, traité, utilisé). In English this is usually translated as the simple past ("The doctor examined/prescribed...") more than "has".
target_language_example: Le médecin a recommandé du repos.
native_language_example: The doctor recommended rest.

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people or things are identical in some way. It often comes before a noun, as in le même livre ('the same book'), and changes for gender and number: la même, les mêmes. It is often followed by que to compare: le même ... que ('the same ... as').
target_language_example: Nous avons le même professeur de français.
native_language_example: We have the same French teacher.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: "avoir le même âge que" + person/pronoun (moi, toi, lui/elle, nous, vous, eux/elles) or a name. You can add an adverb like "exactement" (exactly) or "à peu près" (about/roughly).
target_language_example: J'ai le même âge que mon frère.
native_language_example: I'm the same age as my brother.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s age is equal to yours. It’s built with **avoir + âge** (“to be … years old”), plus **le même** (“the same”) and **que moi** (“as me”). You can swap **moi** for another person: *le même âge que toi / que lui / qu’elle / que nous / que vous / qu’eux / qu’elles*; and you can add *à peu près* to mean “about/roughly.”
target_language_example: Elle a le même âge que moi, mais elle est dans une autre classe.
native_language_example: She’s the same age as me, but she’s in a different class.

additional_notes: A more formal/general word for a ship than "bateau". Often used in news, history, and nautical contexts. Common with verbs like "couler" (to sink), "abandonner" (to abandon), and phrases like "être à flot" (to be afloat).
target_language_example: Le navire a quitté le port ce matin.
native_language_example: The ship left the port this morning.

additional_notes: A body part. Very common in everyday phrases: « Essuie-toi le nez ! » (Wipe your nose!), « avoir le nez qui coule » (to have a runny nose), and « respirer par le nez » (to breathe through your nose). In expressions like « avoir le nez dans l'écran », it means having your face very close to the screen (being glued to it).
target_language_example: J'ai le nez bouché, je respire mal.
native_language_example: My nose is blocked, I’m breathing badly.

meaning: black; the black one (the item in black).
additional_notes: Often refers to the color black in general or to a specific black item (e.g., a black shirt, dress, or pen) depending on context. With the verb "aller" (as in "Le noir te va bien"), it means black suits you / looks good on you.
target_language_example: Je préfère le noir pour les vêtements.
native_language_example: I prefer black for clothes.

additional_notes: Used to identify what someone/something is called: le nom de la ville (the name of the city), le nom de notre fille (our daughter’s name). Often used with verbs like être (C’est le nom de… ?), savoir (Sais-tu le nom de… ?), dire (Peux-tu dire le nom de… ?), and vouloir (Je veux le nom de…).
target_language_example: Tu connais le nom de ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you know the name of this restaurant?

meaning: “the name of the” (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the name belonging to someone or something: le nom du film, le nom du père, le nom du compositeur. It’s the contraction of "le nom de" + "le" → "le nom du". For a feminine noun, use "le nom de la"; for plural, "le nom des".
target_language_example: Quel est le nom du restaurant ?
native_language_example: What is the name of the restaurant?

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk about how many there are (often in statistics or trends). It takes singular agreement: "Le nombre de touristes a augmenté" (not "ont augmenté").
target_language_example: Le nombre de participants a diminué cette semaine.
native_language_example: The number of participants decreased this week.

meaning: "the new" (male person/thing), i.e. the new one.
additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun to mean “the new …” (le nouveau film, le nouveau président). It can also be a noun phrase meaning “the new guy/new person” in a group or job (e.g., Le nouveau arrive demain. / Êtes-vous le nouveau secrétaire ?). Feminine: la nouvelle; plural: les nouveaux / les nouvelles.
target_language_example: Le nouveau est très sympa, mais il est encore en formation.
native_language_example: The new guy is really nice, but he’s still in training.

meaning: ours (the one(s) that belong to us).
additional_notes: A possessive pronoun used to replace a noun already known from context. It agrees with the thing possessed: le nôtre (masc. singular), la nôtre (fem. singular), les nôtres (plural). Often used in comparisons: « le même que le nôtre » (“the same as ours”).
target_language_example: Ce vélo est le nôtre, pas le leur.
native_language_example: This bike is ours, not theirs.

meaning: bread (as a general or specific loaf).
additional_notes: Often refers to a loaf of bread in everyday situations (cutting it, passing it at the table: « Passe-moi le pain. »). In a broader sense, it can mean bread as a staple food in general (« Le pain a permis… »). Common with verbs like « couper le pain » (to cut the bread) and « rompre le pain » (to break bread, sometimes literally, sometimes meaning to share a meal).
target_language_example: Tu peux me passer le pain, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the bread, please?

additional_notes: A common public green space in a town or city. Masculine noun: le parc (singular), les parcs (plural). Often used with location/distance phrases like « être situé… » (to be located) or « se trouver… » (to be located/found).
target_language_example: Le parc est situé au centre-ville.
native_language_example: The park is located downtown.

additional_notes: Refers to past time or past events. Common in set phrases like « C’est du passé » / « C’est le passé » (“That’s in the past / It’s over”). With « vivre dans le passé », it means being stuck in old memories or old ways of thinking.
target_language_example: Il faut laisser le passé derrière soi.
native_language_example: You have to leave the past behind you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the person in charge at work or in a place (like a shop, restaurant, or company). It can mean your direct boss, or the owner/manager. Feminine: "la patronne".
target_language_example: Le patron n'est pas là aujourd'hui, il revient demain.
native_language_example: The boss isn't here today; he'll be back tomorrow.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the country” (a nation): quitter le pays = to leave the country. In some contexts (especially with “dans le pays de…”, or in stories like “le pays des géants”), it can mean a land/realm/region. It can also mean “the countryside” in contrast to the city, depending on context.
target_language_example: Je veux visiter le pays l'année prochaine.
native_language_example: I want to visit the country next year.

additional_notes: Masculine singular form. It can stand on its own to mean "the little/small one," as in choosing between two things. Before a noun or a person's name, petit often means "little," "small," or sometimes "young," and can sound affectionate: le petit Bryan = "little Bryan."
target_language_example: Je préfère le petit.
native_language_example: I prefer the small one.

additional_notes: The meal you have in the morning. Often used with verbs like prendre (to have/eat): « prendre le petit-déjeuner ». Can also refer to the food itself. Note the hyphen and accent: petit-déjeuner.
target_language_example: On prend le petit-déjeuner à 8 heures.
native_language_example: We have breakfast at 8 o'clock.

additional_notes: The usual French word for the morning meal. Often used with verbs like prendre (to have/eat): « prendre le petit déjeuner »; sauter (to skip): « sauter le petit déjeuner ». In hotels/restaurants you might ask if it’s included: « Le petit déjeuner est-il inclus ? ».
target_language_example: On prend le petit déjeuner à 8 h.
native_language_example: We have breakfast at 8 o’clock.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: definite article + adjective + noun. Used to refer to a specific boy (already known, mentioned, or obvious from context). In stories it can also be used more generally for “the little boy” as a character. Feminine equivalent: « la petite fille ».
target_language_example: Le petit garçon cherche sa maman.
native_language_example: The little boy is looking for his mom.

meaning: the people; the population (especially as a political/social group).
additional_notes: Often used in politics and history to mean “ordinary people” or “the nation’s citizens” seen as a collective (e.g., “le gouvernement du peuple…”). It can also refer to a specific nation/ethnic group (“le peuple chinois”, “le peuple américain”). Usually takes singular agreement in French when treated as one group: “Le peuple a choisi…”.
target_language_example: Le peuple demande plus de justice.
native_language_example: The people are demanding more justice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you’re going to do (the plan), how something is organized, or a strategy. Very common in questions like « C’est quoi, le plan ? » / « Quel est le plan ? » meaning “What’s the plan?” You can also talk about changes: « le plan a changé » (“the plan changed”). « le plan B » means “Plan B” (a backup plan).
target_language_example: On fait quoi ce soir ? C'est quoi, le plan ?
native_language_example: What are we doing tonight? What's the plan?

additional_notes: used to form the superlative: le/la/les plus + adjective or adverb means "the most" or "-est" depending on the English word (for example, le plus beau = "the most beautiful"). After a verb, it means "most" (for example, plaire le plus = "please the most"). In le plus ... possible, it gives the idea of "as ... as possible." French also often uses this form where English would say "more" when comparing two things.
target_language_example: C'est le sport que j'aime le plus.
native_language_example: It's the sport I like the most.

le plus beau jour de ma vie

target_language_multi_word_term: le plus beau jour de ma vie
meaning: the best/most beautiful day of my life.
additional_notes: A very strong, emotional way to say a day was the happiest or most wonderful in your life. Often said about a wedding, the birth of a child, or a big personal moment. You can change the possessive: "de ta vie" (of your life), "de sa vie" (of his/her life), "de notre vie" (of our life).
target_language_example: Notre mariage, c’était le plus beau jour de ma vie.
native_language_example: Our wedding was the best day of my life.

meaning: the tallest / the biggest; the greatest (most important).
additional_notes: Superlative of « grand » (tall/big/great). Used with masculine singular nouns (e.g., « le garçon le plus grand »). For feminine, it becomes « la plus grande »; for plural, « les plus grands / les plus grandes ». Can also be used in fixed expressions like « avec le plus grand soin » = “with the greatest care.”
target_language_example: Après Taro, Jiro est le garçon le plus grand.
native_language_example: After Taro, Jiro is the tallest boy.

additional_notes: Superlative of proximity: *proche* = close/near, *le plus proche* = the closest one. It agrees with the noun: **le** plus proche (masc.), **la** plus proche (fem.), **les** plus proches (plural). Common for asking where the nearest place/object is (*le supermarché le plus proche*, *le bureau de poste le plus proche*). With people it can mean emotionally closest: *De qui es-tu le plus proche ?* = Who are you closest to?
target_language_example: Où se trouve le supermarché le plus proche ?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest supermarket?

additional_notes: Superlative form of the adjective *rapide* (“fast/quick”). Use it to compare more than two things/people: *C’est le plus rapide* (“It’s the fastest”). It agrees in gender/number with what it describes: *le plus rapide* (masc. sing.), *la plus rapide* (fem. sing.), *les plus rapides* (plural). You can use it after a noun: *le moyen le plus rapide* (“the fastest way”), or on its own when the noun is understood: *Le plus rapide.* (“The fastest one.”).
target_language_example: C’est le plus rapide pour aller à l’aéroport.
native_language_example: It’s the fastest way to get to the airport.

meaning: as soon as possible; as early as possible.
additional_notes: Used to say you want something done without delay. Very common with commands and requests (e.g., Venez…, Rendez…, Téléphonez…) and with verbs like commencer (to start) or réparer (to fix). You can also shorten it to “au plus tôt” (“as soon/early as possible”).
target_language_example: Envoie-moi les documents le plus tôt possible.
native_language_example: Send me the documents as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used to urge someone to do something with maximum speed (often like “as soon as possible” when talking about coming back or arriving). It commonly follows an imperative (Cours…, Marche…) or a verb of action (revenir, venir, finir).
target_language_example: Envoie-moi les documents le plus vite possible.
native_language_example: Send me the documents as quickly as possible.

meaning: "the (meeting/gathering) point" / "the designated location for…" (e.g., le point de rendez-vous).
additional_notes: Used with a noun after « de » to specify a designated spot: « le point de rendez-vous » (meeting point), « le point de rassemblement » (assembly point), etc. In these contexts it refers to the exact place people are supposed to meet or gather.
target_language_example: Donnez-moi le point de rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Give me the meeting point.

meaning: (non standard) intended to mean “the starting point” (standard French: « le point de départ »).
additional_notes: « Le point de partir » is not idiomatic/grammatical in standard French because « partir » is a verb (“to leave”), and French uses the noun « départ » (“departure”) in this fixed expression: « le point de départ ». If you want natural French, use « le point de départ » for the starting point/basis of a trip, plan, project, or argument. The example below includes « le point de partir » only to match your requested term exactly.
target_language_example: Dans ce document, « le point de partir » est défini à la page 2 (formulation non standard).
native_language_example: In this document, “the point of leaving/starting point” is defined on page 2 (non-standard wording).

meaning: fish (the animal or fish as food).
additional_notes: Usually means “the fish” in context, and can also refer to fish in general as a category (often as food). For an unspecified amount as food, French commonly uses the partitive: « du poisson ». With « le poisson », it can sound generic (“fish, as a food/category”) or specific depending on context.
target_language_example: Elle adore le poisson.
native_language_example: She loves fish.

additional_notes: Used for a physical bridge you cross (over a river, road, valley, etc.). The plural is usually "les ponts." It’s also used in some fixed names like "le pont de Golden Gate" (the Golden Gate Bridge).
target_language_example: On traverse le pont à pied.
native_language_example: We’re crossing the bridge on foot.

meaning: power; authority; the ability to do something.
additional_notes: Usually means political or social power/authority (influence, control), but it can also mean an ability/capacity ("avoir le pouvoir de" + infinitive = "to be able/allowed to"). Often used in general statements: "Le pouvoir corrompt".
target_language_example: Il a le pouvoir de changer les choses.
native_language_example: He has the power to change things.

additional_notes: Uses the expression « par cœur » to mean “from memory / by heart.” Common with « apprendre … par cœur » (to memorize) and « connaître … par cœur » (to know by heart).
target_language_example: Je dois réciter le poème par cœur demain.
native_language_example: I have to recite the poem by heart tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used for the first person or thing in a sequence, in time, or in rank. Before a noun: le premier jour = the first day. Used on its own, it can mean 'the first one' or simply 'first'. It agrees with gender and number: la première, les premiers, les premières.
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé le premier.
native_language_example: I arrived first.

additional_notes: Used in contests/competitions to mean the highest prize or award. Common verbs with it: décrocher/obtenir/gagner le premier prix (“to win first prize”). Often followed by de + event/category: le premier prix de la compétition, le premier prix de piano.
target_language_example: Elle a gagné le premier prix du concours.
native_language_example: She won first prize in the contest.

meaning: the first train (usually the earliest train of the day).
additional_notes: Used when talking about catching the earliest available train, often in the morning (e.g., « prendre/attraper le premier train », « le premier train du matin »). It can mean the first scheduled departure on a route that day, not necessarily the first train ever.
target_language_example: Demain, je prends le premier train pour arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, I’m taking the first train to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone is the first person to perform an action. It is followed by an infinitive: « le premier à + verbe » (e.g., « le premier à arriver » = the first to arrive). It agrees with the person/thing described: « le premier à… » (masc. sing.), « la première à… » (fem. sing.), « les premiers/les premières à… » (plural).
target_language_example: Tom fut le premier à arriver.
native_language_example: Tom was the first to arrive.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the amount of money something costs. Common in shopping and negotiating (e.g., ask to lower the price). Also used in general statements about how price relates to supply/demand.
target_language_example: Quel est le prix de ce billet ?
native_language_example: What is the price of this ticket?

meaning: the problem; an issue or difficulty to deal with.
additional_notes: Very common and neutral. Use it for anything from a small technical issue to a serious situation. You can talk about its seriousness (la gravité du problème), find/spot it (repérer le problème), examine it (examiner le problème), and solve it (résoudre le problème).
target_language_example: On a trouvé le problème, maintenant il faut le résoudre.
native_language_example: We found the problem; now we have to solve it.

meaning: 'the next' (the one that comes after this one).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to refer to the next scheduled/closest one: le prochain train/vol/bus, le prochain village. It agrees with the noun: le prochain (masc.), la prochaine (fem.), les prochains/les prochaines (plural).
target_language_example: On prend le prochain métro.
native_language_example: We’ll take the next subway.

meaning: the next train (the one that leaves/arrives after the current time).
additional_notes: Used when asking about schedules or making plans at a station. You can specify a destination: "le prochain train pour Paris". In questions, French often drops "est": "À quelle heure est le prochain train ?" = "What time is the next train?"
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, le prochain train pour Lyon part de quel quai ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what platform does the next train to Lyon leave from?

additional_notes: Used for someone who teaches (especially in school or university). In French, *professeur* can mean a schoolteacher as well as a university professor. Often shortened informally to *le prof*. Feminine form: *la professeure* (also commonly *la professeur* or *la prof* depending on region/context).
target_language_example: Le professeur explique la leçon.
native_language_example: The teacher explains the lesson.

meaning: the project; a planned piece of work/initiative.
additional_notes: Used for an organized plan or undertaking (at work, school, politics, tech, etc.). Common with verbs like commencer/terminer/abandonner un projet and phrases like un projet est en cours (ongoing) or en discussion (being discussed).
target_language_example: On lance le projet lundi.
native_language_example: We’re launching the project on Monday.

meaning: the president (head of a country or organization).
additional_notes: Used for the person who leads a country (e.g., le président français) or an organization/meeting (e.g., le président du club). Often followed by "de" to specify which one: "le président de la République", "le président du conseil". "Président" can also be a title used without the person’s first name.
target_language_example: Le président du club a commencé la réunion à 18 h.
native_language_example: The club president started the meeting at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Means a group of people in general (“the public”) or the people watching/listening to a performance or event (“the audience”). Often used with singular verb forms in French (e.g., « Le public est… »), even though it refers to many people.
target_language_example: Le public a applaudi pendant plusieurs minutes.
native_language_example: The audience applauded for several minutes.

meaning: the neighborhood; a district/area of a town or city.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a part of a city where people live or a specific area/section of town. In expressions like « dans tout le quartier », it means “throughout the whole neighborhood” (everyone nearby can see/hear/know).
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé un bon café dans le quartier.
native_language_example: I found a good café in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Most often means a written report/document (e.g., “finir le rapport,” “résumer le rapport”). In questions like “C’est quoi le rapport ?” or “Quel est le rapport avec… ?”, it means “what’s the connection/what does that have to do with…?” Note: French “rapport” is a false friend—English “rapport” usually means a good relationship, which in French is more like “une bonne entente” / “de bons rapports (avec quelqu’un)”.
target_language_example: Quel est le rapport avec ce que tu viens de dire ?
native_language_example: What does that have to do with what you just said?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the remaining part of something already mentioned. Very common in expressions like « le reste de + noun » (the rest of + noun) and can also stand alone (« le reste » = what’s left).
target_language_example: Je garde un morceau et tu peux prendre le reste.
native_language_example: I’ll keep a piece and you can take the rest.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to refer to what remains after a part has been taken, used, or considered. It can refer to things (le reste de la boîte, le reste de la maison) or time (le reste de sa vie, le reste de la journée). Note that in speech and writing, "de" may contract with the following article (e.g., "le reste du gâteau" = "le reste de + le gâteau").
target_language_example: On gardera le reste de ce gâteau pour demain.
native_language_example: We’ll save the rest of this cake for tomorrow.

meaning: "the rest of the" (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to refer to what remains of something. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun: le reste de la journée (the rest of the day), le reste de la pizza (the rest of the pizza). For masculine singular, you’d use "le reste du"; for plural, "le reste des".
target_language_example: Je travaille le reste de la journée.
native_language_example: I’m working the rest of the day.

additional_notes: Used to refer to everything that happens from now until you die. Common in phrases like « Tu as le reste de ta vie devant toi » (“You have the rest of your life ahead of you”) and « passer le reste de ta vie avec… » (“to spend the rest of your life with…”). Note the possessive changes with the person: « le reste de ma vie », « le reste de sa vie », etc.
target_language_example: Tu as le reste de ta vie devant toi.
native_language_example: You have the rest of your life ahead of you.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (le reste du voyage, le reste du chemin) to mean what remains of something. For a feminine noun, use "le reste de la" (le reste de la journée). Before a vowel or silent h, use "le reste de l'" (le reste de l'eau).
target_language_example: Je garde le reste du gâteau pour demain.
native_language_example: I'm keeping the rest of the cake for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male monarch. Often appears in formal, historical, or news contexts, and can be followed by a place or title (e.g., « le roi d’Angleterre » = the King of England). Feminine: « la reine » (the queen).
target_language_example: Le roi arrive au palais ce soir.
native_language_example: The king is arriving at the palace tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens in the end (the outcome of an action, event, effort, test, etc.). Often followed by "de" to show the cause: "le résultat de ..." (the result of ...).
target_language_example: Au final, le résultat n'était pas celui qu'on espérait.
native_language_example: In the end, the result wasn’t what we were hoping for.

additional_notes: Used for sand in general (beach sand, desert sand, sand blown by the wind, etc.). It’s a masculine noun: le sable. You commonly see it with prepositions like sur (on) or dans (in): sur le sable, dans le sable. With an unspecified quantity, French often uses the partitive (du sable), but you’ll still use le sable when referring to sand as a defined substance or in general statements.
target_language_example: Le sable sur la plage est très chaud.
native_language_example: The sand on the beach is very hot.

additional_notes: Common word for a bag (plastic bag, shopping bag, backpack, etc.). Used with a specific bag known from context: Où est le sac ? = “Where is the bag?” Can be modified: un sac en plastique (a plastic bag).
target_language_example: Tu peux porter le sac, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you carry the bag, please?

additional_notes: In a home, *le salon* is the main room where people relax, sit on the sofa, watch TV, and receive guests. Don’t confuse it with *la salle à manger* (dining room). *Salon* can also mean a “salon” (e.g., hair salon or an event), but in everyday home contexts it usually means “living room.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve dans le salon après le dîner.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in the living room after dinner.

additional_notes: Used literally for blood in the body or from a wound. Common in fixed expressions and idioms (e.g., “Ça me fait bouillir le sang” = “It makes my blood boil,” i.e., it makes me very angry). Note: in many everyday contexts French also uses the partitive “du sang” (“there was blood”), but the definite form “le sang” is used for blood as a general substance or concept (“Le sang circule…”).
target_language_example: Le sang circule à travers les veines.
native_language_example: Blood circulates through the veins.

additional_notes: Used for something hidden or kept private (a fact, plan, or explanation). Common with verbs like garder (to keep), connaître (to know), découvrir (to discover), révéler / dévoiler (to reveal). Often followed by de + noun to specify what it’s about: le secret de + [something].
target_language_example: Je te dirai le secret, mais promets de ne rien dire.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you the secret, but promise not to say anything.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or explain what something means: *le sens de cette phrase/ce mot/cette image*. In more concrete contexts, *le sens de* can also mean the direction or orientation of something (e.g., *le sens de la marche* = direction of travel).
target_language_example: Quel est le sens de ce mot ?
native_language_example: What is the meaning of this word?

additional_notes: Uses the noun "sens" meaning "meaning" or "purpose" (not just physical direction). Common in philosophical or reflective contexts; you can also hear "le sens de ma/ta/sa vie" for "the meaning of my/your/his/her life."
target_language_example: Il se demande quel est le sens de la vie.
native_language_example: He wonders what the meaning of life is.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is unique in a group. Often followed by a noun: « le seul moyen » (“the only way”). It can also stand alone to mean “the only one”: « Tu es bien le seul » (“You really are the only one”). Changes with gender/number: « la seule », « les seuls », « les seules ».
target_language_example: C'est le seul moyen d'être sûr.
native_language_example: It's the only way to be sure.

meaning: the only one to / the only one who can.
additional_notes: Used to say that one person (or thing) is unique in doing something. It’s followed by an infinitive (often with pouvoir, avoir, être, etc.). It agrees in gender/number: le seul à (m. sing.), la seule à (f. sing.), les seuls à (m. pl.), les seules à (f. pl.). You can negate it: ne pas être le seul à… (“not be the only one to…”).
target_language_example: Il est le seul à pouvoir le faire.
native_language_example: He is the only one who can do it.

le seul à ne pas être invité à

target_language_multi_word_term: le seul à ne pas être invité à
meaning: the only one not to be invited to
additional_notes: Used to say someone was uniquely excluded from an event. Structure: **le seul** (“the only one”) + **à ne pas être** (“to not be”) + **invité à** (“invited to”). Adjust for gender/number as needed: **la seule**, **les seuls/les seules**; and the past participle agrees: **invité** (m.), **invitée** (f.), **invités/invitées** (pl.). Typically followed by the event: **à la fête / à la soirée / au mariage**.
target_language_example: Il a été le seul à ne pas être invité à la fête.
native_language_example: He was the only one not invited to the party.

meaning: his/hers/its/theirs (the one that belongs to him/her/it/them).
additional_notes: "Le sien" is a possessive pronoun (masculine singular) that replaces a noun: "Mon bureau… le sien" = "my office… his/hers." It agrees with the thing owned (masc. sing. = le sien), not with the owner. Other forms: la sienne (fem. sing.), les siens / les siennes (plural). It can refer to different people depending on context (his, hers, theirs).
target_language_example: Je prends mon manteau et il prend le sien.
native_language_example: I’m taking my coat and he’s taking his.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning the absence of sound or speech. Often used with verbs like garder le silence (to keep silent), régner (to reign/prevail: “silence fell”), or in more abstract phrases about dignity/wisdom (in silence).
target_language_example: Après l'annonce, le silence a régné dans la salle.
native_language_example: After the announcement, silence filled the room.

additional_notes: Usually means the surface you walk on. Indoors it’s the floor; outdoors it’s the ground/soil. Common with verbs like regarder (look at), balayer (sweep), and être recouvert de (to be covered with).
target_language_example: J’ai fait tomber mes clés par terre : elles sont sur le sol.
native_language_example: I dropped my keys on the ground: they’re on the floor/ground.

additional_notes: A very common noun used when talking about daylight and times of day. Often used with verbs like se lever (to rise) and se coucher (to set): « Le soleil se lève » / « Le soleil se couche ».
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, le soleil brille.
native_language_example: Today, the sun is shining.

additional_notes: A simple present-tense statement about sunny weather. It can be used literally (about the weather) or more figuratively to mean things are going well (“the sun shines for everyone”). For questions, you often invert the verb: “Le soleil brille-t-il dehors ?”
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, le soleil brille et il fait doux.
native_language_example: Today, the sun is shining and it’s mild.

meaning: 'the sun is' (used to describe the sun).
additional_notes: "Le soleil" means "the sun". "est" is the verb "to be" (il/elle/on est). You use "le soleil est" before an adjective (e.g., grand, rouge, important) or before a place phrase with "dans/au-dessus de" to say where the sun is.
target_language_example: Le soleil est très chaud aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The sun is very hot today.

meaning: “the sun …” (commonly: rises = se lève; sets = se couche).
additional_notes: This is the fixed way to talk about sunrise/sunset in French: **le soleil se lève** (the sun rises) and **le soleil se couche** (the sun sets). The **se** is part of these verbs in French (reflexive form), even though English doesn’t use “itself.”
target_language_example: Le soleil se couche tard en été.
native_language_example: The sun sets late in summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about sunrise as a general fact, a regular event, or something happening now. The verb is reflexive: « se lever » = “to rise / to get up.” You can change the time: « Le soleil se lève à 6 h. » (at 6).
target_language_example: On part tôt, quand le soleil se lève.
native_language_example: We’re leaving early, when the sun rises.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the highest point (peak) of a mountain. Often used with verbs like voir (to see), atteindre (to reach), and être couvert de (to be covered with).
target_language_example: Après trois heures de marche, nous avons atteint le sommet de la montagne.
native_language_example: After three hours of hiking, we reached the top of the mountain.

additional_notes: Refers to sound in general, the sound produced by something ("le son de la radio"), or the audio/volume setting on a device ("Mettre le son", "baisser le son"). Common with adjectives like "fort" (loud) and "faible" (quiet/low).
target_language_example: Le son est trop fort, tu peux le baisser ?
native_language_example: The sound is too loud—can you turn it down?

meaning: breathless; with your breath taken away (or held).
additional_notes: Literally “(the) breath cut off.” Used to describe being unable to breathe normally for a moment because of strong emotion (shock, fear, amazement) or from physical effort. Often appears as: « avoir le souffle coupé » (to be breathless / have your breath taken away) or « attendre, le souffle coupé » (to wait, holding your breath).
target_language_example: En voyant le prix, j’ai eu le souffle coupé.
native_language_example: When I saw the price, it took my breath away.

meaning: the show; the performance (a play, concert, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for an event people watch, especially in the performing arts (concert, theater, comedy show). In fixed phrases like « Que le spectacle commence ! » it means “Let the show begin!” Can also refer more broadly to a “spectacle” (something impressive to watch), but the common beginner meaning is “show/performance.”
target_language_example: Êtes-vous prêts pour le spectacle ?
native_language_example: Are you ready for the show?

meaning: the system (an organized way things work; an organization; a computer/technical system).
additional_notes: Used for a structured set of rules/processes (e.g., school/healthcare/the political system), a technical setup (IT system), or “how things work” in a place (“connaître le système” = know the ropes). In phrases like “Nique le système”, it refers to “the system” as an institution and the tone is vulgar/defiant, but the term “le système” itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas bien le système, tu peux m’expliquer ?
native_language_example: I don’t really understand the system—can you explain it to me?

additional_notes: Most commonly means a painting/artwork (like one hanging on a wall). It can also mean a board used for writing ("le tableau" in a classroom) or a chart/table in documents, depending on context.
target_language_example: J’aime beaucoup le tableau : les couleurs sont magnifiques.
native_language_example: I really like the painting: the colors are beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the language called Tamazight. In French, languages are often used with the definite article (le / la / l’): e.g., le français, l’anglais. You can use it with verbs like parler (to speak), apprendre (to learn), lire (to read), pratiquer (to practice).
target_language_example: J'apprends le tamazight en ligne.
native_language_example: I'm learning Tamazight online.

additional_notes: French uses the same word for both 'time' and 'weather'. In expressions like avoir le temps and prendre le temps de, it means 'time' or 'enough time'; with words like beau, mauvais, changer, or permettre, it means 'weather'.
target_language_example: Tu as le temps de prendre un café ?
native_language_example: Do you have time to grab a coffee?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say whether someone has enough time to do something. Often in the negative: « ne pas avoir le temps de + infinitive » = “not to have time to…”. Can also be used in questions and the future: « Tu as le temps de… ? » / « Vous aurez le temps de… ».
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas le temps de t'appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to call you tonight.

meaning: "the weather is…" or "time is…" (it depends on context).
additional_notes: Le temps can mean either (1) "weather" (talking about conditions outside: Le temps est horrible / Le temps est à la neige), or (2) "time" in a general or abstract sense (Le temps est précieux; Le temps est écoulé). In English, you usually choose either “The weather is…” or “Time is…”, not “The time is…” unless you mean the clock time.
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, le temps est très froid.
native_language_example: Today, the weather is very cold.

meaning: "lost time" (time that was wasted or missed).
additional_notes: Often used with rattraper: rattraper le temps perdu = “to make up for lost time” (by working harder, going faster, etc.). It can also express regret: Le temps perdu ne se rattrape jamais (“Lost time can never be made up”).
target_language_example: Après sa maladie, il a essayé de rattraper le temps perdu.
native_language_example: After his illness, he tried to make up for lost time.

meaning: “the time it takes for him/it to…” / “by the time he/it…”; also appears in the fixed phrase “le temps qu’il fait” = “the weather (outside).”
additional_notes: Used to express a delay before something happens, often followed by the subjunctive: “Le temps qu'il comprenne…” ≈ “By the time he understands…” / “It’ll take him a while to understand…”. In expressions like “Prenez le temps qu'il vous faudra”, it means “as much time as needed” (“whatever time you need”). Note: in “le temps qu’il fait”, the meaning is idiomatic (“the weather”), not “the time that it does.”
target_language_example: Le temps qu'il arrive, on aura déjà fini.
native_language_example: By the time he gets here, we’ll already be done.

meaning: "the time that" / "the amount of time that" (how long something takes).
additional_notes: Used before a clause to talk about duration: *le temps que + verb* = “the time it takes for…” / “the amount of time that…”. Common in expressions like **Peu importe le temps que ça prend/prendra** (“No matter how long it takes”).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas le temps que ça va prendre.
native_language_example: I don’t know how long it’s going to take.

additional_notes: Means "tea" as a drink. Used with the definite article (le) when speaking about tea in general or as the item being discussed/served. In "prendre le thé," it often means having tea (and sometimes a small snack) as an afternoon break or social moment.
target_language_example: Je prends souvent le thé après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: I often have tea after lunch.

meaning: yours (the one that belongs to you).
additional_notes: "Le tien" is a possessive pronoun used instead of repeating the noun: *mon stylo → le tien* (“my pen → yours”). It agrees with the thing possessed, not the person: masculine singular = **le tien**; feminine singular = **la tienne**; masculine plural = **les tiens**; feminine plural = **les tiennes**. Often used with *lequel/quel* (“which/what one?”): *Lequel est le tien ?*
target_language_example: Je prends le mien, et toi, tu prends le tien.
native_language_example: I’m taking mine, and you’re taking yours.

additional_notes: Used for the roof of a house/building (also of a car). In sentences it often appears with building-related verbs like réparer (repair), renforcer (reinforce), arracher (tear off), or with damage words like défoncé (caved in/damaged).
target_language_example: Il faut réparer le toit avant l'hiver.
native_language_example: We need to repair the roof before winter.

meaning: a trip around the world; (figuratively) to go viral / be shared worldwide.
additional_notes: "Faire le tour du monde" literally means "to make the tour of the world" and most often means traveling around the world. It can also be used figuratively to say that news, a photo, or a story spread everywhere (went around the world).
target_language_example: Cette vidéo a fait le tour du monde en deux jours.
native_language_example: That video went around the world in two days.

meaning: everything on the line; an all-or-nothing move (go all in).
additional_notes: Most often used with the verb "jouer": "jouer le tout pour le tout" = to risk everything to try to win/succeed. It suggests a last-ditch effort where you have little to lose or you’re ready to bet it all.
target_language_example: Pour sauver l’entreprise, ils ont décidé de jouer le tout pour le tout.
native_language_example: To save the company, they decided to go all in.

additional_notes: A common travel noun. Used with verbs like prendre (to take), rater (to miss), attraper (to catch), partir (to leave/depart), arriver (to arrive). Often mentioned with la gare (the station) and le quai (the platform).
target_language_example: On va prendre le train de 9 h 15 à la gare.
native_language_example: We’re going to take the 9:15 train at the station.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (était) + past participle (parti) to express the past perfect idea (“had left”) in a past context. Often used with time markers like lorsque/quand (“when”) to show one past event happened before another. Parti agrees with the subject: le train était déjà parti (masc.); la voiture était déjà partie (fem.).
target_language_example: Désolé, le train était déjà parti quand on est arrivés.
native_language_example: Sorry, the train had already left when we arrived.

meaning: work; the job; the task/work to be done.
additional_notes: Often refers either to work in general (employment) or to a specific piece of work/a task (e.g., a project, an assignment). With verbs like faire/finir/terminer, it usually means “the work/the task.”
target_language_example: Je dois finir le travail avant ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to finish the work before tonight.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term for an earthquake. It’s masculine (le). Often used with verbs like provoquer (cause), secouer (shake), détruire (destroy), arriver (happen/occur), and ressentir (feel).
target_language_example: Après le tremblement de terre, les gens sont sortis dans la rue.
native_language_example: After the earthquake, people went out into the street.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a phone in general or a specific phone depending on context (e.g., "C'est le téléphone de qui ?" = “Whose phone is this?”). Common with verbs like décrocher (to pick up/answer), sonner (to ring), fonctionner (to work), and expressions like "au téléphone" (on the phone).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas répondre : le téléphone ne fonctionne pas.
native_language_example: I can't answer: the phone isn't working.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "sonner" for a phone ringing. Used to describe a completed event (often with a time marker like "quelques minutes plus tard") or an event that interrupts another action in progress (often with "pendant que" + imparfait).
target_language_example: Je lisais quand le téléphone a sonné.
native_language_example: I was reading when the phone rang.

additional_notes: "Sonna" is the simple past (passé simple) of *sonner*. It’s common in stories and written narration, but in everyday speech you usually say *le téléphone a sonné* (passé composé).
target_language_example: Au moment où je m'endormais, le téléphone sonna.
native_language_example: Just as I was falling asleep, the phone rang.

additional_notes: Used for wind in weather or as a force that blows (souffler) and can carry things away (emporter) or knock things over (renverser). You’ll often see it with verbs like « souffler » (to blow) and adjectives like « violent » (strong/violent).
target_language_example: Attention, le vent est très fort aujourd'hui !
native_language_example: Watch out, the wind is very strong today!

additional_notes: A common weather phrase. "souffler" means "to blow" (also "to breathe" or "to blow out" a candle). You can add details like where/from where: "Le vent souffle sous la porte" (under the door), "Le vent souffle de l'est" (from the east), or intensity: "Le vent souffle fort" (the wind is blowing hard).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, le vent souffle très fort sur la côte.
native_language_example: Today, the wind is blowing very hard on the coast.

additional_notes: Refers to the abdomen area. Common in phrases like « sur le ventre » (on your stomach/belly, i.e., lying face down), « avoir le ventre plein » (to have a full stomach), and in the idiom « avoir les yeux plus gros que le ventre » (to take more food than you can eat).
target_language_example: Après le déjeuner, j’ai le ventre plein.
native_language_example: After lunch, I have a full stomach.

additional_notes: "Vieil" is the form of "vieux" used before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel sound (often a vowel or silent h), like "homme". You’ll also hear "un vieil homme" (“an old man”).
target_language_example: J'ai aidé le vieil homme à traverser la rue.
native_language_example: I helped the old man cross the street.

additional_notes: Masculine noun (vin). With the definite article, **le vin** can mean wine as a general category (e.g., as a drink) or a specific wine understood from context (e.g., the bottle on the table). Often contrasts with **du vin** (some wine) and **un vin** (a particular wine/a type of wine). Common with verbs like **boire** (to drink), **aimer** (to like), **apporter** (to bring), **goûter** (to taste).
target_language_example: Aimes-tu le vin français ?
native_language_example: Do you like French wine?

additional_notes: A masculine noun for someone who steals (female: "la voleuse"). Often used with "arrêter" (to arrest/stop) and in the common shout "Arrêtez le voleur !" = "Stop the thief!". "Voleur" usually means thief; for an armed robbery you may also hear "un braqueur".
target_language_example: La police cherche le voleur depuis hier.
native_language_example: The police have been looking for the thief since yesterday.

meaning: the trip; the journey (travel from one place to another).
additional_notes: Used for a trip or journey in general (by any means: car, train, plane, etc.). Often appears with adjectives like long/court/ennuyeux and in expressions like « bon voyage ! » (have a good trip).
target_language_example: Le voyage en train dure trois heures.
native_language_example: The train trip takes three hours.

additional_notes: A possessive pronoun used to replace a noun: *le vôtre* = “yours” for a masculine singular thing (with *le*). Often used in comparisons (*que le vôtre* = “than yours”) or questions (*Où est le vôtre ?* = “Where is yours?”). Agree with what is owned: *la vôtre* (feminine singular), *les vôtres* (plural), and it also changes with who owns it (*le mien* = mine, *le sien* = his/hers).
target_language_example: J’ai pris mon sac et j’ai laissé le vôtre sur la table.
native_language_example: I took my bag and left yours on the table.

additional_notes: Very common borrowing from English. Used with the masculine article: le week-end. Often appears with prepositions like pendant/durant le week-end (during the weekend), avant le week-end (before the weekend), and with verbs like passer le week-end (to spend the weekend).
target_language_example: On se voit le week-end ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other this weekend?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend most recently before now. Often placed at the end of the sentence as a time expression. "Week-end" is a common borrowed word in French; you may also hear "le dernier week-end" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Je me suis reposé le week-end dernier.
native_language_example: I rested last weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend that is coming up (the one after this week). Often placed at the end of the sentence as a time expression. You can also hear/see the spelling "le weekend prochain" (without the hyphen).
target_language_example: On se voit le week-end prochain ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other next weekend?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend that comes next (the upcoming weekend). Often placed at the end of the sentence as a time expression: « On se voit le week-end prochain. » You can also use it alone as a short reply or to confirm plans: « Le week-end prochain ? »
target_language_example: On fait un barbecue le week-end prochain.
native_language_example: We’re having a barbecue next weekend.

meaning: 'it to me' / '...to me' (pronoun combo meaning “... it to me”).
additional_notes: Used with commands (the imperative) when you tell someone to give/show/pass something to you. French attaches object pronouns with hyphens: verb + direct object pronoun + indirect object pronoun: « Expliquez-le-moi » = “Explain it to me.” The « le » can also change to « la » (it/her) or « les » (them): « Donne-la-moi », « Montre-les-moi ».
target_language_example: Donne-le-moi tout de suite.
native_language_example: Give it to me right away.

meaning: to go get him/it; to fetch him/it.
additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it” (masculine), referring to something already known from context. With verbs like "aller", "venir", "falloir" (e.g., "Allez le chercher", "Elle est venue le chercher", "Il faut aller le chercher"), it commonly means “go and get/fetch/pick up” rather than simply “look for.”
target_language_example: J'arrive, je vais le chercher.
native_language_example: I’m coming, I’m going to get it (or: him).

additional_notes: This is the tu form of connaître with the direct object pronoun le placed before the verb. Le can refer to a masculine person or thing, so the exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Tu le connais depuis longtemps ?
native_language_example: Have you known him for a long time?

additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (often referring to a fact, story, or what someone just said). With people, "le" can also mean "him". The pronoun comes before the verb: "Je ne peux pas le croire" = "I can’t believe it."
target_language_example: Je n'arrive pas à le croire.
native_language_example: I can’t believe it.

additional_notes: From the verb dire (to say/tell) in the future tense: je dirai = “I will say/tell”. The pronoun le (“it”) comes before the verb: je le dirai = “I’ll say it / I’ll tell you (it)”. Often used with an indirect object (à maman, à tout le monde) or with te/vous in the pattern: je te/vous le dirai = “I’ll tell you (it)”. Negation wraps around the verb: je ne le dirai pas / je ne le dirai jamais.
target_language_example: Je te le dirai plus tard.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you later.

additional_notes: `le` is the direct object pronoun meaning “it,” “that,” or sometimes “so,” placed before `dire`. It refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. Depending on the sentence, English may use “say it,” “say that,” or “say so”; with another pronoun, `me le dire` can mean “tell me.”
target_language_example: Je n'ose pas le dire.
native_language_example: I don't dare say it.

meaning: to say it earlier / to have said it sooner.
additional_notes: "Le" means "it" (referring to something already known from context). With a pronoun like "le", French puts it before the verb: "le dire" = "to say it". This phrase often appears with the conditional perfect to express regret: "J'aurais dû le dire plus tôt" (I should have said it earlier).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, j'aurais dû le dire plus tôt.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, I should have said it earlier.

additional_notes: Used with a direct object pronoun (often "le" = "it") before "dire", and "à" introduces the person you’re telling: « le dire à mes parents » = “tell it to my parents.” In questions you’ll often see « Comment/Quand/Pourquoi le dire à… ? ».
target_language_example: Je vais le dire à Marie ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell Marie tonight.

meaning: to tell no one (not to tell anyone).
additional_notes: Used with a negation: **ne ... le dire à personne** = “not to tell it to anyone / to tell no one.” **Le** is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” and comes before the verb (**le dire**). Common patterns include: **ne pas vouloir le dire à personne**, **ne pas devoir le dire à personne**, **partir sans le dire à personne**, **se souvenir de ne le dire à personne**. In formal negation you may also see **ne ... à personne** (without *pas*) in some styles.
target_language_example: Tu ne dois le dire à personne.
native_language_example: You mustn’t tell anyone.

additional_notes: “Le” is a direct-object pronoun that replaces what you’re saying (a fact, an opinion, a whole sentence). It’s very common after verbs like dire: « Je le dis » (“I’m saying so / I’m telling you”), « Je te/le lui dis » (“I tell you/him/her”), « Puisque tu le dis » (“If you say so”). Often translated naturally as “I’m telling you” rather than a literal “I say it.”
target_language_example: Je te le dis franchement : ça ne marchera pas.
native_language_example: I’m telling you honestly: it won’t work.

meaning: it/this again; it/this one more time (i.e., do it again).
additional_notes: This sequence is intended to express repeating an action with a direct object pronoun (“le” = “it”). In standard written French, the pronoun is normally hyphenated to the verb (e.g., « Explique-le encore une fois. », « Lis-le encore une fois. »).
target_language_example: Explique le encore une fois, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Explain it one more time, please.

additional_notes: Used when le stands for a thing, action, or idea already understood from context. In French, the object pronoun comes before the infinitive, so you get le faire where English says do it.
target_language_example: On va le faire ensemble.
native_language_example: We're going to do it together.

additional_notes: “Le” is an object pronoun meaning “it” (the thing/action previously mentioned). It usually refers to doing something (an action), not a physical object. Word order: verb + object pronoun (“faire” → “le faire”). Often used after another verb like “pouvoir,” “devoir,” “vouloir,” “falloir”: “Je peux/dois/veux le faire maintenant.”
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas le faire maintenant.
native_language_example: I can't do it now.

additional_notes:
Used to say you will do something on your own rather than have someone else do it. 
- le = “it” (the object)
- faire = “to do/make”
- moi-même = “myself” (emphatic)
Common with modal/auxiliary verbs: je peux/veux/dois/devrais/vais le faire moi-même.
target_language_example: Merci, mais je vais le faire moi-même.
native_language_example: Thanks, but I’m going to do it myself.

additional_notes: "le" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (the thing you’re talking about). "faire" = "to do/make". Used to ask someone to perform a task on your behalf. With questions or polite forms: "Peux-tu le faire pour moi ?" (casual) and "Pourriez-vous… le faire pour moi ?" (more formal).
target_language_example: Tu peux le faire pour moi, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you do it for me, please?

meaning: to do it immediately; right away (on the spot).
additional_notes: "Sur-le-champ" means "immediately / at once" and is often used after the verb: "Fais-le sur-le-champ." You can use it with many verbs (not just "faire"): "venir sur-le-champ" (come right away), "partir sur-le-champ" (leave immediately).
target_language_example: Je vais le faire sur-le-champ.
native_language_example: I'm going to do it right away.

meaning: to do it all by yourself (alone).
additional_notes: "Le" refers back to a previously mentioned thing (it = le). "Faire" means "to do/make". "Tout seul" emphasizes that you do it without help; for a woman you often hear "toute seule".
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je vais le faire tout seul.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to do it all by myself.

additional_notes: Used with the verb faire in the present tense (fais = 'do/make') plus the direct object pronoun le ('it'). Word order: the pronoun goes before the verb (je le fais = I do it; tu le fais = you do it). It can also replace an entire action already understood from context (e.g., plus tôt que je ne le fais = earlier than I do).
target_language_example: Je le fais pour t’aider.
native_language_example: I’m doing it to help you.

meaning: "don’t do it" (informal shortening of "ne le fais pas").
additional_notes: This is the negative imperative of "faire" with the object pronoun "le" (= it): "(Ne) le fais pas." In everyday speech, French often drops "ne", so you may hear "Le fais pas" instead of "Ne le fais pas." It can also appear in other persons as "tu le fais pas" (= you don’t do it).
target_language_example: Le fais pas, tu vas le regretter.
native_language_example: Don’t do it—you’ll regret it.

meaning: 'do it' (subjunctive form, as in 'that someone do it').
additional_notes: Made of the direct object pronoun **le** (“it”) + **fasse** (subjunctive of **faire**, “to do/make”). It’s used after triggers like **il faut que...** (“it’s necessary that...”) or **vouloir que...** (“to want that...”), often implying a wish/need for someone to do a specific thing previously mentioned. Example pattern: **Je veux qu’il le fasse.** = “I want him to do it.”
target_language_example: Il faut que je le fasse aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have to do it today.

additional_notes: “Fera” is the simple future of *faire* (to do/make). The pronoun *le* (“it” or sometimes “him”) goes before the verb: *Il le fera* = “He will do it.” With negation: *ne le fera pas* = “won’t do it.”
target_language_example: Je le ferai demain.
native_language_example: I’ll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Formed with the direct object pronoun **le** (“it”) + **ferai** (future tense of *faire*, “to do/make”): **je le ferai** = “I’ll do it.” **Le** refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. In the negative, it’s usually **je ne le ferai pas** (“I won’t do it”).
target_language_example: D’accord, je le ferai demain.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or "him" depending on context), placed before the verb. "Ferais" is the conditional form of *faire* (je ferais = I would do), used for hypothetical situations, doubts, or something imagined rather than certain.
target_language_example: À ta place, je le ferais tout de suite.
native_language_example: In your place, I would do it right away.

additional_notes: "Le" is an object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" (replacing a masculine noun or a baby/child/pet referred to as "he"). "Garder" often means: keep (don’t throw away: « Je vais le garder »), keep for yourself (« Garde-le pour toi / Veuillez le garder pour vous »), keep/hold onto (« Vous pouvez le garder » = you can keep it), look after/babysit (« Je ne pourrai pas le garder demain »), or keep someone awake (« le garder éveillé »). Word order: the pronoun usually comes before the verb (je le garde, on peut le garder ?).
target_language_example: Si tu veux, tu peux le garder jusqu’à demain.
native_language_example: If you want, you can keep it until tomorrow.

meaning: 'to keep it secret' / 'to keep it confidential'.
additional_notes: Used when “le” refers back to something already mentioned (a fact, plan, message, etc.). Often appears with modal verbs (pouvoir, devoir) and in polite requests (Veuillez...). Word order is fixed here: object pronoun “le” + infinitive “garder” + adjective “secret”.
target_language_example: Tu devrais le garder secret.
native_language_example: You should keep it secret.

additional_notes: Used to strongly insist that something is true or to reassure someone. In this common structure, **te** = "to you" and **le** = "it/that" (what you’re swearing about). You can also say **Je le jure** ("I swear it") without **te**.
target_language_example: Je te le jure, je n’ai rien fait.
native_language_example: I swear to you, I didn’t do anything.

additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (referring to a fact/claim). It usually goes before the verb: « Je peux le prouver. » = "I can prove it." You can also add an indirect object: « te le prouver » = "prove it to you". In questions: « Pouvez-vous le prouver ? » = "Can you prove it?"
target_language_example: Je vais le prouver demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to prove it tomorrow.

meaning: to do it again; to redo it.
additional_notes: “Le” is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it” (something already mentioned). “Refaire” means “to do again / redo,” and it’s often used when repeating a task, restarting an activity, or fixing something by doing it over. In other tenses: « Je l’ai refait » (I did it again), « Je vais le refaire » (I’m going to redo it).
target_language_example: J’ai raté l’exercice, je vais le refaire.
native_language_example: I messed up the exercise, I’m going to do it again.

meaning: to meet him / to meet it.
additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” (or sometimes “it”), placed before the verb. With an infinitive, it comes right before the infinitive: "Je veux le rencontrer" (“I want to meet him”). In questions, it stays in the same place: "Tu veux le rencontrer ?"
target_language_example: Je vais le rencontrer demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to meet him tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb savoir plus the direct object pronoun le (“it/that”) to say you know a fact or piece of information. It changes with the subject: je le sais (I know), tu le sais (you know), il/elle le sait (he/she knows), etc. In questions: Comment tu le sais ? = How do you know (that)? In the negative: Je ne le sais pas = I don’t know (it/that).
target_language_example: Je le sais, mais je ne peux pas te le dire.
native_language_example: I know, but I can’t tell you.
