additional_notes: Used to say someone is doing poorly, often because of illness, exhaustion, injury, or emotional distress. It can also describe a situation or thing that is in poor condition (more figurative). Often used with "être" (Il est mal en point) or "trouver" (Je l’ai trouvé mal en point).
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, j’étais vraiment mal en point.
native_language_example: After the hike, I was really in bad shape.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: « avoir le mal de mer » = to be seasick. Often appears with « contre » when talking about remedies: « des médicaments contre le mal de mer ».
target_language_example: J'ai le mal de mer, je préfère rester sur le pont.
native_language_example: I’m seasick; I’d rather stay on deck.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: « J’ai mal à la tête » (My head hurts / I have a headache). With a specific headache, use the article: « un mal de tête » (a headache), « le mal de tête » (the headache), « du mal de tête » after some verbs like « souffrir de » (to suffer from).
target_language_example: J’ai un mal de tête, je vais prendre un cachet.
native_language_example: I have a headache, I’m going to take a pill.

additional_notes: Used to say you miss your home/country while you’re away. Often used with the verb « avoir »: « avoir le mal du pays » (to be homesick).
target_language_example: Depuis que je suis à l’étranger, j’ai le mal du pays.
native_language_example: Since I’ve been abroad, I’ve been homesick.

meaning: harm to (someone), typically in « faire du/de mal à (quelqu’un) » = to hurt/to harm (someone).
additional_notes: Used most often with « faire »: « faire du mal à quelqu’un » can mean to hurt someone physically or emotionally. In negative sentences, « du » often becomes « de »: « ne pas faire de mal à … ». Common fixed expression: « Il ne ferait pas de mal à une mouche » = He wouldn’t hurt a fly.
target_language_example: Je ne ferai jamais de mal à personne.
native_language_example: I will never hurt anyone.

meaning: a headache; to have a headache.
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: avoir mal à la tête = “to have a headache.” You can change the body part: avoir mal au ventre (stomachache), avoir mal au dos (back pain), etc. Often asked as a question: Tu as mal à la tête ?
target_language_example: J'ai mal à la tête, je vais prendre un comprimé.
native_language_example: I have a headache; I'm going to take a pill.

meaning: a mentally ill person (often offensive as an insult).
additional_notes: Literally “mental patient / mentally ill.” In everyday speech, calling someone "un malade mental" can sound harsh and stigmatizing (similar to “a mental case”); it’s often used as an insult. In neutral/medical or respectful contexts, French more often uses wording like "une personne atteinte de troubles mentaux" or "une personne souffrant de troubles psychiques" (or "une personne avec un trouble mental").
target_language_example: Traiter quelqu’un de « malade mental » est très insultant.
native_language_example: Calling someone a “mentally ill person” is very insulting.

meaning: "despite the rain" / "in spite of the rain".
additional_notes: Used to say something happened even though the rain was a difficulty. It can go at the start of the sentence ("Malgré la pluie, ...") or after the verb ("... malgré la pluie"). In general, "malgré" is followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., "malgré le froid", "malgré ça").
target_language_example: Malgré la pluie, ils sont allés au marché.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, they went to the market.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or someone decides to do something despite obstacles, doubts, or what was said before. It often sums up a contrast: a negative point + malgré tout + the final result/decision.
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, mais je vais sortir malgré tout.
native_language_example: I'm tired, but I'm going to go out anyway.

additional_notes: A formal/legal document (issued by a judge or authority) that authorizes police to search a place (home, office, etc.) and sometimes to seize evidence. Often used with verbs like obtenir/demander/avoir un mandat de perquisition.
target_language_example: La police a obtenu un mandat de perquisition pour fouiller l'appartement.
native_language_example: The police obtained a search warrant to search the apartment.

additional_notes: This is the verb phrase "manger" (to eat) in the present tense: "il/elle/on mange" = "he/she/one eats." "Souvent" (often) usually goes after the verb. "Du poisson" means "(some) fish" in general (not a specific fish). You can swap the subject: "Je mange souvent du poisson" (I often eat fish).
target_language_example: Il mange souvent du poisson le vendredi.
native_language_example: He often eats fish on Fridays.

additional_notes: Common, flexible phrase used to say you need/want/should eat (some unspecified food). Often appears with modals or polite questions: « Il faut… » (you have to), « je veux… » (I want to), « tu devrais… » (you should), « pourrais-je… ? » (could I…?), « voulez-vous… ? » (would you like to…?). You can add details after it, e.g., « quelque chose de salé / de sucré » (something salty/sweet).
target_language_example: On va manger quelque chose avant le cinéma.
native_language_example: We’re going to eat something before the movie.

meaning: “is/are … missing?” / “is there … missing?”; also “do you miss …?” (with a person as the subject).
additional_notes:
This is the question form (inversion) of **il manque** (“… is missing / lacking”). With **manquer**, French often flips what English does: the **thing/person that is missing** is the subject, and the person who feels the lack is an **indirect object**.
- **Combien de chaises manque-t-il ?** = “How many chairs are missing?”
- **Tom te manque-t-il ?** literally “Is Tom missing to you?” = “Do you miss Tom?”
The **-t-** is just a linking sound used in inversion when needed; it doesn’t change the meaning.
target_language_example: Tom te manque-t-il ?
native_language_example: Do you miss Tom?

additional_notes: Used for reversing a car (“en marche arrière” = in reverse). As a fixed expression with the verb “faire” (“faire marche arrière”), it also means to backtrack or change your mind/decision after moving forward with something.
target_language_example: Il a mis la voiture en marche arrière.
native_language_example: He put the car in reverse.

additional_notes: Short for **ne marche pas** in casual speech (the **ne** is often dropped). With devices/machines, **ça/il/elle marche pas** usually means “it doesn’t work.” With a person/animal, it can mean “(he/she) doesn’t walk.” Context tells you which meaning fits.
target_language_example: Mon ordinateur marche pas aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: My computer isn’t working today.

additional_notes: Literally “to walk on four paws/legs.” Used for babies, animals, or adults moving on hands and knees. Often interchangeable with "ramper" (to crawl), but "à quatre pattes" specifically means moving on hands and knees (on all fours).
target_language_example: Le bébé commence à marcher à quatre pattes dans le salon.
native_language_example: The baby is starting to crawl in the living room.

additional_notes: Used to accept an offer or confirm an agreement, often said on its own after negotiating (like “Agreed” / “Done”). You can also say it as a question ("Marché conclu ?") to check that the other person agrees. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Tu me le prêtes pour le week-end ? — Marché conclu.
native_language_example: Will you lend it to me for the weekend? — It’s a deal.

meaning: the black market (illegal buying and selling).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition « au »: « au marché noir » = “on the black market.” Refers to trade that happens illegally (often to avoid taxes, bans, or regulations).
target_language_example: On trouve parfois des billets de concert au marché noir.
native_language_example: You can sometimes find concert tickets on the black market.

additional_notes: Used to describe two people as being married to each other. Very common in wedding/ceremony phrases like « Je vous déclare maintenant mari et femme » (“I now pronounce you husband and wife”). Can also be used as a question or emphasis (« Mari et femme ? ») meaning “Husband and wife? (Really?)”.
target_language_example: Après la cérémonie, ils étaient officiellement mari et femme.
native_language_example: After the ceremony, they were officially husband and wife.

additional_notes: A neutral, formal term used in legal, political, and social discussions. Often appears with verbs like être légal (“to be legal”), légaliser (“to legalize”), soutenir (“to support”), or interdire (“to ban”).
target_language_example: Dans ce pays, le mariage homosexuel est légal depuis 2013.
native_language_example: In this country, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013.

additional_notes: Used for protective equipment worn over the face to filter dangerous gases or smoke. Often appears with articles: « un masque à gaz », « le masque à gaz ».
target_language_example: Les pompiers portent un masque à gaz quand il y a beaucoup de fumée.
native_language_example: Firefighters wear a gas mask when there’s a lot of smoke.

meaning: "the match was canceled" / "the match has been canceled."
additional_notes: Used to say a sports game/event won’t happen. This is the passive voice in the passé composé: **a été** (has been/was) + past participle **annulé** (canceled). You’ll often see it with an article: **Le match a été annulé**. You can also say **Le match est annulé** (“The match is canceled”).
target_language_example: Le match a été annulé à cause de la pluie.
native_language_example: The match was canceled because of the rain.

additional_notes: In French, "football" usually means soccer (not American football). "Match de foot" is a very common shorter version in everyday speech.
target_language_example: On va voir le match de football ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to watch the soccer game tonight?

meaning: from morning to night; all day long.
additional_notes: Most often used as **du matin au soir** (“from morning to night”) to emphasize something happens throughout the whole day. You’ll also see **de… à…** with times (e.g., *de 9 h à 17 h*).
target_language_example: Il travaille du matin au soir.
native_language_example: He works from morning to night.

meaning: a sore loser (someone who takes losing badly).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who reacts badly when they lose (gets angry, complains, makes excuses, refuses to accept the result). Often used with "être" (Il/Elle est mauvais(e) perdant(e)). With a man: "mauvais perdant"; with a woman: "mauvaise perdante". You can also say "un/une mauvais(e) perdant(e)" to talk about the person as a noun.
target_language_example: Ne l'invite pas à jouer : il est mauvais perdant.
native_language_example: Don't invite him to play: he's a sore loser.

additional_notes: Used to say that something harms health. Often follows "être" (e.g., "X est mauvais pour la santé"). You can intensify it with adverbs like "très" (very) or "vraiment" (really).
target_language_example: Trop de sucre est mauvais pour la santé.
native_language_example: Too much sugar is bad for your health.

additional_notes: Used for a plant that grows where you don’t want it (in a garden, lawn, fields). Very often used in the plural: « des mauvaises herbes ». Literally “bad herb/plant,” but the natural English translation is “weed.”
target_language_example: Cette plante est une mauvaise herbe.
native_language_example: This plant is a weed.

additional_notes: Refers to being irritable or unhappy (the opposite of "bonne humeur"). Common with verbs like "être de mauvaise humeur" (to be in a bad mood) and "être en (très) mauvaise humeur" (to be in a (very) bad mood).
target_language_example: Je suis de mauvaise humeur ce matin, je n’ai pas assez dormi.
native_language_example: I’m in a bad mood this morning; I didn’t sleep enough.

additional_notes: Common in gardening contexts for plants that grow where you don’t want them and can take over a garden. Often used with verbs like pousser (to grow) and envahir (to invade/overrun).
target_language_example: Il faut enlever les mauvaises herbes avant qu’elles n’envahissent tout le potager.
native_language_example: We have to pull out the weeds before they take over the whole vegetable garden.

additional_notes: Plural is very common in French (des maux de tête), even if you mean just “a headache.” Often used with verbs like avoir (avoir des maux de tête), souffrir de (souffrir de maux de tête), causer (causer des maux de tête), and with remedies (un médicament contre les maux de tête).
target_language_example: J'ai des maux de tête depuis ce matin.
native_language_example: I've had headaches since this morning.

meaning: to master (be highly proficient in) a foreign language.
additional_notes: « Maîtriser » signifie avoir une très bonne maîtrise/commandement d’une compétence. Pour une langue, cela implique un niveau élevé (comprendre, parler, lire et écrire avec aisance), pas seulement « savoir se débrouiller ». On l’emploie souvent avec des verbes comme « exiger » ou « requérir » pour souligner l’effort et le temps nécessaires.
target_language_example: Maîtriser une langue étrangère exige du temps et de la pratique.
native_language_example: Mastering a foreign language requires time and practice.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb « se brosser les dents »: « Je me brosse les dents » (I brush my teeth). The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: « tu te brosses… », « il/elle se brosse… », « nous nous brossons… », « vous vous brossez… », « ils/elles se brossent… ». In French you usually say « les dents » (the teeth), not « mes dents » (my teeth), because it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Je me brosse les dents avant de me coucher.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth before going to bed.

meaning: to come pick me up; to come get me.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like venir/aller (e.g., « viens me chercher », « ils vont venir me chercher »). In this context, « chercher » means “to go and get someone,” often by car or from a specific place (school, station, home), not “to look for me.”
target_language_example: Tu peux venir me chercher à la gare à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Can you come pick me up at the train station at 6 p.m.?

additional_notes: From *se demander* (“to wonder / to ask oneself”). Usually used with **je**: *Je me demandais si…* It’s a polite, slightly tentative way to introduce a question or request (often similar in tone to “I was wondering if you could…”). Follow with a clause: *Je me demandais si tu avais le temps…*
target_language_example: Je me demandais si tu pouvais m’aider ce soir.
native_language_example: I was wondering if you could help me tonight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a polite question or request. It comes from **se demander** (“to wonder”) in the **imparfait**: *je me demandais...* Often followed by something like *... pouvais venir*, *... avais le temps*, etc. This version uses **tu**; with **vous** you’d say: *Je me demandais si vous...*
target_language_example: Je me demandais si tu pouvais m’aider ce soir.
native_language_example: I was wondering if you could help me tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the object pronoun me before demander. With a subject, it means someone asks or is asking you something: il me demande = 'he asks me / is asking me'. In negative commands, ne me demande pas means 'don't ask me'. Be careful: demander usually means 'to ask', not 'to demand'.
target_language_example: Elle me demande si je peux l'aider.
native_language_example: She's asking me if I can help her.

meaning: “I wonder … / I’m asking myself …” (usually in: « je me demande ce que/si… »).
additional_notes: In real French this is normally not used alone: you usually say « Je me demande ce que … » (“I wonder what …”) or « Je me demande si … » (“I wonder if …”). The verb is « se demander » (to wonder / to ask oneself). « me » changes with the subject: « je me demande », « tu te demandes », « il/elle se demande », etc.
target_language_example: Je me demande ce que tu fais ce soir.
native_language_example: I wonder what you’re doing tonight.

additional_notes: This is a fragment you’ll most often see in the full phrase: « Je me demande ce qu’il + verb… ». « se demander » literally means “to ask oneself,” but in English it’s usually “to wonder.” « ce qu’il » introduces an indirect question meaning “what he…”.
target_language_example: Je me demande ce qu'il fait ce soir.
native_language_example: I wonder what he's doing tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb **se demander** to express curiosity or uncertainty. It’s usually part of a longer sentence, most often **Je me demande ce que…** (“I wonder what…”). You can change the subject: **Il/Elle se demande ce que…** (“He/She wonders what…”). Often followed by a clause like **…tu fais**, **…c’est**, **…il veut**, etc.
target_language_example: Je me demande ce que tu fais ce soir.
native_language_example: I wonder what you’re doing tonight.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern "Je me demande ce qui…" to introduce an indirect question about "what" (as the subject of the verb that follows). It’s often followed by a verb in the third person: "Je me demande ce qui se passe" (I wonder what’s happening). If you’re wondering about an object ("what" + subject + verb), you usually use "ce que": "Je me demande ce que tu fais" (I wonder what you’re doing).
target_language_example: Je me demande ce qui ne va pas.
native_language_example: I wonder what’s wrong.

additional_notes: Used after a subject (often "je") to introduce an indirect question about a place: "Je me demande où…" = "I wonder where…". Literally it’s like "I ask myself where…". Note: French "demander" usually means "to ask" (not "to demand").
target_language_example: Je me demande où il habite.
native_language_example: I wonder where he lives.

additional_notes: Most often used as part of **je me demande pourquoi…** (“I wonder why…”), literally “I ask myself why…”. With a different subject, it can also mean **“asks me why”**: **il/elle me demande pourquoi…** (“he/she asks me why…”).
target_language_example: Je me demande pourquoi il est en retard.
native_language_example: I wonder why he’s late.

meaning: "I wonder who has / who did" (introduces an indirect question).
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb **se demander**: **Je me demande qui a + past participle / complement**. It introduces an indirect question (so you keep normal word order, not question inversion): *Je me demande qui a pris mon sac.* You can also change the subject: *Il se demande qui a...*
target_language_example: Je me demande qui a pris mes clés.
native_language_example: I wonder who took my keys.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern « Je me demande si je… » to introduce an indirect yes/no question you’re asking yourself (doubting, thinking aloud, being unsure). It’s followed by a normal statement word order (no inversion), e.g. « Je me demande si je peux venir. »
target_language_example: Je me demande si je peux venir demain.
native_language_example: I wonder if I can come tomorrow.

meaning: “will you tell me?” / “tell me, will you…?”
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase *dire* (“to tell/say”) in the simple future (*diras*) with subject–verb inversion (*tu*) to form a question. It often introduces a question to someone, sometimes with a rhetorical feel (“tell me…”). You’ll also commonly see the non-inverted form: *Tu me diras… ?*
target_language_example: Me diras-tu la vérité ?
native_language_example: Will you tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Formed with the object pronoun me and dire. In French, object pronouns usually come before the infinitive, so me dire often corresponds to English tell me, especially after verbs like pouvoir, devoir, or vouloir.
target_language_example: Tu peux me dire ton nom ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me your name?

additional_notes: This is typically an incomplete fragment used before a relative pronoun: most often "me dire ce que + clause" (tell me what + clause) or sometimes "me dire ce qui + verb" (tell me what/which thing + verb). In everyday French you’ll almost always see it as "Dis-moi ce que…" / "Pouvez-vous me dire ce que…".
target_language_example: Tu peux me dire ce que tu veux manger ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what you want to eat?

me dire ce qu'il se passe

target_language_multi_word_term: me dire ce qu'il se passe
meaning: to tell me what’s going on (what’s happening).
additional_notes: Used to ask or insist that someone explain a situation. It often appears as a question (e.g., « Tu peux… ? », « Pouvez-vous… ? ») or with obligation (e.g., « Tu dois… », « Vous devez… »). « il se passe » is an impersonal way to say “is happening.”
target_language_example: Tu dois me dire ce qu'il se passe.
native_language_example: You have to tell me what’s going on.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to tell you information: **dire (à quelqu’un) + ce que + clause**. Here, **me** = “to me” (I’m the person being told), and **ce que** introduces what is being said (e.g., *ce que c’est / ce que ça signifie / ce que vous avez entendu*). Often appears in polite requests with **Veuillez…** (“Please…”).
target_language_example: Peux-tu me dire ce que tu as fait hier ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what you did yesterday?

additional_notes: Used after an imperative or a request (e.g., "Peux-tu… ?") to ask someone to tell you something. "ce qui" is used when "what" is the subject of the following verb (thing + verb): "Dis-moi ce qui se passe" (what is happening). If "what" is the object, you usually use "ce que": "Dis-moi ce que tu veux" (what you want).
target_language_example: Peux-tu me dire ce qui ne va pas ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what's wrong?

me dire ce qui s'est passé

target_language_multi_word_term: me dire ce qui s'est passé
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to explain an event. Often appears in questions with polite or informal forms: « Peux-tu… ? » (informal singular), « Pouvez-vous… ? » or « Voulez-vous… ? » (polite/plural). « ce qui s'est passé » literally means “what happened” (the thing that happened).
target_language_example: Tu peux me dire ce qui s'est passé hier soir ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what happened last night?

me dire ce qui se passe

target_language_multi_word_term: me dire ce qui se passe
meaning: tell me what’s going on / what’s happening.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to explain a situation. It’s often a request for clarification and can sound worried, annoyed, or urgent depending on tone. Common variants: « Tu peux me dire ce qui se passe ? » (casual), « Vous pouvez me dire ce qui se passe ? » (polite/formal), « Tu veux bien… ? / Vous voulez bien… ? » (more polite: “would you mind…?”). Literally “(to) tell me what is happening.”
target_language_example: Je suis inquiet : tu peux me dire ce qui se passe ?
native_language_example: I’m worried—can you tell me what’s going on?

meaning: “tell me how” (to do something / how something happened).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question with **comment** (“how”). Often followed by an infinitive (**comment faire…**) or a full clause (**comment tu as fait… / comment il faut…**). With **Veuillez me dire…**, it becomes a polite request (“Please tell me…”).
target_language_example: Tu peux me dire comment on va à la gare ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how to get to the train station?

additional_notes: Uses the indirect object pronoun “me” (= to me). The full verb phrase is “dire la vérité à quelqu’un” (to tell someone the truth). In questions/requests you’ll also see: « Dis-moi la vérité » (Tell me the truth).
target_language_example: S'il te plaît, tu peux me dire la vérité ?
native_language_example: Please, can you tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or demand a location. Often appears in questions with polite forms like « Pouvez-vous / Pourriez-vous me dire où… ? » and is followed by a full clause (subject + verb): « …où tu habites », « …où je peux prendre un train ».
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me dire où se trouve la station de métro ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the subway station is?

meaning: to tell me something; (in questions) to mean anything to me / to ring a bell.
additional_notes: Literally “to tell me something.” Very common after verbs like vouloir/devoir: « Tu dois me dire quelque chose » (You have to tell me something). In questions like « C’est censé me dire quelque chose ? », it’s often rhetorical: “Is that supposed to mean anything to me?” Related expression: « Ça me dit quelque chose » = “That sounds familiar / It rings a bell.”
target_language_example: Tu veux me dire quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Do you want to tell me something?

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “will you tell me,” with inverted word order (direz-vous) that sounds formal or literary. Often used as an aside to introduce a possible objection or question from the listener, similar to “you may ask” or “you might say.”
target_language_example: Mais, me direz-vous, pourquoi partir si tôt ?
native_language_example: But, you may ask, why leave so early?

additional_notes: This is the negative imperative of *dire* used with an indirect object pronoun: *(Ne) me dis pas…* = “Don’t tell me…”. In casual speech, *ne* is often dropped (*Me dis pas…*), which makes it sound more informal. With *tu*, you may also see it in statements/questions like *Tu ne me dis pas… ?* (“You’re not telling me…?” / “You’re not going to tell me…?”).
target_language_example: Me dis pas ça, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t say that to me, please.

additional_notes: Used when you recognize something (a name, face, place, object) but can’t quite remember where you’ve seen/heard it. Pattern: « [Nom/visage/objet] me dit quelque chose » (informal singular) or « … me dit quelque chose » with « votre » for polite/formal. Often implies partial recognition: you feel you know it, but you don’t know from where.
target_language_example: Ce prénom me dit quelque chose, mais je ne sais plus d’où.
native_language_example: That first name rings a bell, but I can’t remember where from.

meaning: "doesn't ring a bell / means nothing to me"; or "doesn't tell me anything."
additional_notes: In French, **(ça) me dit quelque chose / (ça) ne me dit rien** is a very common way to say something is (or isn’t) familiar to you: *Votre nom ne me dit rien* = “Your name doesn’t ring a bell.” With a person as the subject, it’s more literal: *Personne ne me dit rien* = “Nobody tells me anything.” In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *ça me dit rien*.
target_language_example: Ce film ne me dit rien, je ne le connais pas.
native_language_example: That movie doesn’t ring a bell; I don’t know it.

meaning: "gives me" / "makes me" (causes me to feel or have something).
additional_notes: "Me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to me" and it usually comes before the verb: "(quelqu’un/quelque chose) me donne (quelque chose)". Very common with feelings/physical effects: "me donne faim" (makes me hungry), "me donne envie" (makes me want to), "me donne le hoquet" (gives me the hiccups).
target_language_example: Ce film me donne peur.
native_language_example: This movie scares me (gives me fear).

me donne la chair de poule

target_language_multi_word_term: me donne la chair de poule
additional_notes: Used when something makes you feel strong chills on your skin—often from fear, disgust, or creepiness (sometimes also from emotion or cold). Structure: « (Quelque chose / quelqu’un) me donne la chair de poule » = “(Something/someone) gives me goosebumps.” You can change the pronoun: « te donne… », « lui donne… », etc.
target_language_example: Ce film d’horreur me donne la chair de poule.
native_language_example: That horror movie gives me goosebumps.

additional_notes: “Me” is the indirect object pronoun (“to me”) and usually goes before the verb: « Vous pouvez me donner… ? » It’s used in many common expressions, e.g. « me donner congé » = to dismiss/fire me or give me leave, and « me donner ta parole » = to give me your word (promise).
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner ton numéro, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you give me your number, please?

additional_notes: "Me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me.” It usually goes before the verb: peux-tu me donner un indice ? / vous pourriez me donner un contrat. With things like contrat, it can mean “offer/award me a contract,” not literally hand it to you.
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner un conseil ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of advice?

me donner un coup de main

target_language_multi_word_term: me donner un coup de main
meaning: 'to give me a hand'; to help me.
additional_notes: Common, friendly way to ask for help. The pronoun changes depending on who is being helped: me donner / te donner / lui donner / nous donner / vous donner / leur donner un coup de main. Often used in questions and requests (e.g., Peux-tu… ? / Tu veux… ? / Viens…).
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner un coup de main avec ces cartons ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with these boxes?

meaning: "give me a" (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Common request pattern: (Peux-tu/Pouvez-vous) + me donner une + noun. Use "me" for "to me"; "une" is the feminine singular "a/an" (for masculine nouns, use "me donner un"). Can be used for objects (une tranche de pain), information (une description, une estimation), or a chance (une dernière chance).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me donner une minute ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a minute?

additional_notes: This can be either object pronoun + faire ("make me" / "do something to me") or the "me" form of se faire. In the pattern me faire + infinitive or past participle, it often means "get/have something done to oneself" or "be on the receiving end" of an action: me faire comprendre = make myself understood, me faire crier dessus = get yelled at, me faire enregistrer = get checked in.
target_language_example: Je vais me faire couper les cheveux demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to get my hair cut tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Faire confiance à quelqu’un" means “to trust someone.” Here, "me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me,” so it literally corresponds to “to give me trust.” Common in requests or reassurance: "Tu dois me faire confiance" (You have to trust me), "Merci de me faire confiance" (Thanks for trusting me). You can swap the pronoun: "te faire confiance" (trust you), "lui faire confiance" (trust him/her), "leur faire confiance" (trust them).
target_language_example: Je sais que c’est difficile, mais tu peux me faire confiance.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard, but you can trust me.

meaning: “I make/do to myself” (from *se faire*), used in reflexive expressions.
additional_notes:
*Me fais* is the **1st-person singular** form of the reflexive verb **se faire** (je **me fais** …). It often appears in common set phrases where the English translation is more natural than the literal one:
- **Je me fais comprendre ?** = “Am I making myself understood?”
- **Je me fais du souci** = “I worry / I’m worrying” (literally “I’m making myself worry”)
- **Je me fais une règle de…** = “I make it a rule to…”
target_language_example: Je me fais du souci pour toi.
native_language_example: I’m worried about you.

meaning: "don’t … me" / "you don’t … me" (literally: “don’t make/do … to me”).
additional_notes: From the verb *faire* (tu **fais**) with the object pronoun **me** (“me”) in the negative. Very often used without **ne** in speech: **(Ne) me fais pas…** = “Don’t … me.” It can be followed by a noun/phrase (e.g., *me fais pas peur* = “don’t scare me”) or be part of set expressions like **faire confiance à** = “to trust” (*Tu ne me fais pas confiance ?* = “You don’t trust me?”).
target_language_example: Me fais pas attendre !
native_language_example: Don’t keep me waiting!

additional_notes: Used with the verb faire + an indirect object pronoun (me) to show what someone/something does to you or makes you feel/do. Common patterns: (1) faire + infinitive: « Il me fait rire » = he makes me laugh; « Il me fait faire ceci » = he makes me do this. (2) faire + noun: « Il me fait peur » = he scares me. (3) faire + adjective/feelings: « Il me fait (me) sentir… » = he makes me feel…. In negatives: « ne me fait pas… ».
target_language_example: Ce film me fait pleurer à chaque fois.
native_language_example: This movie makes me cry every time.

additional_notes: Used with a body part as the subject: "[body part] + me fait mal" = "my [body part] hurts." For other people: "te fait mal" (hurts you), "lui fait mal" (hurts him/her), "nous fait mal" (hurts us), etc. Often used with "avoir mal" too: "J’ai mal à la tête" = "My head hurts."
target_language_example: J’ai mal au dos : il me fait mal depuis hier.
native_language_example: My back hurts: it’s been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with "faire" + infinitive to say something causes a feeling: "[Someone/something] me fait me sentir + adjective" (e.g., heureux/heureuse, mieux, bizarre, chez moi). You can change "me" to another object pronoun: "te fait te sentir" (makes you feel), "le fait se sentir" (makes him feel), etc. In everyday French, people also often say "me fait sentir" (without the second "me"), especially in speech.
target_language_example: Cette musique me fait me sentir calme.
native_language_example: This music makes me feel calm.

additional_notes: Used when something brings someone or something else to mind. It comes from *faire penser à* (to make [someone] think of). The object pronoun changes with the person: *me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur fait penser à*; and the verb agrees with what is doing the reminding (*ça me fait…*, *ces photos me font…*).
target_language_example: Ce parfum me fait penser à mes vacances.
native_language_example: This perfume reminds me of my vacation.

additional_notes: Usually appears in the pattern il me faut + noun/thing: il me faut de l'aide = i need help. Literally, it is more like something is necessary for me. In questions, me faut-il ... ? is a formal inversion meaning do i need to ... ? / must i ... ?
target_language_example: Il me faut plus de temps.
native_language_example: I need more time.

additional_notes: Used with the impersonal verb falloir, most commonly in the full structure: « Il me faut un/une + noun » = “I need a …”. « me » means “to me”. Choose « un » with masculine nouns and « une » with feminine nouns. You’ll often hear it in requests (shops, cafés, travel).
target_language_example: Il me faut un billet pour Paris, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I need a ticket to Paris, please.

meaning: "has (done/said/given) it to me" — a cluster of object pronouns (**me** + **l’**) followed by **a** (3rd person singular of *avoir* in the passé composé).
additional_notes: **me** = “to me” (indirect object pronoun), **l’** = “it” (direct object pronoun, short for *le* or *la*), **a** = “has” (from *avoir*). This sequence is followed by a past participle: *On me l’a dit* (“They told me”), *Il me l’a donné* (“He gave it to me”). **l’** is used because *le/la* elide before a vowel sound (here, **a**).
target_language_example: On me l'a souvent dit.
native_language_example: I've often been told that.

additional_notes: Common pronoun order with **dire** in the passé composé: **[subject] + me + l’ + a + dit**. **me** = “to me,” **l’** (le) = “it/that,” **a dit** = “said/told.” You can change the subject: *Il/Elle me l’a dit* = “He/She told me.” Note: in correct French typography it’s often written with an apostrophe: **me l’a dit**.
target_language_example: Mon père me l'a dit.
native_language_example: My father told me (it/that).

additional_notes:
Used with different structures:
- **laisser + adjective**: *me laisser seul(e)* = “leave me alone.” (Agreement: **seul** for a man, **seule** for a woman.)
- **laisser + infinitive**: *me laisser faire / vivre / aider* = “let me do it / live / help.”
- **laisser + noun**: *me laisser un message* = “leave me a message.”
In polite requests you may see **veuillez**: *Veuillez me laisser…* = “Please leave…”
target_language_example: Peux-tu me laisser seul ?
native_language_example: Can you leave me alone?

additional_notes: object-pronoun combination placed before the verb (or before the infinitive it goes with). le usually means "it" (sometimes "him"), and me means "to me"; with some verbs, English may instead use "from me," as in me le piquer = "steal it from me."
target_language_example: Tu peux me le montrer ?
native_language_example: Can you show it to me?

meaning: to tell me it / to tell me (that).
additional_notes: This is the verb "dire" (to say/tell) with two object pronouns: "me" (to me) + "le" (it/that). With an infinitive, the pronouns come before the verb: "me le dire" = "tell it to me." In a conjugated form, they also go before the verb: "Tu dois me le dire" (You have to tell me). "Le" often refers to an idea or information already understood from context (like "it" or "that" in English).
target_language_example: Tu peux me le dire franchement.
native_language_example: You can tell me honestly.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "manquer" in the pattern "[someone/something] me manque" = "I miss [someone/something]". The person who feels the missing is an indirect object (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur), and the thing/person missed is the subject. Example: "Tu me manques" = "I miss you."
target_language_example: Tu me manques déjà.
native_language_example: I miss you already.

meaning: 'show me' (demonstrate to me / point out to me).
additional_notes: "Montrer" means "to show." With "me," it means the action is done to you: someone shows you how to do something ("me montrer comment...") or shows you where something is ("me montrer où..."). Used in polite requests with "pourrais-tu...", "veuillez...", or "soyez assez aimable de...".
target_language_example: Peux-tu me montrer ton passeport, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you show me your passport, please?

meaning: to show me how to do that.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for a demonstration or step-by-step help. It’s built from: "me" (to me) + "montrer" (to show) + "comment" (how) + "faire" (to do) + "ça" (that/this). Often appears in polite question forms like "Peux-tu… ?" (informal), "Pourrais-tu… ?" (polite informal), and "Pouvez-vous… ?" (formal). You can replace "ça" with "cela" (more formal) or with a specific task: "…comment faire une omelette".
target_language_example: Tu peux me montrer comment faire ça, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you show me how to do that, please?

meaning: to talk to me; to speak to me.
additional_notes: "Me" is an object pronoun meaning "to me" and it comes before the verb: "Tu peux me parler" (You can talk to me). Often followed by "de" to introduce the topic: "me parler de ..." = "talk to me about ...". In polite questions you may see "pourriez-vous me parler...".
target_language_example: Tu peux me parler de tes projets quand tu veux.
native_language_example: You can talk to me about your plans whenever you want.

meaning: to speak to me in that tone (of voice).
additional_notes: Used to complain that someone is speaking rudely, disrespectfully, or angrily. Often appears in indignant questions/exclamations with oser: « Comment oses-tu/osez-vous me parler sur ce ton ?/! ». You can change the indirect object pronoun/person: te/lui/nous/vous parler sur ce ton.
target_language_example: Comment oses-tu me parler sur ce ton ?
native_language_example: How dare you speak to me in that tone?

additional_notes: Used with the verb plaire: the thing/person you like is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is an indirect object (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur). So "Cette cravate me plaît" = "I like this tie" (literally: "This tie pleases me"). In the negative: "ne me plaît pas" = "I don’t like it". Common pattern: "Ça me plaît" (I like it).
target_language_example: Ce film me plaît beaucoup.
native_language_example: I like this movie a lot.

meaning: to lend me; to loan me.
additional_notes: Used with the verb prêter (“to lend”) plus the indirect object pronoun me (“to me”). Structure: prêter + [thing] + à + [person] → me prêter [thing] (“lend me [thing]”). Very common in polite requests: « Pourrais-tu / Pourriez-vous me prêter… ? ». Also appears in the fixed expression « prêter main forte (à quelqu’un) » = “to give (someone) a hand / help out.”
target_language_example: Tu peux me prêter dix euros, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you lend me ten euros, please?

additional_notes:
From the verb *rappeler*.
- **X me rappelle Y** = “X reminds me of Y” / “X makes me think of Y.”
- **X me rappelle quelqu’un** = “X reminds me of someone.”
- **Quelque chose qui me rappelle à toi** = “something that makes you think of me” (literally “that reminds me to you”).
Note: *se rappeler* means “to remember” (e.g., *Je me rappelle* = “I remember”), which is different from *me rappeler* (“remind me”).
target_language_example: Cette chanson me rappelle mon enfance.
native_language_example: This song reminds me of my childhood.

meaning: to cheer me up; to lift my spirits.
additional_notes: Used when someone helps you feel better emotionally (less sad, discouraged, or stressed). The structure is: remonter le moral à quelqu’un (e.g., me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur). Often said with verbs like essayer de (try to), venir pour (come to), or merci de/pour (thanks for).
target_language_example: Après cette mauvaise nouvelle, mon amie m’a appelé pour me remonter le moral.
native_language_example: After that bad news, my friend called me to cheer me up.

meaning: "makes me" / "renders me" (causes me to feel or become something).
additional_notes: From the verb **rendre** + an indirect object pronoun (**me**). Very commonly used in patterns like **Ça/Cela/Cette chose me rend + adjective** ("It makes me happy/crazy/sad/envieux"), or **Quelqu’un me rend + noun phrase** in the sense of "makes things + adjective" (e.g., *me rend la vie facile* = "makes life easy for me"). Word order: pronoun comes before the verb (*me rend*, *me rendait*, *m’a rendu*).
target_language_example: Ce travail me rend stressé.
native_language_example: This job makes me stressed.

meaning: “drives me crazy” / “makes me mad” (annoys me a lot).
additional_notes: From *rendre* (“to make/turn”) + *fou* (“crazy”). Used with a subject that causes the feeling: *Ça/Il/Elle me rend fou* (“It/He/She drives me crazy”). Change *me* to other object pronouns as needed (e.g., *te, le, la, nous, vous, les*). Agree *fou* with the person affected: *me rend folle* (if the speaker is female).
target_language_example: Ce bruit me rend fou.
native_language_example: That noise drives me crazy.

me rendrait plus heureux que de

target_language_multi_word_term: me rendrait plus heureux que de
additional_notes: Used to compare two actions or situations: one would make the speaker happier than doing something else. It’s typically followed by an infinitive after « de » (e.g., « que de rester », « que de partir »). Note: « rendre » here means “to make (someone) + adjective,” not “to render” in the usual English sense.
target_language_example: Ça me rendrait plus heureux que de rester ici.
native_language_example: That would make me happier than staying here.

additional_notes: In most of these examples, se rendre à + place means 'to go to' or 'make one's way to', often a bit more formal than aller. With a person + adjective, rendre means 'make' or 'cause': me rendre heureux = 'make me happy'. The pronoun changes depending on who is involved (me, te, se, nous, vous).
target_language_example: Je dois me rendre à l'aéroport tôt demain.
native_language_example: I have to go to the airport early tomorrow.

meaning: to do me a favor; to help me out.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone politely to help you by doing something. The indirect object pronoun changes with the person: me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur (e.g., Tu peux nous rendre un service ? = Can you do us a favor?). Common polite variants include: Tu pourrais… ? / Tu veux bien… ? / Voulez-vous… ?
target_language_example: Tu peux me rendre un service et fermer la fenêtre, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and close the window, please?

meaning: to visit me (to come see me).
additional_notes: "Rendre visite à [quelqu’un]" means to pay someone a visit (often at their home, but also at work). The pronoun changes depending on who is being visited: me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur rendre visite. Common with "venir" (venir me rendre visite = come visit me).
target_language_example: Mes amis viennent me rendre visite ce week-end.
native_language_example: My friends are coming to visit me this weekend.

additional_notes: Form of the verb **rendre**. With an object pronoun (**me**) it often means **“make me”** + adjective: *Tu me rends heureux/malade/nerveux* (“You make me happy/sick/nervous”). In *Tu me rends un service ?*, **rendre un service** means **“do a favor”**. With the reflexive verb **se rendre** (*je me rends…*), it means **“to go”** or **“to head”** somewhere: *Je ne me rends nulle part* (“I’m not going anywhere”).
target_language_example: Arrête, tu me rends fou !
native_language_example: Stop, you’re driving me crazy!

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to say again which school (or institution) they’re talking about: « Pourrais-tu / Pourriez-vous me répéter de quelle école… ? » = “Could you repeat which school…?” Often followed by « tu es diplômé(e) » / « vous êtes diplômé(e) » (“you graduated”), with -e added for a woman (diplômée). « Pourrais-tu » is informal (tu); « Pourriez-vous » is more formal/polite (vous).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, pourriez-vous me répéter de quelle école vous êtes diplômé ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you repeat which school you graduated from?

additional_notes: Used with "sembler" to give your personal impression or opinion: "Ça/Cela me semble + adjective" (It seems + adjective to me). Very common also as "Il me semble que..." (It seems to me that...). "Semble" is the 3rd person singular of "sembler"; it doesn’t change, because the subject is "ça/cela/il".
target_language_example: Il me semble que c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: It seems to me that it's a good idea.

additional_notes: Usually seen in je me sens + adjective/adverb, meaning "I feel..." (for example, je me sens bien / mieux / fatigué). In other contexts, me can be the object pronoun, as in tu me sens ? = "can you feel me?". sens is a present-tense form of sentir.
target_language_example: En ce moment, je me sens un peu stressé.
native_language_example: At the moment, I feel a little stressed.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *se sentir* (to feel), often in the 1st person: *Je me sens bien* = “I feel good.” It can describe how you feel physically or emotionally, and it’s a common answer to *Ça va ?* / *Comment tu vas ?* (“How are you?”).
target_language_example: Après une bonne nuit de sommeil, je me sens bien.
native_language_example: After a good night’s sleep, I feel good.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se sentir en sécurité** (“to feel safe”). **Me** is the reflexive pronoun for “I”; it changes with the subject: **je me sens**, **tu te sens**, **il/elle se sent**, **nous nous sentons**, **vous vous sentez**, **ils/elles se sentent**. Often used with places or situations: *ici, à la maison, avec toi, la nuit*, etc.
target_language_example: Avec toi, je me sens en sécurité.
native_language_example: With you, I feel safe.

additional_notes: From the verb "se sentir" (to feel). "Tellement" means "so/so much" and intensifies what comes next. This phrase is usually followed by an adjective or description: "Je me sens tellement fatigué(e)" (I feel so tired). Make the adjective agree with you: fatigué (male), fatiguée (female).
target_language_example: Je me sens tellement fatiguée aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I feel so tired today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **se sentir** (“to feel”), usually in the pattern **Je me sens très + adjective**: *Je me sens très fatigué(e).* You can change the subject and reflexive pronoun: *Tu te sens très… / Il se sent très… / Elle se sent très… / Nous nous sentons très…*.
target_language_example: Je me sens très fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I feel very tired today.

meaning: "I feel a bit…" (used to say how you feel).
additional_notes: From the verb "se sentir" (to feel). It’s usually followed by an adjective or phrase: "Je me sens un peu fatigué(e)" (I feel a bit tired) or "Je me sens un peu mieux" (I feel a bit better). Agree the adjective with the speaker: fatigué (m), fatiguée (f).
target_language_example: Je me sens un peu malade aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I feel a bit sick today.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **se sentir** (to feel). It’s usually followed by an adjective or phrase describing your state: **je me sens vraiment bien / fatigué(e) / stressé(e)**. Agreement: **fatigué** (male) / **fatiguée** (female). Often used to emphasize how you feel with **vraiment** (“really”).
target_language_example: Je me sens vraiment fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I feel really tired today.

additional_notes: Used with "je" as "je me souviens" = "I remember." Often followed by "de" + noun/pronoun ("Je me souviens de toi" = "I remember you") or "de" + infinitive ("Je me souviens de t'avoir vu" = "I remember seeing you"). In the negative, "Je ne me souviens plus (de...)" means "I don't remember anymore."
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne me souviens plus de son nom.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't remember his/her name anymore.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **se souvenir de** = “to remember.” It’s usually used as **je me souviens de + noun/pronoun** (Je me souviens de ce film.) or **je me souviens de + infinitive** (Je me souviens de l’avoir vu.). In speech, you often replace the thing remembered with **en**: *Je m’en souviens.* (“I remember it/that.”).
target_language_example: Je me souviens de ton nom.
native_language_example: I remember your name.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se souvenir de** = “to remember.” It’s usually used with a subject in front (e.g., **Je me souviens de ce…**). Very often it continues as **de ce que + clause** (“I remember what… / I remember that…”) or **de ce moment / de cette fois** (“that moment/that time”).
target_language_example: Je me souviens de ce que tu as dit.
native_language_example: I remember what you said.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the first-person singular past tense of reflexive or pronominal verbs: je me suis + past participle. In English, this may translate as simple past ('I stopped') or with 'myself' when needed ('I dried myself'). After words like et or mais, French can omit je: et me suis séché = 'and dried myself'.
target_language_example: Je me suis lavé les mains avant de manger.
native_language_example: I washed my hands before eating.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb s’asseoir (to sit down): « je me suis assis » (said by a man) / « je me suis assise » (said by a woman). Uses être as the helping verb because it’s reflexive.
target_language_example: Je me suis assis près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I sat down near the window.

meaning: "I had a really good time" / "I had fun."
additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb **s’amuser** (“to have fun”). It’s built with **être**: *je me suis…* and the past participle agrees with the subject: **amusé** (male speaker), **amusée** (female speaker), **amusés/amusées** (plural). **bien** adds the idea of “really/well.” Often used to talk about enjoying an event: *Je me suis bien amusé à la fête.*
target_language_example: Hier soir, je me suis bien amusé au concert.
native_language_example: Last night, I had a really good time at the concert.

additional_notes: Used with the subject "je": "Je me suis cassé la jambe." French often uses the definite article with body parts ("la jambe") where English uses a possessive ("my leg"). With "être" in the passé composé, the past participle agrees if the reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous) is a direct object: "Je me suis cassé la jambe" (cassé), but "Je me suis cassée la jambe" for a woman.
target_language_example: Je me suis cassé la jambe en skiant.
native_language_example: I broke my leg while skiing.

additional_notes: Passé composé of the reflexive verb « se couper ». Used when you accidentally cut yourself: « Je me suis coupé le doigt. » If the speaker is female, it usually agrees: « Je me suis coupée ». Often followed by a body part (le doigt, la main) or used alone when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Je me suis coupé en cuisinant.
native_language_example: I cut myself while cooking.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb « s’endormir » (to fall asleep). You’ll most often see it as « je me suis endormi » (male speaker) or « je me suis endormie » (female speaker): the past participle agrees with the subject here. Often used with time expressions like « hier soir », « tout de suite », « pendant le film ».
target_language_example: Je me suis endormi pendant le film.
native_language_example: I fell asleep during the movie.

meaning: "I got" / "I had (something) done" / "I ended up" (used with *se faire* in the past).
additional_notes: *Me suis fait* is part of the past tense (passé composé) of **se faire**: **je me suis fait…**. It’s commonly used in two patterns: (1) **je me suis fait + adjective** = “I got (hurt/ready/etc.)” → *Je me suis fait mal* (“I hurt myself / I got hurt”). (2) **je me suis fait + infinitive** = “I got/had something done (to me)” or “I got myself (into a situation)” → *Je me suis fait voler mon téléphone* (“My phone got stolen / I got my phone stolen”), *Je me suis fait couper les cheveux* (“I had my hair cut”). It often describes something that happened to you (sometimes unpleasant).
target_language_example: Je me suis fait mal au dos.
native_language_example: I hurt my back.

me suis imaginé que je pourrais

target_language_multi_word_term: me suis imaginé que je pourrais
meaning: "I imagined/thought that I could" (that I might be able to).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption or expectation you had that turned out to be uncertain or wrong. It’s the passé composé of "s’imaginer" (a reflexive verb): "je me suis imaginé(e)". Add -e if the speaker is female: "je me suis imaginée". Often followed by "que" + a conditional verb like "je pourrais" (I could / might be able to).
target_language_example: Je me suis imaginé que je pourrais finir ce soir, mais c’est plus long que prévu.
native_language_example: I thought I could finish tonight, but it’s taking longer than expected.

additional_notes: Passé composé of the reflexive verb « se lever » with « être »: « je me suis levé ». It can mean getting up (out of bed) or standing up (from sitting), depending on context. Agree the past participle with the subject: « je me suis levé » (male speaker), « je me suis levée » (female speaker).
target_language_example: Je me suis levé tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: I got up early this morning.

meaning: "I got up early" / "I woke up early".
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb *se lever* (to get up). It’s built with *être*: *je me suis…*. The past participle agrees with the subject: *je me suis levé* (male speaker), *je me suis levée* (female speaker). *tôt* means “early.”
target_language_example: Je me suis levé tôt pour prendre le train.
native_language_example: I got up early to catch the train.

meaning: “I started to / I began to” (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular past form of **se mettre à + infinitive** (“to start doing”). It’s reflexive, so it uses **être** in the past: **je me suis mis / je me suis mise** (add **-e** if the speaker is female). Typically followed by an infinitive: **Je me suis mis à travailler** (“I started working”).
target_language_example: Je me suis mis à apprendre le français l’année dernière.
native_language_example: I started learning French last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "se réveiller" = “to wake up.” It uses "être" as the helping verb because it’s a reflexive verb: je me suis… You may also see gender/number agreement: "je me suis réveillée" (speaker is female), "nous nous sommes réveillés/réveillées".
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillé tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: I woke up early this morning.

additional_notes: Comes from the reflexive verb « se sentir » (to feel). Used with « je » in the passé composé: « je me suis senti(e) ... ». It’s usually followed by an adjective or a state: « bien » (good), « mal » (bad), « fatigué(e) » (tired). Agreement: « senti » (male / default) and « sentie » (female).
target_language_example: Je me suis senti très fatigué après le travail.
native_language_example: I felt very tired after work.

additional_notes: Idiom used to say someone or something is really irritating you. It’s built with an indirect object pronoun: "Ça me tape sur les nerfs" (It gets on my nerves), "Il/Elle me tape sur les nerfs" (He/She gets on my nerves). You can change "me" to "te/lui/nous/vous/leur" depending on who is annoyed.
target_language_example: Arrête de faire ça, ça me tape sur les nerfs !
native_language_example: Stop doing that, it’s getting on my nerves!

additional_notes: Informal spoken negative form of "Ne me touche pas" (often said without "ne"). Used as a strong command to tell someone to stop touching you. "Me" is the object pronoun (me) and "touche" is "touch" in the tu-form (toucher). Can be intensified with words like "toi !" or followed by details: "avec tes sales mains" (with your dirty hands).
target_language_example: Me touche pas, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t touch me, please.

meaning: “is cheating on me” or “is deceiving/fooling me.”
additional_notes: From the verb "tromper". With a person as the subject, it can mean cheating on someone romantically ("Ma petite amie me trompe" = my girlfriend is cheating on me). It can also mean deceiving/misleading someone (including your senses: "Mon odorat ne me trompe jamais" = my sense of smell never fools me). Don’t confuse with "je me trompe" (reflexive), which means “I’m mistaken / I’m wrong.”
target_language_example: Je pense qu’il me trompe depuis des mois.
native_language_example: I think he’s been cheating on me for months.

additional_notes: “Me” is the direct object pronoun (“me”) placed before the infinitive verb: *tuer* (“to kill”). It can be literal (someone wants to murder you) or used figuratively/exaggerated in everyday speech to mean “(someone) will be furious with me / it will be the end of me,” e.g., *Mon père va me tuer* (“My dad’s going to kill me” = he’ll be really angry).
target_language_example: Si ma mère voit ça, elle va me tuer.
native_language_example: If my mom sees that, she’s going to kill me (i.e., be furious).

additional_notes: Literally refers to someone seeing you. The pronoun me comes before voir in French. Depending on context, it can mean to see you, come see you, visit you, or meet with you.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir me voir demain ?
native_language_example: Can you come see me tomorrow?

me voir de temps en temps

target_language_multi_word_term: me voir de temps en temps
meaning: to see me from time to time; to visit me occasionally.
additional_notes: Used to say someone comes to visit you sometimes, but not regularly. Often used with venir (to come): « venir me voir de temps en temps ». You can change the pronoun: « te voir / le voir / la voir / nous voir / vous voir / les voir de temps en temps ».
target_language_example: Si tu passes dans le coin, viens me voir de temps en temps.
native_language_example: If you’re in the area, come see me from time to time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s closest friend. It agrees with the friend’s gender: meilleur ami (male), meilleure amie (female). Often used with a possessive: mon/ton/son meilleur ami.
target_language_example: C'est mon meilleur ami depuis le lycée.
native_language_example: He’s been my best friend since high school.

additional_notes:
Used to compare something (often implied by context) with “mine.” 
- “le mien” = “mine” (masculine singular). It changes with gender/number: “la mienne” (fem. sg.), “les miens” (masc. pl.), “les miennes” (fem. pl.).
- You can add emphasis with “bien / beaucoup”: “bien meilleur que le mien” = “much better than mine.”
target_language_example: Ce stylo est meilleur que le mien.
native_language_example: This pen is better than mine.

additional_notes: Used for a girl/woman who is someone’s closest friend. Because "amie" is feminine, use it when referring to a female best friend, or when addressing a woman as someone’s best friend ("Tu es la meilleure amie"). With a male best friend you’d say "meilleur ami". Often used with possessives: "ma/ta/sa meilleure amie".
target_language_example: J’ai passé le week-end avec ma meilleure amie.
native_language_example: I spent the weekend with my best friend.

meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée

target_language_multi_word_term: meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée
meaning: “the best thing that has happened to me.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is the best event/experience in your life. The wording is a bit formal/literary because it uses the subjunctive ("qui me soit arrivée") after a superlative ("la meilleure"). "Arrivée" agrees with "chose" (feminine). Often said as: « C’est la meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée. »
target_language_example: C’est la meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée.
native_language_example: It’s the best thing that has happened to me.

additional_notes: Used to express good wishes in greetings and messages (often for the New Year, weddings, birthdays, or congratulations). You can say it alone ("Meilleurs vœux !") or add details: "meilleurs vœux de bonheur" (best wishes for happiness), "meilleurs vœux à toute la famille" (best wishes to the whole family). "Transmets mes meilleurs vœux à…" means “Pass on my best wishes to …”.
target_language_example: Meilleurs vœux pour la nouvelle année !
native_language_example: Best wishes for the New Year!

meaning: “thanks, my …” (followed by a form of address).
additional_notes: Used when thanking someone while addressing them directly: an affectionate nickname (mon ami, mon cœur, mon chou) or a title (mon commandant). The possessive adjective agrees with the person/thing you’re calling them: mon (masc.), ma (fem.), mes (plural). Note: you often still use **mon** before a feminine noun starting with a vowel or silent h: **mon ange**, **mon amie**.
target_language_example: Merci, mon ami, c’est très gentil !
native_language_example: Thanks, my friend, that’s very kind!

additional_notes: A stronger, more emphatic way to say “merci.” Often used on its own, or followed by a name (“Merci beaucoup, Charlie.”) or “de” + infinitive to thank someone for doing something (“Merci beaucoup d’avoir participé.”).
target_language_example: Merci beaucoup pour votre aide !
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help!

additional_notes: A polite, slightly emphatic way to say thanks. Often used on its own, with a title (e.g., "monsieur"), or to politely refuse: "Non, merci bien" / "Merci bien, mais…".
target_language_example: Merci bien, mais je n’en ai pas besoin.
native_language_example: Thanks very much, but I don’t need it.

meaning: “thank you for…” (followed by an infinitive verb).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for doing something: merci d’accepter / merci d’appeler. The verb after d’ is in the infinitive (accepter, appeler, être, avoir fait). With a completed action, French often uses the past infinitive: merci d’avoir + past participle (merci d’avoir été honnête, merci d’avoir fait le déplacement). Related phrase: merci d’avance = “thanks in advance.”
target_language_example: Merci d'avoir fait le déplacement.
native_language_example: Thank you for making the trip.

meaning: “thanks for having…” / “thank you for…” (followed by a past infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something they already did. It’s followed by the past infinitive: d’avoir + past participle (e.g., merci d'avoir écouté = thanks for listening). In everyday French you can also say “merci de + infinitive” (merci de venir), but “merci d'avoir + past participle” emphasizes that the action is completed.
target_language_example: Merci d'avoir accepté de me voir.
native_language_example: Thanks for agreeing to see me.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a state/quality (être + adjective/noun phrase), e.g. Merci d’être mon ami / Merci d’être si compréhensif, or for an action where the verb takes être as the auxiliary in the past tense (être + past participle), e.g. Merci d’être venu(e)(s), passé(e)(s). With être, the past participle agrees with the person being thanked: Merci d’être venu (m.), venue (f.), venus (m. pl./mixed), venues (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Merci d'être passé me voir.
native_language_example: Thanks for stopping by to see me.

meaning: “thanks for coming” (said to a man or a mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for showing up or coming to see you. It’s built from merci de + infinitive (“thanks for” + verb). Agree the past participle with who you’re addressing: merci d’être venue (to a woman), merci d’être venus/venues (to several people).
target_language_example: Merci d'être venu me voir.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming to see me.

meaning: “thanks for coming” / “thank you for coming” (said to a woman).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone (female) for having come/for coming. It agrees with the person you’re speaking to: to a man you’d say « merci d’être venu »; to several people « merci d’être venu(e)(s) » (e.g., « merci d’être venus » to a mixed group).
target_language_example: Merci d'être venue ce soir, ça me fait plaisir.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming tonight, I’m happy you’re here.

meaning: “Thank you for coming.” (addressed to a group)
additional_notes: Used to thank several people for attending/coming, often in speeches or when welcoming guests. The construction d’être venus is a past infinitive meaning literally “for having come.” Agreement: venus (mixed/masculine plural) vs venues (all-female group). Common additions: merci d'être venus ce soir / si nombreux / si vite.
target_language_example: Mesdames et messieurs, merci d'être venus ce soir.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for coming this evening.

additional_notes: Used before a noun or an infinitive. With a noun, it means "thanks for" (merci de ta patience = thanks for your patience). With an infinitive, it can mean "thanks for doing..." or, in polite requests/instructions, "please do..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Merci de m'aider avec ce projet.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me with this project.

meaning: “thank you for having … (done something to/for me)” / “thanks for …”
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific past action. It’s usually followed by a past infinitive: **merci de m’avoir + past participle** (e.g., *merci de m’avoir accompagné* / *merci de m’avoir aidé*). The object pronoun **m’** (= *me*) comes before **avoir**. In natural English, you typically translate it as **“thanks for + -ing”** rather than “thanks for having…”.
target_language_example: Merci de m'avoir accompagné.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming with me / Thanks for accompanying me.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for an action that involves you: merci de + infinitive, with the object pronoun me (“me/to me”). Often followed by a verb in the infinitive (merci de me soutenir) or a past infinitive to thank for something already done (merci de me l’avoir dit = “thanks for having told me / thanks for telling me”). Note: before a vowel sound, me usually contracts to m’ (merci de m’aider), but the uncontracted form is kept before consonant sounds (merci de me soutenir).
target_language_example: Merci de me soutenir.
native_language_example: Thanks for supporting me.

meaning: “please don’t …” (polite request to not do something).
additional_notes: Common on signs, instructions, and emails to politely ask people not to do an action. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: « Merci de ne pas + infinitif » (e.g., fumer, ouvrir, laisser). It’s literally “thank you for not…,” but it functions like “please don’t…”.
target_language_example: Merci de ne pas parler trop fort dans le train.
native_language_example: Please don’t talk too loudly on the train.

meaning: “thank you for having … (to us)” / “thanks for …” (followed by a past infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something they did: **merci de** + **past infinitive** (**avoir** + past participle) when the action is completed. It’s usually followed by a verb, e.g. *merci de nous avoir aidés / prévenus / invités*. Agreement: the past participle often agrees with **nous** when it’s the direct object placed before the verb (e.g. *merci de nous avoir invités* / *invitées*).
target_language_example: Merci de nous avoir aidés hier soir.
native_language_example: Thank you for helping us last night.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing (often a noun): merci de votre patience, collaboration, gentillesse, fidélité, etc. This is more formal than “merci pour …”. Use “merci de ton/ta …” with someone you address as “tu”.
target_language_example: Merci de votre aide, c’est très apprécié.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, it’s very much appreciated.

meaning: "thanks for" (followed by a noun or noun phrase).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing: Merci pour + le/la/les + noun (Merci pour le cadeau / Merci pour la soirée). For a verb, you usually use « merci de + infinitive » (Merci de m’avoir aidé).
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help.

meaning: 'thanks for the' (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing: **merci pour + noun**. **La** is the feminine singular “the” (e.g., *la musique, la danse, la cigarette, la carte postale*). For masculine nouns, use **merci pour le**; for plural, **merci pour les**. (You’ll also see **merci de + infinitive**: *Merci de venir* = “Thanks for coming.”)
target_language_example: Merci pour la gentillesse !
native_language_example: Thanks for the kindness!

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing or action. Use it before a masculine singular noun: merci pour le conseil (the advice), merci pour le lien (the link), merci pour le repas (the meal), merci pour le whisky. With a feminine noun, use “merci pour la …”; with plural, “merci pour les …”; before a vowel sound, “merci pour l’ …”.
target_language_example: Merci pour le coup de main !
native_language_example: Thanks for the help!

additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely, especially in formal or professional situations. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (votre + noun), e.g., votre aide, votre attention, votre soutien. For feminine singular nouns, use “merci pour votre” as well (votre is the same), e.g., votre patience. For plural, use “merci pour vos …” (e.g., vos efforts).
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide, je l’apprécie beaucoup.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help; I really appreciate it.

additional_notes: A polite/formal way to thank someone (using "votre" for one person you address as "vous" or for several people). Often said on its own, or followed by a brief explanation (e.g., "mais…").
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide, je peux continuer tout seul maintenant.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help; I can continue on my own now.

meaning: “Damn!” / “Oh shit!” (an exclamation of surprise, annoyance, or frustration).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar (contains “merde” = “shit”). Used as a standalone reaction, often with fillers like bah/ben/bon/oh. Avoid in polite or professional situations; a milder option is “mince alors !” or “zut alors !”.
target_language_example: Merde alors, j’ai oublié mes clés !
native_language_example: Oh shit, I forgot my keys!

additional_notes: Often refers to your personal belongings: « Je vais prendre mes affaires. » It can also mean “my business / my concern” in the expression « Ce ne sont pas mes affaires » = “That’s none of my business.” Note: « affaires » looks like English “affairs,” but in French it commonly means “things, belongings, matters,” not necessarily romantic affairs.
target_language_example: Attends, j'ai oublié mes affaires dans la voiture.
native_language_example: Wait, I forgot my stuff in the car.

additional_notes: "Mes" means "my" (plural). "Amies" is the plural feminine form of "ami(e)" (friend), used when the group is all women/girls. If it’s mixed or all men/boys, you typically use the masculine plural: "mes amis". You can also say "une de mes amies" = "one of my (female) friends."
target_language_example: Mes amies arrivent ce soir.
native_language_example: My (female) friends are arriving tonight.

additional_notes: Plural possessive phrase used to talk about your friends or to address a group of people warmly (like “my friends!”). For a mixed group or unknown gender, French commonly uses the masculine plural “amis.” For an all-female group, you can say “mes amies.”
target_language_example: Merci d'être là, mes amis !
native_language_example: Thanks for being here, my friends!

meaning: 'my friends are' / 'my friends have' (with a past participle).
additional_notes: Used to describe your friends with an adjective or location (Mes amis sont ici / en danger), or to form the passé composé with the verb être for certain verbs of movement/change (Mes amis sont passés = 'my friends came by / dropped in'). Agreement: with être in the passé composé, the past participle usually agrees with the subject (passés for masculine plural, passées for feminine plural, passé(e)(s) for mixed/unknown).
target_language_example: Mes amis sont arrivés tard hier soir.
native_language_example: My friends arrived late last night.

additional_notes: Used when talking about your belongings you travel with (suitcases, bags). Often heard in travel contexts (airport, train, taxi). Note: French usually uses the plural “bagages,” even if it’s just one suitcase.
target_language_example: Je peux déposer mes bagages ici ?
native_language_example: Can I leave my luggage here?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "mes" (my) with the body part "bras" (arms). Often used when talking about pain, movement, or position (e.g., "Mes bras me font mal"), and in expressions like "ouvrir les bras" (to open one’s arms / to welcome with an embrace).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas lever mes bras.
native_language_example: I can’t raise my arms.

additional_notes: "Mes" is the plural possessive adjective for "my" (used before plural nouns). "Chaussures" is plural; in French, clothing items are often talked about in the plural. You can also say "ma chaussure" for one shoe.
target_language_example: Je ne retrouve plus mes chaussures.
native_language_example: I can’t find my shoes anymore.

meaning: "my hair is" / "my hairs are" (talking about your hair).
additional_notes: In French, "cheveux" (hair) is usually plural, so you use "mes" (my) and the plural verb "sont" (are): "Mes cheveux sont + adjective" (longs, mouillés, gris, propres). In English you typically say "my hair is" (singular). Make the adjective plural to match "cheveux" (often adding -s).
target_language_example: Mes cheveux sont trop courts pour faire une queue de cheval.
native_language_example: My hair is too short to make a ponytail.

additional_notes: Used to talk about schoolwork you have to do outside of class. You’ll often hear it with verbs like faire (to do), finir/terminer (to finish), and expressions like être en train de (to be in the middle of) or venir de (to have just). Note: devoir can also mean "duty" or "obligation," but in the plural (devoirs) it commonly means "homework."
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas jouer maintenant : je dois finir mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I can’t play now: I have to finish my homework.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own children in general. "mes" is the plural form of "my" (before a plural noun), and "enfants" means "children". Often used with family-related verbs like "s'occuper de" (look after), "veiller sur" (watch over), "apprendre" (learn), or "arriver" (arrive).
target_language_example: Mes enfants vont à l'école à huit heures.
native_language_example: My kids go to school at eight o'clock.

additional_notes: Used to apologize politely. Common in the set phrase « Je (vous) présente mes excuses… » (“I offer you my apologies…”) followed by « pour… » (“for…”) + a noun/infinitive (e.g., « pour le retard » / « pour avoir répondu tard »). On its own (« Mes excuses. ») it’s a brief, formal-ish way to say “Sorry.”
target_language_example: Mes excuses, je suis en retard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late.

additional_notes: Plural possessive phrase: "mes" (my) + "frères" (brothers). Used to talk about your brothers in general (e.g., "Mes frères habitent ici") or to address them directly (often followed by a comma): "Mes frères, écoutez-moi !"
target_language_example: Mes frères viennent dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: My brothers are coming for dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate someone on good news or an achievement. Often said as "Toutes mes félicitations !" or "Encore toutes mes félicitations" for extra emphasis. You can also use it in messages via someone else: "Transmettez-lui mes félicitations" ("Please pass on my congratulations").
target_language_example: Mes félicitations pour ton nouveau travail !
native_language_example: Congratulations on your new job!

additional_notes: "Mes" means "my" (plural), and "parents" means "parents". Used to talk about your mother and father together. In speech, "Mes parents ?" can be a surprised/confirming question ("My parents?").
target_language_example: Je vais dîner avec mes parents ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm having dinner with my parents tonight.

additional_notes: Used to describe your parents’ state, situation, or location. It’s the plural form of "mon parent est" (rare) and uses "sont" because "parents" is plural. You can add an adjective ("vieux"), a past participle used like an adjective ("divorcés", "morts"), or a place/status ("là").
target_language_example: Mes parents sont en vacances cette semaine.
native_language_example: My parents are on vacation this week.
