additional_notes: Used for emphasis to show you witnessed something yourself. Very common in the expression « de mes propres yeux » (= “with my own eyes”). « propres » here means “own” (not “clean”), and it agrees with « yeux » (masculine plural).
target_language_example: Je l’ai vu de mes propres yeux.
native_language_example: I saw it with my own eyes.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "mes" (my, plural) + "yeux" (eyes). Used literally for vision or eye discomfort (e.g., burning, sensitive to light), and figuratively in expressions like "sous mes yeux" meaning "right in front of me / before my eyes."
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas lire sans lunettes : mes yeux sont fatigués.
native_language_example: I can’t read without glasses: my eyes are tired.

additional_notes: Used to describe your eyes (color, state, how they feel, or a figurative description). Follow it with an adjective (bleus, fatigués, ouverts) or an expression like "remplis de larmes". Note agreement: "yeux" is masculine plural, so adjectives are usually masculine plural (bleus, douloureux, fatigués).
target_language_example: Mes yeux sont secs aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: My eyes are dry today.

additional_notes: A very formal way to address an audience at the start of a speech or announcement (e.g., on a plane, at an event). It’s often followed by a comma and then what you want to say. Note: the usual spelling is “Mesdames et Messieurs” (both capitalized), though it may appear with different capitalization.
target_language_example: Mesdames et Messieurs, le spectacle va commencer.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, the show is about to begin.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to address an audience or group (e.g., at a speech, announcement, or presentation). It can come at the beginning or end of a sentence. Often used with greetings like « bonsoir » or to get attention (« Écoutez… »).
target_language_example: Mesdames et messieurs, bienvenue à notre conférence.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to our conference.

meaning: “a measure of” (a step taken, or a measured amount).
additional_notes: Often used in fixed phrases like **une mesure de sécurité** (“a safety measure”) or **par mesure de sécurité** (“as a safety precaution”). It can also mean a measured quantity: **une mesure de riz** (“a measure/serving of rice”). Related but slightly different: **prendre la mesure de + noun** means “to grasp/assess the extent of” something (e.g., *Je prends la mesure de ta situation*).
target_language_example: Par mesure de sécurité, on a fermé la porte.
native_language_example: As a safety precaution, we closed the door.

meaning: literally: “measure to do it” (not a natural French expression).
additional_notes: As written, this phrase is not idiomatic in French. If you mean “able to do it,” the common expression is **en mesure de le faire** (“in a position/able to do it”): *Je suis en mesure de le faire.* If you mean “a measure/step to do it,” French usually uses **une mesure pour le faire** or **des mesures pour le faire** (“a measure/measures to do it”).
target_language_example: Je suis en mesure de le faire demain.
native_language_example: I’m able to do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Affirmative command with the verb *mettre* ("to put/place") in the *tu* form: *mets*. The direct object pronoun *le* ("it") is attached with a hyphen in positive commands: *Mets-le…* ("Put it…"). Often followed by a place (*dedans*, *sur mon bureau*). It can also mean "charge it" in contexts like paying: *Mets-le sur mon compte* ("Put it on my account").
target_language_example: Mets-le dans ton sac, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Put it in your bag, please.

additional_notes:
This is the imperative for “tu” of **se mettre** (“to put oneself / to get oneself / to start”). It’s used a lot with a place or position (**Mets-toi de côté / là**) and with prepositions:
- **se mettre à + noun/infinitive** = to start doing something (**Mets-toi au boulot !**)
- **se mettre en + noun** = to get into a state/position (**Mets-toi en garde**)
- **se mettre à + position** = to get into a posture (**Mets-toi à quatre pattes**)
It can also appear in fixed expressions like **Mets-toi bien ça dans le crâne** (“Get it into your head”).
target_language_example: Mets-toi à l’aise et raconte-moi tout.
native_language_example: Make yourself comfortable and tell me everything.

additional_notes: Imperative form of **mettre** (“to put/place”), addressed to **vous** (either several people, or one person politely). **-le** is a direct object pronoun meaning **“it”** or **“him”** (masculine), depending on context. Often followed by a place/direction: *mettez-le ici / dehors / sur la table*.
target_language_example: Mettez-le sur la table, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Put it on the table, please.

meaning: "put yourself" / "get yourself" (often: "start" or "get into" a position or state).
additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of **se mettre** for **vous** (to one person formally or to several people). Common patterns: **mettez-vous à + infinitive** = “start doing …” (e.g., *Mettez-vous à travailler*), **mettez-vous au + noun** = “get to …” (*au travail* = “to work”), **mettez-vous à genoux** = “kneel down,” **mettez-vous en + clothing/state** = “put on / get into” (*en pyjama*), **mettez-vous dans + place/light** = “move/stand into” (*dans la lumière*).
target_language_example: Mettez-vous au travail tout de suite.
native_language_example: Get to work right away.

meaning: to bring (someone) up to date; to inform (someone).
additional_notes: Used to update someone on the latest situation or news. Very common with an indirect object pronoun: « me/te/vous/lui/nous/leur mettre au courant ». Often followed by « de » to specify the topic: « Je vais te mettre au courant de la situation. »
target_language_example: Laisse-moi te mettre au courant de la situation.
native_language_example: Let me bring you up to date on the situation.

meaning: to give birth (to a baby); to bring into the world.
additional_notes: Used mainly for childbirth, often with a direct object: « mettre au monde un enfant / un bébé ». It can be used about the mother (« Elle va mettre au monde… ») or in a more formal/medical tone. Less commonly, it can also mean to bring something new into existence (e.g., an invention), but the usual meaning is “to give birth.”
target_language_example: Elle va mettre au monde une petite fille en avril.
native_language_example: She is going to give birth to a little girl in April.

meaning: to get (people) to agree; to reach an agreement.
additional_notes: Often used as **se mettre d’accord** (“to agree / come to an agreement”): *On s’est mis d’accord sur une date.* Without **se**, it can mean “to make people agree” or “to settle a dispute”: *Il a mis tout le monde d’accord.* Also common: **mettre quelqu’un d’accord avec quelqu’un** (“to get someone to agree with someone”).
target_language_example: Il faut mettre d'accord les deux parties sur le prix avant de signer.
native_language_example: We need to get both parties to agree on the price before signing.

meaning: to move/step aside; to get out of the way.
additional_notes: Often used with the reflexive pronoun (se mettre de côté = to step aside). Common in polite requests with veuillez/voudriez-vous, especially to ask someone to clear space or let others pass. Also note: in other contexts, mettre de côté can mean “to set aside/save (money, objects)”—but here it’s about physically moving aside.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, pouvez-vous vous mettre de côté, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you step aside, please?

meaning: to trick / rip (someone) off; to mess someone around.
additional_notes: Informal. Often used as « On m’a mis dedans » (= “I got tricked / ripped off”). You can also use it with a person: « Il m’a mis dedans ». Literally it can mean “to put inside,” but in everyday speech the idiomatic meaning (“to con/trick”) is very common.
target_language_example: Attention, ce vendeur essaie de te mettre dedans.
native_language_example: Careful, this seller is trying to rip you off.

meaning: to make (someone) angry; to get angry.
additional_notes: Used as (1) transitive: « mettre quelqu’un en colère » = to make someone angry, and (2) reflexive: « se mettre en colère » = to get angry (often suddenly). Commonly appears in phrases like « ça me met en colère » (that makes me angry).
target_language_example: Ça me met en colère quand on me coupe la parole.
native_language_example: It makes me angry when people interrupt me.

meaning: to endanger; to put (someone/something) in danger.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object: « mettre quelqu’un/quelque chose en danger » (“to endanger someone/something”). You can also say « se mettre en danger » to mean “to put yourself in danger / take risks.” Often used in warnings, rules, and safety contexts.
target_language_example: Ne pas mettre les enfants en danger.
native_language_example: Do not put the children in danger.

meaning: to doubt; to call into question.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object (something you doubt): « mettre en doute + nom/pronom ». Common in more formal contexts (news, debates, writing): « mettre en doute la version officielle », « mettre en doute ce qu’il a dit ».
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas mettre en doute ta parole, mais j’ai besoin de preuves.
native_language_example: I don’t want to doubt what you’re saying, but I need proof.

meaning: to warn; to put (someone) on guard.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone about a danger or risk. Common patterns: « mettre quelqu’un en garde » (warn someone) and « mettre quelqu’un en garde contre + noun » (warn someone against/about something). Often used in formal or written contexts; in everyday speech you can also use « prévenir » (to warn).
target_language_example: Je veux te mettre en garde contre les arnaques en ligne.
native_language_example: I want to warn you about online scams.

additional_notes: Used for publishing content (a photo, video, document, article, website) on the internet. Often followed by a direct object: mettre une vidéo en ligne. Related noun: la mise en ligne (uploading/going online). Common alternative: téléverser (Canada) for “upload.” Note: télécharger can mean “download” (and sometimes “upload” in older/incorrect usage), so it can be confusing.
target_language_example: Je vais mettre en ligne les photos ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to upload the photos tonight.

meaning: to start; to turn on; to set in motion.
additional_notes: Used for starting a device, machine, or system (turning it on or getting it running). Can also be used more generally for starting a process or putting something into operation. Conjugates like a normal verb: je vais mettre en marche, tu vas mettre en marche, il/elle va mettre en marche, nous allons mettre en marche, etc.
target_language_example: Je vais mettre en marche la machine.
native_language_example: I’m going to start the machine / I’m going to turn the machine on.

meaning: to tear/sash something to pieces; to dismantle completely; (figuratively) to tear an argument apart.
additional_notes: Used for physically destroying something (a document, an object) or for completely dismantling something (a machine, a plan). Can also be figurative: to totally refute/tear apart an argument or idea. Common pattern: « mettre + [object] + en pièces ».
target_language_example: Il va mettre en pièces le contrat.
native_language_example: He is going to tear the contract to pieces.

meaning: to set up; to put in place; to implement.
additional_notes: Used for creating or organizing something so it can function (a system, plan, policy, organization, measures). Very common with things like "un système", "un plan", "une stratégie", "des mesures". In politics or work contexts it often means “to implement” rather than physically placing objects.
target_language_example: On doit mettre en place un plan pour aider les étudiants.
native_language_example: We need to set up a plan to help students.

meaning: to put into practice; to apply (a plan, idea, advice).
additional_notes: Used when you start using something concretely in real life (a method, rule, lesson, advice). Often followed by a direct object: « mettre en pratique une idée / un conseil / une théorie ». Close to « appliquer ».
target_language_example: J'essaie de mettre en pratique ce que j'ai appris en cours.
native_language_example: I'm trying to put into practice what I learned in class.

meaning: to set off; to get started; to start up (a machine).
additional_notes: Often used reflexively (se mettre en route) meaning “to set off / get going” (leave and start traveling). With machines or systems, it can mean “to start up” (e.g., a generator).
target_language_example: On devrait se mettre en route avant qu'il ne fasse nuit.
native_language_example: We should set off before it gets dark.

meaning: to implement; to put into practice.
additional_notes: Used for carrying out a plan, policy, decision, project, or strategy (often in formal/professional contexts). Common pattern: mettre en œuvre + un plan/une politique/une stratégie/une mesure/un projet. In the passive: être mis(e) en œuvre = to be implemented.
target_language_example: Nous allons mettre en œuvre un nouveau plan de sécurité dès lundi.
native_language_example: We’re going to implement a new safety plan starting Monday.

meaning: to put an end to; to end (something).
additional_notes: Used with "à" + a noun/infinitive: "mettre fin à la grève" (end the strike), "mettre fin à cette situation" (put an end to this situation). The thing being ended is the object of "à"; you can replace it with a pronoun: "y mettre fin" = "put an end to it".
target_language_example: On doit mettre fin à ce malentendu.
native_language_example: We need to put an end to this misunderstanding.

meaning: to put an end to; to stop; to end.
additional_notes: Used with a noun (or noun phrase) to mean bringing something to a conclusion, often something ongoing or negative: mettre fin à une dispute, une guerre, une mission, tout ça. It’s fairly formal/neutral; in everyday speech you can also say arrêter (to stop) depending on the context.
target_language_example: On doit mettre fin à cette dispute avant qu’elle ne s’aggrave.
native_language_example: We need to put an end to this argument before it gets worse.

meaning: to put your hand (on); (in set phrases) to get hold of; to pay/chip in.
additional_notes: Usually appears in set expressions rather than alone. **mettre la main sur / dessus** = “to lay hands on, to get hold of, to find/obtain.” **mettre la main à la poche / au portefeuille** = “to pay, to contribute money” (often reluctantly: “to cough up”).
target_language_example: Personne ne veut mettre la main à la poche.
native_language_example: Nobody wants to chip in (to pay).

meaning: to get hold of; to find; to obtain (sometimes: to catch).
additional_notes: Often used when something is hard to locate or acquire: documents, an object, information, etc. It can also mean to catch someone (e.g., the police catching a suspect). Conjugate « mettre » as needed: « je mets la main sur… », « j’ai mis la main sur… ».
target_language_example: Je vais enfin mettre la main sur mes clés.
native_language_example: I’m finally going to find my keys.

meaning: to put pressure (on someone); to pressure someone.
additional_notes: Used when someone is pushing you to do something, perform, decide, etc. Common patterns: « mettre la pression à quelqu’un » or « mettre la pression sur quelqu’un ». Very common reflexive form: « se mettre la pression » = to put pressure on yourself.
target_language_example: Arrête de me mettre la pression, je vais le faire à mon rythme.
native_language_example: Stop putting pressure on me, I’ll do it at my own pace.

additional_notes: Used for preparing the table before a meal (putting out plates, cutlery, glasses, napkins, etc.). Often used with "peux-tu... ?" / "je vais..." to ask someone to do it or to say you’re going to do it. Not the same as "dresser la table" (more formal) or "mettre le couvert" (set the place settings).
target_language_example: On mange dans dix minutes, tu peux mettre la table ?
native_language_example: We’re eating in ten minutes—can you set the table?

meaning: to set (something) on fire; (figuratively) to set things off / cause a big stir.
additional_notes: Literal use: "mettre le feu à + nom" = to set something on fire (often in warnings, threats, or descriptions of arson). Figurative use: "mettre le feu" can mean to ignite excitement, controversy, or intense reactions (e.g., in media or on social networks). Common pattern: "mettre le feu à + lieu/objet"; can also be used without an explicit object when context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Elle a menacé de mettre le feu à notre maison.
native_language_example: She threatened to set our house on fire.

additional_notes: Usually used with a place: « mettre les pieds à/dans + lieu ». Very common in the negative: « ne pas mettre les pieds (quelque part) » = “not to set foot (somewhere)” / “not to go there at all.”
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus mettre les pieds dans ce café.
native_language_example: I don’t want to set foot in that café anymore.

meaning: to put on the table; (figuratively) to put forward for discussion.
additional_notes: Literal use: physically placing something on a table (object pronouns can go in between: « Je le mets sur la table. »). Figurative use: to bring up an idea, proposal, or topic openly in a conversation/meeting: « mettre une question/un sujet sur la table ».
target_language_example: Je voudrais mettre sur la table cette question avant de décider.
native_language_example: I’d like to put this question on the table before deciding.

meaning: to put an end to; to stop (something).
additional_notes: Used with "à" + noun/infinitive: "mettre un terme à la guerre" (end the war), "mettre un terme à ceci/cela" (put an end to this/that). Fairly formal; in everyday speech you can also say "arrêter" or "mettre fin à".
target_language_example: Ils ont décidé de mettre un terme au conflit.
native_language_example: They decided to put an end to the conflict.

meaning: to update; to bring up to date.
additional_notes: Used for updating software, devices, files, or information (e.g., données, logiciel, appareil). It can also be reflexive: « se mettre à jour » = to get up to date/caught up (learn the latest info, update your knowledge). Often appears with « il faut… » (you need to…) or polite requests: « Pourriez-vous… ? ».
target_language_example: N'oublie pas de mettre à jour l'application avant le voyage.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to update the app before the trip.

meaning: to kick someone out; to throw someone out (also: to fire someone).
additional_notes: Literally “to put (someone) at the door,” but it’s used idiomatically. You can use it for being forced to leave a place (a home, a party, a store) or being dismissed from a job. Often said with a direct object: « On l’a mis à la porte. »
target_language_example: Le patron a décidé de mettre à la porte l’employé qui arrivait toujours en retard.
native_language_example: The boss decided to fire/kick out the employee who was always arriving late.

meaning: to put a price on; to offer a reward (a bounty) for
additional_notes: Used when an authority or organization sets an official price or reward for something—very often a bounty for capturing or finding a person ("mettre quelqu’un à prix"), or a price for an object (especially in sales/auctions). You may also see it in the passive (« Il a été mis à prix »), but the active form is « mettre à prix ».
target_language_example: La police a mis à prix le chef de gang.
native_language_example: The police put a bounty on the gang leader.

additional_notes: From the verb *mourir* (to die): *ils/elles meurent* = “they die.” The phrase *mourir de faim* is used to talk about starving (often literally, especially in news or serious contexts). It can also be used more loosely to mean “I’m starving,” e.g. *Je meurs de faim*.
target_language_example: Sans aide, beaucoup de familles meurent de faim.
native_language_example: Without help, many families die of hunger.

additional_notes: Mostly used in sports to talk about the break in the middle of a match: « à la mi-temps » (“at halftime”). Note: « à mi-temps » (without « la ») usually means “part-time” (e.g., « travailler à mi-temps »).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la mi-temps.
native_language_example: We’ll meet up at halftime.

additional_notes: In everyday French, the appliance is most often said as **un micro-ondes** (masculine, usually with an -s even when singular). You’ll also see **au micro-ondes** = “in the microwave.” Without the -s, **micro-onde** can refer more literally to a “microwave” as a type of wave, but for beginners it usually means the kitchen appliance.
target_language_example: Je vais réchauffer la soupe au micro-ondes.
native_language_example: I’m going to heat up the soup in the microwave.

additional_notes: Refers to the appliance used to heat food quickly. Commonly used with prepositions like « au micro-ondes » (“in the microwave”) and verbs like « passer/mettre au micro-ondes » (“to microwave”).
target_language_example: Je réchauffe la soupe au micro-ondes.
native_language_example: I’m reheating the soup in the microwave.

meaning: '(had) better to' (in *faire mieux de + infinitive*); or 'better from/of' (in *mieux de ta part*, *mieux de lui*).
additional_notes:
Most often appears in fixed patterns:
- **faire mieux de + infinitive**: a strong suggestion/advice meaning **“(you/we/he) had better …”**. Common in the conditional: *tu ferais mieux de… / nous ferions mieux de…*.
- **(s’attendre à) mieux de + someone**: means **“(to) expect better from someone”**: *Je m’attendais à mieux de ta part.*
On its own, **mieux** = “better” and **de** links to an infinitive or indicates “from/of” someone, but the full meaning depends on the pattern above.
target_language_example: Tu ferais mieux de partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You’d better leave now.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation to avoid an action. Often appears after expressions like « C’est mieux de ne pas… » or « Il est mieux de ne pas… » (more common: « Il vaut mieux ne pas… »). Follow it with an infinitive: « mieux de ne pas + verbe ».
target_language_example: C’est mieux de ne pas répondre tout de suite.
native_language_example: It’s better not to reply right away.

additional_notes: Used to add a stronger, improved option or idea right after what you just said. Often follows a suggestion or statement: "On peut prendre le train — mieux encore, on peut y aller à vélo." Can also introduce a positive surprise.
target_language_example: On peut se retrouver demain, ou mieux encore, ce soir si tu es libre.
native_language_example: We can meet tomorrow, or better yet, tonight if you’re free.

additional_notes: Used to say or hope that a situation or performance will improve in the future. Often follows verbs like "être," "aller," or "faire" (e.g., "Ce sera mieux...", "Ça ira mieux...", "faire mieux..."). Can sound encouraging or slightly critical depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis en retard — je ferai mieux la prochaine fois.
native_language_example: Sorry I’m late — I’ll do better next time.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things, meaning that one is superior to the other. It can compare qualities, results, or how well someone does something: « mieux que le tien » (better than yours), « mieux que cela » (better than that), « nager mieux que Marie » (swim better than Marie). Can also be used in expressions like « mieux que tout » (better than anything / best of all).
target_language_example: Ce restaurant est mieux que celui d’hier.
native_language_example: This restaurant is better than yesterday’s one.

meaning: "better than me" (I’m the point of comparison).
additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s ability, performance, knowledge, etc. with yours. Often follows a verb or an adverb of degree: « parler mieux que moi », « connaître mieux que moi ».
target_language_example: Tu comprends ça bien mieux que moi.
native_language_example: You understand that much better than me.

meaning: "better than that" (more than that; not as bad as that).
additional_notes: Used to say someone deserves more, is worth more, or should do better than what is being suggested or happening. Often with verbs like mériter (to deserve), valoir (to be worth), and connaître (to know): « Il mérite mieux que ça » = he deserves better; « Tu ne me connais pas mieux que ça ? » = don’t you know me better than that?
target_language_example: Allez, tu peux faire mieux que ça !
native_language_example: Come on, you can do better than that!

additional_notes: Used to say one option is preferable to another, often in advice, proverbs, or warnings. Common patterns: "Mieux vaut + infinitive" (Mieux vaut partir maintenant.), and "Mieux vaut ... que ..." (Mieux vaut être en avance que en retard.). It can also be followed by a noun: "Mieux vaut la vérité."
target_language_example: Mieux vaut prendre un parapluie que d’être trempé.
native_language_example: It’s better to take an umbrella than to get soaked.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a warning: choose not to do something because it’s wiser/safer. It’s often followed by an infinitive (e.g., mieux vaut ne pas + parler / discuter / savoir). You can also add a person: “Mieux vaut ne pas lui en parler.”
target_language_example: Mieux vaut ne pas répondre tout de suite.
native_language_example: It’s better not to reply right away.

additional_notes: Most often used with « au »: « au milieu de la + [noun] » = “in the middle of the …”. Common fixed phrases include « au milieu de la nuit » (in the middle of the night) and « au milieu de la rue » (in the middle of the street). Note: French « milieu » can mean “middle,” not just English “milieu” (= environment).
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillé au milieu de la nuit.
native_language_example: I woke up in the middle of the night.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that it’s very late/early (deep in the night). Often said with intensifiers like "en plein milieu de la nuit" (= right in the middle of the night) to stress that something happened at an inconvenient hour.
target_language_example: Je me suis réveillé(e) en plein milieu de la nuit à cause du bruit.
native_language_example: I woke up in the middle of the night because of the noise.

meaning: "the middle of nowhere" (a very remote place).
additional_notes: Most often used as "au milieu de nulle part" (= in the middle of nowhere). "Nulle part" means "nowhere". You can use it to say something is far from towns, people, or everything else: "On est au milieu de nulle part."
target_language_example: Le restaurant est au milieu de nulle part.
native_language_example: The restaurant is in the middle of nowhere.

additional_notes: Literally means “a thousand legs.” In everyday French it refers to a centipede (sometimes used loosely for similar many-legged creatures). It can also be used figuratively or humorously (e.g., “un mille-pattes humain” = someone/thing like a “human centipede”).
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé un mille-pattes dans la salle de bain.
native_language_example: I found a centipede in the bathroom.

additional_notes: A warm, emphatic way to thank someone (stronger than "merci"). You can say it by itself ("Mille mercis !") or follow it with "pour" + noun/verb to say what you’re thanking them for ("Mille mercis pour votre aide"). Often used in polite contexts (with "votre"), but it isn’t slang.
target_language_example: Mille mercis pour votre aide, c’est très gentil.
native_language_example: Thank you so much for your help, that’s very kind.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a very large number of people (not necessarily an exact count). Common pattern: "des milliers de + noun" (e.g., des milliers de personnes / de gens). Note that "millier" is usually used in the plural here: "des milliers de…"
target_language_example: Des milliers de personnes sont venues au concert.
native_language_example: Thousands of people came to the concert.

meaning: a million dollars (often: “un million de dollars”).
additional_notes: Usually used with an article or number: “un million de dollars” (a million dollars), “deux millions de dollars” (two million dollars). Note the plural: “millions” takes -s when the number is more than one (deux millions), but not with “un million”. “Dollar(s)” is often plural in English; in French it stays singular after “un” and plural after larger numbers.
target_language_example: Cette maison coûte un million de dollars.
native_language_example: This house costs a million dollars.

meaning: from one minute to the next; very quickly / at any moment.
additional_notes: Most often used as **d’une minute à l’autre** (“from one minute to the next”) to say something changes quickly or can happen at any time. Similar phrases: **d’un moment à l’autre**.
target_language_example: Tout peut changer, minute à l'autre.
native_language_example: Everything can change from one minute to the next.

meaning: staging; a setup (something arranged to look real).
additional_notes: Often used for theater/film to mean the way a scene is staged or directed. In everyday speech, it can mean a fabricated situation meant to create an impression ("It was all staged"). Common with "Ce n'était qu'une mise en scène" (It was just a setup) and "Pourquoi toute cette mise en scène ?" (Why all this show?).
target_language_example: Tout ça, c'était une mise en scène pour me faire peur.
native_language_example: All that was staged to scare me.

meaning: update (a new version or the act of updating).
additional_notes: Common for software, phones, apps, or information being brought up to date. Often used with verbs like « faire une mise à jour » (to do an update), « installer une mise à jour » (to install an update), or « une mise à jour est disponible » (an update is available).
target_language_example: Une mise à jour est disponible : vous voulez l’installer maintenant ?
native_language_example: An update is available: do you want to install it now?

meaning: “began to …” (literary past tense of « mettre à + infinitive »).
additional_notes: « Mit » is the passé simple (simple past) of « mettre » for il/elle/on, used mostly in writing (stories, novels), not in everyday speech. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive: « il mit à rire » = “he began to laugh.” In conversation you usually say « il s’est mis à + infinitive » (passé composé).
target_language_example: À cette nouvelle, il mit à pleurer.
native_language_example: At this news, he began to cry.

additional_notes: This is from the pattern **se mettre à + infinitive** = “to start/begin to do something.” **Mit** is the **passé simple** (literary past) form of *mettre* used in books and stories: *elle se mit à pleurer* = “she began to cry.” In everyday speech you usually say **s’est mis / s’est mise à pleurer** (passé composé).
target_language_example: En entendant la nouvelle, il se mit à pleurer.
native_language_example: On hearing the news, he began to cry.

additional_notes: From the verb pattern « se mettre à + infinitive » = “to start/begin to + verb.” « mit » is the passé simple (literary past) of « mettre » (3rd person singular), so you’ll mostly see it in stories and books. In everyday speech, French usually uses « il s’est mis à pleuvoir » (passé composé).
target_language_example: Tout à coup, il se mit à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to describe how someone (or a group) lives day to day: habits, activities, values, and overall living conditions. Often followed by an adjective (mode de vie sain/actif) or linked to a person/group (son/notre/votre mode de vie). Common with verbs like changer (to change) or menacer (to threaten) in broader contexts (e.g., "our way of life").
target_language_example: Après son déménagement, elle a complètement changé de mode de vie.
native_language_example: After moving, she completely changed her lifestyle.

meaning: 'Me, I’m…' / 'As for me, it’s…' (used to state your own situation/opinion, often in contrast to others).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French to highlight *moi* (“me”) as the topic and often imply contrast: **Moi, c’est + description**. It can sound more natural in English as “As for me…” or “Me, I…”. Also appears in the broader pattern **[person/thing], c’est + description** (e.g., *Toi et moi, c’est terminé*).
target_language_example: Moi, c'est pareil, je n'ai pas envie de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: As for me, it’s the same—I don’t feel like going out tonight.

meaning: “Me, I…” (used to emphasize or contrast what *I* think/do).
additional_notes: Used with a pause/comma to highlight the speaker, often to contrast with others (“Moi, je…, mais lui…”). Common in spoken French for emphasis. Similar idea to “Quant à moi, …” (“As for me…”) but “moi, je” is more conversational.
target_language_example: Moi, je préfère rester ici.
native_language_example: Me, I’d rather stay here.

meaning: “As for me, I don’t …” (emphatic/contrastive “I” in a negative sentence).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize the speaker (“me, I…”) often to contrast with someone else’s actions/opinions. Usually followed by a verb in the negative (ne…pas / ne…jamais / ne…plus, etc.). The comma is common in writing: “Moi, je ne …”.
target_language_example: Moi, je ne veux pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: As for me, I don’t want to go out tonight.

meaning: 'As for me, I am…' / 'Me, I’m…' (emphatic 'I am').
additional_notes: Used to emphasize or contrast the speaker with others (a common French pattern called left-dislocation): "Moi, je suis…" = "I, personally, am…" You’ll often hear it in speech to insist, clarify, or oppose another point of view. In "Ne vous moquez pas de moi, je suis sincère", "de moi" means "of me" (= "at me"), and the following "je suis" is just "I am" (not the set phrase "moi, je suis").
target_language_example: Moi, je suis fatigué, alors je rentre.
native_language_example: Me, I’m tired, so I’m going home.

meaning: “Me, I…” (emphatic way to say “I … to you / you …”).
additional_notes: Used in spoken French to strongly emphasize the subject (“moi”) before a normal sentence starting with “je”. It often contrasts with someone else (like “As for me…” / “I, for my part…”). “te” is the object pronoun meaning “you” (can be “to you” or “you” depending on the verb: je te parle = I speak to you; je te vois = I see you). In writing, it’s usually punctuated: “Moi, je …”.
target_language_example: Moi, je te dis la vérité.
native_language_example: Me, I’m telling you the truth.

meaning: “Me, I’m going to…” / “As for me, I’m going to…” (strong emphasis on what *I* will do).
additional_notes: Used to contrast your choice or plan with someone else’s, or to insist on your own point of view. Common in spoken French: the stressed pronoun "moi" is repeated with "je" for emphasis (not strictly necessary in formal writing). Often followed by an infinitive ("je vais partir") or another verb phrase.
target_language_example: Moi, je vais rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: Me, I’m going to go home.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that this is *your* preference/opinion, often contrasting with what others want. The comma reflects a spoken pause: “Moi, …”. It can sound a bit insistent depending on tone; a softer alternative is “Je voudrais…”. Often appears with “Quant à moi, je veux…” (“As for me, I want…”).
target_language_example: Moi, je veux juste un café, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Me, I just want a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to stay/come/do something with you. The comma shows that “moi” is being emphasized (“with me”). “S'il te plaît” uses the informal “tu” form; in more formal situations you’d say “moi, s'il vous plaît.”
target_language_example: Viens avec moi, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Come with me, please.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you’re talking about yourself, often after a preposition: avec moi-même (with myself), en paix avec moi-même (at peace with myself), fidèle à moi-même (true to myself). Related forms: toi-même (yourself), lui-même/elle-même (himself/herself), nous-mêmes/vous-mêmes (ourselves/yourselves), eux-mêmes/elles-mêmes (themselves).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un moment pour moi-même.
native_language_example: I need a moment for myself.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that *you* personally do something, often to stress independence or that you won’t delegate: *Je le fais moi-même.* It’s the stressed pronoun *moi* + *même* (“self/same”). With other people: *toi-même* (yourself), *lui-même/elle-même* (himself/herself), *nous-mêmes* (ourselves), *vous-mêmes* (yourselves), *eux-mêmes/elles-mêmes* (themselves). In a sentence like *Je préfère moi-même*, it usually implies “I prefer it myself / personally,” but often you’ll hear *Moi, je préfère…* or *Je préfère le faire moi-même* for clarity.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je vais le réparer moi-même.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll fix it myself.

additional_notes: Used to add yourself to what someone else just said. It often comes right after the idea you’re agreeing with (e.g., “Je ressens la même chose, moi aussi.”). You can also hear it as a short answer by itself (“Moi aussi !”). Be careful: “aussi” can mean “also/too” or “as well,” and “moi” is the stressed form of “je” used for emphasis.
target_language_example: J’aime le chocolat, moi aussi.
native_language_example: I like chocolate too.

additional_notes: Used to agree with what someone just said by adding that the same thing is true for you. Common in spoken French; the comma is optional ("Moi aussi je..."). You can also drop "je" and use it alone: "Moi aussi !"
target_language_example: — Je suis fatigué. — Moi aussi, je suis fatigué.
native_language_example: — I'm tired. — Me too, I'm tired.

additional_notes: Used to say you are the same as someone else, usually in response to what they just said ("I am…" → "Moi aussi, je suis…"). You then add an adjective or noun. Remember agreement: adjectives can change for gender/number (e.g., content/contente). In speech, you often hear it without the comma: "Moi aussi je suis…"
target_language_example: Moi aussi, je suis fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Me too, I'm tired today.

meaning: “Me, what he/it …” (a spoken fragment used to introduce your point).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it’s a common spoken structure where you start with "moi" (“as for me/me”) and then continue with "ce qu’il…" (“what he…/what it…”). It’s used to emphasize the topic before the verb, similar to: “Me, what I want is…”. In writing you often add a comma after "Moi": "Moi, ce qu’il…". The "il" can refer to a person (“he”) or be impersonal (“it”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Moi ce qu'il me faut, c'est du temps.
native_language_example: Me, what I need is time.

meaning: 'to me what…' (as in “tell/ask/explain to me what…”).
additional_notes: This is usually not a fixed phrase by itself: it’s the indirect object pronoun "moi" (me) used with "ce que" (what/that which). It appears after an imperative verb with a hyphen: "Demande-moi ce que…" / "Explique-moi ce que…". With "vous" instead of "moi": "Demandez-moi ce que vous voulez."
target_language_example: Dis-moi ce que tu as compris.
native_language_example: Tell me what you understood.

meaning: “Me, what I…” / “As for me, what I…” (used to introduce your personal opinion or preference).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French to put emphasis on yourself as the topic: “moi ce que je pense… / moi ce que je veux…”. It’s typically followed by a verb (aime, préfère, pense, veux, etc.). In more neutral or formal French, you can use “Pour ma part, …” or simply start with “Ce que je…”. In writing, it’s often punctuated with commas: “Moi, ce que je…”.
target_language_example: moi ce que je préfère, c’est rester à la maison.
native_language_example: Me, what I prefer is staying at home.

meaning: “Me, what I have to…” / “As for me, what I need to…” (a sentence starter).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to emphasize your own point of view ("moi" = “me/I, personally”). It’s normally followed by a verb phrase to complete the thought, often with "faire": "moi ce que je dois faire, c’est…". This is a common spoken structure (left-dislocation) and sounds incomplete if not finished.
target_language_example: Moi, ce que je dois faire, c’est appeler le médecin.
native_language_example: Me, what I need to do is call the doctor.

meaning: “Me/I—what you…” (a spoken sentence starter used to emphasize or contrast your viewpoint).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French as a topic-shifting/emphatic frame: **moi ce que tu + verb…** It sets up “as for me / from my point of view, what you …” and is typically followed by your evaluation or reaction. In careful writing, commas are often added (**Moi, ce que tu…**), but in speech it’s frequently said as one flow. You’ll usually continue with a clause like **moi ce que tu dis, je…** or **moi ce que tu fais, ça…**.
target_language_example: Moi ce que tu dis, je ne le crois pas.
native_language_example: Me, what you're saying, I don't believe it.

meaning: “Me / as for me… what you have…” (a spoken-style lead-in used to introduce your point before completing the sentence).
additional_notes:
This is an incomplete fragment you’ll mostly hear in speech, usually with pauses/commas: “Moi, ce que tu as…, c’est …” It combines:
- “Moi, …” = “As for me / me, …” (topic shift or contrast)
- “ce que” = “what / that which”
- “tu as” = “you have”.
It’s typically followed by the main idea (“…c’est …”, “...ça m’impressionne”, etc.). Written French would normally include commas: “Moi, ce que tu as, c’est …”
target_language_example: moi ce que tu as c’est de la patience.
native_language_example: What you have is patience, as far as I’m concerned.

meaning: “Me/as for me: whatever you want.” (i.e., “I’m fine with whatever you choose.”)
additional_notes: Spoken, elliptical reply. *moi* is used to mark your point of view (“as for me”), and *ce que tu veux* literally means “what you want,” functioning idiomatically as “whatever you want.” Often said with an implied pause after *moi* in natural speech, but it can appear without punctuation in writing. A fuller version would be: *Moi, je veux bien ce que tu veux* / *Moi, ça me va, ce que tu veux.*
target_language_example: — On fait quoi ce soir ? — moi ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: — What do we do tonight? — Whatever you want, I’m fine either way.

meaning: “Me, what you…” / “As for me, what you…” (used to start a sentence, setting up contrast or emphasis).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it introduces a clause and is normally followed by a verb phrase: “moi ce que vous + verbe…”. In writing it often appears with a comma after “moi” (“Moi, ce que vous…”). It’s used to highlight the speaker’s perspective or reaction to what the other person says/does.
target_language_example: moi ce que vous proposez, ça me va.
native_language_example: As for me, what you’re suggesting works for me.

meaning: "Me, what’s going on is…" / "The thing is…" (introducing an explanation from my point of view).
additional_notes: This is a spoken, slightly dislocated structure, typically punctuated with commas: "Moi, ce qui se passe, c’est que…" It’s used to introduce an explanation or background from the speaker’s perspective. Used alone, "moi ce qui se passe" feels incomplete—you normally continue with "c’est que…" or a full clause.
target_language_example: Moi ce qui se passe, c’est que j’ai perdu mon téléphone.
native_language_example: The thing is, I lost my phone.

additional_notes: Used to agree with a negative statement (someone says they don’t do/like/have something, and you say you don’t either). It can stand alone as a full reply (“Moi non plus.”). Word order can vary in longer sentences, but the meaning stays the same.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas faim. — Moi non plus.
native_language_example: I'm not hungry. — Me neither.

meaning: "(to) me something" (usually in phrases like "Donne-moi quelque chose" = "Give me something").
additional_notes: This is not usually used on its own. It’s a common sequence in speech when an indirect object pronoun "moi" (to me) is followed by the direct object "quelque chose" (something), especially with commands or requests: "Donne-moi quelque chose", "Apporte-moi quelque chose", "Dis-moi quelque chose".
target_language_example: Donne-moi quelque chose à boire, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me something to drink, please.

additional_notes: Used after an imperative verb (like procure, trouve) to mean “get/find me something to eat.” The indirect object pronoun moi (“to me”) comes before the thing (quelque chose à manger). Often said as: Procure-moi / Trouve-moi quelque chose à manger. Formal/plural forms: Procurez-moi / Trouvez-moi…
target_language_example: Trouve-moi quelque chose à manger, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Find me something to eat, please.

meaning: “me who… / I’m the one who…”, used to emphasize that *I* am the person doing something.
additional_notes: Often used in the pattern **c’est moi qui + verb** (or **ce n’est pas moi qui…**, **est-ce moi qui…**, **que ce soit moi qui…**) to put emphasis on who does the action. The verb in the following clause usually matches **moi** (1st person): *C’est moi qui ai commencé* (“I’m the one who started”). You can also use the same structure with other pronouns: *lui qui*, *elle qui*, *nous qui*.
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas moi qui ai cassé le verre.
native_language_example: I’m not the one who broke the glass.

meaning: “me, who did it / who has done it” — emphatic “I” used in a cleft-like structure to stress that *you* (not someone else) are the one who performed the action.
additional_notes: Commonly used in the emphatic pattern **« C’est moi qui l’ai + participe passé »** (“I’m the one who has/had done it”). **moi** is the stressed form of “I/me” used for emphasis; **qui** introduces the relative clause; **l’** is the object pronoun **le/la** (“it/him/her”) shortened before a vowel; **ai** is the auxiliary **avoir** (1st person singular, present). The term **moi qui l’ai** is typically followed by a past participle (e.g., **fait, vu, pris, dit**).
target_language_example: C’est moi qui l'ai fait.
native_language_example: I’m the one who did it.

meaning: Incorrect / nonstandard French (ungrammatical mix of “moi” = me and “sommes” = are).
additional_notes: *Moi sommes* is not used in standard French because **sommes** goes with **nous** (“we”), not **moi** (“me”). If you mean “I am…,” say **je suis…** (or for emphasis **Moi, je suis…**). If you mean “we are…,” say **nous sommes…**.
target_language_example: ❌ Moi sommes prêt.
native_language_example: ❌ Me are ready. (incorrect English; mirrors the French error)

moi sommes dans la même classe

target_language_multi_word_term: moi sommes dans la même classe
meaning: Intended meaning: “We are in the same class.” (but the French as written is incorrect).
additional_notes:
⚠️ **Grammatically incorrect in French.** *Sommes* is the 1st-person plural form and requires the subject **nous** (we), not **moi** (me). Correct versions:
- **Nous sommes dans la même classe.** = “We are in the same class.”
- **Moi, je suis dans la même classe que toi.** = “Me, I’m in the same class as you.” (emphatic)
If you see **moi sommes...**, it will usually be a learner mistake or intentionally incorrect speech quoted for effect.
target_language_example: Il a écrit : « moi sommes dans la même classe » (mais c’est incorrect).
native_language_example: He wrote: “moi sommes dans la même classe” (but it’s incorrect).

additional_notes: This sequence usually appears inside a full sentence, most commonly: « Laisse-moi te montrer … » (Let me show you …) or « Je vais te montrer … » (I’m going to show you …). On its own, « moi te montrer » sounds incomplete; « moi » can also be used for emphasis (“Me, show you?”) but then it’s typically set off by a pause/comma: « Moi, te montrer ? ».
target_language_example: Laisse-moi te montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: Let me show you how it works.

meaning: 'me a call' (as in: 'give me a call').
additional_notes: You’ll almost always see this with a verb, especially in the imperative: « Passe-moi un coup de fil » or « Donne-moi un coup de fil » = “Give me a call.” Here « moi » means “to me,” and « un coup de fil » is a common way to say “a (phone) call” in everyday French.
target_language_example: Passe-moi un coup de fil ce soir.
native_language_example: Give me a call tonight.

target_language_multi_word_term: (donner / filer) un coup de main (à quelqu’un)
meaning: to give someone a hand; to help.
additional_notes: Very common way to ask for or offer help. Used with verbs like "donner" (neutral) or "filer" (more informal). The person helped is usually an indirect object pronoun: "Donne-moi un coup de main" (Help me), "Tu peux lui donner un coup de main ?" (Can you help him/her?). In writing, "donne-moi" is commonly hyphenated; you may also see "donne moi".
target_language_example: Donne moi un coup de main !
native_language_example: Give me a hand!

meaning: 'me a minute' → used to mean 'give me a minute / wait a minute'.
additional_notes: Usually used with an imperative verb before it: **Accorde-moi une minute** (Give me a minute), **Attends-moi une minute** (Wait for me a minute), **Excusez-moi une minute** (Excuse me for a minute / one moment). Note the hyphen in writing: **-moi** (informal *tu*) and **-moi** with **Excusez-/Accordez-** (polite *vous*).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi une minute, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: Excuse me for a minute, I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to compare prices. Pattern: « moins cher que … » = “cheaper than …”. With « le/la/les moins cher/ chère(s) », it means “the cheapest” (superlative). Adjective agreement: « cher » → « chère » (fem.), « chers/chères » (plural).
target_language_example: On peut prendre le train : c’est moins cher que l’avion.
native_language_example: We can take the train: it’s cheaper than flying.

meaning: at least once a week (usually said as: « au moins une fois par semaine »).
additional_notes: In standard French, to say “at least once a week,” you normally use « au moins une fois par semaine ». To say “less than once a week,” you would usually say « moins d’une fois par semaine ».
target_language_example: J’essaie de faire du sport au moins une fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I try to exercise at least once a week.

additional_notes: Usually used with an article: **le mois dernier** = “last month” (a specific time in the past). **Dernier** agrees with **mois** (masculine), so it stays **dernier**. Compare: **la semaine dernière** (feminine) and **l’année dernière**.
target_language_example: Le mois dernier, je suis allé à Paris.
native_language_example: Last month, I went to Paris.

additional_notes: Means the month after the current one. In French, « prochain » often comes after the noun: « le mois prochain ». You can use it for future plans and dates.
target_language_example: Je pars en vacances le mois prochain.
native_language_example: I’m going on vacation next month.

meaning: “Oh my God!” (an exclamation of surprise, shock, annoyance, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as a strong interjection (often with “Ah” or alone: “Mon Dieu !”). It can express many emotions depending on tone: surprise (Mon Dieu, qu’est-il arrivé ?), frustration (Ah mon Dieu…), or emphasis when reacting to someone (Mon Dieu, Will !). More polite/less religious alternatives include “Oh là là !” or “Mon Dieu” can be softened to “Mon Dieu…” in speech.
target_language_example: Mon Dieu, j’ai oublié mon passeport !
native_language_example: Oh my God, I forgot my passport!

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male friend, or to address someone directly as "my friend." For a female friend, French uses mon amie.
target_language_example: Paul est mon ami depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: Paul has been my friend for a long time.

additional_notes: Used with a female friend (une amie). Even though amie is feminine, French uses **mon** (not *ma*) before a feminine word that starts with a vowel sound (like *a-* in *amie*) to avoid two vowels in a row. Compare: *ma sœur* (my sister), but *mon amie* (my female friend).
target_language_example: Elle s'appelle Claire : c'est mon amie.
native_language_example: Her name is Claire: she's my (female) friend.

additional_notes: Used to address someone you love (partner, spouse), like “darling/sweetheart.” You can say it when speaking directly to them (“Joyeux Noël, mon amour !”) or when talking about your love/affection (“mon amour pour toi”). It’s affectionate and intimate; in more formal situations you’d avoid it.
target_language_example: Tu me manques, mon amour.
native_language_example: I miss you, my love.

additional_notes: “Anniversaire” usually means “birthday” in everyday speech. With extra context, it can also mean an anniversary, especially in phrases like “anniversaire de mariage” (wedding anniversary). You often use it with “c’est” to say when it is, and with “pour” to say “for my birthday” (gifts, plans, etc.).
target_language_example: Pour mon anniversaire, je vais dîner au restaurant.
native_language_example: For my birthday, I'm going to have dinner at a restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to talk about money that belongs to the speaker. Often appears with verbs like donner (give), prendre (take), gaspiller (waste), mériter (earn/deserve), or confier (entrust). You can emphasize the amount with tout mon argent (“all my money”).
target_language_example: Je n'ai plus mon argent sur moi.
native_language_example: I don't have my money on me anymore.

additional_notes: Used to give or ask for your personal opinion. Often appears in set phrases like « C’est mon avis » (That’s my opinion), « demander mon avis » (ask for my opinion), « exprimer mon avis » (express my opinion), or « à mon avis » (in my opinion).
target_language_example: Mon avis, c’est qu’on devrait partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: My opinion is that we should leave earlier.

meaning: my lawyer; my avocado (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Avocat" can mean either "lawyer" or "avocado." In a sentence like "Parle à mon avocat", it almost always means "my lawyer" because of the verb "parler à" (to speak to someone). Pronunciation and context usually make the meaning clear.
target_language_example: J'ai rendez-vous avec mon avocat demain.
native_language_example: I have an appointment with my lawyer tomorrow.

meaning: my job / my work (often: my work duties).
additional_notes: "Boulot" is common, everyday (slightly informal) French for "job/work". "Mon boulot" often means "my job" in the sense of the tasks I’m supposed to do ("I’m just doing my job" / "Let me do my job"). In more formal contexts, you can use "mon travail" or "mon emploi".
target_language_example: Je dois finir mon boulot avant midi.
native_language_example: I have to finish my work before noon.

additional_notes: "Bureau" can mean a room where you work (an office) or the piece of furniture you work at (a desk). The context usually makes it clear: "au deuxième étage" = office; "vieux / neuf" or "utiliser" could be either depending on what’s being talked about. "Mon" agrees with the masculine noun "bureau" (even if it refers to a room).
target_language_example: Je suis dans mon bureau, je t’appelle dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I’m in my office; I’ll call you in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your (male) cat. Grammatically it’s the masculine singular possessive adjective mon (“my”) + chat (“cat”). Note: you also use mon with a feminine noun that starts with a vowel sound (e.g., mon amie), but chat is masculine anyway. In casual speech, people may shorten it to mon p’tit chat (“my little kitty/sweetheart”), but mon chat itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Mon chat dort sur le canapé.
native_language_example: My cat is sleeping on the couch.

additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to a man (or boy). It can sound affectionate, polite/formal, or sometimes slightly ironic depending on tone. For a woman, you’d usually say "ma chère"; in plural, "mes chers" / "mes chères".
target_language_example: Merci, mon cher, c’est très gentil.
native_language_example: Thank you, my dear, that’s very kind.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: *mon* = “my” (used with masculine singular nouns and before a vowel sound), *chien* = “dog.” You can swap the owner: *ton chien* (your dog), *son chien* (his/her dog), *notre chien* (our dog), etc.
target_language_example: Mon chien est très gentil.
native_language_example: My dog is very nice.

additional_notes: Used when talking to someone you’re close to (partner, child, close friend), often in questions or exclamations: « Ça va, mon chou ? ». Literally “my cabbage,” but it functions like an English pet name, not a food-related phrase.
target_language_example: Bonne nuit, mon chou.
native_language_example: Good night, sweetie.

additional_notes: A term of endearment used when speaking to (or about) someone you love. Often said to a romantic partner; can also be used affectionately within family. Feminine form: "ma chérie". You’ll also hear "chéri(e)" on its own.
target_language_example: Tu es prêt, mon chéri ?
native_language_example: Are you ready, my darling?

additional_notes: Used to talk about your cousin who is a man/boy. For a female cousin, say « ma cousine ». When speaking directly to the cousin, you can also use it like a form of address (often in a humorous or old-fashioned way).
target_language_example: Mon cousin habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My cousin lives in Lyon.

meaning: “my ass!” (vulgar: “yeah right / bullshit”) or literally “my ass/butt”.
additional_notes: Very vulgar. Literally refers to your butt/ass (e.g., *Mon cul saigne.*). As an exclamation after a word or sentence (*Arrête, mon cul !*; *Excuse-moi, mon cul !*; *Mon cul, ouais !*), it means you don’t believe it, you reject it, or you’re calling it nonsense—similar to English “my ass!”, “yeah right!”, “bullshit!”. Also appears in phrases like *bouger mon cul* (“get my ass moving”). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Tu vas m’aider ? Mon cul !
native_language_example: You’re going to help me? My ass!

meaning: "my heart" (literal or as an affectionate name like "my dear/sweetheart").
additional_notes: Used literally to talk about your physical heart (health, heartbeat): « Mon cœur bat… ». Also very common figuratively to express strong feelings (love, sadness, longing). As a term of endearment when addressing someone (« Au revoir, mon cœur »), it’s affectionate and intimate—similar to “sweetheart” or “my dear.”
target_language_example: Tu me manques, mon cœur.
native_language_example: I miss you, sweetheart.

additional_notes: Used literally to describe your heartbeat (slowly, fast, irregularly, strongly), often in health or medical contexts: « Mon cœur bat au ralenti/rapidement/de façon irrégulière/fort. » It can also be used figuratively to express strong emotion or love: « Mon cœur bat pour toi. »
target_language_example: Quand je monte les escaliers, mon cœur bat très vite.
native_language_example: When I climb the stairs, my heart beats very fast.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the time when you were a child, often in memories or when comparing past and present (e.g., "depuis mon enfance" = "since my childhood"). Note: "enfance" often means "childhood" in general, not exactly "infancy" (0–2 years).
target_language_example: J'ai beaucoup appris pendant mon enfance.
native_language_example: I learned a lot during my childhood.

meaning: "my child"; also "my dear child" when addressing someone.
additional_notes: Literally means “my child” (mon + enfant). It can refer to your child (“Mon enfant est curieux…”) or be used as a direct form of address, often affectionate or comforting (“Ne pleure plus, mon enfant.”). In contexts like “Elle porte mon enfant”, it means someone is carrying/expecting your child (pregnant).
target_language_example: Viens ici, mon enfant, je vais t'aider.
native_language_example: Come here, my child, I’m going to help you.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase used to refer to your male child. It is made from mon ("my") + fils ("son").
target_language_example: Mon fils habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My son lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Used to describe your son’s state, identity, or situation. **Mon** means “my” (used before a masculine singular noun like **fils**). **Est** is the 3rd-person singular of **être** (“to be”). Pronunciation note: **fils** is usually pronounced like *fee* (the final -ls is silent), and **est** is pronounced like *eh*.
target_language_example: Mon fils est très fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: My son is very tired today.

additional_notes: A possessive noun phrase for the speaker's male sibling. mon means 'my' before a singular masculine noun, and frère means 'brother'.
target_language_example: Mon frère habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My brother lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Used to state where your brother is (mon frère est à Paris / dehors / à son bureau) or to describe him (mon frère est riche). The next word often indicates location with “à” + place, or an adjective.
target_language_example: Mon frère est malade aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: My brother is sick today.

meaning: "my guy" / "my buddy" (addressing a male), or "my boyfriend" (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Very common informal way to address a man or boy, especially when warning/scolding or speaking casually (similar to “my guy,” “buddy,” “man”). Depending on context, it can also refer to a romantic partner (“my boyfriend”). Literally it’s “my guy.”
target_language_example: Ça va, mon gars ?
native_language_example: You alright, my guy?

meaning: "my boy" (a way to address a boy/young man).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to a boy or young man, often to get his attention or to scold/admonish him. Depending on tone and context, it can sound affectionate (to a child) or patronizing/condescending (to a teenager or adult).
target_language_example: Écoute-moi, mon garçon, ce n'est pas prudent.
native_language_example: Listen to me, my boy, it's not safe.

meaning: (informal) “buddy / big guy / champ” (used when addressing a boy or man).
additional_notes: Used as a familiar form of address, often from an older person to someone younger (a child, teen, or younger adult). It can sound affectionate and encouraging (“Well done, champ”), but depending on tone/context it can also feel patronizing. Feminine equivalent: « ma grande ».
target_language_example: Allez, mon grand, courage !
native_language_example: Come on, champ—hang in there!

additional_notes: Used to talk about your grandfather. "Grand-père" is masculine; with the possessive "mon" (my). Before a vowel sound, French also uses "mon" for feminine nouns (e.g., "mon amie"), but "grand-père" is always masculine. In casual speech, you may also hear "papi" for "grandpa."
target_language_example: Mon grand-père habite près de chez nous.
native_language_example: My grandfather lives near our house.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your bed as a place (aller/dans mon lit = to go to/in my bed) or as an object you can make (faire mon lit = to make my bed). In French, "lit" can be masculine even though you sleep "in it": dans mon lit.
target_language_example: Je vais dans mon lit.
native_language_example: I'm going to bed.

additional_notes: Used by a woman to refer to her husband. Like other possessives, it agrees with the noun: mon mari (my husband), ma femme (my wife), mes enfants (my children). Even though "mari" is masculine, "mon" is also used before feminine nouns starting with a vowel sound (e.g., mon amie).
target_language_example: Je sors ce soir avec mon mari.
native_language_example: I’m going out tonight with my husband.

additional_notes: Used to describe your husband with a job, status, relationship, or adjective. The adjective usually agrees with “mari” (masculine singular): mon mari est jaloux / mon mari est malade. For “he is + noun” (job/role), French often drops “a”: Mon mari est boulanger (= My husband is a baker).
target_language_example: Mon mari est très patient.
native_language_example: My husband is very patient.

additional_notes: Used to talk to or about your closest friend. "Mon" is the masculine singular "my". "Ami" is masculine; for a female best friend, you usually say "ma meilleure amie" (note the feminine forms "ma", "meilleure", "amie"). You can also say it about someone you consider your best friend ("Je le/la considère comme mon/ma meilleur(e) ami(e)").
target_language_example: C'est mon meilleur ami depuis le lycée.
native_language_example: He’s been my best friend since high school.

additional_notes: Used to say what your name is or refer to your name in a document/list. "Mon" agrees with the noun: "nom" is masculine, so it’s "mon" (not *ma*). Often appears in introductions: "Mon nom est…" or more commonly "Je m'appelle…".
target_language_example: Mon nom est Martin, enchanté.
native_language_example: My name is Martin, nice to meet you.

additional_notes: A formal or neutral way to introduce yourself. Often used in writing, presentations, or official contexts; in everyday conversation, people also commonly say “Je m’appelle …”.
target_language_example: Bonjour, mon nom est Claire Martin.
native_language_example: Hello, my name is Claire Martin.

additional_notes: Used when giving or referring to your phone number. You can swap « mon » with other possessives: « ton/votre/son numéro de téléphone ». Common with verbs like « donner » (to give) or « oublier » (to forget).
target_language_example: Laissez-moi vous donner mon numéro de téléphone.
native_language_example: Let me give you my phone number.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your uncle (your mother’s or father’s brother, or your aunt’s husband). "Mon" is used because "oncle" is masculine singular. You can use it for family talk and also as a direct address: « Désolé, mon oncle. »
target_language_example: Mon oncle habite à Lyon, et je le vois souvent.
native_language_example: My uncle lives in Lyon, and I see him often.

additional_notes: "Passe-temps" is a masculine noun meaning an activity you do for fun in your free time. It’s often followed by "est de" + infinitive to say what your hobby is (e.g., "Mon passe-temps est de lire"). You can also say "Mon passe-temps préféré" for "my favorite hobby."
target_language_example: Mon passe-temps, c'est de cuisiner le week-end.
native_language_example: My hobby is cooking on the weekend.

mon passe-temps est de collectionner les

target_language_multi_word_term: mon passe-temps est de collectionner les
additional_notes: Used to talk about a hobby/activity you do for fun. After this phrase, you typically name a plural thing you collect (les timbres, les insectes, les pièces, etc.). In natural speech you’ll also hear: « Mon passe-temps, c’est de collectionner… » or simply « Je collectionne… ».
target_language_example: Mon passe-temps est de collectionner les pièces de monnaie.
native_language_example: My hobby is collecting coins.

meaning: “my little …” / “my dear” (affectionate way to address someone).
additional_notes: Used as a term of endearment when talking to someone: « Merci, mon petit » (“Thanks, my dear”). It’s often followed by a noun like « mon petit chat » (my kitty) or « mon petit gars » (my little guy), or a name: « Mon petit Lucien ». It can also be literal with things: « mon petit secret » = “my little secret.” For a female addressee you usually say « ma petite » (or « mon petit + noun/name » depending on gender/word form).
target_language_example: Viens ici, mon petit, je vais t’aider.
native_language_example: Come here, my dear, I’m going to help you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your romantic partner (male). It’s possessive: mon = “my” (used before a masculine noun like ami). The feminine equivalent is ma petite amie (“my girlfriend”).
target_language_example: Mon petit ami arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: My boyfriend is arriving in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your younger brother. "Petit" here means younger (not necessarily small). You can say "C’est mon petit frère" to introduce him. Contrast: "mon grand frère" = my older brother.
target_language_example: Je vais chercher mon petit frère à l'école.
native_language_example: I'm going to pick up my little brother at school.

meaning: my point of view; my opinion.
additional_notes: Used to state your personal perspective on a topic. Often followed by "sur" (on/about): "mon point de vue sur..." It can also be used as a short reply to disagree or qualify something: "Pas de mon point de vue" = "Not from my point of view / Not in my opinion."
target_language_example: De mon point de vue, c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: From my point of view, it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to address a male friend in a casual, friendly way (like “buddy” or “mate”). It can also refer to “my friend” in general: *une fête chez mon pote Aaron* = “a party at my friend Aaron’s place.” For a female friend you’d usually say *ma pote* (informal) or more commonly *mon amie* (neutral).
target_language_example: Salut, mon pote, ça va ?
native_language_example: Hey buddy, how’s it going?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first person you loved romantically. Often said about a past relationship (e.g., with the imperfect « était » for a description, or « a été » to sum up that it was your first love). Changes with gender/number: « ma première amour » is sometimes heard, but the standard form is « mon premier amour » because « amour » is masculine in the singular; in the plural it’s often feminine (« mes premières amours »).
target_language_example: Même si on ne se parle plus, il restera mon premier amour.
native_language_example: Even if we don’t talk anymore, he’ll remain my first love.

additional_notes: A basic family expression for talking about your father. Mon is the possessive form used with the masculine singular noun père.
target_language_example: Mon père travaille à la maison le vendredi.
native_language_example: My father works from home on Fridays.

meaning: "my father has" / "my father (did)" (used before a verb in the past).
additional_notes: Very common pattern: subject + "a" (present of avoir) + past participle to form the passé composé. In English this is often translated as simple past ("my father suggested") even though French uses "has" + past participle. Use "mon père" before a consonant sound; before a vowel sound you say "mon père a" (liaison: "père a" sounds like "pèr-a").
target_language_example: Mon père a acheté une nouvelle voiture.
native_language_example: My father bought a new car.

additional_notes: Used to describe your dad (job, origin, personality, situation, etc.). It’s followed by an adjective (e.g., « occupé »), a noun with an article (e.g., « un archéologue »), or a place of origin with « de/du/de la/des » (e.g., « du Donegal »).
target_language_example: Mon père est très gentil.
native_language_example: My father is very kind.

additional_notes: Uses the verb mourir (“to die”) in the passé composé: est mort (literally “is died,” meaning “died/has died”). You’ll often see it with time expressions like il y a… (“…ago”) or cela fait… que… (“it’s been … since …”). Change the subject as needed: ma mère est morte (my mother died/is dead), mon grand-père est mort (my grandfather died).
target_language_example: Mon père est mort il y a deux ans.
native_language_example: My father died two years ago.

additional_notes: Used to describe your father in the past. "était" is the imperfect (l’imparfait) of "être" and is common for past states, descriptions, or background information (e.g., how someone was, what something was like).
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, mon père était très patient.
native_language_example: When I was little, my father was very patient.

additional_notes: Used to say what your father used to be / was (profession, role, identity). The verb tense "était" is the imperfect (imparfait), common for background description in the past. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun or job title: "Mon père était un acteur." (For a feminine noun, you’d say: "Ma mère était une …").
target_language_example: Mon père était un professeur de mathématiques.
native_language_example: My father was a math teacher.

additional_notes: Use this to talk about a long-term ambition or goal. It’s followed by an occupation/role (often without an article): « Mon rêve est de devenir pilote / professeur ». You can also specify details: « ...acteur à Hollywood ».
target_language_example: Mon rêve est de devenir médecin.
native_language_example: My dream is to become a doctor.

additional_notes: "Mon" means "my" (used before a masculine singular noun). "Sac" is a general word for a bag (handbag, backpack, shopping bag, etc.). Use it when talking about your own bag; for a more specific bag you can say "mon sac à dos" (my backpack) or "mon sac à main" (my handbag).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je crois que c'est mon sac.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I think that's my bag.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your job in general or the work/tasks you personally have to do. "Mon" agrees with the masculine noun "travail" (even before a vowel sound). Often used with verbs like aimer/adorer (to love), faire (to do), terminer/finir (to finish).
target_language_example: Je dois retourner à mon travail après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: I have to go back to my work after lunch.

additional_notes: "Mon" means "my" (used with masculine singular nouns). "Téléphone" can mean a phone in general, but in everyday French it often refers to a mobile phone. You can use it to ask where it is, request it back, or talk about it ringing or not working.
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon téléphone à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my phone at home.

additional_notes: Means your personal mobile phone. In France, people often just say "mon portable"; "téléphone portable" is a bit more explicit. You can swap "mon" for another possessive: "ton/ses/notre" etc.
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon téléphone portable à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my cell phone at home.

additional_notes: Informal and familiar term of address, often used with friends or someone you know well (usually a man/boy). It can sound affectionate, comforting, or sometimes slightly patronizing depending on tone. Literally means "my old (one/guy)", but it’s used like "my friend" rather than talking about age.
target_language_example: Allez, courage, mon vieux, ça va s’arranger.
native_language_example: Come on, buddy, it’ll work out.

additional_notes: Very common informal interjection to reject or mock what someone just said (often sarcastic). You can say it alone ("Mon œil.") or after a word/claim to contradict it ("Du tennis, mon œil !" = "Tennis, yeah right!"). Note: outside the idiom, it can also mean the literal "my eye" (e.g., "Mon œil a gonflé." = "My eye swelled up.").
target_language_example: Il a dit qu’il avait tout compris… mon œil !
native_language_example: He said he understood everything… yeah, right!

additional_notes: Often used after prepositions like au/du/dans le ("to the / from the / in the") to mean "across/around the entire world." It’s commonly used when talking about spreading a message, being known, or something coming from everywhere.
target_language_example: Cette chanson est connue dans le monde entier.
native_language_example: This song is known worldwide.

additional_notes: Used as part of a sentence, usually with an article or demonstrative before it: **le monde est…** (“the world is…”), **ce monde est…** (“this world is…”), **un autre monde est…** (“another world is…”). In phrases like **dans le monde**, it means “in the world” (worldwide).
target_language_example: Le monde est grand, mais on peut s'y sentir seul.
native_language_example: The world is big, but you can feel lonely in it.

meaning: “(the) world knows that …” / “everyone knows that …” (usually: “tout le monde sait que …”).
additional_notes: On its own, “monde sait que” sounds incomplete in French. The natural, common phrase is “tout le monde sait que …” (“everyone knows that …”). You can also say “le monde sait que …” (“the world knows that …”), but it’s less common and more rhetorical.
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que Paris est une ville chère.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that Paris is an expensive city.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural with the article: « les montagnes russes ». With the verb « faire » it means “to go on / ride roller coasters” (« faire des montagnes russes »). You can also say « monter sur les montagnes russes » for “to get on / ride the roller coaster.”
target_language_example: On a fait des montagnes russes au parc d’attractions.
native_language_example: We went on roller coasters at the amusement park.

meaning: "get in the car" (said to one person).
additional_notes: From the verb "monter" (to get in/go up) + "dans" (into) + "la voiture" (the car). It’s often used as an instruction/command. "Monte" is the informal singular imperative (to a friend/child); for a polite or plural command, use "Montez dans la voiture."
target_language_example: Monte dans la voiture, on est en retard.
native_language_example: Get in the car, we’re late.

meaning: to stand guard; to keep watch.
additional_notes: Used for people (soldiers, police, security guards, etc.) who are watching a place or person to protect it or make sure nothing happens. Can also be used figuratively. Often used with a location: «monter la garde devant la porte / à l’entrée / près du bâtiment».
target_language_example: Un policier doit monter la garde devant l’ambassade.
native_language_example: A police officer has to stand guard in front of the embassy.

meaning: to go to your head (make you dizzy or conceited).
additional_notes: Used with things like alcohol, strong smells, heat, success, praise, or power. It can mean (1) a physical effect (it makes you dizzy) or (2) that someone becomes arrogant because of success/attention. Common patterns: « L’alcool m’est monté à la tête »; « Le succès lui est monté à la tête ».
target_language_example: Le succès lui est monté à la tête et il est devenu insupportable.
native_language_example: Success went to his head and he became unbearable.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of *montrer* + *moi* (“to me”). It’s written with a hyphen in the affirmative imperative: *Montre-moi…* (“Show me…”). You can make it softer with *s’il te plaît* (“please”) or more formal with *s’il vous plaît*.
