target_language_example: Montre-moi où c’est sur la carte, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Show me where it is on the map, please.

additional_notes: Imperative: "montre" (show) + "moi" (to me). "ce que" means "what/that which" and "tu as" means "you have". Used to ask someone to reveal or present something (often what they’re holding, carrying, hiding, or what’s inside something). It can sound demanding, especially with an exclamation point. "Ta bagnole" is informal for "your car."
target_language_example: Allez, montre-moi ce que tu as dans ton sac.
native_language_example: Come on, show me what you have in your bag.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to demonstrate a method or explain the steps. "Montre" is the tu-command form of "montrer" (to show), "moi" is an indirect object pronoun (to me), and "comment" means "how". Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "faire") or by a full clause (e.g., "tu fais").
target_language_example: Montre-moi comment utiliser cette application.
native_language_example: Show me how to use this app.

meaning: “Show me your …” (addressing someone you use tu with; for a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Imperative of montrer (“to show”) + moi (“to me”) + ta (“your”, feminine singular). Use before a feminine noun: ta blessure (your injury), ta montre (your watch). For a masculine noun, use “montre-moi ton …”; for plural, “montre-moi tes …”.
target_language_example: Montre-moi ta photo, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Show me your photo, please.

meaning: 'show me your' (addressing one person, masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Command form: "montre" (tu-form imperative of montrer) + "moi" (to me). "Ton" is the possessive adjective for "your" used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., ton bras) or before a vowel/silent h (e.g., ton épaule). With a feminine noun starting with a consonant, use "montre-moi ta"; with plural, "montre-moi tes"; to be more formal, use "montrez-moi votre / vos".
target_language_example: Montre-moi ton passeport, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Show me your passport, please.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "montrer" (to show) with a direct object (quelque chose = something). You can add who you show it to with "à" (or an indirect object pronoun like me/te/nous/vous): "montrer quelque chose à Layla" / "me montrer quelque chose". Common in polite speech: "Je voulais vous montrer quelque chose."
target_language_example: Je peux te montrer quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Can I show you something?

additional_notes: Imperative of **montrer** + indirect object pronoun **moi** (“to me”). Used to ask someone to show something, explain how to do something, indicate a place (often with **où**), or demonstrate an attitude (e.g., **Montrez-moi du respect !** = “Show me some respect!”). **Montrez** is the **vous** form, so it’s polite (or used for addressing more than one person).
target_language_example: Montrez-moi votre passeport, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Show me your passport, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to show you something that belongs to them. It’s an imperative: montrez (you, polite singular “vous” / plural) + moi (to me). The word after it is usually a noun: Montrez-moi votre passeport. Use "votre" before a singular noun (votre main). Before plural nouns, use "vos" (Montrez-moi vos papiers). For an informal singular "you" (tu), you’d say: "Montre-moi ton/ta/tes..."
target_language_example: Montrez-moi votre billet, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Show me your ticket, please.

additional_notes: Literally “dead from hunger.” Used with être: « Je suis mort de faim » = “I’m starving.” If the speaker is female, it becomes « morte de faim ». As a noun with un/une (« un mort de faim »), it can mean a very poor person, often as an insult (“a loser/nobody”).
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, j’étais mort de faim.
native_language_example: After the hike, I was starving.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago someone died, often in biographies or obituaries: « mort il y a deux ans » (“died two years ago”). « il y a » means “ago.” The past participle agrees with the person: « morte il y a… » (female), « morts/mortes il y a… » (plural). You may also see the more formal « décédé(e) il y a… ».
target_language_example: Mon grand-père est mort il y a cinq ans.
native_language_example: My grandfather died five years ago.

additional_notes: Used for the secret code you type to access an account, website, device, or Wi‑Fi. Often appears in instructions and notifications: « entrer votre mot de passe » (enter your password), « changer de mot de passe » (change password), « votre mot de passe a été modifié » (your password has been changed).
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon mot de passe, je ne peux plus me connecter.
native_language_example: I forgot my password, I can’t log in anymore.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a very literal translation that follows the original wording closely. Often appears with verbs like « traduire » (to translate) or « traduire … mot à mot ». It can be a recommendation (not to translate word for word) because a natural translation may need rephrasing.
target_language_example: Ce proverbe ne se traduit pas mot à mot.
native_language_example: This proverb can’t be translated word for word.

additional_notes: Used for an internet service/app that helps you find information on the web (e.g., Google). Often appears with a specific one ("un moteur de recherche comme Google") or with "utiliser" ("Quel moteur de recherche utilises-tu ?").
target_language_example: J’utilise un autre moteur de recherche parce que celui-ci ne marche pas bien.
native_language_example: I use another search engine because this one doesn’t work well.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural (les/des mots croisés) to talk about crossword puzzles as an activity or the puzzles in newspapers. Common with verbs like faire (to do/solve): faire des mots croisés.
target_language_example: Je fais des mots croisés dans le train.
native_language_example: I do crossword puzzles on the train.

meaning: to starve (to death); to be extremely hungry.
additional_notes: Literally “to die of hunger.” It can be used literally (people lacking food) or figuratively as exaggeration to mean “I’m starving.” Commonly appears conjugated (e.g., « je meurs de faim », « il va mourir de faim »), but the infinitive « mourir de faim » is also used after modal verbs (e.g., « devoir », « préférer »).
target_language_example: Tu dois mourir de faim.
native_language_example: You must be starving.

meaning: a way to; a means of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to express the method/possibility for doing something: "un moyen de + infinitive" (a way to do), "le seul moyen de..." (the only way to...), "aucun moyen de..." (no way to...). Often refers to ability or possibility rather than a specific tool.
target_language_example: On cherche un moyen de réduire les coûts.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a way to reduce costs.

additional_notes: Used to talk about any way of getting from one place to another (car, bus, train, bike, etc.). Often appears with an adjective or in comparisons: « le moyen de transport le plus sûr » (the safest mode of transport). You can also say « sans moyen de transport » (without transportation).
target_language_example: On cherche un moyen de transport pour aller à l’aéroport.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a way to get to the airport.

additional_notes: Refers to the Western art-music tradition (e.g., Bach, Mozart, Beethoven). Often used with partitive articles to talk about listening to it: « écouter de la musique classique ». You can also use it after « passionné de » (passionate about) or in the phrase « À propos de musique classique… » (Speaking of classical music…).
target_language_example: J'aime écouter de la musique classique quand je travaille.
native_language_example: I like listening to classical music when I work.

additional_notes: From the verb « mener » (to lead). It’s usually followed by an adjective or description: « mener une vie saine/simple/normale/heureuse ». You can also use it in the imperative to give advice: « Mène une vie heureuse. »
target_language_example: Depuis qu’il a déménagé, il mène une vie plus calme.
native_language_example: Since he moved, he’s been living a calmer life.

additional_notes: This is simply the noun **mère** (“mother”) + **est** (“is”). In everyday speech you’ll usually see it with a determiner or possessive: **ma mère est…** (my mother is…), **ta mère est…**, **votre mère est…**, **la mère est…**. Sometimes **Mère** is used without an article as a title or in a more formal/literary style (e.g., talking about “Mother” as a role).
target_language_example: Ma mère est au travail aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: My mother is at work today.

meaning: "(My/our) mother has died" / "(my/our) mother is dead."
additional_notes: Uses the verb être + morte (feminine of mort). In context it’s often part of a full sentence like « Notre mère est morte » (Our mother has died). For a male: « père est mort ». You can add time expressions like « il y a six ans » (six years ago).
target_language_example: Notre mère est morte il y a six ans.
native_language_example: Our mother died six years ago.

meaning: primary care doctor (the doctor in charge of your ongoing care).
additional_notes: Common in France to refer to your regular/main doctor (often a general practitioner) who follows you over time and coordinates your care (referrals, renewals, etc.). Often used with possessives: mon/ton/votre médecin traitant; and in questions like « As-tu un médecin traitant ? ».
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas encore de médecin traitant.
native_language_example: I don’t have a primary care doctor yet.

additional_notes: Used to say something is identical or to agree that you feel/think the same. Very common with the article: « la même chose » (“the same thing”). You can also reply « Même chose pour moi » (“Same for me / Me too, same here”).
target_language_example: On a choisi le même restaurant : c’est la même chose qu’hier.
native_language_example: We chose the same restaurant: it’s the same thing as yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things and say they are identical. Very often you’ll see it with an article: « la même chose que » (e.g., « C’est la même chose que… »). It’s followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause to say what it’s the same as.
target_language_example: C’est la même chose que hier.
native_language_example: It’s the same thing as yesterday.

meaning: 'same time' (most often used in the phrase "en même temps" = 'at the same time').
additional_notes: Usually appears as **en même temps** to mean **at the same time/simultaneously**, and sometimes to add a contrast like **"at the same time, however"**. You can also see **en même temps que + noun/pronoun** (at the same time as) or **en même temps que + clause** (while). On its own, "même temps" is uncommon without a preposition.
target_language_example: Je travaille et j'écoute de la musique en même temps.
native_language_example: I work and listen to music at the same time.

additional_notes: Used with articles and prepositions like: « le même âge » (the same age) and « du même âge » (of the same age). Often appears after « avoir »: « On a le même âge. »
target_language_example: Mon frère et moi, on a le même âge.
native_language_example: My brother and I are the same age.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something doesn’t happen or isn’t true at all, often implying surprise or criticism. Very common in speech; you may see it with the informal omission of “ne” (e.g., “Il y a même pas…” instead of “Il n’y a même pas…”). Often placed before an infinitive or verb: “Je ne sais même pas…” / “Tu n’imagines même pas…”.
target_language_example: Je n’ai même pas eu le temps de te répondre.
native_language_example: I didn’t even have time to reply to you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition or contrast that doesn’t change the main point. Often followed by the subjunctive when it refers to something uncertain or hypothetical (e.g., « Même si ça doit me coûter cher… »). With a real fact, it can be close to “even though” (e.g., « Même si tu as raison… »).
target_language_example: Je vais venir, même si je suis fatigué.
native_language_example: I’m going to come, even though I’m tired.

additional_notes: A very common contraction (elision) of the indirect/direct object pronoun **me (m’)** + the verb **avoir** in the present (**a** = “has”). Used before a past participle in the **passé composé**: **Il/Elle m’a + past participle** (e.g., *Il m’a aidé* = “He helped me / He has helped me”).
target_language_example: Elle m’a appelé ce matin.
native_language_example: She called me this morning.

meaning: to repay/settle what I owe (to someone); to pay someone back (often in a moral sense).
additional_notes: Used with a person (auprès de vous/toi) to express that you want to repay a debt or show gratitude for what they did for you. It’s fairly formal and can imply a sense of obligation ("I owe you"). You’ll often see it in polite requests: « Permettez-moi de m’acquitter auprès de vous. »
target_language_example: Après tout ce que vous avez fait, je veux m’acquitter auprès de vous.
native_language_example: After everything you’ve done, I want to repay you.

meaning: "has never" / "never has" (past tense negative, 3rd person singular).
additional_notes: Part of the French negative pattern **ne ... jamais** = “never.” Here **n’** is **ne** shortened before a vowel, and **a** is **avoir** (“has”) used to form the **passé composé** (3rd person singular: *il/elle/on a*). Typical structure: **Il/Elle/On n’a jamais + past participle** (e.g., *Il n’a jamais fait* = “He has never done”). It can combine with other negatives: **n’a jamais rien dit** = “never said anything.” In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped (*Il a jamais fait ça*), which is more informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Il n'a jamais fait ça.
native_language_example: He has never done that.

additional_notes: Negative form of a with ne ... pas. Before a vowel, ne becomes n'. Very common in the passé composé: n'a pas + past participle, as in il n'a pas gagné = 'he didn't win' or 'he hasn't won'.
target_language_example: Il n'a pas compris la question.
native_language_example: He didn't understand the question.

meaning: "has nothing" / "didn't … anything" (negative with "avoir" in the 3rd person singular).
additional_notes: "n'a" is the 3rd person singular of "ne ... a" (negation with "avoir"), and "rien" means "nothing." Commonly used with a past participle to mean "didn't … anything": "Elle n'a rien vu" = "She didn’t see anything." Note that in everyday speech/writing, "ne" is often dropped: "Elle a rien vu" (informal).
target_language_example: Elle n'a rien vu.
native_language_example: She didn’t see anything.

additional_notes: Used to negate a past experience with **je** + **ne … jamais**. It often appears with the helper verb **avoir** (**je n'ai jamais + past participle**): *Je n'ai jamais dit…* (“I’ve never said…”), *Je n'ai jamais connu…* (“I’ve never known/met…”). In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *J’ai jamais dit ça* (informal).
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais visité Paris.
native_language_example: I have never visited Paris.

additional_notes: This is the negative passé composé with "ne... jamais" (never) and the verb "dire" (to say): "je n'ai jamais dit ...". Often followed by what you supposedly said (a word, a phrase, or a full clause with "que"). In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "j'ai jamais dit" (more informal).
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais dit que je viendrais.
native_language_example: I never said I would come.

meaning: "I've never heard of / I've never heard about."
additional_notes: Usually appears in a full sentence with a subject and the preposition **de**: **Je n'ai jamais entendu parler de ...** ("I've never heard of ..."). It uses the negative form **ne... jamais** ("never") and the past tense **ai entendu** ("have heard"). You can change the subject: **Il/Elle n'a jamais entendu parler de...**, **On n'en a jamais entendu parler** ("We/People have never heard of it").
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais entendu parler de ce film.
native_language_example: I've never heard of that movie.

meaning: "have never had" / "never had" (for "je" in the past).
additional_notes: This is the negative passé composé of "avoir" with "je": **je n'ai jamais eu** + noun (or **je n'ai jamais eu à** + infinitive). It expresses that you have *never had* something or *never experienced* something up to now. In full: **Je n'ai jamais eu de voiture.** (You can also say **Je n'ai jamais eu** on its own if the object is understood.)
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais eu de problème avec ça.
native_language_example: I’ve never had a problem with that.

additional_notes: Used with "je" in the negative past (passé composé) of "avoir": "Je n'ai jamais eu de + nom". After a negation (ne…jamais), "un/une/des" usually becomes "de" (or "d'" before a vowel): "Je n'ai jamais eu de voiture / d'argent". For other subjects, it changes: "tu n'as jamais eu de…", "il/elle n'a jamais eu de…", "nous n'avons jamais eu de…".
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais eu de carte bancaire.
native_language_example: I've never had a bank card.

meaning: "I have never … anything" / "I never … anything" (strong negative).
additional_notes: This is a common negative pattern built around the verb "avoir" in the 1st person singular: "je n'ai…" + "jamais" (never) + "rien" (anything/nothing). It’s used to say you have never done/seen/had anything of that kind: "Je n'ai jamais rien vu" = "I’ve never seen anything." In everyday spoken French, "ne" is often dropped: "J’ai jamais rien vu."
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais rien compris à ce film.
native_language_example: I never understood anything about that movie.

meaning: "have never seen" (used with "je": "Je n'ai jamais vu…").
additional_notes: This is the negative perfect tense of "voir" (to see) with "ne … jamais" = "never", formed with "avoir" in the passé composé: "Je n'ai jamais vu" = "I have never seen". In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "J'ai jamais vu…" (more informal).
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais vu ce film.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen that movie.

additional_notes: Negative form of the passé composé with "je": "Je n'ai pas dit…" = "I didn’t say…" or "I haven’t said…" depending on context. "ne" becomes "n'" before a vowel sound, and "ai" is the present of "avoir" used to form the past tense; "pas" goes around the helping verb (n' + ai + pas). Commonly used to deny, correct, or clarify something: "Je n'ai pas dit ça" (I didn’t say that).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas dit que c'était vrai.
native_language_example: I didn’t say it was true.

meaning: "I have nothing" / "I didn't … anything" (with *ne … rien* = "not … anything").
additional_notes: This is the negative pattern **ne + verb + rien**. Here it appears with **avoir** in the 1st person singular: *je n'ai rien…* In English it often becomes “I didn’t … anything” depending on the verb that follows (e.g., *Je n'ai rien vu* = “I didn't see anything”). In speech, **ne** is often dropped: *J'ai rien fait* (informal).
target_language_example: Je jure que je n'ai rien fait.
native_language_example: I swear I didn't do anything.

additional_notes: Contraction of ne + ai. It appears with je to form je n'ai..., the negative of j'ai (“I have”). It is usually completed by another negative word such as pas, plus, or rien: je n'ai pas..., je n'ai plus..., je n'ai rien....
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas le temps.
native_language_example: I don't have time.

additional_notes: This is a common fragment from the structure **ne ... que** meaning **only**: **Je n'ai qu'une + noun** = “I only have one + (feminine noun)”. **n'** is the shortened form of **ne** before a vowel (ai). Use **qu'un** with a masculine noun: *Je n'ai qu'un frère.*
target_language_example: Je n'ai qu'une question.
native_language_example: I only have one question.

meaning: "you have not" / "you did not" (negative form of "tu as").
additional_notes: Used to negate a verb with "tu" (you, informal singular). It’s "ne" + (verb) + "pas"; before a vowel, "ne" becomes "n'" and "as" is from "avoir" (present: tu as). Common in the passé composé: "tu n'as pas répondu" = "you didn’t answer". In everyday speech, the "ne/n'" is often dropped: "Tu as pas répondu" (informal).
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas oublié ton passeport ?
native_language_example: You didn’t forget your passport, did you?

additional_notes: Used with **tu** in the negative past (passé composé): **tu n'as pas changé**. **n'** is the shortened form of **ne** before a vowel sound. You can swap the subject: **je n'ai pas changé** (I haven’t changed), **il/elle n'a pas changé** (he/she hasn’t changed), **vous n'avez pas changé** (you haven’t changed, formal/plural). Often said to someone you haven’t seen in a while (sometimes sincerely, sometimes teasing).
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas changé depuis le lycée !
native_language_example: You haven’t changed since high school!

meaning: "don’t have" / "haven’t" (you do not have) — also used for "don’t" in "tu n'as pas besoin / le droit / à…".
additional_notes: This is the negative form of "tu as" (you have): "tu n'as pas…" In spoken French, the "ne" is often dropped: "t'as pas…" It’s used literally for possession ("You don’t have…") and very commonly with set phrases like "tu n'as pas besoin de…" (you don’t need…), "tu n'as pas le droit" (you’re not allowed), and "tu n'as pas à + infinitive" (you don’t have to / you’re not supposed to…).
target_language_example: Non, tu n'as pas besoin de ça.
native_language_example: No, you don’t need that.

additional_notes: Used with "tu" in the negative form of "avoir" (to have): "Tu n'as pas de + noun". In negatives, "un/une/des" usually becomes "de" (or "d'" before a vowel): "Tu as un vélo" → "Tu n'as pas de vélo". Often used without "ne" in casual speech: "T'as pas de...".
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas de monnaie ?
native_language_example: Don’t you have any change?

meaning: 'you just have to' / 'you only need to' (to...).
additional_notes: Usually part of the full phrase "Tu n'as qu'à + infinitive" to suggest an easy solution or give advice. In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "T'as qu'à...". Other forms: "Vous n'avez qu'à...", "Il/Elle n'a qu'à...".
target_language_example: Tu n'as qu'à lui demander.
native_language_example: You just have to ask him/her.

meaning: to have nothing to do with; to have no connection with; to be unrelated to.
additional_notes: Used to say two things are unrelated or irrelevant to each other, or to deny involvement. It’s the negative form of « avoir à voir avec ». In real speech it’s often conjugated (e.g., « Ça n’a rien à voir avec… »), but the dictionary form is « n'avoir rien à voir avec ».
target_language_example: Je te le dis clairement : n'avoir rien à voir avec cette affaire, c’est ne pas y être mêlé du tout.
native_language_example: I’m telling you clearly: to have nothing to do with this matter means not being involved in it at all.

meaning: “not … any / not … of it / not … about it” (ne + en).
additional_notes: Used when a verb takes the pronoun **en** (“some,” “any,” “of it/them,” “about it”), and it’s negated with **ne … pas/jamais/plus/rien**. **n’** is the shortened form of **ne** before a vowel sound: **ne + en → n’en**. The exact English translation depends on what **en** refers to: quantity (**Je n’en ai pas** = “I don’t have any”), replacing **de + noun** (**Je n’en veux pas** = “I don’t want any/of it”), or **de + topic** with verbs like **parler de** (**Je n’en ai jamais parlé** = “I never talked about it”). Note: the apostrophe in **n’en** may sometimes appear as a straight apostrophe (**n'en**) in plain text.
target_language_example: Elle n'en a jamais rien dit.
native_language_example: She never said anything about it.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" in the 1st person singular: "je n'en ai pas". "En" replaces something previously mentioned (often introduced with "de" or a quantity): "Tu as du café ? Non, je n'en ai pas." It can also be followed by another word like "besoin": "Je n'en ai pas besoin" = "I don't need it/any."
target_language_example: Tu as des billets ? Désolé, je n'en ai pas.
native_language_example: Do you have tickets? Sorry, I don't have any.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être (je suis, tu es, etc.) in a negative sentence: ne ... pas. The pronoun "en" means "of it / about it / from it" and refers back to something already mentioned. Often heard as "Je n'en suis pas" meaning "I'm not" (e.g., not ready, not at that stage, not one of them), with the rest understood from context.
target_language_example: Tu es prêt ? — Je n'en suis pas.
native_language_example: Are you ready? — I'm not.

meaning: “you are not” (negative form of « tu es »).
additional_notes: Used with « tu » to make a negative statement: « tu n'es pas + adjective/noun/past participle ». In speech, the « ne » is often dropped: « t'es pas… ». Agreement note: « tu n'es pas obligé » (to a man) vs « tu n'es pas obligée » (to a woman).
target_language_example: Non, tu n'es pas celui que je recherche.
native_language_example: No, you’re not the one I’m looking for.

additional_notes: Contraction of **ne + est** ("is"). Used in negation with **ne ... pas** (or other negative words like **rien**, **nul**, etc.). **Ne** becomes **n'** before a vowel or silent *h*: *Il n'est pas là.* Also appears in the tag question **n'est-ce pas ?** ("isn't it?/right?").
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas facile.
native_language_example: It's not easy.

meaning: "isn't it?", "right?" (a question tag asking for confirmation).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a statement to check/seek agreement (like “..., right?”). It can also start a question: "N'est-ce pas + noun/phrase ?" = “Isn’t that...?” The verb form in the tag doesn’t change with the subject (unlike English tags). More formal than "hein ?" or "non ?".
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h, n'est-ce pas ?
native_language_example: We’ll meet up at 6 p.m., right?

additional_notes: This is a negative question with inversion: "ne ... pas" + verb "être" + subject pronoun "elle". It’s used when you expect (or hope) the answer is yes, similar to a tag question: "It’s wonderful, isn’t it?" Often refers to a feminine noun (elle = she/it), e.g., la vie / une robe.
target_language_example: Cette robe n'est-elle pas magnifique ?
native_language_example: This dress is gorgeous, isn’t it?

additional_notes: This is the negative pattern **ne + (verb être: est) + jamais**. In speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Il est jamais là* (informal). With other verbs you’ll see the same structure: *Je ne viens jamais* (“I never come”).
target_language_example: Il n'est jamais en retard.
native_language_example: He is never late.

additional_notes: Used to make a negative sentence with « être » (to be): « ne … pas » surrounds the verb, e.g. « il n'est pas… ». Often shortened in speech to « il est pas… ». You also see it with other subjects: « ce n'est pas… », « on n'est pas… ».
target_language_example: Il n'est pas venu.
native_language_example: He didn’t come.

additional_notes: Negative of "(il/elle) est là" (he/she is here/there). Used to say someone is absent or not in the expected place. You can replace the subject: "je ne suis pas là" (I'm not here), "ils ne sont pas là" (they aren't here). In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "il est pas là".
target_language_example: Désolé, le responsable n'est pas là pour le moment.
native_language_example: Sorry, the manager isn't here at the moment.

additional_notes: Used with a singular subject like il, elle, or ce. The pattern ne... plus means 'no longer' or 'not anymore', and là can mean 'there' or sometimes 'here' depending on context.
target_language_example: Mon livre n'est plus là.
native_language_example: My book is no longer there.

additional_notes: This is the **être** form of the restriction pattern **ne...que** (= 'only'). With **être** in the present tense, it appears as **n'est que** (with an apostrophe). It’s used to limit what something/someone is: **Ce n'est que + noun/phrase**. Note: in formal writing you may also see **Ce n’est que...** with a curly apostrophe; the meaning is the same.
target_language_example: Ce n'est que le début.
native_language_example: It's only the beginning.

meaning: “if it hadn’t been for … / were it not for …” (except for).
additional_notes: Very formal/literary expression (rare in everyday speech). Used to introduce an exception or a factor that prevented something: "… n'eût été + noun" or "… n'eût été que + clause". In modern, everyday French you’ll usually hear: "sans …", "s’il n’y avait pas eu …", or "si ce n’était pas pour …".
target_language_example: Tout se serait bien passé, n'eût été ce retard.
native_language_example: Everything would have gone well, if it hadn’t been for that delay.

meaning: “any / no matter (which, who, where…)” (used with an interrogative word), or as an exclamation meaning “Nonsense!” / “Whatever!”.
additional_notes: Most often appears as n’importe + question word: n’importe qui (anyone), n’importe quoi (anything), n’importe où (anywhere), n’importe quand (anytime), n’importe comment (any way), n’importe lequel/laquelle/lesquels/lesquelles or n’importe quel / quelle / quels / quelles (any). On its own, « N’importe ! » can mean “Nonsense!” or “Whatever!”, depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: N'importe !
native_language_example: Nonsense! / Whatever!

additional_notes: Used when it doesn’t matter which one you choose: « Ça peut être n'importe lequel. » With negation for emphasis, « pas n'importe lequel » means “not just any one / not any old one” (something special or specific). It agrees in gender/number: n'importe lequel (m. sg.), n'importe laquelle (f. sg.), n'importe lesquels / lesquelles (pl.).
target_language_example: Ça peut être n'importe lequel.
native_language_example: It can be any one.

additional_notes: Means “in any place” with no restriction. Often used in sets like “n’importe qui/où/quand” (anyone/anywhere/anytime). Can also appear in imperatives like “Va n'importe où…” meaning “Go anywhere…”.
target_language_example: Tu peux te connecter n'importe où avec ton téléphone.
native_language_example: You can log in anywhere with your phone.

additional_notes: Means it can happen at any moment, with no particular time specified. Often used with other "n'importe + question word" phrases like "n'importe où" (anywhere) or "n'importe qui" (anyone).
target_language_example: Tu peux m'appeler n'importe quand.
native_language_example: You can call me anytime.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (n'importe quel + noun) to mean “any/whatever,” with the idea of no preference or no restriction. Common in fixed expressions such as « à n'importe quel moment » (at any moment), « à n'importe quel prix » (at any cost), and « par n'importe quel moyen » (by any means). Other forms: « n'importe quelle » (fem. sg.), « n'importe quels/quelles » (plural).
target_language_example: Je veux la vérité, à n'importe quel prix.
native_language_example: I want the truth, at any cost.

additional_notes: Means it doesn’t matter which person. Common as a subject (« N'importe qui peut entrer. »), after verbs like demander à (« Vous pouvez demander à n'importe qui. »), and in phrases like « ce/cela pourrait être n'importe qui » (“it could be anyone”). With negatives, it can mean “not just anyone”: « Je ne le dirai pas à n'importe qui. » = “I won’t tell just anyone.”
target_language_example: Cela pourrait être n'importe qui.
native_language_example: It could be anyone.

additional_notes: Literally means “no matter what.” Use it after a verb to mean “anything/whatever”: « Demande-moi n’importe quoi » (Ask me anything), « Ça pourrait être n’importe quoi » (It could be anything). In « faire n’importe quoi », it means doing things carelessly/incorrectly (“to do anything / make a mess of it”). Said on its own (« N’importe quoi ! »), it’s a common, informal way to say “Nonsense!” / “That’s ridiculous.”
target_language_example: Tu peux choisir n'importe quoi.
native_language_example: You can choose anything.

meaning: “anything to/for (do something)” (to show you’d do whatever it takes).
additional_notes: Often followed by a person or goal to show strong willingness or commitment. Common pattern: « Je ferais n’importe quoi pour + personne/objectif » = “I’d do anything for + person / to achieve + goal.” Note: « n’importe quoi » alone can also mean “nonsense,” but with « pour » it usually means “anything/whatever it takes.”
target_language_example: Je ferais n'importe quoi pour t'aider.
native_language_example: I’d do anything to help you.

meaning: "not there" / "not to it" / "not about it" (negative with "y").
additional_notes: "n'y" is the combination of "ne" (negation) + the pronoun "y". "Y" usually means "there" (a place) or "to it / in it / about it" (replacing something introduced with à, dans, sur, etc.). In everyday spoken French, "ne" is often dropped, but "y" stays: "J'y ai pas pensé."
target_language_example: Je n'y suis jamais allé.
native_language_example: I've never been there.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir in the expression “il y a” (“there is/there are”). With negation it’s commonly “il n’y a pas …” (“there isn’t/aren’t …”), often followed by “de” before a noun: “Il n’y a pas de problème.” In writing you’ll often see the typographic apostrophe (’), but the plain apostrophe (') is also common.
target_language_example: Il n'y a pas de café aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There isn’t any coffee today.

meaning: "there isn't / there aren't" (negative of "il y a").
additional_notes: Usually part of the full phrase "il n'y a pas". Often followed by "de" + noun: "Il n'y a pas de café." = "There is no coffee." You may also see it in questions/short answers: "Il n'y a pas de problème."
target_language_example: Il n'y a pas de métro ici.
native_language_example: There isn't a subway here.

meaning: “there is no / there isn’t any” (used in: “il n’y a pas de …”).
additional_notes: This is the negative form of “il y a” (“there is/there are”). It’s usually used as “il n’y a pas de + noun” to say something doesn’t exist or isn’t available. Note that in correct French spelling, this appears with curly apostrophes: “n’y a pas de”. Before a vowel or silent h, “de” often becomes “d’”: “il n’y a pas d’eau”.
target_language_example: Désolé, il n'y a pas de bus après 22 h.
native_language_example: Sorry, there are no buses after 10 p.m.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "il y a" (there is/there are) to express that only one thing (or a limited set) exists or is available: "Il n'y a que deux solutions." It’s closely related to the common pattern "ne … que" = "only". In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Y a que deux solutions."
target_language_example: Il n'y a que deux bus aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There are only two buses today.

additional_notes: Used in the common structure « il n'y a rien » (literally: “there has nothing there”), meaning nothing is present or nothing exists. Often followed by extra info like « ici » (here) or an infinitive: « il n'y a rien à dire/faire » (“there’s nothing to say/do”). You can reinforce it with « rien du tout » (“nothing at all”).
target_language_example: Non, il n'y a rien ici.
native_language_example: No, there’s nothing here.

meaning: "have never (there/it)" — a 1st-person singular passé composé negative fragment with « y » (there/to it/about it).
additional_notes: Sentence fragment built from: ne + y + ai (avoir, 1st person singular, passé composé auxiliary) + jamais. Used before a past participle when the main verb takes « avoir »: « Je n’y ai jamais pensé » (I never thought about it) or « Je n’y ai jamais travaillé » (I never worked there). « y » usually replaces « à + place/thing » (there, to it, about it). With verbs that use « être » in the passé composé, you wouldn’t use « ai » (e.g., « Je n’y suis jamais allé(e) » = I’ve never gone there).
target_language_example: Je n'y ai jamais pensé.
native_language_example: I never thought about it.

additional_notes: Negative form of "être" (to be) in the imperfect tense: "ne ... pas" + "étais" + "là". Used to say someone was absent or not present (physically or emotionally) over a period of time. Changes with the subject: "je n'étais pas là" (I wasn’t there), "tu n'étais pas là" (you weren’t there), "il/elle n'était pas là" (he/she wasn’t there), "nous n'étions pas là" (we weren’t there), etc.
target_language_example: Désolé, je n'étais pas là hier soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I wasn’t there last night.

additional_notes: Used to negate être in the imperfect tense: ne + était/étaient + pas. Often means someone/something wasn’t in a certain state, place, or habit “at that time” in the past. In speech, the “ne” is frequently dropped: "il était pas là".
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il n'était pas là.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he wasn’t there.

meaning: 'no / not any / none' (negative), used as part of the two-part negation with a verb.
additional_notes: In standard French, this idea is usually expressed as **ne … aucun(e)**: **ne** comes before the verb and **aucun(e)** typically comes before the noun (or can stand alone). **Aucun** agrees with the noun: **aucun** (masc.), **aucune** (fem.). Common pattern: **ne + verb + aucun(e) + noun** → *no / not any*. In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped (informal), but in writing you usually keep it. Note: the exact string **ne aucun** will typically appear with a conjugated verb between them (e.g., *n’ai aucun*, *n’ai aucune*).
target_language_example: Je n’ai aucun problème.
native_language_example: I have no problem.

additional_notes: Negative form of *boire* (“to drink”) using **ne … pas**. With **tu** it can be a question (*Tu ne bois pas ?* “You don’t drink?”) or a statement (*Tu ne bois pas.* “You don’t drink.”). Used as a negative command: **Ne bois pas !** (“Don’t drink!”), often with **trop** (“too much”).
target_language_example: Ne bois pas trop ce soir.
native_language_example: Don’t drink too much tonight.

additional_notes: Imperative with negation of **bouger** (“to move”). Used to tell one person to stay where they are or not make any movement; can be urgent (e.g., safety, warning) or simply asking someone to hold still. For multiple people: **ne bougez pas**.
target_language_example: Ne bouge pas, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: Don’t move, I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Negative form of the verb comprendre (to understand). It’s used with different subjects: je ne comprends pas (I don’t understand), tu ne comprends pas (you don’t understand), il/elle ne comprend pas (he/she doesn’t understand). In casual spoken French, the ne is often dropped: je comprends pas.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne comprends pas la question.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand the question.

additional_notes: This is the negative form of connaître (“to know” a person/thing, to be familiar with). It’s usually used with a direct object: Je ne connais pas ton nom. In casual speech, French often drops “ne”: Je connais pas. Also note the set phrase connaître de vue (“to know/recognize by sight”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne connais pas cette rue.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know this street.

additional_notes: From the verb *croire* (“to believe/think”) in the negative: *ne … pas*. Often used to disagree or say something is unlikely (*Je ne crois pas* = “I don’t think so”), or with an object: *Je ne crois pas ça* (“I don’t believe that”). With *en*, it means belief in something: *Je ne crois pas en Dieu* (“I don’t believe in God”). In casual spoken French, *ne* is often dropped: *Je crois pas*.
target_language_example: Tu penses qu’il va venir ce soir ? Je ne crois pas.
native_language_example: Do you think he’s coming tonight? I don’t think so.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt, disbelief, or disagreement. After *ne crois pas que*, French typically uses the subjunctive: *Je ne crois pas qu’il vienne* / *Je ne crois pas que ce soit vrai*. (In casual speech, *ne* is often dropped: *Je crois pas que…*).
target_language_example: Je ne crois pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don’t think that’s a good idea.

ne crois pas que ce soit

target_language_multi_word_term: ne crois pas que ce soit
meaning: "I don't think it's…" / "I don't believe that it's…"
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disagreement. With negation (ne…pas), **croire que** is typically followed by the **subjunctive**, so you often see **ce soit** (subjunctive of *être*) instead of *c'est / c'était*. Often completed with an adjective or noun phrase: *Je ne crois pas que ce soit vrai / une bonne idée / possible.*
target_language_example: Je ne crois pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don't think it's a good idea.

additional_notes: Used with the conditional of devoir (je devrais) to give advice, express what is (not) recommended, or what is (not) supposed to be necessary: « Je ne devrais pas + infinitive ». In speech, the « ne » is often dropped: « Je devrais pas… » (more informal), but in careful French you keep « ne … pas ».
target_language_example: Tu ne devrais pas parler comme ça au professeur.
native_language_example: You shouldn't talk to the teacher like that.

additional_notes: Negative form of **devoir** in the conditional (**devrait**) to express advice, recommendation, or a moral/social rule. Often followed by an infinitive: **ne devrait pas + verbe**. In speech, **ne** is frequently dropped: **Il devrait pas…**
target_language_example: Il ne devrait pas revenir ici.
native_language_example: He shouldn’t come back here.

additional_notes: Built from the conditional of devoir (devrait = “should/ought to”) plus negation ne…pas and être (“to be”). Used to express that something is not desirable or not how it should be: X ne devrait pas être + adjective/noun/adverbial phrase (e.g., secret, ainsi).
target_language_example: Ça ne devrait pas être si difficile.
native_language_example: It shouldn’t be so difficult.

ne devriez pas vous y rendre

target_language_multi_word_term: ne devriez pas vous y rendre
additional_notes:
Formal/polite advice or warning using the conditional of devoir (devriez): “you should/ought to.”
- vous = formal/plural “you.”
- y = “there” (replaces a place mentioned earlier).
- se rendre (à + place) = “to go (to).” Often used in notices or more formal speech.
target_language_example: Vous ne devriez pas vous y rendre seul.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t go there alone.

additional_notes: This is the negative imperative of "dire" (tu-form): "Ne + verb + pas". Used to tell someone not to say something: "Ne dis pas ça" (Don’t say that). In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Dis pas ça."
target_language_example: Ne dis pas ça, ce n’est pas gentil.
native_language_example: Don’t say that, it’s not nice.

additional_notes: Negative imperative of *dire* (“to say”), used to tell someone not to say something. Often implies the comment is inappropriate, rude, hurtful, or badly phrased. You can add details: *Ne dis pas ça comme ça* (“Don’t say it like that”), *Ne dis pas ça devant lui* (“Don’t say that in front of him”).
target_language_example: Ne dis pas ça, c’est méchant.
native_language_example: Don’t say that, it’s mean.

additional_notes: Uses the negative structure **ne … rien** (“not … anything”) with **dire** (“to say”). Often used as a negative command: **Ne dis rien !** (“Don’t say anything!”). In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **Dis rien.** It can also appear as a statement: **Je ne dis rien** (“I’m not saying anything”).
target_language_example: Ne dis rien, je vais m’en occuper.
native_language_example: Don’t say anything, I’ll take care of it.

meaning: “must not” / “don’t have to” / “shouldn’t” (negative of devoir, “to have to / must”).
additional_notes: Used with the verb devoir in the present tense (je dois, tu dois, il/elle doit, etc.) inside the negation ne … pas. Often expresses a prohibition or strong advice not to do something (like “must not”), but in some contexts it can also mean “don’t have to” (lack of obligation). In everyday spoken French, “ne” is often dropped: Tu dois pas…
target_language_example: Tu ne dois pas parler pendant le film.
native_language_example: You must not talk during the movie.

additional_notes: This is the negative form of **devoir** (to have to / must) in the 3rd person singular: **ne + doit + pas** (“he/she/it must not”; also used with **on** = “one/people/you (general) must not”). It expresses a prohibition or something that is not allowed/expected, and in some contexts can also be strong advice (“shouldn’t”). Note: this is different from “doesn’t have to / doesn’t need to,” which is often expressed with **ne pas avoir à** (or sometimes **ne pas devoir** depending on meaning).
target_language_example: On ne doit pas dire du mal des morts.
native_language_example: One must not speak ill of the dead.

additional_notes: This is the negative of devoir ("to have to / must"): "(subject) ne doit/doivent pas + infinitive". It can express prohibition/rules ("must not") or a strong expectation ("are not supposed to / shouldn't"), depending on context. In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Ils doivent pas…"
target_language_example: Les étudiants ne doivent pas utiliser cette toilette.
native_language_example: Students must not use this toilet.

meaning: to be one (to be united / inseparable).
additional_notes: Often used with plural subjects: « Ils ne font qu’un » = “They are one / they’re inseparable.” You can also say « ne faire qu’un avec + noun » to mean “to be one with” something (e.g., nature, the crowd). Here « ne… que » means “only,” but the whole expression is idiomatic and usually translates as “to be one” rather than “to make only one.”
target_language_example: Après des années ensemble, ils semblent ne faire qu'un.
native_language_example: After years together, they seem to be as one.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tu) not to do something. It’s the negative imperative of faire: ne + verb + pas. Often followed by an infinitive (Ne fais pas ça. / Ne fais pas attention.) or by a noun phrase (Ne fais pas de bruit. / Ne fais pas de tort.). For more formal or plural "you," use "ne faites pas."
target_language_example: Ne fais pas ça, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t do that, please.

additional_notes: Negative command with "tu" (fais = "you do"). In speech, French often drops the "ne": "Fais pas ça." It can also be used as a statement: "Je ne fais pas ça" = "I don’t do that."
target_language_example: Ne fais pas ça, c'est dangereux.
native_language_example: Don’t do that, it’s dangerous.

meaning: “doesn’t do / doesn’t make” (negation of faire, 3rd person singular: il/elle/on ne fait pas).
additional_notes: This is the standard French negation ne...pas around the verb faire in the 3rd person singular (il/elle/on fait → il/elle/on ne fait pas). Often appears in fixed expressions like ne fait pas partie de (“is not part of”) and ne fait pas grand-chose (“doesn’t do much”). In casual spoken French, ne is often dropped: il fait pas.
target_language_example: Taiwan ne fait pas partie de la Chine.
native_language_example: Taiwan is not part of China.

meaning: only; does nothing but; just (keeps) doing.
additional_notes:
From the pattern **ne + faire + que**. It limits the action to *only that*.
- **Ça ne fait que commencer** = “It’s only just beginning.”
- **Il ne fait que ça** = “He does nothing but that / That’s all he does.”
Often used to emphasize that something is ongoing or that things are getting started.
target_language_example: Elle ne fait que se plaindre.
native_language_example: She does nothing but complain.

additional_notes: From the verb **faire** (“to do/make”) in the negative: **ne … rien** = “not … anything” → “nothing.” Used to say someone does nothing, or that no action is being taken: **Si on ne fait rien…** (“If we don’t do anything…”). In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **Il fait rien.**
target_language_example: Je suis inquiet : il ne fait rien pour chercher du travail.
native_language_example: I’m worried: he isn’t doing anything to look for a job.

additional_notes: Used to form the negative imperative with the verb faire (vous form): ne + faites + pas. It can be a polite request to one person (vous), or a command to multiple people. Often followed by an infinitive or object: « Ne faites pas attention… » (Don’t pay attention…), « Ne faites pas ça » (Don’t do that).
target_language_example: Ne faites pas ça, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please don't do that.

additional_notes: Negative command using the formal/plural imperative of faire (faites). Used to tell one person politely (vous) or more than one person not to do something. For an informal singular command (to one friend/child), you’d say: « Ne fais pas ça. » Often strengthened with « s’il vous plaît », « je vous en prie », or « par pitié ».
target_language_example: Ne faites pas ça, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please don’t do that.

additional_notes: Usually used with an impersonal subject: « il ne faut pas + infinitive » to give general advice or a rule (similar to “you mustn’t/shouldn’t…” in English). Often shortened in speech to « faut pas » (dropping « ne »).
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas fumer ici.
native_language_example: You mustn’t smoke here.

additional_notes: Standard French negation: ne + verb + pas. Used to say a device/machine isn’t working, or that something (a plan, method, idea) won’t work. In everyday speech, people often drop “ne” and say “Ça fonctionne pas,” but the full form is common in writing and more formal speech.
target_language_example: Désolé, l’ascenseur ne fonctionne pas aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, the elevator isn’t working today.

additional_notes: This is the negation of **être** (“to be”) in the **passé simple**: **il/elle/on ne fut pas…**. It’s mostly found in written/literary French (stories, history, formal narration). In everyday speech, you usually use **n’était pas** (imperfect) or **n’a pas été** (passé composé).
target_language_example: Ce ne fut pas facile, mais il a réussi.
native_language_example: It wasn’t easy, but he succeeded.

additional_notes: Used as a negation and typically placed as **ne ... guère** around a verb. It is more formal/literary than **ne... pas** and often conveys “not much” or “almost not.” In modern spoken French, **ne** is often dropped, but with **guère** this sounds quite formal (*Je comprends guère*).
target_language_example: Je ne guère comprends ce qu’il veut dire.
native_language_example: I hardly understand what he means.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to mean 'to never do' something, often after verbs like regretter, craindre, or essayer. With a conjugated verb, French usually uses ne ... jamais around the verb: Je ne vais jamais là-bas.
target_language_example: J'essaie de ne jamais oublier mes clés.
native_language_example: I try to never forget my keys.

meaning: 'not it / not him / not her' (in a negation).
additional_notes: Used when you negate a verb (often with "ne ... pas") and replace the direct object with the pronoun "le / la", which becomes "l'" before a vowel or silent h. The pronoun comes before the verb: "Ils ne l'ont pas dit" = "They didn’t say it."
target_language_example: Je ne l'ai pas vu.
native_language_example: I didn’t see him/it.

additional_notes: Negative passé composé: ne...pas surrounds the auxiliary verb (a), and l' is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it” (short for le/la before a vowel sound). Used to deny that a specific action (previously mentioned) was done. Most commonly with il/elle/on: il/elle/on ne l'a pas fait = he/she/we/people didn’t do it.
target_language_example: Non, il ne l'a pas fait.
native_language_example: No, he didn't do it.

meaning: fragment meaning “don’t/didn’t … it/him/her” (used with another negative word like pas, jamais, plus).
additional_notes: This is not usually used alone. It’s a common fragment in French negation: **ne + l’ + ai**. **l’** is the shortened form of **le/la** (“him/it/her”), and **ai** is “I have” (from **avoir**), also used as the auxiliary in the **passé composé**. Typical patterns include **Je ne l’ai pas** (I don’t have it / I didn’t), **Je ne l’ai jamais** (I never did), **Je ne l’ai plus** (I don’t anymore). In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **Je l’ai pas**.
target_language_example: Je ne l'ai pas.
native_language_example: I don’t have it / I didn’t (do it).

additional_notes: Uses the negative pattern **ne ... jamais** = “never.” **l'** is the direct-object pronoun “him/it” (short for **le** or **la**) placed before the auxiliary **ai**. Commonly said without **ne** in speech: **Je l'ai jamais vu** (informal spoken French).
target_language_example: Je ne l'ai jamais vu, mais j'en ai entendu parler.
native_language_example: I've never seen him/it, but I've heard about him/it.

meaning: "you have never … it/him/her" (negative passé composé with a direct object pronoun).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment you normally complete with a past participle: « Tu ne l'as jamais vu. » The « l' » is the direct object pronoun (short for « le » or « la ») meaning “him/it” or “her/it.” « ne … jamais » is the standard way to say “never” in French; in casual speech, « ne » is often dropped (« Tu l'as jamais vu »). Note: in French typography the apostrophe is often curly (« l’as »), but here we keep the straight apostrophe to match the exact term.
target_language_example: Tu ne l'as jamais vu ?
native_language_example: You’ve never seen him/it/her?

additional_notes: Used with "tu" in a negative construction with "avoir": ne + l’ (direct object pronoun = "it/him/her") + as ("have", tu form) + pas. Often appears in the passé composé when followed by a past participle (e.g., "tu ne l’as pas fait" = "you didn’t do it"), but can also be used without an explicit main verb to mean "you don’t have it" (e.g., "tu ne l’as pas" = "you don’t have it"). In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "tu l’as pas".
target_language_example: Non, tu ne l'as pas fait.
native_language_example: No, you didn’t do it.

additional_notes: Fixed negative form of « l’est » (“is it/that”). The pronoun « l’ » usually refers back to something already mentioned (often an adjective, status, or idea): « Elle est prête ? — Non, elle ne l'est pas. » Often used with « ce » or « ça »: « Non, ça ne l'est pas. » Can also appear in questions or hypotheticals: « Et si elle ne l'est pas ? »
target_language_example: Elle est prête ? Non, elle ne l'est pas.
native_language_example: Is she ready? No, she isn’t.

meaning: "don’t … it/her" (negative command with the object pronoun "la").
additional_notes: Used mainly in negative imperatives: "Ne la + verb(ez) pas" = “Don’t + verb + it/her.” The pronoun "la" refers to a feminine singular thing (“it”) or to “her,” and it comes before the verb (e.g., "Ne la réveille pas" = “Don’t wake her up.”). In other tenses you’ll see "ne" before the verb and "la" still before the verb (e.g., "Elle ne la vit plus" = “She didn’t see her/it anymore”).
target_language_example: Ne la laisse pas ici.
native_language_example: Don’t leave it here.

additional_notes: Not a standalone expression: this is the beginning of a negative construction with the object pronoun le. In full sentences, ne comes before le and the verb, and another negative word usually comes after the verb, such as pas, jamais, or plus: ne le fait pas, ne le saura jamais. le can mean him, it, or sometimes so/that, depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ne le comprends pas.
native_language_example: I don't understand it.

additional_notes: Uses French negation **ne … pas** with **faire** (“to do/make”) and the object pronoun **le** (“it”). In the imperative it means **“Don’t do it!”**; in a statement it means **“you don’t do it / I don’t do it”** depending on context (**je/tu**). In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **Le fais pas ! / Je le fais pas.**
target_language_example: Ne le fais pas, c’est dangereux.
native_language_example: Don’t do it, it’s dangerous.

additional_notes: This is a verb fragment from **penser** (to think) with the object pronoun **le** (= “it/so,” referring to an idea or situation). It’s most commonly used with **pas**: **Je ne le pensais pas** (“I didn’t think so / I didn’t think it”). In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **Je le pensais pas**.
target_language_example: Je ne le pensais pas, mais tu as raison.
native_language_example: I didn’t think so, but you’re right.

additional_notes: This is the negative form of **(le) savoir** (“to know it/that”). **ne … pas** wraps around the verb: *je ne sais pas* (“I don’t know”). **le** is an object pronoun meaning “it” and often refers to an idea or fact already understood from context (similar to “that” in English). In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je le sais pas* (informal).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne le sais pas.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know.

additional_notes: Used when "les" (“them”) is the direct object pronoun in a negative sentence. "Les" goes before the verb, and the negation is completed with a second word like "pas", "jamais", "plus", etc.: « Je ne les vois pas » (“I don’t see them”). In speech, "ne" is often dropped: « Je les vois pas ».
target_language_example: Je ne les vois pas aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I don’t see them today.

meaning: "not to him/her" (used with a verb in the negative).
additional_notes: Used when the verb takes an indirect object pronoun (lui = “to him/to her”). In standard negation, the pronoun comes before the verb: ne lui + verb + pas (e.g., « Je ne lui parle pas. »). In negative commands, « ne » comes before the pronoun: « Ne lui dis pas… ».
target_language_example: Je ne lui réponds pas tout de suite.
native_language_example: I’m not replying to him/her right away.

additional_notes: This is a common negative pattern in the passé composé: ne + indirect object pronoun (lui = to him/to her) + ai (I have) + jamais (never). It usually needs a past participle after it (e.g., dit, parlé, donné): « Je ne lui ai jamais parlé. » In everyday spoken French, « ne » is often dropped: « Je lui ai jamais parlé » (but that’s informal and considered incorrect in careful writing).
target_language_example: Je ne lui ai jamais dit la vérité.
native_language_example: I have never told him/her the truth.

meaning: “not … me / myself” (the start of a negative sentence before a vowel sound).
additional_notes: This is a combination of **ne** (negation) + **me** (“me / to me / myself”), where **me** becomes **m’** before a verb starting with a vowel or silent **h** (elision): *ne m’écoute pas, ne m’appelle pas*. In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped (*M’écoute pas*), but it’s common in writing and more formal speech. It’s not a complete negation by itself—you usually see it with **pas**, **plus**, **jamais**, etc.
target_language_example: Je ne m'en souviens pas.
native_language_example: I don’t remember it.

additional_notes: This is a common French negation pattern: ne + indirect object pronoun (me → m’ before a vowel) + auxiliary verb (here, a) + jamais (“never”). It’s used in the passé composé to say something has never happened, e.g. “He has never loved me,” “She has never talked to me about you.” With feminine subjects you may see agreement on the past participle when the direct object is “me” (Elle ne m’a jamais aimée.), though many learners focus first on the core pattern.
target_language_example: Il ne m'a jamais répondu.
native_language_example: He has never replied to me.

additional_notes: Built with the negation pattern **ne ... que** meaning **“only”** (not “not”). It restricts what someone eats: *ne mange que des légumes* = “eats nothing but vegetables.” You can add adjectives or details after **des légumes** (e.g., *des légumes frais*, *que je cultive moi-même*).
target_language_example: Il ne mange que des légumes depuis un mois.
native_language_example: He has only been eating vegetables for a month.

additional_notes: From the verb « marcher » (“to work” for machines/devices, or “to function”). Used with « ne … pas » for negation. Common in speech with dropped « ne »: « Ça marche pas. » Often said as an exclamation when something fails: « Ça ne marche pas ! »
target_language_example: Désolé, mon téléphone ne marche pas aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, my phone isn’t working today.

additional_notes: This is a grammatical chunk, not a fixed expression. ne starts a negation, and me means 'me' before the verb. It is usually followed later by another negative word such as pas, jamais, or rien: ne me force pas = 'don't force me', vous ne me devez rien = 'you don't owe me anything'.
target_language_example: Ne me parle pas comme ça.
native_language_example: Don't talk to me like that.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to say something, often in a firm or annoyed way. It’s the negative imperative of "dire" (to tell/say): "dis" (tell) + "me" (to me) + "pas" (not). Often followed by "que" + a full clause (Ne me dis pas que…) or by "de" + infinitive (Ne me dis pas de…).
target_language_example: Ne me dis pas que tu as oublié encore une fois.
native_language_example: Don’t tell me you forgot again.

meaning: "doesn’t tell me anything" / "doesn’t ring a bell"; also "doesn’t appeal to me".
additional_notes: Used most often with a subject like "ça" ("Ça ne me dit rien") to mean you don’t recognize something (it doesn’t sound familiar) or you’re not interested in doing it (it doesn’t tempt you). In more literal contexts, it can also mean "no one tells me anything" ("Personne ne me dit rien"). You may also hear the stronger form "ne me dit rien du tout" (not at all).
target_language_example: Ce nom ne me dit rien, tu es sûr que je le connais ?
native_language_example: That name doesn’t ring a bell—are you sure I know it?

additional_notes: Used to say something is not a problem for you. Very common in answers like « Non, ça ne me dérange pas. ». It can refer to an action or situation (« Ce que tu fais ne me dérange pas. »). In everyday speech, people often drop « ne »: « Ça me dérange pas. ».
target_language_example: Tu peux ouvrir la fenêtre, ça ne me dérange pas.
native_language_example: You can open the window; I don't mind.

meaning: “don’t do that to me” / “don’t (make) me …” (negative command).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to do something that affects you: **Ne me fais pas + noun/phrase** (e.g., *ce coup-là* “that trick,” *la leçon* “a lecture,” *la morale* “a moral lesson”). It’s the negative imperative of **faire** with **me** (“to me”). With a verb after it, you often see **Ne me fais pas + infinitive** (e.g., *Ne me fais pas attendre* “Don’t make me wait”).
target_language_example: Ne me fais pas attendre, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t make me wait, please.

additional_notes: Negative informal command (tu form) of *laisser* addressed to one person. Often followed by an adjective/adverb (*ne me laisse pas tranquille* = don’t leave me alone) or an infinitive (*ne me laisse pas partir* = don’t let me leave). Also used on its own as a plea: *Ne me laisse pas !* = Don’t leave me!
target_language_example: S’il te plaît, ne me laisse pas seul ce soir.
native_language_example: Please, don’t leave me alone tonight.

meaning: (1) “doesn’t concern me / isn’t my business”; (2) “don’t look at me.”
additional_notes: With « regarder » + an indirect object (« me/te/lui… »), French can mean “to concern” (e.g., « Ça ne me regarde pas » = “That’s none of my business”). As an imperative (« Ne me regarde pas ! »), it’s the literal “Don’t look at me!” Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Ce qu’ils font après le travail, ça ne me regarde pas.
native_language_example: What they do after work is none of my business.

ne me rendrait plus heureux que de

target_language_multi_word_term: ne me rendrait plus heureux que de
meaning: "nothing would make me happier than to…"
additional_notes: Used to express a strong preference or wish. It’s part of a negative comparison: « Rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que de + infinitive » (“Nothing would make me happier than to + verb”). Often used with the conditional (« rendrait ») to sound polite or hypothetical.
target_language_example: Rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que de passer plus de temps avec toi.
native_language_example: Nothing would make me happier than spending more time with you.

meaning: "I don't feel (well / up to it)" (as in "I don't feel...").
additional_notes: This is usually part of a full sentence with the subject: « Je ne me sens pas… ». It uses the reflexive verb « se sentir » (= to feel). Very commonly followed by an adverb/adjective: « Je ne me sens pas bien » (I don’t feel well), « Je ne me sens pas prêt(e) » (I don’t feel ready), « Je ne me sens pas à l’aise » (I don’t feel comfortable).
target_language_example: Je ne me sens pas bien aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I don't feel well today.

meaning: "have never" (said by "I"; used before a past participle).
additional_notes: This is a common negative pattern in the passé composé: **ne + (reflexive pronoun) + auxiliary (suis) + jamais**. It’s used with pronominal verbs like *se tromper*, *se plaindre*, *se sentir*: *Je ne me suis jamais trompé.* In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je me suis jamais trompé* (more informal/less careful).
target_language_example: Je ne me suis jamais senti aussi fatigué.
native_language_example: I have never felt this tired.

meaning: “don’t follow me” / “I didn’t … (myself)” (negative with *suivre* or a reflexive verb in the past).
additional_notes:
This is a common negative pattern that depends on the verb.

1) With *suivre* (tu suis = “you follow”), in the negative imperative it means “Don’t follow me!”: *Ne me suis pas !* / *Ne me suis pas comme ça !* (“Don’t follow me like that!”).

2) With *je me suis …* (passé composé of a reflexive verb), it means “I didn’t …”: *Je ne me suis pas confessé* (“I didn’t confess”). Reflexive verbs use *être* in the past (*je me suis…*), and *ne…pas* wraps around the auxiliary (*ne me suis pas*).
target_language_example: Ne me suis pas, je rentre chez moi.
native_language_example: Don’t follow me; I’m going home.

additional_notes: Used to express negation of place/destination (“nowhere”). In standard French, the negation is typically written as "ne … nulle part" with "ne" before the verb and "nulle part" after it (e.g., "Je ne vais nulle part"). In casual speech, "ne" is often dropped ("Je vais nulle part"), but in writing and careful speech it’s usually kept.
target_language_example: Je ne vais ne nulle part ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m not going anywhere tonight.

meaning: 'doesn't speak' / 'doesn't talk' (used with a negative word like pas, jamais, plus, personne, que, etc.).
additional_notes: In French negation is usually two parts: ne + a negative word. With parler, you’ll see: ne parle pas (doesn’t speak), ne parle jamais (never talks about / never speaks), ne parle à personne (doesn’t talk to anyone), ne parle que de… (only talks about…), and the more formal/literary ne… point (not). In everyday speech, ne is often dropped (e.g., Elle parle pas).
target_language_example: Je ne parle pas bien français, mais j’essaie.
native_language_example: I don't speak French well, but I'm trying.

additional_notes: This is the common French negation: **ne + verb + pas**. With **il/elle** it usually means someone *doesn’t speak* (a language) or *doesn’t talk*: *Elle ne parle pas anglais.* In the negative command (imperative), it means *don’t speak / don’t talk*: *Ne parle pas !* You can add what not to talk about with **de**: *Ne parle pas de lui.*
target_language_example: Ne parle pas si vite, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t speak so fast, please.

meaning: "Don’t talk like that." / "Don’t speak like that."
additional_notes: A negative command in the informal "tu" form, used to tell someone to stop speaking in a rude/disrespectful way or using an inappropriate tone. You can specify the target with "à + person" (Ne parle pas comme ça à ta mère.) or what they’re saying with "de + person/thing" (Ne parle pas comme ça de ta tante.).
target_language_example: Ne parle pas comme ça à ton professeur.
native_language_example: Don’t talk like that to your teacher.

additional_notes: Built from negation (ne…pas) + parler de (“to talk about”). It can be used as (1) a statement: « Je ne parle pas de… » = “I’m not talking about…”, or (2) a negative command: « Ne parle pas de… ! » = “Don’t talk about…!” (informal singular ‘tu’). With a name, you usually add « de » + the name: « Ne parle pas de maman. »
target_language_example: Je ne parle pas de toi, je parle de la situation.
native_language_example: I’m not talking about you; I’m talking about the situation.

additional_notes:
From the verb *partir* (to leave). **Ne … pas** is the standard negation. 
- As an instruction to one person (negative command): **Ne pars pas !** = “Don’t leave!” 
- In a statement with a subject: **Je ne pars pas.** = “I’m not leaving.” 
In everyday speech, people often drop *ne*: **Pars pas !** / **Je pars pas.**
target_language_example: Ne pars pas maintenant, attends-moi.
native_language_example: Don’t leave now—wait for me.

additional_notes: basic French negation. Before an infinitive, ne pas goes directly before the verb: ne pas parler = not to speak. With a conjugated verb, ne usually comes before the verb and pas after it: je ne sais pas. In everyday spoken French, ne is often dropped, but the full form is standard.
target_language_example: Essaie de ne pas rire.
native_language_example: Try not to laugh.

meaning: 'to not have' / 'not to have' (often used to say you did not do something).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as a negated infinitive in the past: **ne pas avoir + past participle** (the *infinitif passé*), meaning **“to have not…” / “not having…”** and often translates naturally as **“not to have (done)”** or **“not (having) done.”** Example patterns: *regretter de ne pas avoir…* (“to regret not having…”), *s’excuser de ne pas avoir…* (“to apologize for not having…”).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de ne pas avoir appelé plus tôt.
native_language_example: I’m sorry I didn’t call earlier.

additional_notes: Used to say that something did not happen in the past, in an infinitive form (often after another verb or expression). Common after verbs like regretter (to regret), être content(e) (to be happy), penser (to think), or in structures like après/pour + infinitive: « Je regrette de ne pas avoir été là » (I regret not having been there).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de ne pas avoir été plus clair.
native_language_example: I’m sorry I wasn’t clearer.

meaning: not to do that; don’t do that.
additional_notes: Uses French negation (ne…pas) with the verb faire (“to do/make”) and ça (“that”). In speech, the “ne” is often dropped: Pas faire ça. You’ll most often see it as an instruction with the infinitive (e.g., rules, reminders), while the direct command is: Ne fais pas ça ! (to one person/“tu”) or Ne faites pas ça ! (formal or plural/“vous”).
target_language_example: Attention : ne pas faire ça à la maison.
native_language_example: Warning: don’t do that at home.

meaning: “not to … it / him” (negative infinitive with the object pronoun le).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: **de ne pas le + infinitive** (“to not + verb + it/him”). In French, object pronouns like **le** come **before** the infinitive: *ne pas le regarder* = “not to look at him/it.” **Le** can mean “him” or “it” depending on context (for a person or a masculine noun/idea).
target_language_example: J'essaie de ne pas le dire.
native_language_example: I’m trying not to say it.

additional_notes: Uses the negation pattern "ne … pas" with the object pronoun "le" (= it). With an infinitive, pronouns come before the infinitive: "ne pas le faire" (not to do it). In everyday spoken French, "ne" is often dropped: "pas le faire".
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, donc je vais ne pas le faire ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m tired, so I’m not going to do it tonight.

additional_notes: This is the negative infinitive of venir (“to come”). It’s used after another verb or expression, often with de: e.g., dire à quelqu’un de ne pas venir (“to tell someone not to come”), décider de ne pas venir (“to decide not to come”), promettre de ne pas venir (“to promise not to come”). In a full sentence you usually see it after a conjugated verb: Il peut ne pas venir (“He may not come”).
target_language_example: J’ai décidé de ne pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I decided not to come tonight.

meaning: to not go there / to not go (to it).
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun **y** (“there”, “to it/to them”) to avoid repeating a place or destination already mentioned. It’s the negative infinitive of **y aller** (“to go there/to go to it”). In conjugated speech you’ll usually hear forms like **je n’y vais pas** (“I’m not going there”).
target_language_example: Je préfère ne pas y aller ce soir.
native_language_example: I’d rather not go there tonight.

additional_notes: This is the negative infinitive form of the verb “être” (to be): “ne … pas” surrounds the infinitive “être”. It commonly appears after another verb or expression (e.g., pouvoir, préférer, sembler, risquer): “ça pourrait ne pas être…” = “it might not be…”. In everyday spoken French, “ne” is often dropped (“pas être”), but in writing and careful speech “ne pas être” is standard.
target_language_example: Ça pourrait ne pas être suffisant.
native_language_example: It might not be enough.

additional_notes: Used with the negation "ne…pas" before an infinitive ("être"). Often follows verbs like "essayer de…" (try to…), "espérer…" (hope to…), or "veiller à…" (make sure to…). You can add details like "à nouveau demain" (again tomorrow).
target_language_example: Je vais partir plus tôt pour ne pas être en retard.
native_language_example: I'm going to leave earlier so I won’t be late.

ne pas être invité à la

target_language_multi_word_term: ne pas être invité à la
meaning: to not be invited to the (event/occasion introduced with « la »).
additional_notes: Expression built from the negation « ne… pas » + « être invité(e) » + « à la » (used before a feminine noun: « la fête », « la réunion », etc.). Agree « invité » with the subject: « invité » (masc. sg.), « invitée » (fem. sg.), « invités/invitées » (plural). In everyday speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Je suis pas invité(e) à la… ».
target_language_example: Je vais rester à la maison : ne pas être invité à la fête, c’est dommage.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay home: not being invited to the party is a shame.

additional_notes: This is the verb *penser* (“to think”) in the negative: **ne … pas** goes around the verb (je **ne** pense **pas**). Without a subject, **Ne pense pas !** is an imperative meaning “Don’t think (like that)!” With a subject, it’s a statement: **Je ne pense pas (ça)** = “I don’t think so/that.”
target_language_example: Je ne pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don’t think that’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used after a subject (often "je" or "il/elle") to express a negative opinion or doubt: "Je ne pense pas que…" / "Il ne pense pas que…". It is very commonly followed by the subjunctive ("Je ne pense pas qu’il vienne"). In careful French you keep "ne"; in everyday speech people often drop it: "Je pense pas que…".
target_language_example: Je ne pense pas que tu aies raison.
native_language_example: I don’t think you’re right.

ne pense pas que ce soit

target_language_multi_word_term: ne pense pas que ce soit
meaning: "(I) don’t think that it is / that this is."
additional_notes: Used after a negative of *penser que* (“to think that…”). In French, *ne… pas penser que* is typically followed by the subjunctive, so you get *soit* (subjunctive of *être*). Often appears as **Je ne pense pas que ce soit…** + adjective/noun: *Je ne pense pas que ce soit vrai / une bonne idée.* In casual speech, *ne* is often dropped: *Je pense pas que ce soit…*
target_language_example: Je ne pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Standard written French uses a two-part negation: **ne** goes before the conjugated verb and **personne** usually goes after it: *Je ne vois personne.* In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Je vois personne.* **Personne** can also be the subject meaning “no one”: *Personne ne vient.* Note: the contiguous sequence **« ne personne »** is generally not used as a standalone phrase; the correct pattern is **ne ... personne**.
target_language_example: On n’emploie pas « ne personne » tout seul : on dit « ne ... personne » (ex. : Je ne vois personne).
native_language_example: You don’t use “ne personne” by itself: you say “ne ... personne” (e.g., “I don’t see anyone”).

additional_notes: 3rd-person singular present of ne pas pouvoir. It is used with a singular subject (il, elle, on, ce, or a singular noun). In everyday French, you will often see ne peut pas; leaving out pas is more formal/literary and is especially common with negative words like aucun, nul, or rien, and in phrases like il ne peut y avoir...
target_language_example: Il ne peut pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: He can't come tonight.

additional_notes: Negative form of peut (from pouvoir), usually meaning that he/she/it/one cannot do something. It is commonly used with il, elle, on, or something like ça. In everyday spoken French, ne is often dropped: il/elle peut pas.
target_language_example: Marie ne peut pas rester ce soir.
native_language_example: Marie can't stay tonight.

meaning: “can’t be” / “cannot be” (impossible; cannot happen or be true).
additional_notes: Built from: ne…pas (negation) + peut (can) + être (to be). Often followed by a past participle to form the passive: ne peut pas être + participe passé (“cannot be + done”), e.g., exécuté, réparé. It can also express disbelief: “Ça ne peut pas être vrai” (“That can’t be true”).
target_language_example: Désolé, ce document ne peut pas être envoyé aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, this document can’t be sent today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pouvoir in the negative form ne…plus to say someone/something is no longer able to do something: « ne peut plus + infinitive » (e.g., « cela ne peut plus durer »). In spoken French, « ne » is often dropped: « ça peut plus durer ». Note: « ne peut plus » is 3rd-person singular (il/elle/on/ce/cela/ça). For “I can no longer,” it’s « je ne peux plus ».
target_language_example: Cela ne peut plus durer.
native_language_example: This can’t go on any longer.
