meaning: "can’t (do) anything" / "can’t (verb) anything" (3rd person singular: "he/she/it can’t … anything").
additional_notes: Common negative pattern: **ne + pouvoir + rien**. **Rien** means “nothing/anything” in negative clauses. With a second verb in the infinitive, **rien** usually goes **before the infinitive**: *Elle ne peut rien faire.* With other infinitives it’s the same: *Il ne peut rien dire / rien sentir.* In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Il peut rien faire.* Note: **ne peut** is 3rd person singular; for “I can’t” you’d use *je ne peux rien …*.
target_language_example: Elle ne peut rien faire.
native_language_example: She can’t do anything.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (here: être) in the negative: ne + pouvoir (can) + pas + infinitive. In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Ça peut pas être vrai." Can also appear in passive constructions: "ne peut être + past participle" (e.g., "ne peut être mise en doute" = "cannot be questioned").
target_language_example: Ce résultat ne peut être correct.
native_language_example: This result cannot be correct.

additional_notes: This is the negative form of **pouvoir** (“to be able to / can”) in the **ils/elles** form: **ils/elles peuvent** = “they can”, **ils/elles ne peuvent pas** = “they can’t.” In spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **Ils peuvent pas**. You can also use it in short answers: **Non, ils ne peuvent pas.**
target_language_example: Désolé, ils ne peuvent pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, they can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: This is the negative of the verb phrase **pouvoir être** (“to be able to be”). It’s used with **ils/elles** (or any plural subject) and is often followed by a past participle to form a passive meaning: **ne peuvent pas être + participe passé** = “cannot be + past participle” (e.g., *ne peuvent pas être vues* = “cannot be seen”). For singular, you’ll see **ne peut pas être** (“cannot be”).
target_language_example: Ces documents ne peuvent pas être partagés.
native_language_example: These documents cannot be shared.

meaning: “can’t / cannot” (with a subject: je/tu … ne peux).
additional_notes: Used with the verb pouvoir (“to be able to”). Most often it’s part of a full negation: je/tu ne peux pas… (“I/you can’t…”), but it can also take other negative words (ne peux jamais…, ne peux plus…, ne peux rien…). In some set phrases like “plus que tu ne peux imaginer” (“more than you can imagine”), the “ne” is often *expletive* (it doesn’t make the meaning negative).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Built on the verb **pouvoir** (“to be able to”): **(je/tu/il/elle/on) ne peux/peux/peut même pas + infinitive / noun / clause**. It expresses that something is impossible or too much to handle: “I can’t even do/say/believe it.” In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: **je peux même pas…**
target_language_example: Je ne peux même pas répondre maintenant.
native_language_example: I can’t even reply right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to do something or you’re not allowed to do it, depending on context. It commonly appears with a subject: *je ne peux pas* (I can’t), *tu ne peux pas* (you can’t), *il/elle ne peut pas* (he/she can’t), *vous ne pouvez pas* (you can’t). In everyday spoken French, *ne* is often dropped: *je peux pas*.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: This is the negative form of **pouvoir** in the **je** form: **je ne peux pas + infinitive**. In real sentences you usually include the subject (e.g., *Je ne peux pas faire ça*). It’s formed with **ne … pas** around the verb (*peux*). In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Je peux pas faire ça.*
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas faire ça aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I can’t do that today.

additional_notes: Negative form of pouvoir (“to be able to / can”) + faire ça (“do that”). Used to refuse or say something is not possible/allowed. Often said as: « Je peux pas faire ça » (spoken French drops “ne”). You can change the subject: « je/tu/il/elle/on ne peut pas faire ça ».
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas faire ça aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t do that today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pouvoir (je peux = I can) in the negative (ne ... pas) plus the direct object pronoun le (“it” for a masculine noun, or “him”). The pronoun le goes before the verb: je ne peux pas le faire = I can’t do it. In speech, ne is often dropped: je peux pas le faire.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas le faire maintenant.
native_language_example: I can’t do it right now.

meaning: "I can't" + "(to) myself/me" (used before a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern with "je": "Je ne peux pas me + infinitive". It’s the negative of "je peux me..." and is used before reflexive verbs (verbs that use "se"), e.g. "me lever" (get up), "me souvenir" (remember), "m’habiller" (get dressed). In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je peux pas me...".
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas me souvenir de son nom.
native_language_example: I can't remember his name.

additional_notes: Built with the negation "ne…pas" + the verb "pouvoir" ("peux" = "I can") + an infinitive ("parler"). It’s used to say you’re unable or not allowed to speak/talk. In conversation, "ne" is often dropped: "Je peux pas parler."
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas parler maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable or not allowed to remain somewhere, often because you have to leave soon. It’s the negative of pouvoir (can) + rester (to stay). You can add a time limit: « Je ne peux pas rester longtemps / jusqu’à… ». With other subjects: « tu ne peux pas rester », « on ne peut pas rester ».
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas rester, j’ai un rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t stay; I have an appointment.

additional_notes: Used with a direct object introduced by « à » (a person, message, question, email, etc.). The verb changes with the subject: « je ne peux pas répondre à… », « tu ne peux pas répondre à… », « il/elle ne peut pas répondre à… ». In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « je peux pas répondre à… ».
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas répondre à ton message tout de suite.
native_language_example: I can’t reply to your message right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you really dislike someone or something, or you can’t tolerate a situation (noise, heat, waiting, etc.). Most common as "Je ne peux pas supporter…" or with an object pronoun: "Je ne peux pas le/la/les supporter" (him/her/them). In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je peux pas supporter…". Note: French "supporter" often means "to tolerate/put up with," not "to support" (help).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas supporter ce bruit.
native_language_example: I can’t stand this noise.

additional_notes:
This is a common fragment that appears inside a longer sentence, usually with “je” before it and another verb after it: “Je ne peux pas te + [verb]” = “I can’t + [verb] + you.”
- “ne … pas” makes a negative.
- “peux” is from “pouvoir” (I can / I’m able to).
- “te” means “you” (object pronoun) and goes before the verb it belongs to.
In everyday spoken French, “ne” is often dropped: “Je peux pas te …”.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas te voir ce soir.
native_language_example: I can’t see you tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pouvoir in the negative: « je ne peux plus + infinitive ». It means you no longer have the ability or possibility to do something (because of a change, a limit, a rule, etc.). In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « je peux plus ». With a different verb, it changes by person: « tu ne peux plus », « il/elle ne peut plus », etc.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux plus venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come tonight anymore.

meaning: "can’t do anything / can’t do a thing" (literally: "can do nothing").
additional_notes: This is the negative form of "pouvoir" (to be able to): "ne … rien" means “not … anything / nothing.” It’s most often used as "je ne peux rien" (I can’t do anything) or "tu ne peux rien" (you can’t do anything). With "pour + someone" ("je ne peux rien pour vous/lui"), it commonly means “I can’t do anything to help you/him.” In everyday spoken French, the "ne" is often dropped: "je peux rien."
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux rien faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t do anything today.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to say that something stops happening or is no longer true. In a full sentence, it normally appears as ne ... plus around the verb: Je ne mange plus. With an infinitive, both words come before it: de ne plus revenir.
target_language_example: Elle a décidé de ne plus fumer.
native_language_example: She decided to stop smoking / to no longer smoke.

meaning: to never again; to not … anymore ever again.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (or a conjugated verb with ne… plus… jamais) to say you will stop doing something and will never do it again. Structure: ne + verb/infinitive + plus + jamais. Example with infinitive: "décider de ne plus jamais + infinitif"; with conjugated verb: "Je ne lui parle plus jamais."
target_language_example: Après ça, j’ai juré de ne plus jamais revenir ici.
native_language_example: After that, I swore I would never come back here again.

meaning: not / not at all (literary or old-fashioned negation; equivalent to « ne … pas »).
additional_notes: « Point » can replace « pas » in a negative construction: « ne + verb + point ». It is mostly literary/archaic or very formal. In modern everyday French you normally use « ne … pas » (and often drop « ne » in speech). Note: « ne point » as an exact sequence is relatively uncommon because a verb usually comes between them (e.g., « ne … point »), but it can occur when the verb is omitted/understood in context or in stylized writing.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, mais ne point répondre serait impoli.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but not replying would be rude.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *porter* (“to wear”). In the negative, French typically uses **pas de** (or **pas d’** before a vowel) instead of *pas un/une/des*: *Il ne porte pas de chapeau* = “He isn’t wearing a hat.” The verb changes with the subject/tense (e.g., *je ne porte pas de…*, *il/elle ne porte pas de…*).
target_language_example: Je ne porte pas de manteau aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm not wearing a coat today.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of pouvoir (je pourrais, tu pourrais, etc.) with the negative ne...jamais to express impossibility, often hypothetical or polite: « Je ne pourrais jamais faire ça. » In casual spoken French, the « ne » is often dropped: « Je pourrais jamais… »
target_language_example: Je ne pourrais jamais oublier ce jour-là.
native_language_example: I could never forget that day.

additional_notes: This is the negation of the imperfect tense of *pouvoir* (*il/elle ne pouvait pas*). It describes an ongoing or repeated inability in the past, or something that was not possible at that time. Often used with negatives like *plus* (no longer), *rien* (nothing), or in the structure *il ne pouvait y avoir…* (“there couldn’t be…”).
target_language_example: Sans argent, il ne pouvait rien faire.
native_language_example: Without money, he couldn’t do anything.

additional_notes: This is the negative imperfect of **pouvoir**: **ne … pas** + **pouvait** (“could”). It describes a past inability or impossibility (often a situation/background), and is usually followed by an infinitive: **ne pouvait pas + verbe** (e.g., *ne pouvait pas venir* = couldn’t come). With **ça/ce**, it can also mean “that couldn’t be / it wasn’t possible” (*Ça ne pouvait pas être vrai.*).
target_language_example: Marie ne pouvait pas imaginer passer un an en Corée.
native_language_example: Marie couldn’t imagine spending a year in Korea.

additional_notes: Usually used as the discontinuous restriction pattern « ne ... que », meaning 'only' rather than a true negation. In normal sentences, other words usually come between ne and que, so the exact contiguous string « ne que » is most often seen when the expression is being cited or discussed. Ne typically goes before the conjugated verb, and que goes before the word or phrase being limited: « Je n'ai que cinq euros » = 'I only have five euros.' In informal spoken French, the ne is often dropped.
target_language_example: La tournure « ne que » signifie « seulement » en français.
native_language_example: The expression "ne que" means "only" in French.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to mean that no thing is involved: ne rien dire = to say nothing / not say anything, ne rien faire = to do nothing. In French negation, ne comes before the verb or infinitive and rien comes after it.
target_language_example: Je préfère ne rien acheter aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'd rather not buy anything today.

meaning: to say nothing / not to say anything.
additional_notes: Uses the French negative pattern with *ne ... rien* (“nothing”): *Je ne dis rien* = “I’m not saying anything.” With *pour* it can mean “to talk without saying anything meaningful”: *parler pour ne rien dire*. Often used in legal contexts: *Vous avez le droit de ne rien dire* (“You have the right to remain silent”).
target_language_example: Je préfère ne rien dire pour éviter les problèmes.
native_language_example: I’d rather say nothing to avoid problems.

meaning: "(I/you/he, etc.) don’t know" / "don’t know how to".
additional_notes: Used with a subject pronoun: « je/tu/il/elle/on ne sais/sait pas… ». In questions like « Tu ne sais pas + infinitive ? », it often means “You don’t know how to…?” and can sound critical depending on tone/context. In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Je sais pas. »
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas où il est.
native_language_example: I don’t know where he is.

additional_notes: Used with a subject pronoun, most often as **je ne sais (pas)** (“I don’t know”) or **tu ne sais (pas)** (“you don’t know”). In modern spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **je sais pas**. Common extensions: **je ne sais plus** (“I don’t know anymore”), **je ne sais pas** + question word (**ce que**, **qui**, **quand**, etc.).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne sais pas où il est.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know where he is.

additional_notes: Usually used with a subject, most often: « Je ne sais même pas… » (“I don’t even know…”). Built from the negation « ne … pas » around « savoir » (“to know”) plus « même » (“even”) for emphasis. In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Je sais même pas. »
target_language_example: Je ne sais même pas où il habite.
native_language_example: I don’t even know where he lives.

additional_notes: From the verb "savoir" (to know). Used with different subjects: "je ne sais pas" (I don’t know), "tu ne sais pas" (you don’t know), "il/elle ne sait pas" (he/she doesn’t know). Often followed by a question word: "je ne sais pas où/qui/quand/pourquoi...". In everyday speech, the "ne" is often dropped: "je sais pas".
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas où il est.
native_language_example: I don’t know where he is.

additional_notes: Used with a subject (often "Je") and usually followed by "que" or "qui": "Je ne sais pas ce que…" = “I don’t know what…”, "Je ne sais pas ce qui…" = “I don’t know what/which (thing)…” In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je sais pas ce que…"
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: I don’t know what you want.

meaning: "don’t know what…" (as in "I don’t know what...").
additional_notes: Used inside the full structure « Je ne sais pas ce que… » to introduce an unknown thing: « Je ne sais pas ce que c’est » (I don’t know what it is), « Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux » (I don’t know what you want). In everyday speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Je sais pas ce que… ».
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I don’t know what you mean.

ne sais pas ce que tu

target_language_multi_word_term: ne sais pas ce que tu
meaning: "(I) don’t know what you…" (start of a sentence).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment you’ll usually see as part of a longer phrase like: « Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux / ce que tu dis / ce que tu fais » (“I don’t know what you want / what you’re saying / what you’re doing”). In correct French it normally includes the subject « je » before it.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: I don’t know what you want.

meaning: "(I) don’t know what/which…" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Most often used as part of a full sentence like: « Je ne sais pas ce qui se passe. » Here « ce qui » means “what/which” when it is the subject of the next verb (what is happening = what + happens). If you’re asking about the object (what someone did/said), you usually use « je ne sais pas ce que… » instead.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce qui s’est passé.
native_language_example: I don’t know what happened.

meaning: "(I) don’t know how" (used to start a clause).
additional_notes: This is part of the negative form of *savoir* (“to know”): *je ne sais pas…* (“I don’t know…”). *Comment* means “how,” so it’s typically followed by a verb or a full clause: *Je ne sais pas comment le faire* (“I don’t know how to do it”). In casual spoken French, *ne* is often dropped: *Je sais pas comment…*
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas comment dire ça en français.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to say that in French.

meaning: "don’t know what"; also "a certain something" (hard to describe).
additional_notes: Most often used as part of **je ne sais pas quoi** (“I don’t know what” / “a certain something”). It can introduce an indirect question: *Je ne sais pas quoi dire* (“I don’t know what to say”). It can also mean an indefinable quality: *Elle a un je ne sais pas quoi de charmant* (“She has a certain something charming about her”).
target_language_example: Il y a un je ne sais pas quoi dans cette chanson qui me rend nostalgique.
native_language_example: There’s a certain something in this song that makes me feel nostalgic.

meaning: "I don't know if I…" ("I’m not sure whether I…").
additional_notes: This is a sentence starter used before adding a verb: « Je ne sais pas si je + verb… » (e.g., « …viens », « …peux », « …dois »). It uses the negation « ne … pas » with « savoir » (to know) and « si » meaning “whether/if.” In everyday speech, people often drop « ne »: « Je sais pas si je… ».
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas si je peux venir demain.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with a subject like « je » or « tu »: « je ne sais rien » = “I don’t know anything.” This is the common French negation pattern « ne … rien » (“not … anything”). In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Je sais rien. » Often followed by « de + [person/thing] » or « à propos de + [topic] »: « je ne sais rien de lui » (“I don’t know anything about him”).
target_language_example: Je ne sais rien de cette histoire.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about this story.

meaning: "(I) know nothing about …" / "(I) don’t know anything about …"
additional_notes: Used with the verb *savoir* in the negative: **(Je) ne sais rien de + noun/topic**. In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je sais rien de…*. You can change the verb to match the subject (e.g., *Il ne sait rien de…*, *Nous ne savons rien de…*).
target_language_example: Je ne sais rien de cette histoire.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about this story.

additional_notes: Negative form of savoir ('to know'). This exact form is used with il/elle/on. When followed by an infinitive, it usually means someone doesn't know how to do something or lacks the skill to do it.
target_language_example: Il ne sait pas nager.
native_language_example: He doesn't know how to swim.

additional_notes: Negative form of sait (“knows”), from savoir. It normally comes after a subject: il/elle/on ne sait = “he/she/one doesn't know.” It is often followed by words like rien (“anything/nothing”), pas, or a clause explaining what is not known.
target_language_example: Il ne sait pas où aller.
native_language_example: He doesn't know where to go.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer sentence with a subject: "(Il/Elle/On) ne sait ce qui…" = “(He/She/People) don’t know what…”. It’s commonly used with situations or events: "ne sait ce qui se passe" (doesn’t know what’s happening). In formal writing you may see "ne sait" without "pas"; in everyday speech it’s more often "ne sait pas ce qui".
target_language_example: Elle ne sait ce qui s’est passé hier soir.
native_language_example: She doesn’t know what happened last night.

additional_notes: Usually used in the full expression « On ne sait jamais » to mean that something is uncertain and it’s wise to be prepared (often like “just in case”). It can also appear after an action: « Prends un parapluie, on ne sait jamais. »
target_language_example: Prends ton chargeur, on ne sait jamais.
native_language_example: Take your charger—you never know (just in case).

additional_notes: Used with the verb savoir (to know a fact). It’s the 3rd person singular present tense: il/elle/on ne sait pas… Often followed by a question word (qui, où, ce que, etc.): « Il ne sait pas qui tu es. » In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Il sait pas. »
target_language_example: Marie ne sait pas précisément où elle est née.
native_language_example: Marie doesn't know precisely where she was born.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *savoir* in the negative: **ne … rien** = “nothing / anything” (in a negative sentence). **Ne sait rien** is the 3rd person singular form (“he/she doesn’t know anything”). It is often followed by **de / du / de la / des** or **sur** (“about”) to specify what someone knows nothing about. With **on**, you get **On ne sait rien** (“We don’t know anything / Nothing is known”). In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Il sait rien*.
target_language_example: Il ne sait rien sur elle.
native_language_example: He doesn’t know anything about her.

meaning: "didn't know" / "didn't used to know" (imperfect of *savoir* in the negative).
additional_notes: Used with a subject like *je* or *tu*: *je ne savais pas* = “I didn’t know”, *tu ne savais pas* = “you didn’t know.” The imperfect (*savais*) often describes a past state or ongoing situation (what someone knew/didn’t know at the time), rather than a one-time discovery. In casual speech, *ne* is often dropped: *je savais pas*.
target_language_example: Je ne savais pas que c'était si loin.
native_language_example: I didn't know it was that far.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself. This is the negative pattern ne + se used before a pronominal verb, usually with another negative word after the verb such as pas, plus, or jamais: ne se fait pas, ne se produit plus. In everyday spoken French, ne is often dropped: ça se fait pas.
target_language_example: Ça ne se voit pas d'ici.
native_language_example: You can't see it from here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will not be the case in the future. It’s the negative form of *sera* (he/she/it will be): *ne … pas* wraps around the verb (*ne sera pas*). Often seen with *ce/ça*: *Ce/Ça ne sera pas…* = “It won’t be…”. In casual speech, *ne* is often dropped: *Ça sera pas long.*
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ça ne sera pas difficile.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it won’t be difficult.

additional_notes: This is the negative conditional of *être* (serait = would be). It’s used for hypothetical situations (“it wouldn’t be easy”), for polite/soft suggestions (“I wonder if it wouldn’t be better like that”), and in questions where the speaker expects it might be true (“Wouldn’t he be in love with you?”). It also appears in set phrases like *ne serait pas de refus* (“wouldn’t be unwelcome / I wouldn’t say no”).
target_language_example: Ce ne serait pas mieux demain ?
native_language_example: Wouldn’t it be better tomorrow?

additional_notes: Uses the French negative pattern **ne ... jamais** (“never”) around the verb. **seras** is the future tense of **être** for **tu** (“you” singular/informal). Often part of a longer sentence (e.g., followed by an adjective or noun). In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *tu seras jamais...*
target_language_example: Tu ne seras jamais seul ici.
native_language_example: You will never be alone here.

additional_notes: Used with the verb servir (à) to say something has no use or point. Often appears as « Ça ne sert à rien » (“There’s no point”) or with an infinitive: « [Faire/Parler/Essayer] ne sert à rien » (“[Doing/Speaking/Trying] is pointless”).
target_language_example: Inutile d’insister : ça ne sert à rien.
native_language_example: No use insisting: there’s no point.

meaning: “there’s no point in / it’s no use (doing something)”.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: « (Ça/Il) ne sert à rien de + infinitive ». Common to say something is useless or won’t help. You can also use it with a noun: « Ça ne sert à rien. » = “It’s useless / It’s no use.”
target_language_example: Ça ne sert à rien de t’inquiéter.
native_language_example: There’s no point in worrying.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (tu) not to be in a certain state, followed by an adjective or noun phrase: « Ne sois pas + adjectif ». It’s the negative imperative of être for tu: sois / ne sois pas. (For vous: « Ne soyez pas… ».) Adjectives agree with the person you’re speaking to: « gênée » (to a woman), « gêné » (to a man).
target_language_example: Ne sois pas inquiet, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Don’t be worried, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used after triggers like « il se peut que / il se pourrait que / il semble que / pourvu que / que… » where French typically requires the subjunctive. It almost always appears with « que » and in the pattern « ce/ça ne soit pas… » (“that it isn’t…”).
target_language_example: J'espère que ce ne soit pas trop tard.
native_language_example: I hope it isn’t too late.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb être (“to be”) with the subject nous (“we”), or with a subject like “toi et moi” (= “you and I”), which often takes the nous verb form. In full negation, ne goes before the verb and pas goes after: nous ne sommes pas…
target_language_example: Nous ne sommes pas prêts aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We are not ready today.

additional_notes: Negative form of sont ("are"), used with plural subjects such as ils/elles or plural nouns. In French, ne ... pas usually goes around the verb. In everyday spoken French, the ne is often dropped: sont pas.
target_language_example: Mes amis ne sont pas ici.
native_language_example: My friends are not here.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être ("to be") in the negative: ne + sont + pas. It’s the 3rd‑person plural form ("they are"): ils/elles ne sont pas… . "Des" is the plural indefinite article ("some/any") before a plural noun: ne sont pas des + noun (e.g., des poissons). In casual speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Ils sont pas des…".
target_language_example: Ces livres ne sont pas des romans.
native_language_example: These books are not novels.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **être** in the **ils/elles** form (**sont**) to say that some people/things are not the ones being talked about: **ils/elles ne sont pas les …** + noun. In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **Ils sont pas les…**
target_language_example: Ils ne sont pas les responsables.
native_language_example: They are not the ones responsible.

additional_notes: This is the restrictive pattern **ne… que** (= “only/just”) with **être** in the 3rd person plural: **ils/elles ne sont que des + noun** (“they are only just + plural noun”). It downplays what something is (“nothing more than…”). In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **Ils sont que des…** (still means “only/just”).
target_language_example: Ces problèmes ne sont que des détails.
native_language_example: These problems are only details.

additional_notes: Used with "vous" as a negative imperative (command/request) of the verb "être" (to be): "Ne soyez pas + adjective/noun". It can address one person formally or multiple people. For an informal singular command, you’d usually say "ne sois pas".
target_language_example: Ne soyez pas trop dur avec vous-même.
native_language_example: Don’t be too hard on yourself.

additional_notes: From the verb « suffire » (to be enough). Used in negative sentences with « ne … pas »: « Ça ne suffit pas » = “That’s not enough.” Often followed by « à + infinitive » to mean “isn’t enough to (do something)”: « ne suffit pas à vous faire taire » = “isn’t enough to make you be quiet.” You can also use « de + infinitive » in some patterns: « Ça ne suffit pas de… » = “It’s not enough to…”. Note: « suffit » is 3rd-person singular (il/elle/on/ça) while « suffisent » is plural (ils/elles).
target_language_example: Non, ça ne suffit pas.
native_language_example: No, that’s not enough.

additional_notes: Usually appears with je and another negative word: je ne suis pas = "I am not", je ne suis plus = "I am no longer / am not anymore". By itself, ne suis is normally just part of a larger negative expression with être.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas prêt.
native_language_example: I'm not ready.

additional_notes:
This is the negation pattern **ne … pas** with **suis**.
- With **je**: **je ne suis pas …** = “I am not …” (verb **être**, to be). Example: *Je ne suis pas contre.*
- Without a subject, it can be a **negative command**: **Ne suis pas … !** = “Don’t follow … !” (verb **suivre**, to follow), as in *Ne suis pas ses conseils !*.
In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Je suis pas contre.* / *Suis pas ses conseils !* (more informal).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas d’accord avec toi.
native_language_example: I don’t agree with you.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re uncertain. It’s the 1st-person singular of "être": "je ne suis pas sûr" (often shortened in speech to "je suis pas sûr"). If the speaker is female, add -e: "je ne suis pas sûre". Common patterns: "Je ne suis pas sûr de + infinitive" (I’m not sure (about) doing...) and "Je ne suis pas sûr que + subjunctive" (I’m not sure that...).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas sûr de comprendre.
native_language_example: I’m not sure I understand.

meaning: "am not a" (used to say what you are not).
additional_notes: This is a negated form of the verb être with je: « Je ne suis pas un/une + noun ». Use « un » before a masculine noun and « une » before a feminine noun. In everyday spoken French, « ne » is often dropped: « Je suis pas un... ». You can’t normally use « ne suis pas un » by itself; it needs a subject (usually « je ») and a noun after it.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas un expert, mais je peux t’aider.
native_language_example: I’m not an expert, but I can help you.

additional_notes: This is a common negative pattern in the passé composé: ne + object pronoun (t’ = te) + auxiliary (ai) + jamais. It must be followed by a past participle (e.g., vu, entendu, oublié). In casual spoken French, "ne" is often dropped: "Je t’ai jamais vu(e)."
target_language_example: Je ne t'ai jamais vu ici.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen you here.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself. In negative sentences, ne is the first part of negation (usually with pas), and te means "you" when speaking to one person (as an object pronoun or reflexive pronoun). Together they come before the verb: Ne te lève pas = "Don't get up"; Je ne te vois pas = "I don't see you."
target_language_example: Je ne te comprends pas.
native_language_example: I don't understand you.

additional_notes: From "déranger" (= to bother/disturb). Used to tell someone not to go to any trouble (e.g., not to get up, not to do something for you). In questions it often appears as "Ça ne te dérange pas ?" (= “Do you mind?”) and in polite requests as "Si ça ne te dérange pas" (= “If you don’t mind”).
target_language_example: Ne te dérange pas, je vais le faire moi-même.
native_language_example: Don’t bother, I’ll do it myself.

meaning: "I won’t let you" / "I won’t leave you" (depending on context).
additional_notes: This is the negative future of "laisser" (je laisserai) with the object pronoun "te" (you). It’s an incomplete phrase on its own—usually followed by a verb or complement: "Je ne te laisserai pas partir" (I won’t let you leave) or "Je ne te laisserai pas seule" (I won’t leave you alone). In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je te laisserai pas…"
target_language_example: Je ne te laisserai pas tomber.
native_language_example: I won’t let you down.

additional_notes: Negative imperative of *se mêler de* (“to meddle in / interfere with”). Used to tell someone (tu) to stay out of something; it can sound quite sharp or scolding. Often followed by a noun (*Ne te mêle pas de ça*) or by *ce qui…* (*Ne te mêle pas de ce qui ne te regarde pas*).
target_language_example: Ne te mêle pas de mes affaires.
native_language_example: Don’t meddle in my business.

additional_notes: This is the negative of the near-future form with *aller*: **(subject) + ne + aller + pas + infinitive**. It expresses that something is not going to happen (often equivalent to “won’t”). Example: *Il ne va pas venir* = “He isn’t going to come / He won’t come.” (Note: *Ça ne va pas* without an infinitive can also mean “It’s not going well,” but that’s a different use.)
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ça ne va pas durer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s not going to last.

meaning: "isn't going well / isn't OK"; or (imperative) "don't go".
additional_notes: From the verb aller (to go). With a subject like "ça" or a person ("Tom"), it often means something is wrong: "Ça ne va pas" = "It’s not going well / It’s not OK"; "Tom ne va pas bien" = "Tom isn’t doing well." As a reaction, "Mais ça ne va pas ?" can mean "What’s wrong with you? / Are you crazy?" With an imperative, it’s simply a negative command: "Ne va pas plus loin" = "Don’t go any further," "Ne va pas travailler" = "Don’t go to work."
target_language_example: Ça ne va pas aujourd’hui, je suis malade.
native_language_example: I’m not doing well today; I’m sick.

meaning: "I’m not going to" / "I’m not about to".
additional_notes: Used with the verb aller to form the near future in the negative, most often with je: « je ne vais pas + infinitive » (I’m not going to + verb). In everyday speech, ne is often dropped: « je vais pas ».
target_language_example: Je ne vais pas attendre toute la journée.
native_language_example: I’m not going to wait all day.

meaning: “are not going” / “are not going to …” (negative of “tu vas …”).
additional_notes: Used with **tu** (2nd person singular) in the negative: **tu ne vas pas + infinitive** = “you’re not going to …” (near future). It can also appear in expressions like **tu ne vas pas bien** (“you’re not doing well”). In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **tu vas pas…**.
target_language_example: Tu ne vas pas comprendre tout de suite.
native_language_example: You’re not going to understand right away.

additional_notes: Usually appears with another negative word after the verb, such as pas, plus, or rien: ne veut pas = doesn't want, ne veut plus = doesn't want anymore. Veut is the 3rd-person singular form of vouloir, so it means he/she/it doesn't want, depending on the subject. In expressions like ça ne veut rien dire, it means 'that doesn't mean anything.'
target_language_example: Il ne veut pas venir avec nous.
native_language_example: He doesn't want to come with us.

additional_notes: Negative form of veut (from vouloir, “to want”) in the present tense, most often with il/elle/on: “he/she/it/one doesn't want.” It can be followed by an infinitive (ne veut pas parler), by de + noun (ne veut pas de nous), or by que + clause (ne veut pas que tu...). In everyday spoken French, ne is often dropped: veut pas.
target_language_example: Il ne veut pas venir avec nous.
native_language_example: He doesn't want to come with us.

additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the French negative pattern **ne … pas** (“don’t want”) or with another negative word like **ne … rien** (“don’t want anything”). Example: **Tu ne veux pas venir ?** In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **Tu veux pas… ?** / **Tu veux rien ?**
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go out tonight.

additional_notes: This is the negation of the verb *vouloir* (to want) in the present tense: *je ne veux pas* (I don’t want), *tu ne veux pas* (you don’t want). It’s often followed by *de/d’ + noun* (*je ne veux pas d’une dispute* = I don’t want an argument). In everyday spoken French, *ne* is frequently dropped: *je veux pas*, *tu veux pas*.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "vouloir" (to want) in the negative: "je ne veux pas de + noun". After a negation in French, "un/une/des" often becomes "de" (or "d’" before a vowel): "Je veux du café" → "Je ne veux pas de café". In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je veux pas de…".
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas de café, merci.
native_language_example: I don’t want any coffee, thanks.

additional_notes: Used inside the pattern « Je ne veux pas que tu + subjunctive verb » to express that you don’t want someone else to do something. The verb after « que tu » is usually in the subjunctive (e.g., « que tu viennes », « que tu fasses », « que tu sois »).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas que tu partes maintenant.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to leave now.

meaning: "I don't want to be" (followed by a noun/adjective/verb).
additional_notes: This is a common verb pattern: **ne + vouloir (je veux) + pas + être**. It uses the French negation **ne … pas** around the conjugated verb (**veux**). In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Je veux pas être…*. You can change the subject to match the person: *je ne veux pas être*, *tu ne veux pas être*, *il/elle ne veut pas être*, etc. After **être**, you can add an adjective (*…fatigué*), a noun (*…un problème*), or sometimes an infinitive with **en train de** (*…en train de déranger*).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas être en retard.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be late.

additional_notes: Built from negation + vouloir: "ne ... plus" means "no longer / not anymore." It’s followed by either an infinitive ("ne veux plus jouer" = don’t want to play anymore) or a noun/pronoun with "de" ("ne veux plus de moi" = don’t want me anymore). In casual speech, "ne" is often dropped: "tu veux plus".
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus en parler.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about it anymore.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment built around the negative of vouloir (to want): ne … plus jamais = “no longer / never again.” It’s followed by te (“to you”) and then an infinitive verb, e.g. te voir (see you), te parler (talk to you), te revoir (see you again). Often used to express a strong decision or rejection.
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus jamais te voir.
native_language_example: I never want to see you again.

meaning: (You) don’t come / don’t come (here) / don’t come (over).
additional_notes: This is the negative of the verb "venir" (to come) in the "tu" form: "tu viens" → "tu ne viens pas" (you’re not coming). It can also be used as a negative command (imperative): "Ne viens pas !" = "Don’t come!" You can add a place after it: "Ne viens pas ici" (Don’t come here), "Ne viens pas à Paris" (Don’t come to Paris).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, alors je ne viens pas ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m tired, so I’m not coming tonight.

meaning: “(I) don’t see.” (can mean “I can’t see” or “I don’t understand / I don’t get it.”)
additional_notes: Used with the verb voir (“to see”) in the negative. Often said alone as « Je ne vois pas » to mean “I don’t see what you mean / I don’t get it.” It can also be literal: “I can’t see (it).” In full sentences you’ll often hear « je ne vois pas de quoi tu parles » (“I don’t see what you’re talking about”). In casual speech, the “ne” is often dropped: « je vois pas ».
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne vois pas ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t see what you mean.

additional_notes: This is the negation of **vouloir** (“to want”) in the imperfect: **je/tu il/elle voulais/voulait**. French negation is usually **ne ... pas**, placed around the verb: **tu ne voulais pas**. Common patterns: **ne voulais pas + infinitive** (Tu ne voulais pas y aller.), **ne voulais pas + de + noun** (Tu ne voulais pas de livres.), and **ne voulais pas que + subjunctive** (Tu ne voulais pas que je vienne.). In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: **Tu voulais pas…**
target_language_example: Je ne voulais pas te déranger.
native_language_example: I didn’t want to bother you.

additional_notes: It’s the negative form of the imperfect tense of "vouloir" (to want): "il/elle voulait" = "he/she wanted" or sometimes "he/she would". "Ne ... pas" makes it negative: "il ne voulait pas" can mean either (1) he didn’t want to (lack of desire) or (2) he wouldn’t (refusal). Often followed by an infinitive ("ne voulait pas reconnaître"), by "de" + noun ("ne voulait pas de nous" = didn’t want us), or by "que" + subjunctive ("ne voulait pas que..." = didn’t want [someone] to...). It can also be used for things that won’t work: "Le moteur ne voulait pas démarrer" = the engine wouldn’t start.
target_language_example: Je lui ai proposé de venir, mais il ne voulait pas.
native_language_example: I suggested he come, but he didn’t want to.

meaning: "have never" (to/with you) — used with "je" as in "je ne vous ai jamais…"
additional_notes: This is a common negative pattern in the passé composé: "je ne vous ai jamais" + past participle. "ne … jamais" means “never,” and "vous" is the object pronoun (“you,” formal or plural). In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je vous ai jamais…" (still means “I never…”).
target_language_example: Je ne vous ai jamais menti.
native_language_example: I have never lied to you.

meaning: "haven’t (done) … to you" / "didn’t (do) … to you" (formal or plural “you”), in the past tense.
additional_notes: This is a common fragment in the negative passé composé with avoir. It comes after the subject (often "je") and before the past participle: "Je ne vous ai pas + participe passé" (e.g., vu, entendu, appelé). "Vous" is the object pronoun meaning "you" (polite singular or plural). In full speech/writing, French negation is "ne … pas"; in casual speech, "ne" is often dropped ("Je vous ai pas vu").
target_language_example: Je ne vous ai pas vu hier.
native_language_example: I didn’t see you yesterday.

meaning: “if you don’t mind” / “(I hope) I’m not bothering you.”
additional_notes: Uses the formal/polite object pronoun vous. Often appears as a question (“Je ne vous dérange pas ?” = “Am I bothering you?”) or in the set phrase “Si ça/cela ne vous dérange pas, …” to politely ask permission (“If you don’t mind, …”). Literally means “doesn’t bother you.” Note: French déranger usually means “to bother/disturb,” not English “derange” (mental disturbance).
target_language_example: Si ça ne vous dérange pas, je vais ouvrir la fenêtre.
native_language_example: If you don’t mind, I’m going to open the window.

additional_notes: A reassuring, polite/formal way to tell someone not to worry. Uses "vous" (for one person formally or for several people). Often followed by "pour ça" (= about that). Informal equivalent: "Ne t’en fais pas."
target_language_example: Ne vous en faites pas, tout est sous contrôle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is under control.

additional_notes: Negative imperative of s’inquiéter (“to worry”) used to reassure someone. Uses vous, so it’s for speaking politely to one person, or to more than one person. Often followed by a reason: « Ne vous inquiétez pas, tout va bien. » or « Ne vous inquiétez pas pour moi/pour ça. »
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, je vais m’en occuper.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Used to state a time. With "à" it means "at nine" (à neuf heures). With "vers" it means "around nine" (vers neuf heures). In schedules, "de neuf heures à cinq heures" means "from nine to five." Often said alone as an answer to "À quelle heure ?"
target_language_example: On se voit à neuf heures.
native_language_example: See you at nine o’clock.

additional_notes: Used for a hole or dip in the road surface caused by wear/weather. Common with verbs like « éviter » (to avoid) or « tomber dans » (to hit/fall into). Literal words mean “hen’s nest,” but the real meaning is “pothole.”
target_language_example: Attention, il y a un nid-de-poule juste après le virage.
native_language_example: Careful, there’s a pothole right after the turn.

additional_notes: Used to talk about altitude/elevation measured relative to the ocean’s surface. Common in geography and weather contexts: au niveau de la mer (at sea level), au-dessus du niveau de la mer (above sea level), sous le niveau de la mer (below sea level).
target_language_example: Cette ville est à 300 mètres au-dessus du niveau de la mer.
native_language_example: This city is 300 meters above sea level.

additional_notes: Used to describe photos/films/prints that are not in color ("en noir et blanc" = "in black-and-white"). It can also be used figuratively to mean something is seen in an overly simple, either/or way ("voir les choses en noir et blanc").
target_language_example: Je préfère les photos en noir et blanc.
native_language_example: I prefer black-and-white photos.

additional_notes: Means the fruit of the coconut palm; used both for the whole coconut and for coconut as an ingredient (often introduced with à: gâteau à la noix de coco = coconut cake). In everyday French, you may also see coco alone, but noix de coco is the standard full term.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un jus de noix de coco, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like coconut juice, please.

additional_notes: Used on forms or when identifying someone to ask for or provide a person’s entire name (first name(s) + last name(s), and sometimes middle names). Often appears as a form label: « Nom complet ».
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me donner votre nom complet, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you give me your full name, please?

meaning: "name of"; used to say what someone/something is called.
additional_notes: Most often appears in set phrases like **du nom de** (“named/called …”), **sous le nom de** (“under the name … / known as …”), and **le nom de + noun** (“the name of …”). In exclamations like **Nom de Dieu !**, it’s a swear word equivalent to “God damn it!” (very rude/informal).
target_language_example: Ce jeu est connu sous le nom de « baduk » en Corée.
native_language_example: This game is known as “baduk” in Korea.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to show anger, frustration, or shock—similar to “damn it!” or “for God’s sake!” It’s considered blasphemous and quite rude/strong, so avoid it in polite situations. You can also hear it inserted into a sentence for emphasis (e.g., ending a question). Related but different: « au nom de Dieu ! » literally “in the name of God,” often meaning “for God’s sake!”
target_language_example: Nom de Dieu, arrête ça tout de suite !
native_language_example: For God’s sake, stop that right now!

additional_notes: Used to ask for or give someone’s surname, especially on forms or in identification contexts. Often paired with “prénom” (first name). In questions it may be shortened to just “Nom de famille ?” meaning “Last name?”
target_language_example: Sur le formulaire, écrivez votre nom de famille en majuscules.
native_language_example: On the form, write your last name in capital letters.

meaning: maiden name (a woman’s family name before marriage).
additional_notes: Used on forms or in questions to identify someone by their birth family name. Often appears in questions like « Quel est votre nom de jeune fille ? » or « Nom de jeune fille de votre mère ? ». Not used for men; you’d say « nom de naissance » (birth name) if you want a gender-neutral term.
target_language_example: Quel est votre nom de jeune fille ?
native_language_example: What is your maiden name?

meaning: 'name is' (used to say what someone/something is called, or under what name it’s registered).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in "mon nom est …" ("my name is …"). In everyday speech, French more often uses "Je m'appelle …". You can also see it in questions like "Sous quel nom est … ?" meaning "Under what name is it?" (e.g., whose name it’s registered under).
target_language_example: Bonjour, mon nom est Alex.
native_language_example: Hello, my name is Alex.

nom est connu de tous dans

target_language_multi_word_term: nom est connu de tous dans
meaning: “(Someone’s) name is known to everyone in …”
additional_notes: A common pattern is: « Son/Mon/Le nom de X est connu de tous dans + place/group ». It means the person is famous or well-known within that place or community. « de tous » = “by everyone” (i.e., “to everyone”). You can also say « … est connu de tous » without adding a place if it’s understood.
target_language_example: Son nom est connu de tous dans le quartier.
native_language_example: His/Her name is known to everyone in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a quantity. With a specific count, it’s often followed by a number (e.g., « un nombre de 20 personnes » = a number of 20 people). Used without a number (often at the start of a sentence), « nombre de + plural noun » means “many / a large number of” and is fairly formal. Related: « bon nombre de » = quite a few.
target_language_example: Nombre de personnes sont arrivées en retard.
native_language_example: Many people arrived late.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective or noun. As an adjective it describes a place/object where smoking is not allowed (une zone/le coin non-fumeur). As a noun it describes a person who doesn’t smoke (un/une non-fumeur/non-fumeuse). Often contrasted with fumeur (“smoker”).
target_language_example: Désolé, c'est un restaurant non-fumeur.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s a non-smoking restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with negation to add something that is also not true: «Je ne… pas non plus» = “not… either.” It can answer a negative statement: «Moi non plus.» = “Me neither.” Usually placed near the end of the clause after the negated verb or complement.
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas faim non plus.
native_language_example: I’m not hungry either.

meaning: “No, it’s …” (used to contradict, correct, or push back on what was just said).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to disagree with someone or correct their assumption, followed by what it actually is. Common continuations include: a noun/pronoun (Non, c'est pour toi.), an adjective (Non, c'est réel.), or a phrase/clause (Non, c'est la première fois.; Non, c'est fini.). In casual speech it’s often clipped and emphatic.
target_language_example: Non, c'est fini.
native_language_example: No, it’s over.

meaning: "No, I'm the one who…" (emphasizing that *I* am the person responsible/concerned).
additional_notes: Used to correct someone or to take responsibility, often in apologies or when disagreeing politely. The structure "c'est moi qui + verb" puts strong emphasis on "moi" (me): "C'est moi qui ai tort" = "I'm the one who's wrong." In speech you’ll also hear "Non, c’est moi qui…" as a quick, modest response.
target_language_example: Non, c'est moi qui ai fait l'erreur.
native_language_example: No, I'm the one who made the mistake.

additional_notes: A common spoken way to disagree or correct someone. "C'est pas" is the informal shortened form of "ce n'est pas" (dropping "ne"). It’s usually followed by an adjective or noun phrase: "Non, c'est pas fini" (it’s not finished), "Non, c'est pas ça" (that’s not it). In more formal speech/writing, use "Non, ce n'est pas…"
target_language_example: Non, c'est pas la bonne adresse.
native_language_example: No, it’s not the right address.

meaning: "No, it was…" (used to correct or contradict).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to disagree with what was just said or to clarify what really happened/what something really was. Often followed by a description: « Non, c'était autre chose. » In casual speech you’ll often hear « c’était pas… » instead of the more formal « ce n’était pas… ».
target_language_example: Non, c'était pas ça, je parlais de demain.
native_language_example: No, that wasn’t it—I meant tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct something that was just said or assumed. Very common in conversation; often followed by a noun (“… ça”), an infinitive phrase, or an expression like “du tout” (not at all).
target_language_example: Non, ce n'est pas ma faute.
native_language_example: No, it’s not my fault.

non, ce n'est pas ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: non, ce n'est pas ce que
additional_notes: Used to correct a misunderstanding before completing the thought with a clause (typically subject + verb): "non, ce n'est pas ce que je pense / je veux / tu crois". Built from "ce n'est pas" (“it isn’t”) + "ce que" (“what/that which”). Often followed by a verb of thinking/believing/wanting (penser, croire, vouloir, etc.).
target_language_example: non, ce n'est pas ce que je pense.
native_language_example: No, that’s not what I think.

additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct something in the past. It’s the imperfect tense of "ce n’est pas" (it’s not): "ce" (it) + "n’était" (was) + "pas" (not). Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or phrase: "Non, ce n’était pas moi" (No, it wasn’t me), "Non, ce n’était pas un accident" (No, it wasn’t an accident), "Non, ce n’était pas comme ça" (No, it wasn’t like that).
target_language_example: Non, ce n'était pas une blague.
native_language_example: No, it wasn’t a joke.

additional_notes: Used when answering a question about a female person and correcting/contrasting (e.g., “Not me/him—her”). Often followed by a verb: “Non, elle n’a rien dit.” It can also stand alone as an incomplete sentence: “Non, elle.” = “No, her/she (did).”
target_language_example: —C’est toi qui as appelé ? —Non, elle.
native_language_example: “Was it you who called?” “No, her.”

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a sentence to answer “no” and then continue with information starting with **il**. **Il** can mean “he,” but it’s also often **impersonal** (refers to a situation, not a person), especially in common patterns like **il fait** (weather: “it’s…”), **il faut** (“it’s necessary / I have to…”), and **il y a** (“there is/are…”).
target_language_example: Non, il ne peut pas venir aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: No, he can’t come today.

meaning: "No, he is…" / "No, it is…" (to correct someone).
additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct what someone just said, then you continue the sentence (often with a place or situation: "ici", "à la maison", "dans la famille…", or ownership: "à nous"). "Il" can mean "he" or "it" depending on what you’re talking about (a person, an animal, an object).
target_language_example: Non, il est au travail, pas à la maison.
native_language_example: No, he’s at work, not at home.

meaning: “No, he/it doesn’t…” (start of a negative sentence with il + ne).
additional_notes: Used to answer “no” and immediately continue with a negative statement beginning with **il ne…**. **Ne** becomes **n’** before a vowel or mute h: **il n’a…**, **il n’existe…**, **il n’y a…**, **il n’y en a…**. This is just the beginning of the full negative structure (often with words like **pas, rien, plus, jamais**).
target_language_example: Non, il n'y a pas de problème.
native_language_example: No, there isn’t a problem.

meaning: “no, there isn’t / there aren’t …” (to say something doesn’t exist or isn’t available).
additional_notes: Used to answer a question negatively before continuing with an “il n’y a …” sentence. Very often followed by “pas de + noun” (Non, il n’y a pas de réseau) or by “personne” meaning “nobody” (Non, il n’y a personne). You can also omit “pas” with “personne” and similar negative words: “Il n’y a personne.”
target_language_example: Non, il n'y a pas de place aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: No, there aren’t any seats today.

additional_notes: Used to start a negative reply about what a man (il = he) does or would do. It introduces the French negation structure **ne ... pas** (or other negative words): **Non, il ne + verb + pas**. In speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Non, il fait pas…*. Before a vowel or silent h, **ne** becomes **n’**: *Non, il n’est pas…*.
target_language_example: Non, il ne veut pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: No, he doesn’t want to come tonight.

meaning: 'No, I…' (with 'j'' = 'je' before a vowel or silent h).
additional_notes: Used to start a reply that refuses, corrects, or clarifies what you’re doing/thinking. 'Je' becomes 'j'' before a vowel sound: j’aime, j’attends, j’en veux, j’y tiens. Often followed by a verb; in casual speech you may hear 'j’aime pas' instead of the more formal 'je n’aime pas'.
target_language_example: Non, j'aime pas ça.
native_language_example: No, I don’t like that.

meaning: “No, I have…” / “No, I…” (to start a reply).
additional_notes: Used to begin a negative answer and then add what you did/have done (often in the passé composé: "j’ai" + past participle). It can also be followed by another negative: "Non, j’ai rien dit" (“No, I didn’t say anything”). Note: in proper French spelling, "Non" is usually capitalized at the start of a sentence ("Non, j’ai…"), but the key term here is the exact sequence "non, j'ai".
target_language_example: non, j'ai rien vu.
native_language_example: No, I didn’t see anything.

meaning: “No, I have…” / “No, I’ve got…” (used to refuse and immediately give a reason or state).
additional_notes: Used to answer “no” and then add an explanation with the verb avoir (“to have”): Non, j’ai du boulot (I’ve got work), Non, j’ai faim (I’m hungry), Non, j’ai rendez-vous (I have an appointment). French often uses avoir for states: j’ai faim/soif (I’m hungry/thirsty), j’ai besoin de… (I need…).
target_language_example: Non, j'ai du boulot.
native_language_example: No, I’ve got work.

meaning: “No, I…” (starting a reply to disagree or correct).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to answer “no” and then continue with what you (je) do/think/said. Often followed by standard French negation in the rest of the sentence (e.g., « Non, je ne… pas » / « Non, je n’en… plus »).
target_language_example: Non, je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: No, I don’t agree.

meaning: "No, I … it/him." ("je le" = "I" + direct object pronoun "le" = "him/it/that")
additional_notes: "Non, je le…" is a sentence starter used to answer and then continue with a verb. "Le" is a masculine singular direct object pronoun placed before the verb: "Je le connais" = "I know him/it." It can refer to a man, a masculine noun, or sometimes an idea/statement (roughly "that/so"), e.g., "Je le pense" = "I think so." In careful/written French, negation is "ne … pas" ("Je ne le connais pas"), but in everyday speech "ne" is often dropped: "Je le connais pas." With "être," French often uses "Je ne le suis pas" / spoken "Je le suis pas" = "I’m not (him/that)."
target_language_example: Non, je le connais pas.
native_language_example: No, I don’t know him/it.

meaning: “No, I don’t / I’m not / I haven’t …” (the start of a negative sentence).
additional_notes: Used to begin a refusal, correction, or contradiction. "n'" is the elided form of "ne" used before a vowel or silent h (e.g., j'ai, j'aime, j'en sais, j'irai, j'étais). It is normally completed by a second negative word such as "pas" (not), "rien" (nothing), "personne" (nobody), etc.: "non, je n'ai pas…", "non, je n'en sais rien."
target_language_example: non, je n'aime pas ça.
native_language_example: No, I don’t like that.

meaning: "No, I haven't…" / "No, I don't have…" (starting a negative reply with "I have").
additional_notes: Used to begin a negative answer with the verb **avoir** in the present: **je n'ai** (= *je ne ai*). It’s almost always followed by another negative word, e.g. **pas** (not), **jamais** (never), **rien** (nothing), **pas encore** (not yet): *Non, je n'ai pas… / Non, je n'ai jamais… / Non, je n'ai rien…*. The **ne** becomes **n'** before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Non, je n'ai pas le temps aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: No, I don't have time today.

meaning: “No, I haven’t” / “No, I didn’t” (a negative reply using the verb avoir).
additional_notes: Used to answer questions like “Have you…?” or to deny having done something, with ne…pas around the auxiliary avoir (j’ai → je n’ai). It’s often followed by a past participle: je n’ai pas fait / je n’ai pas eu / je n’ai pas fini. In everyday speech, “ne” is often dropped: “Non, j’ai pas…”.
target_language_example: — Tu as fini ? — Non, je n'ai pas fini.
native_language_example: — Have you finished? — No, I haven’t finished.

additional_notes: Used to answer negatively with the verb "avoir" (to have). Often followed by a noun: "Non, je n'ai pas faim" (I’m not hungry), "Non, je n'ai pas confiance" (I don’t trust / I don’t have confidence). With a noun you typically use "de/d’" after "pas" ("je n’ai pas de temps"), but some fixed expressions don’t ("je n’ai pas faim", "je n’ai pas soif").
target_language_example: Non, je n'ai pas le temps aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: No, I don’t have time today.

meaning: “No, I don’t / I can’t / I didn’t … (about it / any).”
additional_notes: This is the start of a negative sentence with the pronoun “en”. “En” usually replaces something introduced with “de” (e.g., de ça = about it; de café = (some) coffee; de trois = three of them). It’s commonly used with negatives like “ne…pas” (not any), “ne…plus” (no longer), “ne…rien” (nothing about it): « Je n’en veux pas » = “I don’t want any (of it).” The exact meaning depends on the verb/expression that follows (avoir envie de, pouvoir, savoir, être, vouloir, etc.).
target_language_example: Non, je n'en ai pas besoin.
native_language_example: No, I don’t need it (any).

additional_notes: "Non" is "no". "Je n'…" is negation ("I don't / I'm not"), and "n'" is used before a vowel sound (arriverai, crois, suis, tiens, vais). "Y" is a common pronoun meaning "there" or "to it/to that" (replacing a place or something introduced with "à"). Examples: « Je n'y vais pas » = “I’m not going there.” / « Je n'y crois pas » = “I don’t believe it.” / « Je n'y suis pour rien » = “It’s not my fault / I had nothing to do with it.”
target_language_example: Non, je n'y pense pas.
native_language_example: No, I’m not thinking about it.

meaning: “No, I don’t…” / “No, I’m not…” (start of a negative answer).
additional_notes: Used to begin a reply where you contradict or refuse something and then continue with a negative sentence using ne…pas (or another negation). Often followed by a verb: “Non, je ne sais pas.” In casual speech, people may drop “ne” (e.g., “Non, je sais pas”), but “Non, je ne…” is the standard form.
target_language_example: Non, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: No, I can’t come tonight.

meaning: "No, I didn't" / "No, I don't have it" (with "it/him/her" = l').
additional_notes: Used to answer a question with a negative in the past tense (passé composé): ne + auxiliary (ai) + pas. The object pronoun l' (= le or la, meaning “it / him / her”) comes before the auxiliary: « Je ne l'ai pas vu(e) ». Add -e in « vue » if the direct object is feminine (la) and comes before the verb.
target_language_example: — Tu as vu Marie ? — Non, je ne l'ai pas vue.
native_language_example: — Did you see Marie? — No, I didn't see her.

additional_notes: This is the start of a negative sentence: **ne … pas** around the verb. **Le** is a direct object pronoun placed **before** the verb (it can mean “it,” “him,” or “that,” depending on context). You then add the verb: *Non, je ne le connais pas* (“No, I don’t know him/it”), *Non, je ne le crois pas* (“No, I don’t believe it”), *Non, je ne le suis pas* (“No, I’m not”). In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Non, je le connais pas*.
target_language_example: Non, je ne le comprends pas.
native_language_example: No, I don’t understand it.

meaning: “No, I can’t.” / “No, I’m not able to.”
additional_notes: Used to refuse or say you’re unable to do something. Often followed by an infinitive (Non, je ne peux pas venir.) or a pronoun (Non, je ne peux pas le faire.). In casual speech, the "ne" is often dropped: "Non, je peux pas."
target_language_example: Non, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: No, I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to deny something about yourself with the verb être (“to be”). The full structure is: Non + je ne suis pas + adjective/noun (e.g., marié(e), prêt(e), comme ça). You can also stop at “Non, je ne suis pas.” when the rest is understood from context. Note that adjectives/past participles often agree with the speaker: prêt (masc.) / prête (fem.), marié (masc.) / mariée (fem.).
target_language_example: —Tu es fatigué ? —Non, je ne suis pas fatigué.
native_language_example: —Are you tired? —No, I’m not.

meaning: “no, I don’t want to / I don’t want it.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb *vouloir* (“to want”) in the present tense: *je veux* (“I want”). The negative is formed with *ne … pas*: *je ne veux pas* (“I don’t want”). In casual spoken French, *ne* is often dropped: *Non, je veux pas.* You can add an infinitive after it (*je ne veux pas voir* = “I don’t want to see”) or stop the sentence if the context is clear.
target_language_example: Non, je ne veux pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: No, I don’t want to go out tonight.

meaning: “No, I am…” (a correction or clarification about who/what you are).
additional_notes: Used to correct someone or contradict an assumption, then state identity, role, state/condition, opinion, or what you’re doing. Follow with a noun/adjective (“Anglais”, “bien”), a job (“cascadeur”), a relationship (“son père”), a prepositional phrase (“en train de lire”, “pour la paix”), etc. In formal contexts you can also say “Non, je ne suis pas…” when denying what you are not.
target_language_example: Non, je suis étudiant, pas professeur.
native_language_example: No, I’m a student, not a teacher.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or contradict, then state what you intend to do next with "je vais" + infinitive (near-future). In speech, "je ne vais pas…" is often shortened to "je vais pas…" (dropping "ne"). You can also use "j’y vais / je vais y aller" to mean “I’m going there / I’m going to go there.”
target_language_example: Non, je vais rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: No, I'm going to go home.

meaning: 'No, I want…' (to refuse/correct and state what you want).
additional_notes: Used to contradict what someone suggested or assumed: first you say "Non" (no), then "je veux" (I want). It’s usually followed by a noun ("je veux la paix" = I want peace) or an infinitive verb ("je veux rentrer" = I want to go home). "Non, je veux." can also stand alone to mean "No, I do want to."
target_language_example: Non, je veux rester ici.
native_language_example: No, I want to stay here.

meaning: "No, but…" (used to object, correct, or qualify what was said).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French as a discourse marker at the start of a reply. It often introduces a disagreement or a correction ("Yes, but…" / "No, but…"), and can also be used for emphasis or mild annoyance ("Non mais !" = "Come on!" / "Seriously!").
target_language_example: Non, mais attends, je vais t'expliquer.
native_language_example: No, but wait, I’m going to explain.

meaning: “No, don’t …” (used to start a negative command).
additional_notes: Used to stop someone or tell them not to do something. In French negative commands are formed with **ne** + verb + a negative word: most often **ne … pas** (Non, ne crie pas.), but also **ne … rien** (don’t say anything), **ne … jamais** (never), **ne … plus** (no longer), etc. With object pronouns, the pronoun goes between **ne** and the verb: **Non, ne me touchez pas** (“Don’t touch me”).
target_language_example: Non, ne t’inquiète pas !
native_language_example: No, don’t worry!

additional_notes: Repeating « non » adds emphasis (stronger than a single « non »). It’s common in speech to disagree, refuse, or stop someone: « Non, non, laisse tomber. » You can repeat it more times for even stronger emphasis.
target_language_example: Non, non, je ne veux pas.
native_language_example: No, no, I don’t want to.

meaning: "No, no, I…" (used to correct, refuse, or reassure).
additional_notes: A common spoken lead-in before explaining your position (often with "je…"). Repeating "non" adds emphasis and can sound reassuring ("No, no, I'm fine"), corrective ("No, no, I don't think so"), or politely stopping someone to clarify. Intonation matters: it can be gentle or firm depending on context.
target_language_example: Non, non, je vais le faire moi-même.
native_language_example: No, no, I’ll do it myself.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse, correct someone, or reassure them that something is fine/not necessary. Often said quickly in conversation; punctuation varies ("Non non non" / "Non, non, non"). Tone can range from firm ("absolutely not") to calming ("no, it’s okay").
target_language_example: Non, non, non, merci — je n’ai pas besoin d’aide.
native_language_example: No, no, no, thanks—I don’t need help.

additional_notes: Repeating « non » several times adds strong emotion: firm refusal, disagreement, alarm, or protest. You can repeat it more or fewer times (« Non, non ! », « Non, non, non ! ») depending on how strong you want it to sound; punctuation like « ! » makes it even more emphatic.
target_language_example: Non, non, non, non ! Ne fais pas ça !
native_language_example: No, no, no, no! Don’t do that!

additional_notes: Used to begin a sentence after saying “Non,” followed by the subject pronoun “on.” In everyday French, “on” very often means “we” (instead of “nous”), especially in conversation: “Non, on continue.” It can also mean “people in general / you” depending on context.
target_language_example: Non, on ne peut pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: No, we can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Used when answering and immediately correcting/negating a specific detail: time (Non, pas au début.), degree (Non, pas si mal.), frequency (Non, pas souvent.), possession (Non, pas le tien.). Often followed by a word/phrase being negated. With “du tout,” it becomes stronger: “Non, pas du tout” = “No, not at all.”
target_language_example: Non, pas aujourd’hui : demain.
native_language_example: No, not today: tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny something, disagree, or reassure someone (often like “No, not at all!”). You can also use just “pas du tout” after a question (e.g., “Tu es fâché ? — Pas du tout.”).
target_language_example: Tu veux que je t’aide ? — Non, pas du tout, merci.
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you? — No, not at all, thanks.

meaning: “No, what…?” / “Wait, what…?” (often expressing surprise, disbelief, or protest before a question).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French to react strongly before asking for an explanation (e.g., « Non, qu'est-ce que c'est ? », « Non, qu'est-ce que tu fais ? »). The expression is compositional (« non » + « qu'est-ce que »), but the overall effect is idiomatic in tone (similar to “Wait, what…?”).
target_language_example: Non, qu'est-ce que tu fais ?
native_language_example: No, what are you doing?

meaning: “no, you…” (used to contradict or correct someone).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to disagree with what someone said or is about to do: “Non, tu…” is often followed by a verb (frequently with ne…pas for “don’t / can’t / won’t”). It can sound firm or corrective depending on tone.
target_language_example: Non, tu ne touches pas à ça !
native_language_example: No, you don’t touch that!

meaning: “No, you …” (starting a negative sentence with “tu n’…”).
additional_notes: Used to contradict or refuse something: “Non, tu n’…” introduces a sentence in the negative with “tu” (you, informal singular). The “ne” part of negation is shortened to “n’” before a vowel or silent h: tu n’as pas…, tu n’en as pas…, tu n’iras pas…. It’s usually followed by another negative word like pas (not), jamais (never), rien (nothing), plus (no longer/not anymore), etc.
target_language_example: Non, tu n'as pas raison.
native_language_example: No, you’re not right.

meaning: “No, you don’t…” / “No, you’re not…” (starting a negative reply).
additional_notes: Used to begin a firm correction or refusal. It’s followed by French negation: most often **ne … pas** (Non, tu ne vas pas…), but also **ne … jamais** (never), **ne … plus** (no longer), **ne … rien** (nothing), **ne … nulle part** (nowhere), etc. In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped (Non, tu vas pas…), but in writing and careful speech it’s kept.
target_language_example: Non, tu ne peux pas entrer ici.
native_language_example: No, you can’t come in here.

meaning: "No, you don't… / No, you didn’t…" (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Used to start a correction or contradiction. It introduces a negative sentence with "vous" (you = formal singular or plural). In full negation, "ne" is typically paired with a second negative word such as "pas": "Non, vous ne comprenez pas." With object pronouns, they come after "ne" (e.g., "vous ne l'avez pas fait").
target_language_example: Non, vous ne pouvez pas entrer ici.
native_language_example: No, you can’t come in here.

meaning: "No, that… / No, it…" (used to contradict or correct).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to disagree with what was just said, often followed by a verb phrase: "Non, ça ira" (No, it’ll be fine), "Non, ça ne l’est pas" (No, it isn’t). "Ça" refers to a situation/thing previously mentioned (like “that/it”).
target_language_example: Non, ça ne marche pas comme ça.
native_language_example: No, it doesn’t work like that.

meaning: “No, it doesn’t / won’t …” (starting a negative sentence about “that/it”).
additional_notes: Used to say “No” and then immediately start a negation with **ça** (“that/it”) + **ne** + verb, usually completed by a negative word like **pas** (not), **plus** (no longer), **jamais** (never), **rien** (nothing), etc.: *Non, ça ne marche pas.* In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Non, ça marche pas.*
target_language_example: Non, ça ne fonctionne pas comme ça.
native_language_example: No, it doesn’t work like that.

additional_notes: Common spoken reply to refuse politely (especially when someone offers something: "Non, ça va, merci") or to reassure someone that everything is OK. Intonation and follow-up change the meaning: "Non, ça va très bien" = "No, I'm doing very well"; "Non, ça va pas" or "Non, ça va pas du tout" = "No, I'm not OK at all." You may also hear it repeated: "Ça va, ça va" = "It's fine, it's fine."
target_language_example: Tu veux un café ? Non, ça va, merci.
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee? No thanks, I’m fine.

meaning: "Come on!" / "Seriously!" (an exclamation showing protest, surprise, or annoyance).
additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence to react strongly to what someone did/said: "Non mais !" or "Non mais ça va pas ?" It’s very common in spoken French and usually sounds irritated or incredulous. Although it literally looks like “no, but…”, it often doesn’t function as a real contrast like English “no, but”.
target_language_example: Non mais, tu te prends pour qui ?
native_language_example: Seriously, who do you think you are?

additional_notes: A polite way to refuse or decline an offer (help, a cigarette, an invitation, etc.). Often said on its own ("Non merci !") or followed by an explanation ("Non merci, ça va." / "Non merci, je me débrouillerai."). You can add "monsieur/madame" or a name to sound more formal or personal.
target_language_example: — Tu veux un café ? — Non merci, ça va.
native_language_example: — Do you want a coffee? — No thanks, I'm good.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true and that there is an additional point. Very often followed by a second part: "non seulement … mais aussi/mais encore …" ("not only … but also …").
target_language_example: Non seulement il est en avance, mais en plus il a apporté des fleurs.
native_language_example: Not only is he early, but he also brought flowers.

additional_notes: "Nos" is the plural form of "notre" (our). Use "nos amis" for a mixed group or an all-male group; for an all-female group, say "nos amies".
target_language_example: Ce soir, nos amis viennent dîner à la maison.
native_language_example: Tonight, our friends are coming over for dinner at our place.

additional_notes: "Nos" is the plural form of "notre" and is used before a plural noun, regardless of whether the group includes boys and/or girls. "Enfants" can mean "children" (plural) or more generally "kids". Used to talk about children belonging to the speaker and one or more other people (often a couple or family).
target_language_example: Nos enfants vont à l'école ici.
native_language_example: Our children go to school here.

meaning: these days; nowadays (most often in: « de nos jours »).
additional_notes: Literally means “our days,” but it’s usually used in the fixed expression « de nos jours » to talk about modern times / the present day. It’s common at the start of a sentence to set the context (like “Nowadays, …”).
target_language_example: De nos jours, on travaille souvent à distance.
native_language_example: Nowadays, people often work remotely.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: "nos" (our) + "vies" (lives). Used to talk generally about the course or experience of life (often in broad statements: "dans nos vies" = "in our lives"). Note the singular is "notre vie" (our life).
target_language_example: La musique fait partie de nos vies.
native_language_example: Music is part of our lives.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "notre" (our) with the singular noun "famille". Common in phrases like "dans notre famille" (in our family) or when talking about family traditions, reputation ("le nom de notre famille"), or family unity/conflict.
target_language_example: Dans notre famille, on dîne ensemble le dimanche.
native_language_example: In our family, we have dinner together on Sundays.
