additional_notes: Often used as a request/instruction (e.g., for a verification code, an invite code, or a QR/login code). Uses the polite/plural form "votre" (your) and is typically addressed to someone you don’t know well or to multiple people. You may also hear "Partagez votre code avec moi" (imperative: “Share your code with me”).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous partager votre code avec moi ?
native_language_example: Can you share your code with me?

additional_notes: Used to talk about an organized group that shares political ideas and participates in elections and government. Often used with verbs like appartenir à (to belong to), rejoindre (to join), and former/créer (to form/create).
target_language_example: Elle ne veut pas adhérer à un parti politique.
native_language_example: She doesn’t want to join a political party.

additional_notes: Used in the common structure: **[subject] est parti(e) il y a + duration**. With **être**, *parti* agrees with the subject: **parti** (masc.), **partie** (fem.), **partis/parties** (plural). Here **il y a** means **“ago”** (time before now), not “there is/there are.” Note: the exact string **parti il y a** is masculine singular; for a female subject you would normally say **partie il y a**.
target_language_example: Il est parti il y a trois jours.
native_language_example: He left three days ago.

additional_notes: This is a fragment most often used inside a larger question like: « Est-ce qu’il y a quelque chose de particulier que tu veuilles ? » It uses « particulier » (“particular/specific”) + « que tu veuilles » (subjunctive of vouloir: “that you want”). You’ll often see it with « quelque chose de » before it.
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose de particulier que tu veuilles manger ?
native_language_example: Is there anything in particular you want to eat?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a portion of something (“une partie de la ville” = an area/part of the city) or to say someone/something belongs to a group or whole (“faire partie de” = to be part of/belong to). Very common with quantities: “la plus grande partie de” = most of.
target_language_example: Je fais partie de cette association depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve been part of this organization for two years.

additional_notes: Most often used in the expression « faire partie de la + noun » = “to be part of the / to belong to the” (a group, organization, country, etc.). It agrees with the subject: je fais / tu fais / il fait / nous faisons / ils font partie de…. Use « de la » before a feminine singular noun; compare « du » (masc. sing.), « de l’ » (before a vowel/h mute), « des » (plural).
target_language_example: Je fais partie de la même équipe que toi.
native_language_example: I’m part of the same team as you.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase « faire partie de » (“to be part of / belong to”). It can be literal (a family member) or figurative (someone treated like family). You can add words like « presque » (“almost”) to soften it: « Il fait presque partie de la famille. »
target_language_example: Après toutes ces années, il fait vraiment partie de la famille.
native_language_example: After all these years, he’s really part of the family.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a section of something: « cette partie du bois » = “this part of the woods.” Often appears in the expression « faire partie du/de la/des » = “to be part of (a group/whole).” « du » is the contraction of « de + le » (so it’s used with masculine singular nouns).
target_language_example: Elle fait partie du groupe depuis hier.
native_language_example: She’s been part of the group since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used when someone departs without acknowledging others. You can also say: « partir sans dire au revoir à quelqu’un » (to someone) or « partir sans dire au revoir à tout le monde » (to everyone).
target_language_example: Êtes-vous sûr que vous voulez partir sans dire au revoir ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave without saying goodbye?

meaning: to leave immediately; to leave at once.
additional_notes: Used to insist on urgent/immediate departure. Common in rules, orders, or formal instructions. Note: “sur-le-champ” does not literally mean “on the field” in English here; it means “right away / on the spot.”
target_language_example: Si tu n'es pas d'accord, tu peux partir sur-le-champ.
native_language_example: If you don’t agree, you can leave right away.

additional_notes: Uses the verb « partir » (to leave/depart) + « tout de suite » (right away). Often used with obligation/advice: « Je dois… » (I have to…), « Tu dois… » (you have to…), « Il faut… » (it’s necessary…), « Vous feriez mieux de… » (you’d better…).
target_language_example: On est en retard : il faut partir tout de suite.
native_language_example: We’re late: we have to leave right away.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens or exists in many countries/places globally. Often placed at the end of the sentence for emphasis: « … partout dans le monde ». You can also use it alone as a short statement meaning “worldwide.”
target_language_example: On trouve ce plat partout dans le monde aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You can find this dish all over the world today.

meaning: “can you manage to…?” / “are you able to…?”
additional_notes: From the verb *parvenir à* (“to manage to / to succeed in doing”). It’s the inverted question form with *tu* (common in writing and more formal speech): *Parviens-tu à + infinitive ?* In everyday conversation, you’ll often hear *Tu parviens à… ?* or *Tu arrives à… ?*.
target_language_example: Parviens-tu à finir ce travail avant ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can you manage to finish this work before tonight?

meaning: "not ..., but I ..." (contrast: something is not the case, but the speaker states what they do/feel/will do).
additional_notes: Used to link a negated clause ending in "pas" to a contrasting clause introduced by "mais je". Very common pattern: "Je ne + verbe + pas, mais je + verbe..." (the "ne" may be omitted in informal speech). Comma is optional but frequent in writing.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas, mais je le ferai.
native_language_example: I don’t want to, but I’ll do it.

meaning: not aware; not up to date (on something).
additional_notes: Used with "être": "(ne) pas être au courant (de ...)" = to not know about something / to not be informed. Very common in conversation; the "ne" is often dropped in speech ("Je suis pas au courant"). Often followed by "de" + noun or "que" + clause.
target_language_example: Je suis pas au courant de la réunion de demain.
native_language_example: I didn’t know about tomorrow’s meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say something is unnecessary. It’s often followed by an infinitive (Pas besoin de parler. / Pas besoin de faire ça.) or a noun (Pas besoin de chaussures.). You can also say: « Tu n’as pas besoin de… » (= you don’t need to…).
target_language_example: Pas besoin de t’inquiéter, je m’en occupe.
native_language_example: No need to worry, I’ll take care of it.

meaning: 'not what' / 'not that which' (used in a negative sentence).
additional_notes: Used with the negation "(ne) ... pas" before "ce que" to mean “not what.” In speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je sais pas ce que..." = "Je ne sais pas ce que...". Common with verbs like dire, savoir, croire, comprendre: "(Ne) me dis pas ce que je dois faire" = “Don’t tell me what I should do.”
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you mean.

additional_notes: This is usually a fragment used inside a longer sentence, most often after “ce n’est pas” (it’s not) or “ce n’est pas du tout” (not at all): “Ce n’est pas ce que je voulais” = “That’s not what I wanted.” It’s followed by a verb (voulais, pensais, pensais dire, etc.).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: That’s not what I meant to say.

additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct what someone thinks/said, usually as part of a longer sentence: “C’est pas ce que tu crois” (“That’s not what you think”). In formal French you often see “Ce n’est pas ce que tu …” (with “ne”).
target_language_example: C’est pas ce que tu crois.
native_language_example: That’s not what you think.

additional_notes: Usually appears inside a longer negative sentence like « Ce n’est pas ce que vous pensez » (“That’s not what you think”). In full form, French typically uses « ne … pas » for negation (often « n’est pas » here), and « ce que vous … » means “what you …” when followed by a verb.
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas ce que vous voulez.
native_language_example: That’s not what you want.

additional_notes: Usually appears inside a full sentence with negation, most often: « Ce n’est pas ce qui s’est passé » (“That’s not what happened”). « ce qui s’est passé » means “what happened” (literally “that which happened”), and « pas » negates it. In spoken French, you may also hear it as « C’est pas ce qui s’est passé » (dropping « ne »).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas ce qui s'est passé hier.
native_language_example: That’s not what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with a verb like voir/savoir/comprendre (often in questions) to say you don’t see/know/understand what is happening: « Tu ne vois pas ce qui se passe ? » = “Don’t you see what’s going on?” The core expression is « ce qui se passe » (“what’s happening”). Note: « se passer » means “to happen,” and is a false friend with English “to pass.”
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce qui se passe ici.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what’s happening here.

meaning: “not like that” / “don’t do it like that.”
additional_notes: Used to correct someone’s way of doing something (how they speak, look, enter, shout, etc.). Often said as an instruction or reprimand: « Ne + verb + pas comme ça ! » or « (Ne) + verb + pas comme ça. »
target_language_example: Ne me touche pas comme ça !
native_language_example: Don’t touch me like that!

additional_notes: Used before a noun to show absence or non-existence: pas de guerre = 'no war'. Very common in negative sentences such as il n'y a pas de... ('there is/are no...'). After pas, French usually uses de before the noun instead of un/une/des.
target_language_example: Il n'y a pas de problème.
native_language_example: There is no problem.

meaning: no harm; no damage; (would) do me no harm.
additional_notes: Used most often in the phrase « (ne) faire pas de mal (à quelqu’un) » = “(not) to hurt someone / (not) to do harm.” It can also be used with « ça/ne me ferait pas de mal » to mean “it wouldn’t hurt (me)” in the sense of “it would be good for me” (e.g., some coffee, compassion, a change of scenery).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je ne te ferai pas de mal.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I won’t hurt you.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to accept a request (like “sure” or “that’s fine”). Often said alone as a full reply: « Pas de problème. » In casual speech you’ll also hear « Y a pas de problème » (= « Il n’y a pas de problème »).
target_language_example: Tu peux m’aider demain ? — Pas de problème.
native_language_example: Can you help me tomorrow? — No problem.

meaning: “You’re welcome / no problem.” Also: “nothing to (do something)” / “not enough to (do something).”
additional_notes: Often used alone as a reply to thanks: « —Merci ! —Pas de quoi. » It can also be followed by an infinitive to mean “nothing to …” (e.g., « Pas de quoi rire ! » = “Nothing to laugh about!”). With « ne … pas de quoi + infinitive », it can mean “not enough (money/means) to …” (e.g., « Je n’ai pas de quoi manger. » = “I don’t have enough to eat.”).
target_language_example: —Merci pour ton aide ! —Pas de quoi.
native_language_example: —Thanks for your help! —No problem.

meaning: “(I don’t know/see) what you’re talking about.”
additional_notes: Used almost always with a verb like **je sais pas / je vois pas / j’ai aucune idée**: **Je (ne) sais pas de quoi tu parles** = “I don’t know what you’re talking about.” The structure **de quoi** means “what / about what.” The missing **ne** (je sais pas…) is very common in speech and informal writing. Can also be accusatory: **Tu sais pas de quoi tu parles !** = “You don’t know what you’re talking about!”
target_language_example: Désolé, je vois pas de quoi tu parles.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t see what you’re talking about.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to say “it’s fine/you’re welcome.” Very common in spoken French. You’ll also hear it with different levels of formality: “Pas de souci !” (neutral), “Pas de souci, boss.” (more casual). Related expression: “Ne te/vous fais pas de souci” = “Don’t worry.”
target_language_example: — Tu peux m’aider demain ? — Pas de souci !
native_language_example: — Can you help me tomorrow? — No problem!

meaning: "Not that / none of that." (refusing a topic or behavior)
additional_notes: Used to shut down or refuse something: a subject of conversation ("On parle pas de ça") or someone’s attitude/behavior ("Pas de ça avec moi" = “don’t do/say that with me”). Often said in a firm tone; common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Pas de ça ici, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: None of that here, please.

pas dire du mal des morts

target_language_multi_word_term: pas dire du mal des morts
meaning: not to speak ill of the dead.
additional_notes: A common saying (often as: « Il ne faut pas dire du mal des morts » / « On ne dit pas du mal des morts ») meaning you shouldn’t criticize someone after they’ve died. « Dire du mal de quelqu’un » means “to speak badly of someone / to badmouth someone.”
target_language_example: Je sais qu’il a fait des erreurs, mais il ne faut pas dire du mal des morts.
native_language_example: I know he made mistakes, but you shouldn’t speak ill of the dead.

additional_notes: Used to strongly reinforce negation. Often appears after a negative verb ("je n’aime pas du tout" = "I don’t like it at all") or alone as a short reply meaning "not at all / no, not at all". Can also be used politely to reject thanks or an apology: "—Merci ! —Pas du tout."
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas du tout d’accord.
native_language_example: I don’t agree at all.

additional_notes: Used with ne...pas to say something hasn’t happened up to now (often implying it may happen later). Common in questions (e.g., Tu as fini ou pas encore ?) and in statements (e.g., Je n’ai pas encore mangé.).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas encore reçu ta réponse.
native_language_example: I haven't received your reply yet.

additional_notes: Used with negation: (ne) pas + infinitive. In careful writing you’ll see **ne pas faire ça**; in everyday speech and informal writing, **ne** is often dropped: **pas faire ça**. Often used after another verb (e.g., *vouloir*, *laisser*): *Je ne veux pas faire ça* (“I don’t want to do that”).
target_language_example: Je préfère ne pas faire ça maintenant.
native_language_example: I’d rather not do that now.

meaning: not much; not a lot; not much of anything.
additional_notes: Means “not much / not a lot” and is very common in both spoken and written French, often referring to quantity, activity, knowledge, or importance. It frequently appears with negation, and in speech the "ne" is often dropped: "Je sais pas grand-chose" (instead of "Je ne sais pas grand-chose"). It can also be used alone as a short answer: "Pas grand-chose." = “Not much.”
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas grand-chose sur les hommes.
native_language_example: I don’t know much about men.

meaning: 'no need / don't bother' (and with valoir: 'not worth it').
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t necessary or doesn’t justify the effort. Very common in speech, often as **C’est pas la peine (de + infinitive)** = “No need to…” / “Don’t bother…”. With **(ne) pas valoir la peine**, it means “not worth it”: **Ça (n’)en vaut pas la peine** / **Ça ne vaut pas la peine de + infinitive**.
target_language_example: C’est pas la peine de venir si tu es malade.
native_language_example: No need to come if you’re sick.

meaning: no need to / don’t bother to.
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t necessary or worth doing. Often said on its own as an instruction or reassurance (short for something like « Il n’y a pas la peine de… »). Followed by an infinitive verb: « pas la peine de + infinitive ». Can sound firm (“don’t bother…”) or comforting (“no need to…”), depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Pas la peine de t’inquiéter, tout va bien.
native_language_example: No need to worry, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used mainly with être, especially in set phrases like « ce n’est pas le cas » (“that’s not the case”) or informally « c’est pas le cas ». Often used in questions/conditions: « Et si c’est pas le cas ? » = “What if that’s not the case?”
target_language_example: Si ce n’est pas le cas, dis-le-moi tout de suite.
native_language_example: If that’s not the case, tell me right away.

additional_notes: This is the negative of "le faire" (“to do it”), with the object pronoun "le" = “it.” In careful/formal French you’ll often see "ne pas le faire"; in everyday speech and informal writing people commonly drop "ne": "(ne) pas le faire". It often follows verbs like "dire de" ("to tell [someone] to"), "pouvoir" ("can"), or "vouloir" ("want"): "Je peux pas le faire" = “I can’t do it.”
target_language_example: S’il te plaît, ne le fais pas — je t’ai dit de pas le faire.
native_language_example: Please don’t do it — I told you not to do it.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not in that place ("là-bas" = over there). Often appears with the full negation "ne ... pas" (e.g., "Je ne suis pas là-bas"), but in casual speech "ne" is frequently dropped (e.g., "Je suis pas là-bas").
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne suis pas là-bas en ce moment.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm not there right now.

meaning: 'not bad'; also 'quite a lot' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “not bad / pretty good” when reacting to a result, idea, or performance: « C’est pas mal ! ». In « Même pas mal. », it’s a set phrase meaning “It doesn’t hurt at all / Not even!” (often said after getting hurt). In questions like « Ça fait pas mal ? », it means “Does it hurt (a lot)?” Note: « pas mal de + noun » means “quite a lot of / many”: « pas mal de monde ».
target_language_example: Ton dessin est pas mal !
native_language_example: Your drawing is pretty good!

meaning: quite a lot of; a fair number/amount of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun or an uncountable noun to mean “many” or “a lot of.” Often implies “more than you’d think” or “a decent amount,” but not necessarily an extreme quantity. Very common in everyday speech; you can also hear it without “ne” in negatives (e.g., « Il n’y a pas mal de… » is rarer than « Il y a pas mal de… »).
target_language_example: On a pas mal de travail aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We have quite a lot of work today.

meaning: quite a few things; a lot of things.
additional_notes: Means “many/quite a lot of things” (more than you might expect). Often used in everyday speech. With verbs like avoir/faire/expliquer: “On a pas mal de choses…” = “We have quite a few things…”, “Ça explique pas mal de choses.” = “That explains a lot.” You can also say it alone as a short answer: “Pas mal de choses.” = “Quite a few things.”
target_language_example: J'ai encore pas mal de choses à faire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I still have quite a few things to do today.

additional_notes: Used with negation (ne…pas / ne…plus / ne…jamais, etc.) to say that something is also not true: “not … either.” It often corresponds to English “either” after a negative statement (or “neither” as a short reply). Example pattern: « Je ne … pas non plus » = “I don’t … either.”
target_language_example: Je ne m'y attendais pas non plus.
native_language_example: I wasn't expecting it either.

additional_notes: This sequence is usually part of a larger negative structure rather than a fixed expression by itself. After a verb, *ne ... pas que* introduces a clause: *je ne savais pas que...* = 'I didn't know that...'. In *il n'y a pas que...*, it means 'not only' or 'not just'.
target_language_example: Je ne pensais pas que ce serait si difficile.
native_language_example: I didn't think it would be so difficult.

meaning: "I don’t think it’s…" / "I don’t think that it’s…"
additional_notes: Used after verbs like *croire* or *penser* in the negative: *Je crois/pense pas que ce soit…* It introduces doubt/uncertainty, so French uses the subjunctive (*soit* = subjunctive of *être*). Very common in spoken French because *ne* is often dropped (formal: *je ne crois/pense pas que ce soit…*).
target_language_example: Je pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used in negative sentences with a verb like vouloir, aimer/plaire, croire, penser, trouver, etc., followed by a clause starting with que + tu. Very often you’ll see it without "ne" in speech: "Je pense pas que tu…" (more informal) = "Je ne pense pas que tu…". After "je ne pense/crois pas que…", French often uses the subjunctive (e.g., "pas que tu aies…"), though in everyday speech you may also hear the indicative.
target_language_example: Je ne pense pas que tu aies raison.
native_language_example: I don’t think you’re right.

meaning: "not just that / not only that"; sometimes "not that (it...)".
additional_notes: Often used in spoken French (with no "ne") to say something is more complicated than it seems: "C’est pas que ça." It can be a standalone reply, or followed by "mais..." to add another reason/detail: "Pas que ça, mais...". It can also start a clause meaning "Not that it matters/Not that anyone cares": "Pas que ça intéresse qui que ce soit."
target_language_example: Je fais pas que ça, j’ai aussi du travail à finir.
native_language_example: I’m not only doing that; I also have work to finish.

additional_notes: Used to firmly refuse or say something is not acceptable. Common patterns: **Pas question de + infinitive** (Pas question de partir.) and **Pas question que + subjunctive** (Pas question que tu viennes.). Often heard in spoken French; you may also see **Il n’est pas question de/que...** for the same idea.
target_language_example: Pas question que je te laisse faire ça.
native_language_example: No way I’m letting you do that.

meaning: “not so / not that” (as much, as … as).
additional_notes: Used to soften or correct an exaggeration: "pas si + adjective/adverb" = "not so + adj/adv" (e.g., pas si simple = not that simple). Often appears with "que" for comparisons: "pas si … que" = "not as … as". Can also be used alone as a brief correction: "Pas si bien." = "Not that well."
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas si fatigué que ça.
native_language_example: I’m not that tired.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to slow down physically (speaking, running, etc.) or to slow down mentally/figuratively ("hold on", "one thing at a time"). Often said on its own as an exclamation: « Pas si vite ! » You can also add a name after it: « Pas si vite, Paul ! »
target_language_example: Pas si vite, on n’a pas fini !
native_language_example: Not so fast, we’re not finished!

additional_notes: A strong warning said as an exclamation, often to protect something that belongs to you. Common with « à + noun/pronoun »: « Pas touche à mon vélo ! » (= Don’t touch my bike!). Can also be said alone: « Pas touche ! ». Colloquial, often used with kids or jokingly, but can be serious too.
target_language_example: Pas touche à mon téléphone !
native_language_example: Hands off my phone!

additional_notes: Used to soften or limit something: quantity/intensity ("Pas trop fort !" = not too loud/strong) or degree ("pas trop moche" = not too ugly). In casual speech it can also mean "not really" (e.g., "Ça va ? — Pas trop." = Not really / Not so great). Often used with adjectives or adverbs, and also with verbs to mean “don’t … too much” ("Serre pas trop" = don’t squeeze/tighten too much).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, mais pas trop.
native_language_example: I'm tired, but not too much / not really.

meaning: not a word; don’t say a word.
additional_notes: Used to insist on total silence or secrecy (often as an order or warning): « Pas un mot ! ». You’ll also see « ne dis pas un mot » / « ne dites pas un mot » (singular/plural “you”), and « pas un mot de plus » (“not another word”). In « C’est pas un mot », the « ne » is omitted in casual speech; formally: « Ce n’est pas un mot ».
target_language_example: Pas un mot à personne, d’accord ?
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone a word, okay?

additional_notes: Often added to the end of a statement to check that the other person agrees or to confirm something you believe is true. Literally it means “not true?”, but in everyday speech it functions like “right?” or “isn’t that so?”. It can also be used alone to ask for confirmation: « Pas vrai ? » = “Really?” / “Is that true?”.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h, pas vrai ?
native_language_example: We’re meeting again at 6 p.m., right?

meaning: not to go there / not to go.
additional_notes: It’s the negative form of « y aller » (“to go there”). « y » is a pronoun meaning “there” (to that place/event). In full form you often see « ne … pas »: « Je ne peux pas y aller. » In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Je peux pas y aller. »
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas y aller ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go there tonight.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the structure **ne ... pas être**. When **être** is in the infinitive after another verb (often a modal like **devoir** = must/should or **sembler** = seem), **pas** comes right before **être**: *Il ne doit pas être là* (“He must not be there”). In casual speech, **ne** is often dropped: *Il doit pas être là*.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas être en retard.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be late.

additional_notes: Usually said with full negation: « ne pas être en retard ». « être en retard » = “to be late”; add « ne … pas » to make it negative. Often used as an instruction or goal: « Il ne faut pas être en retard. »
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas être en retard pour le train.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be late for the train.

additional_notes: A noun for an activity you do in your free time for pleasure (e.g., photography, fishing). Often used with "avoir" (avoir un passe-temps), with a possessive (son/mon passe-temps), or with "préféré" (favorite hobby). It can also describe something that started as a casual hobby: "Ça a commencé comme un passe-temps."
target_language_example: Je fais de la cuisine comme passe-temps le week-end.
native_language_example: I cook as a hobby on the weekend.

additional_notes: Imperative of **passer** + the indirect object pronoun **moi** (“to me”). Used to ask someone to hand you something: **Passe-moi le marteau.** It can also mean “put me through (to someone)” on the phone or in an office context: **Passe-moi ton supérieur.** Often followed by **le/la/les** or a name.
target_language_example: Passe-moi la clé, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Pass me the key, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to give you an object. It’s the informal imperative of *passer* (tu-form): **passe** + indirect object pronoun **moi** (“to me”) + **le** (“the”, masculine singular). Before a vowel or silent *h*, **le** becomes **l’**: *Passe-moi l’eau.*
target_language_example: Passe-moi le stylo, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Pass me the pen, please.

additional_notes: Used with passer + (amount of time) + à + infinitive to say you spend time doing an activity: « Je passe beaucoup de temps à lire. » It can also be followed by a place with à + noun to mean you spend a lot of time somewhere: « Il passe beaucoup de temps à la plage. » (Je passe / tu passes / il-elle-on passe / nous passons / vous passez / ils-elles passent.)
target_language_example: Je passe beaucoup de temps à étudier le français.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time studying French.

meaning: still acceptable; (I) can still live with it.
additional_notes: Used to say something is just barely OK, tolerable, or not too bad—often with "ça" ("Ça passe encore."). It can suggest you’re not fully satisfied, but you’ll accept it. Common in casual spoken French.
target_language_example: La chambre est petite, mais ça passe encore pour une nuit.
native_language_example: The room is small, but it’s still OK for one night.

meaning: to pass in front of; to go ahead of (someone).
additional_notes: Used for physical movement: *passer devant la maison* (“to pass in front of the house”). With a person, it often means going ahead of them (sometimes like cutting in line): *Il a passé devant moi.* You can also use it more generally to mean something comes before/has priority: *Le travail passe devant le plaisir.*
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je peux passer devant ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I go ahead (in front)?

additional_notes: Used to talk about being with someone for a period of time (socially, with family, dating, etc.). Conjugate "passer" (je passe, tu passes, il/elle passe, nous passons, vous passez, ils/elles passent) + "du temps" + "avec" + a person (avec toi, avec mes amis, avec ma fille). Often used with "vouloir" (want to) or "pouvoir" (can/could).
target_language_example: J'aimerais passer du temps avec toi ce week-end.
native_language_example: I'd like to spend time with you this weekend.

meaning: 'to spread the word' / 'to pass the message along'.
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to tell other people some information. Very common with the causative "faire": "Fais/Faites passer le mot" (Tell people / Spread the word), "J’ai fait passer le mot" (I spread the word), "Je lui ai fait passer le mot" (I passed the message on to him/her).
target_language_example: Tu peux passer le mot à tout le monde ?
native_language_example: Can you spread the word to everyone?

meaning: to pass the time; to kill time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something while waiting or when you don’t have anything specific to do. Often follows "pour" (pour passer le temps) or is used with "ça" (Ça fait passer le temps = That helps pass the time).
target_language_example: On peut jouer à un jeu pour passer le temps pendant le trajet.
native_language_example: We can play a game to pass the time during the trip.

meaning: to cross someone’s mind; to occur to someone.
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun: « Ça me passe par la tête » (It crosses my mind). Often used in the negative to mean “it never even occurred to me”: « Ça ne m’a jamais passé par la tête de… » / « Ça ne m’a jamais passé par la tête. »
target_language_example: Ça ne m’a jamais passé par la tête de quitter ce travail.
native_language_example: It never even crossed my mind to quit this job.

additional_notes: Uses **passer** to mean “to spend” (time). Structure: **passer + (duration) + avec + person**. You can change the duration: *passer du temps avec* (spend time with), *passer moins de temps avec* (spend less time with). Note: **passer** looks like English “to pass,” but here it means “to spend (time),” so it’s not translated literally.
target_language_example: J’aimerais passer plus de temps avec mes amis.
native_language_example: I’d like to spend more time with my friends.

meaning: to make a few phone calls.
additional_notes: Uses the verb passer with coup de fil (literally “phone call”). Very common for talking about calling several people quickly to arrange something or get information. You can change the quantity: passer un coup de fil (make a call), passer deux/trois coups de fil (make two/three calls).
target_language_example: Je vais passer quelques coups de fil pour organiser le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I'm going to make a few phone calls to set up the appointment.

additional_notes: Common everyday way to say you’re going to call someone, often implying it won’t take long. You can use it with an indirect object: « Je dois passer un coup de fil à Marie. »
target_language_example: Je dois passer un coup de fil à Marie ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to give Marie a quick call tonight.

meaning: to move on (to something else); to move on from something.
additional_notes: Used when you stop focusing on a situation, topic, or person and continue with something new. Can mean changing the subject (« On peut passer à autre chose ? ») or turning the page emotionally after a breakup, disappointment, etc. Common in advice or suggestions: « Il est temps de… », « Il te faut… », « Pourquoi ne pas… ? »
target_language_example: Il est temps pour moi de passer à autre chose.
native_language_example: It’s time for me to move on.

meaning: "do you spend...?" / "are you having...?" (question form of *tu passes*)
additional_notes: This is the verb *passer* in the 2nd-person singular present (*tu passes*), with inversion (*passes-tu*) to form a question. Often used with time: *passer du temps* (to spend time), *passer Noël* (to spend/celebrate Christmas), *passer du bon temps* (to have a good time). Note: it can look like English “pass,” but here it often means “spend” or “have (a good time).”
target_language_example: Combien de temps passes-tu ici chaque semaine ?
native_language_example: How much time do you spend here each week?

meaning: “Pass/hand me …” or (on the phone) “Put me through to …”.
additional_notes: Imperative (vous form) of *passer* + indirect object pronoun *moi* (“to me”). It’s used with an object: *Passez-moi ce magazine* (“Hand me that magazine”) or with a person/department in a phone context: *Passez-moi la réception* / *Passez-moi Burke* (“Put me through to reception / Burke”). In the imperative, the pronoun comes after the verb with a hyphen: *passez-moi*.
target_language_example: Bonjour, passez-moi le service client, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Hello, put me through to customer service, please.

additional_notes: Used with avoir + passé (past participle of passer) to talk about how long you spent somewhere or with someone: « J’ai passé beaucoup de temps ici/avec eux. » In English you say “spend time,” not “pass time,” so this can be tricky for beginners.
target_language_example: J'ai passé beaucoup de temps à apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I spent a lot of time learning French.

additional_notes: From the verb "passer" (to spend) + "la nuit" (the night). Used to say where someone stayed overnight (e.g., in a hotel, outside, in prison) or sometimes who they stayed with ("passer la nuit avec quelqu’un" = spend the night with someone). In the present/past: "Je passe la nuit…" / "J’ai passé la nuit…"; with a location often uses "à", "dans", "sur", "chez" (e.g., "chez un ami").
target_language_example: On a passé la nuit chez des amis.
native_language_example: We spent the night at some friends’ place.

additional_notes: This is the past participle phrase of **passer** (often used in the **passé composé**: *j’ai passé…*). Depending on the noun that follows, it can mean different things: **passé du temps** = spent time; **passé un examen** = took an exam (not necessarily passed it); **passé un bon moment** = had a good time; **passé une commande** = placed an order. The exact meaning comes from context. Note: **passé quelque chose** is a template-like phrase ("passed/spent something") where *quelque chose* stands in for the object.
target_language_example: J’ai passé quelque chose au bureau avant de rentrer chez moi.
native_language_example: I dropped something off at the office before going home.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "passer" (to spend) to talk about spending a period of time somewhere or in a situation: "passer + duration + en prison". It’s usually in the past tense (e.g., "a passé" / "ont passé") to say someone served time in prison.
target_language_example: Mon oncle a passé trois ans en prison quand il était jeune.
native_language_example: My uncle spent three years in prison when he was young.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase « passer un bon moment » = “to have/spend a good time.” « Passé » is the past participle (used with « avoir »): « J’ai passé… / On a passé… ». Often used to ask how someone’s evening/event was: « Vous avez passé un bon moment ? ».
target_language_example: On a passé un bon moment au restaurant.
native_language_example: We had a good time at the restaurant.

meaning: 'had a really great time' (spent a very good time).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **passer un bon moment** = “to have a good time.” It’s very common with **avoir** in the past: **j’ai / on a / il a / nous avons passé...**. You can add details with **avec** (with someone) or time expressions like **hier soir** (last night).
target_language_example: On a passé un très bon moment au restaurant hier soir.
native_language_example: We had a really great time at the restaurant last night.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **passer** to talk about how you spent a period of time: **passer une bonne journée / une bonne soirée / de bonnes vacances**. In questions, you’ll often see: **Tu as passé une bonne journée ?** Note: **passer** here means “to spend / to have (a good time),” not “to pass.”
target_language_example: J’espère que tu as passé une bonne journée.
native_language_example: I hope you had a good day.

meaning: 'had a nice evening' (spent a pleasant evening).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "passer" to talk about how your evening went. It’s commonly used as a question after an event: "Vous avez passé une bonne soirée ?" (formal/plural) or "T’as passé une bonne soirée ?" (informal). You can add intensifiers like "vraiment" (really).
target_language_example: Merci, j’ai passé une bonne soirée avec vous.
native_language_example: Thanks, I had a nice evening with you.

additional_notes: A harsh, offensive insult. Literally “poor idiot,” but it’s usually said to insult someone (sometimes with contempt or anger), not to express pity. Avoid using it in polite conversation; you may hear it in arguments or in movies.
target_language_example: Arrête de faire le pauvre con !
native_language_example: Stop being such an idiot!

additional_notes: Used when talking about the legal punishment of executing someone for a crime. Commonly heard in opinions and debates with expressions like « être pour/contre la peine de mort » (to be for/against the death penalty).
target_language_example: Beaucoup de gens sont contre la peine de mort.
native_language_example: Many people are against the death penalty.

additional_notes: Used to ask about a duration (minutes, hours, days, etc.). It often comes at the beginning of a question (Pendant combien de temps… ?) but in casual speech it can be left at the end: Tu restes ici pendant combien de temps ?
target_language_example: Pendant combien de temps restes-tu à Paris ?
native_language_example: How long are you staying in Paris?

meaning: for hours; for a long time.
additional_notes: Used with an action or state that lasts over a continuous period of time. It often suggests it felt long (e.g., crying, talking, waiting). You can replace "des heures" with other durations: "pendant deux heures" (for two hours), "pendant des jours" (for days).
target_language_example: On a attendu pendant des heures à l'aéroport.
native_language_example: We waited for hours at the airport.

additional_notes: Used to situate an action or situation in time: something happened in the period when a war was taking place. Often refers to World War II in historical contexts, but it can mean any war depending on context.
target_language_example: Pendant la guerre, ils ont dû quitter leur maison.
native_language_example: During the war, they had to leave their home.

additional_notes: Used with "pendant" to say something happens within a period of time. "Les vacances" can mean school breaks or holiday periods; you’ll often specify which ones: "les vacances scolaires" (school vacation), "les vacances de Noël" (Christmas holidays), etc.
target_language_example: Pendant les vacances, je dors plus et je vois mes amis.
native_language_example: During vacation, I sleep more and I see my friends.

additional_notes: Introduces an action or situation happening at the same time as another. Usually followed by a full clause (subject + verb): « pendant que je coupe », « pendant que c’est chaud ». Often used to contrast two simultaneous actions (one person does X while another does Y).
target_language_example: Je vais préparer le dîner pendant que tu mets la table.
native_language_example: I’ll make dinner while you set the table.

additional_notes: Used to express a duration (how long something lasts). Often follows a verb: "rester/vivre/voyager" + place + "pendant trois jours". For ongoing actions or situations, it means the action continued over that time period.
target_language_example: On a travaillé pendant trois jours pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: We worked for three days to finish the project.

meaning: for a moment; for a while.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a short period of time. Often follows an action/state (e.g., attendre/rester/se reposer pendant un moment). It can also come at the beginning of a sentence ("Pendant un moment, ...") to mean "for a while" in that period.
target_language_example: Attends ici pendant un moment, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: Wait here for a moment; I’ll be right back.

meaning: for an hour; during an hour.
additional_notes: Used with "pendant" to express duration (how long something lasts): pendant + time period (une heure, deux jours, trois semaines). It can stand alone as a short answer to “Combien de temps ?” (“How long?”).
target_language_example: J'ai travaillé pendant une heure.
native_language_example: I worked for an hour.

meaning: for a week; during a week.
additional_notes: Used to express duration: something lasts for one week (pendant + length of time). Often translated as “for” with a time period (pendant une heure, pendant trois jours).
target_language_example: Je serai à Lyon pendant une semaine.
native_language_example: I’ll be in Lyon for a week.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a mistaken assumption about someone (often before being corrected). It’s a common pattern: « Je pensais que vous étiez + (noun/adjective) ». « vous » is formal or plural “you”. « pensais » is the imperfect of « penser » (I was thinking / I thought).
target_language_example: Je pensais que vous étiez le professeur.
native_language_example: I thought you were the teacher.

meaning: "I thought I had told you to …"
additional_notes: Used to say you believed you had already told someone to do something. Most common as: « Je pensais vous avoir dit de + infinitive » (polite you). With friends you’ll often hear: « Je pensais t’avoir dit de… ». Note the past infinitive « avoir dit » = “to have told.”
target_language_example: Je pensais vous avoir dit de fermer la porte.
native_language_example: I thought I had told you to close the door.

additional_notes: "Pensait" is the imperfect past (3rd person singular) of "penser" (to think). It often describes an ongoing or background belief/thought in the past and is followed by "que" + a full clause: "[il/elle/on/nom] pensait que + [proposition]".
target_language_example: Marie pensait que Tom dormait.
native_language_example: Marie thought that Tom was sleeping.

meaning: "does he think" / "is he thinking" (inverted question form).
additional_notes: "pense-t-il" is the verb "penser" + "-t-" + "il" used in formal written questions (inversion), especially after question words: "Que pense-t-il ?" (What does he think?), "Pourquoi pense-t-il ça ?" (Why does he think that?), "À quoi pense-t-il ?" (What is he thinking about?). The "-t-" is inserted for pronunciation when a verb ends in a vowel sound (here "pense") and the subject pronoun is "il"/"elle"/"on".
target_language_example: Qu'en pense-t-il, au juste ?
native_language_example: What does he think about it, exactly?

additional_notes: Often part of a longer sentence like « Je pense pas que… » (informal) or « Je ne pense pas que… » (more formal). It introduces an opinion you don’t believe; in full sentences, it commonly triggers the subjunctive in the clause that follows (e.g., « Je pense pas qu’il soit là. »).
target_language_example: Je pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used (most often as part of « Je ne pense pas que ce soit… ») to express doubt or a negative opinion about something. After « ne… pas penser que », French typically uses the subjunctive: « ce soit » is the subjunctive of « c’est / c’est être » (from « être »). You’ll often follow it with an adjective or noun: « …que ce soit possible / vrai / une bonne idée ».
target_language_example: Je ne pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: This is the verb "penser" (to think) + "que" (that). The apostrophe shows elision: "que" becomes "qu'" before a vowel sound (e.g., qu'il, qu'on). It introduces a clause: « Il pense qu’il a raison. » You can change the subject and verb: « Je pense que… / Tu penses que… / Ils pensent que… ».
target_language_example: Je pense qu'on peut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I think we can leave now.

additional_notes: A common fragment used after a subject (often omitted in this entry), e.g. « Je pense qu'il… » = “I think that he/it…”. « qu'il » is a contraction of « que il ». « il » can mean “he” (a male person) or “it” (referring to something with a masculine noun, or used impersonally like “it” in English).
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il a raison.
native_language_example: I think he's right.

additional_notes: Fragment built from **penser que** (“to think that”) + **on** (“we/people/one/you” in general). **qu'on** is the elision of **que on** (used before a vowel sound). It typically appears inside a longer sentence, often after a subject like *il*. Related forms: *je pense qu’on*, *tu penses qu’on*, *ils/elles pensent qu’on*.
target_language_example: Il pense qu'on va réussir.
native_language_example: He thinks we’re going to succeed.

meaning: "(I/he/she) thinks that we should…" (to suggest an idea).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a suggestion or opinion, often in a longer sentence: « Je pense qu'on devrait + verb » (I think we should...). « qu'on » is a contraction of « que + on » (“that + we/one/people”). « devrait » is the conditional of « devoir » and sounds softer/more polite than « doit ».
target_language_example: Je pense qu'on devrait partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: I think we should leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone believes or thinks. This is the third-person singular form of penser + que, so it commonly means 'he thinks that,' 'she thinks that,' or 'it thinks that,' depending on the subject.
target_language_example: Elle pense que tu as raison.
native_language_example: She thinks that you are right.

meaning: "(he/she) thinks that it's a…" / "(I) think that it's a…" (introducing a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes:
This is a sentence fragment you’ll typically see inside a longer sentence.
- « pense » is the 3rd-person singular present of « penser » (to think): « il/elle/on pense ». With « je », you’d use « je pense ».
- « que » means “that” here.
- « c'est » means “it’s/that’s” (informal spelling without the curly apostrophe: « c’est »).
- « une » is “a/an” used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., « une idée », « une solution »). For a masculine noun, use « un »: « …c'est un problème. »
Note: This entry uses the exact spelling « c'est » as given in the term; in normal French typography you’ll often see « c’est ».
target_language_example: Il pense que c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: He thinks it's a good idea.

meaning: "(I/he/she) think that what…" (used to introduce an idea about something).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase on its own; it’s usually the start of a longer sentence: « Je pense que ce que tu as dit est important. » It combines « penser que… » (“to think that…”) + « ce que… » (“what / that which…”). You’ll often see it followed by a verb phrase: « ce que tu fais », « ce que j’ai dit », etc.
target_language_example: Je pense que ce que tu as dit est vrai.
native_language_example: I think that what you said is true.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or suggestion: « penser que… » = “to think that…”. « ce serait » is the conditional of « c’est » (“it is”), meaning “it would be” (often used to sound more polite or less certain). The subject can change: je pense que ce serait…, il/elle pense que ce serait…, etc.
target_language_example: Je pense que ce serait une bonne idée de partir tôt.
native_language_example: I think it would be a good idea to leave early.

meaning: "(I) think that I…" (used to introduce what you believe about yourself).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the full phrase "Je pense que je…" followed by a verb (often in the present tense): "Je pense que je suis… / je vais… / je peux…". It’s used to express an opinion or uncertainty about yourself; for a more certain tone you can use "Je sais que je…" (I know that I…).
target_language_example: Je pense que je vais rentrer tôt ce soir.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to go home early tonight.

additional_notes: Usually used after the subject: “Je pense que je peux …” to introduce an opinion or belief about what you’re able to do. You can follow it with a verb in the infinitive (e.g., “venir”, “le faire”) or with a time phrase. Note: “pense” is the present tense of “penser” for “je” (I).
target_language_example: Je pense que je peux venir demain.
native_language_example: I think I can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report someone’s belief or opinion about you. It’s typically followed by an adjective or noun (e.g., « stupide », « de son côté ») or by a past participle/phrase describing your state. With « penser que », French usually uses the indicative: « je suis » (not the subjunctive).
target_language_example: Elle pense que je suis en retard.
native_language_example: She thinks I'm late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believe you’re about to do, often followed by an infinitive: « Je pense que je vais partir » (I think I’m going to leave). In speech, « que » is sometimes dropped: « Je pense je vais… ». Change « pense » depending on the subject (e.g., « tu penses que tu vas… », « il/elle pense qu’il/elle va… »).
target_language_example: Je pense que je vais prendre un café.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to have a coffee.

additional_notes: This is the pattern **penser que + [clause]**. **Pense** is “thinks” (present tense, 3rd person singular: *il/elle pense*), **que** is “that,” and **les** is “the” (plural). Often used to give someone’s opinion or belief: *Il/Elle pense que les…* (“He/She thinks that the…”). You’ll also see **On pense que…** meaning “People think that…” / “It’s thought that…”.
target_language_example: Elle pense que les prix vont augmenter.
native_language_example: She thinks that prices are going to go up.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment, not a complete phrase by itself. It usually needs a subject before it (e.g., "Il/Elle pense que nous..."). "pense" is the present tense of *penser* (to think) for *il/elle/on* (he/she/one). It is typically followed by a full clause starting with "nous" (we).
target_language_example: Elle pense que nous avons raison.
native_language_example: She thinks that we are right.

additional_notes: A phrase fragment: **pense** is the 3rd-person singular of *penser* (“to think”). It’s typically used with a subject (e.g., *Il/Elle pense que…*). **que** means “that,” and **nous avons** is “we have.” Often followed by what “we have” (e.g., *assez de temps*, *une solution*).
target_language_example: Il pense que nous avons assez de temps.
native_language_example: He thinks we have enough time.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer sentence with a subject before it: e.g. « Je pense que nous devrions… » (I think we should…). « devrions » is the conditional form of « devoir » and is often used to make a suggestion or give polite advice (“we should / we ought to”).
target_language_example: Je pense que nous devrions partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I think we should leave now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *penser* + *que* to introduce an opinion, followed by what “we can” do. Often appears as **Je pense que nous pouvons...** (“I think we can...”) or **Il/Elle pense que nous pouvons...** (“He/She thinks we can...”).
target_language_example: Je pense que nous pouvons partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I think we can leave now.

meaning: "(I/he/she) think(s) that you…" or (imperative) "think that you…"
additional_notes:
This is often part of a longer sentence:
- "Je pense que tu…" = "I think that you…"
- "Il/Elle pense que tu…" = "He/She thinks that you…"
It can also be an instruction (imperative): "Pense que tu…" = "Think/Remember that you…". In speaking, French commonly drops "ne" in negatives: "Je pense que tu n'as pas…" → "Je pense que tu as pas…" (informal).
target_language_example: Je pense que tu as raison.
native_language_example: I think you’re right.

additional_notes: Often used to give advice or make a suggestion. Very commonly appears as **Je pense que tu devrais + infinitive** (e.g., *Je pense que tu devrais dormir*). It can also be used after other subjects: *Il/Elle pense que tu devrais...*
target_language_example: Je pense que tu devrais parler au professeur.
native_language_example: I think you should talk to the teacher.

meaning: "(he/she) thinks that you are..." (often part of a longer sentence).
additional_notes: This is usually not used on its own; it’s a fragment you’ll most often see after a subject like "Il/Elle" (he/she): "Il pense que tu es…" = "He thinks you are…". "pense" is the 3rd-person singular of "penser" (to think). After "que" (that), French keeps a normal subject + verb order: "tu es" = "you are".
target_language_example: Il pense que tu es fatigué.
native_language_example: He thinks that you are tired.

meaning: “think that you …” (as in “I think that you …”).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it’s typically part of a longer sentence like « Je pense que vous avez raison. » It uses the verb « penser » + « que » to introduce what you think. « pense » is the 1st/3rd person singular present (je/il/elle/on pense). With « vous », the full sentence is often « Je pense que vous… » (I think that you…).
target_language_example: Je pense que vous avez raison.
native_language_example: I think you’re right.

pense que vous avez besoin de

target_language_multi_word_term: pense que vous avez besoin de
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment often followed by what is needed: a noun (e.g., « de l’aide », « du temps ») or an infinitive (« de partir », « de faire »). « pense » is 3rd person singular of « penser » (he/she thinks). The « de » at the end must be completed: « avoir besoin de + [noun/verb] ». You can change the subject: « Je pense que vous avez besoin de… » (I think you need…).
target_language_example: Je pense que vous avez besoin de plus de temps.
native_language_example: I think you need more time.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of a longer sentence, often with a subject before it: "Je pense que vous devriez…" (= I think you should…). "Vous devriez" is the conditional of "devoir" and is a polite way to suggest or recommend something. Uses "vous" for formal or plural "you".
target_language_example: Je pense que vous devriez consulter un médecin.
native_language_example: I think you should see a doctor.

additional_notes: This is a fragment built from **penser que** (“to think that”) + **ça** (“that/it/this”). It’s usually followed by a verb: **Je pense que ça va** (“I think it’s going OK / I think I’m fine”). On its own, it sounds incomplete; you normally need a subject before it (je/il/elle) and more words after **ça**.
target_language_example: Je pense que ça va marcher.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to work.

additional_notes: From the verb penser + à. Use it with a noun or an infinitive: penser à + nom (“think about something”) or penser à + infinitif (“think about doing / remember to do”). In the imperative (Pense à...), it often means “remember to... / make sure you...”.
target_language_example: Pense à prendre ton passeport.
native_language_example: Remember to take your passport.

meaning: to think of / to have an opinion about.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or express an opinion about someone or something. Very common in questions like « Qu’est-ce que tu penses de… ? » (What do you think of…?). Can also appear in structures like « quoi penser de… » (what to think of…).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas trop quoi penser de tout ça.
native_language_example: I don’t really know what to think of all that.

meaning: to intend/plan to do; to think you will do (something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after « penser » to express an intention or expectation: « Je pense faire… » = “I’m planning to…” / “I think I’ll…”. Common in the imperfect (« Je pensais faire… » = “I was planning to…”) and with negation (« Je ne pensais pas faire ça » = “I didn’t think I would do that”).
target_language_example: Je vais penser faire les courses après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to plan to do the grocery shopping after work.

meaning: to think about; to have in mind
additional_notes: Used with a person, thing, or idea you have in mind: penser à quelqu’un / à quelque chose. It can also be used before an infinitive to mean thinking of doing something or remembering to do something, depending on context. Compare with penser de, which usually asks for an opinion about something.
target_language_example: Vous devriez penser à votre avenir.
native_language_example: You should think about your future.

additional_notes: Used to suggest changing your focus (often to stop worrying or obsessing) or simply to talk about shifting to a different topic. With "à" after "penser": "penser à" = "to think about." In "Ça me fait penser à autre chose", it can mean "That makes me think of something else" (it reminds me of something different).
target_language_example: Après cette mauvaise nouvelle, j’essaie de penser à autre chose.
native_language_example: After that bad news, I’m trying to think about something else.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone what they think, believe, or have in mind. It’s an inversion question (verb + "-tu"), common in writing and more formal than simply "Tu penses… ?" Often followed by an infinitive ("penses-tu pouvoir…") or by "que" + a clause ("penses-tu que…").
target_language_example: Penses-tu venir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you think you’ll come tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion, belief, or guess. It’s the inverted question form of "tu penses que…" (you think that…). Common in writing and more formal speech; in casual conversation you’ll often hear "Tu penses que… ?" with rising intonation. The clause after "que" is a full statement (e.g., "Tom a raison").
target_language_example: Penses-tu que Tom a raison ?
native_language_example: Do you think Tom is right?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion about what you should do or what you might do/want. It’s an inversion question: "penses-tu" = "do you think", followed by "que" + a clause. After "que", French often uses the subjunctive in many contexts (e.g., "Penses-tu que je doive…?"), though in everyday speech you may also hear the non-inverted form: "Tu penses que je…?"
target_language_example: Penses-tu que je devrais lui envoyer un message ?
native_language_example: Do you think I should send him/her a message?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for advice or their opinion. It’s the inverted-question form of "Tu penses que je devrais…?" and is followed by an infinitive (e.g., faire, y aller, le dire). "Devrais" is the conditional of "devoir" and makes the question sound polite/soft (like “should” rather than “must”).
target_language_example: Penses-tu que je devrais attendre encore un peu ?
native_language_example: Do you think I should wait a little longer?

additional_notes: Used to challenge or express surprise/disbelief about someone’s intention or plan. Built from: penser à (“to think about/consider”) + sérieusement (“seriously”). Often followed by an infinitive (acheter, te remarier) or a noun.
target_language_example: Penses-tu sérieusement à quitter ton travail sans rien trouver d’abord ?
native_language_example: Are you seriously thinking about quitting your job without finding anything first?

additional_notes: Used to ask (often with doubt, surprise, or challenge) whether someone truly believes something. It’s an inverted-question form: « penses-tu » = « do you think? », and « vraiment » adds emphasis (“really”). It’s typically followed by a full clause with « que » + subject + verb.
target_language_example: Penses-tu vraiment que c'est une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you really think that it's a good idea?

additional_notes: From the verb *penser* (to think). *Tu penses que...* = “you think that...”. In casual questions, French often keeps normal word order: *Pourquoi tu penses que... ?* = “Why do you think that...?” (more formal: *Pourquoi penses-tu que... ?*). Often used after *si* (“if”): *Si tu penses que c’est mieux...* = “If you think it’s better...”.
target_language_example: Tu penses que c’est une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or belief. It’s the verb penser in the vous form + subject inversion (common in formal writing and careful speech): « Pensez-vous que… ? ». In speech, you’ll also hear « Vous pensez que… ? » (less formal) and sometimes « pensez-vous » inserted as a parenthetical: « Pourquoi, pensez-vous, a-t-il dit cela ? ».
target_language_example: Pensez-vous que c’est une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or belief. It’s the formal/inverted question form of « Vous pensez que… ? ». Often followed by « que » + a full clause; after expressions of doubt or possibility, French may use the subjunctive (e.g., « pensez-vous que… soit / puisse »).
target_language_example: Pensez-vous que ce soit une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you think that’s a good idea?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask someone’s opinion about you or what you should do. It’s an inversion question (pensez-vous) followed by que. Often used with the conditional for advice: « Pensez-vous que je devrais… ? ». After « pensez-vous que », French typically uses the subjunctive when expressing doubt/uncertainty, but in everyday speech you’ll also hear the indicative depending on context.
target_language_example: Pensez-vous que je puisse vous aider ?
native_language_example: Do you think I can help you?

additional_notes: Used to ask for advice/opinion. It’s a polite/formal question because it uses **vous** and inversion (**pensez-vous**). It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb: *Pensez-vous que je devrais partir ?* (“Do you think I should leave?”).
target_language_example: Pensez-vous que je devrais attendre encore un peu ?
native_language_example: Do you think I should wait a little longer?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion or expectation about what *they* can/will do. It’s a formal question using inversion (*pensez-vous*). After *pensez-vous que…*, French often uses the subjunctive (e.g., *pensez-vous que vous puissiez…?*), especially in more careful/formal speech.
target_language_example: Pensez-vous que vous puissiez m’aider demain ?
native_language_example: Do you think you could help me tomorrow?

additional_notes: Question form of "penser sérieusement à" + noun/infinitive. Used to ask if someone is truly considering a plan or possibility, often with surprise or skepticism. Register is neutral; "pensez-vous" is fairly formal—more casual: "Tu penses sérieusement à… ?"
target_language_example: Pensez-vous sérieusement à déménager à l’étranger ?
native_language_example: Are you seriously considering moving abroad?

additional_notes: Formal/polite way to challenge or question someone’s belief. Used to introduce a clause (often with the indicative, but the subjunctive is also common when expressing doubt or judgment: « Pensez-vous vraiment que votre projet soit réaliste ? »).
target_language_example: Pensez-vous vraiment que ce soit une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you really think that it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used with the verb *penser* + *que* to introduce what someone believed or assumed. In your examples it’s in the past (*a pensé que*, *ont pensé que*, *avons pensé que*), where *pensé* is the past participle used with *avoir*. After *penser que*, French typically uses the indicative (not the subjunctive).
target_language_example: J’ai pensé que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *penser* + *à* to mean thinking about someone/something, considering an idea, or remembering to include someone (e.g., *penser à nous* = think of us / remember us). In the past tense, you’ll often see it as *j’ai pensé à…*, *ils ont pensé à…*.
target_language_example: J’ai pensé à toi en voyant ce film.
native_language_example: I thought of you when I saw that movie.

additional_notes: Used for someone passing out (often from pain, shock, heat, illness, etc.). In French, "connaissance" here means "consciousness/awareness" (not "knowledge"). Common in medical or emergency contexts; you can also say "Il/Elle a perdu connaissance" (He/She fainted).
target_language_example: Il a failli perdre connaissance pendant quelques secondes.
native_language_example: He almost lost consciousness for a few seconds.

meaning: 'to lose sight of' / 'to lose track of' (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used literally (you can’t see someone/something anymore) or figuratively (you stop being in contact or no longer know what’s happening). Very common with people: « On s’est perdus de vue » = “We lost touch.” Also used for losing track while looking for someone in a crowd: « Je t’ai perdu de vue ».
target_language_example: J’ai perdu de vue mon ami après le lycée.
native_language_example: I lost touch with my friend after high school.

additional_notes: Used when talking about reducing body weight (health/fitness/diet goals). Conjugate "perdre" (je perds, tu perds, il/elle perd, nous perdons, vous perdez, ils/elles perdent) + "du poids" (some weight).
target_language_example: Je fais du sport pour perdre du poids.
native_language_example: I exercise to lose weight.

meaning: to waste time; to lose time.
additional_notes: Often used to say something is pointless or inefficient: « Je ne veux pas perdre du temps » (I don’t want to waste time). You can also use it with « à + infinitif »: « Tu perds du temps à expliquer ça » (You’re wasting time explaining that). Literally ‘to lose time,’ but in English it’s usually ‘to waste time.’
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas perdre du temps avec ça.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste time with that.

meaning: to lose hope; to give up hope.
additional_notes: Used to say someone stops believing that a good outcome is possible. Very common in the negative, especially as encouragement: « Il ne faut jamais perdre espoir » / « Ne perds pas espoir » (“Don’t lose hope”).
target_language_example: Il ne faut jamais perdre espoir.
native_language_example: You must never lose hope.

meaning: To lose face; to be publicly embarrassed or lose respect.
additional_notes: Used when someone risks humiliation, shame, or a loss of reputation (often in front of others). It can be used with an indirect object: « faire perdre la face à quelqu’un » = “to make someone lose face.”
target_language_example: Il refuse de s’excuser parce qu’il ne veut pas perdre la face.
native_language_example: He refuses to apologize because he doesn’t want to lose face.

meaning: to lose your head (panic); to go crazy.
additional_notes: Used when someone panics or stops thinking clearly: « Ne perds pas la tête ! » It can also mean “to lose your mind” or “to go crazy.” With « pour + quelqu’un », it often means “to be crazy about someone” (fall hard for them): « Il a perdu la tête pour elle. »
target_language_example: Quand j’ai vu mon passeport disparaître, j’ai failli perdre la tête.
native_language_example: When I saw my passport disappear, I almost lost my head.

meaning: to lose one’s life; to die (often in an accident or conflict).
additional_notes: A formal/neutral euphemism used in news reports, official statements, or serious contexts. Often refers to death resulting from an event (accident, disaster, war), rather than simply saying "mourir". Conjugates like "perdre" (e.g., "a perdu la vie", "ont perdu la vie").
target_language_example: Plusieurs personnes ont perdu la vie.
native_language_example: Several people lost their lives.

meaning: to lose control; to panic; to lose it.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression (literally “to lose the pedals”). Used when someone gets overwhelmed, flustered, or stops thinking clearly and can’t manage the situation. Often used in everyday speech to describe stress, confusion, or overreaction.
target_language_example: Quand j’ai vu l’examen, j’ai commencé à perdre les pédales.
native_language_example: When I saw the exam, I started to panic / lose control.

additional_notes: Used when someone can’t stay calm or keep waiting anymore. Often with "avec" + a person ("perdre patience avec quelqu’un") or in the negative/imperative: "Ne perds pas patience" (Don’t lose patience).
target_language_example: Je commence à perdre patience avec ce service.
native_language_example: I’m starting to lose patience with this service.

additional_notes: Used when you can’t find where you are or how to reach your destination. It conjugates like "perdre" (je perds, tu perds, il/elle perd, nous perdons, vous perdez, ils/elles perdent) and the possessive changes with the subject: "perdre mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur chemin". The dictionary form is "perdre son chemin"; in real speech it often appears conjugated (e.g., "j’ai perdu mon chemin").
target_language_example: Il a perdu son chemin en rentrant chez lui.
native_language_example: He got lost on his way home.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity isn’t worth it or won’t lead anywhere. Often used with **ne pas** (don’t waste your time) or **faire perdre son temps à quelqu’un** (to waste someone’s time). You can specify what you’re wasting time on with **avec**: *perdre son temps avec…* or with an infinitive: *perdre son temps à…*.
target_language_example: Tu vas perdre ton temps : perdre son temps à attendre ne sert à rien.
native_language_example: You’re going to waste your time: wasting your time waiting is pointless.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with "avoir": "j’ai perdu du poids" (I lost weight / I’ve lost weight). In questions you’ll see inversion ("As-tu…?", "Avez-vous…?") or "est-ce que" ("Est-ce que tu as perdu du poids ?").
target_language_example: J’ai perdu du poids ces derniers mois.
native_language_example: I’ve lost weight in the last few months.

additional_notes: Past participle of *perdre* used with *avoir*: *il/elle a perdu son…* = “he/she lost his/its…”. *Son* is a possessive meaning “his/its” (and sometimes “her” before a vowel sound: *son équilibre*, *son amie*). Common phrases: *perdre son équilibre* (lose balance), *perdre son sac* (lose one’s bag), *perdre son chemin* (lose one’s way), *perdre son sens* (lose its meaning), *perdre son sang-froid* (lose one’s cool), *perdre son travail* (lose one’s job).
target_language_example: J'ai perdu son numéro de téléphone.
native_language_example: I lost his phone number.

meaning: lost in thought; absorbed in his thoughts.
additional_notes: Common with verbs like être or sembler: « Il est / Il semblait perdu dans ses pensées. » It can also be used as an appositive/aside in a sentence: « Jack faisait les cent pas dans la pièce, perdu dans ses pensées. » The adjective perdu agrees with gender/number (perdue, perdus, perdues). The possessive can vary: « perdu dans mes/tes/ses/nos/vos/leurs pensées ».
target_language_example: Il est perdu dans ses pensées.
native_language_example: He is lost in thought.

meaning: "Allow me to…" (polite/formal way to introduce what you’re about to do or say).
additional_notes: Uses the formal command (imperative) of permettre: permettez (to you, formal/plural) + moi (me). Common in speeches, meetings, and polite conversation before presenting, rephrasing, summarizing, introducing yourself, leaving, etc. Followed by an infinitive verb: « Permettez-moi de + infinitive ». In informal situations you’ll more often hear « Laisse-moi… » / « Laissez-moi… » or simply « Je vais… ».
target_language_example: Permettez-moi de vous poser une question.
native_language_example: Allow me to ask you a question.

additional_notes: Used with the formal/polite “vous” to introduce a request or offer: *Permettez-moi de vous + infinitive* (accompagner, demander, présenter, etc.). Very common in formal speech, customer service, speeches, and introductions.
target_language_example: Permettez-moi de vous aider avec vos bagages.
native_language_example: Allow me to help you with your bags.

additional_notes:
Very polite/formal phrase used when introducing someone to another person or group. 
- "Permettez-moi" = polite imperative "allow me" (vous-form).
- "de vous présenter" = "to introduce (someone) to you".
Usually followed by the person/people being introduced: "Permettez-moi de vous présenter Monsieur Kato."
target_language_example: Permettez-moi de vous présenter notre nouvelle collègue, Sophie.
native_language_example: Allow me to introduce our new colleague, Sophie.

additional_notes: An official document showing you’re allowed to drive. Often used with verbs like avoir (to have), obtenir (to obtain), and passer (to take the driving test/qualify for the license): « passer son permis de conduire » = to take the driving test / work toward getting your license. Common in admin or police contexts (e.g., « Permis de conduire et carte grise »).
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon permis de conduire à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my driver’s license at home.

meaning: an elderly person; an older adult.
additional_notes: Polite, neutral term for an older person. Often used in everyday contexts (giving up a seat, services for older adults). You can also say "une personne âgée" (feminine) or "un personne âgée"? (No—"personne" is always grammatically feminine, so it’s always "une personne âgée" even when talking about a man).
target_language_example: Dans le bus, il a proposé son siège à une personne âgée.
native_language_example: On the bus, he offered his seat to an elderly person.

meaning: no one else; nobody else (and in some contexts: anyone else).
additional_notes: Means “no one/nobody else,” most often in negative contexts (ne…personne), e.g., « Je n’ai personne d’autre » = “I have no one else.” It can also be used as the subject: « Personne d’autre ne… » = “No one else…” The « d’ » is the shortened form of « de » before a vowel.
target_language_example: Je n'ai personne d'autre à qui parler.
native_language_example: I have no one else to talk to.

additional_notes: Used when 'no one' is the subject before the verb. In standard French it is followed by ne + verb, without pas: personne ne sait. Compare je ne vois personne ('I see no one') when it comes after the verb. Personne can also mean 'person' in other contexts.
target_language_example: Personne ne comprend la question.
native_language_example: No one understands the question.

additional_notes: Uses French negation with **ne** after the subject and before the verb. **Personne** here means “nobody” (not “a person”), and it’s followed by a verb in the singular: *personne ne connaît…*. Often used to emphasize that nobody has the knowledge (sometimes followed by comparisons like *…mieux que toi* = “better than you”).
target_language_example: Personne ne connaît cette histoire mieux que ma grand-mère.
native_language_example: No one knows this story better than my grandmother.

additional_notes: Used in French negation: **personne ne** + verb means “nobody/no one.” **le** is an object pronoun meaning “it” (for a masculine noun) or “him.” In the passé composé, **personne** can trigger agreement: *Personne ne l’a vu(e)* (agreement depends on what **l’** refers to). Note that **personne** looks like English “person,” but with **ne** it means “no one.”
target_language_example: Personne ne le sait encore.
native_language_example: No one knows it yet.

additional_notes: Used to negate the subject: **personne** = “no one,” with **ne** to form a negative sentence. It’s followed by a verb, and **me** is the object pronoun (“me / to me”). In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Personne me comprend* (informal speech), but in writing you usually keep **ne**.
target_language_example: Personne ne me répond quand j’appelle.
native_language_example: No one answers me when I call.

additional_notes: Used to start a negative sentence: **Personne ne + verb + nous** = “Nobody/No one + verb + us.” The **ne** is part of French negation with *personne* (and is often dropped in casual speech: *Personne nous croit*). The object pronoun **nous** (“us”) comes before the verb: *Personne ne nous croit* = “Nobody believes us.”
target_language_example: Personne ne nous aide ici.
native_language_example: Nobody helps us here.

additional_notes: Built with French negation: **personne** (nobody) + **ne ... peut** (can). It uses **pouvoir** conjugated as **il/elle/on peut**. In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Personne peut...* but in writing and formal speech, keep **ne**.
target_language_example: Personne ne peut tout faire tout seul.
native_language_example: No one can do everything alone.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people were able to do something in the past. It’s the negative pronoun personne (“no one”) with ne + the imperfect of pouvoir (pouvait) for ongoing/possible ability in the past. Often followed by an infinitive: personne ne pouvait + verb (e.g., entendre, voir, refuser). In informal speech, ne is often dropped: Personne pouvait…
target_language_example: Personne ne pouvait entrer sans billet.
native_language_example: No one could enter without a ticket.

additional_notes: Used to say that no one has the information. It’s a negative structure: "personne" (nobody) + "ne" + verb ("sait" = knows). Often followed by a question word like "ce que" (what), "qui" (who), "quand" (when), "ce qui" (what [as subject]), etc.
target_language_example: Personne ne sait où il est allé.
native_language_example: Nobody knows where he went.
