It’s commonly followed by a noun: votre attention (your attention), votre numéro (your number), votre signature (your signature), votre autographe (your autograph). In everyday speech, people often also say: « Est-ce que je peux avoir votre … ? » or « Je peux avoir votre … ? ».
target_language_example: Puis-je avoir votre nom, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I have your name, please?

meaning: “Can I count on…?” / “Can I rely on…?”
additional_notes: A polite way to ask if you can depend on someone or something. Uses subject–verb inversion: “puis-je” = “may I / can I”. Follow it with a person (“sur toi / sur vous”) or a noun (“sur votre aide”, “sur ta venue”).
target_language_example: Puis-je compter sur vous demain matin ?
native_language_example: Can I count on you tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: "Puis-je…?" is a formal/polite way to ask permission (“May I…?”). "Emprunter" means “to borrow” (something you will give back). It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: Puis-je emprunter ce parapluie ? / Puis-je l’emprunter ?
target_language_example: Puis-je emprunter votre stylo, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I borrow your pen, please?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission to borrow something owned by the person you’re speaking to. “Puis-je” is an inversion form meaning “may I / can I” (quite formal). “Emprunter” means “to borrow” (you’ll give it back). “Ton” is “your” for a masculine singular noun (ton vélo) or for a noun starting with a vowel/h (ton échelle). For a feminine noun, use “ta” (ta voiture); for plural, “vos” (your, formal/plural) or “tes” (your, informal plural).
target_language_example: Puis-je emprunter ton stylo, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: May I borrow your pen, please?

additional_notes: A polite, fairly formal way to ask permission to borrow an item. Then add the noun: votre + masculine singular noun (votre stylo, votre téléphone). For a feminine noun it’s also votre (votre voiture). With multiple people or “you” plural, use votre → votre becomes vos (Puis-je emprunter vos clés ?). More casual: Je peux emprunter votre… ?
target_language_example: Puis-je emprunter votre chargeur, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I borrow your charger, please?

additional_notes:
Very common polite request. 
- "Puis-je" is a formal way to say "may I / can I" (more formal than "Est-ce que je peux...").
- "en" replaces a previously mentioned thing (often introduced with "de" or an amount), like "some" in English: "Des biscuits ? Puis-je en avoir ?" = "Cookies? Can I have some?"
- You often add a quantity: "puis-je en avoir un/une" (one), "quelques-uns/quelques-unes" (a few). The choice of "un/une" and "quelques-uns/quelques-unes" depends on the gender and number of the thing you’re asking for.
target_language_example: Il reste des fraises ? Puis-je en avoir quelques-unes ?
native_language_example: Are there any strawberries left? May I have a few?

additional_notes: A very polite/formal way to ask what you’re allowed to do or how you can help. It uses inversion ("puis-je" = "can I"). Often used in questions like: « Puis-je faire autre chose ? », « Que puis-je faire ? ».
target_language_example: Puis-je faire quelque chose pour vous ?
native_language_example: Can I do something for you?

additional_notes: “Puis-je… ?” is a formal/polite way to ask “Can I…?” (inversion of “je peux… ?”). “Le” is the direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it” and it comes before the verb (puis-je le + verb). Common in polite questions: “Puis-je le prendre ?” (Can I take it?).
target_language_example: Puis-je le voir, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I see it/him, please?

meaning: "May I…?" (polite/formal), used before a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: This is a very polite, formal question form using inversion: "puis-je" = "may I / can I". The "me" is the reflexive pronoun used with many French verbs (e.g., me joindre, me permettre, me reposer). In everyday speech, people often say "Est-ce que je peux me… ?" or "Je peux me… ?" instead.
target_language_example: Puis-je me présenter ?
native_language_example: May I introduce myself?

additional_notes:
Very polite/inverted question form of “je peux parler… ?”. Often followed by:
- à + person: “Puis-je parler au directeur ?” (to the manager/director)
- avec + person: “Puis-je parler avec Tom ?” (with Tom)
You’ll also commonly hear it on the phone or in formal settings when asking to speak to someone.
target_language_example: Bonjour, puis-je parler à Marie, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Hello, may I speak to Marie, please?

additional_notes: A polite, fairly formal way to ask about paying. Uses inversion (puis-je = "can I") and is often followed by how you want to pay: avec la carte (by card), en espèces (in cash), en euros (in euros), par chèque (by check). In everyday speech, people also say: "Est-ce que je peux payer… ?"
target_language_example: Puis-je payer en espèces ?
native_language_example: Can I pay in cash?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask permission or request something. Literally it’s an inverted question: "puis-je" = "can I" + "prendre" = "to take". Used for things like asking to take a day off (prendre un jour de congé), ordering/requesting (prendre votre commande), or asking what amount you might gain/put on (prendre des kilos = gain weight). In casual speech, people often say "Est-ce que je peux prendre…?" or "Je peux prendre…?"
target_language_example: Puis-je prendre un café, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I have a coffee, please?

meaning: “may I / can I (to) you…?” (polite way to ask permission).
additional_notes: Used to form a polite question with inversion: "puis-je" = "can/may I" (from "pouvoir"). It’s normally followed by an infinitive ("puis-je te parler… ?"). "te" is the indirect object pronoun meaning “to you” (informal singular). For “to you” formal or plural, use "puis-je vous… ?".
target_language_example: Puis-je te poser une question ?
native_language_example: May I ask you a question?

meaning: "May I talk to you?" (polite way to ask to speak to someone).
additional_notes: "Puis-je" is an inversion form of "je peux" and sounds formal/polite (common in customer service or serious situations). "Te" is the informal "you" (tu). You’ll often add a time phrase like "un instant / une minute / rapidement". If you want a more formal version with "you" = "vous", say: "Puis-je vous parler ?"
target_language_example: Puis-je te parler un instant, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: May I talk to you for a moment, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask for permission or possibility. "Puis-je" is an inverted form of "je peux" (can I) and is common in writing or formal speech. Use it with a noun or object you want to use: "Puis-je utiliser + [object] ?"
target_language_example: Puis-je utiliser votre ordinateur un moment ?
native_language_example: May I use your computer for a moment?

additional_notes: Polite, formal way to ask permission. Inversion “puis-je” (= “can I / may I”) is more formal than “est-ce que je peux…?” or “je peux…?”. “Votre” addresses someone you don’t know well (more polite than “ton”). You can soften the request with “s’il vous plaît” and add a short duration: “un instant / une seconde”.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, puis-je utiliser votre téléphone un instant, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I use your phone for a moment, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/inverted question form of "je peux voir…?". Used to ask permission to look at something (a menu, document, ticket, item, etc.). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: "Puis-je voir le menu ?", "Puis-je voir celui-ci ?"
target_language_example: Puis-je voir votre passeport, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I see your passport, please?

additional_notes: Used by staff or authorities (e.g., ticket inspectors, police, reception) to politely ask to check a document or item. It’s an inverted question form of “je peux… ?” and is more formal. Typically followed by a noun like billet (ticket), carte d’identité (ID), permis de conduire (driver’s license), etc.
target_language_example: Puis-je voir votre passeport, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I see your passport, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/inverted question form of "je peux" (“can I”). It’s usually followed by a verb: "puis-je vous présenter…" (may I introduce you…), "puis-je vous aider ?" (may I help you?), "puis-je vous donner…" (may I give you…). "vous" is the formal/plural “you” and can be either the direct object (“touch you”) or indirect object (“give you”, “serve you”).
target_language_example: Puis-je vous aider à porter ces sacs ?
native_language_example: May I help you carry these bags?

additional_notes: A very polite way to offer help, often said by staff in shops, hotels, or customer service. It uses inversion for questions (puis-je = “can I/may I”). “Vous” is the formal “you” (or plural “you”). You can specify the help with “à” + infinitive: “Puis-je vous aider à trouver… ?” (“May I help you find…?”) or “En quoi puis-je vous aider ?” (“How can I help you?”).
target_language_example: Puis-je vous aider à trouver votre réservation ?
native_language_example: May I help you find your reservation?

meaning: "May I ask you…?" / "Can I ask you…?" (polite).
additional_notes: Very polite, formal way to ask permission to ask a question. Uses inversion (puis-je = can I), and vous for a formal/plural "you". Often followed by a question: « Puis-je vous demander où sont les toilettes ? ». Note: « demander » usually means "to ask" or "to request," not "to demand."
target_language_example: Puis-je vous demander votre nom, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I ask your name, please?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to offer someone something (often a drink or food). Uses inversion for questions: « puis-je » = « can I/may I ». « vous » is the formal/plural “you.” Often followed by « du/de la/des » or « quelque chose à boire/à manger ». You may also hear « Que puis-je vous offrir ? » = “What can I get you?/What may I offer you?”
target_language_example: Puis-je vous offrir un café ?
native_language_example: May I offer you a coffee?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask for a conversation. Used with “vous” (formal ‘you’ or plural ‘you’). Often followed by details like “une seconde / une minute” (for a second/minute), “dehors” (outside), or “seul à seul” (in private, one-on-one).
target_language_example: Puis-je vous parler un instant, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I speak to you for a moment, please?

meaning: May I see you? / Can I meet with you? (formal/polite)
additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask to speak with someone (“vous” = you, formal or plural). Often followed by a time or place: dehors (outside), demain (tomorrow), en privé (in private), un instant/une seconde (for a moment). In everyday speech, people often use “Est-ce que je peux vous voir… ?” or “Je peux vous voir… ?”.
target_language_example: Puis-je vous voir après la réunion, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I see you after the meeting, please?

additional_notes: A noun for a sweater you pull over your head (often just shortened to "un pull" in everyday French). Common with colors and comparisons: "un pull-over bleu", "le plus cher", "le même que". Used when shopping: "Puis-je essayer ce pull-over ?"
target_language_example: Il fait froid : je vais mettre mon pull-over.
native_language_example: It’s cold: I’m going to put on my sweater.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize annoyance, anger, or (sometimes) strong emotion like relief: « ce putain de… », « quel putain de… ». It’s extremely rude/vulgar in French (stronger than “damn”), so avoid it in polite situations. It usually comes right before a noun: « ce putain de temps », « la putain de porte ». Often used with « ce/cet/cette/ces » or « quel(le)(s) ».
target_language_example: J’en ai marre de ce putain de bruit.
native_language_example: I’m sick of this fucking noise.

meaning: Very strong vulgar swearword: “fucking shit!” / “for fuck’s sake!”
additional_notes: Used to express intense anger, frustration, or contempt. Extremely offensive and not appropriate in polite conversation. Often said as an exclamation on its own or added to an insult (e.g., “Va te faire foutre, putain de merde.”).
target_language_example: Putain de merde, j’ai encore raté le train !
native_language_example: Fucking shit, I missed the train again!

additional_notes: Refers to a man who has children and family responsibilities, often implying a respectable, responsible role. Common with être: « Je suis père de famille. » It can also be used after en (« en père de famille ») meaning “like a responsible family man / in a sensible, prudent way.”
target_language_example: Il agit en père de famille et pense d’abord à ses enfants.
native_language_example: He behaves like a responsible family man and thinks of his children first.

meaning: 'father is' (used to describe what someone's father is/does).
additional_notes: Often appears inside a longer sentence, especially with relatives like « dont » (whose): « une fille dont le père est avocat » = “a girl whose father is a lawyer.” You’ll usually add a job, nationality, or adjective after « est ».
target_language_example: C’est un garçon dont le père est professeur.
native_language_example: He’s a boy whose father is a teacher.

additional_notes: A very common pattern is with a possessive: « Mon père est mort. » Using « être » + « mort(e) » describes a state (is dead). With « mourir » (to die), French uses « être » in the past tense: « Mon père est mort » (he died / he is dead). « mort » agrees with the person: « ma mère est morte » (feminine).
target_language_example: Mon père est mort il y a dix ans.
native_language_example: My father died ten years ago.

meaning: to lose it; to flip out (suddenly get very angry or panic).
additional_notes: Very informal idiom. Literally evokes “blowing a fuse” (as in an electrical circuit). Used when someone suddenly snaps, gets furious, or can’t handle the stress anymore. Often used in the past tense: « Il/Elle a pété les plombs. » A close synonym is « péter un câble ».
target_language_example: Je vais péter les plombs si ça continue.
native_language_example: I’m going to lose it if this keeps up.

additional_notes: Usually appears in the pattern ne... qu' to mean 'only' or 'just'. qu'un is the form used before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel sound (qu'un = que + un). In everyday speech, the ne is often dropped: C'est qu'un boulot = Ce n'est qu'un boulot.
target_language_example: Ce n'était qu'un malentendu.
native_language_example: It was only a misunderstanding.

meaning: “only a / only one” (feminine), often in the **ne…que** restriction pattern.
additional_notes: **qu'** is the shortened form of **que** before a vowel sound (like **une**). **qu'une** commonly appears in **ne…que** (= “only”): *On n'a qu'une idée* (“We only have one idea”). It can also follow **c'est** to mean “it’s only…”: *C'est qu'une enfant* (“She’s only a child”).
target_language_example: C'est qu'une enfant.
native_language_example: She’s only a child.

additional_notes: Most often used with the restrictive pattern **ne ... que** (= “only/just”): *Je ne l’ai vu qu'une fois* (“I’ve only seen him once”). It can be used about past events (*je ne l’ai rencontré…*) or future actions (*je ne le demanderai qu'une fois*). Note the elision: **que + une** → **qu'une**.
target_language_example: Je ne l'ai rencontré qu'une fois.
native_language_example: I only met him once.

meaning: contraction of « que à » (often in « n’avoir qu’à » = “just have to / only need to”).
additional_notes: « Qu’à » is used instead of « que à » before a vowel sound. Very common in the pattern « (ne) … avoir qu’à + infinitive » to give a simple suggestion or instruction: « Tu n’as qu’à… » = “You just have to… / All you need to do is…”. It can also appear in fixed expressions like « n’en faire qu’à sa tête » (“to do only what one wants / be stubborn”).
target_language_example: Tu n'as qu'à cliquer ici.
native_language_example: You just have to click here.

additional_notes: A formal inversion question: « Qu’ » = « Que » (what) before a vowel, + « a » (has) + « -t- » for pronunciation, + « elle » (she) + « dit » (said). Used to ask what a woman/girl said; in everyday speech you’ll often hear « Elle a dit quoi ? » (more informal).
target_language_example: Qu'a-t-elle dit exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly did she say?

meaning: “what has he…?” / “what did he…?” (formal inverted question).
additional_notes: Used to ask a question with subject–verb inversion: que + a + t + il (= que a-t-il). The -t- is inserted for pronunciation when a verb ending in a vowel is followed by il/elle/on (a-t-il, a-t-elle, a-t-on). Common in writing and formal speech; in everyday conversation you often hear: « Qu’est-ce qu’il a… ? » or « Il a… quoi ? ».
target_language_example: Et qu'a-t-il répondu ?
native_language_example: And what did he reply?

meaning: “What did he do?” / “What has he done?”
additional_notes: A question in the passé composé (“a fait” = “has done/did”). This uses formal question inversion: “a-t-il” = “has he/did he” (the extra “-t-” is added for pronunciation). Common in writing or formal speech; in everyday speech you often hear: “Qu’est-ce qu’il a fait ?” or “Il a fait quoi ?”
target_language_example: Qu'a-t-il fait cette fois ?
native_language_example: What did he do this time?

meaning: “what does he have…?” / “what has he…?” (question form).
additional_notes:
Contraction of « que a-t-il »: « que » + « a » becomes « qu’a ». It uses inversion (« a-t-il ») to form a question. Common patterns include:
- « qu'a-t-il de + adjectif/nom ? »: asks what is special/remarkable about him (e.g., « Qu'a-t-il de spécial ? »).
- « qu'a-t-il de plus que… ? »: asks what he has more than someone else.
- « qu'a-t-il à voir avec… ? »: means “what does he have to do with…?”
target_language_example: Qu'a-t-il à voir avec ça ?
native_language_example: What does he have to do with that?

additional_notes: Uses the near-future tense: aller (vous allez) + infinitive (faire). The “qu’” is short for “que” before a vowel: “Que allez-vous faire ?” → “Qu’allez-vous faire ?”. Often followed by “de + [person/thing]” to mean “What are you going to do with him/her/them/me/us?” (e.g., Qu’allez-vous faire de moi ?).
target_language_example: Qu'allez-vous faire après le travail ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do after work?

additional_notes: Contraction of **que + as + tu** ("what" + "have" + "you"). Used to ask what someone has done/said/felt, usually with the **passé composé** (e.g., *Qu'as-tu fait ?*). It’s a common **inversion** question structure; **que** becomes **qu’** before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Qu'as-tu fait hier soir ?
native_language_example: What did you do last night?

meaning: "what did you do?" / "what have you done?"
additional_notes: A direct question using inversion (as-tu) in the passé composé: *faire* (to do) with *avoir* → *tu as fait*. Used to ask what someone did (often with a time phrase: *hier soir*, *tout ce temps*). With *de* + noun/pronoun (e.g., *Qu'as-tu fait de ma femme ?*), it often means “What did you do with/to …?” and can sound worried or accusatory depending on context.
target_language_example: Qu'as-tu fait pendant les vacances ?
native_language_example: What did you do during the vacation?

meaning: "what have you…?" / "what did you…?" (formal or plural).
additional_notes: Inversion of « vous avez » used to form a question, typically in the passé composé: « qu'avez-vous + participe passé ? ». It addresses one person formally (vous) or more than one person. A more neutral/less formal alternative is « Qu’est-ce que vous avez… ? »; with tu: « Qu’as-tu… ? ».
target_language_example: qu'avez-vous décidé ?
native_language_example: What did you decide?

additional_notes:
Used to ask about someone’s actions in the past, addressing one person formally (vous). Often followed by: 
- « Qu'avez-vous fait ensuite ? » = what you did next
- « Qu'avez-vous fait d’autre ? » = what else you did
- « Qu'avez-vous fait de + noun/pronoun ? » = what you did with something/someone (e.g., « Qu'avez-vous fait de lui ? » can imply “What did you do with him?/What happened to him?” depending on context).
target_language_example: Qu'avez-vous fait après le cours ?
native_language_example: What did you do after class?

meaning: “What did you do with…?” / “What have you done with…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what happened to someone or something, often with an accusatory, suspicious, or worried tone (implying it’s missing, has been taken, or has been mishandled). This is the formal or plural form (vous). Informal singular equivalent: « qu’as-tu fait de… ? »
target_language_example: Qu'avez-vous fait de toutes mes affaires ?
native_language_example: What did you do with all my stuff?

meaning: “what do you have to…?” (asking what someone has to say/think/do/hold/gain).
additional_notes: Formal question with inversion (“avez-vous”). It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., « qu'avez-vous à dire ? » = what do you have to say?) or certain set expressions with « à » like « à l’esprit » (in mind), « à la main » (in your hand/at hand), and « à y gagner » (to gain from it). In everyday speech, you’ll often hear « Qu’est-ce que vous avez à… ? » or « Vous avez quoi à… ? ».
target_language_example: qu'avez-vous à dire à ce sujet ?
native_language_example: What do you have to say about this?

meaning: "what did you have?" / "what had you...?" (formal question).
additional_notes: Contraction of « que aviez-vous ». « aviez-vous » is the formal/inverted question form of « vous aviez » (“you had/you used to have”). Used in polite/formal contexts (often written). Can also appear before another verb in the past: « Qu'aviez-vous fait ? » (“What had you done?”).
target_language_example: Qu'aviez-vous commandé ?
native_language_example: What did you order?

additional_notes: A clause meaning “(the thing) that she said.” It often appears after a word like **ce** to form **ce qu’elle a dit** (“what she said”): *Je n’ai pas compris ce qu’elle a dit.* Note the contraction **que + elle → qu’elle** to avoid two vowels in a row. On its own, you’ll more commonly use **elle a dit** (“she said”) as a complete clause, while **qu’elle a dit** typically depends on something before it (e.g., **ce** or a noun).
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas compris ce qu'elle a dit.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what she said.

additional_notes:
Contraction of « que » + « elle » → « qu'elle ».
Used after a main clause to introduce what she wants (often after verbs like « savoir », « dire », « demander », etc.). Depending on context, it can mean either “that she wants” (a relative clause) or “what she wants” (after something like « ce que » is implied or understood).
target_language_example: Je sais qu'elle veut partir.
native_language_example: I know that she wants to leave.

meaning: "What about…?" / "How about…?" (asking about the situation/status of someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to ask for an update or clarification about someone/something, often after discussing something else: « Et qu'en est-il de… ? » = “And what about…?”. Typically followed by « de + noun » or « de + stressed pronoun » (de vous / de toi / de lui / d’elle / de nous / d’eux). Fairly formal/neutral in tone; in casual speech, « et … alors ? » or « et … ? » may be used instead.
target_language_example: On a réglé ton problème ; et qu'en est-il de ta sœur ?
native_language_example: We solved your problem; and what about your sister?

additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the question patterns qu'est-ce que or qu'est-ce qui to ask "what...?". On its own, qu'est is not normally used as a complete expression.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu cherches ?
native_language_example: What are you looking for?

additional_notes:
Used at the start of many questions, usually followed by:
- **qu'est-ce que + subject + verb**: *Qu'est-ce que vous faites ?* (“What are you doing?”)
- **qu'est-ce qui + verb**: *Qu'est-ce qui va se passer ?* (“What is going to happen?”)
In casual spoken French, you may hear shortened forms like *Qu'est-ce t'as fait ?* (instead of *Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ?*).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qui va se passer ?
native_language_example: What is going to happen?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to mean “what…?” before a subject + verb. Fixed question structure: « qu'est-ce qu' + subject + verb ? » (e.g., « qu'est-ce qu'il… ? », « qu'est-ce qu'on… ? »). In very informal speech, « qu'est-ce qu'il y a ? » is often reduced to « qu'est-ce qu'y a ? ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il a voulu dire ?
native_language_example: What did he mean?

meaning: 'What's wrong with her?' or 'What does she have?'.
additional_notes: Literally “what is it that she has?”. Used to ask about her condition (“What’s wrong with her?”) or what she has/has on/has with her, depending on what follows: aux yeux (with her eyes), dans la tête (in her head/what’s she thinking), à la main (in her hand), de spécial (special). In speech, it’s often shortened to « Elle a quoi ? ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'elle a ? Elle a l'air malade.
native_language_example: What's wrong with her? She looks sick.

meaning: “what is he…?” / “what is it…?” / “what does he…?” (question opener with il).
additional_notes: Introduces a question where « il » means “he” or an impersonal “it” (e.g., about a situation). It’s part of the structure « Qu’est-ce que + subject + verb… ? » used to ask what someone is doing, wants, means, etc. Very common in speech; can sound like « kesk’il… ». Note: in careful writing it’s usually capitalized at the start of a sentence (« Qu’est-ce qu’il… ? »), but the fixed multi-word term is « qu'est-ce qu'il ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il veut dire ?
native_language_example: What does he mean? / What is he trying to say?

meaning: "What's wrong with him?" / "What does he have?" / "What's so special (about him/it)?"
additional_notes:
Used to ask what the problem is or what someone has (a symptom, a trait, an advantage, an idea). Often followed by a detail: 
- "Qu'est-ce qu'il a au visage ?" = what’s going on with his face?
- "Qu'est-ce qu'il a en tête ?" = what does he have in mind?
- "Qu'est-ce qu'il a de + adjective ?" (de bon / de spécial / de génial) = what’s good/special/great about him/it? (what makes him/it so ...?)
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il a de si intéressant, ce livre ?
native_language_example: What’s so interesting about this book?

additional_notes: Very common way to ask what is happening, often because something seems wrong, unexpected, or urgent. Literally “what is it that is happening,” but used idiomatically as “what’s going on?” Can be used on its own or to address someone directly (e.g., adding a name or “les gars”). Note the informal contraction in speech/writing: « qu'est-ce » (from « que est-ce »).
target_language_example: Attends, qu'est-ce qu'il se passe ?
native_language_example: Wait, what’s going on?

meaning: 'what's wrong/what happened?' / 'what’s there?' / 'what does it say?' (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Very common question built on **il y a** (“there is/are”). Use it to ask:
- **What happened / what’s wrong?**: *Qu'est-ce qu'il y a ?* / *Qu'est-ce qu'il y a eu ?*
- **What does it say (written)?**: *Qu'est-ce qu'il y a marqué ?* / *Qu'est-ce qu'il y a écrit ?*
- **What is he doing there?**: *Qu'est-ce qu'il y fait ?* (**y** = “there” or “in it”)
- **What does he know about it?**: *Qu'est-ce qu'il y connaît ?* (**y** = “about it / in it”).
In casual speech it’s often shortened: **Qu'est-ce qu'y a ?**
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il y a écrit sur la porte ?
native_language_example: What does it say on the door?

meaning: "What’s the matter?" / "What is it?" / "What’s going on?" / sometimes literally "What’s there?"
additional_notes: Very common question whose meaning depends on context. On its own ("qu'est-ce qu'il y a ?"), it usually means "What’s wrong?" or "What’s going on?" You can also add a complement to ask what is present somewhere: "qu'est-ce qu'il y a dehors ?" (what’s outside?), "qu'est-ce qu'il y a là-dessous ?" (what’s underneath?), or "qu'est-ce qu'il y a d'autre/de mieux ?" (what else/better is there?). Literally it’s like "what is it that there is," but in natural English you usually translate it as "What’s the matter?" or "What’s going on?"
target_language_example: Dis-moi, qu'est-ce qu'il y a ? Tu as l’air inquiet.
native_language_example: Tell me, what’s wrong? You look worried.

additional_notes: Literally “what is it that we have.” Used when you’re looking at something and taking stock (“So, what have we got here?”), or to ask what the situation/problem is (often said by a doctor/teacher/parent: “So, what’s the matter/what’s happening?”). Commonly followed by ici/là (“here/there”) or d’autre (“else”).
target_language_example: Bon, qu'est-ce qu'on a aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: So, what have we got today?

meaning: “What can we do?” / “What can we do about it?”
additional_notes:
A very common question used to ask for options, solutions, or help. Literally “what is it that we can do,” with the general subject on = “we/people/you” depending on context. You can add details:
- Qu'est-ce qu'on peut faire pour toi ? = How can we help you?
- Qu'est-ce qu'on peut faire d'autre / de plus ? = What else / what more can we do?
target_language_example: Il n'y a plus de billets—qu'est-ce qu'on peut faire ?
native_language_example: There are no tickets left—what can we do?

meaning: 'what…?' / 'what is it that…?' (question opener before a vowel sound).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a direct question, followed by a subject + verb: « Qu'est-ce qu'il faisait ? » = “What was he doing?” It’s the shortened form of « qu’est-ce que », used before a vowel sound (qu’est-ce qu’il…, qu’est-ce qu’elle…). Often interchangeable with inversion (more formal): « Que faisait-il ? ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'on mange ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are we eating tonight?

meaning: 'What is she…?' (used to start a question about what she is doing/saying, etc.).
additional_notes: This is the question starter "qu'est-ce que" + "elle" (she). It’s usually followed by a verb: « Qu'est-ce qu'elle fait ? » = “What is she doing?” You can use it when you don’t do subject–verb inversion (instead of « Que fait-elle ? »).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'elle veut dire ?
native_language_example: What does she mean?

additional_notes: A common question asking for the content of what a woman/girl said. Often followed by details: d'autre (else), exactement (exactly), sur moi (about me). In careful writing you may see: « Qu'a-t-elle dit ? » (more formal/inverted).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'elle a dit au professeur ?
native_language_example: What did she say to the teacher?

meaning: “what … has he/it …?” / “what did he/it …?” (question starter with **il** = “he/it”).
additional_notes: Contraction of **qu’est-ce que + il** → **qu’est-ce qu’il**. Used to introduce a question when the subject is **il** (“he/it”), followed by a verb: **qu'est-ce qu'il + verb … ?** Example patterns: *qu'est-ce qu'il fait ?* (“what is he doing?”), *qu'est-ce qu'il a dit ?* (“what did he say?”). Note: For “What happened?”, standard French is **Qu'est-ce qui s'est passé ?** (not *qu'est-ce qu'il s'est passé ?*).
target_language_example: qu'est-ce qu'il lui a fait ?
native_language_example: What did he do to him/her?

meaning: “What is he saying?” / “What does he say?”
additional_notes: A very common way to ask what a man (il) is saying. Often used by itself as a question (Qu’est-ce qu’il dit ?) or with an extra detail: d’autre = “else” (Qu’est-ce qu’il dit d’autre ?). For a woman, use: Qu’est-ce qu’elle dit ?
target_language_example: Je n'entends pas bien : qu'est-ce qu'il dit ?
native_language_example: I can’t hear well—what is he saying?

meaning: "What is he doing?" / "What does he do?"
additional_notes: Common way to ask a question with *qu'est-ce que* + subject + verb. In these examples it usually means "What is he doing?" (right now), especially with context like *là-bas/là-haut* or *au juste* ("exactly"). Without context, it can also mean "What does he do?" (as a job), but you'd often add something like *dans la vie ?* to make that clear.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il fait dehors à cette heure-ci ?
native_language_example: What is he doing outside at this time?

additional_notes: A very common way to ask what is happening (often because something seems wrong or surprising). It’s neutral (not slang). You can add a place or time: « qu'est-ce qu'il se passe en bas ? » (downstairs), « …là ? » (there), « …maintenant ? » (now). In faster or more standard speech, you may also hear « qu'est-ce qui se passe ? » (same meaning).
target_language_example: Maman, qu'est-ce qu'il se passe ?
native_language_example: Mom, what’s happening?

meaning: "what did he … to you?" / "what did he … you?" (start of a question).
additional_notes: Used before a verb to ask what a man (il = he) did/asked/took from someone (t' = short for te, “to you”). It’s the shortened form of « Qu’est-ce qu’il te… ». In full questions you’ll usually see it followed by an auxiliary like « a » or « est »: « Qu’est-ce qu’il t’a demandé ? », « Qu’est-ce qu’il t’est arrivé ? ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il t'a dit exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly did he say to you?

meaning: “what is he going to…?” (asking what he will do / what will happen to him).
additional_notes: Used to start a question about what a man/boy is going to do or what’s going to happen next. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (faire, devenir, arriver, etc.) or by a pronoun + infinitive (lui faire). Very common in spoken French. (Variants: qu’est-ce que je vais…, qu’est-ce qu’elle va…, qu’est-ce qu’ils vont….)
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il va dire à ses parents ?
native_language_example: What is he going to say to his parents?

additional_notes: A common way to ask what a man/boy wants (his intention, request, or goal). Often followed by an infinitive (Qu'est-ce qu'il veut faire ? = What does he want to do?) or by a clause with "que" + subjunctive to ask what he wants someone to do (Qu'est-ce qu'il veut que je fasse ? = What does he want me to do?). Adding "lui" (Qu'est-ce qu'il veut, lui ?) can sound more pointed: "What does he want, him?" / "What’s his problem?"
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas : qu'est-ce qu'il veut exactement ?
native_language_example: I don’t understand: what does he want exactly?

meaning: “What is he doing …?” / “What has he come to do …?”
additional_notes: Fixed question pattern used to challenge or question someone’s presence or actions: **Qu’est-ce que + subject + venir + infinitive ?** After **vient**, you normally add an infinitive (often **faire**, but also **dire**, **chercher**, etc.), and optionally a place word like **ici / là / là-dedans**. It often carries a slightly critical or suspicious tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il vient faire ici ?
native_language_example: What has he come to do here? / What is he doing here?

additional_notes: Used to begin a question meaning “what” when the subject is ils (“they”). It’s the common spoken pattern: Qu’est-ce que + subject + verb. The verb tense changes the meaning (present, past, future): Qu’est-ce qu’ils font ? / Qu’est-ce qu’ils ont fait ? / Qu’est-ce qu’ils feront ?
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'ils veulent exactement ?
native_language_example: What do they want exactly?

additional_notes: Common spoken question asking about what “they” (ils) are doing. Often followed by a place or time word (ici, là, là-haut, maintenant). Can also be used in a broader/critical sense with a complement, e.g., “Qu'est-ce qu'ils font de nous ?” = “What are they doing with/to us?”
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'ils font ici ?
native_language_example: What are they doing here?

meaning: “what did they … to you / for you?” (question starter).
additional_notes: Used to start a question in the past tense with “they” (ils) and an indirect/direct object pronoun “to you” (t’ = te). It’s short for “Qu’est-ce que ils t’ont … ?” and is followed by a past participle: demandé (asked), dit (said), donné (given), fait (done).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'ils t'ont raconté ?
native_language_example: What did they tell you?

meaning: "What are they going to…?" (start of a question).
additional_notes: Used to ask what “they” (ils) are about to do. It’s followed by an infinitive: « Qu'est-ce qu'ils vont faire ? » (“What are they going to do?”). This uses the near-future « aller + infinitive » (ils vont + verb). « Qu’est-ce que » introduces a question without inversion; in speech it’s often pronounced with a /k/ sound: « qu’est-ce qu’ils vont… ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'ils vont dire quand ils l'apprendront ?
native_language_example: What are they going to say when they find out?

additional_notes: Very common question starter: « qu'est-ce que » + subject. Here the subject is « on », which can mean “we,” “you” (informal/general), “people,” or “one,” depending on context. It’s typically followed by a verb: « qu'est-ce qu'on fait ? » = “What do we do?” In expressions like « qu'est-ce qu'on y peut ? », « y » means “about it/there,” giving “What can we do about it/What can we do?”
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'on y peut ?
native_language_example: What can we do about it?

meaning: "what do we have?" / "what’s going on?" / "what’s wrong?" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “what is it that we have.” Used to ask (1) what’s available / what options there are (« Qu'est-ce qu'on a comme options ? »), (2) what you’ve got/what’s there (« Qu'est-ce qu'on a là ? »), or (3) what the matter is / what’s happening (« Qu'est-ce qu'on a ? »), often said to someone who seems unwell or upset. In careful writing this is commonly spelled with apostrophes: « Qu'est-ce qu'on a ? ».
target_language_example: Tu as l’air fatigué… Qu'est-ce qu'on a ?
native_language_example: You look tired… what’s wrong?

meaning: "what are we" / "what are we supposed to be/do" (start of a question).
additional_notes: This is the question pattern **qu’est-ce que + subject + être**. Here **on** often means **“we”** (or sometimes “people/one”), and **est** is singular because **on** is grammatically singular in French. It’s very commonly followed by **censé(e)(s)** or **supposé(e)(s)**: *Qu'est-ce qu'on est censé faire ?* = “What are we supposed to do?” In *Qu'est-ce qu'on est ?*, it can mean “What are we?” (e.g., what are we to each other?) or “What are we?” (identity/classification), depending on context.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'on est censés faire ?
native_language_example: What are we supposed to do?

meaning: "What do we do?" / "What are we supposed to do?"
additional_notes: A very common question to ask what to do next, what the plan is, or how to handle a situation. It can refer to the present moment (Maintenant, qu'est-ce qu'on fait ?), the next step (Qu'est-ce qu'on fait après ?), or what to do with something (Qu'est-ce qu'on fait avec ça ?). "On" here usually means "we" in everyday French (instead of "nous"). Tone can range from neutral planning to worried/urgent depending on context.
target_language_example: Bon, qu'est-ce qu'on fait maintenant ?
native_language_example: So, what do we do now?

meaning: “What are we going to…?” / “What’s going to happen (for us)…?”
additional_notes: Used to start a question about what “we” (on = we/people in general) are going to do, often expressing concern, uncertainty, or trying to figure out the next step. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (faire, devenir, dire, etc.), sometimes after a modal like pouvoir: « qu'est-ce qu'on va pouvoir faire ? ». In speech, « qu'est-ce qu'on » is often pronounced roughly like “kesskon”.
target_language_example: qu'est-ce qu'on va faire avec ça ?
native_language_example: What are we going to do with that?

meaning: What are we going to do?
additional_notes: Common way to ask what the next step or solution is, often showing worry, confusion, or urgency. Uses “on” (= “we” in everyday French) instead of the more formal “nous”: “Qu’est-ce que nous allons faire ?”. Can be followed by “avec + person/thing” (what are we going to do with her/him/it?) or “de + pronoun” (what are we going to do about them?).
target_language_example: Il pleut et on n’a pas de parapluie… qu'est-ce qu'on va faire ?
native_language_example: It’s raining and we don’t have an umbrella… what are we going to do?

additional_notes: Used to ask 'what' at the start of a direct question, usually followed by normal subject-verb order: qu'est-ce que tu fais ? It is very common in spoken and everyday French. A more formal alternative is inversion, as in que fais-tu ?
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu veux manger ?
native_language_example: What do you want to eat?

meaning: 'What is it?' / 'What is that?' (also: 'What does that mean?').
additional_notes: Common question to ask what something is. Often followed by a noun: « Qu'est-ce que c'est, un jeu ? » = “What is a game?” You’ll also hear emphatic/annoyed versions like « Qu'est-ce que c'est que ça ? » (“What is that?” / “What’s this supposed to be?”) and with « supposé »: « Qu'est-ce que c'est supposé dire/vouloir dire ? » = “What is that supposed to mean?”
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, qu'est-ce que c'est ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is it?

meaning: “what is it supposed to…?” (often: “what’s that supposed to mean?”).
additional_notes: Used to question the purpose or meaning of something, typically with a verb after it: « Qu'est-ce que c'est censé dire / prouver / signifier / être ? ». « Censé » means “supposed to” or “meant to” and agrees with « c’ » (= « cela »). Often carries a skeptical or annoyed tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que c'est censé faire, ce bouton ?
native_language_example: What is this button supposed to do?

additional_notes: A question used to react to or ask about something you’re seeing/encountering, often with surprise, annoyance, or disbelief. It’s commonly followed by a noun phrase with a demonstrative (ce/cet/cette/ces): « Qu’est-ce que c’est que ce truc ? » = “What is this thing?” More neutral alternatives are « Qu’est-ce que c’est ? » or « C’est quoi ? » (informal).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que c'est que ce bruit ?
native_language_example: What is that noise?

additional_notes: Used to ask for identification or clarification about something in the past (a noise, an event, an object, a situation). Often used on its own, or with add-ons like « déjà » (“again / remind me”): « Qu'est-ce que c'était déjà ? » = “What was it again?” You can also add « que ça » or « ça » for emphasis: « Qu'est-ce que c'était que ça ? » / « Qu'est-ce que c'était ça ? » = “What was that?”
target_language_example: J’ai entendu un bruit… qu'est-ce que c'était ?
native_language_example: I heard a noise… what was that?

meaning: "what does that…?" / "what is that…?" (used to start a question).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the meaning, cause, or nature of something previously mentioned. It’s a more formal/neutral alternative to "qu’est-ce que ça". It’s typically followed by a verb: "Qu’est-ce que cela signifie ?" (What does that mean?), "Qu’est-ce que cela implique ?" (What does that involve/entail?).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que cela veut dire exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly does that mean?

meaning: "What am I…? / What did I…?" (start of a question with “I”).
additional_notes: Used to form a question with “je” (I). It comes from the common question pattern “Qu’est-ce que + subject + verb… ?”. Here, “je” becomes “j’” before a vowel or silent h: j’attends, j’oublie, j’écris, j’ai… Often translates as “what do I…?” or “what am I going to…?” depending on the tense.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que j'ai fait ?
native_language_example: What did I do?

meaning: “What did I…?” / “What have I…?” (used to ask what you did/said/missed, often with surprise or confusion).
additional_notes: Introduces a question where « j’ai » is typically followed by a past participle (passé composé): « qu'est-ce que j'ai dit/fait/raté ? ». Often conveys surprise, confusion, or mild frustration—especially with « encore » (“again”): « Qu'est-ce que j'ai encore fait ? ». Literally “what is it that I have…”, but the natural English rendering is usually “What did I…?”. Note: correct spelling is « Qu'est-ce que j'ai fait ? » (not « j'ai fais », which is a common mistake).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que j'ai encore dit ?
native_language_example: What did I say again?

meaning: "What have I done?" / "What did I do (with it/them)?"
additional_notes: A common question meaning you’re confused, worried, or regretful about something you did. It can also be used when you can’t find something: "Qu'est-ce que j'ai fait de + [thing/person] ?" = "What did I do with ...? / Where did I put ...?" Adding "encore" (again) emphasizes annoyance: "What have I done now?"
target_language_example: Oh non… qu'est-ce que j'ai fait de mes clés ?
native_language_example: Oh no… what did I do with my keys?

meaning: 'What do I have?' / 'What's wrong with me?'.
additional_notes: Literally "what is it that I have". Used to ask what you have (in your pocket, with you, etc.) or, by extension, what is the matter with you/me. Often followed by extra details: "Qu'est-ce que j'ai d'autre ?" (What else do I have?), "Qu'est-ce que j'ai dans ma poche ?" (What do I have in my pocket?), "Qu'est-ce que j'ai à y gagner ?" (What do I get out of it?/What’s in it for me?).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que j'ai dans mon sac ?
native_language_example: What do I have in my bag?

meaning: “what do I … with it/them?” or “what do I … about it/them?”
additional_notes: This is the start of a question and it must be completed with a verb: e.g., « Qu'est-ce que j'en fais ? » (What do I do with it?), « Qu'est-ce que j'en pense ? » (What do I think about it?). The pronoun « en » usually refers to “of it / about it” or replaces something introduced by « de » (e.g., « de ça », « de ce livre »), and sometimes can mean “some/any” depending on the verb. Word order: « Qu’est-ce que + subject + en + verb ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que j'en fais, de ces papiers ?
native_language_example: What do I do with these papers?

meaning: "What do I … about it?" / "What can I do about it?" (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: This is the start of a question pattern: « Qu'est-ce que j'y + verbe ? » The pronoun « y » usually means “about it” / “to it” / “there” and refers back to something already mentioned. Common with verbs like « connaître » (Qu'est-ce que j'y connais ? = What do I know about it?), « gagner » (What do I get out of it?), and « pouvoir » (What can I do about it?). Often used rhetorically to show you don’t know, don’t benefit, or can’t change anything.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que j'y peux si ce n'est pas de ma faute ?
native_language_example: What can I do about it if it’s not my fault?

meaning: “What was I…?” (often used to ask what you were supposed/expected to do, say, or be).
additional_notes:
Used at the start of a question. Built on the imperfect tense "j’étais" (“I was”), so it typically refers to a past situation or expectation. Very often followed by:
- "censé / censée" = supposed/expected to (common)
- "supposé / supposée" = supposed to
Note: "sensé" (without "c") usually means “sensible/meaningful”; it’s frequently written by mistake when people mean "censé". Remember agreement: "censé/supposé" change with gender (censé/censée, supposé/supposée).
target_language_example: qu'est-ce que j'étais censé dire ?
native_language_example: What was I supposed to say?

meaning: “what am I…?” / “what do I…?” (to start a question about yourself).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question with “je” (I), followed by a verb: “Qu’est-ce que je fais ?” = “What am I doing?” It’s a very common, neutral way to form questions in spoken French. Before a vowel sound, “que” becomes “qu’” (qu’est-ce que).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que je peux faire pour t'aider ?
native_language_example: What can I do to help you?

meaning: "What am I saying?" / "What do I say?"
additional_notes: A question used either (1) literally to ask what you should say (often followed by à + someone: « qu'est-ce que je dis au médecin ? », « qu'est-ce que je dis aux autres ? »), or (2) rhetorically to react to what you just said (« qu'est-ce que je dis là ? » = “What am I saying?”). With « toujours », it can mean “What do I always say?” In « Vas-y, qu'est-ce que je dis ? », it can be used to prompt someone to repeat/confirm what you always say (“Go on—what do I say?”).
target_language_example: Je suis perdu… qu'est-ce que je dis au médecin ?
native_language_example: I’m lost… what do I say to the doctor?

meaning: "What should I / do I have to ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask what you are supposed/expected to do. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: « Qu'est-ce que je dois faire ? / dire ? / répondre ? ». Uses the verb « devoir » (je dois = I must / I have to / I should). A more formal alternative is « Que dois-je ... ? ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que je dois faire maintenant ?
native_language_example: What should I do now?

meaning: “What am I supposed to do?” / “What should I do?”
additional_notes: A common way to ask for instructions or guidance. Literally “what is it that I must do,” but in everyday English it’s usually “What should I do?” You can add time words like maintenant (now), alors (then/so), ensuite (next), or specify an object with de + noun: Qu'est-ce que je dois faire de ça ? = “What should I do with that?”
target_language_example: Je suis perdu : qu'est-ce que je dois faire ?
native_language_example: I'm lost—what should I do?

meaning: 'What am I doing?' / 'What should I do?'
additional_notes: Very common question using the pattern « qu’est-ce que + subject + verb » to mean “what…?”. It can be literal (asking what you’re doing), but is also often used rhetorically to express confusion, doubt, or “What am I supposed to do now?” (often with « ici », « maintenant », « alors »). It can also take complements: « qu'est-ce que je fais avec toi ? » = “What am I doing with you?” / “What should I do with you?”, « qu'est-ce que je fais de toi ? » = “What am I going to do with you?” / “What should I do with you?”.
target_language_example: Mon Dieu, qu'est-ce que je fais ?
native_language_example: Oh God, what should I do?

meaning: "What would I do…?" / "What on earth would I do…?"
additional_notes: A question in the conditional (je ferais = “I would do”), often used rhetorically to express uncertainty or dependence: « Qu'est-ce que je ferais sans toi ? » (“What would I do without you?”). It can be followed by a complement like « en tournée » (on tour), « d'autre » (else), « de vous » (with you/what would I do with you), or « sans toi/vous » (without you).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que je ferais sans toi ?
native_language_example: What would I do without you?

additional_notes: Used to ask what you are able/allowed to do or say. Commonly followed by an infinitive (dire, faire, répondre, etc.). Often expresses uncertainty or helplessness, especially in phrases like “Qu’est-ce que je peux y faire ?” (“What can I do about it?”).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que je peux faire pour t'aider ?
native_language_example: What can I do to help you?

additional_notes: A common question used to ask what action you should take, or how you can help someone. Often followed by: d'autre / de plus (“else / more”), or pour + person (“for you”): « Qu'est-ce que je peux faire pour toi/vous ? ». « Je peux » means “I can” (ability/possibility).
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, qu'est-ce que je peux faire pour vous aider ?
native_language_example: I'm sorry—what can I do to help you?

meaning: 'what am I…?' (used to ask what you’re supposed to do/understand, etc.).
additional_notes: This is the start of a question meaning “What am I…?” It’s very often followed by **censé(e)** or **supposé(e)** + an infinitive: **Qu'est-ce que je suis censé(e) faire ?** = “What am I supposed to do?” The ending agrees with the speaker: **censé / supposé** (male) vs **censée / supposée** (female). Note: **sensé** (with an *s*) means “sensible/reasonable” and is often a misspelling of **censé** in this structure.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que je suis censée faire ?
native_language_example: What am I supposed to do?

additional_notes: Used to ask what you are expected to do/say in a situation, often when you’re unsure, confused, or frustrated. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: « Qu’est-ce que je suis censé faire/dire ? ». If the speaker is female, you often see « censée » (with -e).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que je suis censé faire dans cette situation ?
native_language_example: What am I supposed to do in this situation?

meaning: “What am I going to…?” (used to ask what you will do/say/become next).
additional_notes: Introduces a question about your next action, what will happen to you, or what you should do—often with uncertainty, worry, or needing to decide. It is typically followed by an infinitive (faire, dire, mettre, devenir, etc.). Very common with pronouns like "en" (Qu'est-ce que je vais en faire ? = What am I going to do with it?) or an indirect object like "leur" (Qu'est-ce que je vais leur dire ? = What am I going to tell them?).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que je vais faire sans toi ?
native_language_example: What am I going to do without you?

additional_notes: A common, often emotional way to ask what to do next (worry, panic, frustration). It can also mean “What am I going to do with…?” when followed by de + noun/pronoun: Qu'est-ce que je vais faire de ça/de vous ? Adding moi emphasizes “me” (what about me?).
target_language_example: Je suis en retard… qu'est-ce que je vais faire ?
native_language_example: I’m late… what am I going to do?

meaning: "What can I … for you?" / "What did I tell you?" (question starter: “What … I … you?”).
additional_notes: Used to start a question where the speaker (je) is doing/saying something to “you” (vous). It’s typically followed by a verb: qu’est-ce que je vous offre ? (What can I offer you?), qu’est-ce que je vous sers ? (What can I get you to drink/serve you?), qu’est-ce que je vous disais ? (What was I telling you?). Very common in polite situations because vous is formal/plural “you.”
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que je vous apporte ?
native_language_example: What can I bring you?

meaning: “what do you…?” (with “tu” contracted to “t’” before a vowel sound).
additional_notes: Common spoken/colloquial form of “Qu’est-ce que tu… ?” used to ask questions. “t’” is the contraction of “tu” before a verb beginning with a vowel or silent h (e.g., t’aimes, t’as, t’écris). Often avoided in careful writing in favor of “Qu’est-ce que tu… ?”.
target_language_example: qu'est-ce que t'aimes ?
native_language_example: What do you like?

meaning: “what have you…?” / “what did you…?” (informal spoken form of « qu’est-ce que tu as »).
additional_notes: « t’as » is a contraction of « tu as ». Very common in speech and casual writing. Often followed by a past participle to form a question in the passé composé: « qu'est-ce que t'as mangé ? » = “What did you eat?” In careful writing, use « qu’est-ce que tu as… ? ». Note: in standard French you’d write « qu'est-ce que t'as dit ? » (not *dis*) and « qu'est-ce que t'as fait ? » (not *fais*).
target_language_example: qu'est-ce que t'as mangé ?
native_language_example: What did you eat?

meaning: "What did you do?" / "What have you done?"
additional_notes: Very common spoken (informal) way to say « Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ? ». Uses the contraction « t'as » = « tu as ». Often used to ask what someone did earlier (neutral) or to react to something they did (can sound accusing: “What have you done?!”).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que t'as fait pour te retrouver dans cette situation ?
native_language_example: What did you do to end up in this situation?

meaning: Informal: “what do you have…?” / “what’s wrong (with you)?”
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of « qu’est-ce que tu as ». Used to ask what someone has on them or what’s happening (often: what’s wrong). It’s frequently followed by a complement: « au bras » (on your arm), « sur ta chemise » (on your shirt), « à dire » (to say), or « d’autre » (else). More formal: « Qu’est-ce que tu as… ? »
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que t'as ? Tu as l'air fatigué.
native_language_example: What’s wrong? You look tired.

meaning: Informal: “What’s wrong with you / Why are you …?” or “What do you have …?”
additional_notes: Spoken, informal contraction of « Qu’est-ce que tu as à… » (t’as = tu as). With a noun/body part/place, it often means “What’s the matter with …?” or “What do you have … (in/on)?”: Qu'est-ce que t'as à la main ? (“What do you have in your hand?”), Qu'est-ce que t'as à la tête ? (“What’s wrong with your head?” / “What’s the matter with your head?”). With à + infinitive, it commonly means “Why are you …?” / “What are you … for?” and can sound challenging/accusatory: Qu'est-ce que t'as à me mater ? (“Why are you staring at me?”). A more neutral/formal alternative is « Pourquoi tu… ? » or « Qu’est-ce que tu as ? » (“What’s the matter?”).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que t'as à la main ?
native_language_example: What do you have in your hand?

meaning: “what do you … about it?” (informal: “what do you … of it?”).
additional_notes: Colloquial start of a question, usually followed by a verb: « Qu'est-ce que t'en dis ? » (What do you say about it? / What do you think?), « Qu'est-ce que t'en penses ? » (What do you think of it?), « Qu'est-ce que t'en sais ? » (What do you know about it?). Here « t' » = « tu » and « en » often means “about it / of it” and refers to something already mentioned. More standard: « Qu'est-ce que tu en … ? » or « Qu'en …-tu ? ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que t'en penses, toi ?
native_language_example: What do you think about it?

additional_notes: Common spoken way to ask someone’s opinion. Here, "t'" = "tu" (you) and "en" means "about it / about that" (referring to something already mentioned). More neutral/full form: "Qu'est-ce que tu en penses ?" Also common: "Tu en penses quoi ?"
target_language_example: J'ai changé le plan pour demain : qu'est-ce que t'en penses ?
native_language_example: I changed tomorrow’s plan—what do you think about it?

additional_notes: Very common question starter used before a verb: « Qu'est-ce que tu + verb… ? » (informal singular “you”). It corresponds to English word order like “What do you want/like/choose…?” Often translates naturally as “What are you…?” or “What do you…?” depending on the verb. More formal: « Qu'est-ce que vous… ? ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight?

additional_notes: A common way to ask someone what they like. It can stand alone (Qu'est-ce que tu aimes ?) or be followed by an infinitive (Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire ? = “What do you like to do?”) or by a topic/context (Qu'est-ce que tu aimes dans la musique ? = “What do you like in music?”).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu aimes manger au petit-déjeuner ?
native_language_example: What do you like to eat for breakfast?

meaning: “what have you … ?” (asking what someone has done/decided/eaten/written, etc.).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question: "Qu'est-ce que" = “what”, and "tu as" is the start of the past tense with avoir (passé composé) for "tu" (“you have”). You typically finish it with a past participle: "Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ?" (“What did you do?”). In speech, it’s often shortened to "Qu’est-ce que t’as … ?".
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu as préparé pour le dîner ?
native_language_example: What did you prepare for dinner?

meaning: 'What did you do?' / 'What have you done?'
additional_notes: A very common way to ask what someone did in the past (passé composé: "tu as fait" = "you did / you have done"). Often said with emotion (surprise, worry, anger), and it can be a rhetorical question after something happened.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What did you do this weekend?

meaning: "What do you have…?" / "What’s the matter with you?"
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone has (on them, in a place, or as a problem/symptom), usually followed by extra information: a place (dans ton sac), a body part (à l’œil), or a time (en ce moment). It can also mean “What’s wrong with you?” depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu as au bras ?
native_language_example: What’s wrong with your arm? / What do you have on your arm?

meaning: "What do you have on your …?" / "What’s wrong with your …?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about something on a body part (a ring, bracelet, mark, injury, etc.) or what’s bothering it. The pattern is: « Qu’est-ce que tu as au + [masculine singular body part] ? » where « au » = « à + le » (e.g., au bras, au cou, au doigt, au poignet, au visage). With feminine body parts you’d use « à la » (e.g., à la main), and with plural « aux » (e.g., aux yeux).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu as au doigt ?
native_language_example: What do you have on your finger?

meaning: "What do you have to…?" / "Why are you…?" (often challenging).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone has to do/say/offer, or to challenge/criticize someone’s behavior. Often followed by an infinitive: « Qu'est-ce que tu as à me dire ? » (“What do you have to tell me?”). It can also be followed by a noun in set expressions like « Qu'est-ce que tu as à la tête ? » (“What have you got on your head?”). Tone can sound accusatory depending on context.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu as à me parler comme ça ?
native_language_example: Why are you talking to me like that?

meaning: "What are you waiting for?" / "What do you expect (from me/us)?"
additional_notes: Built with **attendre**, which can mean **to wait** or **to expect** depending on context. On its own (no object), it usually means “What are you waiting for?” and can sound impatient or urging someone to act. With **de + person/pronoun** (e.g., *Qu'est-ce que tu attends de moi ?*), it means “What do you expect from me?” Note: **attendre** is a false friend of English **attend** (go to an event).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu attends pour partir ?
native_language_example: What are you waiting for to leave?

meaning: “What do you think…?” / “What do you think you’re doing?” (often challenging or annoyed, depending on tone).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French to question or challenge someone’s idea, assumption, or behavior. Often followed by an infinitive (Qu'est-ce que tu crois faire ? = “What do you think you’re doing?”) or by a clause with que (Qu'est-ce que tu crois qu'il va se passer ? = “What do you think is going to happen?”). On its own (Qu'est-ce que tu crois ?), it can mean “What do you think?” or “What did you expect?” depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu crois faire ?
native_language_example: What do you think you’re doing?

meaning: "What are you saying?" / "What did you say?" (often surprised or skeptical).
additional_notes: Direct question using informal "tu". Depending on tone, it can be a simple request to repeat, or show disbelief/annoyance. With "de ça" (Qu'est-ce que tu dis de ça ?), it often means "What do you think about that?" or "What do you say to that?" With "là" (Qu'est-ce que tu dis là ?), it emphasizes "right now/there" and can sound more critical.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu dis ? Je n'ai pas bien entendu.
native_language_example: What did you say? I didn’t hear well.

meaning: "What do you ... about it?" / "What do you ... of it?" (asking your opinion, conclusion, or knowledge).
additional_notes: This is the start of a question pattern followed by a verb: « Qu'est-ce que tu en penses ? » (What do you think about it?), « Qu'est-ce que tu en dis ? » (What do you say about it?), « Qu'est-ce que tu en sais ? » (What do you know about it?), « Qu'est-ce que tu en conclus ? » (What do you conclude from it?). The pronoun « en » often means “about it / of it / from it” and refers back to something already mentioned.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu en penses, toi ?
native_language_example: What do you think about it, you?

meaning: “What do you think about it?” / “What’s your opinion?”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion about something that was just mentioned.  “en” refers back to “it/that” (an idea, plan, situation, etc.). You can add “toi” for emphasis (“you, what do you think?”). Often preceded by connectors like “Alors,” “Donc,” or “Et”.
target_language_example: J'hésite entre ces deux restaurants : qu'est-ce que tu en penses ?
native_language_example: I’m hesitating between these two restaurants—what do you think?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is attempting to do or say, often because you don’t understand their intention or message. It’s made of: « Qu’est-ce que » (what) + « tu essaies de » (you’re trying to) + infinitive verb (dire, faire, prouver, etc.). Can also be followed by an indirect object: « de me dire » = “to tell me”.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu essaies de m'expliquer ?
native_language_example: What are you trying to explain to me?

meaning: "What are you doing?" / "What are you up to?" (often with surprise or annoyance).
additional_notes: Literally it’s “what is it that you are making/fabricating?”, but in everyday French it often means “what are you doing?”—especially when the speaker thinks you shouldn’t be there, you’re doing something strange, or they don’t understand what you’re doing. Very common with a place word: « Qu’est-ce que tu fabriques ici / là-haut / par ici ? » (“What are you doing here / up there / around here?”).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu fabriques dans ma chambre ?
native_language_example: What are you doing in my room?

meaning: “What are you doing?” / “What do you do?” (informal singular).
additional_notes: A very common way to ask someone (one person you address as tu) what they’re doing right now, what they usually do, or what they’re doing at a specific time (e.g., demain soir). Often expresses surprise or concern (“Wait—what are you doing?”). More formal: « Qu’est-ce que vous faites ? » More neutral/standard: « Que fais-tu ? »
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What are you doing this weekend?

additional_notes: Used to express surprise, impatience, or reproach that someone is still doing something or is still in a place. Often followed by a location or situation: « ici / là » (here/there), « debout » (up/awake), etc. In more formal situations, you’d use « Qu’est-ce que vous faites encore… ? ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu fais encore au bureau à cette heure-ci ?
native_language_example: What are you still doing at the office at this hour?

additional_notes: A very common question to ask why someone is in a place (often expressing surprise). Informal singular "tu"; for a more formal or plural version, use "Qu'est-ce que vous faites ici ?". You can add details after it, e.g., "Qu'est-ce que tu fais ici, à Rome ?".
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ici si tôt ?
native_language_example: What are you doing here so early?

meaning: “What are you doing there / here?” (often: “What are you doing here?!”).
additional_notes: A common spoken question expressing surprise or suspicion about someone being in a place or situation. "là" can mean “there” or “here” depending on context; in these examples it often implies “here” (e.g., outside, so late/early). You can add details like "dehors" (outside), "si tard" (so late), "si tôt" (so early). "toi" adds emphasis: “you, what are you doing here?”
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu fais là à cette heure-ci ?
native_language_example: What are you doing here at this time of night?

additional_notes: Used to ask why someone is in a particular place, or what they’re doing there. With cities, French uses "à" (à Paris, à Rome). You can also use it for events/places like "à la fête" (at the party) or "à l’école" (at school).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu fais à Lyon ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What are you doing in Lyon this weekend?

additional_notes: A common way to ask what someone was doing in the past. Uses the imperfect tense (faisais) to focus on an ongoing/repeated action or a situation in progress. Depending on tone/context, it can sound neutral ('What were you doing?') or surprised/critical ('What on earth were you doing?'). Often followed by extra details: « Qu'est-ce que tu faisais là-bas ? » ('What were you doing over there?').
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu faisais quand je t'ai appelé ?
native_language_example: What were you doing when I called you?

meaning: “What the hell are you doing?” (informal, often annoyed).
additional_notes: Uses the informal verb "ficher" to mean "to do" (like "faire"), but it’s slang and can sound rude or confrontational depending on tone. It’s almost always said with "tu". For a neutral version, say: "Qu’est-ce que tu fais ?" You can add details: "qu'est-ce que tu fiches ici/chez moi/à cette heure ?"
target_language_example: Mais qu'est-ce que tu fiches ?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing?

meaning: “What the hell are you doing?” / “What are you doing?” (very informal, can be rude).
additional_notes: Uses the verb « foutre » in the slang sense “to do / to be up to.” It’s common in spoken French to show annoyance, surprise, or impatience, but it can sound aggressive—use « Qu’est-ce que tu fais ? » in polite/neutral situations. Often followed by a place or situation: « … ici / là / dans la cuisine / en caleçon », etc.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu fous dans ma chambre ?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing in my room?

meaning: “What the hell are you doing here?” (very informal / can be rude).
additional_notes: Uses the verb « foutre » (here: « tu fous ») as a slang, often aggressive way to say « faire » (“to do”). It’s confrontational and can sound rude, like “What are you doing here?!” / “Why are you here?!” A neutral alternative is « Qu’est-ce que tu fais ici ? ».
target_language_example: Mais qu'est-ce que tu fous ici, d'abord ?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here, anyway?

meaning: “What the hell are you doing here?” / “What are you doing here?” (rude, slang).
additional_notes: Very informal and often confrontational. Uses the verb "foutre" ("fous"), which is slang and can be vulgar depending on tone and context. It’s stronger than "Qu’est-ce que tu fais là ?" (neutral: “What are you doing here?”). "Là" means “here/there” depending on context.
target_language_example: Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu fous là ?
native_language_example: And you—what the hell are you doing here?

meaning: “What are you …ing to them?” / “What did you … to them?”
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a question. **qu'est-ce que** is a very common way to ask “what” in French, and **tu leur** means “you (to) them.” You must complete it with a verb (and often an object/complement), e.g. **qu'est-ce que tu leur as dit ?** (“What did you tell them?”) or **qu'est-ce que tu leur donnes à manger ?** (“What are you feeding them?”). In casual speech, **qu'est-ce que** is often pronounced roughly like “keske.”
target_language_example: qu'est-ce que tu leur as dit ?
native_language_example: What did you tell them?

meaning: “what … to him/her?” / “what did you … to him/her?” (used to ask what you did/said/want with that person).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a question and must be followed by a verb. **lui** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” or “to her.” Common completions include: *qu'est-ce que tu lui as dit ?* (what did you tell him/her?), *qu'est-ce que tu lui veux ?* (what do you want from him/her?), *qu'est-ce que tu lui trouves ?* (what do you see in him/her?). Depending on tone/context, it can sound accusatory or confrontational.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu lui veux ?
native_language_example: What do you want from him/her?

meaning: “What did you … to him/her?” (question starter in the past tense, followed by a past participle).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone said/did/gave/told/replied to another person, with the indirect object pronoun « lui » (= to him/to her). It must be completed with a past participle in the passé composé: « qu'est-ce que tu lui as dit / donné / raconté / répondu ? ». Word-for-word it resembles “what is it that you to him/her have…”, so it isn’t translated literally into natural English.
target_language_example: qu'est-ce que tu lui as répondu ?
native_language_example: What did you reply to him/her?

meaning: "what are you … me?" (opening of a direct question meaning "what are you [verb]-ing/telling/showing/asking] me?").
additional_notes: Very common spoken pattern introducing a question addressed to someone; it must be followed by a verb (often in the present): « qu'est-ce que tu me dis ? », « qu'est-ce que tu me demandes ? », « qu'est-ce que tu me montres ? ». Adding « là » often makes it more emphatic, skeptical, or accusatory (roughly “what are you telling me there/now?”).
target_language_example: qu'est-ce que tu me demandes ?
native_language_example: What are you asking me?

meaning: "What are you (… ) to us?" / "What are you (… ) us?" (start of a question).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete question starter that must be followed by a verb: e.g., « Qu'est-ce que tu nous amènes ? » (What are you bringing us?), « Qu'est-ce que tu nous caches ? » (What are you hiding from us?). « qu'est-ce que » = “what”; « tu » = “you” (informal singular); « nous » = “us / to us / from us” depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu nous racontes ?
native_language_example: What are you telling us?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion. Often followed by "de + noun/pronoun" (Qu'est-ce que tu penses de lui ? = What do you think of him?) or by an infinitive to ask about someone’s plan/intentions (Qu'est-ce que tu penses faire ? = What are you planning/thinking of doing?). You can also add "que" to ask what someone thinks about a whole idea (Qu'est-ce que tu penses que c'était ? = What do you think it was?).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu penses de ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: What do you think of this restaurant?

meaning: 'What are you talking about?' / 'What are you saying?' (often: 'What nonsense!')
additional_notes: A common, fairly informal way to question what someone just said—often showing surprise, disbelief, or disapproval. Adding "là" makes it more pointed: "Qu'est-ce que tu racontes là ?" = 'What are you talking about?' / 'What are you going on about?'
target_language_example: Mais qu'est-ce que tu racontes ? Je n'ai jamais dit ça !
native_language_example: What are you talking about? I never said that!

additional_notes: A direct question using the common spoken form "Qu'est-ce que... ?" + "tu". It can be neutral (genuine curiosity) or confrontational/annoyed depending on tone and context (similar to English "What are you staring at?"). "Regarder" means "to look/watch" (more active than "voir" = "to see").
target_language_example: Hé, qu'est-ce que tu regardes ? Il n'y a rien à voir ici.
native_language_example: Hey, what are you looking at? There's nothing to see here.

additional_notes: Used to ask what information someone has. Often followed by de + noun/pronoun (de lui, de ça, de tout ça, des femmes) or sur + person/topic (sur lui). Tone depends on context: it can be neutral (“What do you know about him?”) or challenging (“What do you know about that?”).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu sais de cette histoire ?
native_language_example: What do you know about this story?

additional_notes: Used to ask what information someone has about a person/thing/topic. Structure: "qu'est-ce que" (what is it that) + "tu sais" (you know) + "sur" (about). You can switch to formal/plural: "qu'est-ce que vous savez sur ... ?" Note: many speakers more naturally say "qu'est-ce que tu sais de ... ?"; "sur" is also correct, often used for topics or when emphasizing "about/on."
target_language_example: qu'est-ce que tu sais sur ce type ?
native_language_example: What do you know about that guy?

meaning: “what are you going to…?” (introduces a question about what someone is going to do/say/become).
additional_notes: Used with the near future (aller + infinitive): « Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ? » = “What are you going to do?” It is normally followed by an infinitive (faire, chercher, devenir) and can include object pronouns before the infinitive (« Qu'est-ce que tu vas en faire ? », « Qu'est-ce que tu vas lui dire ? »). Depending on tone, it can express curiosity, surprise, worry, or disapproval. Note: « foutre » is slang/rough for “do” (« Qu'est-ce que tu vas foutre… ? »).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire avec ça ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do with that?

meaning: What are you going to do?
additional_notes: A very common way to ask about someone’s plans or what they intend to do. It uses the near-future tense: "tu vas + infinitive" (you’re going to + verb). You can add details: "Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire samedi ?" (this Saturday), "là-bas" (over there). With "de + pronoun/name" it means what you’re going to do with someone/something: "Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire de lui/de moi ?" = "What are you going to do with him/me?" (often implies deciding their fate/what to do about them). Add "alors" = "so/then", "hein" for emphasis, and "patron" = "boss" (informal address).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tonight?

meaning: "What do you want?" / "What would you like?"
additional_notes: Very common way to ask someone what they want. Often followed by extra information: qu'est-ce que tu veux me dire ? (what do you want to tell me?), qu'est-ce que tu veux pour Noël ? (what do you want for Christmas?). Depending on tone/context, it can sound neutral or a bit abrupt/annoyed (like “What do you want?”).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu veux manger ce soir ?
native_language_example: What do you want to eat tonight?

meaning: "What do you mean?" / "What are you saying?"
additional_notes: Common way to ask for clarification in spoken French. Often followed by **par** + noun/pronoun to specify what you mean: **Qu'est-ce que tu veux dire par “famille” ?** (“What do you mean by ‘family’?”). **Par là** means “by that / by it” (referring to what was just said).
