meaning: to put (someone) in their place; to put back where it belongs.
additional_notes: Often used about correcting or scolding someone who is being rude, arrogant, or overstepping ("Il fallait le/la remettre à sa place"). It can also be literal (putting an object back in its proper spot). Object pronouns are common: le/la/les remettre à sa place.
target_language_example: Il parlait très mal au serveur, alors je l’ai dû remettre à sa place.
native_language_example: He was talking very rudely to the waiter, so I had to put him in his place.

meaning: “goes back to / dates back to the last time that …” (used to say when something last happened).
additional_notes: This expression is most idiomatic with **à**: **(Ça) remonte à la dernière fois que + clause**. Without **à**, it can sound incomplete or less standard, but it may still appear in casual speech if the speaker omits **à**. Typically used with **ça** (or **cela**) as the subject to refer to a past event or memory.
target_language_example: Ça remonte la dernière fois que j’ai vu Paul.
native_language_example: It goes back to the last time I saw Paul.

meaning: to cheer someone up; to boost someone’s morale.
additional_notes: Used when you try to make someone feel better after they’re sad, stressed, or discouraged. It’s often followed by an indirect object: « lui remonter le moral » (cheer him/her up), « te/vous remonter le moral » (cheer you up). In everyday French you also hear « Ça va te remonter le moral » (“That’ll cheer you up”).
target_language_example: On va aller prendre un café pour te remonter le moral.
native_language_example: We’ll go have a coffee to cheer you up.

meaning: to go back in time; to travel back in time.
additional_notes: Used literally for time travel, and also figuratively to mean going back to earlier times (e.g., remembering the past or looking at old photos). Often used with "si" (if) or in storytelling: "Si je pouvais remonter le temps…"
target_language_example: Si je pouvais remonter le temps, je changerais cette décision.
native_language_example: If I could go back in time, I would change that decision.

additional_notes: Used for scheduled appointments (doctor, work, etc.) and also for planned meetings, including a date. Common verbs: avoir un rendez-vous (to have an appointment), prendre rendez-vous (to make/book an appointment), annuler un rendez-vous (to cancel), donner rendez-vous à quelqu’un / se donner rendez-vous (to arrange to meet someone).
target_language_example: J’ai rendez-vous chez le dentiste à 15 h.
native_language_example: I have a dentist appointment at 3 p.m.

additional_notes: Imperative of *rendre* + *moi* (“to me”). Used to demand that something be returned: *Rendez-moi ce livre !* It also appears in fixed expressions like *rendez-moi un service* (“do me a favor”). *Rendez* is used when speaking to more than one person or to one person formally (vous).
target_language_example: Rendez-moi mes clés, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me back my keys, please.

additional_notes: Very common for scheduled appointments (doctor, dentist, etc.) and planned meetings. Often used with "avoir" ("J’ai rendez-vous à 15 h" = I have an appointment at 3 p.m.) or "prendre" ("J’ai pris rendez-vous" = I made an appointment). It can also be used like an instruction to meet somewhere: "Rendez-vous au tribunal" = Meet at the courthouse. Don’t confuse with the verb phrase "se rendre" ("Où vous rendez-vous ?" = Where are you going?).
target_language_example: J’ai rendez-vous avec le médecin demain matin.
native_language_example: I have an appointment with the doctor tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a scheduled meeting with a person or group. Very common for medical appointments ("prendre rendez-vous avec" = to make/book an appointment with) and for work/official meetings ("avoir rendez-vous avec" = to have an appointment with).
target_language_example: Demain matin, j'ai rendez-vous avec ma conseillère.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning, I have an appointment with my advisor.

meaning: To realize/become aware (most often as « se rendre compte (de) ») / to report or give an account of (as « rendre compte de »).
additional_notes: Most common: « se rendre compte (de) » = “to realize / become aware (of)”. It typically takes « de » + noun (« se rendre compte de l’erreur ») or « que » + clause (« se rendre compte que… »). You’ll also see « s’en rendre compte », where « en » replaces something previously mentioned (“realize it/that”). Without « se », « rendre compte (de) » means “to report on / give an account of”: « rendre compte du résultat », often in formal/professional contexts.
target_language_example: Vous devez rendre compte du résultat.
native_language_example: You must report on the result.

additional_notes: Used most often with an indirect object introduced by "à": "rendre hommage à quelqu’un". Refers to showing respect/admiration, typically in a formal or public way (speech, ceremony, memorial, artistic work). In English you generally don’t say “render homage”; prefer “pay tribute (to)” or “honor.”
target_language_example: Je voulais leur rendre hommage lors de la cérémonie.
native_language_example: I wanted to pay tribute to them during the ceremony.

meaning: to return the favor; to do the same back (in kind).
additional_notes: Used when you want to repay someone for what they did—often something nice ("return the favor"), but it can also mean retaliation ("pay them back"). Conjugate "rendre" and keep "la pareille" fixed: je te/la lui rends la pareille, on va leur rendre la pareille. The person you’re paying back is typically introduced with an indirect object pronoun (te, vous, lui, leur).
target_language_example: Après tout ce que tu as fait pour moi, je vais te rendre la pareille.
native_language_example: After everything you’ve done for me, I’m going to return the favor.

meaning: to do someone a favor; to help out.
additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object: rendre service à quelqu’un (to do someone a favor). Very common as a polite request: Tu peux me rendre service ? (informal) / Vous pouvez me rendre service ? (formal). Often implies a small, practical help.
target_language_example: Tu pourrais me rendre service et m'envoyer ce document ?
native_language_example: Could you do me a favor and send me this document?

meaning: to do someone a favor; to help someone out.
additional_notes: Used when you help someone with a task or problem. Often followed by an indirect object: « rendre service à quelqu’un » (to do someone a favor). You can also say « Tu peux me rendre un service ? » to politely ask for help.
target_language_example: Tu peux me rendre un service et m’envoyer ce document ?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and send me that document?

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object (a person): rendre visite à quelqu’un / rendre visite à + noun. It emphasizes visiting a person (often at their home), not visiting a place. Common patterns: aller rendre visite à…, venir rendre visite à…, être venu(e) rendre visite à….
target_language_example: Je vais rendre visite à mes grands-parents ce week-end.
native_language_example: I'm going to visit my grandparents this weekend.

rendre visite de temps en temps

target_language_multi_word_term: rendre visite de temps en temps
meaning: to visit from time to time (occasionally).
additional_notes: You normally specify who/where you’re visiting with "à": "rendre visite à quelqu’un" / "rendre visite à un endroit". The sequence "de temps en temps" means "from time to time / once in a while" and is often placed at the end of the sentence. Note: in real usage, speakers would typically say "rendre visite à X de temps en temps"; omitting "à + person/place" can sound incomplete unless the context is clear.
target_language_example: J’aime rendre visite de temps en temps à mes grands-parents.
native_language_example: I like to visit my grandparents from time to time.

additional_notes: Used for visiting a person (often at their home or in a place where they are). The structure is always **rendre visite à + person** (à Pierre, à ma tante, à eux). For visiting a place, you usually use **visiter** (e.g., visiter Paris).
target_language_example: Je vais rendre visite à mes grands-parents ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my grandparents this weekend.

meaning: to go to / get to the train station.
additional_notes: In real French you normally say **se rendre à la gare** (reflexive): *je me rends…, tu te rends…, il/elle se rend…, nous nous rendons…, vous vous rendez…, ils/elles se rendent…*. It’s a somewhat formal way to say **aller à la gare** (“to go to the station”). Often used with transport: **en bus** (“by bus”), **en métro** (“by metro”).
target_language_example: Tu peux te rendre à la gare en bus.
native_language_example: You can get to the train station by bus.

meaning: "Do me" / "give me" (imperative), often in "Rends-moi un service" = "Do me a favor."
additional_notes: This is the command form (tu) of *rendre* + *moi* (“to me”). In everyday French, it’s very common in the fixed expression **rendre un service (à quelqu’un)** = “to do someone a favor.” It can also mean “give/hand back to me” when talking about returning something: *Rends-moi mon livre.*
target_language_example: Rends-moi mon stylo, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me back my pen, please.

meaning: Give me back my… / Return my… (to me).
additional_notes: Used to demand that someone gives something back. Built from the imperative of **rendre** (to give back/return) + **moi** (to me) + **mon** (my, masculine singular; use **ma** for feminine, **mes** for plural). Often said in an annoyed or urgent tone: *Rends-moi mon peigne !*
target_language_example: Rends-moi mon téléphone, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me back my phone, please.

additional_notes: Most commonly appears in the reflexive verb **se rendre compte (de + noun)** = “to realize/be aware of.” You’ll also often see **s’en rendre compte** (“to realize it/that”), where **en** replaces something previously mentioned. Note: **rends compte** is the **tu**/**je** present form within these reflexive patterns (e.g., **je m’en rends compte**, **tu t’en rends compte**).
target_language_example: Je m’en rends compte maintenant.
native_language_example: I realize it now.

meaning: "visited" (someone) (past tense), as in "rendre visite à quelqu’un".
additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **rendre visite à + person** = “to visit someone” (focuses on visiting a person, not a place). **Rendu** is the past participle of *rendre* and is used with **avoir**: *j’ai rendu visite à…* (I visited…).
target_language_example: J’ai rendu visite à ma grand-mère samedi.
native_language_example: I visited my grandmother on Saturday.

additional_notes: Used with a person or possessive to mean going to that person’s place: « Je rentre chez moi » (I’m going home), « On rentre chez nous » (We’re going home), « Il rentre chez Paul » (He’s going to Paul’s place). « Rentrer » is the verb “to return/go back,” and « chez » means “at/to someone’s place.”
target_language_example: Je rentre chez moi après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going home after work.

meaning: Go home. / Go back to your place.
additional_notes: Imperative (command) of "rentrer" + "chez toi" (to your home/your place), used when speaking to one person you address as "tu". For a more polite or plural version: "Rentrez chez vous." You can add "maintenant" for emphasis: "Rentre chez toi maintenant."
target_language_example: Il est tard, rentre chez toi.
native_language_example: It’s late, go home.

additional_notes: From the verb rentrer (“to return/get back”). With “à la maison” it means returning home. In context it can be an instruction (Rentre à la maison ! = Go home!) or describe someone’s return (Papa rentre à la maison demain. = Dad is coming home tomorrow).
target_language_example: Rentre à la maison avant la nuit.
native_language_example: Come home before nightfall.

meaning: to go back home / to return to (someone’s) place.
additional_notes: Used with a person after "chez": rentrer chez moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles (“go back to my/your/his/her/our/your/their place”). It can also be used with a name: rentrer chez Marie (“go back to Marie’s place”). In everyday French, it often just means “to go home.”
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, je vais rentrer chez moi.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going to go home.

meaning: to go back home (to his place).
additional_notes: "Rentrer" means to return/go back (often home). "Chez lui" means "to/at his place" (for a man). You can change the pronoun: "rentrer chez elle" (her place), "rentrer chez moi" (my place), "rentrer chez nous" (our place), "rentrer chez vous" (your place), "rentrer chez eux/elles" (their place). In the passé composé: "il est rentré chez lui" = he came/got back home.
target_language_example: Il vient juste de rentrer chez lui.
native_language_example: He just got back home.

meaning: to go back home; to return to my place.
additional_notes: Used when you’re away and want/need to return home. « rentrer » = to go back/come back (often to a usual place), and « chez moi » = at my place/home. You can swap the pronoun: rentrer chez toi (your place), rentrer chez lui/elle (his/her place), rentrer chez nous/vous/eux/elles.
target_language_example: Il est tard, je vais rentrer chez moi.
native_language_example: It’s late; I’m going to go back home.

meaning: to go back home (to your place).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "rentrer" (to go back/come back) + "chez" + a stressed pronoun. "chez toi" means “at your place / to your place” when used with a verb of movement. You can swap the pronoun: "rentrer chez moi" (my place), "chez lui/elle" (his/her place), "chez nous/vous/eux/elles". Often used to tell someone to go home: "Il est temps de rentrer chez toi."
target_language_example: Après le cours, je vais rentrer chez toi pour te rendre ton livre.
native_language_example: After the class, I'm going to go back to your place to return your book.

additional_notes: Used when addressing one person formally (vous) or multiple people. With verbs like "aller", "vouloir", "devoir", you often see the infinitive: "Vous devriez rentrer chez vous". "Rentrer" often implies returning home (going back), while "aller chez vous" is simply going to your place.
target_language_example: Après le travail, vous pouvez rentrer chez vous.
native_language_example: After work, you can go home.

meaning: to crash/bump into (someone or something); (figuratively) to go at someone / lay into them.
additional_notes: Common in everyday spoken French. For a physical collision, it often means “to hit/crash into” (e.g., in a car accident). Figuratively, it can mean to confront someone aggressively or tell them off; with an indirect object pronoun it’s frequent: « Je lui suis rentré dedans » (context-dependent).
target_language_example: Il m’a rentré dedans avec son vélo.
native_language_example: He crashed into me with his bike.

meaning: to go home; to return home.
additional_notes: Used with the verb rentrer (“to go back/come back”) + à la maison (“home”). It means going back to where you live (or where you’re staying). Common with devoir (must/have to), vouloir (want), and aller (going to): « Je vais rentrer à la maison. »
target_language_example: Je vais rentrer à la maison après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to go home after work.

meaning: Go home / go back to your place.
additional_notes: Imperative of « rentrer » (to go back/return), used either for (1) one person with « vous » (polite/formal) or (2) several people. « chez vous » means “to your home/at your place.” Often used as an instruction/command.
target_language_example: Il est tard, rentrez chez vous maintenant.
native_language_example: It’s late—go home now.

meaning: went home; returned to his place.
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "rentrer" with "être": "il est rentré chez lui" = "he went/returned home." "Chez lui" means "at his place/home" (for a man). You can change it: "chez elle" (her place), "chez moi" (my place), "chez toi" (your place, informal), "chez nous" (our place), "chez vous" (your place, formal/plural), "chez eux/elles" (their place).
target_language_example: Il est rentré chez lui vers minuit.
native_language_example: He went home around midnight.

additional_notes: Past participle of "rentrer" used with "être" in the passé composé: "être rentré(e) à la maison" = to have returned home. It agrees with the subject: rentré (m.), rentrée (f.), rentrés (m. pl.), rentrées (f. pl.). Often used with a time: "Je suis rentré(e) à la maison à 20h."
target_language_example: Je suis rentré à la maison après le travail.
native_language_example: I came back home after work.

meaning: hit (and knocked down) by a car.
additional_notes: Uses the passive voice: « être renversé » = to be knocked over/struck (often a pedestrian or cyclist hit by a vehicle). In other contexts, « renverser » can also mean “to tip/knock over” (e.g., a glass), but with « par une voiture » it means being hit by a car.
target_language_example: En traversant la rue, il a été renversé par une voiture.
native_language_example: While crossing the street, he was hit by a car.

additional_notes: Used when you want to reset and begin again as if nothing had been done yet (a project, a relationship, a plan, a game, etc.). Often implies going back to the beginning and rebuilding step by step. Conjugates like repartir (je repars, tu repars, il/elle repart, nous repartons).
target_language_example: Si ça ne marche pas, on va repartir à zéro et on essaiera autrement.
native_language_example: If it doesn’t work, we’ll start over from scratch and try a different way.

additional_notes: An informal singular command (imperative) meaning “rest” or “get some rest,” addressed to one person you call tu. From the verb se reposer (“to rest”); it literally means “rest yourself.” You can add words like bien (well), un peu (a little), ici (here), pendant un moment (for a moment) to specify how/where/for how long.
target_language_example: Tu as l’air fatigué : repose-toi un peu.
native_language_example: You look tired: rest a little.

meaning: “Rest in peace.” (said about someone who has died.)
additional_notes: Used as a respectful expression after someone’s death (like “RIP”). Often appears as a wish with the subjunctive: « Qu’il/elle repose en paix. » You can also address the deceased directly: « Repose en paix. »
target_language_example: Nous ne t'oublierons jamais. Repose en paix.
native_language_example: We will never forget you. Rest in peace.

respecter le code de la route

target_language_multi_word_term: respecter le code de la route
meaning: to follow/obey the rules of the road (traffic laws).
additional_notes: Used when talking about driving and road safety. "Respecter" here means to obey or comply with rules. "Le code de la route" is the set of traffic laws (signs, speed limits, right of way, etc.).
target_language_example: Pour éviter une amende, il faut respecter le code de la route.
native_language_example: To avoid a fine, you have to follow the rules of the road.

additional_notes: Used to say you must comply with rules (laws, school rules, game rules). Very common with obligation expressions like « devoir » (must) and « devoir/ falloir » or « il est important de… ». You can specify which rules with « les règles de… » (e.g., « les règles de la circulation » = traffic rules).
target_language_example: Au travail, il faut respecter les règles de sécurité.
native_language_example: At work, you have to follow the safety rules.

additional_notes: Used to compare similarity in appearance or general resemblance: « X ressemble à Y ». You can use it for people, animals, objects, or even situations/ideas (« Ça ressemble à un plan » = “That looks like a plan”). Note the accent: « à ».
target_language_example: Ça ressemble à un plan.
native_language_example: That looks like a plan.

additional_notes: From the verb **ressembler à** (“to look like / to resemble”). It’s followed by a person or thing: **Il/Elle ressemble à un/une…**. Use **à un** with masculine nouns and **à une** with feminine nouns (e.g., *Elle ressemble à une actrice*). Note: French uses **à**, even though English says “resemble” (no “to”).
target_language_example: Il ressemble à un professeur avec ces lunettes.
native_language_example: He looks like a teacher with those glasses.

additional_notes: From the verb **ressembler à** (“to look like / to resemble”). You use **ressembler à + noun** to compare appearance or impression. It agrees with the subject: **il ressemble à…**, **elle ressemble à…**, **ça/cela ressemble à…**. Use **à un** for masculine nouns and **à une** for feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Ce dessin ressemble à une photo.
native_language_example: This drawing looks like a photo.

additional_notes: General term for the fast-food industry/style of eating (burgers, fries, etc.). Often used with verbs like manger/consommer (to eat/consume) or with restaurant (un restaurant de restauration rapide).
target_language_example: On évite la restauration rapide pendant la semaine.
native_language_example: We avoid fast food during the week.

additional_notes: From **rester** (to remain) + **-t-** (linking sound) + **il** (he/it). Used in formal/written French to form questions like **Reste-t-il des billets ?** = “Are there any tickets left?” It often means “is there any … left?” or “do we have any … left?” depending on context. With time: **Combien de temps nous reste-t-il ?** = “How much time do we have left?”
target_language_example: Reste-t-il du café, ou faut-il en acheter ?
native_language_example: Is there any coffee left, or do we need to buy some?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to remain in the same place. It’s the imperative (command) form of *rester* for *tu*: **(tu) reste ici**. For more than one person, you’d say **restez ici**.
target_language_example: Reste ici, s'il te plaît, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: Stay here, please, I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Used when someone is sick, resting, or advised not to get up. Often appears with advice verbs like "devoir" (must) and "(re)commander / conseiller" (recommend/advise): « Tu devrais rester au lit. »
target_language_example: J'ai de la fièvre, donc je vais rester au lit aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have a fever, so I'm going to stay in bed today.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone stays in the current place instead of leaving. Very common with modal verbs like devoir (must), pouvoir (can), and devoir/ falloir for obligation: « Je peux rester ici ? » / « Nous devons rester ici. ». You can change the place word: « rester là » (stay there), « rester chez moi » (stay at my place).
target_language_example: Je vais rester ici jusqu'à demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay here until tomorrow.

meaning: to stay/remain there; to stay put.
additional_notes: Used for staying in a specific place or position. Often implies not moving or not leaving ("Stay there!"). Can also carry an impatient or admonishing tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu vas rester là.
native_language_example: You’re going to stay there.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that you want to extend your stay/time in a place. Very common with polite question forms like « Est-ce que je peux… ? », « Puis-je… ? » (formal), or « Pourrais-tu… ? » (to a friend), and with « Veuillez… » for polite instructions/requests.
target_language_example: Je peux rester un peu plus longtemps, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I stay a little longer, please?

additional_notes: Used to say you will not go out and will remain at your home. Common with near-future plans: « Je vais rester… ». Also used for advice/instructions (e.g., from a doctor): « On te conseille de rester… ».
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, je vais rester à la maison parce qu'il pleut.
native_language_example: Today, I'm going to stay at home because it's raining.

meaning: delay because of the… (feminine noun follows).
additional_notes: Common in travel/transport announcements to give the reason for a delay. It’s usually followed by a feminine noun: « la météo » (the weather), « la grève » (the strike), « la circulation » (traffic). For a masculine noun, you’d say « retard à cause du … » (e.g., « du trafic »). Note: French « retard » means “delay” (not the English insult/slur “retard”).
target_language_example: Nous avons un retard à cause de la météo.
native_language_example: We have a delay because of the weather.

additional_notes: Used literally (stop breathing for a moment, e.g., underwater or from surprise). It can also be used figuratively to mean “to wait anxiously/in suspense” for something to happen. Conjugate the verb: je retiens mon souffle, il/elle retient son souffle, nous retenons notre souffle, etc.
target_language_example: Je vais retenir son souffle quelques secondes.
native_language_example: I’m going to hold my breath for a few seconds.

meaning: back to square one; back to the starting point.
additional_notes: Used when a plan or process fails and you have to start over from the beginning. Often appears after verbs like « être » (être de retour à la case départ) or alone as a comment: « Retour à la case départ. » The image comes from board games: going back to the starting square.
target_language_example: On a perdu le dossier, alors c’est retour à la case départ.
native_language_example: We lost the file, so it’s back to square one.

meaning: to come back here next week.
additional_notes: Used to talk about returning to this place (“ici”) during the following week (“la semaine prochaine”). Often appears with the near future tense: « aller + infinitif » (e.g., « Tu vas revenir… » / « Vous allez revenir… »). In questions, you’ll see « tu » (informal singular) vs « vous » (formal singular or plural).
target_language_example: Je vais revenir ici la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: I'm going to come back here next week.

meaning: to come back to (a topic); to go back on/reconsider (a decision); to return to (a place, esp. Earth).
additional_notes:
Common uses:
1) **Revenir sur + noun** = to return to a subject and talk about it again: *revenir sur une déclaration, un point, un détail*.
2) **Revenir sur + décision/choix/promesse** = to go back on it (change your mind, undo it): *On ne peut pas revenir sur son choix.*
3) With places, especially **revenir sur Terre** = to return to Earth (from space).
target_language_example: Avant de conclure, je voudrais revenir sur un point important.
native_language_example: Before we wrap up, I’d like to come back to an important point.

meaning: to come back/return to; (revenir à soi) to come to (regain consciousness).
additional_notes: Used with a destination: « revenir à la maison » = to go back home. With « soi » (or an indirect object like « lui »): « revenir à lui / à soi » = to regain consciousness or come back to your senses. You may also see « revenir » without « à » when it’s followed by a time: « Il revient à cinq heures » = He’s coming back at five o’clock.
target_language_example: Je vais revenir à la maison après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to come back home after work.

meaning: come back right away / be right back.
additional_notes: "Reviens" is the tu (informal singular) command form of "revenir" (to come back). In the examples with "je reviens tout de suite", it means “I’ll be right back” (common when stepping away briefly). For a formal command to one person, use "revenez tout de suite"; for “come back” to someone you’re on first-name terms with, "reviens" is natural.
target_language_example: Je vais aux toilettes, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: I'm going to the bathroom; I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Used for the level at street entrance in a building. In France, floors are often counted as: rez-de-chaussée (RDC), then 1er étage (one floor up), 2e étage, etc. Common on signs and in addresses/elevators.
target_language_example: L’appartement est au rez-de-chaussée, juste à côté de l’entrée.
native_language_example: The apartment is on the ground floor, right next to the entrance.

meaning: “received a / got a” (past tense: *avoir* + *reçu* + a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used in the past with *avoir*: *j’ai reçu un…* (I received/got a…), *il/elle a reçu un…* (he/she received/got a…). Often followed by a message, call, treatment, welcome, etc. Feminine is *reçue* (e.g., *elle a reçu une lettre*).
target_language_example: J’ai reçu un e-mail ce matin.
native_language_example: I got an email this morning.

additional_notes: Used to restrict something to one thing/person: « rien que pour nous » = “just for us / only for us.” It can also mean “merely/by the mere fact of,” especially with an infinitive: « Rien que de voir… » = “Just seeing…”. In the fixed phrase « la vérité, rien que la vérité », it means “the truth and nothing but the truth.”
target_language_example: Je veux rester à la maison, rien que ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to stay home, just tonight.

meaning: just for; only for (for the sole purpose/benefit).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize exclusivity: something is done only for a particular purpose ("rien que pour te voir" = just to see you) or reserved only for someone ("rien que pour elle" = just for her). You can also use "rien que" without "pour" to mean "just/only" ("rien que te parler" = just talking to you).
target_language_example: Je suis venu rien que pour te dire merci.
native_language_example: I came just to say thank you.

additional_notes: Means “nothing else” after a negative (often with ne…pas/plus, but in speech you may hear it without ne: « J’ai rien d’autre. »). In questions, it often means “anything else?”: « Vous n’avez rien d’autre ? » = “Don’t you have anything else?” / “Do you have anything else?” Can also follow a verb like penser à: « penser à rien d’autre » = “to think of nothing else.”
target_language_example: Je n'ai rien d'autre à ajouter.
native_language_example: I have nothing else to add.

additional_notes: Used to say you have no other tasks/activities planned (often implying you’re free or just killing time). Very common with the informal negation that drops "ne": "J’ai rien d’autre à faire"; in more formal French you may hear "Je n’ai rien d’autre à faire." It can also be used as a question: "Vous n’avez rien d’autre à faire ?"—often with a slightly critical or surprised tone (“Don’t you have anything better to do?”).
target_language_example: On peut aller se promener : j’ai rien d'autre à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We can go for a walk: I have nothing else to do today.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean “nothing about” (rien de + noun): « Rien de nouveau » = “Nothing new.” With a past participle (rien de + past participle), it means “nothing (to be) … / nothing …ed planned, prepared, etc.”: « Rien de prévu » = “Nothing planned.” Often used with ne: « On ne sait rien de… » = “We don’t know anything about…”.
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien de spécial à dire.
native_language_example: I have nothing special to say.

meaning: nothing more; no more than that.
additional_notes: Used to limit or downplay what you just said: “that’s all.” Common after a statement (“Je veux juste être ton ami, rien de plus.”) or alone as a short reply (“Rien de plus, merci.”). With a negative it often means “I won’t say anything else” (“Je ne dirai rien de plus.”).
target_language_example: Je suis venu pour discuter, rien de plus.
native_language_example: I came to talk, nothing more.

meaning: “nothing like that / nothing of the kind”; also “nothing beats…”
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) to say something like that doesn’t exist or won’t happen (often with ne): « Rien de tel ne se produira » = “Nothing like that will happen.” (2) to say something is the best way to get an effect: « Rien de tel pour… » = “Nothing like it / Nothing beats … for …”. On its own (« Rien de tel. ») it can mean “Nothing like that / Not at all.”
target_language_example: Pour se détendre après le travail, rien de tel qu’une promenade.
native_language_example: To relax after work, nothing beats a walk.

meaning: to say nothing; not say anything.
additional_notes: Used with negation to mean “say nothing.” Common patterns: **sans rien dire** (“without saying anything”), **ne rien dire** (“to say nothing”), **je ne peux rien dire** (“I can’t say anything”), and in informal speech the **ne** is often dropped: **je peux rien dire**. Also **Ça ne veut rien dire** means “That doesn’t mean anything / That makes no sense.”
target_language_example: Il est resté silencieux sans rien dire.
native_language_example: He stayed quiet without saying anything.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the negation **ne … rien** with the verb **dire** in the past tense: **(ne) + avoir + rien + dit**. In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **Elle t’a rien dit ?** = **Elle ne t’a rien dit ?**.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, je ne t’ai rien dit parce que je ne savais pas.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I didn’t tell you anything because I didn’t know.

meaning: nothing at all; not anything (at all).
additional_notes: Used for strong emphasis with "rien" (nothing), often in negative sentences: "Je ne … rien du tout" = "I don’t … anything at all." You can also use it alone as an emphatic answer: "Rien du tout." = "Nothing at all." In expressions like "plus rien du tout" it means "nothing left at all." In "un/une rien du tout," it means "a tiny insignificant thing" (often said about an object or a very small amount).
target_language_example: Tu as mangé quelque chose ? — Non, rien du tout.
native_language_example: Did you eat anything? — No, nothing at all.

meaning: 'nothing' (as the subject of a negative verb).
additional_notes: Used when "rien" (= nothing) comes before the verb: "Rien ne + verbe...". In this structure, "ne" is used without "pas" (unlike most negations). Often followed by other words like pronouns or the verb: "Rien ne s'est passé" (Nothing happened), "Rien ne me retient" (Nothing is holding me back), "Rien ne vaut..." (Nothing is worth/equals...).
target_language_example: Rien ne m'empêchera d'essayer.
native_language_example: Nothing will stop me from trying.

rien ne me rendrait plus heureuse que de

target_language_multi_word_term: rien ne me rendrait plus heureuse que de
additional_notes: A strong way to say what would bring you the greatest happiness. Uses the conditional "rendrait" (“would make”) and a comparison "plus … que" (“more … than”). It’s followed by "de" + an infinitive (e.g., "de te voir" = “to see you”). You can change "heureuse" to match the speaker: "heureux" (male speaker), "heureuse" (female speaker).
target_language_example: Rien ne me rendrait plus heureuse que de passer la soirée avec toi.
native_language_example: Nothing would make me happier than spending the evening with you.

rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que de

target_language_multi_word_term: rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que de
additional_notes: A strong, heartfelt way to say that one thing is your greatest wish. Uses the conditional rendrait (“would make”), so it often sounds polite/romantic. After que, you usually use de + infinitive (de te voir…, de t’aider…, de passer du temps avec toi…). You can change heureux to match the speaker: heureux (male), heureuse (female), and change me to another person (te, le/la, nous, etc.).
target_language_example: Rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que de passer la journée avec toi.
native_language_example: Nothing would make me happier than spending the day with you.

meaning: 'nothing to' (followed by an infinitive) / 'nothing about' (with a noun phrase).
additional_notes: Commonly used in the pattern "(ne)... rien à + infinitive" to say there is nothing to do/offer/fear/etc.: "Je n’ai rien à dire". In informal speech, "ne" is often dropped: "J’ai rien à dire". With verbs like "piger/comprendre", "rien à + [noun clause]" means 'nothing (at all) about/ of what...': "Je ne comprends rien à ce que tu dis" = 'I don’t understand anything you’re saying.'
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien à ajouter.
native_language_example: I have nothing to add.

meaning: 'nothing to do' / 'no business (being here)'; also 'no way!'
additional_notes: Used with a subject + negation: "(Il/Elle) n’a rien à faire ici/là" = “He/She has no business being here/there” (doesn’t belong, shouldn’t be there). Said on its own as an exclamation ("Rien à faire !") it can mean “No way!” / “Forget it!” / “Nothing can be done about it,” depending on context. Often used after a condition: "Si tu… , rien à faire !" = “If you…, no way!”
target_language_example: Tu veux entrer sans billet ? Rien à faire !
native_language_example: You want to come in without a ticket? No way!

meaning: “I don’t give a damn / I don’t care at all.” (very vulgar)
additional_notes: Very informal and aggressive; “foutre” is vulgar. Used alone as an exclamation (“Rien à foutre !”) or with “de + noun/pronoun” to mean you don’t care about something/someone (“Rien à foutre de ça / de lui / de ma vie”). In polite conversation, use “Je m’en fiche” or “Je m’en moque.”
target_language_example: Rien à foutre de ce qu’ils pensent, je fais ce que je veux.
native_language_example: I don’t give a damn what they think; I’ll do what I want.

additional_notes: Used in the expression **(ne) ... avoir rien à voir (avec ...)** to say something is unrelated or not involved: **Ça n’a rien à voir** = “That has nothing to do with it / That’s not the point.” You can add **avec + noun/pronoun**: **Ça n’a rien à voir avec toi** = “It has nothing to do with you.” Often used to deny responsibility or connection: **X n’a rien à voir là-dedans** = “X has nothing to do with it (in this matter).”
target_language_example: Ce problème n’a rien à voir avec toi.
native_language_example: This problem has nothing to do with you.

additional_notes: You usually see this inside a larger sentence, especially with a verb like traverser (to cross) or passer (to get across): traverser la rivière à la nage = “to swim across the river.” The expression à la nage means “by swimming.”
target_language_example: Ils ont traversé la rivière à la nage.
native_language_example: They swam across the river.

additional_notes: Refers to rice with the bran removed (as opposed to "riz brun" = brown rice). Often used when choosing a side dish or specifying what kind of rice you want.
target_language_example: Je vais prendre du poulet avec du riz blanc, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have chicken with white rice, please.

additional_notes: Used for a circular road intersection where you drive around a central island and take an exit (“Prends la deuxième sortie au rond-point”). It’s also sometimes used as a meeting point (“On se retrouve au rond-point”).
target_language_example: Au prochain rond-point, prends la première sortie.
native_language_example: At the next roundabout, take the first exit.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a car’s extra tire/wheel kept for emergencies (like a flat). Often found in the trunk (le coffre). In everyday speech you may also hear "roue de rechange".
target_language_example: On a crevé, mais heureusement on a une roue de secours.
native_language_example: We got a flat, but luckily we have a spare tire.

additional_notes: A noun meaning the cosmetic you put on your lips. Often used with "un/du/le" (un rouge à lèvres, du rouge à lèvres, le rouge à lèvres). You can also talk about marks left by it: "une trace/des traces de rouge à lèvres".
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon rouge à lèvres dans la salle de bains.
native_language_example: I forgot my lipstick in the bathroom.

additional_notes: A common general term for tape that sticks (often like Scotch tape). Usually used with the partitive: du ruban adhésif (“some tape”). In everyday speech you may also hear simply du scotch (informal/brand-based).
target_language_example: Tu peux me passer du ruban adhésif, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me some tape, please?

meaning: out of stock; sold out (temporarily unavailable).
additional_notes: Used mainly in shopping contexts to say a product isn’t available right now. Most often appears as "être en rupture de stock" (to be out of stock), on signs/websites or in customer service. It implies the item may be restocked later (unlike "ne plus être en vente", no longer sold).
target_language_example: Je voulais ces chaussures, mais elles sont en rupture de stock.
native_language_example: I wanted those shoes, but they’re out of stock.

meaning: rule of the game; rule to follow.
additional_notes: Most often used in the plural: « les règles du jeu » (“the rules of the game”). Can be literal (actual game rules) or figurative for the rules/conditions in a situation (e.g., at work, in politics). In the singular (« règle du jeu »), it often refers to one specific rule/principle.
target_language_example: La règle du jeu est simple : chacun son tour.
native_language_example: The rule of the game is simple: everyone takes turns.

additional_notes: Job title for the person who leads the editorial team of a newspaper, magazine, or other publication and makes the final decisions on what gets published. Often used with "du/de la/des" (rédacteur en chef du journal) or "à" to indicate the publication (rédacteur en chef à Rolling Stone). Feminine form: "rédactrice en chef".
target_language_example: Tom a été nommé rédacteur en chef du journal local.
native_language_example: Tom was appointed editor-in-chief of the local newspaper.

meaning: to reduce to ashes; to burn down completely.
additional_notes: Used for something destroyed by fire (a building, a forest, etc.). Often implies total destruction and is common in news reports or formal writing. Literal: "to reduce into ashes."
target_language_example: L'incendie a tout réduit en cendres.
native_language_example: The fire reduced everything to ashes.

additional_notes: “Répondre” is followed by “à” before the thing/person you answer (répondre à une question / à quelqu’un / à ça). In everyday French, you often use it with “ça” (“that”) to refuse or say you don’t have to answer.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas répondre à cette question maintenant.
native_language_example: I can’t answer this question right now.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "répondre" with the preposition "à" (répondre à + noun/pronoun). Very common in questions and negative statements: "Je ne peux pas répondre à cette question"; polite request: "Pouvez-vous répondre à cette question ?".
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne sais pas répondre à cette question.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know how to answer this question.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "répondre" with the preposition "à" (répondre à + noun/pronoun). Common in formal contexts like interviews, court, or school; often appears with verbs like "refuser de" (to refuse to) or "pouvoir" (to be able to).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous répondre à la question, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you answer the question, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a social media service (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, etc.) or the general concept of a social network. Often used with verbs like "utiliser" (to use), "publier sur" (to post on), "être sur" (to be on), and "s'inscrire à" (to sign up for). Plural: "les réseaux sociaux".
target_language_example: Ce réseau social est très populaire.
native_language_example: This social network is very popular.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *résoudre*: *j’ai résolu*, *tu as résolu*, *il/elle a résolu*. Uses *avoir* as the helping verb. *Résoudre* often translates to “to solve” in everyday contexts (a problem, an issue).
target_language_example: On a enfin résolu le problème.
native_language_example: We finally solved the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you (or someone) will find a solution to a specific issue. Conjugate "résoudre" to match the subject (je dois résoudre…, nous devons résoudre…). Often used with can/can't, must/have to, need to: "Je peux / je ne peux pas", "Je dois", "Il faut".
target_language_example: On va résoudre ce problème ensemble.
native_language_example: We’re going to solve this problem together.

additional_notes: Used to talk about finding a solution to a difficulty or issue. Often appears with helper verbs like « pouvoir » (As-tu pu…? = Were you able to…?), « finir par » (ended up managing to…), and « parvenir à » (to manage to…). You can specify the type of problem with « le problème de/du… » (e.g., « le problème du logement » = the housing problem).
target_language_example: On doit résoudre le problème avant demain.
native_language_example: We have to solve the problem before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb réussir + à + infinitive to say someone was able to do something (often after effort or difficulty). It’s usually in the past (a réussi à / as réussi à / j’ai réussi à), but can also be present (je réussis à…). Don’t confuse with réussir un examen (“to pass an exam”).
target_language_example: J’ai enfin réussi à finir mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I finally managed to finish my homework.

additional_notes: Imperative of "se réveiller" (to wake up). Used to tell one person to wake up; it uses "toi" because it’s addressed with "tu". For a more formal or plural version, use "réveillez-vous".
target_language_example: Réveille-toi, on est en retard !
native_language_example: Wake up, we’re late!

meaning: the American Dream (the idea of success and a better life in the U.S.).
additional_notes: Usually refers to the cultural idea that anyone can achieve prosperity through hard work and opportunity in the United States. Often used in discussions about society, immigration, and the economy (e.g., “Qu’est-il arrivé au rêve américain ?”). In other contexts, it can simply mean “an American dream” in a literal sense, but the common meaning is the well-known concept.
target_language_example: Il est venu aux États-Unis pour réaliser le rêve américain.
native_language_example: He came to the United States to achieve the American Dream.

meaning: “dream is to become …” (as in “My dream is to become …”).
additional_notes: Usually used with a possessive: « Mon rêve est de devenir … » (“My dream is to become …”). « rêve » is a noun (“dream”), « est » is “is”, and « devenir » means “to become” and is followed by a job or identity (médecin, professeur, artiste, etc.). You can also say « Mon rêve, c’est de devenir … » for emphasis in spoken French.
target_language_example: Mon rêve est de devenir médecin.
native_language_example: My dream is to become a doctor.

meaning: to be about; to concern; to be a matter of.
additional_notes: Usually used impersonally: "il s'agit de ..." (not *je m'agis*). Common for clarifying what something is about: "De quoi s'agit-il ?" (What is it about?/What’s going on?). Takes "de" + noun or "de" + infinitive: "Il s'agit de comprendre" (It’s a matter of understanding).
target_language_example: Il va s'agir de trouver une solution rapidement.
native_language_example: It’s going to be a matter of finding a solution quickly.

meaning: “it’s about / it’s a matter of” (most often used in « il s'agit de… »).
additional_notes: Almost always used in the impersonal construction « il s'agit de + noun/infinitive » to specify what something is about or what the issue is. Common in negatives (« il ne s'agit pas de… » = “it’s not about…”) and in conditional contexts (« s'il s'agit de… » = “if it’s a matter of…”). Note: the apostrophe in « s'agit » is required.
target_language_example: Non, il ne s'agit pas de ça.
native_language_example: No, it’s not about that.

meaning: to have fun; to enjoy oneself.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (amuser = “to amuse,” s’amuser = “to amuse oneself” → “to have fun”). Very common with purpose: « pour s’amuser » (“for fun / just to have fun”). Also used to say people seem to be having fun: « Ils ont l’air de bien s’amuser » (“They seem to be having a good time”).
target_language_example: On va s'amuser ce soir !
native_language_example: We’re going to have fun tonight!

meaning: "is called" / "is named" (for a person or thing).
additional_notes: From the verb "s'appeler" (to be called), used to ask or say someone’s name. Common in questions like "Comment s'appelle-t-il ?" (What’s his name?) or statements like "Il s'appelle…" (His name is…).
target_language_example: Elle s'appelle Marie.
native_language_example: Her name is Marie.

meaning: to work things out; to come to an agreement; to sort itself out.
additional_notes: Used when you think a problem can be resolved or a compromise can be found (often in negotiations: price, schedule, plans). With a subject like « ça / tout », it means things will end up being okay: « Ça va s'arranger » = “It’ll work out.”
target_language_example: Pour l'heure, ne t'inquiète pas : ça va s'arranger.
native_language_example: For now, don’t worry: it’ll work out.

meaning: “(oneself) from it / away / out of it” (se + en, used with many verbs).
additional_notes:
“S’en” is the combination of the reflexive pronoun “se” (myself/yourself/himself…) + “en” (“of it/from it/some”). It appears in lots of common verb phrases, and the exact English translation depends on the verb:
- s’en aller = to go away/leave
- s’en sortir = to get out of it / get by / make it through
- s’en foutre (informal) = to not care at all
- s’en douter = to suspect it / to have guessed
In a sentence, “s’en” is placed before the verb (or before the auxiliary in compound tenses): Il s’en va, Il s’en est sorti.
target_language_example: J'espère qu'il s'en sortira.
native_language_example: I hope he’ll get through it / make it out of it.

additional_notes: Very common way to say you’re leaving/going away from a place or situation. It’s built from the pronoun se (reflexive) + en (roughly “away/from here”) + aller (“to go”), and it conjugates like a reflexive verb: je m’en vais, tu t’en vas, il/elle s’en va, nous nous en allons, vous vous en allez, ils/elles s’en vont. Frequently used to express necessity or intention: il faut/on doit s’en aller = “we have to leave.”
target_language_example: Il faut s'en aller.
native_language_example: We have to leave.

meaning: to not care (at all); to not give a damn.
additional_notes: Very informal and often considered vulgar because it uses the verb « foutre ». Used to say you don’t care about something: « Je m’en fous » (I don’t care), « Il s’en fout » (He doesn’t care), « On s’en fout » (We don’t care). The « en » refers to “about it/that.” A more polite alternative is « Ça m’est égal » or « Je m’en fiche ».
target_language_example: Arrête de me demander : je vais m'en foutre, et toi tu vas t'en foutre aussi.
native_language_example: Stop asking me: I'm not going to care, and you won’t care either.

meaning: to take care of it; to handle it.
additional_notes: Refers to dealing with a task/problem/situation. "s'" is the reflexive pronoun (linked to the subject) and "en" replaces "de + [thing]" (="of it/about it"). Common with devoir/falloir/aller: "Il faut s'en occuper" (It needs to be taken care of), "Je vais m'en occuper" (I'll take care of it).
target_language_example: Il faut s'en occuper.
native_language_example: It needs to be taken care of.

meaning: "gets by / manages / copes"; "makes it through" (a situation).
additional_notes: From the verb "s'en sortir". It’s used to talk about how someone is doing in a difficult situation (a problem, a challenge, financially, emotionally, etc.). Very common with adverbs like "bien" (well) or "mal" (badly): "Elle s'en sort bien." = “She’s managing well.” The "en" refers to “out of it/out of that situation” and doesn’t translate directly into English.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas comment il s'en sort avec tout ce travail.
native_language_example: I don’t know how he manages with all that work.

meaning: to get by; to get out of a difficult situation; to manage.
additional_notes: Very common pronominal verb used for overcoming trouble or coping with something difficult. Often used with contexts like problems, money, school, addiction, etc. Conjugates like a reflexive verb: je m'en sors, tu t'en sors, il/elle s'en sort, nous nous en sortons, vous vous en sortez, ils/elles s'en sortent. Past: je m'en suis sorti(e).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, on va s'en sortir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll manage / we’ll get through it.

meaning: Pronoun sequence used with the auxiliary être in compound tenses (e.g., passé composé) to express “to have gotten/been … from it/there/of it,” depending on the verb and context.
additional_notes: This is not generally used alone; it appears as part of a larger verb phrase in a compound tense: se + en + être (conjugated) + past participle. “En” refers back to something previously mentioned (“of it,” “from it,” “from there”). Common fixed patterns include: s’en être sorti(e) (to get through it / manage), s’en être allé(e) (to have gone away). In the infinitive (as in the entry term), you’ll see: s’en être + past participle (e.g., s’en être sorti).
target_language_example: Il dit que tout va bien maintenant, après s'en être sorti.
native_language_example: He says everything is fine now, after having gotten through it.

meaning: to get along (with each other); to be on the same wavelength.
additional_notes: Used mostly with people to express compatibility or ease of agreement: "On va (bien) s'entendre" = "We’ll get along (well)." Also common as "s'entendre avec quelqu'un" (to get along with someone). In other contexts, "s'entendre" can mean "to hear oneself" (e.g., a voice carries), but in the examples here it’s about getting along.
target_language_example: Je crois qu'on va bien s'entendre.
native_language_example: I think we’re going to get along well.

meaning: “(he/she/it) has” in the passé composé for reflexive/pronominal verbs (se + est).
additional_notes: Contraction of “se” (or “s’” before a vowel) + “est” (3rd person singular of “être”). Used to form the past tense of pronominal/reflexive verbs: e.g., “s’est passé” (happened / went), “s’est cassé” (broke). Often translates to English “has” or “got” depending on the verb and context, not literally “is itself.”
target_language_example: Il s'est réveillé très tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He woke up very early this morning.

additional_notes: Used in more formal questions with inversion ("-il-"): *s’est-il passé* = “did it happen / has it happened.” Most often appears after a question word: *Que s’est-il passé ?* (“What happened?”), *Comment cela s’est-il passé ?* (“How did it happen?”). You can also ask *S’est-il passé quelque chose ?* (“Did anything happen?”). In everyday speech, people often avoid inversion and say *Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?* instead.
target_language_example: Alors, que s'est-il passé ?
native_language_example: So, what happened?

additional_notes: Past tense of **se passer** (“to happen/to go”), used with events or experiences (a flight, a trip, an exam, a meeting). It agrees with the subject: **Ça s'est bien passé** (It went well), **Le vol s'est bien passé** (The flight went well), **Tout s'est bien passé** (Everything went well). Often used in questions to check how something went: **Ça s'est bien passé ?**
target_language_example: Votre voyage s'est bien passé ?
native_language_example: Did your trip go well?

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of **se passer** = “to happen.” Used with an impersonal subject like **ça**, **quelque chose**, or **qu’est-ce qui**: **Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?** (“What happened?”). In questions, **qui** is usually correct (subject), not **que**. Although it looks like English “passed,” it usually does **not** mean “passed (an exam)” here.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce qui s'est passé hier soir.
native_language_example: I don't know what happened last night.

additional_notes: Used to say that an event occurred (often something unexpected). It’s built on the verb phrase "se passer" (to happen) in the passé composé: "il/elle s’est passé". You can also say "Il s’est passé quelque chose" (Something happened) or make it a question: "Il s’est passé quelque chose ?" / "Qu’est-ce qu’il s’est passé ?" (What happened?).
target_language_example: Il s'est passé quelque chose pendant la nuit.
native_language_example: Something happened during the night.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French, but informal. It’s a relaxed word order meaning the same as: « Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ? ». Often used as a standalone question (especially when reacting to something unexpected).
target_language_example: S'est passé quoi ? Tu as l’air stressé.
native_language_example: What happened? You look stressed.

meaning: takes care of; looks after; handles.
additional_notes: From the pronominal verb "s’occuper de" (to take care of / deal with). It is followed by a person or a thing: "s’occuper de moi" (take care of me) or "s’occuper de ces choses" (handle these things). Often used either for caring for someone (emotionally/practically) or managing a task. The "s’" changes with the subject: je m’occupe de…, tu t’occupes de…, il/elle s’occupe de…, nous nous occupons de…, vous vous occupez de…, ils/elles s’occupent de….
target_language_example: Elle s'occupe de moi.
native_language_example: She takes care of me.

meaning: to take care of; to look after; to handle/deal with (something or someone).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb: s'occuper (de). Conjugates with a reflexive pronoun + de + noun/pronoun: je m'occupe de…, tu t'occupes de…, il/elle s'occupe de…, nous nous occupons de…, vous vous occupez de…, ils/elles s'occupent de…. Meaning varies by context: caring for a person/animal (look after), taking charge of a task/problem (handle it), or dealing with someone’s situation/case; in phrases like « s'occuper de votre cas », it can sound ominous/threatening depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, je vais m'occuper de tout : je vais s'occuper de ça tout de suite.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to take care of everything: I’m going to deal with that right away.

meaning: to get started (on it); to get down to it.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb used when you finally begin doing a task or make an effort. The pronoun "y" refers to what you’re starting (e.g., work, homework, cleaning). Common patterns: "Faut/Il faut s'y mettre" (We/you have to get started), "Il est temps de s'y mettre" (It’s time to get started), "On va s'y mettre" (We’re going to get started), imperative: "Mets-toi-y !" (Get to it!).
target_language_example: Il est temps de s'y mettre : on commence par la cuisine.
native_language_example: It’s time to get started: we’ll start with the kitchen.

meaning: to go about it; to handle/do something (the way you do it).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the method or approach for doing a task. The "y" refers to what you’re dealing with ("it/that"), often mentioned earlier or understood from context. Very common in questions like "Comment vais-je m’y prendre ?" (= How am I going to go about it?). In "savoir s’y prendre", it means "to know how to do it / to be good at handling it".
target_language_example: Comment vas-tu s'y prendre pour ouvrir ce fichier ?
native_language_example: How are you going to go about opening this file?

additional_notes: Past perfect (plus-que-parfait) form of **se mettre d’accord (avec quelqu’un / sur quelque chose)**. Used to say an agreement had already been reached before another past moment or before what followed in the conversation: *On s'était mis d'accord* = “We had agreed.” Variants include **je m'étais mis(e) d'accord**, **on s'était mis d'accord**, **ils/elles s'étaient mis(es) d'accord**.
target_language_example: Je croyais qu'on s'était mis d'accord sur l'heure.
native_language_example: I thought we had agreed on the time.

additional_notes: Contraction of si + il. It usually means 'if he' or 'if it', depending on context. After verbs like voir, savoir, or se demander, English may also use 'whether'. It also appears in fixed patterns like s'il y a ('if there is/are').
target_language_example: Je me demande s'il est déjà parti.
native_language_example: I wonder if he's already left.

meaning: “please” (informal; said to one person you address as tu).
additional_notes: Used to make a request or to soften an order. Literally means “if it pleases you.” You use **s'il te plait** when speaking to one person informally (**tu**). For formal situations or when addressing someone as **vous**, use **s'il vous plait**. Note: in standard French spelling, **plaît** takes a circumflex (s'il te plaît), but the form **s'il te plait** is commonly seen without it.
target_language_example: S'il te plait, ouvre la porte.
native_language_example: Please open the door.

meaning: “please” (informal; to one person you address as tu).
additional_notes: Used to make a request more polite. You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence: “S'il te plaît, …” / “…, s'il te plaît.” Literal meaning is “if it pleases you.” For a more formal or plural “please,” use “s'il vous plaît.”
target_language_example: Tu peux répéter, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that, please?

meaning: "please, don’t…" (polite request to not do something).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone (tu) not to do/say something. It’s typically followed by a verb in the negative form: ne + verb + pas (or another negative word). Example pattern: « S’il te plaît, ne + verb + pas ».
target_language_example: S'il te plaît, ne parle pas si fort.
native_language_example: Please, don’t speak so loudly.

additional_notes: Used to make a request more polite. Can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence. The « vous » makes it formal or addressed to more than one person; for informal singular, use « s'il te plait ». It can also be used alone to get attention politely (similar to “Excuse me / please?”). Note: the common spelling is « s'il vous plaît » (with a circumflex on « plaît »), but this entry keeps « s'il vous plait » as requested.
target_language_example: Répondez s'il vous plait.
native_language_example: Please answer.

additional_notes: A polite expression used when making requests, giving polite instructions, or ordering something. It uses vous, so it is formal or addressed to more than one person. The informal singular version is s'il te plaît.
target_language_example: Fermez la porte, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: "Please don’t…" (polite request to not do something).
additional_notes: Used to start a polite negative request or instruction. It’s followed by a verb in the negative: “ne + verb + pas” (e.g., « S’il vous plaît, ne bougez pas. »). This is the formal/polite version (with « vous »).
target_language_example: S'il vous plaît, ne vous inquiétez pas.
native_language_example: Please, don’t worry.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to contact you if there is new information or a new development. Very common after a request like "Appellez-moi…" or "Je te/vous appelle…". Literally: "if there is something new."
target_language_example: Envoie-moi un message s'il y a du nouveau.
native_language_example: Send me a message if there’s any news.

additional_notes: Used to refer to or address a king, queen, emperor, etc. The possessive changes with the monarch’s gender: « Sa Majesté » for a woman (queen) and « Son Majesté » for a man (king). Often treated as a third-person noun in formal speech: « Sa Majesté attend. »
target_language_example: Sa Majesté recevra les invités à midi.
native_language_example: Her Majesty will receive the guests at noon.

additional_notes: Means “his/her credit card” depending on who owns it. Use **sa** with a feminine noun like **carte** (even if the owner is a man). In the examples, expressions like **exploser/épuiser sa carte de crédit** are figurative: to “max out” or “blow through” a credit card/credit limit (spend a lot).
target_language_example: Il a perdu sa carte de crédit et il a appelé la banque.
native_language_example: He lost his credit card and called the bank.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" depending on who owns the room (it agrees with the noun "chambre," which is feminine). Often used for someone’s bedroom, especially at home or in a hotel (e.g., "ramenez-la à sa chambre" = "take her back to her room").
target_language_example: Elle lit dans sa chambre tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She reads in her room every evening.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun "chemise," which is feminine, not with the owner). In context it often refers to someone taking off, tearing, ironing, hanging up, or tucking in their shirt. If the owner is a man, you still say "sa chemise" because "chemise" is feminine.
target_language_example: Il a enlevé sa chemise parce qu’il avait trop chaud.
native_language_example: He took off his shirt because he was too hot.

additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective that agrees with the noun "famille" (feminine singular), not with the owner. So it can mean either "his family" or "her family"—you know which from context. You can use it with verbs like parler de (talk about), connaître (know), manquer à (to be missed by), and soutenir (support).
target_language_example: Elle veut passer le week-end avec sa famille.
native_language_example: She wants to spend the weekend with her family.

meaning: his/her way of thinking; his/her mindset.
additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" depending on who you’re talking about (it agrees with the noun "façon"). You can swap the possessive: "ma/ta/notre/votre/leur façon de penser" (my/your/our/your/their way of thinking). Often used to comment on someone’s viewpoint or attitude: "Sa façon de penser est + adjective".
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas sa façon de penser.
native_language_example: I don’t understand his/her way of thinking.

meaning: his wife; her wife (rarely: its wife).
additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun that follows, not the owner). Since "femme" is feminine, you use "sa". Often the surrounding context tells you whether it means "his wife" or "her wife".
target_language_example: Elle a invité sa femme à dîner.
native_language_example: She invited her wife to dinner.

additional_notes: "Sa" is the feminine form of "his/her" and is used before feminine nouns like "femme" (wife). It can refer to a man’s or a woman’s spouse: French chooses "sa" based on the noun (femme), not on the owner. "Est" is the verb "to be" (il/elle est = he/she is).
target_language_example: Sa femme est médecin.
native_language_example: His wife is a doctor.

additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (it depends on who the owner is). It agrees with the noun possessed: "fille" is feminine singular, so you use "sa". (For plural: "ses filles" = "his/her daughters".)
target_language_example: Sa fille a dix ans.
native_language_example: His/Her daughter is ten years old.

meaning: his/her youth; the time when he/she was young.
additional_notes: Refers to someone’s younger years. Use the possessive adjective to match the person: sa (his/her), ma (my), ta (your), notre (our), leur (their), etc. Often used to talk about memories, dreams, or to ask people to consider someone’s age/immaturity.
target_language_example: Il raconte souvent des histoires de sa jeunesse.
native_language_example: He often tells stories about his youth.

additional_notes: “Sa” is a possessive adjective meaning “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun’s gender, not the owner’s). “Main” is feminine, so it’s always “sa main” (= his hand / her hand). Common expression: “demander sa main” means “to ask for her hand (in marriage).” Note: French “main” means “hand” (false friend with English “main”).
target_language_example: Il a pris sa main et il lui a souri.
native_language_example: He took her hand and smiled at her.

additional_notes: “Sa” means “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun “main,” which is feminine). “Gauche” means “left” here (not “awkward”). You’ll also hear: “la main gauche” = “the left hand,” and “ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur main gauche” depending on whose hand it is.
target_language_example: Il s’est blessé à sa main gauche.
native_language_example: He injured his left hand.

additional_notes: "Sa" is the possessive adjective for a feminine singular noun (here, "maison"). It can mean "his" or "her" depending on who owns it (not the gender of the house). Use "son" instead before a vowel sound: "son ancienne maison".
target_language_example: Il cherche sa maison sur la carte.
native_language_example: He’s looking for his house on the map.

meaning: his/her illness (the illness of someone previously mentioned).
additional_notes: “Sa” means “his” or “her” depending on what is owned (here: “maladie” is feminine), not on the person’s gender. Common with verbs like “se remettre de” (to recover from), “guérir de” (to cure/be cured of), “récupérer de” (to recover from), and with adjectives like “grave” (serious).
target_language_example: Après sa maladie, il a dû reprendre le travail doucement.
native_language_example: After his illness, he had to go back to work gradually.

additional_notes: "Sa" can mean "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun "amie," which is feminine, not with the owner). "Meilleure" is the feminine form of "meilleur" (best). Used for someone’s closest friend who is a woman/girl; for a male best friend you’d say "son meilleur ami."
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec sa meilleure amie.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with his/her best friend.

additional_notes: "Sa" is the possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (it depends on who died, not on the speaker). It’s used to talk about someone’s death, often in time expressions like "avant sa mort" (before his/her death) or "après sa mort" (after his/her death).
target_language_example: Après sa mort, sa famille a déménagé.
native_language_example: After his/her death, his/her family moved.

additional_notes: Refers to a third person's mother. In French, sa can mean both 'his' and 'her'; context tells you which one. Sa is used here because mère is feminine.
target_language_example: Il téléphone souvent à sa mère.
native_language_example: He often calls his mother.

meaning: his girlfriend (or her girlfriend, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Petite amie" means "girlfriend" (a romantic partner). "Sa" can mean "his" or "her" because it agrees with the noun "amie" (feminine), not with the owner. For a male partner, you say "son petit ami".
target_language_example: Il a invité sa petite amie à dîner.
native_language_example: He invited his girlfriend to dinner.

additional_notes: Literally “his/her place,” using the possessive adjective **sa** (feminine singular). It’s used for a physical place (a seat on a bus, a spot in a line, where something belongs: *Sa place est ici*) and also for someone’s role/position (*prendre sa place* = “take his/her place,” i.e., replace them). The possessive changes with the owner: **ma place** (my), **ta place** (your), **sa place** (his/her), **notre place**, **votre place**, **leur place**.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je crois que c’est sa place.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I think that’s his/her seat.

additional_notes: “Sa” is a possessive adjective meaning “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun: *poche* is feminine). You’ll often see it in literal contexts (*dans sa poche* = “in his/her pocket”, *de sa poche* = “from his/her pocket”). It also appears in the common idiom *connaître [un endroit] comme sa poche* = “to know [a place] like the back of one’s hand.”
target_language_example: Elle a sorti ses clés de sa poche.
native_language_example: She took her keys out of her pocket.

meaning: his/her proposal; his/her offer; his/her suggestion.
additional_notes: Refers to a plan, idea, or offer made by someone (the person is marked by the possessive adjective: sa = his/her). Often used with verbs like accepter/refuser/décliner (accept/refuse/turn down) and expressions like faire objection à (object to) or mériter réflexion (be worth thinking about). In plural, you’d say ses propositions.
target_language_example: Nous avons discuté de sa proposition avant de donner une réponse.
native_language_example: We discussed his/her proposal before giving an answer.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to emphasize that something belongs uniquely to someone: "sa propre chambre" = "his/her own room". It agrees with the noun, not the owner: masculine singular = "son propre"; feminine plural = "ses propres"; masculine plural = "ses propres". Often adds emphasis/contrast (e.g., risking "sa propre vie" = "his/her own life").
target_language_example: Chacun a sa propre façon de faire les choses.
native_language_example: Everyone has their own way of doing things.

additional_notes: “Sa” means “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun, not the person). Since “santé” is feminine, you use “sa” even when talking about a man. Common in phrases like “s’inquiéter de sa santé” (to worry about his/her health), “préoccupé(e) par sa santé” (concerned about his/her health), “au prix de sa santé” (at the cost of his/her health), “sa santé a décliné” (his/her health declined), “sa santé est défaillante” (his/her health is failing).
target_language_example: Après l’opération, sa santé s’est améliorée.
native_language_example: After the operation, his/her health improved.

meaning: his/her sister (depending on who owns it).
additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective that agrees with the noun ("sœur" is feminine), not with the owner. So "sa sœur" can mean "his sister" or "her sister" (and sometimes "their sister" if referring to a singular group like a company/organization). For "your sister" use "ta sœur" (informal singular) or "votre sœur" (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Il vient avec sa sœur.
native_language_example: He’s coming with his sister.

meaning: "his/her head" (also used in expressions about being stubborn).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: someone’s head (sa = his/her/its, depending on who you’re talking about). Often appears in the expression « n’en faire qu’à sa tête », meaning “to do only what one wants” / “to be stubborn, not listen to others.”
target_language_example: Il n’en fait qu’à sa tête et refuse d’écouter les conseils.
native_language_example: He just does what he wants and refuses to listen to advice.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **sa** can mean “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun *vie* (feminine), not with the person). Commonly seen in the expression **sa vie durant** = “all his/her life / throughout his/her life.”
target_language_example: Elle a vécu dans ce village toute sa vie.
native_language_example: She lived in this village her whole life.

additional_notes: Refers to the town/city someone was born in. The possessive adjective changes with the person: ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur ville natale. Common with verbs like quitter (to leave), revenir (to return), habiter loin de (to live far from), retourner (to go back).
target_language_example: Il habite loin de sa ville natale.
native_language_example: He lives far from his hometown.

meaning: his/her/its car (the car belonging to her/him/it).
additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (or "its") and it agrees with the noun that follows. Since "voiture" is feminine, you use "sa" (not *son*), even if the owner is male. Context tells you whether it’s "his" or "her."
target_language_example: Elle a garé sa voiture devant la maison.
native_language_example: She parked her car in front of the house.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" depending on who owns the voice (it agrees with the feminine noun "voix," not with the speaker’s gender). Often used to describe the sound or tone of someone’s voice (e.g., "se fit douce" = "became soft/gentle"), or to express annoyance ("me court sur les nerfs" = "gets on my nerves").
target_language_example: J’ai reconnu sa voix tout de suite.
native_language_example: I recognized his/her voice right away.

additional_notes: A common everyday noun for a bag worn on your back. You’ll often see it with colors/adjectives (un sac à dos bleu) and with possessives (mon/ton/son sac à dos).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon sac à dos à l'école.
native_language_example: I forgot my backpack at school.

additional_notes: A small bag (often carried by women) used to carry personal items. Common with possessives: « mon/ton/son sac à main ». It’s masculine: « un sac à main », « ce sac à main ».
target_language_example: J’ai laissé mon sac à main sur la chaise.
native_language_example: I left my handbag on the chair.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is alive and not injured after danger, an accident, or a difficult situation. Common with verbs like « être », « rentrer », « revenir », « arriver », « repartir », « ramener »: « rentrer sain et sauf », « ramener quelqu’un sain et sauf ». Agreement is possible: « saine et sauve » (feminine), « sains et saufs » (masc. plural), « saines et sauves » (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Je suis soulagé que vous soyez sain et sauf.
native_language_example: I’m relieved that you’re safe and sound.

additional_notes: Said about a woman or girl who got through something without harm. It agrees in gender and number: masculine singular is « sain et sauf », plural « sains et saufs » (mixed/masc) or « saines et sauves » (all female). Often used after danger, an accident, a trip, etc.
target_language_example: Après l’accident, elle est rentrée saine et sauve.
native_language_example: After the accident, she got home safe and sound.

meaning: "safe and sound"; unharmed (plural masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like rentrer, revenir, arriver, s’en sortir to say people made it back/through something without injury. It agrees with the people: sain et sauf (1 man), saine et sauve (1 woman), sains et saufs (men/mixed group), saines et sauves (women).
target_language_example: Après la tempête, ils sont rentrés sains et saufs.
native_language_example: After the storm, they got home safe and sound.

additional_notes: Inversion of the verb "savoir" + "tu" to form a question, meaning “do you know…?” and often used like “can you…?” for skills/ability. Commonly followed by an infinitive: "Sais-tu nager ?" = “Can you swim?” More formal than "Tu sais… ?".
target_language_example: Sais-tu cuisiner ?
native_language_example: Can you cook?

additional_notes: Question form of tu sais, using inversion with savoir. It means "do you know...?" when speaking to one person informally. This inverted form is common in writing and more formal speech; in everyday spoken French, tu sais...? or est-ce que tu sais...? is often more common.
target_language_example: Sais-tu où il habite ?
native_language_example: Do you know where he lives?

additional_notes: Uses subject–verb inversion ("sais-tu") to form a question; it’s a fairly formal/standard way to ask if someone knows some information.
