Note: in practice, both **se rappeler + direct object** and **se rappeler de + complement** are used; usage varies by register and region.
target_language_example: Je dois me forcer à se rappeler les noms quand je rencontre quelqu’un.
native_language_example: I have to make myself remember names when I meet someone.

meaning: to go/get to (a place); to surrender.
additional_notes: Often used with a destination: « se rendre à + lieu » (to go to / get to). In the context of conflict or police action, « se rendre » means “to surrender” (to give up, stop resisting): « Il va se rendre » / « Ne vous rendez pas ». In the travel/mobility sense it commonly appears in questions about time or directions: « Combien de temps faut-il pour se rendre à… ? » / « Quel est le chemin pour se rendre à… ? ».
target_language_example: Combien de temps faut-il pour se rendre à Boston ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to get to Boston?

additional_notes: Used with a destination (often a feminine noun) after « à la »: « se rendre à la gare / à la banque / à la mairie ». It’s a slightly formal way to say « aller à… ». Note: « se rendre à + person/authority » can also mean “to surrender/turn oneself in to” (e.g., « se rendre à la police »).
target_language_example: Je dois se rendre à la gare avant 18 h.
native_language_example: I have to go to the train station before 6 p.m.

meaning: to rest; to take a break.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb used when someone rests or takes time to recover: « Je dois me reposer. » It often follows verbs like « conseiller de » (to advise to) or « laisser » (to let). Note: « se reposer sur + [person/thing] » means “to rely on” (e.g., « On ne doit pas se reposer sur le rapport. »).
target_language_example: Je lui ai conseillé de se reposer.
native_language_example: I advised him to rest.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **se retrouver**. It’s used (1) when someone ends up in a situation or place (often unexpectedly): *Il se retrouve seul* (“He finds himself alone”), and (2) to talk about meeting up again: *On se retrouve à 18h ?* (“Shall we meet at 6?”). In questions like **Où se retrouve-t-on ?**, it means “Where are we meeting?”
target_language_example: Après le film, on se retrouve devant le cinéma.
native_language_example: After the movie, we’ll meet in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb « se revoir ». Used with a plural/reciprocal subject (nous, vous, on, ils/elles) to mean you’ll meet/see one another again. Often said at the end of a conversation to imply you’ll see the person again soon (like “see you again”).
target_language_example: On se revoit demain ?
native_language_example: Will we see each other again tomorrow?

additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb « se sentir » (to feel), here in the 3rd person singular present (il/elle/on se sent). Commonly followed by an adjective: « Il se sent bien / fatigué / blessé / exclu ». Can describe physical condition or emotional state, and can also be used for groups/countries (« La Chine se sent forte »). In questions: « Comment on se sent ? » = “How do we/you feel?”
target_language_example: Il se sent fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: He feels tired today.

additional_notes: Imperfect past (3rd person singular) of the pronominal verb « se sentir » (to feel). Used to describe someone’s physical/emotional state over a period of time or as background in a story. Common patterns: « Il/Elle se sentait + adjectif » (He/She felt…), « se sentait comme ça » (felt like that), « se sentait différent(e) de… » (felt different from…).
target_language_example: Le lendemain matin, Bill se sentait vraiment bien.
native_language_example: The next morning, Bill was feeling really good.

meaning: to feel (emotionally/physically); to feel oneself (to be in a certain state).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb ("sentir" + "se"). Used to describe someone’s state or feelings: se sentir bien/mieux/mal (to feel good/better/bad), se sentir seul(e) (to feel lonely), se sentir piégé(e) (to feel trapped), se sentir aimé(e) (to feel loved). Conjugates with être in compound tenses (e.g., je me suis senti(e)). Often followed by an adjective or comme ("se sentir comme..." = to feel like...).
target_language_example: Tout le monde veut se sentir aimé.
native_language_example: Everyone wants to feel loved.

meaning: to stick together; to support each other (especially in a difficult time).
additional_notes: Used to encourage solidarity and mutual help when things are tough. Literally “to squeeze/press each other’s elbows,” but it’s an idiom meaning to stand united (family, friends, teammates, coworkers). Often said with il faut / on doit / c’est le moment de… to rally people.
target_language_example: Dans cette période difficile, on va se serrer les coudes.
native_language_example: In this difficult time, we’re going to stick together.

meaning: to use; to make use of.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (se servir) followed by **de** + a noun/pronoun: **se servir de quelque chose**. Often implies using something as a tool or resource. Conjugates like other -ir verbs: *je me sers de..., tu te sers de..., il/elle se sert de..., nous nous servons de..., vous vous servez de..., ils/elles se servent de...*.
target_language_example: Je vais me servir de mon téléphone pour traduire.
native_language_example: I’m going to use my phone to translate.

meaning: “is located” / “is situated” (to be found in a place; also: to rank/stand in a position).
additional_notes: Used mainly to give a location (physical place on a map): *se situer + sur/dans/à/en/au/aux* (e.g., *se situe au centre-ville*, *en Asie*). It can also be used figuratively for a ranking or position in a list/competition (e.g., *se situe au fond du panier* = “is at the bottom of the table”).
target_language_example: Le musée se situe près de la gare.
native_language_example: The museum is located near the train station.

additional_notes: Used in the passé composé with reflexive or pronominal verbs for a plural subject (they / plural nouns). In English, it often just corresponds to a simple past form like "stopped," "sat down," or "got lost," rather than a separate word for "se."
target_language_example: Ils se sont réveillés très tôt.
native_language_example: They woke up very early.

meaning: “got married” / “were married” (said about two or more people).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb se marier (“to get married”). Used with plural subjects: Ils/Elles se sont mariés = “They got married.” With a mixed group or all men, use mariés; with all women, mariées. Often followed by a time expression (en secret, il y a quelques années, en octobre, le mois dernier).
target_language_example: Ils se sont mariés à Paris l'année dernière.
native_language_example: They got married in Paris last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb "se moquer de" = to make fun of someone/something. Structure: "se moquer de + person/thing" (e.g., "se moquer de moi", "se moquer de sa tenue"). In other tenses you’ll see forms like "ils se moquent de..." (present) or "ils se moquaient de..." (imperfect).
target_language_example: Ils se sont moqués de son accent.
native_language_example: They made fun of his accent.

additional_notes: Passé composé of the reflexive verb **se rencontrer** (“to meet each other”). Used with **être**: *ils/elles se sont…* The past participle agrees with the subject: **rencontrés** (masc. plural), **rencontrées** (fem. plural). You’ll also see other forms: *je me suis rencontré(e), tu t’es rencontré(e), ils/elles se sont rencontrés/rencontrées*.
target_language_example: Ils se sont rencontrés à Paris en 2020.
native_language_example: They met in Paris in 2020.

additional_notes: From the verb "se soucier de" (a reflexive verb). It’s used to say someone cares/ worries about something or someone. Common pattern: "se soucie de + noun" (Elle se soucie de sa famille) or "se soucie de + question word" like "ce que / quand" (Qui se soucie de ce qu’ils pensent ?). Often used in the negative to mean "not to care": "Je ne m’en soucie pas" (= I don’t care about it).
target_language_example: Elle se soucie de ma santé.
native_language_example: She cares about my health.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: *se souvenir de* + noun/pronoun/infinitive (e.g., *Je me souviens de toi* / *Je me souviens d’avoir fermé la porte*). Often used in the present as *je me souviens* (“I remember”). Contrast with *se rappeler* (often used without *de*: *Je me rappelle ton nom*).
target_language_example: Il éprouve des difficultés à se souvenir des noms.
native_language_example: He has difficulty remembering names.

meaning: to kill oneself; to commit suicide.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (used with "se"). Conjugates like regular -er verbs: je me suicide, il/elle s’est suicidé(e). Often used after verbs like décider de / tenter de ("to decide/try to commit suicide").
target_language_example: Il a menacé de se suicider, mais on a réussi à l’aider.
native_language_example: He threatened to kill himself, but we managed to help him.

meaning: "was standing" / "was positioned" (past tense of se tenir).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something being in a certain posture or position at a given moment. Often followed by an adverb or place phrase: se tenir debout (to stand), se tenir sur une patte (to stand on one leg), se tenir au milieu de… (to be in the middle of…). It can refer to people, animals, or objects/vehicles.
target_language_example: Il se tenait près de la porte, sans rien dire.
native_language_example: He was standing near the door, without saying anything.

additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb « se terminer » (to end/finish). Used to talk about how something ends (a story, a movie, a night, a situation). Often in questions like « Comment ça se termine ? » (“How does it end?”). Common pattern: « Ça se termine + bien/mal » (“It ends well/badly”).
target_language_example: Le film se termine à minuit.
native_language_example: The movie ends at midnight.

meaning: “is standing / is located”; also “keeps (oneself) …” (informed/ready); “(it) makes sense” (Ça se tient).
additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb se tenir (il/elle se tient). Common uses: (1) physical position/location: Il se tient sur la colline. / Un garde se tient dehors. / Où se tient-il ? (2) with an adjective: se tenir prêt = to be ready. (3) with au courant de: se tenir au courant de… = to keep up to date about…. Fixed expression: Ça se tient = “That makes sense / It’s consistent.”
target_language_example: Il se tient prêt à partir.
native_language_example: He’s ready to leave.

additional_notes: Imperfect (past) form of **se trouver**. Commonly used to say where someone/something **was** at a certain time: **Il se trouvait à Paris.** It can also mean “happened to be” (by chance): **Il se trouvait là au bon moment.** Often used with places (**où / là / ici / à bord / dans…**).
target_language_example: À ce moment-là, elle se trouvait dans sa chambre.
native_language_example: At that moment, she was in her room.

additional_notes: From the verb **se trouver**. Commonly used to say where something is situated (more neutral/formal than **être**). It often appears with place words like **ici, là, à…, devant, derrière, près de**, etc. In descriptions, French may invert the order: **Devant ma maison se trouve un lac** (= “In front of my house there is a lake”).
target_language_example: Le musée se trouve près de la gare.
native_language_example: The museum is located near the train station.

additional_notes: Question form (formal) of **il se trouve** from **se trouver** (“to be located / to be found”). The **-t-** is added for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (e.g., *trouve-t-il*). Used to ask where something/someone is, or whether something is present/on a list: *Votre nom se trouve-t-il sur la liste ?* = “Is your name on the list?”
target_language_example: Où se trouve-t-il exactement ?
native_language_example: Where exactly is it located?

meaning: is located in downtown / in the city center.
additional_notes: Used to give the location of a place. "se trouve" is a common, fairly formal way to say "is located / can be found" (often for buildings, offices, stations, etc.). "au centre-ville" means "in the city center" (literally: "in the town/city center").
target_language_example: L'hôtel se trouve au centre-ville, près de la gare.
native_language_example: The hotel is located downtown, near the train station.

meaning: “the … is located / is found / is (in a certain state)” (with *se trouver*).
additional_notes: Used with a noun after it (*se trouve le/la/les…*) to say where something is, where it sits within something, or what condition it’s in. Very common in questions: *Où se trouve le… ?* (Where is the…?), *Dans quelle direction se trouve le… ?* (In what direction is the…?), *En quel état se trouve le… ?* (What condition is the…?). Word order is inverted (verb before subject) in formal questions.
target_language_example: Où se trouve le musée, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Where is the museum, please?

additional_notes: Form of the verb "se trouver" (present tense, 3rd person plural). It’s commonly used to say where people or things are, often as a more neutral/formal alternative to "être" (to be): "Où se trouvent… ?" = "Where are…?"
target_language_example: Les toilettes se trouvent au fond du couloir.
native_language_example: The toilets are at the end of the hallway.

meaning: to be located; to be found
additional_notes: Commonly used to say where someone or something is: se trouver quelque part = to be / be found somewhere. With a noun object, it can also mean to find or get something for oneself, as in se trouver un travail or se trouver un appartement. In the location sense, it is usually not translated literally as 'to find oneself'.
target_language_example: Mon livre doit se trouver quelque part dans la chambre.
native_language_example: My book must be somewhere in the room.

additional_notes: Most often used with an impersonal subject: « Ça se voit » = “It shows / You can tell.” Common in the negative too: « Ça ne se voit pas » = “You can’t tell / It doesn’t show.” Used to comment on something noticeable (feelings, changes, effort, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu as beaucoup travaillé : ça se voit.
native_language_example: You worked a lot—you can tell.

meaning: "you can tell by… / it shows in…"
additional_notes: Used mainly in the pattern "Ça se voit au + noun" to say that something is noticeable from a sign or feature (e.g., the face, the look, the smile, the accent). Here "au" is the contraction of "à + le". Literally it’s close to “it’s seen in/on (the),” but the natural English meaning is “you can tell by / it shows in.”
target_language_example: Ça se voit au visage qu’il est fatigué.
native_language_example: You can tell by his face that he’s tired.

additional_notes: Used literally (moving your head from side to side) and often to show disagreement, refusal (“no”), disbelief, or disapproval. Commonly used with "pour dire non" (to say no) or in the past tense: "J’ai secoué la tête."
target_language_example: Elle va secouer la tête pour dire non.
native_language_example: She is going to shake her head to say no.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week immediately before the current one. Often said as **la semaine dernière** (“last week”), especially after time expressions like **toute**: *toute la semaine dernière* = “all last week”. You can also use it with **de** to mean “from last week”: *les robes de la semaine dernière* = “the dresses from last week.”
target_language_example: On s’est vus la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: We saw each other last week.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week after the current one. Often comes after a preposition like pour (for/by next week) or la (until next week): e.g., pour la semaine prochaine = for/by next week. You can also say la semaine prochaine to mean “next week.”
target_language_example: On se voit la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: See you next week.

additional_notes: Used almost always with **faire**: **faire semblant de ne pas + infinitive** = “to pretend not to …” (often meaning to ignore something on purpose). It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., *entendre, connaître, voir, remarquer*).
target_language_example: Elle a fait semblant de ne pas me voir.
native_language_example: She pretended not to see me.

meaning: “does it seem (to you)?” (formal/written inversion) ; also “so it seems / apparently” when used parenthetically.
additional_notes: Formed from « sembler » + inverted subject pronoun « il » with a linking -t- (euphony): « semble-t-il ». Used mostly in formal or written French in questions with inversion, often after « cela/ça »: « Cela vous semble-t-il juste ? » = “Does that seem fair to you?” It can also be used parenthetically (« …, semble-t-il, … ») to mean “apparently / so it seems.”
target_language_example: Cela vous semble-t-il juste ?
native_language_example: Does that seem fair to you?

additional_notes: Most often used as **il semble que + clause** to express an impression or uncertainty (“it appears that…”). In modern French, it commonly takes the **subjunctive** after *que*: *Il semble que ce soit vrai.* (You may also hear the indicative in some contexts, especially in speech.)
target_language_example: Il semble que Marie soit en retard.
native_language_example: It seems that Marie is late.

additional_notes: Form of the verb « sembler » + « être » to express an impression/appearance (not certainty). Common patterns: « Ça/Cela semble être + noun/adjective » (“It seems to be…”). With a person: « Il/Elle semble être + adjective/noun » (“He/She seems to be…”). You can also say « Il me semble (que)… » = “It seems to me (that)…”.
target_language_example: D'après les indices, cela semble être la bonne solution.
native_language_example: Based on the clues, it seems to be the right solution.

additional_notes: Used to talk about practical judgment and basic reasoning. Often appears in fixed expressions like « manquer de sens commun » (to lack common sense) and « être dépourvu de sens commun » (to be devoid of common sense).
target_language_example: Ça, c’est du bon sens commun !
native_language_example: Now that’s good common sense!

additional_notes: Used with "avoir" (to have): "avoir le/un sens de l'humour". "Le" is general (“a sense of humor” as a trait), while "un" often describes a particular kind: "un curieux sens de l'humour" (“a strange/odd sense of humor”). Often appears in teasing questions like "Où est passé ton sens de l'humour ?" (“What happened to your sense of humor?”).
target_language_example: Elle a beaucoup de sens de l'humour, même au travail.
native_language_example: She has a great sense of humor, even at work.

additional_notes: Used in philosophical or personal discussions about why we exist or what makes life worthwhile. In French, "sens" can also mean "direction," but here it means "meaning/purpose." Often used with verbs like "chercher" (to look for), "comprendre" (to understand), and "se poser des questions" (to ask oneself questions).
target_language_example: Je me demande parfois quel est le sens de la vie.
native_language_example: I sometimes wonder what the meaning of life is.

meaning: upside down; all messed up / in chaos.
additional_notes: An idiom meaning things are in complete disorder or turned upside down. Used for rooms/houses/situations ("La maison est sens dessus dessous") and sometimes for a person who feels disoriented or shaken ("Il est sens dessus dessous"). Often used with être: "Tout est sens dessus dessous."
target_language_example: Après la fête, l'appartement était sens dessus dessous.
native_language_example: After the party, the apartment was a complete mess.

additional_notes: Question form of the verb **sentir** ("to feel" or "to smell") with **inversion** (**sens + -tu**) for "do you…?". Used to ask if someone feels something physically (pain, a touch, a vibration) or notices a smell. (Different from **se sentir** = "to feel (well/bad)" about your general state.)
target_language_example: Sens-tu l’odeur de fumée ?
native_language_example: Can you smell the smell of smoke?

additional_notes: From the verb *sentir* (“to feel” or “to smell”) + *un peu* (“a bit”). By itself, **sens un peu** is usually incomplete and needs context (e.g., *Tu sens un peu la fumée ?* “Do you smell a bit of smoke?”). If you mean “I feel a bit…”, beginners more often use **je me sens un peu…** (with *se sentir* = “to feel”).
target_language_example: Je me sens un peu fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I feel a bit tired today.

additional_notes: From the verb "sentir" (to smell). You use it to describe a nice odor: "X sent bon". (Opposite: "X sent mauvais" = smells bad.)
target_language_example: Ce gâteau sent bon !
native_language_example: This cake smells good!

meaning: "do you feel…?" / "can you smell…?" (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: From the verb "sentir" in the present tense with inversion for a question ("sentez" + "vous"). It can mean either physical/emotional feeling ("Vous sentez-vous bien ?" = Do you feel well?) or smelling/perceiving an odor ("Sentez-vous la fumée ?" = Do you smell smoke?). With "en" ("Vous en sentez-vous à la hauteur ?"), it’s part of the expression "s’en sentir à la hauteur" = to feel up to it / capable of it.
target_language_example: Sentez-vous une odeur de gaz ?
native_language_example: Do you smell a gas smell?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of seven years ("depuis sept ans" = for seven years) or someone’s age ("Il a sept ans" = He is seven). Also appears in time expressions like "il y a sept ans" (seven years ago).
target_language_example: Elle a vécu ici pendant sept ans.
native_language_example: She lived here for seven years.

meaning: seven o’clock (7:00); also “seven hours” depending on context.
additional_notes: With a time of day, it usually means 7:00. Often used with prepositions like « à sept heures » (at seven) or « vers sept heures » (around seven). Without context, it can also literally mean a duration of seven hours.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à sept heures devant le café.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at seven o’clock in front of the café.

additional_notes: Question form (inversion) of the future tense of être: « il sera » → « sera-t-il ? ». « il » can mean “he” or “it,” depending on what you’re talking about. Often used with quand (“when”) to ask about timing (Quand sera-t-il prêt ?).
target_language_example: À quelle heure sera-t-il là ?
native_language_example: What time will he be there?

additional_notes: A formal question form in the future tense (inversion): sera (will be) + -t- (linking sound) + il (it/he) + publié (published). Used to ask when something (a book, magazine issue, etc.) will come out/be released. For “she,” use: sera-t-elle publié(e) (agreement often written: publiée for a feminine subject).
target_language_example: Quand sera-t-il publié ?
native_language_example: When will it be published?

additional_notes: Future tense of être ("sera" = "will be") + "bientôt" ("soon"). Used to say something will happen/arrive/be ready in the near future. Often followed by a time/event (Ce sera bientôt le Nouvel An.) or by an adjective (Ce sera bientôt prêt.)
target_language_example: Le repas sera bientôt prêt.
native_language_example: The meal will be ready soon.

meaning: 'will be back in' (after a certain amount of time).
additional_notes: Used to say someone will return after a duration. This is the 3rd-person singular future of "être de retour" (to be back): "il/elle/on sera de retour" + "dans" meaning "in" (in 10 minutes). The time expression after "dans" can be: une seconde, dix minutes, une heure, quelques heures, moins de dix minutes, etc. Note: for "I will be back in…", use "je serai de retour dans…".
target_language_example: Il sera de retour dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: He’ll be back in ten minutes.

meaning: “would you be…?” / “could you be…?” (polite, formal “vous” form).
additional_notes: This is the conditional of être (to be) with vous, used to ask a polite question or make a soft request. Often followed by an adjective or description: Seriez-vous intéressé(e)…? (“Would you be interested…?”), Seriez-vous prêt(e)(s)…? (“Would you be ready…?”). It can also be used to confirm someone’s identity: Seriez-vous Tim Norton ? (“Would you be Tim Norton?” = “Are you Tim Norton, by any chance?”). Agreement changes with who you’re addressing: intéressé (male singular), intéressée (female singular), intéressés/intéressées (plural).
target_language_example: Seriez-vous disponible demain matin ?
native_language_example: Would you be available tomorrow morning?

meaning: to hug (hold someone tightly in my arms).
additional_notes: Most often used as **serrer quelqu’un dans ses bras** (“to hug someone”). The possessive changes with the subject: *dans mes bras* (my), *dans tes bras* (your), *dans ses bras* (his/her), etc. You can also say *Je l’ai serré(e) dans mes bras* (“I hugged him/her”).
target_language_example: Je veux te serrer dans mes bras.
native_language_example: I want to hug you.

additional_notes: Used for greetings, introductions, or congratulations. Often appears as "serrer la main à quelqu’un" (to shake someone’s hand). In polite instructions you may see "Veuillez vous serrer la main" (Please shake hands with each other).
target_language_example: Je vais lui serrer la main après la réunion.
native_language_example: I’m going to shake his hand after the meeting.

meaning: to grit your teeth; to clench your teeth (and push through).
additional_notes: Used literally (clenching your teeth) or figuratively to mean enduring something difficult, painful, or annoying and continuing anyway ("hang in there"). Often used with "il faut" or in the imperative: "Serre les dents !"
target_language_example: J’ai mal, mais je vais serrer les dents et continuer.
native_language_example: It hurts, but I’m going to grit my teeth and keep going.

additional_notes: From the verb "se servir de" = "to use". "Sers-toi de ..." is the imperative for "tu" (telling one person you’re on first-name terms with to use something), often with body parts or tools: "Sers-toi de ta tête" = "Use your head." For a more formal/plural command, use "Servez-vous de ...". Not to confuse with "Servez-vous !" (without "de"), which often means "Help yourself!" (e.g., to food).
target_language_example: Sers-toi de ce couteau pour couper le pain.
native_language_example: Use this knife to cut the bread.

additional_notes: Used mainly in the negative: « ça ne sert à rien » = “it’s pointless / it’s no use.” You can also use it with an infinitive: « Ça ne sert à rien de + verb » (“There’s no point in doing …”). With « sinon »: « … sinon ça ne sert à rien » = “otherwise it’s pointless.”
target_language_example: Ça ne sert à rien de s'inquiéter maintenant.
native_language_example: There's no point in worrying now.

meaning: “there’s no point in / it’s no use (doing something)”.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say an action is useless: **(Ça) ne sert à rien de + infinitive**. Very common with **ça** (“that/it”): *Ça sert à rien de…* (informal spoken) or more correct: *Ça ne sert à rien de…* / *Il ne sert à rien de…*.
target_language_example: Ça ne sert à rien de s’inquiéter.
native_language_example: There’s no point in worrying.

additional_notes: From the verb "servir" (to serve). "Servez-vous" can be (1) the present tense for "vous" meaning "you serve" (formal singular or plural): "Quels plats servez-vous ?" It can also be (2) an imperative meaning "Help yourself" / "Serve yourself" (often said when offering food): "Servez-vous une part de gâteau."
target_language_example: Servez-vous, il y a du pain sur la table.
native_language_example: Help yourself—there’s bread on the table.

additional_notes: Refers to a government intelligence or security agency. Often used with an article ("le service secret") or in the plural ("les services secrets") to talk about secret services in general. Depending on context, it can mean intelligence gathering, internal security, or protective services.
target_language_example: Il travaille pour le service secret.
native_language_example: He works for the secret service.

additional_notes: “Ses” is the plural possessive adjective meaning “his/her” (it can refer to either a man or a woman). It’s used before a plural noun, like “amis” (friends), and the meaning is understood from context (who “ses” refers to).
target_language_example: Il parle souvent de ses amis d’enfance.
native_language_example: He often talks about his childhood friends.

additional_notes: "Ses" is a possessive adjective that means "his", "her", or "their" (plural owners), depending on context. It’s used with plural nouns like "chaussures" (shoes). For "his/her shoe" (singular), use "sa chaussure".
target_language_example: Il a oublié ses chaussures dans l’entrée.
native_language_example: He forgot his shoes in the entryway.

additional_notes: “Ses” means “his/her” (also “its” or “their” depending on context). With the plural noun “cheveux” (hair), French uses “ses” for both masculine and feminine owners: ses cheveux = his hair / her hair. Often used in descriptions (long/short, clean, gray) or with body-related verbs (se brosser les cheveux, se couper les cheveux).
target_language_example: Elle se brosse ses cheveux tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She brushes her hair every evening.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe hair color, texture, or length. "Ses" means "his" or "her" (it depends on who owns the hair, not on the gender of the person speaking). "Cheveux" is plural in French, so you usually use the plural verb form "sont" and plural adjectives: "Ses cheveux sont longs/gris."
target_language_example: Ses cheveux sont courts et bouclés.
native_language_example: His/Her hair is short and curly.

additional_notes: Used with a possessive adjective (ses = “his/her/their”) to talk about someone’s homework. Often used with the verb faire: faire ses devoirs = “to do one’s homework.” Note that it agrees with the (plural) noun devoirs, not with the owner’s gender.
target_language_example: Elle lui fait faire ses devoirs avant le souper.
native_language_example: She makes him/her do his/her homework before dinner.

additional_notes: A phrase fragment you’ll usually see inside a full sentence, often after a verb like faire: « Il fait ses devoirs immédiatement après le dîner. » Here, « ses devoirs » means “his/her homework” (not “duties”), and « immédiatement après » means “immediately after / right after / right afterwards,” followed by what comes next (e.g., a meal, class, an event).
target_language_example: Elle fait ses devoirs immédiatement après le cours.
native_language_example: She does her homework right after class.

meaning: his/her fingers in his/her hair (often: to run one’s fingers through one’s hair).
additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like « passer » or « faire courir »: « passer/faire courir ses doigts dans ses cheveux » = to run his/her fingers through his/her hair (often from stress, thinking, or to fix hair). The possessives change with the person: « mes doigts dans mes cheveux », « tes doigts dans tes cheveux », etc.
target_language_example: Il a fait courir ses doigts dans ses cheveux avant de répondre.
native_language_example: He ran his fingers through his hair before answering.

additional_notes: "Ses" is a possessive adjective meaning "his/her/their" (it agrees with the noun: enfants is plural, so ses). It can refer to one person’s children (his/her) or multiple people’s children (their); the context tells you which. Often appears with verbs like aimer (to love), penser à (to think about), léguer à (to leave/inherit to), choisir des noms pour (to choose names for).
target_language_example: Elle parle souvent de ses enfants.
native_language_example: She often talks about her children.

additional_notes: “Ses” is a possessive meaning “his” or “her” (it depends on who owns the glasses). “Lunettes” is plural in French, so you normally say it in the plural, like in English (“glasses”). Used for eyeglasses; for sunglasses you often say “ses lunettes de soleil.”
target_language_example: Elle ne peut pas lire sans ses lunettes.
native_language_example: She can’t read without her glasses.

additional_notes: "Ses" can mean "his", "her", or "their" depending on context; it agrees with the plural noun "lunettes" (glasses), not with the owner. Common with verbs like "mettre" (put on), "enlever/ôter/retirer" (take off/remove), and "perdre" (lose).
target_language_example: Il a perdu ses lunettes de soleil.
native_language_example: He lost his sunglasses.

additional_notes: "Ses" is a possessive determiner meaning "his", "her", or "its" (singular owner), and it agrees with the plural noun "mains". Used to talk about someone’s hands in general: "ses mains étaient…" (his/her hands were…), "il/elle a levé ses mains" (he/she raised his/her hands).
target_language_example: Elle s'est lavé les mains, puis elle a séché ses mains avec une serviette.
native_language_example: She washed her hands, then she dried her hands with a towel.

additional_notes: “Ses” is a possessive meaning “his/her” (or “its/their”) and agrees with the plural noun “parents” (not with the owner’s gender). So it can refer to either someone’s mom and dad, or more generally someone’s family/relatives depending on context.
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, je voyageais souvent avec ses parents.
native_language_example: When I was little, I often traveled with his/her parents.

meaning: 'his/her/its own' (emphasizing that they belong specifically to that person/thing).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun: ses propres + nom (ex. ses propres vêtements, ses propres problèmes). It adds emphasis, like “their very own” or “their own (not someone else’s)”. The singular forms are: son propre (masc.), sa propre (fem.), ses propres (plural).
target_language_example: Elle veut avoir ses propres idées.
native_language_example: She wants to have her own ideas.

additional_notes: "Ses" is a possessive adjective meaning "his/her/its" (singular owner) or "their" (plural owners). It agrees with the noun "vêtements" (plural), not with the owner’s gender. Often used with verbs like ôter/retirer (to take off) or mettre (to put on).
target_language_example: Il a mis ses vêtements dans l’armoire.
native_language_example: He put his clothes in the closet.

additional_notes: "Ses" means "his" or "her" (you know which from context), and "yeux" is the plural of "œil" (eye). Often used literally (looking at someone’s eyes) or figuratively to talk about emotions you can see in someone’s gaze: "Je l’ai lu dans ses yeux" = "I could read it in his/her eyes."
target_language_example: On voyait la joie dans ses yeux.
native_language_example: You could see the joy in his/her eyes.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "ses" (his/her/their, plural) with "études" (studies). Often refers to someone’s period of education or academic program: "faire ses études" (to do/complete one’s studies), "finir ses études" (to finish), "pendant ses études" (during), "se concentrer sur ses études" (to focus on), "des difficultés dans ses études" (difficulties). The owner changes with context: ses = his or her or their.
target_language_example: Après ses études, elle a trouvé un travail à Paris.
native_language_example: After her studies, she found a job in Paris.

meaning: all alone; alone in the world.
additional_notes: Means being completely alone or isolated (literally or figuratively). It agrees with the person: « seule au monde » (feminine), « seuls au monde » (plural). Often used for emphasis, like “completely alone.”
target_language_example: Depuis son déménagement, il se sent seul au monde.
native_language_example: Since his move, he feels all alone.

seul à ne pas être invité à la

target_language_multi_word_term: seul à ne pas être invité à la
meaning: "the only one not invited to the…"
additional_notes: Used to say someone is the only person who didn’t get invited to an event (often with a feeling of exclusion). It’s a pattern you complete with the event: « …à la fête / à la réunion / à la soirée ». Grammar notes: « seul » agrees with the person (seul, seule, seuls, seules). After « seul(e)(s) », French often uses « à + infinitive »: « seul à ne pas être invité… ». You can also replace « invité » with « invitée(s) » depending on gender/number.
target_language_example: J’étais le seul à ne pas être invité à la fête.
native_language_example: I was the only one not invited to the party.

meaning: one-on-one; in private (just the two of us).
additional_notes: Used to insist that no one else should be present—often with verbs like parler (to talk), voir (to see), or nouns like entretien (meeting/interview). It can be said as a standalone request: « Seul à seul. » (= “Privately.” / “Just us two.”).
target_language_example: J’aimerais te parler seul à seul après la réunion.
native_language_example: I’d like to talk to you one-on-one after the meeting.

additional_notes: Used in a relative clause, usually as **la seule chose qui + verb** to introduce what is unique/only. Example: **La seule chose qui me manque, c’est toi.** (Note: you’ll most often see **la** because *chose* is feminine.)
target_language_example: La seule chose qui m’inquiète, c’est le temps.
native_language_example: The only thing that worries me is the weather.

meaning: “only I could …” / (most often) “if only I could …”.
additional_notes: On its own, this word order is unusual in modern French. You most often see it as part of the wish/regret expression **si seulement je pouvais…** (“if only I could…”), followed by an infinitive or a full clause: *Si seulement je pouvais venir…* / *Si seulement je pouvais t’aider…*. In more natural phrasing, French often prefers **je pouvais seulement…** (“I could only…”).
target_language_example: Si seulement je pouvais partir plus tôt !
native_language_example: If only I could leave earlier!

meaning: “so (well) that,” expressing a result; also “that well” in “pas si bien que ça.”
additional_notes: 1) As a conjunction, **si bien que + clause** introduces a consequence/result: *Il pleuvait, si bien que je suis resté chez moi.* → “It was raining, so I stayed home.” 2) In expressions like **(ne) pas … si bien que ça**, it means “(not) that well / not so much”: *Je ne le connais pas si bien que ça.* → “I don’t know him that well.” 3) **Si bien que ça ?** is a short question meaning “That good/well?”
target_language_example: Il me tient en laisse, si bien que je ne peux pas respirer.
native_language_example: He keeps me on a leash, so I can’t breathe.

meaning: so long; for so long (so much time).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the duration of an action/state. Often comes after a verb: attendre si longtemps (wait so long), réfléchir si longtemps (think for so long). In questions like « Qu'est-ce qui prend si longtemps ? », it means “Why is it taking so long?”
target_language_example: Je ne t’ai pas vu depuis si longtemps.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in so long.

meaning: so little; so few (so not much).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a small quantity or degree. With an adjective/adverb it means “so little” (e.g., si peu sûr = so not confident). With a noun, it often appears as “si peu de + noun” meaning “so little/few of …” (si peu de choses = so few things).
target_language_example: Il parle si peu en classe.
native_language_example: He speaks so little in class.

meaning: so late (at such a late time).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize how late the time is, often when apologizing for calling/coming late ("Désolé d'appeler si tard"). You can also soften it with "pas si tard" (= "not that late") or "pas si tard que ça" (= "not that late, really").
target_language_example: Je suis désolé d'arriver si tard.
native_language_example: I'm sorry to arrive so late.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize how early something happens or is done. Often placed after the verb (e.g., se lever si tôt, rentrer si tôt). Don’t confuse with « aussitôt » (“as soon as / immediately”).
target_language_example: Pourquoi es-tu arrivé si tôt ?
native_language_example: Why did you arrive so early?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize speed, often in questions or statements of surprise. It can describe how fast something happens (Tout est allé si vite.) or how fast someone does something (Comment t'es arrivé si vite ?).
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu es parti si vite ?
native_language_example: Why did you leave so quickly?

si, pour une raison quelconque, cela

target_language_multi_word_term: si, pour une raison quelconque, cela
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical situation (“if…”) where the speaker doesn’t know or specify the cause (“pour une raison quelconque” = “for some reason”). It’s often followed by a verb describing what might happen: cela arrive / devait arriver / devait avoir lieu / devait survenir (“that happens / were to happen / were to take place / were to occur”).
target_language_example: Si, pour une raison quelconque, cela ne marche pas, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If, for some reason, it doesn’t work, call me.

additional_notes:
Used to introduce a condition, often in set phrases like:
- « Si c'est ce que tu crois » = “If that’s what you think.”
- « Si c'est ce que vous voulez, d'accord » = “If that’s what you want, OK.”
- « Si c'est comme ça » = “If that’s how it is / If that’s the way it is” (often sounds resigned or accepting).
target_language_example: Si c'est ce que vous voulez, d'accord.
native_language_example: If that’s what you want, OK.

si c'est ce que tu veux

target_language_multi_word_term: si c'est ce que tu veux
additional_notes: Used to accept or go along with someone’s preference/decision. It can sound neutral or slightly resigned depending on tone and context. Often paired with “d’accord”, “très bien”, “OK”, etc.
target_language_example: On peut partir plus tôt, si c'est ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: We can leave earlier, if that’s what you want.

additional_notes: Expression with « si » + imperfect (« c’était ») used to introduce a hypothetical, uncertain, or imagined situation. Often paired with the conditional: « Ce serait… si c’était… » (“It would be… if it were…”). Very common in « si c’était le cas » = “if that were the case,” and « comme si c’était… » = “as if it were…”.
target_language_example: Ce serait bien si c'était vrai.
native_language_example: It would be nice if it were true.

additional_notes: Often used after a negative or general statement to introduce the only exception: "nothing/no one..., except..." It can also mean "if not" when correcting or qualifying what was just said (e.g., "It’s true—if not surprising").
target_language_example: Je n'ai rien mangé aujourd'hui, si ce n'est une pomme.
native_language_example: I didn’t eat anything today, except an apple.

meaning: “if it’s not” / “if that isn’t the case.”
additional_notes: Introduces a condition where something is not true, often in questions or when setting up an alternative. Common with « le cas »: « Si ce n’est pas le cas… » (“If that’s not the case…”). Note: without « pas », « si ce n’est » can also mean “except (for)”, but « si ce n’est pas » is the literal conditional (“if it’s not…”).
target_language_example: Si ce n'est pas Ian, qui est-ce ?
native_language_example: If it’s not Ian, who is it?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like demander, savoir, se demander to introduce an indirect yes/no question about a female subject (elle). Often followed by another verb: « si elle peut / si elle a / si elle veut ».
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas si elle vient ce soir.
native_language_example: I don’t know if she’s coming tonight.

additional_notes: Used after **si** (“if/whether”) with **elle était** (imparfait of *être*). Common in: (1) **indirect questions**: *Il a demandé si elle était…* = “He asked whether she was…”; (2) **comme si** (“as if”), often describing an unreal/imagined situation: *comme si elle était…* = “as if she were…”.
target_language_example: Je me demandais si elle était déjà partie.
native_language_example: I was wondering if she had already left.

additional_notes: Rather formal/literary. Used to strongly confirm what was just said, similar to “indeed” or “certainly” in English. Don’t confuse with **si** alone, which means “yes” when answering a negative question (e.g., *Tu n’as pas faim ? — Si !*).
target_language_example: — Il n'a jamais aidé. — Si fait, il a beaucoup aidé.
native_language_example: — He never helped. — Yes, he did; he helped a lot.

meaning: "if ever" / "if by any chance" (often: "just in case").
additional_notes: Used to introduce a possibility that may or may not happen. Very common in practical instructions or precautions: "Si jamais il appelle..." (= If he happens to call...). It can also express a hypothetical situation with an implied consequence, sometimes sounding like a warning: "Si jamais il est innocent, gare !" (= If it turns out he’s innocent, watch out!).
target_language_example: Si jamais tu passes par ici, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If you happen to be in the area, call me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition or hypothesis with je (“I”). Very common at the start of conditional clauses: si je peux... (“if I can...”), si je savais... (“if I knew...”); in polite expressions, si je peux me permettre means “if I may.”
target_language_example: Si je finis tôt, je t'appelle.
native_language_example: If I finish early, I'll call you.

meaning: "if I" + "it/him" (introduces a condition with a direct object).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a conditional clause: **si** = "if", **je** = "I", **le** = "him/it" (direct object pronoun). The verb usually comes right after (**si je le connais** = "if I know him/it"). In many examples it’s followed by the conditional (e.g., **je le ferais** = "I would do it") or used with **voir**/**savoir** (e.g., **je vais voir si je le…** = "I’m going to see if I…").
target_language_example: Je te rappelle si je le peux.
native_language_example: I’ll call you back if I can.

meaning: "if I don't / if I do not" (start of a negative condition).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition with a negated verb: "si je ne + verb" (e.g., si je ne rentre pas = if I don’t come back). In French negation is usually "ne ... pas" around the verb, but in formal/literary French you may sometimes see "ne" without "pas" (e.g., si je ne vous aimais = if I didn’t love you).
target_language_example: Si je ne comprends pas, je te demanderai de répéter.
native_language_example: If I don’t understand, I’ll ask you to repeat.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or ability, often when offering help or checking whether something is possible: "Je vais voir si je peux…" (I’ll see if I can…). It can stand alone at the end of a sentence to mean "if I can" (e.g., "Je m'en occupe, si je peux."). Also appears in stronger phrases like "Pas si je peux l'empêcher" = "Not if I can help it" (I’ll try to prevent it).
target_language_example: Je viendrai demain, si je peux.
native_language_example: I’ll come tomorrow, if I can.

additional_notes: Often used to express a hypothetical or wish. Commonly appears after expressions like « comme si… » (“as if…”) and can be followed by an infinitive (e.g., « si je pouvais venir »).
target_language_example: Si je pouvais, je resterais à la maison aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: If I could, I would stay home today.

meaning: 'if I may say so' (a polite hedge).
additional_notes: Used to soften a comment, add a respectful tone (especially with titles like « Votre Excellence » / « Madame »), or sometimes to signal a slightly bold, witty, or ironic remark. « Puis » is a formal/literary form of « peux » (“can”). Often placed after the comment: « …, si je puis dire. »
target_language_example: C’est une solution plutôt originale, si je puis dire.
native_language_example: It’s a rather original solution, if I may say so.

meaning: 'if I … you' (introduces a condition with 'te' = 'you' as the object).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a conditional clause: **si** = “if”, **je** = “I”, **te** = “you” (informal singular object pronoun). **Te** comes before the verb: *si je te vois* (“if I see you”), *si je te quitte* (“if I leave you”). Often followed by another clause giving the result.
target_language_example: Si je te rappelle ce soir, réponds, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: If I call you back tonight, please answer.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen only if it’s required. Often placed at the start of a sentence ("Si nécessaire, ...") or at the end ("... si nécessaire"). Can also be used alone as a short reply meaning “if needed.”
target_language_example: Appelez-moi si nécessaire.
native_language_example: Call me if necessary (if needed).

additional_notes: Introduces a condition. In everyday French, on very often means 'we' instead of nous. In general statements, it can also mean 'you', 'one', or 'people'. With the imperfect, as in si on changeait..., it often makes a suggestion: 'what if we...?' or 'how about...?'
target_language_example: Si on part tôt, on évitera les embouteillages.
native_language_example: If we leave early, we'll avoid the traffic jams.

meaning: “How about we…?” / “What if we went…?” (a suggestion).
additional_notes: Used to make a friendly suggestion for an activity, often as a question. It literally uses the imperfect of aller (“we were going”), but it functions like “shall we…?/how about…?”. Often appears with “Et” at the start: “Et si on allait… ?”.
target_language_example: Si on allait au cinéma ce soir ?
native_language_example: How about we go to the movies tonight?

meaning: 'if we' / 'if you' + a reflexive verb ('if we/you ... ourselves').
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition with the subject "on" and a reflexive verb (verb used with "se"). In everyday French, "on" often means "we" (and sometimes "you" or "people in general" depending on context). The "se" changes form with the subject (je me, tu te, on se, nous nous, vous vous, ils/elles se). Examples: si on se dépêche (if we hurry), si on se comprend (if we understand each other), si on se disperse (if we split up), si on se lance (if we get started).
target_language_example: Si on se dépêche, on arrivera à l’heure.
native_language_example: If we hurry, we’ll arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to soften a request or preference (“preferably”), often placed at the end of the sentence. Can refer to timing ("as soon as tomorrow, if possible"), quantity ("one or two more, if possible"), or a condition ("less than a year old, if possible").
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me l’envoyer aujourd’hui, si possible ?
native_language_example: Can you send it to me today, if possible?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition: if an event happens, if there’s a problem, or if anything changes. Very common with verbs like "arriver" (to happen), "survenir" (to occur), "clocher" (to be wrong). In spoken French, "Si quelque chose, ..." can be short for "If anything (happens/changes), ...".
target_language_example: Si quelque chose ne va pas, appelle-moi tout de suite.
native_language_example: If something isn’t right, call me right away.

additional_notes: Used to say “in case something happens/changes,” often in instructions or offers of help: « Appelle-moi si quoi que ce soit change/survient. » You can also use it in questions: « Si quoi que ce soit se produit, puis-je compter sur toi/vous ? » (toi = informal singular, vous = formal or plural).
target_language_example: Préviens-moi si quoi que ce soit arrive pendant mon absence.
native_language_example: Let me know if anything happens while I’m away.

additional_notes: Often introduces something you wish were true, usually followed by the imperfect or pluperfect: « Si seulement c'était… » (If only it were…), « Si seulement j'avais su… » (If only I had known…). It can also mean “even if only / at least” in the sense of a minimal condition: « …si seulement vous en êtes capable » (…if you can at least manage it).
target_language_example: Si seulement je pouvais y aller avec toi.
native_language_example: If only I could go there with you.

additional_notes: Expresses a strong wish or regret about something that isn’t true right now (often something difficult or impossible). Typically followed by an infinitive (e.g., parler, voler, être). You can change the subject: si seulement tu pouvais… / si seulement on pouvait…
target_language_example: Si seulement je pouvais venir avec vous ce soir !
native_language_example: If only I could come with you tonight!

additional_notes: Introduces a condition with tu: 'if you...'. Used in both real possibilities and hypothetical situations, depending on the tense that follows.
target_language_example: Si tu veux, on peut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: If you want, we can leave now.

meaning: "if you have" (talking to one person informally).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition (something is true only if the other person has something: time, a moment, a question, hunger, etc.). "Tu" is informal singular (friends, family, kids). With a noun, it’s very common: "si tu as le temps" (if you have time), "si tu as une question" (if you have a question). Often followed by an instruction or suggestion.
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin d'aide, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If you need help, call me.

additional_notes: Used to offer help or leave the door open for someone to ask for something later. You can follow it with a noun (si tu as besoin de quelque chose = if you need something) or an infinitive verb (si tu as besoin de parler = if you need to talk). Often used with an imperative or offer: Appelle… / Dis-moi… / Je suis là…
target_language_example: Dis-moi si tu as besoin de quelque chose.
native_language_example: Tell me if you need something.

si tu as besoin de moi

target_language_multi_word_term: si tu as besoin de moi
additional_notes: A common conditional phrase to offer help or availability. Often paired with an imperative (Appelle…, Réveille-moi…) or a promise (Je serai là…). Word order can be either: “Appelle si tu as besoin de moi” or “Si tu as besoin de moi, appelle.” In everyday French you may also hear “si tu as besoin” (implied “of me”) or “si tu as besoin de quelque chose” (if you need something).
target_language_example: Je suis là si tu as besoin de moi.
native_language_example: I'm here if you need me.

si tu as besoin de quoi que ce

target_language_multi_word_term: si tu as besoin de quoi que ce
additional_notes: In real French, this is almost always completed as: « si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit » (“if you need anything / if you need something, whatever it is”). Used to offer help or availability. « avoir besoin de » = “to need”. « quoi que ce soit » is a common set phrase meaning “anything (at all)”.
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If you need anything, call me.

si tu as quelque chose à dire

target_language_multi_word_term: si tu as quelque chose à dire
additional_notes: Used to challenge someone to speak up (often because they seem to be hinting, criticizing, or talking behind someone’s back). Commonly followed by an imperative like dis-le / dis-le-moi en face (“say it / say it to my face”). Can sound confrontational depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Si tu as quelque chose à dire, dis-le clairement.
native_language_example: If you have something to say, say it clearly.

meaning: "if you are" (used to start a condition).
additional_notes: "Si" introduces a condition, and "tu es" uses the informal singular "you" (tu) with the verb "être" (to be). It’s followed by a description/state: si tu es là (if you’re here), si tu es heureuse (if you’re happy), si tu es prête (if you’re ready). It can also be part of a longer form like "si tu es allé(e)..." = "if you went / have been...". Common pattern: "Si tu es…, (alors) …" = "If you’re…, (then) …".
target_language_example: Si tu es fatigué, on peut rentrer.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, we can go home.

additional_notes: Used to start a condition with si (“if”). tu = “you” (informal singular). le is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (a masculine thing/idea) or “him” (a man/boy), and it goes before the verb: si tu le veux (“if you want it”), si tu le laisses (“if you leave it”), si tu le tues (“if you kill him/it”).
target_language_example: Si tu le finis aujourd’hui, on peut sortir demain.
native_language_example: If you finish it today, we can go out tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to show you accept what someone says, often with doubt, irony, or mild skepticism. Can also be a short standalone reply (“Si tu le dis.”). Tone depends on context; with emphasis (“Si tu le dis !”) it can sound more sarcastic.
target_language_example: — Je te jure que je vais changer. — Si tu le dis.
native_language_example: — I swear I’m going to change. — If you say so.

additional_notes: Used to start a conditional clause with a negative verb (si + tu + ne...). In everyday French, "ne" is often used with another negation word (e.g., "pas", "plus", "jamais"): "si tu ne viens pas" = "if you don't come". The result/main clause can come after or before it: "Si tu ne leur dis pas, je le ferai" / "Je le ferai si tu ne leur dis pas".
target_language_example: Si tu ne comprends pas, je peux répéter.
native_language_example: If you don't understand, I can repeat.

si tu ne le fais pas

target_language_multi_word_term: si tu ne le fais pas
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition (“if…”). "tu" = you (informal singular). "ne…pas" makes the verb negative, and "le" is an object pronoun meaning “it” (referring to something already mentioned). Often followed by a consequence in the future/imperative (e.g., "tu devras…", "je le ferai") or in the conditional ("je le ferais").
target_language_example: Si tu ne le fais pas aujourd’hui, on n’aura pas le temps demain.
native_language_example: If you don’t do it today, we won’t have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often used to make a suggestion or invitation softer and more polite, implying it’s up to the other person. It can also be used like English “I mean / you know” (e.g., « Si tu veux, oui. » = “Yes, if you like / yes, I guess.”). In speech it’s sometimes shortened to « si tu veux » said quickly.
target_language_example: On peut se retrouver à 18h, si tu veux.
native_language_example: We can meet at 6 p.m., if you want.

meaning: “If you want, you can …” (it’s up to you / you’re allowed).
additional_notes: Used to offer someone a choice or give permission in a friendly way. Often introduces a suggestion: “If you’d like, you can…”. Can also sound slightly indifferent depending on tone (like “do what you want”).
target_language_example: Si tu veux, tu peux prendre ma place.
native_language_example: If you want, you can take my seat.

additional_notes: Used with "si" + imparfait ("étais") to talk about unreal or unlikely situations. It’s often followed by the conditional to say what would happen: "Si tu étais…, tu ferais/tu serais…". Also common in "comme si tu étais…" = "as if you were…".
target_language_example: Si tu étais plus tôt, on pourrait partir maintenant.
native_language_example: If you were earlier, we could leave now.

additional_notes: Used with vous, which can mean either plural 'you' or formal singular 'you'. si vous often introduces a condition ('if you...'), but after verbs like se demander, savoir, or dire, it can mean 'whether you...'.
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin d'aide, appelez-moi.
native_language_example: If you need help, call me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition in polite/formal address (vous): "If you have X, then…" Common with besoin (need) or une question (a question): « si vous avez besoin… », « si vous avez une question… ». Often paired with a request or instruction in the next clause.
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin d'aide, appelez-moi.
native_language_example: If you need help, call me.

meaning: 'if you need' (something) / 'if you need to' (do something).
additional_notes: Used to politely offer help or make something conditional: "Si vous avez besoin de + noun" (If you need + a noun) or "Si vous avez besoin de + infinitive" (If you need to + verb). "Vous" is the formal/plural 'you'. Often followed by "quelque chose" (something) or "de l'aide" (help).
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin de quelque chose, appelez-moi.
native_language_example: If you need anything, call me.

si vous avez besoin de moi

target_language_multi_word_term: si vous avez besoin de moi
additional_notes: Used to offer help/availability politely (vous = formal or plural “you”). Often paired with a reassurance like “je suis là” (I’m here) or an instruction like “appelez-moi” (call me). You can also say “si tu as besoin de moi” to one person informally.
target_language_example: Je suis au bureau si vous avez besoin de moi.
native_language_example: I’m at the office if you need me.

si vous avez besoin de quelque chose

target_language_multi_word_term: si vous avez besoin de quelque chose
additional_notes: Used to offer help politely: you’re telling someone to contact/ask you (or someone else) in case they need anything. Uses "vous" (formal or plural "you"). Often followed by an instruction like "appelez-moi" (call me) or "dites-moi" (tell me). You can also say "si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit" for “if you need anything at all.”
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin de quelque chose, appelez-moi.
native_language_example: If you need something, call me.

si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce

target_language_multi_word_term: si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce
additional_notes: This is most commonly said as **« si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit »** (with **soit**), meaning “if you need anything/whatever you need.” It’s a polite offer of help, often followed by **n’hésitez pas à…** (“don’t hesitate to…”). Without **soit**, it sounds incomplete in standard French.
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit, n’hésitez pas à me contacter.
native_language_example: If you need anything, don’t hesitate to contact me.

additional_notes: A polite, formal/suggested default ("vous") used to invite questions. Often follows an offer of help or an instruction: "Contactez-moi / appelez-moi / venez me voir si vous avez des questions." You can add "des" (some/any) without changing the meaning much; in English it’s usually “any questions.”
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, n'hésitez pas à me contacter.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, don’t hesitate to contact me.

meaning: "if you (can/do) it" (starting a condition with polite/plural 'you' + 'it/him').
additional_notes: Used to begin an "if" clause (si...) where "vous" is the subject (polite or plural "you") and "le" is the direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "him." In French, object pronouns like "le" usually come before the verb: "si vous le pouvez" = "if you can (do) it," "si vous le trouvez" = "if you find it." The verb comes right after "le".
target_language_example: Si vous le voulez, on peut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: If you want, we can leave now.

additional_notes: Used to politely offer an option or to introduce a condition (often like “if you want” or “if you’d like”). It can sound like a softener meaning “if you prefer / it’s up to you,” as in offers and invitations: « Vous pouvez venir si vous voulez. »
target_language_example: On peut partir maintenant, si vous voulez.
native_language_example: We can leave now, if you’d like.

meaning: “if you don’t mind”; a polite “please” (asking someone to do something).
additional_notes: Used with "vous" to sound polite/formal when making a request or giving an instruction: "Si vous voulez bien + infinitive" (e.g., signer, venir, patienter). It can also be used alone as a courteous prompt ("Si vous voulez bien."). With emphatic punctuation ("Si vous voulez bien !"), it can sound impatient or like a firm "please!" depending on tone.
target_language_example: Si vous voulez bien patienter un instant, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: If you don’t mind waiting a moment, I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition with the polite/formal or plural “you” (vous). Often followed by an adjective or noun: si vous êtes prêts (if you’re ready), si vous êtes étudiant (if you’re a student).
target_language_example: Si vous êtes fatigués, vous pouvez vous asseoir.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, you can sit down.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a conditional clause: si = “if” + ça = “that/it” (often referring to a situation or idea). Common in polite phrases like: « Si ça ne t'embête pas » (“If you don’t mind”), « Si ça t'intéresse » (“If you’re interested”), « Si ça vous va » (“If that works for you”).
target_language_example: Si ça marche, on part demain.
native_language_example: If it works, we’ll leave tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often used after the verb être: « être signe de + noun » to say something is evidence/indication of something else. Common with abstract nouns (fatigue, stress, culpabilité, etc.).
target_language_example: Son sourire est un signe de confiance.
native_language_example: His/Her smile is a sign of confidence.

additional_notes: Common way to say “website” in French. Often used with possessives and prepositions: « sur un site web » (on a website), « le site web de l’entreprise » (the company’s website). In casual speech and writing, you may also see « site internet » or just « site ».
target_language_example: Tu peux trouver les horaires sur le site web de la mairie.
native_language_example: You can find the hours on the city hall’s website.

additional_notes: Used to state a length of time ("depuis six ans" = for six years; "pendant six ans" = for six years) or an age difference ("six ans plus âgé(e) que" = six years older than). "Six ans ?" can be used alone as a surprised question: “Six years?”
target_language_example: J'habite ici depuis six ans.
native_language_example: I've lived here for six years.

additional_notes: Means either a duration (six hours) or a time on the clock (six o’clock). Context usually makes it clear: with “par jour” or “plus de”, it’s a duration; with “vers” (around) or when talking about meeting/arriving, it’s a clock time. You can also say “à six heures” (at six o’clock).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à six heures devant le café.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at six o’clock in front of the café.

additional_notes: Used to tell time. In French you often say “X heures et demie” for “half past X.” Since “heure” is feminine, it’s “demie” (with -e).
target_language_example: Il est six heures et demie.
native_language_example: It’s six thirty.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (pendant six mois, depuis six mois, ça fait six mois) or a point in the future/past (dans six mois, six mois plus tard). Often paired with time expressions like depuis (since/for), pendant (for/during), dans (in), environ (about), and plus tard (later).
target_language_example: Je reviens dans six mois.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in six months.

additional_notes: Used before a noun or adjective to question or mock a label: « les soi-disant experts » (“the so-called experts”). It can also be used alone as a skeptical reply: « Soi-disant. » (“Yeah, right.” / “Supposedly.”).
target_language_example: C'est un soi-disant spécialiste, mais il ne sait rien.
native_language_example: He’s a so-called specialist, but he doesn’t know anything.

additional_notes: Reflexive/emphatic pronoun meaning “oneself.” Used to emphasize the subject or the person concerned, often in general statements (e.g., faut tout faire soi-même = you have to do everything yourself). Also used with verbs like se connaître soi-même (“to know oneself”) or parler de soi-même (“to talk about oneself”). In practice, it often varies by person: moi-même, toi-même, lui-même, elle-même, nous-mêmes, vous-mêmes, eux-mêmes, elles-mêmes.
target_language_example: Il est difficile de se connaître soi-même.
native_language_example: It’s difficult to know oneself.

meaning: care of (used mainly in « prendre soin de » = “to take care of”).
additional_notes: Most common in the expression « prendre soin de + [person/thing] » meaning to look after someone/something or to be careful with it. You can use it for health (« Prenez soin de votre dos ») or for objects (« Il prend soin de sa voiture »).
target_language_example: Je prends soin de mes plantes tous les jours.
native_language_example: I take care of my plants every day.

meaning: 'care of him' (as in 'take care of him').
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase **prendre soin de + person**: **prendre soin de lui** = “to take care of him / look after him.” Often appears in instructions or thanks: **Prends/Prenez (bien) soin de lui** (“Take (good) care of him”).
target_language_example: Pendant qu'il est malade, je vais prendre soin de lui.
native_language_example: While he's sick, I'm going to take care of him.

meaning: "care of you" / "care for you" (as in *prendre soin de toi* = "to take care of you").
additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb *prendre*: *prendre soin de toi* = “to take care of you.” Very common as a friendly closing: *Prends soin de toi* / *Prenez soin de vous* (“Take care”). *bien* can add emphasis: *Prends bien soin de toi* (“Take good care of yourself”).
target_language_example: Je prendrai soin de toi pendant ton absence.
native_language_example: I’ll take care of you while you’re away.

additional_notes: Most often used in the expression « prendre soin de vous » (imperative: « Prenez soin de vous ! ») as a friendly way to say “Take care (of yourself)” when saying goodbye or wishing someone well. « vous » can be singular (formal “you”) or plural (“you all”).
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide — prenez soin de vous !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help—take care!

additional_notes: Used in a medical context to refer to the hospital unit where critically ill patients receive constant monitoring and specialized treatment. Common phrasing: « être en soins intensifs » = to be in intensive care.
target_language_example: Mon père est en soins intensifs depuis hier.
native_language_example: My father has been in intensive care since yesterday.

additional_notes: Imperative form (tu) of « être » + « gentil »: « sois gentil(le) avec + person » = telling someone to be kind to someone. Use « gentil » when speaking to a boy/man, « gentille » to a girl/woman (e.g., « Sois gentille avec ta sœur. »).
target_language_example: S'il te plaît, sois gentil avec moi.
native_language_example: Please, be nice to me.

additional_notes: "Sois" is the tu-form of être (to be). Used (1) as an imperative to tell someone to be present: "Sois là !" = "Be there!" and (2) after expressions like "je veux que...", "j'espère que..." to express a wish/requirement that someone be present (subjunctive): "Je veux que tu sois là" = "I want you to be there."
target_language_example: Je veux que tu sois là demain matin.
native_language_example: I want you to be there tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Informal version of the negative imperative with **tu**: **Ne sois pas…** → **Sois pas…**. It’s used to tell someone not to be a certain way or not to do something like being late: **Sois pas bête / Sois pas en retard**. With an object pronoun, it can mean “don’t be it/that way”: **Le sois pas** (= **Ne le sois pas**).
target_language_example: Sois pas inquiet, ça va aller.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’ll be fine.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form addressed to one person you call “tu” (informal singular). Often followed by advice or a warning: “Sois prudent et…” / “Sois prudent quand/quant à…” You can make it more polite with “je te prie” or “s’il te plaît.” Feminine form: “Sois prudente.” Plural or formal “vous” form: “Soyez prudent(s)/prudente(s).”
target_language_example: Sois prudent quand tu traverses la rue.
native_language_example: Be careful when you cross the street.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 70 in French (especially in France): literally “sixty-ten.” Also used in quantities and percentages (soixante-dix poules = seventy hens; soixante-dix pour cent = seventy percent).
target_language_example: J’ai soixante-dix euros sur moi.
native_language_example: I have seventy euros on me.

additional_notes: In natural French you usually include the article: **Le soleil brille.** You can use it to describe sunny weather or a bright day. Common variations: **Le soleil brille aujourd’hui.** / **Le soleil brille dans le ciel.**
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, le soleil brille et il fait chaud.
native_language_example: Today, the sun is shining and it’s hot.

additional_notes: Literally “rising sun.” Can describe the sun in the morning (often in poetic/visual descriptions), and is also used in the fixed expression “le pays du soleil levant” to refer to Japan (“the Land of the Rising Sun”).
target_language_example: On a pris une photo du soleil levant depuis la plage.
native_language_example: We took a photo of the rising sun from the beach.

meaning: “the sun rises” / “the sun is coming up.”
additional_notes: In natural French you usually say **« le soleil se lève »** (with **le**). **Se lever** literally means “to get up” and is used for people (getting up in the morning) and for the sun (rising). Often used with time: **« Le soleil se lève à 6 h. »**
target_language_example: Le soleil se lève tôt en été.
native_language_example: The sun rises early in the summer.

additional_notes: Refers to a very deep state of sleep (sleeping very soundly). Often used with verbs like « plonger dans » (to fall into) or « être dans » (to be in): « plonger dans un sommeil profond », « être dans un sommeil profond ».
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, il est tombé dans un sommeil profond.
native_language_example: After the hike, he fell into a deep sleep.

additional_notes: Used to ask questions by inverting the subject and the verb (être): "Nous sommes…" → "Sommes-nous… ?" Often followed by a place/state/time expression: "Sommes-nous dans… ?", "Sommes-nous en… ?" Can also appear in reflexive questions like "Nous sommes-nous déjà vus ?" (= Have we seen each other before?).
target_language_example: Sommes-nous prêts à partir ?
native_language_example: Are we ready to leave?

additional_notes: This is usually part of a full sentence with the subject: « Nous sommes dans la même classe » (“We’re in the same class”). « sommes » is the “we” form of « être » (to be). « la même » means “the same” (feminine singular to match « classe »).
target_language_example: Nous sommes dans la même classe cette année.
native_language_example: We’re in the same class this year.

additional_notes: Usually used with the reflexive pronoun: « nous nous sommes rencontrés » = “we met.” It’s the passé composé of « se rencontrer » and uses « être », so the past participle agrees (e.g., « rencontrés » for a mixed/masculine group, « rencontrées » for an all-female group).
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes rencontrés à Paris.
native_language_example: We met in Paris.

additional_notes: Used with “nous” to mean “we all …”. In compound tenses with être (especially reflexive verbs), “tous” often comes right after the auxiliary: “nous nous sommes tous + past participle” = “we all + verb” (e.g., we all sat down / we all fell asleep). It can also be in the present tense: “nous sommes tous …” = “we are all …” (e.g., “dans le même bateau” = “in the same boat”).
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes tous retrouvés au même endroit.
native_language_example: We all ended up in the same place.

additional_notes: Means the highest point of a mountain. Often shortened to just "le sommet" when the context is clear. You may also hear "le pic" or "la cime" for “peak,” depending on the context.
target_language_example: Nous avons atteint le sommet de la montagne au lever du soleil.
native_language_example: We reached the summit of the mountain at sunrise.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun, not the owner). Use "son ami" for a male friend of either a man or a woman. (For a female friend: "son amie".) It can also mean "her boyfriend" in context.
target_language_example: Je l’ai vue au cinéma avec son ami.
native_language_example: I saw her at the movies with her friend (male)/boyfriend.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun: anniversaire is masculine). Most often, "son anniversaire" means someone’s birthday, but it can also mean the anniversary of an event (e.g., son anniversaire de mariage = his/her wedding anniversary).
target_language_example: On fait une fête pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: We’re having a party for his/her birthday.

meaning: his money / her money / its money.
additional_notes: "Son" is the possessive adjective used with a masculine singular noun like "argent" (money), even if the owner is a woman: "Elle dépense son argent" = "She spends her money." For a plural owner, use "leur argent" (their money).
target_language_example: Il ne veut pas prêter son argent.
native_language_example: He doesn’t want to lend his money.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" depending on who you’re talking about (it agrees with the noun "bureau," which is masculine). "Bureau" can mean a workplace office (going to/leaving the office) or a desk (on the desk, at the desk), so the context tells you which.
target_language_example: Je t’appelle quand je suis de retour à son bureau.
native_language_example: I’ll call you when I’m back at his/her office.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (not "its") depending on who owns the object; it’s used because "chapeau" is masculine singular. It can appear with verbs like mettre (put on), enlever/retirer/ôter (take off), or when something happens to the hat (e.g., the wind blows it away).
target_language_example: Elle cherche son chapeau partout.
native_language_example: She’s looking for her hat everywhere.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "son" + "chien" (dog). "Son" is used with masculine singular nouns like "chien" (even if the owner is a woman). In context, it can mean "his dog" or "her dog" depending on who you’re talking about.
target_language_example: Elle cherche son chien partout.
native_language_example: She’s looking for her dog everywhere.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (or "its") depending on who owns the thing; it agrees with the noun that follows. Since "comportement" is masculine, you use "son" (not "sa"), even if it’s a woman’s behavior. Often used when judging or describing how someone acts.
target_language_example: Son comportement au travail est très professionnel.
native_language_example: His/Her behavior at work is very professional.
