You can change it depending on the person: « me fera du bien » (will do me good), « lui fera du bien » (will do him/her good), « vous fera du bien » (will do you good, formal/plural). « fera » is the future tense of « faire » (will do/make).
target_language_example: Prendre l’air frais te fera du bien.
native_language_example: Getting some fresh air will do you good.

meaning: 'Are you kidding me?' / 'Are you messing with me?' (rude).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. From "se foutre de (quelqu’un)" = to make fun of / to mess with someone. "Gueule" is a rude word for "mouth" (often used for animals), so the whole phrase is confrontational; you’ll often hear it as a question: « Tu te fous de ma gueule ? »
target_language_example: Tu te fous de ma gueule ? Tu m’as dit que c’était gratuit !
native_language_example: Are you kidding me? You told me it was free!

meaning: to join us (come with us / be part of our group).
additional_notes: Uses the verb **se joindre à** = “to join (a person/group).” Here it’s in the **tu** form with the reflexive pronoun **te** (“you join yourself to us”). Often used to invite someone or ask them to participate: **Tu veux/Veux-tu te joindre à nous ?** (“Do you want to join us?”). Similar to **venir avec nous** (“come with us”).
target_language_example: On va dîner au restaurant ; tu veux te joindre à nous ?
native_language_example: We’re going to have dinner at the restaurant; do you want to join us?

meaning: 'to you' + 'it/him/her' (two object pronouns used together before the verb).
additional_notes: **te l'** is a fixed sequence of two French object pronouns: **te** (to you) + **l'** (short for **le** or **la**, meaning it/him/her before a vowel or silent *h*). It typically comes right before the verb or auxiliary: *Je te l'ai dit* (“I told you (it)”). The **l'** does not indicate gender by itself; it stands for **le** or **la** depending on what is being referred to.
target_language_example: Je te l'ai dit hier.
native_language_example: I told you yesterday.

meaning: “told you (it)” / “said it to you” (with an implied he/she/one/they as the subject).
additional_notes: Common spoken/written chunk within a full sentence like « (Il/Elle/On) te l’a dit ». « te » = “to you” (informal singular indirect object pronoun), « l’ » = “it” (le/la shortened before a vowel), « a dit » = passé composé of « dire » (“to say/tell”). Used for confirming, asking, or reporting that someone told you something (e.g., « Elle te l’a dit ? » = “Did she tell you?”).
target_language_example: Elle te l'a dit, n'est-ce pas ?
native_language_example: She told you, didn’t she?

meaning: "(I) have … it to you" — used in phrases like "I told you / I showed you / I gave it to you."
additional_notes: Common French pronoun cluster with **je** in the passé composé: **Je te l’ai + past participle**. **te** = "to you" (informal singular object pronoun), **l’** = "it" (short for *le* or *la* before a vowel), **ai** = "have" (from *avoir*). It’s not a complete sentence by itself: it normally requires a past participle such as *dit* (told), *donné* (given), *montré* (shown), *envoyé* (sent).
target_language_example: Je te l'ai dit hier.
native_language_example: I told you yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone that you already said something. It appears within the passé composé: « je t’ai dit » = “I told you.” Here, « te » = “to you” and « l’ » = “it/that” (short for « le ») and both object pronouns come before the auxiliary verb: « Je te l’ai dit. » In casual speech, it’s often pronounced/written « J’te l’ai dit. »
target_language_example: Oui, je te l'ai dit.
native_language_example: Yes, I told you.

additional_notes: Used when you’re pleased or relieved to hear someone say something. Structure: entendre + [object] + dire = “to hear [someone] say.” Here, te = “you” and l’ = “it/that” (the thing being said). Often appears after expressions like « Je suis heureux de… », « J’aime… », « Je veux… », « Ça fait du bien de… ».
target_language_example: Ça me rassure de te l'entendre dire.
native_language_example: It reassures me to hear you say it.

meaning: “I won’t leave you” / “I won’t let you (do something).”
additional_notes: This is an informal spoken/written shortening of **(Je) ne te laisserai pas...** (“I won’t ... you”). French often drops **ne** in casual speech, and **je** may be omitted in very informal contexts (songs, texts). **laisser** can mean “to leave” or “to let,” so the exact meaning depends on what follows (e.g., *te laisser partir* = let you leave; *te laisser seul* = leave you alone).
target_language_example: Je te laisserai pas tomber.
native_language_example: I won’t let you down.

additional_notes: A formal/inverted question using the reflexive verb « se laver » (to wash oneself): « tu te laves les mains » = “you wash your hands.” In questions, French can invert the subject and verb: « te laves-tu… ? ». « les mains » is definite (“the hands”) even though English usually says “your hands.” More common in everyday speech: « Tu te laves les mains ? »
target_language_example: Te laves-tu les mains avant de cuisiner ?
native_language_example: Do you wash your hands before cooking?

additional_notes: a combination of two pronouns placed before the verb. Most often, te means 'to you' and le means 'it' or 'him' (for example, je vais te le dire = 'I'm going to tell it to you'). With reflexive verbs, te can mean 'yourself' instead (tu peux te le permettre = 'you can allow yourself that').
target_language_example: Je vais te le montrer demain.
native_language_example: I'll show it to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Future tense of dire (“to tell/say”) with two object pronouns: te = “to you” and le = “it” (a thing/idea previously mentioned). Commonly used in negatives (je ne te le dirai pas/jamais) and with emphasis (Mais jamais je ne te le dirai).
target_language_example: Je te le dirai demain.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Made of object pronouns + infinitive: **te** = “to you” and **le** = “it” (a masculine thing/idea). These pronouns come **before** the infinitive **dire**. Very common in sentences like **« Combien de fois faut-il te le dire ? »** = “How many times do I have to tell you?”
target_language_example: Je vais te le dire après le cours.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you after class.

additional_notes: From the verb *dire* (“to say/tell”) with two pronouns: *te* = “to you” and *le* = “it/so.” Most often heard as **je te le dis** (“I’m telling you”) to insist or emphasize what you’re saying. It can also appear in set, conversational phrases like **Si je te le dis !** (“You have no idea!”) or **Voyons si je te le dis !** (“As if I’d tell you!”).
target_language_example: Je te le dis, ça va marcher.
native_language_example: I’m telling you, it’s going to work.

additional_notes: Usually part of a longer sentence like « Je te le promets. » The pronouns « te » = “to you” (informal singular) and « le » = “it/that” (a masculine direct object, often referring to a promise about something just mentioned). In full: « Je te le promets » = “I promise you (I will).”
target_language_example: Je te le promets, je vais t'aider demain.
native_language_example: I promise you, I’m going to help you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with an object: te montrer + quelque chose ("to show you something") or te montrer + comment + verb ("to show you how to..."). In a different structure, se montrer means "to show oneself / to appear" (e.g., "Comment oses-tu te montrer ici ?" = "How dare you show your face here?").
target_language_example: Je vais te montrer où c’est.
native_language_example: I’m going to show you where it is.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "montrer" (to show) with the indirect object pronoun "te" = "to you" (informal singular). You can swap "te" for "vous" for formal/plural ("vous montrer quelque chose"). Often used to invite someone to look at or see something: "Viens, je veux te montrer quelque chose."
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, je vais te montrer quelque chose.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to show you something.

additional_notes: `te` is the indirect object pronoun meaning “to you” (informal singular), and it goes before the verb: *Je te parle* (I’m talking to you), *Il te parle* (He’s talking to you). In questions it stays in the same place: *Tu m’écoutes quand je te parle ?*
target_language_example: Je te parle, écoute-moi !
native_language_example: I’m talking to you—listen to me!

meaning: 'to talk to you' / 'to speak to you'.
additional_notes: "Te" is the object pronoun used with "tu" (informal 'you'). So "te parler" is used when speaking to someone you address as "tu" (a friend, family member, child, etc.). With formal/plural "vous", you would say "vous parler".
target_language_example: Je peux te parler un instant ?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a moment?

meaning: to talk to you about something.
additional_notes: Used when you want to bring up a topic with someone you address as “tu” (te = “to you”). It often introduces something important or personal. Common with verbs like avoir besoin de / devoir / pouvoir / vouloir / vouloir (conditional: je voudrais) + te parler de…
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux te parler de quelque chose après le cours ?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you about something after class?

meaning: to talk to you in private (one-on-one).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a confidential conversation away from other people. Often phrased politely as a question (e.g., « Est-ce que je peux… ? », « Puis-je… ? ») or to express preference/need (« J’ai besoin de… », « Je préférerais… »). The « te » is the informal object pronoun “to you” (use « vous parler en privé » for a formal or plural “you”).
target_language_example: Après la réunion, je dois te parler en privé.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I need to talk to you in private.

additional_notes: From the verb plaire. French often uses this structure where the thing liked is the subject: ça te plaît ? literally means “does that please you?” = “do you like that?” Te means “to you” for one person informally.
target_language_example: Ce restaurant te plaît ?
native_language_example: Do you like this restaurant?

meaning: to ask you a few questions.
additional_notes: Literally “to put/place a few questions to you,” but it’s the normal way to say “ask you a few questions.” Used with permission/softening phrases like « Je peux… ? », « Je veux juste… », « Je veux seulement… ». You can swap « te » (to you, informal singular) for « vous » (to you, formal or plural): « Je peux vous poser quelques questions ? ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je peux te poser quelques questions ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you a few questions?

additional_notes: Very common way to say “to ask (someone) a question.” Literally “to pose you a question.” Here, te = “to you” (informal singular). With a more formal or plural “you,” use vous: Je dois vous poser une question. Often used with polite starters like Je voudrais / Je voulais / Laisse-moi…
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, je peux te poser une question ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you a question?

meaning: (I) ask/beg you; used to mean “please” (more insistent).
additional_notes: Most often used as **je te prie (de...)**. It can soften a request (**Parle-moi, je te prie.**) or make it sound more urgent/insistent (**Je te prie de le faire.** = “I’m asking/begging you to do it.”). **Te** is the informal “you” (tu). With **vous**, it becomes **je vous prie (de...)** (more formal).
target_language_example: Je te prie de m’écouter un instant.
native_language_example: Please listen to me for a moment.

additional_notes: Used in polite, fairly formal requests, usually as part of « Je te prie de + infinitive » (to one person you say “tu” to). For a more formal or plural “you,” use « Je vous prie de… ». Common in writing and official-sounding speech (letters, notices): « Je te prie de m’excuser. »
target_language_example: Je te prie de me répondre dès que possible.
native_language_example: Please reply to me as soon as possible.

additional_notes: "Te" is the direct object pronoun meaning "you" (informal singular) and it comes before the verb: je vais te protéger (I’m going to protect you). In negatives, it still stays before the verb: nous ne pouvons pas te protéger (we can’t protect you). The verb is "protéger" (to protect); you may also see "toi-même" added for emphasis/reflexive meaning: te protéger toi-même (protect yourself).
target_language_example: Je suis là pour te protéger.
native_language_example: I’m here to protect you.

meaning: to introduce you; to run (as a candidate).
additional_notes:
Two common patterns:
1) présenter qqn à qqn = “to introduce someone to someone” (Je veux te présenter un ami = I want to introduce a friend to you).
2) se présenter à une élection = “to run/stand for election” (Tu devrais te présenter aux élections = You should run in the elections).
target_language_example: Laisse-moi te présenter ma sœur.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to my sister.

meaning: to take you home; to give you a ride home.
additional_notes: Used when offering to escort someone back to their place (often by car, but not necessarily). Literally “to bring you back to your home.” The pronoun changes with the person: me ramener chez moi (take me home), le/la ramener chez lui/elle (take him/her home), nous ramener chez nous (take us home), vous ramener chez vous (take you home, formal/plural).
target_language_example: Si tu es fatigué, je peux te ramener chez toi après le dîner.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, I can take you home after dinner.

meaning: to take/bring you back home; to drive you home.
additional_notes: Used when someone escorts you home (often by car, but it can be any way). It literally means “to bring you back to the house/home.” You can swap the object pronoun: me/nous/le/la/les ramener à la maison (e.g., "Je vais la ramener à la maison.").
target_language_example: Je vais te ramener à la maison.
native_language_example: I’m going to take you home.

meaning: "take you home" / "drive you back to your place."
additional_notes: From the verb *ramener* (“to bring back”). This phrase is used when someone offers to accompany you back to where you live—often by car, but it can also just mean walking you home. The pronoun *te* is informal “you” (to a friend, family, child). More formal: *je vous ramène chez vous*.
target_language_example: Si tu veux, je te ramène chez toi après le dîner.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll take you home after dinner.

additional_notes: From the verb "se rappeler" (to remember). It’s used with the reflexive pronoun "te" for "tu": "Tu te rappelles… ?" = "Do you remember…?" In negatives, French uses "ne … pas": "Tu ne te rappelles pas" = "You don’t remember." You’ll often also see "(se) rappeler de" before a noun or person: "Tu ne te rappelles pas de moi ?" = "You don’t remember me?"
target_language_example: Tu te rappelles de son nom ?
native_language_example: Do you remember his name?

additional_notes: From se rappeler (“to remember”), in the inverted question form. Used to ask if someone remembers a thing (Te rappelles-tu ce que…?), a person/event (Te rappelles-tu du…?), or a time/situation (Te rappelles-tu quand/lorsque…?, Te rappelles-tu comment…?). In everyday speech, people also often say: “Tu te rappelles… ?”.
target_language_example: Te rappelles-tu où on a garé la voiture ?
native_language_example: Do you remember where we parked the car?

meaning: to cheer you up; to lift your spirits.
additional_notes: Used when someone is sad, discouraged, or having a hard time. The base expression is « remonter le moral (à quelqu’un) » = to boost someone’s morale/spirits. The object pronoun changes depending on who you’re cheering up: me remonter le moral (cheer me up), lui remonter le moral (cheer him/her up), nous remonter le moral (cheer us up), etc.
target_language_example: Je vais te remonter le moral après cette journée difficile.
native_language_example: I’m going to cheer you up after this difficult day.

additional_notes: "Te" is the object pronoun (you, informal singular) placed before the infinitive "rencontrer". Used when talking about meeting someone (first time or not), e.g. "Content(e) de te rencontrer" (“Nice to meet you”) or "Ils aimeraient te rencontrer" (“They’d like to meet you”).
target_language_example: Je suis ravi de te rencontrer enfin.
native_language_example: I’m delighted to finally meet you.

meaning: (1) “make you” (+ adjective); (2) “surrender” (in “te rendre” = “give yourself up”); (3) “go to” (in “te rendre à” = “go/arrive at”).
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- rendre + someone + adjective: “to make someone [adjective]” (Te rendre fière = make you proud).
- se rendre: “to surrender / give yourself up” (Tu devrais te rendre = You should surrender).
- se rendre à + place: “to go to / head to” (Te rendre au Palais = go to the Palace).
Note: “rendre” often does NOT mean English “to render.”
target_language_example: Je veux te rendre heureux.
native_language_example: I want to make you happy.

additional_notes: Part of the reflexive verb **se rendre compte de** (= to realize / to become aware of). **Tu te rends compte ?** is common in speech to show surprise or emphasis (“Can you believe it?”). Often followed by **que + sentence** or **de + noun/infinitive**: *Tu te rends compte que…* / *Tu te rends compte de ce que tu dis ?*
target_language_example: Tu te rends compte de ce que tu as fait ?
native_language_example: Do you realize what you did?

additional_notes: Reflexive form of *se reposer* used with **tu**. Often follows verbs like **aller** (*aller te reposer* = go rest) or **devoir** (*tu devrais te reposer* = you should rest). Can also mean to take it easy or recover (e.g., after being tired or sick).
target_language_example: Après le travail, tu peux te reposer un peu.
native_language_example: After work, you can rest a bit.

additional_notes: Used with the infinitive revoir (“to see again”) plus the direct object pronoun te (“you”). Often follows verbs like vouloir (to want), espérer (to hope), penser (to think), e.g., Je veux / J’espère / Je ne pensais plus te revoir.
target_language_example: J’espère te revoir bientôt.
native_language_example: I hope to see you again soon.

additional_notes: Usually comes from **se sentir** (reflexive): **tu te sens…** = “you feel …” (often about health or mood: *Tu te sens bien / mieux ?*). Without the reflexive meaning, **je te sens** literally means “I feel/sense you,” and in conversation it can mean “I get you / I feel you,” which is informal.
target_language_example: Tu te sens mieux aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Do you feel better today?

meaning: “do you feel…?” (talking to one person, informal “you”).
additional_notes: Inversion form of *tu te sens…* used to ask a question. It’s the verb *se sentir* (“to feel”), with the reflexive pronoun *te*. Often followed by an adjective (bien, malade, chanceux) or by *de* + infinitive to ask if someone feels up to doing something (*Te sens-tu de… ?*).
target_language_example: Te sens-tu prêt à partir ?
native_language_example: Do you feel ready to leave?

meaning: to hug you (to hold you in my arms).
additional_notes: Literally “to hold you tight in my arms.” Used to express affection, comfort, or reassurance. You can change the pronoun and possessor: « le/la serrer dans mes bras » (hug him/her), « te serrer dans mes bras » (hug you), « te serrer dans ses bras » (hug you in his/her arms).
target_language_example: Viens ici, je veux te serrer dans mes bras.
native_language_example: Come here, I want to hug you.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se souvenir (de)** = “to remember.” **Tu te souviens (de + noun)** = “You remember (…)
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de son nom ?
native_language_example: Do you remember his name?

additional_notes: This is the inverted-question form of « se souvenir de » (to remember): « Tu te souviens de… ? » is the more common spoken word order, while « Te souviens-tu de… ? » sounds more formal/literary. It’s followed by « de » + a noun (« de ce jour-là ») or « de » + an indirect question (« de quoi », « de la ville où… »).
target_language_example: Te souviens-tu de l’adresse du restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you remember the restaurant’s address?

additional_notes: This is part of the verb **se souvenir de** (“to remember”). It’s used with **tu**: **Tu te souviens de + noun** (Do you remember + noun?) or **Tu te souviens de + infinitive/past event**. Before a vowel, **te** becomes **t’**: *Tu t’en souviens ?* In the past, it’s usually **tu t’es souvenu(e) de …**.
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de mon prénom ?
native_language_example: Do you remember my first name?

additional_notes: From the verb **se tromper** (“to be mistaken”). Used to tell someone they are incorrect: **Tu te trompes.** You can soften it with **Je crois que tu te trompes** (“I think you’re mistaken”). With **de**, it means “to mix up / be wrong about”: **Tu te trompes de numéro** (“You have the wrong number”).
target_language_example: Désolé, mais je pense que tu te trompes.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I think you’re mistaken.

additional_notes: "Te" means "you" (object pronoun) and comes before the verb in the infinitive: "vouloir te tuer" (to want to kill you), "forcer quelqu’un à te tuer" (to force someone to kill you). Often used literally (violence) or as a strong threat; in casual speech it can also be hyperbole ("I’m going to kill you!" meaning "I’m furious"), depending on context.
target_language_example: Si tu recommences, je vais te tuer !
native_language_example: If you do it again, I’m going to kill you!

meaning: "looks good on you" / "suits you" (said about clothes or colors).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "aller à" meaning "to suit" (not "to go"). Used to compliment how something looks on someone: "Ça te va bien" = "That suits you / looks good on you." It can refer to an item of clothing (un pull, une chemise) or a color (Le noir te va bien).
target_language_example: Cette veste te va bien !
native_language_example: That jacket looks good on you!

meaning: "looks really good on you" / "suits you very well."
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone on how an item of clothing, jewelry, a hairstyle, a color, etc. suits them. Built from aller (va) + indirect object pronoun te (“to you”) + très bien (“very well”). You can change the pronoun: me va très bien (suits me very well), lui va très bien (suits him/her very well), vous va très bien (suits you—formal/plural).
target_language_example: Cette couleur te va très bien !
native_language_example: That color looks really good on you!

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address as tu. te is the direct object pronoun 'you', so te voir means 'to see you'. For formal speech or when talking to more than one person, French uses vous voir instead.
target_language_example: Je suis content de te voir.
native_language_example: I'm happy to see you.

additional_notes: This is a fragment of the verb phrase **(je) te vois**: **te** is the direct object pronoun meaning “you” (singular, informal), placed before the verb. It’s commonly used after **je** (“I”) and can appear in clauses like **si je te vois…** (“if I see you…”).
target_language_example: Si je te vois demain, je te dirai bonjour.
native_language_example: If I see you tomorrow, I’ll say hello.

additional_notes: Used to present something in its real/true state or manner: *tel que tu es* = “as you are,” *tel que c’est* = “as it is.” It can also mean “as (we know it)” in expressions like *tel que nous le connaissons*. In conversation, *Tel que ?* means “How exactly?” / “In what way?”. Agreement note: *tel* agrees in gender/number when needed (tel, telle, tels, telles) before *que*, but the fixed multi-word term is written *tel que* (the *tel* part changes form).
target_language_example: Tu es parfait, tel que tu es.
native_language_example: You are perfect, as you are.

additional_notes: Means “such a thing” (often implying something vague or unspecified). It’s the feminine form of *tel* because *chose* is feminine: *une telle chose*. You may also see the plural *de telles choses* (“such things”). Common in negatives or exclamations: *Je n’ai jamais vu une telle chose !*
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais entendu une telle chose !
native_language_example: I’ve never heard such a thing!

additional_notes: The usual, correct form is **de temps en temps** (often shortened in speech to sound like “d’temps en temps”). It means something happens occasionally, not regularly.
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma de temps en temps.
native_language_example: I go to the movies from time to time.

additional_notes: Refers to time when you are not working, studying, or busy. Often used with pendant (during) or avoir (to have): « pendant mon/son temps libre », « avoir du temps libre ». You can also say « du temps libre » (some free time) or « beaucoup de temps libre » (a lot of free time).
target_language_example: Je lis souvent pendant mon temps libre.
native_language_example: I often read in my free time.

meaning: “in time for” (usually: « à temps pour », often with « juste » = “just in time for”).
additional_notes: In this pattern you typically say « (juste) à temps pour + noun/event » to mean you arrive/return before something starts (e.g., a holiday, a meeting). « temps pour » by itself is uncommon; it’s normally part of « à temps pour ».
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé juste à temps pour le début du film.
native_language_example: I arrived just in time for the start of the movie.

additional_notes: Most often used as **de temps à autre** (“from time to time”). It’s an adverbial phrase meaning something happens occasionally, not regularly.
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma de temps à autre.
native_language_example: I go to the movies from time to time.

additional_notes: Used for a storm with heavy snowfall and strong winds. Common with verbs like « avoir » (to have: Nous avons eu une tempête de neige) and « être pris(e)(s) dans » (to be caught in: Nous avons été pris dans une tempête de neige). « Pris » agrees with who is involved: « pris » (masc./mixed plural), « prises » (fem. plural).
target_language_example: On est restés à la maison à cause de la tempête de neige.
native_language_example: We stayed home because of the snowstorm.

meaning: to tend to; to be prone to.
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: "avoir tendance à" + infinitive to describe a usual habit or typical behavior (often something you do without meaning to). You can also use it for general tendencies: "Les gens ont tendance à…".
target_language_example: J’ai tendance à oublier mes clés quand je suis pressé.
native_language_example: I tend to forget my keys when I’m in a hurry.

meaning: to hold out your hand; to offer help (to reach out).
additional_notes: Literal use: physically holding out your hand (to shake hands, help someone up, give/receive something). Figurative use: offering support or help: « tendre la main à quelqu’un ». Often used with an indirect object: « Je lui tends la main. »
target_language_example: Quand quelqu’un a besoin d’aide, il faut lui tendre la main.
native_language_example: When someone needs help, you should lend them a hand.

meaning: to hold out / extend your arms.
additional_notes: Often used literally (to reach for someone or something), and sometimes figuratively to show welcome or to invite a hug (e.g., « Il lui a tendu les bras » = he opened/held out his arms to her). Note: « tendre » looks like English “tender,” but here it means “to stretch/extend.”
target_language_example: Elle va tendre les bras pour attraper le bébé.
native_language_example: She is going to hold out her arms to catch the baby.

meaning: “hold/keep (yourself/yourselves)” (polite or plural “you”), used for commands and instructions.
additional_notes: Form of the verb *tenir* addressed to **vous** (either one person formally or several people). Common in imperatives like: *tenez-vous prêt* (get ready), *tenez-vous tranquille* (keep still/quiet), *tenez-vous à distance* (keep your distance), *tenez-vous la main* (hold hands). In questions like *D’où tenez-vous cette information ?*, it means “Where did you get/obtain that information?” (with *vous* as “you,” not reflexive).
target_language_example: Tenez-vous à l’écart, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please stand back / keep away.

meaning: to keep (someone) informed; to stay up to date.
additional_notes: Used as either: (1) reflexive "se tenir au courant (de ...)" = to keep yourself up to date (with/about something), often news, changes, trends; (2) with an object "tenir quelqu’un au courant" = to keep someone informed. Very common in emails/messages: "Je vous/te tiens au courant" (I’ll keep you posted).
target_language_example: Je voulais vous tenir au courant des derniers changements.
native_language_example: I wanted to keep you informed about the latest changes.

meaning: to hold on; to hang in there; to stand firm.
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone to keep going in a difficult situation (like “Hang in there!”), or to say you are resisting/holding out (against pressure, cold, pain, stress, etc.). Often used in the imperative: « Tiens bon ! » (to one person) / « Tenez bon ! » (formal or plural).
target_language_example: Il faut tenir bon, ça va bientôt s'arranger.
native_language_example: We have to hang in there; it’s going to get better soon.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun (lui/leur) or with "à" + person: "tenir compagnie à quelqu’un". It means to stay with someone so they’re not alone (often to comfort them or keep them occupied).
target_language_example: Je peux te tenir compagnie pendant que tu attends le médecin.
native_language_example: I can keep you company while you wait for the doctor.

meaning: to take into account; to consider.
additional_notes: Used to say you must consider a fact before deciding/acting. Often followed by de + noun (tenir compte de sa santé). Very commonly used with en to refer back to something already mentioned: en tenir compte = to take it into account.
target_language_example: On va tenir compte de ton avis avant de décider.
native_language_example: We’re going to take your opinion into account before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to say you are considering a factor before deciding or acting. Most often followed by a noun or pronoun: « tenir compte de ton avis » (take your opinion into account). To introduce a full clause, French often uses « tenir compte du fait que + [sentence] » (take into account the fact that...).
target_language_example: Il faut tenir compte de la météo avant de partir.
native_language_example: We need to take the weather into account before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has traits from a family member (often physical appearance or personality): « Il tient de sa mère. » = “He takes after his mother.” It can also mean “to have something of / to verge on” in expressions like « Ça tient du miracle. » = “It’s almost a miracle.”
target_language_example: Elle semble tenir de son père : elle a les mêmes yeux.
native_language_example: She seems to take after her father: she has the same eyes.

meaning: to stand up; to stay on your feet.
additional_notes: Used for being upright on your feet, often implying effort (because you’re tired, weak, dizzy, etc.). With the reflexive form (se tenir debout), it means “to stand” (position yourself upright): « Tu peux te tenir debout ? » Without reflexive, it often means “to manage to stay standing / not collapse”: « Tu arrives encore à tenir debout ? ».
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, je n’arrivais plus à tenir debout.
native_language_example: After the hike, I couldn’t stay on my feet anymore.

meaning: to hang in there; to keep going (despite difficulty).
additional_notes: Used when you’re tired, stressed, in pain, or going through a hard time, but you manage to continue. Common in spoken French. Often with a subject (Je/Il/Elle/Tu vas tenir le coup ?) or with « il faut » (Il faut tenir le coup. = We have to keep going).
target_language_example: Je suis épuisé, mais je vais tenir le coup jusqu’à ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m exhausted, but I’m going to hang in there until tonight.

meaning: to keep your word; to do what you promised.
additional_notes: Often appears as « tenir sa parole » (keep one’s promise/word) or « tenir parole à quelqu’un » (keep your word to someone). It refers to following through on a commitment.
target_language_example: Il a promis de venir et il va tenir parole.
native_language_example: He promised to come and he’s going to keep his word.

meaning: to keep quiet; to hold your tongue.
additional_notes: Means not saying something (often a secret) or stopping yourself from speaking. The possessive changes with the subject: tenir ta langue (you, informal), tenir votre langue (you, formal/plural), tenir sa langue (his/her/one’s), tenir leur langue (their). Often used after a request/order: « Tiens ta langue ! »
target_language_example: Elle aurait dû tenir sa langue.
native_language_example: She should have held her tongue.

meaning: to care about; to be attached to; to be keen to; to insist on.
additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun to mean you value something/someone: « Je tiens à mes amis » (I care about my friends). With « tenir à + infinitive », it means to be keen to do something: « Je tiens à venir » (I’m keen to come). With « tenir à ce que + subjunctive », it means to insist that something happen: « Je tiens à ce que tu viennes » (I insist that you come). Not the same as « tenir » = to hold.
target_language_example: Je tiens à te remercier pour ton aide.
native_language_example: I really want to thank you for your help.

meaning: to be close to someone’s heart; to matter a lot.
additional_notes: Used to say something is very important to someone. Most often with an indirect object pronoun: « Ça me tient à cœur » (It matters a lot to me). You can also use it with an infinitive: « tenir à cœur de + infinitive » (e.g., « Ça me tient à cœur de… »), or with a noun phrase: « tenir quelque chose à cœur » (e.g., « Je tiens ce projet à cœur »).
target_language_example: Ça me tient à cœur de t’aider : c’est important pour moi.
native_language_example: It really matters to me to help you; it’s important to me.

additional_notes: Used in medical contexts to talk about measuring/checking someone’s blood pressure (mesurer/vérifier/prendre la tension artérielle). You’ll often hear it with possessives: ma/ta/votre tension artérielle, and with adjectives like normale, élevée, basse.
target_language_example: Le médecin va prendre ma tension artérielle.
native_language_example: The doctor is going to take my blood pressure.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (informal singular "tu") to get their stuff together or take their belongings. "Affaires" is plural and can mean personal items (bags, clothes, etc.) or, more generally, one’s business/concerns depending on context.
target_language_example: N'oublie pas tes affaires avant de partir.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your things before leaving.

additional_notes: "Tes" is the informal singular possessive adjective meaning "your" (used when talking to one person you address as "tu"). It agrees with the noun: use "tes" before a plural noun ("amis" = friends). For "your friend" (singular), say "ton ami" (male friend) or "ton amie" (female friend).
target_language_example: Je vais sortir avec tes amis ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going out with your friends tonight.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to someone you address as tu. Note the plural form: cheveux is almost always plural in French even when referring to all the hair on someone’s head. It often comes up in compliments (Tes cheveux sont beaux.) or asking about a new haircut/style (Tu as fait quelque chose à tes cheveux ?).
target_language_example: J’adore tes cheveux, tu as changé de coupe ?
native_language_example: I love your hair—did you change your haircut?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address as "tu" (informal singular). Often appears with verbs like "faire" or "finir": « faire tes devoirs » = to do your homework. With « toi-même / par toi-même », it means doing it yourself (without help).
target_language_example: Tu peux sortir après avoir fait tes devoirs.
native_language_example: You can go out after doing your homework.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase used when speaking to one person (tu). “Tes” is used before a plural noun starting with a consonant sound (enfants). With a vowel sound, use “tes” as well (e.g., tes amis). In formal/polite speech (vous), use “vos enfants”.
target_language_example: Tes enfants aiment l’école ?
native_language_example: Do your children like school?

additional_notes: "Tes" is the informal singular "your" (used with someone you address as "tu"). "Lunettes" is plural in French, so you use plural forms like "tes" and "sont" even though in English you might say "a pair of glasses." Often used with verbs like mettre (put on), enlever (take off), casser (break).
target_language_example: N'oublie pas tes lunettes avant de sortir.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your glasses before going out.

meaning: your hands (addressing one person with tu).
additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive (tes). With a noun like mains (plural), tes is used (not ton/ta). Common in commands or instructions: « Laisse tes mains… » / « Mets tes mains… »
target_language_example: Garde tes mains sur la table, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Keep your hands on the table, please.

additional_notes: Used with the informal singular "tu" to talk to one person about their mother and father. "Tes" is the possessive adjective for "tu"; it changes with the noun: "ton père" (your father), "ta mère" (your mother), "tes parents" (your parents).
target_language_example: Tes parents viennent te chercher à quelle heure ?
native_language_example: What time are your parents coming to pick you up?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s parents or ask where/what condition they are in. It’s the informal singular “tes” (not polite/plural “vos”). Often followed by an adjective (sympas, riches), a place (à la maison), or a situation/state (en route, en vie).
target_language_example: Tes parents sont au courant ?
native_language_example: Do your parents know?

additional_notes: Used when speaking informally to one person ("tu"). It’s the possessive adjective "tes" + plural noun "yeux" (eye/eyes). Common in instructions or advice: "Ferme tes yeux" (Close your eyes), "Protège tes yeux" (Protect your eyes).
target_language_example: Regarde-moi dans tes yeux.
native_language_example: Look me in the eyes.

additional_notes: Used when offering someone a choice of drinks. In questions you’ll often hear: « Vous voulez du thé ou du café ? » Note: « du café » uses the partitive article (some coffee), which is standard when offering/asking for food or drinks in general.
target_language_example: Vous voulez du thé ou du café ?
native_language_example: Would you like tea or coffee?

additional_notes: Used to specify the type of tea. Often appears with partitive articles when ordering or talking about an unspecified amount: « du thé vert » (some green tea). In a café you can also order simply: « Un thé vert, s’il vous plaît. » Opposite/common contrast: « thé noir » (black tea).
target_language_example: Je prends du thé vert sans sucre, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have green tea without sugar, please.

meaning: “hold on / stay / keep yourself (in a position).”
additional_notes: Imperative ("tu" form) of **se tenir** (“to hold oneself / to stay / to stand”). It’s often followed by an adverb or a phrase: **Tiens-toi bien** (“Hold on tight / Brace yourself”), **Tiens-toi à distance de…** (“Keep your distance from…”).
target_language_example: Tiens-toi tranquille, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stay still/quiet, please.

meaning: Hang in there; hold on (don’t give up).
additional_notes: Imperative form (spoken to one person) of "tenir bon". Used to encourage someone to endure, keep going, or stay strong through a difficult moment; can also imply “hold on” a little longer (e.g., until someone returns). You can also hear it with "Tiens bon !" or "Tiens bon, encore un peu."
target_language_example: Je sais que c’est dur, mais tiens bon : on y est presque.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard, but hang in there: we’re almost there.

meaning: A corkscrew (tool for removing a cork from a bottle).
additional_notes: Used when talking about opening wine or other corked bottles. It’s a common household/kitchen item; you’ll often hear it in questions like « Où est le tire-bouchon ? » or « On a besoin d’un tire-bouchon. »
target_language_example: Tu peux me passer le tire-bouchon, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the corkscrew, please?

meaning: To stick out your tongue; (informal) to be broke/short of money.
additional_notes: Literal wording is “to pull the tongue,” but it usually means physically sticking your tongue out (often to tease someone or because you’re exhausted). In informal speech, it can also mean you’re financially struggling (“Je tire la langue en ce moment” = “I’m broke right now”).
target_language_example: Arrête de tirer la langue, ce n’est pas poli !
native_language_example: Stop sticking your tongue out, it’s not polite!

meaning: to take advantage of; to make the most of.
additional_notes: Usually used as **tirer parti de + noun/pronoun** (or **tirer parti de + infinitive**) meaning to benefit from a situation, resource, or opportunity. Common in slightly formal or written French. Example: *tirer parti de son expérience* (benefit from one’s experience).
target_language_example: On peut tirer parti de cette occasion pour apprendre quelque chose de nouveau.
native_language_example: We can take advantage of this opportunity to learn something new.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "tirer sur" (to shoot at). "Tirer dessus" is used with an object pronoun (me/you/him/her/us/them): "Il m’a tiré dessus" = "He shot at me." In these examples, "tiré" is the past participle (passé composé: "a tiré"). It usually implies using a gun (or weapon) and does not necessarily mean the person was hit.
target_language_example: On m’a tiré dessus, mais je n’ai pas été blessé.
native_language_example: They shot at me, but I wasn’t hurt.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **tirer sur + [person/thing]**. In crime/violence contexts it means to use a gun and shoot at someone (whether or not you hit them). In other contexts, **tirer sur** can also mean “to pull on” (e.g., *tirer sur la porte* = pull on the door), but with a person (*sur lui / sur elle / sur quelqu’un*) it usually means “shoot at.”
target_language_example: La police dit qu’il a tiré sur un passant.
native_language_example: The police say he shot at a passerby.

meaning: “Knock knock” (sound/word said when knocking at a door).
additional_notes: Used to imitate the sound of knocking or to announce yourself at a door. Can be said as a standalone “Toc toc.”; with “!” it sounds more insistent, and with “?” it can sound tentative or like you’re checking if someone’s there.
target_language_example: Toc toc ! Il y a quelqu’un ?
native_language_example: Knock knock! Is anyone there?

meaning: “you” with emphasis (like “you, you…” / “you’re the one who…”).
additional_notes: Uses dislocation for emphasis: "toi" is placed first to highlight or contrast the person, and the sentence continues with the normal subject pronoun "tu". Often used to stress a difference from others ("You, on the other hand...") or to insist on a quality ("You really are..."). Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Toi, tu comprends toujours tout très vite.
native_language_example: You, you always understand everything really fast.

additional_notes: Used to put strong emphasis on the person you’re talking to (often to praise, tease, accuse, or express surprise). It’s a common French structure where the stressed pronoun (toi) is repeated with the normal subject pronoun (tu). Because it uses tu/toi, it’s in the informal/familiar register (with "vous" you’d say: « Vous, vous êtes… »).
target_language_example: Toi, tu es vraiment sympa !
native_language_example: You, you’re really nice!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you (and not someone else) do something or are concerned: « Fais-le toi-même » = do it yourself. Also used in comparisons like « comme toi-même » (as yourself). Can appear after a preposition: « en toi-même » = within yourself / deep down.
target_language_example: Tu dois le décider toi-même.
native_language_example: You have to decide for yourself.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that *you* should do something or experience it directly (not someone else): *Dis-lui toi-même* (“Tell him yourself”), *Va voir toi-même* (“Go see for yourself”). Also used after prepositions like *sur* or after an infinitive to mean relying on/ protecting yourself: *Ne compte que sur toi-même* (“Only rely on yourself”), *te protéger toi-même* (“to protect yourself”). Can also mean “be yourself”: *Reste toi-même*.
target_language_example: Fais-le toi-même, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Do it yourself, please.

additional_notes: Used to include the person you’re speaking to in something that also applies to someone else. Often comes after a statement ("Il a peur, et toi aussi") or after a wish/greeting ("Bonne chance à toi aussi !"). It can also be used alone as a short reply meaning "you too" ("Ouais, toi aussi.").
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, et toi aussi.
native_language_example: I’m tired, and you are too.

meaning: 'you too' (with emphasis), introducing what also applies to you.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the same thing is true for the listener as well. Common in spoken French to repeat the subject for emphasis: “Toi aussi, tu…” (= “You too, you…” / “You also…”). The comma is optional; you may also hear “Toi aussi tu…”.
target_language_example: Toi aussi, tu peux venir avec nous.
native_language_example: You can come with us too.

additional_notes: Uses the stressed pronoun toi (“you”, informal) + et (“and”) to highlight the person you’re speaking to: “you and X…”. Often followed by a noun or another pronoun (toi et moi, toi et ta sœur). When it’s the subject, French commonly uses a plural verb, often with vous to match the addressee: “Toi et Paul, vous venez ?”.
target_language_example: Toi et moi, on part maintenant.
native_language_example: You and I are leaving now.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that it’s only the two of you (often like “just you and me”), or to highlight a bond/comparison (“you and me are the same”). In standard written French, you may also see the more formal subject form “toi et moi, nous…”.
target_language_example: Ce soir, c’est toi et moi : on va régler ça ensemble.
native_language_example: Tonight, it’s you and me: we’re going to sort this out together.

meaning: 'you and me, we…' (to emphasize the two of us as a pair).
additional_notes: Common spoken pattern used to spotlight the relationship or situation between you and the other person: “You and me, we need to talk / we can do this.” The subject pronoun is usually “on” (very common in speech) even though it means “we” here; you could also say “toi et moi, nous…”. It often introduces something personal, serious, or uniting (or sometimes a subtle warning: “Toi et moi, on va parler.”).
target_language_example: Toi et moi, on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: You and me, we’re going to find a solution.

meaning: “you and I, we’re …” (introduces what you two are/have in common).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a comparison or relationship between two people: *Toi et moi, on est pareil* (“You and I, we’re the same”). **On est** is common spoken French for **nous sommes** (“we are”). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (*pareil*, *des amis*, *faits/faites du même bois*). Agreement can change in expressions like *faits/faites* depending on gender/people referred to.
target_language_example: Toi et moi, on est dans la même équipe.
native_language_example: You and I, we’re on the same team.

meaning: “you and I are …” (talking about you and me together).
additional_notes: Uses the stressed pronouns toi and moi as a combined subject, followed by the 1st-person plural of être (sommes). In everyday French, you’ll also often hear: “Toi et moi, on est …” or “Toi et moi, nous sommes …”.
target_language_example: Toi et moi sommes dans la même équipe.
native_language_example: You and I are on the same team.

meaning: 'you who' / 'you (the one) who…' (to emphasize who did something).
additional_notes: Used to single out or emphasize the person being talked to as the one who did/does something. Very common in cleft sentences like « C’est toi qui + verbe » (“It’s you who…”). After « toi qui », the verb is usually in the same person as « tu » (e.g., « toi qui as… », « toi qui es… »).
target_language_example: Toi qui as appelé, tu peux rappeler plus tard ?
native_language_example: You who called—can you call back later?

meaning: “you, who have it / who did it” (addressing someone directly).
additional_notes: Used to single someone out and emphasize that they are the person who has/has done something. It’s usually followed by a past participle or more information: “Toi qui l’as vu…” (= you who saw it…). “l’” is a pronoun meaning “it/him/her” depending on context.
target_language_example: Toi qui l'as vu, tu peux me dire ce que tu en penses ?
native_language_example: You, who saw it, can you tell me what you think of it?

meaning: “yourself a bit” (used after an imperative with a reflexive verb: “... a little / ... a bit”).
additional_notes: This is not usually used alone. It appears in commands with -toi (imperative + reflexive pronoun), e.g. « Approche-toi un peu » (“Come a bit closer”). « un peu » softens the command (like “a bit / a little”), and can suggest a small adjustment or “for a moment,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Calme-toi un peu.
native_language_example: Calm down a bit.

additional_notes: Used for the process of starting to feel romantic love for someone. Common pattern: "tomber amoureux/amoureuse de + [person]" (amoureux for a man, amoureuse for a woman). You can also use it without "de" when speaking generally: "Tomber amoureux prend du temps."
target_language_example: Es-tu en train de tomber amoureux de moi ?
native_language_example: Are you falling in love with me?

meaning: to fall into; to fall for (a trap, mistake, bad habit).
additional_notes: Used literally for physically falling into something (a hole, water), and often figuratively for ‘falling into’ a situation or trap: tomber dans un piège (fall into a trap), tomber dans l’erreur (be mistaken), tomber dans l’excès (go too far). After "dans" you usually put a noun phrase. Conjugates as "tomber" (e.g., je tombe dans, il/elle tombe dans, nous tombons dans, etc.).
target_language_example: Il va tomber dans le piège.
native_language_example: He is going to fall into the trap.

additional_notes: A common, fairly informal idiom meaning to lose consciousness suddenly (often from heat, stress, pain, etc.). Used with conjugated tomber: « Je suis tombé(e) dans les pommes », « Il/Elle est tombé(e) dans les pommes ». The literal words (“to fall into the apples”) don’t help with the meaning.
target_language_example: Il faisait très chaud et elle a failli tomber dans les pommes dans le métro.
native_language_example: It was very hot and she almost fainted on the subway.

meaning: to come out of nowhere; to be totally unexpected (literally: “to fall from the sky”).
additional_notes: Often used to say something is surprising or unforeseen: Cette invitation est tombée du ciel (“This invitation came out of nowhere / I wasn’t expecting it”). It can also be used literally for something actually falling from the sky.
target_language_example: Cette invitation est tombée du ciel !
native_language_example: This invitation came out of nowhere!

meaning: to break down; to stop working (machine/vehicle).
additional_notes: Used for things like cars, computers, elevators, electricity, etc. Often used in compound tenses with "être" (e.g., "Je suis tombé(e) en panne"). A common related expression is "être en panne" (to be broken / not working): "Mon téléphone est en panne".
target_language_example: Ma voiture va tomber en panne si on continue comme ça.
native_language_example: My car is going to break down if we keep going like this.

additional_notes: Used to talk about becoming pregnant (the start of a pregnancy). It’s a common, neutral expression. For being pregnant (state), use « être enceinte ». Often used with a time expression (e.g., « Elle est tombée enceinte l’année dernière. »).
target_language_example: Elle va tomber enceinte cette année.
native_language_example: She is going to get pregnant this year.

meaning: to get sick; to fall ill.
additional_notes: Uses "tomber" (to fall) with an adjective to mean "become" that state. Common for suddenly becoming ill, often in the near future: "Je vais tomber malade" (I’m going to get sick). Related: "être malade" = to be sick (state), vs "tomber malade" = to become sick (change).
target_language_example: Si tu sors sans manteau, tu vas tomber malade.
native_language_example: If you go out without a coat, you’re going to get sick.

meaning: to come across / run into (by chance); to fall onto (physically).
additional_notes: Très courant pour exprimer une rencontre ou une découverte par hasard : « Je suis tombé(e) sur un bon prof » (= I happened to come across a good teacher). Peut aussi être littéral (chute sur quelque chose) : « Il est tombé sur le canapé ». Selon le contexte, peut suggérer que quelque chose « tombe sur » quelqu’un (ennuis, mauvaises nouvelles) ou même « tomber sur quelqu’un » au sens de se jeter sur / attaquer / prendre à partie.
target_language_example: Même là-bas, on peut tomber sur de mauvais professeurs.
native_language_example: Even there, you can come across bad teachers.

meaning: to come at just the right time; to be perfect timing.
additional_notes: Used when something happens exactly when it’s needed or would be most helpful. Often said about a person arriving, a call/message, good news, or an opportunity: « Tu tombes à pic ! » = “You’re here at the perfect moment!”
target_language_example: Tu viens de tomber à pic : j’allais justement te téléphoner.
native_language_example: You arrived at the perfect time: I was just about to call you.

additional_notes: Common way to say someone fell in love. It uses the past tense (passé composé) with être: « il/elle est tombé(e) amoureux/amoureuse de … ». The adjective agrees with the subject: tombé amoureux (male), tombée amoureuse (female), tombés/tombées (plural). You can also use the infinitive: « tomber amoureux/amoureuse de … ».
target_language_example: Il est tombé amoureux de sa meilleure amie.
native_language_example: He fell in love with his best friend.

meaning: “came across / ran into” or “fell onto / landed on; hit/struck”.
additional_notes: Past participle of **tomber sur**. Commonly means **to come across (by chance)**: *Je suis tombé sur un vieux ami* (“I ran into an old friend”). It can also be literal: **to fall onto** something/a body part (*tomber sur le ventre*), or **to hit/strike** something (*tomber sur une mine* = “hit a mine”). In *Êtes-vous tombé sur la tête ?*, it’s often figurative: “Are you crazy?/Have you lost your mind?”
target_language_example: Je suis tombé sur cette annonce par hasard.
native_language_example: I came across this ad by chance.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **tomber sur + noun** = to come across (by chance) or to run into/encounter. **Tombé** is the past participle (used with *être*): *Je suis tombé(e) sur un…* = “I came across a…”. Use **tombée** if the speaker is female. Often followed by a noun like *un ami, un article, un problème*.
target_language_example: Je suis tombé sur un article intéressant en ligne.
native_language_example: I came across an interesting article online.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « tomber amoureux/amoureuse de » = “to fall in love with.” Agreement changes with the speaker: « tombé amoureux de » (man), « tombée amoureuse de » (woman). In the present tense: « je suis amoureux/amoureuse de… » = “I’m in love with…”. Followed by a person/thing you love (often with a name or pronoun like « toi », « lui », « elle »).
target_language_example: Elle est tombée amoureuse de lui pendant le voyage.
native_language_example: She fell in love with him during the trip.

additional_notes: Usually used with “à la …” to mean “at nightfall / at dusk,” often referring to the moment it starts getting dark. Common in narratives and more formal than “le soir” (in the evening).
target_language_example: On partira à la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: We’ll leave at nightfall.

additional_notes: "Ton" means "your" when talking to one person you address with "tu" (informal singular). "Aide" is a feminine noun, but it still takes "ton" (not *ta*) because it starts with a vowel sound: *ton aide*. Common in phrases like *sans ton aide* (without your help), *merci pour ton aide* (thanks for your help), and *j’ai besoin de ton aide* (I need your help).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de ton aide pour porter ces cartons.
native_language_example: I need your help to carry these boxes.

additional_notes: Used to talk to one person (tu) about their (male) friend. It also appears before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel sound: ton amie (your (female) friend), ton école (your school). For a plural group: tes amis (your friends).
target_language_example: J'ai vu ton ami hier au café.
native_language_example: I saw your friend yesterday at the café.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person informally (tu) about their birthday. You can ask the date with « Quand est ton anniversaire ? » or more formally « Quand ton anniversaire a-t-il lieu ? ».
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu veux faire pour ton anniversaire ?
native_language_example: What do you want to do for your birthday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to someone’s opinion. Often appears with verbs like « demander » (to ask for) and « donner » (to give): « On t’a demandé ton avis ? » / « Peux-tu donner ton avis ? ». « avis » is masculine, so it takes « ton » (not « ta »). You can swap the possessive: « mon avis », « son avis », « votre avis », etc.
target_language_example: J'aimerais connaître ton avis sur ce restaurant.
native_language_example: I'd like to know your opinion about this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used when speaking informally to one person you call “tu.” The noun “chien” is masculine, so it takes “ton” even if the dog is female. For “your dog” when addressing someone with “vous,” use “votre chien.”
target_language_example: Ton chien est très gentil, il adore jouer.
native_language_example: Your dog is very nice; he loves to play.

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive adjective "ton" (used with someone you call "tu"). "Fils" means "son". In more formal or plural situations, you’d use "votre fils". "Ton" is used before a masculine singular noun like "fils".
target_language_example: Comment va ton fils ?
native_language_example: How is your son?

meaning: your brother (addressing one person you’re speaking to).
additional_notes: "Ton" is the possessive adjective meaning "your" used with a singular masculine noun (like "frère") and also before a vowel sound. It’s used when you’re talking to one person (tu). For more formal/polite speech to one person, use "votre frère".
target_language_example: Parle à ton frère, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Talk to your brother, please.

additional_notes: “Ton” is the possessive adjective meaning “your” when talking to one person informally (tu) and before a masculine singular noun like “manteau.” For a woman’s coat you’d still say “ton manteau” because “manteau” is masculine. In polite speech (vous), use “votre manteau.”
target_language_example: Mets ton manteau, il fait froid dehors.
native_language_example: Put on your coat, it’s cold outside.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address with "tu" (a friend, child, someone your age in an informal context). For a formal/polite situation or someone you address with "vous," use "votre nom." Often appears in questions like "C'est quoi ton nom ?" or prompts like "Écris ton nom."
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, c’est quoi ton nom ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s your name?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive “ton” (to one person you address as “tu”). For polite/formal or plural “your,” use “votre numéro de téléphone.” Often used when asking for someone’s contact info: “Donne-moi…” (more direct) or “Est-ce que je pourrais avoir…” (more polite).
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner ton numéro de téléphone ?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

meaning: your point of view; your opinion.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s perspective or opinion (often in discussions). You can swap the possessive to match the person: mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur point de vue. It’s neutral and common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je respecte ton point de vue, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I respect your point of view, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase used when speaking to one person informally (tu). It refers directly to that person's father. For formal speech or when speaking to more than one person, use votre père.
target_language_example: J'ai parlé avec ton père hier.
native_language_example: I spoke with your father yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to describe your father’s state, location, or situation. Often followed by an adjective (en vie), a place/status (au front), or a phrase like "au courant" (aware/informed). In questions it may appear after "Est-ce que…" (e.g., "Est-ce que ton père est… ?").
target_language_example: Je crois que ton père est déjà parti.
native_language_example: I think your father has already left.

additional_notes: "Ton" is the possessive adjective for "your" used before a masculine singular noun (sac). In context it can be a handbag, backpack, or any bag. You may also see it in expressions like "Vide ton sac !" which literally means "Empty your bag!" but often means "Say what you really think" / "Spit it out."
target_language_example: N'oublie pas ton sac avant de partir.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your bag before you leave.

additional_notes: "Ton" is the informal singular "your" (used with "tu"). "Travail" can mean your place of employment (job/work) or the tasks you have to do. Common with verbs like "faire" (to do) and "quitter" (to leave).
target_language_example: Je finis ton travail et ensuite on sort.
native_language_example: I’ll finish your work and then we’ll go out.

additional_notes: “Ton” is the possessive adjective meaning “your” when speaking to one person (tu) and the noun is masculine singular (“téléphone”). It’s used for a phone/telephone (often a cellphone in everyday speech). For a female noun you’d use “ta …” (ta voiture), and for plural “tes …” (tes clés).
target_language_example: Où est ton téléphone ?
native_language_example: Where is your phone?

additional_notes: "Ton" is the informal singular "your" (used with friends, family, kids, etc.). "Visage" means "face" (often a bit more neutral/polite than "gueule"). It’s common in expressions like "Je peux le voir sur ton visage" (“I can see it on your face”). In some contexts (e.g., with "Dégage !"), talking about someone’s face can sound rude or insulting.
target_language_example: Je vois la fatigue sur ton visage.
native_language_example: I can see the tiredness on your face.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or confirm someone’s actual/legal name, especially if they use a nickname, username, or false name. Literally “your true name” (ton = your, vrai = real/true, nom = name).
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas ton vrai nom, seulement ton pseudo.
native_language_example: I don’t know your real name, only your username/nickname.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state how old someone is, often by comparing them to the listener (e.g., "Il a ton âge" = "He’s your age"). In "À ton âge...", it means "At your age..." and is often used to make a general comment about what people are like at that age.
target_language_example: Je pensais qu’elle avait ton âge.
native_language_example: I thought she was your age.

additional_notes: Used mostly with the verb « être » to describe someone (usually a man or boy) not wearing a shirt: « être torse nu ». It agrees in gender/number: « torse nu » (masc. sing.), « torse nue » (fem. sing.), « torse nus » (masc. plural), « torse nues » (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Il fait trop chaud : je suis torse nu.
native_language_example: It’s too hot: I’m shirtless.

additional_notes: Short for “Ne touche pas.” Often used as a warning or when telling someone to stop touching something. You can add “à + [thing]” to say what not to touch: “Touche pas à mon sac.”
target_language_example: Touche pas à ça, c’est fragile.
native_language_example: Don’t touch that, it’s fragile.

additional_notes: Expression said after mentioning a hope or good luck, to ward off bad luck. In everyday speech, the conjugated form « Touchons du bois ! » is very common, but the infinitive « toucher du bois » is also used (often after « il faut » / « on va » / « je vais »).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais eu d’accident, il faut toucher du bois.
native_language_example: I’ve never had an accident—we’d better knock on wood.

meaning: to hit rock bottom; to reach your lowest point.
additional_notes: Used literally for physically reaching/touching the bottom (e.g., in water), but most often used figuratively for a very difficult situation when things can’t get much worse. Often used with "avoir l’impression de" (to feel like) or in past tense: "j’ai touché le fond".
target_language_example: Après avoir perdu son travail, il a eu l’impression de toucher le fond.
native_language_example: After losing his job, he felt like he had hit rock bottom.

meaning: to be coming to an end; to be nearing its end.
additional_notes: Used to say that something (a trip, a meeting, a class, a period of time, a season, etc.) is almost finished. The verb is conjugated to match the subject: « Les vacances touchent à leur fin » (the vacation is coming to an end). Often used in a slightly formal or narrative tone.
target_language_example: La réunion va toucher à sa fin, on va conclure.
native_language_example: The meeting is going to come to an end; we’re going to wrap up.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective or adverb to say that something hasn’t changed: it remains equally (often surprisingly) the same as before. Common in descriptions and questions: « toujours aussi + adjectif/adverbe ».
target_language_example: Après toutes ces années, il est toujours aussi drôle.
native_language_example: After all these years, he’s still just as funny.

meaning: always like that / always this way.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens the same way every time, or to describe someone’s usual behavior or attitude. Often in questions ("Tu es toujours comme ça ?") to mean "Are you always like this?" Sometimes implies mild criticism or surprise depending on tone.
target_language_example: Il répond toujours comme ça quand on lui pose une question.
native_language_example: He always answers like that when you ask him a question.

additional_notes: Used to say romantic feelings remain. It’s commonly used with "avoir" (e.g., "J’ai toujours des sentiments pour toi") or as a yes/no question ("As-tu/Éprouves-tu toujours des sentiments pour lui ?"). "Toujours" here means "still" (not "always").
target_language_example: Elle a toujours des sentiments pour son ex.
native_language_example: She still has feelings for her ex.

meaning: "still in" / "always" + en (in, while, in the process of).
additional_notes: “Toujours” can mean “always” or “still,” depending on context. When followed by “en,” it often introduces (1) a place: “toujours en Australie” = “still in Australia,” (2) a state/condition: “toujours en retard” = “always/still late,” or (3) an action with “en + gerund”: “toujours en travaillant” = “always while working.” The exact English translation depends on what comes after “en.”
target_language_example: Elle est toujours en train de parler.
native_language_example: She’s always talking.

additional_notes: Used to complain or comment that someone is late every time (or very often). Common with "être" (Tu es toujours en retard) or "arriver" (Elle arrive toujours en retard). Can also be said alone as a remark: "Toujours en retard."
target_language_example: Mon frère est toujours en retard le matin.
native_language_example: My brother is always late in the morning.

meaning: 'is/was always (in the middle of) doing' (constantly doing).
additional_notes: Used with être (est/était/etc.) + toujours en train de + infinitive to say someone is constantly doing something, often with an annoyed or critical tone. It can describe something happening repeatedly or as a habitual behavior, not just right this second.
target_language_example: Tu es toujours en train de regarder ton téléphone !
native_language_example: You're always looking at your phone!

additional_notes: Used to say someone hasn’t died (often when their status is uncertain or you’re checking if someone is alive). It’s commonly used with the verb « être »: « Il/Elle est toujours en vie. »
target_language_example: Il est blessé, mais il est toujours en vie.
native_language_example: He’s injured, but he’s still alive.

additional_notes: Used to complain or comment that a person, expression, story, answer, technique, etc. never changes. It can stand alone like a short remark (“Toujours la même !”), but it often appears with a noun: “toujours la même histoire / réponse / technique.” Gender changes with what it refers to: masculine “toujours le même” or plural “toujours les mêmes.”
target_language_example: Tu dis toujours la même chose !
native_language_example: You always say the same thing!

meaning: "always something to" (do/say), often implying constant criticism/complaints.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: « toujours quelque chose à + infinitif ». Very common with verbs like « redire » (to complain/criticize) and « reprocher » (to accuse/blame), suggesting someone is never satisfied: they always find something to criticize. It can also be neutral (e.g., « discuter » = to discuss) depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a toujours quelque chose à critiquer.
native_language_example: He always has something to criticize.

additional_notes: Used with the verb vouloir (to want) in the past: most often with avoir + voulu, e.g. j’ai toujours voulu… (I’ve always wanted…), il a toujours voulu… (he has always wanted…), il avait toujours voulu… (he had always wanted…). It expresses a long-standing desire up to that point in time.
target_language_example: J’ai toujours voulu apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to learn French.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir in the passé composé: j'ai toujours été / il a toujours été. It describes a state or characteristic that was true at all times up to the time you’re talking about (often implying it’s still true). "Été" is the past participle of "être" (to be).
target_language_example: On a toujours été proches.
native_language_example: We have always been close.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary avoir (j’ai / tu as / il a / nous avons, etc.) + toujours + été (past participle of être) to describe a state or situation that has been true for a long time, often up to the present: « Ça a toujours été comme ça. »
target_language_example: J’ai toujours été timide.
native_language_example: I have always been shy.

meaning: 'have always been like that / this way.'
additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" in the past tense to say someone has been a certain way for as long as you can remember. It’s most commonly heard as part of a full sentence like "Il a toujours été comme ça" or a question like "Tu as toujours été comme ça ?". "Comme ça" means "like that/like this" (often referring to someone’s personality, habits, or behavior).
target_language_example: Elle a toujours été comme ça : très timide.
native_language_example: She’s always been like that: very shy.

additional_notes: Used for a magician’s trick or illusion (a performance). Often with "faire" or "montrer": "faire un tour de magie" (to do/perform a magic trick), "montrer un tour de magie" (to show a magic trick).
target_language_example: Il fait un tour de magie avec des cartes.
native_language_example: He performs a magic trick with cards.

meaning: To beat around the bush; to avoid saying something directly.
additional_notes: Used when someone is being indirect or evasive instead of getting to the point. Often said as an impatient suggestion: « Arrête de tourner autour du pot » (“Stop beating around the bush”).
target_language_example: Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-moi la vérité.
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me the truth.

meaning: to go around in circles; to get nowhere.
additional_notes: Used literally (walking/driving in circles, pacing) and figuratively (making no progress on a problem, repeating the same points). Often implies frustration: « On tourne en rond. »
target_language_example: On est en train de tourner en rond avec ce projet, il faut prendre une décision.
native_language_example: We’re going around in circles with this project; we need to make a decision.

meaning: To move on (from something); to turn the page.
additional_notes: Often used figuratively about leaving the past behind (a breakup, a failure, a difficult period) and starting fresh. Also used literally as an instruction when reading ("Please turn the page").
target_language_example: Après ce que j’ai vécu, j’essaie de tourner la page.
native_language_example: After what I went through, I’m trying to move on.

additional_notes: Used literally (to face away): « Tournez le dos. » It can also be figurative, meaning to abandon, reject, or ignore someone/something: « Il m’a tourné le dos. » Often takes an indirect object with « à »: « tourner le dos à quelqu’un/quelque chose ».
target_language_example: Comment oses-tu me tourner le dos ?
native_language_example: How dare you turn your back on me?

meaning: “all (of us/them) …” + plural noun (often “all are …” or “all have …”).
additional_notes: Used with a plural noun after a verb like être or avoir: « on est tous des … » = “we’re all …”; « ils ont tous des … » = “they all have …”. It agrees with the subject: tous (masc./mixed) vs toutes (fem.).
target_language_example: On a tous des rêves.
native_language_example: We all have dreams.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to refer to a whole group of things/people close to the situation or already known from context: tous ces cris (all these screams), tous ces problèmes (all these problems). For feminine plural, use "toutes ces" (e.g., toutes ces idées).
target_language_example: Pourquoi il y a tous ces gens devant la porte ?
native_language_example: Why are there all these people in front of the door?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific group of people you can see/identify in the situation. "Tous" = all, "ces" = these (plural), "gens" = people. Often used in questions or complaints: "Que font tous ces gens ici ?"
target_language_example: Pourquoi tous ces gens attendent devant la porte ?
native_language_example: Why are all these people waiting in front of the door?

additional_notes: "Tous" means “all,” "ces" means “these,” and "livres" means “books.” Used to refer to a specific set of books that are present or already known in the context. It can be the subject (Tous ces livres sont à toi.) or an object after de (se débarrasser de tous ces livres).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas porter tous ces livres en même temps.
native_language_example: I can’t carry all these books at the same time.

additional_notes: "Truc" is a very common, informal word meaning "thing/stuff" (often when you don’t know the exact name or it’s not important). "Tous ces trucs" refers to a group of items (physical or abstract: facts, tips, etc.). Often used in questions like "C'est quoi tous ces trucs ?" (What’s all this stuff?).
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu gardes tous ces trucs dans ton sac ?
native_language_example: Why do you keep all this stuff in your bag?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by what follows in the relative clause with « qui » (e.g., « …qui parlent anglais »). « Ceux » is masculine plural; for feminine use « toutes celles qui ». You can also use « tous ceux qui » as the subject of a sentence.
target_language_example: Tous ceux qui veulent venir doivent s'inscrire.
native_language_example: All those who want to come must register.

meaning: "all those who have" (people who have done something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by what they have done (past action), typically followed by a past participle: « tous ceux qui ont aidé / fait / pris… ». Often used in thanks, speeches, or general statements. Feminine form: « toutes celles qui ont… ».
target_language_example: Je remercie tous ceux qui ont travaillé sur ce projet.
native_language_example: I thank all those who worked on this project.

additional_notes: Used for exactly two people or things (not more). Often placed after the pronoun or noun it refers to: « vous êtes tous deux… », « Tom et Mary sont tous deux… ». Can also come after the verb for emphasis: « Nous aimons Tom tous deux » (= we both like Tom). Feminine form: « toutes deux » (two females or feminine nouns).
target_language_example: Ils ont tous deux terminé le travail.
native_language_example: They both finished the work.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun. It usually means 'all the' (tous les passagers = all the passengers), and in recurring time expressions it often means 'every' (tous les jours = every day). The feminine form is 'toutes les'.
target_language_example: Tous les enfants dorment déjà.
native_language_example: All the children are already asleep.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually or regularly each year. It’s interchangeable with "tous les ans" / "toutes les années" in many contexts; you can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence: "Tous les ans, ..." or "..., tous les ans."
target_language_example: Tous les ans, je prends une semaine de vacances en août.
native_language_example: Every year, I take a week of vacation in August.
