additional_notes: Used for exactly two people or things. It often comes after the noun or pronoun it refers to: nous tous les deux = both of us. For two feminine people or things, use toutes les deux.
target_language_example: On peut venir tous les deux demain.
native_language_example: We can both come tomorrow.

meaning: every two days; every other day.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a regular frequency. It literally means “all the two days,” but in practice it means something happens once every two days (often the same as “every other day”).
target_language_example: Je fais du sport tous les deux jours.
native_language_example: I work out every other day.

additional_notes: Used to express a habitual action that happens on Sundays. Often goes with the imperfect for past habits (e.g., « Elle jouait… ») or with the present for current routines.
target_language_example: On déjeune chez mes grands-parents tous les dimanches.
native_language_example: We have lunch at my grandparents' every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or confirm complete information about something. Usually appears with verbs like donner / dire / raconter / savoir / avoir: « Donne-moi tous les détails. » The form stays the same in most contexts (tous = masculine plural; détails is plural).
target_language_example: Raconte-moi tous les détails de ton voyage.
native_language_example: Tell me all the details about your trip.

additional_notes: Uses "tous" (all) + "les" (the) + "enfants" (children) to talk about every child in a group in a general way. It’s often followed by a verb in the plural: "Tous les enfants dorment."
target_language_example: Tous les enfants de la classe sont là aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: All the children in the class are here today.

additional_notes: Literally “all the men.” It can mean “all men/mankind” in a general sense. Watch out for the pattern “Tous les hommes ne … (pas)”: it usually means “Not all men …” (e.g., “Tous les hommes ne sont pas comme toi” = “Not all men are like you”).
target_language_example: Tous les hommes ont besoin de respect.
native_language_example: All people need respect.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about men as a group. In French it often implies a broad generalization (like “All men are the same”). Grammatically: *tous* (plural “all”) + *les hommes* (“men”) + *sont* (“are”, 3rd person plural of *être*). If you mean “all humans/people,” French more commonly uses *tous les êtres humains* or *tout le monde* rather than *tous les hommes*.
target_language_example: Tous les hommes sont différents, mais chacun mérite du respect.
native_language_example: All men are different, but everyone deserves respect.

additional_notes: A general statement about equality, often used with contexts like "devant la loi" (before the law) or "devant Dieu" (before God). Note: in French, "les hommes" can mean “men” specifically, but it is also often used in older/formal contexts to mean “human beings / people.”
target_language_example: Dans une démocratie, tous les hommes sont égaux en droits.
native_language_example: In a democracy, all people are equal in rights.

additional_notes: Usually means something happens daily. It is sometimes also used more loosely in expressions like ce n'est pas facile tous les jours, meaning something is not easy day after day or all the time.
target_language_example: Je vais à l'école à pied tous les jours.
native_language_example: I walk to school every day.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens regularly each morning (a routine/habit). Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also go near the verb for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je bois du café tous les matins avant de partir.
native_language_example: I drink coffee every morning before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens monthly (a repeated schedule, payment, subscription, etc.). You can place it at the end of the sentence or after the verb: « Je suis payé tous les mois. »
target_language_example: Je paie mon loyer tous les mois.
native_language_example: I pay my rent every month.

meaning: all the means; every possible way (to do something).
additional_notes: Refers to using every method or resource available to reach a goal. Common patterns: « tous les moyens possibles » (“every possible means”) and « se donner tous les moyens de + infinitive » (“to give oneself all the means to…”). In « Tous les moyens sont bons », it often implies “anything goes” / “any means are acceptable,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Pour finir le projet à temps, on va essayer tous les moyens.
native_language_example: To finish the project on time, we’re going to try every possible way.

meaning: all the same; all alike (usually said critically).
additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people/things have no real differences: “They’re all the same.” Often sounds dismissive or complaining (e.g., “Les hommes sont tous les mêmes.” = “Men are all the same.”). It agrees with gender/number: tous (masc. plural) / toutes (fem. plural) + les mêmes. You’ll often see it with a pronoun or subject: “Ils sont tous les mêmes”, “Vous êtes tous les mêmes”.
target_language_example: Ils promettent beaucoup, mais au final, ils sont tous les mêmes.
native_language_example: They promise a lot, but in the end, they’re all the same.

additional_notes: Means something happens each evening (as a routine). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: « Tous les soirs, ... » / « ... tous les soirs. ». Note: in French, « soir » is evening; « nuit » is night (as in nighttime).
target_language_example: Je fais mes devoirs tous les soirs.
native_language_example: I do my homework every evening.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of exactly three people (or things) together. Often placed after the subject or object it refers to: « Je vous reconnais tous les trois » (I recognize all three of you). You can also say « nous trois / vous trois / eux trois » in similar contexts.
target_language_example: On va y aller tous les trois après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: The three of us are going to go there after lunch.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of students. Often used as a subject: « Tous les étudiants sont… » (“All the students are…”). You can also modify it with words like « presque »: « presque tous les étudiants » = “almost all the students.”
target_language_example: Tous les étudiants doivent arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: All the students must arrive on time.

additional_notes: Means the entire human race, without exception. Often used in general statements (science, ethics, rights). You’ll also see the singular: "tout être humain" = "every human being."
target_language_example: Tous les êtres humains ont besoin de dormir.
native_language_example: All human beings need to sleep.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun (or a mixed-gender plural group): tous mes fichiers, tous mes frères. For feminine plural, use "toutes mes" (e.g., toutes mes affaires). Before a singular noun, use "tout mon" (m.) or "toute ma" (f.).
target_language_example: Tous mes amis habitent loin d'ici.
native_language_example: All my friends live far from here.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "tous" (all) + "mes" (my, plural) + "amis" (friends). You can swap in other possessives (e.g., "tous tes amis" = all your friends) or other nouns (e.g., "tous mes voisins" = all my neighbors). Also note: "tous" is pronounced like /tu/ (the final -s is silent).
target_language_example: Tous mes amis habitent près d’ici.
native_language_example: All my friends live near here.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “all our …”. It agrees with the noun: feminine plural is « toutes nos » (ex. toutes nos affaires). In speech and writing it often appears with a noun right after it: « tous nos objectifs », « tous nos livres ».
target_language_example: On doit ranger tous nos vêtements avant de partir.
native_language_example: We have to put away all our clothes before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has or affects every one of their items/people/things: « tous ses doigts » (all his fingers), « tous ses caprices » (all his whims). « ses » can mean his, her, or its (it agrees with the plural noun that follows). With a feminine plural noun, use « toutes ses » (e.g., « toutes ses idées »).
target_language_example: Elle connaît tous ses voisins.
native_language_example: She knows all her neighbors.

additional_notes: Often used in religious contexts to describe God (“Dieu tout-puissant” = “Almighty God”). It can also be used as an exclamation (“Dieu tout-puissant !” = “Almighty God!” / “Oh my God!”). As an adjective, it agrees with the noun: tout-puissant (m. sg.), toute-puissante (f. sg.), tout-puissants (m. pl.), toutes-puissantes (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Le roi se croyait tout-puissant.
native_language_example: The king thought he was all-powerful.

additional_notes: Used to give an upper limit (maximum), often with numbers or time expressions. It can be placed after the quantity/time (“une semaine tout au plus”) or before a phrase (“tout au plus dans une heure”). Often implies “and probably less.”
target_language_example: J’en ai pour dix minutes, quinze tout au plus.
native_language_example: I’ll be about ten minutes—fifteen at most.

additional_notes: Used as a quick, friendly way to say there’s no problem or that something is OK. It can also confirm that an answer or plan is correct (like “yep, that’s right”). Often heard in casual speech; especially common in some regions (e.g., Switzerland/Belgium).
target_language_example: Pas de souci, tout bon !
native_language_example: No worries, all good!

additional_notes: Used to compare people or things and highlight similarity. It can introduce a comparison inside a sentence ("Ses sœurs, tout comme lui, …") or stand alone as a short answer to mean "Just like him/your dad."
target_language_example: Elle adore le chocolat, tout comme moi.
native_language_example: She loves chocolate, just like me.

meaning: exactly like (someone); the spitting image of.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is a perfect copy of someone else, especially in looks or personality. Very common patterns: « C'est toi tout craché » (You're exactly like yourself/your past self) and « Son père tout craché » (His/Her father, exactly). You may also hear « du X tout craché » meaning “pure X / typical X” (e.g., « Du Bobby tout craché »). It’s informal and « tout craché » stays invariable (no agreement).
target_language_example: Avec sa manière de parler, c'est sa mère tout craché.
native_language_example: The way he talks, he's the spitting image of his mother.

meaning: all the same; still; nonetheless; anyway (expresses contrast or mild objection).
additional_notes: Used to add a nuance like “even so” or “come on” in a polite-to-neutral way. Often expresses surprise, insistence, or disagreement (e.g., “I’m not going to pay ten dollars, come on!”). It can also soften a statement by acknowledging the opposite point first: “Not really an improvement, but still impressive.”
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas parfait, mais c’est tout de même une bonne idée.
native_language_example: It’s not perfect, but it’s still a good idea.

additional_notes: A very common adverb phrase for doing something without delay. In some contexts, especially when speaking to customers or guests, it can also mean 'in just a moment' or 'I'll be right with you.'
target_language_example: Je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Common in directions and navigation. Used after a verb like aller/continuer/marcher/conduire to mean “go/keep going straight (ahead), without turning.” Can also describe something that is perfectly straight (e.g., une ligne tout droit), but in beginner contexts it’s often for giving directions.
target_language_example: Continuez tout droit jusqu'au carrefour.
native_language_example: Keep going straight until the intersection.

additional_notes: Used after a verb (dire, parler, lire, penser) to mean you say/read/think something aloud so others can hear it. Often translates as “out loud” rather than “very high.” Common in phrases like « parler tout haut » (speak loudly) and « penser tout haut » (think aloud).
target_language_example: Tu peux répéter tout haut, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you repeat it out loud, please?

additional_notes: “Tout” is used as an intensifier meaning “very” with an adjective: “tout petit(e)” = “very small/tiny.” It agrees in gender/number with the noun (“tout petit” masc., “toute petite” fem.). In the phrase “se faire tout petit”, it means “to make yourself small” → to be discreet/keep a low profile so you won’t be noticed.
target_language_example: Sami a un tout petit appartement au Caire.
native_language_example: Sami has a tiny apartment in Cairo.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize proximity (stronger than just près). Often appears on its own ("Tout près.") as a short answer, or with de/d’ici: "tout près d’ici" (very close to here).
target_language_example: La station de métro est tout près d'ici.
native_language_example: The subway station is very close to here.

additional_notes: Used for being alone or doing something without help. It often translates as "alone," "by yourself," or "on your own." The form changes to match the person: toute seule, tout seuls, toutes seules.
target_language_example: Je peux le faire tout seul.
native_language_example: I can do it on my own.

additional_notes: Used to make something sound straightforward or obvious (“just do it”). It can also emphasize inability or refusal: “ne pas pouvoir tout simplement…” = “simply couldn’t…”. With adjectives, it often acts as an intensifier meaning “simply/absolutely”: “tout simplement génial” = “simply brilliant.”
target_language_example: Je n'ai tout simplement pas le temps aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I just don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who looks very happy or pleased (often after good news). It can come after a verb like « être » (Il est tout sourire) or describe someone in a scene (Elle arrive, tout sourire).
target_language_example: Quand il a vu ses amis, il était tout sourire.
native_language_example: When he saw his friends, he was all smiles.

meaning: completely/entirely; (with a person) entirely yours / at your service.
additional_notes: Common patterns: **tout à fait** = “completely,” “absolutely,” “quite” (strong agreement: *Vous avez tout à fait raison.*). With a person/pronoun (**tout à toi / tout à vous**), it means “entirely yours” or “at your disposal/at your service” (often used politely: *Je suis tout à vous.*).
target_language_example: Je suis tout à vous si vous avez des questions.
native_language_example: I’m at your service / I’m here for you if you have questions.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens unexpectedly or quickly. It can go in the middle of the sentence (often after the verb) or at the beginning: “Tout à coup, …”.
target_language_example: Tout à coup, il s'est mis à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, it started raining.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or confirm something ("Oui, tout à fait." = “Yes, absolutely/Exactly.”). With adjectives or verbs it intensifies meaning: "tout à fait + adjective" = “completely/entirely” ("Il a tout à fait raison." = “He’s absolutely right.”). Often sounds a bit more formal/polite than "oui" alone.
target_language_example: —Tu es d’accord ? —Oui, tout à fait.
native_language_example: —Do you agree? —Yes, absolutely.

meaning: completely; entirely; quite; (also) exactly / absolutely (to strongly agree).
additional_notes: Often used as an intensifier meaning “completely/entirely” (Je suis tout à fait choqué). With adjectives/adverbs it can mean “quite” depending on context (tout à fait normal = perfectly/quite normal). As a stand-alone reply, it means “Exactly/Absolutely” to strongly agree: « — Tu es d’accord ? — Tout à fait. » In informal speech it can also intensify criticism (Tout à fait pourri = totally crappy).
target_language_example: — Tu veux partir maintenant ? — Tout à fait.
native_language_example: — Do you want to leave now? — Absolutely.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is fully true or applies: "tout à fait exact/normal/impossible". In conversation, "Tout à fait." can mean strong agreement ("Absolutely"), and with a negative it often softens meaning: "pas tout à fait" = "not quite / not entirely."
target_language_example: — Tu es d’accord ? — Oui, tout à fait.
native_language_example: — Do you agree? — Yes, absolutely.

meaning: “later (today / in a little while)” or “a little while ago.”
additional_notes: A very common time expression for a moment close to now, either in the near future or the recent past. The meaning depends on context: future in sentences like « Je te rappelle tout à l'heure » (I’ll call you later), and past in « La fille qui était là tout à l'heure » (the girl who was here a little while ago). Used alone (« Tout à l'heure. ») it can mean “see you later / talk later.”
target_language_example: Je suis en réunion, je te rappelle tout à l'heure.
native_language_example: I’m in a meeting; I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Most often used as **en tout cas** (not usually *tout cas* alone). It’s a transition that means “anyway / in any case,” often to conclude, correct, or move the conversation along: *En tout cas, merci !*
target_language_example: En tout cas, je dois y aller.
native_language_example: Anyway, I have to go.

meaning: all that time; the whole time.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a duration that has just been mentioned or is understood from context, often implying “during that entire period.” Common with questions like Où étais-tu tout ce temps ? and with pendant: pendant tout ce temps (“during all that time”).
target_language_example: Je t’ai attendu tout ce temps.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for you all this time.

additional_notes: Usually appears in patterns like "tout ce qui" and "tout ce que" to mean "everything that/what". It refers to things or ideas in a general sense, not people.
target_language_example: J'ai oublié tout ce que tu m'as dit.
native_language_example: I forgot everything you told me.

additional_notes: Used before a relative clause with verbs/adjectives that normally take **de** (e.g., **avoir besoin de** = “to need”, **parler de** = “to talk about”). **dont** replaces **de + which/that**. So **tout ce dont il a besoin** = “everything he needs.”
target_language_example: J'ai tout ce dont j'ai besoin pour le voyage.
native_language_example: I have everything I need for the trip.

tout ce dont nous avons besoin

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce dont nous avons besoin
additional_notes: Uses the structure **tout ce dont + (subject) + avoir besoin** to mean “everything that (someone) needs.” **dont** replaces **de + something** because **avoir besoin** is followed by **de** (avoir besoin de…). You can change the subject: *tout ce dont j’ai besoin* (everything I need), *tout ce dont tu as besoin*, etc.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : on a tout ce dont nous avons besoin pour le voyage.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we have everything we need for the trip.

tout ce dont vous avez besoin

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce dont vous avez besoin
additional_notes: Used to say someone has all the necessary things (objects, information, help, etc.). The structure "tout ce dont" means "everything that" with "de" ("dont") because French uses "avoir besoin de" = "to need" + "of". You’ll often see it in questions (Avez-vous… ?) and instructions (Prenez…).
target_language_example: Voici tout ce dont vous avez besoin pour commencer.
native_language_example: Here is everything you need to get started.

additional_notes: Relative construction: tout ce que + clause = “everything that…”. Before a vowel sound, ce que contracts to ce qu’ (elision), hence tout ce qu’. Typically followed by a subject + verb: tout ce qu’il/elle/on… . Depending on context it can also mean “all I have/need/left” (e.g., Tu es tout ce qu’il me reste.).
target_language_example: Cette ville a tout ce qu'on peut désirer.
native_language_example: This city has everything one could want.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing what a man has done/knows/touches, etc. It’s the structure: tout (everything) + ce que (what/that which) + il (he). The "e" in "que" drops before a vowel: que + il → qu'il. Often followed by a verb: « tout ce qu'il a fait » (everything he did), « tout ce qu'il touche » (everything he touches), « tout ce qu'il faudra » (everything that will be necessary).
target_language_example: Je comprends tout ce qu'il dit.
native_language_example: I understand everything he says.

additional_notes: Used to say you have (or there is) everything necessary for a task or situation. Very common with avoir/il y a: « J’ai tout ce qu’il faut » (I’ve got everything we need), « Il y a tout ce qu’il faut ici » (There’s everything we need here). Can also imply “don’t worry, we’re prepared.”
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, j'ai tout ce qu'il faut pour le dîner.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ve got everything we need for dinner.

meaning: “everything that we / you / people (in general)” (“all that one”).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause meaning “everything that…,” with the subject on. In everyday French, on often means “we” (instead of nous), but it can also mean “people/you in general.” Very common in phrases like tout ce qu’on peut (“everything we can”) and tout ce qu’on a fait (“everything we did / have done”).
target_language_example: On fait tout ce qu'on peut.
native_language_example: We do everything we can.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the complete set of things someone has. It’s a relative clause: "tout" (everything) + "ce que" (that which/what) + "on a" (we/you/people have). In more formal French, you may also see "tout ce que nous avons" (all that we have).
target_language_example: On a vendu tout ce qu'on a pour payer les factures.
native_language_example: We sold everything we have to pay the bills.

additional_notes: Used before a clause to refer to the complete set of things, ideas, or actions: 'everything that ...' or 'all that ...'. Common with verbs like dire, vouloir, croire, and faire.
target_language_example: J'ai oublié tout ce que tu m'as expliqué.
native_language_example: I forgot everything that you explained to me.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to all the things you previously said. Common in phrases like "C'est tout ce que j'ai dit" (that's all I said), "Je retire tout ce que j'ai dit" (I take back everything I said), and in questions like "Tu as entendu tout ce que j'ai dit ?" (Did you hear everything I said?).
target_language_example: Désolé, je retire tout ce que j'ai dit.
native_language_example: Sorry, I take back everything I said.

additional_notes: A relative clause meaning “everything that I did.” Often used after another phrase, e.g. C’est… (“That’s…”), Pour… (“For…”), Avec… (“With…”), to refer back to all your actions/efforts. Can be adapted: tout ce que tu as fait (everything you did), tout ce qu’il/elle a fait, etc.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé pour tout ce que j'ai fait.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for everything I've done.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone/something is your only possession or your entire amount of something. Often follows a form of "être" (Ils sont tout ce que j’ai. = They’re all I have.) or "donner" (Je te donne tout ce que j’ai. = I’m giving you everything I have.).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas beaucoup d'argent, mais je te donne tout ce que j'ai.
native_language_example: I don’t have much money, but I’m giving you all I have.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything someone possessed/owned or had available at a time in the past. Often appears in sentences like: “C’est tout ce que j’avais (à dire)” = “That’s all I had (to say).” You can also use it alone as an incomplete sentence for emphasis (“Tout ce que j’avais.” = “Everything I had.”). Grammar note: j’avais is the imperfect of avoir, describing a past state (what you had at that time).
target_language_example: J'ai perdu tout ce que j'avais pendant le voyage.
native_language_example: I lost everything I had during the trip.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing everything you do, say, can do, etc. It’s often followed by a verb: « tout ce que je peux » (all I can), « tout ce que je sais » (all I know), « tout ce que je veux » (all I want).
target_language_example: Je te dirai tout ce que je sais.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you everything I know.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all the things you say (often as the object of a verb like croire, critiquer, répéter, etc.). Common in emphasis or complaints: «Il critique tout ce que je dis» (he criticizes everything I say), «Vous retournez tout ce que je dis contre moi» (you use everything I say against me). Often seen in the pattern «tout ce que + subject + verb» = “everything that …”.
target_language_example: Elle note tout ce que je dis pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: She writes down everything I say during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all of your actions/activities in a general way. Often appears in patterns like: « C’est tout ce que je fais » (“That’s all I do”), « Je réussis tout ce que je fais » (“I succeed in everything I do”), and « Tout ce que je fais, c’est… » to emphasize or explain your motivation.
target_language_example: Je pense à toi dans tout ce que je fais.
native_language_example: I think about you in everything I do.

additional_notes: Commonly used after a verb to mean you’re doing the maximum possible: e.g. « Je fais tout ce que je peux » (“I’m doing all I can”). « Tout ce que » means “all that / everything that,” and « je peux » means “I can.” You can change the subject: « tout ce que tu peux » (all you can), « tout ce qu’on peut » (all we/one can).
target_language_example: Je fais tout ce que je peux pour t’aider.
native_language_example: I’m doing all I can to help you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or promise a full account of your knowledge about something (often with verbs like dire/t'expliquer: « Je vais te dire tout ce que je sais. »). It can also be said alone as a sentence fragment (« Tout ce que je sais. ») meaning “That’s all I know.”
target_language_example: Je vais te raconter tout ce que je sais sur cette histoire.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you everything I know about this story.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having/getting/doing whatever you want. Often comes after verbs like avoir (to have), faire (to do/make), offrir (to offer), or être (to be): «J’ai… tout ce que je veux», «Je peux… tout ce que je veux». In «Je lui fais faire tout ce que je veux», it means “I make him/her do whatever I want” (faire faire = to make someone do). In «Tu es tout ce que je veux», it means “You’re everything I want” (romantic/strong emphasis).
target_language_example: Avec ce travail, je peux acheter tout ce que je veux.
native_language_example: With this job, I can buy everything I want.

tout ce que je veux, c'est

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que je veux, c'est
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that this is your only/main desire or request. The structure is: "Tout ce que je veux, c'est + noun/infinitive/clause". It’s often followed by a noun (un baiser), a person (toi), or an infinitive (être libre). In speech you may also hear: "Tout ce que je veux, c’est que + subject + verb" (All I want is for…).
target_language_example: Tout ce que je veux, c'est un peu de temps.
native_language_example: All I want is a little time.

additional_notes: Built with **tout ce que** (“everything that / all that”) + **je voulais** (“I wanted”). It refers to a complete set of things (or sometimes even a person) that matched what the speaker wanted. You can extend it with another verb: **tout ce que je voulais voir/faire/dire** (“everything I wanted to see/do/say”).
target_language_example: Ce voyage était tout ce que je voulais.
native_language_example: That trip was everything I wanted.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing the totality of things “we” do, say, see, ask for, can, etc. It’s often followed by a verb: « tout ce que nous demandons / disons / voyons / pouvons ». Don’t confuse it with « tout ce que nous avons » (“everything that we have”).
target_language_example: Tout ce que nous voulons, c’est un peu de temps.
native_language_example: All we want is a little time.

meaning: 'everything that you' / 'all that you' (introduces a clause about what you do, say, have, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the totality of things connected to the listener ("tu") and is followed by a verb: tout ce que tu possèdes (everything you own), tout ce que tu diras (everything you say), tout ce que tu demandes (everything you ask for). Often appears in promises or conditions (Je ferai tout ce que tu veux/diras).
target_language_example: Je comprends tout ce que tu dis.
native_language_example: I understand everything you’re saying.

tout ce que tu as dit

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que tu as dit
additional_notes: Used to refer to the complete set of things someone said. Structure: "tout" (everything) + "ce que" (what/that which) + subject + past tense ("tu as dit" = you said). Can be the object of a verb (Je me rappelle…) or the subject of a sentence (Tout ce que tu as dit était vrai).
target_language_example: J'ai noté tout ce que tu as dit pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: I wrote down everything you said during the meeting.

tout ce que tu as fait

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que tu as fait
additional_notes: Built on the structure **tout ce que + subject + verb** (“everything that…”). Here it uses the **passé composé** (**tu as fait**) to talk about completed actions. It’s common in emotional contexts, especially **gratitude** (Merci pour tout ce que tu as fait…) or **reproach/shock** (Après tout ce que tu as fait ?).
target_language_example: Je n’oublierai jamais tout ce que tu as fait pour nous.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget everything you did for us.

additional_notes: Often used to refer to everything someone has (money, items, resources) or everything they can offer in the moment (effort, arguments, things to say). In questions like « C’est tout ce que tu as ? », it can mean “Is that all you’ve got?” (sometimes challenging or disappointed). In « tout ce que tu as à dire », it means “all you have to say.”
target_language_example: Donne-moi tout ce que tu as.
native_language_example: Give me everything you’ve got.

tout ce que tu as à faire est

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que tu as à faire est
meaning: 'all you have to do is' (followed by de + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to say the solution is simple: “all you need to do is…”. It’s followed by **de** + an infinitive (verb in the “to…” form): *Tout ce que tu as à faire est de demander.* You can change **tu** to **vous** for a more formal/polite version: *Tout ce que vous avez à faire, c’est de…* (very common in speech).
target_language_example: Tout ce que tu as à faire est de cliquer sur ce bouton.
native_language_example: All you have to do is click that button.

additional_notes: Built with the very common structure **tout ce que + subject + verb** = “everything that/what + …”. Here, **ce que** introduces a relative clause (“that/what you say”). In questions like **C’est tout ce que tu dis ?**, it can sound like “Is that all you have to say?” depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Je crois tout ce que tu dis.
native_language_example: I believe everything you say.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to share all the information they have about a person/thing/topic. It often follows verbs like dire (tell), savoir (know), expliquer (explain): « Dis-moi tout ce que tu sais sur… » / « Je veux savoir tout ce que tu sais. ». The structure is compositional: tout (everything) + ce que (what/that which) + tu sais (you know).
target_language_example: Explique-moi tout ce que tu sais sur cette affaire.
native_language_example: Explain to me everything you know about this case.

additional_notes: Literally “all that you want.” Used with verbs like fournir (provide), manger (eat), avoir (have), faire (do) to say there are no limits: “as much as you want / whatever you want.” In some contexts (e.g., "Tu peux me faire tout ce que tu veux"), it can mean “You can do whatever you want to me,” which may sound strong depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Prends tout ce que tu veux dans le frigo.
native_language_example: Take anything you want from the fridge.

additional_notes: Uses the structure **tout ce que + subject + verb** = “everything that …”. Here **tu voulais** is the imperfect of *vouloir* (“you wanted”). You can swap the person/tense: *tout ce que je veux* (everything I want), *tout ce qu’il voulait* (everything he wanted), etc. Often used as an object: *J’ai fait tout ce que tu voulais.*
target_language_example: J’ai acheté tout ce que tu voulais au supermarché.
native_language_example: I bought everything you wanted at the supermarket.

meaning: "everything that you" / "all that you" (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause meaning "everything that you ...". It’s followed by a verb: "tout ce que vous voulez" (everything you want), "tout ce que vous pouvez" (everything you can). Here, "vous" is either polite singular (to one person) or plural (to several people).
target_language_example: Je ferai tout ce que vous me demanderez.
native_language_example: I will do everything you ask me.

meaning: "everything that you have" / "all that you have".
additional_notes: Built on the very common pattern **tout ce que + subject + verb** (“everything/all that …”). **Vous avez** is the formal/plural “you have,” so it can address one person politely or several people. Depending on context, it can mean “all you bought/wrote/went through” or, in a question, “is that all you have?” (implying “is there anything else?”).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir si c’est tout ce que vous avez préparé.
native_language_example: I want to know if that’s everything you prepared.

additional_notes: Used to mean the total of what someone possesses at that moment. Common in requests or demands (Donnez-moi tout ce que vous avez.) and in questions meaning “Is that all you’ve got?” (Est-ce tout ce que vous avez ?). Can be expanded with details like sur vous (“on you/with you”).
target_language_example: Donnez-moi tout ce que vous avez, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me everything you have, please.

tout ce que vous avez à faire est

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que vous avez à faire est
additional_notes: Used to say something is the only requirement or the simplest step to achieve a result. It’s followed by either “de + infinitive” (Tout ce que vous avez à faire est de demander.) or “c’est de + infinitive” in a very common variant (Tout ce que vous avez à faire, c’est de demander.). “Vous” is the formal/plural “you”; with “tu” you get “tout ce que tu as à faire, c’est de …”.
target_language_example: Tout ce que vous avez à faire est de remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: All you have to do is fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (politely/formally, with "vous") to share all the information they have about something. Often appears after verbs like "dire" (to tell) or "me dire" (tell me). "Tout ce que" means "everything that/which," and "vous savez" means "you know."
target_language_example: Dites-moi tout ce que vous savez sur cet incident.
native_language_example: Tell me everything you know about this incident.

additional_notes: Means “everything that you want.” Used after verbs like dire (say), donner (give), prendre (take), demander (ask), avoir (have), être (be): e.g., “Dites… / Prenez… / Demandez…”. Uses the formal/polite “vous”; with friends you’d usually say “tout ce que tu veux”.
target_language_example: Choisissez tout ce que vous voulez.
native_language_example: Choose anything you want.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all things that fit a condition or description. It’s followed by a verb clause ("…tout ce qui + verb"). Often used with verbs like éviter (avoid), aimer (like), faire (do), or with expressions like "tout ce qui passe" (everything/anything that comes along).
target_language_example: Je garde tout ce qui peut servir plus tard.
native_language_example: I keep anything that might be useful later.

meaning: "everything that is" / "everything that's …" (i.e., all that exists or all things of a kind).
additional_notes: Used to refer broadly to all things that match a description or category. It’s often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: « tout ce qui est nécessaire » (everything that’s necessary), « tout ce qui est romantique » (everything that’s romantic). In some contexts it can mean “everything around/in/near …” when followed by a place phrase (e.g., « tout ce qui est autour de lui »).
target_language_example: J’ai rangé tout ce qui est sur la table.
native_language_example: I put away everything that’s on the table.

tout ce qui est en mon pouvoir

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce qui est en mon pouvoir
meaning: everything I can (do); everything in my power.
additional_notes: A fairly formal set phrase used to promise you’ll do your best or take all possible action. Often followed by an infinitive with pour: « …pour aider / pour vous aider » (…to help / …to help you). You can also use other possessives: « tout ce qui est en ton/son/notre/votre/leur pouvoir ».
target_language_example: Je ferai tout ce qui est en mon pouvoir pour résoudre ce problème.
native_language_example: I will do everything I can to solve this problem.

meaning: everything that happened; all that happened.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a whole sequence of events in the past (often something important, surprising, or upsetting). It can follow prepositions like après (“after”), pour (“for/about”), or be the object of verbs like voir (“to see”) and savoir (“to know”).
target_language_example: On devrait parler de tout ce qui s'est passé hier soir.
native_language_example: We should talk about everything that happened last night.

additional_notes: Refers to the whole situation, set of things, or information being talked about, usually close in the conversation/context. Often points back to what was just mentioned (events, actions, details). You can also say “tout ça” in a more casual style.
target_language_example: Tout ceci est très compliqué à expliquer.
native_language_example: All of this is very complicated to explain.

meaning: "all that" / "all of that" (everything being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to information, events, or details already mentioned or understood from context. Often appears in questions like « Qu’est-ce que tout cela veut dire ? » (= “What does all of this mean?”).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas tout cela.
native_language_example: I don't understand all of this.

additional_notes: Means a large amount of money being talked about in the situation. Uses "tout" (all) + "cet" (this/that, masculine singular before a vowel sound) + "argent" (money). You’ll often see it in questions about spending, owning, finding, or receiving money.
target_language_example: Tu vas faire quoi avec tout cet argent ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do with all that money?

meaning: Incorrect French; often an attempted way to say “everything” or “every thing.”
additional_notes: **tout chose** is ungrammatical because **chose** is feminine (**la chose**), so the determiner/adjective must agree: **toute chose** (formal/literary, “every thing”) or more commonly **tout** (“everything”) / **toutes les choses** (“all the things”). You may see **tout chose** only as a learner error or in nonstandard/incorrect usage (sometimes marked [sic]).
target_language_example: « Tout chose a son importance. » (incorrect; correct: « Toute chose a son importance. »)
native_language_example: “Everything has its importance.”

additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun to mean an entire thing or the full duration/amount of something: tout le trajet = the whole trip, tout le truc = the whole thing. Related forms are toute la (feminine) and tous les (plural).
target_language_example: J'ai regardé tout le film.
native_language_example: I watched the whole movie.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all people in general. It often takes a singular verb in French: for example, tout le monde est là = everyone is here. Literally it is 'all the world,' but the usual meaning is 'everyone.'
target_language_example: Tout le monde connaît cette chanson.
native_language_example: Everyone knows this song.

additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone/everybody" and is grammatically singular, so it takes the singular verb form ("a" = "has"). Used to say that every person in a group did something: "Tout le monde a + past participle" (passé composé).
target_language_example: Tout le monde a oublié son nom.
native_language_example: Everyone forgot his name.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of rire (a ri = laughed). Often followed by "de + person/thing" to mean "to laugh at": "Tout le monde a ri de moi" (Everyone laughed at me). You can also add an exception with "sauf": "Tout le monde a ri, sauf Tom" (Everyone laughed except Tom).
target_language_example: Tout le monde a ri de lui pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: Everyone laughed at him during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with the passé composé of être (a été) to describe how everyone was at a past moment or over a past period. Even though it refers to many people, "tout le monde" is grammatically singular, so adjectives often stay singular masculine by default: « Tout le monde a été gentil. » (You may also hear plural agreement in informal speech, but singular is the standard.)
target_language_example: Tout le monde a été très patient pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: Everyone was very patient during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people in general. Although it refers to many people, "tout le monde" is grammatically singular, so you use the singular verb: "a" (has). You can change the tense as needed: "tout le monde avait" (everyone had), "tout le monde aura" (everyone will have).
target_language_example: Tout le monde a des jours difficiles.
native_language_example: Everyone has tough days.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people in general. It’s typically followed by a plural noun (des + noun): Tout le monde a des défauts. (Note: literally “all the world has…”, but it means “everyone has…”.)
target_language_example: Tout le monde a des qualités et des défauts.
native_language_example: Everyone has strengths and weaknesses.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about people. It’s made of: tout le monde (everyone) + a (has) + un/une (a). Choose un for masculine nouns and une for feminine nouns: « tout le monde a un frère » / « tout le monde a une histoire ». Even though « tout le monde » refers to many people, the verb stays singular (a).
target_language_example: Tout le monde a un endroit préféré.
native_language_example: Everyone has a favorite place.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about what people like. Literally "all the world likes," but in everyday French it means "everyone" (people in general). You can follow it with a noun (Tout le monde aime le pain.) or with an object pronoun (Tout le monde l’aime. = Everyone likes it/him/her.).
target_language_example: Dans cette ville, tout le monde aime le marché du samedi.
native_language_example: In this town, everyone likes the Saturday market.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about what people like. Here, **les** is the plural definite article (“the” / “some”), so it’s followed by a plural noun: *les chips, les frites, les glaces*. You can also change **les** to **le/la/l’** for singular: *Tout le monde aime le chocolat.*
target_language_example: Tout le monde aime les bons desserts.
native_language_example: Everyone likes good desserts.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person, thing, law, story, etc. is widely known. "Tout le monde" = "everyone" (singular idea), and "connaît" is the present tense of "connaître" (to know/be familiar with). Often followed by a direct object (e.g., son nom, la loi).
target_language_example: Dans ce quartier, tout le monde connaît le boulanger.
native_language_example: In this neighborhood, everyone knows the baker.

additional_notes: Used to mean all the people who are inside a place or within a group: « Tout le monde dans le bâtiment… », « Tout le monde dans ma famille… ». Even though it refers to many people, « tout le monde » is grammatically singular, so verbs usually agree in the singular: « Tout le monde dans la salle est… ». (Common variant: « tout le monde de + group » = “everyone in/from that group”: « Tout le monde de ma famille… ».)
target_language_example: Tout le monde dans la classe comprend la leçon.
native_language_example: Everyone in the class understands the lesson.

additional_notes: Used to make a general recommendation, opinion, or (sometimes strong) instruction about what all people should do. "Tout le monde" = everyone; "devrait" is the conditional of "devoir" (to have to / should), making it sound like advice rather than a strict obligation ("tout le monde doit"). Often followed by an infinitive: "Tout le monde devrait + verbe".
target_language_example: Tout le monde devrait respecter les règles.
native_language_example: Everyone should respect the rules.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation that applies to all people (“tout le monde” = everyone; “doit” is the 3rd person singular of “devoir,” meaning “must / have to”). It’s typically followed by a verb in the infinitive: “tout le monde doit + infinitive” (e.g., payer, participer).
target_language_example: Ici, tout le monde doit montrer une pièce d’identité.
native_language_example: Here, everyone must show an ID.

additional_notes: “Tout le monde” means “everyone/everybody” and it takes a singular verb: tout le monde est / a / fait. It’s often followed by an adjective (Tout le monde est prêt.), a place (Tout le monde est ici.), or a phrase like “au courant” (aware) or “en retard” (late).
target_language_example: Tout le monde est prêt à partir.
native_language_example: Everyone is ready to leave.

additional_notes: This is the formal French question structure using inversion: subject + verb + -il/-elle. Here, the subject is “tout le monde” (“everyone”), and “est-il” means “is (he/it)?” even though it refers to a group of people. It’s common in writing and formal speech. In everyday conversation you’ll often hear: “Est-ce que tout le monde est … ?” or simply “Tout le monde est … ?”.
target_language_example: Tout le monde est-il prêt à partir ?
native_language_example: Is everyone ready to leave?

additional_notes: A common way to say that everybody is pleased with the situation (often as a conclusion: “and everyone’s happy”). Can also be used as a question ("Tout le monde est content ?") to check that everyone is okay with the decision. Note: French "content" usually means "happy" or "pleased," not "content" (as in "not dissatisfied") in the English sense.
target_language_example: On a changé l’horaire, et maintenant tout le monde est content.
native_language_example: We changed the schedule, and now everyone is happy.

additional_notes: Used to check attendance or to announce that everyone has arrived. Often said as a question (Est-ce que tout le monde est là ?) or as an exclamation (Tout le monde est là !).
target_language_example: On peut commencer : tout le monde est là.
native_language_example: We can start: everyone is here.

additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone." "Fut" is the passé simple (simple past) of "être" (to be), mostly used in literature and formal storytelling; in everyday speech you usually say "tout le monde était" (everyone was) or sometimes "tout le monde a été" (everyone has been/was). Often followed by an adjective: "Tout le monde fut surpris" (Everyone was surprised).
target_language_example: Pendant l'annonce, tout le monde fut choqué.
native_language_example: During the announcement, everyone was shocked.

additional_notes: Used to talk about all the people in the place you’re in. Often followed by a verb in the 3rd person singular (e.g., « Tout le monde ici comprend… »).
target_language_example: Tout le monde ici est très gentil.
native_language_example: Everyone here is very nice.

meaning: “everyone” + “him/her/it” (direct object pronoun, elided before a vowel/silent h).
additional_notes: “Tout le monde” means “everyone” (literally “all the world”). “l’” is the elided form of “le” or “la” and must be followed by a verb starting with a vowel or silent h (e.g., l’attend, l’a vu, l’adore). It refers to someone/something already clear from context.
target_language_example: Tout le monde l'a vu.
native_language_example: Everyone saw him/her/it.

additional_notes: **Tout le monde** means “everyone.” The **le** is a direct-object pronoun placed **before** the verb and usually refers to a masculine singular person or thing (“him” or “it”). Pattern: **Tout le monde + le + verb** (e.g., *Tout le monde le sait* = “Everyone knows it”).
target_language_example: Tout le monde le sait.
native_language_example: Everyone knows it.

additional_notes: Used to say that a fact is common knowledge. "le" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (the thing being talked about). Often used for emphasis (sometimes with words like "évidemment"). Can be used as a statement or in a question: "Est-ce que tout le monde le sait ?" = "Does everyone know?"
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tout le monde le sait déjà.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everyone already knows it.

meaning: “everyone … to me / … me” (everyone + “me” as the object).
additional_notes: Used to say that everybody does something to you, or feels something about you. **Tout le monde** = “everyone.” **Me** is an object pronoun meaning “me/to me,” placed **before** the verb: *Tout le monde me connaît* (“Everyone knows me”). With **connaître** (to know a person), the 3rd person singular is often written **connaît** (with a circumflex).
target_language_example: Tout le monde me regarde.
native_language_example: Everyone is looking at me.

tout le monde ne peut pas être

target_language_multi_word_term: tout le monde ne peut pas être
additional_notes: Used to say that a quality, role, or achievement isn’t possible for all people. In standard French, this often implies "not everybody" rather than "nobody". You typically complete it with a noun or adjective: « Tout le monde ne peut pas être + adjectif/nom ».
target_language_example: Tout le monde ne peut pas être médecin.
native_language_example: Not everyone can be a doctor.

additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone" (literally "all the world"). It’s followed by the 3rd-person singular form of the verb: "tout le monde peut" (not *peuvent*). It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "Tout le monde peut apprendre…" = "Anyone can learn…"
target_language_example: Avec un peu de pratique, tout le monde peut y arriver.
native_language_example: With a bit of practice, anyone can do it.

additional_notes: Used to say something is common knowledge (known by all people in a group, or by people in general). Often followed by a clause with que/ce que/qui/ce qui: « Tout le monde sait que… » (Everyone knows that…), « Tout le monde sait qui… » (Everyone knows who…), « Tout le monde sait ce qui… » (Everyone knows what…).
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que ce restaurant est très bon.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that this restaurant is very good.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement presented as common knowledge. The verb is usually present tense (sait), even when what follows is about the past: « Tout le monde sait que je l'ai pris. » Can also be used ironically or sarcastically to mean “as if everyone knows.”
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que c'est difficile.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that it’s difficult.

additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone." "Savait" is the imperfect past of "savoir" (to know), often used for a general state or background information in the past. You’ll often see it with "que" + a clause ("Tout le monde savait que...") or with a direct object ("Tout le monde savait la chanson").
target_language_example: Quand il est arrivé, tout le monde savait déjà la nouvelle.
native_language_example: When he arrived, everyone already knew the news.

additional_notes: Used before a reflexive verb (or a verb used reflexively). With "tout le monde" (singular in French), you still use "se". Depending on the verb, it can mean everyone does something to themselves (e.g., "tout le monde se calme" = everyone calms down) or to each other (e.g., "tout le monde se connaît" = everyone knows each other).
target_language_example: Après la réunion, tout le monde se dépêche de rentrer chez soi.
native_language_example: After the meeting, everyone hurries to go home.

tout le monde se mit à

target_language_multi_word_term: tout le monde se mit à
additional_notes: Past simple (literary) of "tout le monde s’est mis à". Used in stories and written narration to show that everyone began doing something at the same time. It’s followed by an infinitive: "se mit à + infinitive" (e.g., applaudir, rire, parler).
target_language_example: Quand il est entré, tout le monde se mit à crier.
native_language_example: When he came in, everyone started shouting.

additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone" (literally "all the world"). "Sera" is the future tense of "être" (to be): it’s used to talk about how everyone will be later (e.g., happy, tired, there, at home, aware). Often followed by an adjective (fatigué, heureux) or a place/state (là, à la maison, au courant).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tout le monde sera prêt à temps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everyone will be ready on time.

meaning: "everyone is going to" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used with the near future (futur proche): **tout le monde va + infinitive**. It means that everyone will do something soon or is expected to do it. The verb **va** is from **aller** (to go) and stays **va** because **tout le monde** is grammatically singular even though it means many people.
target_language_example: Tout le monde va comprendre bientôt.
native_language_example: Everyone is going to understand soon.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people in general. "Tout le monde" = "everyone" (literally "all the world"), and "veut" is the present tense of "vouloir" (to want). Often followed by an infinitive: "tout le monde veut + verb" (e.g., "tout le monde veut réussir").
target_language_example: Tout le monde veut avoir du temps libre.
native_language_example: Everybody wants to have free time.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (voulait) to describe what everyone wanted at that time in the past. Common patterns: + infinitive (Tout le monde voulait danser.) and + que + subjunctive (Tout le monde voulait que vous fassiez cela.).
target_language_example: Tout le monde voulait partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: Everyone wanted to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to describe a state or situation that applied to everyone at a particular time in the past. It’s the phrase "tout le monde" (everyone) + the imperfect of "être" (was/were), often followed by an adjective or description: "tout le monde était fatigué" (everyone was tired).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, tout le monde était prêt.
native_language_example: When I arrived, everyone was ready.

additional_notes: This is a sentence starter: *tout le monde* = “everyone,” *était* = “was,” and *en* often introduces a state or situation. It’s usually followed by a noun phrase like *en retard* (late), *en colère* (angry), *en vacances* (on vacation), or by *en train de* + infinitive to mean “was (in the middle of) doing …”.
target_language_example: Tout le monde était en retard.
native_language_example: Everyone was late.

additional_notes: Used to refer to everything remaining besides what was just mentioned. Common in comparisons (e.g., “more important than everything else”) and when talking about what’s left over (e.g., food, items, tasks).
target_language_example: Je m’occupe du dossier, et tu fais tout le reste.
native_language_example: I’ll take care of the file, and you do everything else.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very often or continuously. It can be neutral, or it can suggest annoyance depending on context.
target_language_example: Il est tout le temps en retard.
native_language_example: He's late all the time.

additional_notes: This is usually heard/written with punctuation as **« Tout le temps, si ! »**: **tout le temps** = “all the time/constantly,” and **si !** is the special French “yes!” used to contradict a negative statement or question (replying “Yes, I do!” to a negative claim). In natural French, you’d typically include a comma (**Tout le temps, si !**) or place **si** first (**Si, tout le temps !**), but the fixed string **« tout le temps si »** can appear as-is in informal writing or when quoting.
target_language_example: —Tu ne m’appelles jamais. —Je t’appelle tout le temps si !
native_language_example: —You never call me. —Yes I do, I call you all the time!

additional_notes: Means the entire amount of money someone has. The possessive changes with the owner: tout mon argent (all my money), tout ton argent (all your money), tout leur argent (all their money). Often used with verbs like dépenser (to spend), perdre (to lose), voler (to steal).
target_language_example: Il a perdu tout son argent.
native_language_example: He lost all his money.

additional_notes: A fairly formal way to mean “everyone/anyone,” often used for general statements, rules, or things that apply to all people. It’s close to “tout le monde,” but sounds more official and emphasizes “each individual person.” Usually used as a subject: “Tout un chacun + verb.”
target_language_example: Tout un chacun peut comprendre ce message.
native_language_example: Anyone can understand this message.

additional_notes: Refers to a whole set of things, ideas, or a situation already mentioned or visible from context. Very common in everyday French; ça is the usual spoken form of cela.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas tout ça.
native_language_example: I don't understand all that.

additional_notes: Used to sum up a situation (“tout ça” = “all that / all of this”) and then explain the reason, purpose, or responsibility. Very common with: « grâce à … » (thanks to), « à cause de … » (because of, usually negative), and « pour … » (for). The comma is optional in writing; in speech there’s often a short pause: « Tout ça c’est… ».
target_language_example: Tout ça, c'est grâce à toi.
native_language_example: All of that is thanks to you.

additional_notes:
Built on the common expression **avoir l’air** (= to seem/to look). You can follow it with:
- an adjective: **Tout a l’air normal / en ordre / bon.**
- **de + infinitive**: **Tout a l’air de bien se passer.** (= Everything seems to be going well.)
Note: In correct French spelling, it’s **Tout a l’air** (with an apostrophe), not *a l'air*.
target_language_example: Tout a l'air en ordre.
native_language_example: Everything seems to be in order.

additional_notes: A very common, fully compositional phrase: tout = "everything" and est = "is." It is used to describe the overall state or quality of things, often followed by an adjective or fixed expression, as in tout est différent, tout est possible, or tout est en ordre.
target_language_example: Tout est prêt pour demain.
native_language_example: Everything is ready for tomorrow.

meaning: “That’s all there is to say.” / “Everything has been said.”
additional_notes: Used to conclude a discussion or signal that no more explanation is needed (often meaning “case closed” or “nothing more to add”). It can be a full standalone sentence: « Tout est dit. » Similar idea to « Voilà, c’est tout. »
target_language_example: Je t’ai expliqué la situation : tout est dit.
native_language_example: I’ve explained the situation—that’s all there is to say.

meaning: to mess everything up; to ruin everything.
additional_notes: Very informal and can sound crude because of “foutre” (roughly like “to fuck up”). Used when someone is about to spoil a plan/situation completely. You can change the tense/person: je vais/tu vas/il va tout foutre en l’air, etc.
target_language_example: Fais attention : tu vas tout foutre en l'air !
native_language_example: Be careful: you're going to mess everything up!

meaning: “everything will be fine / all will be well.”
additional_notes: A reassuring phrase used to comfort someone or express hope about the future. Literally “everything will go well” (future tense of aller: ira). Often said on its own or with a softener like « Ne t’inquiète pas, tout ira bien. »
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tout ira bien demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine tomorrow.

meaning: everything goes well / everything is going fine.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "se passer" (= to happen). Often used to reassure someone ("Everything’s going fine?") or to express a hope/condition: "Si tout se passe bien…" = "If all goes well…".
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout se passe bien pour l'instant.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is going fine for now.

meaning: “everything will go well / everything will be fine.”
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or express optimism about how a situation will turn out. Built from: tout (“everything”) + se passera (future of se passer, “to happen/go”) + bien (“well”). Often follows verbs like espérer (to hope), parier (to bet), être sûr (to be sure), or is said on its own as encouragement.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : tout se passera bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine.

meaning: everything is fine / everything’s going well.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to ask/check if things are OK. Very common in conversation; can describe a situation (Tout va bien.) or be used as a question with intonation or with "Est-ce que" (Tout va bien ? / Est-ce que tout va bien ?). Often paired with time markers like "pour l’instant" (for now) or "j’espère que" (I hope that).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is fine.

meaning: "Everything will be fine" / "It will all work out."
additional_notes: A very common reassurance when someone is worried or scared. Uses the near-future idea with "aller" (va) + infinitive: "se passer" = "to happen". Often said on its own, or followed by something comforting: "Tout va bien se passer, je te le promets." You may also hear the shorter version: "Ça va bien se passer."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : tout va bien se passer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine.

meaning: Everything is fine / all is well.
additional_notes: A very common reassurance or check-in. Use it to say things are OK ("Tout va bien.") or to ask if someone is OK ("Tout va bien ?" / "Tout va bien pour vous ?" = more polite). You can also add context: "Tout va bien ici ?" (Is everything OK here?).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is fine.

meaning: earlier today / a little while ago (or later today / in a little while, depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a moment close to now but not exact. With phrases like « Désolé(e) pour tout à l'heure » or « Merci pour tout à l'heure », it usually means “earlier today / a little while ago.” In other contexts it can mean “later today / in a little while” (e.g., « Je te rappelle tout à l'heure. » = “I’ll call you back later.”).
target_language_example: On en reparle tout à l'heure, d'accord ?
native_language_example: We’ll talk about it later, okay?

additional_notes: Feminine form of "tout seul". Used to say someone did something without help ("by herself") or that she is alone ("on her own"). Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence: "Elle l’a fait toute seule."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : tu n'es pas toute seule.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re not alone.

meaning: “anyway; in any case” (usually in « de toute façon »).
additional_notes: Most often used as the set phrase « de toute façon » to mean that something won’t change the outcome (“anyway / regardless”). It can appear at the start or end of a sentence: « De toute façon, … » / « …, de toute façon. »
target_language_example: De toute façon, il est trop tard.
native_language_example: Anyway, it’s too late.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean the entire thing or every part of it: « toute la région », « toute la maison », « toute la famille ». It agrees in gender/number (compare: « tout le » masculine singular, « toute l’ » before a vowel/h, « tous les / toutes les » plural).
target_language_example: J’ai passé toute la journée à travailler.
native_language_example: I spent the whole day working.

meaning: the whole family; everyone in the family.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that all family members are included. Often the subject of a sentence: "Toute la famille est…". "Toute" agrees with "famille" (feminine singular), but the meaning is collective (all the people in the family).
target_language_example: Toute la famille vient dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: The whole family is coming for dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Means something lasts for the entire day. Often used with a verb in the past or present: « J’ai travaillé toute la journée » (I worked all day). With « Ça a pris / ça prendrait toute la journée », it means “it took/would take all day.”
target_language_example: On a attendu toute la journée.
native_language_example: We waited all day.

additional_notes: Means “throughout the morning” (from morning until around noon). Often used with the passé composé or imparfait to show a duration: « J’ai attendu toute la matinée » / « Il pleuvait toute la matinée ». Feminine agreement: toute + la matinée.
target_language_example: J'ai travaillé toute la matinée, puis je suis allé déjeuner.
native_language_example: I worked all morning, then I went to have lunch.

additional_notes: Means “throughout the whole night,” often to say something lasted from evening until morning. It can describe an activity (danser, parler), a feeling/state (pleurer), or staying awake (veiller) for the entire night.
target_language_example: On a travaillé toute la nuit pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: We worked all night to finish the project.

additional_notes: Means the entire duration of the week. Often used with or without "pendant" ("pendant toute la semaine" = "for the whole week"). Agreement: "tout" matches the feminine noun "semaine" → "toute".
target_language_example: Je travaille de nuit toute la semaine.
native_language_example: I work nights all week.

additional_notes: Used to mean something lasts for the entire evening (from the start of the evening until it ends). Often placed after the verb: « Il sera là toute la soirée. »
target_language_example: On a regardé des films toute la soirée.
native_language_example: We watched movies all evening.

meaning: "your whole life ahead of you" (plenty of time; you’re still young).
additional_notes: Used with a person/object pronoun to say someone has lots of time ahead (often because they’re young): « toute la vie devant + elle/lui/moi/toi/nous/vous/eux ». Commonly appears as « avoir toute la vie devant soi » (generic “oneself”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu as toute la vie devant toi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you have your whole life ahead of you.

meaning: the whole city / everyone in the city.
additional_notes: Can mean (1) physically all over the city (as in « J’ai fait toute la ville » = I went all around the city), or (2) all the people in the city (as in « Toute la ville en parle » = everyone is talking about it). « Toute » agrees with « ville » (feminine singular).
target_language_example: Après la rumeur, toute la ville le sait.
native_language_example: After the rumor, the whole city knows it.

additional_notes: Means “for my entire life” (duration up to now) or “in my entire life” (often after a superlative: *le plus… de toute ma vie* = “the most… in my whole life”). It can also be used emotionally to mean “it’s my whole life” (*C’est toute ma vie.*)
target_language_example: Je rêve d’habiter à Paris toute ma vie.
native_language_example: I dream of living in Paris all my life.

meaning: his/her entire life; all his/her life.
additional_notes: Means for someone’s whole lifetime (from birth up to now or until death, depending on context). Possessive agrees with the person: toute ma vie (my whole life), toute ta vie (your whole life), toute sa vie (his/her whole life), toute notre/votre/leur vie. Often placed after the verb to indicate something lasted a lifetime.
target_language_example: Elle a travaillé en France toute sa vie.
native_language_example: She worked in France her whole life.

meaning: your whole life; all your life.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize duration from now (or from some point in life) until death. Often appears after a verb like rester (to stay), passer (to spend), être (to be), se souvenir de (to remember), etc. Can be made formal or changed in person: toute ma vie (my whole life), toute sa vie (his/her whole life), toute votre vie (your whole life, formal/plural).
target_language_example: Tu ne peux pas éviter cette conversation toute ta vie.
native_language_example: You can’t avoid this conversation your whole life.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “all these / all those,” often with emphasis (e.g., time: toutes ces années; things: toutes ces provisions; questions: toutes ces questions). It agrees with the noun: masculine plural is tous ces (tous ces livres).
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à croire que tu aies gardé toutes ces lettres.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you kept all these letters.

additional_notes: Refers to a long period of time up to now (often with emotion, nostalgia, or emphasis). It can stand alone for dramatic effect (“Toutes ces années.”) or be used after a preposition like après (“après toutes ces années” = “after all these years”).
target_language_example: Toutes ces années, j’ai pensé à toi.
native_language_example: All these years, I’ve thought about you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a set of specific things already known or visible in context. Often implies “all this stuff” (information, objects, details). Agreement: feminine plural (toutes) + demonstrative (ces) + plural noun (choses).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas parler de toutes ces choses maintenant.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about all these things right now.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun. It often means "all the," and in some general statements it can correspond to English "every." The masculine plural form is "tous les."
target_language_example: Toutes les fenêtres sont ouvertes.
native_language_example: All the windows are open.

meaning: both (of them), when referring to two females.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the statement applies to the two people/things together. It agrees in gender and number: masculine mixed group = « tous les deux », feminine = « toutes les deux ». It can be placed after the subject or after the verb: « Elles sont toutes les deux… », « Elles ont toutes les deux… ».
target_language_example: Vous pouvez venir toutes les deux si vous voulez.
native_language_example: You can both come if you want.

additional_notes: "Toutes" is the feminine plural of "tout" (= all). Used with a plural feminine noun: "toutes les + noun". Be careful with negation: "Toutes les filles ne sont pas ainsi" often means "Not all girls are like that" (it doesn’t necessarily mean that none are like that).
target_language_example: Toutes les filles de la classe sont arrivées en avance.
native_language_example: All the girls in the class arrived early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens each night (a repeated routine or habit). Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also appear at the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je prends une tisane toutes les nuits avant de dormir.
native_language_example: I have an herbal tea every night before going to sleep.

additional_notes: "Toutes" agrees with the feminine plural noun "portes". Common in home/security contexts with verbs like "verrouiller" (to lock) and "fermer" (to close/shut). You can also specify a place: "toutes les portes de la maison" (all the doors in the house).
target_language_example: Avant de partir, vérifie que toutes les portes sont bien verrouillées.
native_language_example: Before leaving, check that all the doors are properly locked.

additional_notes: Means the complete set of answers (e.g., to a question, quiz, or problem). Often used with verbs like connaître/avoir (“to know/have all the answers”) and can be followed by “à + [question]” (e.g., “toutes les réponses à cette question”).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas toutes les réponses, mais je peux essayer de t'aider.
native_language_example: I don't have all the answers, but I can try to help you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything you own/do in a feminine plural category: toutes mes recettes, toutes mes plantes, etc. It’s the feminine plural form of "tout" and must agree with the noun that follows. For masculine plural nouns, use "tous mes" (e.g., tous mes livres).
target_language_example: J’ai perdu toutes mes clés.
native_language_example: I lost all my keys.

additional_notes: Used before a plural feminine noun: toutes ses + noun (e.g., toutes ses erreurs = all his/her mistakes). It refers to everything belonging to one person. The possessor can be "his" or "her"—French uses "ses" based on the noun being possessed (plural), not on the owner’s gender. With masculine plural nouns, use "tous ses".
target_language_example: Elle a oublié toutes ses affaires à la maison.
native_language_example: She forgot all her things at home.

meaning: all one’s strength; with all one’s might.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize maximum physical or mental effort. Often appears in phrases like « de toutes ses forces » (“with all his/her strength”) or with verbs like « épuiser » (to use up/exhaust) and « concentrer » (to focus). The possessive changes with the person: « toutes mes forces », « toutes tes forces », « toutes leurs forces », etc.
target_language_example: Elle a poussé la porte de toutes ses forces.
native_language_example: She pushed the door with all her strength.

meaning: all kinds of; all sorts of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean a wide variety. It agrees with the feminine plural "sortes" (so it stays "toutes sortes de"), and the noun that follows is usually plural but can be singular depending on meaning (e.g., "toutes sortes de choses"). Often implies diversity rather than an exact list.
target_language_example: On y trouve toutes sortes de restaurants, du plus simple au plus chic.
native_language_example: You can find all kinds of restaurants there, from the simplest to the fanciest.

meaning: all kinds of things; all sorts of things.
additional_notes: Used to say there is a wide variety of items/ideas/activities (often without listing them). You can also use the same pattern with a noun: “toutes sortes de livres” (all kinds of books).
target_language_example: On peut faire toutes sortes de choses ici.
native_language_example: You can do all kinds of things here.

additional_notes: Used mainly in medical/scientific contexts to say a substance or medicine may be safe (or less harmful) in small amounts but becomes harmful if the dose is increased. Often contrasts with an implied lower dose (e.g., « à faible dose »).
target_language_example: Ce médicament est efficace à faible dose, mais toxique à plus forte dose.
native_language_example: This medicine is effective at a low dose, but toxic at a higher dose.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. After train, de often gives the place the train comes from (train de Paris = train from Paris) or its scheduled time (train de huit heures = the eight o'clock train). In sentences like empêcher le train de rouler, de belongs to the verb pattern empêcher ... de + infinitive, not to train itself.
target_language_example: Le train de Marseille arrive à 18 heures.
native_language_example: The train from Marseille arrives at 6 p.m.

meaning: in the middle of singing; in the process of singing.
additional_notes: Usually used with « être en train de » to emphasize an action happening right now: « Je suis en train de chanter. » Without « être », « en train de chanter » can appear after another verb (e.g., « Je l’ai surpris en train de chanter » = “I caught him singing”). It does not refer to an actual “train” here.
target_language_example: Je suis en train de chanter, je te rappelle plus tard.
native_language_example: I'm in the middle of singing; I'll call you back later.

meaning: in the middle of sleeping (sleeping right now).
additional_notes: Usually used in the expression « être en train de + infinitive » to emphasize an action in progress: « Je suis en train de dormir » = “I’m sleeping (right now).” By itself, « train de dormir » is typically incomplete without « en » and a form of « être » (suis, es, est, etc.).
target_language_example: Chut, je suis en train de dormir.
native_language_example: Shh, I’m sleeping (right now).

meaning: “in the middle of doing” (used in: être en train de + infinitive).
additional_notes: Almost always used with être: « Je suis en train de faire… » = “I’m (in the middle of) doing…”. It emphasizes an action happening right now (more strongly than the simple present). « train » here does not mean a “train” (the vehicle).
target_language_example: Je suis en train de faire mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I’m doing my homework (right now).

meaning: in the middle of playing (currently playing).
additional_notes: Usually used as part of the structure « être en train de + infinitive » to emphasize an action in progress: « Je suis en train de jouer » = “I’m playing right now / I’m in the middle of playing.” On its own, « en train de jouer » can appear after a noun or in a short answer (e.g., « Il est en train de jouer »).
target_language_example: Je suis en train de jouer, je te rappelle après.
