It can mean you didn’t want something ("tu ne voulais pas de livres" = you didn’t want any books) or you didn’t want to do something / didn’t want someone to do something ("tu ne voulais pas que je vienne" = you didn’t want me to come). Often used to question or challenge someone about a past preference or refusal.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu ne voulais pas venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you want to come with us?

meaning: "you have" / "you did" (to us), used before a past participle in the passé composé.
additional_notes: "Tu" = you (informal singular). "Nous" is the direct object pronoun (us) placed before the verb. "As" is the present tense of "avoir" used to form the passé composé: tu nous as + past participle (tu nous as trouvés / aidés / trompés). If "nous" refers to people and comes before the verb, the past participle often agrees: trouvés (masc./mixed) or trouvées (fem.).
target_language_example: Tu nous as oubliés au restaurant.
native_language_example: You forgot us at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Uses the subject pronoun tu (informal “you”) + negation ne…pas around the verb être (“to be”): tu n’es pas = “you aren’t/you’re not.” Used before an adjective or noun phrase: Tu n’es pas faible (“You’re not weak”). In casual speech, ne is often dropped: Tu es pas…
target_language_example: Tu n’es pas en retard.
native_language_example: You’re not late.

additional_notes: From parler with tu, used for one person you know well or speak to casually. It can mean either "you speak" or "you talk," depending on context. In questions, French often keeps the same word order: Tu parles aussi allemand ? = "Do you also speak German?" With de, it often means "you’re talking about" something: Tu parles du divorce ?
target_language_example: Tu parles trop vite.
native_language_example: You speak too fast.

additional_notes: Used to ask or confirm who/what someone means. Often followed by a person or thing (Tu parles de papa ?), or by a question word (Tu parles de qui ? = Who are you talking about?). In "Comment tu parles de ma sœur ?", it can mean "How are you talking about my sister?" (i.e., watch how you speak about her).
target_language_example: Tu parles de quel film ?
native_language_example: Which movie are you talking about?

additional_notes: From the verb *penser* (“to think”), used with **tu** (you, singular informal). Common in questions: **Tu penses que… ?** (“Do you think that…?”), **Pourquoi tu penses ça ?** (“Why do you think that?”). With **penser à** it means “to think about”: **À quoi tu penses ?** (“What are you thinking about?”).
target_language_example: Tu penses que ça va marcher ?
native_language_example: Do you think it’ll work?

additional_notes: Literally “you think that.” Used to ask for someone’s opinion or what they believe/expect: Tu penses que + clause. In questions it often means “Do you really think…?” or “Do you expect…?” In more formal French, you may hear “Penses-tu que… ?” instead of “Tu penses que… ?”.
target_language_example: Tu penses que ça va marcher ?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to work?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion/guess about what something is. Addressed to one person you call "tu" (friends, family, kids). Often followed by a noun, an adjective, or a clause: "tu penses que c'est quoi ?" / "tu penses que c'est vrai ?" / "tu penses que c'est une bonne idée ?" For a more formal/polite version, use "vous pensez que c’est…"
target_language_example: Tu penses que c'est une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you think it's a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask (often with surprise, doubt, or challenge) what someone believes about you. It’s followed by a verb: « Tu penses que je + verbe… ? » (e.g., « Tu penses que je mens ? »). Uses « tu », which is informal; with someone you don’t know well, use « Vous pensez que je… ? ».
target_language_example: Tu penses que je vais accepter ça ?
native_language_example: Do you think I’m going to accept that?

meaning: "are you thinking about…?" / "do you have … in mind?"
additional_notes: Used with the verb *penser à* + a noun/pronoun/infinitive to ask what someone is thinking about or considering. Often translates as “think about” or “think of” in English (e.g., *Tu penses à une réponse ?* = “Do you have an answer in mind?”).
target_language_example: Tu penses à quoi, là ?
native_language_example: What are you thinking about right now?

additional_notes: Uses informal singular tu, so it is used when speaking to one person you know well, a child, or someone your age in a casual context. It can express ability, permission, or possibility. Peux is the tu form of pouvoir.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir avec nous ce soir.
native_language_example: You can come with us tonight.

meaning: "You can count on me" (you can rely on me).
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that you’ll help or support them, or that you’re dependable. In speech it can sound very warm/encouraging; you can add emphasis like “je t’assure” (“I promise”) or “tu sais ?” (“you know?”).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : tu peux compter sur moi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you can count on me.

meaning: 'you can do' / 'you are able to do'.
additional_notes: Used to say what someone is able or allowed to do. Often followed by an infinitive (Tu peux faire mieux. = You can do better.) or by a noun phrase (Tu peux faire une chose pour moi. = You can do something for me.). In context it can also sound like a suggestion/permission: "You can (go ahead and) do...".
target_language_example: Tu peux faire ça demain si tu veux.
native_language_example: You can do that tomorrow if you want.

tu peux faire mieux que ça

target_language_multi_word_term: tu peux faire mieux que ça
additional_notes: Used to encourage or challenge someone to improve their effort or performance; depending on tone it can be motivating, teasing, or mildly critical. Often said with "Allez" ("Come on").
target_language_example: Allez, tu peux faire mieux que ça : essaie encore une fois.
native_language_example: Come on, you can do better than that: try one more time.

meaning: “can you do that?” / “you can do that.”
additional_notes: Uses the informal “tu” to ask about ability or permission. In questions, intonation or a tag like “n’est-ce pas ? / non ?” can make it sound like “You can do that, right?” Depending on context it can mean either capability (“Are you able to do that?”) or permission (“Is it allowed to do that here?”).
target_language_example: Tu peux faire ça demain ?
native_language_example: Can you do that tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used with the informal singular subject pronoun **tu** (“you”). **Le** is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it” (for a masculine noun) or “him.” In French, object pronouns like **le** usually come **before** the verb (e.g., *Tu peux le prendre.* = “You can take it.”). Very common in requests/questions: *Tu peux le… ?* (“Can you … it?”).
target_language_example: Tu peux le répéter ?
native_language_example: Can you repeat it?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is able to do something, or to encourage them (“You can do it!”). In a question ("Tu peux le faire ou pas ?"), it asks whether they’re able/willing to do it. Very common in spoken French; informal because it uses "tu" (to be more polite, say "Vous pouvez le faire").
target_language_example: Allez, tu peux le faire !
native_language_example: Come on, you can do it!

additional_notes: Used to ask someone you address as tu to do something for you. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: “Tu peux me + infinitive… ?” The object pronoun me (“me/to me”) comes before the infinitive (e.g., tu peux me aider = can you help me).
target_language_example: Tu peux me montrer où est la boulangerie ?
native_language_example: Can you show me where the bakery is?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for information. It’s the informal “you” (tu) and can sound direct; to be more polite, you can add “s’il te plaît” or use the formal version “vous pouvez me dire… ?”. Often followed by an indirect question: “ce que…”, “qui…”, “où…”, “d’où…”, etc.
target_language_example: Tu peux me dire où est la station de métro la plus proche ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the nearest subway station is?

meaning: “you can speak” / “can you speak?” (ability or permission).
additional_notes: Used either as a statement (ability: “You can speak German.”) or as a question asking if someone is able/allowed to speak (“Can you speak?”). Often followed by a language (parler allemand) or a place/context to mean permission (ici = “here”). In speech, rising intonation can make it a question even without “?”.
target_language_example: Tu peux parler plus fort, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you speak louder, please?

meaning: "you can't" / "you can't (do it)" (informal for "tu ne peux pas").
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: the "ne" in negation is often dropped ("tu ne peux pas" → "tu peux pas"). Used both as a statement ("Tu peux pas.") and in questions that can sound surprised or challenging ("Comment ça, tu peux pas ?" = "What do you mean you can't?").
target_language_example: Désolé, tu peux pas entrer sans billet.
native_language_example: Sorry, you can't come in without a ticket.

meaning: you can stay; you may stay.
additional_notes: Used to give permission or say it’s okay for someone to remain somewhere. Often followed by details like duration (cette nuit, un instant, autant de temps que tu veux) or conditions (si tu veux).
target_language_example: Tu peux rester ici jusqu’à demain matin.
native_language_example: You can stay here until tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to give permission or say it’s OK for someone to stay in this place. Often followed by a time expression: « ce soir » (tonight), « aussi longtemps que tu veux / tant que tu veux » (as long as you want). « Tu peux… » can sound like permission (“you may…”) or possibility (“you can…”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu peux rester ici cette nuit.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you can stay here tonight.

additional_notes: Used when the verb is reflexive (it uses se), like se joindre (to join) or se rendre (to go/get to). In French, the reflexive pronoun (te) comes before the infinitive after peux: « Tu peux te joindre (à nous). », « Tu peux te rendre à la gare… ». In English you usually just say “you can + verb” without “yourself.”
target_language_example: Tu peux te laver ici.
native_language_example: You can wash up here.

meaning: "can you come" / "could you come" (asking someone to come).
additional_notes: Literally “you can come.” Used to make a request or invitation in an informal (tu) context. Add details like time/place/activity: un peu plus tôt (a bit earlier), chez moi/à la maison (to my place/home), dîner (for dinner). For extra politeness, add “s’il te plaît” or use “tu pourrais venir… ?”.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir m’aider deux minutes ?
native_language_example: Can you come help me for two minutes?

additional_notes: Uses informal singular “tu” (“you”). It’s the present tense of “pouvoir” + “être” and can express ability/possibility (“you can be…”) or reassurance/permission depending on context (“you can be calm/you’re okay to…”).
target_language_example: Tu peux être fier de toi.
native_language_example: You can be proud of yourself.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: « tu peux + verbe » (e.g., « Tu peux venir ? » = Can you come?). Also common in set phrases like « autant que tu peux » (“as much as you can”) and « si tu peux » (“if you can”), sometimes with a challenging tone: « … si tu peux ! » (“… if you can!”).
target_language_example: Tu peux m'aider, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please?

meaning: “you could” / “could you…?” (polite suggestion, possibility, or request).
additional_notes: From *pouvoir* (“can/to be able to”) in the conditional: *tu pourrais*. Often used to soften what you say (more polite than *tu peux*). It can express (1) possibility/ability: *Tu pourrais être…* (“You could be…”), (2) a suggestion/advice: *Tu pourrais faire…* (“You could…”), or (3) a polite request in a question: *Tu pourrais… ?* (“Could you…?”).
target_language_example: Tu pourrais m'aider avec ça, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you help me with this, please?

meaning: “could you … for me?” / “you could … me” (polite request).
additional_notes: From *pouvoir* (“can/could”). **Tu pourrais me + infinitive** is commonly used to make a polite request: *Tu pourrais me rappeler ?* (“Could you call me back?”). It can also suggest a possibility: *Tu pourrais me remplacer* (“You could replace me”). Often followed by an infinitive like *aider, rappeler, présenter, remplacer, tenir*.
target_language_example: Tu pourrais me dire où est la gare ?
native_language_example: Could you tell me where the train station is?

additional_notes: "Pourras" is the simple future of "pouvoir" (to be able to) for "tu" (you, informal singular). It’s used to talk about what someone will be able/allowed to do later, or to make a polite request in the future sense (often like English "could you...?" depending on context).
target_language_example: Tu pourras m'appeler ce soir ?
native_language_example: Could you call me tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s preference. In questions, spoken French often keeps normal word order ("Tu préfères…?") instead of inversion ("Préféres-tu…?"). Typically followed by two options with "ou" (or), or by "quoi" (what).
target_language_example: Tu préfères qu'on parte maintenant ou plus tard ?
native_language_example: Do you prefer that we leave now or later?

meaning: Not a standard French phrase on its own (literally: “you that I”).
additional_notes: You normally wouldn’t say *tu que je* by itself in French; it doesn’t form a correct standalone expression. **Que je** is common in other structures (e.g., comparisons like *plus grand que je (le suis)*, or subordinators like *avant que je…*). If you meant “you and I,” the natural French is **toi et moi**.
target_language_example: En français, on ne dit pas « tu que je » ; on dirait plutôt « toi et moi » ou « plus … que je ».
native_language_example: In French, you don’t say “tu que je”; you’d rather say “toi et moi” or “more … than I (am)”.

meaning: Nonstandard/incomplete fragment; usually intended as part of « Tu veux que je fasse… ? » meaning “you want me to do … ?”
additional_notes: « tu que je fasse » is not a correct standalone phrase in French and sounds like an error/fragment. In natural French you would say « Tu veux que je fasse… ? » or « Tu veux que je fasse ça ? ». The part « que je fasse » is the subjunctive of *faire* (« je fasse ») used after verbs expressing will/request (vouloir que, demander que, etc.). The example below includes the exact string « tu que je fasse » but is marked as unnatural.
target_language_example: *Tu que je fasse la vaisselle ?* (forme incorrecte; on dirait plutôt : « Tu veux que je fasse la vaisselle ? »)
native_language_example: *You that I do the dishes?* (incorrect fragment; more naturally: “Do you want me to do the dishes?”)

meaning: Ungrammatical fragment; intended meaning is usually « tu as quelque chose à… » = “you have something to … (do/say/etc.).”
additional_notes: « tu quelque chose à » by itself is not correct French because it’s missing the verb « avoir » (conjugated as « as » with « tu »). The correct pattern is: « tu as quelque chose à + infinitif » (e.g., « tu as quelque chose à faire ») or « tu as quelque chose à + pronom » (e.g., « tu as quelque chose à me dire »).
target_language_example: On dit « tu as quelque chose à faire », pas « tu quelque chose à faire ».
native_language_example: You say “you have something to do,” not “you something to do.”

meaning: you—whoever you are; you, whoever it may be.
additional_notes: Expression built around « qui que ce soit » = “anyone at all / whoever it may be.” Used to refer to an unknown/unspecified person; with « tu » it directly addresses an unidentified addressee (“you, whoever you are”). Often appears in slightly formal/literary or emphatic phrasing; in everyday speech you might also hear « toi, qui que tu sois… ».
target_language_example: Tu qui que ce soit, arrête de frapper à la porte !
native_language_example: You—whoever you are—stop banging on the door!

meaning: Not a standard French expression as written; likely an (incorrect) attempt to use **quoi que ce soit** (“anything at all / whatever”).
additional_notes: **Tu quoi que ce soit** is not idiomatic French on its own. The fixed, useful part is **quoi que ce soit** = “anything at all / whatever.” With **tu**, French normally needs a verb, e.g. **Tu veux quoi que ce soit ?** (“Do you want anything at all?”) or **Si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit…** (“If you need anything at all…”). If you see **tu quoi que ce soit** in writing, it’s most likely a mistake or a truncated/fragmentary sentence.
target_language_example: En français, « tu quoi que ce soit » n’est pas une tournure correcte ; on dira plutôt : « Si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit, appelle-moi. »
native_language_example: In French, “tu quoi que ce soit” isn’t a correct phrasing; you’d rather say: “If you need anything at all, call me.”

meaning: 'you’re coming back/going home' or 'you enter (information)' (informal 'you get in/come in').
additional_notes: "Rentrer" has two common beginner meanings: (1) to return/go back, often with "chez" or "à la maison" (e.g., "Tu rentres chez toi ?"), and (2) to input/enter data (e.g., "rentrer tes informations"). In conversation, it can also mean to come inside/get in (e.g., "Tu rentres avec Gina" = you go back/come in with Gina, depending on context).
target_language_example: Tu rentres à quelle heure ce soir ?
native_language_example: What time are you coming home tonight?

meaning: you’re going home / you’re coming back home.
additional_notes: Uses the verb *rentrer* (to come back/return). Depending on tone and punctuation, it can be a statement (*Tu rentres à la maison.*) or a question (*Tu rentres à la maison ?* = “Are you going home?”). Often used for returning home (after work, school, going out).
target_language_example: Tu rentres à la maison après le travail ?
native_language_example: Are you going home after work?

tu ressembles de plus en plus à

target_language_multi_word_term: tu ressembles de plus en plus à
meaning: "you look/are more and more like" (you resemble more and more).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is increasingly starting to look like (or act like) another person/thing over time. The verb pattern is **ressembler à + noun/pronoun** (e.g., *à ta mère*, *à ton père*). You can also use it for behavior/personality, not only physical appearance.
target_language_example: Tu ressembles de plus en plus à ton père !
native_language_example: You’re looking more and more like your dad!

meaning: “you look like a … / you resemble a …”.
additional_notes: Used with **ressembler à + noun** to compare someone’s appearance (or sometimes behavior) to something/someone. It can be a compliment (*un ange*) or an insult (*un chien*), depending on the noun and tone. Note: French uses **à** (“to”), but English typically says **“look like”** rather than “resemble to.”
target_language_example: Avec cette coupe de cheveux, tu ressembles à un acteur.
native_language_example: With that haircut, you look like an actor.

additional_notes: "Tu" is the informal singular "you" (used with friends, family, kids). "Restes" is the present-tense form of "rester" (to stay/remain). Often followed by "avec" + person: "Tu restes avec moi" = "You stay with me." Note: it looks like English "rest", but it usually means "stay," not "rest."
target_language_example: Tu restes ici ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you staying here tonight?

meaning: you stay here / you’re staying here.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "rester" (to stay/remain) in the present tense: "tu restes" = "you stay." It can be a simple statement ("You’re staying here") or a firm instruction ("You stay here"), especially on its own or with emphasis like "Non" or "Toi". Often appears after "je veux que..." or "j’ai besoin que..."; in that case French uses the subjunctive, but the form is the same here: "que tu restes."
target_language_example: Désolé, tu restes ici pendant que je vais chercher la voiture.
native_language_example: Sorry, you stay here while I go get the car.

additional_notes: Often followed by an infinitive to ask if someone knows how to do something: « Tu sais conduire ? » = “Can you drive?” In the negative (« tu sais pas… »), it means “you don’t know how to / you can’t”: « Tu sais pas conduire » = “You can’t drive.” It can also be used as a conversational filler meaning “you know…”, especially in speech.
target_language_example: Tu sais nager ?
native_language_example: Can you swim?

meaning: "you can do" / "you know how to do".
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability or skill. Often followed by an infinitive: « Tu sais faire du vélo ? » (“Can you ride a bike?”). In « ce que tu sais faire », it means “what you can do” (your skills). Common in questions like « Tu sais faire quoi ? » / « Qu’est-ce que tu sais faire ? ».
target_language_example: Tu sais faire la cuisine ?
native_language_example: Can you cook?

additional_notes: Literally means "you know". In speech, intonation decides whether it is a statement or a question ("do you know...?"), and it is also often used as a conversational filler like English "you know". Use it with tu; with vous, say "vous savez".
target_language_example: Tu sais, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: You know, I prefer to stay at home.

meaning: “you know…” (beginning of a sentence; incomplete on its own).
additional_notes: In real French, this is usually followed by something like **que** (“that/what”) or **qui** (“who”): **tu sais ce que…** = “you know what… / you know that…”. By itself **tu sais ce…** sounds unfinished and very conversational, like you’re about to add the important part.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: You know what I mean?

meaning: 'you know what…' (introduces a question or something you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used in informal speech with "tu" to ask about or introduce information: "Tu sais ce qu’il a dit ?" = "Do you know what he said?" The apostrophe (qu’) is used before a vowel sound: qu’il, qu’on, qu’était, etc. In more formal situations, you’d use "vous savez ce que…".
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qu'il te faudrait ?
native_language_example: Do you know what you would need?

meaning: "Do you know what he…?" / "You know what he…" (lead-in before a clause).
additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize information about what a man did/said/what will happen, often as a question: “Tu sais ce qu’il a fait ?” = “Do you know what he did?” It’s commonly followed by a verb phrase (a fait, a dit, va se passer, etc.). In speech, it can also be rhetorical, like “You know what he did?!”
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qu'il a dit au prof ?
native_language_example: Do you know what he said to the teacher?

meaning: "you know what we…" (used to introduce an idea or suggestion).
additional_notes: This is usually the start of a sentence and needs to be completed (e.g., with a verb): « Tu sais ce qu'on pourrait faire ? » It’s common in spoken French as a conversational lead-in, similar to “you know what…” in English. « tu sais » is informal and used with friends; in more formal situations you’d avoid it or use « vous savez ».
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qu'on pourrait faire ce soir ? On pourrait aller au cinéma.
native_language_example: You know what we could do tonight? We could go to the movies.

meaning: "you know what…" (introduces what I'm about to say/ask).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to lead into a statement or a question, often to get the listener’s attention or to set up something (sometimes rhetorical): “Tu sais ce que je pense ?” / “Tu sais ce que je vais faire ?”. Can also be said with a pause: “Tu sais ce que…”.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je veux manger ce soir ?
native_language_example: You know what I want to eat tonight?

meaning: “do you know what it is?” / “you know what it’s like…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone understands a thing, concept, or experience. Often rhetorical, challenging, or emphatic (like “Do you even know what it is?” / “You know what it’s like…”). Common variants: “Tu sais ce que c’est, X ?” and “Tu sais ce que c’est que X ?” (“Do you know what X is?”).
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que c'est le mariage ?
native_language_example: Do you know what marriage is?

meaning: “You know what I’ve…?” / “Guess what I…?” (used to introduce something you did/decided/realized, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as a lead-in to announce something (often with suspense or emphasis). It’s typically followed by a past participle because "j’ai" is the auxiliary verb for the passé composé: "Tu sais ce que j'ai fait/décidé/découvert… ?" It can be a genuine question or a rhetorical way to grab someone’s attention.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que j'ai découvert ?
native_language_example: You know what I discovered?

tu sais ce que j'ai fait

target_language_multi_word_term: tu sais ce que j'ai fait
meaning: "Do you know what I did?" / "You know what I did?"
additional_notes: Used to introduce a story or reveal something you did. Often said as a rhetorical question to build suspense or to emphasize a point (sometimes with a reproachful tone, e.g., reminding someone of what you did for them). In casual speech it’s common without inversion: "Tu sais…?"
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que j'ai fait hier soir ? J'ai appelé le restaurant pour réserver.
native_language_example: Do you know what I did last night? I called the restaurant to book a table.

meaning: "you know what I…" (often used to introduce a question or suggestion).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French to set up what you’re about to say: a question (Tu sais ce que je regarde ?), advice (Tu sais ce que je ferais à ta place ?), or what you should do (Tu sais ce que je devrais faire ?). It’s often rhetorical—more like “You know what?” than checking if the person really knows. You can also use the formal version: « vous savez ce que je… ».
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je pense ? On devrait partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You know what I think? We should leave earlier.

tu sais ce que je pense

target_language_multi_word_term: tu sais ce que je pense
additional_notes: A direct statement meaning the other person already knows your opinion. Often used to introduce or emphasize an opinion, and it can sound a bit confrontational depending on tone. You’ll often hear it followed by **de + [person/thing]** (“about”): *Tu sais ce que je pense de lui/d’elle/de ça.* It can also be used as a rhetorical question: *Tu sais ce que je pense ?*
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je pense : ce n’est pas une bonne idée.
native_language_example: You know what I think: it’s not a good idea.

tu sais ce que je veux

target_language_multi_word_term: tu sais ce que je veux
additional_notes: Often used as a lead-in to emphasize a desire or to set up a question (sometimes rhetorical): "Tu sais ce que je veux ?" It can sound insistent or a bit confrontational depending on tone, like reminding someone they already know.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je veux : qu’on se parle franchement.
native_language_example: You know what I want: for us to speak honestly.

meaning: "Do you know what you…?" (often: "Do you realize what you…?")
additional_notes: Used with "tu" (informal ‘you’) to start a question about the other person’s actions/words/plans: "Tu sais ce que tu fais/dis/vas faire…?" Very often it’s rhetorical and expresses surprise, annoyance, or a warning (similar to “Do you realize what you just said/did?”).
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que tu viens de promettre ?
native_language_example: Do you realize what you just promised?

meaning: “Do you know what that…?” / “Do you realize what that…?”
additional_notes: Used in speech to introduce a question about the meaning, cost, effect, or consequences of something: « Tu sais ce que ça coûte / implique / représente / veut dire ? ». Often used rhetorically to emphasize a point (similar to “Do you realize…?”), not just to ask for information.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que ça change si on part plus tôt ?
native_language_example: Do you know what it changes (what difference it makes) if we leave earlier?

tu sais ce que ça veut dire

target_language_multi_word_term: tu sais ce que ça veut dire
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows the meaning of a word, expression, sign, or situation. Often said as a check for understanding; can also be rhetorical (implying “this has a meaning/implication”). You’ll also see it as a polite question: « Est-ce que tu sais ce que ça veut dire ? » (same meaning).
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que ça veut dire, « à bientôt » ?
native_language_example: Do you know what “à bientôt” means?

additional_notes: Conversational lead-in before a question, suggestion, or remark, often rhetorical: "Tu sais ce qui est le plus... ?" It uses "tu" (informal); the formal version is "vous savez ce qui". Often followed by a verb: "tu sais ce qui m’énerve ?"
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qui serait génial ? On partirait plus tôt.
native_language_example: You know what would be great? We’d leave earlier.

meaning: "you know what is…" / "you know what…" (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French as a lead-in, usually followed by an adjective or noun phrase: "Tu sais ce qui est drôle/important/difficile ?" It uses "tu" so it’s informal (with "vous": "Vous savez ce qui est…"). Often used to set up a point or ask a rhetorical question.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qui est vraiment important ? Prendre du temps pour toi.
native_language_example: You know what’s really important? Taking time for yourself.

meaning: "do you know how/what…?" or "you know what … is/are like."
additional_notes: Literally “you know how.” Used either (1) as a question asking for information (“Do you know how/what…?”), often followed by a full clause (e.g., *Tu sais comment il s’appelle ?*), or (2) to refer to shared experience: “You know what they’re like” (*Tu sais comment ils sont*). In the second use, *comment* is closer to “what … are like” than to “how.”
target_language_example: Tu sais comment on dit ça en français ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to say that in French?

meaning: “you know what (I mean / I’m talking about).”
additional_notes: Used in conversation to refer to something understood from context. It often introduces an explanation or a (sometimes slightly teasing) rhetorical question: “Tu sais de quoi j’ai envie ?” = “Guess what I feel like / You know what I’m craving?” You’ll also hear it continued with “je veux parler” (“I want to talk about”).
target_language_example: Tu sais de quoi je parle : de ce problème au travail.
native_language_example: You know what I’m talking about: that problem at work.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether someone knows the location of a person/thing, or where someone is going. Often followed by a clause (où + subject + verb): « Tu sais où il est ? » You can also use it on its own (« Tu sais où ? ») meaning “Do you know where?” in context. Informal alternative: « Tu sais où c’est ? » = “Do you know where it is?”
target_language_example: Tu sais où on peut se garer ?
native_language_example: Do you know where we can park?

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of something they already know, or to emphasize what you’re about to say. It’s very common in conversation and is followed by a full clause (subject + verb): “Tu sais que + …”.
target_language_example: Tu sais que j’ai cours demain matin.
native_language_example: You know that I have class tomorrow morning.

meaning: “you know that it’s …” (often used to introduce or emphasize an explanation).
additional_notes: Mostly used in spoken, informal conversation to remind someone of something before adding information. It’s typically followed by an adjective, a noun phrase, or a full clause: "tu sais que c'est important", "tu sais que c'est mon frère", etc. Note the different structure "tu sais ce que c'est" (“you know what it is”), which has a different meaning.
target_language_example: Tu sais que c'est important, alors fais attention.
native_language_example: You know it’s important, so be careful.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of a fact about you, or to emphasize what you’re about to say. Very common in conversation; it can sound a bit insistent depending on tone. Often followed by a verb phrase (e.g., "tu sais que je cherche...", "tu sais que je dis...").
target_language_example: Tu sais que je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: You know that I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: A direct, personal sentence using **tu** (informal “you”), said to a friend/partner/close family member. Often used to reassure someone, remind them of your feelings, or introduce emphasis (sometimes followed by **pas vrai ?** = “right?”).
target_language_example: Tu sais que je t'aime, même quand on se dispute.
native_language_example: You know I love you, even when we argue.

additional_notes: Used to say (or suspect) someone has information about a topic, often implying there may be a secret or important detail. Very common in questions with a topic marker: « Tu sais quelque chose sur… ? / à propos de… ? / là-dessus ? »
target_language_example: Tu sais quelque chose sur cette histoire ?
native_language_example: Do you know anything about this story?

meaning: "you know who" (referring to a person you both know, often without naming them).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to hint at someone without saying their name (for secrecy, suspense, or because it’s obvious). It can introduce an indirect question ("Tu sais qui j’ai vu ?" = "Do you know who I saw?") or be said alone to mean "you-know-who."
target_language_example: Je l’ai croisé hier… tu sais qui.
native_language_example: I ran into him yesterday… you-know-who.

meaning: “you know what?” (to introduce something you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to grab attention or build suspense before giving news, a surprise, an opinion, or a decision (“You know what? I’m leaving.”). It can also be a real question meaning “What do you know about…?” especially with extra context: “Tu sais quoi sur lui ?” = “What do you know about him?” Often followed by a pause or comma: “Tu sais quoi, maman ?”
target_language_example: Tu sais quoi ? J’ai décidé d’apprendre le français.
native_language_example: You know what? I decided to learn French.

additional_notes: Used to say how someone appears based on what you observe (their behavior, tone, or expression). Often followed by an infinitive (tu sembles comprendre) or an adjective (tu sembles surpris). Less direct than stating something as a fact; it expresses an impression.
target_language_example: Tu sembles fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You seem tired today.

additional_notes: Often used after a past verb (e.g., « je savais que… ») to express the future from a past point of view: « Je savais que tu serais ici » = “I knew you’d be here.” It can also be used for hypothetical situations: « Si tu venais, tu serais content » = “If you came, you’d be happy.”
target_language_example: Je pensais que tu serais en retard.
native_language_example: I thought you’d be late.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone will be like or where they will be in the future, often to reassure or make a promise (Tu seras bien.) or in time clauses with quand/lorsque (“when”), e.g., quand tu seras grand (“when you’re grown up”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tu seras prêt demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’ll be ready tomorrow.

additional_notes: “Tu sois” is the subjunctive present of “être” with “tu.” It usually appears after “que” in sentences that express necessity, doubt, emotion, or purpose (e.g., « Il faut que tu sois… », « pour que tu sois… »). You also see it in set patterns like « où que tu sois » = “wherever you are / may be.”
target_language_example: Je veux que tu sois prêt à huit heures.
native_language_example: I want you to be ready at eight o’clock.

meaning: "your name is" / "you're called" (used to ask someone's name).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb s'appeler (“to be called”). It’s the informal singular “you” (tu). Often used in questions like « Tu t'appelles comment ? » or « Comment tu t'appelles ? ». A more formal/polite version is « Vous vous appelez comment ? » / « Comment vous vous appelez ? ». You can answer with « Je m'appelle … ».
target_language_example: Salut ! Tu t'appelles comment ?
native_language_example: Hi! What's your name?

meaning: "you ... about it / of it" (a pronoun combo used before a verb).
additional_notes:
This is not a fixed expression by itself: it’s the subject pronoun "tu" + the reflexive pronoun "te" (contracted to "t'" before a vowel) + the pronoun "en". "En" often replaces something introduced by "de" ("about it", "of it", "some"), and the exact meaning depends on the verb that follows:
- "Tu t’en occupes" = you take care of it.
- "Tu t’en rends compte" = you realize it / you’re aware of it.
- "Tu t’en souviens" = you remember it.
Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Tu t'en rends compte ?
native_language_example: Do you realize it?

meaning: "you" + "have" (passé composé) for reflexive verbs; used to say what "you" did (to yourself).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of reflexive verbs: "tu" + "te" → "t'" + "es" (from "être"). It’s followed by a past participle: "Tu t'es levé(e)", "Tu t'es lavé(e)". With reflexive verbs, French uses "être" as the helping verb, and the past participle often agrees with the person (levé / levée) depending on gender and sentence structure.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu t'es arrêté si vite ?
native_language_example: Why did you stop so quickly?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of **se faire** with **tu**. It’s commonly used in two patterns: (1) **tu t’es fait + infinitive** = “you had/got something done” (often something you arranged): *Tu t’es fait couper les cheveux ?* (“Did you get your hair cut?”). (2) **tu t’es fait + past participle / expression** = “you got …” in a passive sense, often something unpleasant or accidental: *tu t’es fait sortir* (“you got kicked out”), *tu t’es fait prendre* (“you got caught”), *tu t’es fait avoir* (“you got tricked”). It can also mean “you made” in the sense of forming relationships: *Tu t’es fait des amis ?* (“Did you make friends?”).
target_language_example: Tu t'es fait voler ton vélo ?
native_language_example: Did your bike get stolen?

additional_notes: Used with the informal singular subject tu before a reflexive or pronominal verb. It often corresponds to English 'you' or 'yourself,' but English does not always translate it literally: tu te dépêches ? = 'are you hurrying?'. Before a vowel or silent h, te becomes t' (for example, tu t'appelles).
target_language_example: Tu te sens bien aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Do you feel well today?

meaning: "you think you are…" / "who do you think you are…?"
additional_notes: From the verb *se croire* (“to think of oneself as / to imagine oneself”). It’s often used as a reproach or challenge, especially in questions: *Tu te crois où ?* (“Where do you think you are?”), *Tu te crois malin ?* (“You think you’re smart?”). It’s typically followed by an adjective (*malin*), a place (*au cinéma*, *sur Facebook*), or a comparison (*au-dessus de tout*, *mieux que moi*).
target_language_example: Tu te crois chez toi ici ?
native_language_example: Do you think you’re at home here?

meaning: 'you get' / 'you make yourself' (something happens to you, often + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with **se faire + infinitive** to show something is done to you or happens to you: **tu te fais tuer** = “you get yourself killed/you get killed.” It can also be used with some nouns to describe what you “put yourself through,” e.g. **tu te fais (trop) de soucis** = “you worry (too much).”
target_language_example: Tu te fais couper les cheveux demain ?
native_language_example: Are you getting your hair cut tomorrow?

tu te fous de ma gueule

target_language_multi_word_term: tu te fous de ma gueule
meaning: "Are you kidding me?" / "Are you messing with me?" / "Are you making fun of me?" (very rude).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used when you feel someone is mocking you, lying to you, or treating you like an idiot. Often said angrily as a confrontation (similar tone to “Are you fucking kidding me?”). "se foutre de" = to mess with / make fun of; "gueule" is a crude word for “mouth/face,” so the whole expression is aggressive.
target_language_example: Tu te fous de ma gueule ? Tu savais très bien que c’était interdit.
native_language_example: Are you kidding me? You knew perfectly well that it was forbidden.

meaning: “Are you kidding?” / “You’re making fun of me.”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "se moquer de" = "to make fun of" / "to mock". In questions ("Tu te moques de moi ?"), it often means “Are you kidding (me)?” said in disbelief or annoyance. It can also be literal: someone is laughing at you, possibly "dans mon dos" (“behind my back”).
target_language_example: Tu te moques de moi ? Je viens de te le dire !
native_language_example: Are you kidding me? I just told you!

meaning: "Who do you think you are?" / "You think you're…?" (accusing someone of acting like they are someone else).
additional_notes: Built on "se prendre pour + noun" = to take yourself for / to think you are (often said sarcastically or angrily). Used to challenge someone who is acting bossy, important, tough, heroic, etc.: "Tu te prends pour ma mère ?" = "Who do you think you are, my mother?"
target_language_example: Tu te prends pour le chef ou quoi ?
native_language_example: Who do you think you are, the boss or what?

additional_notes: Spoken, informal/neutral way to ask someone if they remember. Often used as a tag question at the end of a sentence to remind someone: « …, tu te rappelles ? ». You can follow it with a direct object (« Tu te rappelles ce que je t’ai dit ? ») or with « de » + person/thing (« Tu te rappelles de lui / de moi / de son nom ? »).
target_language_example: Tu te rappelles où on s’est rencontrés ?
native_language_example: Do you remember where we met?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state that someone remembers something. It comes from the verb "se rappeler" (to remember). It’s commonly followed by "de" + a noun ("Tu te rappelles de son nom ?") or "de ce que" + a clause ("Tu te rappelles de ce que nous avons dit ?"). In everyday French, you may also hear "Tu te rappelles …" without "de".
target_language_example: Tu te rappelles de notre première rencontre ?
native_language_example: Do you remember our first meeting?

additional_notes: Very common spoken expression used to make someone notice the importance of something, often with surprise or disbelief. It’s frequently rhetorical (you don’t necessarily expect an answer). More formal: « Vous vous rendez compte ? »
target_language_example: Tu te rends compte ? On a oublié les billets à la maison !
native_language_example: Can you believe it? We forgot the tickets at home!

additional_notes: From the verb **se sentir** (“to feel”), used with reflexive pronouns: *je me sens, tu te sens, il/elle se sent*, etc. It’s commonly followed by an adjective (*tu te sens triste* = “you feel sad”) or an expression like *mieux* (“better”). In questions it can mean “Do you feel…?” or “Are you feeling up to it?” (*Tu te sens d’attaque ?*).
target_language_example: Tu te sens mieux aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Do you feel better today?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "se souvenir de" (to remember). It can be a statement ("Tu te souviens de ta promesse." = You remember your promise.) or a question ("Tu te souviens ?" = Do you remember?). With what you remember, it’s usually followed by "de" + noun ("Tu te souviens de ta promesse ?"), "de" + pronoun ("Tu te souviens de quoi ?"), or sometimes a full clause without "de" ("Tu te souviens combien tu as payé ?").
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de son prénom ?
native_language_example: Do you remember his first name?

meaning: “do you remember … ?” / “you remember …” (talking to one person).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se souvenir de** (“to remember”). **Tu** addresses one person informally. It’s usually followed by a noun (**Tu te souviens de nous ?**) or **de + ce que/quoi** (**Tu te souviens de ce que tu as fait ?**). In speech, you may hear **t’as** (= **tu as**) in the past: **Tu te souviens de ce que t’as fait ?**
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de la première fois qu’on s’est rencontrés ?
native_language_example: Do you remember the first time we met?

tu te souviens de ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: tu te souviens de ce que
additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern **se souvenir de** (“to remember”). **Tu** is the informal “you” (speaking to one person you know). **Ce que** introduces “what/that which” when it’s the object: *Tu te souviens de ce que j’ai dit ?* = “Do you remember what I said?” (often followed by a verb phrase).
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de ce que je t’ai dit hier ?
native_language_example: Do you remember what I told you yesterday?

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase **se souvenir de** (“to remember”). It’s built like: **Tu te souviens de + noun**. When the noun has an article/possessive, French keeps **de**: **Tu te souviens de notre ami ?** (“Do you remember our friend?”). **Tu** is used with friends/family (informal/familiar); with someone you don’t know well, you’d say **Vous vous souvenez de notre … ?**. **Notre** stays the same for masculine and feminine singular nouns (ami, lune), and becomes **nos** for plural.
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de notre professeur de français ?
native_language_example: Do you remember our French teacher?

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **se tromper** (“to be mistaken”). It’s commonly used to correct someone: **Tu te trompes.** = “You’re mistaken.” Note: **tromper** (without *se*) usually means “to deceive” or “to cheat on (someone),” so the meaning changes with the reflexive pronoun.
target_language_example: Tu te trompes : le rendez-vous est demain, pas aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You’re mistaken: the appointment is tomorrow, not today.

additional_notes: Uses the informal subject pronoun tu (to one person you’re on familiar terms with). In the present tense, it can describe a habit (“you work [in general]”) or something happening now (“you’re working [right now]”), depending on context. Often followed by details like avec (“with”), trop (“too much”), le soir (“in the evening”), etc.
target_language_example: Tu travailles aujourd’hui ou tu es en congé ?
native_language_example: Are you working today, or are you off?

tu un inconvénient à ce que je

target_language_multi_word_term: tu un inconvénient à ce que je…
meaning: (As written) not grammatical; intended meaning: “Do you mind if I…?”
additional_notes: As written, « tu un inconvénient à ce que je… » is missing the verb « avoir ». The correct phrasing is « Tu as un inconvénient à ce que je + (subjunctive)… ? » e.g., « Tu as un inconvénient à ce que je parte ? » (subjunctive: je parte). In everyday speech, people often use « Ça te dérange si je… ? ».
target_language_example: « tu un inconvénient à ce que je » n’est pas correct : on dit « Tu as un inconvénient à ce que je ferme la fenêtre ? »
native_language_example: “tu un inconvénient à ce que je” isn’t correct: you say “Do you mind if I close the window?”

additional_notes: Uses tu, the singular informal 'you'. On its own, tu vas can mean 'you are going'; followed by an infinitive, it commonly forms the near future: 'you're going to ...'.
target_language_example: Tu vas venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Are you going to come with us?

additional_notes: Uses the near-future form (aller + infinitive): "tu vas" + "avoir". Often introduces a prediction or warning about what will happen soon (e.g., "Tu vas avoir des ennuis" = "You’re going to have trouble").
target_language_example: Tu vas avoir froid sans ton manteau.
native_language_example: You’re going to be cold without your coat.

meaning: “you’re going to have to” (you will need to; obligation).
additional_notes: Uses the near future: tu vas + infinitive. Here the infinitive is devoir (“to have to”), which is followed by another verb in the infinitive: tu vas devoir + VERB. It’s a common way to tell someone they’ll be required to do something soon or inevitably.
target_language_example: Tu vas devoir partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You’re going to have to leave now.

meaning: "you’re going to do" / "what are you going to do" (near future).
additional_notes: Formed with the near-future tense: aller (tu vas) + infinitive (faire). Used to talk about what someone is going to do soon, or to ask about their plans: « Tu vas faire quoi ? » = “What are you going to do?” Can take an object: « tu vas faire un prêt » (“you’re going to take out a loan”). Often appears in questions with « qu’est-ce que… » or informally with « quoi ».
target_language_example: Tu vas faire quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tonight?

meaning: “What are you going to do?” / “What will you do?”
additional_notes: Very common spoken/colloquial word order (placing the question word at the end). In more formal French you’d usually say: « Qu’est-ce que tu vas faire ? ». Often followed by details like « avec ça ? » (with that) or « maintenant ? » (now).
target_language_example: Tu vas faire quoi ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do this weekend?

meaning: “you’re going to … it/him” (near future with the direct object pronoun *le*).
additional_notes: Used with *aller* + infinitive (the “near future”): *tu vas le + verbe* = “you’re going to + verb + it/him.” *Le* replaces a masculine singular direct object (a thing, an idea, or a man/boy). Common in threats: *Tu vas le regretter !* (“You’ll regret it!”), *Tu vas le payer !* (“You’ll pay for it!”). If the object is feminine, use *la*; plural: *les*.
target_language_example: Tu vas le faire maintenant ?
native_language_example: Are you going to do it now?

meaning: “you’re going to … me” / “you’re going to … to me” (near future).
additional_notes: Used with the near-future tense: **tu vas** + infinitive. **me** is the object pronoun (“me/to me”) and usually goes right before the infinitive: *Tu vas me faire mal* (“You’re going to hurt me”). Often used as a warning about what someone is about to do.
target_language_example: Attention, tu vas me faire tomber !
native_language_example: Careful, you’re going to make me fall!

meaning: "Aren’t you going to…?" / "You’re not going to…?" (informal).
additional_notes: Colloquial way to form a negative question by dropping "ne" from "tu ne vas pas…". Often used to show surprise, doubt, or to prompt someone to do something: "Tu vas pas rester ici ?" = "You’re not going to stay here, are you?" It’s followed by an infinitive verb (prendre, rester, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu vas pas me dire que tu as oublié !
native_language_example: Don’t tell me you forgot!

meaning: "you’re going to" (followed by a reflexive verb: "you’re going to [do something to yourself]").
additional_notes: This is the near future: **aller (tu vas)** + infinitive. The **te** is a reflexive pronoun used with reflexive verbs (e.g., *te détendre, te taire, te rétablir, te débarrasser de…*). In speech, it can sound like a prediction (*tu vas te rétablir* = “you’ll recover”) or a strong warning/order depending on tone (*tu vas te taire ?*).
target_language_example: Tu vas te souvenir de mon nom.
native_language_example: You’re going to remember my name.

meaning: "you’ll see" / "wait and see"; or "are you going to see (someone)?"
additional_notes: Literally "you’re going to see" (aller + infinitive), often used to mean “you’ll see” as a promise, reassurance, warning, or to build suspense: « Attends, tu vas voir. » It can also be a real question about visiting/meeting someone when followed by a person: « Tu vas voir tonton Jay ? » (= “Are you going to see/visit Uncle Jay?”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu vas voir, ça va bien se passer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’ll see, it’ll go well.

additional_notes: Near-future form: aller (tu vas) + infinitive (être). Used to say a future state is expected or about to happen (prediction, announcement, etc.). Often followed by an adjective (Tu vas être content.) or a noun without an article for roles/status (Tu vas être papa. = You’re going to be a dad.).
target_language_example: Tu vas être fatigué demain.
native_language_example: You’re going to be tired tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone that, if they don’t hurry/change something, they will arrive late. Very common with places/events: « en retard au boulot/en cours » (late for work/class) and « en retard pour l’école/pour ta partie » (late for school/your game/match).
target_language_example: Si tu ne pars pas maintenant, tu vas être en retard.
native_language_example: If you don’t leave now, you’re going to be late.

meaning: "you go/you’re going"; often "you’re going to" (near future).
additional_notes: From the verb *aller* (to go), 2nd person singular: *tu vas*. Used for movement (*Tu vas dans le Maryland ?* = Are you going to Maryland?) and very often to form the near future: *Tu vas + infinitive* (e.g., *Tu vas faire quoi ?* = What are you going to do?). In casual speech, *Tu vas quoi ?* is an abrupt reaction meaning “What do you mean?” / “What are you talking about?”
target_language_example: Tu vas faire quoi ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do this weekend?

additional_notes: Literally 'you go well,' but used to ask or state how someone is doing. Most often a question: "Tu vas bien ?" (neutral, common). With emphasis (e.g., "Mais tu vas bien ?") it can also mean "Are you okay?!" or "What’s wrong with you?" depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Après l'accident, tu vas bien ?
native_language_example: After the accident, are you okay?

additional_notes: Common in spoken French with normal word order (subject + verb + question word at the end). More neutral/formal options are "Tu vas où ?" with a polite tone, or "Où vas-tu ?" (more formal/literary). Often used when someone is leaving or heading somewhere, sometimes with surprise or annoyance depending on tone.
target_language_example: Hé, tu vas où comme ça ?
native_language_example: Hey, where are you going like that?

additional_notes: Literally the future of "voir" with "tu". Used both for simple future meaning (you will see/notice something) and as a set phrase meaning “you’ll see” (= wait and you’ll find out / it will become clear).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu verras, tout ira bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’ll see, everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular subject tu, so it is for one person you know well. In everyday French, it is often used as a question without inversion: Tu veux...? = Do you want...? It also appears in expressions like tu veux dire...? meaning do you mean...?
target_language_example: Tu veux un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee?

meaning: “do you want to go” / “you want to go.”
additional_notes: Literally “you want to go.” Used to ask someone if they want to go somewhere or go do an activity. Often followed by an infinitive (aller manger, aller nager, aller voir un film) or a place with à (aller à la plage).
target_language_example: Tu veux aller au café avec moi ?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the café with me?

additional_notes: Literally “you want (to)?” but used to soften a request, often placed at the end like a tag question: « …, tu veux bien ? ». Can also start a request: « Tu veux bien + infinitive… ? ». Tone depends on context: it can sound friendly, insistent, or even irritated (e.g., « Tu veux bien te taire ? »).
target_language_example: Tu veux bien m’aider deux minutes ?
native_language_example: Could you help me for two minutes?

meaning: "you mean" / "do you mean …?" (asking or clarifying meaning).
additional_notes: Used to check you understood correctly, to clarify what someone intended, or to introduce what you think the other person is saying: « Tu veux dire que… ? » = “You mean that…?” In a statement, it can also mean “I know what you mean”: « Je vois ce que tu veux dire. »
target_language_example: Tu veux dire qu’on part à huit heures ?
native_language_example: You mean we’re leaving at eight o’clock?

meaning: "Do you want some…?" (asking if someone wants a food/drink item).
additional_notes: Used in casual conversation with "tu". "Du" is the partitive article (de + le) used with masculine singular or uncountable nouns (du pain, du fromage). In a more formal/polite situation, use "vous": « Vous voulez du… ? ». With feminine nouns it becomes « tu veux de la… ? », and with plural it becomes « tu veux des… ? ».
target_language_example: Tu veux du café ?
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee?

meaning: "do you want to do" / "you want to do".
additional_notes: Common in questions to ask what someone wants to do: « Qu’est-ce que tu veux faire ? » or « Tu veux faire quoi ? ». Uses informal « tu » (to one person you’re on familiar terms with). « faire » is very flexible: it can mean to do, to make, or to have/play (e.g., « faire un bonhomme de neige » = make a snowman; « faire une partie de billard » = play a game of pool).
target_language_example: Tu veux faire un tour avec moi ?
native_language_example: Do you want to go for a walk with me?

meaning: “do you want to … me?” / “would you like to … for me?”
additional_notes: Used to start a question with vouloir (to want) + an infinitive verb: **Tu veux me + [infinitive]?** The **me** is an object pronoun meaning “to me / me,” and it comes **before** the infinitive: *Tu veux me parler ?* (“Do you want to talk to me?”), *Tu veux me raconter… ?* (“Do you want to tell me…?”).
target_language_example: Tu veux me montrer comment ça marche ?
native_language_example: Do you want to show me how it works?

meaning: “Do you mean…?” / “Are you telling me…?” (literally: “you want to tell me”).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone means or to prompt them to explain (often before a clause: « tu veux me dire + que… / ce que… / pourquoi… »). Depending on tone, it can sound neutral (“what do you mean?”) or surprised/skeptical (“are you telling me…?”).
target_language_example: Tu veux me dire que tu n'as jamais été à Paris ?
native_language_example: Are you telling me you've never been to Paris?

additional_notes: Spoken shortcut of **tu ne veux pas** (the **ne** is dropped). Often used to make a suggestion or invitation in a casual way: **Tu veux pas + infinitive ?** It can also mean “you don’t want to…” in statements.
target_language_example: Tu veux pas venir avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Why don’t you come with us tonight?

meaning: “Do you want us to…?” / “Do you want to… (together)?”
additional_notes: Used to propose or suggest doing something together. Built from “tu veux” (you want) + “qu’on” (“that we”). The verb that follows is typically in the subjunctive: “tu veux qu’on aille… ?”, “tu veux qu’on prenne… ?”, “tu veux qu’on soit… ?”. In everyday speech, “ne” is often dropped in negatives (e.g., “tu veux qu’on s’en aille ?”).
target_language_example: Tu veux qu'on aille chez moi ?
native_language_example: Do you want us to go to my place?

meaning: "Do you want me to…?" / "Do you want (someone/something) to…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask what the other person wants to happen, usually followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., « tu veux que je dise… », « tu veux que je fasse… »). It can be a real question or a rhetorical one to criticize an idea: « Tu veux que la folie gagne le pays ? » = “You want madness to take over the country?”
target_language_example: Tu veux que je t’aide à porter ça ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you carry that?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they want you to do something. After "vouloir que", French normally uses the subjunctive: "Tu veux que je conduise ?" (not *"je conduis"). More formal: "Vous voulez que je… ?"
target_language_example: Tu veux que je t’aide avec tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with your homework?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants you to do. It uses the pattern **vouloir que + subjunctive**: *Tu veux que je fasse…* (literally “you want that I do…”). Often followed by a specific task: *Tu veux que je fasse quoi ?* / *Tu veux que je fasse ça maintenant ?*
target_language_example: Tu veux que je fasse la vaisselle ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to do the dishes tonight?

meaning: "do you want me to (for you / to you) …?"
additional_notes: Used to offer or propose doing something, or to check what the other person wants. Pattern: « Tu veux que je te + verbe (subjonctif) … ? » (e.g., je te laisse, je te lise, je te montre). « te » is an indirect/direct object pronoun meaning “to you” or “you,” depending on the verb. Often comes as a question; without « est-ce que », it can sound more direct.
target_language_example: Tu veux que je te montre où c'est ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to show you where it is?

tu veux que je te dise

target_language_multi_word_term: tu veux que je te dise
meaning: "Do you want me to tell you…?" (often: “What do you expect me to say?”)
additional_notes: Literally “you want that I tell you.” Used to introduce what you’re about to say (Tu veux que je te dise un truc ?), or—especially with Qu’est-ce que…?—to show you don’t know what to answer / you’re frustrated or resigned (Qu’est-ce que tu veux que je te dise ? = “What do you want me to say?”). In speech you may hear the shorter form without « que »: « Qu’est-ce tu veux… ».
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu veux que je te dise ? Je n’y peux rien.
native_language_example: What do you want me to say? I can’t do anything about it.

additional_notes: Informal expression used to show disbelief, annoyance, or sarcasm at what someone just said or did. Literally it means “you want to laugh,” but in real use it’s like saying someone’s claim is ridiculous. Often said with a rising intonation as a question: « Tu veux rire ? »
target_language_example: —Je vais finir ce projet en une heure. —Tu veux rire ?
native_language_example: “I’m going to finish this project in an hour.” “Are you kidding?”

meaning: "do you want to know" / "you want to know".
additional_notes: Common way to introduce an explanation or reveal information, often leading into a question: « Tu veux savoir pourquoi ? » (= “Do you want to know why?”). Uses informal « tu » (said to one person you’re on familiar terms with). You can follow it with a question word (pourquoi, comment) or with « ce que… » (“what…”).
target_language_example: Tu veux savoir la vérité ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know the truth?

meaning: “Do you want to…?” (informal), introducing a verb that uses “te” (you/yourself).
additional_notes: Used with the informal subject pronoun “tu” to ask (or challenge) someone: “Tu veux te + infinitive… ?” The “te” is an object/reflexive pronoun needed by certain verbs (e.g., se battre = to fight, se lever = to get up, se joindre à = to join, se fondre = to blend in). In English, you usually just say “Do you want to + verb…?” without translating “te” as “yourself.”
target_language_example: Tu veux te reposer un peu ?
native_language_example: Do you want to rest a bit?

meaning: “Do you want a…?” (asking if someone wants a masculine noun item).
additional_notes: Common informal question to offer someone something. Used with a masculine singular noun: tu veux un beignet ? For a feminine noun, use “tu veux une… ?”. In more polite/formal situations, use “Vous voulez… ?”.
target_language_example: Tu veux un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee?

meaning: “Do you want a…?” (to a friend/one person).
additional_notes: Used to offer something singular and feminine (une + a feminine noun): Tu veux une salade ? / une tisane ? In more formal or polite situations, use « Vous voulez une… ? ».
target_language_example: Tu veux une bière ?
native_language_example: Do you want a beer?

additional_notes: Used to offer or suggest showing something to someone. Often followed by a noun (“tu veux voir ma collection… ?”) or “un truc + adjective” (“tu veux voir un truc cool ?”). It’s conversational and direct; you can add “Est-ce que” for a more neutral tone (“Est-ce que tu veux voir… ?”).
target_language_example: Tu veux voir la photo que j’ai prise ?
native_language_example: Do you want to see the photo I took?

meaning: “do you really want (to)…?” / “do you really mean it?”
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, doubt, or to double-check what the other person wants. It’s often followed by an infinitive (tu veux vraiment y aller ?) or by “que” + subjunctive (tu veux vraiment que je parte ?). Tone depends on context: it can be neutral (just confirming) or slightly challenging (are you sure?).
target_language_example: Tu veux vraiment commander ça ?
native_language_example: Do you really want to order that?

meaning: "Do you want to go (there)?" / "You want to go (there)."
additional_notes: Literally “you want to go there.” Used to ask or state someone’s desire to go somewhere. "y" replaces a previously mentioned place ("there"), and "tu" is informal "you" (singular), used with friends, family, kids, etc. For a more formal/polite version, use "vous voulez y aller ?"
target_language_example: Tu veux y aller ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want to go there tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (one person you address as tu) if they want to become or be something. It’s followed by a noun or adjective (e.g., chef, amie) or by a past participle/adjective like payé(e) (“paid”). For formal or plural, use vous voulez être.
target_language_example: Tu veux être médecin plus tard ?
native_language_example: Do you want to be a doctor later?

additional_notes: From venir. Often used to ask if someone is coming along, joining an activity, or following someone. In a statement, it can mean 'you’re coming' or 'you come.' If it is followed by de + infinitive, it means 'you have just ...' (for example, tu viens de dire = 'you just said').
target_language_example: Tu viens avec nous au cinéma ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us to the movies?

meaning: "Are you coming with me?" / "You’re coming with me."
additional_notes: Literally “you come with me.” Often used either as a question (with rising intonation) to invite someone to come along, or as a firm statement/command meaning “You’re coming with me,” especially in contexts like “Ça suffit, tu viens avec moi.” You can soften it with “Tu veux venir avec moi ?” or “Viens avec moi.”
target_language_example: Tu viens avec moi au café ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with me to the café?

additional_notes: Can be literal (seeing something with your eyes) or used to explain something or check that the other person understands, like "you see" or "see?". Because it uses tu, it is for one person you speak to informally.
target_language_example: Tu vois ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: Do you see what I mean?

meaning: "you see what…" / "you know what…" (to point something out or check understanding).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to introduce an explanation, highlight a consequence, or make sure the other person understands (often like English “you see…/you know…”). It’s usually followed by a clause: « tu vois ce que je veux dire ? » = “you know what I mean?”
target_language_example: Tu vois ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: You know what I mean?

meaning: "you see what I…" (often: "you know what I mean").
additional_notes: Conversational phrase used to check that someone understands. It’s usually followed by a verb, especially: « tu vois ce que je veux dire ? » (“you know what I mean?”). You can also hear « Vous voyez ce que je… » (more formal) or « tu vois ce que j’veux dire ? » (very spoken).
target_language_example: Tu vois ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: You know what I mean?

tu vois ce que je veux dire

target_language_multi_word_term: tu vois ce que je veux dire
additional_notes: Used to check that the other person understands what you’re saying, often at the end of a sentence. Literally “you see what I want to say,” but it’s the common French way to say “you know what I mean.” You can add a tag like “non ?” to seek agreement.
target_language_example: Il faut partir tôt pour éviter les embouteillages, tu vois ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: We need to leave early to avoid traffic, you know what I mean?

meaning: 'you will want' (future tense), often meaning 'whenever you want' / 'as much/long as you want' depending on context.
additional_notes: Future of "vouloir" (to want): "tu voudras" = "you will want". In everyday French it’s very common in set phrases like "quand tu voudras" (whenever you want), "où tu voudras" (wherever you want), "tant que tu voudras" (as long as you want), "autant que tu voudras" (as much as you want), and "comme tu voudras" (as you like / whatever you prefer).
target_language_example: On peut partir quand tu voudras.
native_language_example: We can leave whenever you want.

additional_notes: “Tu” is the informal singular “you” (used with friends, family, kids). “Voulait” is the imperfect past tense of “vouloir,” often used for (1) an ongoing or repeated desire in the past (“you wanted to…”) or (2) a softer, polite-sounding question like “Did you want something?” In questions it can imply “Were you trying to…?” or “Were you planning to…?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu voulais un café ou un thé ?
native_language_example: Did you want a coffee or a tea?

meaning: “you wanted to … me / you were going to … to me”.
additional_notes: Used when addressing someone informally (tu). It’s the imperfect of vouloir (“to want”), often used to refer to an intention or request in the past (“you wanted to talk to me / tell me / show me…”). Typically followed by an infinitive (parler, dire, montrer, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu voulais me demander quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Did you want to ask me something?

additional_notes: Used to ask or confirm what someone had intended to say. The imperfect (voulais) often makes it sound a bit softer or like “you were going to tell me / you meant to tell me,” especially when returning to an earlier topic: « Alors, qu’est-ce que tu voulais me dire ? ».
target_language_example: Tu voulais me dire quelque chose d’important ?
native_language_example: Did you want to tell me something important?

meaning: “you wanted to talk to me” / “did you want to talk to me?”
additional_notes: Literally “you wanted to speak to me.” Often used to check why someone contacted you or to bring up a topic: “Tu voulais me parler de … ?” Uses the imperfect (voulais), which commonly sounds like “were you wanting to…” / “did you want to… (earlier)?” and can feel slightly softer than “tu veux.”
target_language_example: Tu voulais me parler de quoi ?
native_language_example: What did you want to talk to me about?

additional_notes: “Y” is a pronoun that usually replaces a place (“there”) or something you’re involved in. So **tu y es** can be literal (you’re there: *Tu y es en sécurité* = you’re safe there) or idiomatic to encourage/correct someone: **Tu y es presque** (“You’re almost there”), **Tu y es !** (“That’s it!/You got it!”). As a question (**Tu y es ?**), it can mean “Are you there?” or “Do you get it?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu y es presque, ne lâche pas !
native_language_example: You’re almost there—don’t give up!

meaning: (in questions with inversion) “do you … at home?” / “are you … at home?” / “when are you … home?” depending on the verb; literally “you … at home”.
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom on its own: it’s the combination of **-tu** (subject pronoun used in **inversion** to form a question: *viens-tu…?* = “are you coming…?”) + the place phrase **à la maison** (“at home / (back) home”). It most often appears with verbs like *venir, rentrer, revenir, déjeuner* etc. Note: you normally wouldn’t list **tu à la maison** as a standalone term; the core location phrase is **à la maison**.
target_language_example: Quand rentres-tu à la maison ?
native_language_example: When are you coming home?

additional_notes: Imperfect form of être with tu, used for describing a past state, condition, location, or ongoing situation. Tu is singular and informal, so this is used with one person you address as tu, not vous.
target_language_example: Tu étais très calme hier.
native_language_example: You were very calm yesterday.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time (while waiting).
additional_notes: Used when you do an activity just to keep busy, often because you’re waiting or have nothing else to do. Common patterns: « pour tuer le temps » (in order to kill time), « chercher à tuer le temps » (to try to kill time).
target_language_example: On peut prendre un café pour tuer le temps avant le train.
native_language_example: We can have a coffee to kill time before the train.

additional_notes: A noun phrase used for someone paid to murder a specific person. Often used with verbs like « engager » (to hire), « payer » (to pay), « assassiner » (to assassinate), or « tuer » (to kill): « un tueur à gages », « des tueurs à gages ».
target_language_example: La police pense qu'un tueur à gages a été engagé.
native_language_example: The police think a hitman was hired.

additional_notes: Usually said with an article: « Le téléphone a sonné. » It uses the passé composé (a + past participle « sonné ») to describe a completed past action. You can also say « Mon téléphone a sonné » (my phone rang).
target_language_example: Le téléphone a sonné pendant le dîner.
native_language_example: The phone rang during dinner.

additional_notes: Refers to a phone you carry with you (as opposed to a landline). Often shortened to « un mobile » or « un téléphone » when the context is clear. Used with either informal « tu » or formal « vous » (e.g., « As-tu… ? » vs « Avez-vous… ? »).
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon téléphone mobile à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my cell phone at home.

additional_notes: Common way to say “mobile/cell phone” in France. Often shortened to “portable” in everyday speech (e.g., Tu as ton portable ?). Used with verbs like voler (steal), sortir (take out), and être éteint/allumé (be off/on).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon téléphone portable à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my mobile phone at home.

additional_notes: Usually appears as **« Le téléphone sonna »** in stories and novels. **sonna** is the **passé simple** of **sonner** (“to ring”), mainly used in written narration; in everyday speech you’d usually say **« Le téléphone a sonné »**.
target_language_example: Le téléphone sonna au milieu de la nuit.
native_language_example: The phone rang in the middle of the night.

additional_notes: "Téléphoner" is followed by "à" + the person you’re calling (téléphoner à quelqu’un). For the thing you use, French often uses "téléphoner de" (from) or "avec" (with): "Je téléphone de mon portable." / "Je téléphone avec mon portable."
target_language_example: Je vais téléphoner à mes parents ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my parents tonight.

meaning: a private one-on-one conversation/meeting (just the two of you).
additional_notes: Used for situations where two people talk or meet alone, often privately (e.g., to discuss something personal or important). You can say “en tête-à-tête” (= one-on-one) or “un tête-à-tête” (= a one-on-one chat/meeting). It can be plural: “des tête-à-tête”.
target_language_example: Après la réunion, j’aimerais te parler en tête-à-tête.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I’d like to talk to you one-on-one.

meaning: head down; with your head lowered (often: without thinking).
additional_notes: Literally “lowered head.” Used (1) physically: looking down, often showing sadness, shame, or submission ("marcher la tête baissée"); and (2) figuratively: doing something recklessly or blindly ("foncer tête baissée" = rush in headfirst). Can also be used as a short command: "Tête baissée !" = "Keep your head down!"
target_language_example: Il s’est lancé tête baissée dans ce projet sans réfléchir.
native_language_example: He jumped into this project headfirst without thinking.

meaning: a scatterbrain; an airhead (a forgetful person).
additional_notes: An informal, often teasing (but still insulting) expression said about someone who is very absent-minded or forgets things easily. Used as an exclamation ("Tête de linotte !") or with "être/avoir" ("Tu es / Tu as une tête de linotte").
target_language_example: J’ai encore oublié mes clés : quelle tête de linotte !
native_language_example: I forgot my keys again: what a scatterbrain!

meaning: top of the list; first in line (highest priority).
additional_notes: Used mostly in the expression « être en tête de liste » to mean someone/something is ranked first or has priority (e.g., for a waiting list, candidate list, to-do list). Often implies you’ll be handled next or are the main candidate.
target_language_example: Bonne nouvelle : vous êtes en tête de liste, on vous contacte cette semaine.
native_language_example: Good news: you’re at the top of the list; we’ll contact you this week.

meaning: a stubborn person; a real mule-head (insult).
additional_notes: An informal, often mildly insulting way to say someone is very stubborn and won’t change their mind or do what they’re told. Common in exclamations ("Quelle tête de mule !", "Une vraie tête de mule !") or when speaking directly to someone ("Avance, tête de mule !"). The noun phrase is grammatically feminine ("une tête de mule"), but it can refer to a man or a woman.
target_language_example: Arrête d’insister, quelle tête de mule !
native_language_example: Stop insisting—what a stubborn mule-head!

additional_notes: Informal and insulting (sometimes said jokingly between friends, but can be rude). Used to call someone stupid or to complain about someone’s behavior: « Quel/Quelle tête de nœud ! » or « Espèce de tête de nœud ! ». Often preceded by « quelle » / « quel » or « espèce de ». Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Arrête de faire le tête de nœud et écoute-moi deux minutes.
native_language_example: Stop being an idiot and listen to me for two minutes.

meaning: one-on-one; in private (just the two of you).
