additional_notes: Often used with "en" ("en tête à tête") to mean talking/meeting privately with only two people present: "Je dois te parler en tête à tête." It can also describe a close contest or duel (sports/politics): "Le championnat a été un tête à tête."
target_language_example: On peut se voir en tête à tête demain après le cours ?
native_language_example: Can we meet one-on-one tomorrow after class?

additional_notes: Used to say something happened earlier today in the morning (often earlier than expected). It commonly comes after the verb: « Il a appelé tôt ce matin. » You can intensify it with « très »: « très tôt ce matin ». It can also be used alone as a short time answer: « — Quand ? — Tôt ce matin. »
target_language_example: J'ai reçu un message tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: I got a message early this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens early during the morning (often soon after waking up). You can make it stronger with "très" ("très tôt le matin" = "very early in the morning").
target_language_example: On se retrouve tôt le matin, vers 7 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet early in the morning, around 7 a.m.?

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen at some point in the future, even if you don’t know exactly when. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (“Tôt ou tard, …”), or after the verb/clause (“…, tôt ou tard.”).
target_language_example: Tu finiras par comprendre, tôt ou tard.
native_language_example: You’ll end up understanding, sooner or later.

additional_notes: Very common spoken contraction of « tu es ». Used with adjectives or nouns: « T’es fatigué(e) », « T’es une bête ». Mostly appears in informal writing (texts, dialogue) to reflect speech.
target_language_example: T’es prêt(e) ?
native_language_example: Are you ready?

additional_notes: A common loanword in French for a short-sleeved casual shirt. The plural is usually written "des T-shirts" (often with a hyphen). Used after clothing verbs like "porter" (to wear).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un T-shirt pour le match.
native_language_example: I bought a T-shirt for the game.

additional_notes: Used for an unplanned event, often something that causes damage or injury (e.g., a car crash or a household mishap). In French, you commonly say "avoir un accident" (to have an accident) or "un accident de voiture" (a car accident).
target_language_example: Il a eu un accident de voiture hier soir.
native_language_example: He had a car accident last night.

meaning: an accident involving (something); a (type of) accident.
additional_notes: Use **un accident de + noun** to say what kind of accident it was: **un accident de la circulation / de la route** (a traffic/road accident), **un accident de ski** (a skiing accident), **un accident de chasse** (a hunting accident), **un accident de travail** (a work accident). In English you usually say “a traffic accident” or “a skiing accident” rather than “an accident of…”.
target_language_example: Il a eu un accident de voiture sur l’autoroute.
native_language_example: He had a car accident on the highway.

meaning: a road traffic accident (a car crash).
additional_notes: Used to talk generally about an accident involving vehicles on the road. Common in news/police/insurance contexts. You can also hear/see: "accident de voiture" (car accident), and "accident de la circulation" (traffic accident, more formal).
target_language_example: Nous avons appelé les secours après un accident de la route.
native_language_example: We called emergency services after a road traffic accident.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an accident involving a car. You’ll often hear it with verbs like « avoir » (to have/be in) or « faire » (to have/cause): « avoir un accident de voiture », « faire un accident de voiture ». You can add an adjective like « grave » (serious): « un accident de voiture grave ».
target_language_example: Heureusement, personne n’a été blessé dans un accident de voiture.
native_language_example: Fortunately, nobody was hurt in a car accident.

additional_notes: Literally one male friend: un is the masculine form of 'a/an', and ami means 'friend'. Use une amie for a female friend. In many contexts, English just says 'a friend' unless the person's gender matters.
target_language_example: J'ai un ami à Paris.
native_language_example: I have a friend in Paris.

additional_notes: Used to indicate who the friend is connected to; the person comes after "de" (often with a possessive like "mon/ma/mes" or a name): "un ami de mon père", "un ami de Marie". In the plural: "des amis de ...".
target_language_example: C'est un ami de mon père.
native_language_example: He's a friend of my father.

meaning: a friend of mine (one of my friends).
additional_notes: Uses the pattern "un/une + noun + à moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux" to mean “one of my/your/his/her/our/your/their …”. It often introduces someone without specifying which one. Very close in meaning to "un de mes amis" (= one of my friends). Feminine: "une amie à moi".
target_language_example: Un ami à moi vient dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: A friend of mine is coming over for dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or length of time. With numbers, "an" often becomes plural: "deux ans" (two years). In the expression "il y a…", it means "…ago": "il y a un an" = "a year ago".
target_language_example: Je suis resté en France un an.
native_language_example: I stayed in France for a year.

meaning: an angel; (figuratively) a very kind, sweet, or patient person.
additional_notes: Used literally for an angel (religious/mythical being) or as a compliment: "Tu/T’es un ange" = “You’re an angel” (thanks for being helpful, patient, etc.). Also appears in comparisons like "dormir comme un ange" (sleep very peacefully) or "ressembler à un ange" (look like an angel).
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide, tu es un ange.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help, you’re an angel.

meaning: an animal; (figurative, often negative) a brutal or wild person.
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a literal animal. In comparisons with "comme" (e.g., "comme un animal") or with words like "enragé" (rabid), it can be figurative and negative, implying someone is acting savagely, cruelly, or without control. Pronunciation note: the final "n" of "un" links to the vowel sound in "animal" (often heard as "un-nanimal").
target_language_example: Je vivais comme un animal.
native_language_example: I lived like an animal.

additional_notes: A common way to say “camera” in French (literally “photo device”). Often used with the verb prendre: prendre des photos = to take pictures.
target_language_example: As-tu un appareil photo�a0?
native_language_example: Do you have a camera?

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for a place to live, usually one unit in a larger building. Common with verbs like trouver (to find), louer (to rent), habiter/vivre (to live), and with descriptions like de luxe (luxury) or très joli (very nice).
target_language_example: Nous cherchons un appartement près du métro.
native_language_example: We’re looking for an apartment near the метро/subway.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a telephone call in everyday French. Often used with verbs like recevoir (to receive/get a call) and attendre (to be expecting a call). You can specify who it’s for with pour: « Un appel pour le Colonel. »
target_language_example: J'attends un appel de mon médecin.
native_language_example: I'm expecting a call from my doctor.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning a tree in general. Often appears in everyday spatial phrases: contre un arbre (against a tree), derrière un arbre (behind a tree), dans un arbre (in a tree). Also used with verbs like abattre un arbre (to cut down a tree) and percuter un arbre (to hit a tree with a vehicle). In figurative/poetic contexts it can be used metaphorically (e.g., comparing someone to a tree: strong, rooted).
target_language_example: Je me suis dissimulé derrière un arbre.
native_language_example: I hid behind a tree.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for the natural phenomenon (often after rain). Plural: des arcs-en-ciel (often invariable in everyday use).
target_language_example: Après la pluie, on a vu un arc-en-ciel au-dessus de la ville.
native_language_example: After the rain, we saw a rainbow over the city.

additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun to mean one more or a different one. It changes with gender and number: une autre, d'autres, les autres. It can also stand alone as a pronoun: Tu en veux un autre ? = Do you want another one?
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un autre livre.
native_language_example: I'm going to take another book.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an alternative way of doing something or an alternative solution. Often followed by "de" + infinitive ("un autre moyen de sortir" = another way to get out) or by "par lequel" to specify the means ("un autre moyen par lequel je puisse te payer" = another way I can pay you).
target_language_example: On peut essayer un autre moyen si ça ne marche pas.
native_language_example: We can try another way if it doesn’t work.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a refill or an additional drink. Often followed by “de + drink” (un autre verre de bière / de vin). In a restaurant/bar it’s a polite request with verbs like « pouvoir »: « Puis-je / Pourrais-je avoir un autre verre ? » It can also literally mean a different physical glass, but most often it means another serving to drink.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je peux avoir un autre verre de vin, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have another glass of wine, please?

additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering a refill (one more glass). You can say it as a request (Puis-je avoir… ?) or an offer (Tu veux… ?). Also works with other drinks: un autre verre d’eau, un autre verre de bière.
target_language_example: Je prendrai un autre verre de vin, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have another glass of wine, please.

additional_notes: Most often means an aircraft you travel in: «monter dans un avion» = to board/get on a plane. It can also refer to other types of aircraft (e.g., military) and to «un avion en papier» (a paper airplane).
target_language_example: On prend un avion demain matin.
native_language_example: We’re taking a plane tomorrow morning.

meaning: a wanted notice (bulletin to help find someone).
additional_notes: Used for an official announcement—often by the police or organizations like Interpol—asking the public to help locate a person (sometimes also a missing person or suspect). You can say « émettre un avis de recherche » (issue) or « lancer un avis de recherche » (launch).
target_language_example: La police a publié un avis de recherche pour retrouver l'enfant disparu.
native_language_example: The police published a wanted notice to find the missing child.

meaning: a lawyer (also: an avocado, depending on context).
additional_notes: Most often means “a lawyer” in legal contexts (e.g., “Avez-vous un avocat ?” = “Do you have a lawyer?”). In food/shopping contexts, it can mean “an avocado” (e.g., “Prends un avocat.”). Not a close cognate of “lawyer”; it can look like English “advocate,” but in everyday French it usually refers to a lawyer.
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un avocat.
native_language_example: I need a lawyer.

additional_notes: Means a bath (the act of bathing in a bathtub) and can also refer to the bathwater. Most commonly used with the verb "prendre" (to take): "prendre un bain" = "to take a bath". Often contrasted with "une douche" (a shower).
target_language_example: Après le sport, je prends un bain chaud.
native_language_example: After working out, I take a hot bath.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: un beau jardin, un beau garçon. It can also mean "nice," "lovely," or "fine" depending on the noun and context. Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, French usually uses un bel instead. In some expressions, it can be ironic, as in un beau pétrin = "quite a mess."
target_language_example: C'est un beau cadeau.
native_language_example: It's a beautiful gift.

additional_notes: Used to say something is needed quickly or is very important. Often followed by a noun (or noun phrase): « un besoin urgent de volontaires / de vacances ». You can change the subject: « J’ai / Tu as / On a un besoin urgent de… ».
target_language_example: Nous avons un besoin urgent de soutien.
native_language_example: We have an urgent need for support.

additional_notes: Masculine singular form of bon used before a noun. Most often it simply means "a good," but with some nouns it can also suggest a respectable or fairly large amount, like "a solid" or "a good-sized." The feminine form is une bonne.
target_language_example: C'est un bon livre pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: It's a good book for learning French.

additional_notes: Used to describe a friend you appreciate or trust. The adjective usually comes before the noun here: un bon ami (masculine). Feminine: une bonne amie. You can add à moi / à toi / à lui, etc. to mean “a friend of mine/yours/his…”.
target_language_example: Tom est vraiment un bon ami ; il m'aide toujours quand j'en ai besoin.
native_language_example: Tom is really a good friend; he always helps me when I need it.

meaning: a good boy; a good lad / a good guy (male).
additional_notes: Literally “a good boy.” Used to praise a male (often a child, but it can also be said to an adult in a friendly or slightly patronizing way). In the imperative, it’s used as a request/command: « Sois un bon garçon » = “Be a good boy.” For a girl: « une bonne fille » (or more commonly for children: « une bonne petite fille »).
target_language_example: Allez, sois un bon garçon et écoute le professeur.
native_language_example: Come on, be a good boy and listen to the teacher.

meaning: a good time; a good moment (to do something).
additional_notes: Common in expressions like « passer un bon moment » (“to have a good time”) and questions like « Quand est-ce un bon moment pour toi/vous ? » (“When is a good time for you?”). In « depuis un bon moment », it means “for a long time / in quite a while,” not “since a good moment.”
target_language_example: On peut se parler plus tard ? Ce soir, c’est un bon moment pour toi ?
native_language_example: Can we talk later? Is tonight a good time for you?

additional_notes: Used in greetings and small talk. With "passer" it means "to have/spend a good weekend" (e.g., "Tu as passé un bon week-end ?"). With "souhaiter" or "passer" in the imperative, it’s a common way to say "Have a good weekend!" (formal: "Passez un bon week-end" / "Je vous souhaite un bon week-end"; informal: "Passe un bon week-end").
target_language_example: Bon, je te laisse : passe un bon week-end !
native_language_example: Alright, I’ll let you go: have a good weekend!

additional_notes: Used with faire or construire: faire/construire un bonhomme de neige = “to make/build a snowman.” Literally “a little man of snow.”
target_language_example: Les enfants font un bonhomme de neige dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The kids are making a snowman in the garden.

meaning: a bit of; a piece of; (with time) a while.
additional_notes: Literally “an end of,” but in everyday French it commonly means “a bit/piece of” something (often food: un bout de gâteau) or “a while/quite some time” with time expressions (un bout de temps, Ça fait un bout de temps). With time, it often suggests a fairly long time in a casual way.
target_language_example: On va marcher un bout de chemin, puis on prendra le bus.
native_language_example: We’ll walk part of the way, then we’ll take the bus.

additional_notes: Used for any small sheet of paper, often something informal (to write a note, a phone number, etc.). In phrases like « C’est juste / Ce n’est qu’un bout de papier », it can also mean “just a piece of paper” to downplay the importance of a document.
target_language_example: Tu as un bout de papier pour que je note l’adresse ?
native_language_example: Do you have a piece of paper so I can write down the address?

additional_notes: Means a very young child. Common in family contexts: « avoir un bébé » = to have a baby (give birth / become a parent), « attendre un bébé » = to be expecting a baby. Can also be used in comparisons like « comme un bébé » (e.g., to fall/cry/sleep like a baby).
target_language_example: Ils ont eu un bébé l'année dernière.
native_language_example: They had a baby last year.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning something you give to someone (often for a birthday, holiday, or to thank them). Used with verbs like offrir (to give) and faire (to give): offrir un cadeau à quelqu’un, faire un cadeau à quelqu’un. You can specify who it’s from with de la part de: un cadeau de la part de Marie.
target_language_example: Elle a offert un cadeau à Tom.
native_language_example: She gave Tom a gift.

additional_notes: Used to say who gave the gift: « un cadeau de + person » (a gift from + person). For the occasion, use « un cadeau de Noël / d’anniversaire » (“a Christmas/birthday gift”). To say who it’s for, add « pour + person »: « un cadeau de Noël pour toi ».
target_language_example: C'est un cadeau de mes parents.
native_language_example: It's a gift from my parents.

additional_notes: Used to say a present is intended for a particular person. Structure: (avoir/acheter) + un cadeau pour + [person]. With a noun: « pour Sandrine / pour ma petite amie ». With a pronoun: « pour elle / pour lui ».
target_language_example: J'ai un cadeau pour toi.
native_language_example: I have a gift for you.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering coffee, or suggesting a casual coffee meet-up (prendre un café = to have a coffee). Also note the spelling: un café (coffee / a café) vs un caffe (not French).
target_language_example: On se retrouve pour un café après le travail ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet up for a coffee after work?

additional_notes: A masculine noun for a large vehicle used to carry goods (e.g., un camion de livraison = a delivery truck). Used with common verbs like conduire (to drive), percuter (to hit/collide with), and monter dans (to get into).
target_language_example: Il y a un camion garé devant la maison.
native_language_example: There’s a truck parked in front of the house.

additional_notes:
Used to be intentionally vague while still pointing to something specific.
- With an abstract noun: means “a certain amount/degree” (e.g., un certain effort = some effort).
- In "en un certain sens": means “in a way / in a certain sense.”
- Before a person’s role/name: suggests an unnamed but identifiable person (often with a hint of mystery or “you know who I mean”).
target_language_example: Cela a demandé un certain effort.
native_language_example: That required a certain amount of effort.

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified amount of time (not exact), often suggesting it may take longer than expected. Common with verbs like prendre (to take) and with pendant to mean “for a while.”
target_language_example: Je vais rester ici un certain temps avant de rentrer.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for a while before going home.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article meaning "a" or "an." "Un chat" refers to one cat in general (not a specific cat). The plural is "des chats" (some cats).
target_language_example: J'ai un chat noir à la maison.
native_language_example: I have a black cat at home.

additional_notes: A common, basic noun: "un cheval" (a horse), "le cheval" (the horse). Used literally (an animal) and in common expressions, e.g. "fort comme un cheval" (as strong as a horse) or "Je pourrais manger un cheval" (I’m so hungry I could eat a horse). Plural: "des chevaux".
target_language_example: Dans ce parc, on peut voir un cheval et des poneys.
native_language_example: In this park, you can see a horse and ponies.

additional_notes: A friendly compliment meaning someone is a good person. In this expression, "chic" means "nice/kind" (not "stylish"), and "type" means "guy". Often used with emphasis: "vraiment un chic type" = "really a great guy." Mostly informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide : tu es vraiment un chic type !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help: you’re really a great guy!

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "un" = "a" (masculine singular) + "chien" = "dog". The plural is "des chiens" (some dogs).
target_language_example: J’ai un chien à la maison.
native_language_example: I have a dog at home.

meaning: a wink; a quick (often playful) signal with one eye.
additional_notes: Literally a quick closing of one eye. It can also be used figuratively to mean a “nod” or “reference” to something (e.g., in a film or book): *un clin d’œil à…* (“a nod to…”).
target_language_example: Il m’a fait un clin d’œil pour me dire que c’était une blague.
native_language_example: He winked at me to tell me it was a joke.

meaning: a fairy tale; (figuratively) a dreamlike, perfect story.
additional_notes: Literally “a tale/story of fairies.” Used for actual fairy tales (stories with magic, princesses, etc.) and also figuratively to describe something that seems unrealistically wonderful ("like a fairy tale"). Common with "comme" or "sembler" (e.g., "comme un conte de fées", "ça semble être un conte de fées").
target_language_example: Leur mariage ressemblait à un conte de fées.
native_language_example: Their wedding felt like a fairy tale.

additional_notes: Basic meaning is 'a hit' or 'a blow'. Depending on context, it can also mean one attempt or one go (en un coup = 'in one go'). In the casual expression boire un coup, it means 'have a drink'.
target_language_example: On va boire un coup après le travail ?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a drink after work?

additional_notes: Often used with the verb jeter: « jeter un coup d'oeil (à) » = “to take/have a quick look (at).” With y (« Jetez-y un coup d'oeil »), it means “have a quick look at it/there.”
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d'oeil à mon email ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my email?

additional_notes: Often used with the verb « jeter »: « jeter un coup d'œil (à…) » = to take a quick look (at…). « Jetez-y un coup d'œil » means “take a quick look at it,” where « y » replaces what you’re looking at. Common in everyday speech and can be a polite suggestion (« Ça mérite un coup d'œil » = it’s worth a look).
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d'œil à mon email avant que je l’envoie ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my email before I send it?

meaning: a quick/sudden burst of (something); a quick swipe/strike of (something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe a brief action or sudden event: *un coup de chiffon* (a quick wipe with a cloth), *un coup de vent* (a gust of wind). It also appears in common expressions like *prendre un coup de vieux* (“to suddenly feel/look older”). The word *coup* can also mean “blow/strike,” depending on the context.
target_language_example: Je donne un coup de fil et j’arrive.
native_language_example: I’ll make a quick phone call and I’ll come right away.

meaning: a gunshot (a shot fired from a gun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the sound/event of a firearm being fired (often heard: *entendre un coup de feu*, *un coup de feu retentit*). It can refer to one single shot; plural: *des coups de feu* (“gunshots”).
target_language_example: On a entendu un coup de feu près du parc.
native_language_example: We heard a gunshot near the park.

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to talk about a phone call. Used with verbs like donner/passer: « passer un coup de fil » = to make/place a call; « donner un coup de fil » = to give someone a call. Often means a quick call.
target_language_example: Je te donne un coup de fil ce soir.
native_language_example: I’ll give you a call tonight.

meaning: a hand; a bit of help.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or offer help with a task. Very common in spoken French with verbs like donner/avoir/fil(er) un coup de main (to give/get/lend a hand).
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner un coup de main pour porter ces cartons ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand carrying these boxes?

meaning: a kick (a blow with the foot).
additional_notes: Literally “a blow of foot.” Often used with the verb donner: donner un coup de pied à [person/thing] = to kick [someone/something]. You can also say donner un coup de pied dans [something] (to kick something) or donner un coup de pied pour [verb] to show purpose (e.g., to boost yourself up).
target_language_example: Il m’a donné un coup de pied dans la jambe.
native_language_example: He kicked me in the leg.

meaning: a punch (a punch with a fist).
additional_notes: Literally “a blow of (the) fist.” Commonly used with verbs like donner/mettre/asséner un coup de poing à quelqu’un (“to throw/land a punch on someone”). You can also say au visage (“in the face”), dans le ventre (“in the stomach”), etc.
target_language_example: Il lui a donné un coup de poing au visage.
native_language_example: He punched him in the face.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb phrase « jeter un coup d’œil (à …) » = “to take/have a quick look (at …)”. Very common for asking permission or offering to check something briefly: « Je peux jeter un coup d’œil ? » / « Je vais jeter un coup d’œil à … ».
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d’œil à mon email avant que je l’envoie ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my email before I send it?

additional_notes: A masculine noun (un couteau / le couteau). Used for everyday table settings (fork and knife) and also in more serious contexts like crime reports. Plural: des couteaux.
target_language_example: Peux-tu me passer un couteau, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me a knife, please?

meaning: a dead end (street); a dead end (situation).
additional_notes: Used literally for a street that does not continue (no through road). Figuratively, it means an impasse or situation with no way forward. Masculine noun: un cul-de-sac; plural: des culs-de-sac.
target_language_example: On s'est trompés de route : c'est un cul-de-sac.
native_language_example: We took the wrong road: it’s a dead end.

additional_notes: Refers to a detective hired by a private person (not the police) to investigate or follow someone. Often used with verbs like engager or employer (to hire). You can also say une détective privée for a woman.
target_language_example: Ils ont engagé un détective privé pour retrouver leur chien.
native_language_example: They hired a private investigator to find their dog.

additional_notes: Most often means a paid job position (similar to “un boulot,” but more neutral/formal). Common with verbs like trouver (to find), chercher (to look for), avoir (to have), and expressions like un emploi à temps partiel (a part-time job) or un emploi près de chez moi (a job near my home).
target_language_example: Elle a enfin trouvé un emploi dans une petite entreprise.
native_language_example: She finally found a job at a small company.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a place in a general way (often with an adjective: un endroit charmant/sûr/dangereux). It can be a real location (un musée) or a more abstract one (le monde est un endroit dangereux). Often interchangeable with « un lieu », but « endroit » feels more everyday.
target_language_example: On cherche un endroit tranquille pour déjeuner.
native_language_example: We're looking for a quiet place to have lunch.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with a location. It’s usually followed by a verb (e.g., vivre, rester, travailler) to describe what you can do in that place.
target_language_example: Je cherche un endroit où je peux étudier au calme.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a place where I can study quietly.

additional_notes: Can refer to a young person in general or to someone's child (son or daughter). In some contexts, calling someone un enfant can suggest they are childish or immature.
target_language_example: Nous avons un enfant de cinq ans.
native_language_example: We have a five-year-old child.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: un excellent boulot / un excellent travail / un excellent cadeau. With a feminine noun, use **une excellente** (e.g., une excellente idée). In the plural: **d’excellents / d’excellentes**.
target_language_example: C’est un excellent restaurant.
native_language_example: It’s an excellent restaurant.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering an illustration to clarify an explanation or point: « donner un exemple » = “to give an example.” Often appears in questions like « Vous voulez un exemple ? » or « Tu peux me donner un exemple ? ». With pronouns: « m'en donner un » = “give me one (example).”
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un exemple pour comprendre.
native_language_example: I need an example to understand.

additional_notes: Used with avoir: "avoir un faible pour quelqu’un/quelque chose". It means you feel a special fondness or attraction, or you’re easily won over by someone/something (not necessarily serious love; can be affectionate or slightly biased). Often implies you can’t resist or you tend to be more lenient.
target_language_example: J’ai un faible pour le chocolat noir.
native_language_example: I have a weakness for dark chocolate.

additional_notes: Means a movie in general. Often used with common verbs like voir/regarder un film (to see/watch a movie), aller voir un film (to go see a movie), and tourner un film (to shoot/make a film). You can specify the type with de + genre, e.g., un film de Noël (a Christmas movie).
target_language_example: On va regarder un film ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to watch a movie tonight?

additional_notes: Common informal word for a police officer. Often sounds casual or slightly pejorative depending on tone/context; in polite situations, prefer "un policier / une policière" or "un agent de police".
target_language_example: Il a dit qu'il était un flic, mais je ne l'ai pas cru.
native_language_example: He said he was a cop, but I didn’t believe him.

additional_notes: Means “a boy” (male child) or more generally “a young man/guy,” depending on context. It can also be used about someone’s child (“un garçon ou une fille ?” = “a boy or a girl?”). In some contexts, “garçon” can mean “waiter,” but that meaning usually appears when addressing staff (e.g., « Garçon ! ») or in restaurant context.
target_language_example: Il y a un garçon dans la classe.
native_language_example: There’s a boy in the class.

additional_notes: Masculine singular form used before a noun. It often means big or large in physical size, but with abstract nouns it can mean great or strong (for example, un grand sens des responsabilités = a strong/great sense of responsibility). With people, it can mean tall or grown-up depending on context. The feminine form is une grande.
target_language_example: Nous avons un grand jardin.
native_language_example: We have a big garden.

additional_notes: A warm, emphatic way to thank someone. Often used alone (spoken or written) or followed by “pour…” + noun/infinitive: “Un grand merci pour votre aide.” In writing you may also see “Un grand merci à tous !” (thanks to everyone).
target_language_example: Un grand merci pour ton message !
native_language_example: A big thank you for your message!

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to express that there are many of something. It’s a slightly formal, written-style way to say "beaucoup de". The verb usually agrees with the plural idea (e.g., "Un grand nombre de personnes ont...").
target_language_example: Un grand nombre de touristes visitent la ville chaque été.
native_language_example: A large number of tourists visit the city every summer.

additional_notes: "Gros" is an adjective meaning "big/large" (size or importance) and it agrees with the noun: un gros risque (a big risk), un gros tube (a large tube), un gros problème (a big problem). With a person ("un gros type"), it often means "a big/heavy guy" and can sound rude or insensitive depending on context. For a woman, you’d say "une grosse" (e.g., une grosse erreur).
target_language_example: On a eu un gros problème hier soir.
native_language_example: We had a big problem last night.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone extremely intelligent or exceptionally talented (often in science, art, music, etc.). It can also be used more casually as a compliment for someone who found a clever solution: « Tu es un génie ! »
target_language_example: Tu es un génie : tu as trouvé la solution en deux minutes !
native_language_example: You’re a genius—you found the solution in two minutes!

additional_notes: Basic way to say an adult male person. un is the masculine singular indefinite article ('a'/'an'). In some contexts, it can also emphasize number: 'one man.' homme begins with a silent h, so it behaves like a vowel-starting word.
target_language_example: J'ai vu un homme dans la rue.
native_language_example: I saw a man in the street.

meaning: a good, decent man (a respectable person).
additional_notes: "Bien" here describes someone’s character, not that he is physically "well". You can also say "C’est quelqu’un de bien" (“He/She is a good person”).
target_language_example: Tout le monde dit que c’est un homme bien.
native_language_example: Everyone says he’s a good, decent man.

meaning: "a man of…" (used to describe a man by his quality, character, or type).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **un homme de + noun/phrase**. It can describe: (1) a **trait/quality** (*un homme de foi* = a man of faith; *un homme de raison* = a rational man), (2) a **temperament** (*un homme de feu* = a fiery/passionate man), or (3) a **kind/type/origin** (*un homme de Cro-Magnon*). Often followed by an abstract noun (foi, raison), but it can also be followed by a more detailed phrase (*un homme de grande taille* = a tall man). Feminine: **une femme de…**.
target_language_example: C'est un homme de parole.
native_language_example: He’s a man of his word.

meaning: "a man who" (introduces a description about a man).
additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause describing a man: "un homme" + "qui" + verb. "Qui" refers back to "un homme" and is the subject of the following verb (e.g., "un homme qui travaille"). Often used with "connaître" (to know) or "être" (to be).
target_language_example: C'est un homme qui comprend vite.
native_language_example: He's a man who understands quickly.

additional_notes: “Riche” means “rich/wealthy” and agrees with the noun: “un homme riche” (a rich man). You can use the same pattern with other nouns (e.g., “une femme riche” = a rich woman).
target_language_example: C'est un homme riche, mais il est très simple.
native_language_example: He’s a rich man, but he’s very down-to-earth.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: un hot-dog. Used when ordering or identifying the food; in a request you can say “Un hot-dog, s’il vous plaît.” Plural: des hot-dogs.
target_language_example: Je prends un hot-dog, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a hot dog, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe a male person admired for bravery, achievements, or for helping others. It can be literal (a real-life hero) or figurative/ironic ("You’re a hero" for doing something helpful). For a female hero, say "une héroïne".
target_language_example: Il a sauvé un enfant de la rivière : c'est un héros.
native_language_example: He saved a child from the river: he's a hero.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article un (“a”). In conversation, you’ll often hear it when asking if there’s a hotel nearby: « Y a-t-il un hôtel… ? » or « Où il y a un hôtel ? ». « Tenir un hôtel » means “to run/own a hotel.”
target_language_example: Nous cherchons un hôtel pas trop cher.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a hotel that isn’t too expensive.

additional_notes: “Bon marché” means “inexpensive/affordable” (not “good market”). It usually comes after the noun: un hôtel bon marché, des vêtements bon marché. For “cheap” in the sense of “low quality,” French often uses “de mauvaise qualité” instead.
target_language_example: Je cherche un hôtel bon marché près de la gare.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a cheap hotel near the train station.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used to call someone stupid or to say someone seems stupid ("passer pour un idiot" = "to look like an idiot"; "prendre quelqu’un pour un idiot" = "to take someone for an idiot"). Strong and rude in many contexts; in formal situations avoid it. Feminine: "une idiote".
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas un idiot : je comprends très bien.
native_language_example: I'm not an idiot: I understand perfectly well.

meaning: a drawback/disadvantage to the fact that…
additional_notes: Used to point out a problem with a situation introduced by a clause. The verb after « à ce que » is typically in the subjunctive (e.g., « à ce que tu viennes »). Often appears in the negative as « Il n’y a pas d’inconvénient à ce que… » = “There’s no harm in / no drawback to …”.
target_language_example: Je vois un inconvénient à ce que tu viennes plus tôt.
native_language_example: I see a drawback to you coming earlier.

un inconvénient à ce que je

target_language_multi_word_term: un inconvénient à ce que je
additional_notes: Usually used in the full pattern « (Il n’y a pas / Y a-t-il) un inconvénient à ce que je + subjunctive… ? » meaning “Is there any problem with me…?” or “There’s no problem with me…”. After « à ce que », French typically uses the subjunctive: « …à ce que je parte / que je vienne / que je fasse… ». More natural/complete as « un inconvénient à ce que je… » rather than on its own.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il un inconvénient à ce que je prenne une photo ?
native_language_example: Is there any problem with me taking a photo?

un inconvénient à ce que je me

target_language_multi_word_term: un inconvénient à ce que je me
meaning: an objection / any problem with me (doing something).
additional_notes: This is a fragment that typically appears in the pattern: « (Ne pas) voir / avoir d’inconvénient à ce que + [subjunctive] » = “to (not) mind / to (not) have any objection to …”. After « à ce que », French normally uses the subjunctive (e.g., « je me joigne », « je me mette », « je me gare », etc.). Note: « inconvénient » is a noun meaning “drawback / inconvenience / objection”; it can be a false friend with English “inconvenient” (adjective).
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous voyez un inconvénient à ce que je me joigne à vous ?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I join you?

un inconvénient à ce que je vous

target_language_multi_word_term: voir un inconvénient à ce que…
meaning: to mind / to object to… (literally: “to see a drawback in the fact that…”)
additional_notes: Polite way to check whether something would be a problem: « Voyez-vous un inconvénient à ce que… ? » = “Would you mind if…?” After « à ce que », French uses the subjunctive: « …à ce que je vous appelle », « …à ce que nous partions ». Common negative variant: « Vous n’y voyez pas d’inconvénient à ce que… ? » (with « y » referring to the situation).
target_language_example: Voyez-vous un inconvénient à ce que je vous appelle demain ?
native_language_example: Would you mind if I call you tomorrow?

meaning: a moment; a second (a very short time).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to wait briefly (often with verbs like « excuse-moi » or « attends »), or to say something will happen very soon (« dans un instant » = “in a moment”).
target_language_example: Attends un instant, j'arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, I'm coming.

meaning: a game; (sometimes) play/just a game (not serious).
additional_notes: Usually means a game (a pastime, board game, video game, etc.). In expressions like « C’est (comme) un jeu » or « Tu crois que c’est un jeu ? », it can imply “this is just a game / you’re not taking it seriously” (often said to criticize or warn). With « jouer à », it names the game or activity: « jouer à un jeu ».
target_language_example: Pour lui, tout est un jeu, mais pour moi c’est sérieux.
native_language_example: For him, everything is a game, but for me it’s serious.

additional_notes: In these examples, it means at an unspecified time in the future: 'one day' or 'someday.' It can also literally mean 'one day' as a time unit depending on context.
target_language_example: Un jour, j'irai à Paris.
native_language_example: One day, I'll go to Paris.

meaning: "one day, he..." (introducing a moment in a story; sometimes "someday, he...")
additional_notes: Used to set the scene and start a new event in a narrative: *Un jour, il + verb...* (= “One day, he + verb...”). Depending on context, *un jour* can mean a specific day in the past (“one day”) or an unspecified day in the future (“someday”), especially with future forms like *il faudra*.
target_language_example: Un jour, il a décidé de tout changer.
native_language_example: One day, he decided to change everything.

additional_notes: Used for time off from work or school (vacation/leave). Common with the verb « prendre »: « prendre un jour de congé » = to take a day off. You can also say « demander un jour de congé » (to request a day off).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un jour de congé demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to take a day off tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or estimate a short amount of time, often meaning “about a couple of days” rather than exactly 48 hours. Can be used with verbs like donner (give), rester (stay), or in time estimates with dans (in): « dans un jour ou deux » = “in a day or two.”
target_language_example: Je reviens dans un jour ou deux.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a day or two.

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting. Often used with souhaiter (“to wish”): « Je te/vous souhaite un joyeux Noël. » You can also say it by itself (« Un joyeux Noël ! ») or with « à + person » (“to”): « Un joyeux Noël à vous tous/toutes. »
target_language_example: Je te souhaite un joyeux Noël et une bonne année !
native_language_example: I wish you a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year!

additional_notes: Basic way to say 'a book.' Livre is a masculine noun, so it takes un. Without the article, livre means 'book' in general.
target_language_example: J'achète un livre pour ma sœur.
native_language_example: I'm buying a book for my sister.

additional_notes: Often used with avoir: « avoir mal à la tête » = to have a headache. « avoir un mal de tête » is also common. You can add adjectives: « un gros mal de tête » (a bad headache).
target_language_example: J’ai un mal de tête, je vais me coucher tôt.
native_language_example: I have a headache; I'm going to bed early.

additional_notes: In France, "football" usually means soccer. If you mean American football, you often specify "football américain" (as in "un match de football américain"). "Match" is commonly used for sports games, especially team sports.
target_language_example: On va au stade pour voir un match de football ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to the stadium to watch a soccer match tonight.

meaning: a lot; as much as possible (the maximum).
additional_notes: Very common informal shortening of «(un) maximum». Often used as «un max de + noun» = “a lot of …” (J’ai un max de boulot.). Can also be an exclamation meaning “as much as possible!” or “a lot!” (Un max !). In slang, «se faire un max de …» can mean “to make/earn a lot of …” (money, etc.).
target_language_example: J’ai un max de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have a ton of things to do today.

meaning: a good guy; a decent guy.
additional_notes: “Mec” is informal for “guy” (like “dude”). Adding “bien” means the person is kind/reliable/respectable (“a good one”), not “good-looking.” You can say it directly to someone: « T’es un mec bien. »
target_language_example: Il m’a aidé sans rien demander : c’est vraiment un mec bien.
native_language_example: He helped me without asking for anything: he’s really a good guy.

additional_notes: Used for a note someone sends or leaves for you. With verbs like envoyer (send) and laisser (leave). You can also hear it as a notification: « Vous avez un message. »
target_language_example: Je t’envoie un message ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m sending you a message tonight.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun: un million de prisonniers (“a million prisoners”), un million de façons (“a million ways”). Very often it’s an exaggeration meaning “loads/so many,” especially in phrases like un million de fois (“a million times”) or un million de questions (“a million questions”).
target_language_example: J’ai un million de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have a million things to do today.

additional_notes: A literal amount of money. Often used in the idiom « la question à un million de dollars » (“the million-dollar question”), meaning a very important or hard question; « à un million de dollars » can also mean “worth a million dollars.”
target_language_example: Si je gagnais un million de dollars, je partirais faire le tour du monde.
native_language_example: If I won a million dollars, I would go travel around the world.

meaning: a miracle; something extraordinary or seemingly impossible.
additional_notes: Used literally for a religious/supernatural miracle, and very often figuratively to mean “it would take a miracle” (something extremely unlikely) or to emphasize that something amazing happened. Can be said alone (“Un miracle !”) as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Réussir sans travailler, ce serait un miracle !
native_language_example: Succeeding without studying would be a miracle!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (pendant un mois = for a month; depuis un mois = for a month/for the past month) or a time point relative to now (dans un mois = in a month; il y a un mois = a month ago). Often appears with contractions: d’un mois (de + un), tout un mois = a whole month.
target_language_example: Je pars en vacances dans un mois.
native_language_example: I'm going on vacation in a month.

additional_notes: Refers to a short period of time. Depending on the verb, English may translate it as "a moment," "for a moment," or "for a while": donne-nous un moment = "give us a moment," parler un moment = "talk for a moment."
target_language_example: Attends un moment, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a portion of something (food, material, an object): un morceau de gâteau (a piece of cake), un morceau de papier (a piece/scrap of paper). It’s followed by a noun. Often shortened in speech with en: Tu en veux un morceau ? (Do you want a piece of it?).
target_language_example: Je peux avoir un morceau de pain, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I have a piece of bread, please?

additional_notes: Used for any small piece of paper you can write on (a slip, scrap, etc.). Common with verbs like donner (to give), écrire (to write), noter (to note down).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un morceau de papier pour noter ton numéro.
native_language_example: I need a piece of paper to write down your number.

meaning: a word; (by extension) a quick word/message.
additional_notes: Literally means “a word.” In phrases like « J’ai un mot à te dire », it often means “I have something (quick) to tell you” or “Can I have a word with you?” You can also use « Juste un mot » to mean “just a word” / “one quick thing.”
target_language_example: Avant de partir, j’ai un mot à te dire.
native_language_example: Before you leave, I have a word to say to you (I have something to tell you).

additional_notes: Used for a secret word/code to access an account, device, Wi‑Fi, etc. Very common with verbs like choisir/créer/entrer un mot de passe (choose/create/enter a password).
target_language_example: Veuillez choisir un mot de passe plus robuste.
native_language_example: Please choose a stronger password.

meaning: a way to (do something); a means of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a method/solution to achieve a goal. Often appears in phrases like « trouver un moyen de… » (to find a way to…), « il y a un moyen de… » (there’s a way to…), or in questions « Y a-t-il un moyen de… ? » (Is there a way to…?).
target_language_example: Il faut trouver un moyen de résoudre ce problème.
native_language_example: We need to find a way to solve this problem.

additional_notes: Means a medical doctor. Used with verbs like voir/consulter un médecin (to see/consult a doctor), envoyer quelqu’un chercher un médecin (send someone to get a doctor), or se faire examiner par un médecin (get examined by a doctor). Plural: des médecins.
target_language_example: J'ai pris rendez-vous chez un médecin pour demain.
native_language_example: I made an appointment with a doctor for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a name” (someone’s name, the name of something). It can also mean “a noun” in grammar contexts. With il/elle me faut + un nom = “I need a name.”
target_language_example: On doit choisir un nom pour le bébé.
native_language_example: We have to choose a name for the baby.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to describe something as new: un nouveau plan, un nouveau modèle. Before a vowel sound or silent h, French usually uses un nouvel instead (for example, un nouvel ami).
target_language_example: J'ai acheté un nouveau téléphone.
native_language_example: I bought a new phone.

meaning: a new (before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or silent h).
additional_notes: "Nouvel" is the masculine singular form of "nouveau" used before nouns that begin with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u) or a silent h: "un nouvel ami", "un nouvel étudiant", "un nouvel emploi". Before a consonant, you usually use "un nouveau" ("un nouveau livre"). Feminine: "une nouvelle".
target_language_example: On cherche un nouvel appartement.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a new apartment.

additional_notes: “Nouvel” is a form of “nouveau” used before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel or silent h (like “ordinateur”). You’ll also see: “un nouveau téléphone” (consonant start) and “une nouvelle voiture” (feminine).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un nouvel ordinateur pour le travail.
native_language_example: I need a new computer for work.

meaning: an eye; (in common expressions) a look / watch.
additional_notes: Very common in fixed expressions: **garder un oeil sur (quelqu’un/quelque chose)** = “to keep an eye on (someone/something)” (watch, supervise); **jeter un oeil (sur/à)** / **jeter un oeil** = “to take a look (at)” (often a quick look). Note: the standard spelling is **un œil** (plural **yeux**), but **un oeil** is sometimes used when ligatures aren’t available.
target_language_example: Je garderai un oeil sur lui.
native_language_example: I’ll keep an eye on him.

additional_notes: A common masculine noun. The article changes with context: un oiseau (a bird), l’oiseau (the bird), des oiseaux (some birds/birds). The initial vowel sound means you say and write l’oiseau (not *le oiseau*).
target_language_example: Il y a un oiseau sur la branche.
native_language_example: There is a bird on the branch.

additional_notes: Literal use: a physical pack/packet (e.g., *un paquet de cigarettes*). Very common informal use: means “a lot of / loads of,” especially with money, problems, questions, etc. Often used with slang nouns too (e.g., *fric* = money, *clopes* = cigarettes).
target_language_example: On a un paquet de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We have loads of things to do today.

meaning: one more step; one step further (literally or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used for physical movement ("one more step") and also metaphorically for progress toward a goal ("one step closer"). Often appears in warnings/threats with an implied consequence: "Un pas de plus, et..." = "One more step, and..." You can also see it in negatives like "Pas un pas de plus !" ("Not one more step!").
target_language_example: Encore un pas de plus et on arrive au sommet.
native_language_example: One more step and we’ll reach the top.

additional_notes: A noun for an activity you do regularly for fun in your free time. Common with avoir (to have): « J’ai un passe-temps » / « As-tu un passe-temps ? ». Plural: « des passe-temps ».
target_language_example: J’ai un passe-temps : la photographie.
native_language_example: I have a hobby: photography.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: un petit poisson = a small fish. It can describe physical size, a small amount, or make something sound more modest, friendly, or casual, as in un petit coup de main ?
target_language_example: Je voudrais un petit café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a small coffee, please.

additional_notes: The standard word for “breakfast.” Often used with the verb prendre (“to have”/“to take”): prendre un petit-déjeuner. You can also use it when offering breakfast (Veux-tu un petit-déjeuner ?) or promising/owing someone breakfast (Je te/vous dois un petit-déjeuner = “I owe you breakfast,” meaning you’ll treat them).
target_language_example: On peut prendre un petit-déjeuner ici ?
native_language_example: Can we have breakfast here?

additional_notes: Literally “a little friend,” but it means a romantic partner (boyfriend). Often used when asking if someone is dating someone. Note the informal spoken form: “T’as un petit ami ?” (instead of “Tu as…”).
target_language_example: Elle a un petit ami depuis deux mois.
native_language_example: She’s had a boyfriend for two months.

meaning: a little boy; a young boy.
additional_notes: Used to describe a male child. Often implies he’s small/young; in some contexts it can also mean someone is acting or looks like a child ("You look like a little boy"). Feminine: "une petite fille" (a little girl).
target_language_example: J'ai vu un petit garçon qui cherchait sa maman.
native_language_example: I saw a little boy who was looking for his mom.

meaning: a short while; a little bit (of time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a brief duration, either in the past or the near future. Often appears after verbs like rester (stay), attendre (wait), revenir (come back), emprunter (borrow), surveiller (watch). Can also be used alone as a polite request: « Juste un petit moment. »
target_language_example: Attends un petit moment, j’arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, I’m coming.

additional_notes: Used to mean a small amount or degree. Common with verbs like parler (Je parle un petit peu…), with requests to soften them (baisser un petit peu…), and to downplay something (Ça va faire un petit peu mal). Often interchangeable with "un peu"; "un petit peu" can feel slightly more gentle or emphatic.
target_language_example: Attends un petit peu, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Wait a little bit, please.

meaning: a little something (a small gift, snack, or unspecified thing).
additional_notes: Used when you don’t want to name the exact thing, or when it’s not important to specify. Often said when offering or bringing something small (a present, a treat, a bite to eat/drink). In questions like « Vous avez un petit quelque chose, là ? », it can mean “Do you have something (small) there?” or “Do you have a little something (to eat/drink)?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je vais te préparer un petit quelque chose à manger.
native_language_example: I’m going to make you a little something to eat.

additional_notes: Used to soften or moderate an adjective/adverb ("un peu dingue" = "a bit crazy"), or to indicate a small amount. Often sounds more polite/less strong than saying something directly. Can also be used alone as a short answer: "Un peu." = "A little."
target_language_example: Je suis un peu fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm a little tired today.

additional_notes: Used to soften or limit what follows: with verbs (Je joue un peu = I play a little), with adjectives (un peu raide = a little stiff), and in polite requests (réduire un peu le prix = lower the price a bit). It can also stand alone in replies, like Ouais, un peu = Yeah, a little.
target_language_example: Je suis un peu fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm a little tired today.

meaning: "a little (bit) of" (+ noun starting with a vowel or silent h).
additional_notes: "Un peu" means "a little / a bit." Before a noun, you usually say "un peu de"; it becomes "un peu d'" in front of a vowel sound (e.g., eau, alcool, expérience, air, intimité, italien). Used with uncountable nouns and also with languages: "un peu d’italien" = "a little Italian."
target_language_example: J’aimerais un peu d'eau, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a little water, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or talk about a small amount of water. Common in polite requests with "Puis-je avoir... ?" (May I have...?) or "Je vais te chercher..." (I’ll go get you...). Often implies you don’t need much.
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux avoir un peu d'eau, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I have a little water, please?

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean a small amount of something, often with uncountable nouns or abstract ideas: un peu de bière, un peu de peur, un peu de bon sens. In everyday English, it is often translated simply as "some" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un peu de sucre dans mon café.
native_language_example: I'd like a little sugar in my coffee.

meaning: a little (bit) of coffee; some coffee.
additional_notes: Common when offering or asking for a small amount of coffee. "Un peu de" is used with uncountable nouns like café (coffee) to mean “a little/some.” In questions you’ll often hear it alone: "Un peu de café ?" = “Some coffee?”
target_language_example: Après le déjeuner, je prends un peu de café.
native_language_example: After lunch, I have a little coffee.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or describe a small quantity of milk, especially in cooking/drinks. Often follows verbs like ajouter (to add), mettre (to put), donner (to give), or boire (to drink). You can also use it after "avec" (with): "avec un peu de lait". Contrast: "du lait" = some milk (unspecified amount), while "un peu de lait" emphasizes a small amount.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café avec un peu de lait, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with a little milk, please.

additional_notes: Used to suggest taking a small amount of rest or downtime. Common with the verb prendre (“to take”): Prends/Prenez un peu de repos (“Get some rest”). Also works as a noun phrase meaning “some rest” in general: Un peu de repos nous ferait du bien (“Some rest would do us good”).
target_language_example: Après le voyage, j’ai besoin d’un peu de repos.
native_language_example: After the trip, I need a bit of rest.

meaning: “a little bit of respect” / “show some respect.”
additional_notes: Often used as a reproach or demand when someone is being rude or disrespectful. Common in imperatives like « Montre un peu de respect » (“Show some respect”) or as a standalone exclamation « Un peu de respect ! » (“Have some respect!”). « Quand même » adds the idea of “come on / at least.”
target_language_example: Un peu de respect, s'il te plaît !
native_language_example: Show a little respect, please!

additional_notes: Used to say you need (or got) some sleep, often implying it wasn’t much. Common with verbs like « avoir besoin de » (to need) and « dormir » (to sleep): « J’ai besoin d’un peu de sommeil. »
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un peu de sommeil avant de conduire.
native_language_example: I need a little sleep before driving.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or describe a small quantity of sugar, often in drinks (coffee/tea) or cooking. "Un peu de" is a common way to mean “some/a little” with an uncountable noun like "sucre".
target_language_example: Je voudrais un peu de sucre, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a little sugar, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a small amount of time (duration). Common with verbs like gagner/économiser (to save) and prendre (to take): « gagner/économiser un peu de temps » = “save a little time.”
target_language_example: Donne-moi un peu de temps pour réfléchir, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a little time to think, please.

meaning: a little (bit of) tea; some tea.
additional_notes: Used to offer or suggest a small amount of tea. "Un peu de" means “a little/some” with an uncountable noun like "thé". In polite offers you may hear "Tu veux… ?" (informal) or "Voudriez-vous… ?" (formal).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un peu de thé, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a little tea, please.

additional_notes: Used to offer or ask for a small amount of wine. With a mass noun like vin, French uses "un peu de" (not "un peu du" in the general sense). Can be a statement (Je bois un peu de vin), an offer (Prenez un peu de vin), or a question (Tu/Voulez-vous un peu de vin ?).
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on peut prendre un peu de vin.
native_language_example: After dinner, we can have a little wine.

meaning: a little late; slightly behind schedule.
additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived later than expected, but not by much. Often follows "être" (e.g., "Je suis un peu en retard") or describes an arrival with "arriver" ("Il est arrivé un peu en retard"). You can use it in a polite question to point out lateness: "Vous n’êtes pas un peu en retard ?"
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis un peu en retard, il y avait des embouteillages.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m a little late—there was traffic.

meaning: 'a little more' / 'a bit more' (slightly more; a little longer/farther/higher, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a small increase or adjustment (e.g., slower, more patient, more careful) or to indicate a small amount beyond a point in time/space/quantity (e.g., "un peu plus d'un an" = a little more than a year; "un peu plus à gauche" = a bit more to the left).
target_language_example: Tu peux attendre un peu plus, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you wait a little longer, please?

meaning: a little more (of); a little over/more than.
additional_notes: Used either to ask for/add more of something (often with food/drinks: "un peu plus de + noun") or to give an approximate quantity meaning "a bit more than" with numbers ("un peu plus de 40 ans" = a little over 40).
target_language_example: Il me faut un peu plus de temps.
native_language_example: I need a little more time.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or state you need extra time. Common with verbs like "il me faut..." (I need...), "il nous faut..." (we need...), and "j'ai besoin de..." (I need...).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me donner un peu plus de temps, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little more time, please?

meaning: a little longer; a bit longer.
additional_notes: Used to say that something should continue for a short additional amount of time. Often follows a verb (dormir un peu plus longtemps, rester un peu plus longtemps) or can start a sentence meaning “if (it went on) a little longer…” (Un peu plus longtemps et…).
target_language_example: On peut attendre un peu plus longtemps ?
native_language_example: Can we wait a little longer?

meaning: a little later; a bit later.
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something later than now, usually soon (minutes/hours). Common with calls, returning, or continuing a conversation: « Je te rappelle un peu plus tard » / « Je reviens un peu plus tard ».
target_language_example: Je t’envoie le document un peu plus tard.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the document a little later.

additional_notes: Used to soften criticism or say something is slightly excessive (too small/salty/short, etc.). It can describe adjectives ("un peu trop petit"), quantities ("un peu trop de sel"), or someone’s behavior in questions like "Elle n’en ferait pas un peu trop ?" meaning “Isn’t she overdoing it a bit?”
target_language_example: Ton commentaire était un peu trop dur.
native_language_example: Your comment was a bit too harsh.

additional_notes: Used after C’est / C’était / Ça a été to politely say you enjoyed doing something: meeting someone, seeing someone, talking, helping, etc. Follow with an infinitive (de + verb): un plaisir de te voir, un plaisir de vous rencontrer. Common in formal or polite conversation, especially with vous.
target_language_example: Ça a été un plaisir de vous aider.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to help you.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of a longer phrase with an infinitive: « C’est un plaisir de vous rencontrer / de vous voir / de vous parler. » It’s polite/formal because of « vous » (you). On its own, « un plaisir de vous… » can sound incomplete unless the verb is understood from context.
target_language_example: C’est un plaisir de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to meet you.

additional_notes: Used in polite or formal situations when meeting someone, especially with "vous" (you, formal/plural). Often said as "C’est un plaisir de vous rencontrer" or shortened to "Un plaisir de vous rencontrer." In the past, you may hear "C’était/Ça a été un plaisir de vous rencontrer" meaning "It was a pleasure meeting you" (often at the end of a meeting).
target_language_example: Bonjour, je m’appelle Claire — un plaisir de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: Hello, my name is Claire — it’s a pleasure to meet you.

meaning: a plan; an idea/strategy; (also) a map/floor plan.
additional_notes: Most often means a plan/strategy (“Nous avons un plan”). With "plan de secours," it means a backup plan. In some contexts, "un plan" can also mean a map (e.g., a city map) or a floor plan, depending on what someone is asking for.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, j’ai un plan.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have a plan.

additional_notes: Literally means “a hair,” but it’s commonly used in everyday speech to mean “just a little” (often with adjectives/adverbs: « un poil trop grand », « un poil tordu »). In « ne pas changer d’un poil », it means “not change at all / not one bit.”
target_language_example: Tu peux parler un poil plus lentement ?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a (male) police officer. The feminine form is "une policière". You can also say just "policier" after another determiner: "ce policier" (this officer), "un policier" (a police officer).
target_language_example: Il y a un policier devant la station de métro.
native_language_example: There is a police officer in front of the метро station.

meaning: a bribe (money/gift offered to influence someone).
additional_notes: Used for illegal/secret payments or gifts given to obtain a favor (often from an official). Common with verbs like accepter/recevoir (to accept/receive), offrir (to offer), and nier/avouer/refuser de reconnaître (to deny/confess/refuse to admit).
target_language_example: Le policier a refusé de reconnaître avoir reçu un pot-de-vin.
native_language_example: The police officer refused to admit having received a bribe.

meaning: a problem; an issue; a trouble/fault (with something).
additional_notes: Used for anything from an abstract issue ("La corruption était un problème") to a concrete malfunction ("un problème avec les freins"). Common patterns: "Il y a un problème" (There’s a problem), "un problème avec + noun" (a problem with…), "Ça/Cela peut être un problème" (That can be a problem).
target_language_example: Désolé, il y a un problème avec ma carte bancaire.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s a problem with my bank card.

meaning: a problem with; an issue with.
additional_notes: Used to say something is wrong with something (a technical or practical problem) or that you object to something ("Do you have a problem with…?"). Often used with avoir/il y a: "J’ai un problème avec…", "Il y a un problème avec…".
target_language_example: On a un problème avec la connexion internet.
native_language_example: We have a problem with the internet connection.

additional_notes: A very vulgar intensifier placed before a noun (e.g., « un putain de sourire », « un putain de psychopathe ») to express strong emotion like anger, contempt, or admiration. Often translated as “a fucking / a damn / a hell of a…”. Avoid in polite situations; it can sound aggressive and offensive.
target_language_example: C'est un putain de problème.
native_language_example: It's a fucking problem.

meaning: an appointment; a meeting/date (arranged in advance).
additional_notes: Used for scheduled meetings of many kinds: a doctor’s appointment (un rendez-vous chez le médecin), a business meeting, or a romantic date. Common verbs: prendre un rendez-vous (to make/book an appointment), demander un rendez-vous (to ask for an appointment), annuler un rendez-vous (to cancel), avoir un rendez-vous (to have an appointment).
target_language_example: J'ai un rendez-vous à 15 heures, alors je dois partir.
native_language_example: I have an appointment at 3 p.m., so I have to leave.

meaning: an appointment; a meeting (also: a date).
additional_notes: Used for planned meetings: with a doctor, client, or friend. With context it can mean a romantic date (e.g., un rendez-vous avec quelqu’un). Often used with verbs like avoir/prendre/fixer un rendez-vous (to have/make/schedule an appointment).
target_language_example: J’ai un rendez-vous chez le médecin à 15 h.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment at 3 p.m.

additional_notes: Often used to mean something very small or insignificant: *un rien l’énerve* (“the slightest thing annoys him”). Common set phrases: *pour un rien* (“for no reason / over nothing”), *un rien de…* (“a touch of…”, e.g., *un rien de sucre* = “a tiny bit of sugar”), and *trois fois rien* (“next to nothing”).
target_language_example: Il s’énerve pour un rien.
native_language_example: He gets upset over nothing.

additional_notes: Used for a dream you have while sleeping, but also figuratively for a wish/goal (“Mon rêve…”), something ideal (“Tu es un rêve.” = “You’re a dream.”), or something that feels unreal (“Ça doit être un rêve.” = “This must be a dream.”). You can also say it as an exclamation (“Un rêve !”) to show amazement.
target_language_example: Ça doit être un rêve.
native_language_example: This must be a dream.

additional_notes: Most often used with the verb **jouer**: **jouer un rôle important dans + noun** (to play an important role in + something). You can also hear **avoir un rôle important dans** (to have an important role in). The **dans** introduces the area/context (a project, a company, someone’s life, history, etc.).
target_language_example: L’éducation joue un rôle important dans la réussite.
native_language_example: Education plays an important role in success.

additional_notes: A common food item; used with fillings introduced by "au/à la/aux" (e.g., "un sandwich au fromage") or "avec" (e.g., "un sandwich avec du jambon"). In French, "sandwich" is masculine: "un sandwich", "le sandwich".
target_language_example: Je prends un sandwich au thon, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a tuna sandwich, please.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning something hidden or private. Very common with verbs like "avoir" (to have), "cacher" (to hide), and "confier" (to tell/share in confidence): "J’ai un secret" / "Je vais te confier un secret". In questions, it can express suspicion or curiosity: "Un secret ?" / "C’est un secret ?".
target_language_example: Ne le dis à personne : c’est un secret.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone: it’s a secret.

meaning: a favor (something you do to help someone).
additional_notes: In these examples, "un service" is usually used with verbs like "demander" (to ask) and "rendre" (to do/return) to mean a personal favor: "demander un service" = to ask a favor; "rendre un service" = to do someone a favor. It can also mean a "service" in the broader sense (a service provided), but the "ask/do a service" pattern strongly points to "favor."
target_language_example: Tu peux me rendre un service et fermer la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and close the window?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is just one person/thing (often in contrast with many): « un seul coq », « un seul avait lu ». It can stand alone as a pronoun: « Un seul suffira / suffit » (“Only one will be enough”). Common in set phrases like « pas un seul instant » (“not even for a single moment”) and instructions like « un seul à la fois » (“one at a time”).
target_language_example: Je n’en veux qu’un seul, merci.
native_language_example: I only want one, thanks.

meaning: a sign of; a gesture of.
additional_notes: Used with a noun after de to show what kind of sign/gesture it is: un signe de faiblesse (“a sign of weakness”), un signe de tête (“a nod”), un signe de la main (“a wave”). With body parts you’ll often see the article: de la main, de la tête.
target_language_example: C'est un signe de respect.
native_language_example: It's a sign of respect.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like faire (fais-moi un sourire = “give me a smile”), avoir (“to have” a smile), or with adjectives to describe the kind of smile (un sourire reconnaissant = “a grateful smile”). In phrases like Allez, un sourire!, it’s a friendly way to encourage someone to smile (often for a photo).
target_language_example: Fais-moi un sourire, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me a smile, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s facial expression as friendly and inviting. You can change the intensity: « un sourire accueillant » (a welcoming smile), « un sourire chaleureux » (a warm smile). « Accueillant » agrees with the noun: « un sourire accueillant » (masc.), « une expression accueillante » (fem.).
target_language_example: Le serveur avait un sourire très accueillant quand nous sommes entrés.
native_language_example: The waiter had a very welcoming smile when we walked in.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Stylo" is very common in everyday situations (class, office). You’ll often hear it in questions like "Tu as un stylo ?" (Do you have a pen?) or instructions like "Prenez un stylo" (Take a pen).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un stylo pour signer ce document.
native_language_example: I need a pen to sign this document.

meaning: a lot of; lots of; a bunch of.
additional_notes: Literally “a pile of,” but very commonly used to mean “many/much” in everyday speech. It’s followed by a noun (un tas de + nom): un tas de questions, un tas de problèmes. Often slightly informal in tone compared with beaucoup de.
target_language_example: On a un tas de choses à faire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: We have a lot of things to do today.

additional_notes: Used when requesting, calling, taking, or sharing a taxi. Common with verbs like appeler (call), prendre (take), and partager (share). In French, "taxi" is masculine: un taxi, le taxi; plural: des taxis.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, où est-ce que je peux prendre un taxi ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where can I get a taxi?

additional_notes: Used before a noun to emphasize its degree or nature: "un tel + nom" = "such a + noun". It often expresses surprise, admiration, criticism, or strong feeling: "un tel emploi" (such a job), "un tel endroit" (such a place). Feminine: "une telle"; plural: "de tels / de telles".
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais vu un tel spectacle !
native_language_example: I’ve never seen such a show!

additional_notes: Used before a noun: « un tel + nom » means “such a + noun” (often to emphasize the type or degree): « un tel succès » = “such success.” It can also mean “a certain” when you don’t want to specify exactly which person/thing: « un tel monsieur Dupont » = “a certain Mr. Dupont.” Sometimes it’s used on its own as a pronoun: « Un tel ne ferait pas ça. » = “Someone like that wouldn’t do that.” Feminine: « une telle »; plural: « de tels / de telles ».
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas comment un tel problème est arrivé.
native_language_example: I don’t understand how such a problem happened.

meaning: a turn; a short trip/round (a quick walk or drive).
additional_notes: Often used with **faire un tour** = “to go for a quick walk / go for a spin / have a look around.” You can specify what kind of round with **un tour de + noun**: **un tour de manège** (a ride on a carousel/ride) or **un tour de la ville** (a tour/drive around the city). Depending on context, **un tour** can mean “a turn” (your turn) or “a quick outing.”
target_language_example: On fait un tour et on revient ?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a quick walk and come back?

meaning: a job; work (a task to do).
additional_notes: Most often means a job/employment (“chercher un travail”, “trouver un travail”). It can also mean work as a task or piece of work to do (“un travail urgent à faire”).
target_language_example: Elle cherche un travail depuis deux mois.
native_language_example: She has been looking for a job for two months.

additional_notes: Literally “a shaking of the ground.” It’s a common, neutral term used in news and everyday speech. You’ll often hear it with verbs like avoir lieu (to take place), se produire (to happen), or frapper/toucher (to hit/affect): « Il y a eu un tremblement de terre » = “There was an earthquake.”
target_language_example: Cette nuit, un tremblement de terre a frappé la région.
native_language_example: Last night, an earthquake hit the region.

meaning: a hole; (figuratively, in « boire comme un trou ») someone who drinks a lot.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: a hole/opening (in the ground, in fabric, etc.). Common set phrase: « boire comme un trou » = “to drink like a fish” (very heavy drinking).
target_language_example: Il y a un trou dans ma chaussette.
native_language_example: There’s a hole in my sock.

additional_notes: Informal, very common way to refer to an object, idea, or matter when you don't name it precisely. Like English "thing" or "something." Depending on context, truc can also mean a tip or trick, but in these examples it means "thing/something."
target_language_example: J'ai un truc à te demander.
native_language_example: I have something to ask you.

additional_notes: “Un truc” is a very common informal way to say “a thing / something” when you don’t know, don’t remember, or don’t want to specify the exact word. It’s often followed by “à” + infinitive to mean “something to do” (un truc à dire, à régler, à manger, etc.). In questions like “T’as pas un truc à nous dire ?”, it can imply “Isn’t there something you need to tell us?”
