additional_notes: Most often used with "ça" or "cela" to mean something will work out or function: "Ça va marcher ?" = "Will it work?". Literally, "marcher" means "to walk", so in context (especially with a person/animal as the subject) it can mean "is going to walk".
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ça va marcher.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’ll work.

additional_notes: This is the near future ("aller" + infinitive): "ça va prendre..." = "it’s going to take..." (often about time). In the imperative, "Va prendre..." tells someone to go do something: "Va prendre ton bain" (go take your bath), "Va prendre l’air" (go get some fresh air). You’ll also see it inside common expressions like "prendre une raclée" (to get a beating).
target_language_example: Ça va prendre cinq minutes.
native_language_example: It’s going to take five minutes.

meaning: 'is going to' + a reflexive verb (near future), like 'is going to get/handle/improve'.
additional_notes: This is the start of the near-future tense: **aller (va)** + infinitive. Here it’s followed by a reflexive verb starting with a vowel, so **se** becomes **s'** (e.g., *va s'en remettre*, *va s'en occuper*, *va s'améliorer*). The full pattern is **il/elle/on va + s' + infinitive** (or **je vais / tu vas / nous allons / vous allez / ils vont**).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça va s'arranger.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s going to work itself out.

meaning: 'it'll work out' / 'it'll be okay' (things will get better or be resolved).
additional_notes: From the verb "s'arranger" (to work out / to get sorted out). Very common with "ça" or "tout": "Ça va s'arranger" / "Tout va s'arranger" to reassure someone after a problem. Also used about situations resolving themselves (a conflict, a mistake, a delay, etc.).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça va s'arranger.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’ll work out.

meaning: 'is going to take care of' / 'is going to handle'.
additional_notes: This is the near future (aller + infinitive) of **s'occuper de** (“to take care of / deal with”). It’s used with a subject: **il/elle/on va s'occuper de** + noun/pronoun (often **ça** = “that”). The **s'** is a reflexive pronoun and changes with the subject (je **m'**occupe, tu **t'**occupes, etc.). Note: **s'occuper de** is a false friend with English “to occupy”.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, il va s'occuper de ça.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, he’s going to take care of that.

additional_notes: Used in the near future tense: **aller (present)** + **se + infinitive**. It means someone/something is about to do an action to itself or that will happen "by itself" (common with things breaking, expanding, etc.). Changes with the subject: **je vais me… / tu vas te… / il/elle/on va se… / nous allons nous… / vous allez vous… / ils/elles vont se…**.
target_language_example: Attention, ça va se renverser !
native_language_example: Careful, it’s going to tip over!

additional_notes: From the verb phrase « se passer » (“to happen,” “to take place”). « va se passer » is the near future: « aller » (va) + infinitive (se passer). Often used in questions like « Qu’est-ce qu’il va se passer ? » (“What’s going to happen?”). Not the same as English “to pass.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : rien ne va se passer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: nothing is going to happen.

additional_notes: Part of the near-future pattern aller + infinitive. Here va is the il/elle/on form of aller, and te means singular informal 'you'. In sentences like Il va te chercher or Ça va te plaire, te comes before the infinitive and means 'you' as the object of the next verb.
target_language_example: Ça va te faire rire.
native_language_example: It's going to make you laugh.

additional_notes: Extremely offensive and sexually explicit (literally refers to anal sex). Used to tell someone off aggressively; avoid in polite conversation. You may see it shortened or censored (e.g., “va te faire…” or “va te faire e*****”).
target_language_example: Si tu continues à m’insulter, je m’en vais — mais ne me dis jamais « va te faire enculer ».
native_language_example: If you keep insulting me, I’m leaving — but never tell me “go f**k yourself.”

additional_notes: A very vulgar insult used to tell someone off. Literally uses the verb phrase *se faire foutre* (“to get fucked / to be told off”), but it’s best translated as “go fuck yourself.” *Va* is informal singular (to one person you address as *tu*). Plural/formal versions: *allez vous faire foutre* (to several people or to *vous*). Not appropriate in polite situations.
target_language_example: Si tu n’es pas content, va te faire foutre.
native_language_example: If you’re not happy, go fuck yourself.

additional_notes: A very informal, insulting way to tell someone to go away. Literally “go get yourself seen,” but the real meaning is closer to “piss off” / “get lost.” Often used in the imperative with “tu”; you may also hear “va te faire voir ailleurs” (“get lost somewhere else”). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Oh, va te faire voir !
native_language_example: Oh, get lost!

additional_notes: Formed with the near-future tense: aller (conjugated) + infinitive venir. It can refer to a planned/expected arrival (“who’s going to come”). The subject can change (je vais venir, ils vont venir, etc.).
target_language_example: Je pense qu’il va venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I think he’s going to come tonight.

additional_notes: Uses aller (va) + infinitive (être) to talk about what will happen soon or what you expect will be the case. Changes with the subject: je vais être, tu vas être, il/elle/on va être, nous allons être, vous allez être, ils/elles vont être.
target_language_example: Demain, ça va être compliqué.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it’s going to be complicated.

additional_notes: Refers to repeated movement in two directions or frequent traffic/activity (people, cars, waves, etc.). Often used with adjectives like constant and with "de" to specify what is moving: "le va-et-vient des clients". Usually singular with a hyphenated form.
target_language_example: Le va-et-vient des touristes devant l'hôtel a commencé tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: The comings and goings of tourists in front of the hotel started early this morning.

meaning: Extra “-t-” used in questions after a verb ending in a vowel (e.g., va-t-il? = does he go?/is it going?).
additional_notes: This “-t-” is added for pronunciation (a liaison sound) in subject–verb inversion, mainly before il/elle/on: va-t-il, va-t-elle, va-t-on. It has no meaning by itself; the meaning comes from the verb (aller: va… = goes/is going; aller can also mean “to suit/fit” as in Ça me va). You don’t use it if the verb already ends in -t or -d (e.g., part-il ?).
target_language_example: Comment va-t-on y aller ?
native_language_example: How are we going to get there?

meaning: “is she/it going?” (formal question form of « elle va »).
additional_notes: This is subject–verb inversion used to ask a question in a more formal/written style. The extra « -t- » is only added for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (va) and the subject starts with a vowel (elle): « va-t-elle ». Depending on context, « aller » can mean “to go” (Où va-t-elle ?), “to be doing/how is she?” (Comment va-t-elle ?), or “to fit/suit” (Cette jupe me va-t-elle ? = Does this skirt fit/suit me?).
target_language_example: Où va-t-elle après le travail ?
native_language_example: Where is she going after work?

additional_notes: Imperative (“tu” form) of the verb phrase “s’en aller” (to leave/go away). Often used as an order and can sound rude or angry depending on context and tone. You’ll also commonly see it written “va-t’en” (with an apostrophe).
target_language_example: Va-t-en, je dois étudier.
native_language_example: Go away, I have to study.

meaning: "does it suit him?" / "is he going?" (formal question: "is/does ... he/it ...?").
additional_notes: "Va-t-il" is the inverted question form of "il va" (present tense of aller). It can mean "Is he going? / Where is he going?" or, with "aller" meaning "to suit" (common with clothes, a menu, etc.), "Does it suit him/you?" In writing, French adds a "-t-" between two vowels: "va-t-il", "a-t-il".
target_language_example: À quelle heure va-t-il arriver ?
native_language_example: What time is he going to arrive?

meaning: "goes to the" / "is going to the" (he/she/it goes to a masculine singular place).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **aller** in the present tense: **il/elle/on va** = "he/she/one/we go(es)". **Au** is the contraction of **à + le**, so it’s used before **masculine singular** nouns: *au collège, au café, au concert, au centre-ville*. For plural, you’d use **aux** (*aux magasins*), and for most feminine nouns **à la** (*à la gare*).
target_language_example: Il va au marché ce matin.
native_language_example: He’s going to the market this morning.

additional_notes: With clothes, colors, or styles plus an indirect object pronoun (me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur), it means something suits someone or looks good on them. With a person as the subject, it means someone is fine or doing well.
target_language_example: Cette chemise te va bien.
native_language_example: That shirt looks good on you.

meaning: Go and get (fetch); go pick up.
additional_notes: Imperative form addressed to one person you’re familiar with (tu). It’s made of va (from aller, “to go”) + chercher (“to look for / to get”). In everyday French, va chercher often means “go get” something or someone (from another room, from outside, etc.), not just “go search.”
target_language_example: Va chercher ton manteau, il fait froid dehors.
native_language_example: Go get your coat; it’s cold outside.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "aller" to say something (often clothes, but also a job/role/mission) fits someone extremely well. Pattern: "Ça/Cette robe/ce travail + me/te/lui/vous + va comme un gant." Similar idea to English "fits like a glove."
target_language_example: Ce costume me va comme un gant.
native_language_example: This suit fits me perfectly.

additional_notes: Informal spoken French for ne va pas, with ne omitted. In commands it means 'don't go'; with subjects like ça or elle, it can also mean 'isn't okay', 'isn't doing well', or 'doesn't go/work'.
target_language_example: Ça va pas du tout.
native_language_example: Things aren't going well at all.

meaning: “go and get …” (often used as a rude insult, like “go fuck yourself”).
additional_notes: Literally “go (and) make yourself …”, but it’s normally followed by another verb/phrase (e.g., va te faire foutre / va te faire voir / va te faire niquer). In practice it’s frequently used as an aggressive, very vulgar way to tell someone off, especially with niquer.
target_language_example: Va te faire voir !
native_language_example: Get lost!

additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive. Used to tell someone to go away or express contempt/anger. Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start a fight. Often addressed directly with “toi,” or followed by a name/insult.
target_language_example: Si ça ne te plaît pas, va te faire foutre.
native_language_example: If you don’t like it, fuck off.

meaning: fits you very well / suits you very well; (also) is doing very well.
additional_notes: From the verb "aller". With clothing/colors, "(ça) va très bien (à + someone)" means it looks good on someone: "Ce manteau vous va très bien" = "That coat suits you very well." With people/things, it means someone/something is doing fine/very well: "Elle va très bien" / "Sa famille va très bien." You can also use it as an answer about how things are going: "Oui, ça va très bien."
target_language_example: Cette couleur te va très bien.
native_language_example: That color suits you very well.

meaning: "goes to the" / "go to the" (with a feminine destination).
additional_notes: Form of the verb aller (to go) + à la (“to the” before a feminine singular noun). It can describe someone going somewhere (Elle/Il va à la…) or be an instruction (Va à la… = “Go to the…”). Common with places and activities: à la librairie (to the bookstore), à la messe (to Mass).
target_language_example: Elle va à la bibliothèque après l’école.
native_language_example: She goes to the library after school.

additional_notes: "Vais-je" is the 1st person singular of aller (je vais) used in inversion to form a formal/literary question: "Vais-je + infinitive ?" = "Am I going to + verb?" In everyday speech, people more often say "Est-ce que je vais... ?" or "Je vais... ?".
target_language_example: Vais-je devoir payer maintenant ?
native_language_example: Am I going to have to pay now?

additional_notes: Used with the near future: **je vais + infinitive**. Here, **vais** is the **je** form of *aller* (to go), and it’s followed by **essayer de + infinitive** (to try to do something). Change **vais** to match the subject: *tu vas essayer de… / il va essayer de… / nous allons essayer de…*.
target_language_example: Je vais essayer de parler français plus souvent.
native_language_example: I'm going to try to speak French more often.

meaning: “I’m going to do / I’m going to make.”
additional_notes: This is the near future in French: **aller (to go) + infinitive**. **Je vais faire…** = “I’m going to do/make…”. For the negative, you normally say **Je ne vais pas faire ça** (“I’m not going to do that”). Often followed by an activity (**faire du golf**) or a fixed phrase like **faire de mon mieux** (“do my best”).
target_language_example: Je vais faire les courses ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to do the grocery shopping tonight.

additional_notes: A fragment built with je vais + infinitive to talk about the near future. Here, le is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" or sometimes "him," and in French it comes before the infinitive: je vais le prendre = "I'm going to take it."
target_language_example: Je vais le lire ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to read it tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the near future: aller (vais) + infinitive (dire). The direct object pronoun (le = it/him) goes before the infinitive: « vais le dire ». The person you tell it to comes after « à » (a name or stressed pronoun like « à lui / à elle »).
target_language_example: Je vais le dire à Marie.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell it to Marie.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the full sentence "Je vais le faire" (near-future tense: aller + infinitive) to express an intention or something you’re about to do. "Le" means "it" (a previously mentioned thing). You can emphasize who will do it with "C’est moi qui vais le faire" ("I’m the one who’s going to do it").
target_language_example: T’inquiète, je vais le faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to do it tonight.

meaning: “I’ll take care of it.” / “I’m going to handle it.”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **s’occuper de** (“to take care of / deal with”). **Je vais m'en occuper** is a very common way to say you’ll handle something. **en** replaces **de + [thing]**: *Tu peux t’occuper de ça ? — Oui, je vais m'en occuper.* In full, you’ll often see it as **Je vais m'en occuper.**
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je vais m'en occuper ce soir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it tonight.

meaning: 'I’m going to take' / 'I’m going to have'.
additional_notes: Used with the near future tense: **je vais + infinitive**. **Prendre** is very common and can mean 'take' (a bus/taxi), 'take' (medicine), or 'have' (food/drink): *Je vais prendre le bus / un taxi / mes médocs / un café*.
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un café avant de partir.
native_language_example: I’m going to have a coffee before leaving.

additional_notes: Often used with an implied subject: « Je vais rester ici. » It uses the near-future tense: « je vais » (I’m going) + infinitive (« rester », to stay) + place (« ici », here). You can change the subject: « Tu vas rester ici ? » (Are you going to stay here?).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, je vais rester ici.
native_language_example: I’m tired, I’m going to stay here.

meaning: "I’m going to (do something) to/for you" (je vais + te…).
additional_notes: Used with "je vais" to talk about the near future: "Je vais te + verb" = "I’m going to + verb + you". "Te" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" or "you" (depending on the verb) and it comes before the verb: "Je vais te dire" (I’m going to tell you), "Je vais te laisser" (I’m going to leave you/let you). Often followed by another pronoun: "Je vais te le dire" (I’m going to tell it to you).
target_language_example: Je vais te montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: I’m going to show you how it works.

meaning: "I’m going to tell you" / "I’ll tell you."
additional_notes: Usually used after "je": "Je vais te dire…" It uses the near future (aller + infinitive) and the object pronoun "te" (= "to you"). Often introduces what you’re about to say, sometimes like a conversational lead-in ("Let me tell you...").
target_language_example: Je vais te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Often used to introduce what you’re about to explain or reveal. It’s a fragment that needs something after it (a clause): « … ce que je pense / ce que tu dois faire ». Grammar: « vais » = (je) vais (near future with aller), « te » = “to you”, « dire » = “to tell”, « ce que » = “what/that which”. You can change « te » depending on who you’re talking to (vous, lui, leur) and « vais » depending on the subject (je vais, on va, il/elle va, etc.).
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que je pense.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you what I think.

vais te dire ce que je

target_language_multi_word_term: vais te dire ce que je
meaning: "I’m going to tell you what I…" (to introduce what you think/mean/know).
additional_notes: This is a common sentence starter, usually preceded by "Je" ("Je vais te dire ce que je…"). It’s followed by another verb to complete the idea: "…pense" (think), "…veux" (want), "…sais" (know). In speech, "Je" is often shortened to "J’" before a vowel: "J’vais te dire…" (more casual).
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que je pense.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you what I think.

additional_notes: This is the near future tense: **je vais + infinitive**. Here it’s **je vais donner** (“I’m going to give”), with **te** (“to you”) placed before the verb. Used when you’re about to give someone something (an object, information, a hand, a call, etc.). In speech, it can sound like "j’vais te donner".
target_language_example: Je vais te donner mon numéro.
native_language_example: I’m going to give you my number.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future construction aller + infinitive: je vais dire = “I’m going to say/tell.” The object pronouns come before the verb: te = “to you” and le = “it” (masculine; la for feminine, les for plural). Often used to introduce an explanation or answer.
target_language_example: Je vais te le dire, mais promets-moi de ne le répéter à personne.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you, but promise me you won’t repeat it to anyone.

additional_notes: Common near-future structure: present tense of "aller" (vais) + infinitive (montrer). "Te" means "to you" (informal singular). For "you" formal or plural, use "vais vous montrer".
target_language_example: Attends, je vais te montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: Wait, I’m going to show you how it works.

additional_notes: Literally "(I) am going to kill you." It’s usually said as the full sentence: « Je vais te tuer. » Built with the near-future: « je vais + infinitive ». « te » is the object pronoun meaning “you” (one person). This is a very strong threat in French; sometimes used jokingly/exaggerated among friends (like “I’m gonna kill you!”), but it can also be taken literally—use with great caution.
target_language_example: Je vais te tuer si tu touches à mon téléphone.
native_language_example: I’m going to kill you if you touch my phone.

meaning: “I’m going to see…” / “I’ll go see…” (near future of *voir*).
additional_notes: Formed with *aller* (present) + infinitive: *je vais voir* + person/thing. It can mean “go visit/see someone” (*je vais voir Patsy*), or “go check/find out” (*je vais voir ce que je peux faire* = “I’ll see what I can do”).
target_language_example: Attends une minute, je vais voir si le magasin est encore ouvert.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, I’m going to see if the store is still open.

additional_notes: Usually appears in the pattern je vais vous + infinitive, where vais is from aller and vous is the object pronoun. It often translates naturally as either "I'm going to ... you" or simply "I'll ... you." Here, vous means "you" (formal singular or plural) and comes before the main verb: Je vais vous le dire = "I'm going to tell you / I'll tell you."
target_language_example: Je vais vous montrer la photo.
native_language_example: I'm going to show you the photo.

additional_notes: Usually appears with the subject: “Je vais vous dire…”. Uses “vous” (formal you or plural you). Common to introduce what you’re about to explain or reveal.
target_language_example: Je vais vous dire quelque chose d’important.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you something important.

additional_notes: Usually said as **« Je vais vous montrer… »**. It uses the near-future structure **aller + infinitive**: **vais** (from *aller*, “to go”) + **montrer** (“to show”). **vous** means “you” (formal singular or plural).
target_language_example: Je vais vous montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: I'm going to show you how it works.

meaning: "(I) am going to go there" / "(I) have to go."
additional_notes: This is usually short for "je vais y aller" (near future of aller: "I’m going to go"). The pronoun "y" means "there" (to that place) or "to it" (to that situation/thing). In casual speech, "je" is often dropped: "Vais y aller".
target_language_example: D'accord, je vais y aller maintenant.
native_language_example: Okay, I’m going to go there now.

additional_notes: Used most often with the subject pronoun: « Je vais être en retard » (I’m going to be late). You can change « vais » depending on the subject: « tu vas être en retard », « il/elle va être en retard », « nous allons être en retard », etc. « en retard » means “late/behind schedule.” Note: French « retard » means “delay/lateness” and should not be confused with the English insult “retard.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je vais être en retard de dix minutes.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm going to be ten minutes late.

additional_notes: Used with the subject “je” as “je vais bien” to say you’re fine or doing well, often as an answer to “Ça va ?” or “Comment ça va ?”. It can also reassure someone (like “I’m okay, really”). In speech, it’s often shortened to “ça va” or “je vais bien, merci.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je vais bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m fine.

additional_notes: A noun phrase used for a vehicle designed to travel in space. It’s usually masculine: « le vaisseau spatial » (note: sentence 1 should be « Le vaisseau spatial… », not « La… »). Often used in sci‑fi or when comparing something futuristic: « On dirait un vaisseau spatial ! »
target_language_example: Ils ont vu un vaisseau spatial dans le film.
native_language_example: They saw a spaceship in the movie.

meaning: was worth it / was worth the effort.
additional_notes: From "valoir la peine" = "to be worth it" (literally, "to be worth the trouble/effort"). Used to say something was worthwhile after doing it. Often appears as "Ça valait la peine de + infinitive" (Ça valait la peine d'attendre = It was worth waiting) or "en valoir la peine" (le voyage en valait la peine = the trip was worth it). Tense changes: "vaut la peine" (present), "valait la peine" (imperfect/past).
target_language_example: Même s’il faisait froid, la promenade valait la peine.
native_language_example: Even though it was cold, the walk was worth it.

meaning: to be worth it / to be worth the effort.
additional_notes: Used to say something is worth doing or worth the trouble. Commonly conjugated with a subject like "ça": "Ça vaut la peine." You can also use "valoir la peine de" + infinitive: "Ça vaut la peine de réessayer." In the negative: "Ça ne vaut pas la peine" = "It’s not worth it."
target_language_example: Ça vaudra la peine de partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: It will be worth leaving earlier.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, cost, or trouble. Common in questions and negatives: « Est-ce que ça vaut le coup ? » (Is it worth it?), « Ça ne vaut pas le coup. » (It’s not worth it.). In the past: « Ça valait le coup. » (It was worth it.). You can also use it in the infinitive after another verb (e.g., « Ça va valoir le coup. » / « Ça peut valoir le coup. »).
target_language_example: Ça va valoir le coup d'essayer.
native_language_example: It’s going to be worth trying.

meaning: to be better (than); it’s better to.
additional_notes: Used to compare options or to give advice. Often followed by "que" for a comparison ("Ça vaut mieux que...") or used impersonally as "Il vaut mieux + infinitive" meaning "It’s better to..." In everyday speech you may also hear "Vaut mieux..." without "Il".
target_language_example: Il faut savoir quand valoir mieux se taire.
native_language_example: You have to know when it’s better to keep quiet.

meaning: "are you going to" / "do you" (question form, with "tu").
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of "tu vas..." (from aller, "to go"). Often used to ask about a future action: "Vas-tu partir ?" = "Are you going to leave?" It can also simply ask what someone is doing/choosing: "Quelles chaussures vas-tu mettre ?" = "Which shoes are you going to wear?" With a place it can mean "Are you going (to)…?": "Vas-tu à la réunion ?" = "Are you going to the meeting?" Common in writing and more formal than just "Tu vas… ?".
target_language_example: Vas-tu venir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming tonight?

meaning: “are you going to do …?” (asking what someone will do).
additional_notes: This is a question using inversion (verb + “-tu”) with the near future: “aller” (vas) + infinitive (faire). It’s used to ask about someone’s plans or intended actions: “Que vas-tu faire ?” = “What are you going to do?” You’ll often add an object or details after “faire” (e.g., “ce soir”, “à ce sujet”, “pour Noël”).
target_language_example: Alors, que vas-tu faire ?
native_language_example: So, what are you going to do?

meaning: 'you're going to have to' (you will need to).
additional_notes: Used with "tu" understood: "(Tu) vas devoir + infinitive". It’s the near future (aller + infinitive) combined with "devoir" to express obligation/necessity soon or in the near future. Often used in spoken French, especially in instructions or warnings.
target_language_example: Tu vas devoir partir tôt demain.
native_language_example: You're going to have to leave early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with "tu" to form the near future: "tu vas faire ..." = "you’re going to do ...". Very common in questions like "Tu vas faire quoi ?" (What are you going to do?) and "Comment tu vas faire ?" (How are you going to do it?/How will you manage?).
target_language_example: Tu vas faire quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tonight?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself. It most often appears inside a longer pattern like tu vas me + infinitive, meaning 'you are going to ... me' or 'you'll ... me' (for example, tu vas me voir = 'you’re going to see me'). If you meant a command, standard French usually uses va me + infinitive, not vas me.
target_language_example: Tu vas me téléphoner ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you going to call me tonight?

meaning: "do you go?" / "are you going?" (2nd person singular question).
additional_notes: "Vas-tu" is the inverted question form of "tu vas" (you go/you are going), from the verb "aller" (to go). It’s used to ask about where someone goes, how often, or whether they are going somewhere. It can be followed by a place ("Vas-tu au cinéma ?"), by an adverb ("Vas-tu souvent… ?"), or by "y" to mean "there" ("Y vas-tu ?").
target_language_example: Vas-tu à l’école demain ?
native_language_example: Are you going to school tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to urge or encourage someone to do something, often before another verb: Vas-y, réponds. Depending on tone, it can sound supportive, impatient, or challenging. This is the informal singular form; with vous, use allez-y.
target_language_example: Vas-y, essaie encore.
native_language_example: Go ahead, try again.

meaning: "Go ahead, go ahead" / "Come on, come on" (urging or encouraging someone).
additional_notes: Repeated for emphasis. Used a lot in spoken French to push someone to act, to give permission ("go ahead"), or to show impatience/pressure ("come on!"). Very common and informal; tone depends on context and can sound supportive or annoyed.
target_language_example: Vas-y, vas-y, dis-lui la vérité !
native_language_example: Come on, come on, tell him the truth!

meaning: is worth it; is worth the effort.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is worth doing: « Ça vaut la peine de + infinitive » (e.g., « Ça vaut la peine d’essayer. »). You can also use it to say something is worth it in general: « Ça vaut la peine. »
target_language_example: Ce film vaut la peine d’être vu.
native_language_example: This movie is worth seeing.

meaning: is worth it / is worth doing.
additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, money, or trouble. Often followed by "de" + infinitive: "Ça vaut le coup de + verb" (It’s worth + -ing). Can also be used on its own: "Ça vaut le coup" (It’s worth it).
target_language_example: Ça vaut le coup d'essayer une fois.
native_language_example: It’s worth trying once.

meaning: is worth (doing); it’s worth it to.
additional_notes: Comes from the verb phrase « valoir le coup » (“to be worth it”). It’s most often used with a subject like « Ça » or « C’ »: « Ça vaut le coup de + infinitive » (It’s worth + -ing). You can also use other subjects: « Ce film vaut le coup d’être vu » (This movie is worth seeing). In the negative: « Ça ne vaut pas le coup de… » (It’s not worth…).
target_language_example: Ça vaut le coup de visiter ce musée.
native_language_example: It’s worth visiting this museum.

additional_notes: From the verb *valoir* (“to be worth”). Often used in the full form **il vaut mieux + infinitive** (“it’s better to…”): *Il vaut mieux partir tôt.* In speech, **il** is often dropped: *Vaut mieux partir.* You can also use **vaut mieux que + subjunctive** (“it’s better that…”): *Vaut mieux que je parte / que tu répondes.* The short form **Vaut mieux pas** is a very common, informal-sounding way to say “Better not.”
target_language_example: Vaut mieux qu’on rentre maintenant, il se fait tard.
native_language_example: We’d better go home now; it’s getting late.

additional_notes: From the verb *valoir* (“to be worth”). Used to compare two options: **X vaut mieux que Y** (“X is better than Y”). Very common in proverbs and general statements. You can use nouns (**La santé vaut mieux que la richesse**) or infinitives (**Prévenir vaut mieux que guérir**). The plural is **valent mieux que** (e.g., *Ces solutions valent mieux que celles-là*).
target_language_example: Dans ce cas, il vaut mieux que tu partes tôt.
native_language_example: In that case, it’s better that you leave early.

meaning: “it’s better that I …” (used to give advice).
additional_notes: Most often appears as **il vaut mieux que je + verb** (“it’s better that I + verb”). The verb that follows is typically in the **subjunctive** (e.g., *que je parte, que je fasse*). Used to suggest the best course of action.
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux que je parte maintenant.
native_language_example: It’s better that I leave now.

additional_notes: "vend" is the present tense of "vendre" (to sell) for il/elle/on (he/she/one). "des" usually means "some" or "(plural) a/an" before a plural noun (des légumes = some vegetables). Used to say what someone sells.
target_language_example: Elle vend des livres au marché.
native_language_example: She sells books at the market.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or availability on Friday evening. In French, "soir" is the evening/night period; depending on context, it often matches English "Friday night" (e.g., going out) or "Friday evening" (e.g., dinner).
target_language_example: On se voit vendredi soir ?
native_language_example: Are we seeing each other Friday night?

meaning: "do you come" / "are you coming"? (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Inversion of the verb and subject pronoun to form a question: "venez" (you come/are coming) + "vous". Used for formal "you" (one person) or plural "you". Often appears in questions about where someone comes from ("Venez-vous de… ?" = "Are you from…?") or whether they’re coming ("Venez-vous ou non ?").
target_language_example: Venez-vous avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us tonight?

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) addressed to “vous” (one person formally or several people). Used to ask/tell someone to accompany you; can be followed by a destination: « Venez avec moi à… ».
target_language_example: Venez avec moi au bureau, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Come with me to the office, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that you will accompany someone. Very common in questions like « Je peux venir avec toi/vous ? » (“Can I come with you?”). Object pronouns (toi, vous, lui, eux, etc.) usually follow « avec ».
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux venir avec vous ?
native_language_example: Can I come with you?

additional_notes: Used to invite, ask, or tell someone to accompany you. Very common with questions or polite requests like « Tu pourrais venir avec moi ? » and « Tu veux bien venir avec moi ? ». You can swap the pronoun: « venir avec toi » (with you), « venir avec lui/elle » (with him/her), « venir avec nous/vous/eux/elles » (with us/you/them).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu peux venir avec moi au magasin ?
native_language_example: Can you come with me to the store?

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to join your group. "Venir" is "to come" (toward the speaker), and "avec nous" means "with us." Often used in questions or polite invitations: "Peux-tu venir avec nous ?" / "Voudriez-vous venir avec nous… ?"
target_language_example: Si tu veux, tu peux venir avec nous au cinéma.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come with us to the movie theater.

meaning: to come and get / to come pick up (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used when you go somewhere specifically to collect someone/something (e.g., pick up a child, fetch a package, pick someone up by car). It’s often followed by a direct object: « Je viens chercher mon colis. » You can also use pronouns: « Je viens le chercher. » (= I’m coming to get it/him.)
target_language_example: Je viens venir chercher mon colis cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I’m coming to pick up my package this afternoon.

additional_notes: With a person, place, or thing after de, this expression shows origin, source, or cause. It can mean where someone is from, where something comes from, or what is causing something: Ça vient de moi = "it's because of me / it's coming from me." Note: venir de + infinitive is a different common pattern meaning "have just".
target_language_example: Ça doit venir de moi.
native_language_example: It must be coming from me.

meaning: to help; to come to someone’s aid.
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object to express providing assistance, often in a serious, urgent, or practical situation. Common patterns: « venir en aide à quelqu’un » and « venir en aide à + pronoun » (lui/leur/me/te/nous/vous).
target_language_example: Au lieu de lui venir en aide, il est resté planté là en la regardant.
native_language_example: Instead of helping her, he just stood there staring at her.

additional_notes: Used for movement toward the speaker or the place being talked about as 'here'. It's a straightforward combination of venir + ici.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir ici une minute ?
native_language_example: Can you come here for a minute?

meaning: to come see me; to come visit me.
additional_notes: Used to invite or request that someone come to your place (or come to meet you) for a visit. The pronoun changes with the person: venir te voir (come see you), venir le/la voir (come see him/her), venir nous voir (come see us), venir vous voir (come see you/formal or plural), venir les voir (come see them). Often follows another verb: pouvoir venir me voir (can come see me), devoir venir me voir (should come see me), demander de venir me voir (ask to come see me).
target_language_example: Tu veux venir me voir ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come see me this weekend?

meaning: to come right away; to come immediately.
additional_notes: Used to insist on urgency. You’ll often hear it in commands or requests: « Viens/Venez tout de suite ! » (imperative) or « Tu peux venir tout de suite ? / Vous pourriez venir tout de suite ? » (polite request). « Tout de suite » can also be used alone to mean “right away.”
target_language_example: Vous pourriez venir tout de suite ? C'est urgent.
native_language_example: Could you come right away? It's urgent.

additional_notes: Used when an idea, memory, or word suddenly occurs to you. Commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: « ça me vient à l'esprit » (it comes to mind), « rien ne me vient à l'esprit » (nothing comes to mind).
target_language_example: Ton nom ne veut pas venir à l'esprit.
native_language_example: Your name won’t come to mind.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of a full sentence with an article: « Le vent souffle. » You may also hear « Le vent souffle fort » (the wind is blowing hard) or « Le vent souffle du nord » (the wind is blowing from the north). Note: French « vent » means “wind” (not the English “vent” = an air outlet).
target_language_example: Le vent souffle très fort ce soir.
native_language_example: The wind is blowing very hard tonight.

additional_notes: Past participle of venir (“to come”) + ici (“here”), used with être in the passé composé: je suis venu(e) ici, tu es venu(e) ici, il est venu ici, elle est venue ici, etc. Means someone came to this place (often “here,” where the speaker is).
target_language_example: Je suis venu ici pour te voir.
native_language_example: I came here to see you.

meaning: “came here to” / “came here in order to” (expresses purpose).
additional_notes:
Used with a subject + venir (conjugated) + ici + pour + infinitive to state why someone came.
- Past tense agreement in compound forms: venu (m. sg.), venue (f. sg.), venus (m. pl.), venues (f. pl.).
- Often interchangeable with « venir ici afin de… » (more formal) or « venir ici pour + noun » (e.g., « pour le travail »).
- « ici » can sometimes be replaced by « là » depending on context.
target_language_example: Il est venu ici pour te voir.
native_language_example: He came here to see you.

meaning: came to see me; came to visit me.
additional_notes: Past participle phrase used in the passé composé of « venir me voir » (“to come see/visit me”). With « être » as the auxiliary: « il est venu me voir », « tu es venu me voir ». The past participle agrees with the subject when needed (venu/venue/venus/venues). The pronoun « me » precedes the infinitive « voir ».
target_language_example: Il est venu me voir hier après-midi.
native_language_example: He came to see me yesterday afternoon.

additional_notes: Littéralement, un petit ver qui vit dans le sol. Peut aussi s’employer figurativement comme insulte (« Vous êtes un ver de terre. ») ou dans des expressions comme « une vie de ver de terre » pour évoquer une existence misérable et rabaissée.
target_language_example: La poule a mangé un ver de terre.
native_language_example: The hen ate an earthworm.

verrais-tu un inconvénient à ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: verrais-tu un inconvénient à ce que
meaning: 'Would you mind if…?' / 'Would it be a problem if…?'
additional_notes: A polite way to ask permission or check if something would bother someone. Uses the conditional of voir (verrais-tu = would you see) to soften the request. The verb after « à ce que » is in the subjunctive: « …à ce que je fasse / jette / parte / rentre ». You can also use « verriez-vous… » for formal situations.
target_language_example: Verrais-tu un inconvénient à ce que j'ouvre la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Would you mind if I opened the window?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or offer a serving of water. Common request: « Un verre d'eau, s’il vous plaît. » In everyday speech, you may also see « verre d’eau » with a typographic apostrophe; both refer to the same phrase.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a common serving size. Pattern: « un verre de + [drink] » (un verre d’eau, un verre de jus). Often heard when ordering or offering a drink: « Tu veux un verre de lait ? »
target_language_example: Je voudrais un verre de lait, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of milk, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one serving of wine (the drink) in a glass; very common when ordering (often with an article: « un verre de vin »). You can specify the type: « un verre de vin rouge/blanc » (red/white wine).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un verre de vin blanc, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of white wine, please.

verriez-vous un inconvénient à ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: verriez-vous un inconvénient à ce que
meaning: “Would you mind if…?” / “Would you have any objection to…?”
additional_notes: Very polite, formal way to ask permission. It’s built on the conditional of voir (“verriez-vous…”) and is typically followed by “à ce que” + a verb in the subjunctive: “Verriez-vous un inconvénient à ce que je parte… ?” (literally, “Would you see a drawback if I…?”).
target_language_example: Verriez-vous un inconvénient à ce que j’ouvre la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Would you mind if I opened the window?

additional_notes: Used when you secure a door by locking it (often with a lock, latch, or deadbolt). Common alternatives are « fermer la porte à clé » (lock the door with a key) and « fermer à clé » (lock up). In instructions you’ll often hear the imperative: « Verrouille la porte ! » (informal) / « Verrouillez la porte ! » (formal or plural).
target_language_example: N’oublie pas de verrouiller la porte en partant.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to lock the door when you leave.

meaning: "toward the" (in the direction of a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward something: a place (vers la ville), a side (vers la gauche), etc. It’s made of vers (“toward”) + la (“the” for feminine singular nouns). Compare: vers le (masculine singular) and vers les (plural).
target_language_example: On va vers la gare.
native_language_example: We’re going toward the train station.

meaning: towards the right; to the right.
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement in space (e.g., on a map, in a building, while driving). Common with verbs like tourner (to turn), aller (to go), regarder (to look), se diriger (to head).
target_language_example: Tournez vers la droite au prochain feu.
native_language_example: Turn right at the next traffic light.

meaning: "toward the" / "in the direction of the" (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to show direction or movement toward something: vers le haut (upwards), vers le plafond (toward the ceiling), vers le Nord (toward the North). You can use it after verbs like aller (to go), regarder (to look), partir (to leave), lever (to raise). Note: unlike à + le → au, there is no contraction here—it's always vers le.
target_language_example: On marche vers le centre-ville.
native_language_example: We’re walking toward downtown.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction (not a fixed location): looking/moving “up” toward something higher. Often follows verbs like regarder (to look), lever (to raise), monter (to go up), or can be used alone as a direction.
target_language_example: Lève la tête et regarde vers le haut.
native_language_example: Lift your head and look up.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction (where someone/something is heading), often with verbs like se diriger (to head), aller/partir (to go/leave), or filer (to dash off). You can also say it alone on a map or as a short instruction: « Vers le nord. »
target_language_example: On marche vers le nord pour rejoindre le village.
native_language_example: We’re walking toward the north to reach the village.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement in the direction of the south. Common with movement verbs like aller, marcher, voler, se diriger. You can also say simply "au sud" for a location (in the south), but "vers le sud" emphasizes heading that way.
target_language_example: Nous allons vers le sud pour les vacances.
native_language_example: We're going south for vacation.

meaning: 'does he want' / 'does he really want it?' (question form).
additional_notes: This is the verb–subject inversion used to form a question in more formal French: "veut" (wants) + "-il" (he) with a hyphen. It’s equivalent to "Est-ce qu’il veut… ?" or the informal spoken order "Il veut… ?". Used with a following infinitive or object: "Où veut-il aller ?" (Where does he want to go?), "Le veut-il ?" (Does he want it?).
target_language_example: Veut-il venir avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Does he want to come with us tonight?

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning of a word, phrase, sign, or situation. Often appears in questions: « Qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ? » (What does that mean?) and « Que veut dire… ? » (What does … mean?). « Ce qui veut dire… » means “which means… / that is to say…”.
target_language_example: Ça veut dire quoi, « rendez-vous » ?
native_language_example: What does “rendez-vous” mean?

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning or consequence of something. Commonly introduced by **ce qui veut dire que...** (“which means that...”) or **ça veut dire que...** (“that means that...”) to draw a conclusion or clarify what was implied.
target_language_example: Il n'a pas répondu, ce qui veut dire que ça ne l'intéresse pas.
native_language_example: He didn’t reply, which means that he’s not interested.

additional_notes: Used in spoken French to ask for the meaning of a word/phrase: "Ça veut dire quoi ?" (very common). More formal/neutral equivalents are "Qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ?" or "Que veut dire … ?" You can replace "quoi" with the word you’re asking about: "Ziri, ça veut dire quoi ?"
target_language_example: « Bizarre », ça veut dire quoi ?
native_language_example: What does “bizarre” mean?

meaning: "wants to talk to you / wants to speak to you."
additional_notes: Built from *vouloir* (to want) + *te* (to you, informal singular) + *parler* (to talk/speak). It’s often used to say someone is asking to see you or has something to tell you: *Le patron veut te parler* (The boss wants to talk to you). With a formal or plural “you,” say *veut vous parler*.
target_language_example: Le professeur veut te parler après le cours.
native_language_example: The teacher wants to talk to you after class.

meaning: 'wants to see you' (wants to meet/speak with you).
additional_notes: Used when someone is asking to meet you or talk to you. Often sounds like a summons when the subject is an authority figure (le directeur, le patron, etc.). You can add details like where/when: « Il/Elle veut te voir en bas / maintenant ». Adding « toi » emphasizes *you* specifically: « Il veut te voir toi, pas moi ».
target_language_example: Le médecin veut te voir tout de suite.
native_language_example: The doctor wants to see you right away.

additional_notes: Common combination of vouloir + être. This exact form, veut être, is the present-tense third-person singular: it is used with il, elle, on, or a singular noun subject. It is often followed by an adjective, noun, profession, or role.
target_language_example: Mon fils veut être pilote.
native_language_example: My son wants to be a pilot.

additional_notes: Question form of tu veux, using inversion. It is used to ask whether someone wants something or wants to do something. It can sound a bit more formal, direct, or literary than everyday tu veux ... ?
target_language_example: Veux-tu venir avec nous ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us?

additional_notes: Formed with **vouloir** (veux) + **tu** + **aller**. The **-tu** is an **inversion** used to ask a question (a slightly more formal/neutral way than *Tu veux aller… ?*). Often followed by a place (*Où veux-tu aller ?*) or an infinitive to say “go do something” (*Veux-tu aller prendre un verre ?*).
target_language_example: Veux-tu aller au café après le travail ?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the café after work?

additional_notes: A common way to offer something. It uses inversion for questions: *veux-tu* = “do you want?”. *Du* is the partitive article (*de + le*) meaning “some” (typically with masculine singular or uncountable nouns): *du beurre, du ketchup, du citron*. For feminine nouns you’d use *de la* (*veux-tu de la salade ?*), and before a vowel/h mute *de l’* (*veux-tu de l’eau ?*).
target_language_example: Veux-tu du café ?
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee?

meaning: "do you want to do" (asking what someone wants to do/make).
additional_notes: Formed with the verb *vouloir* (to want) + inversion (*veux-tu* = “do you want?”) + an infinitive. Very common in questions about plans/choices: *Que veux-tu faire ?* (“What do you want to do?”). It can also be used before a noun phrase where *faire* means “to do” or “to make”: *faire la liste* (“make the list”), *faire des études* (“do studies / study”).
target_language_example: Que veux-tu faire ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What do you want to do this weekend?

additional_notes: A common, polite/informal question using inversion (verb + -tu) with "tu". Often followed by: "avec" + person (Veux-tu jouer avec moi ?), "en ligne" (online), or "à" + game/activity (jouer à cache-cache, jouer à un jeu).
target_language_example: Veux-tu jouer avec moi après l'école ?
native_language_example: Do you want to play with me after school?

additional_notes: Question formed with inversion: « veux-tu… ? » = “do you want…?” (addressing one person informally) and « manger » = “to eat.” Often used on its own (« Veux-tu manger ? ») or with what to eat: « Veux-tu manger un morceau / un bout ? » = “Do you want to eat a piece / have a bite?” You can also add timing: « Quand veux-tu manger ? » = “When do you want to eat?”
target_language_example: Quand veux-tu manger ?
native_language_example: When do you want to eat?

meaning: "Do you want to… (with me as the object)?"
additional_notes: This is the verb "vouloir" (to want) in a yes/no question using inversion: "veux-tu…?" = "do you want…?" It’s usually followed by an infinitive, and "me" means "me" (the person receiving the action): "Veux-tu me parler ?" (Do you want to talk to me?), "Veux-tu me rencontrer ?" (Do you want to meet me?). In everyday speech you’ll also often hear "Tu veux…?" instead of the more formal-sounding inversion.
target_language_example: Veux-tu me dire la vérité ?
native_language_example: Do you want to tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants to happen or what they want someone else to do. It’s the inverted question form of "tu veux que…" and it’s normally followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "Veux-tu que je vienne ?").
target_language_example: Veux-tu que je t’aide avec tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with your homework?

additional_notes: Used to offer to do something (or ask for instructions). It’s the inverted-question form of "Tu veux que je…" and is followed by a verb in the subjunctive: "Veux-tu que je demande / garde / laisse / prévienne / recommence / rentre / répète / traite… ?" In more formal/polite speech you can also say: "Voulez-vous que je… ?"
target_language_example: Veux-tu que je t’aide avec ça ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with that?

meaning: "do you want me to be" (asking what role/state someone wants you to have).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants or expects you to be (a person, role, or condition). It uses inversion for a question (veux-tu = "do you want") and the subjunctive after "vouloir que" (que je sois, from être). You can change "sois" to match the subject: que tu sois, qu’il/elle soit, que nous soyons, etc.
target_language_example: Veux-tu que je sois plus discret(e) ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to be more discreet?

meaning: "Do you want me to (do something) for you?"
additional_notes: Used to offer to do something for someone or ask for their preference. Literally "do you want that I to you..."; it’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., je te montre, je te prenne, je te réveille). "Te" means "to you" or "you" as an object, depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Veux-tu que je te prépare un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to make you a coffee?

additional_notes: Question form with inversion: "veux" (you want) + "tu" (you) + "savoir" (to know). Often followed by a question word or clause: "Veux-tu savoir pourquoi…?" (why), "qui…?" (who), or "ce que…" (what). More formal/neutral than "Tu veux savoir… ?"
target_language_example: Veux-tu savoir ce qui s'est passé ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know what happened?

meaning: "Do you want a…?" (asking if someone wants one item).
additional_notes: Uses inversion for a question: "Veux-tu…?" = "Do you want…?". "Un" is the masculine singular article (a/an/one). Before a feminine noun, use "veux-tu une…?".
target_language_example: Veux-tu un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee?

meaning: "do you really want to...?" (emphasizes doubt or surprise).
additional_notes: Formed with verb–subject inversion (veux + tu) to ask a question. Commonly followed by an infinitive: "Veux-tu vraiment faire/voir/savoir... ?" You can make it more neutral/less direct with: "Est-ce que tu veux vraiment... ?"
target_language_example: Veux-tu vraiment partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you really want to leave now?

additional_notes: "Veux" is the 2nd-person singular (tu) form of *vouloir* (to want). It’s typically followed by an infinitive: *Tu veux aller… ?* = “Do you want to go…?” Often used in questions with *où* (where) or *pourquoi* (why): *Où tu veux aller ?*
target_language_example: Tu veux aller au cinéma ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the movies tonight?

meaning: “(you) mean”; “to mean” (as in: what do you mean?).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "vouloir dire" (literally “to want to say”), used to ask for clarification or to check understanding: "Qu’est-ce que tu veux dire ?" = “What do you mean?” / "Tu vois ce que je veux dire ?" = “You see what I mean?” Often appears inside "ce que ... veut dire" (“what ... means”). In fast speech you may hear contractions like "c’que j’veux dire".
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used with the verb vouloir (here: je veux) + en savoir plus (to find out more) + sur + noun/topic. You can change the subject and tense: tu veux en savoir plus sur…, il/elle veut en savoir plus sur…, etc.
target_language_example: Je veux en savoir plus sur ce cours de français.
native_language_example: I want to know more about this French course.

additional_notes: From the verb "vouloir" (to want): "tu veux faire + infinitive" is a very common way to say what someone wants to do. It’s often used in questions like "Qu’est-ce que tu veux faire ?" (What do you want to do?) and can also express refusal or preference: "C’est la dernière chose que je veux faire" (That’s the last thing I want to do). You’ll frequently add another verb after it: "Tu veux faire quoi ?" / "Tu veux faire ça ?"
target_language_example: Tu veux faire quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: What do you want to do tonight?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "vouloir" (to want). "Veux" is the "tu" form (you, informal singular). It’s followed by an infinitive ("faire") + an object ("quelque chose" = something). For other subjects: "je veux…", "il/elle veut…", "nous voulons…", "vous voulez…", "ils/elles veulent…".
target_language_example: Tu veux faire quelque chose ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want to do something tonight?

additional_notes: Used mainly with "je": "Je veux juste…" to mean you only want one thing or to soften your request (like "I just want to…" / "I only want to…"). It’s the verb "vouloir" (je veux = I want) + "juste" (just/only).
target_language_example: Je veux juste te poser une question.
native_language_example: I just want to ask you a question.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *vouloir* (here: *je veux* = “I want”) + *parler à* (“to talk to” someone). You change *veux* depending on the subject: *je veux parler à…*, *tu veux parler à…*, *il/elle veut parler à…*. It’s followed by a person: *parler à Marie*, *parler à lui/elle*, *parler à mes parents*.
target_language_example: Je veux parler à ton professeur.
native_language_example: I want to talk to your teacher.

additional_notes: Informal spoken/written French for ne ... veux pas, with ne often dropped in everyday speech: je veux pas, tu veux pas. It is used with vouloir to say someone does not want something.
target_language_example: Je veux pas y aller maintenant.
native_language_example: I don't want to go there now.

meaning: "(I) don’t want you to…" (start of a sentence).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment you’ll usually see as part of **je (ne) veux pas que tu + verb (subjunctive)**: *Je (ne) veux pas que tu partes.* In casual speech/writing, **ne** is often dropped: *Je veux pas que tu…* It introduces what you don’t want the other person to do.
target_language_example: Je veux pas que tu t’inquiètes.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to worry.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a full sentence with a subject, most often: « Je ne veux pas être … » (standard). In everyday spoken French, « ne » is often dropped: « Je veux pas être … », which matches the fragment « veux pas être ». Use it before a noun/adjective/verb to say what you don’t want to be/do.
target_language_example: Je veux pas être en retard.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be late.

meaning: "(you) want us to…" / "do you want us to…?"
additional_notes: Built from "tu veux" (you want) + "que" + "on" (we/people). Very common to suggest or propose doing something together: "Tu veux qu'on + verb (subjunctive) ?" (e.g., "qu'on aille", "qu'on fasse", "qu'on regarde"). It can also be used to ask what someone wants another person/group to do.
target_language_example: Tu veux qu'on aille au cinéma ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want us to go to the movies tonight?

additional_notes: Uses the tu form of vouloir (“veux”) followed by que and usually a subjunctive verb: Tu veux que je parte ? = “Do you want me to leave?” This pattern is used when the person who wants something is different from the person doing the action.
target_language_example: Tu veux que je t'aide ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you?

meaning: '(I) want it to be…' (used to introduce the subjunctive).
additional_notes: This is a common chunk from the verb pattern **vouloir que + subjunctive**. **Veux** is the **tu/je** form of *vouloir* in the present (*je veux / tu veux*), and **que ce soit** is the subjunctive of *c’est* (*être*). It’s typically followed by an adjective or noun phrase: *Je veux que ce soit clair / prêt / une surprise.* You can change the subject: *Je veux que tu viennes* (I want you to come).
target_language_example: Je veux que ce soit plus simple.
native_language_example: I want it to be simpler.

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants you to do: « Tu veux que je + verbe ? ». It usually comes after « Tu » (or « Vous »): « Tu veux que je… ? / Vous voulez que je… ? ». After « vouloir que », French normally uses the subjunctive (e.g., « que je fasse », « que je vienne », « que je t’aide »).
target_language_example: Tu veux que je t’aide ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person (tu): it’s shorthand for "Tu veux que je fasse… ?" It introduces what you want someone to do, and it triggers the subjunctive in French: "que je fasse" (from "faire"). You can replace "veux" with other forms: "Tu veux que je fasse…", "Vous voulez que je fasse…" (formal/plural), "Il/Elle veut que je fasse…".
target_language_example: Tu veux que je fasse quoi ?
native_language_example: What do you want me to do?

meaning: "(Do you) want me to … (for you / to you)?"
additional_notes: This is a common sentence start in questions like: « Tu veux que je te rappelle ? » (“Do you want me to call you back?”). It’s built from: « veux » (want), « que » (that), « je » (I), « te » (to you). After « vouloir que », French typically uses the subjunctive: « tu veux que je te dise… », « tu veux que je t’aide… ». The « te » becomes « t’ » before a vowel or silent h: « veux que je t’aide ».
target_language_example: Tu veux que je te montre où c’est ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to show you where it is?

meaning: "do you want me to tell you (something)?"
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone wants you to say something, often followed by a question word: « Tu veux que je te dise quoi ? » (“What do you want me to tell you?”). It can also introduce your opinion or a frank remark, sometimes in a slightly rhetorical way: « Tu veux que je te dise ? Je n’ai pas envie. » (“You know what? I don’t feel like it.”).
target_language_example: Tu veux que je te dise la vérité ? Je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: Do you want me to tell you the truth? I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Usually appears inside a longer sentence, most often as part of je veux que tu... = "I want you to...". After que tu, the following verb is normally in the subjunctive: je veux que tu viennes, je veux que tu fasses, etc. On its own, this is a sentence fragment rather than a complete expression.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu viennes demain.
native_language_example: I want you to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer sentence: **Je veux que tu ailles + place/verb** (“I want you to go …”). After **je veux que…**, French uses the **subjunctive**: **tu ailles** (from **aller**, “to go”). You can replace **tu** with another subject: **je veux qu’il/elle aille**, **je veux que nous allions**, etc.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu ailles à l’école demain.
native_language_example: I want you to go to school tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is the pattern **vouloir que + subjunctive**. It’s usually preceded by **Je**: **Je veux que tu fasses …** (“I want you to do …”). The verb **faire** becomes **tu fasses** (subjunctive) after **que**.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu fasses tes devoirs ce soir.
native_language_example: I want you to do your homework tonight.

meaning: “(I) want you to … (to/for me) …” (used to introduce what you want someone to do).
additional_notes: This is a fragment you’ll most often see in the pattern: « Je veux que tu me + verb (conjugated in the subjunctive) ». After « je veux que », French typically uses the subjunctive: « Je veux que tu me téléphones » (not *tu me téléphones* in the indicative in careful French). « me » is an object pronoun meaning “me/to me,” placed before the verb.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu me dises la vérité.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me the truth.

additional_notes: This is typically part of a longer sentence, most often: « Je veux que tu me dises … » (I want you to tell me …). It uses « vouloir que + subjunctive »: « dises » is the subjunctive form of « dire » (to say/tell). You usually follow it with what you want the person to tell you (e.g., « la vérité », « ce que tu penses »).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu me dises la vérité.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me the truth.

additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **je veux que + [subject] + verb (subjunctive)**. Here, **prennes** is the **subjunctive** form of *prendre* (“to take”) used after *vouloir que* (“to want that…”). It’s usually followed by what you want the person to take: *Je veux que tu prennes ce livre / le bus / ta carte d’identité.*
target_language_example: Je veux que tu prennes ton parapluie.
native_language_example: I want you to take your umbrella.

additional_notes: Built with the pattern **vouloir que + subjunctive**. Here, **veux** = "(I) want" and **que tu restes** uses the subjunctive of *rester* (tu **restes**) after *vouloir que*. Often followed by a reason: *Je veux que tu restes avec moi.*
target_language_example: Je veux que tu restes ce soir.
native_language_example: I want you to stay tonight.

additional_notes: Usually appears with the subject: « Je veux que tu saches… ». After « je veux que », French uses the subjunctive: « tu saches » (from « savoir », to know). Used to introduce important information or reassurance.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu saches que je suis là pour toi.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I’m here for you.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer sentence: « Je veux que tu sois … » + adjective/noun (ex: content, là, médecin). After « je veux que … », French uses the subjunctive; « sois » is the subjunctive form of « être » (to be) for « tu ».
target_language_example: Je veux que tu sois là à 8 heures.
native_language_example: I want you to be there at 8 o’clock.

meaning: “(I) want you to …” (introduces a verb in the subjunctive).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **Je veux que tu + verb (subjunctive)**. The **te** is a reflexive pronoun (“yourself”) used with reflexive verbs (e.g., *te reposer*, *te lever*, *te dépêcher*). After **je veux que**, French normally uses the **subjunctive**: *tu te reposes*, *tu te lèves*, *tu te dépêches*, etc. On its own, **veux que tu te** is incomplete—you need a verb after it.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu te reposes.
native_language_example: I want you to rest.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of a full sentence like “Je veux que tu viennes.” After “vouloir que” (“to want that”), French typically uses the subjunctive: “tu viennes” (from “venir”). You can swap the subject: “Je veux que vous veniez” (formal/plural), “Je veux qu’il/elle vienne,” etc.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu viennes ce soir.
native_language_example: I want you to come tonight.

meaning: '(I) want you to…' (introduces what you want someone to do).
additional_notes: This is usually part of the full structure: « Je veux que vous + verb (subjunctive) ». « vous » is the polite/formal or plural “you.” In French, after « vouloir que », the next verb typically goes in the subjunctive (e.g., « fassiez », « veniez », « soyez »).
target_language_example: Je veux que vous veniez demain.
native_language_example: I want you to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Fragment from the verb pattern "vouloir que + [subjunctive]". Here, "veux" = "I want" (from *vouloir*), and "vous alliez" is the subjunctive form of *aller* for "you" (formal or plural). Used when one person wants another person to do something: "Je veux que vous alliez..." + place/time.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous alliez à l’hôtel tout de suite.
native_language_example: I want you to go to the hotel right away.

meaning: “(I) want you to … (to/for me) …” (start of a sentence).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment, most often from “Je veux que vous me …” (“I want you to … / I’d like you to … for me …”). After “veux que”, French typically uses the subjunctive: “Je veux que vous me disiez…”, “Je veux que vous m’appeliez…”. If you don’t need “que + subjunctive”, you can also say “Je veux vous + infinitive”: “Je veux vous voir.”
target_language_example: Je veux que vous me disiez la vérité.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used with the pattern **(je) veux que + [subjunctive]** to express what you want someone else to do or say. **vous** is formal or plural “you”; **me** means “to me”; **disiez** is the subjunctive form of **dire** (“to say/tell”) for **vous** after **que**.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous me disiez la vérité.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Usually appears as "Je veux que vous sachiez…". It uses "vouloir que" + the subjunctive: "savoir" → "que vous sachiez". "Vous" is formal singular or plural (talking to one person politely, or to several people).
target_language_example: Je veux que vous sachiez que je suis désolé.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I’m sorry.

additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **vouloir que + subjunctive**. Here, **veux** = “(I) want” (present tense of *vouloir*), and **vous soyez** is the subjunctive of *être* (“that you be”). It’s used when expressing what you want someone to do or be: *Je veux que vous soyez à l’heure* (I want you to be on time). Often followed by an adjective, a place, or a state.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous soyez prêts à partir.
native_language_example: I want you to be ready to leave.

additional_notes: Built with **vouloir** (here: **veux**) + **que** + the **subjunctive**: **(que) vous veniez**. The subject of **veux** is implied by context (most often **je** or **tu**). A very common full sentence is: **Je veux que vous veniez.**
target_language_example: Je veux que vous veniez demain.
native_language_example: I want you to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Built from **vouloir** (to want) + **quelque chose** (something). **Veux** is present tense for **je** or **tu**: *je veux quelque chose* = “I want something”; *tu veux quelque chose ?* = “Do you want something?”. For polite requests, French often uses **je voudrais quelque chose** (“I would like something”).
target_language_example: Tu veux quelque chose à boire ?
native_language_example: Do you want something to drink?

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase « vouloir savoir » (“to want to know”), used with « tu »: « tu veux savoir… ? » = “do you want to know…?”. Often followed by a direct question (« Qu’est-ce que tu veux savoir ? ») or by « ce que » (“what/that which”): « tout ce que tu veux savoir » = “everything you want to know”. You can also see it in « Si tu veux savoir, … » = “If you want to know, …”.
target_language_example: Tu veux savoir pourquoi je suis en retard ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know why I'm late?

additional_notes: As written, this is incomplete in French. You’ll most often see it as **je veux savoir…** (“I want to know…”) or **(tu) veux savoir ce que…** (“(you) want to know what…”). To say “I want to know what you think,” you need **ce que**: *Je veux savoir ce que tu penses.*
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu penses.
native_language_example: I want to know what you think.

additional_notes:
Fragment built from: 
- "veux" = "(I) want" (1st person singular of *vouloir*) 
- "savoir" = "to know" 
- "ce que" = "what/that which".
It’s usually followed by a full clause: *Je veux savoir ce que tu fais.* You can change the subject/person: *tu veux savoir ce que…*, *il/elle veut savoir ce que…*, *vous voulez savoir ce que…*.
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu penses.
native_language_example: I want to know what you think.

meaning: '(you) want to know what you…' (used to start a sentence).
additional_notes:
This is a sentence fragment. It typically appears after a subject like "Je" (I) or "Tu" (you):
- "Je veux savoir ce que tu penses." = "I want to know what you think."
"veux" is from "vouloir" (to want), and "ce que" means "what/that which". It is usually followed by a verb (penses, fais, veux, as dit, etc.).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu penses.
native_language_example: I want to know what you think.

additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **[person] + vouloir (veux/veux/voulez/veut…) + savoir + comment + clause**. It’s used to ask about the way something happens or is done. For “I want to know how…”, use **je veux savoir comment…**.
target_language_example: Tu veux savoir comment ça marche ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know how it works?

additional_notes: A common way to start an indirect question about a place. It’s usually part of a longer sentence, e.g. « Je veux savoir où + subject + verb ». « Veux » is the present tense of « vouloir » (to want): « je veux » (I want), « tu veux » (you want).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir où tu habites.
native_language_example: I want to know where you live.

additional_notes: Made of: « veux » (I want, from *vouloir*) + « savoir » (to know) + « qui » (who). Often followed by a verb clause: « Je veux savoir qui vient. » You can change « veux » to match the subject (e.g., « tu veux savoir qui… », « il/elle veut savoir qui… », « vous voulez savoir qui… »).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir qui a appelé.
native_language_example: I want to know who called.

additional_notes: Made of the verb *vouloir* (“to want”) conjugated as **veux** (used with **je** or **tu**) + **simplement** (“simply/just”). Often used to soften a request or clarify that you only want one simple thing. With other subjects: **il/elle veut simplement**, **nous voulons simplement**, **vous voulez simplement**, **ils/elles veulent simplement**.
target_language_example: Je veux simplement te parler.
native_language_example: I just want to talk to you.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment usually used as: « Je veux simplement que vous + verb (subjunctive) … ». After « je veux que… », French typically uses the subjunctive (e.g., « que vous soyez », « que vous fassiez », « que vous veniez »). « simplement » softens the request (“just/simply”).
target_language_example: Je veux simplement que vous soyez à l’heure.
native_language_example: I just want you to be on time.

additional_notes: Used with the implied subject « je »: « Je veux simplement être… » (“I just want to be…”). « veux » is the 1st-person singular present of « vouloir » (to want). You can change the subject/conjugation: « tu veux simplement être… », « il/elle veut simplement être… », etc. Often followed by an adjective or noun: « …heureux/heureuse », « …moi-même », « …tranquille ».
target_language_example: Je veux simplement être moi-même.
native_language_example: I just want to be myself.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address with "tu". It’s often said with the subject implied: "(Je) veux…". You can change "veux" for another tense/person (e.g., "je vais te montrer…", "je voudrais te montrer…") and switch "te" to "vous" for formal/plural: "Je veux vous montrer quelque chose."
target_language_example: Viens, je veux te montrer quelque chose.
native_language_example: Come, I want to show you something.

meaning: 'want to see' (you want to look at something).
additional_notes: Formed with "vouloir" (to want) + "voir" (to see). Used to offer/show something or ask if someone wants to see it: "Tu veux voir… ?" = "Do you want to see…?" In questions it’s often spoken casually; you can add "Est-ce que" for a more neutral tone ("Est-ce que tu veux voir… ?").
target_language_example: Tu veux voir les photos de mon voyage ?
native_language_example: Do you want to see the photos from my trip?

additional_notes: From vouloir (to want) + vraiment (really). Used to emphasize that the desire is genuine or strong, often in questions to confirm or challenge someone: « Tu veux vraiment… ? » You can change the subject: « je veux vraiment… », « il/elle veut vraiment… ». In statements it often means “I truly/really want to…”.
target_language_example: Tu veux vraiment partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you really want to leave now?

additional_notes: Used with "tu" as the subject: "tu veux" (you want) + "y" (there/to it) + "aller" (to go). "Y" replaces a place or something introduced with "à" (e.g., "à Paris" → "y"). You can change the subject: "je veux y aller", "on veut y aller", "vous voulez y aller", etc.
target_language_example: Tu veux y aller maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you want to go there now?

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern **vouloir + infinitive**. **Veux** is the present-tense form of *vouloir* for **tu** (“you want”): *tu veux être…* (“you want to be…”). With **je**, it becomes *je veux être…* and is often spoken/written informally as **j’veux être…**.
target_language_example: Tu veux être médecin plus tard ?
native_language_example: Do you want to be a doctor later?

meaning: viceroy; a ruler who governs in the king’s place.
additional_notes: Used as a title for a high-ranking official appointed by a king/queen to govern a territory (often a colony). You can address someone directly with it like a title: « Oui, vice-roi ? » = “Yes, Viceroy?”
target_language_example: Le vice-roi arrive demain au palais.
native_language_example: The viceroy is arriving at the palace tomorrow.

additional_notes: Imperative command using vous (to one person politely/formally, or to several people). Common in security checks (airport, courthouse), by police, or before entering certain places. Singular informal would be: « vide tes poches ».
target_language_example: Avant de passer le contrôle, videz vos poches, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Before going through security, please empty your pockets.

additional_notes: Used when talking about religious/spiritual beliefs about what happens after someone dies. Very often appears with « croire à / en » (to believe in) or in questions like « Y a-t-il une vie après la mort ? ».
target_language_example: Elle ne croit pas à la vie après la mort.
native_language_example: She doesn’t believe in life after death.

additional_notes: Made of **vie** (“life”) + **est** (“is”). It often appears after a possessive adjective: **ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur vie est…** (“my/your/his/her/our/your/their life is…”). Also common in fixed expressions like **(ta/votre) vie est en jeu** (“your life is at stake”).
target_language_example: Ma vie est différente maintenant.
native_language_example: My life is different now.

additional_notes: Refers to the personal part of someone’s life that isn’t public (relationships, family matters, personal information).
